## Volume front matter

**Patrologia Latina, volume 180.** *The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library of all Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III: Second Series.*

**Volume 180 of the Patrology:** Eugenius III, Roman pontiff; Bishop Ulger; Abbot Oger; Abbot William; Abbot Hermann; Canon Alger; Monk Teulf; Monk John; Arnulf of Doeriis; Henry of Saltrey. Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, Rue d’Amboise, near the Paris gate commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge, 1855.

## Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III.** A chronological reissue of all monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed through the first twelve centuries of the Church, corrected with the greatest care by comparison of the most accurate editions with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the fullest editions completed in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly placed within the text and headings at the top margin of each page identifying its subject; expanded with doubtful and apocryphal works that nevertheless possess some authority for ecclesiastical tradition; and enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which the reader may see at a glance what each Father wrote on any topic; the other of Holy Scripture, through which the reader may discover which Fathers, and where in their works, commented on each particular text of each biblical book.

This is the most accurate edition and readily preferable to all others if one considers clearness of type, quality of paper, completeness of text, perfection of correction, the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient form of the volumes and its consistency throughout the series, modest price, and especially this single methodical and chronological collection, first assembled in this library, of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works of every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series,** in which appear the Latin Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers from Gregory the Great to Innocent III; edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Library of the Universal Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and one Greek-Latin. The Latin edition, of 260 volumes, is sold for 1,300 francs; the Greek-Latin edition, of 300 volumes, for 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all Western and Eastern authors; the latter are supplied there in Latin translation alone.

## Notice on Hermann, abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, III, 240–41.)

1. Hermann was Benedictine abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai from 1127 to 1137. It is uncertain how many years he survived after resigning office. His *Narrative of the restoration of the abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai*, addressed to all the fathers, brethren, and sons of that monastery, survives. Luc d’Achery first published it in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 358 ff. (new edition, II, p. 888), together with additions by other writers, pp. 922 and 926, covering 1127 to 1160. Vossius, when the work was still unpublished, wrote: “Much is read in it about the kings of France and counts of Flanders, and about how the bishopric of Tournai was separated from that of Noyon.”

2. His *Treatise on the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ*, addressed to Stephen, archbishop of Vienne in Gaul, was first published by Casimir Oudin among the *Sacred Short Works of Several Ancient Writers of Gaul and Belgium*, Leiden, 1692.

3. D’Achery published Hermann’s three books *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary of Laon* at the end of Guibert of Nogent’s works, p. 526. The first two books pursue those miracles; the third, and longest, treats the diocese of Laon, embellished by Saint Norbert and Bishop Bartholomew and enriched with monasteries. Bartholomew held office from 1113 to 1150; see the Sammarthani, *Gallia Christiana*, II, p. 620 ff. Hermann also testifies that he wrote a life of Saint Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, and prefixed it to Ildefonsus’s three books on virginity. Pierre de Marca praises Hermann as an unimpeachable witness for the genealogy of that Bartholomew (*Marca Hispanica*, IV, p. 455).

## Hermann’s treatise on the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ

### Notice preceding the following treatise

(Gallandi, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, XIV, p. 381, Venice, 1781, folio.)

Hermann, or Herimann, third abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai after Segard, who died 30 January 1127, was born to his father Ralph. After scarcely completing nine years of government, he fell into paralysis, voluntarily relinquished the helm, and resigned into the hands of Simon, bishop of Tournai. It is said that after resigning he was sent to Rome and soon set out for Jerusalem. What happened to him on that journey is unknown: some teach that he died a captive, others a martyr. While abbot he wrote the short work *On the Lord’s Incarnation* for Stephen, archbishop of Vienne. Oudin edited it from a codex of the abbey of Vicoigne among the short works of certain writers of Gaul and Belgium, and we have reproduced it from there. It everywhere breathes piety and no ordinary talent. The codex was copied in 1149, as its conclusion states.

### Preface [Col. 0009A–0011C]

Brother Hermann, least of all monks, to his reverend father and lord Stephen, by God’s grace archbishop of Vienne: may you rejoice eternally with Christ, from Christ, through Christ, and in Christ.

For the kindness by which you deigned so gladly to receive and keep with you one who came from a distant region—from the city of Tournai, situated in Frankish territory and known to be the metropolis of Flanders—I give your fatherhood thanks, not such as I ought, but such as I can; and I pray that the Lord, for whose love you did this, may repay you for me. Since your majesty deigned to ask that I show you the small work which my littleness composed on the Lord’s Incarnation, behold, I gladly obey your command. I ask that whatever has been wrongly said in it may be corrected by you, and whatever is good may be approved by you.

Know, however, that I have put nothing of my own into it. Rather, I have gathered as if into one vessel what I had read in holy doctors, especially in the book of Lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, composed on this matter and called *Why God Became Man*. Moreover, Lord Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man of pious memory, first monk and first abbot of our monastery, blessed Martin of Tournai—he who made my father, my three brothers, and me monks, and whom I, though unworthy, succeeded as third abbot in the government of the same monastery—used to give our brothers in chapter every year, on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, a beautiful and lengthy sermon on that Incarnation. He began in the morning and extended it almost to the sixth hour. Since I was then a young man of receptive intelligence, I committed quite a few of his words to memory; I shall now relate them both to you and to everyone willing to read. Thus, after the Gospel had been pronounced according to custom, “When she was betrothed,” etc. (Matthew 1), he used, as it seems to me, to begin in this manner:

# PL 180, section 0001 — batch 002

## Chapter I. The necessity of the Incarnation of the Son of God

Dearest brethren, as we are about to celebrate with annual devotion the birth of our Redeemer, we ought carefully and diligently to consider for what reason or necessity he assumed the weakness of our flesh and at the same time endured the disgraces of the Passion. Not only believers but all unbelievers are accustomed to examine this question: the latter add objections, while the former devoutly and religiously search out the reason for this mystery.

“What necessity,” they ask, “was there that God should be made flesh and enclosed in a woman’s womb for nine months; then be nourished by his mother’s milk like other infants, and swaddled while crying; and finally die so contemptibly, mocked, spat upon, and hung among thieves?” When we answer them with the Apostle’s saying that, because of the exceeding love with which God loved us (Ephesians **[source prints ‘XXIV’]**), he sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8), to redeem us and lead us out of the devil’s power, who held us captive through the first parent’s sin, they immediately add:

“What reason was there for God to descend from heaven to earth and undergo so many sufferings and mockeries for that purpose, especially when the Psalmist says of him, ‘Whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth’ (Psalm 134:6)? If all things are placed in his will and no one can resist his will (Esther 13:9), why did he not, while remaining seated in heaven upon the throne of his majesty, command that captive man be freed from the devil’s hand and lifted to heaven with the angels, just as when he said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light (Genesis 1:3)?

“For just as some very powerful king, able by a mere command to rescue and restore to liberty his servant captured by other servants, would be judged not merciful but excessively foolish if he did not wish to free him except by putting himself in chains for him, so also the Lord God, who by a mere nod, not merely a command, could free man from the devil’s power—if it may be said without offense to him—seems foolish and unbelievable in wishing, in order to rescue him, first to discover by personal experience whether milk in his mother’s breasts was bitter or sweet. For both man and devil were created by God; each was God’s servant. If a wicked servant had deceived a simple servant by fraudulent counsel and subjugated to himself one withdrawn from his own lord, was it not just that the wicked servant should be punished for his wickedness and the simple servant liberated from his dominion?”

When they say these things, they do not consider the judgment of Holy Scripture that wisdom conquers malice, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wisdom **[source prints ‘LXXXI’]**). For not strength alone befits God, but sweetness also; and sweetness is shown not only toward friends but toward enemies. “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9). Therefore, that we may examine more carefully why God became man, let us first consider why God created the first man himself.

# PL 180, section 0001 — batch 003

## Chapter II. Why God created the first man

The omnipotent God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is three in persons but one in substance and majesty. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; nevertheless the Father is not the Son or Holy Spirit, the Son is not the Father or Holy Spirit, nor is the Holy Spirit Father or Son. As a certain wise man says, he is above all things, beneath all things, among all things, and outside all things: above all without being raised up; beneath all without being cast down; within all without being enclosed; outside all without being excluded. He presides above all, sustains beneath all, fills within all, and embraces outside all. His power, riches, and wealth can neither increase nor diminish: he was not richer when he made the whole world, and would not be poorer if the world perished and returned to nothing.

He made the world from no necessity but from goodness alone, as that noble consul Boethius sang:

> O thou who governest the world by everlasting reason,
> maker of earth and heaven, who commandest time
> to move from age to age, and, remaining steadfast, givest all things motion;
> whom no external causes compelled to fashion
> a work from flowing matter, but the indwelling form
> of the highest good, free from envy. From a heavenly model
> thou leadest all things forth, thyself most beautiful, bearing the beautiful
> world in thy mind, etc.

It pleased this supreme King, our Lord God, to build for himself a city, that heavenly city of which the Psalm says, “Glorious things are spoken of thee, city of God” (Psalm 86:3). He made its walls not from his own substance but from nothing. He gave its citizens understanding, by which they might know him as Lord and Creator and know themselves as his servants and creatures; by obeying him without labor or difficulty, they might happily remain in perpetual blessedness with him.

He did not appoint them all equal in one rank. For Isaiah says to the one set over the rest: “Every precious stone was thy covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (**source citation: Ezekiel XVIII:13**). Explaining this in the homily on the ten drachmas, blessed Gregory says: “Behold, he named nine stones, because there are indeed nine orders of angels, over all of whom that one angel was set.” Unable to bear the greatness and excellence of his glory and brightness, he swelled against his Creator, as Isaiah again says to him: “How hast thou fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who didst arise in the morning, who didst say in thy heart, ‘I shall ascend to heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne; I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High’” (Isaiah 14:12).

When he proudly swelled against his Creator, other angels did not fail to join him and to be proud with him against the Lord. But the just Judge, unwilling to leave disorder in his city, at once cast down from heaven those precious stones of heavenly virtues which had raised themselves against their Maker. Thus those who had first been angels are now called devils; the Lord himself attests this in the Gospel: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

If anyone asks how the evil and ruinous pestilence of pride could ascend or creep into such lofty angelic dignity, who first authored it, or how a creature of such high station could be corrupted or infected, let him read the aforesaid Lord Anselm’s book *On the Fall of the Devil*, where he discusses why God did not give the devil perseverance; there he will find much that is useful. Another wise man, asked this question, replied briefly and elegantly in four verses:

> Why ask whence evil, when all things were created good?
> Things that are evil are evil through their own defect.
> For though sweet apples are free from defect,
> they nevertheless quickly draw corruption from themselves and through themselves.

When the proud angels had fallen and abused the free will they formerly possessed, those who remained faithful to their Creator were so strengthened and confirmed by him in the perfect, unchangeable firmness of that same free will that they have no further will to sin or be proud. This is also mystically indicated at the beginning of Genesis. After “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), the second day’s creation repeats that God called the firmament “heaven” (Genesis 1:8). Explaining this, Gregory says that the angelic powers which remained with God when their companions fell were confirmed in such firmness that, by comparison with it, they seem formerly to have been weak and feeble; but on the second day—that is, in this subsequent confirmation—they rightly deserve to be called heaven because of their firmness.

Thus the glorious city of the supreme King suffered a grave ruin and its wall was broken through in no small part. Long after that fall the prophet Daniel said of those who remained: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10). Who can estimate or conceive the beauty of that house or city while it remained whole with all its citizens? Therefore, lest that ruin or breach should for long disfigure so beautiful a city, the heavenly builder resolved to create some creature for its restoration. If someone asks why he did not restore it from the angels who had fallen, he will easily understand, on seeing the difficulty of human restoration in what follows, that fallen angels cannot be restored at all.

God therefore created man, but not with the height of dignity in which he had made angels, lest perhaps man too, unable to bear his glory, should become proud against God and perish. He willed man to consist of a rational soul and flesh: by the rational soul he resembles angels; by flesh from earth’s mud he is continually urged to humility, seeing himself through it equal to beasts. Yet God made him happy and immune from every weakness, need, and corruption, so that, if he refused sin, he would never die; but if he disobeyed his Creator, he would at once become subject to death.

Because man was made from earth, God placed him in an earthly place, paradise. He gave him rational understanding and imposed no obedience except that he should not eat from one tree. He foretold with a threat that death would immediately follow contempt, but that if man observed the command he would in due time be lifted from earth and placed in heaven with angels. He added as companion a woman made from his side—that is, from himself—to bear his offspring, and taught both what they should do.

The devil envied man, formed from earthly mud, his ascent to the place from which the devil knew that he, though so splendid, had fallen. As everyone knows, through a serpent he seduced the woman and through her persuaded the man to eat the forbidden fruit. He thus subjected both to himself and tried to nullify—indeed rejoiced that he had nullified—God’s plan for man. Behold, then, man made in God’s image and placed over every creature under heaven: “Though he was in honor, he did not understand” (Psalm 48:21); indeed “he would not understand, that he might do well” (Psalm 35:4). By God’s just judgment he was compared to irrational beasts and made like them (Psalm 48:21). In this present life, living a short time, he is filled with many miseries (Job 14:1); dying, he is led into infernal darkness.

What then shall the wretched man do? Where shall he turn? How can he rise and free himself from the devil’s hand or servitude? Certainly he cannot rise by himself. Let him cry to the Lord and say: “O Lord, for I am thy servant, and the son of thy handmaid” (Psalm 115:16); “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8); “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God” (Psalm 58:2).

# PL 180, section 0001 — batch 004

## Chapter III. It was fitting that after sin man should not be redeemed unless satisfaction were made to God

What will the Lord God do? It is certainly true that “whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6); yet he neither can nor ought to do anything unjustly. If he commanded the devil to let out of hell the man whom the devil had unjustly and enviously deceived, the devil could answer: “It is true, Lord, that I deceived him through envy; but if you take him from me by force, you treat me unjustly. I did not subject him to myself by force as my possession, for I could have done nothing to him by violence. You commanded him not to eat from the tree; I advised him to eat. You foretold that if he ate he would die; I told him he would not die. He believed me rather than you and freely despised your command on my advice. Since I did not make him sin by force but only advised him to sin, it will be unjust if you take him forcibly from me. Let him instead contend with me; as he freely subjected himself to me, so let him, if he can, snatch himself from my hands.” The devil could certainly object this to God.

Even if some pity or mercy—which is impossible—moved the devil toward man, his pity would not help man. If he said, “Lord God, I am sated with the miseries and punishments of unhappy man; I repent of deceiving him through envy and permit you to bring him from hell—indeed ask you to place him with the angels in heaven,” none of that goodness would benefit man. Man owed the devil nothing and was not in the devil’s hand or power by right. He sinned against God, despising his Lord’s command; God therefore placed him in God’s prison, hell, though by just judgment he delivered him to the torturer whom he had foolishly believed. If man could somehow be reconciled to God, so that God forgave anger and remitted sin, then, whether the devil wished it or not, man could easily be led out of hell.

But this reconciliation cannot happen without some satisfaction for sin. Even if moved by mercy God forgave man and led him from hell, would it be just or fitting to place him, still foul and stained and washed by no satisfaction, with those pure and glorious angels who never offended God? Where then would be the Apostle’s saying, “What fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Every sound mind sees this is unfitting. Therefore man must make some satisfaction capable of appeasing God. What that satisfaction must be may be seen by an example.

Suppose a very powerful king expels one of his princes from the kingdom as stubborn and rebellious. If that man later wishes reconciliation with his king and lord, he must first restore in full whatever he took, or, if he cannot restore it, return something equally valuable. Then he must satisfy, under the laws of the court and judgment of the king’s nobles, for the obstinacy and pride by which he rebelled. So long as he retains and does not return what he took, no satisfaction is fitting, worthy, or honorable to the king. If the king pardoned a man retaining his goods and allowed him to return, people would say he pardoned because he could not make him amend or subject him otherwise; such satisfaction or reconciliation would become the king’s disgrace and reproach.

Likewise, man, expelled from paradise and exiled in hell for guilt, if he wishes reconciliation with the Lord God and restoration to grace, must first restore in full what he took from God, or something equally valuable. Then he must satisfy for the pride by which he despised his Creator’s command and clung to God’s enemy. Unless he satisfies in this order, his satisfaction will not honor God. Let us see what he took from God when he ate of the forbidden tree.

# PL 180, section 0001 — batch 005

## Chapter IV. What man took from God by eating from the forbidden tree

As was said, God created man in order to restore from his race the ruin of the heavenly city. Blessed Gregory, in the homily on the ten drachmas already mentioned, says that we believe as many elect human beings will ascend there as elect angels remained there. When man sinned by transgressing the divine command, he therefore took from God as many souls as God had intended to lift to heaven with angels. If he wishes reconciliation and return to paradise, he must first repay the loss he caused: namely, as many persons as God planned to lift to heaven, and persons as clean and free from every sin as Adam was before sin. Or, if he cannot give so many clean and spotless persons, he must give what is equally valuable. Otherwise his satisfaction, as said, will not honor God.

If, before what was taken has been restored, God moved by mercy forgave man’s sin and joined him with angels in heaven, justice would not make it fitting for God to join to his sons and friends—who always served him as their sweetest father, never offended him, and never transgressed his command—their ravisher, thief, and murderer, who had carried off, stolen, and killed so many men. Let man therefore restore to God what he took, that he may receive grace. But how shall he give God so many humans such as Adam was before sin? Apart from the multitude, he will not find in the whole human race even one such man. When Adam sinned, he lost innocence and purity and became sinful and unclean. As he became, so he generated: sinful and unclean he could generate only sinners and unclean people. As Job says, “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14:4). In the whole line of human generation there is not one person without sin, much less a multitude of thousands.

If a sinful person offered himself to God in death for other people’s sins, he could not justify even himself, much less others. Even holy Isaac, born of holy parents, if he had been killed by his father’s hands in obedience to God’s command, could not have freed himself from hell; neither could holy Abel, praised by God’s voice. Therefore man cannot repay in any manner what he took from God.

Can he at least pay something equally valuable? Certainly not. Although the law given through Moses commands sacrifices of beasts and birds, the Apostle says, “It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). All goats and bulls, indeed all field beasts and birds of heaven, and, to say more, the whole world with sun, moon, and stars, cannot be compared with one human being, even unclean and sinful, nor redeem him. Man is made in God’s image, although by sinning he corrupted it in himself; he has a rational soul; at the end of the world he will rise and come to judgment; afterward he will live forever, though in punishments. Man can therefore repay neither the loss done to God nor something equally valuable, from the whole world or his own race.

But if God made some new just and clean man, as he made Adam, and that man offered himself to God as sacrifice for all human sins, could he be a sufficient victim? Not at all. One man, such as Adam was before sin, could redeem only Adam or one man like him; the blood of one such person could be the redemption only of one human person. Even if, impossibly, it could redeem all, human nature would not be restored by that blood to its former dignity. It would be just for human nature to be subject to and serve the one by whom it knew itself redeemed. But then it would not have been restored to its former dignity. When Adam was made, he was subject to no one but God alone, although David says of the substance of his flesh, “Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6). If he were subject to another, he would be lower than his former dignity and not equal to angels, who are subject to none but God.

Moreover, why should that new and just man die when he committed no sin? Death is only punishment for sin, and if Adam had not sinned he would never have died. That new, holy person, free and immune from all sin, ought not be punished for a sinner; the sinner ought to undergo sin’s punishment. The same might be said and thought of any angel, if an angel became man. Thus the Psalm says, “A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem?” (Psalm 48:8). Angels are our brothers, equal to us in soul, through which God made us in his image. If a brother—that is, an angel, so holy and glorious—cannot redeem us, how shall man redeem, conceived of unclean seed and born in sins? “He shall not give his own propitiation and the price of his soul’s redemption” (ibid.). What then shall he do? “And he shall labor forever” (ibid., 9).

It is evident, then, that neither angel nor any new man, much less an old and sinful man, can redeem the human race. No creature at all, not even the whole world, can make worthy satisfaction for the first human sin. But what angel, man, and whole world cannot do, God, who is omnipotent, can do; for “whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6). If he willed, he could surely redeem us—what neither angel, man, nor any other creature can do.

But I have already said that, for sin, only the nature which sinned ought to die; God did not sin and therefore ought not to die. This redemption, then, can be accomplished only by God, yet it ought to be accomplished only by a human being. Since only God can accomplish it and only a human being ought to accomplish it, it is necessary that God become human in order to accomplish it. Thus let the Psalmist’s words be fulfilled: “The Lord sent redemption to his people” (Ps. 110:9); unless it is sent from heaven, it will not be found on earth. Hence it is said again: “He looked down from his holy height; from heaven the Lord looked upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the fettered and to release the children of the slain” (Ps. 101:20–21).

Although God consists in three persons, the Trinity need not itself be incarnate. Whichever of the three persons is incarnate, God is incarnate, since each person, separately and in itself, is true God. We must therefore ask to which person incarnation is most fitting. There is no need to dwell long on this. It is more fitting that the Son offer himself to the Father as a sacrifice for us and entreat the Father than that the Father entreat the Son. Moreover, if the Father were incarnate and were a son of the Virgin, there would be two Sons in the Trinity: the Son of God the Father, and God the Father himself, who would be the son of the Virgin. This would create a certain confusion of persons, and, whenever the Son was discussed, it would be uncertain whether the speech concerned the Son of God or the son of the Virgin. The same would happen if the Holy Spirit were incarnate.

It is therefore far more fitting and appropriate that the Son be incarnate, while remaining one person in the Trinity without any confusing uncertainty: Son of God and son of the Virgin. Because he is begotten from the Father, he remains true God; because he is born from the Virgin, he is true human being. Otherwise, unless he made himself a new human being from our race, his nature would have no relation to us and he ought not to die for us, because he would not have been born from the nature which had sinned. But now, because he takes true flesh from Adam’s flesh without sin—not conceived and born from male seed but from the Holy Spirit—although he did not commit sin and no deceit was found in his mouth, and therefore did not deserve to die, yet through fellowship in and participation in our humanity he can, rightly and fittingly, if he wills, die for his brothers, who are of the same race and share the same nature with him.

Hence the Apostle says: “It was fitting that he, for whom and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering. Therefore he had to become like his brothers in every respect, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make expiation for the sins of the people” (Heb. 2:10, 17). When he says that he had to become like his brothers in every respect, he does not mean that he had to die for sin as others die, but only because of mercy and participation in our humanity.

## Chapter V. The fitting and becoming redemption of human nature

Let us now consider how fittingly and becomingly the redemption of human nature follows. We said above that human nature must first restore to God what it took from him: as many human beings as he had determined necessary to restore or complete his city, or something of equal value. Is not the Son of God, one God with the Father, better not merely than those persons necessary for restoring the building of the heavenly city, but also than all angels and archangels—indeed, than every creature in the whole world? Is not the creator of every creature better than every creature? Is not almighty God, who made all things by a command alone and, if they perished, could remake all things in an instant by a command alone, better and of greater worth than everything he made?

When, therefore, he offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for us and, accepting death, gave his life for our sins, was not what he rendered for us worth a hundred thousand times, without limit, more than all those human beings whom, as we said, Adam had taken from God when he sinned? How could God the Father refrain from forgiving the human race its sin, remitting its former wrath, and restoring paradise, when he saw his beloved Son, equal and coeternal with himself, hanging on the cross for them, hands stretched out toward him, paying so great a redemption?

Accordingly the Apostle says in the same Epistle: “In the days of his flesh, he offered prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7). He therefore mercifully paid for us what he did not owe for himself, saying with the prophet David: “Then I paid what I had not taken” (Ps. 68:5). Isaiah likewise says: “He was wounded for our sins, crushed for our crimes; the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:5). He accepted for us the discipline of death and suffering, and the passion which we had deserved for our sins; through it he reconciled us to God the Father, to himself, and to the Holy Spirit—that is, to the holy Trinity, which is one God—and, as a merciful mediator, restored peace between God and us in his blood. For he is the priest through whom and by whom we were reconciled; he is the victim by which we were reconciled; he is the God to whom we were reconciled.

## Chapter VI. A satisfaction worthy of God is made through the incarnation

Since through Christ Jesus, mediator of God and human beings, human nature has rendered to God a price worth far more than all the people it had taken from him, let us now see how it makes satisfaction also for the contumacy and contempt by which it transgressed his command. Above we set out the proper order of satisfaction to a king: a prince who had been expelled and was to be reconciled must first pay the king in full what he took from him, or its equivalent; then the measure of satisfaction for contempt of royal majesty and contumacy must be considered.

As was said above, God made the human being from two natures, spiritual and bodily: spiritually according to the soul, bodily according to the flesh made from the clay of earth. According to the soul, rational and immortal, the human being was made in God’s image and likeness; according to the flesh made from earth, the human being was not made in God’s likeness, for God has neither eyes nor ears nor any bodily member, because he is the supreme and unbounded Spirit. Thus what is read in the Psalms, “Your hands, Lord, made and formed me” (Ps. 118:73), and again, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayers” (Ps. 33:16), with many similar phrases, must not be taken simply according to the letter but understood figuratively. “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Otherwise God would have wings as well, since it is read of him: “He mounted the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17:11).

Therefore the Anthropomorphite heretics, who say that the human being was made in God’s image according to the body, must either show that a human being flies, because God is said to have flown, or acknowledge the foolishness of their excessive literal-mindedness. Only rational creatures, namely angels and human beings, bear God’s likeness, even though angels are not said to have been made in God’s image. Isaiah says: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:13). Explaining this, blessed Gregory says: “It must be noted that he is called not made in God’s likeness but the seal of likeness, so that, as his nature is subtler, the image of God is intimated as more subtly and more like expressed in him.”

Thus, in the angel, who has nothing bodily but is spirit alone, the image of God is expressed more closely than in a human being who carries an earthly body. Yet the same blessed Gregory says in his exposition of Ezekiel that, in comparison with that supreme and unbounded Spirit who is God, even angels can be called bodily. According to the soul, then, the human being was made in God’s image and is like the angels—indeed, equal to them; according to the body he is lower than the angels, as the Psalmist testifies: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6).

By the rational understanding given him by God, Adam ought to have known that he was lower than the angels. Through pride he tried to be higher than the angels and like God. For the woman, believing the serpent when it said, “God knows that on whatever day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:4), ate with that intention and persuaded her husband to eat, because she hoped that they would become gods. Hence God himself says: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:22). What great pride: that a human being made from the clay of earth should try to excel the angels and be equal to God his creator! The sin of the proud angel and of the proud human being is thus one and the same. For this reason, by God’s just judgment, equal punishment follows equal guilt: the former is cast from heaven and the latter from paradise.

We believe that the angel fell without any hope of recovery, although Origen is said to have written that, just as our Savior restored fallen humanity, so after the resurrection, when judgment was finished, he would free the fallen angel as well. But now that, through the mediator Jesus Christ, the human being has paid God what was taken from him—the price, namely, of Christ’s blood, which is worth more than what was taken—there remains the duty of making worthy satisfaction for the contumacy and pride by which he swelled against God.

What satisfaction could be worthier or more fitting for the human being’s contumacy, who proudly wished to be like God, than that the Son of God should humbly become human? Because the human being foolishly wished to be God, God mercifully became human. Hence the blessed Apostle says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery” (Phil. 2:5–6). See how distinctly he marks the human being’s pride and Christ’s humility. The human being tried by robbery to be equal to God and thought he could attain this by eating the forbidden fruit; Christ, however, was equal to God not by robbery but by nature. Though in the form of a servant—indeed God’s servant—the human being proudly wished to exalt himself to God’s likeness; Christ, though in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. 2:7).

Adam, under no necessity, transgressed God’s command and scorned to keep his obedience. Christ, however, saying, “I came not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), became obedient to the Father through the hardships and distresses of many tribulations. He kept that obedience unbreakably, not merely for a time but unto death—and not a pleasant, sweet, or honorable death, but a harsh and shameful death, namely the death of the cross. Thus he himself, knowing all this and drawing near to his passion, prayed for everyone while commending the disciples—indeed, the whole human race—to God the Father: “For their sake I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19). It is as if he said: “For them I offer myself, who am worth more than all the human beings whom they took from you; for them, though I was God, your only-begotten Son, I became human and am obedient to you unto death. Therefore let my prayer for them rise like incense before you, and may the lifting up of my hands on the cross make for them an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2), “so that, every stain of original sin having been forgiven, they too may be sanctified.”

Thus, “offering with loud cries and tears, he was heard because of his reverence”; and, when the sacrifice was completed and satisfaction fully performed, he said, “It is finished,” bowed his head, and gave up the spirit (John 19:30). Yet what is more wonderful, sweet to remember, and worthy of constant meditation and veneration is this: he not only rendered to his Father for us his blood, whose price is greater than that of every creature which is not God, but through the power of that same sacrifice restored to him in full all the human beings whom the first parent had taken from God. For the Apostle says that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death (Rom. 6:3). Catholic faith holds that every baptized believer is freed from every stain of original sin, wholly cleansed and purified, and is of the same merit as Adam was before he sinned.

If someone asks why, although original sin is forgiven, its penalty—death—is neither forgiven nor removed but remains fixed, blessed Augustine answers this question in his book *On Free Will*: “The whole sum of our salvation is in faith, for without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), and “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). Faith, as the Apostle says, is “the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). If Jews and pagans saw that those baptized no longer died, all would run to baptism even without being called, not out of love for the Christian faith but to avoid bodily death; faith would thus lose its proper merit.

There are two deaths: the first of the flesh, the second of the soul. As Revelation says, “The conqueror shall not be harmed by the second death” (Rev. 2:11; the supplied citation reads XII, 2). The first human incurred both when he ate from the forbidden tree: in the present, death of the flesh; in the future, death of the soul, that is, condemnation. Our Redeemer, however, set his single death, the death of the flesh, against our double death; through it he freed us from both, destroying ours through his own, as he says through the prophet Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death” (Hos. 13:14).

If we consider more carefully, two deaths can also be found in the soul alone: one in the present, another in the future. When anyone commits a grave sin, the soul dies in that person. Blessed Augustine says that just as the soul is the life of the body, God is the life of the soul. When the soul leaves, the body remains dead; when God departs because of sin, the soul dies. David prayed against this death of the soul: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy say, ‘I have prevailed against him’” (Ps. 12:4–5). So long as we resist the adversary and fight him, whatever temptations to crime he may bring against us, we do not die because of them; rather, they work for us a crown and salvation. But if, yielding and conquered, we allow the enemy to say, “I have prevailed against him,” then alas: in the living and wanton body the soul lies dead. Hence the Apostle says: “The widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:5).

After this first death of the soul, which happens in the present, the second follows in the future; unless the soul rises here through repentance, death—that is, eternal condemnation—receives it when it leaves here. Of this condemnation the Gospel says of the guilty man to the king’s servants: “Cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13). Unless a person falls here through sin into the inner darkness of the heart, the blindness of mind, that person is not after death cast into the outer darkness of hell. Thus through inner darkness one falls into outer darkness, because through the death of sin the unhappy soul incurs the death of condemnation.

Of this death the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die forever” (John 11:25–26). In the Gospel, three dead persons are said to have been raised by the Lord because of the varieties of this first death, that is, sins: the girl in the room, the young man outside the gate, and Lazarus four days in the tomb. They signify that sinners, according to the kind or quality of their crime, will be raised by private, public, or long-lasting repentance. From all these kinds of death the soul is freed in baptism; putting off the old human being, it is made a new human being and a child of God through the washing of regeneration. It comes forth from baptism with the same cleanness and holiness which Adam had before he sinned. “To all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

Yet bodily death remains, lest people come to baptism to escape the body’s death rather than the soul’s. But the time will come when “the last enemy shall be destroyed” (1 Cor. 15:26), namely at the resurrection. When the full number has been gathered, all those needed to complete the perfection of that glorious heavenly city, Jerusalem, each person will receive not one but two white robes: the perfect immortality of soul and body. Thus “our corruptible nature shall put on incorruption and our mortal nature shall put on immortality”; then the saying written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:53–54). Rejoicing forever, we shall see how God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). Amen.

## Chapter VII. How the ancient Fathers, before and after the Law, desired the coming of the incarnation

So then, dearest brothers, we have heard why God, made human, worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Now, if you please, let us hear how the ancient Fathers, believing in him before the Law and under the Law, desired his coming; how they sighed with tears to see him; and how they foretold the mystery of his incarnation by words and deeds. Anyone who wishes to look carefully can find in the ancient Scriptures everything we have now said about the Lord’s incarnation. But because it is not easy to repeat all the testimonies of divine Scripture, let us consider the first text which Moses sets down and see how it agrees with what has been said above.

“In the beginning,” he says, “God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). By “heaven” he wishes the heavenly creation, that is, the angels, to be understood; by “earth,” the earthly creation, that is, human beings. But because he had intended to tell not of angels but of the human being, he leaves heaven aside for the moment and adds: “But the earth was empty and void” (Gen. 1:2). That is, human nature, created good by God, became through the sin of the first-formed human being utterly empty of every good and devoid of virtues, so that no trace of its former dignity or purity remained in it. “And darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Gen. 1:2). By “the deep” the human heart can be understood, as Jeremiah says: “The heart of the human being is crooked and unsearchable; who can know it?” (Jer. 17:9). Just as none of us can penetrate the depth of the abyss or reach its end, so we cannot easily discern or know the height, ingenuity, or cunning of the human heart. Thus the person whom we see outwardly flattering us most may sometimes be the one against whom we must inwardly be most on guard, because we do not understand that person’s deceits or tricks.

Darkness, therefore, was upon the face of the deep, because after the first human being’s sin so great an ignorance of divine knowledge covered human hearts that, leaving their Creator, they believed their own works or inventions to be gods, and scarcely any of them knew why human beings had been made or by whom. “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. 1:2): through the mouths of the prophets, instructed by the Holy Spirit, who foretold that salvation would be restored to the human race through the waters of baptism. See how briefly, by the emptiness and void of earth and by the darkness of the deep, Moses describes the ignorance of the whole world. It was so great that, except for a few people or prophets within Judaea, hardly anyone knew why he had been born.

But when this darkness had covered the world for five thousand years and more, and the time had come of which David says, “You will arise, Lord, and have mercy on Zion, for the time to show her mercy has come” (Ps. 101:14), God said, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1:3). What is this light, if not the Son of God—God from God, light from light? He was indeed with the Father, not made but begotten; angels saw him, for the sight of his brightness illumined them, but human beings could not see him because the density of darkness covered their eyes. A blind person cannot see the brightly shining sun because he has no eyes with which to see it. It is not the sun’s fault that it is not seen, but the blind person’s. Likewise, human beings could not see that preeminent light because they had lost the sight by which God is seen.

This light was with the Father but was not made, because the Son of God was neither made nor created but only begotten from the Father. Since the human being, fixed in the mud of so profound a depth, could not see the light of such greatness, God said, “Let there be light.” It is as if he said: “Because miserable humanity, oppressed by the murk of darkness, cannot see my Son, coeval and coequal with me, I will that my Son, through whom all things were made, should condescend to it and become such a light as it can see with bodily eyes: that is, he should be incarnate and become human. Since the human being cannot see God, who is spirit, let God become human and be seen by human beings as human, so that, by seeing the human being and recognizing that this one is God, humanity may gradually return and ascend from the vision of the human being to the vision of God.” “And there was light” (Gen. 1:3), that is, “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14).

“While all things held their deep silence, and night in its course had reached its midpoint, the almighty Word of God came from the royal thrones of heaven” (Wis. 18:14). Although this was said of God’s vengeance carried out at midnight in Egypt, when all the firstborn were slain, it can fittingly be understood also of the Lord’s incarnation. For two voices sounded in the world: first the voice of the prophets proclaiming that Christ would come, then the voice of the apostles announcing that he had come. These two voices were signified by the two seraphim of whom Isaiah says that one cried to the other, saying, “Holy, holy,” and so forth (Isa. 6:3). What the prophets foretold would happen, the apostles proclaimed as accomplished.

At the time of the Lord’s birth, however, the prophets had for the most part already died, their prophecy had nearly fallen silent, and the apostles’ preaching had not yet sounded; thus between the voices there was a deep silence. Before Christ’s coming it had also been said: “God is known in Judaea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:2). When he came, night in its course had reached its midpoint, because so great a murk of night and darkness—that is, ignorance—had grown that neither the Jews who read the prophets nor the Gentiles recognized him. As John says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:10–11).

Therefore, in such a thickness of darkness, a sudden light shining from heaven came to enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, fulfilling Isaiah’s words: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light; light has risen upon those who dwell in a land of the shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2). This light is also signified by the candle which holy Church, in a most beautiful custom, has a new one made and lit every year on the vigil of Easter. The number of the year of the Lord’s incarnation is inscribed on the candle itself, so that even children may plainly understand that it is made in remembrance of the new light which shone from heaven upon earth.

The darkness which is appointed to be recalled for the three days before Easter also signifies the darkness of which we have spoken, which Christ’s coming illumined. It is fittingly observed for three days because of the three times which preceded that light: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace. The time before the Law ran from the beginning of the world, that is, from Adam to Moses; the time under the Law from Moses to John. For the Lord himself defines it in the Gospel: “The Law and the prophets were until John; from then the kingdom of God is proclaimed” (Luke 16:16).

It is also fitting that darkness continues in the time of grace, even though Christ has now been born, because from righteous Abel to Christ’s passion, however piously and justly the saints lived, when they died they were compelled to go into darkness and hell, though they were by no means punished by fire or torments as the wicked were. Hence, although the Fathers before Christ were most approved, holy Church does not customarily celebrate a feast-day for any of those who died before Christ suffered, except Saint John the Baptist, the Innocents, and the seven Maccabean brothers; for all alike were led to hell. When we celebrate the feast of any saint, we rejoice with that saint and praise God because he has raised the saint’s soul, freed from the body, to heaven. But how can a solemnity be made for those whose souls were led to hell? They seem more to call for compassion than rejoicing.

But after Christ descended to hell, the people of the saints who walked in darkness saw a great light and were brought out by the Lord with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. At once the Apostle’s saying was fulfilled: “The darkness has passed and the true light now shines” (1 John 2:8).

These three times are also signified by the three Masses which we are about to celebrate on this present feast of the Lord’s Nativity. The first Mass, at night, signifies the time before the Law, when, apart from a few patriarchs, the night of ignorance covered faith or knowledge of the Lord’s incarnation. The second Mass, when dawn appears, signifies the time under the Law, when in the Psalms and prophets, much of the former night having been removed, the brightness of the sun about to be born begins to appear. The third Mass, in daylight, denotes the time of grace, when “a light rose in darkness for the upright of heart.” Thus the angel who announced that birth to the shepherds appeared in brilliance of light—something never before recorded—showing that the former darkness was now to be wholly driven away by the ray of the new sun.

After God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3), it rightly follows: “And God saw that the light was good, and he divided the light from the darkness” (Gen. 1:4). God’s seeing is approving and praising. He therefore saw that the light was good: he was pleased with and praised all that this true sun did, saying over him when he was baptized in the Jordan and when transfigured on the mountain, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17; 17:5). And he divided the light from the darkness (Gen. 1:4), saying to him: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as the footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

Or we may understand the light here as his apostles, who by participation in the true light themselves became light, as the Lord says to them: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). He divided them from darkness, saying: “You are not of the world, but I chose you from the world; therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19). And elsewhere: “I came to divide a man against his father and a daughter against her mother,” and so forth (Matt. 10:35). “And he called the light day and the darkness night” (Gen. 1:5). The Lord shows that he calls himself day when he says to the apostles: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11:9), for that day had twelve apostles. The apostles too are called days, as the psalm says: “Day pours forth speech to day” (Ps. 18:3), and again: “Days shall be formed and none shall be in them” (Ps. 138:16). No one is ignorant that the wicked are called night and darkness.

Immediately Moses adds about Christ’s passion: “And there was evening and morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). David briefly shows that evening and morning mean passion and resurrection when he says: “Weeping will linger at evening, and joy at morning” (Ps. 29:6)—for the apostles, who were saddened while Christ suffered and rejoiced when he rose. And in Christ’s person: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2). Notice how fittingly he did not say “there was evening and morning, the first day,” as he says of subsequent days, but “one day” (Gen. 1:5). This has great force against heretics who said that God and the human being were two persons. Thus “there was evening and morning, one day” means more aptly: although Christ suffered and died not in his divinity but in his humanity, and rose through the power of divinity, he must not be said to consist of two persons but of two natures. God must not be separated from the human being in him, because God and human being are one day, that is, one Christ. Accordingly the holy Fathers instituted that Christ’s blood in the sacrament of the altar should never be consecrated from unmixed wine, but that water should always be mixed with wine in the chalice, intending wine to signify Christ’s divinity and water his humanity.

## Chapter VIII. On Blessed Mary, eternally destined to take part in the accomplishment of the incarnation

After briefly anticipating these matters concerning Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and our redemption, Moses again, after the work of the six days, uttered a memorable saying concerning the dwelling-place in which he rested—that is, his most blessed mother, our lady Saint Mary—when he said: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the human being whom he had formed” (Gen. 2:8). If this is understood literally only of the paradise in which Adam was placed, it seems strange that it is said to have been planted “from the beginning.” For the trees were made not in the beginning but on the third day, when God commanded: “Let the earth bring forth living grass and a tree bearing fruit” (Gen. 1:12). If trees were first made on the third day, how can this paradise be said to have been planted from the beginning?

But if it is understood figuratively of our Lady, every question is resolved. The Lord truly planted her from the beginning. Since her Son himself says in the Gospel, “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13), it is plain that she whom he planted, fixed and rooted more deeply, cannot be uprooted. The Lord planted her from the beginning because, before he made anything from the beginning, she was ordered from eternity and “from ancient times, before the earth was made” (Prov. 8:22). God had immovably proposed and determined in his foreknowledge to restore the human race through her fruit.

Holy Church often calls her paradise, when in her praise it sings the Song of Songs: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard” (Song 4:13). Paradise means a place of delights. What place can be understood as more a place of delights than that womb in which, for nine months, the bread of angels and their delight remained enclosed? Therefore the Lord God planted from the beginning a paradise of delight, in which he placed the human being whom he had formed: that is, from the beginning he prepared a royal hall in which, when he formed the man, he would place his Son, equal and coeternal with himself. But how did he plant this paradise, and what kind of paradise did he plant? Clearly one lacking no cause of delight. When a rich king wishes to build himself a hall where he may rest when weary and dwell more frequently, he naturally chooses a suitable place: watered by streams, planted with trees, defended by the nature of the site, joined to woodland, and enclosed by an abundance of gardens.

Let us see whether anything was lacking to that heavenly court, our Lady. This paradise was watered, for “a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Genesis 2:6); and shortly after, “A river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there was divided into four heads” (Genesis 2:10). What is this spring or river going out from the place of delight? It is surely that of which Isaiah says: “On that day there shall be an open fountain to the house of David, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zechariah 13:1). It went out from the place of delight, namely from holy Mary’s womb, watering the whole surface of the earth—that is, washing the sinners of holy Church and refreshing the just with sweet drink: “He led me beside waters of refreshment” (Psalm 22:2), and “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of thy house, and thou shalt give them drink from the torrent of thy delight” (Psalm 35:9).

It divides into four heads because it allotted to each Evangelist what and how much he should say of himself. It wonderfully identifies them: “The name of one is Phison; it surrounds all the land of Havilah, where gold is born, and the gold of that land is best” (Genesis 2:11–12). Since gold is more precious than all metals and Christ’s divinity more precious than his humanity, Phison circling the land producing gold fittingly signifies John, who contemplated and spoke more deeply than the others about Christ’s divinity. “The name of the second river is Gehon; it surrounds all Ethiopia” (Genesis 2:13). We read that Matthew was sent to preach in Ethiopia, travelled through it in preaching, converted it to faith, and suffered there; Gehon therefore rightly signifies him. “The third river is Tigris; it goes against the Assyrians” (Genesis 2:14). Luke, we read, was Syrian by birth; after conversion he went against the Assyrians by writing his Gospel against his ancestral error, and may therefore be signified by Tigris. The fourth river is Euphrates, circling Babylon and Alexandria, where Mark preached, wrote his Gospel, and suffered; Mark may thus fittingly be signified by Euphrates.

This paradise, therefore—the Mother of God, enclosed garden, sealed fountain, well of living waters (Song 4:12, 15)—is surrounded like a spring day by rose flowers and lilies of the valleys (Ecclesiasticus 50:8), and like cinnamon and balm constantly breathes the sweetest fragrance (Ecclesiasticus 24:20). Let us see by what strong defense it is protected. The Song of Love says: “Thy neck is like the tower of David, built with its battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, every armor of the mighty” (Song 4:4). The neck is between head and body and joins head to body. Our Lady is therefore fittingly understood as the neck of holy Church, mediatrix between God and humanity: in bearing God’s Word incarnate she joined Christ to Church as head to body, and divinity to our humanity.

She is called a tower of David because that David, the strong-handed king, raised and fortified her against Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, entered her to fight him, as the Gospel says, “Jesus entered a certain castle” (Luke 10:38). From her he conquered the castle to be invaded; sending soldiers before him, he said, “Go into the castle opposite you, and you will find an ass”—that is, human nature—bound by Babylon’s king; “loose her and bring her to me” (Matthew 21:2). From this tower he defeated the strong man who had guarded his court in peace and, as Isaiah testifies, sat among his rivers saying, “As eggs left behind are gathered, so I gathered the whole earth; none moved a wing, opened a mouth, or chirped” (Isaiah 10:14). From this tower the true David came forth, ruddy and beautiful in appearance (1 Samuel 16:12): ruddy from blood sprinkled from side, feet, and hands; beautiful because “fairer in form than the children of men” (Psalm 44:3). He struck proud Goliath in the forehead, killed him with his own sword, took all his armor and distributed his spoils. Returning victorious to his soldiers, he said, “Take courage, I have conquered the world” (John 16:33), and “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31).

This tower was built with battlements, namely principal virtues or gifts of the Holy Spirit protecting her, as Gabriel said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1:35). “A thousand shields hang from it, every armor of the mighty” (Song 4:4): the thousand, a perfect number, means that she was filled with every virtue, and the angel rightly calls her “full of grace” (Luke 1:28). “Every armor of the mighty” confirms that all virtues with which mighty men, the saints, were individually armed by God’s gift, she alone universally had hanging, implanted, and fixed in herself.

Who can conceive how angelic companies appointed for her service continually attended her? The Song says: “Behold Solomon’s bed; sixty mighty men surround it, of Israel’s strongest, all holding swords and most skilled in war” (Song 3:7). What is more fittingly signified by the bed than the womb in which the true Solomon, peaceful king whose face all earth desires, lay sweetly and rested nine months, then went forth as bridegroom from a chamber? Sixty mighty men surround this bed: not fewer than sixty—that is, perfect and infinite legions of highest virtues and powers—were sent to her service, ready to obey a command and instantly drive away approaching enemies.

This paradise of delight was planted by God from the beginning. Into it he placed the man whom he had formed: that is, he joined his Son, the Word coeternal with himself and made flesh, to the womb of the blessed Virgin. “That he might work and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Isaiah explains what work he might do: “That he may do his work; his work is strange to him” (Isaiah 28:21). What is so foreign to God as to cry and be nourished with a woman’s milk? What is so strange to God as to die? Foreseeing this work Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard thy report and feared; I considered thy works and was terrified” (Habakkuk **[source prints I:5]**). Again the Lord himself says through Isaiah, “Be astonished and wonder, for I do a work in your days which none will believe when it is told” (Isaiah 29:9). Isaiah likewise says, “Lord, who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53).

God began to work this work when he was made flesh in his mother’s womb, for he became man in order to redeem man. The phrase “and keep it” needs no explanation: both before he was incarnate in the blessed Virgin, while enclosed in her, and after he was born from her, he always kept her in every holiness and purity—she who

> Had a mother’s joys with virgin honor,
> and was seen to have no equal before, nor any after.

No tongue can speak, nor mind conceive, how she burned with sweetness of divine love while carrying God enclosed in her womb. David, who contemplated God only through a mirror and in an enigma, nevertheless says from great devotion, “How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord!” (Psalm 30:20). What then should be thought of her in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily for so long? In her, as a wise man says, the abundance of all virtues produced a certain heavenly and ineffable harmony; for without the spiritual song of sweet modulation, one must not believe that God remained in her even one hour.

No one should wonder that I have said she can be signified by paradise or Solomon’s bed. Blessed Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine* that it does no harm, and indeed helps, if the same sense is understood in different ways, provided it does not depart from Catholic meaning and love of God and neighbor. No one disputes that Solomon’s bed figures holy Church, because in it the Lord rests, according to “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble, quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2). If he rests upon the humble, who can be found humbler than she? When the angel said she would become the Lord’s mother, she called herself his handmaid: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to thy word” (Luke 1:38). In her song, passing over every other virtue, she says, “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). Since God dwelt spiritually in her soul through incomparable humility and bodily in her flesh through assumed humanity, I see no reason why she should not more properly be called Solomon’s bed than any other faithful member of holy Church.

If someone says that the exposition of the ancient Fathers is enough and that a new or unfamiliar one ought not be added, we answer with Ruth the Moabitess, who, oppressed by poverty, said to her mother-in-law Naomi: “If you command, I shall go into the field and gather the ears left behind the backs of the reapers” (Ruth 2:3).

## Chapter IX. The same place of Holy Scripture may be expounded in various ways; again on the Blessed Virgin Mary, a great encomium of her

Thus we also gather ears left by reapers’ hands, imitating Isaiah: “It shall be as one gathering ears in the valley of Rephaim” (Isaiah 17:5). The reapers are the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church, to whom the Lord says, “Pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:38), and elsewhere, “I sent you to reap what you did not labor for” (John 4:38). Because the days of man are short and they were prevented by death, they could not reap the whole field—that is, expound all Old Testament Scripture. They left us many ears to gather, namely many meanings to be understood in different ways.

If anyone wishes to rebuke us for searching these out, let him see that he is not unlike Boaz in goodness. Encouraging Ruth to persist in her begun work, Boaz ordered his young men not to trouble her; indeed, he ordered them to cast out from their sheaves and deliberately leave some for her, so that she might gather without shame. She gathered to evening, threshed what she had gathered with a rod, and found three measures of barley. This typifies for us that, if we think we have understood in Scripture something worthy of memory, we should immediately examine it carefully with the rod, that is with the rectitude of subtle testing, lest it be found to contradict, however little, the sayings of ancient Fathers. Rather, it should be restrained to the measure of three measures: faith in the holy Trinity and practice of the three virtues, faith, hope, and charity.

That Ruth, by the very gathering of ears, gained Boaz’s familiarity and later was lawfully joined to him in the marriage bed, and deserved such honor that the Lord Jesus Christ himself descended from her stock, mystically urges us that if we strive spiritually to imitate her acts, we too shall be led through them to the Lord’s love. No one, then, should be blamed for expounding an Old Testament saying differently from what he finds in the ancients, provided he mixes in nothing contrary to them; for the ancient doctors themselves did not always expound the same saying in one and the same way.

Blessed Augustine, explaining “Thou sendest forth springs in the valleys; waters shall pass between the mountains” (Psalm 103:10), says that the mountains are the apostles. Blessed Gregory, much later in the homily *In the Fifteenth Year*, treats the same verse and says that mountains are the proud and valleys the humble. Though proud persons and apostles differ greatly, neither doctor contradicts the other: the Holy Spirit speaks through and in both, and from each mouth, though differently, works edification in the minds of neighbors.

We therefore should not be blamed if we refer the earth’s creation to the re-creation of human nature. The creation of the first man suitably applies in many places to the second man, Christ. The first was made on the sixth day, the second in the sixth age. The first was made not from nothing but from earth’s mud; the second was formed by God from the Virgin’s flesh in her womb. From the first sleeping man’s side God built woman; from the second’s side, dead on the cross, flowed blood and water, by which Church is built. Unless one is reborn by baptismal water and joined to Christ by receiving his blood, he cannot call himself member or child of Christ or Church. From Adam and Eve we are all born according to flesh; from Christ and Church we are all spiritually reborn.

Consider the words Adam spoke of Eve: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). Bones mean the strong in Church, flesh the weak. To show that the strong must not despise the weak, after “bone of my bones” the Lord added “flesh of my flesh.” Those called “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10:28) may be understood as Christ’s bones; the weaker are those told, “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:23). To the bones he says, “Carry neither purse nor bag nor shoes” (Luke 10:4); to the flesh, “Now let him who has a purse take it, likewise a bag” (Luke 22:36). Though Paul says that he endured the cross for the joy set before him, despising shame (Hebrews 12), Christ compassionately says to the weak, lest sudden fear drive them to despair, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death,” and “Father, if possible let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:38–39). Thus he joins himself to them: “flesh of my flesh.” He compares himself especially to a hen, who compassionates her chicks more than other birds, becoming hoarse in voice and bristly in feathers. Hence he allowed Peter, the chief and first pillar of Church, to fall by denying him three times, that after rising he might learn to condescend to the fallen: “And thou, once converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22:32).

“Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). The Apostle explains, “This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:32). Christ left his father and mother, that is, the Synagogue from whose stock he was born according to flesh, and cleaved to his wife, holy Church; bridegroom and bride, head and body, Christ and Church, are one flesh. This union happened in the glorious and most noble chamber of the blessed Virgin’s womb. God foretold her coming in his curse upon the serpent: “I shall put enmities between thee and the woman, thy seed and her seed. She shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel.” The serpent’s head is pride: by pride it was cast from heaven and cast man from paradise, for “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15). She crushed this head, pride, both herself and through her seed, her Son: herself by saying, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:38), her Son by humbling himself, though God, becoming obedient even to death (Philippians 2:8).

Enough of Adam and Eve. Let us give one example of how Noah foreshadowed the Lord’s Passion, and end the sermon.

## Chapter X. How naked Noah figures Christ’s Passion

“Noah planted a vineyard; drinking wine he became drunk and was naked in his tent” (Genesis 9:21). In this place Noah signifies the Lord, who planted the vineyard, namely the Jewish people, of whom the Psalm says: “Thou hast brought a vineyard out of Egypt; thou hast cast out nations and planted it” (Psalm 79:9). Isaiah likewise says of it: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a fertile hill, and I expected it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:1–2).

The wine Noah drank signifies the love which the Lord had for the Jewish people. Although he redeemed the whole world by his blood, he testifies that he came especially for them, saying in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). This wine was so powerful that in drinking it he became drunk. The Apostle explains: because of the exceeding love with which God loved us (Ephesians 2:4), he sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3). Just as a drunken person, having lost his senses, does not consider what he does, so the Lord, because of the exceeding force of love, did what no one would have believed he would do, nor would have thought belonged to the excellence of his majesty: to be born of a woman, nourished on her milk, struck with fists, spat upon, crucified, and to die. He endured all these things as though drunk.

Lest anyone think it incredible that we have said drunken Noah bore the figure of the Lord, let him consider the Davidic saying: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, as a mighty man drunken with wine” (the source prints Psalm XVII:65). The Song of Love also says, “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). Drunken with wine—that is, burning with the excess of his love for us—he was naked in his tent, because among the Jewish people, who ought properly to have been his tent and house, he was dishonored and spat upon; he was physically stripped of his garments by Pilate’s soldiers and hung naked on the cross.

Ham, his younger son, who mocked his father’s nakedness, signifies the unbelieving people: seeing Christ hanging naked on the cross, they mocked him and shook their heads, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the beloved Christ of God” (Mark 15:31). Shem and Japheth, his elder sons, signify the prophets and apostles. Seeing him naked—in prophetic spirit, as prophets, or bodily, as apostles—they did not despise him but honored him.

One of these was Isaiah, who, seeing him naked beforehand, says: “He has neither form nor beauty; we saw him and there was no appearance, and desired him: despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity. His face was as though hidden and despised, and therefore we did not esteem him. Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows; and we thought him as it were a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isaiah 53:2–4). The Apostle Paul agrees: “We preach Christ crucified, to Jews indeed a scandal and to Gentiles folly, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).

When Noah awoke, he cursed not the son who mocked him but Canaan, that son’s son; the two who honored him he blessed. So Christ, rising from the dead and ascending to heaven, glorified with himself the prophets and apostles and all who believed their preaching, but commanded the unbelieving seed to be punished. The Psalm says: “He struck his enemies in their hind parts; he gave them everlasting reproach” (Psalm 77:66). He struck his enemies in their descendants: upon the descendants of those who crucified him he cast, in this present life, the sentence of dispersion and captivity, and in the future the dart of eternal condemnation. Since much has been said of Christ’s Incarnation and Passion and it is time to end such a lengthy sermon, let us again turn our eyes to our Lady, mother of mercy; through her blessed fruit we were saved, and in her let us end our speech.

## Chapter XI. The author turns to the Blessed Virgin and begs her as mother of mercy

She is truly the mother of whom it is said: “Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all living” (Genesis 3:20).
