That Eve is rightly called mother of the dying, because through her fault we all incurred the sentence of death; this Mary is mother of the living, because through her we all recovered life lost. Following the Apostle, who says, “As in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22), we too may say of his glorious mother: as through Eve all die, so through Mary all are made alive. Paradise’s gate was closed to all through Eve and opened again through the Virgin Mary.

Of her the Lord’s saying may fittingly be understood: “Let us make him a help like himself” (Genesis 2:18). Just as the Lord made other bodily creatures by command alone, but seemed to wish to make man—the man formed in his image, by whom we may understand Christ—as if not without counsel, saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), so he created woman as if by counsel: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a help like himself” (Genesis 2:18). No one doubts this was said literally about Eve; yet it can no less fittingly be understood of the spouse and mother of God, holy Mary, and through her of holy Church.

Although Isaiah says, “Shall I, who make others bring forth, not bring forth? says the Lord; and shall I, who give generation to others, be barren? says thy God” (Isaiah 66:9), before blessed Mary he was in a sense barren: though as God he made all things, he had not generated anyone in the way in which he later generated the Son. But when God said, “Let us make him a help like himself,” he joined our flesh as bride to his only-begotten Son in the blessed Virgin’s womb as in a bridal chamber; and, as Adam said, “They shall be two in one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), he joined God and man in the one Christ. At once, barrenness removed, God began to generate those children of whom John says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:12–13).

Behold, then, how fittingly the words “Let us make him a help like himself” are understood of our Lady. God is the Father of created things, and Mary the mother of recreated things. God, who created all things from nothing, willed to repair them in their corrupted state ‘without Mary’ [so the supplied text; the immediately following sentences instead describe Mary’s role in the restoration]. God created all things, and Mary gave birth to God; because she bore God’s Son, Mary became God’s spouse.

Mary bore not God alone; after him and through him she bore many children of God, who daily cry devoutly, “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). The good Son of Mary does not disdain to call those children brothers: “I shall declare thy name to my brethren” (Psalm 21:23), and “Go, announce to my brethren” (Matthew 28:10). Thus Mary’s Son is our brother and, consequently, Mary is also our mother. O what we owe Mary! Through Mary God became our Father, because through her God’s Son became our brother. Through Mary our Creator became our Father; through Mary our Judge became our brother.

What then need we fear when our Judge is our brother and our Judge’s mother is also our mother? If our Judge is perhaps angry with us because of sins, let us not despair, for his mother is our mother too. Let the pious mother please the pious Son for guilty children; let the good mother reconcile the angry brother to miserable brothers.

That good servant of hers, Lord Anselm, often mentioned above, wrote of her in a prayer addressed to her as follows: “We remember, and it is delightful to remember, how, appearing to a servant of yours at his last hour and asking whether he knew you, when he replied trembling, ‘Not at all, Lady,’ you sweetly said: ‘I am the mother of mercy.’ Where then should the wretched more rightly and confidently bewail their calamities than with you, who deserved to be mother of our Redeemer and Judge?

“The golden urn, in which by God’s command manna was placed—the bread of angels which human nature ate through you—prefigured you. Therefore, pious mother, offer this bread to your hungry children; and, that they may be able to receive it worthily, heal in them the palate of the inner man. Although your Son himself says, ‘Who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him’ (John 6:55), a saying of one of his stewards greatly terrifies us: ‘Who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself’ (1 Corinthians 11:29). For we know truly that we are entirely unworthy of so great a mystery, having offended him in many things. Therefore, although we desire him, our conscience grievously reproaching us inwardly, we fear to receive him.

“But fleeing to you, our mediatrix, who after God are our sole hope, we confess our sins to you, and beg you to be mediatrix and intercessor between us and God. But what shall we wretches do? Straits press us on every side. When we offend God’s Son, we also offend his mother, whom he loves greatly. How, then, do we seek reconciliation to the Son through the mother when we likewise offend the mother?”

But because we offend both, let us flee to the mercy of both and ask to be reconciled to each through the other. Good mother, reconcile to thy good Son thy guilty children. Good brother, reconcile to thy good mother thy guilty brothers. Thou art good and she is good; thou art sweet and she is sweet.

Good Lord and good Lady, sweet brother and sweet mother, we beg your mercy: grant that we may remember this present feast of the Nativity of the pious brother and of the childbirth of the pious mother in such a way that through that feast you may lead us to eternal feasts, where we may see you, rejoice in seeing you, and, rejoicing, praise you through all ages of ages. Amen.

This book of Holy Mary of Casa Dei [Note: now Vicoigne, a monastery of the Premonstratensian order] was written in the year of the Incarnate Word 1149.

## Hermann, abbot: Three books on the Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon and the deeds of Bishop Bartholomew and Saint Norbert

See *Patrologia Latina*, volume 156, column 961, Appendix to Guibert of Nogent.

## Narrative of the restoration of the abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai, by Hermann

### Notice preceding the following short work

(Dom Luc d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, edition of de la Barre, II, p. 888.)

We received the narrative or history of the restoration of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai, a Benedictine foundation of very ancient origin which we are publishing, from the most learned and highly skilled student of antiquities, the Discalced Carmelite Joseph Ignatius of Saint Anthony, born of the illustrious family of the lords of Rebec. He copied it and adorned it with brief notes which gave me much light; by them several words and various places in the text are explained.

The author Hermann first appears as monk and afterward as abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai. In the prologue he explains why he undertook this work. He frankly admits that, because the abbey had remained ruined for many centuries or undergone varying disasters and reversals, he was often wrapped in darkness when writing the narrative. He found scarcely any ancient documents, since that noble religious house had been wholly stripped, its buildings destroyed, of precious ornaments, charters, and revenues. Thus only with the greatest labor could he acquire any knowledge of the earlier and ancient age and of the former Fathers who had inhabited the monastery. To weave history’s thread and observe chronological order, he adds to monastic affairs the actions of popes, kings, princes, and rulers.

The learned reader will undoubtedly observe distinctive matters in this narrative, especially those which Hermann affirms happened in his time as an eyewitness and hearer. I add nothing here; if you wish, read the appended notes.

Hermann begins his work with Samson, archbishop of Reims, and with Innocent II governing the Catholic Church while he was at Rome. He himself testifies in the preface: “Lest I wholly perish from the weariness of so long a time in the Lateran palace, I undertake to write the order of the restoration of our church,” etc. I think he ends with the words, “and from their companionship it would have been better than if they had been buried separately.” What follows from number 103 to the end I judge to be another person’s account. Since Hermann was conspicuous for great humility and other virtues, it is not credible that he would have broken out into so much praise of himself. That continuator ends his account in 1160.

### Prologue

Brother Hermann, the least servant of them all, to his most beloved lords, fathers, brothers, and sons, all the monks of the monastery of blessed Martin of Tournai: may you continually remember the heavenly Zion beside the rivers of Babylon.

For the affection you have shown me from my childhood, and for the sincere obedience which, so long as I chose to be your abbot [Note: Col. 0039. “I chose to be.” That is, he resigned the office of abbot in 1136, at the end of that year or the beginning of the next, having presided for about ten years, as stated below.], you have always rendered me without any scruple, whether I was present or absent, I give thanks to God and to you all; and I pray for his mercy, that the Lord himself may reward you on my behalf. Since some among you have often asked me to make known, by committing it to writing, the manner of the building—or restoration—of our church, both to those now living and to those to come, I willingly wish to satisfy their request. I know that knowledge of the predecessors has often benefited posterity, whereas ignorance of them has very often caused no small loss.

You know that, from the time when I was a young man, I wished to do this very thing, and even set some matters down in writing; but, considering that the first founders of our church were still alive, I feared the charge of flattery if I seemed to write their deeds while they themselves yet lived, and so I destroyed what I had begun. But now, since the first two have died and I have succeeded as the third abbot, and since I see that of the earlier monks none, or few, survive; and since I know also that the fiftieth year of our restoration has now passed, I can more confidently comply with your request. For if I delay any longer, many things which ought to have been recorded may gradually be consigned to oblivion as time passes.

Therefore, as you know, after the recent Christmas of the Lord, when I was returning from Rome with our lord Samson, Archbishop of Reims, I brought to Tournai the letters of Pope Innocent, commanding the people of Tournai to elect a bishop of their own and to be wholly released from obedience to the Bishop of Noyon. When Lord Absalon, Abbot of Saint-Amand, had accordingly been elected bishop, I was immediately asked to return to Rome on his behalf. And while I await the pope’s reply, I find that I have remained at Rome from the octave of Easter until the octave of Pentecost. Therefore, lest I utterly fail from the weariness of so long a time, or waste away in idleness in the Lateran palace, I begin to write the account of the restoration of our Church [Col. 0041], and desire to send it to you when written. I earnestly entreat you that, if perhaps—as I greatly fear—it should happen that I die at Rome as the excessive heat grows stronger, you may commend the soul of your servant to the Lord in your prayers.

I especially exhort your fraternity continually to devote itself to two things: religious observance and mutual affection. By these two, with God’s favor, you will be able to prosper both inwardly and outwardly. Whenever we held these two firmly, we mocked and despised the storms raging outwardly in the world, and by despising them trod them underfoot. But whenever we permitted them, even slightly, to grow cold among us, we found that outward prosperity brought us no advantage. But this preface is now sufficient; let the most truthful account now follow.

Here ends the Prologue.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0041]

[Col. 0041A] Concerning the restoration of the church of Saint Martin of Tournai.

1. While King Philip, son of Henry, son of Robert, son of Hugh Capet—who expelled from the kingdom the kings descended from the illustrious Charles and obtained the sovereignty—held the sceptres of the Frankish realm, there was a certain cleric named Odo, born in the city of Orléans, son of Gerard and Cecilia. From childhood he devoted himself diligently to literary studies; within his youth he acquired so much learning that he was judged second to none among the Franks of his time. Thus he was considered more worthy of the title of master than of pupil.

He first taught scholars in the city of Toul; then he was summoned by the canons of Blessed Mary in the city of Tournai and appointed master of their school. Governing it for almost five years, he spread the reputation of his name so widely [Col. 0041B] that crowds of clerics from France, Flanders, Normandy, and even distant Italy, Saxony, and Burgundy flocked daily to hear him. Thus, if you went through the streets of the city and saw groups engaged in disputation, you would have believed that all its citizens, abandoning every other occupation, were devoted to philosophy alone.

If, moreover, you approached the school, you would see Master Odo sometimes walking about while teaching his pupils in the manner of the Peripatetics; sometimes seated like the Stoics and resolving various questions; and, in the evening hours, disputing before the doors of the church until deep into the night, pointing out to his pupils with his finger the courses of the stars and demonstrating the varieties of the zodiacal [Col. 0041C] or Milky-Way circles. Since many gifts were given to him, one person among the rest gave him a gold ring upon which this fitting little verse was engraved:

> A golden ring befits Odo of Orléans.

Although he was skilled in all seven liberal arts, he excelled especially in dialectic, and it was particularly for this that crowds of clerics sought him out. He also wrote two small books on it. The first, extremely useful for recognizing and avoiding sophisms, he entitled *The Sophist*; the other he called the *Book of Complexions*. He also composed a third work, *On Thing and Being*, in which he resolves the question whether “thing” (*res*) and “being” (*ens*) are one and the same. In these three little books, and in his other writings when occasion arose to mention his own name, he called himself not Odo but Odard, as everyone then called him.

2. It should nevertheless be known concerning this master that he taught this same dialectic to his pupils not, like certain moderns, “in the word” (*in voce*), but, in the manner of Boethius and the ancient doctors, “in the thing” (*in re*). Therefore Master Raimbert, who at the same time taught dialectic to his clerics “in the word” in the town of Lille, and very many other masters, greatly envied and disparaged him, declaring their own lectures superior to his.

> [Note: Col. 0041C. “In the word.” These are called Nominalists; the others Realists.]

For this reason some clerics, troubled as to whom they ought rather to believe, hesitated. They saw that Master Odard did not depart from the teaching of the ancients; yet certain of them, eagerly pursuing, by human curiosity and in the Athenian manner, either to learn or to hear something new, praised the others instead—especially because they said that their lectures were of greater value for the exercise of disputation, eloquence, indeed talkativeness and fluency.

Accordingly, one of the canons of that church, named Gualbert—who later became our monk, and afterwards an abbot in the diocese of Châlons—was disturbed by so great a diversity of opinions and misguided clerics. He secretly approached a certain deaf and dumb diviner, famous in the same city for fortune-telling, and began by signs and gestures to inquire to which master greater credence ought to be given. Immediately that man—marvellous to relate!—understood his question. Drawing his right hand through the palm of his left like a plough cutting the earth, and extending his finger toward Master Odo’s school, he indicated that Odo’s teaching was most correct. Then, extending his finger toward the town of Lille and, bringing his hand to his mouth, blowing it away, he signified that Master Raimbert’s lecture was nothing but wordy chatter.

I have said this not because I think diviners should be consulted, or that they should be believed contrary to the divine command, but in order to refute the excessive presumption of certain proud men. Seeking nothing but to be called wise, they prefer that their invented novelty be read in the books of Porphyry and Aristotle [Col. 0043A], rather than the exposition of Boethius and the other ancients. Indeed, Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in the book he wrote *On the Incarnation of the Word*, calls clerics of this kind not dialecticians but heretics of dialectic: “They think,” he says, “that universal substances are nothing but a breath”; and he says that they rightly deserve to be blown out of the number of the wise.

3. Although Master Odard [Note: Col. 0043D. “Odard.” Odard the bishop ought not therefore be removed from the catalogue of the bishops of Cambrai, since he is the same person as Odo.] was everywhere praised for his learning, the dignity of religious seriousness was nevertheless so strong in him that he was no less celebrated and renowned everywhere for that reason. Whenever he followed last, as was his custom, the company of nearly two hundred clerics proceeding before him to church, you could scarcely have found stricter religious observance in any monastery of the most rigorous monks [Col. 0043B]. No one dared speak with his companion; no one laugh; no one even whisper. No one presumed to turn his eyes in the slightest either to the right or left. When they came to the choir, anyone seeking Cluny for the sake of more abundant strictness would have sought in vain.

It is superfluous to say anything of visits from women, disordered hair or clothing, or the abuse of similar things which we today see practised everywhere, since such plagues would without doubt either have driven him from the school or caused him to abandon the mastership of the school. His severity was so great, moreover, that at lesson-time he permitted no layman at all to enter the cloister. Before his arrival, knights and citizens had been accustomed to use the canons’ cloister for hearing and deciding secular lawsuits; but he had now expelled them all so completely that he would not permit even Everard, the most powerful castellan of that city, to remain there for even an hour on such business. Everard had at that time, by military valor, forcibly captured and added to the dominion of Tournai the castle of Mortagne, previously altogether impregnable, although Odo knew that he gave him no small offence by this.

> [Note: Col. 0043D. “Mortagne,” commonly so called, on the River Scheldt, between Tournai and the town of Saint-Amand of Elnone. Everard’s successors took the name of Mortagne from this place.]

For he feared nothing less than the unjust anger of rich or powerful men, and he said that it was a great disgrace for a wise man to depart even slightly from the path of rectitude for the favor or goodwill of princes. For such conduct he was loved and deservedly honored not only by the canons but also by Lord Radbod, then the venerable bishop of that city [Col. 0043D], and by all the citizens. Although some said that he exercised this strictness not for the sake of religion but rather from the custom of ancient philosophy, the reader may readily discern what manner of man he was after his conversion, since he is known to have been so rigorous in secular life. But enough has now been said concerning what he did in the schools; let us come to the beginnings of his conversion.

4. When he had presided over the school of Tournai for nearly five years [Col. 0044A], a certain cleric offered him Saint Augustine’s book *On Free Choice of the Will*. The master bought it only to augment his library, and threw it into a chest with his other books, since, still devoted to worldly wisdom, he took more pleasure in reading Plato than Augustine.

Nearly two months later, while reading Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy* with his pupils, he came to the fourth book, in which Boethius discusses free choice. Remembering the book he had bought, and considering whether he might find in it anything worthy of remembrance, since it was known to be entitled on that subject, he called his servant and ordered it brought to him. Opening it when it had been brought, and reading two or three pages, he gradually began to delight in the beauty of its style. Immediately, therefore, calling the clerics together—being wholly free from envy and wishing them to share in the treasure he had discovered—he said: “Truly, until now I did not know that Augustine possessed eloquence so great and so delightful.”

Having said this, he at once began the book itself from the beginning and read it to them eagerly, not only then but also the next day, carefully explaining the more obscure places. Then, as they read, they came to the third book, in which the aforesaid doctor compares sinful souls to a slave expelled from his former rank because of his crimes and assigned to clean a sewer. Such souls lose heavenly glory because of their wicked deeds, yet in some manner adorn this world, like a foul sewer, so long as they live in it.

When Master Odard read this judgment aloud to his pupils, he was inwardly pierced with an overwhelming sorrow of heart. Drawing deep sighs from the bottom of his breast, he said: “Alas, how forcefully this judgment presses upon us! Truly, it seems to apply to us as properly as if it had been written for us alone. For we adorn this foul world with whatever small learning we possess; but after death we shall not be worthy of heavenly glory, because we render no service to God and do not employ our learning in his service. Rather, in the vanity of the world and for worldly praise, we make wicked use of it.” Having said this, he rose and entered the church, wholly bathed in tears.

The entire school was suddenly disturbed, and the community of canons also was shaken by great astonishment. Thereafter he gradually began to absent himself from the schools [Col. 0044D], to frequent the church more than usual, to distribute his accumulated money among all the poor, but especially needy clerics, and to attempt the rigor of fasts. Often he would close bread within his fist and cut off with a knife what projected outside it, retaining for food no more than remained within his fist. And behold: a man formerly of milky complexion and robust appearance was suddenly worn down by the mortification of fasting. Within a few days he became so thin, lean, dry, and frail, his bones standing out, that those accustomed to seeing him thought him changed into another man [Col. 0045A], and many could scarcely recognize him.

The report at once spread through the entire region that the great Odo would very soon renounce the world. Four of his clerics followed and attached themselves to him, promising that wherever he went they would follow him inseparably. They received from him the answer that he would do nothing without their common consent. We have learned that they were called by these names: Odo, abbot, whose anniversary is on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July; Gerbert, who died on the fourth day before the Ides of April; Rodulf, who likewise died on the fourth day before the Kalends of March; William, who died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May; and Lamfrid, their fifth companion, who fell away in flight and perished.

Immediately the abbots of the whole province, both monks and canons, came individually to Tournai and each invited Master Odo and his companions to his own church. The master’s clerics, however, preferred to embrace the order of canons rather than monks, because canons followed a more tolerable rule than monks both in liturgical offices and in daily food and clothing. Accordingly, they went sometimes to Mount Saint-Eligius and sometimes to Gautenies, where canons of a stricter life lived, in order to visit and carefully explore in which place it would be more suitable for them to remain. But divine providence had already ordered otherwise concerning them.

5. At that time there was outside the southern gate of that city a small church, built on a little hill in honor of Saint Martin [Col. 0045C]. Tradition declared that it had once been an abbey, but that during the Vandal persecution it had been destroyed by pagans together with the other Gallic churches and reduced to nothing. Yet some of its lands remained in the district, still called by everyone “the lands of Saint Martin”; but they had come into the hands of laymen, who held them as benefices from the bishop.

The little church itself had been reduced to such desolation that no divine office at all was celebrated in it. The priests who held the parish churches of the same city were unwilling to sing Mass there, since no one came who might make them any offering. Only poor people who possessed absolutely nothing, and who died far from the parish churches without finding anyone to carry them there, were brought to this church because it was nearer [Col. 0045D]. Then a priest from the neighboring church of Saint Piat would come, bury them, and carry away anything that might perhaps have been offered by a faithful person.

6. At the same time, that fiery plague, by divine judgment, grievously afflicted the region itself. The feet of very many people seemed publicly to be burned by an invisible fire called “the fire of hell.” Therefore those burned by this fire were brought daily in crowds, not only from that province but also from distant and remote lands, to the church of Blessed Mary built in the city of Tournai [Col. 0046A], because it had been proven and widely reported that very many had already been healed there by her mercy.

But when that church was filled everywhere with their multitude, and scarcely any who entered could endure the excessive stench—of burning human flesh, or, to speak more suitably, its odor—the canons, compelled by necessity, ordered that those whose legs had already been burned after their feet were consumed, and for whose recovery there was no hope, should be cast out of the church. Thus expelled, since they were not received in the other parish churches either because of the same intolerable odor, they were carried by their neighbors to the aforesaid little church of Saint Martin, being empty and solitary, and there, when they finally died from the burning of the same fire, were buried.

Moved by the horror of this plague, the venerable Bishop Radbod mentioned above assembled the people of the whole province at the same church of Saint Mary. After delivering a general address to all, and while everyone was greatly terrified, he cut the hair of more than a thousand young men and cut off their garments trailing upon the ground and serving lust rather than necessity. He then ordered all to fast for one whole Friday until nightfall, so that even little infants should not suck their nurses’ breasts. Moreover, at the following Exaltation of the Holy Cross, he ordained that all the people, barefoot and bearing the relics of the saints, should make a procession around the whole exterior circuit of the city. Thus all experienced the Lord’s wrath turned to mercy, many prayers and alms having been offered for this purpose [Col. 0046C].

This procession on the aforesaid Exaltation of the Holy Cross is observed around the circuit of that city to the present day.

> [Note: Col. 0045. “Is observed.” This procession is still celebrated annually. On the preceding Sunday, the preacher announces the reason for this procession.]

At times nearly a hundred thousand people of both sexes and every age seem to gather for it from the surrounding regions. Except that they no longer perform it barefoot; rather, soldiers and young men engage in games of various frivolities and horse-races, and more frivolity than religion or devotion is found there on that day, since very many have now, through the passage of time, become ignorant of the necessity or reason for which the procession was instituted.

7. When the elders and citizens of the city saw that the sick persons mentioned above, temporarily consumed by the conflagration of the invisible fire but—as we believe—purified of their sins by the same punishment [Col. 0046D], were being brought to the aforesaid little church of Saint Martin, they shed tears out of compassionate mercy. They said that the treasury of the whole city ought to be brought to Saint Martin, and confidently added that the Lord, through the prayers of those buried there, would soon have mercy on that church and restore it. Their pious faith did not deceive them.

8. A certain old man, Vitalis, poor in possessions but rich in character, saw young people coming there on feast days and engaging in races, various games, and shouting revelry, since the place was spacious and solitary. He rebuked them, saying: “Do not, sweetest children [Col. 0047A], disturb the souls of the faithful who rest here. For truly I tell you: through their prayers the Lord, appeased, will within a short time do something great in this place.”

When the old man frequently made this declaration in the hearing of all, the provost of the canons, a vigorous man named Hermann, mocked him as an old fellow and asked playfully what that great thing was which he so often foretold would happen there. He immediately answered before everyone: “Certainly you will see it with your eyes, but I shall not see it.” The outcome proved this true. The provost, with his brother Siger, precentor of the canons, later became a monk in our monastery and lived many years; he often told us that this had been foretold him by that old man [Col. 0047B].

9. Furthermore, Fastred, advocate of the same city, held the lands of that church as a benefice from the bishop. When he saw his wife Ida, sister of Theoderic of Avesnes, distributing these lands to her peasants for cultivation and habitation, he rebuked her and said that she acted wrongly in distributing Saint Martin’s lands to outsiders, and that before she died she would regret having done so, because divine mercy would soon come to the aid of that little church. The result also proved this true. For after her husband’s death Ida became a religious woman among us; and when she saw us contending against the very peasants to whom she had given the lands for their redemption, she struck her breast with a loud groan [Col. 0047C], confessed herself guilty in this matter, and confessed that this had often been foretold to her by her husband.

Fastred himself also, while frequently riding with his knights and passing before the little church, would raise his hands and eyes toward its doors and say with tears: “Ah, Saint Martin, why do you not look upon this church of yours, so long desolate? I pray you, have mercy upon it now and grant that it be restored.” When his knights heard him often praying in this way, they urged him to bring some monks there from the monasteries of the district. He replied that he could find no one willing to enter into such poverty. “But,” he said, “if I found anyone willing to dwell here and restore this little church, I call God and his saints to witness that I would not leave my children even a foot’s breadth of my entire estate, but would hand over everything I possess to this church.”

Yet before Lord Odo’s arrival he was killed by his enemies on the feast of Saint Medard, and could not see what he had long desired to see. He left behind sons who were not so well-disposed toward the place [Col. 0047D].

10. In the same city of Tournai there lived two knights. One, named Walter son of Hubert, was considered among the more powerful nobles of the province; the other, Radulf of Osmont,

> [Note: Col. 0047D. “Radulf of Osmont”: the father of the author of this history.]

seemed inferior to none of the citizens [Col. 0048A]. A certain young man saw these two knights in a dream standing in the aforesaid church and intending to restore its ancient ruins. When, after awakening, he related this to his mother, she immediately offered a judgment like those of the others: “Believe, my son, that by the Lord’s mercy the same church will soon be restored, and that these two knights will greatly benefit that place.” This subsequently happened just so: for both became monks in the same church of Saint Martin. He for whom they labored is witness to how many labors they performed in it and for it.

11. Therefore, while such reports concerning the restoration of that church were being declared by various persons in the region of Tournai, the citizens saw that Master Odo and his five clerics wished to leave secular life, but had not yet determined where they would go. They approached the aforesaid Bishop Radbod and unanimously asked him to exhort them to remain at that church, promising that the help of the whole city would not fail them.

The bishop rejoiced and, summoning them secretly, made known to them the citizens’ request and added many persuasions. The five clerics replied that they would consent to whatever Master Odo wished; the whole matter of consent or refusal depended upon the master’s judgment. The bishop therefore repeated his entreaties and continually urged him to become the fearless founder of so great a good. But Odo, seeing that there stood there only one church, old and half ruined, feared to undertake so weighty a burden. He left the bishop’s house without giving any definite answer [Col. 0048C]. Yet the bishop did not cease repeatedly to kindle his mind for undertaking this work.

Seeing that he made little progress, the bishop summoned a religious priest named Gislebert, who at that time was honored in that district like some prophet and who now rests buried before the altar in the church of Saint Peter of Elnone.

> [Note: Col. 0048D. “Of Elnone”: in the church of Saint-Amand in Pabula, four leagues from Tournai.]

Joining this man to himself, he again tried with all his strength to inflame the master’s mind. He set before him the apostle’s saying that whoever labors more will receive more reward, and that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21); and he argued that it would be more honorable and advantageous for him before God and men to become himself the new foundation of a church than, by entering a monastery built long ago, to build upon another’s foundation [Col. 0048D].

At last Master Odo, overcome by so many and such darts of argument, answered that he would remain there if the little church were handed over to him free from every exaction by episcopal privilege. The bishop, exceedingly delighted, summoned the community of canons and asked that they kindly grant this. But, as though conjecturing and foretelling the future, they wholly refused to grant it. They said that the inhabitants of the district would desert the mother church and frequent Saint Martin’s monastery because of the religious observance of its inhabitants [Col. 0049A]; thus they themselves would be diminished, while the others would be increased above them.

Seeing that such objections had delayed his petition for several days, and fearing that in these postponements Master Odo might go elsewhere, the bishop summoned the canons again. When he saw that all his requests were poured out in vain, he became somewhat stirred in mind and said: “Come now: in the name of the Lord and by the force of obedience, I command you to say whether I am not permitted to give the church which is in my possession and in no way belongs to your communion to those who may serve God in it and strive to build it for God’s honor.”

Then they, bound by the bond of obedience, knew that the church was in the bishop’s possession, that he was permitted to do what he wished with it, and that by canonical law they could say nothing against it. After taking counsel, they finally said that they would consent to whatever pleased the bishop concerning it, on this condition: that, after any of their parishioners had died in secular life, no one might be buried there without their consent. The bishop, greatly rejoicing, on the following Sunday—which was the sixth day before the Nones of May, the day after the Apostles Philip and James—assembled a very great procession of canons and the entire people. He led the aforesaid Master Odo and his five clerics to the church founded in honor of the most holy confessor and bishop of Christ, Martin. Since it had lost the service of the monks who served it under an abbot, it had formerly been destroyed in a barbarian assault [Col. 0049B]. Before all, he handed it over to them free and confirmed by episcopal privilege; and he left them there to serve God canonically, under the Rule of Saint Augustine and in clerical habit.

These things took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, when Pope Urban presided over the Apostolic See; Renaud was Archbishop of Reims; Lord Radbod was bishop of Tournai and Noyon; Philip ruled the kingdom of the Franks; Henry was emperor of the Romans; the illustrious King William, son of Robert, Count of the Normans, ruled the English—he who, having defeated King Harold with his army, had violently subjected England to himself; and the younger Robert, son of the Frisian, held the county of Flanders [Col. 0049C].

12. This Robert was the son of Count Baldwin [Col. 0049D], who built the church of Saint Peter at the town of Lille, placed canons in it, and ordered that he be buried there. When he died, Baldwin his son, brother of the aforesaid Robert, succeeded him. He built the church of Saint Peter at Hasnon, placed monks there, and ordered that he be buried in it. At the command of his father, Count Baldwin, this Baldwin took in marriage Richilde, widow of Herman, Count of Mons; by her he begot two sons, Baldwin and Arnulf. Thus, after the sedition which had long endured between them had been settled, he held both counties, namely Flanders and Hainaut.

When Leo, then pope of Rome—formerly Bishop of Toul and called Bruno—heard this, he said that the marriage was not lawful because they were near relatives by a line of consanguinity. He prophesied that Baldwin’s descendants would not possess both counties for long. The outcome proved this true. For Baldwin, who lies at Lille, fearing that after his death a conflict would arise between his sons Baldwin and Robert, gave his entire land during his lifetime to Baldwin, and made his nobles promise homage and fidelity. Thus at Oudenaarde, upon the relics of the saints, in the presence of father and son and many princes, that Robert publicly swore that he would in no way harm either Baldwin himself or Baldwin’s heirs concerning the land of Flanders. When he had completed this oath, he left Flanders and withdrew into Frisia [Col. 0050A].

[Col. 0050B] 13. Some years later, however, hearing that his brother Baldwin had died and been buried in the monastery of Hasnon, and that Baldwin’s son Arnulf had become Count of Flanders, Robert secretly summoned certain princes of Flanders and promised many gifts. He entered Flanders and, disregarding the oath he had made, prepared war against his nephew. Arnulf, hearing this, joined King Philip of France to himself, from whose hand he had received the land, and met his uncle Robert with his army at the castle of Cassel. There, after battle was joined and Arnulf was killed, Robert obtained Flanders. Richilde, Arnulf’s mother, was driven out of Flanders with her other son Baldwin and returned to the county of Hainaut. Thus Pope Leo’s prophecy was shown to be true.

[Col. 0050C] Robert immediately sent envoys to Emperor Henry, asking him, if necessary, to be his helper. Among these envoys was Baldwin, advocate of Tournai, who later became a monk of Lord Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. He related that, as they drew near Cologne, they encountered an honorable and unknown matron. When she asked who they were, whence they came, and where they were going, they did not wish to disclose the matter as it stood. She said: “I know that you are envoys of Robert, Count of Flanders, who, violating the oath that he made to his father concerning his brother, killed his brother’s son and invaded his land. You are now proceeding to Emperor Henry in order to obtain his favor and friendship. Know, therefore, that you will have a prosperous journey and the favor of Caesar; Robert himself, with his son, will peacefully possess Flanders. But his grandson, begotten from his son, will die without offspring. A certain handsome young man will succeed him, coming from Denmark, but he too will die without offspring. After him two others will contend for Flanders; one of them will kill the other, and the victor will possess Flanders. His heirs will possess Flanders until the time of Antichrist.”

[Col. 0050D] I heard this story while still a little child from the aforesaid Baldwin, advocate of Tournai, who had been one of the envoys. Now, however, as I incline toward old age, I see with my own eyes that these things are true, just as she said.

14. The aforesaid Robert held Flanders in great peace and was a man of much power, so much so that Philip, king of the French, married his stepdaughter [Note: His stepdaughter: Bertha, daughter of Florentius, count of Holland.], by whom he begot King Louis. William, count of the Normans, married his sister; after killing Harold, king of England, and violently seizing England, he held two principalities, being count of the Normans and king of the English. Thus on his seal [Note: On his seal: A similar seal of William may be found in Selden’s edition of Eadmer’s *Historia Novorum*, p. 166.] he sat on horseback on one side as count, and on the other upon a throne with sceptre as king. By Matilda, daughter of the count of Flanders, he begot three sons: William, namely, who succeeded him first; Robert, to whom he gave the county of Normandy; and a third son, Henry, who at first indeed possessed nothing, so that when his renowned father King William died, he seemed to be no more than a knight among the rest. But remarkable fortune attended him.

For when his brother King William, still young, had reigned for almost ten [Note: “After ten”: rather, after thirteen; see Henry of Huntingdon, book VII.] years and went hunting in a forest, he saw a stag passing by and ordered his knight, named Walter Tirel, to stand opposite him with bow and arrows and not allow the stag to pass on the other side. But the knight, drawing his bow and shooting an arrow at the stag, struck the king in the heart and killed him instantly. Thus Henry, the brother who previously had possessed nothing, succeeded him in the kingdom.

When Henry saw that his brother Robert, count of Normandy, was rebelling against him and claiming the kingdom of England because he was the elder by birth and ought by greater right to have succeeded his brother William, Henry assembled an army, crossed the sea, entered Normandy, and, after battle was joined, defeated and captured his brother Robert. He brought him back to England and kept him confined in a certain castle until the day of his death, though he ordered that everything necessary for bodily needs should be supplied and administered to him as to himself. Thus Henry alone again acquired both the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy, and ordered his father’s seal to be made for himself.

Since I have mentioned this Henry, and there will be no other occasion to speak of him, although I may seem to stray far from the narrative begun, I shall nevertheless relate something worthy of remembrance.

15. Once established in the kingdom, he wished to marry a certain maiden, daughter of David, king of the Scots. He asked Lord Anselm, then the venerable archbishop of the city of Canterbury, to bless her for him and, having blessed her in solemn nuptials, to join her to him in marriage. The archbishop replied that he would not bless her, nor would he advise the king to take her as his wife, because, as he had certainly learned, she had worn the veil of nuns upon her head, by which she had shown herself to be the bride of a heavenly rather than an earthly king.

The king replied that he had promised, and had even confirmed by oath to her father King David, that he would marry her; therefore, in order to keep his oath, he would not give her up unless the matter were decided by canonical judgment. He ordered that, with the archbishop of York summoned, a council of bishops, abbots, and ecclesiastical persons from all England be assembled, to determine such a matter by ecclesiastical judgment.

Accordingly, in a general council [Note: “In a general council”: see Eadmer, book III of the *Historia Novorum*, p. 57; Malmesbury, fol. 88.] the abbess in whose monastery that maiden had been brought up was asked whether she had in truth been consecrated by episcopal blessing according to the custom of nuns, with a veil placed upon her head. The abbess publicly answered before all:

> “Indeed, King David, her father, entrusted her to me, not that she should become a nun, but solely that she might be brought up in our church among our other girls of her own age for protection, and be educated in letters. But when she had already grown up, I was informed one day that King William—brother of my lord King Henry, who was then alive—had come to see her, had already dismounted with his knights before the doors of our church, and had ordered that the doors be opened to him for prayer.
>
> “Hearing this, and greatly terrified lest he, being an unrestrained young king who wished immediately to do whatever came into his mind, might, on seeing the girl’s beauty, inflict some unlawful violence upon her—for he had arrived so suddenly and unexpectedly in order to see her—I led her into a more secluded chamber, explained the matter to her as it stood, and, with her consent, placed a veil upon her head, so that when the king saw it he might be drawn back from an unlawful embrace. Nor did my hope deceive me.
>
> “For the king, as though intending to inspect the roses and other flowering plants, entered our cloister; but as soon as he saw her wearing a veil on her head among our other girls, he left the cloister and departed from the church, plainly showing that he had come only because of her. When, however, King David, the girl’s father, came to our church within that same week and saw the veil upon his daughter’s head, he angrily tore the veil apart, threw it to the ground, trampled it under his feet, and took his daughter away with him.”

The abbess was then asked how old the girl had been at that time. She answered that she may have been twelve years old. Then, at the king’s urging the archbishop to order judgment upon the matter, the bishops and abbots, after taking counsel and reading various chapters of the canons, judged unanimously that marriage should not be forbidden to her on account of such an act, since, so long as she had been below lawful age and under her father’s guardianship, she had not been permitted to do anything without his consent.

When judgment had been rendered, the king asked the archbishop whether he wished to challenge it in any respect. Lord Anselm answered that he would not challenge it, since in truth they had judged rightly according to the decrees of the canons. Then the king said: “Since you approve the judgment that has been pronounced, I want you to betroth the maiden to me.”

And Lord Anselm replied: “I do not condemn the judgment; but if Your Majesty were willing to believe me, I would advise you not to marry her, because, however it happened, she nevertheless wore a veil upon her head, and you could readily find sufficient daughters of kings or counts.”

But as the king persisted in what he had begun, that most holy man added:

> “You indeed, my lord king, will set aside my counsel and do what pleases you; but whoever lives longer, I think, will see that England will not long rejoice in offspring born from her.”

I heard him say this when I was a young man; now, however, I see that it has in great part already come to pass.

16. The king therefore begot by her two sons and one daughter. The sons, already adolescents, were returning from Normandy to England when their ship was wrecked and they perished at sea with many others. Their daughter, with great wealth sent to her by her father, was married by Henry, emperor of the Romans, who celebrated the wedding at Liège with great splendour. But after she had borne him one son, he was overtaken by a swift death and left her a widow.

After being widowed, she married the count of Anjou. When her father suddenly died in the city of Rouen, the nobles of the English established over themselves as king Stephen, count of Boulogne, brother of Count Theobald of Champagne. Thereupon Robert, the son of King Henry by a concubine, greatly indignant, openly rebelled against him. He captured him in battle and confined him in chains in a certain castle which his father had given him; and he ordered his sister to cross quickly to England with her son and take up her father’s kingdom.

She, thinking that she would find all things favourable, crossed over swiftly, but found matters otherwise than she had believed. For the wife of Prince Stephen, rallying supporters to herself, stoutly resisted her. Stephen himself, moreover, after a few days was reconciled to Robert by certain agreements, released from his chains, and again obtained the kingdom of the English. Thus the daughter of King Henry groaned that she had been deceived by vain hope.

We are indeed uncertain about future events. Yet this one thing we plainly see: according to Lord Anselm’s prophecy, England did not long rejoice in the offspring of that queen who had married King Henry after wearing the veil; indeed, devastated and oppressed by prolonged civil strife, it fell from its former riches into great poverty. Therefore the words of wise men and prelates of the Church are not to be despised, but rather revered and feared, since it is manifest that both the aforementioned prophecy of Pope Leo concerning Baldwin, count of Flanders, who married his kinswoman, and the following prophecy of Lord Anselm concerning the king of the English, were true.

Now let us return to those things which the unknown matron foretold to the envoys of Robert, count of Flanders, and briefly explain how true they were.

17. That Robert, as has been written above, gave his stepdaughter to Philip, king of the French, and his sister to William, count of Normandy. Of his two daughters, he gave one to Canute, king of the Danes, by whom Charles was born; the other to Henry, count of Brussels.

When this Henry heard that Everard, castellan of Tournai, had very valiant knights with him, he came to Tournai to see their courage. One day, therefore, as he went out and in youthful fashion exulted in his own strength, he asked one man from the opposing line, named Cosceguin of Forest, to come alone against him alone. That man answered that he would not come, because Henry was his lord and he feared that some chance might cause him to injure him. But the count repeatedly challenged him, and, now calling him cowardly and sluggish, by excessive provocation compelled him to come against him.

At last the knight, provoked by his repeated exhortations, raised his lance, spurred his horse violently, and charged against him. Wishing to unhorse him in a martial game, he drove the lance into his heart and killed him instantly, filling the whole region with immense grief. For at that time this count was of the highest renown and illustrious name, and had expelled all robbers and thieves from his land so thoroughly that no region could be found with greater peace and security than his.

Thus, when he was killed through such rashness or folly and left no offspring, his wife was left a widow and married Simon, duke of Auxatia, near Saxony, bearing him several sons.

18. Robert, count of Flanders, after so nobly marrying off his daughters, left all Flanders at his death to his son Robert. In his time Lord Odo, renouncing the world with his clerics, entered the church of Saint Martin of Tournai and found the count himself, together with his Clementia, a generous helper.

This Clementia, of Burgundian birth, was daughter of William, duke of the Burgundians, and sister of Lord Guy, archbishop of Vienne, who later became pope of Rome, was called Calixtus, and held a general council at Reims in the time of Archbishop Ralph, called “the Green,” who was successor to Manasses and predecessor to Rainald, bishop of Angers.

Clementia bore her husband Count Robert three sons within three years. Fearing that if she bore more children they would contend with one another for Flanders, she employed feminine artifice to prevent herself from bearing further children. This was so avenged by divine retribution that all her sons died long before her, and she herself afterwards, in her widowhood, seeing other counts and suffering many evils from them, lamented too late that she and her offspring had been disinherited.

19. One year after Lord Odo’s conversion, Pope Urban, at the Council of Clermont, urged all bishops to enjoin upon the peoples subject to them that, for the remission of their sins, they should go to Jerusalem and free the Lord’s Sepulchre, together with the city itself, from pagan hands.

Then one might see an innumerable multitude from the western regions, as though by a divine command, leave their native soil and make for Jerusalem. On this occasion the aforesaid Count Robert, together with Godfrey, count of Boulogne; Robert, count of Normandy; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Hugh, count of Vermandois; Baldwin, count of Hainaut; Anselm of Ribemont; Clarenbald of Vendœuvre; and many other princes, left Flanders with the people of God.

After Antioch had been besieged and captured, and many other cities likewise, he finally entered Jerusalem in victory, with God’s help. Having expelled or killed the pagans, admitted Christians, and established a king, he returned to Flanders. Received with great glory, he ruled the province for nearly twelve years.

20. After this, Louis, king of the French and son of his sister, summoned him to besiege a certain castle called Saint-Martin. As he fought courageously in battle according to his custom and drove the king’s enemies farther back, he was exhausted by excessive exertion, carried to bed, and died there three days later. The same king and the princes of the kingdom brought him with great mourning to Arras, where he was buried in the church of Saint Vaast.

After he was buried, the king immediately summoned his son Baldwin, still a youth and not yet made a knight, together with his mother. He restored to him all his paternal land and ordered the nobles of Flanders to render him homage in his presence; then he returned to France. What, then, shall I say about Baldwin, and of what spirit he was even in tender age?

21. After the king departed, Baldwin summoned his nobles, indicated that he wished to keep the peace, asked them to help him in this, and declared that he would do justice upon anyone who first violated it. Yet he compelled none of them to swear peace. The princes promised that they would preserve the peace, and so the court was dissolved, many saying that peace could not easily be maintained by such a boy, because no one would fear him.

22. About two months later, a certain poor woman complained to the count that two cows had been taken from her by a robber, and showed him where the robber lived. The young count immediately pursued the robber, seized him, and led him to Bruges. When everyone pleaded that he should neither hang the knight nor have his eyes torn out, he replied that he would do neither.

At once he ordered a huge bronze vessel, which the common people call a *lebes* or cauldron, to be suspended high in the public marketplace before the eyes of all, filled with water, and heated by a great fire underneath. When the water was boiling fiercely, he had that knight thrown into the cauldron with all his clothing, even girded with his sword, and thus killed him in the boiling water. Immediately such fear seized everyone that thereafter no one in all Flanders dared take anything.

23. One day he was entering the church of Saint Peter at Ghent to hear Vespers, when suddenly a poor woman complained that her cow had been stolen. The count gently asked her to wait for him at the door until he had heard Vespers. But she replied that, because of the multitude of knights and princes surrounding him, she would not afterward be given the opportunity to speak to him. He immediately gave her his cloak, which he had removed, and instructed her to keep it for him until after Vespers.

When Vespers were finished and the princes surrounding the count wished to discuss other affairs, he swore that he would answer no one until the poor woman’s cow had been restored to her. Thus, blessed by her a thousand times, he satisfied her request.

24. In the town called Turholdis [Note: Turholdis, commonly Torhout, near Bruges.], a great market was customarily held every year on the feast of Saint John. The count was told that ten knights, trusting in their kinsmen, had taken something from the pack of a merchant coming to the market. The count immediately sprang up, seized them, and shut them in a house.

Their parents, greatly terrified, quickly came to beg the count’s mercy and urged him to accept whatever sum of money or horses he wished, provided only that he would not hang them. The count, pretending that he would grant their request, told them to wait a little until he had entered the house, spoken to the accused men, and come out again. So he spoke; then immediately entered with a few men and ordered them to hang the accused inside that same house.

When the men pleaded with him to spare them and not cause them to incur the permanent enmity of their parents, he spared them in this manner: he ordered the accused men that whoever among them wished to escape should hang his companion. Thus, after nine had been hanged and the tenth remained, the count ordered him to cast the rope over a beam and, standing on a stool, put a noose made from that rope around his own neck. When this had been done, the count pushed the stool farther away with his foot and left him hanging two cubits above the ground.

Then, returning from the house with his men, he was again entreated by their parents. “Come now,” he said, “go out and take them down; and, once they are down, warn them not to take anything further in my land.” Having spoken, he at once mounted his horse and departed. But when the parents entered the house, they found all their sons hanging and already dead; utterly terrified, they fled.

By deeds of this kind he had frightened all robbers so thoroughly that no one dared not only to steal anything, but even, if he found a costly garment or a golden cup upon the road, to pick it up. Flanders might have called itself fortunate, had it deserved to possess so great a prince for a long time. But after he had established such peace that for a whole year he saw no complaint brought to him, deeming it shameful to sit quietly at home, being a young man of scarcely thirty years, he began to train himself in military arms; and wherever he heard that knights had gathered for battle, he immediately burned to be present with them.

25. At that time the aforesaid Henry, king of the English, entered Normandy, fought against his brother Robert the count, defeated him, and took him to England. Robert’s son William, a boy of ten, disinherited, fled to Baldwin, count of Flanders. Baldwin brought him up and, in the fourteenth year of his age, made him a knight. Urging him to rebel against his uncle, the king of England, who held his father imprisoned, Baldwin began repeatedly to attack Normandy with him.

But King Henry sent word that he should desist from his attacks, otherwise he should know that Henry would come with an army to Bruges. Baldwin immediately sent back word that Henry should not undertake such labour, but should know that Baldwin would meet him at Rouen. Having said this, he immediately followed the messenger with five hundred knights and arrived at the city of Rouen, where the king was staying. Driving his lance into the city gate, he cried out to the citizens that they should tell the king that the count of Flanders was present.

The king, however, since he had two thousand knights with him, saw such noise and boldness and, as a most prudent man, said that he would not go out against a senseless young man. He ordered all his knights under threat that none should dare leave the gate: “For when he is tired,” he said, “he will return and carry nothing away from my land.”

The count, therefore, deeply distressed because he could draw no one out of the city, shouted as he rode around its walls and did not know what he could do; for he was unable to storm so great a city with so few knights. At a distance he saw a herd of stags which the king had enclosed in a nearby wood. The young man cried out: “Even if I can do nothing else, at least I shall free these stags from their enclosure and restore them to freedom.” Having spoken, he immediately ran with his knights, swords drawn, cut down the very strong fence made of stakes which held the stags enclosed, scattered the stags over the fields, and so returned to Flanders without accomplishing any other business.

26. Meanwhile, he gladly retained with him Charles, son of his paternal aunt [Note: His paternal aunt: Adela, daughter of Robert the Elder, count of Flanders.], whom she had borne to Canute, king of the Danes, when Charles came to him after his father’s death. He gave him in marriage the sister [Note: Sister: Margaret, sister of Count Ralph of Péronne, daughter of Rainald of Clermont and the aforesaid Adela.] of Count Ralph of Péronne, and entrusted Flanders to him to guard in Baldwin’s absence. Thus more secure, Baldwin began to visit Normandy frequently.

But this exercise in arms and warfare, although it brought him great delight as a young man, caused immense grief to monks, clerics, and all other wise persons, because all foretold that he could not live long amid so many perils. Nor did their expectation deceive them; indeed, the fear which they feared came upon them. For while he was attacking Normandy too persistently, a certain knight wounded him with a sword above the nose. Yet he did not withdraw from battle because of the wound; overcome by the intense heat of the sun, he grew feverish, and the swelling wound compelled him, against his will, to return to Arras.

There, with physicians summoned, he could easily have been cured if he had been willing to abstain from harmful foods. But because he would not give up goose flesh or similar things, weakened by the wound, he failed and lay in bed throughout the whole year. Yet to avoid boredom he often had himself carried in a litter from place to place. At last, when he saw that he could not escape death, he appointed the aforesaid Charles as his successor and handed Flanders over to him. Thus, becoming a monk at Saint-Bertin, he died within eight days, leaving immense mourning and grief to all the churches and teaching that no one ought to trust in his own strength.

Charles, his kinsman, succeeding him, was not inferior to him in maintaining justice. But in prudence and caution, because he was somewhat more advanced in age, he surpassed him altogether. He also protected the churches so well that he was called “Father of the Churches.” I shall relate one incident that comes to mind, so that his devotion may be known.

27. On the day of the Epiphany, when he saw Abbot John, lord abbot of Saint-Bertin, entering his court at Bruges, he immediately called to him: “Lord abbot, who today sang the principal Mass in the church of Saint-Bertin?”

The abbot replied that there had been no lack of someone to sing it honourably, since there were more than a hundred monks in his convent. The count added: “On so great a feast you ought to have sung it, eaten in the refectory with the brethren, and provided a good refreshment from the gifts made by my predecessor counts for those who kept vigil throughout the night at Matins, rather than sitting in my court.”

The abbot said that he would more gladly have sung Mass than come there, but had been compelled to come because a certain knight was taking from him land which his church had possessed peacefully for more than sixty years. The count added: “And why did you not send word of this to me through your servant? For it is yours to pray for me, but mine to protect and defend the churches.”

Having said this, he immediately summoned the knight and asked why he was troubling the church of Saint-Bertin about land which it had possessed for so long. The knight answered that the church had held the land unjustly, because it belonged to him by right. The count said: “As your father kept silence concerning it, so keep silence yourselves; for I swear by the soul of Count Baldwin that, if I hear any complaint concerning it, I shall do nothing else to you than the count himself did to the man whom he boiled in a cauldron at Bruges.”

The aforesaid Abbot John told me that the count thus secured peace for him.

28. But Flanders was not worthy of such a prince. Wicked men—namely Bertulf, provost of the church of Bruges, and his kinsmen—who denied that they were the count’s servants because of the justice that he administered, secretly banded together and conspired against him.

When this was reported to the count at Ypres, and many warned him not to go to Bruges, he answered that, if God willed, he was ready to die for justice and would not depart from justice. He immediately came with his knights to Bruges, burned a certain fortification which those conspirators had made, and returned to his own house.

The next day, rising very early in the morning and proceeding from the seat of his palace to the seat of the church of Saint Donatian, he ordered Mass to be sung there for him by his chaplain. It was Wednesday in the second week of Lent. When the prayer of Esther was already being read in the Epistle, and the count, prostrate in prayer, was reading psalms from an open psalter, a certain poor woman came up and begged alms of him. Of the thirteen coins which, by custom, the count had placed upon the psalter, she took one from his hand.

After she received it, the same woman cried out to him: “Lord count, beware!” The count raised his head to see what was happening; and behold, Burchard, nephew of the aforesaid provost, had silently approached in armour with drawn sword. He drove the sword into the count’s forehead and, adding many wounds, killed him there before the altar. Having killed one man with him, he put the others present to flight in terror. Immediately the sad news filled the whole region: the glorious Count Charles had been murdered in church.

29. Lord Gilbert, abbot of Saint Peter’s at Ghent, a most truthful and devout man, told me and asserted under the testimony of truth that there was then at Bruges a certain poor cripple, well known to him, to whom the count had often been accustomed to give alms.

When he heard this most grievous report, he came to the church weeping, wailing, and crying loudly. With immense exertion, crawling on hands and legs, he climbed the stone steps to the stone seat upon which the count had been murdered. He found only the count’s body lying there, bloody with gore. Astonished that everyone had so quickly left the body alone, he sat beside it and, uttering deep groans and cries from the excessive grief of his heart, began to smear his legs and shins with the blood flowing abundantly from it—not, as he himself said, because he had any hope of being healed, but solely because of the sweetness and love of the man who had done him such great good.

Suddenly he felt himself perfectly healed by divine mercy. Leaping down the steps like a roe deer, he ran throughout the town and showed himself healed to all the people. This event brought a great cloud of disgrace upon those murderers, and would have brought greater disgrace still, had not that poor man, terrified by their power, ceased publicly proclaiming it by leaping about. For they had amassed great riches from the count’s revenues, over which he had placed them, so much so that, when shortly before his death the count had appointed them a day of hearing at the castle of Cassel, where they might prove by the judgment of his nobles that they were not his servants, Bertulf, provost of that church and Burchard’s uncle, openly brought three thousand knights there with him. The count, fearing that so great a crowd might raise some disturbance, postponed the case to another day.

30. Since the count’s body could not be buried there—for Lord Simon, bishop, whose sister [Note: His sister: Margaret, his uterine sister, born of another father, namely Rainald of Clermont.] the count had married, had heard of so great a crime and wholly prohibited divine service in that church—and since the people of the district would by no means permit it to be transferred to another church, the aforesaid Provost Bertulf, wishing as far as he could to excuse himself of the count’s death, immediately had a costly tomb built for him in the same place of the upper chamber where he had been murdered, from marble columns. His body lay there for almost sixty days.

So great a disturbance suddenly arose throughout Flanders that what is read in the Apocalypse, “After a thousand years the devil shall be released” (Rev. 20:2), seemed to have occurred literally in that province. Wherever two men found a third alone, they either plundered or even killed him. Thus at that time even the simplest person could easily understand openly how great a power had existed in that single prince, who had compelled that untamed people to remain continually at peace as if they were cloistered monks.

31. The princes of Flanders, and especially Baldwin [Note: Baldwin: namely, surnamed “the Cross-Eyed” and “the Bearded.” See Du Cange, Dissertation 21 to the *History of Saint Louis*, where this kinship is explained.] of Ghent, brother of Ivo of Noyon, who is now count of Soissons, saw such disorder. On an agreed day they assembled together, made peace among themselves, and, lest so great a crime should become an everlasting reproach to them if it remained unavenged, gathered an army and advanced upon Bruges.

When those murderers, supported by many helpers, came forth to fight them with a great multitude of horsemen and foot soldiers, Baldwin, protected by cuirass and helmet, cried out in a loud voice:

> “We have not come against you, good men, nor do we seek to storm the castle of Bruges. We wish rather to avenge the unjust death of our lord, lest perhaps it be said that we too are guilty of his betrayal and are thereafter always called traitors. If, then, you come to fight against us, you will declare yourselves accomplices in so great a crime and incur everlasting reproach. Therefore I urge and advise you rather to join us and help us put to shame the traitors of our lord.”

At these words the people shouted aloud and, joining Baldwin, turned against and defeated those with whom they had come. The latter immediately took flight; because they had no other way of escape, they returned to the castle, entered the count’s tower, and were shut up in it, besieged by Baldwin for nearly two months.

32. Meanwhile Louis, king of the French, whom we said above was born of Charles’s maternal aunt, struck by the bitter report concerning his kinsman, came to Arras. Because Charles had died without offspring, he asked the princes of Flanders whom they wished to have as count. Some said that the king himself was the nearer relative and urged him, because he had several sons, to give Flanders to one of them. But the king, as a most prudent man, considered that none of his sons was yet twelve years old; that no one so young could govern so untamed a people without a guardian constantly attached to him; and that the king could not always be personally present. Fearing that some evil might therefore befall them, he wisely refused to place any of his sons over the land.

[Col. 0061A] **33.** There was at that time a certain Baldwin, count of Hainaut, quite valiant in arms as far as his age allowed. His great-grandfather had been that founder of the monastery of Hasnon who, as was said above, had married Richilde, countess of Hainaut, and had held both counties, namely Flanders and Hainaut. By that same Richilde he had begotten two sons: Arnulf, who succeeded his father and was slain by his uncle Robert at Cassel; and Baldwin, who held the county of Hainaut with his mother. Having begotten one son, Baldwin, he set out upon the Jerusalem journey with the other princes at its beginning; from it he has not yet returned, and to this day it has not been possible to learn whether he was killed or captured.

But when his son Baldwin had become count, Clementia, countess of Flanders, persuaded him to take as wife a certain young woman, her niece, and promised that with her she would give him one thousand marks of silver. The young man consented and swore that he would betroth her on the appointed day; and in like manner he publicly received from her, before many witnesses, an oath of betrothal. Before the appointed day, however, disregarding the oath which he had made, the young man married as his wife Yolande, daughter of Gerard, count of Babenberg. Therefore the countess, gnashing her teeth—especially because she saw that her own brother, Guy, archbishop of Vienne, had now become pope of Rome and was called Calixtus—complained to him that her family had been slighted by so insignificant a count.

He immediately sent letters commanding Ralph, archbishop [Col. 0061C] of Reims, not to delay in avenging that perjury. The prelate summoned bishops, abbots, and many other ecclesiastical persons, ordered the count to appear and answer concerning the marriage agreement. Clementia complained that he had promised under oath to take her niece as his wife on the day fixed, adding that she would produce three hundred noble witnesses if he wished to deny it. Baldwin replied that he neither wished nor was able to deny what had been said, since it was established that she had spoken the truth; nevertheless, he had already married another wife, solemn nuptials had been celebrated, and he had been joined to her. He added that he would do whatever should be judged in the matter.

After the judges had long deliberated together, they finally asked for a postponement out of reverence for the lord pope, and requested that so important a case be referred to his judgment at Rome. This was done: the matter was brought to Rome.

> **Note [Col. 0061D].** “To Rome”: that is, to the Roman curia, as I suppose. For Calixtus had not yet been in Rome.

The cardinals assembled and, favoring the pope’s will, decided that the first pledged faith, according to the Apostle, could not be made void without condemnation, and therefore that the woman whom he had first sworn to marry ought to be taken as his wife.

Meanwhile, a cardinal of great authority named Bruno—

> **Note [Col. 0061D].** Bruno: that is, as I suppose, Bruno, bishop of Segni. See the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, chapter 31, p. 497.

—while the others spoke differently, remained altogether silent. When the pope urged him to state his opinion, he answered that he would not oppose what the others had said. But when the pope commanded him under obedience to disclose what he genuinely thought on the matter, [Col. 0062A] he carefully reviewed every point and maintained that in the first union there had been only an oath, whereas in the second there had been an oath, betrothal, a priest’s blessing, solemn nuptials, and finally the union of the two parties: a complete marriage had been made. Citing various chapters of the canons, he added that the second marriage could no longer be dissolved, while penance ought to be imposed upon the count for the earlier perjury.

The pope and cardinals agreed with this judgment. When the messengers returned to France with apostolic letters, Count Baldwin indeed rejoiced that Yolande remained his wife; but the young woman grieved that she had been deprived of marriage to the count. Yet suddenly, through a pitiable turn of fortune—or rather through the mercy of God—[Col. 0062B] she was joined in marriage to Louis, king of the French, and became the mother of Louis, who is now king, and of the king’s other sons. She had grieved that this had not happened earlier; afterward she greatly rejoiced, because she preferred to be called and to be queen of the French rather than countess of Hainaut.

This Baldwin by the aforesaid Yolande begot another Baldwin, and Richilde, wife of Everard, castellan of Tournai. Since Richilde married Everard, prince of this province, it is fitting to say a little about her by way of digression.

**34.** This Richilde, as she was most noble by birth, so was she most beautiful in appearance and exceedingly vigorous in the wicked pursuits of the world. She bore Baldwin, a most handsome and noble youth; but alas, [Col. 0062C] struck by fever in the flower of youth, he made his compact with death and was buried in the cloister of Saint Mary, Mother of God. Dying, Richilde left Everard and Godfrey, handsome sons, and a daughter, Yolande.

While this Everard was still tender in age, he was deeply distressed, with gnashing teeth, that the land of his paternal right was most abundantly subject to evildoers. In indignation and wrath, with sword drawn, his eyes troubled by the harshness of pride and ferocity, he came swiftly and violently upon them with a strong hand; in a short time he expelled them all from his territories, restored his land to peace and peace to his land. After this he took as wife Gertrude, daughter of Lambert, count of Liège, by whom he begot [Col. 0062D] a son, Baldwin. His sister Yolande married Roger, seneschal of Flanders.

**35.** Now let us briefly relate something concerning Baldwin, count of Hainaut, who had succeeded his father Baldwin when the latter died in youth and had married the sister of the count of Namur. He was now a young man and a valiant knight when Flanders was bereaved of Prince Charles.

Hearing that the king of the French had come to Arras and was seeking counsel concerning the appointment of a count for Flanders, Baldwin took with him the noble and wise princes of his own land and approached the king. Before the king’s leading men he publicly complained that his grandfather Baldwin, who had gone to Jerusalem, had unjustly been driven out and disinherited by his uncle Robert of Flanders. He humbly petitioned the king to restore to him his ancestral land and inheritance, adding that he was ready to go wherever the king should appoint a day anywhere in his entire kingdom, and that he would prove by arms and single combat of his own person that no one had a nearer, more rightful, or greater claim to the affair of Flanders.
