The knights who had come with him applauded his request and suggested to the king that great peace throughout the province would result; they added many other arguments relevant to the present business. The most prudent king graciously answered all, called the count his kinsman, and raised his hopes greatly of obtaining what he sought. But because, according to Solomon, “The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord; he will turn it wherever he wills” (Prov. 21:1), the king’s intention turned out otherwise than the count wished.

For while many believed it certain that Flanders would be restored to that count, it was suddenly heard—driven, I know not by what gust of wind—that it had been given to a certain young man, namely William, son of Robert, count of Normandy. At that time William was still shut in custody by his brother Henry, king of the English. He had been born of the daughter of Robert the elder, count of Flanders, as was related much earlier above.

Thus the aforesaid young Baldwin, disappointed in his hope, angrily withdrew from the king’s presence and took up arms against Flanders. A few days later he attacked the town called Oudenaarde and burned it utterly to ashes, so that more than one hundred persons of different sex and age were burned in the church of Saint Walburga.

The king, however, entered Flanders with the new count and came to Bruges. He commanded Lord Simon, bishop of Tournai, to assemble the abbots of that diocese and come as quickly as possible to bury the body of the most glorious Count Charles. What I then saw concerning that body I report confidently. The lord bishop summoned my insignificance together with Lord Absalon, abbot of Saint-Amand. In the presence of many, the tomb which Provost Bertulf, as we said a little before, had caused to be built from marble columns was broken open. The count’s body was lifted out and, with a great procession, carried by the king [Col. 0063D] to the church of Saint Christopher the Martyr, situated in the same town, so that on the appointed day, once the princes and all the people had gathered, the church of Saint Donatian might be reconciled and the body returned there and honorably buried in the ground.

Although more than fifty days had already passed since his death, we feared that the smell of the body might burden its bearers. But the merciful God plainly showed that all had feared in vain: we perceived no harmful odor whatever issuing from it. Indeed, what was still more wonderful, we saw the linen cloth in which the body had been wrapped so white and uncorrupted that we discerned upon it no marks whatever except fresh blood.

What groaning was there, what grief, what cries and lamentation, what a flood of tears was poured forth by the king and all the princes—indeed by the entire people—I pass over, since the devout attention of the reader can readily perceive it even if I say nothing. Five days later that church was reconciled, and, after Mass had been celebrated and the count’s body honorably buried, the king immediately installed the young cleric Lord Roger in the office of provost, since Provost Bertulf had already fled.

When this had been done, the king attacked the tower in which the traitors were still shut up and under siege. But because it was very strong and they resisted manfully, he could not take it so easily. On the following night Burchard and his uncle Bertulf secretly left the tower and fled, leaving all the others in danger of death. When these saw that they resisted in vain, they finally surrendered to the king and allowed him to enter. The king ordered all of them, once captured, to be kept first for three days in the prison of the same tower. Then he had them brought out and taken upward, and caused them to be hurled down one by one from the battlements of that very high tower. Thus he killed thirty men by the fall.

Bertulf and Burchard had already departed from the province and even reached Tournai, but they nevertheless could not escape divine judgment. They were again seized in parts of Flanders and, most shamefully hanged, ended their unworthy lives by a miserable death.

**36.** The king therefore returned to France, leaving William as count in Flanders. At the beginning of his rule, even in the king’s presence, he promised good things to the Flemings, both knights and townsmen, and publicly confirmed by oath that he would preserve their liberty and their laws according to the custom of his predecessors. But once he saw all subject to him, he immediately grew proud. He began to plunder their goods and property; then he compelled even those bound in chains and delivered to custody to ransom themselves.

The Flemings, immediately terrified, being unaccustomed to such treatment and expecting worse evils still, unanimously resolved to rebel and chose death rather than suffer such things. The people of Lille, whom he afflicted most severely, were the first to dare openly resist him.

At that time, in the province of Lotharingia called Alsace, there was a young knight named Theodoric, son of Simon, duke of Alsace. Simon had begotten him by the daughter of Robert the elder, count of Flanders, who had first had Henry, count of Brussels, as husband, but after he was killed near Tournai had married the aforesaid Duke Simon. Knowing that this young man was Charles’s nearest relative, as the son of his maternal aunt, the Flemings secretly sent an envoy to him and asked him to come to Flanders.

Theodoric immediately came to Flanders accompanied by scarcely three knights, and was joyfully received. Resistance to William now became more confident. At William’s renewed request, the king returned to Arras with the archbishop.

> **Note [Col. 0063D].** The archbishop: namely, the archbishop of Reims.

Theodoric was summoned to appear before the archbishop as an invader of another’s right. Refusing to come, he was publicly excommunicated with all his supporters, and divine service was interdicted at Lille, where he was then staying. The king ordered him to leave Flanders as swiftly as possible and return to his own land. He turned a deaf ear and awaited the outcome.

The king and William assembled an army and besieged Theodoric, shut within Lille. Three times in one day, attacking the town in three places, they attempted to enter the gates and overcome those enclosed there; but they accomplished nothing. On the sixth day the king returned without any result to Arras, and thence to France.

Theodoric came out of Lille and traveled through Flanders. Engaging William several times, he was now found inferior, now superior, while all waited anxiously to see which of them would conquer and which be conquered. William again assembled cavalry and besieged Theodoric, shut up in the castle called Alost. But while he strove valiantly in battle to storm the castle, in August he was wounded in the hand beneath the thumb by a foot-soldier. Oppressed by excessive heat, he felt his arm swelling; he secretly summoned Duke Godfrey, who was with him, foretold that he would die immediately, and advised him to take care to withdraw the cavalry from there.

Perceiving the adverse fortune, the duke shrewdly summoned Theodoric through intermediaries and, pretending that he wished to arrange peace between him and William, cautiously led out the army. When he was already far away, he informed Theodoric that William was dead.

Thus William died from a slight wound and was buried at Saint-Bertin beside Count Baldwin. With the king’s consent, Theodoric acquired lordship over all Flanders. After his wife died, he took as wife the sister of the count of Anjou, namely the daughter of Fulk, king of Jerusalem. This outcome proved that the prophecy of the matron had not been false—the prophecy which she had made many years before to Baldwin, advocate of Tournai, and his companions, envoys of Count Robert the Younger.

For Baldwin, son of Count Robert the Younger, died childless. The handsome young man whom she had foretold would come from Denmark was undoubtedly Charles. The two counts whom she added would come after him and contend for Flanders, one of whom would kill the other, were William and Theodoric. But when she finally declared that the victor and his descendants would possess Flanders until the time of Antichrist, we leave this to the knowledge of God and to experience in things to come. This one thing we see: Theodoric is now securely count, rejoicing many people; and he has already promised his daughter to Henry, son of Count Theobald, although the king of France strives to dissolve the marriage, saying that the two are related in the third degree.

But since in speaking of kings and counts we have made too long a digression, let us now, as though we had completed a lengthy journey, return to Lord Odo and his clerics, lest they die of hunger while we wander through various matters.

**37.** When Lord Bishop Radbod withdrew with the procession, five poor clerics remained with poor Martin. Soon, however, with help from the townspeople, they bought one wooden house from a monk who was steward of the court of Saint-Amand of Villemel. A small church having been built beside it, they gradually began to increase, so that in the second year after their arrival eighteen brothers were already found there.

Yet at first they endured no small poverty, so that they had nothing on which to live. Certain devout laypeople publicly carried sacks daily about the city and cried out that aid should be given to the poor of Saint Martin. By such support they passed an entire year.

### The noble conversion of Alulf

**38.** Meanwhile a young cleric named Alulf, son of Siger, precentor of the canons of Saint Mary, forsook secular riches and joined them. When this was reported to his father, he immediately assembled his relatives and came furiously to Saint Martin. Seizing the young man by the hair, throwing him to the ground, and beating him severely, he brought him back home.

The next day, when the youth was thought to be going to the church of Saint Mary, he secretly slipped away and returned to Saint Martin. But his father immediately brought him back again and put him in fetters. When this happened repeatedly—that is, whenever the youth could, he fled to Saint Martin, and his father immediately brought him back—it happened that Lord Haiméric, abbot of Anchin, came to Tournai to visit and encourage those poor men.

When Master Odo asked him what should be done about the youth who was daily being violently taken back by his father, the abbot, being a wise man, seized a suitable occasion and disclosed what he had previously been considering. He said:

> “Truly, good master, this will happen to you not only in the case of this young man, but also in that of your other brothers, unless you become monks. You live near the city, and your younger brothers will easily be deceived by their secular clerical companions and brought back to the world, because you and they wear the same habit. But if you were monks, thereafter they would attempt to bring none of yours back, because the monks’ habit is black whereas that of clerics is white; and clerics hold the monks’ habit in such horror that, once they have seen someone a monk, they will never afterward deign to have him as a companion. Consider also that the life of clerics, even those living by a rule, is softer and more relaxed: they wear linen, frequently eat meat, and on feast days read only nine lessons. Therefore, since you are everywhere accounted famous and celebrated, and have renounced the world, if you wished to believe me, I would advise you and your clerics to seek a stricter rather than a more relaxed order.”

Encouraged by these persuasions of the abbot of Anchin, Master Odo called together his companions, reported the abbot’s advice, and asked their consent. They immediately agreed with his words and, lest delay allow anyone to turn them aside, asked the aforesaid abbot to remain there that night. They promised that on the next day they would become monks.

### Odo, abbot of Saint Martin, and his companions abandon the clerical institution and adopt the Benedictine one. Siger the precentor and Herman the provost, brothers, become monks.

On the following morning, very early, after chapter had ended, twelve clerics went to the altar of Saint Martin. They laid aside their clerical clothing and, through the hand of Abbot Haiméric, received the monastic habit with a blessing and three days’ silence. Thus, although they had sung Matins and Prime in the clerical rite, they sang Terce and all the following Hours, down to the present day, according to monastic custom.

Nor did adoption of this good counsel deceive the master. For that Siger, precentor of the canons, on seeing his young son made a monk, made no further attempt to draw him back; rather, he strongly encouraged him to persevere. Indeed, pricked by God’s prompting, Siger himself forsook worldly riches and became a monk in our monastery together with his brother Herman, provost of the greater church, whom we mentioned much earlier above. He obtained for us the grant of five altars which he had acquired for his other son, named Adam, a canon; these yield us each year more than thirty pounds in money.

When the three days’ silence was completed, Abbot Haiméric advised the monks whom he had made to elect an abbot for themselves. Master Odo attempted to choose one of his companions, but they all rushed upon him and unanimously chose Odo himself. They presented the elect to Lord Bishop Radbod for confirmation. He was consecrated on the following Sunday at Tournai, in the church of Saint Mary, on 4 March, in the third year after his conversion.

The youth of whom we spoke, Alulf, after becoming a monk in our monastery held the office of librarian, or cantor, for forty-seven years. Reading all the books of Saint Gregory repeatedly, and imitating Paterius, he excerpted all the passages of both the Old and New Testaments expounded by Gregory. From them he compiled three codices—

> **Note [Col. 0067D].** These three codices survive in the library of Saint Martin of Tournai in four volumes; in the last of them one reads:
>
> > From the books of Gregory he drew these little works;  
> > through Gregory’s prayers may Alulf rest in peace.
>
> Alulf’s work was published at Paris.

—and added a fourth, containing various and very useful sayings. He gave them the name *Gregorialis*, and in the forty-eighth year after his conversion ended his life in good resolve.

Siger, his father, when he had first become a monk, was sleeping in bed one afternoon and saw in a dream one of the canons of Saint Mary who had died many years earlier. The canon appeared to him and spoke of various things. Since Siger had not forgotten the man’s death, he asked him to reveal how souls fared in the other life. The other immediately replied:

> “Lord Siger, why do you ask about the other life? Truly I tell you: whoever has been poor here for God’s sake will be rich there.”

Siger at once understood that he had seen this for his own consolation. Glorifying God for it, he immediately recounted it to us.

### The monks of Saint Martin abandon their place from love of solitude, but return at the bishop’s command

[Col. 0068A]

**39.** When Lord Odo had become abbot, he began diligently to read with his monks the *Institutes* and *Conferences*, or the *Lives of the Fathers*. Whatever they read, they immediately wished to fulfill in deed. Thus, having zeal for God, though perhaps not according to great knowledge, in the third year after their arrival they began to complain that they had not remained in a good place. There they heard the cries of youths and the songs of girls; there they saw secular clothing, by which their minds were greatly hindered from their purpose. They thought that they ought rather to seek a desert place, where they could more freely devote themselves to divine meditation.

Discussing these and similar matters among themselves every day, and frequently sighing deeply over them, they finally reached a unanimous decision. One night, after singing Matins earlier than usual, when Matins had ended, they loaded their clothes and books onto a wagon. Thus, leaving the church empty before midnight, they all followed the abbot and hastened out of the province as quickly as possible, with none of the citizens aware.

When morning came and the citizens, coming as usual to Saint Martin’s church for prayer, discovered what had been done, they immediately groaned as though the destruction of the city threatened. In sorrow they told one another what they had heard, declared that they had not been worthy of the monks’ fellowship, and finally ran in crowds to the church itself. With tears they went about the places where the monks had slept and eaten, and began, wailing, to proclaim that some new calamity was about to come upon the entire region.

But when they learned through certain religious women living near the church that the monks were going to Noyon in order to ask Lord Bishop Radbod, who was then staying there, for permission to leave, they immediately summoned Everard the castellan, prince of all that region. All the leading men of the city swiftly gathered together; after taking common counsel, they urgently sent word to the bishop that he should have no hope of ever entering Tournai again if he granted them permission.

The messenger, whose horse was severely wearied by spurs, overtook the monks, told the bishop what had occurred, and then delivered the words of the prince and citizens. The bishop immediately burst into tears and replied that the citizens had sent this message needlessly: even if they themselves asked him to permit the monks to depart, he would in no way consent.

He therefore at once sent a messenger ahead along the road by which he expected them to come, to find them out. As they approached, he went to meet them. Seeing that almost thirty of them came on foot, he ordered his knights and clerics to dismount and allow the monks to mount. The monks, however, refused to mount and came on foot as far as the bishop. In the middle of the gate of the city of Noyon they fell at his feet and asked permission to leave.

Immediately, with excessive weeping, the bishop in turn fell at their feet and declared on oath that he would by no means do this. Taking them to his house and keeping them with himself for three days, relieving them from so great a labor and generously refreshing them, he finally compelled them, bound by obedience, to return to Tournai.

When this became known to the citizens, they rejoiced as though they saw the sun returning after darkness, and prepared to meet them at a distance from the city. It happened that they returned on the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, in the year 1095, when, as we said above, Bishop Radbod had established that celebrated procession around the city because of the fiery plague. Therefore the canons, who had already gone out of the city with the holy relics, upon hearing that the monks were returning, went to meet them with the entire procession of almost sixty thousand people and joyfully led them back to the church of Saint Martin.

**40.** From that time our church began gradually, with God’s help, to grow and increase down to the present day. The citizens of Tournai, now made more certain of the monks’ stability, approached the aforesaid bishop. They mentioned the ancient lands of Saint Martin, which, when the monastery had formerly been destroyed, had come into the bishop’s hand and which they held from the bishop’s hand in benefice. They unanimously asked him to restore them to Saint Martin.

At that time Baldwin, the advocate of Tournai whom I mentioned above, had already renounced the world. He had become a monk in the monastery of Bec in Normandy under the venerable Abbot Anselm, afterward archbishop of Canterbury. His brother Ralph, a most valiant knight, succeeded him in the advocacy and received the lands of Saint Martin, together with the advocacy, as a benefice from the bishop’s hand.

The bishop secretly summoned Ralph and began with persuasive words to stir him toward almsgiving. At last he asked him to relinquish those same lands to those poor monks for the sake of his soul. O incredible mercy of the Holy Spirit! The man’s heart was immediately inflamed. He graciously answered everything and, without any delay, restored those lands to the bishop. The bishop in turn, by the authority of his charter, restored them free to Saint Martin.

> **Note [Col. 0069D].** This charter is recorded by Dom Aegidius Duquesne, prior of Saint Martin of Tournai, in his manuscript history of the same monastery.

But since, apart from that charter, we have no testimony from ancient writing that our church was formerly an abbey—except only what is contained in the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop*, where, as he was dying, he summoned Baldered, abbot of Tournai, and commanded him not to return to his own people at Tours—we affirm with less confidence that it was an abbey. Whether it was or was not, we confidently assert that Lord Odo found nothing in it. I will also tell what happened to me in my youth.

**41.** One of our monks, sent to Courtrai to Countess Clementia, found there a certain abbot who had also come to her. Asked by her whence he came, he answered that he was from Saint Martin. That abbot immediately began to inquire where the abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai was and what sort of abbey it was. When the monk said that it was nearby, not ancient but new, and had been built twenty years earlier, the abbot immediately added:

> “Truly, brother, it has been more than three hundred years since the abbey of Saint Martin of Tournai was established. For in our church the charters of Saint Martin of Tournai are still preserved; its monks brought them to us when fleeing the persecution of the Vandals and left them there. I myself have often asked where in the world the church of Saint Martin of Tournai might be, but until now I have not been able to learn.”

When the monk then asked the abbot whence he came, the latter answered that he was abbot of Ferrières. Although earnestly asked to come to Tournai, he replied that he had no leisure. When the monk returned and told us this, he was immediately sent back to Courtrai with another man skilled in letters in order to investigate the matter more fully. But the abbot, who had already departed, was not found. Great sorrow and great uncertainty arose among us concerning where the church of Ferrières was. We searched, but could not discover it.

**42.** Two years later Pope Calixtus convened a general council at Reims. This pope was brother of Countess Clementia; he had previously been archbishop of Vienne and was called Guy. There our hope of hearing something was renewed. Investigation of this affair was assigned to me, although, I think, I was not yet a deacon.

All day I went about the church of Saint Mary. Overwhelmed in so great an assembly, I asked every monk whom I met where Ferrières was, but for three days I accomplished nothing. At times I lost heart, but strength was restored to me by that little verse:

> . . . . Labor conquers all  
> Unremitting . . . . .  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* I.145–146.)

At last I heard that Ferrières was in the diocese of Paris. I cried, “Thanks be to God!” Through Parisian clerics I identified the abbot of Ferrières. I immediately wished to approach him, but the crowd prevented me. At last, when the pope granted the long-desired permission to eat, I joined the abbot. I recalled the words which he had spoken two years earlier at Courtrai to the monk of Saint Martin of Tournai, and rejoiced that he easily remembered them. I asked what was contained in the charters which he had said were preserved with him.

He answered that there was a charter of Charles, king of the French, confirmed by his seal. It stated that King Charles, at the request of Ingelram, count of Châtelland, had given Saint Martin of Tournai the estate called Supas, in the district of Paris, with mills, all waters, appurtenances, witnesses appended at the end, and both the date and place of the gift.

> **Note [Col. 0070D].** Supas: French *Suppres-sur-Loin* [perhaps Supt], in the diocese of Sens.

I asked him to give me that charter, because it was of no use to him. He answered that he would not give it for nothing. I promised him one hundred solidi. He set a day for me to come to him and showed me the route: first to Paris, then to Châtelland, and from there to Ferrières.

I returned joyfully to Tournai, reported what I had heard, and brought the money. Passing through Paris, I came to Ferrières, showed the abbot the coins, and asked him to give me the charter. But, as his monks told me, the abbot feared to offend the knight who held the estate. He answered that after the council he had been unable to find the charter.

Nevertheless, after receiving from me a precious girdle, he had me led to the estate itself, called Supas, which lay two miles away. When I saw the mills and the advantages of the place, I could not hold back my tears. Entering the church, I found a very ancient codex, now almost falling apart and decayed. In it I saw written: “Book of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai.”

As I was leaving, I met an old and decrepit peasant and asked him whose estate it was. He answered:

> “It belongs to the knight Joscelin and certain others.”

I said to him:

> “Please, father, tell me: have you ever heard that it belonged to any saint?”

He replied:

> “We all know that this estate belonged to an abbey called Saint Martin of Tournai, but we do not know where it is. And we wonder what the accursed monks of that abbey are doing, since they do not reclaim such an estate.”

Then I said:

> “And how, father, did you hear that such an estate had been given to so unknown and distant an abbey?”

He replied:

> “I heard that a certain knight of this region, to whom this estate belonged, went as a paid soldier with other knights into that province. There, wounded and despaired of, he became a monk in that abbey. But later he recovered and returned, and through King Charles confirmed his estate to that same abbey of Saint Martin.”

Hearing this, but unable to do anything more, I returned sorrowful; yet I rejoiced in this, that I had become somewhat more certain of the antiquity of our abbey. This makes most certain what I remember having read elsewhere.

43. For Saint Ouen, metropolitan of Rouen, clearly and faithfully describing the deeds of blessed Eligius, relates among other things that he was at first a goldsmith at the court of Lothair, king of the Franks, son of Chilperic, who greatly enlarged the church of Blessed Mary at Tournai [Col. 0071D], and of whom we shall speak later; and that, at this king’s request and with all expenses supplied by him, Eligius fashioned the tomb of blessed Martin of Tours from gold and precious stones. On this occasion and opportunity—nor, as subsequently became clear, without the Lord’s will—it happened that he removed two teeth from the saint’s jaw and kept them for himself as relics.

After a long time, when he obtained, seventh in succession from blessed Eleutherius, the dignity of the episcopal see of the Church of Tournai, and undertook the pastoral care of the peoples of Tournai and Noyon in the year of the Lord 649—over whom he ruled for seventeen years, that is, until the year of the Lord 665—God, who had prompted him to separate the saint’s teeth from the body, was pleased, after he had exercised the priestly office for a few days, that [Col. 0072A] the work should now be done by which the blessed pledges might be held in veneration in the regions of Gaul and might afford very great protection for the salvation of their venerators.

At once, inflamed by divine prompting, he was kindled with wondrous devotion toward the saint. Then, reflecting on the reverence with which the relics ought to be honoured, and that it was not right for them to lie hidden under a bushel, he thought that they would obtain the most distinguished honour and the greatest concourse of people if they were placed in such a location as had hitherto possessed no memorial of any saint, but which thereafter, solely on account of their excellence, would be frequented by the people.

Accordingly, having deposited one tooth at Noyon in the church of Blessed Mary, he brought the other to Tournai. At that time, at the southern approach to that city, there was a very lofty hill [Col. 0072B], covered with woodland and planted with fruit-bearing trees of diverse kinds, where a weary spirit was refreshed as though it rejoiced to have taken possession of a portion of paradise’s pleasantness. It was said that blessed Martin had formerly sat there in person while travelling through Gaul for the sake of preaching; that he had raised a dead man there; and that he had bestowed many benefits of healing upon countless sick persons, through which he converted no small multitude of pagans to the worship of the Lord.

God’s servant Eligius therefore chose this place, chosen beforehand by blessed Martin and consecrated by his presence. Depositing the saint’s tooth there, he built in that place a baptismal house in Martin’s honour, so that, while the ministers of the sacraments celebrated divine praises, a people worthy of God might gather there and receive divine gifts. [Col. 0072C] Not at all forgetting the purpose of his desire, he also constructed dwellings there for monks.

But as time went on and the devotion of the faithful toward that place increased somewhat, seeing some who were inclined to what he had long pondered in his mind—namely, to serve God under a rule and to live the common life—he gathered there a great many persons from different peoples, both slaves and freeborn, lest the prepared dwelling should lack inhabitants; and he set over them an abbot at whose command they should depend. He imposed upon them so strict an institution of life that the life of these monks was almost unique in comparison with the other monasteries of Gaul.

Then nobles began to gather there from every direction, and, committing themselves to the service of almighty God, they assigned even their hereditary possessions to that place. [Col. 0072D] Eligius himself enriched the place with larger estates, assigned lands and sufficient revenues, and with quite diligent care provided everything necessary to the monastery. Some of these things he possessed from episcopal revenues; some he had bought for a price; some he had received as a royal gift; while others had been given to him by the gratuitous generosity of powerful persons.

For he was so dear to King Clovis—during whose third regnal year he had received the pontifical mitre—and to all his leading men, because of the bond of earlier fellowship which he had enjoyed with him in the palace under his father Dagobert and grandfather Lothair, that he obtained without delay whatever he requested from him. [Col. 0073A] Whatever he could acquire, he bestowed wholly upon the aforesaid place, which he had founded last among the regions of Gaul, after the famous monasteries he had established in various places. Thus it came about that, after a short time, the goods assigned there were entirely sufficient for the needs of the brothers serving God in that place. Documents of the possessions conferred upon the Church at this time survive to the present day; and how they came to our knowledge we have judged worthy of setting down here.

44. In the church of Blessed Mary at Tournai there was a canon named Erbald, who administered the office of treasurer there for many years. But after the passage of some years, oppressed by a fatal illness, he fled to the aid of blessed Martin. While we were attending him during his sickness one day and conversing together about the antiquity of this church, he suddenly, sick as he was, [Col. 0073B] added the following response to our conversation:

“Truly, brothers, this place was formerly an abbey; for I have very often read, in exceedingly ancient parchments stored within the precinct of the church of Blessed Mary, descriptions of the ancient possessions and revenues of this church, in which there was also included no small multitude of its male and female slaves.”

These words, or writings, bear witness to the antiquity of the church. Yet he named none of the slaves, female slaves, or possessions individually, because, owing to their long dispossession, he could not readily say what descendants or households from them now existed, or to what successors [Col. 0073C] they had passed under the lordship of those now holding them.

When we reported his words to the canons of Blessed Mary and sought that the truth might be disclosed to us more fully, they replied that no written record naming our possessions was held in their whole library. Yet in former times it could have happened that certain determinations of our boundaries were mixed among the writings belonging to their own church; these, now obliterated by excessive age, appear nowhere. But even if some had existed, while they remained intact Erbald, to whose keeping they had been entrusted, could easily discover them by reading them often—something which never occurred to others.

Hearing this, yet being unable to make any progress, we grieve. Nevertheless, we hold most firmly what we have learned by paternal tradition: namely, that at the time of the Northmen’s persecution certain articles of our church’s equipment and possessions, together with the tooth of blessed Martin—in whose veneration the monastery of monks had been founded by blessed Eligius—came then into the possession of the canons of Blessed Mary, either because they received them for safekeeping or because, for some reason of reciprocal exchange, they subjected them to their own legal right. [Col. 0073D] For even to the present day the tooth is said to be held by them, as is shown by the words set down below.

We do not doubt that Erbald’s words were true, because the custom frequently followed today in writing charters had already taken root in those times. Just as, concerning possessions and altars now given to churches by princes and bishops, we see two chirographs written [Col. 0074A], one of which, sealed with the donor’s own seal-impression, is assigned to the church to which the possession is conveyed, while the other, unsealed, remains at the church where the bishop’s seat is located; so it is plainly evident that the documents of those possessions which this Church formerly held were handed over in the same manner to the canons of Saint Mary.

45. Even in our own times there were elderly men beside the Scheldt, around Helchin and Saint-Ghislain, who said that they had heard from their forebears that this Church had formerly possessed notable revenues within the aforesaid boundaries. Specifying the possessions themselves, they said that these were the altars of the aforesaid villages, meadows, woods, arable lands, male and female slaves, and the other revenues [Col. 0074B] now held there by the bishop, the canons, and the knights holding from the bishop. After the monks had departed, they made the altars of Kortrijk and of Hennuyères into their own freehold; but because this church was restored, the records of its antiquity are not brought to light lest some quarrel or dispute arise between the children of the two churches concerning the recovery of possessions.

They further admit most fully that they possess the privileges of the churches of Saint Quentin in the marketplace and of blessed Peter in the middle of the city, in which communities serving Christ formerly remained and still remain unrestored, and that they hold their possessions.

46. Yet another testimony to its antiquity, which persists to the present time, I judge should by no means be passed over in silence. In ancient times a custom established at that period was observed in churches: the names of the brothers of neighbouring churches, to whom they knew themselves to owe mutual prayers or with whom they had promised fellowship, were placed in writing upon the holy altar, so that the priest might recite them by name while singing the Mass, when he came to the place where it is said: “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids, who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.” [Col. 0074C] Then one of the altar’s ministers, approaching him, presented the names to be recited.

We know that the ancient monks of this monastery had this fraternity of association with the monks of Saint Amand at Elnone. For that written record in which the names of the brothers of Saint Martin were contained together with the names of the brothers of neighbouring churches remained in that same monastery of Elnone until our own times; indeed, some of our people held it in their hands and inspected it with their eyes.

Therefore, relying upon these testimonies, which we have learned either from writings or from succession, we confidently affirm that this place was formerly an abbey. Nor would such distinguished testimonies as those related above have been preserved in vain to the present day, although we acknowledge that not everything has come to our knowledge.

47. The same blessed Eligius, our author, as is read in his Life, likewise buried blessed Piaton the martyr in the district of Medenant within the territory of Tournai, at the place called Siclinium [Col. 0075A].

> [Note: Col. 0075D: *Siclinium*, commonly Seclin-en-Mélantois.]

There, enlarging, according to the measure of his resources and with the aid of almighty God accompanying him, the church constructed after the martyr’s passion, he established the offices of clerics serving the Lord, as we see even to this day. But, leaving it to the people of Siclinium to hand down in records the enlargements of their boundaries, let us turn our pen to recounting the manner of the desolation of our first church.

48. After the city of Tournai had received knowledge of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ from blessed Piaton, about the year 300 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and after the most cruel persecution had ceased—the persecution exercised by Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West, under which the same martyr suffered—and after the churches of Blessed Mary and Saint Martin had been founded [Col. 0075B] and were flourishing in divine peace, both inwardly and outwardly, the people of Tournai began to grow in renown, increase in offspring, expand in possessions, glory in vanity, delight in prosperity, feast luxuriously, and enjoy their own pleasures for six hundred years less nineteen, that is, until the year of the Lord 881.

They made use of these delights not so much happily as they were unhappily deceived by them. For through the vices of desire they neglected true religion, offended God, and incurred his wrath. Suddenly, amid these very times of prosperity, God stirred up the fierceness of most cruel peoples, intending to avenge the anger caused by their offence against peoples of diverse nations. Then the multitude of the Northmen rushed violently onward [Col. 0075C], just as we read that the Vandals had done in the year 453 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the time of the most holy Nicasius, when Merovech reigned over the Franks. They overthrew the fortifications of many cities; slaughtered fathers and mothers of both sexes with their children by sword and fire; and, continuing for almost thirty years to ravage Gaul, among their other crimes they destroyed the walls of the city of Tournai, plundered its buildings, laid waste its citizens and peoples, devastated all its possessions and equipment together with the neighbouring churches, and rendered it wholly uninhabitable.

We have resolved to commit to writing, and make known to posterity, how this happened, so far as we can gather from the writings of chronographers or the statements of modern persons.

[Col. 0075D]

49. In the chronicle of Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, it is found that the Northmen, joined by the Danes, wandering through Francia and Lotharingia in the year of the Lord 881, devastated by iron and fire Arras, Amiens, Corbie, Cambrai, Thérouanne, the territories of the Menapians and Brabanters, and all the land around the river Scheldt—namely Tournai and its borderlands, Ghent, Kortrijk, the abbey of Saint Amand at Elnone in Condé on the bank of the Scheldt, where they established their seat in the first year of the episcopate of Heidilo, bishop of Tournai—the monasteries of Saint Valery and Saint-Riquier, Liège, Maastricht, Tongeren, Cologne, Bonn with its adjacent castles, the town and palace of Aachen, the monasteries of Stavelot, Malmedy, Inda, [Col. 0076A] Prüm, Trier, and Metz.

At that time Tournai was an episcopal see, and it is shown to have held that dignity for three hundred years less sixteen before the period just passed, because from the year of the Lord 484 Saint Eleutherius governed its bishopric. Before him, a few days earlier, Theodore had presided; but nothing is known of his birth, ordination, or the length of his presidency, except that he is remembered to have been killed by a divine shaft—that is, by a thunderbolt.

50. There is also another chronicle of this Northmen’s invasion, composed specifically by a certain monk of Marchiennes. It bears witness to the account just given, expressly writing that Tournai was then plundered and reduced to nothing. It adds that Emmo, bishop of Tournai, was killed by the Northmen in the year of the Lord 860, twenty-one years before this devastation. [Col. 0076B] In this work the same arranger of times sets forth in distinguished style the wars and battles which the Northmen, through their insatiable thirst for shedding human blood, waged while fighting fiercely against the people of Reims, Paris, Orléans, and Compiègne.

51. At that time the monks of Saint Martin, dispersed from the city of Tournai, each left both their own place and the citizens by whose protection they had formerly prospered, strengthened by divine help and enlarged by favour, and scattered to suitable locations where they hoped they would act more conveniently or be of greater benefit. Some of them, scattered through the vast expanses of the world, delighted also in the goods they found everywhere [Col. 0076C] and content with the customs of the places they encountered, neglected—as many testify—to return thereafter to their former desirable places, now reduced to a plain; nor were they willing to undertake the labour of raising those ruins. Instead, they ended their present lives in the places to which they had fled, conveying their hereditary possessions to those places by perpetual donation in return for benefits received.

Some possessions they sold for a price because of the scarcity and inconvenience of their necessities. Others, lacking a guardian and defender, passed into the lordship of secular powers. But a certain portion of those who had greater devotion toward God and sounder judgment turned aside to an abbey situated in the diocese of Paris, in the town called Ferrières. They carried with them some few articles from the equipment of their Church, or those things which they judged would be more useful to themselves. Among these, as we have discovered from the indications reported above about the twentieth year of the second restoration, was especially the chirograph of a certain estate in that region called Supas.

For they possessed that same estate nearby, at a distance of about two leagues, extended by ample holdings and yielding abundant revenues. They therefore turned aside to it, that they might be more suitably maintained from its revenues and might devote themselves more vigilantly to guarding those revenues, so that they might be stronger for their own needs. Since we have said above how they possessed it, we judged it superfluous to repeat the matter here. [Col. 0077A]

They joined that community in order that the vows of their lips—that is, the observance of the Rule, by which they knew they had devoted themselves to God and to his blessed confessor Martin—might at least be repaid in another place by complete observance of regular precepts, since they could not fulfil them in the place where they had indeed been able to promise them.

52. At this time we believe it happened that the canons of the church of Blessed Mary appropriated the tooth of blessed Martin, together with the documents described and certain utensils of this church. Certain things, however, which they could not carry away, they hid beneath the ground around the church precinct, as is said even to the present day.

Hence also that treasure shown in a dream at the head of the chapel of Blessed Mary to a cleric named Bernard, son of Vitalis—of whom mention has been made above, and whom many of us knew—is believed to have belonged to this church. [Col. 0077B] For he saw standing beside him a beautiful-faced maiden, with her hair dressed, adorned in orderly garments, who said:

“Look at the shrines, crosses, Gospel-books, phylacteries, and other ornaments of the Church which I bring into the sunlight.”

After he had gazed at all these things for a long time, the maiden added:

“See that you tell no one that these things have been shown to you; for if you tell it and transgress my command, you will die within thirty days.”

Immediately upon waking, because of the excessive joy of his heart, he could not keep silent about what he had seen. Instead, he recounted it in full and, according to the maiden’s words, died before the thirtieth day, so that, although he went to sleep healthy in the evening, he was found dead in the morning. [Col. 0077C]

But because we do not yet see the revealed treasure, we do not affirm that his dream was true. Yet it is clear, from the fact that he did not reach the thirtieth day, that what it declared was not altogether false. Perhaps the time for revealing it has not yet come, or perhaps he for whom it was laid up has not yet arrived.

Whether or not what was shown to him existed, we have nevertheless learned from the frequent testimony of our predecessors that abundant treasures have been deposited around the church precinct. In our times the places where they are kept have been revealed in dreams to certain persons. One of these is a matron named Hersendis, who indicated two places to us, saying that it had been shown to her that in one there was a well, and in the other [Col. 0077D] a treasure was preserved. We sought the well in the designated place and found it to contain exceptionally clear water; in it we also found certain bronze vessels quite suitable for the Church’s use. But we have not yet dug up the site of the treasure, indicated nearby toward the west; therefore we do not know whether it contains any truth.

53. In the aforesaid persecution, blessed Piaton of Siclinium was carried off to Chartres, where, before coming to Tournai, he had preached the name of Christ. But when those people did not receive his preaching, he sought Tournai, and there upheld the faith of our Lord. Concerning his body, a great dispute survives to our time [Col. 0078A]: we at Siclinium say that it was brought back to the places of his passion, while the people of Chartres, on the contrary, affirm that it is kept among them to this day.

To settle this dispute, it is necessary to acknowledge what we have received from our elders: namely, that, although the body was brought back among us, some portion of it should be believed to have remained there. For at Siclinium, when the chest in which the martyr’s body was kept was opened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1143, it was shown to the people.

> [Note: Col. 0077: “was shown.” By Simon, bishop of Tournai.]

The monks of Saint Martin at Tournai deserved to receive a tooth from his body. Then, restored to its former place, the body is kept with great vigilance, and the Church of Siclinium rejoices that it is not deprived of the martyr’s presence.

54. Among the people of Siclinium there raged that pestilence commonly called the “infernal fire,” so severely that it not only deprived some of their limbs but also took their lives. Many of these were carried by others’ hands to the basilica of the blessed martyr established at Siclinium. [Col. 0078B] The church was disturbed by cries, and all implored the help of God and the martyr’s intercession.

Now upon the shrine in which the blessed martyr’s relics were kept were carved ten Gospel virgins: namely, five wise and five foolish ones (Matt. 25:2). All these, then, displaying the martyr’s affection, pitying the sufferings of the wretched, and carrying out the Lord’s will, wept so that they were believed to be animate. In this event the power of the highest miracle and the presence of blessed Piaton the martyr shone forth. For just as, while living in the body and exhorting peoples to the Christian faith, he had poured out not merely an abundance of tears, but at last his own blood for them, so then he displayed the greatness of his feeling through the images placed beneath him. From the eyes of the prudent virgins drops of blood flowed; from the eyes of the others tears flowed like water. [Col. 0078C] After this miracle the sick experienced divine help and the martyr’s consolation, and those thought to be dying were restored to health.

Having said these things about the presence of blessed Piaton’s body and the antiquity of our abbey, let us return to the matters from which we digressed.

55. Therefore, when Lord Rabodus had restored the ancient lands to our Church, he came to the chapter house and advised Abbot Odo and the other brothers no longer to trust themselves or immediately wish to do whatever they read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, but rather to choose some monastery whose customs they should observe. The bishop’s counsel pleased them. The monastery of Anchin was chosen, which had been built fifteen years before ours and which alone at that time in our province preserved the religion and customs of the monastery of Cluny.

Thus Lord Abbot Odo sought Haimeric, abbot of Anchin, and, because he acknowledged both himself and all his monks to belong to Haimeric—since they had been made and blessed by him—begged him also to teach them how they ought to live. The religious abbot consented, and immediately, appointing priors from among his own monks in our monastery, and willingly teaching some of ours at Anchin with him, he laboured gladly with us. [Col. 0079A] Both he and his brothers became to us fathers in counsel, brothers in aid, and servants in service. Therefore, above all the monasteries of the province, we have always had the greatest familiarity with the people of Anchin, so that all things are common between us, both within and without; and whatever we do for our brothers, living or dead, we have granted that we should do for them, and we receive the same from them in reciprocal exchange.

56. Meanwhile, very many persons of both sexes, renouncing the world, began to come to our church for conversion and to convey to us portions of their resources. The first, as it seems to me, to come for conversion was that noble matron Ida, whose memory I made above [Col. 0079B]. She had been the wife of Fastrad, advocate, who greatly desired to see the restoration of our Church, but, prevented by death, could not see it. Among other gifts, she gave us a house in the city and the lower mill on the little river Maire, which we possess to the present day. Though most noble, she nevertheless never wished to hold among the other religious women any office but that of the lowest servant.

She was the sister of that noble prince Theoderic of Avesnes, who at the same time built from its foundations the monastery of Liessies on his own land; when all its buildings had been completed, he placed monks there and provided abundantly for their food and clothing. Since his name has arisen and there will be no other occasion to relate it, I shall say something about him from which benefit may be gained by any reader wishing to imitate him.

This noble and very powerful Theoderic, while frequently waging war against Baldwin, count of Mons, one day assembled a considerable force, violently entered Baldwin’s territory, and carried off much booty. Among his other acts there, he also burned two monasteries of religious women: those of Saint Waldetrudis at Mons and Saint Aldegund at Maubeuge, because the count had stationed soldiers there to resist him. [Col. 0079C]

57. A certain hermit, living alone in the nearby wood called Broqueroy, saw—as he himself related—not while asleep but awake, at midday, the holy Mother of God Mary seated in heaven upon a lofty throne like a queen. The two aforesaid saints lay prostrate at her feet and sought vengeance upon Theoderic of Avesnes, who had burned their churches. As they complained vehemently and pressed urgently for justice, the holy Virgin replied to them:

“Spare him, I beg you, and do not trouble me, for I do not wish to afflict him at present. For his wife, Lady Ada, performs for me a certain service by which she binds me to herself in such intimate friendship that I cannot allow any burden to be inflicted either upon her or upon her husband.”

When the saints asked what that service was, she replied that it was that angelic salutation [Col. 0080A] which on earth had been the beginning of her joy.

> [Note: Col. 0079: “Salutation.” Note the Rosary of the Blessed Virgin, commonly called the *chapelet*, already in use at that time.]

“Each day she repeats it to me sixty times: twenty times prostrate, twenty times with bent knees, and twenty times standing, whether in church, in her chamber, or in some secluded place: ‘Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb’ (Luke 1:28).”

But when the saints, repeatedly urging many things more insistently, importunately demanded to be avenged, the holy Virgin finally answered them:

“I ask you to grant me a postponement of this vengeance for the present; and I promise you that a time will come when I shall do justice for you against him, while committing no wrong against Lady Ada.”

When I heard this in my childhood, I believed it false; later I did not greatly doubt that it could have been true. For when our abbot Odo, about the twelfth year after his conversion, had been promoted to the episcopate of the city of Cambrai, the blood-relations of that Theoderic, distressed because he had no offspring by his wife, accused them before that bishop of being related in the fourth degree, and on the appointed day confirmed it by oath. Thus, by ecclesiastical judgment, after they had already lived together for more than twenty years, they caused that marriage to be dissolved. [Col. 0080B]

Hardly half a year had passed when the aforesaid Theoderic, going to hunt in the forest, was surrounded by the ambushes of Isaac of Berlemont and killed. He was carried to the monastery of Liessies, which he had built, and buried in the chapter house before the abbot’s seat. Then it became commonly reported that what the hermit said he had heard could have been true: that holy Mary had promised that she would avenge the saints and would commit no wrong against Lady Ada, now separated from him.

That same lady, separated from her husband, immediately abandoned worldly splendour and went to the aforesaid monastery which she had built with her husband. Yet she did not wholly relinquish her property; rather, having built herself a stone house beside the church and unwilling to burden the Church, she lived from her own revenues until the end. She frequently gave the monks what was necessary and told many people that what we have related was true. [Col. 0080C]

The matter was so widely reported that Gosceguin, son of Lady Ada, our first religious woman, who succeeded his aforesaid uncle Theoderic, also repeated those salutations of blessed Mary daily and urged his knights to say them. Therefore, although he did many evil things, he nevertheless ended his life well. For, perceiving that he was suffering from a serious illness, he became a monk in that same monastery and, dying thus, was buried beside his uncle in the chapter house.

Because he had no offspring by his wife Agnes, daughter of Anselm of Ribemont, he appointed as his successor during his lifetime Walter, an excellent young man, son of his brother Fastrad. The aforesaid Agnes, his wife, imitating Lady Ada, abandoned worldly splendour and went to the same monastery. Living from her own revenues, she had gold chalices, candelabra, and many other costly ornaments made for that church. [Col. 0081A]

This Fastrad, whom I have now named as Walter’s father, was the son of Ida, our first religious woman. This same Fastrad, after he had been advocate of Tournai for many years, was struck by illness and became a monk in our monastery, and so died. His wife Richeldis, imitating the aforesaid Ida, her husband’s mother, abandoned the world, took the habit of a religious woman among us, and, though she had been most noble and wealthy, showed no pride whatsoever among the other women for twenty years. Thus living humbly, she died a good death.

Walter, her son, seeing that his father and mother were buried among us, gave us for their souls and his own a mill on the little river Riez. As long as he lived, he was everywhere like a father to our Church. He married Ida, daughter of Everard, castellan of Tournai, by whom he fathered many sons and daughters; and he surpassed all his predecessors in power and wealth. [Col. 0081B] He was first advocate of Tournai; then, succeeding his paternal uncle, he held the castle of Avesnes and almost the entire region called Brabant.

Wishing to live peaceably, repenting of many crimes he had committed, and attempting to mitigate the wars that had endured for many years between the counts of Mons and the princes of Avesnes, he joined the sister of Baldwin, count of Mons, in marriage to his son Theoderic, a young knight; and thus he pacified the whole province.

But the enemy of the human race did not endure that peace for long. This young Theoderic, unwilling to be content with his father’s wealth, roamed everywhere like an unbroken horse. He began to bring back plunder and captives not only from nearby regions but even from distant ones, namely from the territory of the duke of Louvain and the bishop of Liège. At length, one day, elated by frequent victories and advancing too far with a hundred knights, he could not return. Killed by infantry rushing upon him from every side, he was carried back on horses, with great danger, to the monastery of Laeties, bringing great grief to all his friends. [Col. 0081C]

Then his father, struck by excessive sorrow and fearing the various turns of fortune, gave in his lifetime the castle of Avesnes and Brabant to his other son Nicholas, adding to them the castle called Walcourt. To his third son he handed over the advocacy of Tournai. To his fourth son, Everard, whom he made a cleric, he acquired the two archdeaconries of Cambrai and Tournai, the provostship of Nivelles, and many other ecclesiastical honours; and he gave four daughters to wealthy husbands.

As he himself told me many times, he would gladly have become a monk if he could have obtained his wife’s permission. But in the present year, after the feast of All Saints, while he was pleading in the hall of Count Baldwin at the castle of Mons against him concerning the castle of Trelon, which the count wished to take from him, he was struck by sudden paralysis and lost his speech. He was then placed by the countess in the count’s bed, and died the following night. [Col. 0081D]

Thereupon his sons [Col. 0082A] carried him to the monastery of Laeties, where he was buried with his forebears, to the great grief of the whole province, because everyone had been accustomed to call him the father of the poor and of churches. But let these matters suffice. We must now turn to those two knights, Walter and Radulf, whom I mentioned much earlier, and briefly show how true was that dream in which they seemed to stand in the church of Saint Martin and renew its walls.

58. This Walter, as I said before, was called the son of Hubert, and was one of the more powerful nobles of the province of Tournai. When he came to conversion with his wife, he gave us that mill on the little river Maire, where all the grain is ground from which the bread eaten in the monastery is made. He also held [Col. 0082B] a certain piece of land in the forest of Pevele, near Templeuve, which he wished to give us but could not, because he held it as a benefice from Robert the Younger, then count of Flanders. For the count was unwilling to grant freely to the Church so much land as belonged to his benefice or fief.

While efforts were therefore being made to obtain the count’s consent, it happened that the aforesaid knight Radulf had a horse of great value, for which the count wished to give forty marks. Radulf accordingly asked the count to take that horse and give the land as alms to Saint Martin for the sake of his soul. The count agreed, and by the authority of his charter confirmed that same land to our monastery. Thus the aforesaid mill [Col. 0082C] together with that land afterwards yielded us more than a thousand pounds.

Now, once he had become a monk, no one could readily describe how he conducted himself. Though inferior to none of the nobles of the region, he showed himself humbler than all peasants. He was never ashamed, before the eyes of his fellow knights and kinsmen, who wept in astonishment, to carry water to the kitchen, wash bowls and pots, sift flour, light the oven, clean the horses’ stables, and carry away dung. By his example he converted many. He began the new church from the offerings of the faithful and, with God’s help, completed it—as may be seen today—sufficient for one hundred monks.

59. Radulf, however, had two knightly brothers in the city. The elder was Thetbert; the other was called [Col. 0082D] Theoderic the moneyer. Thetbert was the provost of Bishop Rabodus and showed himself faithful to him as to his lord. Therefore the advocate Fastrad, angry with him because he everywhere defended and protected the bishop’s poor peasants, first deceitfully made himself his intimate friend; and, receiving his son at baptism, became his spiritual kinsman. But a few days later, pursuing him as he unsuspectingly hunted hares, he deceitfully kissed him as his spiritual kinsman and immediately killed him unawares, on the feast of the Apostle Saint Bartholomew. At once fleeing the province, he withdrew to his uncle Theoderic of Avesnes and remained with him for nearly three years.

Then Lord Bishop Rabodus gave Fastrad’s advocacy to the knight Radulf of Noyon [Col. 0083A] and entirely disinherited Fastrad because of his crime. Some said that this happened by God’s will, because Radulf, the new advocate, readily restored, at the bishop’s request, the lands of Saint Martin which he held, as was said above; lands which, as Fastrad later asserted many times, he would in no way have restored had he held them at that time.

But after two of Fastrad’s knights had already been killed in vengeance for this crime, Thetbert himself appeared—not in sleep, but to one awake—to a devout citizen of Tournai named Rainer. When the man, greatly terrified, asked whether he was indeed Lord Thetbert and how he fared, he replied that he was the man himself, told him not to fear, and then added:

> “I am indeed in torments for my sins, and especially because after the death of [Col. 0083B] my wife I kept a concubine. But I shall receive mercy, because I was unjustly killed for loyalty to my lord the bishop; and Saint Bartholomew also, upon whose feast I was slain, aids me, because I invoked him at the hour of my death. I ask you, therefore, to go to my brothers and sons, and entreat them, for the sake of my soul, to forgive Fastrad my death and no longer seek to avenge me on my account. For if they do this, it will greatly help my soul in obtaining salvation.”

Rainer replied that he would indeed tell them his commands, but that they would by no means believe him. The dead man then immediately imposed upon him certain signs which he was to tell each of them, and so vanished. Rainer went to the dead man’s brothers and sons, disclosed his commands to them, added the signs, [Col. 0083C] and thus made them more willing to make peace.

Accordingly, after some years, Fastrad came barefoot with his friends, threw himself at their feet, and received both their friendship and his inheritance from the bishop. To confirm the friendship, he gave his daughter Sarah in marriage to Gosceguin, son of Theoderic the moneyer, who had been Thetbert’s brother.

[Note: [Col. 0083] “Moneyer,” because he presided over the mint established by Philip Augustus in the city of Tournai. Thus the *Customs of Tournai*.]

The brothers of the slain man also immediately gave Saint Martin the twenty pounds in coin which they had received from him for the reconciliation.

60. After this, Radulf, Thetbert’s brother, took as his wife a certain young woman, Mainsendis, born of the knights of the province—namely, the daughter of Herman, provost of Saint-Amand of Elnone. By [Col. 0083D] her he had three sons: Theoderic, Walter, and Herman. He entrusted the first, Theoderic, at five years of age to be taught letters; and, at the urging of the canons, he sought and obtained from Bishop Rabodus a prebend for him in the church of Saint Mary, promising thirty marks of silver for it.

When this was announced to the boy in the school, amid the congratulations of the canons, he returned home at evening and refused supper, sitting sadly at the table. His father, thinking that he had been beaten by his teacher, as boys often were, took him aside after supper and asked what was wrong and why he was sad. The boy immediately replied:

> “In the name of the Lord, can I not rightly be sad, when I know that today you have been plunged into hell on my account? Have you not heard that those who buy or sell prebends are excommunicated? Take care, certainly, what you do concerning your soul; for know that I shall leave this province sooner than eat of it.”

Astonished at this, his father said: “Son, do not grieve about this any longer; for I call God to witness that you shall never possess it any more.” He spoke, and immediately sent word to the bishop to do what he wished with the prebend, since his son would not have it.

61. In the same year Radulf was seized with a most severe fever, almost to death. When, by God’s will, he recovered, he secretly approached a monk named Walter, a most prudent man and brother of [Col. 0084B] his wife, and began to seek counsel concerning the salvation of his soul in these words:

> “Since you owe fidelity to God as a monk, and to me as the husband of your sister, I implore you by that same fidelity which you owe to God and to me to advise me how I may be saved. For recently, when I was sick and feared death, I sought counsel from the canons of Saint Mary. They advised me to confess my sins truthfully, receive the Body of the Lord, be anointed with holy oil, and rest assured that I would be saved. I did as they advised; but once I recovered, I again feel myself bound by sins. This does not seem to me to be true confession: to confess sins when I am ill, and when I recover to be defiled by sins again. I therefore beg you, for God’s sake, to advise me what I ought to do.”

The monk replied: “And what advantage will it be to you to hear my counsel, when you will not wish to follow it?”

“Give the counsel,” said the knight, “and if I do not follow it, it shall not be charged against you.”

Then the monk said: “Truly I tell you that, so long as you live in the world as you have lived until now, I do not see how you can be saved. But if you truly wish to be saved, leave the world and take up the monastic life.”

“And how,” said the knight, “shall I do this without the consent of your sister, my wife?”

Then the monk said: “Since the Lord says in the Gospel, ‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother and wife and children for my name’s sake, he cannot be my disciple’ [Col. 0084D] (Luke 14:26), I shall never advise you to lose your soul for my sister’s sake. Ask only her permission; and if she refuses to give it, I advise you to leave her, leaving her a portion of your property, and flee to God.”

Having heard this, the knight thanked him and returned home. Entering his chamber and sitting on the bed, he began to weep most bitterly. Mainsendis came in, saw him weeping, and asked what new event had occurred to make him torment himself thus. He wished to conceal it; but when she pressed him earnestly, he recounted everything that her brother, Lord Walter, monk and provost of Saint-Amand, had said. Then she said:

> “And why do you torment yourself so because of these things?”

“Because,” he said, “if I did not have to leave you, I would truly become a monk as soon as possible.”

She immediately added:

> “Do not refrain from doing good because of me. For as you fear for your soul, so I fear for mine; and on whatever day you leave the world, I too shall leave it. Even now, if you wish, I give you permission and promise to live chastely.”

Then the knight said: “And what shall we do with our three sons?”

The woman replied: “Let us not leave them in the devil’s hand, but rather present them to God with ourselves. For we are wealthy, and wherever we choose we shall gladly be received with them.”

Delighted by these words, Radulf said: “And where do you think it fitting that we should take the religious habit with them?”

[Col. 0085B] At that time Master Odo governed the school of Tournai, and no mention had yet arisen of his conversion. Therefore, not knowing where else to turn, the woman said:

> “It seems to me that we can suitably go to Saint-Amand, for my father was provost there and my brother succeeded him; moreover, I was born and brought up there.”

Radulf agreed. He immediately sent a messenger to the aforesaid Lord Walter the monk, related what had been said, and gave Saint-Amand, through Walter’s hand, a mill situated near Tournai on the little river Marvis. Then he called his wife and said:

> “One who wishes to act rightly ought not delay, because the crafty devil always seeks opportunities by which he may hinder God’s servants from their good purpose. Therefore it seems to me that tomorrow, without delay, we should leave the world.”

Then she said:

> “My lord, this cannot be done so quickly. For I have not yet told you something in confidence: it is now two months since I perceived that I had conceived, and certainly it would not be reasonable for me to leave the world while pregnant. Meanwhile, therefore, let us prepare all that is necessary, so that after I have given birth we may immediately renounce the world. Yet since I have already given you permission, although no witness after God was present, it is surely fitting that we should henceforth do nothing marital or conjugal with one another, but live continently.”

After this, as they themselves related to me many times, they remained in [Col. 0085D] secular life for a whole year and a half. They lay undivided in one bed, yet did nothing carnal—not by their own strength, but because Christ’s grace protected them. Mainsendis was young: when she left the world, she was only twenty-four years old. Thus their fourth son was born, and at baptism was called Radulf.

In the same year Master Odo renounced the world and, with his clerics, entered the church of Saint Martin, as we related above. Mainsendis visited them frequently, often sending them alms; yet no one in the city knew what she and her husband had resolved to do. One Sunday, therefore, intending to hear their Mass and see their procession, she went with her son Theoderic, a young cleric now almost seven years old, [Col. 0086A] to the church of Saint Martin and waited until Mass had been sung. Unbeknown to her, the boy joined those clerics and remained with them.

When Mass ended, the woman sought her son among her neighbors. Thinking that he was playing with other boys, she went home. Once lunch had been prepared, the boy was sought; his mother said that he had gone with her to Saint Martin. No one suspected his conversion. After lunch the knight mounted his horse, went to the house of his brother Theoderic, and searched both there and in the other houses of his relatives for his son, but heard no news of him.

He then went to Saint Martin and found Haimeric, abbot of Anchin, with Abbot Odo. He saw the boy sitting before them and listening to them. The abbots made the knight sit with them and instructed him, as he gladly listened, concerning God’s commands. As evening approached, the knight asked and received leave to depart, and commanded his son to return home with him. Then the boy first disclosed his intention:

> “If you wish, return home and greet my mother and brothers, and tell them to pray for me. For I shall never again enter your house; I shall remain here with these poor men. Nor do I acknowledge any father or mother but God and Saint Martin.”

His father, astonished and believing he spoke in play, said: “Come, for here you would have nothing to eat tonight, nor a bed on which to lie.”

The boy answered: “Even if they have nothing to eat, I shall go around the city and bring them alms which I have begged; at night I shall rest upon the bare ground.”

The father laughed, said that these were childish words, and wished to take the boy away by force. At last Abbot Haimeric, a most prudent man, said:

> “Lord Radulf, if you will believe me, do no violence to the boy now. Leave him with us; for during one night we shall adequately provide what he needs. If this desire comes from God, it will appear tomorrow; but if it comes from childhood, do not compel him, for he will return home willingly.”

The knight consented and returned home, where he told his wife what had happened. She immediately knelt, raised her hands and eyes to heaven, and said:

> “I give thanks to God because he has made my firstborn [Col. 0086D] son a servant of himself. It seems, therefore, my lord, that God wishes us to build that little church from our resources. We shall take this as a sign of the divine will: if the boy perseveres in what he has begun, then let us be certain that what I have said is true; but if he returns, then God wills something else concerning us.”

In the morning the knight again mounted his horse and returned to Saint Martin, where he found the boy persevering most steadfastly in what he had begun. Immediately he summoned his brother Theoderic and his other kinsmen, offered his son—still a boy of seven and not yet of lawful age—to Saint Martin before the altar, and bestowed with him the four mills he possessed on the little river Rieu.

Thereafter, although Radulf remained in the world, he took all care for that little church, providing necessities no less fully than if he had already become a monk.

62. In the same year (1095), through Abbot Haimeric, as was said above, those clerics received the monastic habit. The boy Theoderic then became a monk with them. When the monks, as related above, wished to leave the church and seek deserted places, they wished to leave Theoderic there. But since he would not remain, and, being a boy of eight, could not endure the fatigue of the journey on foot, they placed him with his books upon a cart and took him with them.

When this was reported very early in the morning to Radulf, who was still sleeping in his bed, he immediately rose in haste, went to the church [Col. 0087B] of Saint Mary, quickly summoned the assembly of canons, restored to them their toll, which he had until then held by force, and asked pardon for the violence done to them. He disclosed his purpose: that he would immediately leave the world and follow the monks of Saint Martin who were departing.

Having said this, accompanied by a great crowd of clerics and people, he returned home. Taking his wife by the hand and lifting his eyes to heaven, he said:

> “Lord God, you gave me this wife, and I have kept lawful faith with her, you being my witness, until this present day. But now, for love of you, I leave her and commend her to you.”

After this he took his little sons Walter and Herman, raised them up, and offered and commended them to God. How great was the grief of all, born of tenderness, when they saw the fourth son, Radulf, still nursing, brought with his cradle, drawn from it by his father, raised up, and commended to God.

Then he immediately mounted his horse. To a poor cleric, Rainer, whom he had maintained with him for God’s sake for two years and who did not wish to leave him now either, he gave another horse. Quickly following the monks, he joined them before they reached Seclin. Falling at Abbot Odo’s feet, he asked that he might be permitted to accompany their pilgrimage.

The abbot, astonished at the zeal of so wealthy a man, summoned the monks who were walking with him and began an exhortation from Radulf’s conversion:

> “Behold, we monks thought that we had accomplished something, and yet we have been surpassed by a secular publican, Zacchaeus.”

Thus, going with them to Noyon, he disclosed his purpose to Bishop Rabodus. The bishop, shedding tears in excessive astonishment, kissed him, gave thanks to God, took Radulf by the hand, and placed him in the abbot’s hand. Then he added:

> “Tell me now, good abbot, why do you wish to leave Tournai? Do you think you have made little progress, when you have taken such a sinner from the devil and joined him to God? Return, therefore, joyful and swiftly, for truly through this man God will yet gain another.”

When he returned to Tournai and again lay prostrate at the abbot’s feet, asking to be received, the abbot said:

> “I shall not receive you until you have been tested, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, which says: ‘Test the spirits, whether they are from God’ [Col. 0088A] (ch. 58). Go, then, and publicly seek your livelihood before the people by labor: carrying water to taverns, cutting wood, cleaning horses’ stables, and doing similar things wherever you see a need.”

He willingly carried out the abbot’s command and, setting aside all shame, submitted himself to the most menial tasks.

When Mainsendis, his former wife, saw this, she was not frightened by any fear. Rather, summoning Theoderic the moneyer, Radulf’s brother and the richest man in the whole city, she went to Saint Martin and entrusted her sons to God, placing the youngest, with his cradle, upon the altar—not without the tears of many bystanders. Their uncle Theoderic, moved by pity and with the abbot’s consent, had the children carried to his own house to be nourished, and kept them with him for a long time.

Mainsendis then placed more than two hundred marks of silver, two mills on the Costentin, and all else that her husband had left her, in the hands of Saint Martin. Thus stripped of all things, she fell at the abbot’s feet, asking to be received. The abbot said:

> “You too must first be tested. Go through the city and seek your living by spinning, weaving, and combing wool. If perhaps some man or woman wishes to give you a whole loaf, do not accept it; instead, ask for pieces of bread broken off, as poor people do when they beg alms.”
