The woman rejoiced to be fed on such delights. Having cast off shame, she begged alms publicly, while the matrons who saw this wept and wished through their maidservants to send an abundance of loaves with her to Saint Martin [Col. 0088C].

Such was the conversion of Radulf and Mainsendis, which I do not believe that merciful Jesus can forget.

These, indeed, are the things which he bestowed upon our church: four mills on the Rieu, which are nearer to the Scheldt. He had a fifth upon the Scheldt; but because in autumn, when the water of the Scheldt rose, it was easily swallowed up by its overflow, he later had it wholly destroyed. Yet he ordered the posts to be left and preserved as a testimony to the former mill, for this one reason alone: that no one in future might build another mill below those four as far as the Scheldt; for if one were built, it was clear that they could easily suffer no small loss from it.

He also gave us two mills [Col. 0088D] on the Costentin with the adjacent land, which had come to him by paternal right. Upon it he caused a farmstead to be built, which remains to the present day. He also gave us a herd of mares, whose offspring is still kept in our pastures to this day. From them we have often obtained teams for cultivating our land, and have bred and sold horses of great value. Thus, from them, in various ways, we have already derived benefit of more than a thousand pounds.

With the money which his wife gave, we redeemed lands situated around the church and purchased others in the same district, because when he came to conversion we did not yet possess even a foot of arable land. He had one mill on the Marvis; but when he first resolved to renounce the world, as was said above, he gave it to Saint-Amand, because he wished to become a monk in its monastery called Elnone, since no mention of our monastery had yet been made among people.

63. At that time the venerable abbot of the same monastery of Saint-Amand of Elnone was named Hugh. A few years earlier he had rebuilt from the foundations the church of Saint-Amand, which had accidentally burned, and had constructed it most fittingly with cloister, towers, and offices, as may be seen today.

Filled, then, with the sweetness of charity, he saw that Radulf, with his wife and children, had left the wealthy church of Saint-Amand and sought the poor church of Saint Martin. Calling his monks together in chapter, [Col. 0089B] he said:

> “Behold, dearest brothers, that secular knight Radulf has preferred the poverty of Saint Martin to our riches and has wished to become a monk in a poor church. Let us, therefore, show that we possess the tender heart of charity, and grant half of the mill which he gave us to the poor church of Saint Martin. Thus let us make blessed Martin a sharer in that mill with our patron Saint Amand.”

All consented, and not one showed himself degenerate from paternal charity. Thus the aforesaid Lord Hugh came to Tournai, sought and received, prostrate in body in the chapter house, fellowship and fraternity with the poor monks, and gave them half of that mill. Thereafter he always showed that he had a fatherly heart toward us. For when the monks, with Lord Odo, wished to seek deserted places and left the church of Saint Martin, as was said above, the aforesaid Lord Hugh, abbot of Saint-Amand, sent five of his monks there, lest the church of Saint Martin lack the divine office. Sending them their daily sustenance, he commanded them to remain there until the return of the monks of Saint Martin.

64. Through this Radulf many people of the city of Tournai began to come to conversion and become imitators of his fervor. Among them Henry, a very wealthy man, came to conversion with his wife Bertha, his still-nursing son John, and his two daughters Trasberga and Julitta, in almost the same manner as Radulf. [Col. 0089D] He gave the church a great sum of money, from which the dormitory and other offices were constructed, together with certain lands. Ordered by the abbot publicly to beg alms, he was proved to be a man of truly great fervor and was at last made a monk.

For nearly twenty-two years after his conversion he was cellarer in our monastery and an example of goodness to all. He ended a praiseworthy life with a good death, rendering his spirit to God in the Easter season, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May. His son John, raised in the monastic habit with Radulf, son of Radulf, received all ecclesiastical orders with him. Exercising the priestly office to this day, he has shown himself to be good fruit of a good tree. His mother Bertha and his sisters Trasberga and Julitta lived blamelessly for many years in the religious habit, and they too have now passed from labor to rest.

65. After Henry, one might see, in a wonderful fashion, young men and virgins, old men together with the young, coming from the whole province to conversion after leaving the world. Thus, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, they sold what they possessed and brought the prices of their goods to Lord Abbot Odo. Had that abbot then wished, in the manner of abbots of this age, to retain the money and property given him and expend it upon the church’s needs, he could, as many thought, have enlarged it greatly.

But at that time the aforementioned Everard, castellan of Tournai, rebelled against Robert, count of Flanders. He maintained a large military force and frequently seized many persons, rich as well as poor, from the count’s territory and compelled them to ransom themselves. Oppressed by fetters and hunger, they flocked to Abbot Odo and tearfully begged him to relieve their misery. The abbot, moved by compassion for their weeping, distributed abundantly among them the money brought to him, and thus redeemed many.

66. At the same time a certain devout priest and monk named Radulf, a Norman by birth, who had been one of Abbot Odo’s first five companions, was charged by the abbot with the care of ringing the hours. As is customary for those charged with this office, he had placed his bed in a more secluded part [Col. 0090C] of the church—not in order to guard the church treasury, which did not yet exist, for the abbot would have neither a silver chalice nor a cross nor a gospel-book; but solely in order to attend diligently to the ringing of vigils.

One night, as Radulf himself, a most truthful man, related to us many times, while lying in his bed and keeping vigil in psalms and prayers, he heard in the choir what seemed to be a multitude entering and singing in a restrained voice that Responsory of the Holy Trinity:

> “Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit.”

When the Responsory was completed, he heard two persons approach the altar and add the verse of the Responsory:

> “Blessed are you, O Lord, in the firmament of heaven,”

in a most sweet and prolonged melody. When the verse was finished, he again heard the choir repeat the conclusion of the Responsory, and then fall silent.

When this devout monk had heard it several times and secretly related it to Lord Abbot Odo and certain spiritual elders, all said together that they believed these were the souls of good persons resting there, who gave thanks to God for the restoration of that little church.

67. The aforesaid abbot constantly read the institutions and teaching of the ancient Fathers, and also recalled the line of that secular poet:

> “Tell me, pontiffs: what does gold do in a sanctuary?”  
> —Persius, *Satires* II.69

He did not wish to manufacture golden crosses, but distributed among the needy and oppressed all the money brought to him. Yet he retained all who came to conversion, striving to imitate the saying of the Lord: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37).

He wished to receive no one before he had been tested, and during the very testing imposed burdens so great that he seemed to surpass all the trials of the ancients. For he commanded one man desiring conversion to drag alone beyond the city of Tournai an enormous rock which scarcely several men could move. One might see the man now placing arms and hands, now his whole body, against the rock with all his strength, pouring out streams of sweat from every part, and striving as far as he could to fulfill his master’s command.

He ordered others to remain motionless for several days and nights [Col. 0091B] beneath the eaves of houses, enduring the pouring rains. Yet although he imposed on them such harsh and unbearable burdens, far more people then came to conversion for our church—knights as well as clerics—than we now see coming, when no one is tested; indeed, many are coaxed by flatteries and promises so that they may come.

At that time some of the canons of Saint Mary also converted there: namely, Lord Amand, who held the priorate of the church of Anchin for many years and then became abbot of Marchiennes. By renewing that church, almost destroyed, both inwardly in religious observance and outwardly in wealth, he restored it. There was also Lord Walbert, who, after serving as prior in our church, became abbot after many years in the episcopal diocese of Cambrai, in the monastery called Mont-Saint-Martin, and died there. There was also Lord Gonstard, who held the priorate of our church for many years; and Lord Bernuin.

Had you heard how Abbot Odo tested these four men—first wealthy clerics and later poor monks—you could scarcely have restrained your laughter because of the immense delight. Seeing that they were excessively proud, he ordered them to milk cows and make cheese for several days; and after testing them thus, he gave them the monastic habit.

If we had then wished to receive the altars which they held, perhaps our church might have been richer from them even to this day. But because he had resolved to accept neither altars nor churches nor tithes, and to live only from the labor of their own hands, from farming with teams, and from the increase of their livestock, he wished to possess nothing of the ecclesiastical revenues which they had held. He said that such things ought to be possessed not by monks, but only by clerics. This intention of his did indeed accord with the life and institutions of the ancient monks; later, however, he learned from monks living near cities—whom some call *populares* (“town-dwelling”) or secular—that the institutions of the ancients could not be observed in their entirety.

[Col. 0092A] **68.** For since he wished to draw everyone with him to God, he received so great a multitude of women, not only poor but also wealthy, that no separate monastery existed for them, nor did it seem possible for one to be built. Therefore the abbot, considering that the stone house which had formerly belonged to the aforesaid knight Radulf, and which Radulf’s wife had given him when she came to conversion, was of no small size, partitioned it with walls and arranged in it an oratory, refectory, and dormitory. He installed about sixty converted women there and set over them his own sister, a nun named Eremburgis. [Note: [Col. 0091] Not even a trace of this monastery remains.]

Among the other women he ordered Mainsendis, formerly Radulf’s wife, to reside there also; and in another part of the same city he established an equal number of converted women under another mistress. After some days Mainsendis was brought low by a most severe illness and was compelled to lie in bed in what had once been her own house. Feeling herself increasingly burdened by sickness, she asked the aforesaid mistress, the sister of Lord Abbot Odo, to have her communicated. Because of the immediate necessity, since that house was far from the church of Saint Martin, the lord abbot granted that sick converted women might receive viaticum and absolution from the priest of Saint Piat, who lived nearby.

The mistress therefore sent for Lord Hellinus, a priest, to visit Mainsendis with viaticum. He came most willingly, since in her secular life she had been one of his parishioners and he had received certain services from her. When the priest came, [Col. 0092C] the mistress ordered Mainsendis not to speak to him except concerning her sins. Mainsendis therefore confessed to the priest and received the body of the Lord, while the mistress stood by and heard everything that was said. As the priest departed, Mainsendis begged him to remember her and pray to God for her.

But immediately after the priest’s departure, the mistress approached her and said: “Truly, you are excommunicated, because against my command you spoke to the priest about something other than your sins.” Mainsendis replied: “Truly, lady, I did not think that I had sinned; for when I asked him to pray for me, I did not mean the health of my body, but the remission of my sins.” Then the mistress called the other sisters, declared that she was excommunicated, and ordered that she be expelled outside.

[Col. 0092D] All threw themselves at the mistress’s feet and begged for mercy, but could not obtain it. Although Mainsendis was unable to rise from her bed, by the mistress’s order she was carried outside the house together with the bed and placed beneath the wooden stairway by which one descended into the courtyard, so that the refuse from the kitchen above ran down upon her. There she lay for three days. Though oppressed by illness, she nevertheless rejoiced in spirit, because in the house of which she had once been mistress she was now enduring affliction for God.

But because the gracious God brings consolation after affliction, behold: after three days the aforesaid Henry, now made a monk, was carrying upon his head by the abbot’s command a great bundle of flax for spinning and went to the sisters’ house. Entering the courtyard gate, he saw Mainsendis lying in bed beneath the stairway. Astonished, he asked one of the sisters—who was permitted to speak with him while receiving the flax—why she lay there in such a condition. When he heard the reason, though not daring to speak to Mainsendis, he ventured to say only this, in consolation of her and within hearing of all:

“O Saint Alexis, who lay as a stranger in your father’s house for seventeen years and thereby gained great glory with God, strengthen this handmaid of God, who in the house of which she was once mistress now endures so great an affliction.”

Hearing this, Mainsendis was so cheered that, as she later told me many times, she entirely forgot her illness. When Henry returned and reported to the abbot what he had heard, the abbot immediately ordered that she be brought back inside with the others.

**69.** In the same year scarcity of provisions and the horror of famine severely afflicted the whole region. The abbot began mercifully to give to all poor persons who fled to him whatever he could have, so that nothing remained either in the granary or in the cellar. At last, compelled by necessity and anxiety, he revealed the matter as it stood in chapter to the brothers, who for the whole year had been confined to the cloister, restrained in continual silence, and knew nothing of what was being done outside: namely, that he had received a great multitude of men and women and had nothing from which they might live even for a single day.

All were astonished and wondered that he had done so great a thing [Col. 0093C] without anyone’s counsel. They begged him to entrust the care of external affairs to some prudent man, while he himself should devote himself to teaching and the salvation of souls; that thereafter he should receive no one without the brothers’ counsel; and that he should not test those whom he received by imposing grievous and unbearable burdens according to the manner of the ancients, but should be content with the institutions and Rule of the monastery of Cluny. At that time Cluny alone surpassed all the monasteries of Gaul in renown, religious observance, and charity, and was governed by the venerable Abbot Hugh.

The abbot accepted the counsel of the brothers. At once he appointed Lord Henry cellarer, entrusted the provostship to Radulf, and gave him Walter, son of Hubert, as companion. Entrusting to these three the external provision of the whole church, he permitted them to go out without leave; to the rest he prescribed that they should apply themselves with him to religious observance and silence.

On leaving chapter, they entered the kitchen and sought what could be prepared for the brothers; but they found nothing. Then they went through the city gate. When citizens met them and, as though they had been released from a long imprisonment, asked how matters stood with them, they answered with cheerful faces that all was well. But shortly afterward they made known to them the brothers’ need. Immediately the citizens, consulting with one another—one giving wheat, another rye, another beans—encouraged and exhorted them, and sent them back to the brothers joyful and glad.

[Col. 0094A] Radulf also informed his brother Theoderic of the church’s need and asked him to lend money for purchasing the brothers’ necessities. Theoderic immediately lent him forty marks of silver, which he afterward never wished to receive back; rather, he left them to the church for his soul. He also gave our church a very useful garden on the Scheldt, near Saint Medard, and in many matters always helped us beyond the other citizens. For when the aforesaid Walter later began, by the abbot’s command, to build a church from the alms of the faithful, the same Theoderic immediately gave him one hundred solidi at the outset; for building the refectory, another hundred solidi; and for the cellar, another hundred solidi. How often he sent a full fish-meal to the community, let it be left to Him for whose sake he sent it to count and recount.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] Saint Medard. The Abbey of Saint Medard was destroyed in 1671 and 1672; its regular canons were transferred to the parish of Saint Margaret because of the citadel constructed by Louis XIV.]

**70.** How great a want of bread the poor community endured throughout that entire year can scarcely be believed. There was no mention of wheaten bread or wine, unless perhaps some wealthy person sent it to them; even rye was wholly lacking. Oats alone were ground for them, brought back from the mill; the flour was purified neither by sieve nor bolting-cloth. Instead, hot water was immediately poured over it and bread was made from it. When baked and placed before a monk, it seemed fit to be used as kindling, with stalks protruding; and when it was cut with a knife, a greater heap of straw than of crumbs appeared before the monk. Yet because, according to Solomon, even bitter things appear sweet to a hungry soul (Prov. 27:27), the monks, wasting away with hunger, ate that oat-bread with such eagerness that neither crumb nor straw remained.

[Col. 0094C] Some of them still survive, one being Lord Ascelin, who succeeded Lord Henry in the management of the cellar or in the office of cellarer. He still testifies that at that time he often wondered whether he might ever see the day when the church of Saint Martin would be so rich that he himself might be satisfied with bread alone. Therefore, let whatever successors of ours read this pray for the souls of their predecessors, who, by eating oat-bread with straw, acquired for them through their patience and God’s grace an abundance of wheaten bread.

**71.** Radulf therefore, seeing and knowing that the church was poor, without revenues, and could not easily subsist without agriculture, devoted all his efforts to buying and acquiring land. Accordingly, he established four teams of draught animals for the church and assigned them sufficient land, partly from gifts of the faithful and partly purchased with money. Then he built four houses, or holdings—which we improperly call *curtes*—in the district of Tournai, within scarcely a mile of one another and near the church. The first is called Varnavia, the second Dusiolpetra, the third Longacalix, and the fourth Tintenias. In these four holdings he established ten teams and acquired sufficient land for them.

He built a fifth holding between Namur [Col. 0095A] and Templeuve, on land which, as was said above, he had obtained from Count Robert as a gift to the church in exchange for his horse; a sixth at Canfen; a seventh at Costenten, on land which came to him from his paternal inheritance; an eighth at Audolmansum on the River Scheldt; a ninth at Galren; a tenth at Domerias; an eleventh at Catenias.

**72.** Meanwhile Lord Rabodus, bishop and uncle of Everard, castellan of Tournai—who a few days previously had seized the castle of Tournai itself together with the castle of Mortagne, subjected them to his own lordship, and expelled their lawful heirs, Gerulf of Tournai and Hugh of Mortagne—this Rabodus, a man of noble birth and high worth, took care, among the other things that he commendably did, to restore our monastery, as has been stated above.

But alas! As blessed Job says, God “finds perversity in his angels” (Job 15:15); so this bishop of such high worth began to be accused before the Roman see of having obtained the bishopric by money given to the king. Since he was repeatedly summoned before the pope, he sold certain ornaments of the church of Tournai for his ransom and gave them to his helpers; he sold certain revenues of the altar of Saint Saviour at Bruges to the canons of Saint Donatian; and he alienated other revenues, both of other altars and of episcopal lands.

When it was decreed that he should clear himself of simony together with two bishops, Master Anselm, then the foremost teacher of the school of Laon and famous throughout France for his learning, by his counsel withdrew from him the bishops’ assistance, knowing that they could not safely swear that he was innocent. But when, through many intercessors, he was permitted to clear himself by his own hand alone, Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the apostolic see, saw that he wished to swear. Rising before all, he said: “What are you doing, unhappy man, who seek to kill your soul by swearing falsely? Desist from this oath, and we shall obtain that you are not deposed now, but that, after receiving a delay of two years, you may afterward honourably resign the episcopate voluntarily, ostensibly on grounds of religious life or old age. For if you swear, behold, I foretell to you that you will not leave this year with honour.”

[Col. 0095D] The bishop, as he had begun, placed his hand upon the Gospel-book and swore that he was innocent of simony. Secure after the council, he departed and returned to Tournai. A few days later he went to Bruges. Wishing to be bled because of illness, while the physician was awaited, he entered the inner part of his chamber for a bodily necessity. When he remained there for some time, one of his attendants followed him and saw that he had fallen backward before the seat; he cried out in extreme distress. All immediately entered and found him stricken with paralysis, having lost the use both of his limbs and of his tongue. They lifted him in their hands, carried him to bed, and after a few days mourned him as he died.

He was carried to Tournai and buried in the church of Saint Mary. Lord Balderic, archdeacon of Noyon, succeeded him in the bishopric.

**73.** Radulf persuaded Lord Abbot Odo that, if anyone wished to give altars to our church without simony for the good of his soul, he should not refuse to receive them, following the custom of other religious abbots. The abbot agreed. First, a certain canon of Blessed Mary named Wericus gave us the altar of Esplechin; then Baldwin, the cantor, with his son Tetbert, gave the altar of Samium. Letbert, a canon and father of Lord Walter, abbot of this monastery, gave the altar of Passchendaele; likewise the canon Gerricus together with the knight Wenemar gave certain shares of the altar of Templeuve.

Rabodus, bishop at whose time our monastery was restored, gave the altar of Euregniis. Adam, a canon, at the request of his father Siger, precentor—who, with his brother Hermann, provost, was a monk with us, as was related far above—gave us five altars: Haltra, Sarra, Hisengein, Gudelengein, and Estenputh. The cleric Erpulf gave the altars of Villesbecca and Fivia. The monks of Dunes caused two altars, Beverna and Lendegein, to be given to us in exchange for certain land above the sea which we had from Lord Simon, bishop of Tournai. Desiderius, archdeacon of Tournai and provost of Lille, gave the altars of Guerra and Liedda. Bishop Gerald and the clerics of Ecurt caused the altar of Muscherum to be given to us in exchange for the holding at Bruges. The monks of Lhos caused the altars of Anulino and Alelnis to be given to us by Lord Bishop Gerald in exchange for the holding at Pevela. [Col. 0096C] We possess all these in the bishopric of Tournai.

Letbert, the canon, gave the altars of Zulte and Wachines; Bishop Bartholomew, the altars of Fasti and Proisi; Thomas of Marla, the altar of Froimont. These three are in the bishopric of Laon. In the bishopric of Cambrai are the following: Albert gave the altar of Sirau; Dean Werricus, the altars of Galren and Quarta; Ubald, the altar of Hacheniis; Lord Odo, the first abbot of this place, when he became bishop of Cambrai, the altar of Malda; Odo, priest of Bouniis, the altars of Ostiolo and Papengain; Walter, dean of Tournai and afterward bishop, the altar of Vais.

Tetbald, provost of Rothnac and father of Radulf, archdeacon of Cambrai, came to conversion and gave us the altars of Floresbech, Ormegniis, Balluel, and Saint-Martin Lierda. To the latter altar belonged certain land on the River Tenra, where the aforesaid Provost Radulf built a twelfth holding and constructed an excellent mill. Then Mascelin, provost of the church of Lutos, came to conversion with his wife Mainsende and his son Alexander, and gave us two altars, Boveniis and Branteniis. In those same parishes the aforesaid Radulf added three further holdings, thus completing the number fifteen. He built a sixteenth at Veson, a seventeenth at Merbiis, an eighteenth at Toreliis, a nineteenth at Froiana, [Col. 0097A] and a twentieth near Bruges, at the little church called Saint Trudo’s.

**74.** In the district of Noyon, near the fortress called Torota, [Note: [Col. 0097D] Torota: near Compiègne; from it a noble family took its name, which produced distinguished men in military dress and in mitres.] he found a little church built in honour of Saint Amand, but so empty and poor that he found not even a foot of land, a house, or anything pertaining to sustenance. Delighted with that solitary place, remote from human habitation, he approached Lord Balderic, bishop of Noyon, asked that the little church be given to us, and obtained it.

Then, against the will of many monks of our monastery, who said that he would labour in vain at so great a distance and in so great a solitude, he obtained from Lord Abbot Odo permission to send there a priest-monk, a Norman by birth named Radulf, who could not bear the bodily labour of the community because of infirmity. He sent him there, not forcing him to dig or uproot the forest with a hoe, but supplying him from the property and money of our church. Thus, by God’s granting grace, he advanced the place so far that in a short time he rejoiced to have several persons serving God there, where at first he had found nothing but an empty little church surrounded by brambles.

[Col. 0097C] The canons of Noyon, frequently visiting the place and seeing that it was suitable for those wishing to serve God in solitude, began first to bestow their property there, then to come to conversion and become monks. After making profession, however, they received the monastic blessing from the abbot in the church of Saint Martin. Among them was one Peter, regarded as a kind of father among the other canons. Renouncing the world and becoming a monk, he gave two excellent vineyards situated at Noyon. He began to be of such religious devotion that he made himself an example not only to clerics and knights, but also to the monks of the whole region. Many visited him and listened to his counsel as though it were divinely given. Yet he himself was a guardian of humility: although asked by the abbot and brothers, he would not receive priestly orders; nor would he consent to speak to visitors unless he had first received permission from the prior. He frequently reminded the prior himself of almsgiving to the poor.

**75.** At a certain time, when extreme famine oppressed the entire region and the aforesaid Prior Radulf, concerned for the brothers’ shortage, hesitated to distribute alms to the poor as usual, Lord Peter urged that nothing be diminished from the customary number. Suddenly, when poor people arrived, the servant replied that the bread had run out. Lord Peter said to him: “Go and see whether perhaps some piece of bread remains in the chest.” The servant said that he had left the chest empty that very hour; but Peter urged him to search. Wearied by his insistence, the servant returned to the chest and found it, though he had left it empty a little before, filled with bread to its very top.

[Col. 0098A] Therefore, trusting in Peter’s faith, the same Prior Radulf began to give so abundantly to all poor persons who arrived that bread was denied to no one at all. The more he distributed, the more the small resources of the house seemed to increase by God’s will. Thus, to this day, the aforesaid little church of Saint Amand is greatly loved and frequented by the neighbouring people. Now many persons, both men and women, come to conversion not only from Noyon but also from Compiègne and other nearer places, and bestow many things upon that place. The brothers of Tournai, who had earlier murmured against Provost Radulf because he was sending money from Tournai, now rejoice and praise him because he did not yield to their wishes.

The aforesaid Lord Peter, speaking familiarly with us many times, said that he had been born and baptized on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter and had come to conversion, adding that he believed he would die on that same feast. This indeed happened: on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, passing, as we believe, from labour to rest, he was buried in the cloister near the door of Saint Amand’s church, amid the great grief of the brothers and of the people of the region.

The aforesaid Prior Radulf of Saint Amand, whom we have said was Norman by birth, had three brothers in our church, men of great religious devotion: namely Lords William, Godfrey, and Roger. They had come to conversion with Lord Abbot Odo from the beginning and had borne with him the burden of poverty.

**76.** One of these men just mentioned, Godfrey, was a most skilled scribe and left in our church many books written by him: namely, the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory on Job, divided into six volumes; an excellent history beginning with the Proverbs of Solomon and containing all the prophecies, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Epistles; a missal from which both daily Masses are sung in the community; a Gospel-book; Augustine’s *City of God* and his *Enchiridion*; and many other books. [Note: [Col. 0098D] Books: In 1668 the most illustrious Lord Charles Le Tellier, archbishop of Reims, transferred several manuscript codices among these to his own library.] From the resemblance of the handwriting, these may readily be recognized as written by him.

While this Godfrey was still young, after writing many books, he visited the sick lord abbot while he himself was well and conversed with him. Suddenly he was himself seized with illness and, to our amazement, [Col. 0098D] was carried to bed. After three days he was anointed with holy oil. When the others had left, I, who served the lord abbot, remained with him and asked how he was. He answered that he felt no evil or pain whatsoever. When I urged him to permit himself to be laid upon a hair-shirt on the ground, so that after the example of blessed Martin he might also feel the hardness and roughness of the earth, he immediately agreed willingly.

Once laid down, he asked me to read to him the Catholic faith—that is, “Whoever wishes,” etc. After I had done this, I asked whether he wished the board to be struck and the community summoned for his departure. He replied that he felt nothing amiss, but would gladly see the brothers. I immediately ran and struck the board hastily. The brothers assembled and sang the litany around the sick man. When, with bent knees and my ear at his mouth, I asked whether he saw the brothers and heard what they said, he answered that he both saw the brothers and heard the names of the saints; that he felt no pain, but was in great joy. Having said this, he immediately gave up his spirit, not without grief and loss to our whole church.

His companion in writing books was Lord Gislebert, whom Lord Abbot Odo had educated in the school together with Theoderic, son of Provost Radulf. Gislebert too wrote a history of the entire Old Testament, and two large and very useful books in an ample and clear hand, containing the readings for all Sundays [Col. 0099B] and feasts of the whole year. One is called the summer volume and the other the winter volume. He died on the Purification of Blessed Mary, amid the greatest grief of our whole community.

**77.** When Lord Provost Radulf saw that he had achieved something, though only a little, in accordance with his wish through the little church of Saint Amand in the district of Noyon, he also sought the region of Laon. Seeing there that, because of the war between Thomas of Marla and Roger of Pierrepont, many lands and villages had remained empty and desolate, he gave money to Roger and asked him to give something from that land to our church for the salvation of his soul, where we might prosper through labour. Roger immediately, with the consent of his wife Ermengard, gave us vacant land at a place called Canteliva and confirmed it before Lord Ingelram, then bishop of Laon.

Without delay Radulf built a house there. Seeing that the land was fertile and sufficient, he established four plough-teams there and stocked it with sheep and oxen. Then he approached another prince, Gerard of Chérisy. Having given him a considerable sum of money, he asked him likewise, in imitation of Roger, to give something for his soul to the church of Saint Martin. Gerard then gave us lands which he held at Livry and Brancourt; and because they were held as fiefs of the king, he had them confirmed by Louis, king of the French. This was the first royal privilege which our church possessed.

Thus Radulf built one holding [Col. 0099D] at Livry and another at Brancourt; he also restored a mill which had previously been destroyed. He built a fourth holding, not far from the others, in the village called Moncellis; this, however, consists not of one person’s gift and cultivation, but of many persons’.

After some time, the aforesaid Thomas of Marla saw our holding filled with an abundance of livestock. Led by greed, he plundered it. When, having been excommunicated for this, he sought absolution, he gave us an altar in the village called Foimons in reparation for the plunder, and had it confirmed by the privilege of the bishop of Laon, from whom he held it in fief. Thus he received absolution for that deed. The often-mentioned Provost Radulf built these four holdings in the district of Laon, and by them greatly enlarged our church.

**78.** He also built another holding in the district of Soissons, in the forest of Pinon, and had it confirmed by the privilege of Lord Lisiard, bishop of Soissons. He placed his son Walter there for the work of construction, so that Walter obtained the consecration by the aforesaid bishop of a little stone church there, built in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God, from the alms of the faithful.

**79.** In these houses—or, as we more commonly call them, holdings—which the aforesaid Provost Radulf built in various places, he established more than sixty plough-teams. Thus, with God’s help, he provided from both agriculture and the raising of livestock the necessities of food and clothing for the whole community [Col. 0100B] of our church.

Lord Abbot Odo rejoiced greatly in this and gave thanks to God that He had given him such a man, who had made him wholly free and exempt from external care and disturbance. For, with the external care of our whole church entrusted to Radulf, Odo applied himself so fervently to religious observance and silence that he often did not leave the cloister for an entire month. Continually devoted to reading, he applied all his effort to the writing of books. He rejoiced that the Lord had granted him an abundance of scribes, so that if one entered the cloister, one would commonly see twelve young monks seated in chairs, silently writing on tablets carefully and skilfully arranged.

Accordingly he had copied with such care all Jerome’s books explaining the prophets, all the books of blessed Gregory, and whatever works he could find of Blessed Augustine, Ambrose, Isidore, Bede, and also of Lord Anselm, then abbot of Bec and afterward archbishop of Canterbury, that scarcely a similar library could be found in any neighbouring church. Everyone sought exemplars from our church in order to correct their own books.

At that time our monastery had great renown and religious standing, because in the entire archbishopric of Reims only three churches were found which observed the customs of Cluny: namely, Acquicinum, Affligem, and ours. The monastery of Cluny was then pre-eminent in religious observance throughout the entire kingdom [Col. 0100D] of the French, for the rigor of Cîteaux had not yet sprung up, and no mention of Lord Norbert had yet arisen.

**80.** At that time Lord Lambert became abbot of the monastery of Saint Bertin. Seeing his church so ruined through excessive laxity that scarcely a few monks could remain in it, compelled by the utmost necessity, he sought Lord Hugh, then the most famous abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Cluny. Entrusting himself and his whole church to Hugh’s instruction, he publicly made profession in that monastery. He then brought back with him twelve monks received from Lord Hugh and entrusted the church of Saint Bertin to their governance. With God’s grace aiding them, they advanced so far in a short time that where formerly one could scarcely find twelve monks, later one found one hundred and fifty supplied with every abundance.

Seeing this, the illustrious Count Robert of Flanders, having now returned to his own land after Jerusalem had been captured, placed monks taken from that same monastery of Saint Bertin in the churches of Saint Vedast at Arras and Saint Peter at Ghent, and greatly reformed them. Lord Odo, the venerable abbot of Saint Remigius at Reims, placed in his monastery monks received from the aforesaid abbot of Saint Bertin. Then Louis, king of the French, seeing other churches prosper through the same customs, caused them to be observed by force at the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons. Thus by God’s grace scarcely any monastery is now found in France or Flanders [Col. 0101B] in which the customs of Cluny are not observed.

But while, as has been said, our monastery flourished among neighbouring churches with great renown and prosperity, behold, suddenly the crown fell from our head and the joy of our heart failed.

**81.** For Lord Manasses, archbishop of Reims, summoning the other abbots generally to a council, specifically called among them Odo, abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai. While we wondered what might be reported to us from the council and waited astonished and anxious, suddenly we heard that he had been elected to the bishopric of the see of Cambrai and without delay consecrated by the archbishop and the bishops of the province (A.D. 1105). No one could easily explain what mourning filled our whole community that day, or what sobbing shook our breasts.

Yet scarcely eight days had passed when some consolation was restored to us, because he could not enter the city of Cambrai peacefully, owing to the rebellion and resistance of Bishop Galcher, and so was returned to us by the archbishop. He remained with us for a whole year. Although this digresses from the narrative begun, it seems proper to explain briefly the cause of that rebellion.

**82.** In the life of blessed Gregory we read that, when he had been elected to govern the apostolic see and resisted, the Romans sought the consent of the Emperor Maurice and through him installed the elect upon the papal throne. We also read that blessed Eligius and Saint Audoenus were elected and promoted to the episcopate by Dagobert, king of the Franks. Since the same is read in many other places—that holy men were promoted to episcopal office by kings—behold, suddenly, in the time of the Emperor Henry the Elder, the Roman pope, first called Hildebrand and afterward Gregory VII, forbade anyone to be elected or promoted by the emperor. All who had been promoted by the emperor, or had received staff or ring from the emperor’s hand, were excommunicated and deposed. Throughout his entire realm, but only in the German regions, the divine office was also forbidden.

There arose the greatest disturbance of holy Church, so that many said that the prophecy of King Hezekiah was then fulfilled: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38:17). Bitter indeed was the Church’s bitterness in the time when martyrs were slain by pagans; more bitter in the time of heretics; most bitter in the peace of Christians.

[Col. 0102A] Emperor Henry, unable to endure that the dignity of his predecessors should be taken from him, said that the pope did this not for the Church’s freedom, but rather in order that, under the occasion and pretext of justice, he might collect more money. He elected another pope named Guibert; he had the pope who had excommunicated him excommunicated; and, contrary to that pope’s command, he compelled the divine office to be celebrated in his realm. Then, having gathered an army, he besieged Rome and devastated the whole region.

When Pope Gregory died, Urban succeeded him (A.D. 1095), confirmed what his predecessor had established, and, among the other decrees made at the Council of Clermont, struck Galcher, bishop of Cambrai, with the sword of excommunication because he had obtained the bishopric by money and received staff and ring from the emperor’s hand; he deposed him from episcopal office. But Galcher, supported by royal force, for many years arrogantly presided over the bishopric and, contrary to the pope’s command, ordered the divine office to be celebrated in the city of Cambrai.

When Pope Urban died, Paschal succeeded him. Grieved that Galcher obstinately persisted in prolonged stubbornness, Paschal sent letters commanding, by apostolic authority, Manasses, archbishop of Reims, to gather the bishops of the province and elect and consecrate a bishop for the church of Cambrai without delay. Thus our abbot, Lord Odo, was elected and consecrated. But because Galcher could not be expelled by the archbishop’s authority, our abbot, though now consecrated, was returned to us. He performed episcopal office everywhere, but did not possess entry into the city or the royal revenues.

83. Meanwhile the cunning pope incited Henry, the young son of Emperor Henry, against his father by letters, and urged him to aid the Church of God. Greedy for the kingdom, and rejoicing that by apostolic authority he had found a suitable opportunity, he took up arms fiercely against his father and drove him from the realm, so that, apart from Autbert, bishop of Liège, his father could find [Col. 0102D] no one who would adhere to him. The young man, enraged because his father was being detained against his will by the aforesaid bishop in the city of Liège, gathered an army and prepared to enter Liège by force on the holy day of the Preparation. Therefore, on the preceding Thursday, when the bishop, after Vespers had ended, was according to ecclesiastical custom washing the feet of the canons and celebrating the Lord’s Supper, suddenly word came that the soldiers of the young king had taken the castle called Visé. The men of Liège rushed out with force, and, with the count of Namur leading them, hastened to meet those approaching. But while the army of the new king rashly and precipitately mounted the bridge over the river Meuse, the bridge suddenly broke, and about five hundred mailed and armed soldiers, falling with their horses [Col. 0103A] into the river, were killed. Thus the young king, repenting too late that he had wished to fight against his father on so solemn a day, was compelled to withdraw in great confusion and return to Mainz. But because he had already gained possession of the whole kingdom except Liège, he again gathered his strength and took up arms against his father, until his father, deprived of all the aid of the princes, was shut up by him in a certain castle. There survives a letter:

> [Note: [Col. 0103] Letter. Published by Reiner Reineccius among the letters appended to the *Life of Henry IV*.]

It was addressed by that father to Philip, king of the Franks, and in it he complains of his son. Whoever reads it and does not weep seems to me to have a hard heart.

84. When Henry the elder, father of Henry, died (A.D. 1106), not indeed by arms but through grief of heart, his son, now having obtained the kingdom he had desired, ordered the people of Cambrai [Col. 0103B] to expel the excommunicated Walcher from the city and receive Lord Odo. Then, for the first time, Lord Odo peacefully entered the city of his see and ordered us to elect an abbot. By his counsel we elected our prior, Lord Segard, a religious man devoted to fasting and prayer, who had already held the priorship of our church for many years.

But the aforesaid Henry, having gained the kingdom and yet remaining in his father’s position, and unwilling to lack the dignity of the ancient kings, who had customarily elected bishops, gathered an army and marched toward Rome, saying that he was going there to receive consecration and the crown from the hand of the lord pope. Received by the Romans with great joy and procession, [Col. 0103C] he came to the church of Saint Peter, where the lord pope sat awaiting him. But when, according to custom, he had submitted at the pope’s feet and was raised to kiss him, he immediately revealed the treachery and perfidy long premeditated; giving a signal in the German tongue to his armed soldiers, he violently seized the lord pope—whom he had just kissed—together with all the cardinals who had surrounded him for so festive a procession, led them into his camp, and committed them to custody. He also slaughtered many Romans who had wished to resist him, for he had come with a great army. They, however, having no suspicion of deceit, were altogether unprepared for war; and therefore it was no wonder that they were easily overcome.

The pope, seeing the danger not only to the bishops and cardinals [Col. 0103D] captured with him but to the whole region, which Henry was laying waste as an enemy—not as an emperor but as a tyrant—preferred, in the urgency of necessity, temporarily to alter his judgment rather than fail to provide for those over whose necks the sword hung. He therefore granted the king, and even confirmed by the authority of his privilege, that elections of bishops should take place with his assent, and that he should invest those elected by staff and ring. When the king demanded a guarantee of this concession, the pope placed the body of the Lord in his mouth.

> “This body of the Lord,” he said, “I give you in place of a surety, that I shall not hereafter violate anything that I have promised you concerning these matters.”

Thus the king, rejoicing, [Col. 0104A] released the pope with all whom he had captured and returned to his own land, that is, to Lotharingia. At Liège he took as wife the daughter of Henry, king of the English, whom her father had presented to him with many riches (A.D. 1114). Yet by divine judgment he did not enjoy lasting prosperity: leaving the aforesaid queen a childless widow, he was soon deprived alike of kingdom and life (A.D. 1125).

For after his departure from the city of Rome, various bishops assembled together and, denouncing him as guilty of betrayal of the Apostolic See and declaring that he would be the equal of Judas, who betrayed the Lord after a kiss and by a kiss, struck him with a sentence of anathema. They also called that document which the pope had given him not a *privilegium* (“privilege”) but a *pravilegium* (“perverse privilege”), and decreed void everything that the lord pope had done by dispensation under compulsion of necessity. [Col. 0104B]

85. A certain cleric named Norbert, who had been the emperor’s chaplain during that same captivity, saw the great wickedness of his lord the king. Moved by repentance, he prostrated himself at the feet of the lord pope; having received absolution from him, he abandoned secular life and came to France. Finding in the bishopric of Laon a certain solitary place called Prémontré, he began there to serve God under the Rule of Saint Augustine—or rather under one much stricter and more austere. By God’s grace he advanced in a short time so greatly that we see no one since the apostles who has produced so much fruit in the Church. For although the thirtieth year of his conversion [Col. 0104C] has not yet arrived, we have already heard that nearly a hundred monasteries have been founded by his followers throughout different regions of the world, so that their rule is observed even as far as Jerusalem.

Not to mention others: in the city of Laon, a certain poor church built in honor of Saint Martin was entrusted to him by Lord Bartholomew, bishop of Laon. Norbert placed a few of his brethren there and set over them as abbot a religious man named Walter, to whom God granted such grace that today nearly five hundred brethren are said to dwell in that church itself; and already nearly ten other monasteries have sprung from it. Norbert himself was afterwards made archbishop in the city of Magdeburg, and died in the time of Emperor Lothair, who succeeded Henry. [Col. 0104D] But now let us return to our monastery.

86. When Lord Odo had governed it for about thirteen years, after becoming bishop he left Lord Segard, our prior, to govern it. At that time a very great tribulation came upon us. For the canons of Tournai, once Lord Odo had become bishop, began to forbid us to bury any outsider, saying that our church was not an abbey but rather a chapel belonging to their jurisdiction, and that we would remain in it only as long as they wished. Therefore two archdeacons of Cambrai, namely Anselm and Ralph, son of Lord Theobald our monk, who [Col. 0105A] were attending upon their bishop while he was still dwelling with us, were disturbed by this opposition from the canons of Tournai. With letters of entreaty from Lord Odo, bishop, they went to Rome and brought us a privilege of Pope Paschal. In it he granted that we might freely and without any opposition bury all who wished to be buried with us, provided that they were not excommunicated. They also added, without the knowledge of many of us, that thereafter we should not pay tithes from the labors which we undertook about the monastery, because the lord pope remitted them to us.

When this became known to the canons, they immediately rose against us, stirred up the whole world against us, and grievously harassed our church by arson and plundering. Since the frequently mentioned Ralph was provost of our monastery, while the canons’ provost was Gunther, son of Ralph’s full brother Theobert, [Col. 0105B] uncle and nephew fought one another not only with ecclesiastical but also with secular weapons. It seemed that between the two churches there was being waged not merely a civil war, but something worse than civil war. Yet the lord pope never ceased to extend his aid to us, but piously advised those who frequently resorted to him. Among many other letters, he also sent the following to Baldwin, our bishop.

87. Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, or Tournai: greeting and apostolic blessing. We have already sent your brotherhood a second letter, etc. See Paschal, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, letter no. 353.

[Col. 0105C]

88. The clerics of Tournai, having returned from Rome and disregarded everything which they said the lord pope had promised them, again began to ravage us by arson and even to pay soldiers to plunder our possessions. One day, toward evening, they sent their retainers to plunder our estate of Dusiolpetra. When this was reported to Lord Abbot Segard, he sent ahead a certain monk named Gerulf, who in secular life had been a valiant knight and was related to the leading men of the region, to restrain the audacity of the plunderers. But they came with arms and a crowd of men, plundered the estate, and beat the monk who wished to resist them so severely [Col. 0105D] that he had to be carried on a bed to our church.

His relatives, greatly stirred, assembled after a few days against the clerics and their supporters. Battle having begun, they killed eighteen of their retainers; cutting off the feet of some, they put them all alike to flight. Some of the knights also said that in that battle they had seen Saint Martin in the air, seated on a white horse and driving off the enemy with drawn sword. Although their number was much greater than ours, victory nevertheless fell to our side.

When Lord Abbot Segard saw some of our young men exulting over this victory, he entered the church, prostrated himself before the altar, and began to weep most bitterly, both for the souls of those who had been killed [Col. 0106A] and for the danger to the brethren who had exulted over it. He therefore immediately summoned everyone to chapter and ordered that on the following day the entire community should fast unanimously on bread and water; and that, as on Good Friday, they should rise in the morning barefoot, recite the whole Psalter after Prime, and make a procession. In chapter, too, all were to receive the discipline generally. The result at once showed that this devotion pleased God.

89. For while we were still sitting in chapter, suddenly Everard the castellan, chief man of the whole region, whom we mentioned far above, unexpectedly knocked at the cloister gate and asked permission to enter the chapter. He entered with certain wise men and said:

> “[Col. 0106B] My lords, we are deeply grieved concerning the restoration of this church. Although not yet twenty years have elapsed since it was restored, we are nevertheless very sorrowful at its destruction. For we truly know that the clerics unjustly forbid you the burial of those who are not their parishioners; and, no less unjustly, you wish to take their tithes from them. Although we have given our lands for the salvation of our souls, we could not give you the tithes owed to our lady Saint Mary. Therefore hold what we have given you; but, holy men, do not take away from Saint Mary what we sinners were giving her. [Col. 0106C]
>
> “If you wish to take away from her the right which she has held for five hundred years, I do not know what advantage it has been to you to leave secular life, since, if I may say so without offence to your grace, you will appear more covetous, more rapacious, and worse than we are. For though we take from the poor what is theirs, nevertheless we render to God His tithes. Therefore I beseech you, my sweetest lords, to desist from the obstinacy you have begun. Do not trouble the province for the sake of a singular and unprecedented liberty, but follow the custom of the neighboring abbeys, which are older and richer than yours. We shall cause the clerics, whether willing or unwilling, to grant you the same freedom of burial which those abbeys possess. But if you refuse to heed our prayers, you are indeed stretching your arms against a torrent, for we shall by no means suffer the tithes of our lady to be taken away.”

Our community assented to this speech of the aforesaid prince and yielded to his persuasion. Thus, on an appointed day, neighboring abbots and many other ecclesiastical persons assembling from both sides, it was settled and confirmed by charter that we should give tithes according to the customary practice, and that in respect of burial we should be permitted the same as the church of Saint Amand and the other neighboring churches.

When peace had thus been made, the clerics who had previously tried to overthrow us utterly were again joined to us in such friendship that the aforesaid Provost Gunther, a very vigorous man, exerted every effort to assist our needs and strove to wash away and make amends for the wrongs he had done us in the time of discord by services and help. Thereafter such affection and familiarity existed between us and them that, more than with the other neighboring churches, we were joined to one another by a bond of love. [Col. 0107A] Thus, in the undertaking which they began immediately after the peace had been made, we were to them as brothers and partners. The undertaking was as follows.

90. The city of Tournai formerly had its own bishop. Hence it is read in the Life of Saint Medard that, while he was a boy learning at school, he foretold that a certain companion of his, Eleutherius, would become the supreme bishop of God in the city of Tournai; and later the event proved the truth of this. When, therefore, blessed Eleutherius had become bishop in the city of Tournai and Saint Medard bishop in Vermand, Louis, king of the Franks, whom Saint Remigius had baptized, came to Tournai and asked that same Saint Eleutherius—

> [Note: [Col. 0107D] Eleutherius. Eleutherius and Medard were bishops long after the death of Clovis, and after Remigius’s death.]

—to implore Christ’s mercy for a sin which he had committed and was ashamed to confess. [Col. 0107B] When the man of God did this, he learned from an angel that he had been heard, and brought to the king the crime itself written down. The king, rejoicing, gave thanks to God and to His blessed confessor, left him many gifts, and returned home.

Later it happened that blessed Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, because of extreme old age and weakness, his eyes growing dim, could not fulfill the episcopal office. Owing to their ancient friendship, he therefore asked Saint Medard, bishop of Vermand, to help him in conferring holy orders, consecrating churches, and carrying out the other episcopal duties. Medard consented; often visiting Tournai and preaching the word of God, he won no small favor with the whole clergy and people.

When that same Saint Medard had solemnly buried the deceased blessed Eleutherius, after celebrating Mass [Col. 0107C] in the church of Saint Peter of Blandain, and the clerics of Tournai had assembled to elect a bishop, seeing the religion and integrity of Saint Medard, they chose him as their bishop, as I find written in his Life at Soissons. They said that, just as he had governed both bishoprics well for a time while blessed Eleutherius was still living, so he could do the same after his death.

The holy man resisted and objected, saying that it was neither canonical nor possible for him to hold two bishoprics, and that he would therefore not undertake so great a burden, under whose weight he would fail. The people of Tournai persisted in their resolution, approached blessed Remigius, at that time archbishop of Reims, and asked him [Col. 0107D] to impose upon Medard the care of the church of Tournai. Moved by their prayers, and considering both their devotion and the religious character of blessed Medard, Saint Remigius imposed upon him, under the bond of obedience, the care of the church of Tournai.

Afterwards Saint Medard moved the episcopal see, transferring it from the city of Vermand to Noyon. Thus he held during his lifetime the two bishoprics, namely Noyon and Tournai. After his death, too, his successors, namely the bishops of Noyon, held both bishoprics. Too late the clerics of Tournai repented that they had elected Saint Medard, seeing that what they had granted once they could no longer change. [Col. 0108A]

91. The Life of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, contains that in his time the church of Reims, the metropolitan see, had twelve bishops subject to it: namely those of Senlis, Châlons, Amiens, Beauvais, Soissons, Laon—whose see had not existed in ancient times, but was established by Saint Remigius himself, who gave it some of his own towns together with Laon itself, which had belonged to the diocese of Reims—Noyon, Arras, whom he was also the first to ordain—

> [Note: [Col. 0108D] “Ordained”: that is, restored; for the see had long been vacant.]

—Cambrai, Tournai, Thérouanne, and Boulogne.

92. When blessed Medard had died and been buried at Soissons, Lothair, king of the Franks and son of the aforesaid Louis, [Col. 0108B] built a church over his body. Some years later that same king died and was buried in the same place, leaving four sons as heirs to the kingdom: Charibert, Guntram, Sigebert, and Chilperic. Dividing the kingdom among themselves, Charibert established his seat at Paris, Guntram at Orléans, Sigebert at Reims, and Chilperic at Soissons.

Chilperic took a wife named Audovera, while he had a concubine named Fredegund. Fredegund deceived Queen Audovera by the following trick: she persuaded her that she herself, and no other, should receive from the sacred font the daughter whom she had borne to Chilperic. The deceived woman did so. For this reason she was separated from her husband, and Fredegund the concubine thus entered into marriage. The bishop who baptized the child was condemned to exile.

[Col. 0108C] The Franks who were under Chilperic’s authority went over to Sigebert. Chilperic, fleeing his brother, sought the city of Tournai, which was included in his division. The citizens of that city received him and began to fight against the aforesaid Sigebert, who, having gathered an army, besieged his brother in the city of Tournai. But Fredegund, Chilperic’s wife, fearing that the people of Tournai, wearied by the siege, would hand herself and her husband over to their enemies, summoned two young men of fierce spirit, promising them rewards and honors if they killed King Sigebert. They agreed to her plan, approached the king, and, pretending that they wished to speak with him more privately, called him aside. They then killed him with daggers.

Chilperic [Col. 0108D] came out of Tournai and drew the army to his side. He buried his brother in the village called Lambres, near Douai; gave thanks to the citizens of Tournai; and bestowed many benefactions on the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary for the salvation of his own soul and that of his brother, who had fallen slain unexpectedly. He distributed between the bishop and clergy the royal rights which he possessed in that city. To the bishop he assigned the city’s mint, the *mairia* (mayoral jurisdiction), justice, judicial district, advocacy over the men of Blessed Mary, and the *wionagia* of carts and wagons that brought goods for sale into the city. To the clergy he gave the toll and bridge-toll; [Col. 0109A] and, so that they might buy what was necessary for their clothing from those revenues and have abundant and sufficient sustenance, he subjected to their authority all the land lying between the two small rivers, namely the Rieu and the Marais, so that they might be maintained from its cultivation without want. He also added to them all the mills then on the Scheldt, reserving six of them for the bishop with five ploughlands. The *foragia* of breweries—or what others call the *scyphicationes* of shops—and the revenues from wine vessels, he divided equally between the two parties.

Thus, having enlarged the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary in this fashion, he returned with honor to his own lands. Afterwards, once established in his kingdom, he transferred his brother’s body to Soissons and buried it beside his father in the church of Saint Medard. He himself, [Col. 0109B] after some time, was killed through the cunning of his wife Fredegund by Landric, mayor of the palace, with whom that same Fredegund committed adultery, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent at Paris.

93. After blessed Medard, Augustine presided over the churches of Noyon and Tournai; Gundulf succeeded Augustine; Ebrulf Gundulf; Saint Acharis Ebrulf. In Acharis’s time Saint Amand is recorded as bishop of the Trajectenses, and he built the monastery of monks at Elnone. Saint Eligius followed blessed Acharis. Among the notable monasteries which this saint built throughout Gaul, he also constructed the church of Saint Martin of Tournai in the place where it has now been restored. Saint Mummolenus succeeded Saint Eligius; [Col. 0109C] Gundulf succeeded Mummolenus; Guarulf, Gundulf; Crasmar, Guarulf; Framiger, Crasmar; Hunuan, Framiger; Guido with Enutius, Hunuan; then Elisha; Adelfred succeeded Elisha; Dido, Adelfred; Gislebert, Dido. Gislebert was abbot of Saint Amand of Elnone. It is said that, in exchange for the parish of Saint Martin, which is situated near Elnone in the bishopric of Arras, he gave the bishop of Arras or Cambrai the abbey of Marchiennes, which lies in the bishopric of Tournai.

Pleon succeeded Gislebert; Guandelmar, Pleon; Ronegarius, Guandelmar; Fichard, Ronegarius; Emmo, Fichard. Emmo was killed by the Northmen. Rainelmus succeeded Emmo; Heidilo, Rainelmus. Under Heidilo, the citizens of Tournai withdrew to Noyon because of the devastation and oppression [Col. 0109D] of the Northmen; at that time the monks of Saint Martin in the same city also withdrew to their estate of Supas, situated in the bishopric of Paris. Raubert succeeded Heidilo; Airard, Raubert; Walbert, Airard; Transmar, Walbert; Ralph, Transmar.

After him certain bishops presided whom I think ought rather to be called plunderers than governors, destroyers than rulers, hirelings than shepherds. They squandered the benefices of the church and reduced it almost to nothing, so that of its ancient possessions we see it today holding no more than the bishop’s three mills and his three ploughlands, and, for the canons, the toll, bridge-toll, and their portion of the brewing dues—apart from a few lands and mills which they recovered through the offerings of the faithful. [Col. 0110A] How this happened, we pass on to posterity in the words received from our elders.

94. Fulcher succeeded Ralph in the bishopric. Being of illegitimate birth—namely, born of an obscure father—he was the son of the chief cook of the king of France. Seeking the bishopric, he made the king of Gaul and the nobles of his court guilty of simony and bound them to himself in a favorable alliance. Because his ordination was against the sacred canons, throughout the time that he presided he rebelled against God and holy Church and led in every respect an unworthy life.

Having gained the rank he desired, he demolished three churches in Noyon, with the consent of the king and his magnates, to whom he gave their estates and possessions, so that they might exalt him as their lord and promise lordship and fealty, as they had been accustomed to do to his predecessors. [Col. 0110B] When he had obtained this according to his wish, he decided also to visit the region of Tournai. Coming to Tournai, and having been received by both clergy and people, he demolished two neighboring churches: that of blessed Quentin in the Forum, where canons lived, and that of blessed Peter in the middle of the city, where religious women lived. He did this at the urging of the knights whom he had brought with him, to whom he also distributed their estates in order to win their favor. He also seized certain hereditary lands of Saint Martin which had been devastated in the Northmen’s persecution and still lay uncultivated and without inhabitants. To increase his own damnation, he added to them [Col. 0110C] his own benefices, which his predecessors had received from the king’s hand; and, adding to these the city’s mint, the *mairia*, justice, judicial district, advocacy, *vionagia*, and three of the six mills mentioned above, he brought the bishopric to miserable ruin.

Having also torn apart the goods of the clerics to a great extent, he paid the fitting penalties of vengeance within a short time. For after he had returned from Tournai to Noyon, he was immediately seized by illness. On the following night he saw in a dream that he was standing between the two altars in the presbytery of the episcopal church of Saint Mary at Tournai. He saw, too, a great fire kindled between those altars, and a most beautiful maiden, but clothed in torn garments, standing beside the greater altar. Clapping her hands, she beat her hair and face [Col. 0110D] and, with a great cry and groaning, demanded justice from God against Fulcher, who had torn her garments and stripped her naked. She drove Fulcher himself into the flames of that fire, saying:

> “O cruel tyrant, greedy invader of my church, why have you torn me so? Why have you stained me with such disgraces?”

As Fulcher resisted, lest he be cast into the fire, and said, “Lady of the whole world, I did not return you to this state of dishonor,” the maiden added:

> “As often as you defrauded those who served me of their goods, so often you hurled at me the darts of reproach.”

Awakening immediately from this dreadful vision, he began to cry out violently, and by his cry he roused his whole household. When all had gathered and asked the cause of his outcry, he told what he had seen in his dream [Col. 0111A] and explained that the maiden was the holy Mother of God. She had complained to her Son that he had stripped her church of lands belonging to it, as though they were her own garments, and had given them to the knights of Noyon. He added that he would therefore very soon perish by an evil death and be plunged into the flames of Gehenna.

While all were terrified and awaited the outcome, suddenly a dreadful pain seized his bowels. Stricken with a disease of the skin, as is said of Herod, worms called lice began, before the eyes of all, to boil forth from his body in clusters and cover his throat, face, and whole body. This continued until he gave up his soul. When the dead man’s body had been washed and dressed in garments according to custom, the lice never ceased to boil forth [Col. 0111B] and cover all the clothes. At last the attendants, compelled by necessity, dressed him in other garments, sewed him into a deer-hide, and buried him thus.

Hadulf succeeded Fulcher; Leudulf succeeded Hadulf; Rabodus, Leudulf; Harduin, Rabodus. This Harduin lived in the time of Robert, king of the Franks, son of Hugh Capet. With him ended the line of the kings of France descended from that famous King Charles, who, because of his extraordinary worth, was summoned by the Romans, crowned king, called Charles surnamed the Great, and ruled both Romans and Franks for fourteen years thereafter. His heirs held the kingdom of the Franks through eleven generations.

But Hugh Capet, while duke of Paris, entered Laon by night with an armed force through the treachery and deceit of Ascelin, bishop of Laon. He captured in the tower of Laon his kinsman King Charles, surnamed “the Simple,” bound him in chains, and deprived him of the kingdom. Having gained supremacy, he was crowned with the diadem by Gerbert, archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0111C] and was called king of the Franks. His son, the aforesaid Robert, knowing that Baldwin the Bearded, count of Flanders, was at that time very powerful, betrothed his own daughter Adela, still a little girl, to Baldwin of Lille, the count’s young son, and entrusted her to the father to be brought up.

95. At that time King Robert himself possessed a tower at Noyon, situated within the boundaries of the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, beside the bishop’s court. By means of it he inflicted many evils upon the people of that city. [Col. 0111D] For the knight to whom it had been entrusted by the king for guarding was of a violent disposition, so much so that he wished to appropriate to his own jurisdiction the episcopal dues. He wished to preside over all pleas and judicial cases which ought to have been decided in the bishop’s court, and the bishop was permitted to establish nothing unless he had first arranged it.

Thus, embittering both the bishop and the citizens, he imposed certain services upon them. Since he continued this for a long time and would not amend his ways despite any exhortations of religious men, the bishop, clergy, and people—greatly distressed and no longer able to endure his madness—resolved to resist him altogether and began to seek a means of carrying this into effect. At length it seemed to them that, if the tower were destroyed—for it was the basis of his obstinacy—they would easily obtain peace. [Col. 0112A]

It happened one day that the man who was to guard the fortress was absent by chance, and that no one of his whole household remained except his wife and her maidservants. Seeing, therefore, that a suitable opportunity had arisen to complete the plan already conceived for destroying the tower, the bishop ordered the citizens to take up arms and had them all girded with swords, so that anyone who might meet and resist them under arms could readily be overcome. The bishop then sent deceptive and fraudulent persuasive words to the lady through messengers, saying:

“I have a silk cloth from which I wish to have a chasuble, or a *planeta*, made; but I cannot find anyone who knows how to cut and assemble it as suitably and elegantly as I have learned that you can. Therefore I beg [Col. 0112B] that it may be prepared by your chaste hands. Order the doors to be opened, so that I may come to you and we may jointly consider what work we can seriously undertake.”

Delighted by the bishop’s visit and wholly unaware of the deception he was contriving, she immediately ordered the doors opened. She herself went out to meet him and, leading him into her chamber, made him sit down. After they had conversed together for some time, the bishop, seeing that his own household had assembled with the equipment for demolition, disclosed what he had arranged:

“Because of the vexations and injuries which your husband has repeatedly inflicted upon both my court and the citizens, these men have gathered against this fortress in order to cast it down and level all its defenses to the ground. Let us therefore go out unharmed, lest we be overwhelmed together with [Col. 0112C] its ruins and perish.”

Terrified by these words and as if lifeless, she fell to the ground. The bishop gently consoled her, soothed her grief with persuasive words, took her by the hand, and led her out with him unharmed. The bishop’s servants at once kindled fires everywhere, demolished all the buildings, set up engines for demolition on every side, leveled its immense height to the ground, shattered it from its highest stone to its lowest, and then returned home.

Thus destroyed, it remains unrestored to the present day; yet its traces are visible—namely, its enormous stones. When the king heard what had happened, he was exceedingly angry. Against the bishop, who owed him loyalty, [Col. 0112D] he began to complain of the destruction of his house, openly demanding satisfaction for treachery according to the judgment of his great men. When the king’s court judged that the bishop should be expelled from the kingdom of the Franks and undergo exile, the bishop, fearing the king’s hostility and knowing that none of the princes had greater influence with the king than the count of Flanders, namely Baldwin the Bearded, fled to him.

That count’s son, already flourishing in the first promise of youth, was to marry Adela, daughter of the aforesaid king, as has been said. He also built the church of St. Peter in the town of Lille, installed canons there, and ordered that he be buried there. The bishop laid the cause of his distress before both father and son, poured forth entreaties that they should free him from his present danger, and strive to appease the king’s anger, [Col. 0113A] which had justly flared up. He promised splendid gifts if they restored him reconciled to the king and to his own see and quickly secured the result of his petition.

When the count inquired what recompense in return was to be given for undertaking this embassy, the bishop replied:

“I possess in the region of Flanders, subject to your lordship, very many altars, of which I hand over twelve of the richer ones to be held by you and your sons for three generations; but in the fourth generation let them revert to the bishop. And lest any controversy arise from this between my successors and your descendants, I shall make you a confirming charter, in which I shall record the specified period, the names of the altars, and the witnesses of my court and yours who were present and gave their assent.”

The count, won over by the reward, approached the king, his son’s father-in-law, made petition for the bishop, easily obtained pardon, and quickly restored him reconciled to the king and his own see. He then held the altars assigned to him, whose names are these: those of Kortrijk, Putten, Torhout, Oudenaarde, Hennies, Hulten, Dunza, Nivelle, Rodenbruc, Alenbruc, Mallenghin, and Sclipies. [Col. 0113B]

After the bishop had made this grant, the Flemish magnates asked the count to grant these altars to them as benefices. Having received them, the magnates in turn distributed them as fiefs to the knights serving them; and so they gradually passed wholly from pontifical right into the right of knights. By this arrangement, therefore, the Church of Tournai lost twelve altars. If the bishop of Tournai possessed them freely for his own table, as formerly [Col. 0113C] he did, he could feed many poor persons from them along with himself. Harduin was succeeded by Hugh, Hugh by Baldwin, Baldwin by Rabodo.

96. In the time of this Rabodo, Robert, son of Baldwin of Lille and Adela the king’s daughter, held the county of Flanders; to them the altars had been granted. Bishop Rabodo therefore came to him and asked him, for the sake of his soul, to restore to the Church of Tournai the twelve altars which Harduin had taken from the table of the bishop of Tournai and granted to Count Baldwin the Bearded, Robert’s grandfather; for the time had now passed when they ought to have been restored. Three counts, now deceased, ought to have held them: Baldwin the Bearded, grandfather of this Robert; Baldwin of Lille, [Col. 0113D] his father; and Baldwin of Hainaut, brother of the same Robert.

When the bishop asked him to restore the altars, he sought a delay until he could hear the truth of the matter from his mother. When he consulted his mother, the aforesaid Adela—

> [Note: Col. 0113. Adela. She founded the Benedictine nuns’ abbey called Messines, near Ypres.]

—she, being devout and fearing God, answered: “It is true, my son, that the time has now passed when they had been promised to be restored by your father and grandfather. Since God has restored to you the inheritance which you lost, namely Flanders, and has thereby bestowed great honor upon you, I counsel you also to honor him in this matter and restore her altars to Holy Mary, his mother.”

Moved by these words, the count promised the bishop that he would restore them.
