[Col. 0114A] But before they could be made free from the hands of the knights who held them, he was overtaken by death and did not fulfil his purpose. The bishop too died not long afterward (A.D. 1093), without completing what he had begun. Indeed, to the further impoverishment of the bishopric, he sold the bishop’s arable lands around Tournai to Theoderic the moneyer and other leading men of the region. He disposed of the wood and forest of Helein and St. Genesius, granting each *bonarium* at a rent of four denarii payable to him each year.

Among the other things he did commendably, he also took care to restore our monastery, which was said to have been destroyed long before by barbarians, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092. Rabodo was succeeded by Baldric.

[Col. 0114B] 97. Thus, after the Church of Tournai had for almost three hundred years been deprived of its own shepherd, in the time of Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, whom we have mentioned above, it happened that a canon of the Church of Reims, a man of great integrity named Odo, left secular life and became a monk in that same church of Cluny. After living there most devoutly for several years, Pope Gregory VII ordered Lord Hugh, the abbot, to send him some wise men from among his monks whom he might suitably ordain bishops. Among others Lord Hugh sent him the aforesaid Odo, whom the pope consecrated bishop of Ostia.

After Pope Gregory’s death, Victor succeeded him; and after Victor, the same Odo [Col. 0114C] was elected to the pontificate of the Apostolic See and was named Urban. Since he had been educated in the Church of Reims, he loved it exceedingly above others and strongly desired to restore to it its ancient dignity of twelve bishops. Therefore, after excommunicating the above-mentioned Walter, bishop of Cambrai, for simony at the Council of Clermont, he immediately ordered the people of Arras to elect a bishop of their own. By the authority of his privilege, he granted that the city of Arras should henceforth be free and exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Cambrai, and confirmed that it should always have its own bishop.

He also ordered the clergy of Tournai to come to him and receive the freedom of having their own bishop. [Col. 0114D] The canons immediately sent to Rome two honorable men of their church, namely Elbert and Geldulf; but they found Pope Urban already dead and returned without accomplishing anything. Urban was succeeded by Reiner, abbot of St. Paul, who was called Paschal. During his time, while the clergy frequently visited the Roman court because of the dispute between us and them, the Romans, always eager for novel undertakings, began to incite us to reclaim our own bishop.

But when they had already come to an agreement with us, our bishop Lord Baldric, angered by a certain matter, sent letters of interdiction and, without any hearing or canonical judgment, [Col. 0115A] forbade the divine office in the city of Tournai. Thereupon the aforesaid Gonter, provost of the canons, summoned an assembly and urged them to reclaim their ancient liberty. Immediately two of their number—Walter, who later became illustrious as abbot of St. Martin, and Movinus, precentor of the church—set out for Rome with letters from the chapter. They brought back to Tournai letters of Pope Paschal ordering the clergy, abbots, and other persons of the bishopric to elect their own bishop without delay. They also carried other letters to Lord Ralph, archbishop of Reims, ordering him effectively to press forward that election and consecrate the man elected. Before they had returned, Lord Bishop Baldric died.

98. The people of Noyon, however, knowing that the clergy of Tournai [Col. 0115B] had gone to Rome, acted cunningly and elected Lambert, archdeacon of Tournai, as their bishop. They knew him to be wealthy and trusted that, through his money, the purpose of the people of Tournai could be frustrated. Lambert, elected at Noyon, returned to Flanders. At Kortrijk he assembled the abbots and persons of the bishopric and obtained their support for his election.

Our abbot Lord Segard alone, when asked to assent, replied that such assent ought to be given not at Kortrijk but at Tournai, in the chapter of St. Mary, where the episcopal see was situated; nor would he grant anything unless he saw the dean and provost of the Church of Tournai present. The other persons, being thus stirred against him, returned to Tournai.

Without delay the envoys returned from Rome with the pope’s letters. [Col. 0115C] They thanked our abbot for his answer and, following his counsel, assembled unanimously in their chapter and elected as bishop a certain archdeacon of the Church of Thérouanne, named Herbert. They carried the pope’s letters to John, bishop of Thérouanne, and requested and obtained the release to them of their elect. Then, approaching the aforesaid archbishop of Reims, they asked him to consecrate Herbert in accordance with the pope’s command.

But Lambert had forestalled them. As is said, he had already corrupted the archbishop’s mind with money, so that, acting on his advice, even King Louis, himself bribed, sent two bishops—the bishop of Orléans and the bishop of Paris—to Rome [Col. 0115D] to annul the election of the people of Tournai. When the clergy of Tournai requested the consecration of their elect, the archbishop answered that he would consecrate neither Lambert nor Herbert until the two bishops, envoys of the king whom he had sent to the pope on this same matter, returned from Rome.

Thus the consecration of both elects hung in suspense and uncertainty. Then the bishops returned from Rome and brought the archbishop letters of the pope, in which the pope placed the matter in the archbishop’s hand and oversight. The pope said that the archbishop had informed him that, if the people of Tournai had their own bishop, the episcopal dignity would be greatly diminished and the revenues of the Church of Noyon would by no means suffice for the bishop’s necessities alone.

On receiving these letters, the archbishop summoned the bishops subject to him [Col. 0116A] and fixed a day upon which he was to consecrate Lambert. On that very day King Louis arrived at Reims, called together all the bishops, and urged them carefully to deliberate together concerning the matter.

“For if,” he said, “you see that it is more fitting for the honor of God and the salvation of souls that the Church of Tournai should have its own bishop, I willingly consent; for I see that I lose nothing thereby, and I do not wish in any respect to oppose the will of God or the salvation of souls. Nor do I wish anyone, on my account, to say that this good thing was left undone, or to try to excuse himself before God under the cover of my protection.”

To this Lord John, bishop of Thérouanne, a devout man, replied: “Truly, lord king, by this statement you have freed your soul. Now let our lords the bishops consider what they ought to do.” [Col. 0116B]

Nevertheless, the archbishop persisted in what he had begun and consecrated the aforesaid Lambert bishop over both churches. Many wondered that he preferred to pocket money rather than restore to the Church of Reims its ancient dignity—something he could certainly have done easily, with both the king’s permission and the pope’s authority.

> Yet bold Turnus did not yield in confidence.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.126.)

For courage did not fail Gonter the provost. Rather, taking with him our abbot Lord Segard, he brought their elect Herbert to Rome—not through France, because he feared the king and archbishop, but through Lotharingia—in order to test the pope’s constancy. [Col. 0116C] Lambert likewise, now consecrated bishop and confident in the abundance of his riches, made for Rome, certain that his earlier consecration would profit him little if the pope consecrated the elect of the Church of Tournai.

Both parties therefore appeared before the pope. Now the court favored these, now those; but at last even Rome was overcome by the vastness of money, unwilling that Sallust’s saying should prove false: “Everything is for sale at Rome.” Yet, lest the pope should appear wholly to have failed the people of Tournai, he ordered them by letter to elect an archdeacon for themselves, since he had heard that their archdeacon Lambert had been consecrated bishop of the Church of Noyon. He also ordered the archbishop to forbid him access to all the churches of the bishopric of Tournai.

The archbishop, [Col. 0116D] seeing Roman instability and changeableness, prohibited both clergy and monks in the city of Tournai from celebrating the divine office unless they received Lambert as bishop. Lambert too, wishing to test whether they would receive him, came to Tournai. But certain mockers, on his arrival, stole all the clappers of the bells, so that, when they could not ring, the procession might become more contemptible.

Seeing that he had been received without honor by the canons, the bishop complained of this to the citizens, immediately left the city, and seized all the churches, both monastic and clerical, which they possessed in Flanders. Gonter returned again to Rome, reported all this to the pope, and brought back letters from him to the archbishop, in which the pope sharply rebuked him for the interdict he had imposed on the Church of Tournai, [Col. 0117A] ordered that interdict to be void, and took the church into his own hand and protection so that Lambert should not oppress it.

Upon receiving these letters, the archbishop summoned the bishops of his province and sent the people of Tournai exceedingly sweet and humble letters, strongly exhorting them to concord with their bishop. At length, since help was lacking to them, he bent them to his will. The pope likewise instructed them by letter not to take it ill that, for the time being and because of the scandal of the realm, he still allowed the bishop of Noyon to govern the bishopric of Tournai as well. Thus the clergy of Tournai, having experienced Roman equivocation, became quiet and hoped that after Lambert’s death they might obtain their liberty.

99. After Lambert’s death, the canons of Noyon [Col. 0117B] elected as their bishop a young man named Simon, son of Count Hugh, surnamed the Great. Hugh had set out with the other princes to take Jerusalem and had died on the journey. Since this Simon was the brother of Count Ralph of Péronne, since the illustrious Charles, count of Flanders, had Simon’s sister as his wife, and since the aforesaid Hugh, Simon’s father, had been brother of Philip, king of the Franks—whose son Louis then held the kingdom—the clergy of Noyon elected Simon to the bishopric in order to frustrate the hopes of the people of Tournai.

The people of Tournai immediately consented, through the intervention of the glorious Count Charles, without further objection, certain that, if he wished, Simon could govern the Church of Tournai very well. But because he was still [Col. 0117C] under age and had not yet received ecclesiastical orders, Ralph, archbishop of Reims, delayed consecrating the candidate presented to him, until Simon went to Rome and obtained the pope’s favor. He then presided over both churches.

100. Meanwhile Gonter the provost, while again making for Rome, died in the village called Sarracenas in the diocese of Luni and was buried in the church of St. Mary. He was succeeded by the young Theoderic, son of his father Theoderic.

Lord Odo, bishop of Cambrai, had granted the altar of Malda, for the expenses of the poor, to his brother Lord Benedict, our monk and almoner. He had also composed certain little books: on the canon of the Mass, on a disputation against a Jew, and on the origin [Col. 0117D] of the soul. Burdened by bodily illness, he resigned the bishopric and had himself carried in a litter to Anchin. When our abbot Lord Segard heard this, he immediately went there with his monks and asked that Odo might permit himself to be carried to the church of St. Martin, which he had built from the foundations and where he had first been a monk and first an abbot. But Aluisus, abbot of Anchin, said that he would by no means allow the man whom God had given him to be taken elsewhere.

Thus the same bishop died within eight days and was buried with great honor before the crucifix in the church of Anchin. An image of him in white marble was carved above his tomb. A certain Burchard succeeded him in the bishopric.

[Col. 0118A] 101. Meanwhile, a man of Tournai named Movinus, seeing that he had no offspring, enlarged from his own resources a church situated near Tournai in honor of St. Medard. He asked Bishop Simon to establish religious clerics in it. Favoring his request, Simon made a certain devout canon named Oger of Mont-Saint-Éloi its abbot and handed the church over to him free.

Oger, seeing at once with God’s help and the assistance of the citizens that he could prosper there, nevertheless knew that the place was too narrow for the workshops necessary to a community of brothers. He bought some land on the plain below the River Scheldt and there constructed a stone church in honor of St. Nicholas, with suitable buildings. He gathered there many persons—[Col. 0118B] clergy and laity alike, and also women—and caused the abbey to be called St. Nicholas of the Meadow.

102. At that time an exceedingly severe famine oppressed the whole province, so that many people swelled from hunger. Count Charles also forbade beer to be brewed throughout Flanders because of the shortage of oats, saying that it was better for the rich to drink water than for the poor to perish from hunger. Our abbot Lord Segard, moved by compassion, sold silver chalices and certain other ornaments, and with their proceeds bought bread to feed the poor.

Not long afterward Lord Ralph the Norman died, prior of our church of St. Amand, situated in [Col. 0118C] the district of Noyon. He was buried in the cloister near the door of the church by Lord Theoderic, abbot of St. Éloi at Noyon, who loved him greatly for his religious life. Lord Ralph, our provost, was deeply grieved by his death and himself soon afterward began to be afflicted by a most serious bodily illness. How great was his love for the Church, and how sound and clear his judgment remained even in the sickness of fever, could readily become known to all.

After he had been anointed with holy oil by the lord abbot, while the whole community wept, his four sons laid him on the ground upon haircloth and asked him, following St. Martin’s example, willingly to allow himself to lie on the ground in ashes and haircloth for three or four days. Theoderic, [Col. 0118D] his brother, a rich secular man, hearing that he was so ill, came at once to visit him. Seeing him lying on haircloth, he wept bitterly. Ralph began to exhort him to contempt for the world, saying that worldly riches should be wholly despised:

“For,” he said, “if Adam had lived in riches from the beginning of the world to the present day, and it happened that he died today, it would profit him nothing that he had possessed them for so long.”

Among other things, while still lying on the ground, he asked where Count Charles was and what he was doing. When his sons told him not to inquire into such matters but to concern himself only for his own soul, he answered:

“Truly, we must be altogether concerned for the peace and condition of so good a prince, because in his peace will be the peace of the churches, while in his disturbance [Col. 0119A] the churches too will be disturbed. Therefore, while living I am concerned for him; and even after my death, if by God’s gift I have rest, I should gladly pray for him.”

When afterward he felt that death was now at hand, he asked the brothers standing around him not to abandon, but diligently to cultivate, a certain estate in the bishopric of Laon which he had recently bought from Clarenbald of Roset and which was called Sparciacus, because they could make much progress there.

After this speech, on the Sunday before Christmas, while the community was chanting the Night Office in church, about midnight—almost at the hour at which St. Martin had passed away—his faithful servant Ralph, commending his soul to God and to St. Martin, departed from this [Col. 0119B] world.

Lord Abbot Segard wished to bury him in the chapter house before his own seat, chiefly because Ralph appeared to have built the church in large part, partly from his own resources and partly through his work and skill. But Ralph’s four sons prevented this and asked rather that he be buried with his brothers in the cemetery, saying that burial in the chapter house might be attributed to pride or exaltation, whereas he himself had always served humility rather than exaltation. For although he had been provost of the church for almost thirty years, no one whatever—not merely among the monks or brothers, but even among the servants—could be found whom he had called foolish or stupid, or upon whom he had laid a hand in anger.

Thus the lord abbot, granting their request, buried him with many tears in the cemetery, next to and near the chapel of St. Mary which Ralph himself had built that same year, behind the altar, on that same Sunday before Christmas. [Col. 0119C] With the counsel of all the brothers, he entrusted the provostship to Ralph’s son Hermann.

Mainsendis, formerly Ralph’s wife, lived for nearly twelve years after Ralph’s death. Having completed more than forty years in the habit of a religious woman, she ended her present life and was buried in the same cemetery. Their sons wished their father and mother to be buried in the cemetery rather than in the chapter house or the church because they truly believed that the bodies of good persons were buried there and that it was better for their parents to be among their company than to be buried apart.

[Col. 0119D] 103.

> [Note: Col. 0119. What follows does not appear to have been written by Hermann, but by another.]

Hermann, then, having become provost, began to imitate his father’s manner of life to the extent of his ability, and especially to ensure that humility rather than pride might be discerned in his habit and conduct. After holding the provostship from Christmas until Easter, he saw in a dream that he was speaking with his father and asked whether his father had found complete rest. His father answered:

“Truly, son, if I had been allowed to remain in the cloistered life and the provostship had not been imposed upon me, I would have found perfect rest without any debt.”

Hermann immediately awoke. Believing that he had seen this sort of dream for his correction, [Col. 0120A] he reflected on the apostolic saying: “If you have secular judgments among yourselves, appoint for judgment those who are despised in the Church” (1 Cor. 6:4). He also recalled the saying of Blessed Gregory: those who devote themselves to reading and prayer are the vessels of gold and silver which Moses was commanded to make in the tabernacle of testimony for the service and ministry of the altar; whereas the haircloth coverings with which the tabernacle is covered signify those occupied with external affairs, exposed to rain, showers, and blasts of wind.

Turning these and many similar passages of Holy Scripture over in his mind, he fulfilled in full every obligation owed to the Church without any delay. He then came into the chapter house, prostrated himself at the feet of Lord Abbot Segard, related the dream already mentioned, [Col. 0120B] and asked to be released from the provostship. Insisting strongly, he obtained this. Thereafter, in his customary way, he began to devote himself to copying books and to ecclesiastical psalmody. By God’s gift he was physically sound; he wished to be in no respect inferior or slower than any brother in enduring the silence of the cloister and the labor of both nightly and daily psalmody. Nor did he allow himself to be surpassed by any scribe in the constancy or speed of writing.

For he wrote four breviaries and several books of Blessed Augustine. For such pursuits he was greatly loved by Lord Abbot Segard and Lord Gerbert the prior, so that on Sundays and feast days they even charged him, in their presence, with delivering sermons in chapter to the brothers. For, along with his other gifts, the Lord had granted him understanding of the Scriptures [Col. 0120C] and eloquence in expressing what he understood.

104. After the death of Ralph the provost, Lord Abbot Segard too gradually began to weaken and lose bodily strength. That same year, burdened by a prolonged illness, after the course of a year had elapsed, on the day of the following Christmas—when we had sung at the Mass at dawn, “The light shall shine”—he saw himself failing from excessive exhaustion. He had himself carried before the step of the sanctuary in the greater church. There he was anointed with holy oil and strengthened by receiving the Lord’s body. After Prime he came into the chapter house, absolved the entire community, and asked to be absolved by it. He then returned to his bed, and a few days later, on the third day before the Kalends of February, a Sunday, [Col. 0120D] he gave up his spirit in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127, in the fifth indiction, with epact six and concurrent five. He had presided over this church for twenty-one years.

105. In the same year the glorious Charles, count of Flanders, was secretly murdered by his enemies in the church of St. Donatian at Bruges. After his death, when the legitimate heirs had died, the county of Flanders was granted by King Louis to a young man named William, son of Robert, count of the Normans. Simon, bishop of Tournai, came to him, with the intervention of the same king, his kinsman, and informed him how Bishop Harduin had granted Count Baldwin the Bearded twelve altars from the table of the bishopric of Tournai for a term, as related above. [Col. 0121A] Since the time had now passed when they ought to have been restored, he asked William finally to restore them to the Church of Tournai and to himself.

The count, recognizing from the testimony of many that the bishop’s words were true, immediately, at the king’s prompting, restored them freely to the aforesaid bishop and promised that he would cause him no trouble concerning them. But the count did not long allow the Flemings to remain in their liberty; rather, he gradually began to oppress them and subject them to laws of servitude. Terrified, as though they saw death already at the door, they began first to whisper and then to confer more openly about how they might shake from their necks the intolerable yoke of this new Pharaoh.

In short, they heard that a young man named Theoderic, born of Duke Theoderic and the maternal aunt—

> [Note: Col. 0121. “Maternal aunt”: Gertrude, daughter of Robert the Elder, count of Flanders.]

—of Count Charles, was living in Auxatia. They secretly summoned him. After various fortunes of war, he was wounded in the hand beneath the thumb by a foot-soldier near the castle called Alost and died. Buried at St. Bertin, he obtained, with the king’s consent, dominion over all Flanders.

Simon the bishop asked Theoderic that, just as his predecessor William had recognized the Church of Tournai’s right to the twelve altars, which his predecessors had unjustly held for many years, so he too should recognize it and restore them, as William had restored them before the king. Then the count restored the altars to the bishop, released them freely, and promised never to cause him trouble concerning them. [Col. 0121C] Yet, despite these acknowledgments by the counts, the Flemish magnates who had received them as benefices still would not restore them; and so we lament that the church remains disinherited.

This bishop presided for a long time. He could not recover the altars, but he granted to churches those altars which reverted to him when their holders died. From his own statement and the testimony of many, I learned that he increased the annual revenues of the bishopric and the prebends of the canons of the Church of Tournai by nearly one hundred marks of silver.

106. From the ancient possession granted by King Chilperic, they retain to the present time the toll, bridge-toll, and their share of the market dues. [Col. 0121D] Adding to these the things given to them daily by the faithful, they established very rich prebends, by which they are magnificently maintained. They also devoted their entire attention to buying lands and acquiring altars. Thus it came about that they reclaimed from the knights of Noyon, to whom that bishop had granted them as fiefs, and subjected to their own jurisdiction, the church of Blessed Quentin of the Market—where a community of canons had formerly remained—and Blessed Peter’s in the middle of the city, long inhabited by religious women. These churches, as we stated earlier, had been destroyed by Bishop Fulcher. Along with them they recovered certain of their ancient possessions and so greatly enlarged their boundaries.

[Col. 0122A] 107. Meanwhile, after the death of the religious Segard, of pious memory, who was buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary before the altar, Hermann the third, son of Provost Ralph, succeeded him in governing the monastery. Together with his brothers Theoderic, Walter, and Ralph, he had been excellently instructed in literary learning at the feet of Master Odard. He shone forth as a great preacher of the divine word, outstandingly proclaiming the Gospel and proving from Scriptural testimonies that Christ is the power of God, the Redeemer and Savior of the world. His tongue spoke wisdom especially among princes.

In his time our church was dedicated by Lord Bishop Simon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, the fortieth from the restoration of that monastery. Before ten years of his administration of the monastery had elapsed, [Col. 0122B] he contracted a severe illness called paralysis. Abounding in great gentleness and humility of heart, in accordance with the example of the supreme Master, who said, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29), with no one at all compelling him, but of his own will and humility, he placed the care entrusted to him and the staff of the rule he had undertaken into the hand of the noble and honorable Simon, bishop of Tournai by God’s grace.

108. After him Walter became the fourth to assume the helm of our Church. Born and brought up at Tournai, he was a canon of the episcopal church, a man who, according to the wisdom given him by God, had zeal for God. Knowing in every respect the restoration of our church mentioned above [Col. 0122C]—for he was seven years old at the very time when it began—he was often admonished by Odo himself, the first abbot of this place, to abandon the enticements of the world and, together with the sons of Provost Radulf, his contemporaries, to take the habit of holy religion. But although day after day the abbot wished to kindle his spirit with such addresses, Walter gave no assent whatever. At last, wearied by long admonition, the abbot foretold him, as if in jest, that before he ended his life’s course he would become a monk of St Martin.

But because neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, unless God gives the increase (1 Cor. 3:7), at that time the word of preaching did not prevail in him; rather, for almost forty years thereafter he remained in secular life. [Col. 0122D] Then indeed, seeing that the fitting time had come for the prophecy of Lord Odo to be fulfilled, the Lord struck him with a severe bodily illness; and, when his whole stomach failed, He drew him with His hook away from love of secular life, and he became a monk in the monastery of St Amand at Elnone. Having lived there commendably for two years, and having been made prior there on account of his worth, he was requested by us to be given as our abbot, and we received him. Thus, [in accordance with] the prophecy of Lord Abbot Odo, it is clear that from that time he was not only a monk of St Martin, but also the overseer and servant of that entire house, and steward of all who served Christ within it. He was ordained by Lord Simon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0123A] 1136, in the fourteenth indiction, concurrent III, epact XV.

He also shone with such great reverence among secular persons that, once at the Flemish court, when the countess asked whether he would dare swear concerning a matter under discussion, Roger, provost of Bruges, a religious man of good repute, replied that this was not fitting; rather, that the abbot of Tournai would dare, by his word alone, confirm this very matter with an oath together with all the religious persons of Flanders. Therefore, in the days of this Lord Walter, God looked upon the Church of Tournai, restoring to it its own bishop and its own dignity, lost for so many years.

109. When Lord Simon had already held the episcopate for almost twenty-four years and had no suspicion whatever of decline, it happened that a young canon of St Mary, [Col. 0123B] named Henry, on the Monday in Easter week, the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], in the evening hour, when night was already falling, happened to be passing alone without any fear through the new fabric of the church of St Mary. Suddenly he heard certain voices, like those of a great multitude rushing upon him with terrible violence. He also saw a flaming torch descending upon him, so that it burned a portion of his tunic and of the flesh beneath it, on his arm near the fist.

Immediately terrified, he fell to the ground; and at once, as though caught up in ecstasy, he saw very many people coming toward him and speaking with him—people whom he knew to be already dead, and people whom he recognized as living. Afterwards it seemed to him that he was in a field filled with roses, lilies, and flowers, and with every delightfulness of sweetness. [Col. 0123C] Standing there, exhilarated by the exceeding pleasantness after the terror of his earlier fright had vanished, and as though wholly refreshed and renewed, he saw four persons clothed in white approaching him with candlesticks and censers. They were followed by three venerable men, adorned in episcopal vestments, holding pastoral staffs in their hands and wearing golden mitres upon their heads, on which the name of each was written. On the mitre of the one who walked in the middle was written: “ST ELEUTHERIUS, BISHOP”; on that of the one who walked at the right: “ST ELIGIUS, BISHOP”; and on that of the one standing at the left: “ST ACHARIUS, BISHOP.”

After them followed Lord Gerard, a priest and religious man, clothed in priestly vestments, [Col. 0123D] who had been the faithful administrator of the alms-house of St Mary. Blessed Eleutherius then approached the young man and, as though caressing him, cast his cloak over him. He then showed him the book of his life, which he held in his hand, and ordered him to read it before him. When the youth had read it through, Eleutherius took it back, placed it in his bosom, and returned to the place where he had stood before.

Afterwards Blessed Eligius approached the youth and offered him the book of his life; but the youth, saying that he knew it quite well, refused to read it. St Acharius also showed him what was written in his right hand: “In the name of the Lord Jesus, through me a dead man was raised.” [Col. 0124A] After this, they departed in the order in which they had come.

Having seen these things, the young man returned from ecstasy to himself, rose from the ground, and, returning to his father’s house, lay ill in bed throughout the night. When morning came, he asked to be sprinkled with holy water. Thus refreshed, he showed the burned portion of his clothing and the flesh melted beneath it, and recounted some of what he had seen. On the following Friday, having secretly summoned William, dean of the canons—who afterwards became a distinguished abbot in the Cistercian order—he confessed his sins, received absolution from him, and was enjoined penance. On the next Sunday he received the Body of the Lord; and, after receiving it, he began—marvellous to relate—to read aloud in haste, for all who heard, the Life of Blessed Eleutherius which he had read in ecstasy six days earlier, as though it were the Lord’s Prayer, recalled to memory [Col. 0124B] in its entirety.

Astonished and struck by the novelty of the matter, we assembled.

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] “We assembled.” The continuator of this history appears to have been a canon, later a monk of St Martin at Tournai.]

We began to discuss and conjecture much among ourselves about so wonderful a vision. For although some said that the young man, skilled in composition and versification, could have composed this Life, we, not ignorant of his learning, were certain that he had never been accustomed to such composition. Even if he had composed it, he could in no way have read it so swiftly, from memory and entirely by heart, without a book.

Having therefore taken counsel with religious men, we sent a written account of this vision to our lord Samson, archbishop of Rheims, to Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and to other bishops and abbots assembled with the king of the Franks at Sens, in the octave of Pentecost, to hear and examine the books of Master Peter Abelard. [Col. 0124C]

> [Note: [Col. 0124D] “At Sens.” The Council of Sens was held in 1142, not in 1140, as some maintain. See the note to no. 108.]

We asked their advice concerning what ought to be done. They instructed us henceforth to await the outcome of the divine will.

110. And behold, after a few days, the aforesaid youth, foreknowing from certain signs that Blessed Eleutherius would again reveal himself to him, confessed his sins early in the morning, heard Mass, and received the Body of the Lord. Then he entered with a few others the sacristy in which the shrine of the holy man was placed, in order to pray; and suddenly those outside were told that he had fallen to the ground. Very many entered, and we entered with them. [Col. 0124D] Upon entering, we saw him lying on the ground with his eyes closed, as though lifeless; amazed, we awaited the outcome. And behold, shortly afterwards we heard him reading the account of the elevation of St Eleutherius, and marvelled that he answered many questions which we put to him. Returning from ecstasy, he wrote down what he had read.

After this vision which we had witnessed, being made more certain concerning the first, at which no one had been present, we prayed together to God that, if this vision were from Him, it might also be manifested a third time.

111. Not yet forty days had passed when [Col. 0125A] the aforesaid youth, sensing that the third vision would soon come, again confessed his sins early in the morning on the Friday before the feast of St Lawrence. Having heard Mass and been strengthened by receiving the Body of the Lord, he entered the aforesaid sacristy with a few others in order to pray. Without delay, hearing outside that he had fallen, we ran in and saw him lying on the ground in his customary manner, with closed eyes, as though lifeless.

Scarcely a quarter of an hour had passed when, behold, we heard him reading certain miracles of St Eleutherius. As we questioned him, we were astonished that he answered very many things, among them openly predicting that the Church of Tournai would before long have its own bishop and recover its former dignity. This vision and prophecy gave us signs of future liberty.

112. At that time it happened that many renowned clerics, both from the church of St Mary at Tournai and from its diocese, followed Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, for the sake of conversion. Informed by their report about the ancient dignity of the Church of Tournai, and taught how necessary it was for it to have its own bishop on account of the innumerable multitude of its people, the same abbot took occasion from the youth’s vision. He privately approached Bishop Simon and, setting before him the peril of so many souls living under his care, gently urged him to permit a bishop of Tournai to be ordained.

The bishop, immediately moved by the abbot’s gentle exhortation, consented to his request, but [Col. 0125C] on the condition that during his lifetime he might retain a share of the income of the Church of Tournai. But the clerics of Noyon, hearing of this, approached Radulf of Vermandois and reproached his brother Simon with having sold his bishopric; through Radulf they frustrated and overturned the abbot’s plan.

113. At the same time a dispute arose between Pope Innocent and King Louis, son of the elder Louis, and the above-mentioned kinsmen of the king, namely Bishop Simon and Count Radulf. On account of it, the king and count were deprived of communion and remained so for a year; the bishop, however, was suspended for a time from episcopal office. For the pope consecrated as archbishop of Bourges a certain cleric, a kinsman of his chancellor; because the king refused to accept this, he was deprived of communion.

The count, wishing to marry the sister of Eleanor, queen of the Franks, began to impugn his lawful wife on grounds of consanguinity. But, because he could not be separated from her without canonical judgment, he caused his brother, the aforesaid Simon, together with two other bishops, namely those of Laon and Senlis, to testify under oath that he was related to his wife in such a degree that their marriage bond ought to be dissolved. Once this oath had been sworn, he separated from her and married the queen’s sister. Both women were daughters of the count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine; and the latter was in fact more closely related to him. [Col. 0126A]

The report of this perjury, spread throughout the whole region, was brought to the apostolic hearing also by Count Theobald, prince of Burgundy. The woman whom Count Radulf had repudiated was Theobald’s niece, and the disgrace of the repudiation touched him. When through his envoys he laid this complaint before the pope, the pope bound the count with the bond of anathema and suspended the bishops from episcopal functions for a time.

When this dissension between pope, king, and bishop of Noyon became known, Provost Theoderic, who had succeeded Gunther, burning with desire that his Church might regain its former dignity, privately addressed Lord Herimann, formerly our abbot, and urged him to go to Rome and cautiously explore [Col. 0126B] the pope’s disposition concerning this affair. Lord Herimann, favouring their requests, went to Rome. He showed Pope Innocent the letters which Pope Paschal had formerly sent to the people of Tournai and laid open the entire course of the matter described above. At last he also received letters from the pope, in which he admonished the people of Tournai and commanded them by apostolic authority, after taking counsel with religious and prudent men and laying aside delays, to choose their own bishop; they were to present the person chosen to the metropolitan of Rheims for consecration, and if he refused to carry this out, they were to bring him before the pope’s presence. Lord Herimann presented these letters to the people of Tournai; we appointed a day for the election and summoned persons from the diocese.

[Col. 0126C] 114. Having taken counsel with religious men, we unanimously chose Absalon, abbot of St Amand, a religious man, as bishop for ourselves. The election was immediately notified to the archbishop of Rheims; but he said that he did not dare consecrate him because he feared the king and Count Radulf. Necessity therefore compelled us to send again to Rome. The elect himself, as a wise man, refused to go, fearing—as later happened—that the Roman curia might be bent from its judgment by money, and that this would turn to his disgrace if he suffered rejection.

The clerics of Tournai, joined by Lord Herimann, set out for Rome, showed the pope their letters concerning the election, and, most graciously received by him, awaited day by day [Col. 0126D] his final reply. Suddenly Bishop Simon, who had followed them, was announced to be present. Entering the palace with his clerics, he complained to the pope about the clerics of Tournai, who, having disregarded the fidelity and obedience which they had promised him, had made an election of another bishop against him.

The pope replied that he had released them from the fidelity and obedience which they had promised him and had commanded them to elect their own bishop; therefore they had committed no offence in this matter. Lord Herimann then added, with the pope’s permission to speak, that the clerics of Tournai had brought no accusation against Bishop Simon before the pope, but bore good testimony to him as a noble and praiseworthy man. They had not chosen another bishop through any ill will; but, even if Simon himself were no less worthy than the good Martin, they nevertheless desired that their mother Church of Tournai should recover the former dignity of having its own bishop.

The necessity of this was so great that, although more than nine hundred thousand people of different sexes and ages were included in the bishopric of Tournai, nevertheless, because of the bishop’s absence—as the bishop himself testified—more than one hundred thousand had died within ten years without having been anointed with consecrated oil by the hand of a bishop; and that there were there more than [lacuna], implicated both in homicide and in other crimes, who had not received penance for their sins from a bishop. When Lord Herimann had set forth these and many other matters in the bishop’s presence, none of which the bishop denied, the pope, astonished, confirmed the election of the people of Tournai [Col. 0127B] before all. He promised to complete it; exhorting the cardinals seated about him to assist him in this matter, he rose from his seat and entered the sacristy with them. Our envoys hoped that their case would soon be concluded.

Afterwards, however, the pope detained them for more than fifteen days, until Lord Simon, having distributed five hundred marks of silver among the curial officials, received the favour of the lord pope. Yet, summoning Simon into the sacristy in our presence, the pope commanded him before the cardinals, under peril to his rank, to display no ill will whatever in deed or word toward the people of Tournai, who had made an episcopal election at his command. Thus, reconciling him with our envoys by a kiss, he gave him letters in which he informed us that he had not changed his intention concerning our election but, for the present, was postponing it by counsel until, having convened an assembly of bishops and metropolitans, he might confirm what he had begun. Meanwhile he commanded us to render Simon the customary obedience.

Thus, dismissing our envoys in sadness and giving many people occasion to speak ill, he died in the following year and had Celestine as his successor. Celestine died within one year; he left the apostolic see to Chancellor Gerard, who was called Lucius. He too died similarly within a year, and Eugenius succeeded. He had first been called Bernard, had been a monk in the monastery of Clairvaux, and was afterwards appointed abbot at Rome, in the monastery of St Anastasia, by Pope Innocent.

[Col. 0127D] Since all reported to us that he was not greedy for money, we informed him through intermediaries of our affair and asked what he intended to do. He replied that he would do whatever the abbot of Clairvaux should command him by letter. While uncertain discussions about this matter were renewed among us, suddenly Provost Theoderic of the church of St Mary was overcome by a severe illness, became a monk in this monastery, died, and was buried before the chapter house. In the following year our elect, Absalon, abbot of St Amand, also ended his life. Thus it was shown to us that neither he nor Herbert, archdeacon of Thérouanne, had been predestined by God to become bishop of Tournai; this office was being reserved for another.

Nor were Provost Gunther or Theoderic, his successor and his uncle’s son, though they were most ardent lovers of their Church and powerful enough in secular affairs, deemed worthy of the honour that so great a work should be completed through them; for this honour too had been reserved for another.

115. When those men had thus died and were gone, Letbert, son of Theoderic’s sister, succeeded him as provost. At his prompting another Letbert, surnamed Blandus—afterwards chancellor and then precentor of the church of St Mary—went to Rome with letters from the abbot of Clairvaux. He laid before Pope Eugenius the affair of the Church of Tournai and humbly requested that the pope should at last endeavour to bring to its due conclusion and completion the work which God had reserved for him.

When the pope wished to give him letters ordering the people of Tournai once again [Col. 0128B] to make an episcopal election, Letbert replied that he would never carry such letters, but that if the pope gave him a bishop consecrated by his own hand, he would return with him and the bishop would be received by the people of Tournai with due honour. Why linger over many words? Moved by his urgent petition and steadfast persistence, the pope asked whom he wished to choose from his court. The young man wisely placed his counsel in the mouth of the lord pope.

The pope summoned the cardinals and consulted them about what should be done in so important a matter. By chance Anselm, abbot of St Vincent of Laon, had then come to Rome. He had become a monk in the monastery of St Medard at Soissons; but, because the fame of his religious life and worth was proclaimed everywhere, the monks of St Vincent had sought him and had appointed him abbot. For many years he ruled that monastery commendably, so that in his time ten venerable abbots arose from among his monks in various monasteries.

Coming to Rome in those days for the needs of his Church and being very well known in the papal court, he was first named by the pope himself and immediately chosen by Letbert and his companions. He was presented to the pope to be consecrated. He resisted and objected, saying that he was held by a severe illness and was concerned rather about death than the episcopate. But the pope persisted in his decision and, compelling him by the bond of obedience, solemnly consecrated him on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday. He sent the consecrated man as a new shepherd to the citizens [Col. 0128D] of Tournai under the authority of his letters, released them from obedience to the bishops of Noyon, and by the authority of his privilege decreed that they should always have their own bishop.

116. The same pope also sent letters of intercession to Louis, king of the Franks and also duke of Aquitaine, who, at Eugenius’ urging, was preparing an expedition to Jerusalem against the enemies of the Christian religion. He likewise sent letters to Theoderic, count of Flanders, and to the citizens of Tournai, beseeching all together kindly to permit the bishop whom he had ordained for the honour of God and the salvation of souls to be their bishop, and thereafter to pay him the revenues of the episcopate.

The king, the count, and the citizens, through the intervention of the religious man Alvisus, bishop of Arras, acceded to the pope’s request a few days later. Thus we received the new bishop in the episcopal see. The pope also sent letters to the bishop of Noyon, urging him to bear patiently the fact that the people of Tournai had their own bishop and not to presume to inflict any molestation upon him, whether personally or through anyone subject to him. He commanded the metropolitan of Rheims and the suffragan bishops also to support him and assist him in all things, to admonish the bishop of Noyon to desist from every presumption, and to make peace with him.

But this same Simon was a very gentle man and did not know how to repay evildoers with evil. Consequently, he did not attempt to act by word or deed against the pope’s command; this also accorded with the nobility of his birth. [Col. 0129B]

Thus God ordained that Herbert and Absalon should be elected at Tournai and that Anselm should be consecrated at Rome. Thus God permitted Paschal and Innocent to command that an election be held at Tournai, and Eugenius to perform the consecration at Rome. Thus God arranged that the provosts Gunther and Theoderic should labour for the election, and that Letbert should rejoice in the completed consecration. Others, therefore, laboured according to the evangelical saying, and Letbert entered into their labours. Others sowed; Letbert reaped. Blessed be God, who made his journey prosperous.

The consecration of Lord Anselm as bishop was performed at Rome in the year of the incarnation of the Word of God 1146, [Col. 0129C] the year in which there was a most grievous famine, so that at Tournai a sextary of wheat was sold for fifty-six solidi. Therefore, just as through St Medard we lost the dignity of having our own bishop—when he received from the clergy and metropolitan the charge of the bishop of Tournai imposed upon him—so also through that same saint we recovered our liberty, when God, restoring our own shepherd to us, gave us as bishop a monk of St Medard.

Blessed be God, who entrusted such sons to St Medard to be trained, through whose ministry Christ might display divine gifts among the children of adoption and might will to preserve His Church without wrinkle or stain.

117. At the same time Pope Eugenius sent exhortatory letters into Gaul, urging all vigorous men [Col. 0130A] to go to Jerusalem, to the land which Christ sanctified by his presence, and to defend and bring under Christian dominion those territories trampled by the gentiles. Encouraged by his exhortation, Louis, king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, Conrad, emperor of the Romans and king of the Germans, and several princes joined with them, hastened there with many legions of Christians.

Lord Herimann also, formerly our abbot, greatly desiring with those same princes to behold the glorious sepulchre of the Lord Jesus Christ, set out for Jerusalem in religious array in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation, if I am not mistaken, 1147. What he did on the journey or what became of him, we have nothing certain. Some report that he was martyred for Christ’s name [Col. 0130B] and love of neighbour; others, that he was carried away captive.

118. When Lord Anselm died and was buried in the church of St Mary before the high altar, Gerard, abbot of Villers, succeeded him in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1149. During Gerard’s time, when our Lord Abbot Walter died and was honourably buried before the altar of St John the Baptist by the entire procession of St Mary and the two bishops—the bishops of Tournai and Laon—Lord Ivo succeeded him in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1160, in the eighth indiction, concurrent V, epact XI.

Another manuscript addition.

119. Lord John, called of Nécin, succeeded Ivo and is said to have been a man of great religious devotion. Lord Milo, abbot of Marchiennes, formerly a monk of Soissons and afterwards abbot of that same monastery, succeeded this [Col. 0130C] John. Lord John, called of Sobrengien, succeeded Milo; Lord Amandus succeeded John; Radulf succeeded Amandus; Lord Aegidius, called of La Celle, succeeded Radulf; Simon, called Baras, succeeded Aegidius; Lord John Carpenter succeeded Simon; Lord James of Lille succeeded John. He ruled for one month; may Christ the mighty King be King to him. Lord Aegidius of Warnaria succeeded James; Lord Theoderic of Le Parc succeeded Aegidius; Lord Aegidius II, prior of Muisis, succeeded Theoderic, elected seventeenth abbot in the year 1331.

[TEULF OF MAURINIACUM.]

[Col. 0131]

CHRONICLE OF THE MONASTERY OF MAURINIACUM, IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1147, FROM THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1108 UNTIL THE YEAR 1147, IN WHICH KING LOUIS VII SET OUT FOR THE HOLY LAND, BY TEULF AND OTHER MONKS OF THE SAME PLACE.

(Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 359, from the library of the distinguished Alexandre Petau, Parisian senator.)

FIRST BOOK, THE GREATER PART OF WHICH IS MISSING

[Col. 0131A] Know, O our descendants, that the devil and his angels greatly envied the beginnings of this Church, harassed it with frequent assaults, often stirred up severe tribulations, and tried wholly to extinguish it. But the Lord, the good helmsman, has always rescued His ship as it sailed through this great and broad sea from the whirlings of the waves, the whirlpools of the billows, and the storms of the winds. Even if He sometimes seemed to sleep, nevertheless, roused by the tears and prayers of His little servants, He awakened, commanded the winds and sea to be still, and by His grace brought it about that great calm followed great tempest.

Beware, therefore, O our descendants; beware of enemies so dreadful—enemies who do not pass away when we pass away, who do not sleep [Col. 0131B] when we sleep, who do not die when we die. The multitude of our tribulations has more often found its occasions in the rivalry of abbots and monks, mutually envying and mutually biting one another. For the malignant enemy—than whom there is nothing more malicious—more willingly inflicts a wound from the place by which he more easily brings death.

For an enemy wishing more quickly to destroy an enemy does not cut off hand or foot, does not mutilate ears or nostrils, does not tear out eyes, and does not attack other parts of the body; rather, with a bloody sword he severs the head from the neck, and thus with one wound easily kills all the limbs. So too the devil, seeking to kill the whole community, strives to separate the abbot from the community, like the head from the body, with the sword of discord. For how can the body of a living creature live when its head has been removed? Here I make an end, lest I weary anyone by writing. [Col. 0131C]

[Col. 0132A] [Lacuna.] Ansellus, son of Arenbert, gave us one half of the church of Stripiniacum, as was said at the beginning; Haimo, son of Senechildis of La Ferté-Baudouin, gave the other half, as well as Verruinas. Two noble men, Geoffrey and his brother Isenbard, natives of Pithiviers, gave us Echenvillerum. Guido Trossellus, a most faithful adherent of this place, gave us the churches of La Ferté-Baudouin, with the consent of his wife Adelaide, his father Milo the viscount, and his mother the viscountess, who on the preceding night had seen in a dream that she held an olive branch in her hand.

> [Note: [Col. 0131] Perhaps the son of that famous Milo of Leherii-Mont and the younger brother of Milo, viscount of Troyes. Cf. Suger, *Life of Louis the Fat*, ch. 8.]

When we heard the dream from her, we all said that it fittingly pertained to what was being granted to us by them graciously and by divine disposition. Geoffrey and Bernard, two brothers, gave us the church of Bouvines, together with land and woodland, Elia, our monk and their kinsman, encouraging them to do so. Emmauricus, a distinguished townsman of Étampes, gave us the church of St Julian, where there had formerly been an abbey of nuns, with the consent of his sons and wife. Many monks, even offering much money, wished to take it from us.

Bernodalius, a most noble man of La Ferté, and his wife Mathildis gave us the church of Guineville. She made for us a large silver censer and likewise a gilded silver chalice; she also laid the first foundations of the church and raised it to a certain height. Their son Lisiard the Fleming made for us the great window in the apse. Our Ansellus gave us the first share of the church of St German; the aforesaid Helias the second; Urso and Arnald, sons of Alberea, the third and [Col. 0132C] fourth. The fifth [Col. 0133A] or sixth we did not yet have when we wrote these things, but we did not doubt that it would someday be ours.

Milo, son of Rainard, gave us the church of Bonne. Bernodalius Potinus gave us the church of Serny. Engenulf gave us the church of Verres. Elizabeth of Mâcy gave us the church of Cesiacum; Segoredus, the church of St Ebrulf. Herbert Bornius, most generous toward us—may Christ bless his soul—gave us Belouilla. King Philip gave us the churches of Old Étampes, namely St Martin, St Alban, and St Medard, and confirmed this gift by royal letters. He commanded his son Louis, designated king, to grant the same.

This Louis, taking with him Amaury, lord of Montfort, and Simon of Neauphle, came into our chapter house, humbly requested and received a share in our benefits, granted the gift his father the king had made to us, and placed upon the altar the letters which he held in his hands, thereby confirming his father’s gift. Arraud of Corbeil gave us the church of Bolreto.

We acquired the estate called Mesuns in the following manner—or rather, not an estate, but a wilderness. That land belonged to the nuns of St Eligius, but the multitude of invaders and the frequent raids of plunderers had reduced it to wilderness. Having given suitable money to the abbess and other nuns, and having specified an annual rent, with the consent of all whose consent had to be sought in this matter, we received the aforesaid long-uncultivated land to cultivate. When we sought throughout our community someone suited to so great a task [Col. 0133C] and found no one, that Baldwin whom I mentioned much earlier—whom I also recounted as having laboured so greatly in the work of the monastery and dormitory—again, undaunted by the immensity of the labour, freely offered himself and undertook a burden nearly unbearable for the benefit of his brothers.

With what words shall I recount the labours of this man, with which he again toiled in constructing the settlement? I think that not even he who endured them could easily recount them. He cultivated a place long left uncultivated. Brambles and thorns, stones and brushwood, and all the other debris clinging to the earth’s depths, he uprooted now with the plough, now with hoes, now with other implements of cultivators. He gathered there almost eighty *oblatiarii*—tenant settlers bound to the estate. Certain wicked men, seeing [Col. 0134A] the place prosper in this way, began to harass it and make various unjust claims. Some demanded for themselves, threateningly, payment in bran; others, payment in chickens; others, a protection payment commonly called *tensamentum*. “The road toll is mine,” one would say. One demanded this, another that; and thus they oppressed our Baldwin—truly ours—with continual harassment.

As best he could, one man resisted many. Now by negotiation, now by paying money, he broke the assaults of those who rushed upon him. Compelled by this necessity, at harvest time he travelled almost throughout the whole of the Beauce, shamelessly begging grain from everyone. With some money acquired from this, he softened the tyranny of his attackers and relieved the land of customary burdens. At one harvest season, suffering such severe pain in his shins, calves, and feet that he could travel neither on foot nor by horse, he was not ashamed, in devout boldness, to be carried about the Beauce in the vehicle commonly called a *birotum* [two-wheeled cart] to beg for grain. Indeed, he preferred to blush rather than leave unfinished what he had undertaken. Such was Baldwin’s devotion toward this place.

May God repay him for what he did well, honourably, and faithfully. May God have mercy not only on him, but also on all who have built, advanced, protected, or in any way endowed this place. And upon me too, Teulf, who dictated these things—who do not know whether I ever benefited this place in anything, except that I corrected and marked with accents, as best I could, this entire library, from Genesis to the last Epistle of Paul, Augustine’s *On the Trinity of God*, *On the Words of the Lord according to John*, Gregory’s *Moralia*, and certain other books. [Col. 0134C]

I was precentor for a long time and afterwards tried to govern the priory; but I could not govern it as would have been fitting, hindered partly by ignorance, partly by negligence, and partly by weakness—not of the body, but of character. Whoever reads these things, I beseech you by the sweetest name of my Lord Jesus Christ, with whatever affection you can, say:

> “O God, merciful by nature, compassionate in showing mercy, who have mercy on all, I pray: have mercy on Teulf, unworthy of Your mercy.”

But if you close your heart against me and pass by my prayer with a deaf ear, you will sin against God, who is love, and against me.

PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK.

[Col. 0133]

[Col. 0133D] We read in the book entitled *The Acts of the Apostles* that, in the primitive Church, the people’s devotion was so great and the first fruits of the Christian people flourished so abundantly that, after receiving the faith, no one possessed a house or anything as his own private property; rather, by the law of brotherhood all things were held in common among them. That is, those united in the same fellowship of religion also enjoyed the same fellowship of life. For religious men thought it wicked [Col. 0134D] not to admit as a partner in their substance one who was a participant in grace. Thus it is written there: “All who possessed lands or houses sold them, brought the prices of what they sold, laid them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to each according as he had need” (Acts 4:34–35).

And this custom, indeed, continued in happy succession through certain persons who were more religious within the Church [Col. 0135A] until the times of blessed Urban, pope and martyr. But that man, full of God and following the Lamb by the witness of his blood, prudently ordered—or, by his ordering, provided—that possessions should not be sold, but should be given by the faithful to churches, so that those devoted to divine service and occupied with fasts and prayers might have resources by which they could be supported. From that time, therefore, down to our own age the Church has grown marvellously in earthly wealth. For when, according to Isaiah’s prophecy (45:14), “the labour of Egypt, the trade of Ethiopia, and men lofty in stature”—that is, the princes of this world—came to the Church, they enriched it in diverse places throughout the whole world with so many and such great benefactions of possessions that no human memory and no speech can comprehend them.

This happened especially within Gaul. For Clovis, the first king of the Franks to be baptized by blessed Remigius, archbishop of Reims, deserved to be marked by the title of Christianity; and very many kings after him, with most generous liberality, either founded churches or endeavoured to enlarge with their own gifts those founded by others. The nobles of the realm, wishing to become sharers in the same grace, and men of every rank besides, hastened to this most celebrated work with all the eagerness of their hearts, according to their means. Whence, after some time, it came about that the chaff within the Church swelled with riches, and even professed members of our order—what cannot be said without groaning—trampled religion underfoot and flowed away after their own desires.

Yet he who in Elijah’s time reserved for himself seven thousand men who had not bent their knees before Baal (3 Kings 19:18; Romans 11:4), has preserved in our times certain vessels of mercy: namely, good men and lovers of religion, followers of Christ’s poverty and humility, who have stirred many to admiration and imitation of themselves. Others, however, who did not deserve to attain so great a gift of grace, gave a timbrel that they might receive a psalm, sowing carnal things so as to reap spiritual ones; from their own resources and possessions they more willingly bestowed gifts upon newly founded churches and, as it were, upon Christ’s poor.

Among these was one Ansellus, vigorous in years and counsel. Moved by the religion and companionship [Col. 0136B] of the monks of Flavigny, he first offered to the Flavignian monks the church of Stripiniacum and what he possessed in that estate; and afterward, Christ’s grace going before, he granted the estate of Morigny, in which this church was founded in honour of the Holy Trinity. And because almost everything that occurred from the foundation of this church to our own times was truthfully set forth in the preceding book by a certain Teulf, who was reared in this church from his youth and was later promoted to the abbacy of the monastery of Saints Crispin and Crispinian near the city of Soissons, we have taken a few preliminary samples of what we ourselves have seen and heard, and have taken care to transmit to posterity what we judged necessary.

[Col. 0135] Here ends the prologue.

THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0135C] In the year 1108 of the Incarnate Word, Philip, king of the Franks, was taken from human affairs at the castle of Melun and, according to his own wish and decision, was honourably buried in the monastery of Fleury, situated in honour of Saint Benedict on the river Loire. This man was of remarkable prudence and was both most benevolent and most generous toward this place, which began in his time. Seeing this abbey grow beyond expectation through the gifts of his noble men of Étampes, he, being a man of loftier understanding, bought it, in order that it might possess it as an alms-gift, from Ebrard, from whose fief it depended, and who was regarded as lord of Le Puiset and was setting out for Jerusalem.

He was succeeded in the kingdom by his son Louis, a man of simple nature, great-minded and distinguished in warfare. [Col. 0135D] In love for and enlargement of this church he imitated his predecessor in every respect, as a good son does a good father, except that, in the affair between us and the canons of Étampes, misled by the counsel of certain persons, he went astray for a time.

In the second year of his reign, Rainald, the first abbot of this place, after innumerable conflicts with prosperity and adversity, entered the way of all flesh; buried in our chapter-house, he awaits the last coming [Col. 0136C] of the Saviour. The brothers assembled and, deliberating concerning an election as ecclesiastical custom requires, raised to the abbacy from the priorate that Teulf mentioned in the prologue, a man of good reputation and sufficiently learned. But some of them, exercising their customary fickleness, assailed him with insults and removed him from the promotion before he had been consecrated. Nevertheless, yielding to the counsel of certain wise men, he himself consented to their wishes.

Thus, while different persons held different opinions and deliberation long wavered, as is customary, over the person to be chosen, they finally, by common decree, submitted themselves to a certain Hugh, a young man of considerable distinction and, after the leading men of this region, of illustrious birth. They overcame by ambiguous words the king, who had altogether forbidden this to be done, [Col. 0136D] and brought their elect to Sens for consecration; after reconciling the king through the intervention of Hugh’s friends, they obtained the abbot whom they desired. But before a full year had elapsed, opposed by both friends and intimates, he voluntarily relinquished both himself and the abbey; obtaining the church of Saint Julian near the Tower of Brunhild, he lived there a private life when these things were written.

At that time all Gaul suffered from an excessive famine. For seven consecutive years a shortage of everything necessary for food prevailed so severely that it killed many and reduced innumerable wealthy people to poverty. For this reason, while all were intent upon their own necessities, the benefactions of the men of Étampes, by which this church had been supported from its foundation, entirely failed. All the inhabitants of this place were troubled and exceedingly anxious, both because of the abbot’s absence and because of the scarcity of every kind of thing.

Finally, when they sought persons from other monasteries but could not obtain them, they had recourse to the church of Colombs, with which they had the closest fellowship and intimacy, and demanded, as though by some right, that Thomas mentioned in the preceding book be returned to them. Though young in age, [Col. 0137B] he was endowed with learning. Under Abbot Albert, after renouncing secular schools, he had professed as a monk in this church; and at Colombs he had spent ten years devoted to cloistered life and the study of letters. Soon after the feast-days of Epiphany, having received the blessing according to the rule, he was received with great favour both by his brothers and by all the people. For he was sufficiently lovable and approachable, and all who knew him were moved to compassion that he should be coming into such poverty.

For through the harshness of the times and the abbot’s departure all temporal goods had perished to such an extent that there was utterly nothing of bread, wine, livestock, or any other necessary goods. The matter stood in great danger. You who read this, marvel and praise the constancy [Col. 0137C] of our forefathers, who endured in this place through so many privations and tribulations, and built all these structures which you see from the alms of the poor. No king, no count, none of these great men established anything here.

Thomas, however, upon discovering the intolerable poverty, was first greatly alarmed and then, thinking that flight alone was a remedy, tried to leave. But recognizing himself as a monk of this place, he was strengthened by the counsel of good men. Therefore, in the first year of his consecration, he preached the divine word to the people in the church of Blessed Mary at Étampes—a thing for which he possessed the greatest gift. The magnificent man Ansellus, the king’s steward and counsellor, attended with many nobles and leading men of the castle. [Col. 0137D] On this occasion, having gained his friendship, Thomas often found in him both a prudent counsellor and an excellent helper in this church’s necessities.

For with his help he also drove off Robert of Ocunvilla, a malicious and rapacious man who laid claim to the greater part of the land of Mesuns. In this matter the abbot’s diligence and persistence deserve the highest praise, since he was restrained neither by his recent arrival nor by poverty. Although he did not even possess a horse to ride, he did not abandon his purpose until, having repeatedly assembled and brought the nobles of this castle to judicial hearings, he utterly stripped the claimant of his false hopes.

He blocked the well-worn royal road lying between the church [Col. 0138A] and the vineyards, providing both for propriety and for advantage, although many opposed him and were thereby provoked to hatred. Having won the people to himself by divine preaching, he established a confraternity, through which both part of the church was roofed and that great window situated in the front of the church nave was made, among other works.

The monks of Saint-Yon had long withheld from us an annual payment of seven solidi. Rainald, the abbot before Ivo became bishop, had received a summons to the court at Chartres concerning this matter; and because he neither appeared nor lawfully sent an excuse, he lost the case. But through Thomas’s efforts the monks were again summoned to answer at law; and, what seemed new to some, it was adjudged that the case should be reopened from its beginning. For through the negligence of an individual person a church ought not to lose its own right; when the person has died or changed, his successor may seek justice within the canonical term. [Col. 0138B] The monks defaulted there, and through Pagan, lord of Saint-Yon, and Henry, the venerable prior of Longpont, with several witnesses present, the matter was brought to this conclusion: what had been lost was remitted, and the payment was to be rendered every year, as is more fully contained in the charters made concerning this matter.

But enough of these things. Some matters that required great care and great expense must be recounted. Before Thomas’s arrival, a certain knight named Herbert, when near death, had given this church a very extensive estate called Belotivilla. But because a certain Geoffrey, who had Herbert’s sister as his wife, resisted, it still [Col. 0138C] lay uncultivated. Thomas therefore gave the man ten pounds in money; his wife and her sister, who lived in the household, forty solidi. He then gently stirred up Vulgrin—whose many and great benefactions are recorded in the preceding book—the most distinguished benefactor of this place, who had grown somewhat lukewarm in his affection for us. He supplied him with abundant resources for cultivating the land, beyond, if it may be said, what this place could afford.

Vulgrin, for his part, undertook the matter with all his strength and at great cost built buildings, established plough-teams, and gathered livestock. The undertaking was increasing as we wrote these things, and it nourished our hopes with great expectations that it would free us from the lack of bread which we had suffered almost every year from the beginning.

At about the same time, the abbot, reminded by the brothers that he should go, on the feast of Saint Martin called the winter feast, to the church of Old Étampes dedicated in honour of that confessor—a church which King Philip had given and confirmed by charter—and ought to sing Mass, consented. But, with the canons protesting and rebelling, he was driven away only with difficulty. Employing wise counsel, he avoided a disturbance and went with all speed to the king. He set forth the injury, complained moderately, and was gladly heard. Finally, relying upon the assistance of Ansellus the steward, he obtained that the clerics of Étampes should assemble in the royal court and consent to the gift. The king himself also, which he had not previously done, confirmed the gift by a charter under his own seal. A copy of it [Col. 0139A] is written below.

Thus the gift of the churches of Old Étampes was settled, so far as royal authority was concerned. The abbot, however, deriving hope of attempting greater things from his favourable successes, petitioned the king through Ansellus to ask the archbishop of Sens himself—in whose diocese these churches lay—to approve and confirm his alms-gift. The king approved the request, promised assistance, and instructed the abbot to follow him to Melun, where the archbishop was to meet him.

Daimbert then governed the Church of Sens, a man as noble as he was wise, but one who in affection for this church did not in every respect imitate his predecessor Richer, a man of gentle disposition. When he heard the king’s requests, he began at first to resist most vehemently. He complained that monks were violent and rebellious toward bishops. At length, overcome by the intervention of the king and many nobles, and by reason, he replied that he would need the counsel of his clerics and ordered the abbot to come to him at Sens. He himself sent his archpriest, named Ralph, a lover of this place, to Étampes, to assemble the clerics, hear whether they consented or protested, and report back to him.

Ralph carried out his orders. The clerics having been assembled in the church of Blessed Mary, and giving their assent before many witnesses, he himself reported to the archbishop what he had heard. Thus, with very great difficulties, which for brevity’s sake we omit to write, the abbot obtained [Col. 0139C] the archbishop’s consent to the gift and its confirmation by his own privilege, as ecclesiastical custom requires. Having at last obtained what he wished, he received the gift from the archbishop’s hand and brought back the privilege, which is kept among us, in these words:

> In the name of the Lord. Daimbert, archbishop. Let present and future persons alike know that the venerable brother Thomas, abbot of the monastery of Morigny, humbly approaching our metropolitan see, petitioned us with all devotion and humility that we should grant to him and his successors, to possess in perpetuity, the church of Old Étampes, dedicated in honour of the Lord and in commemoration of blessed Martin, just as King Philip and his son Louis, likewise king, had made a gift of it to him. For those kings had already assigned the same church to the monastery of Morigny by royal liberality, and royal entreaties urged us to confirm that grant.
>
> But we, giving heed rather to the Lord’s saying, “Ask and it shall be given you; knock and it shall be opened to you,” did not permit the petition of our religious brother to be fruitless. Rather, in accordance with the evangelical saying, we opened to one asking in faith and knocking in hope, believing that in one act we could please the divine sight, satisfy royal prayers, and provide for fraternal advantage.
>
> Therefore, to the praise and honour of the Lord, with the consent and will of the brethren—that is, the canons of the same church—we grant to the monastery of Morigny the aforesaid church to possess in perpetuity, [Col. 0140A] on this condition: the present canons shall peacefully retain their prebends as long as they live, unless, with all violence removed, they consent to surrender them to the abbot of Morigny. After the death of each individual, each prebend shall pass into the right and lordship of the abbot of Morigny. Yet the right of the Church of Sens is preserved in every respect, from first things through intermediate things to the last.
>
> Given at Sens in the month of January, in the fifth indiction, in the fourth year of the reign of King Louis.
>
> Daimbert, archbishop, subscribed.  
> Ansellus, archdeacon, subscribed.  
> Hato, archdeacon, subscribed.  
> Tetbaud, archdeacon, subscribed.  
> Girard, archdeacon, subscribed.  
> Burchard, archdeacon, subscribed.  
> Girard, chancellor, wrote.

Such, then, were the king’s gift and the bishop’s assent. With these matters having been so prosperously accomplished, the abbot resolved to go to Rome in order to bring the affair to completion, especially at the urging of a certain canon of Chartres surnamed Pagan, a very wealthy man and a benefactor of this place. Having therefore taken what was necessary for this business, he set out for Rome with our monk Alberic, a simple and good man, and with Pagan also as companion. There, remaining at the Roman curia for a month and more, he deserved to obtain from Pope Paschal II, of good memory, both the protection of the apostolic see and confirmation of this gift.

But matters relating to the churches of Old Étampes appear to have been sufficiently explained. Meanwhile the Lord’s vineyard, planted in a poor place, was growing and multiplying and was stretching out its branches in every direction. At Dourdan, a royal town, it obtained the church of Saint Peter. At Stripiniacum, Guarsadonius, son of our founder Ansellus—who, having set out for Jerusalem, lies at Cluse—and his sister Adelina, who lies in our cloister, gave this church an annual payment of approximately fifty solidi and half the toll-revenue. Bartholomew, then prior of that place, was especially active in bringing this about. At La Ferté-Baudouin, Milo came to us and restored the churches of Bonne which he had given and taken away, and enlarged his gift. King Louis also gave us half the tithe of the toll gathered at Berovilla and forgave, for the soul of his steward Ansellus, the ten solidi of annual rent which we owed the king.
