[Col. 0140D] By royal generosity he also granted us a fair, named for our summer feast, beginning on that feast and lasting an entire week, together with the market and all customary dues.

Guy, viscount of Étampes, the abbot’s closest intimate and a most devoted friend of this place, also gave us the other half of the tithe of the aforesaid toll, the tithe of a mill which he possessed at Old Étampes, and one very useful tenant in the middle of the river Cale at Étampes. This Guy was the son of the great Hugh, lord of Le Puiset, in whose fief this church was founded. Having married the daughter of Marcy, viscount of Étampes, and thereby acquired the viscountcy, when the nobles of the Franks—and especially his relatives—rebelled against King Louis, he adopted sound counsel, urged above all others by our abbot, and through many dangers proved most faithful to the king.

Since an occasion has arisen to speak of this dissension, although it seems wholly unrelated to the present matter, it will not be without value if we offer something from it for the warning of posterity. To make this clearer, we must begin from the origin of the evil.

During the reign of King Philip, Henry, king of the English, son of that great William who had acquired the kingdom of England by military force while duke of the Normans, captured in war his brother Robert when he returned from Jerusalem; having put him in chains, he joined Robert’s county to his own kingdom. Louis, the designated king and still a youth, deceived by the counsel of certain collateral relatives, consented to these actions, although his father—a wise man—opposed him and, with prophetic foresight, foretold the evil which afterwards occurred.

That Henry was almost without equal among the princes of his age in wealth and wisdom of government. Through his sister he also had a nephew named Theobald, count of Chartres, Blois, Meaux, and many other provinces. This count palatine, second to the king within France, puffed up by wealth and noble birth, began from his youth, as if by a hereditary right of war, to harass King Louis. On the occasion of this conflict all France was set ablaze by wars, the nobles of each party desiring it and inflaming the minds of both men to hatred.

Among them Hugh of Crécy, [Col. 0141C] as the tinder of all these evils, surpassed the others in impious counsels and deeds. He was a bold man and ready with his hand, a pretender and concealer in every matter, an oppressor of the poor and a greedy killer of peasants, wishing in one moment to sweep over every crime and disgrace. This man, relentless against the king’s enemies [variant: “an enemy of the king,” or “among the king’s friends”], raged like a minister of the devil and devastated everything he could all around. Men were slain, among them Ansellus, the king’s steward, who was killed at the castle of Le Puiset. All things being thrown into confusion, the kingdom wavered for a while, until he who orders all things from eternity looked down from on high and, sins demanding it, allowed the wicked Hugh to be ensnared in such a way that peace was restored to human affairs and an example of treachery to be avoided was left to posterity.

For Hugh betrayed and captured Milo of Montlhéry, his lord and kinsman, a young man of excellent character and most valiant in arms; having bound his captive in fetters, he consigned him to prison custody. But, according to the divine oracle, he fell into the pit which he himself had prepared. From the very source from which he expected a victory and glory acquired for himself, and unbearable harm for the king, incredible joy arose for the king, while for Hugh himself came loss and perpetual disgrace, the Lord rendering him what he deserved for his deeds.

For when Hugh could neither keep Milo in chains any longer nor dare ransom and release him, since he feared that Milo would become a more bitter enemy to him, he led him through [Col. 0142A] various places and brought him back. Long uncertain what to do, driven by the enormity of his crimes and drawn by the prompting of a most violent demon, he suffocated an innocent man by night in the most shameful and utterly abominable kind of death, commonly called *murt* [murder]. Through the window of the wooden tower in which Milo was confined, he secretly cast out the body, as though Milo himself had wished to escape.

Found in the morning, the body struck all who saw and heard of it with astonishing horror and inexpressible grief. The traitor, however, turned pale; with trembling lips and a face displaying the torment of his mind and hellish conscience most plainly through outward signs, he allowed the body, by divine judgment hastening his ruin, to be carried away and buried at Longpont, a regular monastery and an alms-foundation of Milo’s ancestors. Rumour flew more swiftly than speech, and persons of every sex streamed together from neighbouring towns, villages, and boroughs. All were astonished; stunned by the novelty of an unheard-of crime, they poured forth the most abundant tears and raised a cry to heaven.

King Louis also hurried from the city of Lutetia, called Paris, followed by a vast multitude of nobles and knights. When he was seen weeping, tears, griefs, and groans multiplied, and all demanded vengeance with immense cries. After the man had been most fittingly buried in the cloister, as was proper, their hearts burning and their attack aroused, all rushed together to arms. Led by divine providence, they attacked and captured the neighbouring castle of Gometz. Great terror seized Hugh; all anathematized him; his followers abandoned him; he was stunned within himself and, bound by the testimony of his conscience, lost his strength.

A remarkable and most joyful reversal of affairs occurred. For when the traitor was compelled to clear himself by judicial combat concerning Milo’s death in the court of Amaury of Montfort—one of the most eminent men in this province after the counts palatine, and the man whose little daughter Hugh himself had betrothed—he was abandoned by the man in whom he had placed singular hope and did not dare enter the hazard of battle. Convicted, and confessing his guilt before all, he threw himself at the king’s feet, asked pardon, surrendered his land into the king’s hand, and immediately put on the monastic habit.

The king of England and Count Theobald, as though they had lost the spur by which they provoked King Louis, were astonished [Col. 0142D] and sought peace. What more need be said? After the dreadful storm of wars, the serenity of peace smiled forth: the kings and the count were reconciled. Then God’s mercy looked upon France and sent perfect concord among them; the head of sedition having been extinguished, the security of peace gladdened the hearts of the peasants.

Having truthfully and briefly recounted these things for the information and warning of posterity, the pen must be directed to the matters for which we began.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, Gelasius II, pope of Rome, also called John of Gaeta, left the City in the first year of his pontificate because of circumstances that had arisen. Carried by boat along the coast, he arrived at Marseilles, a city of Gaul. [Col. 0143A] Reared in the papal court from his youth and most excellently equipped by industry and learning, he was planning a council at Reims, the metropolitan see of the kingdom, at which he believed he would settle great matters. But divine judgment, hidden yet never unjust, ordered otherwise: overtaken by a most severe illness, he had himself carried to Cluny, which at that time shone above all monasteries in religion and riches. There he died, freed from the bonds of flesh, and, as befitted the supreme priest, was honourably buried.

There was then a grave and long-established conflict between the supreme pontiff and the king of the Germans—who, by succession from Charles the Great, king of the Franks, was patrician of the Romans—concerning the investiture of bishops and abbots. It had disturbed the Roman see for more than forty years and exhausted nearly all the churches of the whole Latin world. The king had also installed at Rome as a false pope one Burdinus, archbishop of Braga, a learned, courtly, and eloquent man; after introducing him by military force, he returned home and left him in possession of the see. Burdinus was afterwards forcibly captured by Pope Calixtus II at Sutri, led through Rome, made a monk at Cava—the most rigorous monastery situated above Salerno—and confined there.

Those who had come with Gelasius, led as if by a prophetic spirit, had, before leaving Rome, taken counsel with those who remained at Rome and received their consent: if, as happened, the pope should depart this life, they would have authority to elect a pontiff in our regions. After Gelasius had died and been buried, the cardinals and other Romans, with a very great multitude of bishops and nobles who had assembled there, immediately elected in the same place Guy, archbishop of Vienne, an energetic man of incomparable nobility of birth, and clothed him in pontifical insignia. Some, however, murmured because of the novelty of the matter; others, it was said, did so from envy and held another view.

Guy returned to Vienne, arranged his affairs, travelled through Gaul, held a council first at Toulouse and then another at Reims, and entered Rome with the greatest rejoicing, as was fitting. Burdinus having been captured, he obtained the throne of the supreme pontificate against the tyrant’s will. Among the other highest distinctions of his nobility, King Louis had married his great-granddaughter. Rejoicing in Guy’s dignity, while he had recently been elected and was passing through Auvergne on matters necessary to himself, Louis first sent Thomas, abbot of this place, to him as his representative, together with Peter, bishop of Beauvais, and Lord Conon of Palestrina, legate of the apostolic see.

At that time a most foul and turbulent dispute concerning the burial of bodies was being waged between us and the canons of Étampes. Their party was supported by a certain Algrin, a palatine and royal cleric, and by Stephen, chancellor, brother of Ansellus the steward and the king’s most private counsellor, whose judgment then directed—or rather carried along—the kingdom of France. [Col. 0144A] Both were canons of Étampes and therefore supported the canons in this cause as much as they could. While these men oppressed the cause of justice and perverted the king’s heart, our abbot was sent to the lord pope against the king’s wish. Since he could not seek the king’s aid, he had recourse to the queen’s assistance; having requested and obtained letters of intercession, he set out securely.

When they had found the lord pope in Auvergne and suitably settled the matters for which the embassy had been sent, the abbot, having become known at the curia and aided by Conon’s prayers, obtained and carried away, for the strengthening of his party, the privilege whose copy is written below.

Yet, although the abbot was exceedingly praiseworthy in obtaining this privilege, he was filled with sudden and great joy and for a while exulted childishly. Rather than concealing his staff of defence until necessity demanded it, as he ought to have done, he immediately disclosed and publicized to anyone whatever had happened; thus he brought upon himself a most grave and almost unbearable conflict. For when the canons of Étampes heard such things with stunned ears, they thought their church was about to be torn up from its foundations. Running about and crying that they had suffered violence, they fled for help to Algrin, the royal cleric, a military canon, a worldly man, and to Lord Stephen, the king’s chancellor and secretary; they filled the royal court with countless complaints.

These most powerful intercessors, through whose counsel the king and the governance of the kingdom were at that time borne along rather than governed, brought the king over by prayers and their accustomed entanglements of speech, and also bought him with gifts, making him patron and defender of their party. Strengthened by his support, they complained before the archbishop of Sens against the abbot at the castle of Melun during a private conference which the king was holding with certain bishops, the king himself acting as spokesman. In the abbot’s absence, their accusation was more easily and willingly received; with no one to contradict it, the more the monks’ alleged importunity was magnified, the more their cause was depressed.

From there the archbishop sent us grave and thunderous letters, designed to ward off invasions until the Roman pontiff, expected to arrive, should yield to the king’s prayers and himself annul the privilege. Alarmed by these unforeseen disturbances, the abbot first had recourse to God’s help; then he replied by letter to the archbishop’s letters. So that fuller knowledge of this affair may be had, we have resolved to weave the text of those letters into this work below.

To the venerable lord and most dearly beloved father in Christ, Lord D., by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens, Thomas, unworthy minister of Morigny, greeting and due obedience.

We have read in your letters that at Melun the canons of Étampes made the gravest complaints against us: that, so far as lies in our power, we are striving, as they say, altogether to nullify the church of Blessed Mary and the revenues of the canons; that we have appropriated to ourselves a share in the burial-rights of that place; and that we have also encroached upon the boundaries of the parish of that church. [Col. 0145A] We have also felt the words of paternal correction. Although these are more severe than either my case or my person has deserved, nevertheless, returning to myself, I have endeavoured to reflect that I hold a place of penitence in the Church; and I began to ponder that, according to Solomon, “The words of the wise are like nails driven firmly home” (Eccles. 12:11).

It is further written—so I think, for the giving of counsel, not for inspiring terror—that King Louis was present at this complaint; that he wholly favours the party of the clerics, and detests and condemns the harsh and intolerable assaults of monks. We are accordingly urged henceforth so to conduct ourselves in this affair that, perhaps on account of those matters which you touched upon a little earlier, we may not incur the unbearable hatred of the king.

To this our answer is brief. First, because the canons, despising the authority of the Church of Sens, flee to a secular court and hire the king with money against the privilege of the Roman Church, they act against the canons. Secondly, they falsely and wickedly say that we have appropriated a share of the burial-rights of that place and encroached on the parish boundaries. We do none of these things. For we know, both from the teaching of the divine Scriptures and from the oppression of the poor whom we see in our neighbourhood—and indeed only in your diocese—how detestable an evil it is to exact payment for burial: these poor people we see at the graves of the dead weeping more over the loss of their goods than over the bodies of those who have died.

But according to the ancient custom of the Churches, and according to your own ordinance—though we do not yet invoke the privilege of Roman authority—know that we neither now act, [Col. 0145C] nor have acted, otherwise. If there had been any excess on our part, I ought to have been canonically summoned by them, not thus vainly denounced before bishops over matters that had not yet arisen.

Moreover, with your permission, I would say that it was for you, had it pleased your fatherhood, to oppose the staff of defence to their barking—those who think that they lose whatever is given to us by the faithful. This was required both on account of the little and newly founded Church of Morigny, which is yours and which, founded by your predecessor of pious memory, R., has grown from such beginnings; and because, forestalling their snares through a private envoy most faithful to you, I had sent word that the entire matter depended upon your decision.

Finally, what shall I say concerning the king? By the command of the chief Shepherd I have learned both to fear God and to honour the king. Apart from this affair, we have had, and still have, sufficient familiarity with him; and in many matters, if it is lawful to say so, we have been necessary to him. But by what counsels he is often led astray, you, who are the head of your whole region, have at times learned by experience. But, not to linger over many words, let those fear him who are choked by riches and pleasures, or who are occupied with ecclesiastical dignities for their neighbours’ advantage. For we are Christ’s poor. It is a common proverb, my lord: “A naked man cannot be stripped.” No one fears to lose what he desires of his own accord to abandon. To disclose the truth to you: I am prepared to die rather than do anything against the privilege. Farewell.

This was addressed to the archbishop. But the abbot himself swiftly went to the king, since he was very intimate with him, [Col. 0146A] and, both by setting forth the case rationally and by exercising a certain prudent moderation, softened the king’s anger.

Meanwhile the disposer of events, who “takes the wise in their own craftiness,” according to His customary manner looked upon the tribulation of His poor Church; and, after the king had been somewhat humbled—how this came about we have left to be told elsewhere—He compelled him to deal with this matter differently. Now, after a council had been celebrated at Toulouse and the territories of Poitou, Anjou, and Tours had been traversed, the arrival of the lord pope in our regions was already being announced. Cono, Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the apostolic see—of whom we have also spoken above—whom the pope had sent ahead to Reims to arrange necessary matters, was returning to meet him and, because of his customary friendship with the abbot, lodged with us.

Encouraged by his counsel, the abbot arranged to travel with him so that he might have our church dedicated by the lord pope. Lest this seem strange to anyone because it was related in the preceding book that the oratory had been dedicated, let him know that the altar was later moved from the place where it then stood, and that the canonical ruling is: “If an altar has been moved, it must be consecrated anew.” The outer structure also, which the people call the nave of the church, had received its final completion.

But when they had arrived at Orléans and learned that the lord pope was directing his journey by way of Chartres, the abbot, his business unfinished, withdrew from his companions and returned. Yet when the pope learned that King Louis, returning from Normandy with an army, had arrived at Chartres and had burned part of the city, [Col. 0146C] he changed his plan and, intending to pass through Étampes, unexpectedly came to Orléans.

The abbot, astonished at so sudden an event, deliberated for a long time what he should do. Then, as I think, prompted by divine inspiration—for “a man’s steps are directed by the Lord” (Prov. 20:24)—he hastened to the king, who had returned from Chartres to Étampes the next day. He poured out prayers that the king would, by letters sent in advance, ask the pope to dedicate the church of Morigny himself. Without delay, his prayers having been heard, a royal envoy with letters was dispatched in the greatest haste to Orléans with Hugh the monk, then our secretary.

The letters were opened; counsel was taken with the cardinals; and the king’s request was judged one which ought to be granted. Once this was reported, it is impossible to say with what anxious haste the abbot and all of us, caught within the brief interval of only two intervening days, were stirred and harassed. [Col. 0146D]

When the supreme pontiff was received with the greatest reverence at Étampes in the palace, the clerics of Étampes murmuring and maligning us, the enemy who sows tares among the wheat almost ruined the whole undertaking of this good work through one Stephen of Besançon, a most cruel and avaricious man and chamberlain of the lord pope, by whose counsel the private papal court was governed.

The abbot, believing himself as good as dead if so heavenly a gift were torn, as it were, from his hands, assembled the cardinals in the presence of the lord pope, multiplied his prayers with the king and queen, and at last firmly obtained what he sought. What more need be said? Inestimable joy was poured into the hearts of our people and of all our friends. For God arose, and His enemies were scattered. Algrin was amazed, and all our envious men and enemies vanished like smoke before the face of God.

Therefore, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1120, the church of the monastery of Morigny was dedicated by Pope Callixtus II, on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October], with the highest honour and reverence, in honour of the Holy Trinity and the Holy Cross, of blessed Mary ever Virgin, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints of God.

Among the venerable persons present at this holy dedication, the more eminent were Cono, Bishop of Palestrina, legate of all France, [Col. 0147B] of [uncertain: Tentonia], of Germany, and of Saxony; Boso, of the title of St Anastasia, legate of all Spain, through whose aid and industry the island of Majorca and Zaragoza, the most noble city of the Spaniards, were subdued; Tostanus, Archbishop of York; Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres; Galo, Bishop of Saint-Pol in Brittany; Bernerius, Abbot of St Florentin of Bonneval; Stephen, Abbot of St John of Vallée; and many other wise men and excellent persons.

Also present were Louis, king of the Franks, and his wife Adelaide; William the dapifer, who is called seneschal; and his brother Stephen the chancellor, by whose counsel all France was governed; Amaury of Montfort; Guy of Gualardone; and many other magnates and noblemen of the Franks.

An annual remission of sins was also established throughout the district of Étampes on the anniversary of the dedication; and the region was exalted and made joyful. [Col. 0147C] Yet a violent wind coming from the north blew into this house in most frequent blasts, but, God being gracious, did not blow it away.

For after the great and most general council had been celebrated at Reims, the lord pope, intending to enter Burgundy and proceed to Rome with all his retinue, had come from Paris to Corbeil. There the canons of Étampes, because they supplied part of his provisioning, found an opportunity both to speak and to speak against us. They complained to the pope himself concerning the abbot and the monks: that the bodies of their parishioners were violently taken from them, and many other things which ought not to be spoken of; they complained especially about the new privilege.

The pope himself related their complaints to the abbot when the latter met him at Melun out of reverence for him, and invited him to prepare himself so that the question might be discussed before him by pleading the case. Again punishments, again anxieties, again the turmoil of fear and labour arose. The clerics barked; the king supported their side; Lord Stephen, second to the king, pressed the matter; Algrin raged.

On the journey by which they were going the following day to Ferrières, a royal abbey, Lord Stephen came out most openly into dispute and conflict against the abbot. He multiplied terrors, threats, and blows rather than words. The whole aim of him and his accomplices was this: that, if the abbot wished to retain the friendship of the king and of his associates, [Col. 0148A] he himself should tear up the privilege which he possessed.

But the abbot, made stronger and more secure by his poverty, after speaking briefly as the occasion required, finally replied that he was readier to die than to do what was demanded. The pope, his archbishop, and the Roman court were present; he would by no means evade judgment. For, supported by truth, he had prepared the cardinals by acquaintance and services, and had armed them as defenders of justice and of his cause against this importunity.

At that place, when the king and queen were about to take leave of the lord pope and say farewell, magnates, bishops, and many persons had gathered. There, after very many matters had been discussed, with the abbot present and ready to answer anyone who opposed him, the canons, distrusting their case, kept silent and wholly avoided entering into judgment.

Having therefore received leave with goodwill from the lord pope and all the cardinals, the lord abbot went by way of the king, who was at Châteauneuf, and from there entered his home in safety. Nevertheless Algrin, the sworn and publicly declared enemy of the monks, ardent and unyielding in his designs, took with him two canons, Simon the cantor and Philip, companions in his fraud and wickedness, and pursued the lord pope to Sens with certain royal commands.

Thereupon, in a claim of immeasurable emptiness and falsehood, they asserted that they had obtained a contrary ruling containing a privilege against our privilege. Very many, however, believed them and were astonished; [Col. 0148C] but by the ordering of divine providence they incurred the unbearable hatred of the whole people and of all the magnates of Étampes, unless the king’s protection intervened. They were judged impious and utterly criminal by all; they were anathematized by all.

Accordingly an envoy was sent by certain leading men of Étampes to the lord pope to investigate these matters. The abbot, meanwhile, sent a letter concerning this same affair to Lord Grisogonus, chancellor of the lord pope, in these words:

To Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church of God, Thomas, abbot of Morigny, greeting.

When I heard that the envoy of the magnates of Étampes was going to the lord pope, I entrusted letters to him, in which I might greet you and briefly inform you of the unheard-of evils that have hitherto been done against us. [Col. 0148D] I trust in the friendship promised me by you—or rather in that charity which, under one head and in one body, makes us one—that you love what is just and canonical, and that you will give counsel for correcting those things which wound the dignity of the holy Roman Church.

I would more gladly have done this in person, but I have been detained for many reasons, hoping and trusting in Him who does not forsake those who hope in Him, that in your prosperity I may someday see you with greater devotion and service.

Certain canons in our neighbourhood—if indeed they ought to be called canons—live irregularly and shamefully. They sell and buy doves in God’s temple; they make their sons heirs of their prebends; they violently exact a price for baptism and burial from the dead. While you were in our region, they avoided judgment; and when you departed, they fled for assistance to certain men who share in the revenues and crimes of that church.

Through these intercessors, by whose counsels the kingdom of the Franks is disturbed and dishonoured, they deceived the simple ears of the king, as in many other matters; and from our lord—if indeed this can be believed—they secretly extorted a privilege, such as had nowhere and never been heard of. I do not dare to say how they themselves say it was obtained.

I thought that, with God’s help and yours, I had forestalled these snares. But, as I see, “the way of a man is not in his own hand, nor is it for a man to direct his steps.” For “a man’s steps are directed by the Lord” (Prov. 20:24).

They now assert, to the dishonour of our lord [Col. 0149B] pope and of the holy Roman Church, that they possess a privilege against a privilege; and they have become more wicked than usual. Contrary to ancestral custom, to the usage of all Churches, to law, to the canons, and to God, they demand more burdensome burial-dues, and they prevent everyone from being buried elsewhere for the salvation of his soul.

It cannot be said how great a public uproar arises from this, how great the complaints of the nobles, how many insults and curses! This scandal has already sown many murders. All are astonished and amazed that, through you who so severely condemned burial-dues, so great a source of evil could have proceeded. The canons affirm not merely differing but wholly contrary rulings; and, what is an abomination even to hear, they boast that they have crushed one privilege by another privilege.

I therefore beg your Excellency to come to the aid of the souls for whom Christ died, lest the prince of darkness and nocturnal robber find through you an opportunity to seize them. For, so that they might be aided by the prayers of those who live holy and regular lives, people had customarily caused both their own bodies and those of their friends to be carried and freely buried, not only in our place but also elsewhere, in our own times and before our place was founded. How just this is, reason shows, authority confirms, and custom proclaims.

Besides the materials on this ruling which I have seen you have ready at hand, receive what blessed Augustine thinks on this matter. For in his book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, addressed to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, he writes as follows:

> “If a father’s garment and ring, and anything of this sort, are so much dearer to descendants as their affection toward their parents is greater, then the bodies themselves are by no means to be despised—bodies which we surely wear far more familiarly and closely united to ourselves than any clothing whatever. If this is true, then certainly a place provided for burying bodies near the memorial of saints is an act of good human affection towards the funerals of one’s own people. For if there is some religious concern that they be buried, it cannot be no concern at all where they are buried.”

So Augustine. Therefore, concerned for the salvation of your soul, ensure that this envoy may have an opportunity to speak, and urge our lord to provide a remedy for so horrible and grievous an evil. Let him have mercy on those souls which have sought assistance and will be unable to obtain it. Let him have mercy [Col. 0150A] on the poor church which he himself dedicated with his own hand, and for whose oppression—indeed, destruction—the devil has fashioned such engines. Farewell.

The envoy, returning from Tortona, a city of Italy, brought letters from the lord pope in which he said that he had never made one privilege against another; and he directed that, if any dispute existed between monks and canons, they should go to Lord Cono, who was still staying in our regions as his vicar. Thus, when their fraudulent artifice failed, it perished, and the structure whose foundation was falsehood vanished.

But because innumerable small details of these events occur to us, and we have resolved to observe brevity, we leave a fuller and more careful account of this matter to be written and handed down to posterity. You, however, who are sons of the Church of Morigny and love your house, should firmly believe that they possess no privilege against you. If they possess anything, certainly they possess nothing against you.

To crown their persecution, King Louis was tempted by immense promises to destroy the grant of the churches of Old Étampes which both his father and he himself had made. But, God being gracious, he could never be induced by prayers or rewards to commit so great a crime.

Meanwhile, amid these darkest whirlwinds of the greatest disturbances, the Church of God raised its head, and like a mustard seed gave off a stronger fragrance under most frequent crushing. For the abbot was not deprived of the privilege of his customary intimacy with the king. If he had lost any of it, [Col. 0150C] he restored it by frequent interviews and services.

Therefore, first through the inspiration of divine grace, without whose aid no one can act well, and then through the abbot’s industry over a long period, after many prayers and many journeys, he deserved to obtain a general royal writ for the protection of this place and all our possessions, both future and present. King Philip, as was reported, had made the same grant at the beginning of the establishment of this church; but the founding monks of Flavigny had either lost it or, as the more probable opinion held, had taken it away when they departed from here in disagreement.

But Satan always tried to oppose our successes and sought to assault the tower of David which was being built against Damascus. For the royal servants, especially those of Old Étampes, were inflamed to such anger and fury over the judgment made concerning the partition of sons, should a union of our men and royal retainers take place [the text is corrupt: *exarsertur*], that they filled everything with complaints and curses, turned all men against us and all that was ours into the deepest hatred, and would have killed the abbot had they possessed the power.

But the Divinity favourable to us calmed their minds, and not long afterwards reduced that madness to ashes. A certain knight also, named Teudo, when he was approaching his end, gave to this church half of a winepress, a meadow near our garden, and a small plot of land situated before the grange of Belvédère. [Col. 0151A] These were very necessary to us.

We judge these things worthy of record because he gave them, as it were, in investiture of the lands and vineyards lying around the nearby church of St German, and of the whole territory which he held within that parish, on condition that his only little daughter, whom he had, should die without an heir.

When the confraternity of the men and women of Étampes had also been renewed for a second time, all the windows of this church and the stone bridge over the river were completed. Following this example, one Robert, our monk, established throughout the neighbouring district a confraternity very useful for the supply of grain.

Likewise Garsadon, son of Anselm our founder, first at Étampes before many leading men of that place, and afterwards when he was preparing to go to Jerusalem, made a gift in our chapter-house of the estate of Gummarville: if he should die, as in fact happened, upon God’s way, we were to redeem it—for it was under pledge—and possess it in perpetuity.

After his death, when very powerful challengers rose against us, it was demonstrated by most manifest proofs that we had received it from God’s gift rather than from man. For Adelaide, Garsadon’s mother, who at first was most favourably disposed to us concerning this gift, as in other matters, but afterward changed by feminine fickleness, was returning on foot from the house of a certain wealthy man, where she had discussed obstructing this gift. In the middle of a level road, with no obstacle present, she fell and so wrenched her foot that throughout the rest of her life she was unable to walk uprightly.

A certain Stephen, son of Herard, a most powerful man and one most ingenious in malice, who had married this woman’s granddaughter, swore in fury that he would never permit it; that he would make his station in the village; that he would kill the monks. [Col. 0151C] But when he could be overcome by no prayers nor softened by royal threats, struck by divine judgment and brought to his end, before many witnesses he abandoned both his accusation and his life.

More wicked than all enemies was a certain knight named Bonard, a man of profane mind, who had Garsadon’s sister as his wife. He rose against us and first burned that village; then the grange of Mesuns; and afterwards, at the place called Toschetum, situated above Stripiniacum, certain houses, together with six oxen and twenty-six sheep in them, by a nocturnal fire.

He lived, however, in the land of Guy, lord of Rochefort, who was then at Jerusalem; and therefore he could scarcely, or never, be brought to justice. And when, vexed by excessive demonic agitations, he was raving that he would burn not only our possessions but even this church itself unless we abandoned the village, Guy, by God’s favour, unexpectedly arrived on his return from Jerusalem.

When news of his arrival was received, the abbot hastened out to meet him. Having greeted and, as custom required, kissed the man, the abbot asked and obtained from him that he should turn aside to lodge with us and permit himself to be received in procession, since he was returning from Jerusalem. He was received with the greatest honour, and he and all those who had come with him [Col. 0152A] and those who had met him from his castles were most devoutly provided for.

The abbot was silent at that time. But on the following day, which was Sunday, after he had escorted him as far as St Arnulf of Aquilina and there again received him with a procession, the abbot made a complaint concerning Bonard, in the hearing of many magnates who had come there from various regions; and he compelled Guy, bound by the chains of reason and service, to render him justice.

Without delay, on the next day at Rochefort Bonard was brought to justice. In the presence and with the support of Guy, viscount of Étampes, kinsman of that Guy and a most devoted friend of this place, the abbot forgave him what he had done to us outside the law; and Bonard, with his wife and children, withdrew the claim he had been making and granted confirmation of all the things which Garsadon and his father had given us.

Therefore, after excessive labours and expenditure of seventy pounds and more, and after the dismissal of other claims made by certain persons, Gummarville came peacefully into our possession.

In the same district we possess Buxetum, half of which Anselm our founder gave long ago when he was setting out for Spain. Lisiard gave the other half; Bonard, son of Peter, is also named [the syntax and object are uncertain in the source]; and the knights of Étampes gave the tithe of that whole territory. Thus the Church of Morigny acquired there a very great possession through the bountiful gifts of divine favour.

There are other gifts also which, because they are modest and have been recorded elsewhere, we have resolved to pass over in silence.

But the conscience of the abbot and of certain other brothers was troubled [Col. 0152C] because our predecessors had acquired certain churches and tithes not only through gifts but also with money. For at that time, namely at the beginning of the establishment of this Church, the question of simony was not discussed as rigorously as later diligence caused it to be. If, however, any ecclesiastical property was bought from laymen, it was called not purchase but redemption.

But after they had long hesitated over this matter, divine providence brought it about that Lord Cono, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the apostolic see, once more lodged with us. He had with him as a great helper William, bishop of Châlons, who had directed the higher schools and who then, possessing zeal for God above all the bishops of all Gaul, shone in knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

The abbot therefore surrendered into the cardinal’s hand all those things about which he had scruples, so that whatever he wished to do concerning them might be at his disposal. On the next day, these wise men and ecclesiastical stewards summoned the abbot before them and, under obedience, commanded him to receive them from the hand of blessed Peter and to serve God securely in the abbey.

These matters have been related so that our successors may make provision concerning such things and may have no fear regarding what has already been done.

Meanwhile, after the death of William, brother of Ansel the steward, Stephen the chancellor, of whom we have spoken above, brother of both men, became chief officer of the royal household. In preceding generations it had been unheard of [Col. 0153A] for a man performing the office of deacon also to hold, after the king, the chief command of the military. This energetic man, endowed with worldly wisdom and with the revenues of many ecclesiastical benefices, flourished in temporal prosperity above other mortals of our time, through his intimacy with the king—such was the influence he possessed that some said he commanded rather than served him.

But when he had given his niece in marriage to Amaury of Montfort, together with the lordship of Rochefort, which had come to the girl through the marriage, he became puffed up and forgot himself. By most frequent annoyances he made Queen Adela hostile to him; and, as their enmity increased and the king was at last disturbed, he was deprived of his office and expelled from court. Seized, as it were, by a kind of madness, he exerted all his strength [Col. 0153B] to throw the kingdom into disorder, and, relying on the aid of the valiant man-at-arms Amaury, set this country aflame with wars. But when he could not bring his purposes to effect, he returned to himself, relinquished the seneschalship, which he claimed to possess by hereditary right, and was reconciled with King Louis and likewise with Louis’s son Philip, already an anointed king, through the intervention of Queen Adelaide.

Having briefly set forth these matters concerning the man by way of digression, let us pursue those for whose sake we have introduced them. While he flourished at the royal court, and everything after the king depended upon his decision, he was enticed by the promises of Boso, abbot of Saint Benedict. He approached the king, whose chief confidential officer he was, concerning the churches of Old Étampes, and suggested that his father, who lay buried at Saint Benedict’s, had formerly made a gift of those [Col. 0153C] churches to that noble place. Although he could not then bend the king’s heart to his will, Vulgrin, that most intimate friend of ours who was present there, was deeply distressed and hurried to us, relating the affair as he had heard it.

The abbot, astonished and afflicted by the pressure of so grave a dispute, had poured out fruitless prayers before Stephen, who had come to Étampes. He therefore went swiftly to the king; taking with him Count Guy and our Vulgrin, he addressed him in the cloister of Châteauford in these words:

> “I know, lord king, that I have grievously offended the serenity of your piety, in that, as though ungrateful for your generosity [Col. 0153D], I have for a long time placed monks in the churches of Old Étampes. Yet it was not negligence on our part, but poverty, that produced this offence. And lest the delay in this good work should long inflame your anger, I constrain myself; forgetting, out of reverence for you, our own poverty, I intend to establish there monks who will live from our revenues.”

Caught by this argument—for he was ashamed to say that what he had formerly directed to be done should not be done—the king urged Stephen, who was then present, to grant and approve the undertaking, and obtained his consent. Therefore, on the following Sunday, Count Guy and many other magnates of this district accompanying them, the monks of Morigny were admitted into the church of Saint Martin at Old Étampes [Col. 0154A], despite the murmuring of certain clerics, who were nearly resorting to force.

This was, as it were, a very great miracle of our time. For it seemed impossible that this work could be accomplished peacefully. Thus the Church of Morigny, by God’s favour, the king’s generosity, and the abbot’s diligence, quietly took possession of the churches of Old Étampes—something it had long and earnestly desired.

But the enemy of humankind and instigator of all evils, the devil, sowed by night the most shameful tares of discord; and, with divine judgment permitting it, he nearly choked whatever monastic wheat the Lord had sown there in the daytime. Since the clerics could not expel the monks by force, they undertook to do so by cunning contrivances.

When King Louis was having his firstborn son [Col. 0154B] Philip anointed and crowned king with him at Reims, the most noble metropolis of Gaul, and Thomas, abbot of this place, together with Bartholomew, prior of Saint Martin’s, was attending that celebrated assembly, one Hugh, the chief standard-bearer of hostility above all others, who performed the offices of priest and cantor in that church, found an occasion for deception with several accomplices. What is dreadful even to recount, they laid snares. They bribed Hugh with money and the promise of a single prebend, should the monks thus be expelled, and secretly brought him into the church. While they themselves fraudulently hid in the charnel-house—the place within the enclosure of that church which contains the bones of the dead—they came out of hiding and seized the monk while he was alone talking with a boy, as he had often done before (for he was old, foolish, and dissolute) [Col. 0154C], as though he were committing that crime.

Thus these men, whose minds were so corrupt that they seemed actually mad, having banished every regard for humanity, immediately stripped the monk of his clothes. Seizing the church bells, they summoned the people and spread an intolerable calumny. They falsely cried out that all the other monks were like this, and threw everything into confusion. The people, struck by the novelty of an unheard-of outrage, were driven mad. With great cries they attacked the monks’ house; some tried to break it open with clubs, others with stones, and to crush the monks living inside.

But while the monks wept within and cried aloud to God, Christ arose from sleep and rescued the endangered little boat from the storms [Col. 0154D], for certain soldiers of that place were stirred up and repelled the unbridled attack of the people.

It also happened that Henry, archbishop of Sens, passed through Old Étampes in the following week. Our enemies carefully watched for the arrival of the bishop and stationed bands of the mob and of their prostitutes in various places. When he entered that town, a confused clamour rose up, tiresome even to the ears of those less attentive: they demanded that he expel the shameful and incestuous monks and restore their church to the clerics. They now seemed to have the upper hand; and, having corrupted by subsidies certain persons whom we had hoped to be faithful to us in every respect, they tried to win over the king and his court with money, so that he might bring their wishes to effect.

Finally, a day for pleading between the monks and canons was appointed at Pissy, in the king’s presence [Col. 0155A]. This affair seemed unbearable to the abbot and the other brothers, both because of the poverty of this place and because of the disgrace. But that physician who is so mighty as to be almighty, who knows how to make an antidote from poison and to use even evils well, caught those wise men in their own craftiness—for they fell into the pit which they themselves had prepared—and stripped them utterly of their vain hopes, while purifying us through such trials.

For our abbot had long before bound the archbishop to us by many services, so that even as he passed through Old Étampes he denounced the errors and cries of the raging mob, and almost excommunicated them on the spot. The perversity of the clerics and the abbot’s friendship, moreover, [Col. 0155B] made the king hostile to them.

Therefore, when the abbot had assembled at Pissy the most honourable and renowned persons of that time—Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, then famous at the royal court as an outstanding and excellent advocate; Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi at Reims, who had professed in our monastery and had been transferred, through Cono, legate of the Roman Church, from the church of the blessed martyrs Crispin and Crispinian, which he had governed excellently, to that more exalted church; and Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés—while a great crowd of magnates and knights sat around the king, once the matter came into the light of judgment, the wickedness of the plot began to grow pale. Indeed, it would have incurred corporal punishment, had not the authority of the holy canons stood in the way [Col. 0155C].

Those clerics, I mean, having been committed to prison, humbly implored the assistance of the abbot whose death they had so recently and confidently threatened. The angry king summoned all the burgesses and the whole people of Old Étampes to Paris to answer justice, hoping thereby to obtain very great sums of money. Accordingly an immense and intolerable murmur arose: they cursed and denounced the monks, saying that, because of the abbot, who was crafty, and because of them, they were suffering this trouble; and that all the monks would be burned when they returned.

In these dreadful and foul tempests our Vulgrin died, and was buried beside his mother in our cloister, which he himself had built long before [Col. 0155D]. The king took into his own hands all Vulgrin’s goods, including those which he had given us in alms, because he was of the king’s household and had died without an heir.

Amid such narrow passes, like impassable Thermopylae, the abbot, utterly failing in spirit, resolved to leave the abbey and withdraw to a quieter life. But he was strengthened both by the counsel and assistance of his excellent and most religious companion and adviser, Prior Garin.

Garin was born of honourable and noble parents at Épernon. He and the abbot had grown up together as inseparable companions from childhood, and, when they became young men, they came to Étampes for the sake of study. Garin became known and intimate with Albert, then abbot of this place, to whom he was also related by blood. At the urging of one of Albert’s priors, Roger by name—who later shone in the abbey of Colombs as a most brilliant lamp of monastic religion—Garin, at about twenty years of age, bade farewell to worldly affairs and took up the armour of our warfare [Col. 0156A].

Thomas, as though deprived of the better part of himself, could not have lived in the world. Unable for long to bear the restless agitation of an anxious and changeful mind, he followed Garin’s footsteps, glad to have in our order as a guide the man whom he had always had as his companion. When Albert left this abbey and returned to Colombs, taking them with him by permission of this chapter, he bound them there by religious profession. Thomas, having been made our abbot, returned to us and brought back with him his one-hearted companion.

Garin was indeed of excellent character and exceedingly gentle, and had emerged from the world almost wholly untouched by every kind of lust [Col. 0156B]. Having entered upon the paths of monastic life, he was a fervent lover of sobriety, so sparing in food and drink that he was judged incomparable among all monks of our time. Upon this foundation he had built the perfection of his other virtues. He raised the bright standards of chastity so high that, preserving a good conscience before God and a good reputation before his neighbour, he could be suspected by no one, not even an enemy.

Tall in stature, handsome in expression and face, restrained in speech and bearing, he showed outwardly, without affectation and in a natural manner, what he was inwardly; he offered himself to all as a model for life. Many wholly true things might be said about him, were it not that, as we wrote this, he still enlightened us by his presence.

The abbot had entrusted himself wholly to the loyalty and intimate friendship of so great a man. Nor is this surprising: [Col. 0156C] the thirtieth year was already passing since they had professed as monks, and never, even for a moment, had any discord of mind arisen between them. Garin recalled the abbot from faint-heartedness, as he had done in all other troubles. The abbot again presented himself before the king at Paris and, with tears, recounted the perils under which he laboured and the mad frenzy of the reckless populace.

But that gracious Wisdom which “reaches mightily from one end to the other, and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1), in whose hand are the hearts of kings, and which says, “By me kings reign” (Proverbs 8:15), moved King Louis by his prayers to compassion. The king generously relinquished everything Vulgrin had left, reconciled the people whom he had angrily summoned, and sent them home rejoicing [Col. 0156D]. Thus, when God—through whom all things are possible—granted it, after the dreadful clouds of this storm a happy calm of prosperity smiled upon us, though it had seemed impossible to everyone.

Accordingly, with rejoicing hearts, on the solemn day of this church’s own feast which followed these events—namely, on the octave of Pentecost—these ordinances were made and confirmed in the common chapter by Lord Thomas, then abbot of this place, with the agreement of all the brothers.

It was ordained that the anniversary of King Philip should be celebrated solemnly each year, and that the prior of Étampes should provide without delay twenty shillings on that day for the brothers’ refreshment, namely for purchasing fish. For this king was generous to this church, which was founded in his time. He bought it for one hundred pounds from Ebrard, lord of Le Puy, whose fief the property was [Col. 0157A]. He gave us the churches of Old Étampes and bestowed many other gifts through royal generosity.

Likewise an ordinance was made concerning the anniversary of Ansel, son of Arenbert, founder of our place. On that day the prior of Étréchy shall pay ten shillings. The same was ordained concerning Garsadon, son of Ansel: the monk of Buc shall pay ten shillings on that day. Likewise concerning Rainald, the first abbot of this place: the monk of Mézières shall pay ten shillings. The same ordinance shall also be observed for Vulgrin, who bestowed many benefits upon us: the monk of Bellotville shall pay ten shillings.

Thomas, too, the founder of this custom, asked the brothers in the same chapter that this same concession be granted for himself, whether he should die as abbot or former abbot [Col. 0157B]. It was granted and confirmed. The monk of Guillarville shall pay ten shillings on that day. For Thomas acquired and built up that possession for us together with many other possessions.

He also placed it in the hands of the prior and of the whole chapter that, if anyone, through negligence or obstinacy, should fail to render on the above-mentioned days the appointed payment for the brothers’ refreshment, he should be severely corrected without waiting for the abbot and kept in the cloister until he paid the money. Whoever should presume with rash boldness to infringe these ordinances, let him be anathematized. Having drawn out these matters for the instruction of those who shall come after us, the rest remains to be woven.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1129, Honorius II, who had sat on Peter’s throne after Pope Calixtus, died at Rome in the church of Saint Andrew [Col. 0157C], which the blessed and eminent great doctor Gregory had built at his own expense near the slope of Aemilius Scaurus. The cardinals who were present there with the chancellor and had sat beside the sick Honorius set over themselves a certain Gregory, eminent in learning and religion; and, as some say, they clothed him with the pontifical insignia with excessive haste.

They say that this was done as an act of prudent arrangement, in order to frustrate the hopes of a certain Peter, who seemed to aspire to the papacy in a worldly fashion. This Peter was the son of Peter, son of Leo. Leo, having passed from Judaism to Christ at Easter, deserved to be baptized by Pope Leo and to be distinguished by his name. Since this man was very learned, he became influential in the Roman curia and begot a son named Peter, destined to become a man of great renown and great power [Col. 0157D].

At that time there arose the most turbulent dispute concerning investitures between the king of the Germans, who by succession from Charlemagne was patrician of the Romans, and the Roman Church. In this conflict Leo proved so valiant in arms, so prudent in counsel, and so faithful to the Roman Church that the pope entrusted to him, together with the other fortifications of Rome, also that which seems to possess the very likeness of the city—the tower of Crescentius, situated on the Gallic side at the head of the bridge over the Tiber—and held him in especial intimacy. Through this opportunity he increased marvelously from day to day; his position improved, and he was augmented in riches, possessions, and honours.

Among his other offspring—of whom, because of their very great multitude of both sexes, Antichrist, as some said, gloried—he begot this Peter, of whom the discourse is now concerned. Peter, having been educated in letters, was called by some “the forerunner of Antichrist” [Col. 0158A]. For the sake of study he went to Gaul and Paris; on returning home, he assumed the monastic habit at Cluny, a very rich and holy monastery. After being instructed there for some time in regular observances, he was recalled to the curia by Pope Paschal II at his father’s urging. Made cardinal in the time of Pope Calixtus, he was sent with that same Gregory as legate to Gaul, and held councils at Chartres and Beauvais.

After Honorius’s death, relying upon the formidable strength of his brothers and his exceedingly numerous [Col. 0158B] household, and encouraged by the prompting of a certain most learned and, as was thought, most religious old man, bishop of Porto, he seized the summit of the pontificate, with no small part of clergy and people agreeing to him. This was the seedbed of the greatest schism in the Church of God; and, as that secular historian says of other matters:

> “A bad enterprise, but a hope far harsher.”

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Sallust, *Catiline*, 20.13.]

Gregory, who according to the custom of one assuming the bishopric was called Innocent, yielding to the counsels of his supporters, embarked on a ship and departed Rome. He came ashore on the coast of Pisa and was immediately received most willingly by that city and its neighbours.

While these things were happening in Italy, King Louis summoned to Étampes the archbishops of Reims, Sens, Bourges, and Tours, together with the bishops and abbots of his kingdom [Col. 0158C]. After taking counsel, he declared Innocent Roman pope and his own father, together with all his kingdom, because Innocent appeared superior in holiness of life, reputation, and election.

As Innocent came down into Gaul with King Louis’s son Philip, the king humbly met him at Fleury—the monastery of Saint Benedict situated on the Loire—and, bending down according to custom, kissed his foot, joyfully venerating him as the vicar of Christ and Peter. Henry, king of England, then residing in Normandy, moved by this example, hastened to Chartres to see him. Receiving him as pope, he honoured him with very great gifts.

It was decided at court that the journey should proceed from there to the king of the Germans, patrician of the Romans; and, after the first halt at Chartres, they lodged at Morigny. When our lords and friends who stood by—Henry, archbishop of Sens, and Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres—pointed out and urged the poverty of this place [Col. 0158D], the pope would not yield to their entreaties, declaring that he knew the place and the abbot well. For he had stayed with us, together with his adversary Peter, when they were serving as legates in Gaul, and had been carefully entertained for two days.

It happened that our abbot and Prior Garin were then at Aquilina, beyond Saint Leodegar, at the cell of certain hermits. Disturbed by the unexpected news of the arrival of so great a pontiff—who seemed burdensome because he had sent word only on the preceding day and was arriving with a grave and very great multitude—the brothers swiftly sent to the abbot someone to announce these things and urge him to come quickly [Col. 0159A]. But the abbot and prior had intended to go elsewhere that night; when they arose before daylight and had travelled one league, it was a miracle that, while the darkness of night still lasted, they met that very messenger through God’s providence. They hurried quickly and joyfully received the lord pope as he was almost entering Morigny, entertaining him with solemn honour.

On the following day—for he remained with us two days—the abbot humbly approached the pope and court, requesting and obtaining that he should consecrate the altar before the crucifix [Col. 0159B]. Therefore, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1130, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January], the altar before the crucifix in the church of the monastery of Morigny was consecrated by Lord Pope Innocent II in honour of Saint Lawrence and all Christ’s martyrs.

Among the venerable persons present at this holy consecration, the most venerable were:

- Cardinal bishops: William of Palestrina; Matthew of Albano; John of Ostia; Guy of Tivoli.
- Cardinal priests: John of Crema, of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; Peter Rufus, of the title of Saint Clement; Gotielmus, of the title of Saint Cecilia.
- Cardinal deacons: Romanus, of the title of Saint Mary in Portico; Haimeric, chancellor and cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary the New; Guy, of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata.
- Adinulf, abbot of Farfa; Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, at that time the most renowned preacher of the divine word in Gaul; Peter Abelard, monk and abbot, himself a religious man and director of the most distinguished schools, to which learned men flocked from almost all the Latin world; Girard, abbot, a man equally learned and devout; and Sanxon, abbot of Saint-Lucien of Beauvais [Col. 0159C].

Henry, archbishop of Sens, served beside the lord pope in the role of chaplain. Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, preached a sermon to the people. When these things had been carried out with the greatest rejoicing, on the third day the lord pope departed happily with his retinue, giving very great thanks for the hospitality, and went to his meeting at Liège [Col. 0159D].

There Lothair, king of the Alamanni, patrician and emperor of the Romans—who after that Henry who deceitfully captured and imprisoned Paschal II at Rome ruled in Germany by election according to the custom of that people—recognized Innocent as pope and father in the presence of all the archbishops, bishops, and magnates of his kingdom. He promised on oath that he would go with Innocent to Rome and restore him to his proper see.

Returning thence to Gaul, Innocent remained for a long time at Auxerre. When the time of the council which he was to celebrate at Reims on the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist drew near, he first reconciled at Tours Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, Tours, and Maine, a most noble young man of exceptionally vigorous character [Col. 0160A]. Then, returning through the districts of Orléans and Étampes, he honoured Paris by his presence. The whole city went out to meet him as he entered. Such was the man’s graciousness of countenance and affability of speech that he won the goodwill of those who saw him. He was favourably received by King Louis and his son Philip and honourably escorted from the city.

But, as the poet says:

> “All human things hang by a slender thread.”

In the midst of this most radiant calm of prosperity, an unexpected stroke of sudden lightning arose, shaking every heart with the horror of its enormity and casting upon the eyes of the mind dense darkness, no less through astonishment than through grief.

Philip, king and son of the king, that most lovely flower of boys, was about fourteen years old from birth, and had been king for two years and six months. As a royal boy seemingly worthy of rule over the whole world—for he surpassed all mortals of his time and age in physical beauty and the exceptional innocence of his face—he was playing in the city itself on a very swift horse with certain companions on foot. In a narrow street, a pig rushing from the opposite direction ran beneath the feet of the charging horse and threw both horse and rider down upon itself. While his companions fled here and there in terror, he was carried in the hands of poor people to the nearest house; nearly all his limbs broken, he breathed out his last breath on the following day [Col. 0160B].

Thus that tender boy, in whom all hope of the kingdom of the Franks rested [Col. 0160C], was removed from human affairs after being tormented by a terrible death. It cannot be believed how great a grief seized the hearts of all, even those who cared little for the king. His father, angered with certain magnates of the district of the Vexin who did not obey his commands, had summoned from the cities, castles, and places subject to him the provincial soldiers to suppress the rebellion.

Moreover, on that very day the lord pope was arriving at Paris on his way to Reims, followed by a great number of bishops, abbots, learned and noble clerics. Thus, with a multitude of both orders, of every sex and age, gathered together, unbearable mourning and lamentation rose to the stars. With natural feeling, as generally occurs in such a case, some inciting others, the boy’s body was carried to the church of Saint-Denis and buried there [Col. 0160D]. Many magnates, nearly lifeless from excessive grief, were carried by others’ hands to their lodgings.

The incomparable beauty of his appearance and the horror of so sudden a death filled every mind, I know not whether I should say with misery or with pity, and added fuel to grief. There were people who asserted that the beast through which the boy was suffocated had never appeared again, and therefore many thought it had been one of the hostile powers. Such, I think, was the unheard-of departure from this present life of Philip, a guileless and innocent boy, demanded by the sins of others.

Upon hearing the news of this death, the pope was deeply moved in his heart [Col. 0161A]. He sent from his side to console the king the venerable bishops Geoffrey of Châlons and Matthew of Albano, who had been summoned from the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs to Rome by Pope Honorius and appointed bishop. A plan was adopted that the king should go as swiftly as possible to the council and should make Louis, the son born after Philip, king in his stead.

Accordingly King Louis, on Saturday, entered the council with Count Ralph of Vermandois, his kinsman and chief officer of the royal household, and many magnates of the Franks. He ascended the tribunal, kissed the lord pope’s feet, and sat beside him in a chair that had been placed there. He spoke briefly concerning his dead son and moved all to tears.

The pope then turned his gaze toward the king [Col. 0161B] and began thus:

> “It is fitting, most excellent king, that you, who hold authority over the most noble nation of the Franks, should lift the eyes of your mind to the majesty of that highest King through whom kings reign, and should reverence His will in all things. For He who created all things governs all things; possessing knowledge of all things, in the universe He neither does nor permits anything whatever unjustly, though many unjust things are done.
>
> “That most merciful Lord, good king, is accustomed both to console His faithful servants by prosperity and to instruct them through adversity. For, as we read in Holy Scripture—His letter sent from heaven through the Holy Spirit to us dwelling on earth—He wounds and heals (Job 5:18), and ‘chastens every son whom he loves’ (Hebrews 12:6). ‘I,’ He says, ‘will kill, and I will make alive; I will wound, and I will heal’ (Deuteronomy 32:39) [Col. 0161C].
>
> “This is so that man, created in the image of God and cast by the guilt of transgression into the darkness of this mortality, may not love exile as though it were his native country, but may hasten as swiftly as possible to return to that holy heavenly city, Jerusalem, from which he is a pilgrim on earth; whose foundations are upon the holy mountains, that is, upon our apostles; which is above, which is our mother. For we are strangers and pilgrims, as all our fathers were; we have no abiding city here, but seek that which is to come. There, those who vigorously trample down carnal desires here rejoice eternally with God.
>
> “Your son, a boy of simplicity and innocence, has departed to that city. For of such is the kingdom of heaven. David, [Col. 0161D] king, who was an example of virtues to good kings, wept most grievously while his son languished; but after he was told that he was dead, he rose from the ashes and haircloth in which he lay, changed his clothes, washed his hands, and summoned his household to a meal. For it is impossible that what has happened should not have happened; and that man, full of God, knew how greatly he sinned who would oppose divine justice even by a vow.
>
> “Put aside, then, this sorrow of spirit, which carnal affection has produced in you and which you bear in your breast and countenance. For He who has received one to reign with Him has left you several others who may reign afterward. You must also console us—men who are strangers and driven from our own homes [Col. 0162A]—whom you, first of all, received honourably in your kingdom for love of God and Saint Peter, honoured with services, and loaded with benefits. May the Lord render you recompense and everlasting reward, lord king, in that city of which glorious things have been spoken: where there is life without death, eternity without decay, and joy without end.”

By this wonderful antidote of a discourse, the holy apostolic man soothed the wounded heart of the king. Immediately he rose to his feet and, after the Lord’s Prayer had been said silently, as Christian custom requires, absolved the soul of the dead boy. Then, by obedience, he instructed the archbishops, bishops, and abbots to present themselves on the following day, which would be Sunday, dressed in the sacred and festal garments in which they were assembled, and to attend the consecration of the new king [Col. 0162B].

Accordingly, on that day the sun shone more brightly than usual and seemed joyfully to offer its service to the events being performed. Early in the morning, the pope left the bishop’s palace with his court and the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, and went to the church of Saint Remigius, where the king was lodging with his son. He was received there most fittingly with great devotion and a procession of monks.

There, clothed in all the insignia of the Roman pontiff and crowned, as was his custom at sacred and great festivals, with the *phrygium* [papal crown], surrounded by an innumerable multitude of ecclesiastical and military men and of the populace, he came with the boy to be consecrated to the mother church dedicated in honour of blessed Mary. Before the church doors awaited them the king, his magnates, archbishops, certain bishops, abbots, monks, canons, clerics, and fellow students who had flocked to the council from various regions of Gaul and Germany [Col. 0162C].

They entered the church and presented the boy at the altar. With the oil with which Saint Remigius had anointed Clovis, king of the Franks, a Christian—oil presented to him by an angel’s hand—the lord pope consecrated with immense rejoicing the little boy, about ten years old. Some said that never before in France had the celebration of a council and the consecration of a king by the Roman pontiff himself occurred together.

Thus King Louis, having received consolation after lamentation, returned with his wife, son, and court to attend to the affairs of the kingdom. On the following day, however, letters were presented to the pope presiding in the council [Col. 0162D] by a certain archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0161D] Saint Norbert.], from Lothair, king of the Alamanni. In these letters obedience was again promised, and it was announced that he was preparing himself, with all the forces of his kingdom, for the expedition [Note: [Col. 0161D] Namely, the Italian expedition.].

Likewise Henry, king of the English, sent through Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, highly ornate letters and promised faithful obedience. The kings of nearer Spain, the elder Ildefonsus [Note: [Col. 0162D] That is, Alfonso VI, king of Aragon and Navarre.], and of inner Spain, the younger Ildefonsus [Note: [Col. 0162D] That is, Alfonso VII, king of Castile.], greeted the pope through letters sent by the bishops of their provinces [Col. 0163A]. They declared themselves his sons and obedient servants, and earnestly begged aid against the enemies of the Christian name and the invaders of those regions, the Almoravids.

There were also letters, highly relevant both to the joy and admiration surrounding this affair, from the most excellent Carthusian hermits. They were brought by a certain venerable abbot of the Cistercian order and read aloud in the council by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres. The Carthusians were men dwelling an angelic life on the ridges of the Alps, of surpassing religious devotion and incomparable authority [Col. 0164A]. Since we labour for the benefit of posterity, we have decided to insert their letter in this little work. It is as follows:

> To the lord and father most dear and most reverend, Innocent, supreme pontiff of the apostolic see: the poor servants and sons of the Charterhouse offer that peace which the world cannot give, the devoted service of their littleness, and such obedience as, though not necessary, is offered.
>
> Many prayers to the sacred ears of your apostolate, . . .

For the remainder, see among the various letters addressed to Innocent in *Patrologia*, vol. 179.

## PROLOGUE TO BOOK III OF THE HISTORY

[Col. 0163]

[Col. 0163B] As human weakness is instructed by the Word of the Word, so a lamp is not lit by anyone in order to be hidden away or concealed under a bushel. And beyond doubt the generosity of divine compassion bestows the rigour of justice upon certain mortals for this purpose: that, emerging from the innermost recesses of the soul through earnestness in good works into the open, it may be able boldly to rebuke the vicious strength of those who walk about it.

Hence it is that divine Wisdom willed that blessed man—according to the stepmotherly proclamation of the grim-faced Pharaoh—violently exposed in the enigmatic river of dark Egypt, should be preserved by the regard of merciful providence. Thus it might instruct him in deeper mysteries, show him the bush burning without suffering consumption, and through him, by a new manifestation of many signs, soften the hard and unrepentant heart of the hostile Pharaoh; entrust to him the burdensome leadership of a people long exiled; make the waves of the sea yield at his command and the struck rock, contrary to its nature, furnish streams of water; call him, after the rest of the multitude had been dismissed, up the mountain and honour him with the privilege of familiar discourse; deliver to him tablets of the covenant consecrated by a heavenly mystery; and through him prescribe new forms of sacrifice for the ancient people, newly stripped of its garment, and shape the conduct of the nation consecrated to himself according to the measure of his goodness.

[Col. 0163C] There are, I say, many such examples which Scripture itself has set before us. If human frailty keeps them continually before its eyes, it will learn from considering them how to flee the snares of temptations and, by following their example, how to rise into perseverance in good works.

Therefore the manner of life of every holy man living in this world ought to be examined, so that a useful example may be drawn from it. But when the earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, care must be taken that his memory is not allowed to grow obsolete. Although provident death removes him from the world, the fragrance of an honourable reputation should nevertheless represent him through his religious works.

Accordingly, in pursuing the order of this history according to the slight capacity of my weak understanding, I shall first mention Abbot Thomas. Although he is not commemorated by the praise of human speech, his works nevertheless speak for him. Thomas was of humble birth, but he redeemed his natural poverty by no ordinary uprightness of character. When he had most fervently set his hand to the Lord’s plough, and the providence of the heavenly Dispenser had appointed him after Hugh to hold the government of this place, he wished not so much to rule as to be of service. Mindful of the prophetic saying, “Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4), he held the rod in discipline and did not relinquish the staff in consolation.

[Col. 0163D] Both were established in his mind with such balance of discretion—mercy giving just counsel and discipline inflicting punishment piously—that he neither wounded his subjects by excessive harshness nor weakened them by undue gentleness. This man possessed manifold grace in divine gifts; among these he was adorned with the more eminent prerogative of the word of knowledge. Yet he did not wish to use the gift of knowledge as one might an idle tool, nor to place the fruit of profit arising from it in its mere possession. All his diligence concerned divine worship; all concerned the care of the brethren.

What more need be said? In his time he manfully maintained the strictness of the Order; he transformed its buildings from few into many, from very small into very great; wisely acquired what he did not possess, faithfully administered what he had acquired, and most strictly preserved what he had administered. Thus he has attained a celebrated name even to the present day. And, to speak truly, this praise attributed to him will seem small if weighed in the balance of the heart against the multitude of his works.

But lest the sharpness of wine be destroyed by water mixed with it, and a little leaven corrupt the whole lump, let these few words which we have spoken beforehand in his praise be regarded as an interval between the rusticity of our discourse and the loftiness of his speech.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] *idus*, that is, divisions.]

The prologue ends.

THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0165]

[Col. 0165A] At the time when Innocent, after the death of Honorius, had newly been raised to exercise the apostolic office and, after the solemn celebration of the council, returned from France, William, Count of Poitou, who had set out as a pilgrim for St James, was seized by a severe illness and brought to the extremity of death. When the fatal cutting-off provided for him by God drew near—

[Note: [Col. 0165D] Read: *occatio*, that is, a cutting-off, from *occa*, “a harrow,” French *herse*.]

—and he saw that the unavoidable exhalation of his spirit was imminent, he summoned the magnates and leading men of his land and bound them by the compulsion of an oath: they were to join his daughter in marriage to Louis, son of King Louis, and assign his land to them both according to the custom of marriage. William himself, removed from human affairs, was buried in that same church of St James.

[Col. 0165B] Now the son of the aforesaid king, named Louis, was a young man distinguished by elegance of person and splendidly endowed with upright character and piety, keen in quickness of understanding and wisdom.
