That wise Craftsman, so to speak, had brought him forth among his contemporaries as a more fragrant little flower; even in the tenderness of his earliest youth he plainly displayed the disposition of his future worth.

Therefore, as the marriage with the maiden destined for him drew near, his father Louis prepared the necessities for the journey and laboured to bring so great a matter swiftly to completion. Once an imperial summons had been publicly proclaimed everywhere, no small companies of soldiers hastened together, while cities and towns sent forth multitudes of their inhabitants to enlarge the royal retinue. Among them were the chief and most famous magnates: Theobald, Count of Blois; Ralph of Vermandois; William of Nevers; and Rotrou of Perche. By their own will and that of the king they had brought a force of their own soldiers, and rendered honour and reverence to the king as their lord.

[Col. 0165C] Among them also was Geoffrey, bishop of the province of Chartres, not lacking in literary learning and renowned as an administrator and manager of secular affairs. Earlier popes had always held him as a friend and intimate, and, because of the greatness of the worth and distinction with which he was endowed, had entrusted to him the legation of all Aquitaine.

Setting out from Gaul, they came to Bordeaux, and there more splendid preparations were made for celebrating the royal wedding. Nor was the preceding gathering of soldiers sufficient for Louis: he additionally summoned an immense multitude of Poitevins. A general festivity was proclaimed, prompted by the exaltation of their common lord. All came forward and made display without measure or number, as though they had unanimously conspired to empty the royal coffers.

[Col. 0165D] What manifold magnificence of expenditure was displayed there could scarcely be uttered by the tongue of Cicero; nor could that memorable memory of Seneca comprehend the precious variety of royal dishes and luxuries.

Therefore, with all the bishops of Aquitaine standing by together with their archbishop Geoffrey, Louis was joined in lawful marriage to the girl named Aenor. There each was adorned with the placing of golden crowns. There Louis also received the compacts of fealty and homage, and began to hold them as his own.

But because night presses upon day and the turns of human fortune often change, Fortune, which had smiled upon him cheerfully and gladly in the magnificent glory of that honour, finally changed the deceptive colour of her countenance and occupied the culmination of joy with untimely grief. For while all were still dissolved in the abundance and delight of that sumptuous feast, behold: a messenger, arriving in swift course, flew up and announced that King Louis, who had long suffered from severe diarrhoea, had ended his life at Paris.

[Col. 0166A] We do not set forth the life or virtue of this king, because it appears still to be written in people’s minds through memory. But if anyone wishes to know more fully the distress of the illness in which he lay, the eminence of the Christian confession which he maintained while alive and professed when dying, the manner of his death, and also the precious place of his burial, let him diligently consult certain readings composed by the wise man Suger and read on his anniversary.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] See our edition of Suger, under the year 1152.]

But we must return to the matters above.

When, therefore, as we have said, the death of his father was heard, the tender heart of the new bridegroom was thrown into immeasurable confusion; stripping off the garment of joy, he put on the tunic of mourning. The loss of one caused him great sorrow, whom the acquisition of another had greatly gladdened. And he whom the unfamiliar law of a marital union had made depart into a foreign land, the memory of filial affection compelled to return to his native country.

[Col. 0166C] Having therefore taken counsel with magnates and wise men concerning the necessity of returning, all agreed and determined that he should hasten into the regions of Gaul, lest by clinging to lesser matters he lose greater ones. But since marital affection troubled his mind, it seemed fitting to provide some more distinguished man to whom, by royal command, he might entrust the guardianship of his wife.

Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, was chosen; the care of that lady and provision for all her needs were wholly entrusted to him, until a messenger should be sent from the king at the request of them both. Departing from Aquitaine, Louis made for Paris, which is pre-eminent among other cities. There, receiving the sovereignty of the kingdom due to him by hereditary law, he possessed and governed it without opposition from anyone.

[Col. 0167A] The aforementioned Innocent, whose election and certain deeds have been set forth more fully in the preceding book, left the regions of Gaul and entered Rome, whence he had come. But because Peter, an unjust rival, had drawn the greater part of the city to his side, Innocent could not at that time obtain the fullness of the honour due to him. Indeed, with the summit of apostolic dignity in a sense divided in two, Innocent alone possessed the church of St Peter, upon which the dignity of the divine priesthood depended, whereas Peter occupied the seat of the Lateran palace, to which imperial eminence pertains.

From that point the bitterness of that poisonous dissension began to spread more openly everywhere, and the whole city was divided by the increasingly evident streams of the hateful schism. The rustic proverb now seemed true: “It is difficult for the enclosure of one dwelling to contain both a wolf and a lamb.”

[Col. 0167B] Since that division, unless it soon ended, would occasion the greatest harm to the people, the city, and the dignity itself, Innocent yielded place to violence and, adopting the sounder course, went to Pisa.

In that tumult of persecutors there was a certain Gerard of Angoulême, an incitement to envy, a root of sin, nourishment of malice. Relying on this man’s support, Peter had arrogantly seized that honour, and, urged on by him, wished to bring to completion the wrongdoing which he had irrationally begun through him. Gerard had already lived many years, but wickedness still flourished especially in him. Quarrels and dissensions had always pleased him; having expelled every good affection, they possessed his soul as though by hereditary right. Having therefore been habituated to such vice, he could no longer be without it, because—this being the last degree of evils—he loved his evil works. For this reason it was difficult for him to be cleansed from the vice in which he had long lain: he was not merely defiled, but infected.

[Col. 0167C] Since he had maliciously rubbed Peter and his accomplices raw in their wickedness by perverse counsels, he continually made them more hostile to Innocent. Innocent remained at Pisa until Peter, his death bringing the matter to an end, relinquished the dignity of the Apostolic See. Then Innocent returned to Rome and was honourably received with the favour and acclamations of both his own party and the other’s; he was gloriously elevated to the honour of the supreme pontificate, and began fully and wholly to possess what he had formerly held only in part.

After the settlement of the contention which had existed between himself and Peter, he assembled at Rome a principal council of the universal Church, in order decently to arrange and dispose the Church’s urgent needs there. When an incomparable gathering of all the prelates had been made, he—pre-eminent in the splendour of his attire, more reverent in the very appearance of his countenance than others, and likewise more eminent in learned knowledge—rose among them to address the matters which seemed most opportune, and began thus:

[Col. 0167D] “The sum of my address is wholly directed to you, who are not the seed of Canaan but special heirs and all sons of the Most High; who, receiving from the true Judah, as signs of divine generation, the bracelet of continence, the staff of severity and justice, and the ring of perfection, wear these, with discretion, upon arm, hand, and finger; and who, having become one spirit with God, taste nothing else.

“You, I say, whose prudent foresight watches over the care of souls, in whom the dignity of your authentic title implants the property of corresponding action. You know that Rome is the head of the world, and that the height of ecclesiastical honour is received from the permission of the Roman pontiff, as by the custom of feudal right, and is not lawfully held without his permission. You know also that it is his proper office to make the dissentient peaceful, and wisely to arrange and order what is confused.

[Col. 0168A] “For it is impossible for ointment to descend upon the beard if it does not overflow upon the head. A weak head makes the whole body weak. Nor is it customary for a physician suffering the torment of the same illness to cure another sick person. And if the supreme pontiff is separated from God by wickedness, it can scarcely happen that others are reconciled to God through him.

“Therefore, as often as the lethargic enemy rises against the peace given by God on earth to people of good will and attempts to lift its poisonous head against canonical ordinances, so often must it be crushed by that strong woman commended by Solomon through zeal for justice, lest, if it escapes punishment after a first or second conflict, it afterward grow more destructively insolent. For it was said long before our time that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome by reason, but scarcely brought to rest. Though we have often learned this by hearing it, we have now experienced it with the event itself making it manifest.

[Col. 0168B] “And, what cannot be said without tears, we have been preserved to see every sacred law trampled down; power used in place of law; the laws of the fatherland dissolved; justice denied to the living; peace denied to citizens; and the observance of divine worship violated. We ought indeed to have preceded a certain funeral of maternal solemnity with fuller lamentation and most wretched wailing, and, as it were, to have followed the interrupted services of the divine mystery as funeral rites—provoked by the presumptuous impulse of certain persons who did not understand their measure.

“For just as Nimrod once attempted to raise a tower of confusion against the Lord, so these men attempted to raise the profane swelling of their stiff-neckedness against God—because the Holy Spirit is God—and against his Christs. Divided among themselves by differences of error, as though by discordance of tongues, they have been separated from the unity of the Church; and they have sinned against the Holy Spirit because, not retaining unity with their brethren, they have been deprived of the grace of charity.

[Col. 0168C] “For whoever does not love the unity of the Church does not possess the charity of God. The words of Augustine testify that whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however laudably he may think that he lives, does not have life in himself by reason of this crime alone, namely that he is separated from the unity of Christ; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him.

“The blameworthy rashness of such men has therefore supplied cause for our indignation—indeed, our just indignation—not envy. Having broken the bonds of divine ordinance and showing no concern for priestly reverence, they attempted to cast down and annihilate the authority of so great a name and the power of spiritual grace. They ascended there of their own accord, though neither the authority of canonical institutions had raised them nor the will of reasonable men permitted them.

[Col. 0169A] “Therefore, since the precepts of divine law and the inviolable enactments of the holy canons were tools in the peace of the Church, they ought to be weapons in time of war. And those things which have long remained untouched must be seized swiftly in so deadly a necessity.”

With these and similar assertions the lord apostolic imparted the honeycombs of the divine word to the other prelates, showing all by manifest reasoning that Peter Leonis had made himself equal to the vicar of the Apostle Peter, not by the assent of others but by robbery. All the religious men to whom that detestable schism was displeasing unanimously applauded his words with great praise. He answered:

“Since disorderly persons have decreed disorderly things, we destroy whatever he enacted; we depose from rank whomever he exalted; and we deprive of order and depose all whom he consecrated. And all who attained to the office of the altar through Gerard of Angoulême we forbid by apostolic authority to perform it; while permanently remaining in that rank of orders, they shall not ascend to a higher one.”

[Col. 0169B] Having said this, he named individually those whom he knew to be guilty, reproaching them with indignation and rebuke; he violently snatched pastoral staffs from their hands and shamefully stripped from their shoulders the pontifical pallia, in which the highest dignity consists. He also removed without any regard for mercy the rings in which is expressed the Church’s espousal to them.

Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres and, as was said above, legate of all Aquitaine, receiving the lord pope’s command, diligently travelled throughout the whole region of Gaul, including Aquitaine itself. All the altars of holy churches which either Gerard, that author and holder of the sedition, or Gilo, bishop of Tusculum, or their accomplices had consecrated with the blessing of chrismal anointing during the time of that hateful schism, he demolished with his own hands. Leaving no stone upon another which he did not overthrow, he razed them utterly to the ground; and, as reason required, he took care that other altars should be restored in their place.

[Col. 0169C] Abbot Thomas happened to be absent from the special gathering of the aforesaid council because of a certain necessity. Taking this occasion, Archbishop Henry suspended him, although King Louis had sent to that archbishop a letter in his excuse. After the passage of several days, however, a monk of the church named Bartholomew, wise and sprung from noble stock, approached the archbishop. By the persistence of his prayers as well as the demonstration of reason, he made him favourable to the abbot and obtained from him permission for Thomas to perform again the pastoral office.

Returning, Bartholomew reported what he had accomplished; and, greatly gladdening all the monks of Morigny, he secured the abbot’s recovery of his place. This Bartholomew was then prior of Vieilles-Étampes. Along with obtaining pardon for the abbot, on that journey he asked the archbishop to increase the income of the church of St Martin, which had then been fixed at six pounds, to fifteen pounds; this he willingly obtained from him.

[Col. 0170A] But the abbot, broken by the injustice of the frequent troubles inflicted upon him and then desolated by the violence of rising affairs and persecutions, did not remain long in his restored honour. Deceived by the evil counsel of a certain Odo, one of our professed brethren and then abbot of St Rémi, he abandoned the care of his abbey without receiving pontifical permission and without the assent and leave of the community entrusted to him. For the sake of pursuing a more secluded life and spiritual quiet, he withdrew to St Martin of the Fields, a church then most renowned for the strictness of its Order.

Thus, when Thomas had withdrawn from the government of this monastery about mid-Lent, we long remained orphans without a father, and our mother as though a widow. Hearing of Thomas’s removal, the desolation of the abbey, and the future injury to the Order unless help were quickly provided, the king laboured and took pains with great zeal to hasten matters so that the business of election might come under his effective control, lest the burden of need or pressing poverty weary the church stripped of a governor’s prudent care.

[Col. 0170B] Although, in the eyes of secular men, who are bleary-eyed, he was applying himself to a pious work, the execution of that work was neither just nor honourable to our church. For he attempted, at this very point of the approaching election, to draw an abbey which was free and had been emancipated from every obligation since the time of his grandfather through the generosity of Wulgrin, under the constraint of coercive power. He intended that our monks should not have a free voice in their election, but should receive, like subjects, an abbot imposed upon them through the hand and judgement of others.

To bring about this violence, Odo, abbot of St Rémi, and Joscelin, abbot of St Peter at Melun, were sent to us, bringing letters that declared the royal will. The king’s will was that, whichever monk from the community of St Martin they named to us, we should install in Thomas’s place without daring any delay.

[Col. 0170C] The time had now come that was acceptable for carrying out the king’s command, but it was not a day of salvation for our honour. They were now discussing the election when the highest King, for whom to serve is to reign, preferred his own ordinance to that of the earthly king and suddenly overthrew by the event what had been commanded.

For letters useful to us from the Archbishop of Sens were brought into the abbots’ presence. They forbade an election, if one were to be made, and reduced it to nothing if it had been made. Those letters contained the just and reasonable complaint of that archbishop: Thomas had suddenly, foolishly, and without consideration abandoned the government of the abbey, which he had received through the archbishop, without his permission and without the approving consent of the brethren subject to him.

At that time this archbishop had the greatest goodwill toward us; therefore, even though the king opposed us, he supported the advantage of our side.

[Col. 0171A] A second time the king sent to us persons of great reputation: his chancellor Natalis; the abbot of Rebais; Alwin, bishop of Arras; Master Hugh of St Victor, eminent in letters beyond many masters; and several other masters. With a severe command he declared that our election was to depend entirely on their judgement and that our community must not neglect to obey their decision.

But we, seeing with lynx-like eyes what was necessary for us, declared that we were not sons of the bondwoman but of the free woman. Advancing against the adverse force of their opinion, we stopped their mouths, so to speak, by speaking beforehand, as though unanimously proclaiming that we chose Macharius, prior of Longpont, to be our abbot and father. That prior was a nephew of Alberic, bishop of Ostia; in him the branch of probity and wisdom had so sprouted and grown to perfection that he was regarded as familiar to the king and the magnates of France.

[Col. 0171B] Since such a man, and one of such standing, had been chosen by us, those who had come to compel us did not dare in any way to oppose it because of his great authority. Thus we received, with our freedom preserved, him whom we had chosen in order to acquire freedom.

Having crossed the sea of so great a danger, we drowned our rivals, so to speak, overwhelmed with shame in the sea of confusion. Presenting the election that had been made to the king, we received his favourable assent; he extolled with great praise the vigour of our worth and our invincible defence of customary freedom.

Our election was again made known to the Archbishop of Sens, but his consent to the election already made could not be drawn from him. He again objected that Thomas had not been released by him from the office of pastoral care, and that therefore no one could regularly be ordained and substituted in his place.

[Col. 0171C] When these matters were again brought to the king’s attention, unwilling that the church’s trouble—which he had believed finished—should be repeated, he ordered Thomas not to allow his godson to let the monks of Morigny be vexed for so long in this manner, but to go to Sens and leave the pastoral care, having been released from it into the archbishop’s hand.

Thomas, therefore, led to Sens by the prior of St Martin, began to negotiate with the archbishop about his resignation. When he wished to surrender by a book the ministry of pastoral care which he had received by a staff, Henry refused, saying that, just as the assumption of government had been made by delivery of the pastoral staff, so the resignation must be made by surrender of the same. And this was done.

At that very hour Thomas was excluded from the governance of our monastery. Two of our monks who were present, Landric and Robert, presented to the archbishop the election of Lord Macharius. Hearing this, the archbishop burst out in approving laughter.

[Col. 0171D] “When Thomas has been your father until this day,” he said, “by what reasoning did you presume to elect another? And now you present to us as authoritative the very election which we had notified you by letter was invalid in our judgement? Know that the course of your labour up to this point has been spent in vain. Henceforth use your free power: go and make an election according to the rule of your founder.”

Hearing this, the aforesaid monks hastened to return quickly to us and reported to the general chapter what the archbishop had made known to them. Once more the wiser men of the church were summoned for counsel, and the question of what ought to be done was discussed. Our community, so to speak, did not weave the web it had begun with an altered thread. All agreed to the election already made of Macharius and established it with every possibility of change removed.

[Col. 0172A] We therefore sent the aforesaid monks to Cluny and instructed them to request from the abbot of that place that Macharius be released and emancipated from the yoke of obedience. Carrying out the embassy entrusted to them, they came to Cluny and returned with letters concerning the matter for which they had sworn. They requested the archbishop to bless the abbot and showed him the letters of emancipation.

After reading them, the archbishop did not find in them a complete demonstration of emancipation. He therefore postponed the blessing, lest, if he blessed a man still subject, he might thereby bring upon us a greater vexation of trouble than that which we had already endured. He sent us word, therefore, that we should request a fuller emancipation from the abbot of Cluny, asserting that he would never confer the customary blessing upon him unless he knew that he had been more fully released from the yoke of obedience.

The obedience of this journey was again imposed upon Robert of Bruges. Taking royal letters and accompanied by Peter, the king’s chaplain, and Master Simon of Pissy, whom the king was sending to Rome on certain business, he came to Cluny.

[Col. 0172B] Receiving letters drawn up in accordance with his wish, he brought them to the archbishop, who accepted their completeness. Lord Macharius was therefore led to Sens, solemnly blessed by him, entrusted with the care of the pastoral office, sent back to us, and received by us in solemn procession.

In these days certain events occurred worthy of being made clear by their narration. The clerics of Vieilles-Étampes, vomiting forth the madness of their poisonous hearts which they had always harboured since the monks’ introduction, rose in bold opposition against our monks on the vigil of St Martin. They assailed some with dishonourable and shameful words, and others with blows.

Lord Macharius had then gone to Rome. The prior sent a messenger to him and made known everything which the clerics had done. In order to remove utterly from the roots the occasion for their wrongdoing, Macharius obtained on that journey an apostolic privilege concerning their removal from that church, and so prudently expelled them, whether they wished it or not. He also brought with him a privilege concerning the establishment of a confraternity.

[Col. 0172C] In those same days Henry, Archbishop of Sens, reached the end of his life; he was succeeded by the venerable Hugh, then precentor of that church.

At that time also the Church of Bourges, grievously desolated by the death of its pastor, was shaken by the outbreak of the disease of a serious and troublesome schism. The evil of this discord advanced so far that it reached the pope and the king of France. Certain clerics of that church, with the king’s approval, wished to set a certain man of Cahors over themselves. The other party desired to confer the pre-eminence of that honour upon Peter, cousin of Haimeric, the Roman chancellor.

But the pope loved the chancellor and accordingly loved his compatriot for the chancellor’s sake. Therefore, having consecrated Peter as their archbishop, he gave him his full support. Although Peter was to be appointed against the king’s will, the pope sent him to Bourges and deprived the man of Cahors of every ecclesiastical honour.

[Col. 0173A] Seeing that his will could not attain its effect, the king was shaken by no small surge of anger. As though wishing to turn his conceived indignation against the pope’s authority, he forbade Peter entry into all his territory. Innocent, however, drawing the ecclesiastical sword for vengeance, prohibited the celebration of divine offices throughout the king’s entire dominion.

The evil of this discord could not be wholly sweetened throughout all the days of his life. Hence Lord Macharius, having gone to Rome for the sake of peacemaking, obtained very much through the intercession of the cardinals; but, unable to attain the welcome result of reconciliation by prayers or gifts, he returned.

On this return he brought with him a certain privilege containing every acquisition of the other abbots, so that nearly everything of greater authority was enumerated in it individually.

[Col. 0173B] It is certain that through this Macharius many benefits came to our church, and we have judged it fitting to insert some of them here. On the first return from Rome of which we have spoken, he brought with him a portion of the Lord’s Cross, reverently covered with a wrought overlay of precious metal. He also brought three precious cloths, from which certain vestments were made.

This church was further enlarged by him through the establishment of religious life and the Cluniac Order, as well as through shrewd and provident administration of external resources.

The aforesaid Pope Innocent, paying the debt of human condition, died at Rome. Celestine succeeded to his honour; he was also called Master Guido of Castello. He was most worthy of that prelacy, because three things which are reckoned almost the chief among human gifts had come together in him and made him a celebrated master: nobility of lineage, an energy of mind equal in every condition, and manifold learning in letters, to the study of which he was most intensely devoted.

[Col. 0173C] Our king sent envoys to him to make peace. They obtained it through a most gracious petition in such a way that, before them and many nobles—by whose multitude Rome is accustomed to resound—he kindly rose, raised his hand, made the sign of blessing toward this region, and released it from the sentence of interdict.

But death, sparing no one, snatched so great a pontiff from the world by a premature removal in the seventh month of his pontificate. Once he had put off the prison-house of flesh, Lucius, Gerard of Santa Croce, was appointed pope in his place. He too was a most vigorous man, but was overtaken by death even more quickly.

Wishing to provide for the condition of various churches, he took care to send two legates from his side: Alberic of Ostia to France and Haimeric of Tusculum to England. Uprooting what was harmful and building what was useful, they found the abbey of St Benedict in a ruinous condition, owing both to the frivolity of its monks and to the consent of its pastors.

[Col. 0173D] Desiring through humble and pious help to provide assistance at the opportune time, they removed the abbot who presided over it and transferred Lord Macharius there, to reform its condition manfully according to the custom of Cluny. Releasing us, therefore, from obedience to him, they gave us leave and power to choose a father.

Following the intimation of the spirit of counsel which it had brought us concerning this matter, we chose Thevinus, prior of Argenteuil, renowned for manifold praise of wisdom. Of him I can affirm, without any uncertainty of falsehood, that in all his time no person more graceful and handsome was seen in France.

When the king and the aforesaid bishops had confirmed this election, Lord Thoinus went to Sens and was solemnly elevated by the blessing of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, who customarily acts as the archbishop’s vicar in the exercise of his office during the archbishop’s absence.

[Col. 0174C] The aforesaid Pope Lucius, however, after a short time—namely, when he had completed the fifth month of his pontificate—left the things beneath the moon through the inevitable suffering of eclipse [death]. He was succeeded by Eugenius, also called Bernard of Pisa, then a monk of Clairvaux, a man of most continent conduct and life. In the first year of his elevation our abbot foresaw what was necessary for himself, and accumulated a certain sum of money, which would both protect him from the burden of poverty and adequately meet the needs of expenditure. In the second year he adorned the church with a new roof-covering and the boarding of a new ceiling. He did the same for the dormitory. For divine power had bestowed upon this man such grace in administering the affairs of the church that what would be exceedingly difficult for another [Col. 0174D] he regarded as a light matter to accomplish; and whatever his subtle intellect had conceived by effort, he strove to put into effect without the obstacle of delay. Thus the anointing of the Holy Spirit, in whose precepts he had delighted from early age, taught him concerning all things: both to ensure that the established order was firmly observed, and not, after the manner of a foolish man, to allow himself to be overcome by the bustle of external works. Since his foresight brought several benefits to our house, it has seemed good to mention here some principal ones.

Within the abbey walls, then, he built at great expense a noble hall with certain appurtenances; another excellent one at Vieilles-Étampes; a third, of middling size, at La Ferté; and a fourth at Stripiniac, surpassing all those named. [Col. 0175A] Moreover, he bought the tithe of Gomarville and half a ploughland of arable ground, along with many other things which we have judged superfluous to recount, because we have them recorded in the cartulary preserved among us. If, moreover, one turns to the monastery’s necessities, he is known to have adorned it with chalices, books, chasubles, copes, hangings, and many other ornaments.

In the first year in which he presided over us, Thomas, who had once been our Father, while residing at the monastery of Coulombs, was brought to his last day. In the same year Lord Abbot Theoinus, approaching the king, who was staying at Orléans, requested that the privilege which the king’s father had granted our church should, by confirmation in the king’s own decree, be made permanent on his part. Having obtained what he sought, he carried away that decree, [Col. 0175B] embracing everything which the king’s father had given or conceded.

In the same year, too, the city of Edessa, while the vigilance of our people slept, was captured by the enemies of Christ’s cross and suddenly passed under Saracen dominion. Consequently an immeasurable anguish of grief struck to the depths those dwelling in the region adjoining Jerusalem. Envoys therefore came from Antioch and Jerusalem into our region, sent by the leading men of those parts, earnestly beseeching that the unconquerable valor of the Franks might remedy the danger that had occurred and repel those to come. Hearing this, our king, being most compassionate, took pity on the misery of those overseas; and, so that the compassion conceived from it might bear some fruit, he summoned the greater men of his realm at Easter to [Col. 0175C] Vézelay, as necessity required. Addressing them all in a pious manner and recalling the customary valor of the Franks, he said:

“A great disgrace will come upon us if the Philistine begins to reproach the household of David; if a demonic nation begins to possess what a nation devoted to divine worship has held for a long time; if dead dogs mock living valor, especially that of the Franks, whose courage remained free even amid chains; a courage which, however tightly pressed by any necessity, could not endure even an insult inflicted upon it; which readily brought help to friends at the fitting time, and did not cease to pursue enemies even after death. Let that valor, therefore, not grow arrogant, but by courageous assistance raise up the friends of God and of ourselves—that is, the Christians overseas; and let it drive away with severe persecution vile enemies, unworthy even of the name of men. Let us go, men of valor; let us resist worshippers of idols; let us set out for the places which we know were once trodden by the feet of the God-man, and in which he also suffered those things which were worthy of his presence and bodily visitation. God will rise with us, and his enemies shall be scattered; those who hate him shall flee before our face. They shall be confounded, I say, and turned backward, all who hate Zion, if [Col. 0176A] our valor acts manfully and our confidence does not depart from God. Know that a great devotion to this cause already rests upon me. Therefore I earnestly beseech you to strive to strengthen my purpose by your company and help.”

The king’s words were thus fixed deeply in the hearts of many who had assembled. Accordingly, having taken up the crosses with the king himself, they made for Jerusalem after a short time. The more renowned among all those who underwent the hardships of this expedition with the king were: Henry, emperor of the Germans; Robert, the king’s brother; Henry, count of Meaux; Geoffrey [read: Thierry], count of Flanders; Alwin, bishop of Arras; Giraud, bishop of Langres; Gaucher of Mont-Gai; the count of Warenne; Rainald of Tornedor; Manasses of Bulles; and Everard [Col. 0176B] of Breteuil.

The king, wishing to arrange the kingdom’s guardianship by prudent counsel, caused the leading men of France to assemble at Étampes. There he committed the administration of the realm itself to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, a man second to none in the management of secular affairs and also distinguished by the title of literary learning, and to Ralph, count of Vermandois, his kinsman. Before the king departed, Pope Eugenius came into France in order to strengthen by his persuasion what the Spirit of God had inspired. Rejoicing in his blessing, they immediately undertook that pious pilgrimage.

The lord pope, after holding a council at Reims, came to Paris and remained there for some time. Afterwards . . . coming into that city for several days . . . since, as befitted so great a man, he was most lavishly received by . . . [Col. 0176C] the Gallican churches were heavily burdened by this. Our abbot also contributed twenty pounds toward his maintenance, at the urging of the archbishop of Sens. Afterwards the lord apostolic, wishing to return to his own country, subjected to the sentence of anathema all who should dare to disturb the realm before the king’s return.

Our king then pursued the undertaking laboriously, but not wisely: he adopted counsels that should not have been accepted and, walking on an untrodden road, did not guard against thorns being driven into his feet. Hence, after his army had been devastated and his strength weakened, he finally reached Jerusalem with difficulty. Remaining there for a year and more, he was unable to accomplish anything useful, memorable, or . . . worthy of France. Thus, by an obscure . . . from the overseas [Col. 0176D] regions, he made his way . . . and by his departure very much . . . .

But in the fourth [year] after . . . our abbot Thevinus, putting off the tunic of corruptible flesh, was buried before the altar of the abbey, to be endowed and glorified by God with a gift so much greater as he is known to have labored more diligently in adorning His bride.

Holy Father, farewell; to you, a spiritual gift.

ANNO DOMINI 1147. JOHN, MONK OF SAINT LAWRENCE AT LIÈGE

[Col. 0177]

## NOTICE

(Dom Bernard Pez, Preface to vol. IV of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. XVII.)

Whatever may be said about the author of the following little work has been briefly comprised by Reiner, a disciple of John, in book I, chapter 16, *On the Writers of His Monastery*. “John,” he says, “brother of Gislebert both in spirit and in flesh, was a scholastic, distinguished both by learning and office; as a boy, no one ever feared his master’s rod more than Hercules’ club. Alas, how often, while he demands or examines our little works and gazes with his one eye askance at tablets seized in his hooked hands, I thought that I had encountered that one-eyed Polyphemus of Virgil! On one occasion he fell ill and, in a marvellous manner, was made beside himself and above himself; he saw many things worthy of remembrance, which he published in writing for the grace of edification. He also composed two chants, namely, one on Saint Christopher the martyr and one on Saint Mary of Egypt. He rendered the history of Tobit and likewise the Martyrdom of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr in heroic metre, and set the Song of Songs, to some extent, antiphonally to music.” The distinguished and most diligent Father Lombard, who lamented bitterly to me that nothing of these works survives today in his library except the *Vision of the State of Souls after Death*, etc., also noted that John flourished under both abbots named Wazelin. The first ceased to govern the monastery of Saint Lawrence and died in 1147; the second, in 1156.

[Col. 0177]

## VISION OF THE STATE OF SOULS AFTER DEATH, AND MIRACLE OF SAINT LAWRENCE THE MARTYR

(Extracted from a manuscript codex of Saint Lawrence at Liège by the Reverend and Learned Dom Father Celestine Lombard, librarian of that place; published by the Reverend Father Dom Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, part III, p. 5.)

Here begins the Vision of a certain monk concerning the state of souls after death.

[Col. 0177A] § I. At that time there was in this monastery of Blessed Lawrence a brother named John, brother of the monk Gislebert, who composed chants about several saints. Through an incautious bloodletting, the blood inflamed by burning fevers set his brain ablaze. As his illness grew for four days, the feast-day of Blessed Martin the bishop arrived. By order of his abbot, therefore, he was carried into a more secluded cell. And while all, at the fading of daylight, hastened to the office of evening praise, [Col. 0178A] he alone was left there in his bed; those who had undertaken to watch him believed that he had fallen asleep.

But he, having fallen into ecstasy—that is, into a departure from his mind—saw himself as though standing in a certain vestibule, before whose eyes a painting was displayed. Above, he saw the Crucifixion of the Lord arranged; below, scenes from Samson’s deeds: his death and the collapse of the house. While he was looking at these, he felt, as though above his head, a person standing with an ivory rod in his hand and speaking thus with certain persons standing around:

“O how delightful and pleasant it is to direct the mind to divine things, since every wise person could profitably apply his study to the subject matter of such deeds and furnish an eloquence of beauty for the benefit of their souls. This man ought to have had this purpose and this study, if he had taken to heart the salvation of his own soul and the benefit of his brothers.”

The brother heard these words, and it came into his mind that this was Blessed Lawrence. He therefore stood astonished, waiting to hear him say more.

§ II. Then the blessed martyr, directing the rod which he held in his hand at the brother’s head, said: “Which of [Col. 0179B] all the saints has conferred greater benefits upon you? Under whose shelter have you made greater progress? Who fed you? Who taught you? Who set you to serve God? Confess, I say, if you do not wish to end your life in this present illness.”

At this he trembled. “And what,” he said, “can I answer, when I begin to hear such grievous things? What good can I hope for hereafter? Blessed Lawrence is indeed my patron; he received me as a boy, he himself nourished and taught me, and above all the saints I owe thanks to him.”

After he had said this, it occurred to him that perhaps what he saw was an illusion; he began to fortify his forehead with the sign of the cross. To this Blessed Lawrence the martyr replied: “No, brother, you are not being deceived by a phantom; [Col. 0179C] the sign of the cross is familiar to us also. By the sign of the cross God has deigned to work many things through us.” On hearing this, the brother, while all those standing around pitied him, threw himself at his knees, crying out and asking for his mercy.

Then the most kindly Blessed Lawrence the martyr was moved by the wishes of those around him; touching the prostrate man with his rod, he said: “Hope, and do not despair. However you have lived hitherto, or whatever you have done, examination of it will for the present be deferred, and your life in the body will be prolonged by so many years. I shall be an observer and witness of how, from day to day, your amendment, your concern for salvation, and your timely and moderate admonition of the negligent are carried out. Of all these things, I say, I shall be a witness; and if this prolongation of your life proves vain, [Col. 0179D] I shall be a terrible examiner of your negligences and contempt.”

§ III. Restored to hope by these words, and now presuming to speak and lift his head, the brother said: “Behold, my lord, by how great an illness I am oppressed, and, as I am told, by the incurable pain of burning fevers!”

“Why do you doubt,” said Blessed Lawrence the patron, “about present recovery? You shall not die at all from this present affliction.”

The brother answered humbly: “Give me your blessing, most blessed one, after which I shall be unable to doubt my recovery.” Having received it, he rose; now trusting in the grace of his patron, he began, at his bidding, to follow that guide upward. He felt himself ascending through the spaces of the air, especially [Col. 0180A] when he still heard, far below him through an immense stretch of air, the two greater bells of the church sounding in equal resonance for the office of evening. He recognized what this was and perceived that the sound was passing very high through the clouds. While he attended to this, he nevertheless did not forget his ascent; and, following the blessed patron at a very great distance, he sometimes did not see him, and when he feared that he had lost him, he felt him near before him.

His ascent seemed to proceed straight upward until he reached a circle above which he hovered in a marvellous manner. He saw the sphere revolve with a wonderful sound, and a voice resounded, saying: “Who will answer the one who afflicts?” Beneath that sphere he saw the air grow dark, and certain spectres, as though from below, leap upward. But when they heard the sound of the revolving sphere above, they vanished as smoke vanishes, and, in accordance with the devil’s name, flowed downward. That voice or sound was to them as fire, and terrible as lightning from heaven. As the brother watched and marvelled, he remembered that the Venerable Bede says that demons are barred from access above the lunar circle; and, remembering also the Apostle Paul’s words, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places,” he began to consider whether this might be the boundary preventing demons’ access to the higher regions. Concerning the words he had heard, “Who will answer the one who afflicts?” [Col. 0180C] he wished to understand their sense; and he suddenly perceived in his mind this interpretation: that voice is directed against the demons, asking who can resist God or answer him—that is, enter into argument with him. God is called “the one who afflicts” because demons experience him as afflicting them not justly or fairly, but perhaps according to their own strength.

§ IV. Then, as he looked, a very long seat appeared on the eastern side, upon which persons sat in monastic habit. They sat silent and somewhat sad; their feet hung down without footstools. Their faces were half-shaven [*semi-ratae*, as written] and cast down. Yet they had the greatest consolation in this: that, although placed in purgatorial conditions, they were free from the sight and harassment of demons; retaining the blessed hope of [Col. 0180D] their salvation, they were consoled that their dwelling would be somewhat light-filled during their penance.

There were some whom he recognized there, and who saw him, but they dared neither rise from their seats nor speak to him. He also saw his natural father, set farther back, released from the chains by which he had been bound in penal confinement. The brother remained there for a long time and learned about souls what he had not known.

There are two classes of departing souls, according to the diversity of their merits, all of whom will at some time attain salvation. One class consists of souls which, on departing, are immediately reduced under the power of demons, who mock them in their torments and sufferings and threaten them with punishment and everlasting condemnation. The penance of these souls is most grievous, [Col. 0181A] because, so long as they are handed over to these torturers, they have neither angelic visitation nor light nor any hope of salvation. Yet they are not plunged into the lower hell; after some time, both rescue from the company of demons and a lighter penance in other places are granted them.

There is likewise a purification of souls which, by the merit of their life, by the commendation of the faithful, or by the intercession of most blessed patrons, attain peaceful places for their purification. Their lot is most blessed, because they do not lack hope of salvation, angelic visitation at due times, or light. Since the souls whose penance is happy undergo it without demons—neither seeing them nor being terrified by them—might anyone suppose that they suffer? They weigh all that they did on this [Col. 0181B] earth against their salvation, and all that through negligence they did too little in God’s service. How they wish they had been free of these vices and had resisted every sin, even the smallest! How they wish that at all times they had attended divine services and had not been absent even for a moment! In hunger and thirst they weigh what they here indulged by serving the belly with food and drink, through which the bond of the fear of God was loosened and the reins were relaxed for harmful pleasure. In excessive cold they weigh what here burned with the inciting fire. And, to comprehend many things in few words, they pay by diverse sufferings for whatever they here sinned through unlawful desires. They sigh because they are not admitted to divine contemplation, to which, when they ought, they neglected to cleave. Therefore their sufferings now affect them; [Col. 0181C] for the present they draw them away from the sweetness of contemplation by their bitterness and compel them to experience the scourge of God’s wrath. Their eyes—that is, their intentions—are therefore fixed upon the Lord their God until he has mercy and, by angelic visitation, releases them from their suffering. Blessed indeed are the souls who lack sufferings and thirst for God, who is the fountain of life, as the stag longs for springs of water!

But most miserably received are those souls who, for any reason, as human minds are not disposed toward a perfect manner of life, have abandoned their patrons—to whom in this life they were entrusted or to whom they entrusted themselves. For they are either committed to demons when deprived of the intervention of their proper patrons, or, if [Col. 0181D] they are spared, nevertheless exposed to demonic persecutions.

Their persecution is such that, although demons cannot inflict torment upon these wretched souls, they nonetheless do not cease to deprive them of every place of rest, whether on land, at sea, or through the spaces of the air. Souls undergoing purification in this world thirst to hear divine service; it is intolerable pain to them when demonic harassment, fear, or pursuit throws their most salutary desire into confusion.

§ V. The same brother heard an example concerning two monks, lest anyone lightly regard it as nothing to lack his proper patron. One of them, overtaken by sudden and unforeseen death, was snatched away to judgment. Although he had been liable to instability, he nevertheless deserved to be freed through the patronage of a very great patron. Though his sins required that he be condemned, by that patron’s intervention the judge was appeased, and he was handed over to a happy penance and gentle purification without demonic assault.

The other, through impatience of spirit, preferred another to his own place—that is, to his patron—while serving God there, though he did not consider it blameworthy to prefer any saint to his patron. In due course he too died. Guilty among other things of a forward tongue, and because he had counted for nothing [Col. 0182A] the protection of his own patron, he was assigned among the wretched, whose lot of penance is most grievously carried out under demonic harassment; and the number of his years was greatly prolonged.

§ VI. Having learned these and other things about the allotments of souls, the brother remembered his great guide and followed him as he went before. He understood that the guide was not alone, though he saw no one besides him. There was there a very great brightness, compared with which the brother’s soul was almost dark. Since he felt his blessed patron before him—for more often he felt him than saw him—it occurred to him to ask about the harmony of heaven, whether he might hear what he had read in the Scriptures. Answering his thought, the great guide said: “Wait, brother; what you seek will be presented to you shortly.”

While he awaited the promised harmony, he saw raised before his eyes a very large sphere. It was golden in colour, not altogether round but long and extended; its size was like the length and breadth of some very great church, except that a church has rectangularity, not roundness. This round form appeared in the likeness of the heavenly sphere twice as long as it was broad, and it revolved with great speed. From its lower extremity, which inclined toward the southern pole, sounds began to resound in a wonderful manner, as though from bronze pipes—perhaps like harpists playing on their harps in harmony. [Col. 0182C]

As he attended with delight to this gradually swelling harmony, similar voices suddenly began to answer from the upper extremity of the revolving sphere. Thus voices harmonized with voices, producing a concert that human minds cannot estimate or imagine. And while that exultant sound gradually rang out, and the soul hearing it began to be carried away by an ineffable emotion, suddenly the rapt sound and the image of the sphere fell silent and disappeared.

Then the most merciful guide, addressing the brother who was about to return, said: “Be solicitous for yourself, and avoid being overwhelmed by excessive occupations unless there is an unavoidable cause. But if you can properly perform what is imposed upon you, always giving first concern to divine service, all shall go well with you. When you descend through the space of the air, if you are asked about your guide—where he is—answer that Saint Lawrence is your guide. And if demons begin to terrify you with their phantoms, cry out his name in their faces.” Having said this, he disappeared.

§ VII. Somewhat later the brother looked eastward and saw horsemen coming toward him. It immediately occurred to him that it was Saint Maurice [Col. 0183A] who appeared in such form. As he approached with his companions, whose number the brother did not observe—though they may have been six or eight—the brother became entirely certain that it was Saint Maurice. Approaching reverently, and emboldened by confidence, he said to them: “O what strength you had in bodies of such lofty stature and whole youth, soldiers of Christ! You could have resisted your enemies manfully and gained victory over idolaters, had it pleased you to use material weapons.”

To this the most gracious leader replied: “What, brother? Have we not gained victory over the enemies of life? No victory could be more renowned or worthy of praise for us than to strike down the enemy by one’s own hand and, through the death of the body, acquire life for the soul.”

[Col. 0183B] He was clothed in a purple cloak. As the brother looked long upon it, Maurice said: “By this garment, which you inspect so closely, the soldiers of our time were distinguished from common people; and no Roman soldier was permitted to wear a cloak among others except one made of woollen cloth or purple.” It occurred to the brother to wonder whether Blessed Maurice knew him. Answering that thought gently, he said: “I know that you are a monk under the patronage of Blessed Lawrence; but I have a complaint against you. Last year, when you often visited the estate where a little church was built in my name [Note: [Col. 0183D] This is in the district of Wasega, situated in the county of Namur, where there was a little church under the title of Saint [Col. 0184D] Maurice; this estate is still subject to our Church.], and stayed there for three days or more, you never once celebrated the solemnities of Mass, nor even sang the hours of divine service before the altar erected in memory of me.”

[Col. 0183C] Hearing this and knowing it to be true—which he himself had formerly considered, but had neglected from a certain weariness and because his mind was not in that place—the brother offered the sainted martyr this excuse as satisfaction for the fault he recognized: “My lord, do not lay to heart this offense of your servant. If you deign to consider the opposition, affliction, and temptation which I endured in my soul while that estate was under my care, you will not burden your heart against me for this negligence.”

Nodding with a gracious countenance, Blessed Maurice said: “I readily grant you pardon for this offense, because you have paid more than enough penalty for this sin.” And the brother replied: “Since you remember so small an oratory [Col. 0183D] so closely as to observe what is done there, it is remarkable that you do not protect the poor tenants of that estate, or make it manifest to their enemies that you deign to care for that place.”

The blessed martyr replied: “I shall make known to you, not to their enemies, what you do not know.”

Having said this, the brother suddenly saw himself in that very little oratory with Saint Maurice. Saint Maurice stood leaning against the side of the altar that faced the road, holding the brother with his right hand against his side like a nursing child, facing the people who seemed to be standing throughout the church. He ordered the brother [Col. 0184A] to direct his gaze there and attend closely. In the middle of that church stood likewise a poor gathering of both sexes, who seemed to be praying with hands stretched out. One of them lifted up his face and clapped his palms against the altar, saying: “O Saint Maurice, great martyr, why do you not help me? Why do you not avenge me on the robbers who have stripped me of all my goods and seek to seize and kill me naked?”

The saint answered his words, shaking the man whom he held as though to make him attend: “You yourself, so far as lies in your power, are a most wicked robber and companion of thieves; wherever permitted, do you leave any evil undone? Woe to you who plunder, for you too shall be plundered.”

Again, to another who said, “Why do you sleep? Why do you close your ear to our prayers? [Col. 0184B] Why, greatest saint, do you not regard our miseries? Behold, evil men devastate me; together with my money I lose my grain,” the blessed martyr added: “You suffer this deservedly, and it is remarkable that the earth does not swallow you, for you were never faithful to the cause of God, whose man you are and from which you live: sacrilegious in withholding the tithe, a defrauder in rent, evading every duty of service. Therefore you are exposed to every enemy in such a way that every saint disdains to help you.”

Thus he charged them all with what they had done and thereby accumulated their miseries. The brother listened to everything most attentively, knowing that these things had been shown for his sake, so that he might know what he did not know. He marvelled that he was so suddenly in the oratory, all of whose structure he recognized, and that such a manifestation was made so readily by so great a martyr. [Col. 0184C] While he was in this amazement, he suddenly found himself with the saint and his companions where the saint had first spoken to him.

§ VIII. Again the saint, of wonderful condescension and moderation, told him through his inquiry in thought several things which have been omitted to avoid envy and unbelief, not because they would have had much usefulness.

The same brother felt pain in his feet and humbly begged him earnestly to give him a blessing and make the sign of the cross over the pain. The most gracious saint replied: “There is no danger in this pain.” Having been strengthened with a blessing and admonished regarding concern for salvation, he dismissed him as he reverently adored him; and, when he had gone a little way, he disappeared.

The brother, however, suddenly slipping down from the heights, descended more swiftly than speech. In the air, through which demons roamed, were shown to him lying corpses, in which human misery could be seen. There appeared there the bodies of pleasure-loving people, who had lived luxuriously and nourished them in indulgence. He saw these cast down there, some gnawed away as far as the breast, or with the belly alone left. From some, demons tore away certain parts. They mocked one man whom they dragged by the tongue, reproaching him with false testimony, perjuries, and other things; [Col. 0185A] another whom they dragged by the throat, with excessive food and drink; another by the eyes, with impure sight; another by the hands, with unlawful work. O how many men and women were there whose genital parts were torn! Who, seeing this, would not marvel? Who, hearing it, would not amend?

The brother remembered that his blessed patron had charged him, on his return, to name him if asked about his guidance. Trusting in this assurance, he passed through unafraid. But when it came time for him to enter his body, certain dreadful faces and terrible figures began to show themselves, attempting to seize him with hooked hands. He cried in their faces the name of his guide—“Lawrence the martyr!”—and this, like lightning from heaven, drove them wholly away; [Col. 0185B] nor did they appear to him again. He himself suddenly felt, by some order unknown to him, that he was in his body; and, as though waking, he lifted his head and began to look about the cell, marvelling where he was, whence he had come, and what he had seen.

§ IX. He therefore began to ponder what he had seen and told some portions of it to some of the brothers. But because, owing to illness, he could not speak for long, he was ordered to rest until he became better. After he had lain for three days as his illness increased, on the fourth day, as evening drew on, he broke into a sweat and began to discharge from his nostrils a great flow of blood. It continued without interruption throughout the long extent of the night. In the morning he lay like a dead man, emptied of blood, having used neither sleep nor food for almost seven days; for two days, by turns, he was somewhat disturbed, his senses being intercepted by empty images. Human frailty deserves pardon: when the brain is dried out, the body empty, and the blood depleted, it cannot endure without danger to life.

Having therefore been carefully watched, after two days he began, contrary to the expectation of those who had seen him, as though to revive, and to take a little sleep and food. Then, recovering over the following days, as soon as he could, he summoned one brother and had him take down on tablets what he had seen, lest it escape him. Later, rereading it, he committed it to writing, adding this to the narrative:

“As it was not within my power to fall ill, to live, or to die, so it was not mine to see and report, to ascend or descend through the air. One thing is certain: unless I had experienced it, I would not have feared; unless I had seen it, I would not have reported it. Yet I have not presumed to withhold what may perhaps benefit someone. It lies under the judgment of readers to grant it either belief or rejection. Nevertheless, we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal; and it will not be the merit of seeing but of living that is examined.”

BETWEEN THE YEARS OF THE LORD 1148–1152. WILLIAM, ABBOT OF SAINT THEODORIC NEAR REIMS

[Col. 0185]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 167.)

[Col. 0185C] William, abbot of Saint Theodoric, of the Order of Saint Benedict, at Mont d’Or near Reims from the year 1120, thereafter, about 1137, becoming through the influence of his friend Saint Bernard a Cistercian monk at the monastery of Signy, died before Bernard—that is, before 1153. [Note: [Col. 0185] The statement in the most excellent Cave, under the year 1140, that he entered the Cistercian Order in 1153, should be corrected.] On him see Bulaeus, vol. II of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 743, and Oudinus, vol. II, p. 1434 ff.

The following of his writings were published by Bertrand Tissier, or Textor, in vol. IV of the *Cistercian Library*, Bonfontaine, 1669, folio.

1. The treatise or letter to Haimo, prior [Col. 0186C] and the brothers of Mont-Dieu, Carthusians, *On the Solitary Life*, had often appeared among Saint Bernard’s works and under Bernard’s name. Mabillon more plausibly restored it to Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, and presented it under his name, divided into three books. Tissier—and previously Henry of Ghent, chapter 10 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and others cited by Trithemius—were led to attribute it to William by a prologue added by copyists to a volume containing the sustained labours of Guigo and William, and from the prologue to the work of each; in this prologue William also mentions his other little works.

[Col. 0187A] 2. *Mirror of Faith.*

3. *Enigma of Faith.*

4. *Book of Meditations*, formerly published at Louvain in 1546 and at Antwerp in 1550 and 1590, and reprinted in the *Libraries of the Fathers*, for example in the Lyons edition, vol. XXII, pp. 1143–1159. William himself calls the *Meditations* “not altogether useless for forming novices’ minds in prayer.”

5. *On the Nature and Dignity of Divine Love*, likewise published at Louvain and Antwerp, in the *Libraries of the Fathers*, and in the Lyons edition, pp. 1159–1163; also among Saint Bernard’s works, vol. V of Mabillon’s edition, p. 256.

6. The book *On Contemplating God*, likewise among Saint Bernard’s works, vol. V, p. 246. This is the work which in certain codices is entitled the *Book of Bernard’s Soliloquies*. [Col. 0187B]

7. Two books *On the Nature of Body and Soul*, addressed to Theophilus.

8. *Disputation of the Catholic Fathers against the Doctrines of Peter Abelard*, three books, addressed to Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, with a prefatory letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, in which he urges them to attack Abelard’s theology; and both did so. This letter of William, written about the year of Christ 1139, is also found among Saint Bernard’s letters as no. 391 (no. 326 in the Mabillon editions), together with Bernard’s reply, in which he declares that William’s counsel and undertaking meet with his approval.

9. *On the Errors of William of Conches*, concerning whom see above [Col. 0187C] pp. 138 ff., 144 ff., and vol. I, p. 408.

10. An Exposition of the Song of Songs, which he left unfinished because of another work undertaken against Abelard, having reached the words, III.3: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” It begins: “The mouth of the Bridegroom, the inspiration of Christ.”

[Col. 0188A] 11. A Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, mentioned in the appendix to Henry of Ghent, ch. 6.

Besides these works published by Tissier, there survives another Commentary on the Song of Songs by the same William, distinct from the preceding one—and indeed two such commentaries. One was compiled by him from the writings of St Ambrose and printed at the end of the Works of St Ambrose, vol. I, Benedictine edition, pp. 1545–1618. It begins: “Here are celebrated not incentives to impurity, but mysteries of chastity.” The other was drawn from the books of Pope St Gregory, and Casimir Oudin published it among the sacred minor works of several ancient writers of France and Belgium, Leiden, 1692, octavo. It begins: “By the mouth of God the only-begotten Son may be designated.”

One book On the Life of St Bernard, ending with the year [Col. 0188B] 1130, in Surius, 20 August, and frequently published with the Works of St Bernard.

A small work, *Sentences on Faith from St Augustine*. [Note: [Col. 0187] Trithemius also, after William’s *Mirror of Faith* and *Enigma of Faith*, mentions his book *Sentences of Faith*.] Oudin, vol. II, p. 1438, reports that he had handed it to Thomas Blampin for publication in the appendix to the final volume of St Augustine. Yet I find nothing of the kind in the Benedictine Augustine, except, in the appendix to volume VI, pp. 782 ff., “Miscellaneous Sentences of an Uncertain Author,” a short work of a moral rather than dogmatic character.

William himself further testifies that he wrote a little book On the Sacrament of the Altar, also mentioned by Trithemius, ch. 383, and by Charles Visch, p. 137 of the Cistercian Library; Visch adds also a book Against the Errors of Gilbert of Poitiers.

[Col. 0188C] To this William St Bernard not only wrote several letters and from him received several, but also dedicated to him his Apology against the Cluniac Monks, vol. I of the new edition, p. 531, and his book On Grace and Free Choice, p. 609.

[Col. 0187]

## SECOND NOTICE CONCERNING WILLIAM

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine Religious, vol. XII, p. 312. Paris, 1763, quarto.)

### § I. Account of His Life

William [Note: [Col. 0187C] *Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. IX, pp. 187 and 616.], born of noble parents at Liège, came to study at Reims with his brother Simon. The edifying life practised at the abbey of Saint-Nicaise in that city touched both of them, and they embraced the monastic state there. Their merit soon shone through the veil with which they tried to cover it. Both were elected abbots in 1119 [Note: [Col. 0187C] Bernard, *Works*, vol. II, p. 298.]: Simon, of Saint-Nicolas-aux-Bois in the diocese of Laon; William, of Saint-Thierry near Reims. The latter was still only a student at Saint-Nicaise when he first went to see St Bernard and formed with him that close friendship which lasted throughout their lives.

William would gladly, from that time, have settled beside the saint; but Providence continually raised obstacles to this plan, which he retained in his heart as long as he judged its execution possible. Far from weakening its traces, the abbatial dignity only strengthened them. Insensible to distinctions, he continually longed to be freed from an office which he had accepted only reluctantly. His elevation was closely followed by a long and grievous illness. When the news reached St Bernard, he sent his brother Gerard to invite him to Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 0188C] Bernard, *Works*, vol. II, p. 1085.], assuring him that there he would quickly be delivered from all his evils, either by death or by perfect recovery. For a soul attached to the [Col. 0189] earth, the alternative would doubtless have had something frightening in it. It was not so for William. He obeyed without hesitation, came to Clairvaux, and there recovered his health under the saintly abbot’s eyes and through his prayers. This occurred in Lent of the year 1120.

That same year, and shortly after his return, he learned that St Bernard himself was at the point of death. He hurried back as though to receive his last breath. But on his arrival the ominous symptoms had vanished. Bernard’s recovery, which was not long delayed, entirely dispelled William’s fears. One may judge how great these had been from the extraordinary zeal he displayed on every occasion for the interests of that illustrious friend. More jealous of Bernard’s reputation than Bernard himself, he could not see it attacked without the keenest pain. The monks of Cluny criticized the saint’s conduct on certain points; our abbot gave him no rest until he had set his hand to an Apology against their reproaches [Note: [Col. 0189] Bernard, *Works*, vol. I, p. 527.].

William’s attachment to this great man’s person rested upon the highest opinion of his learning and virtue. St Bernard, in return, held the abbot of Saint-Thierry’s merit in high esteem. “How,” he wrote to the abbot of Cuissy (*Ep.* 79), “did you think of consulting someone as far from you as I am, when at your door you have William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, that excellent man who combines rare prudence and equal ability with the sincerest affection for your house?” Oger, a regular canon, having wished to excuse himself to the saint for communicating without his authorization a writing entrusted to him in confidence: “Why,” replied the abbot of Clairvaux (*Ep.* 88), “should my little book fear the eyes of one to whom I would wish to disclose the depths of my heart? You do not sufficiently know my feelings for the abbot of Saint-Thierry. I should have a thousand good things to say to you about him, if the limits of a letter allowed me to enlarge upon the subject.” Bernard then asks Oger to visit this mutual friend, so that together they might examine his work and correct whatever they judged needed correction.

The same sentiments of esteem and deference appear in the letter he wrote to William himself [Note: [Col. 0189] *Ibid.*, p. 603.], urging him to review his treatise *On Grace and Free Choice*. Finally, whoever wishes to see the tenderest outpourings of heart from one friend speaking to another should read the letter (*Ep.* 85) in which Bernard answers William’s complaints concerning the indifference William supposed him to feel. Such was St Bernard’s return of affection toward the abbot of Saint-Thierry.

In 1130 the Benedictines held their first general chapter at Saint-Médard of Soissons. William, one of the presidents of this assembly, distinguished his zeal by the wise regulations which he caused to be made there. One might suppose that on his return he concerned himself only with enforcing them in his own house; nevertheless, it was then that he thought more seriously than ever of withdrawing to Clairvaux. He wrote about it to St Bernard (*Ep.* 86). But the reply was in no way favourable to his plans. The abbot of Clairvaux informed him that he continued in the same opinion which William well knew him to hold: both of them ought to prefer the divine will to their own; William would incur no risk by following this counsel, whereas he would expose himself greatly by sacrificing, to his particular inclination, the care of the souls with which Providence had entrusted him.

William appeared to yield to this advice and indeed forced himself for the following five years to conform to it; but at length the love of private life triumphed in his heart. He abdicated in 1135 and went to seclude himself—not at Clairvaux, where he clearly foresaw that his action would not be approved, but at the abbey of Signy, of the same order, in the diocese of Reims. There, according to the testimony of a writer of the house [Note: [Col. 0189] *Chronicle of Signy*.], he divided all his leisure between study and contemplation.

From the depths of his retirement he did not cease to watch over the interests of religion. Persuaded that a solitary person, more than any other, is bound to defend it according to the measure of his talents, he successfully employed his own to repel the assaults which a new mode of reasoning was beginning to direct against it. It was he who sounded the alarm against Abelard’s attacks, brought Abelard into conflict with the abbot of Clairvaux, and afterwards himself dealt him the final blows. He exercised his zeal no less successfully against other innovators of his time, as will be seen in the detailed account of his writings. There we reserve proof that he was still alive in 1148. Nothing more precise is known concerning the date of his death, except that it preceded that of St Bernard, which occurred on 20 August 1153.

The Chronicle of Signy records it as follows: “William, having fallen asleep holily in the Lord, was buried in the cloister, near the chapter-house door.” But eighty years after his death, Giles, ninth abbot of Signy, caused his bones to be transferred inside the oratory, together with those of Arnoul, abbot of Saint-Nicaise, and Gerard, abbot of Florennes, and placed them in an honourable tomb, *in quadam theca honore debito sepelivit*—“he buried them in a certain shrine with due honour” [Note: [Col. 0190] *Chronicle of Signy*.].

### § II. His Writings

William’s pen produced a great number of writings, nearly all excellent. He himself gave us their catalogue, without prejudice to those composed after he had drawn it up. They were for the most part collected in the fourth volume of the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux*, printed at Bonne-Fontaine in 1669. In describing them, we shall follow the order in which they stand in that collection, though it differs from the order assigned by the author, in which he appears to have published them.

I. The treatise on the Solitary Life, in the form of a letter addressed to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu. This treatise, which some have wished to credit to St Bernard and others to the Venerable Guigo, truly belongs to our author. We shall not repeat here the arguments employed to establish this critical conclusion. It has likewise been shown that the work cannot be dated before 1144, since its prologue is addressed to Haimon, prior of Mont-Dieu, who succeeded Geoffrey in that year. In this prologue William declares that, in composing his work, he had in view less the body of solitaries in that house—too enlightened, in his judgment, to need his instruction—than his brother Stephen, one of them and doubtless the younger. He then lists the books he had composed up to that point and recommends that they read them. This item is indeed lacking in some manuscript copies; but because it occurs in the oldest, nothing requires that it be rejected as an interpolation. This is the observation of Dom Mabillon, who republished the entire prologue, with the treatise, among the works falsely attributed to St Bernard [Note: [Col. 0190] Bernard, *Works*, vol. II, p. 135.].

The body of the work is divided in the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux* into thirty-two chapters, which Dom Mabillon [Col. 0191] reduced to sixteen, with summaries much clearer and more precise. It first presents general principles concerning religious life. “Your profession,” says the author, “is sublime: it rises to heaven and equals the state of angels in purity. You have vowed not merely holiness, but the perfection of all holiness, even the very summit of perfection. Your condition is not to languish in the practice of ordinary precepts, nor to inquire merely what God commands you; but to seek what he desires of you, and in every circumstance to study how to know his will—what is good, what is pleasing in his sight, what is perfect. For others it is enough to serve God; for you, one of your essential duties is to be intimately united with him. For others, it is enough to believe in him, to know that he exists, to love and adore him; for you, to know him, understand him, taste him, and enjoy him is your allotted portion.” He then shows that a newly founded community cannot practise its duties with too much fervour, because its example must serve as a rule for posterity.

Entering upon the particulars of monastic obligations, he distinguishes three states of cloistered life: the animal, the rational, and the spiritual. The first belongs to beginners; the second, to those advanced in virtue; the third, to the perfect. Everything William says concerning these states, which divide his book, is admirable and would lose too much by abridgment. We refer readers eager for instruction and edification to the work itself.

Speaking of the design of cells, our author criticizes those of Mont-Dieu as too sumptuous in his opinion and too little in keeping with the spirit of poverty. He advises that they be demolished or their use changed, being reserved to lodge the sick.

Gerson, in his sermon on the Supper, thinks that one ought to read cautiously what William says concerning the likeness of the righteous person to God. Yet one sees there only the common language of mystics, and it is sufficiently known that their expressions are not always to be taken literally.

This treatise appears in all editions of St Bernard. It is also placed at the beginning of volume VI of the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux*. Finally, it appears after the Rule of St Benedict, together with Hugh of St Victor’s little work *On the Manner of Praying*, in an octavo volume published by Badius Ascensius at Paris in 1521 [Note: [Col. 0191] At the Abbey of La Couture at Le Mans one sees a copy perfectly conforming to this one, dated 1519. There is every appearance that they do not belong to two different editions.]. To make it accessible to those who did not understand Latin, a French translation was made as early as the author’s own century; a manuscript copy is preserved in the library of the Jesuits’ novitiate at Paris. M. Le Beuf published its beginning in volume XVII of the *Memoirs of the Academy of Belles-Lettres* (p. 721). This translation is probably the same as that which Dom Martène says he saw among the manuscripts of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu [Note: [Col. 0191] See *Voyage littéraire*, p. 115.].

In the last century Sieur Lami made a new translation of this treatise, which was very well received and had two Paris editions: the first in 1651, by Antoine Vitré; the second in 1656, by Pierre le Petit.
