Both are in a duodecimo volume which also contains two writings of St Bernard rendered into French by the same translator: namely, that on Conversion of Conduct and the treatise on the Commandments and Dispensation. In a dissertation serving as a preface to this collection, an attempt is made—on frivolous grounds—to claim the work under discussion for Peter, abbot of Celles and later bishop of Chartres.

II. A collection of twelve Meditations on various subjects of piety. Speaking himself of these Meditations in the prologue of the preceding treatise, William says that they are useful for forming the minds of monks in prayer. This judgment is not excessive: the esteem always accorded the work is attested by the multiplicity of editions. It first appeared at Paris, under the name of St Bernard, in 1499, from George Mithelius, in an octavo volume. It was subsequently reprinted at Louvain, sextodecimo, with Guigo’s Meditations, in 1546; at Antwerp in 1550, 1589, and 1590; and at Paris in 1600. There were new editions in all the great Libraries of the Fathers, including that of Lyons, in whose twenty-second volume it appears, not to mention the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux*. We may further note that Jean Guitot translated them into French and published them under the name of St Bernard at Rouen in 1627, in a sextodecimo volume, after the Meditations attributed to St Augustine and those of St Anselm.

III. A book On the Manner of Contemplating God. Older editions of St Bernard, following certain manuscripts, attribute it to that Father under the title *Book of Soliloquies*. The editor of the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux* was the first to restore it to the abbot of Saint-Thierry; but the copy from which he published it was incomplete. Dom Mabillon subsequently issued a complete edition among the works falsely attributed to St Bernard [Note: [Col. 0191] Bernard, *Works*, vol. II, p. 233.]. The work consists of ten chapters, dealing solely with the characteristics of divine love. The author sets forth a spirituality exceedingly refined, yet very solid. It is evident that he took St Augustine’s *Confessions* and *Soliloquies* as his model. We shall be content to extract the following words, in which he forcefully marks the difference between the virtues of paganism and those of Christians:

> “The philosophers of this world once cultivated justice, both by an affection of love and by the performance of its prescribed works, so much so that it was said by them concerning them:
>
> *The good hate to sin through love of virtue.*
>
> But they are convicted of not having loved justice, because they did not know you, from whom proceed the fountain and origin, and to whom return the end and final goal, of true justice; and without whom all human acts of justice are like a menstrual cloth. For they did not have the faith that works through love, though they had a certain affected love and certain works of moral uprightness. Because these did not proceed from the fountain of true justice and did not tend toward the end of true justice, they went astray all the more hopelessly as they ran more vigorously outside the way. For the way, Father, is your Christ, who said: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life.’” [Note: [Col. 0191] *Philosophi mundi hujus olim eam (justitiam) coluerunt, et affectu amoris et effectu operis, in tantum ut diceretur ab eis de eis:*
>
> *Oderunt peccare boni virtutis amore.* [Col. 0192]
>
> *Sed convincuntur justitiam non amasse quia non noverunt te, a quo fons et origo, et in quem finis et recursus verae justitiae, et sine quo omnes justitiae hominum sicut pannus menstruatae. Non enim habebant fidem quae per dilectionem operatur, licet affectatum quemdam amorem et opera quaedam haberent honestatis; quae quia a fonte verae justitiae non prodibant, et ad verae justitiae finem non ibant, tanto desperatius errabant, quanto fortius extra viam currebant. Via enim, Pater, Christus tuus qui dixit: Ego sum via, veritas et vita.*]

[Col. 0193] IV. The treatise On the Nature and Dignity of Love. It is a continuation of the preceding work. It is divided into twenty chapters in the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux*, and into fifteen in the new edition of St Bernard [Note: [Col. 0193] Bernard, *Works*, vol. II, p. 243.]. The author shows by what manner and by what stages one may rise to the perfection of love in this life. It is also found in all editions of St Bernard, beginning with the edition of Jean Tiraqueau.

V. The Physics of Body and Soul, or the treatise On Self-Knowledge. William himself says that he divided this writing into two parts under the name of Theophilus. The first treats of the structure of the human body: it is a rather superficial summary of anatomy. It states that physicians of the time counted 241 bones in the human body, seven pairs of nerves issuing from the brain, and thirty-one pairs plus one unpaired nerve rooted in the nape of the neck. In the second part, concerning the physics of the soul, the author says that animals appear to act by voluntary motion, but that perfect reason is found only in human beings; that the soul differs from the senses; that it is wholly present in every part of the body; that it was created in God’s image; that the vices within it do not belong to its original nature, although they constitute the nature of beasts; and that it was made to use creatures and enjoy God alone. He explains what rectitude of mind is. He makes the difference between the happy and unhappy soul in this life consist in the difference of its love. He ends with a moving depiction of the blessedness of the saints and the miseries of the damned.

VI. The Mirror of Faith. Properly speaking, it is a treatise on the three theological virtues. These virtues, says the author, do not come from us; they are the work of grace. “Therefore, if you will the good, O human being, and if you believe rightly, this depends not on your willing or running, but on God’s mercy. Certainly, if you do not will to believe, you do not believe; and you believe if you will. But you will never believe unless grace first comes before you, because no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him. How does he draw him? Assuredly by creating and inspiring in him the free will by which he freely wills what he wills; that is, so that what he wills belongs to his own will.” [Note: [Col. 0193] *Non ergo volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei quod bene vis, o homo! et quod credis. Equidem si non vis credere, non credis; credis autem si vis: sed non vis nisi a gratia praeveniaris,* [Col. 0194] *quia nemo venit ad Filium, nisi Pater traxerit eum. Quomodo? Utique creando in eo et inspirando ei liberam voluntatem qua libere vult id quod vult, hoc est ut voluntatis ejus sit quod vult.*]

VII. The Enigma of Faith. The excellence and simplicity of faith are the subject of this writing. William acknowledges that this faith is found far more bristling with difficulties in the writings of the holy doctors than in the divine Scriptures. “I do not see in the latter,” he says, “the name ‘Trinity’; nor do I find there that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, except in St John’s epistle, where it is said: ‘There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.’ But this is not found in the old version. Moreover, I speak only of the names, and not at all of the things they signify; for the Scriptures testify that God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are one God. But they do not speak of three persons in the Godhead; likewise, they make no mention of their relations, nor of the famous ‘consubstantial,’ nor of other similar terms which the necessity of repelling the novelties of heretics obliged people to devise. For I am quite certain that, without this necessity, the Fathers would have refrained from them. Yet I reverence and receive these expressions as the standard of faith.”

The author proceeds in the remainder of the book to discuss the mystery of the Trinity, which he explains in a very orthodox manner and much more clearly than the subtle arguments of the scholastics of his time concerning this mystery.

VIII. When Abelard’s books fell into William’s hands in 1139, he was greatly shocked by the doctrine they contained and immediately took up his pen to refute them. He addressed his work to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and to St Bernard in a letter written in that pathetic and vehement style which is never better employed than in defence of religion.

“It is,” he tells them, “with extreme confusion that I find myself forced, by your silence and that of everyone else, to speak to you of an important matter which concerns all the faithful together. Was it for a man of no consequence such as I am to anticipate you, who are my lords and fathers? But on the other hand, how can I be silent when I see the faith of our common hope endangered without anyone opposing it—that faith, I say, which Jesus Christ sealed with his own blood, in whose defence apostles and martyrs shed theirs, and which the vigils and labours of the holy doctors have handed down pure and unstained to the unhappy age in which we live? Yes, I waste away with grief within myself; and my heart’s agitation is such that, to relieve it, I must raise my voice for a cause of which I should count myself happy to be the victim, if necessary and if the occasion arose.

“Do not imagine that trifles are at issue here: the faith of the Holy Trinity, the person of the Mediator, that of the Holy Spirit, the grace of God, the sacrament of our redemption—these are the matters in danger. Peter Abelard is again teaching and writing novelties. His books cross the seas; they travel beyond the Alps; they fly from province to province and from kingdom to kingdom. Everywhere they are enthusiastically praised and defended with impunity, so much so that, it is said, they are esteemed at the Roman court. Therefore I tell you, and the whole Church, that the silence in which you remain may become disastrous. What! Do we count for nothing the faith for which we have renounced ourselves? Fear of offending an influential man banishes from our hearts the fear of offending God. I repeat: forestall the evil while it is only beginning to appear; for if you allow it to grow, you will no longer be able to restrain it. It is time to set out in detail the grounds of my apprehension.”

He then reports Abelard’s errors, dividing them into thirteen heads, the same ones condemned by the Council of Sens. In closing, he protests that he attacks only these errors, not at all the author’s person, whom he had formerly loved and would still wish to love: *Dilexi ego eum et diligere vellem, Deus testis est; sed in causa hac nemo umquam mihi proximus erit vel amicus*—“I loved him, and I would wish to love him—God is witness; but in this cause no one shall ever be near to me or be my friend.”

After this comes the treatise in which he refutes each of these errors individually. Its title is: *Disputation of the Catholic Fathers against the Doctrines of Peter Abelard*. We shall not give an analysis of it, because its arguments have already been used in the examination of Abelard’s doctrine.

William’s letter is found among those of St Bernard, with that saint’s reply, in the editions of Horstius and Dom Mabillon, as well as in the *Bibliothèque de Cîteaux*. The treatise following it appears only in the latter collection.

[Col. 0195] IX. After Abelard there arose a new philosopher who undertook to revive some of his errors and to add others. This was William of Conches, author, among other works, of a *Summa*, or *Compendium of Philosophy*, in four books. A good man who came to Signy to retire there brought this *Summa* with him. William of Saint-Thierry, having read through it, judged that he should again refer it to his oracle, the abbot of Clairvaux. He did so in a letter in which he imputes to the philosopher of Conches several deviations, the details of which will be given in the article on the latter. In this letter one notes the same ardour and force of expression and argument, though not always the same skill in grasping his opponent’s thought as in the work against Abelard.

X. Our author did not treat Abbot Rupert with such scant consideration in the letter he wrote to him to criticize certain expressions in his treatise on the Divine Offices. The subject of their dispute has been described in the account of Rupert, and it has been shown that the abbot of Saint-Thierry’s position was unfounded. But it must be added here that his letter is seasoned with every courtesy and with the most sensitive marks of esteem and charity. The dispute concerned the manner in which Christ’s body is present in the Eucharist. Rupert fundamentally thought as William did; but William had misinterpreted Rupert’s expressions.

XI. Apart from this factual error, William was highly learned in the matter of the real presence. He had long studied it in the sources, examined its proofs and difficulties, and collected, on the one hand, the clearest and most precise authorities of the Fathers for establishing the true view; on the other, those which seemed to him most obscure and most liable to produce disturbance and uncertainty in weak minds. From all this he subsequently composed a small work entitled *On the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ*. But before publishing it, he communicated it to the abbot of Clairvaux, so that Bernard might correct whatever he judged appropriate. This is seen in the letter to the saint placed at the head of the work, of which it is proper to give a summary.

Twelve chapters make up its divisions, apart from the prologue, which seeks to prove that reason ought to allow itself to be guided by faith, rather than presume to guide it. In the first chapter the author shows how great are the perfections which the union of human nature with the Word bestows upon Christ’s body from the moment of the Incarnation: for example, its subtlety and agility, for which proofs are found in the various states through which it has passed—that is, before as well as after its glorification. From this he concludes that nothing prevents one from saying that Christ’s body, especially since it has been glorified, may be in several places at once, although it is not true that this body is everywhere as the Godhead is. For while it is necessary that the Godhead be found in every place, since nothing can subsist outside its presence, it is not likewise necessary that Christ’s body exist everywhere, but only wherever the concern of our salvation requires it to be present.

> “Therefore it is established that Christ’s body can be in different places at one moment of time, but by the law of the creating, not the created, nature. Since it is the nature of created nature to obey in all things the laws of the creating nature, if the latter sometimes permits the former to set aside the order it has prescribed for it, he who established and orders it ought not [Col. 0196] to seem to err or to depart from his own order—especially in the case of that nature which, by virtue of the person, is joined to that Word through whom every creature was made and apart from whom it could in no way exist.”  
> [Note: Col. 0195.]

The second chapter is devoted to showing in what manner Christ’s presence is now necessary to us. The author says that, in the days of his flesh, Christ’s body had to make itself visible and tangible, since otherwise it could not have accomplished the mystery of our redemption. Today, however, that body ought no longer to be perceptible, because, being intended to serve us as food, it must be presented to us under a form that conceals it. This could not have been done more suitably than by giving us that body under the species which occupy the foremost rank among foods—bread and wine.

The third chapter concerns absolute accidents. The fourth concerns transubstantiation: the author does not use this expression, but instead employs that of transmutation, which is equivalent. In the fifth he treats of the spiritual eating of Christ’s body. The sixth turns upon the distinction between Christ’s twofold flesh. This flesh, the author says after St Jerome, is understood in two ways: at one time as that which was crucified and buried; at another as that divine and spiritual flesh of which the Savior himself says, “My flesh is true food.” The faith of the Church, to which the sacrifice belongs, whatever the merit of the person offering it, produces Christ’s body in the sacrament. But it is purity of life and fervor of love that make us participants in the Savior’s spiritual flesh.

The seventh chapter seeks to prove that one of the two fleshes may be eaten without the other. The eighth concerns bodily eating, and establishes two points: first, that this eating is not an absolutely indispensable necessity for salvation, baptism being sufficient in certain circumstances; second, that Christ’s body is not subject to the shameful consequences of digestion. The ninth concerns the various sacraments or mystical signs of Christ’s body. The tenth is a recapitulation of the whole work. In the final two chapters the author examines why the Fathers contain so many obscure expressions concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist. His reason is that the Fathers applied themselves to clarifying doctrines only as they were attacked by heretics; they therefore had to speak less plainly on this doctrine than on others, because in their time it had encountered no contradiction. He concludes by citing various passages from St Ambrose, St Jerome, and St Augustine which seem to conflict, and reconciles them in a very plausible manner.

This work was printed under St Anselm’s name in the older editions of that Father, on the basis of various manuscripts. [Note: Col. 0196, *Anselm, Works*, vol. I, Gerberon edition, in the appraisal of the works.] But because it contains passages borrowed from Rupert’s treatise *On the Offices*, composed in 1111, two years after the holy prelate’s death, this is clear proof that the attribution is false. François [Col. 0197] Titelman, in the octavo edition which he issued at Antwerp in 1532, [Note: Col. 0197, *Magna Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, p. 576, no. 2.] credited it, with equally little basis, to Ernaud, abbot of Bonneval. The editor of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* restored it to its true author from four manuscripts: two from Signy, in which William’s name occurs as many as five times; one from Clairvaux; and one from Igny.

XII. William was engaged in commenting on the Song of Songs when Abelard’s writings were brought to him. He considered himself bound to interrupt that work in order to refute them, and he does not appear to have resumed it. In any case, the work is incomplete both in the manuscripts and in the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. In the preface the author declares that he considers only the moral sense of his text, and it may be said that he successfully carried out his design. We shall speak below of other commentaries he made on the same book.

XIII. The Song of Songs was not the only portion of Scripture that William undertook to explain. We have from him a commentary on St Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. It is divided into seven books and preceded by a fine preface, in which the author says that, since this Epistle is full of great difficulties, he formed the purpose of smoothing them out—not by a continuous explanation derived from his own mind, but by selectively collecting what bears upon them in the writings of the holy doctors, especially Origen, St Ambrose, St Augustine, and those teachers of his own time most devoted to ancient doctrine.

“The chief motive,” he adds, “that led me to this work is the pleasure of contemplating that divine grace which the Apostle is continually occupied in defending against the Jews when writing to the Romans; which the holy doctors, by their writings, have made triumphant over the efforts of heresy; and which each of us must draw to himself by his desires, so as to enter into the dispositions of profound humility and produce works of solid devotion. For those who have wholly devoted themselves to God’s worship must know that this worship is nothing other than piety; that there is no true piety without thanksgiving, and no thanksgiving without knowledge of grace itself. Through frequent meditation upon this truth we become those blessed poor in spirit to whom the kingdom of God belongs, because they have placed all their hope in his help. For grace predestined us before we existed and while we were still in nothingness; it called us when we were far from God; it justified us after turning us back toward him; finally, after justifying us, if we do not fail him by our ingratitude, it is to glorify us.”

This preface ends with a moving prayer to Jesus Christ. Such a favorable beginning invites the reader to become acquainted with the work, and his expectation is not deceived in reading it. He finds there an almost continuous texture of expressions or thoughts of the Fathers, tastefully selected and intelligently applied to the various parts of the Apostle’s text. Let us give a few samples of this Commentary.

On the words, “Where, then, is your ground for boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By the law of works? No, but by the law of faith,” William says:

> “It must be known wherein the law of works and the law of faith differ. For both say, ‘You shall not covet’—a prohibition embracing all sins, of which covetousness is the common source. Both likewise have their sacramental works, which indeed are not alike. To determine the difference between these two laws, we say that it consists in this: the law of works shows the justice of a God who commands, while the law of faith shows us the mercy of that same God who comes to our aid. For what the law of works orders by threatening, the law of faith obtains by believing. By the former God says: ‘Do what I command.’ By the latter one says to God: ‘Lord, give what you command.’ The law commands, in fact, only in order to warn us what faith must do: namely, so that the person to whom the command is addressed may know what he ought to ask for if he cannot fulfill it; and, if he can immediately fulfill it and does so obediently, may know from whom he received that power. Such is the wisdom called piety, through which the Father of lights—the author of every excellent grace and every perfect gift—is honored. For by the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving he is given true worship, so that his servant may glory in him alone and not at all in himself, and so that the true son of faith may know from whom he ought to await what he does not yet possess, and whence comes what he already has. Yet the law of works is holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good. But through this very good sin brought about death, because the commandment both forbids and at the same time incites concupiscence, insofar as it commands and does not help, punishes and does not deliver.”

On the verse, “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11:29), he says:

> “For the gifts of God and the calling are without repentance—that is, they are firmly fixed without change. Whoever belong to this calling are all teachable by God; nor can any one of them say, ‘I believed in order that I might be called.’ But God’s grace goes before them all, because they are called so that they may believe. For all who are teachable by God come to the Son, since they have heard [Col. 0198] and learned from the Father through the Son, who says most plainly: ‘Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me.’ None of these perishes, because of all that the Father gave him he loses no one.”  
> [Note: Col. 0197.]

He explains, in the manner of St Augustine and his disciples, the words, “Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin”:

> “Not only every act, but the entire life of unbelievers is sin. For where knowledge of unchangeable truth is absent, there is false virtue even in the best morals.”  
> [Note: Col. 0198: *Everything that is not from faith is sin. Not every act alone, but the whole life of unbelievers is sin. For where recognition of unchangeable truth is lacking, there is false virtue even in the best morals.*]

These examples may suffice to enable a judgment of the merit of this Commentary.

XIV. Abelard, as was said in the article concerning him, after his condemnation was pronounced at the Council of Sens, published his *Apology*, a work very different from his confession of faith, and no less insulting to his judges than it was at variance with sound doctrine. The artifice with which it was filled, and the air of assurance which its author assumed in it, made good people fear that it might increase the number of his adherents. Hugh of Amiens, archbishop of Rouen, charged William with answering it. In obedience to this order, he composed a work in three books, in which he follows his adversary step by step, shrewdly disentangles his disguises, exposes the atrocity of his insults, and refutes his errors with precise and numerous authorities from the holy Fathers. This answer demonstrates better than any other of William’s works how deeply versed he was in the study of tradition.

[Col. 0199] It is unfortunate that the beginning of the first book is lacking in both the manuscripts and the printed version. This lacuna is ancient; already in the twelfth century, a few years after St Bernard’s death, Geoffrey, his successor, wrote to Cardinal Henry of Albano that the first quire of this work was missing from the Clairvaux copy. [Note: Col. 0199, Oudin, *Writers*, vol. II, cols. 1435–1436.] He did not even know the author’s name, and knew only, as he said, that he was an abbot of the Order of St Benedict. Yet if he had taken the trouble to compare this piece with the letter addressed to the bishop of Chartres and to St Bernard, and with William’s other writings which must have been at Clairvaux, he would easily have judged that it came from the same pen.

Indeed, at first glance one recognizes the style and phrasing of our author; the modest expressions he habitually uses in speaking of himself; the substance of his arguments; several passages which he had used the first time in refuting the same adversary; and, finally, the liveliness that characterized him in controversy. The editor of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* was even better positioned to compare all these writings, and Manrique, [Note: Col. 0199, under the year 1140, ch. 6, book II, §5.] who shares our opinion, urged him to do so. Nevertheless, he contented himself with inserting these three books in his collection under the mere title, *Disputation of an Anonymous Abbot against Abelard*. Duboulay, followed by modern bibliographers, did not hesitate likewise to assign them to William; but they have all confused and treated as one and the same work the two refutations of Abelard composed by William of Saint-Thierry.

Here ends, in the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, the collection of our author’s works. But this collection, as we have already said, does not contain all the productions of his pen. Here are others not found in it.

I. Three commentaries on the Song of Songs, in addition to that of which we have already given an account. The first of these is in truth less William’s work than St Bernard’s. It precedes all the others in date and arose on the following occasion. Our author himself relates that, while ill at Clairvaux, he asked St Bernard to explain the Song of Songs to him according to its moral sense, setting aside the mysteries it contains. The saint did what he asked and, in a series of conversations, unfolded for him the moral teaching of this book. [Note: Col. 0199, *Life of St Bernard*, ch. 12.]

> “Each day,” William says, “after he had left me, I took care to write down the things he had told me, so far as my memory could recall them.”

With Dom Mabillon, we think that this record drawn up by our author is the same as an explanation of the first two chapters of the Song of Songs, which that scholar printed among the spurious works of St Bernard from a manuscript of the Abbey of the Dunes. The style manifestly reveals the abbot of Saint-Thierry.

The second commentary is drawn from the writings of St Ambrose. It was first published under the name of Antoine Démocharès, or Mouchi, at the end of the fifth volume of this Father’s Works, published at Paris in 1569. In that edition the copyist’s name was taken for the author’s, because the manuscript from which the commentary was published was indeed in Démocharès’s hand. But Father Hommei restored it to its true author in his *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* (p. 260), where it is printed. The latest editors of St Ambrose reproduced it more correctly from a copy from the Abbey of Signy, regarded as the original.

The third is extracted from the Works of St Gregory the Great. It was published in 1692 at Leiden in an octavo volume containing other ancient writings, through the care of Casimir Oudin.

II. William did not content himself with admiring St Bernard’s virtues and taking them as the model for his conduct; he also took care to hand down the memory of them to posterity. We possess the book he composed on the Life of that great man, though he carries its history only to the year 1130. His work was successively continued by Ernaud of Bonneval and Geoffrey of Clairvaux. We do not know either why he himself did not carry his work further or the precise time when he began it. Dom Mabillon proves very well that he undertook it only after 1140. It may have been his final composition, which death apparently prevented him from finishing. This book appears in all editions of St Bernard, in Surius under 20 August, and in Bollandus under the same date. Elsewhere we shall speak of the translations that have been made of it.

Such are William’s writings in the public’s possession. His book of *Sentences on Faith* is still preserved in manuscript. Duboulay, knowing this work only from its title, imagined that our author invented the method of treating theology by sentences, and that the first Scholastics took from him the name “sententiaries.” [Note: Col. 0200, E. du Boulay, vol. II, p. 743.] But we have previously named several works by various writers bearing the same title and apparently preceding this one in time. Moreover, as Oudin observes, [Note: Col. 0200, *Writers*, vol. II, p. 1438.] if the historian of the University of Paris had seen the book in question, he would have formed an entirely different idea of it.

It exists in its original at the Abbey of Signy with this inscription: *Sentences on Faith, chiefly from St Augustine and other Fathers*; and it begins with these words: “Essence is a thing which is from those things from which it is, and which subsists in that which remains.” The author treats, after St Augustine and Boethius—and often using their own expressions—of God’s essence and attributes; the Trinity of the divine persons and the unity of their substance; the creation of angels and of humankind; and so forth. But the method he follows in this compilation is very different from that of the Scholastics and sententiarists mentioned by Duboulay. Oudin, who provides us with this notice—for we have not seen the work—adds that he sent a faithful copy of the Signy manuscript to Dom Thomas Blampin, for inclusion in the new edition of St Augustine. Yet this editor does not appear to have used it, for the *Miscellany of Sentences* by an unknown author, found in the appendix to the sixth volume of St Augustine, is a very short work and much more moral than dogmatic.

Another writing of William’s, which has not yet seen the light and which few bibliographers have mentioned, is a treatise *On Divine Relations against the Errors of Gilbert of Poitiers*. The library of the Collège Louis-le-Grand possesses a copy enriched with marginal notes by Father Labbe. Another was at Morigny near Étampes; but we do not know where the manuscripts of that abbey were taken after the misfortune of its destruction. William began this work shortly after the Council of Reims, at which Gilbert’s novelties were proscribed—that is, toward the end of 1148. This is clear from its opening, where he says:

> “Reader, in these sheets you will find four articles which were recently driven out and rejected in the great Church as manifestly opposed to the truth.”

These four articles are refuted with the same force of argument and liveliness found in our author’s other works. [Col. 0201] He ends with praise of the celebrated theologians of his time in these terms:

> “To return to these particular articles now in hand: when such novel doctrines were heard, ought it not to have been considered how many wise and learned men, sound in judgment and doctrine, the Church had possessed not long before these times—men who had plainly thought and taught the contrary? I mean those distinguished men of Laon, Anselm and Ralph; also Master Alberic, first of Reims and afterward archbishop of Bourges; Hugh of Saint-Victor, the most faithful interpreter of the divine word; Robert Pullen, chancellor of the Apostolic See; and very many others, whose presence still, or whose memory recently, is blessed. Their common judgment stands: whatever is in God is God.”

Besides these writings, William composed others which have succumbed to the injuries of time. One especially regrets the large number of letters he wrote to St Bernard and to other distinguished persons with whom he was in correspondence. He himself tells us that he had composed a *Treatise on Universals*, addressed to Master Thierry. [Note: Col. 0201, *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, p. 253, col. 1.]

Duboulay (vol. IV, p. 743) wrongly suspects that our author is that Master William, a monk, to whom Walter of Mortagne wrote a letter (*ibid.*, p. 74) in order to refute his opinion that baptism administered by a heretic to children did them no good before the use of reason. For, first, it is doubtful, as Duboulay himself observes, whether the term “monk” was not a surname rather than a designation of profession. Second, the title “master” then denoted a man who gave public lectures, something our author never did. And even if the title were in itself ambiguous, the beginning of Walter’s letter suffices to determine the sense in which we take it here. It begins:

> “Walter of Mortagne sends greetings to Master William the monk. You have said that you do not believe, etc.”

Does not the word “you have said” prove that Walter was attacking not a written work, but a discourse delivered orally and publicly by a teacher? Finally, it is beyond likelihood that an opinion as absurd as the one rebuked in that letter should have entered the mind of one of the most learned men of the twelfth century.

William was indeed such a man, and in almost every branch of learning suitable to his state. A subtle and exact logician, no one understood better than he the art of pursuing an argument, meeting his adversaries’ objections, and disentangling the sophisms in which they wrap themselves. A natural philosopher, insofar as one could be in that age, his knowledge of natural things equaled that of the ablest men of his time. A profound theologian, he joined to extensive reading of the Fathers a sound and penetrating judgment, which enabled him to perceive the correspondence, application, and fruitfulness of the principles he found scattered throughout their writings. A judicious and sublime mystic in every subject of spirituality he treats, he traverses by the light of faith all the degrees that lead to the height of his subject and goes no further. He speaks to heart and reason together: he raises the latter without making it lose the ground beneath it; he warms the former without inspiring excessive enthusiasm. A wise interpreter of Holy Scripture, he does not force the letter in order to bend it to his private meaning; he does not affect novelty, but always takes tradition as his rule in explaining these deep and rich books. Moreover, he is a clear, methodical, eloquent writer, full of unction where his subjects require it—and, to say all in a word, the author of his century who came nearest to St Bernard.

## PREFACE TO THE WORKS OF BLESSED WILLIAM, PRESENTING HIS LIFE AND A CATALOGUE OF HIS BOOKS

(Dom Tissier, *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, vol. IV, p. 1; from an anonymous writer, from the Life and letters of St Bernard, and from the Chronicle of Signy.)

[Col. 0201]

Blessed William, born at Liège of noble family, was sent to Reims in his youth for the sake of study. Having completed the course of learning, he took the religious habit in the monastery of St Nicasius at Reims; and after some years he was chosen abbot of St Thierry near Reims.

About that time, the fame of the virtues of the holy Father Bernard had already spread far and wide. William went to Clairvaux, entered into a sacred bond with the holy man, and from that day was bound to him in the closest intimacy. Of this William writes much in Book I of the same St Bernard’s Life. There too he says that, while suffering from poor health in his monastery of St Thierry, he was summoned to Clairvaux by St Bernard and brought there by Blessed Gerard, Bernard’s brother; and he declares how greatly he advanced through the holy man’s companionship and conversations.

Their writings demonstrate this mutual love. In the letter preceding the book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, William greets the holy Father thus: “To his dearest one, chosen from among thousands: he who is his own self, his.” In another letter, no longer extant, he says: “His—because he is his.” St Bernard answers him in Letter 86 with an equal greeting. In Letter 85, however, Bernard affectionately reproaches him because he had written that he was less loved by Bernard than Bernard was loved by him:

> “Perhaps what you say is true—namely, that you are loved less by me than you love me. But I am sure that you yourself are not sure of it.”

And below, addressing God:

> “That I love him—that is, William—through your gift and his merit, you know and I feel; but how greatly I love him, you know, and I do not know.”

Finally, St Bernard dedicated his book *On Grace and Free Choice*, as well as his *Apology for the Cistercians*, to William; and William in turn dedicated to Bernard his little work *On the Sacrament of the Altar* and another work against Peter Abelard. These works also show how highly each esteemed the other’s learning. [Col. 0203] The holy Father says that he awaits William’s judgment before publishing or suppressing the aforesaid book. And in Letter 79, when consulted by the abbot of Cuissy, he commended our William’s wisdom in these words:

> “I wonder what led you to seek as your adviser one so far away as I am, when close at hand you have a wise man, of your Order and especially devoted to your house: William, abbot of St Thierry.”

Although there was such unity of heart between them, and William desired to enter the Cistercian Order, St Bernard nevertheless dissuaded him from making that change, as is evident from his Letter 86. William nevertheless prevailed and went to the monastery of Signy, where he spent the remainder of his life. Witnesses are the anonymous author of William’s Life and Abbot Burchard, in the note following the book of St Bernard’s Life; both were contemporaries of these holy men. The Chronicle of Signy says the same, as do various manuscripts of the Order, some of which will shortly be produced.

Before he went to Signy, as he was traveling to Soissons to consult a certain friend, he began to be overcome by a heavy drowsiness on the road. While sleeping beneath a tree near Bazoches, the Blessed Virgin appeared to him, gently embracing and caressing his head, and filling his soul with wonderful sweetness. When he had arrived at Signy, the neighboring abbots, distressed by his withdrawal, tried to recall him through the intervention and authority of Lord Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and by sending an embassy to him; but they did not succeed.

Afterward he was severely troubled by temptation concerning the harshness of the food. But he was strengthened, as Christ once was by an angel, by a monk who had followed him and had formerly been provost of St Thierry. In the same monastery he had as companions two other distinguished men: Arnulf, brother of the lord of Morymome, abbot of St Nicasius of Reims; and Gerard, brother of the lord of Orchimont, abbot of Florennes, who had come to Signy with twelve of his monks.

Once, while our William lay ill in the monastery of Signy itself, a monk attending him, overcome by sleep, saw a venerable lady offering him a fur garment and saying, “Cover him with this.” When the monk asked who she was, she answered, “I am the Lady of Bazoches.” He did not know what this meant, being unaware that the Blessed Virgin had previously appeared to William near Bazoches. William soon recovered after the monk told him of his vision.

At last Blessed William, bringing the course of his life to its holy end, fell asleep in the Lord. His body was committed to burial in the cloister, near the entrance to the chapter house. About eighty years after his death, however, it was translated together with the bodies of the aforesaid Arnulf and Gerard by Lord Giles, ninth abbot of Signy, of whom the aforementioned chronicle says:

> “He raised from the tombs in which they had lain until that time the bones of Lord William, formerly abbot of St Thierry, Arnulf, abbot of St Nicasius, and Gerard, abbot of Florennes; and placed them with due honor in a certain shrine within the wall of the oratory, near the entrance of the church on the side of the cloister.”

The neighboring abbots were present at this translation. Their portraits can still be seen painted there, with their names inscribed beneath them.

A monk formerly intimate with him had asked William that, after his death, he might deign to visit him; Blessed William had promised this. When a year had passed, William appeared to him with two others. Asked how matters stood with him, he said, “It will be well with me.” The monk also asked about himself when he would die; one of William’s companions replied that he ought not yet know this. That monk pondered deeply the words, “It will be well with me,” by which so great a man signified that he had not yet attained glory. Yet it did not follow that he was being punished by purgatorial fire, since many after death are afflicted by the purgatory of desire alone, after the punishment of fire or without it. Now we must speak of William’s writings.

He himself drew up their catalogue in the prefatory letter to the book *On the Solitary Life*, addressed to the Fathers of Mont-Dieu—not in the form commonly seen, namely mutilated and cut off halfway through, but as it is found in the libraries of the Order, and specifically at Signy, where it was written by the author. It begins with that very book, *On the Solitary Life*, which he calls his daily labour; for the other books which he subsequently lists had already been published. They are these: *The Mirror of Faith*, *The Enigma of Faith*, a book *On Contemplating God*, a book *On the Nature and Dignity of Love*, a little book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, *Meditations*, *On the Song of Songs*, down to the passage, “A little while after I had passed by them,” etc.; *Against Peter Abelard*, an *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, *Sentences of Faith*, a book *On the Nature of the Body*, and a book *On the Nature of the Soul*. The same Father afterwards also wrote the first book of the *Life of St Bernard*, whom he rendered immortal.

It has long since been accepted, even by those who prepared the older editions of Bernard’s works, that the book *On the Solitary Life*, addressed to the Fathers of Mont-Dieu and attributed by some to St Bernard, is not his. For all the printed codices have, before that book, this notice: “Thus far you have the works composed by our Lord Bernard.” Consequently, the works following that notice are denied to be St Bernard’s. First among those denied to him is that book, or letter, *To the Brethren of Mont-Dieu*. But every manuscript codex without exception attributes that little work to William, abbot of St Thierry. I have seen the Signy exemplar, which I have used; I have also seen those of Longpont and of Carolocense. Our Henriquez testifies that he saw the one at Dunes; others report others: all of them acknowledge William as their author. Our Manrique likewise unhesitatingly assigns the same book to the same author. Bellarmine too says that the work has Bernard’s spirit, but not his style, and that it is commonly attributed to William. The anonymous writer of William’s Life likewise places that book *On the Solitary Life* in the catalogue of his works. There is also an old codex in the monastery of St Thierry containing a catalogue of the same works, in which this very book, or letter written to the Carthusian, is mentioned. Formerly the very autograph of William was kept at the monastery of Mont-Dieu, as the venerable Lord Ganeron, a monk of that place, testified to me; he possesses a copy transcribed from it.

Finally, since the author of that book claims for himself the twelve other works already listed, if we attribute that book to St Bernard, we must also attribute to him those twelve aforementioned little works, which nevertheless bear William’s name. Therefore the aforesaid book *On the Solitary Life*, addressed to the Fathers of Mont-Dieu, is his.

Some attribute the book *On the Sacraments* to Anselm, but wrongly, because Anselm had already died when that book was published. For Eadmer, Anselm’s disciple, says in his *Life* that Anselm was made bishop in 1093 and lived thirteen years in the episcopate. He therefore died in 1106. But that book *On the Sacrament of the Altar* was written after 1111. For the first part of this book is addressed to Rupert of Deutz, and refutes his words found in Book II, chapter 9, *On the Offices*. But the books *On the Offices* were being written in 1111. For in Book VIII, chapter 4, he recounts a miracle occurring in that very year: “This happened on the holy Sabbath of Easter, on which the year one thousand one hundred and eleven from the Incarnation was inscribed on the Paschal candle,” etc. Anselm could not have refuted a book written after his death.

2. Eadmer, in his catalogue of Anselm’s works, does not mention this notable book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*; why would he have omitted it if Anselm had written it? Finally, in manuscripts this book is everywhere attributed to William, never to Anselm. I had two exemplars from the monastery of Signy; each of them gives the name of William as author five times. So too does the exemplar of Clairvaux. In the monastery of Igny, moreover, the aforementioned letter which refutes Rupert’s error is prefixed to Rupert’s books *On the Offices*, and that same letter is attributed to our William.

Concerning the disputation against Abelard, note that there exists another disputation by a certain abbot against the same man, contained in three books, but incomplete; and portions have long since fallen out of it—portions which Geoffrey, abbot of Hautecombe, once complained had been lost. Yet it remains incomplete to this day. Some have attributed this to our William; but the work which I present here was taken from the monastery of Signy, where it was written by our author himself.

> [Note: [Col. 0203] It is also by William himself. EDIT.]

[Col. 0205] Who that other abbot was is unknown. Nevertheless, to satisfy the curious, it seemed fitting to add it.

[Col. 0205]

## LETTER TO THE BRETHREN OF MONT-DIEU ON THE SOLITARY LIFE

(Printed among the Works of St Bernard in the *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIV, col. 298.)

[Col. 0205]

## MEDITATIVE PRAYERS

(*Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, edited by Bertrand Tissier, vol. IV, p. 22, Bonofonte, 1669, folio.)

### MEDITATION I. The soul contemplates God’s foreknowledge, predestination, and reprobation.

[Col. 0205A]

O depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God: how incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? (Rom. XI.) For, Lord, you have mercy on whom you have mercy; but you bestow mercy on him on whom you will have had mercy. For it depends not on one who wills or runs, but on you, our merciful God (Rom. IX).

Here the earthen vessel springs back from the hand of him who fashioned it; from him who says through the prophet: “I have made, and I will bear” (Isa. XLVI). It springs back from the hand that holds and bears it—though it is about to fall, be broken, and be crushed—and cries: “Why is fault still found? For who has resisted his will?” [Col. 0205B] (Rom. IX.) And it adds: “Why have you made me thus?” (Ibid.) Thus does the earthen and clay vessel, a vessel of dishonour and wrath fitted for destruction, speak to you, O eternal Wisdom, when rather it ought to tremble before you and pray to you, who have power from the same mass of clay to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour.

Yet the vessels of honour and election remain: vessels of mercy, which you prepared beforehand for glory. They do not say this, but acknowledge you as their Creator and potter, and themselves as clay compacted in your hand. If they fall from it, woe to them, for they will be broken, crushed, and reduced to nothing. They know this, and by your grace do not fail. Have mercy, Lord, have mercy: you are our potter, and we are clay. Yet somehow we still hold together; [Col. 0205C] we are still borne in the hand of your power; we still hang upon your three fingers—faith, hope, and charity—upon which you suspend the mass of the earth, that is, the solidity of your holy Church. Have mercy; hold us, lest we fall from your hand. Burn our inmost parts and heart with the fire of your Holy Spirit, and strengthen what he has wrought in us, lest we dissolve and be reduced into [Col. 0206A] our clay or into nothingness.

We were created by you for you, and our conversion is toward you. We acknowledge you as maker and fashioner; we adore and invoke your wisdom in ordering, your goodness and mercy in sustaining and preserving. Perfect us, who made us; perfect us unto the full form of your image and likeness, to which you formed us.

The clay vessel destined for clay says to you, and its voice is that of one falling and breaking: “Why have you made me thus?” A vessel for honour does not say this. For it believes with the heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X), because in your goodness you made all things well: you made this one for honour and that one for dishonour well, giving free choice to each, so that each might do what it does, not under compulsion of necessity but by [Col. 0206B] spontaneous will, and might possess the proper merit of virtue. For virtue is the voluntary assent of a good will to the good.

But since you possess knowledge of all things, you foreknew, O eternal Wisdom, concerning each of the two how each would use free choice and what kind of master each would be over himself and his affairs; and you had grace ready for each who would not receive it in vain. Yet your foreknowledge does not compel them to be what they will be, as though they necessarily will be so because you foresaw that they would be so. Rather, because they were going to be so, you—who know all things before they happen—therefore foresaw this also; and your foreknowledge cannot in any way be deceived.

Your foreknowledge, God, is your very wisdom, which [Col. 0206C] eternally coexists with you from eternity, even if no creature existed. In it are eternally the causes of all things which come to pass in time, including the foreknowledge of the creature to be created in its own time. Yet that creature was not future to you, because in your consubstantial Word itself, through whom all that has been made was made, “life was” (John I): existing in him as life in the manner in which it would be future; wholly future in that manner because in him it was life. But it was life not compelling it to be so, but existing in him as that which would be so.

[Col. 0207A] What then? Is the temporal manner of what will be the cause in God of that which is—that is, of eternity? For if it were not going to be so in time, it seems that it could not be eternally in the Word of God. But your knowledge or foreknowledge, God, is your very Truth, which says: “I am the truth” (John XIV). And just as you, God, do not by foreknowing compel what is future to occur, so neither can you be compelled to foreknow by what will be. For to you nothing is past, nothing future; but you are always what you are. Whatever exists in any way, whether present, past, or future, is life in your Word. “The wicked walk round about” [Col. 0207B] (Ps. XI). Gather yourself, O human being, from the circle of error to the centre of truth.

The clay vessel is thus reduced to its clay: God’s foreknowledge does not compel it to this, because its future condition was not hidden from him. Yet because he foresaw that it would be so, he predestined it to destruction. God’s foreknowledge is also his goodness, prepared from eternity for all, though not to be received by all. Nor is it outside God’s foreknowledge to know by whom it will be received and by whom it will not; this goodness, as has been said, was prepared from eternity for all insofar as concerns God’s goodness, even if no creature existed. For this goodness is the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son. Hence at the creation of the world: “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “was borne over the waters” (Gen. I)—that is, offering himself to all, [Col. 0207C] presenting himself to all by doing good and providing what is useful, which is proper to the Holy Spirit; yet fleeing the ill-disposed soul, into which wisdom cannot enter (Wis. I).

Thus foreknowledge concerning the creature is, as regards God, foreknowledge; as regards human beings, predestination. It is election or reprobation itself. Hence: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XIV). Predestination is the preparation of grace; grace is the effect itself. Why one is taken up into it and another rejected, do not wish to inquire, if you do not wish to err. If you are proud, that is not hidden from God’s foreknowledge; nor do you escape his providence, by which you are predestined to the punishment prepared for the proud. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV). Pride, therefore, is both the merit and the sign of reprobation, just as humility is the merit and sign of election.

[Col. 0207D] Let the clay vessel therefore say: “Why have you made me thus?” that is, “Why have you predestined me to destruction?” And Truth answers: “To speak in your own terms: because I foresaw that you would become a vessel of wrath fitted for destruction—a fool, who did not know, or did not wish, to be saved; proud, scorning to be humbled. Therefore I now make no complaint, but you will go irredeemably to destruction. Yet you do not resist my will, since it is my will that mercy should be near to the wretched—that is, to those who know themselves to be wretched—while the mighty in iniquity should suffer mighty torments. I will have mercy only on the humble: ‘I have mercy on whom I have mercy.’”

[Col. 0208A] Go on and ask: “Why did you not give me humility?” Because I gave you something greater, freedom of choice; and you, like one mighty in iniquity, loved malice more than goodness. Moreover, you have turned your evils against me and strive so to excuse yourself by them that you wish to accuse me. You do not wish your iniquity to be found out so as to be hated; therefore you will go to your place, a vessel fitted for wrath and destruction.

### MEDITATION II. The soul presents itself to God, desiring to be enlightened by him and, with the mind withdrawn from sensible things, to contemplate the most holy Trinity.

“Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. XXXIII).

I am ashamed, Lord God; I am ashamed with a foul and dreadful shame [Col. 0208B] whenever, as I approach you, I find the door of your vision shut against me. I seem almost to hear that terrible voice: “Amen, I say to you: I do not know you” (Matt. XXV). And I who desired to be enlightened by you am so wholly darkened by the pain of my heart and disturbance of my mind that it seems to me I would almost have been better not to approach. For who will console me if you choose to desolate me? Let all my consolations, which are not you or do not come from you, depart and perish. “Woe to one alone,” says Solomon (Eccl. IV). Truly, woe to me alone if you are not with me, or I with you.

Lord, I believe myself blessed and most blessed if I feel that you are with me; but I weary of myself and hate myself whenever I feel that I am not with you. So long as I am with you, I am also with myself; but I am not with myself as long as I am not with you. And woe to me whenever I am not with you, without whom I can never exist. For I could not continue to exist in any manner, whether in body or soul, unless your power were present; I would not desire or seek you except through your grace already present; I would never find you unless your mercy and goodness came to meet me.

But when in all these things I am with you, I feel your grace at work within me: it is good for me that I exist, that I live; my soul boasts in the Lord. But if you are present to me in doing me good while I am absent in thought or affection, then the benefits of your grace around me seem like the attentive and dutiful care of burial about a corpse. If at times I sense you passing by, [Col. 0208D] you do not stay with me, but pass me as I cry after you, like that Canaanite woman (Matt. XV). And when, as though wearied by the importunate cries of my need, you throw back upon my shameful conscience its former uncleanliness as a dog and its present shamelessness, and drive away—or allow to depart—your dog from your table, hungry, starving, and afflicted by the lashes of conscience: shall I then approach any further? Certainly, Lord. For little dogs driven from their master’s house with blows immediately return, and, keeping watch around the house, receive their daily bread. Driven out, I return; shut out, I cry; beaten, I entreat. A dog cannot live without human companionship, nor can my soul without [Col. 0209A] its Lord God.

Open to me therefore, Lord, that I may approach you and be enlightened by you. You dwell in your heavens, and have made darkness your hiding place, dark waters in the clouds of the sky (Ps. XVII); and, as the prophet says, “you have set a cloud in the way, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. III). But I have decayed upon the earth and heaped thick mud against myself, making a shield of my heart. Your heavenly stars do not shine upon me; the sun is darkened; the moon does not give its light.

For in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs I hear your mighty deeds; in your Gospels your sayings and deeds gleam for me; the examples of your servants continually strike my eyes and ears; the Scriptures of your truth shake me with terrors and prick me with promises, constantly pressing themselves upon my sight and beating at the deafness of my ears with their clamour. [Col. 0209B] But through evil habit and excessive dullness of mind I have become hardened; I have learned and grown accustomed to sleep against the brilliance of the sun, not to see what confronts me, and—though placed in the sea—not to hear the roar of the sea or the thunder of heaven: dead in heart.

How long, Lord, how long? How long will you not tear open your heavens and come down, and shake my stupidity in the wrath of your consummation, so that I may not be what I am; so that I may know you ruling Jacob and the ends of the earth; so that at least I may turn at evening, suffer hunger like a dog, and go about your city (Ps. LVIII), which still partly journeys on earth, yet in its greater part already rejoices in heaven—if perhaps I may find those who will receive me, as I fail, into their dwellings, having no bed of my own in which to lay my head?

At times I do indeed hear the voice of your Spirit, but it passes like the whisper of a gentle breeze (III Kings XIX); and I understand it saying: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII). I hear and am shaken; and, rising as though from sleep and shaking myself, I become somewhat less dull. I open my mouth and draw in breath; I stretch out the faculties of my soul that they may cast off sloth; I emerge from the inward places of my nocturnal conscience; I go forth toward the light of the sun of righteousness rising upon me.

But when I wish to turn my sleepy eyes toward him, they are dazzled, being unaccustomed to light and accustomed to darkness. With the trembling and flickering pupil of reason, together with its eyelids, I wipe away as far as I can, by the hand of practice, [Col. 0209D] the rheum of long sleepiness. If, by your gift, I find the fountain of tears which is accustomed soon to rise in the valleys of the humbled and contrite soul, I wash the hands of action and the face of devotion. Then, as the hawk spreads its wings toward the south to feather itself, I stretch out my hands to you, Lord; my soul is before you like waterless earth. And as a desert land, trackless and without water, so do I appear before you in the sanctuary, that I may behold your power and glory (Ps. LXII).

And when I raise the eyes of my mind, the faculty of reason, toward you, O sun of righteousness, what commonly happens to those drunk with sleep or suffering from weak eyes happens to me: seeing one thing, they suppose that there are two or three, until, through continued looking, they begin to understand that the defect belongs [Col. 0210A] to the eyes, not to the thing seen. For when my soul has awakened from the use or pleasure of senses and sensible objects, imagination first confronts it. Imagination darkens, with images of sensible things, the soul accustomed to sensible objects, although the senses are shut; so that, as it had been wholly occupied with sensible things, it can now know or understand nothing except the imagination of sensible things.

Therefore, when awakened suddenly from the sleep of negligence, I look toward God, concerning whom the divine law instructs me, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, God is one” (Deut. VI), and when I ought wholly to direct the gaze of my mind toward him by whom I am to be enlightened, whom I am to adore and pray to, the Trinity of God presents itself to me. Catholic faith, sung into me by my forebears, impressed by habitual use, and commended to me by you [Col. 0210B] yourself and your teachers, sets this Trinity before me. But the foolish imagination of my soul receives and contemplates it in such a way as to dream that the number of the Trinity inheres in the simple substance of divinity—which exists outside all number, yet made all things in weight, number, and measure—and assigns, as it were, a proper place to each of the persons in the Trinity. Thus it imagines that it must pray to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit as though it had to pass from one to another through a third. Thus the mind, clouded in the One, is scattered among the Three, as though it had to distinguish or unite three bodies.

While imagination—that is, the imagining mind—imagines this even unwillingly, or endures the imagined thing unwillingly and in protest, faith comes and reproves it; reason judges through faith; authority condemns it; and all things within me jointly cry out what was said above: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, God is one” (Deut. VI). For while faith, reason, and authority teach me to think of the Father in himself, the Son in himself, and the Holy Spirit in himself, they nevertheless judge that nothing must be admitted in the holy Trinity which introduces a division of substance through time, place, or number, or which seems to imply a confusion of persons. They so affirm the unity of the Trinity as to exclude solitude; they so affirm the Trinity of unity as not to admit plurality of number into the substance of the Godhead.

For your grace, Lord, preceding every merit, every prudent knowledge, and every virtue in us, gives us [Col. 0210D] some small knowledge of ourselves and of you. Grace itself subjects us to humility; humility to authority; authority to faith. Faith instructs reason; reason, through faith, educates—or destroys and rejects—imagination. But reason does not itself instruct faith toward understanding; through faith, it awaits understanding from above, from the Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James I).

This understanding is not that which is gathered from reason or formed by ratiocination, but that which is brought from the throne of your majesty through the merit of faith and shaped by your wisdom. It is altogether like its origin: coming into the mind of your faithful one, it gathers reason to itself and conforms reason to itself; it quickens and enlightens faith.

Therefore the soul, fearful and astonished, stands to pray to its God, always carrying itself in [Col. 0211A] its hands as though to offer itself to you. Fearful amid familiar things, astonished at unfamiliar things, it bears, in seeking you, the seal of your faith; but it has not yet found one to whom it may open that seal. It seeks your face, Lord, your face; it neither knows nor wholly does not know what it seeks. It abhors the phantasms of its heart concerning you as idols. It loves you as faith describes you to it, but the mind is not sufficient to see. Burning with desire for your face, to whom it may offer the sacrifice of its piety and righteousness, offerings and holocausts, it is more troubled when delayed.

And since it does not quickly obtain the enlightenment of your faith, to which it has entrusted itself, at times it becomes so stunned that it scarcely believes itself to believe in you; it comes to hate itself because it seems to itself not to love you. But far be it that she who is so distressed by longing for you should not believe in you, or that she who desires you to the contempt of all that exists, even of herself, should not love you! How long, Lord, how long? Unless you light my lamp and enlighten my darkness, I shall not be delivered from this temptation, nor shall I leap over this wall except in you, my God.

### MEDITATION III. The soul expresses its desire to see God and ranges freely over the object itself which it desires to enjoy.

I no longer dare to gaze upon your face, Lord, whom I desire unto death, because you said to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). Yet although I wish to die in order to see, or to see in order to die, [Col. 0211C] I cover my face like that same Moses, not daring to look upon you against yourself. For thus we read there: “Moreover Moses covered his face, for he did not dare to look upon the Lord” (Exod. III). For perhaps he would have looked upon the Lord against the Lord if he had wished to look upon God, not as to who he was, but as to what he was. For he heard who he was: “I,” he says, “am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (ibid.).

Yet when that same Moses had heard of his death and still burned with the same longing, praying that your glory might be shown to him, you answered: “I will show you all good” (Exod. XXXIII). And, Lord, where is all good except in your face? Thus David too, burning with the same longing, says: “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Ps. XV). Forgive, [Col. 0211D] forgive: my heart is impatient for you. I seek your countenance; through yourself I seek out your face, lest you turn it from me at the end.

For I know and am certain that those who walk in the light of your face do not stumble, but walk securely; all their judgment proceeds from your face. They are those who live, because they live as they read and understand in the pattern of your countenance. Lord, I do not dare to look upon you against yourself, lest I be struck with still greater astonishment. Yet standing before you as poor, beggarly, and blind, as you see me not seeing you, I offer you a breast full of longing for you and my whole self—whatever I am, whatever I can do, whatever I know, and even this very fact that I languish and fail after you. But I do not find where I may find you.

[Col. 0212A] Where are you, Lord, where are you? And where, Lord, are you not? I know certainly, and am most certainly certain, that here and now you are with me: in you we move and are; and from your most health-giving presence my soul burns and faints for your salvation. I know most certainly and truly, I feel most healthfully, that you are with me; I know and feel, adore, and give thanks. But if you are with me, why am I not with you? What stands in the way? What hinders? What intervenes? If you are with me by doing me good, why am I not with you by enjoying you, the good of all my goods?

Is it because of my sins? And where is he who took them away and nailed them to his cross? Is it because I do not love him? Would I not willingly die a hundred and a thousand times for you, Lord Jesus? If this is not enough for you, it is not enough for me either, because nothing is enough for my soul, nor does it seem to itself to love you at all unless it enjoys you. But it cannot enjoy you unless, by your gift and according to its measure, it sees and understands you.

Why then does it not see you? I who now love you unto death would then love you unto eternal life. Some fragrance of yours, Lord, already breathes that life into me. If only it were perfected in me, for the present I would seek no more. For at times you send me, as it were, little morsels of your consolation; but what are they to the desire of my hunger? I beseech you, tell my soul, O its salvation, why you have breathed into it desire for yourself. Is it only that it may torment, tear apart, and kill me? And would that it had killed me! I beseech you, Lord: is this my Gehenna? Let it be so. Let it never cease to torment me, nor let me ever cease [Col. 0212C] to burn in it; let me have no leave to breathe in any respect for one day, one hour, one moment, until I appear in your presence, your glory appears to me, and the eternal festivity of your face shines upon my soul.

Let that ancient Moses have his face veiled toward you, bearing the figure of the people over whom he presided, always fleeing from the face of the Lord. Your Paul—wholly ours because wholly yours—the trumpet of the New Testament, speaking for himself and for his disciples in longing and love for you, says: “We all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (II Cor. III). This man of yours did not flee from your face, but ran toward your face.

Forgive, Lord, forgive my boldness [Col. 0212D] and importunity; we still dare because we burn. Your fire presses us—the fire which you came to cast upon the earth and wished intensely to be kindled (Luke XII). I beseech you by your most almighty goodness, by your ever most gentle patience toward us: allow me still to ask something, and tell my soul what it desires when it desires your face. For it is so blind, so bewildered in relation to myself, that it melts away in desire and does not know what it desires.

Does it wish to see you as you are? And what is “as you are”? Is it what sort you are, or how great? But you are neither of a certain quality nor of a certain quantity, because there is neither quality nor quantity in you, who are what you are. What then is “as you are”? To see this is beyond us, because to see what you are is to be what you are. No one sees the Father except the Son, [Col. 0213A] nor the Son except the Father; for it is the Father’s being to see the Son, and the Son’s being to see the Father.

But he goes on to say: “And to anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI). The will of the Father is not one thing and that of the Son another, but one and the same will, which is the Holy Spirit. Therefore, through the Holy Spirit, the Trinity—God himself—reveals itself to some friend of God whom it has wished especially to honour. But does a human being see God as the Father sees the Son or the Son the Father—whose seeing one another, as has been said, means not that they are two different things, but that they are one God? Exactly so, but not in every respect.

That this may be made somewhat clearer to us, we must consider sight and its natural power: what does physical understanding maintain? Every bodily sense, if it is to be a sense and to perceive, must in some sensible way be altered into that which it perceives: sight into what becomes visible to it, hearing into what is audible, and similarly with the rest. Otherwise it neither perceives nor is a sense. For unless the soul of the perceiver, through the sense reporting the object to reason, is changed by a certain transformation of itself into the thing, or into the quality of the thing, perceived, it neither is a sense nor can perceive.

Accordingly, if the soul perceives God as good through love, which is its sense, and loves him because he is good, it cannot do this unless, sharing by affection in the good itself, it itself becomes good. If we return to the sense of the soul, is this not what Paul says: “Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image”? [Col. 0213C] (II Cor. III.) For this is in some manner the case with the soul’s sense. The soul’s sense is love; by it, whether soothed or offended, it perceives whatever it perceives. Whenever through it the soul is stretched toward something, it is changed by a certain transformation of itself into what it loves. This does not mean that it is the same in nature, but that it is conformed in affection to the thing loved; for it cannot love someone as good because that person is good unless it itself becomes good in that good.

Is this not: “Think of the Lord in goodness”? (Wis. I.) And Wisdom says: “To know you is consummate understanding” (Wis. VI). And the Apostle: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (Phil. II). This is charity: whoever loves abides in God, and God in him (I John IV). O charity, charity, which has brought us so far that, by loving God and the Son [Col. 0213D] of God, we are called—and are—gods and sons of God! Although it does not yet appear what we shall be, when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (I John III).

Lord, it is good for us to be here; we delight to remain here; and would that we might be permitted to die here! But to us who meditate, speak, and write of you, grant, I pray, sober spiritual perceptions, restrained and disciplined words, and a heart burning for you, O Jesus, for the opening of the Scriptures that concern you. Forgive, Lord, forgive; love for your love drives me: you know, you see. I am not an investigator of your majesty, but a beggar of your grace. I beseech you, by the sweetness of your most sweet gentleness, let not your majesty crush me, but let your grace raise me up.

Forgive, I say, because the proper desire of faith is the vision of God: here in an enigma, but there face [Col. 0214A] to face. Do not presume, therefore, or be confident, O human being; do not stop here, whoever you are, a man of desires like Daniel; and do not say, “It is enough.” Whatever you perceive here of God, whatever you see, whatever faith teaches you about him here, is an enigma: one thing more obscure, another more distinctly expressed. Yet how sweet it is when present, how desirable when it seems absent, those who experience it know. For this is the white stone bearing a written name, which no one knows except the one who receives it (Rev. II).

But concerning what will be face to face, it has been said: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). For the one who sees here does not live, but will say: “Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII), then at last hoping that he will live when he sees perfectly. What can sense do here? What can imagination achieve? What can reason do? What can rational understanding do? For though reason, O God, sends us toward you, it does not reach you of itself. Nor does even that understanding which arises from reason concerning lower things exceed the limits of reason or possess the measure needed to reach you.

But the understanding that comes from above bears the savour of what is above: it is nothing human but wholly divine. Where it pours itself out, it brings with it reasons of its own kind, which do not communicate themselves to lower reason except insofar as that reason receives them through the obedience of faith. In the holy Trinity this understanding divides nothing and joins nothing together; but it touches the faithful sense in such manner, measure, and time as the Holy Spirit wills, so that those praying to or contemplating you, having passed beyond all that you are not, may in some measure see you who are, though they do not see you as you are. Yet some intermediate object delights the gaze of the devout mind: it is known neither to belong to the things which you are not, nor, though it is not wholly all that you are, to be foreign to what you are.

For thus the Spirit of the Lord suddenly clothes and changes his quiet and humble one, upon whom he rests, into another man, so that the perception of the beholder does not divide. May unity not confuse the Trinity; may the Trinity not offend the piety of one seeking the one God; the unity of substance does not grieve the charity that rejoices in love for the Father and the Son. In neither case let solitude or plurality disturb it; rather, let the unity of Trinity and the Trinity of unity help it even in this: that with pious and sober understanding it may comprehend, by not comprehending, the majesty of divine incomprehensibility.

Thus, tasting and seeing how sweet the Lord is, it is suddenly so wholly sweetened by tasting his sweetness, so enlightened by living in the light of his truth, so gladdened in the joy of the Holy Spirit by the sudden fullness of the highest good, that, if this is perfected in it, it may be confident that it has obtained eternal life. For “this,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII). Come therefore to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed (Ps. XXXIII).

### MEDITATION IV. The soul asks for the gift of prayer and describes its former state and its final solitude.

[Col. 0215A]

Merciful and compassionate Lord, patient and abounding in mercy: you are gracious, Lord, to all, and your mercies are over all your works (Ps. 144 [145]). You exhort us, Lord—you yourself, and through your Holy Spirit—to pray and to watch in prayer. You exhort and teach us as one who is loving, compassionate, desirous of mercy; and you prepare a ground for us, doing judgment and justice for us, so that, when we pray as we ought, you may as it were have a just ground for showing us mercy. Indeed, you yourself dictated to us the form of prayer, lest you, both judge and advocate, should fail our cause in any respect.
