And you commanded us confidently [Col. 0215B] to ask in your name, and to believe that whatever we ask, we shall receive, and it shall be done for us (John 16; Mark 11). Your goodness prompts this in you, Lord; pressing necessity lies heavily upon us. Yet, though you exhort, we grow sluggish; though you dictate, we neglect; though you promise, we do not believe. But in your abundant mercy and compassion you shake many who are sluggish and negligent; in your patience you overlook the unbelieving. Moreover, because we neither know nor can know how we ought to pray (Rom. 8), you send us your Holy Spirit, to aid our weakness and intercede for us with inexpressible groanings.

Therefore we pray because you exhort us; we ask confidently because you promise; and immediately you come to meet us and hear us praying, finding—by doing—that through which you may be gracious to us. Gracious to all, Lord, you multiply your sweetnesses for us, and your mercies over all your works begin to appear to us. For when you, God who draw near and do not withdraw, begin to approach us, and your consolations to gladden our souls, then at once, by the fragrance and touch of your most health-giving presence, the deadened senses of the soul revive; faith exults, confidence becomes glad, the heart is kindled, tears flow—not tears that extinguish the kindled fire, but that make it rise the higher. And when your Spirit aids our weakness, we weep copious, rich, sweet tears from the affection awakened by your sweetness. When you wipe them away with the compassionate hand of consolation, they flow more abundantly, [Col. 0215D] and become our bread by day and night, a strong and welcome refreshment; for it is sweet to us to weep before you, the Lord our God, who made us, whose people we are and the sheep of whose pasture we are (Ps. 94 [95]).

I—I, Lord—am, as your prophet says, “a man seeing my affliction” (Lam. 3). I am poor and in troubles from my youth; yet, having been exalted, I have been humbled and confounded (Ps. 87 [88]). How many great and grievous tribulations you have shown me; and, turning again, you revived me and brought me up again from the depths of the earth. You multiplied your magnificence; and, turning again, you consoled me (Ps. 70 [71]). For when you had once created me in your paradise, [Col. 0216A] and had given me the tree of life itself as a possession of perpetual right, you willed—or permitted—that I should also stretch out my hand to the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2–3), so that, as though wearied with my inward goods, I might discover what I could do outside, with my Eve—my flesh—consenting to this. I tasted and saw, not your sweetness, but my confusion, so that I saw myself to be one whose shame required a covering; whose nakedness trembled at your coming; whose freedom required the restraining discipline of laws. For I was found naked in your sight of all those things which people thought were within me; shameful in my secret places, where I hid neither myself nor you; in need of a governor, though I had undertaken the governance of others.

Therefore, Lord, I hid [Col. 0216B] myself among the trees of paradise; therefore I fled into my darkness. Fleeing, I went far away—not, however, away from you, but toward you—and remained in solitude.

> [Note: The author seems in these words to describe his withdrawal to the monastery of Signy: “I went far away and remained [Col. 0216D] in solitude,” etc. For he indicates that before that withdrawal he had already dwelt in the paradise of holy religion.]

There I wait for you, who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the storm (Ps. 54 [55]). I set my mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope; like a solitary wild ass, drawing in the wind of my love (Jer. 2). And when, restored wholly to myself, I sit alone and silent, hearing neither the cry of the taskmaster nor the sound of battle, seeing that time favors me and that I am free to be at leisure with myself, I examine myself: who I am, and whence I came. And I find myself one of Adam’s children, by nature a child of wrath (Eph. 2), but by grace a child of your handmaid, holy Church; one of the exiles from paradise, dwelling and laboring in the land of the curse, which you cursed because of Adam’s works. [Col. 0216C] When I have worked it, it does not yield its fruits to me, but produces thorns and thistles. In the sweat of my face I eat my bread, according to that most severe sentence of your righteous judgment, by which you rebuked the proud and accursed who turn aside from your commandments.

O good Creator, how well you had created me! How gloriously you had formed me! How happily you had placed me! For you had created me, Lord, as your Apostle says, for good works (ibid.), which you had prepared for me to walk in; you had formed me in your image and likeness; and you had placed me in the paradise of your delight, that I might cultivate and guard it—cultivate it by exercises in worthy pursuits, guard it lest the serpent should creep in. The serpent crept in, seduced my Eve, [Col. 0216D] and through her made me a transgressor. Therefore, driven from the paradise of a good conscience, I became an exile in a foreign land, in the region of unlikeness.

But, O Lord, who created all things and saw all that you had created, that they were very good (Gen. 1): shall your good thing perish because of my evil work? For you established paradise not for paradise’s sake because of me, but for my sake when you made me a human being upon the earth. Do not repent, O Creator, that you made me human upon the earth; but command, as in the beginning, that I may be a rational human being, having dominion over my earth: that my body [Col. 0217A] may be subject to my spirit, and my spirit to you. Do not repent of the dignity granted to humanity: that I may rule over the beasts of my earth—the fierce, untamed movements of the soul’s affections; also the creeping things, thoughts that crawl upon the ground, harmful or deadly because of the earth’s poison to which they cling continually; the fish of the sea and birds of the sky—that is, thoughts of the spirit of this world, worldly curiosities, investigating and pursuing its loftiness and its daylight; and likewise the cattle, these bodily senses, created with us so that, according to their name, they may help us.

Grant us—you who gave them to us—that they may endure reason’s bridle, the spurs of good zeal, and the stall of discipline, where they may be fed and nourished with their proper food, to be brought forth for use when necessity requires; but do not permit them to run wild in the broad expanse of public error. “He will come,” says the one who promises; the day will come when lion and lamb shall lie down together (Isa. 11), when those things which now harm shall not harm on all your holy mountain. Then the cattle too shall graze in the richest pastures: no longer beasts of our weakness, but instruments of blessed happiness.

Meanwhile, Lord, answer the heavens, and let the heavens answer the earth; and let the earth hear wine, oil, and grain; and let these hear Jezreel (Hos. 2), that is, the seed of God which you have sown in us. For you nourished me, Lord, as the prophet says, and led me into the wilderness, promising that there you would speak to the heart of your servant (ibid.). Already I give you thanks: you have spoken once and again, and many times; and when my soul says to you, “You are my God,” you answer at times gently and kindly: [Col. 0217C] “I am your salvation.”

And now, O desire of my soul: my soul itself, wishing to be free for you for a little while, and to taste and see how gracious the Lord is, prays to your most gracious mercy to make peace and silence for me from all things without and within; that among the things within me you may preserve for me the right which you gave, while outwardly you may make for me a covenant with the beast of the field, the creeping thing of the earth, and the bird of the sky; and may break bow, sword, and war from my earth, so that all my place may become peace, and my dwelling may be in Zion (ibid.). Give me, Lord, the consolation of my solitude, a solitary heart, and frequent converse with you. For I shall not be alone so long as you are with me, my God. [Col. 0217D] But if you forsake me, woe to one alone: for if I fall asleep, there will be no one to warm the sleeper; if I fall, there will be no one to raise the fallen.

But still, O my refuge and strength, lead me into the inner places of your desert, as you led your servant Moses, where the bush burns and is not consumed (Exod. 3); where the holy soul that has deserved to be taken up to this burns wholly in the fullness of the fire of the Holy Spirit, like a seraph wholly burning and not consumed, but purified. Then for the first time it stands more firmly: this is the miracle of all your miracles and the vision of visions. There is a holy place in which no one stands or advances unless, with the sandals of bodily impediments removed, one walks barefoot—that is, with pure and clean affections. There he who is, though he cannot be seen [Col. 0218A] as he is, is nevertheless heard saying: “I am who I am” (ibid.). There, for the present, the face must be covered lest it look against the Lord; but hearing must be trained in the humility of obedience, that it may hear what the Lord its God speaks within it.

Hide me, Lord, meanwhile, in the secret of your tabernacle in the day of these evils; in the secret of your face from the contradiction of tongues. You have indeed laid upon me your sweet yoke and light burden; and when you show me the difference between your service and the service of the world, you gently and tenderly ask whether it is better to serve you, the living God, or foreign gods. I adore the hand that lays it on, kiss the yoke, and embrace the burden; and it is very sweet to me to labor under it. For many masters besides you possessed me, and for a long time, [Col. 0218B] whose yoke is not sweet and whose burden is not light. I desire to be yours by right; I acknowledge your yoke and the light burden which raises me up rather than presses me down.

But as I enter the new discipline of your service, I seem to see new heavens and a new earth; and behold, you make all things new for me (Rev. 21). Teach me, Lord, a rustic person coming from the countryside of the world, the disciplined customs of your city and the gracious refinements of your court. Unform me from the form of the world to which I had conformed myself; conform me to your citizens, lest I appear misshapen among them. Teach me also the language that I did not know (Ps. 80 [81]), which I begin to hear as I go out from the land of Egypt, but which, grown old in a foreign land, I do not understand: namely, the language in which you speak with your children, and they with you. Make me also [Col. 0218C] understand your signs, by which you make those who understand comprehend what your good, pleasing, and perfect will is (Rom. 12).

And now, my soul gives you thanks, sweet Father: when you speak to it, it begins to recognize your voice, though it does not sufficiently understand what you say to it. For your voice never comes empty, because your voice is your grace: not sounding outwardly, but working inwardly with power and sweetness. When I too speak to you, I attend to you, and this also is good for me. Wherever prayer may go, I never pray to or worship you in vain, since even in praying abundant recompense is made to me. Teach me, therefore, Holy Spirit, to pray without ceasing, that you may grant me in you to rejoice without ceasing. [Col. 0218D] For although your poor one weeps when praying—poor in spirit, or mindful of sins, or placed in straits—yet as grief grows more intense, joy grows more intense. Conversely, one who rejoices in the world, when rejoicing more intensely, is then, if possessed of any wisdom, more violently tortured and grieved in the secret places of conscience. A devout and pure prayer, therefore, is never without joy.

## MEDITATION V. He recounts diverse modes of prayer; recalls Christ’s Passion and his own sins.

When I desire to stir, train, and habituate my heart to pray continually and effectively, I would rather be instructed in this discipline by no one than by you, O Lord Jesus, wisdom of God the Father. I consider, therefore, [Col. 0219A] the modes of prayer by which, praying before people on earth, you gave us a model of perfect prayer; and I find that you sometimes prayed alone (Matt. 14), sometimes amid a crowd (John 12), sometimes in exultation of spirit (Luke 10), sometimes in a bloody sweat (Luke 22), sometimes lifted up upon the cross (John 12).

The exultation of spirit and solitude in prayer are most sweet for me to imitate. But unless you go before me in the blessings of your sweetness, I easily find a place, but not so easily a solitary heart. Exultation of spirit comes either from purity of conscience, of which I am not conscious in myself, or from the abundance of your grace, of which I am unworthy. To pray amid a crowd belonged to you, who lacked nothing; yet, when circumstances require it, neither do we [Col. 0219B] avoid it.

I know, Lord, I know that prayer of blood and prayer of the cross would be most necessary for me. For when I feel what prayer has to sweat out in me, and what the cross has to torture, I do not indeed have a bloody sweat, but my heart sweats bloody tears before your eyes. My body finds no cross upon which to be crucified, but my unhappy soul is tortured within itself beyond every pain of the cross. Nevertheless, Lord Jesus, I am crucified with you, somehow, upon the cross of the religious profession which, from your gift, I offer to you daily and continually—for your gifts are gifts bestowed by you. Yet, as I contemplate the Passion of your cross amid the delights of my own cross, I am pierced by the nails of your fear, confounded, and wholly melt away: not from the pain of my cross, which through your grace is now no pain to me, but from [Col. 0219C] the pain of heart with which I consider your work revived in the midst of the years; made glorious in all years before and after by the effect of redemption. Nothing can compensate for it; no death and no life can answer it sufficiently. Yet the world, redeemed through it, despises it.

For by the very force of habit we now count it as nothing to see you crucified, to think of you dead and buried; and—what more deeply pierces hearts—you beaten with slaps and scourges, mocked, spat upon, fastened with nails and lance, crowned with thorns, given gall or vinegar to drink, although upon your cross you thirsted for nothing but our salvation. When you were crucified, the earth trembled; we laugh. Heaven, with its lights, was darkened; we strive to shine in the world. [Col. 0219D] The rocks were split; we harden our hearts. The opened tombs gave back their dead (Matt. 27); we, luxuriating in beds of wantonness, bury your dead.

Three prayers, Lord, as I understand it, you offered to God the Father at the time of your Passion. In them is contained everything that in that Passion had to be accomplished at the price of blood for yourself, for friends, and for enemies. When you prayed for yourself, indeed, you did not labor, because, as the Apostle says, you were heard because of your reverence (Heb. 5). You prayed also for your friends, who remained with you in your temptations, and for your enemies who were crucifying you but did not know what they were doing. Where is prayer for those who sin knowingly?

> [Note: He seems to deny that Christ prayed for those sinning voluntarily; perhaps because, when he prayed for his killers, he excused even them on the ground of ignorance; or because he did not pray specially for such persons as he did for the ignorant, though he may nevertheless have prayed generally for all. Finally, the author must be interpreted in the sense in which Paul (Heb. 10) asserts that no sacrifice remains for those who sin after receiving knowledge of the truth.]

So long as they are such, they are outside the embrace of the Crucified One, who, with hands stretched out upon the cross, seemed even through the shape of the instrument of execution to embrace all those for whom he suffered. Thus, as the Apostle says: “For those who sin voluntarily, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10). Unless repentance removes these sins, unless a bloody sweat is sweated out and the cross tortures, I do not find that those sinning voluntarily and knowingly have any share either in the prayer of him sweating blood or in the sacrifice of him hanging upon the cross.

Alas for me, whom conscience accuses, whom truth does not excuse [Col. 0220B] so that it may say, “For he did not know what he was doing.” Forgive, therefore, Lord, through the price of your precious blood, all my sins into which I have fallen knowingly and unknowingly; and tell your sinner, make known to your poor one, what he should do concerning them, especially concerning those which I committed knowingly. For if you have excluded all who sin knowingly, woe to the whole world, because you will find very few included.

“For those who sin voluntarily,” says the Apostle, “there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishments, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and counted unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said: ‘Vengeance is mine; [Col. 0220C] I will repay’” (Heb. 10).

Truly, Lord, after receiving knowledge of the truth I have sinned voluntarily and greatly, and insulted the Spirit of grace. Having freely received remission of sins in baptism, after receiving knowledge of the truth I returned to them, like a dog to its vomit. But have I trampled you underfoot, Son of God? I have, if I denied you—although I do not suppose that Peter trampled you underfoot, though he happened to deny you; for at that time he loved you most ardently, even while denying you once, twice, and a third time. Have I counted the blood of the covenant unclean? Let anyone who thinks this be anathema. Far be it that my heart should ever think it; far be it that such a confession should ever pass through my mouth!

It is not that Satan has not at times demanded [Col. 0220D] my faith, to sift it like wheat; but your prayer reached even to me, so that my faith in you has never failed. Virtue is the voluntary assent of the mind to the good. You know how willingly I have always given it to faith in you; preserve it for me until the end. I have always believed in you; I have never denied you; I have always loved you, even when I sinned against you. I repent of my sin unto death, but I do not repent of loving you—except that even then I did not love you as I ought. For if I had loved you thus, [Col. 0221A] I would not have sinned.

But alas! How I fear lest the very fact that I loved you then should turn into judgment against me. For if it is so grave to sin after receiving knowledge of the truth, how much graver after tasting your goodness, after receiving the sweetness of your love! For even in my childhood, an unclean child, I already loved you by your grace; and yet I sinned against you not in a childish manner. From then until now I have never ceased to sin, nor have you ceased to do me good. What remains except that it be said to me: “You received good things in your life” (Luke 16)?

But turn, Lord, your judgment into mercy, and condemn sin through sin, so that you, who have just grounds to condemn me, may, for the little love with which I then loved you, receive now, through your grace, the fullness of your love; and so I may come into your judgment and [Col. 0221B] appear in your holy place and before the eyes of your mercy, on the same ground on which that sinful woman appeared, of whom you said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7).

But first deign that the great heat of your perfect love may sweat out from my heart and burn away every poison of sin; that it may search out and wash away with the tears of my eyes every contagion of my conscience; that your cross may torture away whatever the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life have contracted through the long neglect of my life; that whatever has been kindled and buried through the will of the flesh or consent of the mind may perish at the rebuke of your countenance. Lord, let whoever wishes hear this and mock me as I confess; let him see me, your sinful woman, lying at the feet of your mercy, [Col. 0221C] washing them with the tears of my heart and anointing them with the ointment of devout devotion.

Let all my substance, however little it is, whether in body or soul, go into the price of an ointment pleasing to you, which I shall pour over your head—whose head is God—and over your feet, whose lowest part is our nature’s humility. Let the Pharisee murmur; do you have mercy on me, my God. Let the thief who keeps the moneybags gnash his teeth at me: so long as I please you, I do not greatly value whom I displease. Let this anointing of mine be daily—indeed continual—for you, O love of my heart; for when I anoint you, I anoint myself also. For my nature, corresponding to the hardness of inveterate wickedness, has become like a wineskin in frost. Unless it is continually [Col. 0221D] softened by the sweetness of this ointment, it stiffens, hardens, cracks, and spills whatever of your good it seems to possess within.

You said: “She has done what she could” (Mark 14). Grant me, Lord, faithfully to do for you whatever I have, whatever I know, whatever I am, whatever I can do; may I reserve nothing for myself. I have a cause with you, with no human being. I lie at the feet of your mercy; there I shall lie, there I shall weep, until you make me hear your good voice, the judgment of your mouth, the sentence of your justice and mine—because given to me by you: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7). Lord, through all the judgment which the Father has given you, forestall me by this merit and judge me by this judgment; for out of love for your love I would rather be justified and saved by this judgment than magnified and glorified by another. Lord, [Col. 0222A] do not exclude me from the embrace of your redemption, for in every way I desire to share in your cross.

You said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12). Not so, most gracious one. Rather, let vengeance be mine, so that I may repent. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” Command whatever you will; but grant me to understand and to accomplish what you command, you who have already given my heart this readiness: that neither my heart nor body may withdraw in any respect from doing your will. You have known my sitting down and my rising up, and all things of mine, last and first (Ps. 138 [139]). Unform me from the world to which I conformed myself; form and conform me to your grace, to which I have fled, and give my heart a form of repentance pleasing to you. Give me also, Lord, faith pure and devoted, [Col. 0222B] devout, strong, and unshaken, so that, granting grace for grace, you may say even to me: “Go, because your faith has made you well” (Luke 7).

## MEDITATION VI. The soul contemplates the joy of the blessed, heaven—that is, God—and the ark of the covenant—that is, Christ’s humanity.

“I saw a door opened in heaven,” says blessed John, “and the first voice which I heard, as it were of a trumpet speaking with me, saying: ‘Come up here’” (Rev. 4).

O Lord, who created heaven and earth, but cursed the earth because of sin and Adam’s work, and assigned it for habitation to his children—upon it all who dwell are under the curse, since they continually pay the penalties of the ancient curse, while, by turning aside [Col. 0222C] from your commandments, new curses are daily heaped upon them, of whom it is said: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (Ps. 118 [119])—wearied by so many new and ancient curses, by which I am compelled to pay for things I did not seize and am exacted with compound interest for things I did seize: how gladly, how desirously, would I flee from our earth into your heaven, which, once cleansed of pride when the proud one was cast from it, you kept for yourself—if I could find an ascent and an open door.

I hear that none of all the evils we suffer here is there; that there is no morning and evening there—morning, of joy that does not linger; evening, of lingering weeping—whose departure, you know, would delight me greatly; but that there is one day there, festive with the continual glory [Col. 0222D] of your vision, free from all things that can disturb the feast of your countenance. I hear that fire, hail, snow, ice, and stormy winds do not ascend there—those things which, carrying out your word in afflicting us, continually descend upon us here; that there is no death there nor corruption of bodies or souls; that every plague of disturbance has been wholly removed; that there is one strength, one happiness and joy: your love enjoying its good without fear of losing it.

I hear further that this festal day is renowned for the joys and praises of angels, glorious with the crowns of apostles and martyrs, and that the Church of all the good who have pleased you from the beginning is gathered there and has fixed its everlasting dwelling places for this festival day. When we sometimes see two or three gathered in your name on earth, with you in their midst, and see their dwelling together to be so good and pleasant, so full of the ointment of the Holy Spirit that your blessing commanded there is evident to all, how much more so where you have gathered your saints, who ordered your covenant over sacrifices and, having become heavens, proclaim your righteousness (Ps. 9)! [Col. 0223A]

For not that beloved disciple of yours alone found an ascent there, nor was an open door in heaven shown to him alone. You openly proclaimed to all—not through a herald or any prophet, but through yourself—saying: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10). Therefore you are the door. And when you say, “If anyone enters through me,” you seem open to all who wish to enter. But if we who are on earth see an open door in heaven, what good is it to us, who cannot ascend there? Paul answers: “He who ascended is the same one who descended” (Eph. 4). Who is this? Love. For love toward you, Lord, ascends there in us because love in you descended here to us. Because you loved us, you descended here to us; by loving you, we shall ascend there to you.

But you yourself who said, “I am the door,” through yourself I beseech you: open yourself to us, that you may show more clearly whose house’s door you are, when it is open, and for whom. The house whose door it is, as has already been said, is heaven, which the Father inhabits, of whom it is written: “The Lord’s seat is in heaven” (Ps. 10 [11]). [Col. 0223C] For no one comes to the Father except through you, who are the door.

But one of your servants says: Those who still delight in visible beauties and cannot think anything spiritual about God, because they prefer earth to heaven, hold a more tolerable opinion if they believe that God, whom they still conceive bodily, is rather in heaven than on earth. For you, O maker of all things, both places and times, are neither moved by time nor held by place; you are not supported by the bodily heaven lest you fall, nor do you dwell in it so as not to fill heaven and earth. You are everywhere present—if this can be said of one who is without place; everywhere whole—if totality can be predicated in or of you, in whom there is no partiality.

Yet you yourself taught us to say: “Our Father, [Col. 0223D] who are in heaven” (Matt. 6). And this opinion embraces all so fully that all people, even Jews and pagans, are said to hold that God dwells in heaven. But one thing is the judgment of those who hold what is false; another, the judgment of those who express what is true through such names for things that truth may be understood by the intelligent, while those who cannot conceive or understand things as they are may be allowed, by means of the names of things, to form a somewhat more tolerable opinion. Thus the prophet who says, “God is in heaven” (Ps. 113 [115]), shortly afterward says: “He dwells in Jerusalem” (Ps. 124 [125]).

Answer, then, I beseech you, those who stretch toward you and pant after you: “Rabbi, where do you dwell?” You answer at once and say: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me” (John 14); and elsewhere: [Col. 0224A] “On that day you shall know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you” (ibid.); likewise: “I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” (ibid.). Therefore your place is the Father, and you are the Father’s place; and not only that, but we too are your place, and you ours. Since, then, O Lord Jesus, you are in the Father and the Father in you, O supreme and undivided Trinity, you are your own place; you are your own heaven, for, having no source from which you are, you need no support in which to subsist, except from yourself in yourself.

But when you dwell in us, we are indeed your heaven—not one by which you are supported in order to dwell, but one which you support in order that it may be inhabited. And you, existing as heaven for us, are he to whom we ascend in order that we may dwell. Therefore, as I see it, our dwelling in you—or yours in us—[Col. 0224B] is heaven for us. But the heaven of heaven for you is your eternity, by which you are what you are in yourself: the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father; and the unity by which Father and Son are one, namely the Holy Spirit, not as though coming from elsewhere and making himself a middle term, but existing by co-abiding in that very oneness.

The author and orderer of the unity by which we are one in ourselves or in you is the same Holy Spirit, making us children of God through grace, though by nature we were children of wrath, as the Apostle says: “See what manner of love the Father has given us, that we should be called and be children of God” (1 John 3)—by the gift, certainly, which is the Holy Spirit. And shortly afterward: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see [Col. 0224C] him as he is” (ibid.).

The Son’s birth from the Father belongs to the nature of eternity; birth in us is adoption by grace. The former neither comes to be nor makes unity, but is itself unity in the Holy Spirit. The latter is not unity, but comes to be through the Holy Spirit insofar as it is marked by the likeness of God—indeed beyond the measure of human nature, but short of the divine essence. For the Holy Spirit is also called the seed of this birth, of whom the same Apostle says: “Everyone born of God does not sin, because his seed remains in him, and therefore he cannot sin” (ibid.).

But the vision of God will confer upon us the likeness of God itself, by which we shall see God—not what he is, but as he is—and this itself is the likeness by which we shall be like him. For the Father’s seeing the Son is the Son’s being what he is, and conversely. But for us, seeing God is being like God. This unity, this likeness, is heaven itself, in which God dwells in us and we in God. But you are the heaven of heaven, O supreme Truth, who are what you are, who are from yourself for yourself, your own for yourself, sufficient for yourself; lacking nothing, overflowing in nothing. With you there is no discord, no confusion, no change of state, no alteration or shadow of vicissitude; no need, no death; but supreme harmony, supreme clarity, supreme fullness, supreme life. [Col. 0224D]

No ugliness of your creatures is ugly to you; wickedness does not harm, nor does error err. You have appointed to each of your good creatures its own dwellings of virtue or blessedness, which they are wholly destined to attain, whatever necessity may hinder or delay them; and you have fixed limits for the wicked in their wickedness, which they have no power to pass, even if they do not lack the will. [Col. 0225A]

O Lord, this height, this depth, this wisdom, this power—can this be the heaven of which you are the door? Indeed, indeed it is. Hence, when the door was opened, as the same John says: “The ark of the covenant was seen in heaven” (Rev. I). For what is the ark of the covenant recognized in heaven but, as the Apostle says, “the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things” (Eph. III)? For you are truly the ark of the covenant, in whom is stored from the ages, and fulfilled in the last time, everything that from the beginning of the world was testified by all the saints and prophets, by the Law, prophecies, signs, and wonders. [Col. 0225B]

You are the ark overlaid on every side with pure gold, because the glorifying fullness of the wisdom of God rested in you and wholly encompassed you. In you is the golden jar containing manna: your holy and immaculate soul, in which the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily; and Aaron’s rod which had budded: the dignity of the eternal priesthood; and the tablets of the covenant, by which the world has been made heir of your grace, and the nations have been made fellow heirs, fellow members of one body, and fellow partakers of your promise. Above these are the Cherubim of glory: the fullness of knowledge; above them, however, not as surpassing them in dignity, but because they need to be borne and supported by them; overshadowing the mercy-seat—that is, testifying to the incomprehensibility of the mysteries of your propitiating grace.

These good things, hidden from the ages in the heaven of your secret counsel, you showed to a world longing for them at the end of the ages, when you opened yourself, the door in heaven. You opened it when your grace appeared to all people, instructing us; when your kindness and humanity appeared, saving us not because of works of righteousness which we had done, but according to your mercy (Tit. II). Then, heaven being opened, every good thing and all heaven’s sweetness poured itself upon the earth. Then how great was your goodness toward us, O God—you who did not spare your own Son but delivered him up for us all—became openly known to all, when you made known to the world your salvation and revealed your righteousness before the nations, the righteousness which you wrought for us in the blood of your only Son. [Col. 0225C–D] He himself rendered to you the chaste obedience of love concerning our salvation, and to us the love of his obedience.

Then you blessed our land, and from that time it began to yield its fruit. From that time a public road was laid to your heaven, worn by the footsteps of apostles, martyrs, and all the saints, who, receiving from you the example and grace of love, loved you even to contempt of themselves and did not fear to lay down their lives for you. These unsearchable riches of your glory, Lord, lay hidden with you in the heaven of your secret counsel, until, when the side of your Son—our Lord and Redeemer—was opened on the cross by a soldier’s spear (John XIX), the sacraments of our redemption flowed forth. Thus we may no longer put merely a finger or hand into his side, as Thomas did (John XX), but may all enter through the open door even to your heart, Jesus: the sure seat of mercy; even to your holy soul, full of all the fullness of God, full of grace and truth, of our salvation and consolation. [Col. 0226A]

Open, Lord, the door in the side of your ark, that all whom you are to save may enter from before this flood overflowing the earth. Open to us the side of your body, that those who desire to behold the hidden things of the Son may enter and receive from it the flowing mysteries and the price of their redemption. Open the door of your heaven, that your redeemed may see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, though they still labour in the land of the dying; that they may see and long, burn and run—you who have become for them the way by which one goes there, the truth to which one goes, and the life for which one goes: the way, the example of humility; the truth, of purity; the life, eternal life. [Col. 0226B]

You have become all these things for us: merciful Father, gracious Lord, sweet brother. We are your little children, to whom you said, “My little children, yet a little while I am with you” (John XIII); your servants, to whom you said, “You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (ibid.); your brothers, whom you commanded to go where they would see you. O good Father, sweet brother, gracious Lord—good, sweet, and gracious in all that you are, in whom all goodness abounds—open yourself to us, so that your sweetness, which endures from you even to us, may fill us.

Open yourself to me, you who are the door, that through you I may sometimes enter in affection, although I do not yet deserve to enter in full reality, “into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God” (Ps. XLI). For you have at times opened the ear of your servant, so that he has at times caught the sound of rejoicing and confession, the voice of one feasting; but he has not been permitted to proceed. Therefore my soul is rightly sad; rightly you trouble me. But “hope in God, for I shall yet confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God” (ibid.). [Col. 0226C]

Open to me, Lord, so that, since I am an alien and am not yet worthy to be enrolled as a citizen there, it may nevertheless be granted me by you to sojourn there sometimes, if only for a little while; that, seeing, I may see your glory, and depart only when driven out. If I may deserve to ascend there more often, remain there for some time, and return later, I shall become known to your citizens—not citizens who merely rejoice, but like all who dwell there rejoicing—whose joy no words can express, whose sharing is wholly one. Nor will they regard me as a stranger if you command me sometimes to rest among them in some part of that house of yours.

Lord, my heart is restless and impatient for you, and outside you I find no rest for it. Therefore, when I am cast out of heaven, wearied by my life, I sometimes wish to descend alive even into hell—lest I happen to descend there when dying—that I may see what is done there also. But when, at its very threshold, I find written that in hell there is none who will confess you, I pronounce anathema upon it and flee away. I hear within weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth; but let it not happen to me, Lord, to descend so far. [Col. 0226D]

To you, Lord—to you are my eyes always lifted, you who dwell in the heavens; to your house, to your city, Jerusalem, from which you descended to us, bringing with you so wonderful a pattern of it. Inflamed by this, I often run back there eagerly and longingly. If I find you, the door, open, I enter, and it is well with me as long as this is permitted. If I find you closed, I return ashamed. Forbidden to see your glory, I am sent back miserable to my own house and compelled to endure my domestic and familiar poverty. O if I may see! O if I may endure! O if I may someday hear: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV), so that I may enter thus and never go out again. You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is round about you. Perfect what you have done; give what you have promised. [Col. 0227A]

## MEDITATION VII. The soul expresses its desire to see God.

[Col. 0227B]

My heart has said to you: “My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek. Turn not your face away from me; decline not in anger from your servant” (Ps. XXVI). To compare my face with your face, Lord God, searcher and judge of hearts, seems altogether rash and presumptuous. For if you enter into judgment with your servant, the face of my unrighteousness can do nothing but flee from the face of your righteousness. Yet if, by your gift, burning love might excuse me and devout humility assist my poverty, let those who hate flee; I would not flee from your face. The one presumes; the other nourishes confidence. I am not conscious that I possess these things, yet I profess that I am their friend.

For if you ask me as you asked Peter, “Do you love me?” (John XXI), I shall plainly and confidently say: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I wish to love you.” My heart wills this so strongly that it wills nothing as it wills to love you. I also embrace humility, which those who define it define as contempt for one’s own excellence. Yet because I sometimes unknowingly run into certain trifles of distinction, or when they are offered to me do not shake them off quickly enough, I know very well that I am not humble. [Col. 0227C]

There is another kind of humility, namely self-knowledge. If I am judged by it, according to what I know in myself, all is over with me; and, as they say, with an evil omen I have set my foot upon the justice of your judgment. Yet if this is reckoned a virtue before you—if my sin is always before me—I do not judge myself wholly without this virtue. For even against my will, when I am occupied with better things, the foul face of my sins so often thrusts itself before the eyes of my mind that because of them I myself hate myself.

O Lord, why say much about the shameful face of my conscience? Whatever it is, however it may be, its whole face so longs for your face that it despises and scorns all things of this life, even life itself, for love of it; nor does it care at all how it may appear, provided that it sees you. [Col. 0227D]

Thus meanwhile, O vision to be desired, my face seeks you; I seek your face. Do not, I implore you, turn it away from me (Ps. XXVI). But teach me meanwhile, O eternal Wisdom, by the illumination of your own countenance, what this face and face may be. For though longing draws me from the one toward the other, I know neither sufficiently. I know that if it was not granted to the Apostle Paul to see you face to face in this life, nor to your beloved disciple to see you as you are, then it is not sound-minded to hope or seek this which was not granted to one who loved so greatly and was so greatly beloved.

Yet when I hear of “face” and “face” in David, I cannot despair that someone may hope from you what I hear him hope; not because I have forgotten who I am, but because I hope in the indulgence of your mercy. And though I make miserable progress in this, I would not wish to love you less than anyone who loves you. For although what was denied, as it seems, to Moses was by no means despaired of by David (Exod. XXXIII), this same David sings and chants concerning Moses and the other fathers: “For they did not possess the land by their own sword, nor did their arm save them, but your right hand, and your arm, and the illumination of your countenance” (Ps. XLIII). [Col. 0228A–B]

He also says of himself: “Lord, in your favour you bestowed strength upon my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Ps. XXIX). Therefore, sweetest one, turn toward me that face which you once turned away from holy David, and he became troubled, and I shall be consoled—the face by which, before you turned it away from him, you had in your favour bestowed strength upon his beauty. May your right hand, your arm, and the illumination of your countenance possess my land, as they possessed the land of the fathers in whom you were pleased.

For I hear no one speak and converse so often and familiarly of your countenance and your face as David does (Ps. XVI). Nor should one believe that he had no experience of your countenance, when he prays that all his judgment may proceed from before your face and confidently expects to be filled with joy in your countenance. Blessing the blessed people who know jubilation, he says: “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance” (Ps. LXXXVIII). [Col. 0228C]

Consulting, as attentively as I can, that very countenance of yours, O God of my heart, so that my judgment about this matter may proceed from it—with the whole assent of my conscience crying out in agreement—I find that this your countenance and face are knowledge of your truth. Your blessed people, presenting the face of good will to it, celebrate joy in the Holy Spirit and the festival of the great jubilee year in contemplating and enjoying that very truth of yours. In its light they also walk, directing their steps and all that belongs to them according to the judgments of your righteousness.

There is indeed another face and another countenance of your knowledge, of which it was said to Moses: “My face shall not be seen by you, for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII): the vision or knowledge of your divine majesty. In this life it is better known by not knowing; and to know how one does not know it is the highest knowledge of it in this life. [Col. 0228D]

But, O Lord, although you have made the darkness of our ignorance and human blindness the hiding place of this face, yet around you there have been certain holy persons, your tabernacle—namely, your luminous ones—who, shining and burning through companionship with your light and fire, enlightened and inflamed others by word and example. They announced to us the solemn joy of this surpassing knowledge of you in the life to come, when you shall be seen as you are, or face to face. Meanwhile, through them flashes of your truth shone upon the world, and gleams flashed forth, at which those rejoice who have healthy eyes, whereas those are moved and troubled who love darkness more than light. [Col. 0229A]

For the manifestation of your truth here, through whomever it occurs, is like your sun, which you make rise upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matt. V). Remaining in the purity of its nature, it uses the materials of things as it finds them: hardening mud, softening wax, illuminating every eye, both seeing and blind—the seeing eye, so that, illuminated, it may see more; the blind eye, remaining in its blindness. So too you, O Wisdom of God and light of truth: when you came into the world, through whom the world was made, you enlightened every person coming into this world; but the darkness did not comprehend you. Yet to all who received you and the light of your truth, you gave power to become children of God. [Col. 0229B]

## MEDITATION VIII. On the manifold face of the human being, and the kiss and embrace of bridegroom and bride.

O sun of righteousness, your countenance’s light flashing upon all and the splendour of your truth invite your bride, whoever she may be, saying: “Show me your face, my sister” (Song II). Immediately the soul of good will, to whom peace is proclaimed from heaven, who is Christ’s brother and whose soul is called his sister, desires to appear to you in your holy one as he is, and to see light in your light. [Col. 0229C]

If she is a sinner, she shows you the face of her misery, seeking the face of your mercy. If she is holy, she meets you in the face of her righteousness and finds in you the face of her likeness, by which you, the righteous Lord, love righteousness. But one whose forehead is that of a prostitute refuses to be ashamed; fleeing your truth, she encounters your most severe justice. For as many affections as a human soul has, so many faces has it toward you. But you, O Truth, receive them all; lending yourself to all, you remain unchanged in yourself. Devout humility finds in you familiar grace; burning love finds the sweet substance of oil; contrition of a humble heart finds righteousness prepared for it by you; the prostitute’s forehead finds its own confusion.

Thus, O supreme righteousness, mercy and truth meet one another in you (Ps. LXXXIV): when the truth of human righteousness humbly confesses in a righteous soul, and the truth of your righteousness mercifully deals, as is just, with the person confessing in truth. And while that soul offers the kiss of righteous confession, you receive it in the kiss of peace. [Col. 0229D]

This is the kiss of bridegroom and bride. That her face might be found worthy of your kiss, O Lord, your face was spat upon; that hers might appear beautiful and fair, your face was bruised by blows of hands and reeds; yours was filled with reproaches in human eyes, so that hers might appear beautiful and fair in your eyes. Moreover, you made for her a bath of your precious blood, in which the children of God might be washed. You suffered dreadful things for us, who did dreadful things—things for which no face of any penitence could in any degree satisfy the face of supreme righteousness, unless your innocence had been added to what you suffered for us. And because you were the Son, you were heard on account of your reverence.

For my hands, Lord, which did what they ought not, your hands were pierced with nails; your feet for my feet; your eyes for my unlawful sight; your ears for my hearing—all fell asleep unto death. Your side was opened by a soldier’s spear, so that through your wound everything which long corruption had set aflame and buried within my impure heart might at last flow wholly out. At last you died that I might live; you were buried that I might rise again. [Col. 0230A]

This is the kiss of your sweetness to your bride; this is the embrace of love toward your beloved. Woe to one who has not shared in this kiss; woe to one who has fallen from this embrace. The confession of the thief received this kiss upon the cross (Luke XXII); Peter received it when the Lord looked upon him as he denied him, and he went out and wept bitterly. Many also of those who crucified you, turning to you after your Passion, were joined to you by covenant in this kiss. In this embrace Mary—once possessed by seven demons—rejoiced (John XX); from it the treachery of the betraying disciple had fallen. In this embrace tax collectors and sinners were held close, whose table-companion and friend you became (Matt. IX). There are Rahab the converted prostitute, Babylon knowing you, foreigners, Tyre, and dark Ethiopians (Ps. LXXXVI). [Col. 0230B]

But where, Lord, do you draw those whom you embrace and hold close, if not to your heart? Your heart is that sweet manna of your divinity (Heb. IX), which you have within, O Jesus, in the golden jar of your all-wise soul. Blessed are those whom your embrace draws to it; blessed are those whom you have hidden in the hidden place of that hidden heart, in the midst of your heart, and who are overshadowed by your shoulders from human disturbance. They have no hope except beneath your wings, which protect and cherish them.

For those who are hidden in the hidden place of your heart are overshadowed by the shoulders of your power. They sleep sweetly and rejoice in sweet expectation between the two portions: the merit of a holy conscience and the expectation of the reward promised by you; neither failing through faintheartedness nor murmuring through impatience. But those who kiss one another more sweetly also breathe their own spirits into each other, and delight to be suffused with certain fragrances from one another. [Col. 0230C]

Receive, Lord, and do not reject my whole spirit, which I pour wholly into you, and which is wholly fragrant. Pour wholly yours into me, yours which wholly gives off the scent of what it is, so that mine may no longer smell apart from your sweetness, and that your sweet fragrance, O sweetest one, may remain ever more deeply in me.

This is what is done when we do what you commanded us to do in remembrance of you (I Cor. XI). Nothing sweeter and nothing more powerful could have been provided for the salvation of your children. In eating and drinking the incorruptible feast of your body and blood, we, like your clean animals, bring up again as it were to the mouth, from the inward stomach of memory, the sweetness of meditation; and, always chewing it anew with a fresh affection of devotion into the new and everlasting effect of our salvation, we sweetly store again in that same memory what you have done for us and what you have suffered. [Col. 0230D–0231A]

There you say to the longing soul: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX). And as it tastes and sees your sweetness in the great and incomprehensible sacrament, it becomes what it eats—bone from your bones and flesh from your flesh—so that, as you prayed to the Father when about to suffer (John XVII), the Holy Spirit may work here in us through grace what exists eternally by nature in the Father and in you, his Son: that as you are one, so we too may be one in you. This, Lord, is your face toward the one longing for you; this is the kiss of your mouth to the mouth that loves you; this is the embrace of your love toward the embrace of your bride, who sighs for you and says: “My beloved is mine, and I am his; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song I and II). And: “My heart has said to you: My face has sought you” (Ps. XXVI). [Col. 0231B]

For if the face of our soul does not seek your face, it is not its natural face but some bestial mask. Who would not seek it? Who would not become weak for it? Who would not languish? Who would not fail? Who would not die? Have mercy, Lord. I should already have died after it by I know not what death, unless your visitation had guarded my spirit.

Conversely, in the time of your countenance the enemy finds in you a furnace of fire; the sinner, the portion of his cup—snares, fire, sulphur, and tempestuous winds; the proud person, the power which resists the proud; the hypocrite, the light of truth which he hates. And all these, having consciences branded by the individual faces of their private evils, have, as it were, a common face of impenitent wickedness. You receive it in the face of righteousness judging justly, and those who hate righteousness in the hatred of iniquity. [Col. 0231C]

For because they proved unwilling to have God in their knowledge, you delivered them, O God, to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting (Rom. I): things shameful to mention before you, yet done before you shamelessly and irreverently. From their lusts and their daughters, from sins and their sons, and sons of sons, they weave for themselves that tearful, harsh, and long chain, formed from a multitude of sins as though from linked iron rings: at first sweetly clanking, yet binding beyond release, by which they are drawn into hell. There no one will any longer confess you, O God; there is no hope, no return from there.

Concerning them I wonder whether, once placed in hell, they will somehow be given to know how great a good it is to enjoy you. If they are somehow given to know it, I do not think there is a greater torment in hell than to lack your vision. But alas, alas: those who committed horrible deeds will suffer horrible things besides, because your blood, Christ, will not help the impenitent. Rather, they shall be judged guilty of your blood, which they trampled underfoot by sinning and not repenting. [Col. 0231D]

This is the face of your wrath, which the Prophet fears; and he trembles before the face of those whom he awaits, as the Apostle says: “A certain terrible expectation of judgment, and a zeal of fire which shall consume the adversaries” (Heb. X). Lord God, judge of the living and the dead, these are the two flocks at your right hand and your left on the day of your judgment. And between these lots and portions—the lot of death and life, perdition and redemption, wrath and grace—where shall I stand? [Col. 0232A]

O truth, truth: by the glory and majesty of your countenance, do not hide it from me. Rather flash within me all its lightning, that in its light I may see light: namely, what my face is in relation to yours, and yours in relation to mine; whether, as truth is in you, Jesus, so truth may be in me—that I may put off, according to my former manner of life, the old human being who is corrupted according to the desires of error. For, O Truth, I know that I seek you; but whether I seek you truly, I do not know. This is my face toward you: the face of my great misery and my great blindness. [Col. 0232B]

Although your consolations sometimes make my soul glad, I know what I have been; but now I do not know what I am. One thing have I asked of the Lord; this I seek: that as the face of my misery yearns toward you, so the face of your mercy may shine upon me more and more, unto the complete destruction of all my misery and darkness.

## MEDITATION IX. The soul examines, or summons to judgment, its thoughts and affections.

So dense and immense, Lord, is the misery within me that I am not sufficient to examine it part by part, nor to survey the monstrous face of its totality. For behold, as is its custom, its darkness wraps me round. Neither the sight with which I desire to speak to and hear you, the Lord my God, is free, nor is my hearing unencumbered. Thus my own house, the conscience within me, always treats me; thus it casts me out from itself. Is this what is meant: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI)? [Col. 0232C]

And when, with the eyes of my mind darkened, I strive in some groping way toward the goal at which I was aiming, exhausted and shattered in the effort of burning desire, I fall back from your heights into my depths: from you into myself; from myself beneath myself. With the whole mechanism of my endeavour broken down, I become like some empty grain of dust cast from the face of the earth, the sport of winds amid phantasms of thoughts, wills, and affections—as many as the faces of people, the moments of hours, and the rushes or encounters of things and events.

Therefore, although the face of your goodness is always directed toward me in doing good, the face of my misery, always looking upon foolish earth, becomes so wrapped in the darkness of its blindness that it neither knows nor can appear before you, except insofar as it cannot, however it may be, remain hidden from the face of truth which sees through all things. [Col. 0232D]

Therefore, leaving my gift before the altar, angry with myself and shaking myself awake, I arise within myself. With the lamp of God’s word lit in the indignation and bitterness of my spirit, I enter the dark house of my conscience, as though to discover whence come these darknesses, whence this hateful gloom dividing me from the light of my heart.

And behold, there comes upon my eyes something like a plague of flies, almost driving me from the proper dwelling-place of my conscience. Yet I enter as one entering upon my legal right; and behold, a crowd of thoughts so insolent, undisciplined, varied, and confused that the human heart which produced them cannot distinguish them. Nevertheless I sit down as if to judge them. I command them to stand near me, that I may recognize the faces and nations of each, assigning to each its proper place before me. Before I can examine or recognize them, they scatter, and, with some presenting themselves in place of others, seem to mock their judge. [Col. 0233A]

I am indignant and angry with myself. I rise as though to proceed against them more severely by authority, as in my own kingdom. I summon to myself, and make sit with me as though in counsel, those whom I have at times found sure and stable, drawn from the fountains of the Saviour: he himself is judge, accuser, and witness. I set apart the unclean and worst thoughts as unworthy of a hearing, to be condemned without any judgment and punished with the punishment of penance that they deserve. I drive away idle and hateful thoughts as troublesome flies. Meanwhile, I admit businesslike or preoccupying thoughts, as reasonably to be heard and dismissed, assigning to them their times and places.

Those condemned by the judgment of their own conscience receive their sentence without murmuring. The idle thoughts, seeing the matter seriously conducted, scatter or become more sluggish, fearing to disturb what is being done. The businesslike thoughts, seeing themselves neglected and, since their affairs have ceased, useful only briefly, blush to be counted almost among idle thoughts and depart. [Col. 0233B]

Thus, after the mist of thoughts has been dispersed somewhat, I turn to their origin, namely to arrange the discipline of the affections. Because of the necessity of the solitude to which I have fled, I find their entrances and exits in matters of the flesh blocked; if I found them open, I confess my misery, I should regard my weakness as highly suspect. Yet their prince, love, through the grace of him who strengthens me, being continually intent upon that one thing which I seek, reduces their whole multitude to slavery under itself. It gives laws, shapes measures, and fixes boundaries which they may not pass.

Therefore, all mist now dispersed, I turn healthier eyes toward you, O light of truth. Excluding all others, I shut myself in with you, O Truth. Hiding myself in the hiding place of your countenance, I speak to you more secretly and intimately. Opening to you all the recesses of my conscience, casting off Adam’s garment of skins, which you made for him to cover the shame of his confusion, and showing myself naked to you as you created me, I say: [Col. 0233C–D]

“Behold me, Lord: not as you made me, but as I made myself after I fell away from you. Behold my wounds, recent and old. I hide nothing; I lay all before you—your good things and my evils. You created me in your image; you placed me in your paradise; you gave me a named place among the allotted company of your children; from my very impure childhood you stamped upon me the light of your countenance. I fled from paradise; in place of the dwelling you had given me, I found a sewer and wrapped myself in it. I always held the seal of your countenance in affection, but cast it away in action. For, following my lusts and the vanities of my heart, I ruined my youth and nearly entered upon the way of the dog. Yet my spirit always loved you, even when my flesh neglected you.” [Col. 0234A]

“When I fled from these things, I fled to you, and you drew me out from the whirlpool of the world. I made a covenant with you; I swore and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness. And you, opening to me the bosom of your mercy, gathered me into it. Resting there sweetly, I saw and desired the day of humankind. You sent me out, both unwilling and willing; yet you did not let me go from you. If I at times forgot my God and stretched out my hands where I ought not, immediately the torturers in the secret place of my conscience broke all the inward bones of my soul with the rod of your discipline; outwardly, however, sinners built upon my back.

“Thus, falling and rising, dying and reviving, you bore and sustained me for a long time. At last, when I failed both in body and mind and cried to you from the belly of hell, you immediately came to me: you stretched out your hand and drew me from the pit of misery. You restored me to my former state and gave me back a joy in your salvation greater than before.” [Col. 0234B]

“Such I was, Lord; such I am. Behold, I am wholly present before you. My evils that are manifest are hidden neither from you nor from me; yet there are more hidden from me through my blindness or forgetfulness, though open to you. If there is any good in me, none of it is uncorrupted, because the enemy has snatched much away from me; or, if he could not do this, he has corrupted it in some manner—although I myself have done more to myself than the enemy.”

“Behold before you my face, whose name is misery, before your face, O supreme mercy. I do not hide its concealed angles and recesses from you; you know them, O Truth. I pray that this may be truth before you. For I fear no one as I fear myself, lest knowingly or unknowingly I deceive myself. Do I not believe you (*credo te*), believe you (*credo tibi*), believe in you (*credo in te*), my God? Let those who define the boundaries and limits of my faith not mock me. With heart, mouth, hand, and writing, I offer you, O light of truth, a willing and full assent of faith in all that the Catholic Church believes concerning you. Fulfil these bounds of my faith, if they suffice; supply what is lacking, if they do not.” [Col. 0234C]

“But concerning hope I say confidently: I do not truly believe if I hope for something other than what I believe. I believe you; I hope for you; give yourself to me: I seek nothing else. Yet I do not hope unless I love, nor do I love unless I hope. Therefore, Father, because I love miserably, I hope languidly. And while what has grown above the root of faith withers, the root itself also becomes sluggish. Yet I still believe in you, and hope, and love, O eternal life.”

“O homeland, homeland, which I see and greet from afar, where there are no evils and every good thing! Of evils I know that there are no evils there, a truth which long and wearisome experience has perfectly taught me. But of the good things which are there, in proportion as my experience is distant from them, so too is my knowledge a stranger to them. Have mercy, Lord. Behold, I have run and made straight my course; rise to meet me and see” (Ps. LVIII). “Make known to me my end and what is the number of my days, that I may know what I lack” (Ps. XXXVIII). [Col. 0234D–0235A]

“I stand in your faith; I make progress in hope; poor and beggarly, I stand before you for your love. O love, O fire, O charity, come into us. Be our guide and light, a fire burning and consuming in repentance for sins; Paraclete, comforter, advocate, and helper in the causes of our prayers. Show us what we believe; make known to us what we hope; make the face which we may compare with the face of God, so that we may say: ‘My heart has said to you: my face has sought you’” (Ps. XXVI).

## MEDITATION X. Consideration of Christ’s incarnation and Passion.

Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 6). My conversion is toward my Crucified One. His cross is my glory: by it my forehead is marked; [Col. 0235B] my mind is made glad; my life is set straight; death is loved. Let not those who are worthy to see you seated upon the high and exalted throne of your divinity, and filling all the earth with your majesty, despise me for this; for even those mysteries of your human dispensation that are beneath you fill the temple of every contemplation, whatever its greatness.

Let your holy angels have their glory in heaven; yet let them sometimes share their grace with us also on earth. For their blessed perfection still delights to advance through what belongs to us, and finds sweetness when, as the Apostle says, “through the Church the manifold wisdom of God is made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3). Therefore, Lord, forgive us even in this, if your love sometimes [Col. 0235C] draws us so that we desire to see with them what we love with them. We rejoice for them with full charity, since they see what we are not yet worthy to see.

May they happily contemplate, in your wisdom, the majesty of your divinity, which, beholding what is before our middle and what is after it, encloses within the present of its eternity all that whatever it may be of past or future; which reaches mightily from end to end. But it has spread out in charity our middle things, which belong to your human dispensation, disposing all things sweetly for the daughters of Jerusalem—devout souls, yet still weak. Not yet having their senses trained to behold those sublime things, they love to be moved by your lowly things and, as it were, to melt away around things like themselves.

Among these, Lord, may my spirit too someday learn [Col. 0235D] to worship you, who are Spirit, in spirit and truth, when the flesh no longer lusts against it, or does so more slowly. But meanwhile, because it cannot be so vigorously disengaged for what is yours as is fitting for it, arrange for it what is its own as sweetly as befits it. For since I have not yet passed beyond the rudiments of my sensuous imagination, permit and welcome my still-weak soul, through that very imagination of the mind, to exercise its own disposition upon your lowly things: namely, to embrace the manger of the newborn; to adore the holy infancy; to kiss the footprints of him hanging on the cross; to hold and kiss the feet of the risen one; to put my hand into the places of the nails; and to cry out: “My Lord and my God.”

And in all [Col. 0236A] these things, as Job says, “when I visit my form, I shall not sin,” when I pray and adore what I shall see in imagination, what I shall hear, what my hands shall touch concerning the Word of life. For I shall boldly say that, in the sweet ordering of your wisdom, this grace was provided for us from eternity, and that among the chief causes of your Incarnation this was not the least before you: that your little ones in your Church, still needing milk rather than solid food, and unable to think of you spiritually and in your own manner, might have in you a form not unknown to them, which they might set before themselves in the sacrifice of their prayers without scandal to faith, since they were not yet able to gaze upon that brightness of your divine majesty.

Therefore, although we now no longer know you according to [Col. 0236B] the flesh, nevertheless, inasmuch as you sit glorified at the Father’s right hand on high, having become so much better than the angels as you have inherited a name more excellent than theirs, we pray to, adore, and entreat that very flesh of ours—which you did not set aside, but glorified—which is the footstool of your feet. David exhorts us to this and says: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98).

And O blessed temple of the Holy Spirit, from which no oblivion banishes Christ exalted upon the cross, and in which the blood ever flows fresh for the salvation of the believer and lover, and unceasingly accomplishes what the Prophet asks: “Redeem me and have mercy on me” (Ps. 25). For the effect of our redemption is celebrated within us as often as the affection of the suppliant recalls it. But because we cannot even do this as we wish, we therefore dare still further: we place before ourselves an image of your Passion, so that even the eyes of the flesh may have something to see and cling to—not worshipping the likeness of the picture, but the truth of your Passion in the image.

For when we gaze more attentively upon the silent image of your Passion, you seem to us to say from the cross: “Having loved you, I loved you unto the end. Let death and hell bite me into their own death. Eat, my friends, and be drunk, my beloved, unto eternal life.” Thus your cross becomes for us that sheet shown to blessed Peter and let down from heaven by its four corners. Entering into it, along with clean and unclean animals, we rejoice to be lifted into heaven [Col. 0236D] in it; and in it we who are unclean are cleansed.

For through the image of your Passion, Christ, your goodness, contemplated by us in relation to ourselves, suddenly transfers us into an affection for the highest Good. In the work of your salvation you grant us to see its face, no longer through an understanding arising as though from human effort, with the trembling eyes of the mind fleeing your light, but through the tranquil sense of love, the wholesome practice of seeing, and the sweetness of enjoyment—your wisdom sweetly arranging for us what is ours.

For the one who climbs up by another way labors. But one who enters through you, O door, walks on level ground and comes to the Father, to whom no one comes except through you. He no longer labors in the understanding of surpassing knowledge, but is wholly dissolved in the sweetness of a conscience rightly affected. And [Col. 0237A] as the fuller current of the river makes that soul glad, it seems to itself to see you as you are, while it ruminates in the sweetness of contemplating the wondrous mystery of your Passion upon your goodness toward us—how great you are, or what you are. It seems to itself to see you face to face when the face of the highest Good appears to it in the cross and in the work of your salvation; and the cross itself becomes for it a mind’s face rightly disposed toward God.

For what could have been prepared better, what ordered more sweetly, than that a person ascending to his God, who must offer gifts and sacrifices according to the precept of the Law, should not have to ascend by steps to his altar, but should proceed upon the level ground of likeness, gently and with uninjured foot, to a man like himself, who says at the very threshold of entry: “I and the Father [Col. 0237B] are one” (John 10); and should immediately, through the Holy Spirit, be taken up into God in affection, and himself receive God coming into himself and making a dwelling with him—not only spiritually, but also bodily through the mystery of the holy and life-giving body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ?

This, Lord, is your face toward us and ours toward you, full of good hope. Clothe me in this your salvation, and form in me this face of your Christ; for it is impossible that you should turn it away whenever it appears before you in your holy one.

Go, O human being, whoever finds this hidden treasure in the field of your heart: sell all that you possess, and sell yourself into perpetual slavery, that you may possess it by the right of hereditary inheritance; [Col. 0237C] and you shall be blessed, and it shall go well with you. The treasure is in your possession; Christ is in your conscience.

## MEDITATION XI. He sets forth his blindness, desiring to be enlightened by God and to relinquish the pastoral burden.

“God of hosts, turn us again; show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). Since, Lord, by the gift of your grace, I have no face of heart toward things of the flesh, but you have put them behind my back; since you have put the world and whatever belongs to it beneath me: what, I beg you, is the reason that, while with my whole heart I seek you, when I rejoice that I have grasped your face—the only thing my face desires—I suddenly find myself apart from it? Why do you hide it? Do you consider me your enemy? Do you wish to consume me in the sins of my youth [Col. 0237D]? Am I not turned toward you, or are you still turned away from me?

If I am not turned, God of hosts, turn me. And again: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1). You know the gift of your grace in the heart of your poor servant: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready.” Command what you will; make me understand what you command; give me the power, you who gave me the will, and whatever you will shall be done in me or from me. “I have desired to do your will, O God,” and I embrace your law among your commandments in the midst of my heart.

But there is another law of yours, immaculate and converting souls; yet I do not know it, Lord. It lies hidden in the secret place of your countenance, into which I am unworthy to enter. If you would once grant me to enter there so as to see it, I would copy it upon my heart two and three times over with the pen of your Holy Spirit, the swiftly writing scribe, [Col. 0238A] so that I might have somewhere to turn back, and, understanding my works, might thereafter walk simply and confidently.

But now I am like a blind man groping at noon, fearing a snare and a fall wherever I set the foot of my assent. And as to a blind person I am told, “Here or there, this way or that”; but I, like one who does not see, know neither here nor there, neither this way nor that. Send forth to me, Lord, your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles. You say to me: “I am the way by which you shall go; the truth to which you shall go; the life for which you shall go. You know where you are to go, and you know the way.” And I, Lord, do not know where I am going; and how [Col. 0238B] can I know the way?

“You held my hand, and in your will you led me” (Ps. 72). You held my hand when you stretched out your own to one blind, crying after you and weeping, and said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11).

On hearing this, I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart. I came to you, offering you a ready heart: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready,” and saying: “What do you wish me to do?” And you said to me: “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me.” I went away, I ran, I sold all that I had—my very body, my very soul. I gave nothing to the poor, because I had nothing. And to you, Lord, I sold whatever I had, and you are my price.

[Col. 0238C] You know that I kept nothing for myself; or if anything escaped me and still lies hidden in some recess of my conscience, I shall seek it out and faithfully offer it to you. But when I seek my price from you, you charge against me the sins of my youth, the old debt. I beg you, Lord, have patience with me; I have nothing with which to repay you. Thus far I have come; here I stand; I may not go forward.

Sitting therefore beside the road while you pass by, blind, poor, and a beggar, I cry to you: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Matt. 15). And the crowds press upon my face and rebuke me to be silent. But I cry out much more: “Have mercy on me, Son of David.” “I am weary with crying; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in the living God.” Yet you pass by the one crying out. Sometimes you stand for me, but only briefly. You command [Col. 0238D] me to come to you and say: “What do you wish me to do for you?” But I, and all my bones, say to you: “Lord, that I may see” (Luke 18). Yet you pass by. Have mercy on me, Son of David. I cannot follow you, because I am blind. Have mercy on me.

I had from you whatever little reason brought me to you; I do not have the strength that would make me run after you. Have mercy on me, Son of David. Have mercy on me, at least you, my lords, servants of my God, and say to him: “Let him alone, for he cries after us” (Matt. 15). Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; my soul has long dwelt as a stranger in the house of darkness. What have I done? He is the Lord; he shall do what is good in his eyes. I shall sit beside the road. I shall not leave the road. Perhaps some day he will return [Col. 0239A] without the crowds; he will see the one who does not see and have mercy.

For his good word is present in my heart, saying: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord” (Ps. 26). Meanwhile gather yourselves to me, my soul and all that is within me: and the word of God, living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit, joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and there is no creature invisible in his sight, but all my things are naked and open to his eyes. To him is our word.

“I said to the Lord: You are my God; my lots are in your hands.” Let us cast the lot to discover by whose sin this evil has happened to us, [Col. 0239B] so that God turns his face away from his servant. The verdict of my lot is, O God, the discovery of your truth.
