As the Lord lives, if my right hand, if my eye, if my foot causes me to stumble, I will not spare it; rather I will cut it off and cast it from me. Tell me, O Word of God: was not what I did good, when, believing you, I left all things and followed you? All my thoughts and intentions of heart, soul and spirit, joints and marrow answer that it was good.

I add a further question: was not even this good thing done well? The thoughts murmur, and, having received permission to speak, they say: The Lord said to Peter: “Peter, do you love me?” He answered: “You know that I love you.” “Feed my sheep” (John 21). And this he said three times, so that the threefold cord of this judgment may not seem easily [Col. 0239C] broken; for feeding the flock is the proof of love.

**Intentions.** A shepherd who is not a hireling, even if he has laid down his life for the flock, scarcely does enough. But it is most grievous for him to preside where he cannot be of use. There was once a time when King David was so infirm in body that he lay in bed, so chilled by old age that he could not be warmed by garments; yet from his bed he governed the people of God by the word of command alone, and the eyes of all Israel looked to him in every matter. The bewitchment of triviality had not yet obscured good things; the harsh wickedness of the aging world had not yet grown so hot that due reverence was not preserved for retired old men.

But now, when the pastors of the Church are charged with feeding [Col. 0239D] the Lord’s flock in body and soul together; when God chiefly requires the soul, saying, “Seek first the kingdom of God” (Matt. 6), but makes them secure regarding the body as though secondarily, adding, “And all these things shall be added to you” (ibid.): who today would hear anyone preach this? Who spares an old man? Who forgives the infirm? The prudence of the flesh, the spirit of this world, inquisitiveness, sophistication, and other such things are today demanded from the teachers of the Church. Simplicity is ridiculed; religion is despised; humility counts for nothing.

And if the one who presides still seems somehow sufficient to supply the inward things, for whom today is this sufficient unless outward things abound sufficiently as well? Would that sufficiency knew its own limits. Therefore woe to us, because we have sinned. Therefore, as the prophet says: “We gave our hands to Egypt and the Assyrians, that we might be satisfied with bread” (Lam. 5). For, contrary to the Apostle, we have become slaves of men (1 Cor. 7)—of plunderers, moneylenders, and children of strangers who abound in this age. Unless a superior today serves such people at their pleasure; unless he conforms himself to this fashion of the world; unless he flatters people set over his head, and ingratiates himself with his subjects by feigning many things and concealing more: what will he do? What can he accomplish? Where will he find obedience? For today compliance plainly produces scarcely a few friends—and those unstable and fickle—while truth produces open, cruel, and persistent enemies.

But let this for the present be laying down one’s soul for one’s brethren; let it be enduring outwardly the discomforts of this climate in rough haircloths, so that the house of God may remain inwardly in its beauty. But would that the sword did not reach the soul! For we have been stupefied by the bewitchment of triviality and the pressure of desire, and our hearts have been hardened; we have become Ephraim, a heifer trained to thresh. Thus we have departed from ourselves; thus, through the heart’s inclination, we have passed over into things that were necessities, so that those whose duty it is to do them delight, merely through doing them, in things which it is shameful and horrible to endure; indeed, even those for whom they are not imposed seek them out.

Where today is Martha’s complaint that she is left to serve alone? Does not rather Mary’s murmur today fill the whole house, because she is permitted to sit at the Lord’s feet? Therefore, endangered in body and soul, and with our strength worn down through a long campaign and the long practice of labor, we think it lawful [Col. 0240C] now to look toward the hands of royal generosity, that it may at last allow our old age to be called retired and bestow upon it better things than it knows itself to have deserved.

Will Jacob always endure the bleary eyes of his Leah? Will he always serve for Rachel and never attain her? Indeed, everything that perished was exacted from him, while his wages were changed daily, so that he received black animals for white. Within were jealous wives; without, Laban arguing with his sons. Jacob must sometime provide for his own household as well; and it seems just that, at least old and exhausted, he should be permitted to return to his father’s house.

**Joints.** If affairs begin to be conducted in this way, the end has come. For the jointing of the whole body is dissolved; and when unity perishes, parts must arise, a divided kingdom be laid waste, and house fall upon house. A wise householder, setting out on a journey and ordering his household, assigned to each servant authority over his particular work and placed a doorkeeper at the threshold. A house without a doorkeeper is a public inn. Whoever wishes enters and leaves, brings in and carries off.

The house is the Church; the doorkeeper, who is also the door, is Christ Jesus. Whoever does not enter or leave through him is a thief, ascending or descending by another way. He himself became obedient to the Father unto death. Whoever does not keep this rule of obedience has departed from Christ, as the Apostle says: “Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, fainting in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood” [Col. 0241A] (Heb. 12). Neither old age nor infirmity excuses anyone until he who brought him in himself leads him out. Otherwise, if there is a door without a doorkeeper and it stands open to all, what remains except that, as there is equal and free permission to go out, so there is also equal and free permission to come in?

**Marrow.** Alas, alas: “The wicked walk round about; according to your loftiness, O God, you have multiplied the sons of men.” Driven in the circle of error, we are benumbed by a certain dizziness of the head, so that we do not attain the unmoving center and point of unity of truth, which, remaining stable, gives movement to all things. He is Truth. He is the one who said: “I am the truth” (John 13). And: “You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8)—free, assuredly, from the circle of error.

Let us therefore consult the center of truth as to whether the circle in which we revolve is guided by it and through it. If it is guided rightly, it converges upon itself according to its laws; but if not, the error is manifest. Let affections and actions be considered. Let the affection be fixed upon the center of truth, and the rounded circularity of outward action will correspond harmoniously to it. For the whole affection is owed to God. When one faithfully cleaves to him, in whatever direction the circle of action turns, it cannot stray from the straight path, but harmoniously converges upon itself, so that every part corresponds equally to the center of truth.

A point can exist without a circle; but a circle cannot in any way be rightly drawn without a point. Affection is sufficient if the matter does not require, or possibility does not permit, action to be exercised. When the necessity of charity requires action, the truth of charity owes it either to God or [Col. 0241C] to the neighbor; if it is not required, the charity of truth ought to keep us free for itself. And as the whole affection is always owed to God, so then the whole action that is free is owed to him as well. Where the neighbor’s necessity does not demand it, one who scatters away from God, outwardly, anything of affection or action commits sacrilege.

Yet whatever necessity may demand, a person’s will ought not to be so ready that his capability is not examined. Whether it exists or not must be consulted at the center of truth, in truth itself. If it does not exist and he presumes, he does not cleave to the center; and therefore he throws the perfection of the outer circle into confusion. For there are people who never love to cleave to the point of stability, but always to revolve outwardly. These are the wicked who walk round about; these are the sons of men whom the height of God’s judgments multiplies, or permits to be multiplied, in this world, and who become enemies of unity and truth.

Here is the conclusion. If the person who is called upon truly can act, let him fix his affection in truth and not refuse the action of service. If consulted truth replies that he is insufficient and unfit, let him be free inwardly for the stability of truth, lest, placed outwardly as a wheel, he be cast into the precipice of error. Yet the person whom consulted truth absolves, if, when necessity demands, he judges about his own capability without great fear in favor of his own will, is wrapped in great error. For if he errs knowingly, he is guilty of negligence toward his neighbor and of deceit toward truth; and he then has neither action nor affection. He does not err so greatly if he errs unknowingly; but [Col. 0242A] he errs altogether if he is self-assured. Yet one who does not dread the judgment of truth is not wholly alien from truth.

Therefore, as we are about to enter the judgment of truth, let us avoid all the windings of error by a brief and faithful shortcut. And because perhaps we wish not to be able, let us not, as though we might be found false in the judgment of truth, confess ourselves false according to the judgment of our own will. Rather, seeking pardon both in affection and action for this very matter, we shall appear more truthful in the judgment of truth. For we must not act deceitfully before truth, so that our iniquity may be found unto hatred.

**Spirit.** I agree. And this truly is the marrow and center of truth: not to stroke the disease, but to ulcerate the whole poison of inward wickedness.

[Col. 0242B] **Soul.** It is so. For just as it once delighted me to preside, so it is now my will to be subordinate; and my own will makes the excuse of necessity agreeable to me and does not allow me to attend to the need of my brethren.

**Spirit.** Although, O soul full of your brethren’s necessity, compassion is not lacking, nevertheless, as you say, it is your own inclination. Therefore nothing remains except the confession of humility and every effort of virtue, so that, however unfruitful and useless we may appear outwardly, we may not be found wholly empty and barren inwardly. And although the crowds press upon our mouth, let us cry with all our heart and all our mind: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.”

## MEDITATION XII. A confession of sin and a desire to love God are expressed here.

[Col. 0242C]

“Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication; in your truth hear me, in your righteousness” (Ps. 142). Lord, you who are near to all who call upon you in truth, as the Scripture of your truth promises us: as it is true before you that today I have the will to call upon you in truth, so, O Truth, hear me in the multitude of your mercy.

For I have said: now I have begun; let this be your change, O right hand of the Most High. For in my past evils and sins, which are great and innumerable, and in which I have grown old, I have become vile and contemptible to myself; while in the good things, if any seem to have been in me, I myself am most scrupulously suspicious of myself.

[Col. 0242D] Therefore today I come to you, as though my whole past life were dead, to make a beginning in you, O beginning of new life. Whatever good I have done is yours; I entrust it to you; return it to me in the time of your good pleasure. The evils I have committed are mine. Alas, how many and how great they are—most of them have perished from my memory! Would that fitting repentance might also blot them out from yours; yet, because of their horror, they are fixed in my memory far otherwise than any forgetfulness can abolish them. Nevertheless I so hate the memory of them that I often wish I had once forgotten them all utterly.

But you, Lord, do not remember the sins of my youth. They were the firstborn of Egypt, whom you destroyed in Egypt; and what I did in Egypt I had left in Egypt when I departed from there. For afterward you led me long through the wilderness [Col. 0243A], taught me, and guarded me as the pupil of your eye. You corrected me when I sinned; you comforted me when I grieved; you instructed me when I did not know, until you brought me almost to the entrance of the promised land.

Standing there, as you show me the delights of the land of the living, and remembering what was said to Moses, “You shall see it, but you shall not enter into it” (Deut. 34), I am shaken altogether with terror. For if he deserved to hear this for the transgression of one sin, what shall I hear, who am today to bring before you so many and such great sins of my own? Yet today let all my past evils, those I remember and those I do not, and the deserts of them, which have not passed away, come before you as they are before you, O Truth—even while I am silent—by my confession before you today.

But let them be brought forth as though into one little bundle [Col. 0243B] to be burned—or rather into a great and unbearable faggot, unless there is someone to help. I do not examine them; I do not count them, for I cannot. But however much or in whatever manner it is true that I have sinned before you, O Truth: as you know me to be a sinner, so I confess that I am. Let no one lighten them for me; let no one exaggerate them; let no one diminish them; let no one multiply them—not even I myself. For the matter is being dealt with before you, God. I shall not spare myself; do you spare me, Lord.

Yet do not spare me in such a way that from this day you judge me your enemy and write bitter things against me, to consume me in the sins of my past life. O guardian of humankind, do not any longer set me in opposition to you, since I have become too grievous to myself; but take away my sin, which divides [Col. 0243C] me from you. If you forgive, Lord, forgive; if it pleases you to avenge yourself, I too will avenge myself with you. Yet do not crush me with the blow of an enemy. For I am ready for the stripes of your hand, and my pain shall always be before you. For I shall declare my iniquity and consider myself to suffer for my sin.

For I do not entrust myself to the hands of an enemy; rather, with all confidence, I commit myself to yours, which I have often experienced. Therefore, when one hand strikes me, the other caresses; when one throws me down, the other places itself beneath me lest I be dashed to pieces. But sometimes even over the wrath of enemies you stretch out your hand, striking more heavily than any enemy when, angry, you turn your face away from us; and heaven becomes bronze to us and earth iron, [Col. 0243D] and all things hard, all things evil—the things that usually happen when your countenance is turned away.

For your name’s sake, Lord, in this spare your servant. Inflict whatever stripes you will, provided that you always make your face shine upon us and have mercy on us. Yet you are the Lord of avengings, acting freely in forgiving or lightening them. For you have turned our evils upon yourself, and in your Passion, paying what you did not seize, you have prepared your throne for judgment, so that, unjustly judged, you may justly absolve those who are judged in your righteousness.

Therefore your judgments, Lord, will help me; and you will look upon me according to the judgment reserved for those who love your name, as you once judged the sinful woman who loved you: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7). Let your very love today be the advocate in my cause. If [Col. 0244A] I deny it on earth, I fear that it too will deny me in heaven; if I am ashamed of it, it too will be ashamed of me. And indeed I am ashamed of it, because I do not possess it as I ought.

And since today is the day of my judgment, in this also, O Judge of my heart, judge me today, and determine my cause: whether I truly possess the advocate whom I claim. For this is what so darkens my mind’s sight that I utterly hesitate whether I seem to myself to see what I do not see, or not to see what I do see. Certainly I seem to myself to be sure that I always love your love, so much so that I am moved whenever I am reminded of it or remember it. But when I remember you or am reminded of you and am not moved or affected, I fear that perhaps I am convicted of not always loving you, although the most manifest signs of your present power and goodness everywhere and from every side strike or rouse the dullness of my senses to this.

O light of truth, scatter these darknesses for me today and dissolve the mist. Feed me with this bread of life and understanding, and give me to drink of the saving water of wisdom. For in understanding the things that are yours there are both food and drink: some things are those which we exercise and labor to retain and, as it were, chew; others, like drink, pass through us and refresh us in their manner.

For when we seek your love by understanding and sometimes find it, it is the bread of life strengthening the human heart. We often seek it with great labor before we possess it, and eat it in the sweat of our face as the punishment of Adam’s sin. But at other times your Spirit blows where it wills and when it wills, and breathes upon us the grace of your love. We hear its voice because we receive the sense of love; but we do not know by what judgment of your mercy it comes, or by what judgment of your justice it sometimes passes us by, as though greeting us, more sweetly at one time and more lightly at another. This is drink.

Feed me today with your bread, which gives life to the world; and from the things that I inquire about concerning your love, let a more solid understanding be given me. And by the sweetness of your grace, like saving drink, order and moderate the food itself, lest food that is too solid injure rather than strengthen my understanding, which is less capable.

I ask, Lord, whether I possess your love. If I find that I possess it, this alone is what my soul praises in itself and what pleases me; but if not, it is hateful to me, and there is nothing that I may love, since I hate myself. I feel and confess that I possess love for your love, so far that I wish to love nothing at all except in it or for its sake—not even myself. To deserve fully to behold its face, to deserve manifestly to walk in its light and enjoy its delights, I would care nothing at all how, for its sake, I gave myself either to death or to life.

This is what my conscience, called forth and examined in the light of your truth, seems fearlessly to answer me concerning love for your love. But concerning you—whether it always loves you, and loves you sufficiently—it trembles to answer in your judgment. For wherever I see your love in anyone and find evident signs of it, I am wholly gladdened; [Col. 0245A] but though all things everywhere always bear witness to me of the presence of your goodness or power, I am scarcely ever moved by this.

Therefore, if today you ask me what you once asked your blessed Apostle, “Do you love me?” I tremble to answer, “You know that I love you” (John 21); yet I answer with a cheerful and assured conscience: “You know that I want to love you.” Reveal my eyes, Lord, and I shall consider these wonders in your law, in the law of your love.

Perhaps I seem to myself to love your love because, when I sometimes think of you or of it, I in some measure feel, see, and taste it; but you I do not feel, or scarcely feel; I do not see, or scarcely see; most rarely and sparingly do I taste you. But a thing which does not make itself known to its lover through itself is loved with difficulty. For your frequent and great benefits, and your very love, which I most certainly love, send me to you; but when I do not find you, I fall back upon it and rest in it not without hope.

For when I sweetly feel your love in affection, but seek you through the understanding of that love itself, I love what I feel and desire what I seek; and, languishing in desire, I fail. For even if at times, by your gift and in my manner, understanding itself is affected, it is not permitted to swallow the whole savor of the good taste; rather it is, as it were, taken from its mouth, and it falls back into its hunger and ignorance. Nor is it permitted to stand in the light of your countenance until in it it distinguishes and brings to an end the distress of this hesitation.

When, in my meditation, a fire is kindled, and I labour to know what is present to me and what I lack, I begin for myself a way of ascent to you, asking your help in this. I therefore set these ascents in order within my heart. First, a great will seems necessary; then an enlightened will; then an affected will. In everyone who ascends, this will is first great, according to its own capacity; enlightened, according to your gift; affected, according to your measure. Great, insofar as you created it; enlightened, insofar as you made it worthy; affected, as you formed it. Yet you formed it without form; for, since you are neither form nor anything formed, neither can there be any form of your love, so that it may be formed around something as though formed. For he is Wisdom, of whom it is said: “She is a vapour of the power of God, and a certain pure emanation of the glory of the almighty God” (Wisdom 7); and therefore nothing defiled enters into her [Col. 0245D]. For she is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness. Therefore we do not apprehend him whenever we wish; and unless he first comes to us, and unless his grace goes before us, any effort of our understanding advances us little or not at all.

For when the Apostle says that you are “in the form of God” (Phil. 2), the form of your Godhead is the very simplicity of your nature or substance, to which one’s love must be like. For, as a certain wise man says concerning your faith: “Because a thing is as it is, so we ought to attempt to receive faith concerning it”; so this must be understood all the more of your love, inasmuch as charity surpasses faith. (BOETHIUS.) But affection alone discerns this [Col. 0246A].

I have a will for you, or toward you, greater than I can have; and I would rather not exist than lack it. Unless the protection of its shield had long ago crowned me, when men rose against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. Of the grace that enlightens and of charity that affects, I have sometimes felt certain sweet stirrings; but the experience of their fullness remains far from me. And when the will which you have given me is rarely and only slightly enlightened—because of my sins—and is still more rarely affected, through the wretched concurrence in this matter of my efforts and merits, I do not know whether it ought to be called love. Those who define it commonly define love as intense will alone; but those who so define it do not know how to judge the boundaries of your love. If it is called desire, I do not refuse the name. For in truth I desire you. But while my confession appears before you so poor, so wretched [Col. 0246B], my conscience cannot possess joy.

Let whoever wishes laugh at me or mock me: I know what I suffer in this. And I know that no one sympathizes with me in it who has not himself suffered, or does not suffer, the same. My tears shall indeed be my bread by day and by night, so long as it is said to me, “Where is your God?”—that is, so long as there is in my soul any affection in which my God is not, in its own manner; especially love, which ought to be his proper seat within me. This pain will not be relieved for me until he reveals himself to me: when I shall see what I shall love, and with the sure joy of the mind shall love what I see. Yet meanwhile, what I feel in part, I love in part; and unless I felt it to some extent, I should not love it at all.

[Col. 0246C] For when at your table I see your children feasting upon the delights of your love, though fasting I vehemently love your love in them, and sweetly embrace within my heart those who love you. And I see them rejoicing together in my joy, which I have in their joy, and wishing—but unable—to express the measure of their joy. For the affection by which, loving you, they enjoy you can indeed be perceived through a sensible sweetness of a certain spiritual or divine joy; but just as the taste of any food cannot be imparted to anyone except one who tastes it, so that taste can neither be examined by reasoning, nor expounded in words, nor conceived by the senses. It is something divine: an earnest or pledge of the Spirit, by which in this life you, O God, gladden and nourish your poor servant, lest he fail [Col. 0246D] on the way; and by which you announce the joy of eternal life, as you say through Job, your friend, that it is his possession and that he can attain it (Job 36).

For the holy soul is re-formed in the image of the Trinity, in the image of him who created it, even by the very manner of its blessedness. For enlightened and affected will—that is, understanding and love—and the habit of enjoyment are in some manner three persons of affections, as it is said and believed of the Trinity, God; but they are one substance of blessedness, because what is loved is loved only by understanding, is understood only by loving, and is enjoyed only by loving and understanding him whom one deserves to enjoy. For there, to possess or enjoy is the same as to understand or to love.

Happy the conscience whose affections follow the path of ordered charity; advancing toward you with unwavering constancy [Col. 0247A], it thus prospers in its progress through the cooperation of your grace, so that it does not fail until you bring it to completion—you who complete for those who hope in you the abundance of your sweetness which you hide for those who fear you—especially those whose works shine before the sight of the children of men, to your glory, O Father who are in heaven. These are they who love you; when I see such persons and do not find myself among them, I am weary of living. Their wisdom is not from the spirit of this world or from the prudence of this age; but, because they did not know learning, they entered into the power of the Lord, and, poor in spirit, they remember your righteousness alone. For this reason you taught them to proclaim your wonders by their life and conduct.

For these are your simple servants, with whom [Col. 0247B] your discourse is accustomed to be; who, in going toward you, do not place their hope in the chariots of their own intellects or in the horses of their own strength, but only in the name of the Lord. Therefore, as your wisdom sweetly orders all things for them, they reach their appointed end by a short way and with a light burden, where chariots and horsemen fail. They do not fashion or conform your love to themselves by subtle investigation; rather, your love, finding simple material in them, forms them and conforms them to itself both in affection and in effect. Thus, apart from what lies hidden within—namely, glory and riches in the house of a good conscience—the inner light shines forth in their outward countenance, not through artificial effort but as if by a certain natural complexion; so much so that from the graceful simplicity of their face and bearing [Col. 0247C], a certain summons of your charity proceeds, which sometimes pierces even rude and barbarous minds to your love by sight alone.

Indeed, nature returning to its own origin, they become teachable by God without a teacher; and when their spirit, with your Spirit helping their weakness, passes into divine affections, their senses being regulated by a certain spiritual discipline, even their bodies assume certain spiritual appearances, faces more than human and possessing a certain singular grace. Moreover, their flesh, sown in corruption through the pursuits of good discipline, already begins to rise in glory, so that together heart and flesh may rejoice in the living God; and, while the soul thirsts for you, the flesh also thirsts for you in many ways [Col. 0247D].

For the blessed meek possess the earth of their body, which, made fruitful by the pursuits of spiritual exercises [Col. 0248A], even when left to itself and uncultivated through good use, bears fruit spontaneously in fasts, vigils, and labours; ready for every good work without resistance or sloth. When I see these persons, I am wholly affected with love for your love, which works this in them, and which I recognize in them by a certain experience known to those who love. Therefore I love them because they love you, and I love them greatly, just as I love the love by which you are loved, which I love in them. And if I love them in this manner, so that in them and in their natural affection I love nothing but you, since I love that affection itself only because it is full of you; yet if I never love my own affection within myself unless I find myself affected by you—among those whom I love in you and in myself, whom I desire to love only in you—what do I love except you? Absolutely nothing. For [Col. 0248B], even if I perceive that I love them or myself in any other way whatever, in this I hate myself more than I love.

Therefore I find you, Lord, in my love; but would that I might always find you! For since love does not exist unless it loves, and since there is always within me an intense will for you—that is, love pressing me toward you—why am I not always affected by you? Is love one thing, and the affection of love itself another? As I see it, love belongs to nature; loving you belongs to grace; affection is the manifestation of grace. Of this the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12). For so long as the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation oppresses the mind that thinks many things, it is necessary that, however much the soul loves, it should experience both failing and advancing. Unless this affection consoled the one [Col. 0248C] and restrained the other, it would collapse into utter failure, from which no advance could raise it.

Therefore your love is always in the soul of your poor servant, O God, but hidden like fire beneath ashes, until the Spirit, who breathes where he wills, is pleased to manifest it, as and insofar as he wills, for usefulness. Be present, then, be present, holy love; be present, sacred fire. Burn the pleasures of the reins and hearts; consume thoughts broadly as you will, so as to make the material of humility more abundant for the flame of your manifestation. Appear when you will, to disclose the glory of a good conscience and the riches it possesses in its house. Manifest yourself, that you may make it watchful in keeping; hide yourself, lest you make it rash in squandering [Col. 0248D], until he who began may bring to completion, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages.

[Col. 0249]

[Col. 0249]

# DISPUTATION AGAINST PETER ABAELARD, ADDRESSED TO GEOFFREY OF CHARTRES AND BERNARD, THAT THEY MAY DEFEND THE CAUSE OF GOD AND THE CHURCH AGAINST THE ERRORS OF PETER ABAELARD, OF WHICH IT PRODUCES SEVERAL ARTICLES

[Col. 0249A] To the reverend lords and fathers in Christ, GEOFFREY, bishop of the people of Chartres, and BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: life and good days.

“I am confounded, God knows,” etc. See this letter in our edition of the Works of St Bernard, vol. I, col. 531.

# CHAPTER I

At the very threshold of his theology, he defined faith as an estimation of things not apparent and not subject to bodily senses—perhaps thinking either that our common faith is estimation, or that it is lawful for anyone to estimate whatever he chooses concerning it. Blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0249B] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XIII, ch. 1] says: “Faith, he says, is possessed in the heart in which it exists, by the person whose faith it is, not by conjecturing or opining, but by certain knowledge, with conscience affirming it aloud.” Far be it that Christian faith should have such boundaries—namely, estimations or opinions, whether these estimations are those of the Academics, whose judgment is to believe nothing, know nothing, but estimate everything. For a similar hope and a similar charity accompany a similar faith. If faith wavers, hope trembles, and charity does not exist. “For I know,” says the Apostle, “whom I have believed, and I am certain” (2 Tim. 1). But he is ready to suppose concerning everything, who wishes to dispute concerning everything, concerning divine matters equally with secular ones.

# CHAPTER II

Then, after setting forth an excellent and praiseworthy profession concerning faith in the Trinity of three persons in the one substance of the Godhead, he seems shortly afterward to wish to diminish the persons themselves into something less than subsisting persons, when he says:

> “It seems to us that, by the foregoing names of the three persons, the perfection of the highest good has been carefully described; so that, when God is proclaimed to be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we may understand through this distinction that he is the highest good and perfect in all things. For by the name Father is designated the power of divine majesty, by which he can accomplish whatever he wills; by the designation Son or Word is signified God’s wisdom, by which, that is, he is able to discern all things, lest he be deceived in anything; while by the title Holy Spirit is expressed his charity or benevolence, by which he most excellently wills all things to be done or ordered.”

And elsewhere he says more plainly:

> “It should be noted that these three names, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, although, like other names, they are spoken of God improperly, have nevertheless suitably been applied in describing him for the commendation of the highest good [Col. 0251A], by which God’s power, wisdom, and benevolence are designated. For if,” he says, “he were omnipotent and not all-wise, he would not be supremely good. Again, if he were not benevolent, his power would be destructive and useless.”

How far this statement is from that place where to be able is the same as to be wise; to be wise, the same as to be benevolent; and all this, the same as to be. I pass over here his frivolous and inept expressions about God, and the vapid terms concerning the essence of the highest good which strike my ears even to impatience: namely, that God must possess wisdom—that is, must generate the Son—lest he be deceived in anything; that he must possess benevolence—that is, the Holy Spirit—lest his power or wisdom be destructive; as though this were not to be possessed if that danger were not to be avoided. I also pass over what he says there, as though on the authority of blessed Augustine, that God is not omnipotent because he can do only what he wills; we have omitted this for the sake of brevity. I pass over all these things, I say: they are words, and it is easy to meet them with words. Let us come to the issue.

He says that the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are improper in God, but have been added for commendation in the description of the highest good. The description of the highest good of which he speaks might have been understood simply, had we not seen, at the very opening of his account, the scandal of division arise from his description of parts in the unity of the divine essence. For he immediately cuts into three that which is supremely and singularly one: into greater, lesser, and least, as will appear more clearly in what follows. Therefore we say that, when divinity is proclaimed by Catholic Fathers in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, this is a confession of faith, not a description of divinity. If it could be described, it could also be circumscribed. For just as what is described is described through its parts, so what is circumscribed is circumscribed through its whole. Certainly, where parts are found for describing, there must also be a whole for circumscribing. Even if it is spiritual substance, in place of bodily parts and local dimensions it has qualities of spiritual nature, which can indeed be distinguished in their own way for description and comprehended in their own way for circumscription [Col. 0251D].

But that nature is devoid of all such things: there is pure simplicity, simple unity, and identity itself, having neither parts through which it may be described nor qualities by which it may be distinguished. They are three, yet one; one in three, whole in each—if indeed “whole” exists there where there is no part, and if “so much” exists where there is neither quantity nor quality. Among the three, none includes another and none excludes another; but, as has been said, they are three and they are one: one God, one essence, where, as was said above, to be able is to be wise; to be wise is to will; and all this is to be.

Nor, as he says, have these three names of the three distinct persons in God been attached by man or through man for commendation, or employed for a partial description or perfection of the highest good; rather, they are truly, naturally, and eternally in God. They have been announced to human beings so that, when it is heard that one is in three and three are in one, if anyone should suppose that something there can be described or circumscribed, unity may restrain and deter the effort of human reason from proceeding as far as solitude, and Trinity as far as division [Col. 0252A].

Far be it from Catholic faith and proclamation concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that, as this new master says, one should in any respect be said or believed to perfect the highest good in another or toward another, since each individually is to be believed sufficient in himself for the whole fullness of the highest good. Far be it that what is full in each should be superabundant in the three, that what is simple and indivisible one should be distributed in parts, or that what is Trinity should be reduced to solitude. There, the fact that one is from another, or one toward another, is not a dissipation of unity but a distinction of persons; for although one is truly proclaimed in relation to another, there are not there one thing and another thing, but simple unity.

To think this concerning God is, for those who believe, hope, and love in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a pious thing to hear, delightful to speak familiarly, desirable for ardent faith above everything desired to understand, and sweet to enlightened love above everything sweet, whenever some experience of understanding has been attained. For in such matters, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0251D] Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 27], “love itself is understanding.” Yet he does not represent him to us in this way—the one whom Ezekiel calls the sound of the sublime God (Ezek. 1)—when he introduces, in place of the names Father and Son, power, power of discerning, and, from power, both the power of acting and of discerning, as though one thing were related to the whole, as our theologian says.

This is not to deny that in the Scriptures and in ordinary speech and customary exposition, power is often assigned to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and benevolence or charity to the Holy Spirit. But this is according to the logic of faith and the understanding of piety: so that, both regarding omnipotence in effecting and regarding benevolence in showing mercy, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are always understood to be not merely powerful but omnipotent—and yet not three omnipotent beings, but one omnipotent being [Col. 0252D]; likewise wise, or, as he is accustomed to say, all-wise, and all-benevolent—not the Father alone, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit.

For it is said of God the Father that “he has done all whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113); and the Apostle calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1); and “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). Through whichever person of the Trinity something concerning God, or God in some respect, has been made especially known to human beings, divinity has revealed that this person is to be adored in that very respect; and humanity has become accustomed to do so—not that person alone, the others excepted, but as one acting in this regard, with the others cooperating equally and without distinction.

Names of this sort seem less properly to designate the nature of the supreme and surpassing essence when they are uttered with such an addition, by which God is denominated not in what he is toward himself but in what he is toward the creature: namely, when he is called power to do whatever he wills and to discern, or wisdom, that is, the power of discerning. At least when they are uttered absolutely, so that the divine essence is said to be simply supreme power—to which being is the same as being able, being wise, and being benevolent—yet when uttered with such an addition regarding creation, they seem to exist only, as it were, in relation to the creature, or to be toward the creature, as a certain relative quality [Col. 0253B].

But the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are proper there, expressing the reality, as was said above, according to the customary way of thinking and familiar manner of speaking, in accordance with the truth of generation in the truth of begetter and begotten. When divinity is added to these, so that one says God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, the most certain faith in the natural unity of the Godhead destroys every suspicion of plurality, multiplicity, division, and diversity in the truth of substance arising from the Trinity of persons. For although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are spoken relatively—and the Holy Spirit himself is spoken relatively insofar as he is God’s gift—yet, as to the truth of natural coessentiality, no necessity of relation removes any of them beyond the bounds of natural unity [Col. 0253C].

For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are always proclaimed one, although not one person; and the proclamation of this truth, by the authority of Truth itself, brings every understanding of human reason captive into obedience to its faith and confession (2 Cor. 10).

Against his assertion that the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are improper in God, as though they signify something other than what sounds in the names themselves, blessed Ambrose says against the Arians in his book *On the Holy Spirit*: “You hear ‘Son of God’: either erase the name or confess the nature. Why do the tortures of questions delight you? I am permitted to know concerning the Son of God that he was born; I am not permitted to know how he was born.” Again: “These are not bare names, but indications of operative power. For the Father is not the same as the Son; but between Father and Son the distinction of generation is expressed, so that God from God may be understood.”

Therefore the operative power, of which those names are indications, is the unthinkable generation known only to the very persons for whom knowing it is identical with their very being—that is, with being begetter and begotten, Father and Son. Therefore the name of fatherhood is proper, and properly proper, to that Father, from whom it becomes a family name in all those in whom it exists, as the Apostle says: “I bend my knees to the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3) [Col. 0254A].

For there these names are not, as among human beings, father and son through the accidental cause of an accidental begetting; but he who is Father or Son was never not Father and Son: always Father, always Son; not with temporal perpetuity, but with perpetual eternity; not by an accidental change, but by immutable nature. Yet, lest we seem to depart from truth out of love for truth, if he had called the names Father and Son improper because of their mutual relation to one another—namely, because by these names not so much what they are as what they are toward each other appears to be designated—he would have said something. Nevertheless, let us hear what blessed Ambrose says in the same place against those who alleged diversity in the divine nature of Father and Son:

> “When I say ‘begotten,’ I have expressed not a property of nature but the signification of generation. Thus, if I say ‘son’ generally and do not add whose son, one may understand either a son of man, a son of iniquity, the offspring of cattle, or the young of doves; and therefore in the designation ‘sons’ there is no expression of a signified nature. But if I wish to designate a nature, I shall call it either man, horse, or bird, so that the nature may be understood. Therefore, if I desire to designate the divine nature, I ought to name the true God. But when I say ‘son,’ I signify begottenness; when I say ‘father,’ I declare begetting.”

Therefore the names father and son are indeed improper to nature but proper to begetting, signifying father and son in the truth of begetter and begotten. Having removed and rejected these names as improper and as signifying other things, our theologian, having—as he says—found the truth of the Trinity by which the fullness of the highest good is perfected, namely in God the power of acting and discerning, generated wisdom from that power—that is, the power of discerning—and God’s benevolence, and wishing even generation itself to be something significative in God, undertakes to demonstrate from powers themselves and benevolence what the generation of the Son from the Father and the procession of the Holy Spirit from both signify in God. But first the Father and Son must be discussed; then a place must be reserved for the Holy Spirit. For this order seems also proper to their own procedure.

# CHAPTER III

Thus he proposes, in the unity of the divine essence, to demonstrate not so much a distinction, as he promises, as a destruction of the persons; and by what philosophers have said about matter and form, or by an analogy with matter and form, to establish an account of divine generation—namely, what it is for the Son to be, or to be begotten from the Father. He says:

> “A bronze seal is bronze formed in such a way. Therefore the bronze itself, which is the matter of the bronze seal, is essentially the same thing; yet in their properties they are distinct, so that one property belongs to bronze and another to the bronze seal. And although they are essentially the same, the bronze seal is from bronze, not bronze from the bronze seal; and bronze is the matter of the seal, not the seal of bronze.”

Then, after inserting some intervening remarks, he adds:

> “As the bronze seal is from bronze and is in a certain manner generated from it, so the Son has being from the substance of the Father, and accordingly is said to be begotten from him. For, as we showed above, divine power is specially declared by the name Father, just as divine wisdom is declared by the name Son. But divine wisdom is, so to speak, a certain power of God himself, because he can provide against every deception or error. Therefore, since wisdom, as has been said, is a certain power, just as a bronze seal is a certain bronze, it is clear that divine wisdom has its being from divine power, by the analogy in which a bronze seal is said to be from bronze, which is its matter, or a species from a genus, which is said to be, as it were, the matter of the species—as animal is of man. For just as from the fact that something is a bronze seal it necessarily follows that it is bronze, and from the fact that something is a man it follows that it is an animal, but not conversely; so divine wisdom, which is the power of discerning, requires that there be divine power, but not conversely. For just as bronze is related both to the bronze seal and to other things, and animal both to man and to other things, so divine power is related both to discerning and to acting. And just as the bronze seal is said to be from the substance or essence of bronze itself, because to be a bronze seal is to be a certain bronze, and to be a man—that is, a rational mortal animal—is to be a certain animal, so divine wisdom is said to be from the substance of divine power, because to be wisdom—that is, the power of discerning—is to be a certain power. And this is for the Son to be from the Father, or to be begotten: just as philosophers say that a species is begotten, or created, from a genus.”

This is the new theology of the new theologian concerning Father and Son: it clothes the holy simplicity of Christian faith in alien spoils against its will, and makes it more obscure while striving to make it clearer. For when, in the faith of the Trinity, the powers of acting and discerning are presented to us in place of Father and Son, and from the power of acting comes the power of discerning, as a son from a father, a species from a genus, or that which is materialized from matter, the very novelty both of terms and meanings seems to force a harsh discord upon the ears of the faithful. Deprived of the harmonious sound of good names, it recoils, as it were, from understanding: plainly because divine matter is not handled by its own instruments and refuses to be subjected to common craftsmanship [Col. 0255D].

These, I say, are the words and this is the meaning of Master Peter concerning the generation of the Son of God. Thus he expounds that generation which he who said, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53), judged inexpressible. “From the womb,” says God the Father, “before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109). The men of God who spoke in the Spirit of God were accustomed to interpret that womb as the unsearchable secret of God the Father, from whom the Son of God was begotten from eternity. But that secret is now no secret, having been made so accessible to human reason.

I marvel greatly that a man who knows anything should introduce genus and species, which are predicated only of differing things, or matter and that which is materialized, which likewise differ from one another in their own manner, into the essence of supreme and most simple unity; when that nature is nothing but simple one, exists only from itself and for itself, has no cause or rationale of its being except itself, and whatever it is, is from itself, in itself, and through itself—being itself for itself [Col. 0256A]. I marvel also greatly that, while in this theology he often rightly and Catholicly proclaims the Trinity *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), “of one substance,” the Son in every respect like and consubstantial with the Father, what this analogy of bronze and a bronze seal is intended to mean, since it seems wholly designed to make an unequal dissimilarity appear between Father and Son.

For what else does he do when he says that, just as from the fact that something is a bronze seal it necessarily follows that it is bronze, and from the fact that something is a man it follows that it is an animal, but not conversely, so divine wisdom, which is the power of discerning, requires that there be divine power, but not conversely? What does “not conversely” mean? Namely: just as every bronze seal is bronze, but a certain bronze, so wisdom, which is the power of discerning, is power, but a certain power. And just as it does not follow conversely that every bronze is a bronze seal, since a seal is nothing but a certain bronze, so it does not follow conversely that every power is wisdom, since wisdom is nothing but a certain power. This is to say that, just as not all bronze is expended in the bronze seal, so not all power is understood to be present in wisdom [Col. 0256B].

Thus it is easy to see, in the analogy drawn from bronze seal and bronze, the dissimilarity of the similarity; in this cast work, the confusion of many incongruities; and an alien meaning seeking and failing to find a place for itself where it does not belong. For if we compare divine wisdom and power to the bronze seal and bronze—so that wisdom is to power as a bronze seal is to bronze—then, O Israel, the Lord your God is no longer one God, in whom there are greater and lesser: namely, power of such a kind in relation to power, Son in relation to Father, as a certain bronze is in relation to all bronze, as a certain animal is in relation to its genus; part in relation to whole, the materialized in relation to matter.

For this is what he says when he maintains that, because wisdom is a certain power just as a bronze seal is a certain bronze, “it is clear that divine wisdom has its being from divine power, by the analogy in which a bronze seal is said to be from bronze, which is its matter, or species from genus, which is said to be, as it were, the matter of the species.” “For,” he says, “just as bronze is related both to the bronze seal and to other things, and animal both to man and to other things, so divine power is related both to acting and discerning”—so that we are to understand what wisdom does not possess, since it is only a certain power, namely the power of discerning. The Father, then, is richer in power than the Son is in wisdom—he who says: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 15) [Col. 0256D].

Then, teaching what that generation of the Son from the Father is and signifies, and seeking to establish it as significative rather than real, like the names of begetter and begotten themselves—that is, Father and Son—he continues and says:

> “Just as the bronze seal is said to be from the substance or essence of bronze itself, because to be a bronze seal is to be a certain bronze, and to be a man—that is, a rational mortal animal—is to be a certain animal, so divine wisdom is said to be from the substance of divine power, because to be wisdom—that is, the power of discerning—is to be a certain power.”

Then, as though concluding—but from ungranted premises—he says:

> “And this is for the Son to be from the substance of the Father, or to be begotten, just as philosophers say that a species is begotten, or created, from a genus.”

Let others judge these things as they please. But it seems to us that his attempt to diminish subsisting and complete persons, whom the Greeks call *hypostases* (ὑποστάσεις), equal to one another in every respect, alike and consubstantial, into power and half-power, is Sabellian in respect of the destruction of persons; and, in respect of dissimilarity and inequality, is to walk directly into Arius’s judgment. These, however, are ancient and very old heresies of the ancients. But that a dialectician should treat God the Father and Son as he does matter and the materialized, although all such things are far removed from that substance, and should proclaim the Son from the Father as a species from a genus—this is a wholly new heresy and peculiar to him. In this he has appeared in the world, as the Athenians said of Paul, to speak more mildly, as a proclaimer of new gods (Acts 17) [Col. 0257B].

For where now is God the Trinity? Where are the persons of begetter and begotten, and of the one proceeding from both? Where is the unity of which Truth says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10)? For destruction of the persons destroys the Trinity in God; dissimilarity between greater and lesser destroys unity. O God of knowledge, judge of consciences, you know, you see, that I would rather err concerning his words than that he should err in faith; yet, unless another teaches me otherwise, I cannot extract from his words a sounder meaning than that which I understand.

# CHAPTER IV
Let us now come to the Holy Spirit—or rather, let him himself come into us and not permit us to think thoughts alien to him, but make us agree in all things with the truth, the Spirit of truth. Would that he did not say so many things concerning him; would that, at least, he did not write against himself. For in the matters set forth previously, although he often says what gives offense, nevertheless, by saying one thing and then another, he gives some indication that he is not stating definitively what he says. Here, however, with every veil of pretense removed, his opinion runs so freely that he seems altogether even to wish to defend what he says. He says, therefore:

“The Spirit is, as it were, so called from *breathing*. Hence Truth itself says: ‘The Spirit breathes where it wills.’ And the Prophet, using a fitting metaphor, distinguishes the Spirit of the Lord and calls him the Spirit of his mouth (Ps. 32); and therefore by his very name he is declared to proceed from God the Father and the Son rather than to be begotten. For that very beneficence which is denoted by this name is not in God power or wisdom; since being beneficent is not, for anyone, being powerful or wise, but this goodness of his [Col. 0258A] must rather be understood according to the affection or effect of charity itself. But charity, as blessed Gregory testifies, cannot exist between fewer than two. For, he says, no one is said to have charity toward himself, but extends himself toward another in love, so that charity may exist. Therefore God’s proceeding is, as it were, his extending himself toward some thing through an affection of charity, so that he may love it and join himself to it by love. Since, then, both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father, the one begotten and the other proceeding, procession differs from generation in that he who is generated is from the very substance of the Father, since wisdom itself, as has been said, has him as its very being, so that he is a certain power; whereas the affection of charity belongs rather to the beneficence of disposition than to [Col. 0258B] power. Hence it is rightly said that wisdom is from power, the Son from the Father—that is, that he is from the very substance of the Father. But the Spirit, though he is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, and though the Trinity itself is proclaimed *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, of one substance, is nevertheless by no means from the substance of the Father and the Son; for that would be to be begotten from the Father and the Son. Rather, he has proceeding from them; and this is, as it were, God extending himself through charity toward another. For no one can be beneficent toward himself, but only toward another. Yet God, who needs no one, would remain within himself through beneficence if he could be beneficent toward himself by conferring some benefit upon himself.”

This is Master Peter’s theology concerning the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0258C] this is what he proclaims concerning him—and would that it were not against him! At his own pleasure he fashions an image of the supreme essence for himself. But from the form of faith handed down by the apostles, formed through them by the Holy Spirit and commended to all the faithful, he removes what he wishes and adds what he wishes, making all things new: new words, new doctrines, of which he alone is the author for himself.

We must beware that, having as it were set aside from the faith the sacred names of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as improper, he first tries to entangle believers by arguments from other names, by whose supposedly rational consequence he may lead them into the novelty of his notions. For if one treats of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to the rule and form of faith, and according to evangelical and apostolic teaching—these being the names which Truth itself dictated to us when it said, “Baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28)—then faith and understanding of unity in the divine essence immediately disperse, by a single ray of truth, all this darkness of error gathered from every quarter. For, as has already been said above, when we proclaim Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we express the truth of the Trinity; but when we add, God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, certain faith in deity forms in our hearts the truth of the supreme and indivisible unity.

Therefore I do not wish to depart from the good name in which I was baptized and in which I was marked as a Christian; nor do I know how at all to speak about God, or to hear or understand anything, except in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy [Col. 0259A] Spirit. Concerning power, wisdom, and beneficence in God, I believe and am certain only of this: that God the Father is all-powerful, the Son all-powerful, and the Holy Spirit all-powerful; and, as he himself is accustomed to say, the Father all-wise, the Son all-wise, and the Holy Spirit all-wise; the Father all-beneficent, the Son all-beneficent, and the Holy Spirit all-beneficent. These three are one: one powerful, one wise, one good God, who is blessed for ever.

But may what he says about a half-power in God, which he says is in the Son, and about no power at all, which he proclaims to be in the Holy Spirit, always be as far from my heart as it is plainly far from almighty God. Therefore, to answer what he says concerning the Holy Spirit—as the Holy Spirit himself may grant—let us first speak about his very name. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “is so called from breathing. Hence the Lord also says: ‘The Spirit breathes where it wills’ (John 3).” And the prophet, using a suitable metaphor, distinguishes the Spirit of the Lord, calling him the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth, saying: “And by the Spirit of his mouth is all their power” (Ps. 32).

We, then, say what we have received from the Fathers: namely, that God is called Spirit from the more subtle and more noble nature, as the Lord says: “God is Spirit” (John 4). Since, therefore, the Father too is Spirit and holy, and likewise the Son is Spirit and holy, it was necessary that he who is common to both, and is their commonality, should be designated by some name common to both; and whatever is common to both is their charity, embrace and kiss, [Col. 0259C] goodness, sweetness, and joy—and, to sum up all, their divinity. This is not from myself; blessed Augustine says it [Note: [Col. 0259D] Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, ch. 9]:

“God also,” he says, “is Spirit. He did not say, ‘The Spirit is God,’ but ‘God is Spirit,’ so that in this place the very deity of Father and Son is called God, which is the Holy Spirit.”

That fitting metaphor of the Lord’s mouth, however, does not so much, as he says, serve to distinguish between that generation and procession as to declare their complete likeness. For the Spirit of the Lord is read and understood to be of the same mouth as the Word of God and the wisdom of God, which says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24). Concerning procession, moreover, the Son says: “I proceeded from the Father [Col. 0259D] and came” (John 8).

The theologian continues and says: “The beneficence denoted by the name Holy Spirit is not power or wisdom in God, since being beneficent is not, for anyone, being powerful or wise.” Here I wonder how wisdom is to be understood rather as the power of discerning than beneficence as the power of willing good. Yet let us follow his very meaning, and we shall discover that, just as it was sufficiently clear above how, through dissimilarity of essence and inequality of power, he makes the Son unlike and unequal to the Father, so in a similar fashion—or rather, through a vaster interval of dissimilarity—he divides the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

For when he says that the beneficence of God which is denoted by the name Holy Spirit is not any power in God, just as, in relation to the full power which is the Father, the Son is a certain power, what is this except to say that the Son is somehow of the same substance as the Father, whereas the Holy Spirit is in no manner so, since he is not power but beneficence? For the Father’s substance is power both to act and to discern; to it the Son, as wisdom—that is, as power of discernment—is consubstantial, as a half-power is to power, though with a certain mutilated blessedness. But the Holy Spirit, since he is absolutely no power, is wholly alien from consubstantiality in divine glory. Hence he also continues [Col. 0260B] and says: “But this goodness of his must rather be understood according to the affection or effect of charity itself.” This is to say that the procession of the Holy Spirit—or rather of God—by which God proceeds into his creature according to the affection of his charity, which is the Holy Spirit, is not so much substantial as affective.

Hence follows what he says: “But charity, as blessed Gregory testifies, cannot exist between fewer than two. For,” he says, “no one is said to have charity toward himself, but extends himself toward another in love, so that charity may exist. Therefore God’s proceeding is, as it were, his extending himself toward some thing through an affection of charity, so that he may love it and join himself to it by love.” And shortly afterward: “No one,” he says, “can be beneficent toward himself, but only toward another. Yet God, who needs no one, would remain within himself through beneficence if he could be beneficent toward himself by conferring some benefit upon himself.”

Here our theologian openly shows to all how he savors of flesh rather than spirit, of man rather than God. For how unfitting it is for the immutable God to be moved by affection or extended toward something is clearer than light. And if, in defining the Holy Spirit as it were, he calls him God’s beneficence or affection toward creatures, then, if the Holy Spirit is God’s affection or beneficence toward creatures, he is no longer so much the third person in the Trinity as a certain quality of God, just as blessed Augustine says of the Son of God, the wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0259D] Book VI, *On the Trinity*]:

“If God the Father is wise by the wisdom [Col. 0260D] which he himself begot, the Son is his quality, not his offspring.”

Further, what blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0260D] Gregory, Homily 17 on the Gospels, speaks of human love, not divine love.] says concerning charity toward one’s neighbor, from one human being to another, he transfers to God, as though proving from this that God has no charity toward himself or within himself, and that God’s charity is not charity unless by it God extends himself to something else. But the supreme good, contemplated in itself, offers itself to be understood by those who seek devoutly: namely, that God is or is called good or beneficent not so much according to an affection which he has toward creatures, but according to himself. For God is the good of all goods; and even if all other goods, which are good from him or by reason of him, were removed or did not exist, he is not to be understood as less good in himself—that is, as less fully what he is—or as less power, wisdom, or beneficence.

For I do not think that anyone among human beings can be good or beneficent toward another unless he has first been established as good in himself according to the condition of a good mind. But especially in God, charity or goodness consists not in his proceeding into the creature, but he proceeds into the creature from what he is, or from that which is in him. When he says that God in some manner extends himself toward the creature, this must in no manner be thought concerning God, who rather is in every creature in his own way, that is, in the manner in which God is everywhere.

When he says that “God’s charity tends toward another, so that charity may exist, and that God cannot love himself,” we say, with the manifold authority of Holy Scripture and according to the very reason of faith, that God nowhere extends himself by loving, because he loves nothing but himself. And when he loves himself, this means that he is what he is; for, just as he himself is his own good, so he himself is his own love toward himself. But when he loves a human being, this means that he makes that person worthy to receive his love, the Holy Spirit, poured into him, so that God may most rightly and mercifully love himself from that human being and within that human being.

When the spirit of a human being is disposed toward the Holy Spirit, it is made one spirit with him; and in that very thing which is loved, it loves, because when God loves himself in a human being, that is what it means for him to love the human being in himself; this is what it means for the human being [Col. 0261C] to love God, for the human being to be in God, and for God to be in the human being. In this, God is not disposed toward the human being; rather, the human being is disposed toward God, since, as the Apostle says, he is made such by God: “For,” says the Apostle, “God makes us for this very thing” (2 Cor. 5).

Therefore God is not, by proceeding, extended toward a human being through an affection of beneficence—that is, through the Holy Spirit—but the human being, rightly disposed in the Holy Spirit, is gathered and assumed to God. Thus comes about what is written: “For our exaltation is of the Lord” (Ps. 88). For just as the Word of God the Father is not uttered but born, in order that he may be the Son he is, so he who is the Holy Spirit does not depart when he proceeds. For the Son is always in the Father, from whom he is by being born; the Holy Spirit is always [Col. 0261D] in the Father and the Son, from whom he is by proceeding. The Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father, insofar as they are what he is, and they are from the Father, one by being born and the other by proceeding, insofar as they have from the Father that they are what they are. The Father is in each of them insofar as he is what they are.

Here he should humbly have asked, that he might receive; devoutly sought, that he might find; knocked, that it might be opened to him. But he leaps over this and pronounces as though by an authoritative decision: “God’s proceeding is his extending himself toward some thing through an affection of charity.” Therefore this is not the procession of the Holy Spirit but of God, by which God acts in the creature through the affection of his charity, that is, through the Holy Spirit. Therefore he is not one for whom proceeding from the Father and Son is to be what he is; for he does not himself proceed from the Father and the Son, but rather they proceed through him [Col. 0262A] into the creature. And, as has already been said above, the Holy Spirit is no longer so much the third person in the Trinity as a certain quality or disposition of God toward the creature.

Moreover, if the procession of God, or even of the Holy Spirit, as he has defined it, is only into the creature, then when the creature is removed there is no procession; and he whose proceeding is his being depends greatly upon our goods in order to exist. Now it can be thought that the creature does not exist, since once it did not exist and it remains only so long as its Creator wills; but to think that the Holy Spirit does not proceed—that is, does not exist—is blasphemous at first sight.

Yet there certainly is that procession by which God proceeds through the Holy Spirit into the creature. But it is in God, not according to affections but according to effects, by which he is in the creature, so that the creature may exist or may exist well. For by causal goodness, eternally in that procession there is life, in which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and, by proceeding, is the Holy Spirit. It exists through the power of foreknowledge and the grace of predestination; but it occurs in time in the creature, when the Holy Spirit breathes where and when he wills. For there is one procession in God of nature and another of grace. The procession which is of nature is eternal there; it is proper to him for whom always to proceed from the Father and the Son is to exist, even if no creature whatever exists. The procession which is of grace is also there eternally, as has been said, and is common to the whole Trinity; but it takes place through the Holy Spirit, not as through an affection, but when, according to his effects in the way stated above, the goodness of God displays itself in the creature. The former [Col. 0262C] is the Holy Spirit’s own procession from the Father and the Son; the latter takes place through the Holy Spirit, with the Father and Son cooperating. The former indeed is God; the latter is a marvelous work of God.

Then, in what follows, when he is challenged and asked from where he gets this assertion—that while confessing with us that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he adds, “but not from their very substance”—he in turn asks us from where we have the assertion that he proceeds from their very substance. Certainly from the fact that both we and he confess that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. For what is it to proceed from them except to proceed from what they are? And what are they? God. Therefore God proceeds from God: the Holy Spirit proceeds from the [Col. 0262D] Father and the Son, one God with them.

“Certainly,” he says, “but not from their very substance.” And, returning to his philosophical support, he says that there are three things in a bronze seal: bronze, the seal—that is, what can be sealed, as though suited to receiving a seal—and that which seals. The seal is from the bronze, from the very substance of the bronze; namely, because, in order for it to be a seal, some bronze must be taken from the bronze. But that which seals proceeds from the bronze and the bronze seal and has its being from both, yet not from their very substance, since nothing is taken from that substance in order for it to be that which seals. “Thus,” he says, “the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son; yet he is not, or does not proceed, from their very substance.”

That is, just as some bronze is taken from the bronze, from the very substance of bronze, in order that it may be a seal formed in its own manner, so wisdom, both power to act and power to discern, is from the power of God, in order that there may be generation in God, that the Son may be from the Father, that he may be begotten. For this, he says, is to be begotten: to be from the very substance of the begetter. And this is to be from the very substance of the begetter: to be some part of the whole. Therefore, just as a bronze seal is some bronze from the whole bronze, so wisdom is from power—that is, it is a certain power. This, therefore, the Holy Spirit does not have, nor does he deserve to be numbered among the powers of God, as our theologian says, because, he says, God’s beneficence is no power. Nor is he, he says, from the very substance of the Father, which would be to be the Son and to be begotten from the Father; but, according to that prophetic metaphor spoken of above, he proceeds from the mouth of God.

If, when asked what that mouth is, what that procession is, from which or through which the Holy Spirit’s proceeding is his being what he is, he should say that he does not know, he could readily be excused. But whatever that mouth may be, whatever that procession may be, from which or through which each proceeds and each has being what he is—the Son as well as the Holy Spirit—as has already been made manifest from the prophetic Scriptures, certainly in both, namely in the mouth and in the procession, identity of names expresses a complete likeness of realities: namely, the Son’s generation and the Holy Spirit’s procession. Since Scripture declares both to be from the same mouth of the Most High Lord, using the same term, “procession,” they are joined in so great a likeness that, as blessed Augustine says, although each proceeds from the Father, it is an insoluble question in this life why both are not called Son.

But that one is the Son and the other the Holy Spirit, the Lord himself made manifest in the world, saying: “The Father loves the Son” (John 3), and elsewhere: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15). Both, as has often already been said, are also declared to proceed and to proceed from the same mouth. Moreover, blessed Augustine, defining the Son’s birth as far as a human being could, says: “The Son was and is, because he is from him who always is what he is. But for him to be from him who is what he is—that is, from the Father who is—is birth. And always to be from him who always is, is eternity.”

The same must plainly be declared of the Holy Spirit, apart from the names “birth” and “procession,” in this way: The Holy Spirit was [Col. 0263D] and is, because he is from him who always is what he is. But for the Holy Spirit to be from him who is what he is—that is, from the Father—is procession. And always to be from him who always is, is eternity.

Thus we also read that, when the Arians of old, aided or favored by the rulers of this age, attacked the faith of the orthodox because they proclaimed that the Son was born from the substance of the Father, they pressed them, saying: “If he was born from God, he is from within God. If he is not from within God, he is not from God.” But the orthodox replied: “Far be it! For that nature has neither outside nor inside, nor does the Catholic faith hold this. But we believe, and therefore speak, that the Son was begotten from the Father; that is, that the Son is what the Father is and has from the Father, by being born, that which he is.”

Who, apart from the names spoken of above, namely Son and birth, could doubt that the same must be proclaimed concerning the Holy Spirit, so that we may likewise say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father—that is, that the Holy Spirit is what the Father is and has from the Father, by proceeding, that which he is? This is what we believe and confess: that the Son is from the Father, or is begotten from his very substance. We also pronounce anathema upon whoever he may be who denies that the Holy Spirit likewise is or proceeds from the Father—that is, from his substance.

Thus blessed Augustine too, in his entire lengthy work *On the Trinity*, which, as he himself says, he began as a young man and published as an old one, complains, concerning the matter which this new theologian boasts of having discovered, that he was never able to find an expression adequate to his understanding; and that his understanding had always exerted itself more than it had achieved in attempting to distinguish how that generation and procession differ, though both are from the Father. For the procession of the Holy Spirit, which is proclaimed to be from both the Father and the Son, is principally from the Father, from whom the Son also has, by being born, this: that the Holy Spirit himself proceeds from him. Thus the Holy Spirit is the gift of both, not by the relation of gift and possessors, but by the harmony of gift and givers.
