For this reason the aforesaid doctor says that there is such great likeness between that birth and that procession that no human being in this life should suppose that their certain dissimilarity, if there is one, can be found; but in the future, he says, it “will be seen by those who are worthy, when the mind contemplates what cannot here be seen by reasoning.” Therefore Master Peter must be told that, just as it is very safe to be ignorant of some things with such men, so to wish to be foremost in discovering things of this kind is exceedingly vain and dangerous. He must be told that it is not without reason that the holy Fathers so earnestly proclaimed that this birth and procession are alike, but because they are alike according to the mode both of being born and of proceeding. As for the apparent dissimilarity in the names themselves, since God has not yet been pleased to reveal in the world why or how this is so, let him for the present allow only those to know it whose perfect knowledge of it is their very being.

But whereas, as has already been said above, he asks why the Holy Spirit is nowhere found to proceed from the Father and the Son from their very substance, we say rather that nowhere is he found not to proceed from them. For what is it to proceed from them except to proceed from what they are? Indeed, when it is said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, that is literal language; but when it is said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is added, “from their very substance,” that is already figurative language.

Therefore, I beg him, let the Holy Spirit possess his own, that is, his full and equal, kinship with God the Father, alongside the Son—a kinship from which he has excluded him through an all-too-philosophical prejudice, saying and writing: “The Son has such kinship to the Father that he is not only from him and begotten from him, but also from [Col. 0265A] his very substance; whereas the Holy Spirit is from him and proceeds from him, but not from his very substance.”

## Chapter V

And in all these things his fury has not turned away from insults to the Holy Spirit; his hand is still stretched out. For he says that God is mind, according to Cato; and that the Holy Spirit is the soul of the world, according to Plato. I wonder by what spirit he speaks concerning the Holy Spirit, with what presumption, with what confidence, he ventures to say or write so great, so unfamiliar, and unheard-of a thing about God, when he has no author at all for it except himself—not even Plato himself, whom he especially boasts of having as his authority in this matter.

“Plato,” he says, “when he had said that the world is an animal, also declared it to be an intelligent—that is, rational—animal, on this ground: that since its soul surpasses all others, it acts and orders all things within it all the more rationally; since in that soul, as in God, are the causes of all things that come to pass, and to it is assigned a divine providence over all natures, in which all things that have been made are life—even evil things, which are ordered in the best way by its goodness.”

By “world,” however, he means whatever the Creator’s providence contains within itself, that is, absolutely all creation. Concerning this world, then, the new Platonist attempts to establish on Plato’s authority that, besides the instruments of the senses, which it need not possess since nothing remains outside it to which those instruments could have [Col. 0265C] any usefulness, the entire power of soul is fulfilled in it through the Holy Spirit.

He adds still more, which, since it has no authority from Holy Scripture and can have no basis in the rules of faith, is thereby easier for us to reject. But we read that this opinion concerning the soul of the world was long ago rejected by blessed Augustine. Perhaps having encountered someone who held such views, he says, when treating the origin of the soul in his work *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*:

“When it is written that God breathed the breath of life into the face of man (Gen. 2), God must be understood to have made the soul from a creature subject to him, in that he is said to have breathed. If, then, we were to say that God is, as it were, the soul of this bodily world, while the world itself were, as it were, the body of a single living thing, we would rightly say that, by breathing, he made the human soul only a bodily soul, from that air which is subject to him as a part of his body. But since we say not only that the body of the world is subject to God, but that he alone is above every creature, whether bodily or spiritual, we must not believe that he made the soul by breathing either from himself or from bodily elements.”

Likewise:

“Perhaps the soul is from air. Breathing is suited to this element. But it is our breathing, not God’s. Hence we said above that this might fittingly be thought if we believed God to be the soul of the world as of one greatest living thing, so that he breathed it from the air of his own body as our soul is breathed from its own. But since it is certain that God is above every body of the world and above every spirit which he created, by an incomparable distance, how could this rightly be said?”

Likewise:

“The Manichaeans, who think themselves Christians or wish to be thought such, are more detestable than pagan philosophers in their opinion concerning the soul, because those philosophers distinguish the soul’s nature from God’s nature, whereas these people, saying that the soul is nothing other than God’s own substance, indeed altogether that which God is, do not shrink from calling it so shamefully changeable that they think there is no kind of plant or worm in which it is not mingled.”

Likewise, writing to Evodius concerning the Trinity and the dove, he says that no creature whatever was ever joined to God in unity of person, “except,” he says, “the human being alone assumed from the Virgin. Since all things were done for the liberation of that very nature, he was joined to the unity of the person of the Word of God by a wonderful and singular assumption; yet the Word remained unchangeably in his own nature, in which no human fancy should suppose that there is any composition with that in which he subsists.”

Further, if the Holy Spirit is the soul of the world, it follows that he is a part of the world, just as a human soul is a part of the human being. In this way too, the Holy Spirit and this world are one person; and the world must now be worshiped and adored by us, just as in Christ we adore the human being joined to God in unity of person, of whom it is written: “Adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy” (Ps. 28).

We certainly believe and confess that “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1); and, just as from the beginning he was said to be borne over the waters (Gen. 1), so he is continually borne over the changing creature—or, as the truer translation of that Scripture has it, he cherishes it as a bird cherishes its young—containing all things so that they may be, ordering them so that they may be well, preserving their proper orders, giving existence to stones, life to trees, sensation to animals, and discernment to human beings.

But just as the divine presence is absent nowhere, yet is in one way in such creatures and in another way in his saints, so too the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of life, gives life in one manner to those of whom it was said, “It is the Spirit who gives life” (John 6), and in another manner to other living things; in one manner to those who live from him and for whom he himself is life, and in another to those things which live in themselves while he acts, and in which whatever kind of soul they have is in them. For even if, in certain holy human beings, their spirit is sometimes made one spirit with God by participation in grace, nevertheless every creature remains far removed both from participation in the divine nature and from unity of person with God.

## Chapter VI

“It is also asked,” he says, “whether all human beings are saved so entirely by the mercy of God that no one can have a good will unless God’s prevenient grace moves the heart, inspires a good will, multiplies it once inspired, and preserves it once multiplied. If this is so—namely, if a human being can do no good of himself and is unable, by free choice without the aid of grace, to raise himself in any way to receive divine grace, as has been said—then there appears to be no reason why, if he sins, he should be punished. For if he cannot do anything good of himself and was made such that he is more inclined to evil than to good, then if he sins, is he not free from sin? Is God, who made him such, to be praised for such a creation, rather than blamed?”

And after some intervening material he adds and says similar things:

“But because this is not so, but is far otherwise, we must state matters as truth has them. We must say, therefore, that through reason given by God a human being can adhere to the grace set before him; and God does no more for the person who is saved, before he adheres to grace, than for the person who is not saved. But just as one who displays precious stones for sale arouses in onlookers a desire to buy, so God sets his grace before all, counsels through the Scriptures, and incites by examples, so that human beings may adhere to grace through the freedom of choice which they possess. One who is prudent adheres to grace through the freedom of his choice; one who is slothful and carnal, though he can do so through free choice, neglects it, and therefore is neglected by God.

“But the statement or belief that, just as dead Lazarus could not return to life unless God raised him, so a human being cannot rise to good willing unless grace gives life, is made because this giving of life is attributed to grace: for the reason by which a human being discerns and understands that evil must be avoided and good done is from God. Therefore a person is said to act by God’s inspiration because God, through the reason which he gave to the human being, makes him recognize sin itself.”

This is plainly the Pelagian heresy. I suppose that no one who has even slightly become familiar with reading the divine books is unaware of the many volumes and treatises by which holy doctors—Augustine, Jerome, and many others—fought against it, and of how long ago it was anathematized from the thresholds of the Church and the hearts of the faithful.

But the man who dares to say this does not seem to divide the matter equally with God. For God, as he says, makes the human being rational; he himself, which is far better, makes himself alive or active according to reason. Against this the Lord says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0267D] See Augustine, to Evodius, *On the Trinity*.]: “He who said ‘nothing’ made no exception.” And Paul says: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. 2). He whose work it is to give reason has also the work of illuminating the reason given. This is a temptation of an utterly vain mind, far removed from God; this is the presumption of the proud in the thought of their heart. “God,” he says, “does by no means do more for the person who is saved than for the person who is not saved before adherence to grace.”

What, then, does predestination do? What does calling do? Augustine says: “A human being cannot will rightly unless it is given by him who cannot will wrongly.” He says that God merely gives reason and arouses desire. But whoever lives by the Spirit of life knows with complete certainty, because he experiences it most certainly in himself, that, as the same doctor says, neither human reason’s discernment nor even a teacher’s admonition can avail where prevenient grace has not healed the delight so as to free the will, and where it has not given power not only to will but also to accomplish.

Nor, as he slanderously asserts, was human nature made thus by God; rather, through sin it has been corrupted and cast down so that human choice is free only for evil and has no freedom for any good except by grace that liberates it. Accordingly, as blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0268D] Augustine, book *On Free Will*, to Boniface.], “God does many good things in a human being which the human being does not do; and the human being does no good things which God does not do, in order that the human being may do them. For by a just judgment we are all held under another’s sin, from which we are freed in baptism, by another’s faith, through the grace of the Savior. Yet the concupiscence of the flesh remains as punishment for sin, by which we are trained. No one can be freed from it unless freed by unmerited grace; and no one murmurs against this except one predestined to death.”

All these words which we have set forth are those of blessed Augustine, from the book *On Free Will*, addressed to Pope Boniface.

Likewise, in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “Those,” he says, “must be resisted most sharply and vigorously who suppose that, without God’s help, the power of the human will by itself can either accomplish righteousness or advance in preserving it. When they begin to be pressed as to how they presume to assert that this can occur without divine aid, they restrain themselves and do not dare utter that claim, because they see how impious and intolerable it is. [Col. 0268C] But they say that these things do not occur without divine aid because God created man with freedom of choice in the will, and, by giving commandments, himself teaches how a human being ought to live. Thus, they say, he surely helps by teaching, removing ignorance so that a person may know in his actions what he ought to avoid and what to seek; and thus, entering by free choice, naturally implanted, upon the path shown to him, he may deserve to attain blessed—and likewise eternal—life by living steadfastly, justly, and devoutly. But we say that the human will is divinely helped to perform righteousness in such a way that, in addition to man’s having been created with free choice of the will, and in addition to the instruction commanding him how he ought to live, [Col. 0268D] he receives the Holy Spirit, through whom there comes about within him delight in and love for that highest and unchangeable Good which is God. This is so even now, while one walks by faith and not yet by sight, so that, having been given this pledge of a gratuitous gift, he may burn with desire to cleave to his Creator and be inflamed to approach participation in that true light, so that it may be well with him through him from whom he has being. For free choice has power only to sin if the way of truth remains hidden; and when what must be done and striven for begins no longer to be hidden, unless it is also delightful and loved, it is not done, not undertaken, and one does not live well. For, in order that it may be loved, the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy [Col. 0269A] Spirit who is given to us—not through free choice, which arises from ourselves.”

Likewise, in the *Enchiridion*, concerning the free choice of the first man (chapters 105–107): “Thus man ought first to have been made, so that he could will either good or evil: neither without reward if he willed good, nor without punishment if evil . . . Yet even then no merit could have existed without grace. For although sin depended upon free choice alone, free choice was nevertheless not sufficient for retaining righteousness unless divine aid were supplied through participation in the unchangeable Good. For just as dying lies within a person’s power when he wishes—for no one, to say nothing else, is unable to kill himself by not eating—yet the will is not sufficient to preserve life if the aids of food are lacking; so man in paradise was able by his will to kill himself [Col. 0269B] by abandoning righteousness. But in order that the righteousness of life might be maintained by him, willing was too little unless he who had made him helped him . . . Man therefore was so made upright that he could remain in the same righteousness, though not without divine help; and could become perverse by his own choice. Whichever of these he chose, God’s will would be done—either by him or justly concerning him. Accordingly, God’s will was done concerning the man who preferred to do his own will rather than God’s; when, from the same mass of perdition which flowed from that man’s stock, God makes by grace one vessel for honor and another for dishonor by judgment, so that no one may boast in man and, therefore, not in himself.”

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0269C] Next the ungrateful man enters into litigation with God and seems to wish to establish that Christ died in vain. His pupils too mutter this, as though from his own opinion; in the slanders set forth as questions, they say—if he dared so say—that Christ’s coming into the world was unnecessary. For, as you have before you and can read, he attacks the mystery of the salvation common to all, concerning Christ’s passion and death; and, insofar as lies within him, destroying and assailing it, he seems to scatter and tear it apart and cast it to the wind, drawing the sword far out against it. If I speak harshly here, forgive me if I groan harshly where I grieve more deeply.

“It must be known,” he says, “that our teachers after the apostles agree on this: that the devil [Col. 0269D] had lordship and power over man, and possessed him by right, because man freely consented to the devil through the freedom of choice which he possessed. For they say that, if someone conquers someone else, the conquered person is by right made the conqueror’s slave. Therefore, as the doctors say, the Son of God was incarnate by this necessity: that man, who could not otherwise be freed, might by the death of an innocent man be rightfully freed from the devil’s yoke. But, as it seems to us, the devil never had any right in man, except perhaps by God’s permission, like a jailer; nor did the Son of God assume flesh in order to free man.”

“As it seems to us,” he says. Will he then assert something to us better than that upon which all the doctors after the apostles agree and concur? Has something better been revealed to him, [Col. 0270A] or has he himself discovered something better, than what those taught us who learned from the Lord? Is his wisdom deeper? His understanding sharper? His life holier? His authority weightier? “It does not seem so to us,” he says. What if it seemed so to Wisdom itself—to the apostle Paul and the other apostles?

For he almost rails against the Lord himself, saying: “What necessity, what reason, what need was there, for our redemption, that the Son of God, having assumed flesh, should endure so many and such great fastings, reproaches, scourges, spit, and”—as he says shortly afterward, let him himself determine whence he obtained it—“a crown of thorns pressed into his head as far as the brain; finally, the very harsh and shameful death of the cross, and execution among evildoers?” And against the Apostle: “How,” [Col. 0270B] he says, “does the Apostle say that man is reconciled to God through the death of the Son of God (Rom. 5), when God ought to have been angered against man so much the more as human beings sinned more gravely by crucifying his Son than by transgressing his command through the taste of a single fruit?” And much else in this manner.

What shall we say to this man, who believes neither Truth itself, nor the apostles, nor apostolic doctors? Many things may indeed be brought against what he says from the authentic Scriptures, in which, for the simple children of God who believe, hope, and love, the Lord’s trustworthy testimonies shine forth concerning the mysteries of human salvation, granting wisdom to little ones; the Lord’s righteous ordinances, being upright, gladden upright hearts; and the Lord’s judgments are true, justified in themselves. But, as the Apostle says of [Col. 0270C] the wise of this world (1 Cor. 2), all these things are foolishness to him.

Finally, consider the mass of accusations piled up from every side for the assault upon truth; taste the force and flavor of the individual questions in their following order, and you will perceive from what root they spring. He is ashamed of God’s Gospel; the simplicity of the Christian faith has become cheap in his eyes. Would that he at least read God’s Gospel with the goodwill with which he reads Plato. When he reads Plato, where he understands him he splendidly proclaims and extols the philosophical meaning he finds in him; but where he does not understand him, or discovers that Plato says something differently according to the spirit of this world, he always attempts to interpret him in the better sense.

Would that in this too he imitated Plato [Col. 0270D] whom he loves: namely, that Plato, when treating of God, carefully and prudently teaches that, by God’s own revelation, he judges the Creator from the creature and thus forms an opinion or understanding concerning him; while patiently acknowledging the rest as unknown with philosophical reverence, he sends inquirers to the Ideas, which he says exist in the mind of the highest God and contain the original forms and rational causes of all things. He pays them more deference than Peter is willing to pay to those to whom [lacuna] Paul sends us—to the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God, to his incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways (Rom. 11), to his understanding and counsel—all of which this man endeavors to investigate and judge by the power of human reason. Does he believe Plato? I know that he does. “What,” Plato says, “was God’s cause in making the world? His goodness. Because he was good, he envied [Col. 0271A] no one: he made it as well as it could be made.” Seneca says this of Plato.

In saying this, Plato, with reasonable caution and philosophical prudence, calling the whole of creation “the world,” briefly gives the reason for all things made in the world: namely, that all things which are made by so good a Maker are good and are made well. Let us likewise say: What was God’s cause for making the new creation in Christ? His goodness. Therefore the supremely good God made it as it was best that it should be made. If, then, in God’s wisdom “it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise again, and so enter into his glory” (Luke 24), what can the ingratitude of human reason censure in this? Therefore he says in the prophet: “I have made, I will bear,” says the Lord (Isa. 46).

Indeed, although many [Col. 0271B] modes of human salvation lay ready before almighty and wise God, why, as blessed Augustine says, should he reject this one? Or rather, why should he not choose this one above all others, where nothing at all has been diminished from the glory of divinity and so great a good has been effected in the world through the Savior’s humility and passion? This man too would surely embrace the result of the salvation common to all and would not so rashly or curiously scrutinize the methods of salvation, if in believing and loving he gave as much deference to Christ, the Savior of the world, as Plato gave in his estimations to God, the Creator of the world.

Blessed Augustine says: “That the devil had excessive power in the world before Christ’s coming, power to be lost in his passion, the Lord himself testified as the hour of his passion approached, saying: ‘Now is the judgment [Col. 0271C] of the world; now the prince of this world shall be cast out’” (John 12). And again: “‘Behold, the prince of this world comes, and will find nothing in me’” (John 14). For unless the devil had been exercising power in the world, it would by no means have been said, “he shall be cast out.” Nor would he seek anything in the Lord if he had nothing in other human beings.

This power of the devil over man began with the one whom he first deceived; not because God gave the devil power over man, but because, as soon as God justly abandoned sinful man, the seducer seized upon the sinner. The first man, when he had been created with free choice—that is, free, if he wished, to possess perpetual righteousness together with immortality—voluntarily consented to the enemy’s suggestion, [Col. 0271D] though he did not yet suffer what the man suffered who said: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, but in the flesh [I delight] in the law of sin. Yet I see another law resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive into the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7).

Thus the devil’s power over man was not acquired by right, but wickedly presumed and justly permitted by God. By it man became the slave of the one by whom he was overcome, and, caught in the devil’s snares, was led captive by him to do his will—as the Apostle says. For so it is written there: “That they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will” (2 Tim. 2). Although he persecutes all alike, both just and unjust, [Col. 0272A] only those are under his power who live according to his will. This slavery is the slavery of desires, by which a person lives according to the will of the seducer. No one can resist him except in the kingdom of grace. But one in whom he cannot accomplish what he wills is not subject to his will.

Before Christ’s coming almost the entire world was subject to this power, since all the unjust served him. Nor were the few then righteous wholly exempt from it: since all entered this world liable through original sin introduced by the devil, being born from the flesh of sin. The righteous who departed from this age, although they were not in torments with the unjust and the devil, were nevertheless not with God, insofar as they were held in the darkness of not seeing God.

[Col. 0272B] But what righteousness there is in Christ’s blood, by which man is justified before God, and how man’s reconciliation to God occurs through the death of his Son, is a difficult question—not to be debated amid tumult, but to be sought devoutly and humbly in the spirit. For it is itself the mystery of which the Apostle says: “And certainly great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit” (1 Tim. 3). That is: what took place in the flesh of the Lord Jesus, whether by sight or hearing, was made manifest to all; but the righteousness which is through faith in his blood appears in the spirit only to certain spiritual persons.

Yet one who loves does not toil in this matter, because love itself is understanding to him who has the mind of Christ (1 Cor. 2), as the Apostle says that he has it. Feeling in Christ Jesus the good of justifying grace, he also merits to feel this very thing in himself; [Col. 0272C] for he could not feel it in himself unless he first felt it in Christ through the fully illuminating perception of faith. Hence it is written: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 2). This indeed is the faith which, as the Lord says to Peter, flesh and blood do not reveal, but the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 16).

Therefore he says elsewhere to the disciples: “There are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom” (ibid.). To stand in faith belongs to many; but to see in this life the Son of Man in his kingdom belongs to few: to these, with the eyes of faith enlightened, it is revealed not by flesh and blood but by the Father who is in heaven. Whoever has become Christ’s kingdom, and remains in Christ by the understanding of faith, the affection of love, and the effect of life—and has Christ remaining in himself—also sees in this life the Son of Man in his kingdom, and according to the Apostle’s precept knows how to sanctify him in his heart.

[Col. 0272D] This faith is that trustworthy testimony granting wisdom to little ones, contemplating in its mysteries the Lord’s righteous ordinances—upright ordinances “gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord, bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18); the holy fear of the Lord enduring for age upon age; “the judgments of the Lord, true, justified in themselves” (ibid.), more desirable than all things desired, so that they may be understood; sweeter than everything sweet, when they are understood. In this faith, when it is possessed by everyone who possesses it, as the same Prophet says, “the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works” (Ps. 32): there is no question in it, no hesitation, but only an affection that delights.

Far away is the scandal of the cross; its only glory is in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, “who became for us,” as the Apostle says, “righteousness from God, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1). This faith understands what righteousness in Christ’s blood is, what man’s reconciliation to God is, insofar as through love of the crucified one that human being becomes one spirit with God.

[Col. 0273A] Possessing wisdom hidden in mystery, it makes plain to all that this is God’s work. It is not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of spirit and power, so that it may not rest in human wisdom but in God’s power. It is truth, it is light; it hates darkness and comes willingly to the light. Nothing is to be feigned for its sake; nothing is to be concealed within it. It loves to be observed closely; the one who loves it more purely beholds it more closely. For it is God’s work, whose distinctive property is to be loved; and this is chiefly recognized in that whatever belongs to God is understood above all through love.

But Peter’s reconciliation, which he fabricates in God and imposes upon us, may be far from God as it is far from us: namely, the reconciliation of an angry and implacable human being unless satisfied by the death of his innocent Son—although, as Peter himself says, God ought rather to have been angered by the unjust death of his innocent Son than by the taste of a single fruit. But God, in whom there is no iniquity, in whom there is no “is and is not,” but in whom there is “is,” [Col. 0273C] made from eternity all things that would come to be; and whatever was made by him is life in him. He predestined that all good things, by whomever they are done, should be done by himself. As all good things are enclosed within the goodness of the one predestining them, so no evils can escape the order of providence, which justly and rightly disposes all things.

Therefore the goodness of the Creator predestined that the world should be made, and man in the world, so that through man he might restore the ruin caused by angelic transgression. Since he foreknew that man, being free in choice, would sin voluntarily, and that the human race would perish in his sin, he again predestined that another man should be made, Christ the Lord, who could not sin because he would be God; and in him he predestined that the Christian race should be saved and freed from the human race.

These are the two men of whom the Apostle says that the debt of the one proceeded to condemnation for all, but the righteousness of the other to justification of life for all, so that “as through the disobedience of one many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many should be made righteous” (Rom. 5). But in making the first man, God established him with free choice, so that he could will either good or evil: so that, if his will were good, it might have merit before God through the merciful aid of grace; or, if it were evil, it too might have its evil merit, grace justly abandoning it, and God’s justice rightly ordering its evil into its punishment.

Adam was made and placed in paradise; he sinned, [Col. 0274A] and God was angry with him, and enmity came about between God and man. God’s anger, while he tranquilly judges all things, was the just vengeance of sin imposed upon the sinner. The enmity between God and man was nothing other than the enmity customarily existing between righteousness and sin.

But when the time for showing mercy came, God sent his Son to save the world, making him man in order to save man. Having predestined him as Savior of the world, he also foreknew that he would be killed in the world, and predestined what would be accomplished through his death—namely, the salvation of the world. For when the author of sin could not persuade him to sin, he killed him as cruelly as he could, inflicting the punishment of sin upon one who was not a sinner.

And the Lord, who could, if he wished, not die—for he was not merely man but also God, wholly removed from every sin and owing nothing to the penalty of sin, that is, death—voluntarily accepted the death which the enemy thought he had violently inflicted upon him. He transferred to himself the punishment of all sinners to be spiritually regenerated in him, just as Adam had sinned to the punishment of all those to be carnally generated from him.

[Col. 0274B] And he poured into the whole posterity of Christian faith original righteousness through regenerating grace, just as Adam had poured into the whole posterity of the flesh of sin the infecting corruption of original sin through carnal generation; so that the children of grace might live by another’s righteousness, just as the children of wrath died through another’s sin. Thus, in the kingdom of righteousness, no evil remained unordered: for in him who died for sinners no sin of the justified person remained unpunished. So great was the value of the price of that innocent blood that whoever—even among his killers—adhered to Christ through faith might, through his undeserved temporal death, escape the eternal death deserved.

Nor, as Peter complains, was that sacred blood given to the devil as if it were a price of redemption for man; rather, it was permitted to his craving wickedness, so that, when it was shed to his joy, an innumerable multitude of the predestined might be taken away from him through Christ’s justification, lest they perish with him to his joy. Nor was it demanded by God the Father as if in order to make satisfaction, though, when offered, it made satisfaction to him most fully.

For in the cooperation of human salvation the unity of the Trinity clearly declared itself, [Col. 0274D] when, as the Apostle says, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5), and Christ in his blood reconciled us to God, as his blood was poured out—he who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, to cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God (Heb. 9).

For the predestination by which all this was predestined from eternity is the goodness of God, that is, the Holy Spirit: the common love of Father and Son, their common sweetness, common grace, and common mercy. As from ancient time he is continually borne over the flowing creature, not by a needy will but by overflowing goodness. This is the Father’s will concerning human salvation, the Son’s obedience, the love of Father and Son, and divine goodness toward [Col. 0275A] its creature. For the Father’s goodness toward the Son and toward the creature is itself the Father’s command to the Son concerning human salvation; and the Son’s goodness toward the Father—which is the Holy Spirit—is itself Christ’s obedience, in the manner in which it was fitting that this should occur, in saving man.

Christ the man, perfectly disposed toward this goodness, obtained through it a new righteousness by suffering the penalty of sin without sin. Since he was also almighty and good God, he bestowed this righteousness upon the Christian race, which was dying with the human race in its sin. For they too were by nature children of wrath, as were the rest, their nature corrupted by the contagion of original sin. In them, afterward, through regenerating grace, original righteousness obtained a kingdom much more worthy and powerful than original sin had previously reigned in them through carnal generation from the concupiscence of the flesh, coming from Adam.

[Col. 0275B] Thus those who had been children of wrath became children of grace; through the more hidden power of the mystery they were justified in Christ’s blood, not only from original sin but from every sin. Moreover, they deserve to receive the holy Spirit of adoption, bearing witness to their consciences that they are children of God. Therefore, when sin was removed—that is, forgiven—to which righteousness was hostile, God’s and humanity’s reconciliation was made complete, and the end came of wrath, that is, of God’s just vengeance.

But the end of vengeance, though eternal vengeance, comes for those reborn unto eternity, while the sentence of temporal punishment remains in order to train faith in eternity. Hence blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Baptism of Infants*: “The flesh first made was not flesh of sin; in it man did not wish, amid the delights of paradise, to preserve righteousness. Therefore God ordained that after his sin the propagated flesh of sin should struggle against receiving righteousness through labors and hardships. For this reason Adam, cast out of paradise, dwelt opposite Eden, that is, opposite the seat of delights, signifying that flesh of sin must be trained through labors, which are contrary to delights—the flesh which did not preserve obedience amid delights before it became flesh of sin.

[Col. 0275C] “Therefore, just as those first human beings afterward lived justly, and hence are rightly believed to have been freed through the Lord’s blood from the final punishment, yet did not deserve in that life to be restored to paradise; so too flesh of sin, even if a person lives justly in it after sins have been forgiven, does not immediately deserve not to suffer the death which it drew from the propagation of sin. Something of this sort is indicated concerning the patriarch David in the book of Kings (2 Sam. 12). When the prophet was sent to him and, because of the sin he had committed, threatened future evils against him from God’s wrath, David obtained pardon by confessing his sin; the prophet replied that his crime and wrongdoing had been forgiven, and yet what God had threatened followed, so that David was humbled by his son.

“Thus if someone says here: ‘If God had threatened this because of that sin, why, when the sin was forgiven, did he fulfill what he had threatened?’—the entirely correct answer is that that forgiveness of sin was granted lest the man be hindered from receiving eternal life; [Col. 0276A] but the effect of that threat followed so that the man’s devotion might be exercised and proved in that humiliation. Likewise God imposed bodily death on human beings because of sin; and after forgiveness of sins he did not remove it, in order that righteousness might be exercised.” Thus blessed Augustine.

Next, Master Peter—as you will be able to read—passes over without discussion the questions he has raised, questions thorny and full of stumbling blocks, and leaves open for the simpler-minded the pit of perdition dug with great labor. He then seems to return to Catholic doctrine, as though making himself immune if anyone should fall into it. For in the dispensation of the Mediator three things above all are to be understood by the faithful: the mystery of universal redemption and reconciliation; an example of humility for those who were perishing especially through pride; and an incitement to love for those whose love had decayed amid earthly things.

Having only lightly touched upon the first, entirely neglected the second, and devoted himself wholly to the third, he says that this was the design and cause of the Lord’s incarnation and passion: that he might illuminate the world with the light of his wisdom and kindle it to love of himself. As though a proud person could be stirred to love God unless first humbled from self-love, and unless first released by the mystery of redemption from the bondage and chain of sin.

When you have read all that he asks, writes, establishes, amplifies, resolves, teaches, and corrects, it is for your judgment whether, in accordance with the commandment of the Law, he has covered over the pit he dug in such a way [Col. 0276C] that, if anyone’s ox or donkey falls into it, payment cannot justly be demanded from him (Exod. 21). Into this exceedingly dangerous ruin those have certainly already fallen who, following his opinion, strive to maintain—if they dared say it fully—that Christ the Lord suffered in vain and came into the world in vain.

This must not be concealed from them; rather, their danger must be pressed upon them, and they must frequently be confronted with the Apostle’s words: “Test yourselves. Prove yourselves whether you are in the faith. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you—unless perhaps you are reprobate?” (2 Cor. 13). Christ is in those to whom Christ is pleasing. Christ is pleasing to the person who is pleasing to himself only in the faith of Christ Jesus. But faith does not belong to all. Therefore the same Apostle says: [Col. 0276D] “But if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who perish; in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of the invisible God, may not shine upon them” (2 Cor. 4).

Christ’s coming into the world and his passion were necessary to such an extent that the world was to be saved in this particular way; but it had to be done especially in this way because, in the counsel of his wisdom and providence, God had ordained that it should be done in this way most suitably and effectively—as he himself knows.

## CHAPTER VIII

Again, speaking of the person of the Mediator, he separates God from man like Nestorius: “It must be known,” he says, “that although we grant that Christ is the third [Col. 0277A] person in the Trinity, we nevertheless do not grant that this person, who is Christ, is the third person in the Trinity.”

Observe the utterly foolish insolence of one speaking about God. “We grant this,” he says, “we do not grant that,” as though there were or could be anything concerning Christ or in Christ except what he has granted. Next, contrary to the Psalm’s statement, “Israel, there shall be no new god in you” (Ps. 80), he accuses us of having a new God in our faith if we confess that anything exists in God which did not exist from eternity.

This is properly the heresy of the Agnoetae, which formerly appeared in the Church during the time of blessed Gregory. Writing to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, Gregory says among other things: “No one can be an Agnoete who is not a Nestorian.” For just as Nestorius formerly strove to establish that Mary was not *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος), that is, Mother of God, so these people, because the Gospel says concerning the day of judgment that neither the angels nor the Son knows that day and hour (Mark 13), and because the Lord is read to have come to the fig tree seeking fruit on it and not found it (Matt. 21), and because he asked concerning Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11), said that the Son of Man was ignorant of many things.

[Col. 0277B] But, as the same doctor says, the Father alone is said to know the day of judgment because his Son, consubstantial with him, has from the nature which is above the angels the capacity to know what the angels do not know. For the incarnate Only-begotten of God, made for us a perfect man, knows the day and hour of judgment in the nature of divinity, yet does not know it from human nature.

Therefore, what he knows in humanity itself he does not know from humanity itself, because God made man knows the day and hour of judgment only by the power of his divinity. Hence we likewise say that Christ, the Son of Man, is the third person in the Trinity in the very nature of his humanity, though not from that nature itself, according to the union he has with God. For as the incarnate God became Son of Man because of the man assumed, so the assumed man became Son of God because of the God who assumed him.

Therefore the same doctor says in his letter: “God and man know the day and hour of judgment; but man knows it because that man himself is God. The knowledge which he did not possess from the nature of humanity, from which he was a creature together with the angels—this he denied that he possessed together with the angels, who are creatures.”

[Col. 0277C] To this we also say: since in the Trinity, which is God, there are three persons—a point he does not deny—and since Christ, God and man, is one person—a point he also does not deny—yet he by no means grants that this person is the third person in the Trinity, then plainly we have from him a new God: namely, a fourth person in God alongside the Trinity. In our faith a quaternity rather than a Trinity is proposed for adoration.

But, as blessed Augustine says to Evodius [Note: [Col. 0277D] Augustine, Letter 102], “by the assumption of man the number of persons was in no way increased, but the same Trinity remained.” We, however, confess—as does every tongue—that the one whom God [Col. 0278A] exalted, that is, if it is permissible so to speak, “the Lordly man,” and to whom he gave the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings should bend (Phil. 2), that is, so that he should be adored by all as God—we confess, I say, that he is in the glory of God the Father. This means nothing other than that he is the third person in the majesty of the supreme Trinity; but this is so because he himself is the Son of God—that is, joined, or rather united, to the Son of God in unity of person.

Thus we believe that God the Son was born in time and suffered, according to that same unity of person, without any objection that this constitutes a newness in God.

For this reason Blessed Augustine also says in the *Retractations* (ch. 19) that he repents of having said somewhere what we too, a little earlier, said in order to make the matter clear—namely, “the Lordly man” (*Dominicum hominem*)—as though that man were not himself the Lord. Yet, as Augustine himself says elsewhere, from the time that he began to exist, he began to be Lord and God. Just as Christian faith refuses to hear of a division of person in Christ, God and man, so it likewise abhors a confusion or mingling of the divine substance with the human substance. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Trinity and the Dove*, as we have already quoted above:

> “Neither was that sound of the voice by which it was said, ‘You are my beloved Son,’ which immediately ceased to exist, joined into the unity of the Father’s person; nor was that bodily appearance of the dove (Luke 3) joined into the unity of the person of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0278C] any more than was that fire (Acts 2) which manifested the same Holy Spirit and, once its signifying function had been fulfilled, immediately ceased to exist. But man alone—because all those things were done for the sake of freeing human nature itself—was joined into the unity of the person of the Word of God by a wonderful and singular assumption. Yet the Word remained unchangeably in its own nature, in which no human imagination is to suppose anything composite with which it subsists. For man was added to the Word; the Word did not, by a change, depart into man. And thus the Son of God is said to be together with the man assumed. Hence the same Son of God is unchangeable and coeternal with the Father—but in the Word alone. And the Son of God was buried—but in the flesh alone.”

Likewise Pope Leo, in Epistle 11, says concerning Christ:

> “He is wholly God because of the God who assumes, and wholly man because of the man assumed. Yet the Word was not changed into flesh, nor flesh into the Word; rather, each remains in the other, and Christ is one in both—neither divided by diversity nor confused by mingling. Nor is one from the Father and another from the mother, although he is from the Father in one manner and from the mother in another: from the Father before every beginning; from the mother at the end of the ages, so that Jesus Christ might be the mediator of God and men, in whom the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily. For this is not a lowering of the one who assumes, but an advancement of the one assumed: that God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every [Col. 0279A] name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2).”

Although there is one person of God and man, the source of their common glory is one thing, and the source of their common humiliation another. For as, in the Trinity, God the Father and God the Son are of one substance but not of one person, so in the form of the Mediator God and man are of one person but not of one substance. “Nor does it matter,” says St. Leo, “from which substance Christ is named, since, while the unity of person remains inseparably intact, he is both wholly Son of man because of the flesh, and wholly Son of God because of his one substance with the Father.”

Therefore Master Peter says: “We do not concede [Col. 0279B] that Christ, this person—that is, God and man—is the third person in the Trinity.”

But we say, in accordance with the foregoing judgments of the Fathers, that Christ, God and man, this person, insofar as he is God, is the third person in the Trinity. He will say: “Therefore not insofar as he is man.” Certainly; but man too is there, by reason of the inseparable unity whereby he is one person with God. Far be it from us, however, to assert thereby something new in God. For, as Pope Leo holds and Augustine agrees, we say that the man, predestined from eternity to this end and glorified in this at the time of God’s good pleasure, began at once to exist and to be God—although there is but one God.

Yet while the divinity of the Son of God remains unchangeably in its own nature, as Blessed Augustine says, [Col. 0279C] without any composite element with which it subsists, such as any human imagination might suppose, man was added or fitted to him, by a wonderful and incomparable assumption, into unity of person; not created first and then assumed, but created in the very act of assumption. And, as was said, he began at once to exist and to be God—but God by grace, not by nature; in name or person, not in essential substance. Hence the Apostle says: “He gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2).

And Blessed Augustine, in the book *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, says:

> “This unity of the person of Christ Jesus our Lord, consisting thus of both natures, is such that either nature imparts even its own designation to the other—the divine to the human and the human to the divine—as the blessed Apostle [Col. 0279D] shows: ‘Have this mind among yourselves,’ he says, ‘which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, humbled himself,’ etc. (ibid.).”

Therefore, since Christ’s name derives from the fact that God anointed him beyond his companions with the oil of gladness—that is, from the fact that, having become man, he humbled himself—yet it was said of this same Christ that he was in the form of God before the form of a servant had been received by him. For he was not yet Son of man, but Son of God, whose equality with the Father was not robbery but nature.

But if we ask who he is who, though in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, the apostolic voice answers us: [Col. 0280A] Christ Jesus. Therefore that divinity also received the name of this humanity. Likewise, if we ask who became obedient unto death, the most correct answer is: he who, though in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized. Therefore this humanity also received the name of that divinity.

Yet the same Christ appears as a giant of double substance: in one respect obedient, in another equal to God; in one respect Son of man, in another Son of God; in one respect saying, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14); in another, “I and the Father are one” (John 5). For all these reasons we say that Mary, the *theotokon* [θεοτόκον], that is, Mother of God, bore Christ as God and man, one person: man, insofar as he began [Col. 0280B] to exist from her; God, insofar as from her God and man began to exist. Thus we confess the very person of Christ to be the third person in the Trinity: God, Son of God, insofar as he is one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit; man, son of man, insofar as he is one person with God, the Son of God: the former, who is God by nature from eternity; the latter, who, from the time he began to exist, is not merely man but also God by grace through the blessedness of divine coessentiality.

Nevertheless, Christian piety’s safeguard remains intact, in order to avoid the suspicion of a newly arisen God. On this point we recalled above Blessed Augustine’s statement that the Word always remains in its unchangeability, in which no human imagination should suppose any composite element with which it subsists.

## Chapter IX

Let us now pass to other matters. Master Peter also says, concerning the sacrament of the altar, that when the substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of the Lord’s body and blood for the accomplishment of the sacramental mystery, the accidents of the former substance remain in the air. I ask: why in the air? What are they to do there?

It seems to us—if it also seems so to you—that those accidents, or the form of the former substance, which, I suppose, is nothing other than a harmonious concurrence of accidents into one, is, if it is there, in the Lord’s body: not as forming it, but as fitting and modifying it through the power of God’s wisdom working in them, so that, according to the rite of the mystery and the mode of the sacrament, that which could not be so in its own form may become fit for handling and tasting in an alien form—acting outwardly so that it may be handled and received bodily, while inward grace acts so that it may be received incorruptibly, may be savoury to the believer, and may give life and spiritual nourishment to the lover. [Col. 0280D]

Accordingly Blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0279D] Augustine, Supplement to vol. I, p. 394]:

> “What you see upon the altar is bread and a cup; this is what your eyes report to you. But what faith, needing instruction, requires is this: the bread is Christ’s body, and the cup his blood.”

Elsewhere he also says of them: “For they are the same things and are changed into something else; and what in them outwardly lies open to the senses is consumed when received.” Hence he says in the book *Against Faustus* [Note: [Col. 0280D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book XIX, ch. 16]:

> “What else are all bodily sacraments but certain visible words—indeed most sacred, yet nevertheless changeable and temporal?”

Likewise elsewhere:

> “If we direct our attention to the visible things themselves by which sacraments are administered, who does not know that they are corruptible? But if we attend to what is effected through them, who does not see that it cannot be corrupted?”

These, then, are what seem to us to be the divine sacraments: exposed to various mishaps of negligence or ignorance, not the Lord’s body, as Master Peter says. Whatever happens in such matters must be believed utterly remote from every injury to its dignity. [Col. 0281A]

## Chapter X

Next he raises another question, saying: “It is commonly asked how the devil can suggest things to human beings, since he does this neither by words nor by signs.” “To this,” he says, “we answer that he does it through the physical properties of things, stones, or herbs. For just as it belongs to the nature of certain stones to attract iron or extinguish sexual desire, so there are certain stones or herbs by which lust, anger, and other vices are aroused. Therefore, whenever the devil wishes to suggest lust, anger, or other vices to someone, he places near him that stone or herb which he knows possesses such a power.” [Col. 0281B]

This is ridiculous. I judge that he said or wrote it only to provoke laughter, since holy teachers plainly say that this is done rather by spiritual wickedness, through a spiritual power unknown to human beings. Satan certainly did not bring Judas some stone or herb when he put it into his heart to betray the Lord, or when he entered into him—that is, as Blessed Augustine says, made him wholly subject to his own dominion. I am also astonished that a man possessing any wisdom should offer, in support of what he advances concerning the aerial bodies of demons, an authority drawn from the tale of Solomon enclosing demons in a glass vessel. [Col. 0281C]

There are still many things in Master Peter’s theology or philosophy that trouble me, but I have passed over most of them, because unless these trouble you, neither would the others. Now I beseech your Reverence, through him who has appointed you watchmen and pastors in his Church, that in the meantime your prudence may deal with these matters in such a way that those scandalized by them may be satisfied, those wounded in faith may be healed, and those who love and proclaim you in God may not be ashamed because of you, but may glory in the Lord concerning you. [Col. 0281D]

## Chapter XI

He also says that from Adam we derive the punishment, not the guilt, of original sin. Why then are infants baptized? But in baptism, as the Fathers say—as we have said above [Col. 0282A] that Blessed Augustine sufficiently explained—the guilt is forgiven; the punishment remains for the exercise of this life: namely, bodily death and the other tribulations of this life.

## Chapter XII

He says that no sin exists except in consent to evil alone and in contempt of God, which a person has in consenting to sin. Indeed, he says that no concupiscence, no evil pleasure, and no evil will is sin, but nature. “To desire,” he says, “another man’s wife, or to sleep with another man’s wife, is not sin; only the consent in this and contempt of God are sin.” And just as no sin is committed in concupiscence and pleasure, so he says that the sin of consent is not increased by any sinful act. [Col. 0282B]

## Chapter XIII

He says that no sin is committed through ignorance. He says that, if a pagan or Jew rejects Christ’s faith because he believes it contrary to God, he does not sin. He says that those who killed the martyrs because they thought that in this they were rendering service to God did not sin. “For this reason,” he says, “the Jews who stoned Stephen and crucified the Lord did not sin; indeed, they would have sinned more had they spared him against the conscience of their own judgment.”

He says that the concupiscence and pleasure of the flesh are not to be killed in us but hated, just as, he says, the Lord commands father and mother to be hated for God’s sake, not killed, so that we may always have something against which to fight. “For,” he says, “what is rightly done with toil and conflict is what deserves a crown and reward; but what is done with peace and pleasure deserves nothing.” [Col. 0282C]

This is what that moral teacher teaches and writes, knowing little, I think, and inexperienced in what freedom of spirit is. He still teaches and writes very many other things, both spiritual and moral, no less blameworthy or dangerous, which it would take too long to pursue. But for rejecting or overthrowing his teaching, if these things are not enough for someone, nothing will be enough.

*Bernard’s Reply to William. He praises the booklet written against Peter Abelard, etc.*

[Col. 0282D]

Brother Bernard to his dearest William. “Your agitation,” etc. See *Works of St. Bernard*, vol. I, col. 533, Epistle 327.

[Col. 0283]

# Disputation of the Catholic Fathers Against the Doctrines of Peter Abelard

(*Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, vol. IV, p. 238.)

## Notice of Dom Tissier

Andrew of Quercy, our Manrique, and others attribute this *Disputation* to William of Saint-Thierry [Note: [Col. 0283] And with good reason. See what the authors of *Gallia litteraria* discuss concerning this disputation above, col. 197, no. XIV. EDITORS’ NOTE.] Yet above we presented William’s legitimate offspring, contained in a single book and written to Geoffrey of Chartres and St. Bernard, in which Abelard’s errors, not yet known to them, are set forth.

This other work, however, divided into three books and dedicated to the Archbishop of Rouen, was published after St. Bernard had attacked Peter Abelard’s errors and Abelard, in an apology written against him, had falsely charged that he had been unjustly attacked by the holy Father. Thus our anonymous abbot defends Blessed Bernard and demonstrates, from Abelard’s own quoted words, that the errors imputed to him by the most holy Father were truly taught and published by Abelard himself.

By the testimony—indeed, by the very words—of these abbots, William namely and this anonymous writer, the calumny will be refuted of those who say that Blessed Bernard, disputing against Peter Abelard, attacked mere masks and chimeras, rather than the doctrine Abelard upheld. This wrong rebounds upon the Apostolic See and the Council of Sens, before whom the chapters of Abelard’s books were read and condemned.

Those who so readily condemn the holy Father for ignorance and acquit Abelard may perhaps have been led into so perverse a judgment by reading Abelard’s response, published thirty years ago with certain other of his works, in which he condemns errors attributed to him in writing and denies that they are his own. Yet that response ought rather to have been entitled *Peter Abelard’s Retraction of Errors* than *Response to the Calumnies Objected*, since William and the anonymous abbot quote at length the opinions of Abelard himself, very plainly containing the errors of which he was accused.

Nor should anyone be troubled that these errors are not found in Abelard’s recently published works, for the books containing them were not printed. Had they been mixed with his other works, they would have brought certain ruin upon them. Furthermore, we have not published the beginning of that disputation. The first quire is missing from the sole extant copy, which once belonged to the library of Clairvaux; and these words were long ago written at its beginning: “One quire is missing; whoever possesses the sequence of the books should inquire.” But not only has that quire not been found: that codex itself was also removed from that library. Andrew of Quercy possessed it during his lifetime, and I myself copied that very manuscript.

Observe that this anonymous author refutes, in the third book of this work, Abelard’s opinion that God’s grace is offered to all. Yet this is not peculiar to Abelard, but is common to scholastic doctors—indeed, also to the Fathers. Among others it is admirably defended by Prosper, Augustine’s disciple, in his books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*; he extends it even to infants who die without baptism. Certainly neither William nor St. Bernard condemned this opinion in Abelard; indeed, they themselves teach it repeatedly. They did accuse Abelard of Pelagianism because he said that we can do good by the powers of free choice, etc. But we shall address this matter again below in our notes.

## Book I

*(The beginning is missing, as we have already noted. In what survives, Abelard’s doctrine is refuted: he assigns power, in a heretical sense, to the Father alone; wisdom to the Son; and benignity to the Holy Spirit.)*

[Col. 0283A]

> “If we examine both evangelical and apostolic sayings, we understand, according to the proper meaning of the expressions themselves, that the things pertaining to power are especially ascribed to the Father, so that from this too it may be plainly inferred that omnipotence itself is especially designated by the title Father. For the Son says: ‘Things which the Father has set in his own power’ (Acts 1), not ‘which the Son and Holy Spirit [have set].’”

And below, on the same matter:

> “When the Apostle says that he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father (Rom. 6), it is suggested that, according to the Father’s property, as stated, those things which belong to power are more properly to be ascribed to the person of the Father; just as those things which pertain to rational discernment or wisdom—such as judging, which belongs to discrimination—are ascribed to the Son. Hence it is written: ‘The Father has given all judgment to the Son’ (John 4), [Col. 0284A] because power yields to wisdom in the examination of judgment, where equity must be weighed more than the force of power exercised.”

And below:

> “Just as from the foregoing it has already long been declared that divine power is especially denoted by the name Father, so wisdom is signified by the name Son. Divine wisdom is, so to speak, a certain power of God himself.”

And below, concerning the Holy Spirit:

> “Benignity itself, which is denoted by the name Holy Spirit, is not any power or wisdom in God; that is, God’s being benign is not his being powerful or wise. Rather, this goodness of his is to be understood according to the affection or effect of charity itself.”

These things, in the same order and in the same words, although here placed in different passages, were vomited forth by the ancient serpent through him in that devilish theology. What Arius, what Eunomius, what other heresiarch ever thought so ill of God, ever wrote so ill? What are you doing, philosophers of our own country? Why do you turn away your eyes? O most noble young men, flowers of the world, golden vessels of secular learning: why do you learn, say, and write such things? Would that your master’s writings were merely empty, and not so destructive!

The apostolic ordinance is: “Everything not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14). What, then, is that which destroys faith? But lest, in removing this foul mire for too long, we become nauseated, let us reread the preceding matters. He says that the Father is omnipotence. That is true; there is no question here. But when he adds “especially,” he becomes suspect to me: he carries poison. For he intends that the Father has an omnipotence that the Son does not have—that is, that the Father can exist of himself, whereas the Son cannot exist of himself. We shall return later to unravel this deception with a truthful answer.

He says that the wisdom of the Father, which is the Son, is not omnipotence, but something belonging to the Father—that is, a certain power derived from the Father’s omnipotence. He repeats this several times. He says that benignity itself, which is the Holy Spirit, is neither power nor wisdom in God, because being benign is one thing and being wise or powerful another. He says that power yields to wisdom in examination of judgment, where equity is to be considered more than the force of power exercised. He says that the Father placed certain things in his own power which neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit placed there. [Col. 0285A]

To these statements—not so much clever arguments as lies—we must respond, as the order of the argument demands and as God, for whom and about whom we speak, grants us the means. First, I ask why he accuses an abbot, distinguished in holy religion and great in reputation, of inventing falsehoods because he wrote in his theology that the Son is a certain power and the Holy Spirit no power at all. For in his *Apology*, which Peter himself directs against the abbot, he denies saying that the divine wisdom is a certain power of the Father and not the Son; yet he admits having said—and obstinately maintains to be true—that the love of the Father and Son is no power, not the Holy Spirit.

But woe to the contentions of men. Truly, according to Jeremiah, every man has become foolish through knowledge. I, a mere insignificant man of slight reputation and no learning, marvel that so learned and celebrated a master should have become so shamefully entangled in such trifles. Not even an ordinary unlearned person ought to be caught in such paltry webs of aerial spiders. For if the wisdom of God is the Son of God, and conversely, and if the love of the Father and Son is the Holy Spirit, and conversely, I cannot see how the Father’s wisdom can be a certain power while the Son is not, or how the love of the Father and Son can be no power while the Holy Spirit is not. [Col. 0285B]

For although the Father is not wise through the Son, but the Son is wise through the Father—for the Father is from no one, while the Son is from the Father whatever he is—Peter himself nevertheless makes especially clear in his *Apology* how he treats the Father’s wisdom. There, on this chapter, he says:

> “Therefore, just as wisdom, which we understand to be his Son, is a certain power or capacity for discerning or knowing all things, so that he cannot err through ignorance, so his love or benignity, which we call the Holy Spirit, is his best will rather than power.”

Awake, you who sleep on beds of ivory and luxuriate upon your couches, lovers of secular wisdom; see how blind is the audacity of presumption. Here he plainly says that God’s wisdom—that is, the Son of God—is a certain power or capacity of God, namely for discerning or knowing all things. He is silent about doing, lest he ascribe omnipotence to the Son, although it is written: “All things were made through him” (John 1). And he says that God’s love or benignity—that is, the Holy Spirit—is the best will, not power. [Col. 0286A]

What more do you seek? It is plain. He says indeed: “The Father is omnipotence; the Son is a certain power; the Holy Spirit is no power.” Why, then, does he rage against the abbot concerning these propositions, as though the abbot had made them, calling him his accuser? Therefore now, not with the voice of the Jews but by the judgment of orthodox believers, let us all cry together: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26).

But that twisting serpent, now coiling back into rings, now—according to the judge’s sentence—crawling upon its breast while raising itself as much as it can, enters the cavern of a most secret and obscure disputation and hisses unheard-of things, as if on Parmenides’ highest rock. Through his *Apology* he makes his theology worse; he adds new errors to old ones and strives obstinately and contentiously to defend them—which makes a person a heretic. He deceives lovers of novelties and simple hearers by sophistical importunities. He calls a most learned—and, what is greater, most religious—abbot inexperienced in the art which is the mistress of argument, as if he had not read in the Apostle that “the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3).

And especially this, from and in the same Apostle:

> “See to it that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). [Col. 0286C]

Having made this digression because he claims that the abbot fabricated those propositions, reason now compels us to return to the preceding falsehoods and examine them, not with our own strength but under the protection of the holy Fathers. All who know anything clearly recognize that falsehood lies hidden beneath truth and, because it is ugly in itself, always seeks to cover itself beneath truth’s shadow.

It is true that omnipotence belongs to the Father, because the Father is omnipotent and is from no one; and, as Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite says in his *Hierarchy*, “The Father is the fountain of Deity.” The Son, however, is naturally from his Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. But his assigning omnipotence so particularly to the Father as to avoid assigning it to the Son or the Holy Spirit—so as, that is, to distinguish the persons, the Father by omnipotence, the Son by wisdom, which is in itself a certain power, and the Holy Spirit by neither power nor wisdom but benignity alone—is poison, error, heresy; and, to use the words of his master, of whom he boasts more than is right, it is deception. [Col. 0286D]

For the Father has no omnipotence which the Son does not have, because whatever the Father has, the Son has; for from the Omnipotent comes the omnipotent Son. Otherwise that Gospel saying would not be true, where the Son says to the Father: “All mine are yours, and all yours are mine” (John 17). For according to divinity the Son is equal to the Father in every respect, although what he is is from him; because God was born from God, the same as he, yet not he; and where there is natural equality, there is also equal and natural power.

Let us see whether the authority of the holy Fathers accords with this assertion. Hilary, that most splendid sun of Gaul and the chief and strongest overthrower of the Arian heresy, says in Book VII of *On the Trinity*:

> “There is no doubt that equality differs in nothing. Nor is equality ever denied where there is union; yet it is not found there in such a way as to differ. Thus the equality of likeness has neither solitude nor diversity, because every equality is neither diverse nor solitary.”

And a little later in the same work:

> “Therefore the Son is the same in the Father’s nature, for whom to be able to do all things belongs to nature.”

And our Aristotle, Blessed Augustine, likewise says in Book VII of *On the Trinity*:

> “Therefore the Father himself is wisdom; and thus the Son is called the wisdom of the Father, in such a way that, as light from light and both true light, so wisdom from wisdom and both one wisdom may be understood. Therefore also one essence, because there being is the same as being wise. For to wisdom, to be wise; to power, to be able; to eternity, to be eternal; to justice, to be just. The Father and Son together are one essence, one greatness, one truth, one wisdom, and one omnipotence.” [Col. 0287B]

Do you see, O Parisian scholars, that omnipotence ought not properly—that is, for distinguishing the persons—to be ascribed to the Father alone? But lest any cloud, however small, of doubt remain, see what the same master continues on the same matter in the eighth book of the same work:

> “Those things are properly said in that Trinity to belong distinctly to the individual persons which are said relatively to one another: Father and Son, and the Holy Spirit, the gift of both. For the Father is not the Trinity, nor the Son the Trinity, nor is the Trinity a gift. But what the individual persons are said to be in themselves ought not to be said plurally as three, but as the one Trinity itself: thus God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; good Father, good Son, good Spirit; omnipotent Father, omnipotent Son, omnipotent Spirit. Yet there are not three gods, three good beings, or three omnipotent beings, but one God, good and omnipotent—which is the Trinity itself.” [Col. 0287D]

By these testimonies it has, I think, been sufficiently shown that omnipotence ought not properly to be ascribed to the Father alone. But I see what Peter intends here [Col. 0288A] and, God granting, I understand into what thickets of new opinion he is venturing. Though he acknowledges above what is true—namely, that the Son is equally omnipotent with the Father in respect of the effect of operation—he nevertheless ascribes omnipotence specially to the Father, because the Son is not equally omnipotent with him in a certain respect, that is, in respect of the mode of subsisting. He seems to draw this from a certain Maximus, whom I suppose to have been Greek, and whom John Scotus also imitated, even to the point of heresy. Peter uses these words in this place:

> “Whatever pertains to omnipotence ought to be ascribed to the Father as his proper attribute, not only in respect of the effect of operation but also in respect of the mode of subsisting; so that, namely, it may be as Maximus said: that the Father is omnipotent through unbegotten [Col. 0288B] Deity.”

It is as though he said openly: by being God and unbegotten, he is omnipotent in both respects. Therefore he is omnipotent in respect of the effect of operation, just as the Son and the Holy Spirit are; and he is omnipotent in respect of the mode of subsisting, which neither Son nor Holy Spirit can be, because the Father can be from himself, whereas the Son and the Holy Spirit cannot.

Thus, according to you, there is a different mode of subsisting in that simple essence. For the Father subsists in such a manner that he properly possesses this omnipotence, which the Son or the Holy Spirit does not possess. Seneca’s saying can be applied to this falsehood: “Whatever is invented lacks a foundation.” For if this is so, then he deceives—or is deceived—who says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). “I,” “the Father,” and “are” pertain to the distinctness of the persons; “one” pertains to the unity of the essence. But he does not deceive, because he is truth; nor is he deceived, because he is wisdom and omnipotence—not *he who is* the Father, but *that which* the Father is. Therefore, in that simple essence there is no differing mode of subsistence [Note: [Col. 0287] He denies that there is in God a different mode of subsistence; but here he takes “to subsist” to mean “to exist,” not as denoting the property of a hypostasis or person.], where whatever is there is of the same nature; and the Father alone is as great a God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, because each person severally is perfect God, while the whole Trinity together is only one God.

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book VI:

> “In bodily things, one thing is not as much as three things together; and two things are something more than one thing. But in the supreme Trinity, which is God, [Col. 0288D] one is as much as the three together; one is as much as two; and they are infinite in themselves. Thus each is in each, each is in all, all are in all, and one is in all. Whoever sees this, even in part, or through a mirror and in an enigma, should rejoice in knowing God, honor God thus, and give thanks. But whoever does not see it should strive to see through piety, rather than through blindness to slander, even though God is one and yet Trinity.”

Augustine argued these things powerfully and faithfully in order to crush the new enemies of the faith and to display the incomprehensible sublimity of indivisible unity. It is therefore plain [Col. 0289A]—unless it be to those who possess an unwise and unrepentant heart through a spirit of pride and contention, storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment—it is plain, I say, that there is no differing mode of subsisting where being is principally and ineffably one and true.

Finally, the essence of a thing is nothing other than the thing itself; and, as Augustine testifies, God does not subsist relatively, as he rules relatively.
