For, as he says in book VII of *On the Trinity*: “Everything subsists in relation to itself; how much more does God, if it is fitting to say that God subsists.” And since in God being wise or being powerful is nothing other than being—as has been powerfully and plainly demonstrated above by both reasoning and the teaching of so great a doctor—it is an unfitting statement concerning God: “The Father can [Col. 0289B] be from himself.” For he *is* from himself, which the Son is not, because the Son is from the Father. Observe how confused—or desirous of causing confusion—is one who says, even concerning a non-simple thing, “This thing can be this thing.” But lest I be wordy and fail by myself—especially being such a one in such matters—I return to the most eminent teacher, Augustine.

That man of God wrote to Saint Evodius, who had questioned him in letters concerning certain most obscure matters. In them Evodius, as it seemed to himself, had proved by reasoning that God must exist; and, as a river swollen with waters, Augustine burst forth in his second letter to Evodius with these words:

> “You have this in the book *On True Religion*. If you recalled and considered it, it would never seem to you that God must exist by rational necessity, or that it ought to be established by argument that God exists. For even in the reasoning of numbers, which we certainly employ in everyday use, if we say, ‘Seven and three ought to be ten,’ we speak with insufficient care. For ten ought not to be; ten *is*. Concerning what things it may rightly be said that they ought to exist, whether they already exist or do not yet exist, we have, I think, sufficiently discussed in the books I mentioned. A wise human being ought to be: if he is, that he may remain; if he is not, that he may come to be. But God ought not to be wise; he is wise.”

Likewise, he ought not to be powerful, but is powerful; and so with all things. For all that is in him is nothing other than himself; yet this mode of speaking accommodates our weakness.

Hence Hilary, *On the Trinity*:

> “Through that which God has, he signifies that very thing by possessing it; for God is not, in the human manner, composed of parts, such that in him one thing is what is possessed by him and another what he himself is who possesses it. Rather, all that he is is one nature—perfect, absolute, infinite, not constituted from dissimilar elements, but itself living throughout its whole being.”

Peter did not see these things. Trusting in the powers of his intellect and pleasing himself with his own inventions—for the very foolish person is pleased with himself who is pleased with himself—he despised the refined teaching of the holy Fathers, who walk by the path of humility and faith. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, he was cast into the blind pit of this most obscure darkness, so that he might think, teach, and write that, because the Father can be from himself, which the Son cannot, omnipotence ought specially to be ascribed to the Father; [Col. 0290A] to the Son not omnipotence, but a certain power; and to the Holy Spirit none at all, because to him belongs goodness alone.

As I write these things, I am astonished, and all my inward parts tremble. I call God and his angels to witness that those who read these falsehoods as learning, unless they repent, are children of perdition; they have chosen for themselves the lot of curse belonging to those who were makers of falsehood and worshippers of perverse doctrines, and are acquiring for themselves eternal condemnation. But since, I think, devout readers have been sufficiently answered concerning this falsehood by which Peter, in the manner stated above, ascribes omnipotence specially to the Father, let us, guided by the light of faith and authority, examine the remaining points also.

There follows an error no less perverse and a disease of no lesser pestilence, when, as though from a secular furnace, [Col. 0290B] he serves his schoolmen bran-like dross and vomits forth vanities—indeed, lying insanities—by lying concerning the Son of God, in whom is the salvation of the world. For he says that the wisdom of the Father, which is the Son of God, is not omnipotence, but something from the Father—that is, a certain power derived from omnipotence.

But in order that we may see more clearly than light that this is a most wicked and detestable teaching—indeed, not teaching but deception—we must be aided by the foregoing argument and by the luminous authorities of those who see God and, reigning with him through everlasting ages, shine forth, so as to drive away these shadows. For the Son is wholly unlike the Father in no respect and is consubstantial with him in divinity, although he is from him from whom he is. This means nothing other than that he is begotten: one from one, true from true, whole from [Col. 0290C] whole, coeternal from eternal; and thus from him, that he may be in him—where there is no diversity of essence but a property of person.

Therefore the Son is not a certain power derived from omnipotence; rather, he is omnipotence from omnipotence. He is not, I say, something from the Father; for although he is other than the Father, he is not something other than the Father.

Hence Hilary, book VII of *On the Trinity*:

> “The Son of God, who is God, is not something other than God. For when I hear, ‘and the Word was God’ (John 1), I do not hear merely the word spoken, but understand that what God is has been shown to exist; and when it is said, ‘the Word was God,’ the reality signified is of substance. For ‘being’ is not an accidental name, but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and the property of natural kind.”

The same author, in book III of the same work:

> “The Father’s being in the Son and the Son’s being in the Father is the perfect fullness of divinity in each. For the Son is not a diminution of the Father, nor is the Son imperfect as from the Father.”

The same author, concerning the same matter, in book IV:

> “Thus one is from one, and apart from the unbegotten God there is no other unbegotten God; nor apart from the only-begotten God is there any other only-begotten God. Thus each is God, since between one and one—that is, one from one—there is not a second nature of eternal divinity.”

And in book VII:

> “Therefore birth possesses the nature from which it subsists, and the Son of God subsists as nothing other than that which God is.”

But he says this still more plainly in book VIII:

> “This the Church understands; this the Synagogue does not believe; this philosophy does not know: one from one, and whole God and Son from whole; neither that through birth anything is lacking of that whole which he is, nor that, in being born, he did not retain that very whole with himself.”

And in book XII:

> “Your Son and your only-begotten is your own reality: not a portion, not an extension, not some empty name according to the theory of emanations; but Son from you, true God the Father, true God, and begotten from you in the power of your unbegotten nature.”

Do you see then, O purple-clad young men—or at least you, O hooded friends, who investigate the hidden chambers of Solomon—do you see, I say, how far from truth is the man who calls the wisdom of the Father, that is, the Son of God, not omnipotence but a certain power from omnipotence, or something from the Father, when the whole is naturally and eternally the same whole as the Father with the Father, although God the Son was born from the Father? The faith founded upon the firm rock may indeed be attacked, but it cannot be moved.

But lest our discourse become overgrown through such a multitude of weighty words, and lose esteem with strict judges, I shall not now leave unexplored the fact that, speaking of the Holy Spirit, he follows the precipitous path of the same perdition. “Goodness,” he says, “which is the Holy Spirit, is not in God some power or wisdom; because being good is one thing, being powerful another, and being wise another.” Why do you read this, O madmen? Who but a delirious heretic, handed over by God to a reprobate mind, dares to say such things, much less defend them? Who has lied so impiously concerning the consoler of Christ’s orphans, the true teacher of Christ’s apostles, [Col. 0291C] the illuminator of holy souls, whom he leads into all truth?

“Whoever speaks blasphemy against the Father or the Son shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12). For remission of sins properly pertains to the Holy Spirit because he is the gift. Yet this “properly” is not Peter’s but Augustine’s: it does not concern a distinction of person, but a manifestation; for the Father and Son forgive sins through their goodness—that is, through the Holy Spirit—not from debt but by a gratuitous gift.

The Apostle’s utterance is: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11). It is as though he said: from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. For their nature and operation alike are one. The expressions “from him,” “through him,” and “in him” signify one and the same substance, as the Apostle most plainly declared in the concluding phrase: “To him,” he says—not “to them”—“be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

A second Macedonius has lately emerged from hell, intent upon crafty disputations, to preach that the Holy Spirit is not God. For if he is not omnipotent, he is not God; since, if he is God, he is omnipotent: he who blows where he wills, searches the hidden things of God, fills the whole world, makes the apostles drunk, makes the Church fruitful, remits sins, and, one and the same Spirit, distributes gifts of grace to each person as he wills. These are not [Col. 0292A] works of a creature but of the Creator. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not a creature but Creator, since whatever exists is either Creator or creature. If, then, he is Creator, he is omnipotent, all-wise, if one may speak thus, and whatever is to be understood in that ineffable and simple nature: eternal, immortal, incorruptible, immutable, living, wise, powerful, holy, just, good, blessed, Creator.

Augustine, book V of *On the Trinity*:

> “If whatever remains in itself and begets and effects something is the principle of the thing it begets or effects, we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is rightly called a principle, because we do not separate him from the designation ‘Creator.’ For it is written of him that he works, and he works while certainly remaining in himself. For he himself is not changed or turned into any of the things [Col. 0292B] which he works.”

Having set out the things which, according to the Apostle, the Spirit works, Augustine concludes:

> “Who can work such great things except God? Therefore, just as the Son of God, ever begotten from God, is ever God, so also the Holy Spirit, ever proceeding from the Father and the Son, is ever God.”

The same Augustine, in the same book of *On the Trinity*:

> “The Holy Spirit always proceeds, and proceeds not in time but from eternity. But because he proceeded so as to be capable of being given, he was already gift before there was anyone to whom he might be given. For ‘gift’ is understood differently from ‘given.’ A gift may exist before it is given; but something given cannot in any way exist unless it has been given.”

And in the book *Against the Assertions of the Arians*:

> “The Holy Spirit hears from that from which he proceeds. For he knows the Word of God by proceeding from that from which the Word is born, so that he is in common the Spirit of both the Father and the Word.”

And in book VI of *On the Trinity*:

> “Accordingly, the Holy Spirit also consists in the same unity and equality of substance. Whether, then, he is the unity of both, or holiness, or love; or whether he is unity because love, and love because holiness, it is manifest that he is not some third thing belonging to the two, by which each is joined to the other—by which the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter—so that they preserve unity of spirit in the bond of peace, not by participation but by their own essence, not by a gift from some superior being but by their own proper gift. Thus those three are one God: alone, great, [Col. 0292D] wise, holy, blessed, omnipotent, good.”

And below:

> “The Holy Spirit is something common to the Father and the Son, whatever that may be. But that communion itself is consubstantial and coeternal. If it can fittingly be called friendship, let it be so called; but more fittingly it is called love.”

And Saint Hilary, book XII of *On the Trinity*:

> “May I not endure the name of creature even in your Holy Spirit, who is certainly from you and sent through the Son.”

Thus, with sound teaching leading the way, it has been clearly disclosed and confirmed, by the common confession of all regenerated in faith in the Holy Trinity and by the combined testimony of reason and authority, that the Holy Spirit is God. But to be God means to be one, simple, true—indeed, to be. For thus Moses is commanded: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3).

Therefore the man lies to his own ruin and begets for himself the destruction of a just condemnation who says, in that being which is eternally, truly, simply, and ineffably one, that being good is one thing, being wise another, and being powerful another. Augustine, book V of *On the Trinity*: “For God to be is for him to be great.” For the same reason we do not call him three great beings, but one great being; for he is great not by participation in greatness but through himself, because he himself is his own greatness. Let this also be said of God’s goodness, eternity, omnipotence, and wisdom. And in book VI:

> “In God goodness is the same as wisdom, omnipotence, and greatness; and truth is the same as all these things. There, being blessed is not one thing, being omnipotent another, being great another, [Col. 0293B] being wise another, being true or good another, or being at all another. Nor, because he is Trinity, should he be thought triple.”

That heavenly sower of the word treated these matters in those books and in his other works in many ways; but we deliberately pass them over in the interest of brevity.

Nevertheless, lest I seem to inveigh too vehemently against Peter, to whom I was bound in the closest friendship, let it be seen with what iron wedge of falsehood he strives to tear open truth’s very entrails. In his *Apology*—that is, his defence in his own estimation, but in truth his accusation—he advances this opinion of which we speak in these words:

> “Therefore the love of God, or goodness, is his best will to make or, as we have said, to order all things in the best manner; it is not that power of making or ordering them. For nowhere, whether in [Col. 0293C] ourselves or in God, should love or goodness be called power, since to love or to be good is by no means to be powerful. For often those who love more, or are more good, are less able to accomplish what they will; and those who are more favorably inclined are less powerful—rich in affection, poor in effect.”

These are the words of one possessed. What has our condition to do with that exalted reality? Can the incomprehensible immensity of divinity be enclosed within the smallness of a comprehensible creature? Yet it is well that what does not escape me, he does not conceal. He says openly: “For nowhere, whether in ourselves or in God, should love or goodness be called power.” How utterly absurd it is to think this concerning God is proclaimed by what has gone before and by very many other passages, which I would now introduce here, if I did not fear burdening readers with weariness.

None of his predecessors suffered from the disease of so wretched a pestilence. Nor is he content merely to lie concerning the divine essence, unless he also becomes entangled in harmful errors concerning the operation of the same Trinity. He returns to the same subject and repeatedly bubbles over with the claim that omnipotence should specially be ascribed to the Father because the Father has placed certain things in his own power which the Son or Holy Spirit has not placed there.

He seems to draw this from the book of the Acts of the Apostles, where, when the disciples asked when the Son of God would restore the kingdom of Israel, he replied: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). This is as though it were not a most familiar practice of Holy Scripture, to those who love God and feed their souls on the *hyperousios*—that is, supersubstantial—bread, namely the Gospel food that does not perish, that what one person is said to do is done at the same time by the entire holy Trinity.

The Apostle says that the Father “did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8). Did not the Son also hand himself over? Certainly he did. For the same Apostle says of the Son: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2). Again, the Son says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it” (John 2). Did not the Father raise the Son? Yet the Apostle testifies that the Father raised the Son; and Peter says in Acts how “God raised him from the dead, loosing the pains of hell” (Acts 2).

And the fact that the Holy Spirit blows where he wills is not foreign to the Father and the Son, because whatever the Holy Spirit can do, the Father and the Son can do, from whom he has his being, which he is. Therefore those whose essence is one have one power, one will, and one operation. Augustine, book XIII of *On the Trinity*: “Therefore the Father, Son, and Spirit of both together work all things equally and in harmonious unity.” This is proclaimed by faith; this is proclaimed by the authority of the orthodox.

But he will say that Christ says in the Gospel that neither the angels nor the Son of Man knows the day of judgment, but the Father alone does (Matt. 24). This was a principal slander of the Arian heretics: that the Son could not have equality with the Father if he did not have equal knowledge with him. But the excellent shepherds of the Lord’s flock, who kept watch alertly and bravely around the sheepfolds of their sheep, broke all their horns and manfully stopped the mouths of the evening wolves.

Saint Hilary, more subtle and acute than the other ecclesiastical disputants, treats much at length in book IX of *On the Trinity* matters occasioned by this question, of which the few passages set below suffice here:

> “God speaks to Abraham, saying: ‘The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is fulfilled, and their sins are exceedingly great. Therefore I shall go down and see’ (Gen. 18), whether they are brought to completion according to the cry which has come to me; but if not, that I may know.’ You thus have a God who does not know what nevertheless he did not fail to know. For when he knows their sins to be exceedingly great and nevertheless goes down again to see whether they are completed—and, if not yet completed, to know—we understand that he knows what he did not know, but knows it when the time comes to act. The Lord’s knowing, therefore, is not a change from ignorance, but the fullness of time. For he is still awaited, that he may know. And since we cannot understand this of him as though he did not know, although he is still awaited that he may know, it necessarily follows that his knowing what he does not know and not knowing what he knows is nothing other than a dispensation either of speech or of action.”

And, on the same matter, at the end of the same book:

> “Therefore, because the Son says that he does not know the day and the hour, he must not be believed to be ignorant—just as, when according to his humanity he weeps, sleeps, or is sorrowful, God must not be confessed to be subject to tears, fear, or sleep. But just as, without impairing the severity of the Only-Begotten, he must be understood to suffer tears, sleep, hunger, thirst, weariness, and fear according to the weakness of the flesh, so he must be understood to have professed ignorance of the day and hour according to the nature of humanity.”

And Ambrose, in *On the Faith*, addressed to Emperor Gratian:

> “He who made all future things knows them according to the mode in which they are future. If this is true of ages, it must much more be believed concerning the day of judgment, which the Son of God knows as though already made by himself. But if we ask why he was unwilling to specify the times, we shall find it to be not ignorance but wisdom. For it would not profit us to know; so that, because we do not know the fixed times to come in God’s counsel, we may, as though posted on watch and stationed on a lookout, turn aside from the habit of sinning, lest the Lord’s day overtake us amid our vices.”

Augustine, book I of *On the Trinity*:

> “According to the form of a servant, his teaching is not his own but belongs to him who sent him; and ‘of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father.’ For he does not know it because he made them not know—that is, he did not know it in such a way as to disclose it then to the disciples, just as it was said to Abraham: ‘Now I have known that you fear God’ (Gen. 22), that is, now I have made you know, because Abraham himself, tested in that trial, became known.”

Jerome on Matthew 12, concerning the same chapter:

> “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone. In certain Latin manuscripts, ‘nor the Son’ is added, though this is not written in the Greek copies, especially those of Adamantius and Pierius. But because it is read in some, the matter seems to require discussion. For Arius and Eunomius rejoice, as though their master’s ignorance were their disciples’ glory, and say: ‘He who knows and he who is ignorant cannot be equal.’ But since Jesus—that is, the Word of God—made all times, for ‘all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’ (John 1), and since the day of judgment also lies within all times, by what consequence can he be ignorant of a part whose whole he knows? Finally, the Son himself says that knowledge of the Father is greater than knowledge of the day of judgment: ‘All things that are the Father’s have been delivered to me’ (Matt. 11). If, then, all things that are the Father’s are the Son’s, on what grounds did the Father reserve knowledge of one day for himself and refuse to communicate it to the Son? Therefore, because we have proved that the Son does not fail to know the day of consummation, an explanation must be given why he is said to be ignorant. The Apostle writes concerning the Savior: ‘In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge’ (Col. 2). Therefore all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are in Christ, but they are hidden. Why hidden? After the resurrection, when questioned by the apostles concerning the day, he answered more plainly: ‘It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power’ (Acts 1). When he says, ‘It is not for you to know,’ he shows that he himself knows, but that it was not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain [reading uncertain] concerning the Judge’s coming, they might live each day as though they were to be judged the next day. Finally, the following Gospel statement itself compels the same understanding. Moreover, when he says that the Father alone knows it, he includes the Son in the Father; for every father is named in relation to a son.”

Therefore, supported by the teachings and safeguards of these later columns, after the first-fruits, the pure faith of Christ’s children steadfastly maintains that the Lord Jesus said he did not know the day of judgment not from ignorance but from providence and the dispensation of human salvation.

Since, then, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same essence, the same power, and the same wisdom, the Father has not placed certain things in his own power which the Son and Holy Spirit have not also placed there; for there is no true diversity where there is true unity in will, power, and operation. [Col. 0296B] He must therefore be avoided and separated from the fellowship of the faithful who teaches so many and such great doctrines contrary to our faith.

Of the foregoing proposed false vanities and insanities, there remains the final mischief of perversity: he says that power gives way to wisdom in the examination of judgment, where equity is to be examined more than the force of power exercised. In this dispute he has lain stupefied in so deep a sleep and, as though buried by a lethargic disease, remained so; or else I myself have been so bewitched and made foolish by the misfortune of some unknown imprecation that I cannot fully discover what he thinks. For this is so recent an invention and such a profane novelty of expression that I cannot find any holy doctor who has answered this calumny before me.

Nor is this surprising. For they did not anticipate that anyone could ever arise [Col. 0296C] who would say, concerning the examination of the final judgment, that in the Lord Jesus Christ—who is wisdom itself, power itself, equity itself, and truth itself—power would yield to wisdom, as though the former withdrew and the latter succeeded; and that in that judgment equity would be examined more than the force of power exercised.

For both will be present in his judgment: equity will be examined—or, to speak more Catholicly, manifested—and the force of power will be exercised. Of him it is written: “He has prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself shall judge the world in equity; he shall judge peoples in righteousness” (Ps. 9). And: “He shall judge the world in equity, and peoples in his truth” (Ps. 95).

For in the judgment the wisdom or knowledge of God will not increase when the books of each person’s conscience are opened and the book of life is opened—that is, divine foreknowledge, which knows all things together before the foundation of the world. There God-man, God’s power and wisdom, will judge the world, crowning the righteous and condemning the reprobate. Will power not be there, when he who came as a lamb in the first coming will come as a lion in the second? The lion will roar: who will not be afraid? The lion will roar in the examination of sinners, who as a lamb was silent in his passion. “I have been silent,” he says through Isaiah, “I have always kept silence; like a woman in labor I shall speak” (Isa. 42). And through David: “Fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 49). And through Moses: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath and shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” [Col. 0297A] (Deut. 32).

In fear of this wrath, that trembling man cried out in the psalm entitled “For the eighth”: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your wrath” (Ps. 6). Therefore, just as human redemption was accomplished through humble wisdom and wise humility, so the final examination will occur through wise power and powerful wisdom. For wisdom and power are not accidents in Christ Jesus, since Christ himself is wisdom itself, power itself, truth itself, equity itself, the life of the living, and the resurrection of the dead.

Therefore Christ’s power, which Peter removes from the examination of judgment, will then be greatest, when Christ comes in his own majesty, that of the Father, and that of the holy angels; when the powers of heaven are shaken; when the elements are dissolved by heat; when all stand [Col. 0297B] before the Judge’s tribunal, to render account for what each has done through the body, whether good or evil; when they see him whom they pierced; when the wicked person is removed lest he see God’s glory; when all tribes of the earth mourn over themselves; when they say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23); when the goats hear, “Depart, you accursed, [Col. 0298A] into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25); when the mighty suffer mighty torments; when their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched; when the head of the wicked, his power of seduction wholly overthrown, is subjected to his punishments and imprisoned forever; and when the elect are purified by the condemnation of the ungodly.

It is plain, therefore, that in judgment the force of power will be exercised. It may truly be concluded, then, that whoever denies this lies. But since we have long dwelt upon refuting these blasphemies, let us leave to the judgment of readers the matters disputed not through our own small learning but through the teaching of the holy Fathers. If we have said anything true concerning God, it is from God; if otherwise, it is from ourselves. Let us therefore not fear correction for errors. No reprover need be feared by one who loves truth. For either a friend or an enemy will offer the correction. If an enemy mocks, he must be endured. If a friend is mistaken, he must be taught; if he teaches rightly, he must be heard. But let the matters that follow be taken up at the beginning of another volume.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0297]

I know, best Father, how immense, how deep, and how close to a fall is the precipice, [Col. 0297C] and how the audacity of foolish presumption can by no means escape unpunished. This has been proclaimed sufficiently by the teachings of the wise, by ancient examples, and by present ones. Though it is always and everywhere harmful, yet that presumption is held far more hostile and detestable than the rest which, relying on its own powers, presumes to investigate hidden matters concerning divine things, and, puffed up rather than filled with the arrogance of secular learning, refuses to follow the light of faith and disdains to imitate the footsteps of the holy Fathers. For the mysteries of the Christian religion—that is, of truth—are to be brought forth not by the empty philosophy which is of the earth, as the Apostle testifies (Col. 2), but by that wisdom which, according to James, “is from above, first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (James 3). [Col. 0297D] The word of this wisdom, given through the Spirit, runs swiftly: living and effective, more penetrating than every sword; and with the flashing stroke of simple faith it cuts through the earthly, dark, and dense mass of errors—not by human artifice, but by divine power. For God “resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5; Jas. 4). To open the royal gate of paradise, the Son of the supreme Craftsman forged, upon the anvil of the cross with the hammers of his sufferings, not a golden or silver key, but a wooden one. The humility of the Savior paved with the most precious stones of virtues that way which alone leads travelers to the heavenly Jerusalem above, which is our mother, which is “built together as one”; in which no hammer or axe is heard; into which no enemy enters; from which no citizen goes into exile; and in which neither sun nor moon, but Christ, is the lamp. [Col. 0298C]

I have said this because, when ecclesiastical mysteries are handled—when they are discussed—the cleverness of Plato’s and Aristotle’s learning grows feeble, and all the skill of the wise is made foolish before that Scripture whose height mocks the proud, whose depth terrifies the attentive, whose truth feeds the great, and whose gracious accessibility nourishes the small. With this as guide, he truly knows true things about God who truly believes. It is my proof, incapable of being shaken by any impulse, that whatever truth says in the Prophet, the Gospel, or the Apostle cannot waver. Avoiding, therefore, the danger of presumption, I place no confidence in human inventions or in my own powers; but I wish to be guided by that light of which it is said: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord” [Col. 0298D] (Ps. 118), with God granting it, whose Spirit has both founded and illuminated it.

Therefore, conceiving good hope from the Catholic exposition of the matters mentioned above, I place my trust in the Lord my God, because he will perfect and strengthen what he has begun in us. For the fulfillment of past things is the certainty of things to come. More securely, then, and more cheerfully, I shall invade the hiding-places of errors; and I shall refute them not by my own judgment but by divine oracles—that is, by the words of the orthodox. For, as Seneca says, the voice of a man speaking truthfully about God is a divine oracle. Accordingly, I shall faithfully set forth these deadly and condemnable errors, if he who gave the desire also grants its effect. Nor shall I do so in the order in which they have been placed, but in that which divine favor deigns to suggest to me.

[Col. 0299A] Therefore, after the treatment of the holy and indivisible Trinity, in which our highest blessedness consists, I shall disclose in Peter’s own words what he thinks concerning the incarnation of the divine Word. Through that incarnation alone—I mean Christ’s incarnation—we, reconciled in the blood of the Son of God, have access to his Father, our Father, and the Father of lights. In his *Theology* he treats of it in these very words:

> “Man,” he says, “is a corporeal thing, composed of members, and is dissoluble. But God is neither a corporeal thing nor composed of members, so that he can be dissolved. Therefore God is properly to be called neither man nor flesh. Otherwise, conversely, man too would properly be called God. Hence one would have to concede that God is something created, or something which has not always existed, since it is plain that man [Col. 0299B] is a creature and has a beginning.”

Here, with profane mouth, entangled in the error of the Nestorian heresy, he declares that Jesus Christ, insofar as he is man, is not a person in the Trinity; because one would then have to concede that God is something created, or something that has not always existed, since man is plainly a creature and has a beginning. Thus he recoils from calling that man God, because he is a creature and has a beginning. For if he is not in the Trinity, he is not God. Just as whatever is in the Trinity is God—which is nothing other than saying that God is Trinity, or Trinity is God—so whatever is not in the Trinity is not God.

“But,” as the Apostle proclaims, there is “one God,” the Father, “from whom are all things”; and one Lord Jesus Christ, “through whom [Col. 0299C] are all things” (1 Cor. 8); and one Holy Spirit, “dividing to each as he wills” (Rom. 11), breathing where he wills and leading the saints into all truth as he wills. He is the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, eternal life. Whoever worships or adores anything besides him with that worship which among the Greeks is called *latria* (λατρεία, “service” or “worship”) is an idolater, serving the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever.

If, therefore, Peter worships the whole Christ—that is, both insofar as he is man and insofar as he is God—then, because the Christ whom Peter imagines is not in the Trinity insofar as he is man, Peter is an idolater when he worships such a Christ, since he worships a creature. But if he does not worship the whole Christ—that is, both insofar as he is man and insofar as he is God—Peter is not a Christian. For Christ is not divided, and it is written: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98), that is, the earth, that is, his flesh. But I am carried away by excessive impulse and am too hasty. We shall examine these matters a little later with more diligent investigation.

First, it is necessary to draw out more carefully the poison of this impiety; and afterwards, from the treasuries of those who “wait for death as for buried treasure, and rejoice greatly when they find the grave,” to apply an antidote. But before I come to that extraction, I shall, if I can, loosen the snare which he has laid in his customary manner. Moreover, through his familiar friendship with that art of disputation which, according to Martianus, carries a serpent beneath [Col. 0300A] its hooked cloak, he does not forget his “properly,” which he employed above. By this he opens these cisterns, in which there is not water but only mud, and into which foolish and wandering animals fall and die.

For it is his habit to add to a proposition something novel and seemingly acute, which, once conceded, allows him—as though he were an admirable and incomparable craftsman—to destroy the usage of ecclesiastical language. Thus, in the preceding argument, by means of this word “properly,” he assigns omnipotence to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and kindness to the Holy Spirit, in order to make, through terms which there are substantial, a distinction of persons—a thing that cannot in the least be done. So also here, when he says that man is not properly to be called God because, conversely, God would then properly be called [Col. 0300B] man, he prepares a snare which he conceals by fraud. He appears, indeed, to preserve the propriety of the natures, which is good; for neither has divinity been changed into humanity nor humanity into divinity. But he does not deceive those whose enlightened eyes of heart possess that light in which light is seen—for whoever sees the Son sees the Father also. For he strives to conclude through his “properly” that Christ Jesus, insofar as he is man, is not in the Trinity; and the following discussion will show this to be utterly false.

I am not unaware how differently—and wisely—the blessed Augustine uses the term “properly” in his treatise *On the Trinity*. In Book XII he says:

> “Therefore, just as we properly call the only Word of God by the name of wisdom, although universally both the Holy Spirit and the Father himself are wisdom, so the Spirit is properly designated by the name of charity, although the Father and Son are universally charity.”

How carefully Augustine speaks here! He can truly say with the Apostle: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10). For when he had said that the Son is called by the name of wisdom and the Holy Spirit properly by the name of charity, lest he seem thereby to have made a distinction of persons, he prudently adds that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, the holy and one Trinity itself, the threefold unity—are universally called wisdom and charity.

[Col. 0300D] Having said this, so that we may not leave his “properly” unexamined, we must now apply pen, mind, and hand to pierce the concealed corruption and draw out the poison from the wound. In his *Apology*, in his response concerning this chapter, Peter, driven by furies, raves; and he attacks the man of God so intemperately that he asserts not that the man himself speaks what he says, but that Satan speaks through him—Satan who transforms himself into an angel of light. There, after reproaching the venerable abbot, he poured out in these very words the poison that he bore in his breast:

> “When you accuse me,” he says, “of not saying that God and man are one person in the Trinity, you openly profess that this is your view. I want you to recognize how contrary your error is to sound faith. For God and man, these two natures, whether taken separately or together, cannot be called one person in the Trinity.”

And below:

> “Therefore that man assumed by the Word is not to be called one of the three persons in that eternity; rather, the Word itself, to which he is united, is so called. But if it cannot be said of God and man separately that they are some person there, much less is it fitting to say this of the two natures taken together. For those two natures cannot be anything eternal, since one of them lacks eternity.”

And below:

> “Only that which was once in that Trinity always remains a person in the same Trinity, and nothing new enters into that Trinity, because it is not permissible to think that God is recent.”

He repeats these things many times and multiplies words to the point of weariness. While he childishly mocks, he does not, though he judges himself superior, avoid the precipice. Finally, in his conclusion, he does not conceal the fear through which, in irreligious timidity, he falls into error. For thus he says:

> “By every means we must beware lest we maintain that there is there anything which has not always been there; lest we establish anything temporal there which has not always been there; nor establish anything temporal in that eternity, anything composite in that simplicity, anything corporeal in that incorporeality, or anything new in that antiquity.”

See into what a gulf of unbelief, led by his familiar guide, he has plunged headlong. He so sees the propriety of the natures in Christ that he does not attend to the unity of person; and, following the dregs of Nestorianism, he so divides Christ that he is in the Trinity only insofar as he is the Word, but is in no way there insofar as he is man. This is that height of secular knowledge, exalting itself against the humble knowledge of God, which shall be destroyed by weapons powerful through God and hurled into the depths of hell. Of such persons it is written: “And he let them go according to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own inventions” (Ps. 80). For this is not only a vain but also a profane new invention, and whoever says, “Christ, insofar as he is man, is not in the Trinity,” utterly overturns, so far as he can, the most firmly founded Catholic faith. This is no other than saying: insofar as he is man, he is not in the Godhead. For the supreme Trinity is nothing other than [Col. 0301D] true Deity, and true Deity nothing other than the supreme Trinity. Therefore the whole Christ, because he cannot be divided, is one person in that Trinity which is God; but the manner must be considered: namely, not a change of nature but a union of person.

Nor did anything new happen to God Christ: what he eternally possessed in himself, he displayed in himself temporally, when he willed and as he willed. For God always was; nor did he diminish what he was when he made himself what he was not. Nor is the Son of God one person and the son of man another, although one thing is meant insofar as he is Son of God and another insofar as he is son of man. Hence Pope Leo the Great, writing to Bishop Julian against Eutyches:

> “Therefore neither was the Word changed into flesh nor flesh into the Word; but both are in one, and God is in both—not divided through diversity, not confused by mixture; nor is one from the Father and the other from the mother. He is the same before the beginning and the same at the end of the ages.”

Thus he existed from eternity in God’s foreknowledge—before he made the world, when he would make it, and how he would make it; and when he would renew it through the death of his only-begotten Son. That is, it was eternally present in his eternal Word when and how the Word would be united temporally to man and man to the Word, so that God could truly and catholicly be called man and man God—not because humanity was consumed into divinity, but because it was personally assumed by divinity. He could be called this *properly*, that is, in proper speech: not in a fanciful opinion but in a true confession, so that the holy Church might believe in its heart unto righteousness, [Col. 0302B] confess with its mouth unto salvation, and preach for the benefit of the predestined that Christ is both God and man, and man and God; and, whole because he cannot be divided, is one person in the Trinity.

For it is true that the man who hung upon the wood and died upon the wood made heaven and earth; and it is true that the Son of God—God from God and coeternal with the Father—hung upon the wood and died upon the wood. This is Peter’s firm confession, praised by Christ himself: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). And the centurion cries before the cross: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27). Augustine says on this in his book *On the Trinity*:

> “The Apostle Paul says: ‘Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Cor. 2). Therefore he was crucified according to the form [Col. 0302C] of a servant, and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For such was that assumption as would make God man and man God.”

Yet what is said, why it is said, and in what respect it is said, let the prudent, diligent, and pious reader understand with God’s help. Therefore man is to be called God and God man, though Peter shrinks from saying so. For this is why God became man: that man might become God. Thus our teacher says that the assumption was such as made God man and man God. For the Word became flesh so that he who was in the truth of divinity without time might be the same in the truth of humanity in time: wholly one person in the Trinity, because wholly one substance from two and in two natures.

[Col. 0302D] I do not dare, because of the scandal of the weak and of those who understand less well the forms of ecclesiastical speech, to say what Jerome says here, “[Some passage is missing] substance”; but, having my eyes upon the treasures of the house of the Lord, where, according to the Prophet, our salvation lies—that is, upon the teachings of the holy Fathers—I shall investigate more carefully how they, following the spiritual David, overwhelm the enemies of faith with the stones of the sling.

That remarkable Hilary, who, because of the constancy of his Catholic faith, was banished to Phrygia by Constantius Augustus, son of the great Constantine and a most Arian emperor, composed twelve books *On the Trinity*, works of immense subtlety and, after canonical Scripture, incomparable usefulness. In them, as though foreseeing our dangerous times, [Col. 0303A] he discussed at greatest length many matters concerning the question now in our hands. Yet, so that our poverty may be refreshed from the abundance of that divine fountain, a few passages must be excerpted here.

In Book IX of that work he says:

> “The Word made flesh—God and man, Jesus Christ the Lord of majesty—was himself established in himself as mediator for the salvation of the Church. By the very mystery of mediation between God and men, he is one, while he himself, from the natures united into one, is the same reality of each nature.”

The same author, on the same matter in the same book:

> “Our assumption did not bring increase to God; rather, our advancement is the result of his willing to undergo humiliation, since he does not lose what he is as God, and he obtains for man that what God is may be man. Therefore the only-begotten God was born of the Virgin, man according to the fullness of time, intending in himself to advance man into God; as man, speaking and doing all the things that belong to God; then, as God, speaking and doing all the things that belong to man. But these mysteries of heavenly things were established before the foundation of the world: that the only-begotten God should will to be born man, with God remaining in man for eternity.”

Likewise:

> “This, then, will be the confession: that Jesus is in the glory of the Father, and that, having been born man, he no longer remains in the weakness of our body, but in the glory of God; and every tongue shall confess this.”

From the testimony of these words it is plain that the Lord Jesus, even insofar as he is man united to the Word, is in the Trinity: not by a nature, as said above, being assumed into a nature, but [Col. 0303C] by being assumed through unity of person into the glory of God. Hear how the following passage explains this same point. The same author, in the same work:

> “It is natural to God that he lives; and by this it is necessary for us to die to our body, that we may live to God in Christ Jesus, who, taking the body of our sin, now wholly lives to God, our nature’s fellowship being united in the communion of divine immortality.”

And later in the same book:

> “The sum of the argument was this: that the whole Son, namely man and God, should now, through the indulgence of the Father’s will, exist in the unity of the Father’s nature; and that he who remained in the power of nature should also remain in the kind of nature. For this was granted to man: that he should be God. But the assumed man could in no way remain in God’s unity unless, through unity with the Word, he passed into the unity of natural God; so that, through the fact that the Word was God by nature, the Word made flesh should in turn exist in the nature of God.”

Thus he speaks. I have sufficiently found what I sought: that our man in Christ is God, and, united to the Word of God, is one person of the Trinity in the Trinity.

But since it is established by the testimonies of Law and Gospel that every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses, we must inquire what others, filled with the same Spirit, think. Augustine, that cock of the Lord, girded and striking his little body with the wings of contemplation and action, excellently melodious for driving away the nocturnal phantoms, says—as has already been noted above—that the assumption was such as made God man and man God. Therefore it is said that God is man and man is God. Hence the same author in Book IV of *On the Trinity*:

> “Thus indeed it came about that there is there not only the flesh of man in the Word of God, but also the rational soul of man; and that this whole is called both God on account of God and man on account of man.”

The same author in the *Enchiridion*:

> “The grace of God,” he says, “is commended to us in the man Christ without any preceding merits; for not even he himself attained by any merits to being so joined to the true God in so great a unity that, together with him, he should become one person, the Son of God. Rather, from the moment he began to be man, from that moment he was also God.”

The same author, in the book *Against the Assertions of the Arians*:

> “For he shows there to be one person in both natures, lest, if he makes two, there should begin to be a quaternity rather than [Col. 0304B] a Trinity.”

So he says. Why, then, do you speak sophistically here, fine master? If, then, there is in God not a quaternity but a Trinity because God and man are one person in Christ, it follows that the Father and the whole Son—that is, God and man—and the Holy Spirit are one Trinity.

The same author in the same book:

> “If,” he says, “we ask who he is who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God (Phil. 2), the apostolic voice answers: Christ Jesus. Therefore that divinity also received the name of this humanity. Again, if we ask who it is that became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, the most correct answer is: he who ‘being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God.’ Therefore this humanity too received the name of divinity.”

So deeply and so keenly is he intent upon such questions that, while slaughtering Nestorian unbelief, he may seem to inattentive readers to assist the madness of Eutyches. For Nestorius preached two persons in Christ, whereas Eutyches preached one nature; by different heresies dividing, so far as lay in them, the seamless garment of Christ.

In Book V of *On the Trinity*, a work which, as he testifies, he began as a young man and published as an old man, he even uses the term “mixture” to express the union in Christ from two natures:

> “No punishment of sin came upon the spirit of the Mediator even unto the death of the flesh; for he did not abandon it begrudgingly, but because he willed, when he willed, and as he willed—indeed, mingled with the Word of God unto unity. Hence he says: ‘I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again’” (John 10).

And in the Letter to Volusianus:

> “As, in the unity of person, the soul uses the body in order that there may be a man, so, in the unity of person, God uses man in order that there may be Christ. In the former person there is a mixture of soul and body; in this person there is a mixture of God and man.”

But observe how he proceeds by a middle and well-trodden path and safeguards Catholic doctrine. He adds:

> “Provided, however, that the hearer withdraw from the customary notion of bodies, by which two liquids are usually mixed in such a way that neither preserves its integrity—although even in bodies incorrupt light is mingled with air.”

And Hilary, in Book II of *On the Trinity*:

> “God, having become man from the Virgin, took into himself the nature of flesh, so that through the fellowship of this admixture there might come into being the sanctified body of the whole human race.”

Yet, as is evident to pious readers from these very words, this “admixture” or “mixture” is not a confusion of natures, but the true personal unification—or union—of the natures themselves in Christ. Hence the Church sings: “God became man, undergoing neither mixture nor division.” “Mixture” is against Eutyches; “division,” against Nestorius.

Now, indeed, another—that is, a third—witness must be introduced. Saint Jerome, as though foreseeing the subtleties, or perhaps I should say the absurdities, of our time, is bolder than all other authorities in this question: he both names mixture and confirms that the man in Christ is coeternal with God in the unity of person. His words in the Sermon on the Assumption [Col. 0305B] of Blessed Mary, beginning, “You compel me, O Paula and Eustochium,” are these:

> “This Word which was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God the Word—the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary brought forth for us this same Word, made flesh from herself.”

And a little later:

> “For God knows all things and can do all things. Because this is so, he knew and was able, in the Virgin’s womb, without corruption of himself, to mingle and unite himself so that Christ might be one God and man, one person, and one substance.”

And below:

> “And the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, ever-Virgin, incomparable among all virgins, could fittingly receive in herself the admixture of divinity, with each nature preserved.”

And again:

> “It is evident that time did not prejudice the mystery of the united God and man, so that he who had not yet been born of the Virgin Mary was already in him from the beginning [Col. 0305C] of the age through unity of person; as Scripture shows in many places.”

After proving this at greater length by testimonies of Scripture, he concludes:

> “Therefore Christ was already in the Son who led out the people, and Christ was tempted in him, because it is beyond doubt that he always existed in God through the unity of the mystery. Otherwise, unless you believe thus, either Christ will not be God at all, or, contrary to the prophet, God will appear to be recent.”

The same author, a little later:

> “For Christ is one in his flesh, one in spirit, one in mystery; nor does he permit at all that one Son of Man and another Son of God be understood. He is neither prescribed by time nor separated by suffering; but the whole passes into Christ, and Christ into God, so that whatever is the Son of God is called Christ, and whatever Christ suffered in the flesh is believed to have been suffered by God. Therefore we neither worship nor adore the man separately, which would not be lawful; for by assuming man he was increased in nothing in himself, and when the Word became flesh he was neither diminished nor changed.”

Further, the same author on the same subject:

> “The grace of God is in Christ Jesus, in whom God and man are so united in one and the same person that, because of the union of substance, man is often read in the divine writings to be coeternal with God; and then God seems to have suffered with man, although man is not without a beginning and God is not passible.”

What do you say here, prudent men? It is a marvel to me that the mind of this man was so divinely inspired that he sails securely by a direct course between the Syrtes [Col. 0306A] and Charybdis: neither driving the ship into the danger of the Nestorian heresy nor suffering shipwreck in the unbelief of Eutyches, while upholding unity of person from and in both natures, and confirming in that union of person the truth of each substance. It is a marvel to me that for so long a time, and by so many men whose teaching shines in the Church as the moon shines by the sun, no answer has been given to our Abelard, who accuses the abbot because he says that God and the man assumed by God are one person in the Trinity, although man is a corporeal thing, composed of members and dissoluble, whereas God is neither a corporeal thing nor composed of members so as to be dissoluble. Hence, he says, neither God is to be called man nor man God, lest one have to concede that God is something created in himself or something that has not always existed. From this he infers that those two natures, neither separately nor joined together, are one person in the Trinity.

What mind could ever conceive, what tongue utter, what hand write such an impiety? What earth could endure the deadly weight of this poison? The ancient schismatics Dathan and Abiram, whom an opening of the earth swallowed alive, did not offend so greatly. For why are we Christians, if Peter’s assertion is true? How, according to the Apostle, does the body of Christ, which is the Church, grow with the growth of God? (Col. 2.) If Christ, God and man, is not one person in the Trinity, Christ is not one person; for if Christ is one person, Christ is one person in the Trinity. But Christ, God and man, is one person. Although he is from two or in two natures, he is nevertheless one thing, so that, according to Jerome, he is one substance—that is, one individual thing subsisting through itself—because of the union which is such there and nowhere else. For what is a person but a rational and individual substance? Where that substance is, it is not absent; and where it is, it is whole. For if it is divided, it is not that substance.

Just as God from God—Christ with him—is not one [person] but one [thing]; so conversely God united to man is indeed one [person] but not one [thing], because he is God and man. And because he is one, he can be separated by no division. Say, then: while Christ was dying on the cross, was God with him or not? If he was not, why does the Apostle call the Lord of glory crucified? [Col. 0306D] But he was. Therefore, if God was in the dying man, reconciling the world to himself by the death of the cross, fastening the record of transgression to the cross, and magnifying the powers of the air, why should not that same man, who had died through our weakness and risen through the power of God, united to the Word of God, be in the glory of God for the same reason—because he cannot be divided? For what other fruit of the passion is there except, through the glory of resurrection and ascension, the blessed and immortal excellence of deification? Otherwise the promise has been abolished, our faith made empty, and apostolic teaching proved deceptive, which says: “He who descended is the same who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4).

But who could fill all things except he who made all things? And how did he ascend and descend, he who truly is, except in assumed, united, glorified, deified man? And plainly, as he himself says to Timothy, “Great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in the flesh, quickened in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, believed in the world, and assumed into glory” (1 Tim. 3). Let him himself also say in what glory:

> “Christ,” he says, “became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

This apostolic assertion proves that this is said of the Lord Jesus insofar as he is man. For insofar as he is God, he was in the glory of God the Father before the foundation of the world. Hence also in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all” (Heb. 2).

And below:

> “But this man, offering one sacrifice for sins, does not sit for ever at the right hand of God” (Heb. 10).

Christ himself declares in the Gospel of what glory this discourse speaks, saying to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17). But I shall explain this better in the words of the holy Fathers than in my own.

Hilary, in Book IX of *On the Trinity*: “The Son of Man [Col. 0307C] is glorified, and God is glorified in him; and God glorified the glorified God in the man, in himself.” Likewise, in the same work: “God glorified in himself Christ, who was born man. Is that which he glorifies in himself outside himself?” The same author, in Book XI: “Because God has been glorified in Christ, God therefore glorified him in himself, so that, because he now reigns in glory—which is God’s glory—he himself may thereby pass into the glory of God. For God glorified him in himself, that is, in that nature in which God is what he is, so that God may be all in all, and Christ, now whole in God according to that dispensation by which he is man, may remain.” Are you asleep or awake here, excellent Peter? If asleep, wake up, for it is now time for us to rise from sleep. Our *tertiani* [term uncertain] are already becoming drunk on the wine of deification; having drunk from the abundance of God’s house and from the torrent [Col. 0307D] of his delight, they speak to a stunned world of the mighty works of God through the novelty of these things. If you are awake, listen with attentive ears to what the heavenly oracle declares: “Christ himself, as man, according to that dispensation by which he is man, remains wholly in God.” It is not I, but Hilary, whose words these are: a most steadfast pillar of the Church, a distinguished teacher, destroyer of heresies, one who suffered insults of speech, the enmity of kings, the squalor of exile, and chains for Christ; pre-eminent by the prerogative of faith, holiness, and learning. By this single millstone the whole machine of your art is overthrown. Therefore Christ, whole—that is, even according to his humanity—glorified into God, is one person in the Trinity.

Pope Leo too, with the blow of the stone of tin mentioned in the prophet Zechariah (chapter IV), shattered and crushed the idol of this your former invention [Col. 0308A], writing against Eutyches as follows: “Although the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and in him the one and same person possesses both true divinity and true humanity, nor can the solidity of this union be separated by any division, nevertheless we understand the exaltation by which God exalted him and gave him the name above every name to belong to that form which was to be enriched by the increase of glorification. For the form of a servant, through which the impassible Godhead fulfilled the mystery of great godliness, is human humility; and it was anointed into the glory of divine mercy, with divinity and humanity joined together in so great a unity from the very conception in the Virgin that divine things were not performed without the man, nor human things without God. Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty [Col. 0308B] is said to have been crucified, so he who is equal to God from co-eternity is said to have been exalted. Nor does it matter from which substance Christ is named, since, while the unity of the person remains inseparable, he is both wholly Son of Man because of the flesh, and wholly Son of God because of the one Godhead he shares with the Father.”

The same writer, in a sermon on the fast of the seventh month: “The true Son of God, true God, possessing unity and equality with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, deigned also to become true man, uniting humanity to himself in such a way that God remained unchangeable, and communicating deity to the man in such a way that he did not consume him by glorification, but increased him.”

The same writer, in a sermon on the Ascension of the Lord: “To heal the wounds of unbelieving hearts, the marks of the nails [Col. 0308C] and of the lance were preserved, so that it might be held, not by a doubtful faith but by most steadfast knowledge, that the nature which had lain in the tomb would sit upon the throne with God the Father.” And later: “The nature of the human race, exalted in Christ beyond the height of the archangels, was to have no limit to its advancement in any sublimities, unless, received into the fellowship of the eternal Father, it should be made a partner on that throne in whose nature it was joined in the Son.” And in another sermon: “The lowliness of our nature has been advanced in Christ above every host of heaven, above all orders of angels, and beyond the height of all powers, to the fellowship of God the Father.” The same writer, in a sermon on Pentecost: “The Lord ascended above every height of the heavens, to sit at the right hand of God the Father.”

Jerome, to [Col. 0308D] Hedibia: “‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father’ (John XX); and the meaning is: You who seek one dead are not worthy to touch him alive. If you suppose that I have not yet ascended to the Father, but have been secretly taken away by human fraud, you are unworthy of touching me. He said this, however, not to blunt the zeal of one seeking him, but so that she might know that the dispensation of the flesh assumed had been changed into the glory of divinity.”

And Augustine, against the assertions of the Arians: “He himself,” he says, “is one Christ: Son of God by nature, and Son of Man assumed by grace in time. Therefore, after the sons of unbelief, defenders of former errors, have been repelled, the holy Church, the bride of Christ, which is without spot or wrinkle—because Christ washed her in his blood so that she might have no spot, and the Lamb, the fuller, stretched her out [Col. 0309A] upon the cross so that she might have no wrinkle—the Church, I say, faithfully and firmly preaches what she believes, and exhorts: ‘Worship his footstool, for it is holy’ (Psalm XCVIII). For we worship his footstool, because it is holy: that is, his flesh—not because it is a creature, but because it is personally united to the Word of God; that is, it is one person with mind and divinity, namely, the one Christ, Son of God and Son of Man, performing divine things and suffering human things.”

Ambrose, in *On the Faith* addressed to Emperor Gratian: “‘And let all his angels worship him’ (Hebrews I). But let them worship not only his divinity, but also his footstool, because it is holy; for in Christ even the mysteries of the incarnation are to be worshipped, in which, as it were, certain traces of divinity are impressed.” [Col. 0309B] And a little later: “By the footstool the earth is understood; and by the earth, the flesh of Christ, which today we worship in the mysteries and which the apostles worshipped. For Christ has not been divided, but is one; nor, while he is worshipped as the Son of God, is his birth from the Virgin denied.”

Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm XCVIII: “‘Worship his footstool, for it is holy.’ I was made uncertain. I fear to worship the earth, lest he who made heaven and earth condemn me. Again, I fear not to worship the footstool of my Lord’s feet, because the Psalm says to me, ‘Worship his footstool,’ and Scripture says to me, ‘The earth is the footstool of my feet’ (Isaiah LXVI). Wavering, I turn to Christ, because here I seek him himself; and I find how his footstool [Col. 0309C] may be worshipped without impiety. For he received earth from earth, because flesh is earth, and he assumed flesh from the flesh of Mary. And because in that flesh he walked here, and gave us that very flesh [Col. 0310A] to eat for salvation—and no one eats that flesh unless he has first worshipped it—it has been discovered how such a footstool of the Lord’s feet may be worshipped; and not only do we not sin by worshipping it, but we sin by not worshipping it.”

Cassiodorus the senator, likewise, in his *Exposition of the Psalms*: “Although the body assumed by the Word of God is glorious, great, and worthy of worship, nevertheless, because of the humility of its humanity, we fittingly understand it as the footstool of God’s feet. For when he himself says, ‘Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet’ (ibid.), the earthly body which he took from the Virgin Mary is rightly called, I think, the footstool of his feet. By the same comparison it is shown that one should understand it so as not to separate his body from the Godhead by the contemplation of the mind, but to refer it to one [Col. 0310B] person, namely to the Word which became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Therefore we do not worship a recent God when we worship the flesh of Christ; we who believe that Christ came in the flesh from David’s seed according to Paul’s Gospel (Romans II). Nor do we introduce anything composite into that true simplicity, nor anything temporal into that antiquity. We do not say that nature was changed into nature, but that humanity was exalted into God’s glory through the wonderful and ineffable unity of person—through which God is man and man is God; whoever denies this is a heretic. Now, borne up by the grace of the Holy Spirit beyond hope and merit from the most rugged places of stormy and most perilous questions, we halt our course [Col. 0310C] for a little while to rest, intending to pursue the matters which follow later with another beginning.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0309C] The labor of the third book now confronts me, as I imitate those who expound the Holy Trinity and worship the Sun of righteousness who rose on the third day. They divinely fulfilled with Abraham God’s command that said to him: [Col. 0309D] “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Genesis XII); and with Moses, leader of the Hebrew people, having taken up vessels of gold and silver, they withdrew from Egypt with all their household for three days, that they might freely sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness the abominations of the Egyptians.

For it came from the indulgence of divine condescension, not from merit, that I—dull, foolish, and unknown—was able to answer, in the preceding truthful discussions, a man most acute, wise, and famous. And, seeing that I have examined the matter and not doubting that I walk along the paths of the orthodox, I am secure under the Father of orphans and Judge of widows, because I shall not be deprived of the reward of the catholic contest. Therefore, by the help of him whose sayings above have been explained, I shall investigate some matters that follow, [Col. 0310C] not all of them, lest I become wearisome to you, my lord, for whom I chiefly write such things, and to other grave men—O most brilliant lamp of the people of Rouen and morning star of our age—who think of your God with a catholic heart, [Col. 0310D] speak with a catholic mouth, and write more excellently than others with a catholic hand.

Of the many profane and deadly novelties which still remain, which Peter foolishly poured forth while raving in his *Theology*, and more foolishly in his *Apology*, I have selected only three. These both grievously afflict our commonwealth and stir good defenders to a greater fervor of zeal burning in God’s house. The first is that the Son of God is always being born from God. The second is that God cannot do anything except what he does, nor do it in another manner or at another time, nor omit doing what he does. The third is that the grace by which the elect are saved is common to all human beings. These must be answered in order; but first, as I did above, I shall set down [Col. 0311A] his own words—briefly, as far as I can—and, with the Lord’s help, add what authority and reason suggest. For among us reason does not precede authority, but follows it, as we read in the *Sentences* of Prosper, which he carefully excerpted from the words of blessed Augustine and some of which he suitably put into verse.

Peter’s words concerning the proposition advanced in his *Theology* are these—brief indeed, but carrying great weight: “In what is said through the Prophet, ‘Today I have begotten you’ (Psalm II), it is shown that the Son of God is always born from the Father and has always been born.” First, however, I do not see what coherence there can be between these words, “always to be born,” and that the same thing has always—that is, from eternity—been born. For “to be born” and “to have been born” are not the same, as will be shown more clearly [Col. 0311B] in what follows by the testimony of blessed Augustine. Yet I am not unaware that many men of great name now are, and have been, who thought and wrote that the Son of God was always being born. But because they walked simply and did not enter pompously into the house of the Lord, they were not cast out from the bosom of mother Church, since they were the children and heirs of saints greatly cast out for Christ. And, as Augustine says in *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, deacon of Carthage, “error does not make a man a heretic, but the defense of error.”

I think that they thought or think this of the Son of God because the true confession of faith declares that, according to Isaiah, that ineffable generation of the Son of God from the Father neither began nor ceased to be (Isaiah LIII), since it neither had a beginning [Col. 0311C] nor will have an end.

Taking occasion from this proposition, the Arians, damnably blinded by the spirit of pride, harassed Catholics and, as though tossing them with horns, struck at them with these sophistries: If, according to you, the generation of the Son of God from God the Father had neither beginning nor will have end, then the Father always begets the Son. If he always begets the Son, the Son is always begotten from the Father. If the Son is always begotten from the Father, the Son is still being begotten from the Father. If the Son is always begotten from the Father, the Son who is still being begotten from the Father is imperfect. For whatever is still being begotten is undoubtedly imperfect.

The whole aim of their error was that the Son should not be co-eternal with the Father, but should be the most perfect creature of all creatures, made from non-existent things and not [Col. 0311D] begotten from God. Their argument would certainly be altogether insoluble if Christ’s generation were some action. For action looks to a creature, which God acted—that is, made—when and as he willed; and before he made it he did nothing. But the generation of the Son is not action, because it surpasses every action and transcends every creation. For he has always—that is, from eternity—been begotten from the Father: whole from whole, true from true, eternal from eternal, perfect from perfect, God from God. For all things were made through him; which would not be true if Christ were a made thing, since he would not have been made through himself. For no created thing was made through itself.

When, therefore, it is said that Christ’s generation neither began nor ceased to be, neither had a beginning [Col. 0312A] nor will have an end, this is not said in order that the Son of God may be said always to be begotten, but in order that his generation may be shown to be everlasting. And therefore he is called “always begotten,” so that by “always” eternity may be indicated, and by “begotten” perfection. For in that generation there is nothing temporal: nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, nothing different. Eternity excludes earlier and later; identity—that is, consubstantiality, which in Greek is ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of one substance”)—excludes difference.

Therefore the Son is not always being begotten, because if the Son is always being begotten, the Son is now being begotten. If the Son is now being begotten, then he does not escape the constraints of temporality and imperfection. But the Son is timeless and perfect, like the Father from whom he is. [Col. 0312B] Therefore he is always—that is, from eternity; that is, without beginning and without end—because he has always been begotten. For to have been begotten is to be Son, to be God, to be always from the Father.

But so that the reasoning of this statement may be firmer, let us now hear what the divine oracles proclaim concerning this. Hilary, surpassing others in such matters, says in Book II of *On the Trinity*: “God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is God not from someone or through something, but is God begotten; and he who, from perfect generation, is perfect God, does not after birth advance into God through a cause; but in that he was born, he is nothing other in being born than God.” The same author, in Book XII of the same work: “From the eternal Father comes eternal birth. But whatever God always is, is also eternal; yet not everything eternal is unbegotten, because what has been born from eternity [Col. 0312C] has an eternal existence because it has been born. For what has been born from eternity—if it was not born eternal—then the Father too will no longer be eternal. Likewise, if it is always proper to the Father that he is always Father, it must always be proper to the Son that he is always Son.”

From this I confidently infer: therefore it is proper to the Son that he has always been born. Hilary explains this also in the same book: “He who was from eternity and always, must necessarily not have existed without birth; since to have always existed is above time, and always to have been born means that the birth is everlasting. We therefore confess the only-begotten God as begotten, but begotten before eternal times.” And I say: therefore you too, and your companions, in whom Christ is one—not recent, not confused, not divided—who have one heart [Col. 0312D] and one soul in the Lord, who dwell unitedly in the house of the Lord, confess the Son of God to have always been begotten. For if he was begotten before eternal times, then he has always been begotten.

And Hilary, as though driving in a wedge, presses on with the pious undertaking already begun: “What was born before time was always born, because that which is before eternal time always is. Likewise, he must be confessed to have been born before all ages and eternal times, and before the understanding of all things, because through the fact that he was thus born, he always is. Therefore he has always been born, because he permits nothing else to be understood or said about himself except that he has been born.” And I say: the Son of God, therefore, is not still being born. For one who is always being born will never have been born; he will therefore always be imperfect. But he is not imperfect. [Col. 0313A] For the nature of the Son is the nature of the Father. Hence Pope Leo says: “The nature of the Only-begotten is the nature of the Father and the nature of the Holy Spirit.”
