And Hilary, in Book II of *On the Trinity*: “The only-begotten God has in himself the nature of almighty God, since he is born from God; and the full reality of perfect man, since his birth is from the Virgin; subsisting in the nature of God with the truth of a body, and remaining in the nature of God with the truth of a body.” You have here, therefore, that the nature of God took the nature of man, because it took the full reality of perfect man—that is, the whole complete human nature. Where then are those who, following the master of error, make noise in the schools by saying: “Nature did not assume person”—which is true; “nor person person”—which likewise is true; “nor nature nature”—which is false? [Col. 0313B] For the whole nature of divinity is in the Son of God, and the whole Son of God assumed the whole human being. Therefore the whole nature of divinity assumed the whole nature of humanity. Yet the Son alone was incarnate, and in the Son alone the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

We would have other witnesses for making this matter clear, if we were not avoiding weariness. Therefore, to return to the subject: he who was wholly God from the whole God—for otherwise he would not be God—was born from eternity and has always been born.

For confirmation of this assertion Saint Hilary concludes thus: “Therefore, as it is proper to the Father to exist without birth, so it is proper to the Son to exist by birth: this is the property which makes the distinction of persons.” These are Hilary’s words, and blessed Augustine is drawn by the tether of catholic faith to the same meaning. For he says in Book IX of *On the Trinity*: “Indeed, nothing in God is said according to accident, because nothing in him is changeable; yet not everything said is said according to substance. For something is said in relation to another, as Father to Son and Son to Father. This is not an accident, because the one is always Father and the other always Son; and not always in such a way as though, from the time the Son was born, or because the Son never ceases to be Son, the Father does not cease to be Father, but because the Son has always been born.”

Our latter-day men are certainly oppressed by a heavy sleep if, awakened by these words, they do not arise. In them blessed Augustine excludes every bodily notion from fatherhood and sonship, [Col. 0313D] and says that the Son has always been begotten because, just as the Father is always—that is, from eternity—Father, so the Son is always—that is, from eternity—Son.

Therefore the Father begot either a perfect Son or an imperfect one. If imperfect, then he either did not will, or could not, to beget a perfect one. If he did not will it, he is envious; if he could not, he is not omnipotent. Therefore he begot a perfect one. Therefore he is always perfect and has always been begotten. He who has always been begotten was not Son before he was begotten. Therefore he is not always being born, because he would appear imperfect if he were always being born.

Yet I do not doubt that there are certain lovers even of divine reading who think that blessed Augustine yielded to this proposition, that the Son of God is always being born from the Father. For, writing to Pascentius, the Arian count, he says: [Col. 0314A] “What then do we say? If the Son of God was born from the Father, then the Father has now ceased to beget. And if he ceased, he began. But if he began to beget, there was a time when he was without the Son. But he was never without the Son, because the Son is his wisdom, which is the brightness of eternal light. Therefore the Father always begets, and the Son is always being born.”

“You hear,” they say, “that he concludes and says, ‘Therefore the Father always begets and the Son is always being born.’ What remedy, then, do you have, you who deny that the Son of God is always being born?” But it is otherwise. For those who think in this way, not carefully observing what is said and how it is said, are deceived by the obscure construction of the words.

First, people brought out of Egypt’s iron furnace and making their way to the city [Col. 0314B] of habitation ought without doubt to have understood that this man of such keen and illustrious intellect, such learned and spiritual mind, such catholic heart, especially in the cause of God, could never disagree with himself. Then observe the deception of Arian unbelief and the wisdom of the writer replying to it. For the inference, “Therefore the Father always begets and the Son is always being begotten,” does not arise from concessions; rather, it is launched against the adversary as against an evil hunter after words. No catholic and learned scribe in the kingdom of God assents to the first consequence. For the statement “If the Son of God was born from the Father, the Father has now ceased to beget” is utterly false.

I speak to those who know and are skilled in the art of disputation. We cried out in the schools while still boys; and others, I think, cry out even now: the antecedent is true [Col. 0314C] and the consequent false. For it is true that the Son of God was born from the Father; and false that the Father ceased to beget. For he never ceased who never began, as was clearly reasoned above. The consequences that follow—“if he ceased, he began; there was at some time a Father without a Son”—are woven by the deceits of heretical perversity like spiders’ webs. But the following assumption—“the Father was never without the Son, because his Son is his wisdom, the brightness of eternal light”—is most true. Yet this is imposed so that the false conclusion may be inferred: “Therefore the Father always begets and the Son is always being begotten.” This does not follow at all, because that generation was not and is not an action.

For the Arians strove to prove either that the Lord Jesus was not [Col. 0314D] always begotten, and therefore was not co-eternal with the Father, having at some time begun and ceased to be born; or that, if he had always been born, he would always be being born and therefore would appear imperfect. By “always” they understood the continuation, as it were, of some action. But “always” here names not temporal continuation but timeless everlastingness—that is, eternity—which neither had a beginning nor will have an end.

Those therefore are mistaken who think this to be blessed Augustine’s conclusion. He himself makes this clear in the following sentence, or explanation, saying: “Again, it must be feared that generation may be thought imperfect if we say not ‘to have been born’ but ‘to be born.’” But why do we not brandish the shaft [Col. 0315A] which we have held so long in hand, which this master forged, polished, and used to stop the mouths of opponents? This holy man of incomparable prudence and eminent simplicity, now broken by old age and warmed by his Shunammite, revised his books and there treated this proposition most carefully in these words: “Among the things we have written there is also a certain lengthy work, which nevertheless counts as one book, entitled *Eighty-Five Different Questions*.” And shortly after: “As bishop, I collected these and made one book from them. The thirty-seventh of them is entitled *On the Always-Begotten*.”

The proposition which I called above a shaft, and which follows, is expressed in these same words: “It is better to say ‘always begotten’ than ‘always being born.’ For one who is always being born has not yet been born, and has never been born, or never will be, [Col. 0315B] if he is always being born. For to be born is one thing, to have been born another; and consequently he is never Son if he has never been born. But because he is Son because he has been born, he is always Son; therefore he has always been begotten.” To resist this assertion is the act of a self-willed person, one to whom it is said: “If anyone is contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (I Corinthians XI).

Let a third witness also be added, using words so true and manifest that one ought to assent to him with every submission: that great Gregory, who, according to the meaning of his name, kept watch in Christ and excelled others in rank, learning, faith, holiness, and office. He begins Book XXIX of the *Morals* thus: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, in that he is wisdom [Col. 0315C] and power, was born from the Father before times. Or rather, because he neither began nor ceased to be, let us speak more truly: always begotten. For we could not say ‘always being born,’ lest he appear imperfect. But in order that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both ‘begotten’ and ‘always’: so that ‘begotten’ may pertain to perfection and ‘always’ to eternity, in order that by a temporal expression we may in some fashion designate that timeless essence—although even in saying ‘perfect’ we depart greatly from the perfection of that truth, because what has not been made cannot be called perfect.”

To resist such assertions by such great men is not the part of those to whom God has made known his right hand and who have a heart instructed through him in wisdom. [Col. 0315D] Since it has been sufficiently shown that the Son of God has always been begotten and is not always being born from the Father, it remains to examine Peter’s statement that God cannot do anything except what he does, nor at another time. But first, as is our custom, his words must be set down, and truth must afterwards be set against falsehood.

The destroyer of true simplicity and simple truth raves in his *Theology* in these words: “If God must do what he does, then surely it is just that he do whatever he does, or without doubt whatever he ought to do. But if he ought to do it, then certainly he cannot omit doing it. For whatever is just is unjust to omit. And whoever does not do what reason requires sins no less than if he did what in no way accords with reason.” And shortly after: [Col. 0316A] “If only that which God does is good to be done by him, then surely he can do only that which he does, since he can do nothing except what is good to be done by him. By this reasoning, therefore, God seems able only to do what he does, or to omit what he omits, since in each thing done or omitted he has a rational cause why it is done or omitted by him, lest he, who is supreme reason, ought either to will or to do anything contrary to what accords with reason.” And then: “From these arguments drawn from reason and Scripture, it is established that God can do only what he at some time does.”

Then he sets against his own skillet—not Ezekiel’s—his ingenious counterarguments; and he strives, or seems to strive, to crush what he had constructed, with such cunning that he may again establish it more firmly, after eliminating everything that had seemed to oppose his earlier claims. Thus he concludes: [Col. 0316B] “I think it clear to all, from the aforesaid arguments and the resolutions of objections, that God can only do or omit whatever he does or omits, in the manner in which he does or omits it, and only at the time at which he does it, not at another.” But in his *Apology* he is carried much more violently by a spirit of dizziness and is afflicted more unhappily. For, with more careful treatment and as though his forces were gathered into one, he develops this chapter more diffusely than the others and devotes himself wholly to confirming this new invention—or rather, destructive error.

For he sets his mouth in heaven and rises to the height of divine immutability, showing [Col. 0316C] that God’s will and power are the same, saying: “It must be held generally and without doubt that whatever good God has in himself can in no way either increase or diminish in him. And as his power or wisdom is co-eternal with him, so also the will which he has concerning all things to be done or ordered is co-eternal with him.” He speaks truth, but as usual he lays a snare. “For in God to be powerful is not one thing and to will good is another; for, as the foregoing declares, his very being and being God are the same thing; and his will and his power are nothing other than himself.”

Augustine, in Book VII of the *Confessions*: “You are not compelled unwillingly to anything, because your will is not greater than your power. But it would be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself. For God’s will and power are God himself.” [Col. 0316D] See how true are Peter’s propositions; but he must be avoided in this, that from truths he concludes falsehoods. Thus he says: “If, therefore, he can do only what is fitting for him to do or will to do, then surely he can only do and will to do what he at some time does, and only in that way and at that time in which he does it; because it is fitting for him neither to do it nor even to will to do it in another way or at another time.”

He repeats this; he multiplies it by a lengthy pursuit of verbosity—or rather, by curiosity. But what are you doing, O unhappy soul of mine? Do you thus boil over without restraint? Why do you waste the times for reading and prayer? Why do you waste away meditating on such things? Why do you cause even your small sharpness of intellect to grow dull, as though dashing it against a rock? [Col. 0317A] What Augustine, what Gregory, or what man of their kind casts you into the horrible thickness of this rubble? None of them dared say this: “God cannot do except what he does.” Even if this were true, it would have been better kept silent than spoken, much less written.

But now the knot, which I see by God’s gift, must be untied. He treats God’s will in different ways: now according to what it is, now according to the way it relates to created things—that is, sometimes according to essence and sometimes according to action, that is, the creation of things. For with the creation of things began both spaces of places and courses of times. Therefore he remained unchangeable in himself while making changeable things; he always remains unchangeable, governing [Col. 0317B] and making all things. Nothing new happens to him, since he does not know things because they exist, but they exist because he knows them. Nor has he, who is uncircumscribed light, enclosed himself in his creature.

For he is wholly naturally in his Son, because he did not make him but begot him eternally from himself. “‘From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you’ (Psalm CIX),” that is, from my substance before the beginning—that is, without beginning. But he is not in his creature in this way, because he did not beget it from himself but made it from nothing. Therefore all that he made is outside him; for although things are from him, through him, and in him, yet he is above all things and is not contained within any creature. Though he dwells in holy angels and in his elect, he does so not by nature but by grace.

Augustine, to Dardanus (Letter [Col. 0317C] 57): “God, therefore, is everywhere present and everywhere wholly present; yet he does not dwell everywhere, but in his temple, to which he is gracious and propitious by grace.” And later: “For he is said to be everywhere because he is absent from no part of things. He is said to be whole because he does not offer one part of himself as present to one part of things and another part to another part—an equal part to an equal, a lesser to a lesser, a greater to a greater—but is wholly present not only to the whole of creatures but also to every part of it.”

Therefore, as this great doctor’s assertion proves, God is present to the whole universe of things, yet is not contained either in a part of the universe or in its entirety. God is greater than the universe of things, not in bulk but in power, wisdom, goodness, and eternity. [Col. 0317D] Therefore his will and power—which are nothing other than his essence—also exceed the whole universe of things. He is therefore a liar and deceiver who confines God’s will or power—that is, God—within creation, as that man does who says that God can do concerning his creation only what he does, although God’s will precedes the whole universe of things and is the cause of that universe.

Hence the same doctor, in *On Genesis against the Manichees*: “The will of God is the cause of all things that are. For if God’s will has a cause, there is something that precedes God’s will, which it is impious to believe. Therefore, to whoever asks, ‘Why did God make heaven and earth?’ the answer must be, ‘Because he willed it.’ For God’s will is the cause [Col. 0318A] of heaven and earth; and therefore God’s will is greater than heaven and earth. But whoever asks, ‘Why did God will to make heaven and earth?’ seeks something greater than God’s will. But nothing greater can be found. Let human rashness, therefore, restrain itself and not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist. Whoever desires to know God’s will, then, should become God’s friend.”

This, I think, that remarkable philosopher had not read. For if he had read it, I dare not think that afterwards he would have taught things so novel and so harmful. For he says that God has a rational cause, in making or leaving undone things, why they are made or left undone by Him. But, as Augustine testifies, reason contradicts this and says that, in things to be done or left undone, there is no cause higher than the will of God; and he errs who seeks one higher. Therefore God is able to do many things with created things which He does not do. Nor did God receive, nor does He receive, from things a cause determining when or how He should make, order, or govern them; for He Himself is the cause of all things’ existence, and within Himself He possesses the knowledge and power by which all things are ordered. For He Himself is Creator, governor, and ordainer of all things—not only of good things, which all come from Him, but also of evil things, which are not at all from Him and therefore do not truly exist either; since they are not things, but privations of things, or, more properly, corruptions. They exist in nature from nature. For there are no evils except in good things, although there are many good things without evils. Those trained by the words of our supreme disputant—Augustine, I mean—do not doubt such matters. Because there are many statements confirming this assertion, I pass them over for brevity’s sake.

The whole purpose of this labor is to show truly that God’s will, or His power, is not subjected to the law of creation or enclosed within it; and therefore God can do many things with it which He does not do. He therefore lies who says that He cannot. When, then, it is said that God’s will or power cannot be increased or diminished, this is truly said, because it is said according to His essence—which is God—and that cannot be increased or changed. And when it is said that God cannot do evil, this too is truly said, because evil is nothing: it is not a thing, but the corruption of a thing; and God, who is unchangeable, cannot fail to be good. This inability of His is omnipotence. But when it is said that God cannot make it rain except when it rains, or make from His creation anything except what He makes, this is a fallacy. For the statement no longer concerns God’s will or power in the manner discussed above—that is, simply, according to essence, according to what a thing is—but also according to action, that is, according to the effect of things, according to what stands in relation to something else: namely, Creator in relation to creature. For the Creator is the Creator of the creature, and the creature is the creature of the Creator.

We understand and speak of a thing differently according to what it is, and differently according to how it stands in relation to another, although it is the same thing. Aristotle, that most acute discoverer, organizer, and investigator of the categories, showed this to careful readers and wise interpreters; for, treating of the individual categories, he expounded their properties subtly and separately. Since, therefore, the whole universe of things is subject to the Creator and cannot resist His will or power, God can do many things with it which He does not do, He who does nothing contrary to His own will. “For He does whatsoever He wills in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134).

Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “And where is the power which has done whatsoever it willed in heaven and on earth, if He willed to gather the children of Jerusalem and did not do so? Or rather, did even Jerusalem herself not will that her children should be gathered by Him; yet, even against her will, He Himself gathered those of her children whom He willed? For in heaven and on earth He did not will and do some things, while willing but not doing others; rather, He did whatsoever He willed.” Therefore, although God’s will and power are the same in Him, the effect of things nevertheless stands differently: for He can do many things which He does not will to do, He who does whatsoever He wills to do in heaven and on earth. For He can raise up children of Abraham from these stones—that is, make vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath—yet He does not do so from all. But why He does it from some and not from others is a secret with Him; it is an abyss. “For the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Psalm 35).

And since, as Augustine explains at some length in his book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, the work of divine providence is twofold: some causes are eternal and unchangeable in God, while others are implanted in things originally, primordially, causally, by Him who lives for ever; and, according to the prophet, “He created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18). According to the higher causes, whatever has been established is unshaken; according to the lower causes, many things can occur and fail to occur—things which may happen or may not happen. According to the lower causes, wine is pressed from grapes and bread made from flour; according to the higher causes, water is changed into wine, and now five thousand persons are fed with five barley loaves, now four thousand with seven wheaten loaves, by Him who feeds those hungering and thirsting for righteousness with the nourishment of the Old and New Testaments.

But I shall explain the depths of this matter better through the words of the most learned and delightful teacher, blessed Gregory. Thus he says in Book IX of the *Morals*, while expounding the passage, “God, whose wrath no one can resist” (Job 9): “It is very remarkable,” he says, “that no one is said to resist God’s wrath, when the divine utterances testify that many have opposed the indignation of the heavenly judgment.” After mentioning Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, David, and Elijah, he concludes after some discussion:

> “Therefore God’s wrath can be resisted when He who is angry Himself gives aid; and it cannot at all be resisted when He both rouses Himself to vengeance and does not breathe upon the prayer poured out to Him. Thus the statement that God’s wrath can be resisted is made according to the lower cause, as the divine word says to Jeremiah: ‘But if that nation or that kingdom changes its wickedness, then I too will not bring upon it the evil which I said, says the Lord’ (Jeremiah 18). For Jerusalem would not have been destroyed by the Chaldeans if it had exchanged wickedness for goodness. Yet God, remaining unchangeable in Himself, would also have changed that sentence of condemnation. God therefore did not do what He could have done, because He bound neither Himself within the constraints of creation nor free choice under the law of necessity. But the statement that His wrath cannot be resisted belongs to the higher cause, as it was again said to Jeremiah: ‘Therefore do not pray for this people, nor undertake praise and prayer for it, because I will not hear you’ (Jeremiah 7). And again: ‘Though Moses and Samuel stood before Me, My soul is not toward this people’ (Jeremiah 15). It was therefore fixed with Him that Jerusalem and its people should be destroyed. And what was fixed with Him to happen had necessarily to happen according to the higher cause, because His foreknowledge could not be deceived. He knew before the ages what He would do with Jerusalem. But according to the lower cause it was not necessary; for if Jerusalem had changed its wickedness, He too would have changed the sentence. For she had it within herself to do this, if she wished. But He Himself knew before the foundation of the world that she would not wish it.”

The same teacher, in Book XII of the same work, expounding the statement, “You have set his limits, which cannot be passed” (Job 14), says: “It is also fixed for a human being how long he shall live in this mortal life. For although almighty God added fifteen years to King Hezekiah’s life, He then allowed him to die when He had foreknown that he would die. The prophet therefore was not false, because the time of death was made known at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, because the increase in his years of life through God’s bounty was also fixed before the ages, and the span of life unexpectedly added outwardly was established inwardly without any increase in foreknowledge.” Thus he.

It is therefore evident to those who do not possess a contentious spirit that the saying, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (Isaiah 38), was made according to the lower cause, because Hezekiah had deserved it; and that the years were added according to the higher cause. Likewise, according to the higher cause it was true that Jerusalem must be destroyed by the Chaldeans; according to the lower cause it was not true that Jerusalem must be destroyed by the Chaldeans. For this conditional proposition is true: If God has foreknown that Jerusalem will be destroyed by the Chaldeans, then Jerusalem must be destroyed by the Chaldeans. For whatever God has foreknown will occur must occur; otherwise His foreknowledge would be deceived, which is incompatible with truth. Yet this categorical proposition is not therefore true in itself: Jerusalem must be destroyed by the Chaldeans. For Jerusalem could have changed its wickedness if it wished, and then He would have changed the sentence that had been imposed conditionally.

Thus I speak of God’s nature according to the higher cause, but of the nature of things according to the lower cause; as when I say: If David and Peter are predestined to eternal life, David and Peter cannot be damned. But this derives not from themselves, but from God Himself, whose predestination cannot be deceived. Likewise, it is true that, if David had died in adultery and Peter in denial—which could well have happened according to the lower cause—David and Peter would have been damned. But this derives not from God, but from themselves. Necessity therefore does not rest upon things; rather, the relation of things to providence produces conditional necessity. On this point the most eloquent and acute teacher Boethius wrote in Book VI of the *Consolation of Philosophy*; and we, though wholly insignificant in comparison, have treated it more fully, according to our measure, in the *Treatise on Universal Things*, addressed to Master Theodoric.

Therefore, as reason proves and authority confirms, the whole universe of things is subject to the will of the Creator, by whom it was made from nothing. Accordingly, according to the lower cause, He can do many things with it which He does not do, though He does nothing contrary to what has been fixed with Himself. This is the different perspective of understanding and mode of speaking: according to God’s will, power, and providence—that is, according to His essence (for His essence is not one thing and these another thing in Him); and according to that which, if I may say so, He—or they—stand in relation to: the nature of things or their effects. Treating these matters together, the lover of novelties and most subtle academic of the age lays snares to capture little souls given over to vanity, who read too little and understand too little of God’s things. Let this suffice against that invention which spoke wrongly of God.

Of the matters proposed, therefore, one final point remains to be examined, and with it this work shall end. This Peter Abelard, against whose fabricated fictions we write—strengthened by your prayers and by the command of your Holiness, most excellent Father Hugh—pleased certain men distinguished by nobility, study, and learning, and among them some more curious than studious, through vain and empty philosophy. He treated matters pertaining to God not so much catholicly as philosophically; and thus, standing far from the people of whom it is written, “I will praise You among a weighty people” (Psalm 34), he wandered in the wind of subtlety, shamefully opposed to the simplicity of our faith and damnably contrary to truth. In the Egyptian furnace of his works he fashioned little vessels, and brought philosophers—Plato, Virgil, and Macrobius, unshorn and unwashed—to the banquet of the supreme King.

For in his theology, following Plato especially, he says: “Let us now carefully examine Plato’s words concerning the world-soul, so that we may recognize that the Holy Spirit is most perfectly designated in them.” And below: “Plato’s statement that the soul was placed by God in the middle of the world and extended equally through the whole sphere of the entire universe beautifully designates the grace of God offered commonly to all, according to the saying, ‘The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world’ (Wisdom 1:7). Divine acts also agree with this *involucrum*—that is, with the placing of the soul in the middle of the world, namely, with God’s grace offered commonly to all—because our Lord Jesus Christ worked salvation as king in the midst of the earth.”

In calling the course of this temporal order an *involucrum*, he follows John Scotus, who frequently used this unusual word and was himself, because of his subtlety, accused of heresy.

But it is evident to all who read these things and know the truth that he calls the world-soul the Holy Spirit on the basis of philosophical teaching; whereas, according to those philosophers themselves, the world-soul differs greatly from the Creator and from the divine Mind, which they call *nous* (νοῦς, “intellect”); while according to true faith and ecclesiastical teaching, the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, differs from neither, and is coeternal with both.

He therefore says that the grace of God, which he calls the Holy Spirit, is offered commonly to all. In his *Apology*, indeed, he first defends himself vigorously and, anathematizing the Pelagian heresy, thinks and writes catholicly concerning God’s grace; but afterwards, subtle in his accustomed manner and slippery like another Proteus, he escapes and returns to the same position. His own words will prove this better. These are the first:

> “I call the grace of God whatever God ordains from Himself for a person’s salvation, or confers upon that person without the person’s having deserved it. For the Apostle says: ‘A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace’ (Romans 11). But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. Therefore it belongs to God in His elect that He predestined them from eternity, and that He inspired faith in them—things which certainly precede our merits and without which we cannot love Him so as to deserve salvation. For that love itself, which He produces in us through the matters first mentioned, is an effect of God Himself, or His gift; and it must be attributed to His grace before we are even able to merit anything pertaining to salvation. Hence the Apostle says: ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ (1 Corinthians 4).”

These statements concerning God’s grace, spoken by Paul, are words more of truth than of Peter. For what could be said more true, more refined, or more salutary? But stay here with me, I beg you. I have been your friend insofar as I could. As the rule of brotherly love commands, I do not persecute the man but the error. Unless you deceive me, you are bound by the cords of this very assertion of yours. For you say that God’s grace is whatever God ordains for human salvation; that, according to the Apostle, election is by grace, otherwise grace is no longer grace; that through it He predestined His elect from eternity; that through it He inspired faith in them; and that the love itself which He works in us, and without which no one can be saved, must be attributed to God’s grace. According to this very definition of yours, then, I speak with you about God’s grace. Tell me, I pray: is grace, understood in this way, common to all human beings? Does God predestine all human beings to salvation, inspire faith in all, and inspire that love through which they are saved? Most subtle, most renowned, most charming master, teach me. If you are not mad, you will answer: “It is not.”

Therefore this grace is not common to all.

> **[Note: Col. 0323D]** This opinion is not to be maintained; nor is Abelard rightly criticized here for following the contrary opinion. The argument which the author offers is also ineffective and fallacious. For from the fact that not all gifts which may be called by the name of grace are bestowed upon every reprobate person, he wrongly infers that grace is not given or offered to all; for by the same reasoning he would infer that no one possesses God’s gifts, since no one possesses them all. It is enough, therefore, that some grace be granted to the reprobate; if they used it well, they would progressively advance to greater and greater grace, and finally attain salvation. Certainly the Fathers grant grace to the reprobate; among them is St. Prosper, who judges that it is not denied even to infants who die before birth. Since I have cited their words elsewhere, there is no need to repeat them here. For this reason William also did not censure this opinion of Abelard, though he condemned him for Pelagianism because he held that a human being can do good by the powers of nature alone. Abelard’s deception must also be noted here: with the Pelagians he located God’s grace in the law and in free choice. Finally, from both authors—William, namely, and this anonymous writer—it is clear that those err who think Abelard denied free choice; rather, he held erroneous views about grace in order to establish free choice, as is entirely evident from the authors cited above.]

For if it were common, all would be saved—which you by no means concede; otherwise God’s ordination, predestination, inspiration of faith and of love itself would fail, and God’s gift would be frustrated. To think this of God is sacrilegious. But if, which I scarcely believe, you answer, “It is,” reason, catholic preaching, the authority of the Fathers, and the effects of things refute you. For this grace can never be ineffectual: it makes a heart of flesh from a heart of stone, spiritual from animal, enlightened from blind, sound from infirm. By it the Holy Spirit gives a pledge not to all souls but to whichever He wills. This alone the outstanding preacher calls grace; this he defends and proclaims in his Epistles, especially in that to the Romans. By it a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man became kindly, gentle, and a disciple; a wolf became a lamb; Saul became Paul. By it God calls certain persons chosen before the foundation of the world, whose number is fixed and who cannot perish. This comes not from themselves but from God, because He foreknew them and predestined them to be made conformable to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brothers.

Paul knows no other grace; Augustine disputes no other. It is indeed God’s gift that we exist, that we live—indeed, whatever is in us and in every creature. For every creature’s existence, and whatever good is in it, derives from God’s gift, that is, from His goodness. But because the Pelagian heretics, opponents of divine grace, fled to these considerations and called God’s grace what, in the sense just stated, is truly the gifts of nature, catholic writers rightly, subtly, and usefully distinguished gifts of nature from gifts of grace. The gifts of nature are common both to the elect and to the reprobate; the gifts of grace belong to all the elect and to no reprobate persons. Thus, in the usage of ecclesiastical custom, they called grace the effect of that election by which He who has the winnowing fan in His hand and cleanses His threshing-floor separates the grain from the chaff and gathers it into His barn.

But Peter quickly changes his face and, returning to his accustomed position, becomes alien to us. Help now, brothers, I beg you. He is strong; he breaks his bonds; he shines in mastery; I cannot hold him. Without any transition, he says something which seems to me astonishing: “Therefore free choice itself, because it is good, is a gift of divine grace; and so is reason itself, in which free choice consists.” This is true, but you proceed otherwise. For both free choice and the reason in which it consists are common to elect and reprobate alike. You are arguing against us and playing the sophist; we were not discussing grace in that way.

But he becomes more forceful in what follows. For he says:

> “Since, therefore, the Lord grants reason to both elect and reprobate, and shows them the way by which they are to arrive at blessedness, and continually invites us, through His precepts and exhortations, to receive that blessedness which He offers to all: some listen to Him in these matters and obey His precepts, living well in order to receive the rewards offered; others despise them and, remaining in their sloth, shrink from the labor of obedience.”

I wonder whether the man who wrote such things was awake, so nearly does he contradict himself concerning the same matter in almost the same place. See how the mighty preacher and defender of divine grace has vanished more quickly than I expected and, disregarding the proper order of disputation, has left the well-worn paths familiar to him. For he sets a net of falsehood when he asserts that God invites all, by His precepts and exhortations, to receive blessedness, which according to him He offers to all.

I pass over newly born children—both those born among the Gentiles and those born of Christian parents—who are unbaptized and forestalled by death. I pass over the many now living in many places who have not heard the preaching of Christ, without which no one can attain true blessedness. Let him answer, if he can, concerning the innumerable Gentiles, given over to idolatrous worship throughout almost the whole world before the Savior’s coming; for “God was known only in Judea” (Psalm 75). Why, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, did God permit them to go in their own ways (Acts 14)—that is, as though He had said, their ways, not the ways of God’s commandments—so that they would not attain salvation, except by a hidden but never unjust judgment?

He now asks—for it so pleases one who has drained the wells of philosophy’s abyss and who does not now hear, “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor investigate things greater than yourself” (Ecclesiasticus 3)—as a rash investigator of God’s unsearchable judgments, together with Porphyry the philosopher; he asks, I say, together with Julian the Apostate Augustus, who wrote eight books against the Gospels of Christ while on his expedition, why the God of the Christians, who according to them was the Savior of the world, arose in the last times and wrought salvation so late, after innumerable persons had already been damned in hell. Let him hear from the Prophet: “The judgments of God are a great abyss” (Psalm 35). Let him hear from the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and His ways past finding out!” (Romans 11). What remains, then, except that he either disbelieve so many and such great witnesses and cease to be a Christian, or, if he believes, cease to search the unsearchable things and be at peace? Yet whoever wishes faithfully to investigate this depth should read the second chapter, “On the Time of the Christian Religion,” of the little work composed by blessed Augustine (*Epistle* 49, question 2) for the priest called Deogratias.

But Peter disdains to dwell at home with the simple Jacob; rather, like a strong hunter, Esau, he enters the shadowy forests, and from the perverse bow which he has long drawn he shoots the poisoned arrow of this conditional statement. For he says: “The reprobate are prepared for living well just as the elect are—that is, by being taught and admonished and by being given the capacity, so that no excuse may any longer remain.” And, speaking with his opponents, he adds: “But you say that God has not made good will in the reprobate as He has in the elect.” Then he who utterly destroys, by every means, the foundation of catholic firmness, and who, speaking in his own accustomed manner from his own position, destroys it thus: “The reprobate,” he says, “are not to be blamed if they do not live rightly, like the elect, since for the uprightness of life there has been denied them that grace without which they are wholly unable to live rightly.”

This is the very ancient subtle argument of the Pelagian heretics. By this engine they attacked, though they did not overthrow, the singular excellence of grace. Their false benevolence carried them so far that they asserted that infants are born without original sin and proclaimed that they enter the kingdom of heaven without baptism. But no one instructed in catholic doctrine, and especially in the words of blessed Augustine, is ignorant how false these things are.

Peter, therefore, who above had anathematized the Pelagian heresy and had argued against it vigorously, truly, and catholicly, is now enmeshed in such bonds of error that he openly asserts that for his grace offered commonly to all—that is, both elect and reprobate—no preparation of the heart by God is necessary; rather, that this is present in all through free choice, so that each person can receive it; and that God does not make good will in His elect any more than in the reprobate. Yet if He did make it in the elect and did not do the same in the reprobate, the reprobate could rightly excuse themselves concerning the uprightness of life.

See to what dregs this defender of free choice has descended, when the Apostle says: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2). For the grace which we proclaim is such that it makes a person will well what that person did not will, and able to do what that person could not do. For it is not bestowed in such a manner as to remain inactive; it is the inspiration of divine propitiation. It raises those who have fallen, enlightens the blind, makes the weak strong, raises the dead, and brings to eternal life all whom God has predestined. It is not powerless, it does not fail, and it is not common to all. It is poured by God into the hearts of those whose number is certain, none of whom perishes, because no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from the hand of Christ’s Father.

This defense of our assertion must be established by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, so that free choice may be proclaimed without denying grace, and grace may be confirmed without destroying free choice. Augustine, in Letter 1 to Abbot Valentine: “The Lord Jesus,” he says, “did not first come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through Him; afterwards He Himself will judge the world, when He comes to judge the living and the dead. Therefore, if there is no grace of God, how does He save the world? And if there is no free choice, how does He judge the world?” And later in the same letter: “Beware what so great an Apostle says so terribly; and where you find that you do not understand, meanwhile believe the divine utterances: for free choice can neither be converted to God nor make progress in God.”

The same, in Letter 2 to the same person: “The catholic faith does not deny free choice, whether for evil or for good; neither does it attribute so much to it that without God’s grace it can accomplish anything, whether to be converted from evil to good, to make persevering progress in good, or to attain eternal good.”

The same, to Juliana: “Unless it is aided by God’s grace, not even good will itself can exist in a human being.” And in *On the Words of the Lord*: “O evil free choice, unless God’s grace aids it!” And to Optatus: “It would rightly seem unjust that vessels of wrath are made for destruction, if the entire mass had not itself been condemned from Adam. Thus, that persons become vessels of wrath by birth belongs to deserved punishment; but that they become vessels of mercy by rebirth belongs to undeserved grace.” Again, to the same: “The potter, not only just but also merciful, makes other vessels for honor according to grace, not according to debt, since He helps even little children, of whom no merits can be asserted, and prevents older persons with grace so that they may be able to possess some merits.”

The same, in *The City of God*: “The will of God is also called that which He works in the hearts of those obedient to His commandments; concerning which the Apostle says: ‘For it is God who works in you to will’ (Philippians 2).” Where, then, are Peter and his followers, who, trusting in their own strength and in the images of their falsehoods, said: “Preparation of the heart by God is not necessary for human beings; God does not make good will in His elect”? Do you still resist? Hear what grace does in a human being.

Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “Grace alone separates from the lost those whom He had created together in the same mass of perdition derived from the common origin.” And in *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*: “If a person can be without sin by himself, then Christ died gratuitously. But Christ did not die gratuitously. Therefore a person cannot be without sin, even if he wishes, unless he is aided by God’s grace through Jesus Christ our Lord.” And in *On Nature and Grace*: “Just as the eye of the body, even when entirely sound, cannot see unless aided by the brightness of light, so too a person, even when most perfectly justified, cannot live rightly unless divinely aided by the eternal light of righteousness.” Again, in the same work: “The love of God is poured into our hearts not by the capacity of nature nor by the free choice which is in us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

Hear that even the will is prepared by the Lord. Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “For who does not know that Peter’s faith would then have perished if his faithful will had failed, and would have remained if that same will had remained? But because, as it is written, ‘the will is prepared by the Lord God,’ Christ’s prayer for him could not be ineffectual.”

Likewise hear that grace produces a good will in a human being. Augustine, in *On Grace and Free Will*: “The will in us is always free, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. But God’s grace is always good; and through it a person who was formerly of evil will becomes one of good will.” [Col. 0327B] Hear that grace is not ineffectual. For predestination, as Augustine defines it, “is the preparation of grace, while grace is the effect of predestination.” Predestination cannot fail, nor can grace be frustrated: grace not only instills good, but first expels evil. Augustine, addressing Prosper and Hilary, who had questioned him by letters on such matters, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*: “This grace, which is secretly bestowed upon human hearts by divine generosity, is rejected by no hard heart. For it is bestowed precisely so that hardness of heart may first be removed. Therefore, when the Father is heard and teaches inwardly so that one may come to the Son, he removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh.” Hear that grace is not common to all. Augustine, addressing the same persons in the same book: “Faith is not possessed by all, though the capacity to have faith belongs to all. The Apostle does not say, ‘What are you able to have that you have not received, so that you may be able to have it?’ Rather, he says: ‘What do you have that you have not received?’ (1 Cor. 4). Therefore, the capacity to possess faith, just as the capacity to possess charity, belongs to the nature of all human beings; but the possession of faith, just as the possession of charity, belongs to the grace of the faithful.” The same author, addressing Valentinus in *On Grace and Free Will*: “The Pelagians have also dared to say that grace is the very nature in which we were created: that we have a rational mind by which we can understand, having been made in God’s image. But this is not the grace which the Apostle commends through faith in Jesus Christ. [Col. 0327D] For it is certain that we possess this nature in common even with the impious and unbelieving. But the grace of Jesus Christ belongs only to those whose faith it is—that is, to the elect; for faith is not possessed by all.” The same author, on Psalm 77, concerning the same matter: “Although, he says, all the sacraments were common to the ancient fathers, grace—which is the power of the sacraments—was not common to all; just as now, with the faith then veiled having been revealed, the laver of regeneration is common to all baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet grace itself, whose sacraments these are, by which the members of Christ’s body shall reign with their head, is not common to all.”

The same view is held by holy Pope Innocent. Defending Peter’s chair from error, he writes to the same African bishops and the others who had written from the Council of Milevis, [Col. 0328A] as follows: “O perverse doctrine of utterly depraved minds! Observe at last how freedom itself so deceived the first man that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression; nor could he be delivered from this unless, through the providence of regeneration, the coming of Christ the Lord restored to him the condition of his former freedom.”

You who read and understand, see whether Blessed Augustine has anywhere spoken more strictly than Innocent does here about what freedom of choice can accomplish if the grace of God does not assist it. For, as Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, “The first human being sinned and lost both himself and free choice. For he possessed free choice differently before sin, differently after sin; differently through grace, and differently he will possess it when he possesses eternal life. Before sin he possessed it as free, so that he could stand in good if he wished; after sin it was so weakened that he can never rise from evil by himself, but through grace—not grace offered indiscriminately to all, but grace poured out by the Holy Spirit only in the hearts of the elect—it is so improved that he both wills and is able to do good.” But this discussion belongs to another time.

Finally, Blessed Gregory confirms the same points, saying in Book 27 of the *Moralia*: “When, therefore, holy preachers are called to Macedonia and forbidden from Asia (Acts 16), there the line of hidden measures was drawn out, here drawn back. There it is extended so that Macedonia may be gathered within the bounds of the holy Church; here it is withdrawn so that Asia may be left beyond the boundaries of faith.” And later in the same work: [Col. 0328C] “These measures and lines of God’s hidden judgments were being extended when, as we read in the Gospel, one person promises to follow and is rejected, while another asks to be released and is retained.” And in Book 29 of the same work: “Because almighty God has chosen his saints from among the impious, and knows how many elect persons he still has hidden amid the lives of the wicked, he fittingly declares that he has treasures in snow or hail. For treasures are named from *thesis* [Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ θέσεως], that is, from a placing or deposit; and he sees many people long hidden in the coldness of life, whom, when he commands, he brings forth into the open; through heavenly grace he makes them white with the brightness of righteousness.”

Let these testimonies of Catholic disputants concerning grace suffice. The same Peter also wrote another little work, entitled *Know Yourself* (*Scito teipsum*), and called it, if I am not mistaken, his *Ethics*. In it, as in the works mentioned above, forging vain novelties in his private sense of words, on an anvil harmful to the salvation of souls, he argued at length concerning morals contrary to ecclesiastical custom. But we leave it to others to refute him—those incomparably superior to me, who am lowly in the house of my God, and to those like me, in rank of position, sharpness of intellect, labor of study, and ardor of conflict. Yet since, by the favor of the Godhead, I have escaped the shipwrecks of most profound questions with my vessel intact—not through my own little talent, but by the oars of the holy Fathers—I have put my pen back in its case and am joyfully and securely received into the tranquil harbor of reading and prayer, rendering most abundant thanks to Christ my God and to your Excellency. By his inspiration and at your command, I have completed the present work.

[Col. 0329]

## PETER ABAELARD’S RESPONSE AGAINST THE CALUMNIES OF HIS ACCUSERS

This response ought rather to have been entitled: “A Calumnious Retraction of Peter Abaelard’s Errors.” For it is clear from the debates reported above by William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, and by the other anonymous abbot, that the errors condemned in this response were defended and written by Peter Abaelard, as is manifest from his own words quoted by those authors. If he had taught none of these things, what could have been extracted from his books read at the Council of Sens, as related in the *Life of Saint Bernard*, that would have offended the ears of the prelates? Why did he not prove there that he had taught none of the charges or that they could not be found in his writings? This response is therefore calumnious; and Abaelard truly taught the errors here condemned, whether they are condemned by himself or by another in his name.

[Col. 0329A] To all the children of the holy Church, PETER, one of them, but the least among them.

It is a well-known proverb that nothing is so blessed that it cannot be corrupted; and, as Blessed Jerome observes, one who writes many books acquires many judges. I too, though I have written little—or, compared with others, nothing—have been unable to escape the mark of censure. Yet in those matters for which I am gravely accused, God knows that I acknowledge no fault of my own; nor, if there has been any, shall I defend it insolently.

Perhaps I wrote some things in error that ought not to have been written. But I call God, witness and judge, upon my soul that, in the matters of which I am accused, I have presumed nothing from pride or malice. I have spoken much in many schools; [Col. 0329B] my teaching has contained neither stolen water nor hidden bread. I have spoken openly, for the edification of the weak in faith, what seemed to me more salutary. And whatever I wrote, I willingly laid before all, that I might have judges rather than disciples. If anywhere I exceeded through excessive speech—as it is written, “In much speaking you shall not escape sin” (Prov. 10)—an importunate defense has never made me a heretic. I am always prepared to correct or erase my ill-spoken words. In this resolution I shall certainly persevere to the end.

But as I would wish to correct any ill-spoken words of mine, so it is fitting that I repel charges wrongly brought against me. For Blessed Augustine says, “Cruel is the man who neglects his reputation”; and according to Tully, “Silence resembles confession.” Therefore I have judged it fair to reply to the articles drawn up against me, observing the rule which Blessed Gregory, in these words, lays down for believers regarding the tongues of detractors: “We must know that we ought not by our zeal to provoke the tongues of detractors, lest they perish; but when they have been provoked by their own malice, we ought to bear them with equanimity, so that our merit may increase. Yet sometimes they must be restrained, lest, while they spread evil reports about us, they corrupt the innocent hearts of those who might have listened to us for good.”

Let brotherly charity therefore recognize me, however unworthy, as a son of the Church: with it I wholly receive everything that it receives and reject what it rejects. Nor have I ever torn apart the truth of faith, though I am inferior to others in the quality of my conduct. [Col. 0330A] Thus, whatever has been alleged against me through malice or error—that I wrote concerning God that the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power—I abhor, detest, and, as is most just, condemn these words, which are not so much human as devilish, together with their author. If anyone finds them in my writings, I declare myself not only a heretic but even a heresiarch.

I profess that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father, so that they are of the same substance, altogether the same will and power, as the Father; for where the essence is the same, there can be no diversity of will or inequality of power. Whoever asserts that I wrote that the Holy Spirit is not also of the substance of the Father and Son has acted from malice or the greatest ignorance.

I profess that the Son of God alone was incarnate, in order to free us from the slavery of sin and the yoke of the devil, and by his death to open for us the entrance into the heavenly life. I both believe and affirm—and, affirming it, believe—that Christ himself is the true and only Son of God, begotten before the ages from the Father’s substance; and that the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Trinity, proceeds from both the Son himself and the Father.

I say that God’s grace is so necessary for all that neither natural capacity nor freedom of choice can suffice for salvation without it. Grace itself precedes us, so that we may will; follows us, so that we may be able; and preserves us, [Col. 0330C] so that we may persevere. I believe that God does only those things which it is fitting for him to do, and that he could do many things which he does not do. Many deeds done through ignorance must also be imputed as fault, especially when our negligence causes us not to know what it was necessary for us to know—as in the case of the man of whom the Psalmist says: “He was unwilling to understand, so that he might do good” (Ps. 35).

I confess that God frequently prevents evils, because he not only forestalls the outcome intended by evil persons so that they cannot do what they wish, but also changes their will so that they utterly desist from the evil they had planned. I affirm that from Adam, in whom we all sinned, [Col. 0331A] we contracted both guilt and punishment, because his sin became the origin and cause of all our sins. I confess that Christ’s crucifiers committed a most grievous sin in crucifying him.

Many things are said of Christ which must be understood not so much according to Christ the head as according to his body, which is the Church; for example, that spirit of fear which is the beginning of wisdom, the fear which perfect charity casts out. It must be believed that this spirit of fear was never in Christ’s soul, which possessed most perfect charity; though it is not absent from his lower members. For through union with the Word, that soul was of such perfection and such security that it knew itself altogether incapable of committing anything by which it would incur punishments or offend God.

Nevertheless, I acknowledge both in Christ’s soul itself and in his elect angels the chaste fear that remains for ever and ever, properly called the reverence of charity. Hence it is written concerning the heavenly spirits: “The powers tremble.” I profess that the power of binding and loosing was granted to all successors of the apostles equally with the apostles themselves, and to worthy as well as unworthy bishops so long as the Church receives them.

I profess that all are equal in the love of God and neighbor, equally good and equal in merit; and that no merit is lost before God if the affection of good will is hindered from its effect. For an angel, when sent by God, does not become better when he accomplishes what he wills to do; nor does Christ’s own soul become better when it adds execution to its will. Rather, every good person remains equally good whether he has time to act or not, [Col. 0332A] provided that he possesses an equal will to act well.

I confess that God the Father is as wise, the Son as benevolent, and the Holy Spirit likewise, because one person cannot differ from another in any fullness of goodness or glory of dignity. That the coming of the Son at the end of the age can be attributed to the Father has never, God knows, entered my mind or found its way into my words. Likewise, the assertion that Christ’s soul descended to hell not in itself but by power is altogether remote from my words and thought.

I am accused of having written the final article: that neither deed, nor will, nor desire, nor the pleasure that moves it, is sin; that we ought not to wish it extinguished. This too is no less foreign to my statements than to my writings. Yet I received with the greatest astonishment the conclusion which our friend appended to the articles written against me: “These articles are found partly in his book of theology, partly in a book of *Sentences* by the same author, and partly in the book entitled *Know Yourself*.” For no book called *Sentences* can be found to have been written by me. But, like the other articles against me, this too was advanced through malice and ignorance.

If, then, there is any consolation in Christ Jesus, if any bowels of compassion, I beg your brotherly charity not to sin by sprinkling with the poison of slander an innocence which truth frees from blame. For it belongs to charity not to receive reproach against one’s neighbor, to interpret doubtful matters in the better sense, and always to heed that saying of the Lord’s mercy: [Col. 0332C] “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Luke 6).

This is a distinguished confession of faith, except that Abaelard denies having taught or written the contrary errors and charges Saint Bernard and others who attributed the aforementioned errors to him with ignorance or malice. In order more fully to convict those persuaded by Abaelard’s lie to say that the holy Father and other most learned men fought against phantoms when they attacked Abaelard, it seemed fitting to attach to the anonymous abbot’s disputation against Abaelard the testimony of one of his own disciples.

This was Geoffrey, formerly notary to Saint Bernard, who wrote the final three books of Bernard’s *Life* and succeeded him in governance, becoming the fourth abbot of Clairvaux. He had previously been Peter Abaelard’s disciple and hearer. On the occasion of the subject which he was treating, he refutes one of Abaelard’s errors in the following words.

Geoffrey, Sermon 8, *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, on the text, “Purge out the old leaven,” etc.:

“Now in these paschal feasts we must not pass over the fact that we are commanded to devour the head of that same lamb with its feet and entrails; nor does anyone rightly celebrate the Passover who does not devour all these things. We fittingly understand its feet as examples of deeds: one faithfully devours them who effectively imitates them. Its entrails are the affection of its intimate charity, which he displayed to us so greatly that he laid down his life for his friends. Exceedingly unhappy is the one who does not devour them, to whom they have no savor, who is not refreshed, satisfied, or nourished by pondering them again and loving again.

“Yet I remember that I once had a master who, neither himself devouring nor presenting to his disciples anything more of the paschal lamb than its feet and entrails, defrauded both himself and his followers of no small portion of it. For, nullifying the price of redemption, he commended to us in the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion nothing but an example of virtue and an incentive to love. What the Scriptures testify—that the human race was redeemed from the devil’s power by precious blood—he said consisted solely in this: that an example was set before us of striving even unto death for righteousness and truth, and that an incentive, as it were, to love was supplied when, because of love bestowed, an occasion was given for loving in return.

“These things indeed are great and true, but they are not the only things. Blessed be the Lord, who afterwards gave both me and you a better master, through whom he rebuked the former’s ignorance and refuted his arrogance. For he, as a true Hebrew, eagerly devoured and diligently commended to us for devouring the head with the feet and entrails: thus preaching that the suffering Lord must be imitated, and the loving Lord loved in return, while confessing and adoring in this sacrifice’s principal cause—as in the Lamb’s head—human redemption.”

These are Geoffrey’s words in the sermon mentioned above. Because of them, some supposed that he had written a book against Peter Abaelard, from which the preceding words had been taken. But he wrote nothing else against him except the words reported in the sermon just cited.

[Col. 0333]

## ON THE ERRORS OF WILLIAM OF CONCHES, ADDRESSED TO SAINT BERNARD

(*Cistercian Library*, vol. IV, p. 127.)

[Col. 0333A] To Lord BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux, brother WILLIAM wishes the brightness of the eternal vision.

I greatly fear that I am troublesome to you and to your many occupations, especially since I have so often been for you an evil and importunate prophet, announcing devastation. For behold: from the root of the serpent rises a basilisk, obscure indeed in name and without authority, yet infecting the common air itself with deadly poison. For after the theology of Peter Abaelard, William of Conches introduces a new philosophy, confirming and multiplying whatever Abaelard said, and adding still more, with greater shamelessness, from his own resources—many things which Abaelard did not say.

Although the notoriety of this man’s frivolity makes the vanities of his novelties cheap and contemptible among all who know him, his person is not known to everyone reached by his teaching through what he writes. Therefore his teaching itself must be brought forward. Recently a certain brother came to us, fleeing the world and seeking God; among the other books he possessed, he brought one by that man, entitled *Summa of Philosophy*. In it, with the gaping mouth of a great promiser, he promises to teach concerning everything that is and is not seen. Beginning with God, he philosophizes about him as you may read:

“In the Trinity governing all things, the philosophers have said that there are power to govern, wisdom, and will. For if he could but did not know, how did he make things so beautiful? And if he made them unwillingly, then either ignorantly or under compulsion. But what could he not know, who knows even the thoughts of human beings? And who could compel the Omnipotent? Therefore there are in the Godhead power, wisdom, and will. The saints call these three persons, transferring to them terms from common speech because of a certain affinity: calling power the Father, wisdom the Son, and will the Holy Spirit. Power is called Father because he created all things and governs what he created with paternal affection. Wisdom, begotten before the ages, is called Son because, just as a son is temporally from a father, so wisdom is coeternal and consubstantial with power. But the divine will is called Spirit. For spirit properly means breath. Yet because the will of a human being is often perceived in spirit or breath—for one breathes differently when joyful and differently when angry—they called the divine will Spirit, but Holy Spirit by antonomasia.”

Concerning divine generation he says: “When the prophet says, ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isa. 53), he indicates difficulty, not impossibility.” [Col. 0334A] Then, as though about to declare it, he says: “The Father begot the Son—that is, divine power begot wisdom—when he foreknew how to create things and order those created. And because he foreknew this before the ages, he begot wisdom from eternity, and his wisdom is coeternal with him. This is what it means that power begot wisdom from itself and not from another: it possessed this knowledge not from another’s teaching or from the experience of use, but from its own nature. Moreover, for the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and Son means nothing other than that the divine will extends itself from power and wisdom as far as the creation of things.”

Behold a God conceived by thought, just as they say that God conceived by thought the soul of the world. Behold a feigned faith which the Apostle condemns, saying: “And faith unfeigned” (1 Tim. 1). But true faith cries out from the heart in which it dwells to him from whom it comes, and says: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me” (Isa. 38). Teach me what I should answer these opponents of mine; give me your understanding of yourself, which your truth, through illuminating grace, forms in the human reason that your love conforms to itself, so that in it I may understand how wholly without understanding is every human understanding which human reason, by itself, forms concerning you.

So that, when we speak about God, we may preserve not only the pattern of sound faith but also of sound words in faith: just as this philosopher of ours loves to speak from his philosophers, so let us speak, whatever we speak, from our Fathers, teachers, and guides—expressing their meaning in their own words, adhering to their footsteps, and presuming nothing from ourselves. [Col. 0334C] It is exceedingly dangerous to venture in such matters unless manifest authority protects us or the clear reason of faith guides us. The reason of faith is to place all human reason beneath faith, or to bring it captive into obedience to faith; not to be ignorant of the boundaries of faith itself, set by our fathers, nor to go beyond them in anything.

This man, whose words have just been cited, and Peter Abaelard, so far as one can judge from their writings, are of one spirit both in manner of speaking and in resemblance of error. They walk by the same spirit and the same footsteps, insulting the Spirit of grace while they search out the deep things of God with the spirit of this world. They think and say the same things, except that one betrays the other without knowing it: when one sometimes conceals, the other recklessly declares, what both believe.

Let those who read the entire texture of this man’s faith and the philosophy concerning God which he has assumed into his own speech see whether anything in it is wholly sound, or not wholly insane and heretical. [Col. 0335A] Moreover, he asks his readers that, if anything is found there which has not been written elsewhere, it should not immediately be judged heresy. “For,” he says, “it is not heresy simply because it is not written elsewhere, but if it is contrary to faith.” But Paul says: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything besides what we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1). And again, for repetition and confirmation: “As we have told you before,” he says, “so now I say: if anyone preaches to you anything besides what you have received, let him be accursed.”

And what, I ask, is more to be anathematized—what is more, not merely heretical, but pagan—than publicly to deny in speech [Col. 0335B] and writing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? For is it not a denial of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to assert that they are not what they are called by the truth of nature, but are called this only by designation? No one who has acquired even a slight acquaintance with ecclesiastical writings can be unaware with what authoritative severity this has long ago been condemned and anathematized in the ancient councils, treatises, acts, and writings of the orthodox Fathers.

For the moment I pass over the grave mark of Sabellian heresy which he brings down upon his own head when, intending to speak of God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, he instead sets forth God as powerful, wise, and willing—thus saying that the whole of what God is in himself and from himself is relative to the creature. Let us come to the matters he has proposed.

Purporting to teach the human race what it has not known until now, and to lead everyone, as it were, from faith to understanding, he proposes in the Godhead power, wisdom, and will, from which he constructs God as Trinity. That these three things are in the Godhead is evident. But since it is clear that many other things like these are in God, why, after selecting these three in order to construct, as he says, the Trinity which is God, are all the others of the same condition in the Godhead excluded, by a strange pre-judgment, from partnership in so great a dignity? But let us deal seriously with so serious a matter.

Let us ask how power, [Col. 0335D] wisdom, and will are in God—not only these, but also God’s might, truth, charity, goodness, justice, and all other things like them. Surely, as Blessed Augustine says: “Whatever is in God is God.” And still more expressly in *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0335D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, ch. 7]: “Above all, it must be maintained that whatever that most excellent and divine sublimity is said to be in relation to itself is said substantially; but whatever is said in relation to something else is said relatively. And the substance is of such identical force in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever they are said to be in relation to themselves is said, not plurally in their supreme unity, but singly.”

That is: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit—yet not three gods, but one God. The Father is powerful, or power; the Son is powerful, or power; the Holy Spirit is powerful, or power—yet not three powerful beings, nor three powers, but one power and one powerful being. So too with wisdom, goodness, truth, and charity; and with all things which, as stated, are predicated essentially and in relation to themselves of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Essence, then, in the nature of divinity, and all these names which, as stated, are said essentially and in relation to themselves of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, signify nothing but the most simple unity. But the Father’s relation to the Son, the Son’s to the Father, the Holy Spirit’s to each, and each’s to him, together with the relative names themselves, are what multiply the Trinity. [Col. 0336B] Therefore the Trinity is sought in vain where it is not: there is simple unity there. Accordingly, power, wisdom, and will must by no means be proposed in God as though to construct a Trinity. According to the rule of faith and reason already stated, although they may be pronounced plurally in the three persons, nevertheless in the supreme reality and in that nature where to be able is the same as to be wise and to be wise the same as to will, they are one.

Blessed Jerome writes to Pope Damasus as follows concerning the Trinity which, according to Catholic faith, must be proclaimed in the Godhead [Note: [Col. 0335D] In Jerome, vol. IV, and Augustine, Sermon 191 [Col. 0336D] *On Time*]: “Confounding Arius, we declare the one and same substance of the Trinity. Avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three manifest persons by their properties. For we confess not merely names but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases*, that is, subsistences.”

And Blessed Augustine, identifying the persons by their own names, says [Note: [Col. 0336D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VII, ch. 5]: “It is most certainly known from the Scriptures, must be piously believed, and is grasped in an undoubting perception by the mind’s sight, that the Father exists, the Son exists, and the Holy Spirit exists; that the Son is not the same one who is the Father, nor is the Spirit the Father or the Son; and yet that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one essence, not three.” And, discussing essence and relation still more subtly, he says: “There is no essential name in God which belongs to one person in such a way that it does not belong to all three. Nothing belongs to all three in such a way that it is not, in the supreme reality, one.” But regarding those things said relatively of God, one person is never so designated singly that by its very name it is not referred to another. For by a relative term each person is spoken of in itself in such a way that it is not spoken of in relation to itself. Relation, therefore, as stated, makes the Trinity; essence makes unity.

As for the fact that Scripture sometimes assigns certain of these names properly to the Father, others to the Son, and others to the Holy Spirit, we must understand, as the same doctor says, what this means and why it is so. For the whole of that which the nature itself is is found common to the three persons, yet there is sometimes something by which each person may be known distinctly. [Col. 0337A] Thus, although the Father is sometimes designated, as it were, singly as power, the Son as wisdom or truth, and the Holy Spirit as will or charity, one always returns to this: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one power, one wisdom, one whatever they are.

Then he continues and says: “The saints call these three—power, wisdom, and will—three persons, transferring to them terms from common speech because of a certain affinity: calling power the Father, wisdom the Son, and will the Holy Spirit. Power is called Father because he created and governs what he created with paternal affection. Wisdom, begotten of the Father before the ages and yet coeternal with him, is called Son because, just as some son is temporally from a father, so wisdom is coeternal and consubstantial with power. But the divine will is called Spirit. For spirit properly means breath. Yet because a person’s will is frequently perceived in spirit and breath—for one breathes differently when joyful and differently when angry—they called the divine will Spirit, but by antonomasia Holy Spirit.”

Behold how, in a Sabellian spirit, so far as lies in him, he destroys the reality of the persons in the Holy Trinity. It is agreed that the name “person” was devised by human beings.
