For, as Blessed Augustine says, when extensive debate was required against the snares and errors of heretics, this name was devised out of the necessity of speaking about the ineffable: when one asks of the Holy Trinity, “What are the three?” and no fitting name can be found, this term is drawn, by the necessity of answering and customary speech, from among many unsuitable terms, so that they are called three persons—not in order to state the thing as it is, but so that one may not remain entirely silent.

But we say and believe that no one is the author of the divine names themselves—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—except the divine nature itself: begetting, begotten, and proceeding from both. That nature itself is eternity, and everything belonging to that nature is eternal. Therefore, just as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are these from eternity, so they are called these from eternity—not by a human word, but by the Word of God, God the Word, who is with God.

Augustine: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be named by our voices, [Col. 0337D] which are certainly bodily and sound in a bodily manner, except in their own intervals of time, distinguished by a definite separation, which the syllables of each respective word occupy. But in their own substance, where the Three are One, that very reality exists above every creature without any temporal motion, and without any interval of time or place.” Again: “There, through the Word—not the word which is uttered, sounds, and passes away, but the Word which is with God, and the Word is God, and through whom all things were made—the Word equal to Himself and ever unchangeable, He always and unchangeably speaks Himself. For the names which are worthily spoken of God are spoken in one way by the Word of God, in another by the tongue of angels, and in another by the tongue of human beings. For, for them to be spoken by the Word of God is for the thing named to be what it is; for them to be spoken by the tongue of angels is for it to be contemplated and understood as it is; for them to be spoken by the tongue of the inner human being is for the heart to believe unto righteousness; but by the outer human being, for the mouth to confess unto salvation.”

But in striving to maintain that the Son of God is said to be so merely by appellation, he does not, as he claims, say what certain saints say; rather, he contradicts all the saints. Augustine: “We believe that the Son of God was begotten before every beginning whatsoever, that is, without any beginning of His birth, from the substance of the Father: God from God, Lord from Lord; not from nothing, because from the Father; not merely by appellation, because He has the name from the truth of His nature; not from some material, because there was nothing coeternal with God from which an origin might be supplied to the Son. What profit is it to the Son to be called by the name of Only-begotten, if He is deprived of the truth of that title?” Again, [Col. 0338B] Ambrose against the Arians: “Why,” he says, “do the tortures of disputation delight you? You hear ‘Father’; you hear ‘Son.’ Either erase the name, or confess the nature.” Again, on Luke: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Where are the Arians, to whom the Son is displeasing, in whom the Father was pleased? I do not say this, nor does any human being say it; nor does God speak through a human being, nor through angels, nor through archangels; but a voice sent from the Father Himself marked Him out. Therefore whoever does not believe the Son does not believe the Father. For He is the witness concerning the Son.”

Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “Eunomius’ dialectic is laughable. Since he was unable to understand, and unwilling to believe, that the Only-begotten Word of God, through whom all things were made, is Son of God by nature—that is, begotten from the substance of the Father—he said that the Son was not of nature or essence, but of will; namely, because the Apostle calls Him the Son of God’s love.”

He then strives to maintain that the very names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not in God in the truth of begetting, being begotten, and proceeding from both, but have been transferred to God by a certain equivocal analogy. He says: “Power is called Father because it created all things and orders them with fatherly affection. Wisdom is called Son, begotten by the Father before the ages and yet coeternal with Him, because just as a son exists temporally from a father, so Wisdom exists eternally and consubstantially from Power.”

Here it is plain to all how he attacks the faith [Col. 0338D] and opposes the truth: when he says that the Father, as Father, is not related to the Son but to creation—not by nature but by affection; indeed, that there is no Father at all, but that Power is called Father because of the affection to create and govern. Augustine: “That He is Father is relative to the Son; that He is Lord, relative to creation.” He says, moreover, that Wisdom is called Son because, as any son is temporally begotten from his father, so Wisdom is eternally begotten from Power. See the drunken man stumbling and falling. He sets Wisdom in relation to Power as a son to a father; but he sets Power as father not in relation to Wisdom, but to creation. Yet we have neither authority nor rational ground for saying that Wisdom is born of Power. On the contrary, in ordinary human reasoning power is more often and more effectively generated from wisdom than wisdom from power.

As for what he says about the Holy Spirit—namely, by what analogy the very name “Holy Spirit” has been transferred from our common usage to that nature—unless it is that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit, it is so frivolous and ridiculous that I should suppose he said it of the Holy Spirit only in jest or mockery. And I believe that He who dwells in heaven will laugh at him, and the Lord will hold him in derision.

For this merely natural and philosophical man, handed over to a reprobate mind, philosophizes physically about God; and, as above he makes “Father” derive from affection, so he jests that “Holy Spirit” derives from breathing. But sufficient answer, I think, has already been given above to Peter Abelard, who prates the same thing. As for his assertion [Col. 0339B] that the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Father and the Son means nothing other than God’s will proceeding from power and wisdom into the work of creation, blessed Augustine says: “If the Holy Spirit does not proceed except when He is given, then assuredly He would not proceed before there existed someone to whom He might be given; and He is no longer Himself substance, if He exists only because He is given. But He always proceeds in order that He may be, even when He is not given; just as the Son, in being born, has not only that He may be Son, which is said relatively, but altogether that He may be substance itself. And because the Holy Spirit proceeds eternally in such a way as to be capable of being given, He was already a gift before He was given.”

As to his statement, in expounding the divine generation, that the Prophet announced not impossibility but difficulty: whom ought one more readily believe, him or the holy doctors? The judgment is easy. Augustine: “Christ’s generation from a mother is beyond reason; but His generation from the Father is beyond understanding.” Again: “For the Son, seeing the Father is nothing other than being born from the Father; just as seeing the Father at work and working equally with Him are not different things for Him.” Ambrose: “Do you wish to know the divine generation? In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God.” Again: “How the Son is begotten from the Father cannot be known. The mind fails; speech is silent—not only that of human beings but even that of angels. It is above angels, above cherubim, above seraphim, above every understanding. We are commanded to believe; we are not permitted to investigate. Put away arguments where faith is sought. It is permitted to know that He was born; but it is not permitted to know how He was born.”

Let our philosopher therefore confess his ignorance where such great men profess admiration alone. Let him understand that, if the generation of the Son of God—or of the Wisdom of God—is the foreknowledge of creation, then what is temporal is the cause of eternity. Let him understand that in the simplicity of the highest essence there is no numerical plurality of the Trinity and therefore neither consubstantiality of substance nor coeternity of eternity.

Then, describing the creation of the first human being philosophically—or rather physically—he first says that the body [Col. 0340A] was made not by God but by nature, and that the soul was given to it by God; afterward, however, that the body itself was made by spirits, whom he calls demons, and by the stars. In one respect he appears to follow the opinion of certain foolish philosophers who say that absolutely nothing exists except bodies and bodily things; that God is nothing else in the world than the concurrence of the elements and the tempering of nature; and that this itself is the soul in the body. In the other respect he is plainly a Manichaean, saying that the human soul was created by the good God but the body by the prince of darkness.

In the creation of woman it is plain to all readers how foolishly and proudly he ridicules the history of divine authority: namely, that God removed a rib from the first human being in order to make a woman from his rib. [Col. 0340B] Interpreting this in a physical sense, he most arrogantly prefers his own invention to the truth of the history, making light of that great sacrament of which the Apostle says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. But I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Gen. II; Eph. V).

Augustine: “Adam, who was a figure of the One to come, furnished us with an image of realities and a great judgment of the sacrament—indeed, God did so in him. For while asleep he was deemed worthy to receive a wife, who was made from his rib; because the Church was to come from Christ asleep on the cross, from the side of Him sleeping, since from the side of Him hanging on the cross, pierced by the spear, flowed forth the sacraments of the Church. A great sacrament. God could have taken flesh from the man, from which to make the woman, and this might seem the more fitting possibility. For the weaker sex was being made; and weakness ought rather to have been made from flesh than from bone. Yet the woman was formed from bone, that is, from the man’s rib, and flesh filled the place of the bone. He could have made bone in place of bone; for making the woman He could have taken not a rib but flesh. What then do these things signify? The woman was made in the rib as strong; Adam was made in the flesh as weak—Christ in the Church. For His weakness was our strength.”

Had he believed this, he would not ridicule it. But what are we doing? Whoever reproves a scoffer brings injury upon himself. Then, glorying as though mysteries hidden from the ages had been revealed to him, he attacks religious men throughout, without naming them; yet it is sufficiently understood against whom, or against which persons, he speaks: namely, those who celebrate the Passover—that is, who treat of divine things—and, because their poverty of understanding does not suffice for eating the lamb, do not deign, according to the command of the law, to invite him as a neighbor, that is, one abiding in the same faith. But, as I hear from those who knew him, he was indeed once a neighbor, yet has withdrawn so far from those of whom he speaks that, unless he returns to the house from which he apostatized, he ought no longer to partake of the Paschal sacrament, nor be worthy either to be invited or admitted to the eating of the lamb.

[Col. 0341]

# BOOK ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE ALTAR

Falsely ascribed by some to St Anselm, as we have shown in the preliminary notice.

(*Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, IV, p. 130.)

# LETTER OF WILLIAM TO A CERTAIN MONK

[Note: [Col. 0341D] This monk is Rupert, who later became abbot of Tuit.]

Who had written concerning the Body and Blood of the Lord.

[Col. 0341A] To his dearest brother in Christ: may the eyes of your heart be enlightened. I read and reread, dearest brother, your work *On the Offices*, and its reading delights me greatly, both because of its usefulness and because of my very sweet affection for its author. But since the truth of charity and the charity of truth hate the cosmetic of flattery, I seem to see on the face of this beautiful work a single blemish. Although it may for the present be covered or colored among ourselves by a kindly dissimulation, if this work comes into the hands of those who love to find fault even with the good sayings of others, it will become a sign contradicted by many.

For when, in arranging the order of the divine sacrifice under the three heads of matter, intention, and final cause, you were discussing its matter, you said after much else: “But my opponent says to me: Christ, God and man, is living, sentient, and capable of movement in His body. But the body of the sacrifice has no life, no sensation, and is not capable of movement; therefore it is not the body of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0342D] Rupert’s words, book II, *On the Offices*.] To this you reply against your opponent: “I beg you, what life do you seek in the body of the Lord? There is animal life and there is spiritual life. Animal life exercises the five senses: sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch. This is animal life; it is carnal; it is flesh. But the Lord says that the flesh profits nothing.” And after some further words: “Therefore His wisdom ought to administer to us in the sacrifice spiritual life alone: namely sanctification, blessing, mercy and truth, righteousness and peace. This spiritual life is in the body [Col. 0341C] of the sacrifice without its animal life, as the light of the sun is in the body of the moon without its heat.”

First, I do not at all perceive what you call here “the body of the sacrifice.” For when, through the mystical blessings and the invisible working of the Word of God, body has been changed into body and substance into substance, just as at the wedding feast water was changed into wine, only the wine was present into which the water had been changed; so at the table of the altar the body of the Lord alone is present, into which the true substance of bread has truly been changed—except that in that change nothing of the water remained, whereas, for carrying out the instituted rite of the sacred mystery, the visible appearance alone remains from the bread that has been changed. Hence blessed Ambrose says: “Lest there should be horror at blood, therefore you receive the sacrament in a likeness.” [Note: [Col. 0342D] Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*.]

For Christian piety has always abhorred the assertion that the substance of bread remains upon the altar after the consecration of the Lord’s body; and it recently condemned this in Berengar of Tours and his followers. For if this were admitted, then the Word would be said not only to have become incarnate, but also—if such a thing could be said—to have become “inbreaded” (*impanatum*), if, as he said, bread passed into the body of the Lord in such a way as nevertheless not to cease being bread.

Therefore I understand “the body of the sacrifice” to mean nothing other than [Col. 0342B] that body which died and rose again; and we call it not “the body of the sacrifice,” but, as it truly is, the body of the Lord. Whoever does not believe that this is the same body that is sacrificed on the altar places himself among those who went back, saying, “This saying is hard” (John VI). Yet you too sometimes call that body of the sacrifice the body of the Lord. But, with your leave, you draw a conclusion which I do not know whether it fits the body of the sacrifice, but which does not fit the body of the Lord.

For no one except the fool who says in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. XIII), will deny that the body of the Lord—or rather, the Lord Jesus in His body, that very body, I say, in which He is present to us upon the altar, which is none other than the body seated at the right hand of the Father—has movement and sensation and is in every respect of our nature, though of another glory. But if by “the body of the sacrifice” you mean that visible appearance which appears upon the altar, namely on account of its likeness to bodily bread, then your opponent is foolish and inept if he seeks in the appearance of bread what belongs properly to a living body—that is, life, sensation, and movement—rather than what belongs properly to that appearance: roundness, whiteness, and the like.

[Col. 0343A] For that likeness of bread which presents itself to bodily eyes upon the altar, considered by itself, is not the body of the Lord. But since it was something adhering to, or accidental to, the former substance—that is, bread—it remained, when the substance to which it adhered migrated into the Lord’s body, for carrying out the instituted rite of the sacred mystery. This indeed is contrary to the practice and reasoning of worldly wisdom: that, when the substance is removed, an accident of the substance should subsist. But God is not subject to the law of nature; indeed, He Himself is the creator of that law. He can either preserve accidents when the foundation of their substance has been withdrawn, or transfer them to another substance—He who, according to one prophet, hangs the earth upon nothing (Job XXVI), or, according to another, founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers (Ps. XXIII).

He also works wondrously concerning this very body of which we speak that which the weakness of the human soul can scarcely comprehend even concerning His divine substance: He brings it in while the doors are shut and offers it to be touched (John XX); and when it is distributed in the sacrament to the faithful, He makes true of it what is written: “He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little” (II Cor. VIII). In a single moment He sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven and is sacrificed at the table of the altar. Likewise, in one moment, from the rising of the sun to its setting, and from north to south, He is present to all the faithful who faithfully celebrate, in His remembrance, that which He Himself delivered. No one who is in a body can conceive this concerning a body.

Therefore in the mysteries there is the true substance of the Lord’s body, but without its visible appearance; and there is the true visible appearance of bread, but without its substance. Hence blessed Augustine says: “What you see on the altar is bread and a cup, as your eyes report to you; but what faith requires you to be taught is that the bread is Christ’s body, and the cup is Christ’s blood.” And blessed Ambrose: “That they may be what they were, and be changed into something else.” For nothing false is to be supposed in the sacrifice of truth, as happens in the tricks of magicians, where the eyes are deceived by a kind of illusion so that what is seen appears to be something which it is not at all. Rather, the true visible appearance of bread, which was in the bread, now existing apart from its own substance, in a sense sojourns in something foreign, being sustained by Him who made it and transferring it to His own body.

[Col. 0343D] Yet, when transferred to the body of the Lord, it is not related to it as an accident to a substance; for, so far as the Lord’s body is concerned in its substance, that whiteness does not make it white, nor that roundness round, and so with the rest. But because, as blessed Augustine says, what must be understood invisibly must necessarily be celebrated visibly, that appearance is necessarily admitted, by a necessary and pious arrangement, as a kind of instrument for the rite of the mystery and for the assistance of taste. When that rite has been completed, it is consumed in receiving the sacrament. For it was consumable and liable to corruption; and this cannot be true of that Holy One concerning whom the Prophet says: “You will not permit your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV).

Then, when you deny that the body of the sacrifice lives with animal life, I wish you had stated more clearly what you call animal life there. For the Apostle says: “May your spirit and soul and body be preserved unto the day of the Lord” (I Thess. V). According to this distinction, which can be found in every human being, two lives are distinguished, mutually opposed to one another: spiritual and animal.

For when, of these three—spirit, soul, and body—the latter two serve the first, life is spiritual; when the first two serve the last, life is animal. Scripture customarily calls this life animal. Such indeed is the person who does not receive the things of God. Whoever says that Christ’s body lives this animal life does not himself live, and is worse than every animal. But if we restrict the term animality so that we call animal life that by which a body alone is given life and sensation, whoever denies to Christ’s body after the resurrection from the dead the life and senses of our nature, though of another glory, should consider how he can maintain what he says—especially since he takes away from the members the hope of resurrection which he seems to destroy in the head.

This is what offended me, and some of our brethren, in your work. [Col. 0344C] The following passage which you spoke a little earlier also seems to tend toward this meaning. For there it reads: “Therefore whoever eats the visible bread of the sacrifice and, through unbelief, drives away the invisible from his heart, kills Christ, who separates life from the Living One and tears with his teeth the dead body of the sacrifice; and thereby is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” And everything proposed or adduced in that statement concerning the matter of the holy sacrifice seems to accord with this meaning. Whether it needs correction I leave to your judgment and that of your readers.

Now there is one thing I beg of your charity, through Him who is charity: do not judge that I have, as one doubting the soundness of your faith—which is far from my heart and conscience—rashly and boastfully pronounced a censorious judgment upon the work of your study. Rather, before God as witness, I speak with fraternal charity and friendly concern, anxious for your sake. Thus I would have this work, and every work of your study and labor, to be refined and carefully considered before it goes forth into the hands of outsiders, so that one wishing to gnaw at it may find nowhere to set his tooth, and so that no one may encrust a pure vessel. Farewell.

[Col. 0343] (In both manuscripts at hand, the following words follow the preceding letter: “Here ends the letter of Lord William, formerly abbot of St Thierry; but because of an excessive desire for perfection and for the poverty he longed for, he finally became a monk of Signy.”)

The prologue of Lord William to St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, begins.

To his dearest one, chosen from among thousands: he who is his own, to himself. Since recently, at the demand of the matter itself, I had written briefly to a certain brother concerning the sacraments, taking from that a beginning for reflection, I began to compare with one another certain arguments drawn from the sayings of the Fathers. Gathering together certain matters which in their books, and especially in those of blessed Augustine, are wont to trouble some persons concerning this question, I began to test whether I might make anything from them. And when this little work somehow emerged from that compilation, I thought it should be sent before all others to you, to be retained only by you and me, so that, when you have corrected what needs correcting in it, it may be both my work and yours. Since I have made it and you have corrected it, it will be yours even more than mine, if what was not well made by me is well corrected by you.

After the end of the little work, I have separately collected the sayings of the Fathers for the exposition and mutual reconciliation of which I undertook the work itself, although I have scattered them throughout the little work; and, where it was appropriate, I preferred to set down their own words rather than mine. Here ends the prologue.

# THE BOOK OF LORD WILLIAM ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD BEGINS

[Col. 0345A] Since the truth of the Christian faith has, as it were, this special prerogative—that it itself is not to be sought through understanding, but that its understanding is to be sought through it—it restrains every proud or inquisitive investigator: everyone who, amid many varied questions, seeks in faith nothing but his own glory; and everyone who, as though reasoning and reconsidering, tests by certain doubtful deliberations whether that which divine authority commands us to believe ought to be believed.

Blessed are the poor in spirit, who, knowing themselves to be little ones and needing to be nourished with milk until they are fit for solid food, approach faith simply. Faith receives and exercises them; and theirs is the faith which is not everyone’s. For faith is one thing, knowledge another. Knowledge is gathered by reason and understanding; faith is commanded by authority alone. Whoever therefore is willing to believe nothing unless reason or understanding precedes confuses the matter. And, wishing to know everything, he seems, so far as lies in him, to nullify faith by believing nothing.

But one who approaches God must believe that He is (Heb. XI); and “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. X). Therefore, as I am about to write, by His own gift, on the sacraments of the most holy body of our Lord Jesus Christ, I do not think it irrelevant to remind jointly with myself those who think or speak about this and similar matters: not to rely too greatly upon their own judgment, but to set a limit to their prudence; rather, to fix the gaze of the mind upon the matter under consideration and, according to the saying of the most prudent man Boethius, to try to form faith concerning it as the thing itself is. For it is not the part of a rational human being, when treating divine things, to weigh them from realities below God or to confine the immensity of omnipotence within the limits of our possibility; or, as it were by disputing, to wish to shape that nature after the likeness of mutable nature, in which all the causal forms of things flowing away in time stand eternally. In such matters examples for reasoning or arguments for proof must be drawn from above, not from below. Otherwise, whoever does not do this is like, and ought to be considered like, one who attributes the spring to the stream, rather than the stream to the spring.

## CHAPTER I. How one ought to think of the body of the Lord; and that it is in different places at one and the same time, though not everywhere

With this consideration, therefore, we must not think carnally of flesh in the mysteries of Christ according to the flesh. For even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him so no longer (II Cor. V). Nor again, by investigating spiritually, ought we so to attenuate the truth of His flesh as to seem, through reasoning, to destroy its nature, united to the Word of God but not changed into the Word. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Heb. XIII). He glorified that nature in which He shared flesh and blood, in order that He might become a merciful high priest made like His brethren in every respect, in such a way that He did not destroy it; He exalted it in such a way that He did not empty it.

Thus we must think of the Lord’s body as it is: of our nature indeed, but of another glory. For if the body of our lowliness, glorified by resurrection, will be spiritual insofar as it surpasses in spiritual power, incorruption, and glory, how much more will that body in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily—the body of Christ, who rose from the dead as the firstfruits? If it will then happen in us that whatever is mortal is swallowed up by life, and whatever is human is transformed into its better state, so that what is now spirit, soul, and body may then be wholly spiritual, or spirit: how much more did Christ—God and man, the one reality of both natures from their union and lacking neither nature—advance in Himself, when in the power of His resurrection He brought to an end those conditions which belonged to a passible and mortal human being? He advanced that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification, so that, as the Apostle says, He exalted it and gave it [Col. 0346C] a name above every name (Phil. II).

And if the nature of flesh, from the time it was united to that highest nature, has been joined to it in such unity from the Virgin’s conception that divine things were never done without the man, nor human things without God, and through this unity Christ as man could do divine things even in the days of His flesh, how much more, when by the exaltation with which God exalted Him His lowliness was changed into glory, weakness into power, and death into life! For that which seems unacceptable to the reasonings of secular philosophy concerning His humanity glorified through resurrection—that He entered among the disciples, tangible, while the doors were shut (John II)—He had displayed while passible and mortal, when He came forth from the bridal chamber of the virgin womb with nature’s gates shut, to run the course of the human dispensation.

If the power of the Creator and the devotion of faith make it credible that that body could enter and depart through closed doors, I do not see what can make it incredible that that body could do, or have done, other things beyond the nature of bodies. For even our spirit, in which we were created in the image of God, since, according to the image of Him who created it, it stands in a certain manner in the realm of the bodily mechanism over which it rules as the Creator stands in the realm of His creation—so that, as He is wholly present in every place, so it is in its whole body and is wholly present everywhere in it, although human reason does not comprehend how this occurs—why should it seem difficult that the nature of flesh, united to that highest nature so that all that belongs to the flesh became the possession of that highest nature, should be able by divine power, especially after the glorification of the resurrection, to be in different places at the same time?

For, as the Apostle says, “although He was crucified from weakness, yet He lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII). Although rational spirit is admittedly of a worthier and subtler nature than any body whatever, yet I judge that that body which deserved to be exalted above all heavens in Him who is above all is worthier, subtler, and more effective for all that it wills than not only some lower spirits, but even all those who have deserved to be called by the name of heavens. For although its bodily elevation, by which that nature was lifted above the heavens, must undoubtedly be believed, nevertheless the exaltation by which it is believed exalted above the heaven of heavens must most truly be understood thus: that it was glorified above all heavenly things in dignity, glory, and power.

For, as the Apostle says, He “sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high, having become so much better than the angels as He has inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. I). That right hand must certainly be understood as nothing other than that which this Majesty holds as preeminent. Yet I do not say that the nature of the Lord’s body is everywhere, because it is not needed except where He wills and where He works by a definite sacrament of faith the purpose for which it was assumed and glorified: namely, the mystery of human salvation.

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0347D] Book I, *On the Incarnation*, ch. 4.]: “For what is beyond nature must not be interpreted according to the nature of divinity. For although we believe that flesh was assumed by Christ, we must not therefore distinguish the nature of the Word and of flesh. To us it is said: ‘If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.’”

God alone is necessarily everywhere; for, since all things hold together in Him, nothing could exist where He might be absent. Therefore necessity inevitably requires that the presence of His substance and power be everywhere. Thus it is certain that Christ’s body can be in different places in a single moment of time, but by the law of the creating nature, not of created nature.

But since it belongs to the nature of created nature to obey in all things the laws of the creating nature, if it sometimes permits its own established order to be relaxed by Him who instituted and governs it, it ought not to seem to err or deviate from its order—especially in that nature which, through the power of its person, is joined to that Word through whom every created nature was made and apart from whom it could not exist in any way, unless, as the Evangelist says, life were in Him (John I).

Yet if we consider that unity of person by which “although He is God and man, Christ is not two but one” [Note: [Col. 0348D] Athanasian Creed], according to which the Lord Himself says, “No one has ascended into heaven except He who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III), and of which the Apostle says, “Had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II)—if, I say, we consider this unity of person, then through the participation of human nature with God, Christ the man must be believed both to have been and to be in heaven, on earth, and everywhere, even before the Virgin’s conception; just as, through the participation of divine nature with man, God must beyond doubt be believed to have been crucified.

For according to this unity, in one moment when Christ the Lord rested in the tomb, He was in heaven, on earth, and everywhere, but according to divinity alone; in the same moment of time He rested in the tomb, but according to flesh alone; at the same time He was in hell, freeing His own, but according to soul alone; at the same time He sat in heaven at the right hand of the Father, but according to deity alone. And if we ask concerning any of these things, we must plainly answer that Christ the Lord did it, but according to the property of each substance.

But this is not the only presence of His body under discussion. According to that presence of which we began to speak, the Lord is present in His body at one time in different places, in a manner incomprehensible and inexpressible, yet certain by faith, wherever the matter of human salvation requires it. Yet in that manifestation of His body in which, after His resurrection, He ascended into heaven amid the rejoicing of the Apostles’ congratulations and the angelic testimony of the trumpet’s voice, He is contained in some one place—whatever that place may be. No one who does not wish to err should seek it by investigation. There He will remain until the times of the restoration of all things; and only then will He come, as He was seen to ascend into heaven.

## CHAPTER II. How the presence of the Lord’s body is now necessary to us
For just as the necessity of human salvation requires that he be present where there is need, so it also requires that his body be present in the manner needed. For that manifest presence of his, by which Christ lived among men when our nature had to be redeemed by his death—in which he alone [Col. 0349A] was found innocent—is no longer necessary to us. Nor could he otherwise be crucified, unless, through weakness and through the manifestation of flesh and distinction of limbs, he presented himself as one who could be crucified. Yet his presence is necessary to us in the manner in which Truth itself testified it to be necessary, saying: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have abiding life in yourselves” (John 6).

Therefore we must eat the flesh of Christ if we wish to have abiding life in ourselves. For his flesh truly is food, and his blood truly is drink. What is sought by food and drink is supplied in this food alone: namely, that one may hunger no more. And as ordinary food is sought in order that one may live, so the life by which one truly lives is attained only through this food [Col. 0349B]. For this food has been given to confer eternal life upon the soul, not to sustain the ruins of this wretched life, which is a vapour appearing for a little while (James 4). This, then, is the manner in which the presence of his body is necessary to us for salvation and life: namely, that it may be eaten by us, having become our daily bread.

But just as, when his visible presence was necessary to us, the Word, invisible in his own things, was made visible in ours by becoming flesh; so, when the matter of our salvation requires that his flesh be eaten, that flesh which is not itself edible in its own nature must become edible in another nature. This could be done most fittingly in those things which in some manner hold primacy among all the provisions of the human body: bread [Col. 0349C] and wine. For even literally, above all foods bread strengthens the human heart and wine makes it glad. Therefore, by the same condescension and mercy by which he deigned to lift the lost sheep upon his shoulders—that is, to assume our corrupt nature into the unity of his person—he now takes up the earthly substance of bread and, by the power of divine omnipotence, to which the power to do whatever it wills is subject in all things and through all things, transforms it into the reality of his flesh.

## CHAPTER III. On the visible appearance in the sacrament of Christ’s body

When he changes nature into nature, substance into substance, body into body, he causes only that to remain from what has been changed which the matter requires: namely, that when the substance of bread has passed into that [Col. 0349D] substance which sits at the right hand of the Father, it should retain from the quality of its former substance that by which, according to the rite of the mystery, that which was not so by its own nature becomes capable of being handled and tasted.

But, contrary to every principle and understanding of secular philosophy, when the substance of bread has been changed into another substance, he has so transferred unchanged, for a certain service of the mystery, certain accidents adhering to it that the Lord’s body, though whiteness is present, does not become white; nor, though roundness is present, does it become round. Rather, he has preserved all such things in such a way that, although they are present alongside the true body of his humanity, they are not within it. Yet they neither stain nor affect it as accidents affect the substance to which they occur; but, serving outwardly to conceal the Lord’s body in some [Col. 0350A] fashion—which truly remains in its own form and nature—they cause one thing that belonged naturally to bread and did not belong to the Lord’s body, but which the matter of the sacrament required for it, to pass into it through the service of its covering: so that, according to the rite of the mystery, that which was not capable of being handled and tasted by the quality of its own nature may truly become so.

And this, it seems to me, is that visible appearance of bread in the sacrament of the altar. Nor is it more wonderful that God causes accidents to subsist apart from substance than that he himself is substance, receiving no accidents: whatever he is, existing substantially; good without quality, great without quantity, everywhere present without place, subject to nothing, and so with the rest.

## CHAPTER IV. What in the sacrifice is according to nature, and what is above nature

[Col. 0350B]

But it is pleasant to investigate somewhat more closely the common, natural, and naturally possible transformation of natures or forms, so that we may see and understand what, in the holy sacrifice, God—the Creator of all natures—does according to nature and what above nature.

Boethius: “Only those things can be changed and transformed into one another which have a common underlying subject of one matter.” Nor does this apply to all such things, but to those which can both act upon and be acted upon by one another. This is proved as follows. Bronze cannot be changed into stone, nor into a plant; nor can any body whatever be transformed into any other body, unless the things passing into one another have the same matter [Col. 0350C] and can act upon and be acted upon by each other. Thus, when wine and water are mixed, both are such that they communicate action and passion to one another. For the quality of water can suffer something from the quality of wine, and likewise the quality of wine can suffer something from the quality of water.

Therefore, if there is much water but very little wine, they are not said to be mixed; rather, one is destroyed by the quality of the other. If someone pours wine into the sea, the wine is not mixed with the sea but is destroyed in the sea, because the quality of the water, through the multitude of its body, has suffered nothing from the quality of the wine; rather, by its own abundance it has transformed the quality of the wine into itself. But if the natures are moderate and equal to one another, or somewhat unequal, and can act upon or suffer something from one another, then they are mixed and tempered with moderate [Col. 0350D] qualities between themselves.

These things apply to bodies—and not to all bodies, but only to those which, as has been said, can act upon and be acted upon by one another, having a common and identical underlying matter. For every body which subsists in generation and corruption appears to have common matter; but not every body can act upon, or be acted upon by, every other body or in every respect.

But bodies can by no reasoning be transformed into incorporeal things, because they do not share any common underlying matter which, on receiving qualities, may be transformed into one or the other. The Lord’s body, however, has a common underlying matter with bread. Insofar as the Lord’s body could be generated and [Col. 0351A] die, it appears to share common matter with this earthly bread. Insofar as bread has common matter with Christ’s body, it can be transformed into it; nor, when this occurs, is there an utter departure from nature.

For if it is possible for a drop of wine to be transformed by the multitude of the sea into its own nature, so that no trace of it at all remains visible, will it be impossible for the multitude or greatness of Christ’s power—by which Christ Jesus the man is one with God the Father—to transform bread into his own body, by the omnipotent action of the Creator and the most obedient passivity of the creature? And for him for whom it was easy to create both the formed thing and its form from nothing, how will it be difficult to change the formed thing and preserve the form?

Thus, as has been said, for the rite of the mystery and for the aid of taste, with certain things changed and others not changed, our merciful Redeemer has made it possible for us reverently, [Col. 0351B] holy, and truly to eat his body whenever he blesses this bread for us—that is, whenever he transforms it into his body.

## CHAPTER V. On the spiritual eating of Christ’s body

But since it seems absurd and full of horror to the natural man, who does not receive the things that are of God, that a servant should eat his lord, we must consider with all diligence how such food is so necessary to us for true life that without it it is impossible to attain that life. The manner of eating must also be examined more carefully, lest everyone who appears to eat bodily should trust that he has abiding life [Col. 0351C] in himself.

But it has already been said what that life itself is, to which this food gives us life. For no one doubts that through it the life of the soul rather than of the body is sought. It is likewise plain to all that, as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. “God is love” (1 John 4). Therefore the life of the rational soul is the love of God.

Accordingly, this food must nourish us to love him who is himself his own love, and who is possessed where he is loved. For whatever our Redeemer did in the flesh, he certainly did in order to be loved by us—not because he himself needed our love, since he has no need of our goods and is in every respect sufficient to himself [Col. 0351D], but because those whom he had undertaken to make blessed could not be blessed except by loving him. Therefore, not merely by the love with which he first loved us, but by every service of love, he in some manner laboured to deserve to be loved by us: healing our weaknesses, raising the dead, choosing the ignoble things of the world, confounding its strong things, commending hatred of earthly things and love of heavenly things.

For this purpose he came down to us: that, by displaying the benefits of his mercy, he might gather into himself our love, scattered and putrefied among earthly things; refashion it into newness of life; and, having drawn it away and cleansed it from the dregs of those things which cannot be loved together with him, might raise it with himself on high.

Augustine, in the *Confessions*: “Thus that supreme Majesty, surpassing the higher [Col. 0352A] parts of his creation, raised those subject to him to himself. For in the lower parts he built for himself a humble house from our clay, through which he might cast down those to be subjected from themselves and bring them across to himself: ending fear and nourishing love, lest they should go farther in self-confidence, but rather grow weak as they saw before their feet divinity made weak through participation in our garment of skin, and, wearied, should prostrate themselves upon it; while it, rising, might lift them up. For what could wretched man do? Who would free him from this body of death, unless the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? In him, when the prince of this world found nothing worthy of death, he killed him; and thus the bond which stood against us was cancelled. But he willingly tasted death for all, and freed those who, through their whole life, were subject to slavery through fear of death. Thus, in sharing death, the Son of God deigned to become our friend, that we might recognize God as made in some sense like us, and, trusting in him, might leave our enemy and flee to our Redeemer.”

He descended so far to raise us that he did not shrink, for us, from taking upon himself that in which the enemy boasted himself to be greater and more worthy than our nature. For by yielding to him in sufferings and by dying, because he could die he seemed even to the apostate angels to be made a little lower than they; to the one who could not die, he appeared powerless and not dreadful. Thus, as the prophet Hosea says, we were to be drawn [Col. 0352C] with bonds of love (Hosea 11). Thus those who loved themselves even to contempt of God were to be healed, that they might learn to love God even to contempt of themselves. For he called forth in us for our sake what he displayed to us in himself for our sake: namely, that we might learn to love him even to contempt of ourselves, since he first loved us even, in a sense, to contempt of himself.

Without prejudice to the other mystery of our redemption, it was for the sake of this that he took flesh, exposed the flesh he had assumed to the necessities of nature, to injuries, and to sufferings, and did or said whatever he did or said through the flesh or in the flesh. Therefore, when from his flesh he offers so great a motive for loving him, he supplies our souls with a great and marvellous nourishment [Col. 0352D] of life. We receive it with eager mouths when we sweetly gather together and store in the stomach of memory whatever Christ did or suffered for us. And this is the banquet of the flesh and blood of Jesus; whoever shares in it has abiding life in himself.

But then we share in it when, with burning faith working through love, we place again upon the Lord’s table such things as we have received from it: namely, that as he gave himself for our salvation, under no necessity of his own, so we may give ourselves wholly to his faith and love under the necessity of our salvation. For whoever is fed at this banquet does not know how to eat his bread idly, but rises diligently with the strong woman in the night of this age to the lamp of the word [Col. 0353A] of God, that he may eat the labours of his hands, be blessed, and prosper.

Thus the good guest of Christ remains in Christ through the affection of devout love, and has Christ abiding in him through the effect of holy action. Since both are gifts of God, he advances more and more toward the fullness of a greater love for him whom to love perfectly is to be perfectly blessed. He eats this food more who loves more; and by loving more in turn he eats more and more, and loves more and more. Yet in this life we receive only a certain pledge of that love, awaiting its fullness as its reward in the age to come. Behold: this is to eat that flesh of which Jesus says: “He who eats my flesh abides in me, and I in him” (John 6).

## CHAPTER VI. On the twofold body of Christ

[Col. 0353B]

Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “But the flesh of Christ is understood in two ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, ‘My flesh truly is food’; or that flesh which was crucified and buried.”

For from that former flesh, which was crucified, this latter proceeds. And, according to the Psalmist, God brings bread forth from the earth (Psalm 103), when from the field of the earthly body which he assumed from us he brings forth the mystery of the heavenly bread and saving cup by which the Church is refreshed. And as the Lord’s body that died is called in the Gospel a grain of wheat falling into the earth, so in the psalm that mystical flesh is called “the fat of wheat,” to which the Lord, exhorting [Col. 0353C] his disciples, said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have abiding life in yourselves” (John 6).

And in the sacraments, the faith of the holy Church makes the Lord’s body, the sacrifice being in general the same, whatever may be the merit of the person through whom it is made; but the merit of life and the disposition of minds in the hearts of those ministering or receiving make that spiritual flesh through the grace of God. Hence the words: “May it become for us the body and blood of your Son” [Note: [Col. 0353D] In the canon of the Mass.]. “For us,” it says, “may it become.” For without doubt the Lord’s body is always made upon the altar-table whenever that solemn mystery is celebrated by the rite required; but it does not always become so for those through whom it is made.

## CHAPTER VII. That one body of the Lord may often be received without the other

[Col. 0353D] Since, by this reasoning, this flesh is understood in two ways, as one may be understood without the other, so one may also be eaten without the other. Hence likewise the words in the canon: “That as many of us as, by this participation at the altar, receive the most holy body and blood of your Son, may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.” For not all who eat bodily are filled spiritually with that heavenly blessing and grace.

Hence also: “That what we perform in time we may attain in eternal joys.” Likewise: “That what we have received to be taken in visible mysteries, we may attain by invisible effect.” And many statements of this kind. For according to Isaiah, all who love pleasures more than God are sanctified in victims and thresholds, because they cannot enter into the mysteries of truth; and they eat foods of impiety, since they are not holy in body and spirit. Nor do they eat the flesh of Jesus or drink the blood of which he himself speaks: “He who eats my flesh” (ibid.), and the rest.

For those are sanctified at thresholds who in this sacrament attend only to what they receive bodily; and, as they in some way venerate it as holy, so they eat foods of piety. But because they drive piety itself from their hearts, they refuse to receive within the thresholds of their house the sanctification of heavenly grace. They do not become the body of Christ by receiving Christ’s body. Therefore they do not eat that flesh of Jesus of which we spoke above [Col. 0354B], nor drink his blood; but what they eat and drink, they eat and drink unto judgment for themselves.

For just as the sun, by the one heat of its ray, melts wax here and hardens mud there, and, though not diverse in itself, works diversely in things by using the materials of things as it finds them; so Christ’s grace, as far as he is concerned, pours itself into all in one manner, but, finding different minds, works differently in them: mercifully softening one into love of himself, and justly hardening another by withholding mercy. For “he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9).

Augustine: “Such was Judas at the Saviour’s supper: to him the Lord’s morsel, which he received from his hand, was poison. When he received it, the enemy entered into him—not because the morsel was evil, but because an evil man received a good thing [Col. 0354C] evilly.” Judas and Peter both received from the one bread; but what portion has the faithful with the faithless? Peter received unto life; Judas unto death. Thus, according to their differing understanding and differing effect, though Christ’s bread is one, yet in some manner the bread received by Peter was one thing and that received by Judas another; and one may be received without the other.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the bodily eating of the Lord’s body

But enough, I think, has now been said about the spiritual eating of Christ’s spiritual flesh. To sum up much briefly: it is nothing other than to set one’s heart upon his power and carry the matter into deed and effect. And now the order of the subject itself seems to require [Col. 0354D] that we also speak of bodily eating.

Bodily eating is the bodily reception of the Lord’s body, whether worthily or unworthily, whether unto life or unto death. For although the former suffices if an unavoidable necessity compels this, yet the latter must not be omitted. The former is sufficient in itself, because there can be no doubt whatever that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ’s body; nor is he excluded from the fellowship of that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking the cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body.

[Col. 0355A] For he is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he is found to possess that which the sacrament itself signifies. Yet reception of the sacrament must not be neglected, because each doorpost of our house—that is, body and soul—must be marked with the blood of the lamb, lest it be ravaged by the destroyer and lest the scourge draw near to our dwelling.

Moreover, the nature of our flesh, which in its first parent was corrupted by unlawful food and, through original propagation, was wholly infected by sin and the penalty of sin, and handed over to eternal death and corruption, had to be healed by the antidote of another food, as the Christian poet Sedulius says most beautifully:

> You restore ruined humanity, undone by the sweetness of the forbidden apple,  
> with a better food; and by the drink of sacred blood,  
> you drive out the poison instilled by the serpent.

[Col. 0355B] The flesh of Christ, received by the mouth of our flesh, must by no means be judged according to the rule of ordinary foods. For this food is not for the belly but for the mind. It is wholly unlike those foods of which it is said: “Everything which enters the mouth goes into the belly and is expelled into the latrine” (Matthew 15). This is food which does not go into the body, because it is not changed into the nature of the body as other foods are; rather, it changes our body into its own nature, preparing and fitting it for the resurrection to come and for perpetual incorruption. It is in us and where it was—namely, at the right hand of the Father.

For thus its natural property, through the sacrament, becomes the sacrament of perfect unity, when these things received and drunk bring about that both we are in Christ and Christ is in us. Therefore he himself is in us through the flesh; and we are in him, according to that which we are, in God. Thus the cause of our life is that we who are fleshly have Christ abiding in us through the flesh, so that we shall live through him on the same condition on which he lives through the Father.

## CHAPTER IX. On the different sacraments of the Lord’s body, and on the very name “sacrament”

It should be known that the flesh or body of Christ which is sacrificed on the altar of the cross and on the altar, and is eaten bodily, is the sacrament of that flesh or spiritual body of which we have spoken much above. Let no one accuse me of presumptuous novelty because I call Christ’s body the sacrament of Christ’s body. For Paul also says to Timothy that the mystery of godliness is great, which was manifested in the flesh [Col. 0355D] (1 Timothy 3). And blessed Ambrose, in his book to Gratian, says that the Father’s only-begotten appeared to men through the sacrament of the assumed man. The other doctors of the Church say that those who eat unworthily eat Christ’s body only sacramentally.

Yet it has been established above that they do eat Christ’s body, although they do not eat that flesh which gives life through the life-giving Spirit. For, like Judas, they are permitted to rush to their judgment against that flesh, so to speak, of which the Apostle says: “And he reconciled us [Col. 0356A] in the body of his flesh through death” (Colossians 1)—a flesh which is the sacrament of that other flesh. By the wondrous patience of God, they are permitted, by eating Christ’s body unworthily, to crucify Christ again for themselves, as the Apostle says, and to expose him to public shame; and, as it were, to bind him to themselves against his will with unworthy and defiled hands, while they eat his body sacramentally, though he had prepared it as food for eternal life.

Unless they regarded as unclean the blood of the covenant, they would consider it dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God—upon whom they themselves lay bloody hands when they eat without discerning the Lord’s body. Yet gentle Jesus, while it is the time of patience, bears these persons with the same mercy by which he bore the Jews while they mocked, spat upon, and crucified him: persons such as those Jews were, who are, properly speaking, similarly occupied toward him [Col. 0356B].

Thus, as we began to say, one flesh of Christ is the sacrament of the other. For a sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing. A sign is that which, beyond the appearance it presents, causes something else to come to mind. That flesh which is called food because it brings about true life has, in turn, as its sacrament the flesh of Christ which was crucified and rose again. For consideration of why that flesh was assumed and why it was so ordered brings the former flesh to mind; and, received faithfully by the mouth of the body, it brings the former into the refreshment of the mind.

Again, the flesh which was crucified has its sacrament in the visible form of bread; because when its breaking, laying down, [Col. 0356C] and lifting up, and the other things which, although visibly celebrated there, are nevertheless understood invisibly, are considered in the mysteries, it brings to the minds of believers Christ’s death, burial, ascension into heaven, and the whole order of the thing of which it is the sacrament. Moreover, because bread holds primacy among all foods, its visible appearance can be a sacrament of that flesh which is called truly food because it nourishes unto true life.

But Christ’s material flesh, although it is the sacrament of that spiritual flesh, is nevertheless truly Christ’s flesh. That visible appearance of bread, however, considered in itself, is not Christ’s flesh or body, except that it is so called according to that customary usage of Scripture by which sacraments frequently receive the names of those things whose likeness they bear, and therefore of which they are sacraments. “For if sacraments did not possess some likeness of the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all” [Note: [Col. 0355D] Augustine, Epistle 23.].

Because of this likeness, as Christ was called the rock—“The rock,” he says, “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10)—so also that manna which the fathers of the unbelieving Jews ate as a sacrament of the Lord’s body, and died [Col. 0356D] (Exodus 16), may be called the Lord’s body; not because manna was evil, but because they ate it evilly. On this basis the Lord’s body which he took from us and that manna [Col. 0357A] (Numbers 11) are compared and are alike, not in what they are, but in what they signify.

Of what thing the Lord’s body is a sacrament has been sufficiently explained above. Manna likewise bore the type and expressed the likeness of the same thing—not in one respect but in many, which it would now take too long to pursue. Therefore it is rightly called its sacrament. Thus, though manna and the Lord’s body are not one, they nevertheless signify one thing: namely, the bread which came down from heaven.

Augustine: “Manna signified this bread; the altar of God signifies this bread. Those were sacraments; these also are sacraments. They differ in signs; they are alike in the thing which they signify. They all ate the same spiritual food—certainly the same spiritual food, though a different bodily food, because they had manna and we have something else; but spiritually the same as we have [Col. 0357B]. And they all drank the same spiritual drink: they had one thing, we another, in visible appearance; yet it was the same in spiritual power. How, then, the same drink? ‘They drank,’ he says, ‘from the spiritual rock which followed them; and the rock was Christ’ (1 Corinthians 10). The same bread, the same drink. Christ was the rock in the sign; the true Christ is in flesh and Word. ‘This, then, is the bread coming down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die’ (John 6); but this concerns the power of the sacrament, not the visible sacrament. He eats who eats within, not without; who eats with the heart, not one who presses with the tooth. ‘The bread,’ he says, ‘which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world’ (ibid.).” When could flesh grasp what he said, calling bread flesh? That which flesh cannot grasp is called flesh; and for that reason flesh is all the less able to grasp it because it is called flesh.

By the same rationale of likeness, that same body of Christ which was taken from the earth, together with its sacrament, that visible appearance, are sacraments of the other body of Christ, which is the Church, whose head is Christ. For what diversity of members is in a body, such is diversity of graces in the Church; and love reduces both kinds of diversity to unity. For as the diverse members of a body, serving, ministering, and adhering mutually to one another, bring about the unity of the body, so the members of the Church, adhering to their head and mutually to one another under him, [Col. 0357D] bring about the most beautiful unity of their body.

Again, consider the forms in which the Lord chose to commend his body and blood. They are things which are brought into one from many. For bread is made one out of many grains, and wine flows together into one from many grapes. This is a sacrament of the same thing. And although in that holy mystery we are so by the sacrament of likeness, still more are we so through that reciprocal communion of natures: because, having become what we were, he made us what he was—Christ Jesus our head. Thus, by unity of nature and by the love of the Spirit, wherever he is, we also are; and, made his body and his fullness, we receive from him what we are, while we eat his body.

## CHAPTER X. Recapitulation: how one ought to think concerning the sacraments

[Col. 0358A]

Since, therefore, the matter of the sacrament stands thus, we must judge things as they are and weigh spiritual things spiritually. And when we receive the flesh of Jesus from the altar, we must take care diligently not to remain in the flesh in our thought and so fail to be made alive by the Spirit; lest, if we are not made alive by the Spirit, the flesh profit us nothing. For if we remain in thought in the flesh of the Saviour, not only are we not made alive by the Spirit, but we cannot even understand how the flesh of the man Christ can be eaten by a human being, except as those hard-hearted people understood it, to whom Christ’s saying seemed hard and who went back (ibid.).

For they understood it foolishly [Col. 0358B], thinking carnally that he would cut pieces from his body and give them to eat. Therefore we must think of that body of the Lord spiritually and in some divine manner, and discern it humbly—that is, think it different from all other foods—and spiritually eat the spiritual flesh of Jesus in the sacrament of his true flesh, which is received at the altar-table. Again, we must believe that the flesh itself which was crucified and buried is not killed by us, torn apart, or devoured under its sacrament as ordinary flesh is; but is handled incorruptibly, broken incorruptibly, and sacrificed under the appearance of bread, and is never consumed. For it is not impiously killed by us but reverently sacrificed; and in this manner we proclaim the Lord’s death [Col. 0358C] until he comes.

For this is what we humbly do for him here on earth, which he himself powerfully does for us in heaven, as the Son who must be heard for the sake of his own dignity, where he intervenes before the Father for us as an advocate. To intervene for us is, in some manner, to present to God the Father for us the flesh which he took for us and from us. Therefore we sacrifice Christ’s body when, with the sure devotion of faith, we believe that holy body to be holy and sanctifying, and offer this faith in honour of him, since “he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one” (Hebrews 2).

For Christ’s death need not be repeated, because, once accomplished, it is powerful for eternal salvation. Christ died once and became an offering for our sins. What then do we do? Do we not offer daily? Certainly we offer, but as a memorial of his death; and there is one victim, not many. How one and not many? Because Christ was offered once. But this sacrifice is an image of that one. It is always the same; accordingly, this is the sacrifice. Otherwise, because it is offered in many places, are there many Christs? By no means; rather, Christ is one everywhere, existing whole here and whole there. As what is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so it is one sacrifice.

That high priest is the one who offered the victim cleansing us. We offer even now that same victim which, once offered then, cannot be consumed [Col. 0358D]. What we do is done in remembrance of what was done. “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” [Col. 0359A] (1 Corinthians 11). It is not another sacrifice; rather, we always offer the same one. More precisely, however, we enact the remembrance of the sacrifice; and we vow and render to him his gifts in ourselves and ourselves as well. At solemn feasts and appointed days celebrating his benefits, we speak and consecrate the sacred memorial, lest ungrateful forgetfulness creep in through the course of time.

## CHAPTER XI. Why such obscure statements concerning the sacraments are found in the books of the Fathers

For, having somehow escaped from rough ground, it is pleasant to consider more attentively why in the treatises of the holy Fathers there are found concerning this subject such doubtful and thorny statements, and statements which sometimes even seem contrary to one another. [Col. 0359B] Thus not only do those who collect them for the purpose of disputation find in them material for error, but even those who wish to establish the catholic faith from them cannot easily extricate themselves.

“The Apostle says, ‘Heresies must be, that those who are approved may be made manifest’” (ibid.). This is most clearly demonstrated in this matter. The disputes and most subtle discussions of the Arians have now made clear to all an exceedingly obscure doctrine concerning the Trinity. The errors of Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches, and many other heretics have now made clear and evident in the Church of God the grave and perplexing questions concerning the Lord’s Incarnation. Had necessity not compelled holy and learned men to think and express something more profound about the matter under inquiry, timid human minds would always have remained in obscurity [Col. 0359C].

Therefore, because from the beginning of the holy Church almost until our own times this question has been left untouched by everyone, the holy Fathers did not defend what was not attacked, except insofar as they sometimes advanced something concerning it in their treatises when the subject at hand required it. And because this did not answer questions which did not yet exist, it now seems insufficient to restrain them when they arise.

Against these errors, since the attention of those Fathers was not then on guard, they left very much in their writings about the holy sacraments which, though rightly said in their own place and sense, when torn from their contexts by those who delight in disputing or erring, seem in themselves to say something other than they say in the places [Col. 0359D] from which they were taken, and other than the writer intended. They also left many statements on the same subject which, though rightly said, were more obscurely expressed, since, being human, they could not foresee every future calumny of error. When badly understood, these seem to furnish the lost with material for error or contention.

Anyone familiar with the reading of the books of blessed Augustine knows that this happened to him in many cases. Before the Pelagian heresy arose, he had included in books already published not a few propositions which that heresy, when it arose, seized in support of its error, even boasting that a man Catholic in every respect held the same views as itself. Hence he was compelled afterwards to publish several books against that plague, and frequently to confess that his statements, though rightly made, ought nevertheless to have been expressed otherwise in order to avoid the perverse understanding of readers [Col. 0360A]. Anyone who has read his *Retractations* and his other writings can know this. Indeed, something similar seems to have happened to the aforesaid man concerning this matter, namely the sacraments. But one who wishes to err, or to teach error, can corrupt by a bad interpretation anything, however well said.

For, to omit other examples for the moment: who could believe that a most learned man had published in his writings something which, had any ignorant person written it, would without hesitation be rejected and spat upon at first sight? For what is more ignorant than to publish mutually contradictory things in one place? For, when he expounded Psalm 98, he says: “From the flesh of Mary he received flesh, and in that flesh he walked here; and he gave us that very flesh to eat for salvation” [Col. 0360B]. And immediately, a little later: “You will not eat this body which you see, nor will you drink the blood which those who crucify me will shed.”

What is more contradictory? Yet the prudent reader—the one who reads with that ecclesiastical goodwill with which secular writings are read by secular people, among whom the man most praised is he who can show that any author has expressed himself better, without doubting that he himself will rather be considered mistaken if he tries to prove that the author has erred in some point—the reader, I say, who reads the book of an ecclesiastical teacher in this way, if he finds something apparently doubtful and troublesome in it, does not immediately assail it with execration. Rather, from the context of the reading [Col. 0360C] and from the other writings of the same author, he examines, discusses, and reconsiders it; and at last he chooses first to confess that he does not know or understand, rather than to brand that author with error.

Thus Augustine’s statement must be understood: it is both the same body and not the same body. It is the same in material substance, but not the same in visible form. What we have said happened to blessed Augustine, anyone who has spent considerable time among the homes of the ecclesiastical library cannot fail to know also happened to holy Jerome through the Origenists and the same Pelagians, and to other teachers through other heresies.

Moreover, as has already been said, among all the varieties of heresies which, each in its own time, attacked the rock built upon the Rock—and which, while the Rock remained firm in its solidity, were shattered against it like earthen vessels—there was no mention of this question except in the Nestorian heresy alone [Col. 0360D]. Its advocates, wholly separating the divine from the human in the person of Christ, utterly denying that Mary was *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος), that is, “Bearer/Mother of God,” and affirming that she was mother only of a man, were asked whose body they professed the body received from Christ’s table to be. With heretical rashness they twisted to their error the words of the Lord: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man” (John 6), and the rest. From these words they tried to establish that what we receive there is only the flesh of the Son of Man—lest, if they confessed it to be the Lord’s body, they should speak against themselves by agreeing that in Christ, God and man, there is unity of person [Col. 0361A].

They therefore said that this flesh was that of a sanctified man, joined to the Word by a unity of dignity, or as possessing a divine indwelling. Against them, through the efforts of Pope Celestine and Cyril of Alexandria, the Ephesian Synod was celebrated, one of the four which blessed Gregory placed at the summit of authority. There the bishops assembled against the pestilential error of those raving men are found writing thus to Nestorius, the inventor of this evil:

> [Note: [Col. 0361D] Council of Ephesus, letter to Nestorius:] “We approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood; not by receiving common flesh—far be it!—nor the flesh of a sanctified man joined to the Word by a unity of dignity, or as possessing a divine indwelling; but flesh truly life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word himself [Col. 0361B]. For, being life by nature as God, he who is united to his own flesh declared it life-giving. And therefore, although he says to us, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,’ we must not suppose it to be the flesh of one human being like ourselves. For how could human flesh, according to its own nature, be life-giving? Rather, we must understand it as truly made his own—the flesh of him who for our sake both became and was called Son of Man.”

And near the end of the council:

> “If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and the very own flesh of the Word of God the Father, but regards it as the flesh of someone else joined to him by dignity, or as though it possessed a divine indwelling, and does not instead confess it life-giving [Col. 0361C] because it has become the own flesh of the life-giving Word, let him be anathema.”

## CHAPTER XII. On the threefold body of the Lord

Whoever, then, exercises himself in the treatises of the holy Fathers and wishes to proceed through these and similar matters with an unoffended foot, should set before himself as the first outlines of understanding the simplicity of faith on such matters. Since it is clear that the Catholic Fathers proclaim this faith throughout, now more obscurely and now more openly, when he sees their opinions converge in agreement with the faith, let him rejoice at finding the truth; when it is by no means clear to him, let him revere their meaning and blame the slowness of his own understanding.

Moreover, whatever appearance their opinions may display at first sight, if their consequences are found either not to meet, or to exceed, the prescribed boundaries of faith, let him not doubt that they are full of error, since they plainly do not accord with truth. For since the Spirit of truth has already long ago taught us all truth through the apostles and apostolic men, faith is not to be corrected by the test of arguments, but arguments by the test of faith. According to the apostolic command, “every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” must be destroyed, and every understanding brought into captivity in obedience to Christ [Col. 0361D].

Therefore, wherever the prudent reader finds something in books about the flesh or body of Jesus God, let him have recourse to that threefold definition of his flesh or body which I set forth above—not discovered through my presumption or fashioned according to my own opinion, but produced from the judgments of the Fathers—so that he may see and discern how the body or flesh of Jesus is being discussed there, and thus shape his understanding according to the writer’s meaning [Col. 0362A].

For the flesh or body which hung on the wood and is sacrificed on the altar must be thought of in one way; the flesh or body of which whoever eats has abiding life in himself, in another; and his flesh or body which is the Church, in yet another. For the Church too is called Christ’s flesh, as in the words: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2).—“This mystery,” says the Apostle, “is great; but I speak in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. 5).

Not that Christ is described by us as having three bodies, as the fables tell of that Geryon, although the Apostle testifies that the body of Christ is one; rather, a certain regard of faith in understanding or affection produces this distinction. But the thing itself retains the pure truth of its simplicity. For this trinity of the Lord’s body must be understood as nothing other than the Lord’s body itself, considered according to essence, unity, and effect [Col. 0362B].

For the body of Christ, so far as it is in itself, offers itself to all as food of eternal life; it causes those who faithfully receive it to live as one with itself, both through the love of the Spirit and through participation in its own nature, being the head of the body of the Church.
