Furthermore, since in Scripture, as we said above from the words of blessed Augustine, the sacrament often receives the names of those things of which it is the sacrament, this visible thing which is present to the eyes in the sacrament of the Lord’s body is sometimes called in Scripture the body of Christ. In such cases, the prudent reader, who is not untrained in the divine reading of these books, should prudently distinguish what interpretation each passage requires. Whatever course he judges necessary in this matter, let him see without hesitation how he may explain himself from the sayings of the Fathers which we have set below, and from many others which are found scattered throughout all their treatises in this manner [Col. 0362C].

### Diverse statements of the holy Fathers concerning the body of the Lord

**Augustine:** “Until the age comes to its end, the Lord is above; yet the Lord, who is truth, is also here with us. For the Lord’s body in which he rose had necessarily to be in [Col. 0362D] one place, but his truth is spread everywhere.”

**Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Hebrews:** “Christ is one everywhere, wholly present here and wholly present there. For just as what is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so there is one sacrifice.”

**Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*:** “‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,’ etc. It is a figure, commanding that one participate in the Lord’s passion and sweetly and profitably store in one’s memory that his flesh was crucified and buried for us.”

**Likewise, *City of God*:** “Those who are not counted among the members of Christ must not be said to eat the body of Christ [Col. 0363A]. Finally, he himself says: ‘He who eats my flesh,’ etc.—as though saying: ‘He who does not remain in me must not say or suppose that he eats my body.’”

**Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians:** “The flesh of Christ is understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself said, ‘My flesh is truly food’; or as the flesh which was crucified and buried.”

**Likewise, on Isaiah:** “According to the tropological sense, we may say that all lovers of pleasures rather than of God are sanctified in gardens and on thresholds, because they cannot enter into the mysteries of truth and eat the foods of piety, while they are not holy in body and spirit; nor do they eat the flesh of Jesus or drink the blood of which he himself speaks: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood,’ etc.”

**Likewise, on Haggai [Col. 0363B]:** “What is offered on the altar is indeed holy; but you are not so much sanctified by the offerings as you are defiled by dwelling in valleys and being among dead works.”

**Likewise, on Psalm 103:** “‘That you may bring bread forth from the earth, and wine may gladden the human heart.’ From the field of the earthly body which he assumed from us, the Savior brings forth the mystery of the heavenly bread and cup by which the Church is refreshed.”

**Likewise, on Isaiah:** “‘He fed them with the fat of wheat.’ These fats must be understood as nothing other than the mystical flesh to which the Lord invites his disciples, saying: ‘Unless you eat my flesh,’ etc. Thus he was betrayed in the valley of Gethsemane, which means ‘the rich valley of spices.’”

**Augustine, on John:** “The spiritual power of the sacrament is like light: it is received pure by those who are illuminated, and, if it passes through the unclean, it is not defiled. Even if the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil, but it is not contaminated” [Col. 0363C].

**Jerome, on Zephaniah:** “The priests also who serve the Eucharist and distribute the Lord’s blood to his people act impiously against the law of Christ when they suppose that the words of the one pronouncing the invocation, rather than the life, effect the Eucharist; and that only the solemn prayer is necessary, not the merit of the priests.”

**Augustine, on John:** “Judas entered and went out with his holy disciples; he approached the Lord’s supper with them. Judas and Peter both received from one bread; but Peter received unto life and Judas unto death.”

**Likewise, *On Penance*:** “The Lord’s morsel was poison to Judas; when he received it, the enemy entered into him [Col. 0363D]. Not because the thing was evil, but because an evil man received a good thing badly.”

**Likewise:** “Their hearts shall live for ever and ever. For that food is for the heart, not the belly.”

**Ambrose:** “This is not bodily food.”

**Likewise:** “This is not the bread which goes into the body.”

**Augustine, *City of God*:** “‘He who eats my flesh,’ etc. He shows what it is to eat the body of Christ not merely sacramentally but in reality. For this is to remain in Christ: that Christ may remain in him.”

**Likewise, against Faustus:** “What else are bodily sacraments but certain visible words, as it were, of sacrifice—yet mutable and temporal?”

**Likewise, *On One Baptism*:** “If we direct our attention to the visible things themselves through which the sacraments are administered, who does not know that they are corruptible? But if we direct it to that which is effected through them, who does not judge that it cannot be corrupted?” [Col. 0364A]

**Likewise, *On Faith, to Peter*:** “In faith and charity the holy Church does not cease to offer throughout the whole world the sacrifice of bread and wine.”

**Likewise, in a sermon on the sacraments:** “In this sacrament he commended to us his body and blood, which he also made us ourselves. For we too are his body, and through his mercy we ourselves are what we receive. Remember: you did not exist, and you were created; you were brought to the Lord’s threshing floor; through the labors of oxen—that is, those proclaiming the Gospel—you were threshed, when you were held back as catechumens; you were stored in granaries; you gave your offerings, you received greater things, and afterwards you came from the side-chambers to the water [Col. 0364B]; and you are with his Spirit, and you have become the Lord’s bread. Behold what you have received. Therefore, as you see that what has been made is one, be one yourselves by loving one another and holding one faith, one hope, indivisible charity. As there was one thing in many clusters, and now it is wine, so after the pressing of the winepress there is one cup in sweetness. And after those fasts you came into Christ’s vessel as if to a cup; there you are, and we are with you. For we are together; we drink this together, because we live together.”

**Likewise, to Boniface:** “We often speak in such a way that, as Easter approaches, we say that the Lord’s passion will be tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, although he suffered so many years ago and that passion occurred only once. Indeed, on the Lord’s Day itself we say, ‘Today the Lord rose,’ although so many years have passed since he rose. Yet no one is so foolish as to accuse us of lying when we speak thus, because we call these days by resemblance to those on which these events occurred: so that the day is said to be the very day, though it is not that day, but resembles it through the cycle of time; and things which were not done on that day, but long ago, are said to occur on that day because of the celebration of the sacrament [Col. 0364C].

“Was not Christ sacrificed once in himself? Yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed for the people not only throughout all the days of Easter but every day. Nor does one who, when asked, replies that he is sacrificed, surely lie. For unless sacraments possessed some likeness to those things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they commonly receive even the names of the things themselves. Thus, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body; the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; so too the sacrament of faith is faith” [Col. 0364D].

**Likewise, on John:** “The flesh was a vessel. Attend to what it possessed, not what it was. Let the spirit come to the flesh as charity to knowledge, and it is greatly beneficial.”

**Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians:** “Just as the head in animals has members subject to it, some of which are diseased and weak, so our Lord Jesus Christ, being the head of the Church, has as members subject to him all who are gathered in the Church, both saints and sinners: saints subject by their will, sinners subject to him by necessity [Col. 0365A]. Thus even enemies are subject beneath his feet.”

**Likewise, on Hosea:** “Over wheat and wine—the false mysteries of Christ’s body and blood—heretics cut themselves and set up diverse tabernacles for themselves, and they have been overthrown into nothingness. For if God is truth, whatever is contrary to truth is falsehood and is called nothing.”

**Likewise, on Psalm [Col. 0366A] 165:** “‘He gives food to the hungry.’ Someone may suppose that he speaks of the heavenly bread of the mysteries. We do indeed receive it in this sense, because it is truly Christ’s flesh. But let us say it differently: Christ is bread; his flesh is the divine Word and heavenly teaching which refreshes our soul.”

*Here ends the book of Lord William on the Body and Blood of the Lord.*

> [Note: [Col. 0365A] From manuscript codices.]

[Col. 0365]

# MIRROR OF FAITH

(*Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, as above, p. 79.)

[Col. 0365B] Among all the saving ordinances of God our Savior which our God—the God who saves—has set before humankind to be observed for its salvation, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 13), “these three remain: faith, hope, and charity,” and they are especially to be observed by mortal persons who are to be saved.

> [Note: [Col. 0365] Certain material seems to have crept from the margin of the codex into the text, disturbing the sense.]

For the holy Trinity established this trinity in the faithful mind, in its own image and likeness, by which we are renewed after the image of him who created us in our inward person. It is that structure of human salvation, for the building and construction of which in the hearts of believers all divinely inspired Scripture keeps watch. For a human being begins from faith. Indeed, while we are away from the Lord on pilgrimage, the Apostle does not deceive us when he says (Eph. 3) that Christ dwells in our hearts through faith.

Hope too is necessary for our pilgrimage [Col. 0365C]. For it is hope that consoles us on the way. Take away from a traveler the hope of arriving, and the strength for walking is broken. But when we have arrived where we are tending, faith will no longer be. For will we be told, “Believe”? Certainly not, because we shall see God and contemplate him. Nor will hope then be necessary, when the thing itself is present. “For what a person sees, why does he hope for it?” (Rom. 8.) Yet faith and hope will not perish, but will pass into their realities: what was believed will be seen, and what was hoped for will be possessed. Charity, however, will not merely remain; it will be perfect, when what is now loved by believing and hoping will then be loved by seeing and possessing.

Meanwhile, it is easy to observe how necessary these three are for the person who desires to direct himself toward that unbounded light [Col. 0365D]. For the eye must necessarily possess three things if it is already to use itself well, in order to look and see. The eye of the soul is mind or reason, pure and cleansed from every evil; and nothing first brings this about for it except faith. For if it does not believe that it will see what cannot yet be shown to it while sick, since it cannot see unless healthy, it makes no effort toward its health. But what if it believes [Col. 0366B] that matters are as stated, and that if it can see, it will see, yet despairs that it can be healed? Does it not wholly cast itself away and despise itself, and refuse to obey the physician’s instructions—especially because the sick person must find the instructions themselves harsh? Therefore hope must be added to faith.

And what if it both believes that all things are so, and hopes that it can be healed, but does not love or desire the light promised to it, judging itself bound to be content with its own darkness, which has already become pleasant through habit? Does it not nevertheless reject the physician? Therefore the third thing, charity, is necessary—and nothing is more necessary. Thus without these three the soul is not healed so that it can see God, that is, understand him. When, therefore, it has healthy eyes, it remains for it to look [Col. 0366C].

The soul’s looking is reason. But because it does not follow that everyone who looks sees, a right and perfect looking—that is, one followed by vision—is called virtue. For virtue is right or perfect reason. Yet even this looking, though it now turns healthy eyes toward the light, cannot do so unless those three remain: faith, by which one believes the reality to be such that the gaze must be turned toward it so that, once seen, it may make one blessed; hope, by which one presumes that, having looked well, one will see; and charity, by which one desires to see and enjoy.

Then that vision of God follows the gaze, which is the end of the gaze—not because it no longer exists, but because it has nothing further toward which to direct itself. This is truly perfect virtue: reason reaching its end [Col. 0366D], followed by the blessed life. That vision itself is the understanding which occurs in the soul when the soul comes to understand—that is, to see God.

Thus, since the righteous lives by faith (Rom. 1), these three certainly remain for the formation of the life of believers. Hence unbelievers cannot have conduct equal to believers, since they do not possess these three equally with believers. For whoever believes, hopes, and loves things different from believers necessarily also lives differently. For even if our use of certain things seems like that of the Gentiles, we nevertheless use those things very differently, because we refer their use to a different end, giving thanks differently to him of whom we do not believe false and perverse things; and because we refer the same things not to the same end, but to the end of the divine and lawful command: charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith [Col. 0367A].

Indeed, a human being supported by faith, hope, and charity, and holding them firmly, has no need of Scripture except perhaps to instruct others. Thus many live through these three even in solitude without books. Therefore I think that in them has already been fulfilled what was said: “Whether prophecies, they shall be abolished; whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be abolished” (1 Cor. 13). Yet by these instruments there has arisen in them so great a formation of faith, hope, and charity that they grasp the perfect without those things—such perfection as can belong to this life, and as can be grasped through faith, hope, and charity [Col. 0367B].

For the perfection of this life is nothing other than perfectly forgetting, through faith, hope, and charity, what lies behind, and stretching out toward what lies before. For the Apostle says this: “As many of us as are perfect, let us think this” (Phil. 3). Therefore, whoever truly seeks God the Trinity should seek to possess within himself the trinity of these three virtues and should strive to conform himself to their discipline.

Their conscience is a paradise of delight, rich in an abundance of graces and in the chaste delights of holy virtues [Col. 0367C], where the human inhabitant of that paradise converses with God, often sees him, is always seen by him, and often speaks with him. Where these three cardinal virtues are present, they are interconnected and joined to one another in a certain likeness of the Trinity of God, so that each is in all and all are in each: whatever, however much, and in whatever manner a person believes, that also, to that degree, and in that manner, he hopes and loves; he likewise hopes what he believes and loves, and loves what he believes and hopes.

For faith is the name of a virtue, a great and eminent virtue. But faith which does not have hope and charity is not a virtue. Thus demons too believe, and human beings who believe like demons (Jas. 2); except that certain people seem worse even than demons, in that people do not fear where demons tremble [Col. 0367D]. Faith must be certain if hope and charity are to be certain. For just as one cannot rightly believe without hope, nor hope without faith preceding it, so hope cannot have a form different from faith. The good believed shapes the desire of hope, since the believed goodness gives confidence to hope for the good believed.

Therefore, after the likeness of the supreme Trinity, just as faith begets hope, charity proceeds from both—that is, from faith and hope—because what is believed and hoped cannot fail to be loved, and must be loved in the manner in which it is believed and hoped. For just as there the three persons are coeternal and consubstantial with one another, so here faith, hope, and charity are not, as regards the substance of virtue, one earlier and another later in time. They may in a sense appear consubstantial, though according to the form of their differing affections they have, as it were, certain personal distinctions [Col. 0368A]. For the general virtue of a rational mind is right reason, and it has as many species as there are virtues attributed to a rational human being.

Indeed, the one form of virtue belonging to these three virtues—faith, hope, and charity—because it proceeds wholly from faith, is in this life, in which we believe, hope, and love what we do not see, faith, and is called faith. Through it we walk here, as long as we are away from the Lord. In the future life it will wholly be charity, both through the grace of its name and through the merit of perfection. Faith and hope will not perish, but pass into their realities, when what is now believed and hoped will be seen and possessed [Col. 0368B].

For even in this life, insofar as one sometimes advances into that very reality of supreme truth through an affection that tastes of the Lord’s goodness, faith and hope are sometimes not so much conformed to charity as united with it. Thus, as these three progress in walking in the light of God’s countenance, though each retains its own distinctive character, often in the three there is, or appears, but one face: that of charity.

For to those ascending from the valley of tears to the heights of the promises above, this charity, or love, or affection begins here at the beginning of faith, when the sun of righteousness immediately rises for the person first advancing from the darkness of unbelief. Then not only does one begin to believe and hope for what is unseen, but one also loves it insofar as it is believed and hoped [Col. 0368C]. Yet in this life no one whatsoever, however far advanced, should hope for the fullness or perfection of that love, until one arrives there where, for those seeing face to face, all blessedness will consist in possessing what will be loved and loving what will be possessed.

Meanwhile, it belongs to those walking by faith to lean toward and sigh for that place where they hope to breathe again after the weariness of the road and the tedium of pilgrimage. For the appearance of the highest good naturally always arouses and draws every rational understanding to love and know it: the purer it is, the nearer it already is to that good, and the more ardently it desires to see what is promised to the blessed pure in heart; for it is seen only by pure hearts, and hearts are cleansed for seeing it only by faith [Col. 0368D].

Whoever desires to love the Lord his God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind sighs for it; and, so far as he is able, he helps his neighbor—whom he loves as himself—to do the same. But as long as, from the sin of the first human being and the punishment for that sin, there occurs in the children of his flesh, who are also children of grace, what the Apostle says of himself: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person; but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive into the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7); and “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5)—as long as a person is thus, it is evident to all how far he does not love the Lord his God as he is bound to do [Col. 0369A]: namely, with all that he is and all the life he has, when he so often desires so many things outside God in so carnal a manner.

For as long as one lives here, carnal desire can be diminished and restrained, but it cannot be extinguished so completely as to cease altogether. Accordingly, that perfect love which is total, and which is owed to the Lord God according to the commandment of the law, is commanded in this life but is by no one at all perfected in it. Yet it is commanded so that we may not be ignorant of the direction toward which we ought to stretch. To the degree that it advances in us, the desires of the flesh must necessarily diminish, until it is perfected there where no desire remains outside God.

To advance in this here is to walk by faith. Whoever is found advancing in it when leaving this life, we must without doubt believe and hope will be perfected in the future life [Col. 0369B].

But we do not hold a right faith concerning faith unless we faithfully understand before all else whose gift it is. Faith is a matter of free choice, but of a choice set free by grace. For the will of a human being sold under sin cannot be free unless set free by him of whom it is said: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8). Of itself it is free only for sin; by this freedom all sin who sin through delight or love of sin. But by this freedom they have become slaves of sin and free from righteousness, having no freedom to will or accomplish any fruit of righteousness unless, having been made slaves of righteousness, they are set free from sin by liberating grace [Col. 0369C].

Among the children of Adam coming from the mass of ancient condemnation, God justly hardens whom he wills by abandoning him, in owed justice; and he mercifully has compassion on whom he wills by helping him, in unowed mercy. Where a person puts forward a good and free will and receives faith when aided, he raises a question and, when abandoned and rejected, merits condemnation. For he says: “Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9.) Let the person who hopes tremble where the one who despairs dares to speak thus. Let him seek not an explanation but beg for mercy; and from the one who is rejected, had grace not come to his aid, let him learn what he himself deserved.

For, as the Apostle says, “Faith is not for all” (2 Thess. 3). Whose, then, is it? “The foundation of God,” he says, “stands firm, having this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’; and, ‘Let all who invoke the name of the Lord depart from iniquity’” (2 Tim. 2) [Col. 0369D]. For all who from eternity are foreknown in God’s foreknowledge are those who have believed, who believe, and who will believe. They, and no one outside them, are the Lord’s sheep, the sheep of his pasture, who hear his voice (John 10), whom no one snatches from his hand; his people, knowing that the Lord himself is God. They are the true believers, the true worshipers in spirit and truth: foreknown from eternity when they did not exist; predestined that they might be something; called when they had turned away; justified when they were sinners; to be glorified when they become immortal.

Known and foreknown in God’s foreknowledge, therefore, they are made known also to themselves in their own conscience, insofar as they call upon the name of the Lord; and the Holy Spirit bears witness to their conscience that they are children of God. They are also made known to human beings, insofar as they depart from iniquity more than other people do. But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some are for honour, others for dishonour (2 Tim. 2). Why or how this is so belongs to the judgment of the potter, who has power from the same clay to make what he wishes, whether for honour or for dishonour. Nor must the thing fashioned answer back to its potter—man to God, clay to its shaper, creature to its Creator. Though he does all things for a cause or reason known to himself, since he is Lord of all, he freely does with all things what is good in his eyes; and surely, being good, he does all things well.

In this respect, just as the humility of the believer is the surest sign of the Lord’s sheep, which is to be set at the right hand, so the proud questioning of the unbeliever is the sign of the goat to be set at the left. For before God no one is saved unless humble in spirit; no one enters through the door of faith except with bowed head. Faith is the eye of a needle: the huge and crooked camel cannot enter through it unless it has been made lean and straight unto the humility and simplicity of Christ. For the proud and exalted person comes to the door of faith; and, when called to believe and invited to enter, he stands and disputes with the doorkeeper why, when one is admitted, another is excluded. At length, by the just judgment of the doorkeeper, the door is shut against him; and while disputing about those admitted and excluded, he himself is found among the excluded. For he says of each thing he does not grasp: “This saying is hard” (John 6); harder still is he himself. Going away and turning back, he is assigned to the things behind.

But the poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of God, working out his salvation with fear and trembling and not setting his mouth in heaven, comes and weeps; he prays to be admitted; and, when admitted, he worships—always fearful, everywhere trembling before the discretion of the potter, who makes from his clay whatever he wills. Even once entered, he is not secure so long as the perception of his flesh weighs him down. He proceeds with fear, advances with love, burns to understand what he sees, yet fears to search into what he ought not. Thus it is not of the one willing or of the one running, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9), that you will well, O human being, and that you believe.

Indeed, if you do not will to believe, you do not believe; but you believe if you will. Yet you do not will unless grace goes before you, because no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him (John 6). How? Certainly by creating in him and breathing into him a free will, by which he freely wills what he wills—that is, so that the good thing he wills belongs to his own will. For when God inspires us, there comes about in us a voluntary assent of the mind to those things that concern him; and with the heart one believes unto righteousness, while with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10). This is faith itself. Thus it is said: If you will, you believe; but you do not will unless you are drawn by the Father; and if you will, then certainly you will because you are drawn by the Father.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Or do you not know yourselves, that Christ is in you—unless perhaps you are reprobate?” (2 Cor. 13). But how is Christ Jesus in us? Certainly through good will, because there is peace for people of good will: namely, by willing that Christ may dwell through faith in our hearts. For this will is already, in some measure, love of Christ; without it faith in Christ cannot exist at all. Pious faith cannot exist without hope and charity. Therefore the complete absence of good will is a sign of complete reprobation and hardened unbelief, just as its good conscience is the Lord’s faithful testimony that we are children of God and of adopting grace. For why do you not believe, O unbeliever? Certainly because you do not love. You do not believe because you do not love; you do not love because you do not believe. Neither can exist without the other, because each depends upon the other. Begin to love—that is, act so that you may will—and you will begin to believe. You will believe as much as you will, that is, as much as you love. For will is the beginning of love; indeed, love is vehement will. And love for what is believed supplies the capacity for believing. Take an analogy concerning God the Father from carnal affection.

A person trusts the authority of his elders and holds without doubt, though he has learned it by no experience, that he is the son of his father and mother. For the authority of the father and mother whom he believes to be such is so great in his estimation that he neither wishes to disprove it, because they are loved, nor can do so, because they are judged worthy, by one who loves them, of being believed without doubt. You too, heir of God and co-heir with Christ, embrace the grace of divine adoption. Bend your knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named,” that he may give you, “according to the riches of his glory, strength to be strengthened through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell through faith in” your heart (Eph. 3); and acknowledge the dignity of your lineage, lest by unbelief you prove yourself degenerate. For even according to carnal generation, to deny one’s parents is a grave injury against nature.

Acknowledge Grace as your mother. Patiently endure her nourishing you in the lap of authority with the milk of simple history, and eagerly seek her breasts so that you may quickly grow. To grow is to make progress; to decline is to fail. Neither to be born nor to grow according to the flesh belongs to the will; but spiritual birth and spiritual growth belong to the will. Yet in this respect will is the daughter of grace.

Grace begets; grace gives suck; grace nourishes and advances, and brings one all the way to perfection. That is, it brings about charity: a great and rightly disposed will. When charity is at work, the Spirit is much more sweetly and much more certainly present, beyond every carnal affection, to bear testimony to the children of grace that they are children of God, than nature is to testify to the children of human beings that they are children of their parents. But the believer must know what he believes, and by what authority and teacher he believes what he believes. For one who is truly faithful and has good will toward faith by no means chooses, among matters of faith, what he shall believe; rather, without all reconsideration and hesitation, he believes whatever divine authority declares must be believed. Nor does he, fashioning new faiths for himself, embrace those things that seem more fitting to his carnal understanding; but he always seeks to embrace what is true, seeking reasons for it and adapting instruction to it. Nor does he hesitate about these things by judging them according to human reason; rather, he holds them certain, adhering to them in faith and love.

Yet it sometimes happens that some possess a faith than which none can be greater, being ready in its confession to give up their lives, just as, according to the Lord’s testimony, no one has greater charity than to lay down his life for his friends (John 15); and yet, in believing—that is, in thinking about matters of faith—they are darkened and troubled. This is a burden of the human mind, a grievous weakness, and a remarkable blindness. For it is often very easy and desirable for many, if necessity or occasion presses, even to die for the faith; yet in believing—that is, in thinking about the things of faith—it is not easy for them to attain the purity of faith itself.

Nor is it surprising, since those who are often most ready to die for the faith find it exceedingly difficult to live according to faith. Hence it is that, when things belonging to faith are heard in Scripture either historically, handed down morally by holy teachers, or treated in certain mysteries or sacraments, what is said is sometimes received by many believers with an understanding that does not assent, sometimes even with an erring assent, and in every case with great difficulty and scruple. People of weak intellect but still weaker faith, being animal persons, do not perceive, or scarcely perceive, the things of God. Although faith stands opposed to the reason and custom of humankind, they often—indeed, unwillingly—measure the infinity of divine power by the weakness of human understanding or of their own faith, as though human nature and its perception suggested that God can be, can do, or can possess nothing except what a human being thinks he can understand concerning him; they consider the sacraments of faith and the mysteries of the holy Scriptures to be inventions of human fabrication.

But the man of faith and virtue—whoever he may be, predestined unto life, anticipated by grace, and, like Paul, having received mercy so as to be faithful (1 Tim. 1)—though he may sometimes suffer some movement of his fleshly understanding in matters of faith, gives it absolutely no assent. Rather, like the faithful servant of divine authority, he first subjects himself with all earnestness of mind to the discipline of the faith which is learned; then, with every affection of piety, he strives for that faith which is bestowed: first for that which flesh and blood reveal; then for that which none but the Father who is in heaven reveals; first for the knowledge which night declares to night; then for the word which day pours forth to day. He labours to learn not only what is believed, but also the means by which faith itself may be defended against the enemies of faith, so that faith may arise where it is absent and be strengthened where it is present. He also conforms life and conduct, so that what is believed may not only be believed, but also hoped for and loved; understood through love and loved through understanding.

For thus the spirit that believes with God merits the Holy Spirit; grace merits grace; faith merits understanding and the affection of piety, and the understanding of love that brings every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ (2 Cor. 10). Thus, according to what is written, “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 6), the one who believes merits, by loving, to understand what he believes. For just as formerly, before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith that was to be revealed, and the law was our pedagogue in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith (Gal. 3); but when faith came, we were no longer under a pedagogue, but, having received adoption as sons, were found to be children of God, having received in our hearts the Spirit of God, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8): so also in this age of grace, before the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ begins to shine in our hearts, we must be kept and shut up under the authority of that same Gospel unto the grace to be revealed to us in the time when the mercy of God enlightens us. Let authority, therefore, meanwhile be our pedagogue in Christ Jesus, so that by the humility of believing we may merit to be enlightened by grace.

For when enlightening grace comes, we are no longer under a pedagogue, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty (2 Cor. 3). Having received the Spirit of the Son of God, we too become children of God; and, understanding and perceiving that we have God as Father, now with every confidence renouncing authority, we say to it what the fellow-citizens of the Samaritan woman said: “Now we believe, not because of your word; for we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world” (John 4).

Meanwhile, while a place is being prepared for understanding by believing—that is, by thinking upon the things of faith—it is necessary that understanding play its proper role, so that in thought a great place may be given to authority. Therefore, in that which meanwhile can neither be grasped by the senses nor investigated by any reasoning, one must yield most obediently and believe divine authority. Such is the evangelical history of the Saviour’s human dispensation and his deeds, which were then performed for those who lived then, that they might see and believe what they did not see; but for us they are declared to be believed because they happened thus, and through them we must believe what those people also believed.

But if the temptations of carnal perceptions begin to boil up in the heart—scandals against faith, sorrowful hesitations, and dark questions—by which even a faithful mind is sometimes accustomed to be darkened, not so much by the deliberate choice of the will as by the carelessness of a neglected mind or the natural volatility of rational ardour, the mind believes that it ought to be governed and entrusted to no one more than to divine authority: namely, that authority which divinity has established upon so exalted a summit of dignity, and which so many and so great men of God have commended to us by word and writing, life and death. When one piously and humbly rests in that authority, one rests well there, as it were in safety, until, through the working of the Holy Spirit, experience itself—as the prophet says—begins to give understanding to hearing (Isa. 28); until faith obtains that the reality which faith has preceded may shine upon the believer’s affection. Thus faith in Jesus Christ becomes in that person’s heart both an example of humility, an incentive of love, and the sacrament of redemption; so that, as the Apostle says, Jesus Christ may become for him, from God the Father, righteousness, wisdom, sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1).

Then indeed faith is rightly exercised; then faith is worthily considered in relation to faith, although it is no longer so much considered as enacted. For whatever belongs to faith the Holy Spirit in some manner actively works in that soul, when the affection of faith burns in the conscience; enlightening grace shines in the understanding; and the affection of good work shines forth in life.

But if, at the beginning of belief, authority as guide is abandoned, those walking in the perception of their flesh must necessarily perish from the right way; and some even among the number of the faithful are often made to stumble. Although they do not stumble so as to fall, they are nevertheless found to pass on neither without some danger to their way nor without loss to their holy progress in faith. For “the fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13). Another says: “How does God know? Or is there knowledge in the Most High?” (Ps. 72), doubting God’s providence. Another wonders whether God ought to have become human for the salvation of humankind. And there are many things of this kind.

For temptations concerning faith of this sort often try even minds more fervent in religion but still tender in faith. They do not meet them openly face to face, but lie in ambush secretly as though at the side, plucking, as it were, at the garment of faith from behind. They do not say, “Yes, yes; no, no” (Jas. 5), but whisper, “Perhaps, perhaps.” “Perhaps,” they say, “it is so; perhaps it is not. Perhaps it happened otherwise, and was written otherwise, because of something that was not written.” When the judgment of reason looks back, everything is thrown into disorder; and though the garment of faith may be found whole, it is felt to have been tugged and shaken. For there appears to be a reason that attacks and a reason that resists: the former animal and carnally minded; the latter spiritual and judging all things spiritually. The former hesitates, as though about things not experienced; the latter submits all things to authority. Moreover, it bears with difficulty that in some part of itself a matter should become at all doubtful to it, when it has given to that matter an undoubting assent on divine authority and unfeigned faith.

But what does the spirit that believes with God do? It reads for itself both the Gospel words of the Lord and his miracles, and in all things venerates and worships the holy traces of truth. Asked about faith, it says: “You are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. 16). Asked about love, it says: “You know that I love you; and I lay down my life for you” (John 21). And although, by the rule of authority, it believes all things of faith with an undaunted heart unto righteousness and confesses them with the mouth unto salvation, it nevertheless cannot shake from the ear of its heart the whisper, “Perhaps, perhaps,” of temptation. It is not itself speaking this, but it bears with extreme distress that some sense within its own soul speaks it to it. Therefore it groans at the Apostle’s words and is exceedingly suspicious of itself: “Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Christ Jesus is in you, unless perhaps you are reprobate?” (2 Cor. 13). And elsewhere: “No one speaking in the Holy Spirit says, ‘Jesus is accursed’” (1 Cor. 12). To this it most steadfastly adds: “Indeed, if anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: maranatha” (1 Cor. 16).

And yet in all these things it cannot shake from itself some hidden sting in the conscience, as it were the sting of death—not piercing, indeed, but still pricking; at times not even pricking, yet still not departing. It greatly fears lest Christ Jesus not be in some part of it if anything is present in some part of its conscience that is against him, although this very anguish of fear and pain is a manifest proof of true faith. No one feels this except the one who struggles, who already loves what he believes and fears to lose what he already possesses, who is spiritually examined. Common custom of assenting with many people, and profession of confession, do not suffice for such a person; having already experienced something, he begins to know what he lacks. But what does he fear, what troubles him, what grieves him in such matters, except faith?

Therefore the man of God sets himself against himself; examining himself spiritually, he says: “What is this, O soul, in which you trouble me? Do you not stand by faith? Do you not believe?” Setting these two things before himself, comparing them, and reasoning with himself, he lets his heart answer him concerning each. He examines what each is and finds that faith is the voluntary assent of the mind to the things of faith, while believing is to think about those things with assent. Looking around upon all the bounds of his faith, he finds in himself a pure will in the heart, assent in the confession of the mouth, and works of faith in purpose and profession, even to the necessity of martyrdom and death should it happen to arise. Thus, for the present, he gives himself a satisfactory answer regarding faith.

Then, reflecting upon the state of his mind when he thinks about faith, he finds in faith a certain assent of free will, but in thought something opposed to that assent. Examining within himself what this is and what it means, he finds that reason, out of obedience to faith, simply goes into assent; leaving behind the natural path of reasoning in doubtful matters, it proceeds by the way of grace and subjects all things to authority.

And when the mind, drawn away from the way of nature into the way of grace, marvels that by another way it is being led back into its own country, it nevertheless adapts itself to believing—that is, to thinking about matters of faith with simple assent. At once it suffers the force of returning nature; and, desiring to know where it may lend its assent, it reasons even against its will against authority. For although it simply assents to what it is commanded to assent, it nevertheless looks to reason, as though seeking its accustomed way. Although reason is able, when thinking about faith, to subject all things to authority by the balance of judgment, the natural force or movement of reasoning cannot be taken away from rationality. For as the mind naturally always tends toward inquiry after truth, and as the discovery of truth toward which it tends is commonly the end of its seeking, so reasoning, by which truth is found, is commonly the way to finding it.

Therefore, when faith is commanded to it through authority, and it sees itself put off from the end for which it hoped and shut out from the way by which it was accustomed to proceed—unless it rejoices that through this postponement a charity surpassing knowledge is promised to it, believing that there it will most certainly find what is perfect when what is partial has been done away—then, although it is commanded for the present to set authority and faith before reasoning and knowledge, as opinion before certainty and the foolishness of God before the wisdom of this world, it sometimes hesitates and falters, though not unto contradiction. For it seems not so much that reason draws the will as that the will draws reason toward faith. And this continues until, through illuminating grace, faith begins at last to receive understanding of its good, hope its desire, and charity its perception.

Meanwhile these things occur in a person to reveal his weakness, that he may show himself also to himself; and likewise that nature, corrupted by sin and too prone to the perception of its flesh, may be freed from the slavery of the flesh, and, through the working of the Holy Spirit, may gradually be conformed by the exercises of piety to thinking about spiritual and divine things. For it is an undertaking of great exercise, and cannot be accomplished without the great help of God’s grace, to believe and love without hesitation what is declared to be believed, though reason has not been received; and, by love for what is believed, to love believing itself. This must reach such a degree that the greatness of love removes the scruple of suspicion, since even in faith as certain as faith can be, so long as it is faith, there cannot be certain knowledge—nor any knowledge other than that of which the Apostle says: “Now I know in part” (1 Cor. 13).

Whoever does not accept this discipline quickly perishes from the way of grace, is led back onto the way of corrupted nature, becomes animal, fails to perceive the things of God, and begins to believe badly—that is, to think badly about faith. When the tempter mingles with these thoughts, he sometimes removes faith itself from that person’s heart; he goes backward, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. For the enemy attacks faith in the servant of God above all else, to harass, sift, or, if possible, destroy it. He knows well that a conscience devoted to God can in nothing be thrown down more dangerously or grieved more severely than in that which reconciles its face to the face of God; in which the devotion of his servant has its way to God, and the consolation or grace of the Lord his God has its way to the human heart; from which comes the incentive of all that person’s good things; in which is his sole consolation amid his labours and pains.

For faith is the first approach to God, as the Apostle says: “Those approaching God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. 11). Faith is the root of all virtues and the foundation of good works. No virtue exists which is not from faith; nor is anything outside the foundation of faith a building, but rather ruin. For this reason the malice of the ancient serpent first seeks to infect this root and always first attacks this foundation in order to shake it, working, if it can, so that faith may either not exist at all, be imperfect, have the perception of illuminating grace obscured within it, or have the richness of spiritual unction withdrawn from it.

Therefore even now that blasphemous serpent is not afraid to creep into God’s paradise, to assail the minds of the faithful, to hiss blasphemies, and to chant diverse suspicions against faith. But one who now advances in faith should know that the harmful head of that serpent is better crushed by ever more despising it than by answering it point by point and, by the very habit of conversation, adding strength to its shameless malice. For one will not escape the contagion of deadly poison unless one utterly removes from oneself the pestilential breath of that venomous mouth.

For there are two temptations in a human being, or rather two vices inherent in nature itself as a punishment of sin: the concupiscence of the flesh and blasphemy of the spirit. Their origin lies in that first suggestion by the serpent to the first parents of the human race: the desire for forbidden food and blasphemy against God. The serpent said to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from the tree which is in the midst of paradise? For he knew that on the day you eat from it, you will be like gods” (Gen. 3). By these words it was readily persuaded to the believing woman that God had been envious toward humankind; and the woman through the serpent, and the man through the woman, were driven by desire for forbidden food to transgress the divine command. Since the whole of human nature was then in them, the whole of human nature sinned. And so, from that time onward, with flesh desiring against spirit and spirit against flesh, a person sold under sin became powerless over himself, often desiring what he does not will and often thinking about God what he does not will—especially when the instigators of these evils, the spirit of blasphemy and the spirit of fornication, press upon him.

But among all the plagues of temptation, fornication and blasphemy seem to possess this special evil: they struggle and press more fiercely against those who resist them merely by the judgment of reason and exercise of thought, yet are more easily either escaped by fleeing or overcome by contempt. Hence the Apostle says: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6). Every memory of it must altogether be fled or despised, lest even under the pretext of resisting, the conscience of one who remembers be polluted; for at the slightest contact of thought that natural itch of the flesh is immediately stirred. But when the devil tempted him with blasphemy and said, “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4), the teacher of truth opposed nothing except the shield of truth or authority, saying: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid.). Likewise, in the book of Kings, when the servants of the king of Assyria blasphemed the Lord, Hezekiah commanded his own people, saying: “Do not answer them” (1 Kings 18).

One must not answer the spirit of blasphemy in any degree or converse with it, but only oppose to it the shield of faith. Its poisonous malice strives to pollute whatever you bring before it; nor does it seek a reply in order to be satisfied. It seeks only either to grieve the conscience of the believer or to corrupt in some respect the purity of faith.

Of these twin evils, one is the spur of the flesh, the other of the soul. Each is, as it were, a natural reminder in the sluggish; and each derives its origin, as has been said, from him who, through the enchantment of the ancient serpent, desired to be like God. Immediately delivered over to the concupiscence of his flesh, he was ashamed of himself, covering those parts of the body that their Creator had well made without need of covering. Yet each vice must have its own antidote. One medicine is not suitable for all members: what heals the head does not heal the foot, nor does what heals the vices of the flesh heal the vices of the soul.

The temptation of the flesh requires afflictions of the flesh and bodily labours; but the temptation of the soul demands the help of prayer, reading, meditation, and whatever other practices belong to spiritual study. Above all, purity of faith is not attained without true and profound humility of heart, pious devotion, and persevering vigilance in prayer. We must therefore pray frequently and say: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17). For even one who advances in it often suffers troublesome nature, if he lacks aiding grace. For rationality, as has been said, restless and unruly in itself, wherever it has the power to reason, often attacks faith, though not from an intention of contradiction—not because it wishes to oppose faith, but as though faith opposed it.

For just as human reason is accustomed to act in human affairs, it tries, as it were, to break through the middle of the necessity of believing into knowledge of divine things. But, as though climbing up by another way, it stumbles, strikes against an obstacle, and slips, until it returns to the door of faith—to him who said, “I am the door” (John 10)—and, humbled under the yoke of divine authority, enters all the more safely the more humbly it enters. But in some people the greatness of negligence prevents them from perceiving the temptation; in others, dullness of reason; in others, the received certainty of illuminated faith.

For the negligent and dull person is meanwhile satisfied with the faith revealed by flesh and blood, and is not tempted because he is not spiritually examined. Custom of assent or profession of confession suffices for him, although he does not know what faith is. If he knew it, he would certainly take pains to understand what he believes. For there is one faith revealed by flesh and blood and another revealed by the Father who is in heaven—another, and yet not another: the same faith, but a different affection. The former teaches what must be believed; the latter gives faith its own understanding and the full etymology of understanding, when the one who believes reads inwardly, in the affection of the heart, what he believes. The former is the pedagogue, guardian, or author for human weakness; the latter is inheritance itself and the perfection of freedom. The former bears with the negligent and does not exclude the dull, setting before all the form of truth; the latter receives only those fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, and possessing enlightened eyes of heart.

Yet by “dull” we do not mean these simple children of God, with whom he often converses. Their special merit and singular grace consists in meriting to receive faith through God’s revelation—not only that faith which flesh and blood reveal, but also that which the Father in heaven reveals. They are taught by God and learn from the Holy Spirit without any noise of disputing words or thoughts; unless that Spirit himself is present to both teacher and learner, the clamorous reasonings of arguments fail to impart this teaching. Such persons are not negligent but simply and exceptionally vigorous and prudent in faith. They must not be considered dull because of their silence, but singularly wise in what they have received. For they think of the Lord in goodness, and by the perception of love they perceive whatever they believe concerning God; what they perceive is sweet to them. Where reasonings grow weary and fail, they run; and because they walk simply, they walk confidently. They do not walk in the chariots of their own intellects or in the horses of human confidence, but in the name of the Lord—not in learning, but in the powers of the Lord and in his righteousness alone.

Making no judgments and no distinctions within faith, they continually offer every judgment of their reason to be enlightened by the Holy Spirit, directing all their perception toward assent to faith; and they receive its spiritual fruits sweetly and confidently. They think of the Lord in goodness (Wis. 1), because they seek him in simplicity of heart. He is found by them because they do not put him to the test; and he appears to them because they have faith in him. In them is fulfilled what the Lord Jesus Christ says while praying to the Father for his disciples: “And these have truly known that I came forth from you” (John 17). How did they know? What follows explains it: “And they believed that you sent me.” Certainly they truly knew because they truly believed.

But others are dull in relation to faith: some because by nature they neither understand nor can understand; others because, though they can, they are too lazy to make the effort necessary to acquire facility in understanding. We do not, however, praise the simply believing simple person as though to disparage the spiritual examiner. If the latter is not a searcher into majesty, but an emulator of piety and imitator of simplicity, he not only escapes unharmed the snares of temptations but also advances magnificently, having been trained by them. Their grace is of another kind.

For it is one thing to possess a simple faith and simply to receive in the heart the sweetness of its fruits; another to understand what is believed, and always to be ready to give an account of the faith. Simple faith has savour, but does not shine; and it is more removed from temptations. The latter, although it sometimes has savour with labour, nevertheless shines, and is safer against temptations. For though it advances step by step in faith, bearing Christ, who dwells through faith, in the heart, it holds with sure knowledge whatever belongs to faith, while conscience bears witness; and it cherishes in a most firm embrace that faith which flesh and blood revealed to it; it sighs after it, and, when it is granted, breathes sweetly in it—that faith which the Father who is in heaven reveals. And although by the short path of holy simplicity it is often anticipated by the simple person, nevertheless it is not repelled from the fountain of grace, which lies open to all [Col. 0379D].

For sometimes, labouring for itself under Adam’s curse, amid the thorns and thistles of its own land, amid the temptations of its corrupt nature, it eats its bread in the sweat of its cultivation; at other times, while it does not know it, like Jacob it finds the Lord’s blessings in the field of its heart. For the labour of spiritual exercise faithfully spent in faith cannot be empty; nor can the sorrow of delay, expended upon piety, be defrauded of its reward. Often illuminating grace is present to faith as it labours; and thus, as if in an instant, it brings into it knowledge and hope of things unseen, and, in knowledge and hope, love: so that, without any interval of time or distinction of perception, love immediately arises from faith, by means of hope, through knowledge [Col. 0380A]; and faith likewise is strengthened in love through knowledge. Thus, as has already been said above, the knowledge, hope, and love of faith, though understood as three distinct things within faith itself, nevertheless by a certain power of conjunction become one out of three in the power of faith itself: in the believer’s perception, the undivided substance of things hoped for. For what is believed is also known by believing; what is known is hoped for because of the good known in it; and what is hoped for and known is loved.

This ought always to be present in a faithful soul through faith, concerning faith, hope, and charity; yet it cannot always be present to that soul’s understanding. For these are the soul’s special virtues, in which all its strength consists. These are the bones of which the Psalmist frequently speaks, which “the Lord guards in his saints” [Col. 0380B] (Psalm 33). When they are joined to one another, there is made from them “one bone, which shall not be broken” (Exodus 12; Numbers 9; John 19). This is the perfection of faith in this life, concerning which he elsewhere says: “My bone, which thou hast made in secret, was not hidden from thee” (Psalm 139). But when they are divided from one another, they are easily disturbed and greatly disturb the soul; either they are broken, and our enemies reproach us, or they are scattered, and place us beside hell.

When flesh adheres to these bones—that is, the remaining affections of the soul—both the affections draw strength from the bones, and the bones from them draw the health-giving juice of fatness; and there comes about *eucrasia*, that is, the good temperament of the soul. But if they are loosened from one another, the flesh, flowing away, wastes within itself; and the dying bones—faith without [Col. 0380C] works, hope without the consolation of delay, charity without the sweetness of piety—dry up within themselves like ashes. Therefore, when flesh adheres to bones, matters go well both with the bones and with the flesh: the flesh is strengthened by the vigour of the bones, and the bones are nourished by the flesh.

But if bone adheres to flesh, as the same prophet laments in one place, saying, “My bone has cleaved to my flesh” (Psalm 102), it softens into flesh and becomes wholly flesh. That is: if the soul’s affections are conformed to faith, that person lives in the Spirit and walks in the Spirit, and is, as it were, wholly spirit. But if those spiritual virtues dissolve into fleshly affections, he becomes wholly flesh, and it is said of that person: “My spirit shall not remain in this man, [Col. 0380D] because he is flesh” (Genesis 6).

Faith, then, must be nourished with its proper food in this spiritual examiner, and before all things it must be disposed toward God by the spirit of humility, until the very substance of hoped-for things begins to appear to devout devotion. Thus the natural ardour of rationality, as has already been said, may through grace become the ardour of love; and importunate reasoning may become devout contemplation, knowledge of what has been found, and joy in enjoyment. Meanwhile, while nature is exercised and instructed, and taught what it can do without grace, even if by the rational faculty we restrain its natural ardour lest it boil over into contradiction, we scarcely succeed in preventing what is fervent from being fervent. Thus the appetite for natural knowledge cannot but look with some scrupulous hesitation toward believing what it is not permitted to attain by any faculty, whether of reason or of the body, for examination [Col. 0381A].

But do not fear, servant of God: let not your feet be moved; let not your steps be poured out. Unbelievers ask for signs; doubters seek wisdom. But embrace Christ crucified: a stumbling-block to those predestined for ruin, folly to those wise in their own eyes, but to all who are called and to be justified, the wisdom of God and the power of God; because what is foolish in God is wiser, and what is weak is stronger, than all human beings (1 Corinthians 1). If you consult the sense of the flesh, it appears foolish and weak. But if, with the Apostle, you have the mind of Christ, you will understand that the Word of God is supreme wisdom, but that the folly of this wisdom is the flesh of the Word; so that those who were fleshly and could not by the prudence of the flesh attain [Col. 0381B] to the wisdom of God might be healed through the folly of preaching and the simplicity of faith—that is, through the flesh of the Word. Become foolish, that you may become wise; and the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, who created all things, will be illuminated for you: the “making-weak” [Latin *infirmare*] of God for the weak [reading uncertain]. And you will learn how surpassing is the greatness of his power toward us who have believed, according to the working of the might of his strength.

Nor should a momentary and passing trembling in believing terrify the faithful mind, when faith does not lack the testimony of a good conscience, and conscience the testimony of the Holy Spirit—even if questioning should arise under the trial of martyrdom. O faithful soul, innocent nature does not condemn you; it marvels at what is unfamiliar [Col. 0381C], not refusing it, but desiring to know something. See the Lord’s mother, the special sign of faith. Having received the good tidings of our salvation, of her own conception, and the pledge of the Holy Spirit, and most certainly believing that she would become the mother of the Lord, she nevertheless wished to know something—namely, the manner in which this mystery was to be fulfilled—saying: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1). She held the thing by faith; she desired to know the manner. Her faithful soul embraced the fact, strengthened by that very grace with which she was full; but nature, astonished, wondered at the way in which it would occur. For she already felt the Holy Spirit working uniquely within herself, but did not know that he would work in her flesh, without the aid of flesh, the wonders which she believed. To her the angel said [Col. 0381D]: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (ibid.). As though he said: This is the finger of God.

Likewise, concerning the spiritual regeneration of baptism, when Nicodemus asked its manner, the Lord replied: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and thou hearest his voice, but knowest not whence he comes or whither he goes. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3). Concerning the sacrament of his body and blood, when they were scandalized, he also said: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). For one and the same Spirit works all these things as he wills, establishing sacraments of faith: some as bodily and visible signs of a sacred reality, as in baptism and in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; others as sacred things hidden [Col. 0382A] in spiritual understanding, to be investigated under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Of these the Apostle says: “That he might make known to us the mystery of his will” (Ephesians 1).

For the secret of God’s will is most hidden and most high, and is the mystery of all mysteries. He makes it known according to his good pleasure, to whom he wills and as he wills; and, as it is divine, so he reveals it in some divine manner to the one whom he himself makes worthy by his gift. Rather, it is not something divine but God, because it is the Holy Spirit himself, who is the substantial will of God. For this is the will of God by which God does all that he wills, of whom it is written: “The Lord has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Psalm 135). Therefore the Holy Spirit himself, to the person into whom he pours himself, makes known the very will of God in whom it is done; nor is it made known elsewhere than where it is present. For although the eye of human reason cannot hide itself from the charity of his light and truth, nevertheless no one can participate in its sweetness except one who does it and in whom it is done—namely, by willing what God wills [Col. 0382B].

For as no one feels unless he lives, because that which feels is the life only of one who lives, so no one knows that will in whom it is not done—although not all know or feel it in whom it is done, as in infants and the unlearned. For as many who possess a soul do not know what the soul is, so many who possess grace do not know it. But to the one whom he draws to himself, he reveals the outward sacraments, while his own reality—the reality of all sacraments—works in that person as their signification. For it is the Holy Spirit himself who consecrates them, that they may be sacraments of so great a reality; and in revealing them he commends them to the faithful conscience, in which hidden grace works the reality itself.

For God, more inward than all that is within us, entrusted outward sacraments to us in our outward faculties—that is, the bodily senses—through which he might lead what is inward in us into his own inward things. Through the working of bodily sacraments he gradually awakens spiritual grace in us; and for this purpose he had also bent himself down to fellowship with our humanity, that he might make us participants in his divinity [Col. 0382C].

Therefore, at the command of the author of our salvation, the flesh is washed outwardly in the water of baptism, while inwardly the soul is cleansed by the working of the Holy Spirit. Thus human sinners, justified by faith in the Son of Man and Son of God, become children of God [Col. 0382D]. The faithful person also eats bodily, yet incorruptibly, the bodily but incorruptible food of the Lord’s body and blood: bodily enough to be suited to us, incorruptibly enough to raise us; conforming the perception of intellectual reason to God insofar as it unites us to God through the taste of illuminated love.

For, accustomed as we are to temporal things, we must be cleansed by temporal things. Nor, once cleansed, shall we merit the contemplation of eternal things unless, while needing cleansing, we apply faith to temporal things. Yet these temporal things are transient; nevertheless, through the firstfruits of the Spirit they bear the firstfruits of eternal things. They are fitted alike to faith which promises, to truth which is to be fulfilled, to our mortality, and to the eternity to come. This shines forth most especially to us in the person of the Mediator, who, remaining eternal God in himself, was made human in time, so that through the temporal and eternal one we might pass from temporal things to eternal [Col. 0383A].

Therefore, as has been said, we eat the Lord’s body and drink his blood bodily, but are refreshed spiritually; we are washed bodily in baptism, but purified spiritually. Thus our assent of faith had to be gradually trained by certain rudiments of Christian piety. When in it we do not test the Lord our God, but simply and faithfully entrust to him our spirit, he himself begins to entrust himself to us. Thus we are no longer among those of whom the Gospel says that they believed in Jesus, but he did not entrust himself to them (John 2). For it is improperly said of them that they believed in him whom they did not love. To believe in him is, by loving, to go into him. They believed that he was the Christ, but did not love him as Christ. Nor did he entrust himself to those to whose inward eyes he did not appear, by the judgment which he himself knew, in that form in which he cannot fail to be loved by those who can see him [Col. 0383B].

Therefore, in the things of God we ought first, without any reconsideration or hesitation, to give a simple and pure assent of faith. Then, in order to understand what we believe, we must, with every observance and obedience of God’s commandments, entrust our whole spirit and understanding to the Holy Spirit—not so much by the striving of ambitious reason as by the affection of devout and simple love. Thus, more by the pursuits of most humble piety than by the powers of mighty intellect, we shall merit that Jesus begins to entrust himself to us, when, through illuminating grace, the assent of faith becomes a perception of love in the understanding of reason. Then it no longer needs outward sacraments in order to know the mystery of God’s inward will.

Nevertheless, while we live here, our outward faculties are bound by the most sacred observance of those sacraments, and through them our inward faculties, lest they flow out into alien things; for this reason *religio* [religion] received its name from *religando*, “binding again” [Col. 0383C].

For while placed in the body, we had to be restrained and held by the bodily forms of sacraments; by obedience to the wisdom of God that instituted them, we had to be reminded through the bodily forms of bodily sacraments [Col. 0383D], and by their outward significations recalled to their inward grace and to the inward realities signified. For we are sick, languishing from the corruption of nature, and we ought to desire health. Our sickness is the mutability of our mortality; the medicine by which passage is made from here to there belongs to the Mediator. Faith, however, is especially concerned with things performed for us in time, through which our hearts are cleansed, so that they may be found fit for eternal things—not to be believed, but understood.

If we conduct ourselves faithfully in this faith, faith merits truth; and mutability passes into the immutable eternity of the reality believed. Therefore, while we are cleansed here, let us render to the sacraments their proper reverence, and to the realities themselves faith, so that, cleansed and helped by these, we may advance to those things to which both the events themselves ministered and their sacraments minister, and to which faith itself ministers: namely, the contemplation of eternal things [Col. 0384A].

But an unclean soul, an impure conscience, a proud spirit, and a curious boastfulness are rightly excluded from the investigation of divine sacraments or mysteries, because “the spirit of discipline will flee deceit, will not dwell in a body subject to sins, and wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1). But humble piety, faithful love, and a pure conscience—the simple children of God and the poor in spirit—even when they reverently withdraw, are summoned by the Holy Spirit; indeed, they are in some manner drawn to seek these things. For they love, and therefore seek while they seek; and they seek in order to love more deeply.

Therefore, O faithful soul, when more hidden mysteries are presented to your trembling nature within your faith [Col. 0384B], dare to say—not from eagerness to resist, but from love to follow—“How are these things done?” Let your question be prayer, love, piety, and humble desire; not searching out God’s majesty in lofty matters, but seeking salvation in the saving works of God for our salvation. And the angel of great counsel will answer you: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, he will suggest all things to you and teach you all truth” (John 14). For “no one knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit which is within that person; so likewise no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

Hasten, therefore, to become a participant in the Holy Spirit. He is present when invoked, and he is not invoked unless he is already present. When he comes in response to invocation, he comes in the abundance [Col. 0384C] of God’s blessing. He is “a river’s rushing stream, making glad the city of God.” And when he comes, if he finds you humble, tranquil, and trembling at God’s words, he will rest upon you. He will reveal to you what God the Father removes from the wise and prudent of this age; and those things which I, Wisdom, was able to tell the disciples on earth will begin to shine upon you, though they could not bear them until the Spirit of truth came, to teach them all truth. In receiving or learning this truth, it is vain to expect from the mouth of any human being what could not be received or learned from the tongue of Truth itself. For Truth itself says: “God is Spirit” (John 4).

And as those who worship him must worship [Col. 0384D] in spirit and truth, so those who desire to know or recognize him must seek the understanding of faith and the perception of that pure and naked truth only in the Holy Spirit. For in the darkness and ignorance of this life, he himself is light enlightening the poor in spirit; he himself is love that draws; he himself is sweetness that disposes the soul; he himself is the human being’s access to God; he himself is the lover’s love; he himself is devotion; he himself is piety. He reveals to God’s faithful from faith into faith the righteousness of God, when in return for grace he gives grace, and in return for faith from hearing he gives illumined faith.

The Apostle says that there are some “having indeed a form of piety, but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3). The form of faith—something capable of being handed down by human beings to human beings through words and the institutions of ecclesiastical discipline—is available to all people in the assent of good will [Col. 0385A]. Human beings still see in a mirror and in an enigma, and pass through in an image: in the mirror by which we are instructed; in the darker enigma in which we are exercised; and in the simple and manifest image in which we are more sweetly affected. But piety itself, truth itself, is handed down or taught only by the Holy Spirit; nor is it inscribed upon the mind except by God’s finger.

Therefore I believe without doubt that the Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—has divine unity, of one substance and inseparable equality; and therefore that there are not three gods but one God. I believe that God, made human for us, the supreme medicine for healing the swelling of our pride, the profound mystery for our redemption and the loosing of our sins, performed miracles and rose from the dead [Col. 0385B]. If you know what omnipotence is, believe of the Omnipotent that he could do this. If you understand what the highest good and highest goodness are, then, where there was so great a necessity among those perishing, believe of the highest good that he willed it. If you can think what humbled divinity accomplished in the world, think well of the Lord’s goodness: how this work befitted his Godhead.

First, when, for the salvation of humankind, the Father did not spare the Son, nor the Son himself, the highest good, in his own form, made himself known to the world and thoroughly taught humanity to love God as he ought to be loved. For by loving humanity, in a manner even to contempt of himself, he taught humanity to love God even to contempt of itself—humanity which, miserable as it was, did not know how to love except itself, even to contempt of God. This is piety [Col. 0385C]; this is the proper worship of God, by which God must be worshipped by his creature. This is the wisdom which supreme Wisdom brought into the world, creating in it so many glorious martyrs, so many perfect despisers of the world and of themselves.

For this is the wisdom of God, by which God has savour to the wise person: one living from the spirit of his life up to the perception of his love; loving up to the imitation of his likeness; in temporal things perceiving in himself what was also in Christ Jesus our Lord; but in eternal things, and toward God, possessing that perception of which a certain wise man says: “To know thee is perfected understanding” (Wisdom 6). For in the form of the Mediator that ancient definition of wisdom properly shines forth, by which wisdom is defined as the knowledge of human and divine things. It is understood—or rather, as has been said above, felt—up to the savour of loving and the affection of imitating: our Lord Jesus Christ, “though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized,” when he humbled “himself, taking the form of a servant, unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2): who did this, what he did, and for whom [Col. 0385D].

Conformed by recalling, understanding, and loving this supreme wisdom, the person wise in God derives from it a certain wisdom of worshipping God as God. By it he seasons his life, conduct, actions, and all that belongs to him with a certain divine savour before all people, and anoints them with the oil of gladdening grace, so that people, seeing his good works, may glorify the Father who is in heaven.
