He has grace toward friends, patience joined to kindness toward enemies, beneficence toward all whom he can assist, good will toward absolutely all people, and that natural law by which he wills to do to no one what he would not wish done to himself, and wills, as far as he can, to do for everyone whatever he wishes others to do for him [Col. 0386A].

Again, from this wisdom supreme Wisdom separates in its wise person the knowledge—not that which pursues the vanity of this world, but that which serves the faith in which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. This knowledge is a certain disposition or habit of mind for receiving those things which properly belong to faith: namely, those realities brought perceptibly to the mind through its own senses or through another’s—whether through the perceiving subject or another person relating or writing them—such as the temporal deeds of the Lord, conveyed by historical knowledge: his birth, passion, resurrection, ascension, and miracles performed among human beings.

Human reason does not find knowledge of these things within itself, as it finds whatever is divine and eternal; rather, it receives them as things arriving from elsewhere through some mode of learning—by seeing, hearing, or reading [Col. 0386B]. To the mind created for eternity, that it may be capable of eternity through understanding and share in it through enjoyment, eternal and divine things seem joined by a kind of natural affinity. Indeed, even if the mind has perhaps become more foolish through fault, it is never deprived of desire for them. For even if it cannot perhaps think of invisible things, nevertheless knowledge of them is so innate in human reason [Col. 0386C] that it never departs from love or delight in goodness and beauty, blessedness and immutability, except when, in desiring or loving the good, it is deceived by a false good. Although nature has an appetite for these things through creating grace, it does not know them perfectly except through illuminating grace; nor does it grasp them except by God’s gift.

Therefore, when one who turns to the Lord calls them to mind, he easily finds that which is known of God, naturally present in his mind or reason. But temporal things, which are learned temporally and are brought into us from elsewhere, as it were, through the senses, do not adhere to the mind with the same ease until, as faith advances and grace illumines, knowledge of temporal things is transformed into the wisdom [Col. 0386D] of eternal things, and temporal realities put on the grace of eternity. This occurs when Christ Jesus begins no longer to be known according to the flesh, and when his deeds are understood and his works judged in accordance with himself.

For according to the Prophet, who says, “They proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds” (Psalm 64), it is no great matter that God’s works be proclaimed if his deeds are not understood. For all the deeds of the Word are words to us, in which he speaks to us, making himself known to us in his deeds when rightly understood. They are understood not only by mystical interpretations in the thought or discourse of knowledge, but much more sweetly and effectively through the affections of devout love in the meditation or discourse of wisdom. Hence the Apostle says that to one is given by the Spirit a word of wisdom, and to another a word of knowledge (1 Corinthians 12) [Col. 0387A].

Meanwhile, until Christ is formed in us, faith, because its subject is knowledge, naturally desires, as it were, to know whatever it is commanded to believe; and when it cannot, it is disturbed. This knowledge, or mode of receiving the things of faith, is ordered in the recipient’s conscience by supreme Wisdom. First, in obedience to the Lord who says, “Whoever believes shall be saved, but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16), realities which, as has been said, come from without are not denied the hospitality of simple assent in obedience to the one commanding. Then, through the familiarity of good will, they are received, as it were, into civic right and partnership in social life, in communion of the same bread and the same cup [Col. 0387B].

Afterward, the affections are joined as though by mutual marriages, when from understood sensible things intelligible things are understood, and from intelligible things sensible things are commended. For they confer upon one another, as it were, from the abundance each possesses: temporal things commending God and making the omnipotent goodness of God intelligible; while the Lord’s goodness and power establish faith in temporal things, because the good one willed, and the powerful one was able, to do for human salvation what human nature scarcely suffices to believe. For the invisible things of God are especially “clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Romans 2), when the temporal dispensation of the Mediator, rightly believed, through faith or the knowledge that belongs to faith trains and nourishes the believer’s heart to receive eternal things; and eternal things, rightly contemplated, make the testimonies of temporal things exceedingly credible [Col. 0387C].

For the dignity of the work bears witness in the loving heart to the greatness of divine goodness; and the supreme good, understood to some degree in the perception of love, establishes God’s own work as worthy of God. For in this matter, concerning the kingdom of charity, which is in the state of eternity, supreme Wisdom shone upon us according to the capacity of his gift, above the capacity of our understanding, when he who was in the form of God was made in the form of a servant. By what he did he taught those who understand what good awaits us in that region of the highest good. This was indeed done in time; but in him who was in the beginning with God (John 1), his work was life and was eternally with God [Col. 0387D].

From this there flowed into the world a new wisdom, wisdom above every wisdom of this world, making it foolish: namely, that the foolish and weak things of God are stronger than all human beings. This wisdom gives to the wise the sweet savour of mind that perceives the Son’s humility even unto death, even death on a cross; the sufferings endured for us; mockeries, blows, spittings, scourges, thorns, nails, and the rest—things which a soul wounded by charity can scarcely at times remember because of the weight of grief, yet which the affection of love never permits it to forget. From this it comes that the Lord’s temporal works become in the faithful heart certain wondrous sacraments of eternity, and marvellous incitements to imitate those same sufferings: so that one who loves, so far as possible, may burn to love beyond what human weakness can do, and to suffer [Col. 0388A] for him beyond what frail humanity can suffer.

This occurs when, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, the faithful person sanctifies the Lord Jesus Christ in his heart (1 Peter 3), and the Lord himself sanctifies himself in that person (John 17). Would that all who profess faith attained this faith; that all who glory in being numbered among the faithful possessed it! For one must not suppose that anyone can have this faith toward God who is still found keeping faith with this world. Therefore the Apostle says that some, “having rejected a good conscience, have made shipwreck concerning the faith” (1 Timothy 1). For an evil conscience easily suffers shipwreck; and one whose mind has been corrupted by the desire of the flesh or of the world cannot stand soundly or credibly with respect to faith. Hence the Apostle likewise says of certain people: “Corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith” (2 Timothy 3).

But if anyone is truly faithful, then, just as at the slightest injury to the heart or brain, or to those bodily parts in which life is contained, all nature suddenly becomes numb, so at the slightest impact upon faith the entire substance of good will trembles within that person. And as the serpent’s prudence is accustomed to expose the whole body in order to protect the head in which its life is contained, so the faithful person refuses neither to do nor to suffer anything, provided the health of his faith always remains undisturbed [Col. 0388B]. Therefore our Father who is in heaven must be prayed to unceasingly, that, though he sometimes permits our faith to be brought as far as testing, he may not permit it to be brought into temptation as though for rejection [Col. 0388C], but may provide with the temptation an outcome, that we may be able to endure it.

With every pursuit of piety, help from grace must also be sought against the sense of the flesh and nature’s ardour, lest faith grow faint or fail, but bear fruit in patience, until by degrees the grace of the Holy Spirit transforms that entire form of trembling nature into a certain substance of perfect faith, completing in it what David prays: “Cut away my reproach, which I have feared” (Psalm 119). Let the prudent mind enlist the great luminaries of the Church as a fortress of faith to strengthen the heart and illuminate the conscience by faith: the greatest men of spiritual knowledge, supreme wisdom, and proved holiness; their teachings and writings [Col. 0388D], their deeds and martyrdoms. And let it say to itself against the movements of its temptations: “Is this man better, wiser, holier, or more penetrating than those who taught in the world what they had learned from God; who preached it magnificently; who transmitted it to us in eloquent writings; who confirmed it by life and miracles; who consecrated it by death and martyrdom?”

Such thoughts concerning faith, and such wavering of minds and hesitation of thoughts, are especially stirred concerning the Saviour’s humanity and the mysteries of faith revealed to us therein. For concerning God—whether he exists, and whether all created and established things are governed through his providence, having been created and established through his omnipotence—the truth of supreme being shows itself so naturally to every conscience capable of reason and makes itself so manifest [Col. 0389A] that there is no one who does not understand himself to be from God if he knows of himself that he exists. Indeed, not even the fool dares say except in his heart: “There is no God” (Psalm 14)—that is, in a foolish and senseless heart.

For human nature is not found so depraved in any human being who is sufficiently in possession of his mind that he does not understand God to be the Creator of every creature: God who is above every creature, insofar as every creature is from him; beyond every time, for with him there is no time; beyond every place, for with him there is no place; he who, being immutable, moves all things. With him, the author of all movements and moving things, one must unquestionably judge there to be immutable power and the causal reason of all things, both of things to be created and of things to be moved.

[Col. 0389B] He who from eternity predestined, by fixed and immutable causes, all things that are to be, has now, according to the prophet, made all things that are to be. To think these things freely concerning God belongs to few; nevertheless, it belongs to human reason that every rational person naturally possesses these things within himself. Therefore, from the image of the highest truth and highest good, truth—even when unknown—is loved by all people; and only what is believed or understood to be good is desired; eternity and incorruptibility are loved. Accordingly, if anyone raises this question within himself, he soon finds within himself the means to restrain turbulent reasoning; or else, accusing himself of slowness, let him reverence the hidden truth.

But concerning the humanity of the Savior, we cannot teach, nor can we learn from a human being, anything other than: “He who believes will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16). There are indeed many and manifold reasons—reasons themselves of the highest worth—for believing that God either could or ought to do what the Gospel proclamation affirms that he did. But that he did do it: apart from evangelical authority, which is most weighty and venerable for devout ears and minds, what reasons shall we bring forward for unbelievers or doubters? They have not seen him himself—as they say with their mouths while murmuring in their hearts—nor have they seen his works, he who said: “If you do not believe me, believe at least the works” (John 10). They have not seen the apostles performing miracles in his name; nor the signs following those who believed through them, of which he himself said: “These signs shall follow those who believe” (Mark 16).

[Col. 0389D] Although even to this day signs and miracles, both public and private, are not lacking in the Church of God, they occur in their proper places and times—not at the will of doubters or in response to the questions of unbelievers, but as aid to the faithful and consolation for those laboring for faith or in faith. Such things occur either in them or through them, not in order that they may believe, but because they believe. Yet unbelievers love to err: they possess loves which they refuse to overcome, and by them are sent into errors from which they find no way back. Moreover, the fleshly sense within them, which cannot think even of spiritual things except bodily, knows or is able to think much less of those things belonging to the human dispensation in the Lord Jesus Christ except carnally.

[Col. 0390A] Unless the Holy Spirit aids the weakness even of faithful persons who seek devoutly, ask humbly, and knock reverently, it is far easier for a human being to conceive divine things concerning God than to think either divine things in a human being or human things in God. This remains so until, through the help of that same Spirit and through the Lord Jesus Christ sanctifying himself in the hearts of believers, there begins to appear to enlightened faith, in the one and same person of the Mediator, both the divinity which glorifies the things of humanity in its majesty and the humanity which glorifies the things of divinity in its humility. Then there comes to pass in them what the Lord himself once said while praying for his disciples: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God has also glorified him in himself” (John 13).

[Col. 0390B] For according to the measure or progress of inward purity in believers’ hearts, Christ is both glorified in the beauty of his glorified humanity and appears in the glory of his divinity to devout faith in their affections. It does not belong to everyone, nor is it granted to all in this life, what the Lord promises in the Gospel to some by a special prerogative of grace, saying: “There are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom” (Matt. 16). Stephen saw him differently at the very moment of his martyrdom, when, “looking into heaven, he saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7); differently did the one see him to whom, after his resurrection, he said: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20).

[Col. 0390C] Those who are worthy also see him differently through faith when they reflect in solitude, and differently when, through grace affecting them, he is in them through the affection of devotion. For when the soul thirsting for the living God, led by grace, contemplates the glory of the Lord, it encounters the Mediator between God and human beings, both man and God, the image of the invisible God, the Lord Jesus Christ. And when, from the greatness of the goodness by which he became man for us and the power of majesty by which he is God, it senses within itself the radiance of God’s grace and the express image of his substance, there comes to pass what the Apostle says: “We all,” he says, “with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3).

[Col. 0390D] For it loves, and its love is its sense, by which it senses him whom it senses; and in a certain manner it is transformed into that which it senses. For it does not sense him unless it is transformed into him—that is, unless he is in it and it in him.

For as the outward bodily sense relates to bodies and bodily things, so the inward sense relates to things like itself, that is, rational, divine, or spiritual things. The inward sense of the soul is its understanding. Yet its greater, worthier sense, and its purer understanding, is love, if love itself is pure. By this sense the Creator is sensed by the creature; by understanding God is understood, insofar as God can be sensed or understood by a creature. For when the sense or soul of a human being moves itself toward sensing, it is changed by sensing into that which it senses. Otherwise it is not sense. For example, as natural philosophers maintain, the visual power issuing from the brain through the rays of the eyes meets the form or colors of visible things; when it reports these to the mind, the mind itself is conformed to them, and sight comes to be. Otherwise the one seeing would not see. The same must equally be understood of the other senses.

[Col. 0391A] Thus the mind has understanding as its sense: by it it senses whatever it senses. When it senses rational things, reason advances within it; and when reason reports, the mind is transformed into it, and understanding comes to be. But in matters relating to God, the mind’s sense is love: by love it senses whatever it senses concerning God according to the Spirit of life. The Spirit of life, however, is the Holy Spirit, through whom everyone loves whatever is truly to be loved.

[Col. 0391B] For since nothing is loved except because it is good, or thought to be good, it follows that all love, and the whole of love, is owed to the highest good alone; and it always returns to that good, unless held somewhere captive and bound, where it is deceived by a false good.

God’s love relates to our love, to that natural affection of ours, as our own soul relates to our body. If God’s love is in that affection, it lives; if not, it is nothing but a kind of corpse, which does not sense what ought to be sensed. But when a human being lives, and through that love senses what ought to be sensed, he is transformed into that which he senses. Here the affection of the lover has more power than either bodily sense among bodies or understanding among rational beings; and the person becomes one spirit with God, toward whom he is affected.

[Col. 0391C] For the will of the soul has such power to join even bodily things together that, bringing them before the senses, it sometimes holds the senses themselves fixed in those things with such intensity that the will itself becomes love, desire, or lust. With a more fervent violence of intention it so longs after sensed things that it affects—or infects—the very body of the one longing or loving, so as sometimes to alter it into a similar shape, appearance, or color. This was not unknown to the patriarch Jacob (Gen. 30), who by an artful and natural contrivance impressed upon the animals about to be born the colors he wished, lest the wickedness of a barbarous man should deprive him of the reward of his labor.

[Col. 0391D] This is accomplished far more powerfully and worthily when he who is the substantial will of Father and Son, the Holy Spirit, so affects the human will to himself that the soul loving God and sensing by loving is suddenly transformed wholly—not indeed into the nature of divinity, but into a certain form of blessedness above the human yet below the divine: into the joy of illuminating grace and the awareness of enlightened conscience. Thus the human spirit, which a little before could scarcely say in the Holy Spirit, “Jesus is Lord,” now confidently cries among the children of adoption, “Abba, Father” (1 Cor. 12; Rom. 8). Nor does the spirit alone do so: the flesh too, already sensing certain firstfruits of its promised incorruption and glorification, gratefully denies itself to itself, running eagerly after its spirit, as that spirit runs after God.

[Col. 0392A] This is the jubilation of the blessed people who know jubilation, who walk in the light of God’s countenance and exult in his name; for them God is the exaltation of righteousness, and he himself is the glory of their strength. This is the exaltation of the Lord, and of the Holy One of Israel, our king: when we sense concerning him in goodness, who was made like us; and when we sense within ourselves that which is also in Christ Jesus our Lord, as we become like him by gladly suffering with him now and are afterward to become like him by reigning with him. For no greater sweetness can befall a human being in this life than when, in the image of the Creator, a rightly disposed conscience finds itself in the likeness of his goodness.

Whoever desires this sweetness should not regard as burdensome the laborious necessity involved in the exercise of faith. For “tribulation produces patience; patience, tested character; and tested character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5).

[Col. 0392B] For after testing, love is poured forth in the heart; and at once, through the Holy Spirit, its proper sweetness is ordered for the devout mind. There comes to it in this a frequent visitation of God, guarding, as holy Job says, the spirit of his servant (Job 10). What visitation could be sweeter, what consolation greater, what light more divine for children of light who hope while laboring amid the darkness of this life, than sometimes, in the passing flash of illuminating grace, to see with the eyes of the heart, however slightly, the one who shows; to sense the one who promises; to understand what mercy and abundant redemption, what propitiation, are with the Lord; to behold, while laboring in the land of evil, what is promised in the land of good; and before the unveiled face of grace to offer the unveiled face of a good conscience?

[Col. 0392C] O therefore, whoever you are who desire and long to have joy in your faith in this life, be for this brief while no doubtful or hesitant, but a wholly certain judge of your own heart before the Lord your God. In faith, possess certain joy, certain in its foundation and founded upon a good conscience; it shall be yours, and no one shall take it from you. Then, after you have begun to see, strive to see more frequently; to sense more effectually, so that you may begin to know. For from this, a new countenance of faith will already begin to dawn upon its faithful one in the knowledge of God—promising itself only in part in this life, but promising to give itself most fully in the life to come. Of that life the Lord, praying for his disciples, said to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

[Col. 0392D] This knowledge of God is one thing in faith, another in love or charity. The knowledge belonging to faith belongs to this life; that belonging to charity belongs to eternal life—or rather, as the Lord says, “this is eternal life.” For it is one thing to know God as a man knows his friend, another to know him as he knows himself. Common knowledge consists in retaining in one’s memory a mental image conceived from some degree of seeing a known person or known thing, by which the thing itself is thought of when absent or recognized when present. In God, this knowledge belongs to faith: not that there is some likeness of a mental image, but there is a certain affection of devotion. Conceived from the form of faith and entrusted to memory,

[Col. 0393A] whenever it returns to the experience of one remembering, it sweetly affects the conscience of the one reflecting.

But the knowledge mutually possessed by Father and Son is itself the unity of both, namely the Holy Spirit; nor is their knowledge, by which they mutually know one another, other than the substance by which they are what they are. By this knowledge, “No one knows the Father except the Son; and no one knows the Son except the Father, and those to whom they themselves are willing to reveal him” (Matt. 11). These are the Lord’s words. Therefore they reveal to some—namely, to those to whom they will, to those to whom they make themselves known—that is, to those to whom they give the Holy Spirit, who is the common knowledge or common will of both. Those, therefore, to whom Father and Son reveal themselves know as Father and Son know themselves, because they have within themselves the mutual knowledge of the two; because they have within themselves

[Col. 0393B] the unity of both and their will or love, which altogether is the Holy Spirit. Yet this is one thing in the divine substance, in which he is consubstantially one with Father and Son; another in lower matter; one thing in the Creator, another in the creature; one in proper nature, another in grace; one in the giver, another in the receiver; one in the immutability of eternity, another in temporal change.

There, mutual charity, unity, likeness, knowledge, and whatever is common to both, are naturally and consubstantially the Holy Spirit. Here, however, he brings this about in that in which it is brought about, and by bringing it about he is in it through grace. There the mutual knowledge of Father and Son is unity; here it is a human being’s likeness to God, concerning which the apostle John says in his Epistle: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

[Col. 0393C] For there, to be like God will be to see God, or to know him. The one who sees or knows will see or know him to the degree in which he is like him; and he will be like him to the degree in which he knows or sees him. For there, to see or know God is to be like God; and to be like him is to see or know him. This perfect knowledge will be eternal life, joy which no one shall take from its possessor. For that cannot be complete here which can be fulfilled only in the full knowledge of God, since what is known or understood here concerning God cannot be known or understood

[Col. 0393D] as in that life where he will be seen face to face and as he is. This mode of knowledge is not to be expected here from the mouth of any human being, because it could not be learned from the mouth of Truth itself—not because the Lord could not teach it, but because human weakness could not bear it.

Yet he does not wholly withdraw it here from his beloved lovers, so that they may know what they lack. For upon the love of the poor in spirit—needy and destitute, and anxiously reaching toward what they love—the Holy Spirit, the love of God, is borne above: that is, he works his works in them, not through the necessity of need, but through the abundance of his grace and beneficence. This is what was signified when he was borne over the waters (Gen. 1), whatever those waters may have been.

[Col. 0394A] For as the sun is borne over the waters, warming and illuminating them and, by its heat, drawing them to itself with a certain natural force in order to supply rain from them to the thirsty earth in the place and time of God’s mercy, so the love of God is borne over the love of his faithful one, inspiring and doing good, drawing that love to himself as it follows by a certain natural desire and possesses, like fire, the natural force of tending upward. He unites it to himself, so that the spirit of the human being who believes may become one spirit with God.

And because Father and Son are commonly called [Spirit]—for “God is Spirit” (John 4)—and because it was fitting that the Holy Spirit should be called specifically Spirit, since he belongs not so much to one of them as he is that in which the communion of both appears, the Holy Spirit himself communicates the name *spirit* to the human being. Thus, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 6), the man of God may be one spirit with God, both by the grace of the name and by the affection of power.

[Col. 0394B] Nor is it merely one person, but many people, having one heart in him and one soul through the outflow of that highest charity, in whose fountain is what is the unity of the Trinity.

This is the Creator’s wonderful condescension toward the creature: great grace, unthinkable goodness, the creature’s devout confidence toward the Creator, sweet access, and the sweetness of a good conscience. In the embrace and kiss of Father and Son, which is the Holy Spirit, a human being finds himself in some manner in the middle, and is united to God by that same charity by which Father and Son are one; he is sanctified in him who is the holiness of both. The awareness of this good and the sweetness of its experience, as great as it can be in this wretched and false life, is already a true life, though not yet full, and truly blessed; in the future it will be full and fully blessed, and unchangeably eternal.

[Col. 0394C] This will be when Paul knows as he also is known (1 Cor. 13), when what is partial is abolished and what is perfect comes, when God is seen as he is. For in this life it is a dangerous presumption to promise the fullness of this knowledge; and in such matters, as unbelief must be guarded against concerning what must be believed, so rashness must be avoided concerning what is to be understood. Meanwhile, let authority govern faith and truth govern understanding.

Meanwhile, although God cannot be seen or known as he is, the one who is making progress progresses greatly if he receives nothing as God which God himself is not. Thus, whatever bodily or local thing comes to mind, whatever presents the form of a quality or the dimension of a quantity, the faithful mind must reject and disapprove. Let it think upon truth itself as it can, and know and love it with complete certainty. How true it is is clearly recognized from this: it is loved even when unknown. This truth is God, who is that which he is; and from whom, through whom, and in whom is everything that is. This very same thing is the highest good, from whom, in whom, and through whom is whatever good exists.

[Col. 0394D] Remove from truth everything that is true, and from good everything that is good; think, if you can, of truth itself, of good itself. Who thinks of it and does not love it? Surely God is the selfsame reality: to think it and to love it are one and the same. I say, him himself, not thoughts about him. For many think about him who do not love him; but no one thinks him himself and does not love him.

One must always long, insofar as it is granted, to taste how sweet the Lord is. But when a devout and humble mind does not merit admission to that purity because of its impurity, or, if admitted to taste, cannot remain to enjoy it because of its weakness, it should be driven away thence not without the groaning of love and tears of sorrow, and should embrace the Lord’s goodness as discipline: his goodness, in that one unworthy is admitted; his discipline, in that one is instructed by being repelled. Let it endure patiently while it is purified and make itself worthy to be admitted more often and to remain longer,

[Col. 0395A] so that it may someday merit to dwell there eternally: that it may be in Christ where he is, and be with him in the Father in whom he is. This does not belong to this life, but to that life in which he will be seen as he is: he will be seen, known, not believed.

Would that we understood what we are saying. The blessed people who know jubilation and walk in the light of God’s countenance see and understand these things. But we utter mere words; we are wrapped up and impeded by words in relation to that which cannot be expressed by any words, and yet of which something can be said only in words. For words have their own forms when they signify things in speech, and they form images of these in the thought of speaker or hearer. When they signify forms and formed things, they draw the mind from its inward realities outward to the things of which they are signs. But when they are signs of spiritual or divine realities, they indeed send us inward, but in entering they only impede us and cast a mist over the eyes of the mind.

[Col. 0395C] For they infect the mind with their admitted images in such a way that spiritual or divine things can scarcely be thought without them, though spiritual and divine things have absolutely no forms or images.

For example: What is God? A name of awe. What is Lord? A name of power. If you seek the name of the thing itself: “I am,” he says, “who I am” (Exod. 3). This name, as he himself says, has belonged to him from the beginning, because no word has ever come nearer to signifying the reality. Yet it does not express him as he is, because he surpasses what it signifies; and what it signifies is eternal, yet it does not signify it fully except by the coeternal Word. Therefore it is lawful for many people to say much about him; but him himself—to whom except himself? Yet love,

[Col. 0395D] enlightened love, which speaks inwardly to God, does this better; and humble devotion, whose striving is piety, whose approach is prayer, whose finding or understanding is the enjoyment of the thing itself. There affection and grace converse; faith and understanding answer one another; hope and reality meet; mercy and truth encounter one another; righteousness and peace kiss.

But because faith nourishes love and heals the eye of the mind for these things, let us grasp without obscurity what we understand; let us believe without ambiguity what we do not understand; nor let us altogether depart from words, so long as, to those who do not know, what must be received by us through words is brought to us through their ministry—and yet must be believed by us without every form of words. For this reason also the Word of God appeared in human form: so that God, who “at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers by the prophets, in these last days might speak to us in the Son” (Heb. 1).

[Col. 0396A] That is, he spoke effectively, as in his own Word; because what took place temporally and bodily in him he offered, as it were, to be received by the hands of faith. But the Word himself, through whom all things were made, he promised through bodily and temporal things to those being purified; and for those purified he reserved a fuller contemplation and possession in eternal blessedness. There, Christ will not be known according to the human being. Thus here too, those who desire to know him in some degree above the human being should not cling too closely to the words spoken about him, but should cross by them, as by a ship, from faith to sight.

For when it is said that “the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father” (John 17), and that they are in us and we in them, if we understand these things merely verbally,

[Col. 0396B] what do we do except fashion an idol in our hearts? Since every being has a place where it is, if from these words we think of a place or something spatial in God, we wander far from truth. Therefore, as has already been said, whether in words or in the forms of words, one makes no small progress if one receives in the heart no thought as God which God himself is not, so long as God cannot be thought as he is.

But though the Father is one and the Son another, for the Father to be in the Son is for him to be what the Son is; and for the Son to be in the Father is for him to be what the Father is. We, however, are in them through devout affection; they are in us through the most merciful operation of their piety. Yet both those words of the Lord and these words of ours that expound them, habit or reason has taught our mouth to utter and our heart to think whenever we wish; nevertheless, we do not understand them at any time except through the experience of affection and the inward sense of enlightened love, however much we may wish to do so.

[Col. 0396C] Therefore the Lord himself, appearing in human flesh, as he removed from the world the vanity of idols, so, while presenting to human thought God as unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, the flashing radiance of divinity removed from the thought of faith every vain imagining concerning God. For when he taught that understanding divinity is above human beings, he thereby taught human beings in his own manner to think.

Therefore all the deeds and words of the Word of God are one word to us; all that we read, hear, say, or meditate concerning him—whether stirring love or instilling fear—call us to one thing and send us to one thing, concerning which much is said and nothing is said. For one does not attain to that which is unless he whom one seeks comes to meet him, illumines his countenance over us, and enlightens his face, so that in the light of his countenance we may know where to walk.

[Col. 0396D] His countenance, made known to the loving person’s sense, is his will; his face is the knowledge of his truth. Nor is God ever rightly understood unless the understanding of God is formed by this face, or conformed to this face. Nor are perceived things rightly judged unless the judgment of the judge proceeds from that countenance. Nor is anything rightly done, nor does anyone ever live rightly, unless the acts or life of one wishing to live according to God are formed from it. Nor is any merit sought or received from it except by the gift of grace that precedes all merit.

[Col. 0397A] Therefore, O you whom no one truly seeks without finding: since the very truth of seeking you in the seeker’s conscience already bears a response not doubtful, a response of truth found at least in some measure—find us, that we may find you; come into us, that we may go into you and live in you. For truly it belongs not to one who wills nor to one who runs, but to you who show mercy. Inspire first, that we may believe; strengthen us, that we may hope; urge and kindle us, that we may love. Let the whole of us be yours, so that it may be well with us in you, in whom we live and move and are.

[Col. 0397]

## THE ENIGMA OF FAITH

(*Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, vol. IV, p. 93.)

[Col. 0397B] It is the devout confession of human weakness that concerning God we know this alone: that God is. But it is devout indeed to investigate and search out his essence or nature, and those secret decrees of his unsearchable judgment; yet since the earthly mind does not penetrate them, it must confess them to be unsearchable and beyond investigation. Of these, the one belongs to devout will, the other to unsearchable nature.

Hence the Apostle also—whose faith the worldly person does not grasp, and whose utterances no one except his own words can explain—stands astonished while searching and investigating them, and says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. II). Where such strength trembles, let religious faith set a limit to human modesty before omnipotence, and let the weakness of our understanding not extend itself to search out things that do not possess a nature capable of being perceived.

[Col. 0397C] For if, when people behold the brightness of the sun, the power of the observer is overwhelmed by the power of its light—so much so that, whenever the intent gaze of curious contemplation more diligently investigates the cause of the radiant light, the nature of the eyes is drawn back until the sense of sight is deadened, and it happens that by striving more to see, it does not see—what ought we to expect in matters of God and of the Sun of righteousness? Will not folly come upon one who wishes to be wise beyond measure? Will not the very keen light of understanding be seized by the stupor of dull foolishness? For an inferior cause does not understand the cause of a higher nature, nor does the reason of heaven lie subject to human conception. Whatever is subjected to the consciousness of a weak human being will remain within the condition of weakness.

[Col. 0397D] But so far as heavenly reason permits itself to be understood, so far it must be sought, lest, if we are not content with the measure of its indulgence, we lose what has been granted. Is there, then, anything in God that can be perceived? Certainly—if you are willing only what you are able. But if you hope beyond what you are able, you will be unable even to do what you could have done. For vision face to face and full knowledge are granted to no one here; they are promised in the future according to the merit of faith, by which here we believe what we do not see. For meanwhile we possess in faith the light of promised goods; in it, as through a mirror and in an enigma, we behold the image of blessed realities and future goods.

If, then, it is asked whether God can be seen in this mortal life by a mortal human being, we answer: he can—but not with bodily eyes, as we see this sun; nor by the gaze of the mind, as each person sees himself seeking or knowing something; but by faith, fortified by the authority of the canonical Scriptures.

[Col. 0398B] Yet he was seen by the Fathers in a form chosen by will, not fashioned by nature (Augustine, *Epistle* 112). For, as the evangelist John says, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1)—that is, as these things are seen which are called visible. Therefore he immediately adds: “The Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.” No one has ever seen God with these bodily eyes; but through the ineffable declaration of the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, the pure and holy rational creature is filled with ineffable vision. It can understand the one declaring in the way that a word becomes known—not as a sound clattering in the ears, but as an image made known to minds—so that what the Lord said becomes clear to it in inward and manifest light: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14).

[Col. 0398C] For the true desire of devout persons, by which they long to see God, does not, I think, burn to behold that form in which, whenever he wills and as he wills, what he himself is not appears; rather, it burns to behold that substance in which he is what he is. For he can be seen here by the pure in heart, but cannot be comprehended. Yet in this question of seeing God, a manner of living seems to me more effective than a manner of speaking. For whoever has learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be meek and humble in heart will make more progress through reflecting and praying than through reading or hearing, although one sometimes also makes progress by reading and hearing.

But no one should say that he wishes to see God who is unwilling to devote to the purification of the heart the care worthy of so great a matter. For no one can see God and live, because the mind that is taken up into the ineffability of that vision must be drawn away from this life. That vision belongs to another and higher life—the vision promised in the future, though already begun here in all the children of grace.

[Col. 0398D] Therefore the Only-Begotten Son, ineffably declaring the nature and substance of the Godhead, even in this life invisibly shows them to eyes worthy and fit for so great a sight; and whoever can invisibly see God can also invisibly cleave to him. For the invisible and incorruptible God, “who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6), cannot be seen by human beings through that by which the bodily human being sees bodies. Yet if he were inaccessible to devout minds, it would not be said: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). And if he were invisible to devout minds, it would not be said that “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

Let us consider the whole of John’s Epistle. “Beloved,” he says, “we are now children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (ibid.).

[Col. 0399B] Therefore we shall see him to the degree that we are like him, and we shall see him from that by which we are like him—namely, the mind. For even now we do not see him to the degree that we are unlike him. Who, even the most deranged, would say that we shall be made like God in body? This likeness, therefore, is in the inward person, by which the person is renewed day by day in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him. There we become more like him the more we advance in his knowledge and charity; and we see him more nearly and intimately to the degree that, by knowing and loving him, we become more like him.

However great our progress here may be, it remains far from that perfection in which God will be seen as he is, face to face. There charity will attain vastly more than faith believed or hope desired; attainment will find more than thought had conceived. For that is the country of the living and the seeing, of intellectual beings and intelligible realities, where truth is beheld without any bodily likeness and is obscured by no clouds of false opinions.

[Col. 0399C] For there, as in the Trinity which is God, Father and Son mutually see one another, and their mutually seeing one another is their being one, and the one being that which the other is; so those predestined and taken up into this will see God as he is, and by seeing will become like him as he is. And just as in Father and Son their vision is unity itself, so in God and the human being, their vision will be likeness itself.

The Holy Spirit is the unity of Father and Son, and likewise the charity and likeness of God and human being; but in one way in the highest essence, and in another in lower nature. There the glory of the Lord will be seen, not by a signifying vision—whether bodily, as it was seen on Mount Sinai (Exod. 3), or spiritual, as Isaiah saw it (Isa. 6), or John in the Apocalypse (Rev. 1)—but by direct sight; not through a mirror and in an enigma, as here it is seen by persons worthy of this vision, insofar as the human mind can receive it according to the grace of the one who raises it up, but face to face.

[Col. 0400A] Whoever thinks that this can happen to a human being still living this mortal life—namely, that, after every cloud of bodily and carnal images has been removed and dispersed, he may attain the most serene light of immutable truth, and with a mind wholly estranged from the habit of this life cling to it firmly and without wavering—does not understand what he seeks. For this belongs to another life; and whoever wishes to have here all that is to be possessed there shows that he does not have faith. But for the believer merit is gathered; to the one who sees, the reward is rendered.

Let him therefore rather believe the supreme and wholly unfailing authority: that, while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord, and walk by faith, not by sight (1 Cor. 5). Thus, steadfastly retaining and guarding faith, hope, and charity, let him strive toward sight through the pledge of the Holy Spirit which we have received. He will teach us all truth, when [Col. 0400B] God, who raised the Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, will also give life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in us. But before that which is dead because of sin is given life, it is undoubtedly corruptible and weighs down the soul. When, aided, the soul rises beyond this cloud which covers the whole earth—that is, this fleshly darkness which covers all earthly life—it is, as it were, struck by a swift flash of lightning and returns to its weakness, with a living desire to be raised again but without sufficient purity by which it may be fixed there. The more each person can do this, the greater he is; the less he can, the lesser.

But if the human mind has as yet experienced nothing of this kind, although Christ dwells in it through faith, one must persist in diminishing [Col. 0400C] and putting to death the desires of the flesh and of the eyes, and the pride of this life; and, through the moral practice of virtue, add with every diligence strength to faith, until, having been perfectly put to death by that death of which it was said to Moses, “For no man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33), one may begin to live that life of which the Lord likewise speaks when praying to God the Father for his disciples: “And this is eternal life: that they may know thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17).

He who has thus already awakened unto God, stirred by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, and in God’s love has become contemptible to himself in his own sight—who wishes to enter to him but cannot, and, as God shines upon him, looks into himself and finds that he [Col. 0400D] and his sickness cannot be made proportionate to that purity—finds it sweet to weep and to pray to God again and again for mercy, until he may put off all misery; and to pray confidently, having now received the freely given pledge of salvation through God’s only Savior and illuminator of humankind. Knowledge does not puff up such a needy and sorrowing person, because charity builds up. For he has preferred knowledge to knowledge: he has preferred knowing his own weakness to knowing the walls of the world, the foundations of the earth, and the heights of heaven. By adding this knowledge he has added sorrow: the sorrow of his exile through desire for his homeland and for its Maker, his blessed God.

Among this kind of people, in this household of your Christ, O Lord my God, if I groan as one poor among your poor, give me of your bread [Col. 0401A]—and grant that I, seeking your face, O Lord, seeking it again and hungering and thirsting for your righteousness in the contemplation of your face, may be satisfied with your truth, not with a phantom of my own heart. Let it not be that, by rejecting your truth, I spring back and fall again into my own vanity. For I indeed perceive how many fabrications the human heart produces. What is my heart, after all, but a human heart? Yet I pray to you, God of my heart, that none of these fabrications may cling to me as firm truth; but rather that the light of your truth may come to me from that source from which, although cast away from before your eyes and seeking to return from afar by the way which you made for us through the humanity of your Only-begotten, the breath of his truth is sprinkled upon me. I gladly draw in that breath—mutable though it may be—insofar as in it I see nothing [Col. 0401B] mutable: neither in places and times, like bodies; nor in times alone and, as it were, places, like the thoughts of our spirits; nor in times alone and with no image of places, as in certain reasonings of our minds.

For your essence itself, by which you are what you are, has nothing mutable: neither in eternity, nor in truth, nor in will. For there truth is eternal, and charity true; eternity true, and eternity beloved; truth beloved. Therefore, since we have been exiled from unchangeable joy, yet have not been cut off or severed from it so completely that we do not seek eternity, truth, and blessedness even amid these mutable and temporal things—for we do not wish to die, to be deceived, or to be disturbed—there have been divinely sent to us things suitable [Col. 0401C] to our pilgrimage, by which we are reminded that what we seek is not here, but that we must return from here to that place; and unless we depended upon it, we would not seek these things here.

“For when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4): made so very small as to be made, and certainly sent to the place where he was made. He came teaching wonderful things and wonderfully persuading people of them: contempt for visible things through love for invisible things; contempt for oneself through love for God. He came performing unbelievable deeds, and setting before humankind things still more unbelievable to be believed. For the Lord Jesus Christ was humbled in order to teach us humility. He who contains all things was conceived; [Col. 0401D] he who begets all things was born; he who gives life to all things died. After three days he rose and ascended into heaven, and placed at the Father’s right hand the human flesh which he had assumed. This is wonderful; but far more wonderful is that the whole world believed so incredible a thing.

And if we consider the very manner in which the world believed, it too is perceived to be truly divine and found exceedingly wonderful. Christ sent into the sea of this world with the nets of faith a very small number—twelve fishermen, one of whom turned back—men uneducated in the liberal disciplines and altogether unpolished in respect of worldly learning, unskilled in grammar and unarmed with dialectic. Yet through them he filled the Churches with fish of every kind, so that very many even among those worldly wise persons to whom Christ’s cross had seemed shameful mark it upon their foreheads, and establish at the citadel of modesty that of which they had thought shame should be felt. When, therefore, the whole world was sick, the Word of God came to it in this manner, veiled in flesh, to heal it of its destructions, preparing remedies with his hands and scattering them over the diseases of the world: the Gospel of the kingdom, which was to be preached throughout the whole world, and the Scripture of the Old and New Testament, which speaks of him. And he gave it such authority throughout the world as was fitting for the thing through which God wished to make himself known to humankind and to be believed by them. When people humbly believe it and, by believing it, submit to it, [Col. 0402B] that is the faith through which those blessed who are pure in heart are cleansed, to whom the vision is promised; they are cleansed in order that they may see, and are cleansed only through faith.

For since we were not fit to attain eternal things, and the filth of sins weighed us down, contracted through love of temporal things and, as it were, naturally ingrained through the propagation of mortality, we needed cleansing. Yet, in order to be cleansed so as to be made proportionate to eternal things, we could do so only through temporal things, however much we might already have been made proportionate.

For because we have descended into temporal things and are hindered from eternal things by love of them, a certain temporal remedy receives us to be healed. It calls us to salvation not as those who know, but as those who believe; it is prior not by excellence of nature but by the order of time. For into whatever place [Col. 0402C] a person has fallen, there he must bend and lean in order to rise. Bodily forms hold us fast through the love into which we fell by consenting to sin; upon those very forms we must lean in order to rise. Therefore the Son of God, who was in the form of God, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, so that human beings, receiving God in the human being by faith, might, having received power, become children of God. For we do not move by places toward him who is present everywhere, but by good zeal and good conduct. We could not do this unless Wisdom itself had deigned to accommodate itself to our great weakness and to provide us with an example of life, and this only in a human being, since we too are human beings.

But because, when we come to Wisdom, we act wisely, Wisdom herself, when she comes to us, is thought by proud people to have acted foolishly. And because, when we come to her, we are strengthened, she, when she comes to us, seems to have been weakened. But the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings. Therefore, since God heals souls in every way according to the opportunities of the times, which are ordered by him with wonderful wisdom, he has in no way provided more beneficently for the human race than when the Wisdom of God itself—that is, the only Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father—deigned to assume the whole human being: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Thus he showed to fleshly persons, unable to behold truth with the mind and devoted to bodily senses, how exalted a place human nature has among creatures: [Col. 0403A] not merely by appearing visibly, for this he could have done in some ethereal body tempered to the endurance of our sight, but by appearing to human beings in a true human being. For the very nature that was to be liberated had to be assumed; and lest either sex should perhaps think itself despised by its Creator, he assumed a man and was born of a woman. He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and instruction.

For the old servitude had passed away; the time of new freedom had dawned; and it was now timely and salutary to persuade humanity how free its will had been created. By miracles he commended faith in God, whom he himself was; by suffering, faith in the human being whom he bore. The servants of pleasures perniciously sought riches; he chose to be poor. They coveted honors and dominions; [Col. 0403B] he did not choose to be king. Fleshly people considered children a great good; he despised such marriage and offspring. They most proudly recoiled from insults; he endured every kind of insult. They judged injuries unbearable: what greater injury than for the just and innocent one to be condemned? They abhorred bodily pains; he was scourged and tortured. They feared death; he was punished with death. They regarded the cross as a shameful kind of death; he was crucified. By lacking all the things which we lived wrongly in desiring, he made them contemptible. By enduring all the things which we turned aside from the pursuit of piety in desiring to avoid, he cast them down. For no sin can be committed except by desiring the things he despised or fleeing the things he endured.

Thus his whole life on earth, through the human being whom he deigned to assume, was instruction in conduct. When these things are believed without hesitation and, with faith, are pondered so that what is believed may be loved and seen as it is believed, what results except that the heart is purified to see what is promised to the pure in heart?

But divine providence provides not only for individual human beings, as it were privately, but also for the entire human race, as it were publicly. What is done with each individual is known by God himself, who acts, and by those with whom he acts. But what is done with the human race he has willed to be commended through history and prophecy; and faith must be given to both, so that each of the faithful may faithfully entrust his spirit to God, both on account of what he has received individually from God and on account of what has been done with the human race. [Col. 0403D] Faith in temporal things, whether visible or invisible, has force more through believing than through understanding; for unless what is said is believed, it cannot by any reasoning whatever be persuaded.

The chief foundation of this religion, therefore, which is to be followed, is the history and prophecy of the temporal dispensation of divine providence, for the salvation of the human race, which is to be re-formed and restored unto eternal life. Once these have been believed, a way of life reconciled to divine commandments and conformed to examples will cleanse the mind and make it fit to perceive spiritual things which are neither past nor future, but remain always in the same manner and are subject to no change: namely, God himself, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 0404A]

Of visible past things which have passed temporally, there is faith alone, since they are not hoped for as things still to be seen, but are believed as things done and past; for example, that Christ once died and rose again for our sins. This is no longer hoped for as future, but is only loved as accomplished. Things which do not yet exist but are future are believed in such a way that they are also hoped for as things to be seen and loved; such is the resurrection of our spiritual bodies, although they cannot in any way now be shown. But things which are such that they neither pass away nor are future, but remain eternally, are partly invisible, such as wisdom and justice, and partly visible, such as Christ’s now immortal body. Invisible things are beheld when understood and, accordingly, are in a certain fitting manner seen; and when they are seen, they are far more certain than things reached by bodily sense. [Col. 0404B] Yet they are called invisible because they cannot at all be seen by these fleshly eyes.

But those permanent visible things can, if they are shown, be shown even to these bodily eyes, as the Lord showed himself to the disciples after the resurrection (Matt. 28), and after the ascension to the apostle Paul (1 Cor. 15) and Stephen the deacon (Acts 7). We therefore believe these permanent visible things in such a way that, even if they are not shown, we hope that we shall someday see them. Nor should we try to comprehend them by reason and understanding, except insofar as, because they are visible, we think of them as somewhat more distinct from invisible things, imagining them in thought as they occur to us—though they are often otherwise than we imagine them.

But justice, wisdom, and whatever is of this sort we do not imagine in one way and behold in another. Rather, when we rightly understand them, we behold these invisible things by the directed attention of mind and reason, without any bodily forms or masses, without any figures or outlines of limbs, and without any local limits or infinite spaces. [Col. 0404C]

In the same way we behold the very light by which we discern all these things: namely, the form of eternal reason. In it there sufficiently appears to us what we believe without knowing and what we hold as known; what form we recall by bodily sense and what we fashion in thought; what bodily sense reaches; what the mind imagines as like a body; and what understanding contemplates as certain and entirely unlike all bodies. This light, in which all these things are judged, is not spread all around through local spaces, as is the brilliance of this sun or of any bodily light, nor does it illuminate our mind, as it were, by visible splendor. Rather, it shines invisibly and ineffably, yet intelligibly; and it is as certain to us as it makes certain for us the things which we behold in accordance with it. [Col. 0404D]

Now there are three classes of things that are seen. One is bodily, such as this heaven and this earth, and whatever bodily sense sees and touches in them. Another is like bodily things: the things which we imagine in thought, or behold as it were bodies, whether recalled or presented; from this class also come visions which in dreams or in some ecstasy of mind are impressed upon us with these quasi-local dimensions. [Col. 0405A] The third is distinct from both: it is neither a body nor possesses any likeness of a body, such as wisdom, which is beheld when understood by the mind, and in whose light true judgment is made concerning all these things.

In which of these classes ought we to believe the Trinity, God, to be—the Trinity whom we desire to know? Certainly, either in one of them or in none. If in one, then surely in that which is superior to the other two, as wisdom is. But if wisdom is his gift in us and is less than that highest and unchangeable wisdom which is called God’s wisdom, I think we ought not to think the giver lower than his gift. And if there is in us some brightness of his wisdom, which is called our wisdom, however much of it we can grasp through a mirror and in an enigma, we must separate him from all bodies and from everything bodily.

But if this Trinity must be declared to exist in none of these classes, and is invisible in such a way that it is not even seen by the mind, then much less ought we to hold an opinion of it such as to believe it like bodily things or images of bodily things. For it surpasses bodies not in beauty or greatness of bulk, but in the unlikeness and dissimilarity of its nature. And even though it is distinct from comparison with the goods of our minds—such as justice, wisdom, charity, and the rest of that kind, which certainly we do not weigh by bodily bulk or shape in thought as though they had bodily forms, but behold, when we rightly understand them, in the light of the mind without any corporeality or likeness of corporeality—how much more separate is it from every comparison of quantities and qualities? [Col. 0405C]

Yet the Apostle testifies that it is not wholly beyond the reach of our understanding, when he says: “His invisible things are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made; even his everlasting power and divinity” (Rom. 1). Therefore, although we labor to comprehend by knowledge this Trinity in things near to our bodily senses or in what we ourselves are in our inner person, and do not suffice, faithful piety nevertheless burns toward those divine and ineffable things above us. It is not inflated by arrogant confidence in its own powers, but is kindled by the grace and desire of its Maker and Redeemer. [Col. 0405D]

Let a person attend to that understanding by which he desires to grasp God, and see that nothing in his own nature is better; and let him see whether there he beholds any outlines of forms, brightnesses of colors, spacious magnitude, distances between parts, extension of bulk, motions across intervals of places, or anything of that kind. Certainly we find nothing of this sort in that in which we find nothing better in our nature: that is, in our understanding, by which we apprehend wisdom itself insofar as we are capable of it. Therefore we must by no means admit into our thought concerning that which is incomparably better than every better thing in us what we do not find in our own better part.

[Col. 0406A] But such is the power of love that the human mind draws with it, even when it returns either to itself or to the divine nature which is above it, those things which it has long thought about with love and to which it has clung by the glue of care. And because the things it has loved outwardly through bodily senses are bodies, and it has become entangled with them by a kind of long familiarity, it cannot bring them inward with itself, as it were, into the region of bodily nature; it draws their images along with it, scarcely imagining either itself or the divine nature, as has been said, to be anything other than that without which it cannot think it.

For this is the curse, O Lord God, by which you cursed the earth in the work of Adam and his children: when they have worked it, it does not yield its fruit, but produces thorns and thistles for them, so that in [Col. 0406B] the sweat of their face they may eat their bread (Gen. 3). And what shall your little ones do, the children of man—less earthly from earth than heavenly from heaven—the man of your right hand whom you have strengthened for yourself, already possessing the firstfruits of the Spirit and awaiting from these the redemption of their body? For they too groan within themselves, long since freed from sin but not yet from sin’s punishment; going forth weeping under the punishment of the first sinner and casting their seeds. Although they live from your table, they scarcely ever receive their daily bread from your hand except after tearful sweats and thorny compunctions. For their living and life-giving bread is the memory of the abundance of your sweetness: the grace of visitation and of some vision of you; joy in the awareness of your love and goodness.

While the world rejoices, you allow them to weep and mourn, promising desolation to the former but consolation to the latter. You will that they hunger and thirst, yet promise them eternal satisfaction. But you delay for the exercise of love, and again at times grant them some abundance of your visitation and vision, as consolation for the delay. And where, through prevenient grace, you find a pure will and intention, in the hour of your visitation you perfect purity in the faithful mind through the power of your presence and the abundance of your grace. Purity, according to its capacity, merits vision, but, as the Apostle says, “in part; through a mirror, and in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). [Col. 0406C]

For as long as they are pilgrims in the flesh, away from you, their Lord [Col. 0406D] God, they have no capacity for seeing you except in part, insofar as there still lives in them something which, for those who strive to live by seeing you face to face and as you are, the Lord testifies must first be put to death when he speaks to Moses: “For,” he says, “no man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). What is this, except in us the body of sin, the fleshly desires naturally grown together with us? He who said, “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7), earnestly and tearfully begged to be delivered from this. The one who said this did not desire through impatience with this life to die bodily; rather, he desired to be freed from certain desires of the flesh still living in him, [Col. 0407A] from which no one delivers except the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ, pouring out his charity in our hearts through the Holy Spirit whom he gives us (Rom. 8).

For that grace is the law of the Spirit of life, freeing, as the same Apostle says, from the law of sin and death—that is, from the desires of the flesh, which, like filth upon the human being’s inner eye, hinder one from seeing that which is seen only with a pure heart; and freeing us for eternal life, of which the Lord says, “And this is eternal life: that they may know thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17). For the inner eye, made to see God there, is cleansed here, where the vision begins that is perfected there. It begins here through holiness of life and the practice of divine contemplation, where love merits vision, when that which is not seen is believed, hoped for, and loved; it is to be perfected there, where vision will feed love, when all virtue will consist in loving what shall be possessed, and all blessedness in possessing what shall be loved.

For this reason he who was such said, and those who are such say: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for it is far better” (2 Cor. 5). Such are those who walk by faith and, although they are perfect travelers, are not yet those who have arrived: perfect insofar as, forgetting the things behind, they stretch themselves toward the things within; travelers insofar as they are still on the way. O Lord God of my heart and my portion forever, end of all my desire and goal of my intention: among these people—though far below them and unlike them—I have long since begun the way toward you, walking by faith in order to live rightly [Col. 0407C] and practicing the cleansing of the heart in order to see and contemplate you. I have grown old in this, and have not yet begun.

But when I often consider our common faith in you, without which it is impossible to please you, O Lord our God, and in which you have established the salvation of all, and which therefore ought to belong to all, both little and great in the Church of God, it has sometimes seemed good to return to those most happy and golden first times of evangelical simplicity [Col. 0407D], and to that proper style of your Holy Spirit by which, through the ministry of those who could foresee your Only-begotten, our Savior, as about to come in the flesh, or who deserved to see him when he came, the law of the Spirit of life first began to be inscribed upon the fleshly tablets of believers’ hearts.

There I find all things plain: a matter common to wise persons and simple alike, one which exercises the strong without frightening away any of the weak. There returns to mind that prophetic reproach directed against the Jewish people: that they despised the native waters of Siloam, flowing gently in silence (Isa. 8), and went by the way of Egypt to drink the muddy waters of Egypt’s river (Jer. 2). For there, as some lament through another prophet, we are not compelled to buy our water with money [Col. 0408A] or to give our hands to Egypt and the Assyrians so that we may be filled with bread (Lam. 5); rather, we receive everything freely. Divine authority is there present for all, and it is unlawful to contradict it, saying: “Only believe, and you shall be saved; and all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 5).

Therefore, when we hear there, O Lord our God, Truth speaking: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), we immediately believe in you: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For Truth would not say this unless this is what you are. Nor would you command us, O Lord God, to be baptized in the name of one who was not Lord God. Nor would it be said, “in the name,” rather than “in the names,” unless you—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—were one God. For it would not be said in the divine voice: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6), unless you who are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one God. And if you, God the Father, yourself were your Son, your Word, Christ; and if you yourself were your gift and the gift of your Son, the Holy Spirit, we would not read in the writings of truth, “God sent his Son”; nor would you, Only-begotten, say of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and from you: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 19), and, “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15). [Col. 0408B] Therefore the Father is not himself the Son; the Son is not himself the Holy Spirit.

Directing all my attention to this rule of faith, insofar as you enable me, I will seek your face, O Lord; I will seek your face always. O Lord my God, my one hope, hear me, lest, weary, I should cease to seek you; rather, let me always seek you ardently. Give strength to seek, you who have given the will; and, insofar as will suffice, increase the will you have given. May I always remember you, understand you, and love you, until you, O Trinity God, according to the fullness which you know, restore me to your image, in which you created me: me, who faithfully remembers you, soberly understands you, and truly loves you.

Thus here I have, concerning my Lord God, what for the present I sought, without the torments of questions, without the snares of sophisms, without the noise of disputes: namely, that God is, and that he is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is my faith concerning God, because it is the Catholic faith. For I believe what I read or hear, because he who called himself Truth commanded even this very act of believing. For he said: “He who believes shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). [Col. 0408D] And in whom does one believe, if one does not believe Truth?

He is the Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever refuses to believe him and to believe in him is not a Christian. I profess myself a Christian; I believe him in whom I believe; and I believe the Scriptures, in which I trust that I shall have life. This is the foundation which the wisdom of God ordained, the Word of God dictated, and the apostles, as wise builders, laid. Whoever wishes to build upon it must see what he builds upon it; but he may be secure concerning the foundation. For the foundation will stand, but fire will test what is built upon it (1 Cor. 3). As for the composition of the foundation, let him who composed it see to that. Why should I inquire into what cannot be known in this life? For instance, why should I inquire how the Trinity is unity there, or how three are one, when the Lord, the apostles, and before them the prophets taught that this is so of our Lord God and added nothing further?

If the Word and Wisdom of God had wished us to know this in this life, no one could have taught it better than he himself, either personally or through his apostles, in this world. Indeed, I confidently say that our holy Fathers, teachers of the Church after the apostles, would have said nothing further, had it been permitted; nor, as long as they could, did they wish to add anything on this matter. Let us run through the whole sequence of canonical Scriptures, both Old [Col. 0409B] and New Testament: nowhere, so far as the name “Trinity” is concerned, do we read “Trinity, God”; nowhere do we find, except in the Epistle of John, even that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three, where it is said: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5). And this very passage is not found in the ancient translation.

Yet I say this only concerning the name and number, not concerning the meaning or understanding of the Trinity. For, as has already been said, all those Scriptures cry aloud that God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are one God. But nowhere in them are three persons proclaimed in the Godhead; nowhere is their relative predication proclaimed; nowhere is that celebrated *homoousion*, [Col. 0409C] the term “consubstantiality,” or even the term “substance” in its simple sense; nowhere is “relative to something,” nor anything else of that kind. But when heresies began to arise in the Church, terms and names such as these began, for the sake of faith, to be introduced against novelty both of words and of meanings—without, however, changing the ancient meanings or corrupting the canonical Scriptures.

For this reason, the names themselves that were assumed from antiquity came to possess the same authority and reverence among all believers: the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and all the other ancient names of those realities of which both these and the former terms are signs. For in divine names, or in any words by which something is said concerning God, one must attend not so much to the signs themselves—the names or words—as to that which is designated through those signs. The time had come for the Catholic faith to be sifted, so that it might be purified; to be exercised, so that it might be proved. Therefore that ineffable nature of the highest good permitted itself somewhat more indulgently to be brought down into human words, to assist human piety toward God, though not so far as the narrow limits of human reasoning.

For, although such terms are instruments of common reasoning concerning ordinary matters, when they are adopted in a matter of faith they are nothing but stumbling blocks unless they are faithfully fitted to the reason of faith. Nor did the great Lord, and his wisdom which is without number, refuse the numerical name “Trinity” in that which was simply said, “God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit”; nor the new name *homoousion* in that which was said, that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God: other according to their mutual relations, other according to what each is in itself, and one God. [Col. 0410A]
