For before Sabellius arose in the Church, preaching that he who is the Son is himself the Father, and that he who is Father or Son is himself the Holy Spirit, the preaching of faith concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit had no need of the name “Trinity.” But when it was adopted in the matter of faith and Father, Son, and Holy Spirit began to be called three, people began to ask, “Three what?” Even then, and up to the present, no answer has been found that could be given as it ought and according to the reality of the matter. For when “three persons” is said, that is a different line of reasoning, concerning which something will be said later.

Likewise, before Arius arose—who, by asserting inequality and dissimilarity, attempted to force upon us a crowd of gods—the reason of faith did not know the name *homoousion*, although the meaning of the name was not unknown to it, since it had proclaimed it from the beginning. For could believers of that time have been ignorant of what the Lord said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10)? This is *homoousion*, and nothing else.

For, as we have already said, the name is new and, for the time being, necessary in the preaching of the faith; but the reality is the same. Therefore, just as the name Trinity was admitted into the cause of faith against Sabellius, so against Arius the name *homoousion*, “consubstantiality,” was set in opposition. Thus number—if indeed it is number—was found [Col. 0410C] or assumed in that nature which creates all things, which itself created weight, measure, and number, by which it orders all that it created. But what number, or what kind of number? One that neither increases nor diminishes, neither separates nor joins; neither divided nor confused. For just as in a trinity of three human beings there are three human beings, so three gods are not to be reckoned or counted there. For those who are three are one there; and those who are one are three. In that Trinity one is not a third part; nor are two a greater part than one; nor are three together anything greater than each singly, because the greatness is spiritual, not bodily. Therefore, just as the three are not parts of one God on account of the individual perfection of each, so neither are they to be reckoned or conceived as three gods, whether [Col. 0410D] perfect or imperfect.

Where, then, is number? The number which is there both is number and is not number. For there is there something ineffable that cannot be explained in words. When you say Father, Son, Holy Spirit, three seem to be counted; but there is no number of any kind there. If you ask, “What three?” number fails. When you begin to think, you begin to count; when you have counted, you cannot answer what you have counted. Each one there is God. Are there three gods? Far be it! Each one is almighty. Are there three almighty ones? By no means. There are not three gods, not three almighty ones, not three wisdoms, not three wise ones, not three great ones, nor three greatnesses. For all these things are said substantially of God. So great is the force of that highest [Col. 0411A] substance in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of each individually in relation to himself is received in the highest reality not plurally but singly. Thus we say, God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; yet in the sum we do not say three gods, but one.

This is the general rule concerning all things said substantially of God, as has been stated, and also concerning those things said with reference to creation, such as Creator, Lord, and the like. Things of this sort—for example greatness, goodness, and the rest—are accidents insofar as they exist in created things, but not in God. For when these are said of God, he is to be understood, as far as we can, as good without quality, great without quantity, Creator without need, present without position, containing without habit, wholly everywhere [Col. 0411B] without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without change in himself, and suffering nothing.

Therefore, when it is asked what three the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are, this is not asked with respect to what they are to one another, but with respect to what they are; nor can they be called three good beings, three great beings, or anything of this sort any more than three gods can be called so, according to the aforementioned rule concerning substantial divine names. But human weakness presses on, infected by familiarity with numbers and numberable things, and says: “Everything that is said relatively to something is also something in itself, apart from that which it is relatively to something else.” For example, three human beings are a father, a son, and any friend of theirs. In themselves they are three human beings; in relation to one another, they are father, son, and friend [Col. 0411C]. Unless they were what they are in themselves, they could not be what they are in relation to one another. Therefore, those who are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in relation to one another are three somethings or three someones in themselves. What three? What three things? Unless an answer is given here, Sabellius gains the point for which he is called a heretic.

Yet the surpassing excellence of divinity exceeds every capacity of ordinary speech. For if we weigh the matter as it is, beyond doubt there is the Father, there is the Son, there is the Holy Spirit; and the Son is not the same as the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit the same as the Father and the Son. Therefore, there are three. Will you say, “Three essences?” Far be it! For according to the aforementioned rule of divine names, the Father is essence, the Son is essence, the Holy Spirit is essence; nevertheless, there are not three essences but one essence [Col. 0411D]. What, then, are the three? Human words fail; let us take refuge in the words of the Word.

When the Lord was speaking to the Jews about himself and his Father, they said: “Where is your Father?” (John 8). It was as if they said: “You say that there are two, yourself and your Father. We see you; where is your Father?” The Lord answered: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). It was as if he said: “One, because I and the Father are one God; *are*, because the Father and I are two.”

Therefore, just as, when questioned, the Lord says that he and the Father are one, so we, taught by him concerning the Trinity which is God, answer “one” to one who asks, “What three? What three things?” If he is obstinate and persists in asking, “What one?” we say, “One God.” Yet he will not be obstinate if he is a faithful person who further asks [Col. 0412A] who that God is, since there is but one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Father and Son, then, are not one, as Sabellius says, but are one, as the Lord says.

Likewise, unless the Holy Spirit were God, *homoousios*, that is, of the same substance with the Father and the Son, the Lord would by no means say: “God is Spirit” (John 4). And elsewhere: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke 11). Again: “The Lord and his Spirit sent me” (Isaiah 48). And all the Scriptures agree in this: the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son. This is the one—or this is the one reality—which David asks of the Lord and seeks in order to contemplate it, saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek” (Psalm 26). But this one is not one by number, but by nature [Col. 0412B]: namely, a solid selfsame reality, having no parts, but possessing its whole entirety in everything that it is or has—if, indeed, “all,” “whole,” or “entire” can be said where there are no parts.

Whenever several things are called one in the Scriptures and it is not added in what respect they are one—as it is added where “one heart and one soul” are said (Acts 4)—the meaning is the same nature, in no respect dissimilar or discordant. Therefore, insofar as three things are thus, they are one. But truly to be three things in this way belongs to that Trinity alone which is God. For even if there are at times three human beings of the same nature and of the same will or agreement, certainly three human beings are always three human beings; and if they agree in some matters, they disagree in many. But in the Trinity which is God, those who are three are most truly one; they are not three gods, but one God, of one nature and the same essence [Col. 0412C]. For the affirmation of one essence establishes perfect unity.

Therefore, when it is asked concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, if there are three, “What three?” nothing is answered from the authority of the Lord and in accordance with the reasoning of faith better or more fitting to the truth than “one.” Yet the Fathers, because of the necessity of disputation and the difficulty of exposition or conversation, were pleased to admit the plural number, apart from relative names; and, in order to answer “What three things?” with one name, to say “three persons.” But this is to be understood so that no masses, intervals, distances of any dissimilarity, separable distinction [Col. 0412D], or personal confusion are conceived there. Let neither part nor whole be conceived there; let not the Trinity be thought something greater than one person, nor a person something less than the whole Trinity. Although they seem to be delimited from one another, nevertheless, insofar as faith can understand, those three which are called three persons are to be understood as infinite in themselves: each in each, each in all, all in all, and all one.

When human poverty sought, in speaking, to bring forth for human understanding this ineffable reality—which we have ourselves attempted almost ineffably to utter from the perception and words of the holy Fathers—insofar as it held it within the inner chamber of the mind according to its capacity, concerning its Lord God either through devout faith or through whatever understanding, Catholic piety feared to say “three essences,” lest some diversity be understood in that [Col. 0413A] highest equality. For it is most certainly known from the Scriptures, devoutly to be believed, and even apprehended by the mind’s gaze, that there is he who is Father, he who is Son, and he who is Holy Spirit; that the Father is not the same as the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the same as the Son or the Father. Yet, not daring to say “three essences,” it sought what it might say without offense and said “three persons.” By these names it did not wish diversity to be understood, but it did not wish singularity to be understood either, lest God be understood as merely singular; that is, so that not only unity might be understood there from the fact that three persons are said. For even if the reality as it is were not expressed, it would nevertheless not be wholly silent when the question was asked, “What three things?” or [Col. 0413B] “What three?” Rather, something would also be answered according to ordinary speech.

Moreover, by these names of the three persons, speech concerning the ineffable abundance was made more abundant and concise for all the faithful; safer for answering adversaries; and more suited both to subtle inquiry concerning God and to discussion with friends. The confession of faith has a form of sound words and an instrument of language fit for exposition or debate.

Those who define define person in two ways: either “an individual substance of a rational nature,” or “that concerning which, by its form, there is a definite recognition of itself.” The first definition, preferring the name “substance,” offers an unambiguous understanding: namely, admission into the fellowship of those names that are said substantially and in themselves of [Col. 0413C] God. Thus, just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are said, yet there are not three gods but one God, so if person is predicated of God, let Father be called person, Son person, Holy Spirit person, but in the highest reality one person. According to this definition, it is no more permissible to say three persons there than three gods.

According to the other definition, however, when asked what three are, we answer “three persons,” because each of them, by the form of its own designation—whether “person of the Father,” “person of the Son,” or “person of the Holy Spirit”—presents a definite recognition of itself and thus has some capacity for answering “What three?” For “three persons” is answered and said as a common name, just as “three human beings” or “three persons,” as though they were three proper relative terms: namely, the person of the Father, the person of the Son, and the person of the Holy Spirit. Since it is proper to the Father that he begot; proper to the Son that he was begotten; and proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from both: in these properties no separation of nature is understood, but a certain personal recognition [Col. 0413D].

This is enough concerning the name “person,” added by the holy Fathers in the cause and reasoning of faith. For it did not seem unjust to the Church of God that holy Fathers should possess great authority in ordering the doctrine of faith, since they endured great labor for the faith, even to the shedding of their blood and the mortification of their bodies.

Therefore I believe and confess one God in three persons: three persons expressly distinguished under [Col. 0414A] their properties; not names only, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks say, *hypostases*, that is, subsistences. The Father never excludes the person of the Son or Holy Spirit; nor, conversely, does the Son or Holy Spirit receive the name and person of the Father. But the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance and distinguished in persons and names. This is my faith, because this is the Catholic faith concerning our Lord God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. By its understanding—such as understanding can be in matters of this kind—one reaches toward the knowledge of divinity, such as knowledge can exist there: first, by doubting nothing through unbelief concerning what must be believed; then, doubting nothing through unbelief concerning what must be understood; then, defining nothing rashly concerning what must be understood; and afterwards, adhering faithfully and most ardently to truth when it appears [Col. 0414B].

For by three grades of understanding the progress of faith must ascend to God and to the knowledge of him. The first grade is diligently to ascertain what one must believe concerning one’s Lord God. The second is to know how one must likewise think and speak rightly concerning that which is rightly believed. The third is now the experience of realities themselves: to think of the Lord in goodness, as those think who seek him in simplicity of heart.

The first is as easy for one ascending as believing is easy for one willing to believe—yet only for one to whom it has been given. For, as the Apostle says, “faith is not for [Col. 0414C] all” (2 Thessalonians 3). The second, the further it is removed from the nature of realities, is the more difficult; it belongs to those who, as the same Apostle says, through practice “have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil” (Hebrews 5), though it is also presumed upon by the curious. The third belongs to the perfect, who desire to love the Lord their God with their whole heart, their whole soul, and all their mind, already possessing the firstfruits and pledge of the Spirit that they are children of God.

Again, the first grade, founded on authority, belongs to faith and possesses a form of faith grounded in probable testimonies of approved authority. The second belongs to reason—not human reason, but that proper to faith—and it too possesses a form of sound words in the faith wholly consonant with divine [Col. 0414D] authority. Its task is to know not only how to think and speak rationally of God according to the reasoning of faith, but also how this same faith may arise where it is absent, be nourished and aided where it exists, and be defended against enemies. The third already belongs to illuminating and beatifying grace, bringing faith to its end—or rather, perfecting it in love—passing from faith to sight, and beginning that knowledge which is not the knowledge of faith and which begins here in the faithful person along with faith, but of which the Apostle says: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know as I also am known” (1 Corinthians 13).

That is the knowledge which perfect charity begins in this life in order to perfect it in the future. The present knowledge, however, belongs to the faith of this temporal life—or rather, it is faith itself—by which God is known as he can be known through faith; and insofar as he is believed, insofar he is known. It has its beginning in the first grade of understanding, its growth in the second, and is in some manner perfected by failing in the third, when one passes from the faith of one who believes and hopes to the knowledge and joy of one who possesses and enjoys—or begins to possess and enjoy [Col. 0415A].

For these two knowledges differ from one another as much as anything that a human being can think or say about God in accordance with human capacity differs from God as he is in himself. That a human being can think of God better than speak of him, while God himself is far otherwise than a human being can think or speak of him, is clear to all who have even a slight apprehension of God. Yet this first knowledge of God [Col. 0415B] is to know, think, or speak rationally concerning God according to the reasoning of faith.

That such knowledge is often more readily available to many who do not believe as they ought than to many truly faithful persons who believe rightly but are unable to distinguish what they believe, plainly shows that this is by no means the perfect knowledge of truth: it sometimes passes by truth’s truest lovers, yet does not deny itself to many lovers of vanity. Many such persons know much about God, or strive to know it, acting from curiosity merely to know, or seeking their own glory in order to seem knowledgeable or be thought so, rather than seeking God’s glory. For this is the knowledge of God of which the Psalmist says that “night declares it to night” (Psalm 44): that is, human being to human being, flesh and blood to flesh and blood, sometimes unbeliever to unbeliever. It is far removed from that wisdom and Word which day—that is, the spiritual person to the spiritual person, or the Holy Spirit himself in himself to the spirit of every holy person—does not merely declare but pours forth: that is, insinuates by a hidden inspiration with a certain perception of divinity and taste of highest wisdom [Col. 0415C].

Nevertheless, because this knowledge is greatly necessary for the exercise of piety, if it is entrusted to the pursuits of piety and devoutly handled, it ought to be desired by absolutely all people and embraced with every effort. It will not be useless for the progress of faith if it is administered soberly and according to the reasoning of faith. For just as it is exceedingly dangerous to think lofty thoughts in matters concerning God, so it is praiseworthy to think [Col. 0415D] soberly. Thus, if anyone judges that every question concerning the highest, immutable, and unsearchable nature should be tackled not only in speech or writing but even in thought alone, every human mind must be checked and restrained from so monstrous and empty a presumption. Yet the spirit of a faithful person ought rather to be aided and exhorted, not extinguished, in investigating only those matters whose comprehension is not denied to humanity, or matters which a faithful person may by no means be permitted wholly to ignore.

For just as inability to know concerning the Lord God our Creator what is above humanity is not counted as sin, so one who could know certain things but does not make the effort, or one who is not yet able but neglects to devote fitting effort to become able, is judged before God guilty not only of ignorance of God but is also assigned, as a penalty justly due to his merits, that here one who would not know or act when able will be unable when he wishes [Col. 0416A]. Moreover, in the things which he pursues curiously while neglecting God, he is afflicted in the present and in the future cast into outer darkness—whatever that darkness may be—of which the Gospel speaks.

Having once entered upon the way of seeking God, therefore, let us not grow weary; let us not cease. Faithful is he who promised, saying: “Seek, and you shall find” (Luke 11). And the Apostle says: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (1 Corinthians 9). And concerning himself: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have obtained it. But one thing: forgetting what lies behind and stretching myself toward what lies ahead, I press toward the [Col. 0416B] goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus our Lord.” And he added: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this.” What? Namely, that “while we are away from the Lord, walking by faith” (Philippians 3), we are travelers, not those who have arrived. To be a vigorous traveler on the way of faith is the perfection of this life; arrival belongs to another life.

Let us therefore proceed devoutly and humbly on this way in which we walk, reverencing the footsteps of the Fathers who have gone before. While attending to the enigmas of the first knowledge of God, which is through faith, let us invoke him who “made darkness his hiding place,” not in order that he may not be seen, but in order that he may be sought more diligently; and the more diligently he is sought, the more sweetly he will be loved when found. Let us go about and act [Col. 0416C], with his aid and instruction, so that meanwhile, insofar as he grants it, we may know him through faith; afterwards it will likewise be his grace that we pass from faith to sight.

The first elements, as it were, of divine knowledge through faith—by which God is known through faith—are the divine names by which God is named among human beings, together with a fitting form of sound words in the faith. For names are also said to derive from knowledge (*notitia*). In order that we may proceed step by step, as we have already touched upon above, according to the right order of advancing toward God, we must first know concerning the thing to be known what it is, since it can be designated only by some name; then what sort of thing it is, or how it is, so that faith concerning it may be received as the thing itself is.

For just as, according to the principles of literacy, first elements are gathered into syllables, syllables into words, and these, joined together according to the intention of the one joining them, produce some meaning in the reader’s mind, so the divine names by which God is spoken of among human beings, fitted together according to the form of sound words in the faith and the reasoning of faith, produce in the believer’s heart some understanding of faith concerning that hidden reality of divinity [Col. 0416D]. Hence the Apostle Paul, instructing his beloved disciple in the faith concerning the matters in which he ought to be taught, says: “Hold the form of sound words which you have heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus. Guard the good deposit” (2 Timothy 1). From this we learn that, in guarding the deposit of faith and its form, the form of sound words within it must be carefully observed. For there is a form of faith [Col. 0417A], and there is a form of sound words within it.

The form of faith is, concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as has often been said, that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; nevertheless, there are not three gods but one God. The form of sound words in the faith, however, is a particular manner of speaking about God according to these very points which we have set forth: a manner which, on the authority of Christ the Lord, the apostles, and apostolic teachers, the practice of Christian piety long ago established concerning divine names and the things said in the confession of faith concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

This manner of speaking about God has its own discipline, fortified by the rules and limits of faith, in order to teach persons to speak rationally about God according to the reasoning of faith and to prepare them to think and perceive ineffably concerning the ineffable [Col. 0417B]. We say “according to the reasoning of faith” because this manner of speaking about God has certain words proper to it: rational words indeed, but not intelligible except within the reasoning of faith, and not according to the reasoning of human perception.

For what we said shortly before—“God is Father, God is Son, God is Holy Spirit; yet there are not three gods, but one God”—is in some fashion comprehended according to the reasoning of human perception. In human matters, human reason prepares faith for itself; but in divine matters faith comes first, and then itself forms for itself a reason of its own kind. For it is the most right reason to receive faith concerning a thing as that thing is, and to fit to faith the form of speech. Speech or inquiry concerning God loves the humble [Col. 0417C] and simple who seek God in poverty of spirit, whom curiosity does not drive to inquiry, but piety draws. It loves to speak not with hasty and alien words, but with those very words by which the Word of God manifested himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit to the world, in that very character of speech by which the people of God propagated faith in the Trinity throughout the world.

It hates disputes, animosities, novelties, battles of words, and the empty torments of questions; teaching believers rather by experience itself and shaping them through the merit and practice of faith to attain the reward of contemplation. The names which we have called its first elements are either those by which divinity itself revealed itself in the world through itself—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—or those by which, from a different consideration of itself, it caused itself to be named differently among human beings [Col. 0417D].

For a human being, made in the image of God, possesses a natural desire for knowledge of God and of his own origin. Since no human mind, however capable of reason, is permitted by nature itself to doubt that God exists, that he is Creator of all things, and that the power and providence of all things rest with him, human piety and curiosity also labor and strive, as though naturally, in some measure to perceive what he is. Therefore, whether through the invisible things of God understood through the things made, through the natural perception of reason, or through the gift of revealing grace, human beings have given God as many names as they have had considerations concerning him: powerful, wise, wisdom, power, and very many other names of this sort [Col. 0418A].

Although human beings too are often called by these names—for they too are called wise and powerful—no one is called wisdom or power, or anything of this sort, because no one is wise or powerful in the manner in which God is. For to be wise and to be powerful is God’s very being, and he himself is his own wisdom and his own power. The same is to be understood concerning truth, charity, and other names of this sort: namely, names by which God can be called substantially.

The rationale of divine names is not uniform. Some things are said substantially of God; other things are said otherwise. For in created things also everything that exists is either a subject or in a subject—that is, either substance or accident. Yet it is [Col. 0418B] not so in God. Nothing is ever said of God according to accident, though neither is everything always said according to substance. For something is also said relatively.

Here it must first be known that categories of this sort—substance and accident, what is said relatively, genus, species, and the like—are alien to the nature of faith. They are common and ordinary instruments of human reason and art for distinguishing ordinary things; they are wholly unworthy of divine realities and foreign to the form of sound words in the faith. Yet the reasoning of faith, as though accommodating human reason, does not wholly reject or cast away these things brought to it by human beings. Rather, it adopts them and, conforming each to its own rules and fitting them together, reduces their understanding as though captive into the service and slavery of faith [Col. 0418C].

Hence many names which, in ordinary things, are names of accidental properties, when transferred to God—where the reasoning of faith admits nothing according to accident—are found to be predicated substantially. For example, when God is called great without quantity and good without quality, what is understood except that things of this kind are not admitted insofar as they are accidents, yet are admitted, and insofar as they are naturally in God in a manner found nowhere else, are predicated substantially?

But where there is no accident, there is neither substance, nor can there be substance which underlies no accidents or can underlie none. Yet the supreme simplicity of the divine nature can receive absolutely no accidents. If it received them, it would not be simplicity. That nature is truly called simple which does not have something that it can lose; which cannot be seen as mutable through either increase or decrease; which is not one thing as possessor and another as what it possesses. Accordingly, that highest nature is truly simple, because quality or quantity is not one thing in it and substance another; nor is it what it is—whether powerful, wise, or blessed—by participation in something foreign [Col. 0418D].

Therefore “essence” is said more fittingly than “substance,” as will appear more fully in what follows. Yet by customary speech we more frequently use “substance” improperly of God [Col. 0419A]. Perhaps this name can, however, be said of God in another sense, so that he may be understood as subsisting, as it were, through himself, or as underlying, as it were, all things that exist, as their principle, cause, and ground of subsistence. Otherwise, “substance” is said of God altogether improperly.

Therefore, when speaking of God, one must not always speak according to substance, but never according to accident. Nor, when something is said relatively—as Father is said with reference to Son, Son to Father, Holy Spirit to both—is it to be understood according to accident. For the Son never came to the eternal and everlasting Father so that he became Father, as though he had not previously been so. He has always been—or rather, always is—Father; and the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with him, is always from the eternal Father, while the Holy Spirit is always from the Father and Son, coeternal and consubstantial with them [Col. 0419B].

Nor is the Trinity, God, to be understood in any way according to genus and species, although some who think perversely about God fabricate this, attempting to assert that the three persons are as though three species of one essence. Both the reasoning of faith professes, and truth cries aloud—and cannot at all be refuted—that the essence itself is nothing other than the three persons, and the three persons are the essence itself. Therefore the Trinity, God, must not be conceived according to genus and species. Nor, indeed, altogether relatively, except according to the measure of faith. For the relation of one God is no greater than that of one human being. Yet there is there the relation of Father to Son, Son to Father, and Holy Spirit to both, making the Trinity, while beyond every rule of relatives one substance retains its truest and most solid unity.

Let such concepts, then, serve in matters concerning God. For they are not always found useless if administered rationally according to the reasoning of faith. When something of this kind is admitted, one must attend not so much to the thing itself as to what the reasoning of faith intends to make of it. Let us not subject the cause of our faith to human arguments or reasonings, but let all such things be subject to it. Let them serve where they ought; let them not intrude further than they ought. For on the simple way one must walk simply. Let those who profess to live according to the Gospel speak according to the Gospel [Col. 0419D].

To continue now concerning divine names: first, we must carefully observe how they are to be understood—common names as common, singular names as singular. Common names are those predicated substantially of God, such as power, wisdom, charity, God; singular names are those said relatively, such as Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Concerning these one must especially maintain what we said above: whatever that most excellent and divine sublimity is said to be in itself is said substantially; whatever it is said to be in relation to something else is said not substantially but relatively. The force of the same substance is, as it were, in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that whatever is said of each individually in relation to himself is received in the highest reality not plurally but singly [Col. 0420A]. For this reason all names of this sort are called common.

Thus God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit are said; nevertheless, there are not three gods but one God. Great Father, great Son, great Holy Spirit are said; nevertheless, not three great beings but one great being. So must one think concerning power, wisdom, charity, truth, and all divine names which, as has been said, are said of the divine majesty in itself and substantially. When it is called any one of these, what it is—not what kind of thing it is—is declared.

How the proper or singular names refer mutually to one another is evident: Father to Son, Son to [Col. 0419C] Father, Father and Son to Holy Spirit, and the Spirit himself to them. In this way both the names of the highest essence [Col. 0420B], which are in themselves, and the names of the Trinity, by which the three are related to one another, each in its own manner proclaim unity and do not leave the Trinity unspoken. The former, insofar as they are common to the three, show the personal Trinity; insofar as they are always one in the highest reality, they show consubstantial unity. The latter, insofar as each is proper to an individual, show the truth of the Trinity; insofar as they are mutually relative and show by the very name of their singularity that one refers to another, they show the unity of substance.

Now let us proceed to the essence of God and its names, namely those called essential from the essence itself. Their starting-point is what God said when his servant Moses asked his name: “I am,” he said, “who I am” (Exod. 3). Thus, he says, you shall tell the children of [Col. 0420C] Israel: “He who is has sent me to you” (ibid.). For just as “substance” is named from subsisting, so “essence” from being. How substance does not properly apply to God—although Scripture often employs the term improperly—has already been said above. To whom the name “essence” applies more truly and fittingly is obvious to all. For he alone is truly to be called “being” who is unchangeably from eternity, whose being is what he is; and what he is, he always is; and as he is, so he always is. He has in himself no possibility of not being what he is, because neither has he in himself any possibility of being what he is not; and that which is thus is neither preceded by a beginning, enclosed by an end, turned through times, contained by places, nor altered by ages. Nothing is lacking there, because all is in him; nothing is superfluous, because nothing is [Col. 0420D] outside him. Therefore he to whom it belongs by nature always to be able to be what he is is alone, or almost alone, to be called “being.”

Accordingly, it is known most certainly from the Scriptures and is to be believed devoutly that this one is the Father, this one is the Son, this one is the Holy Spirit; yet the Father is not the same as the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the one who is Father or Son. Yet we avoid speaking of three essences there no less than of three gods, since being and being God are not different there, but are the same. Therefore, in accordance with the form of sound words in faith and with the previously stated rule drawn from the reasoning of faith concerning God’s essential names, we call the Father essence, the Son essence, the Holy Spirit essence; yet not three essences, but one essence. [Col. 0421A]

All these names that are called essential from the essence itself bear a certain likeness to their origin and to the thing whose names they are. As the three are there and the three are one, so all these names are one and one is all. For God is designated by one of these names just as by all of them, and not more by all than by one of them. One of those goods signified by so many names is the same as all of them, and all as one. For in God power is the same as willing, wisdom, knowing, and all the rest which, as was said, are predicated of God essentially and in relation to himself. He does not have one manner of power, another of will, another of wisdom, another of knowledge, since he is not one thing in one respect and another in another respect; rather, he simply is what he is. Nor should it be thought or believed that the supreme good is somehow composed [Col. 0421B] of all these goods. It is no less in each than in all; rather, it is wholly in each, and one in all. Otherwise our God would not be simple but multiple. Moreover, all these things are likewise, together and in this same way, each of the individual persons in the Trinity: just as all these things are one in God, so every person in the Trinity is all these things.

The Father is indeed sometimes called power, the Son wisdom, and the Holy Spirit goodness. But when this is said, Catholic understanding must be alert and carefully observe that some things common to all three are sometimes assigned in this way to individual persons, in order, as it were, to weave together and order for human understanding the harmony of divine co-operation. [Col. 0421C] And just as the Trinity of the three persons has one operation, so in all these matters, insofar as they are in God, one undifferentiated operation must be understood, although that same operation does not reach the creature in the same manner, even though it proceeds from God in this same manner. For as God is not powerful in one way, wise in another, and good in another, so neither, insofar as it is in him, does he do in one way what belongs to power, in another what belongs to wisdom, and in another what belongs to goodness—although, in creatures unlike one another, the effect of that undifferentiated operation appears dissimilar.

But when certain divine names of this kind, which, as was said, belong equally by natural unity to all three persons in the Trinity, seem by more familiar and frequent usage to be assigned especially to certain persons in the Trinity—such as those already mentioned: [Col. 0421D] power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, goodness to the Holy Spirit—this is done in order that the persons may be distinguished, not separated. For, apart from the relative names by which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said in relation to one another, the individual names proper to each are indeed proper to each. By whatever name one of them is named, all are named together, because all are found to be one in that by which they are named.

The Son is called not only Wisdom and God, but also the wisdom of God; and the Holy Spirit, the goodness of God. This too must certainly be understood according to the reasoning of faith. For the Son is the wisdom of the Father—not the wisdom by which the Father is wise, since he is himself supremely wise through himself and supreme wisdom—but he is the Father’s wisdom in this sense: since he is wisdom, his being what he is is from the Father, from whom comes to him everything that he is. The Son is from the Father, wisdom from wisdom, one wisdom with the Father; just as he is substance—or rather essence—from essence, one essence with the Father. [Col. 0422A] For if the Son is called the Father’s wisdom in the sense that the Father is wise through him, then the Son will be not so much the Father’s Son as the Father’s quality. And since for God to be wise is to be, and the Father’s wisdom is one essence with the Father, if the Son were the Father’s wisdom in the sense that the Father were wise only by that wisdom which is the Son, the Son would be not so much the Father’s Son as his essence; and, according to Sabellius, the Son himself would be the Father. [Col. 0422B] The same must be understood concerning the goodness called the Holy Spirit.

But lest, because the Father is called power, the Son wisdom, and the Holy Spirit goodness, the persons themselves should somehow be thought separable, the reasoning of faith immediately supplies that these same things, individually proper to the individual persons, are also said commonly of all three. Thus not only the Father is called power, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit; not only the Son wisdom, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit; nor only the Holy Spirit goodness, but also the Father and the Son. And when, concerning the providence of creation, the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, and the goodness of the Holy Spirit are proclaimed, nothing else is to be understood in these names of deity than that the operation [Col. 0422C] of omnipotent, wise, and most kindly deity is proclaimed in such a way that in what is said the co-operation of the Trinity may also be understood. [Note: [Col. 0421D] Words of Pope Leo, Sermon 2 for Pentecost.]

When Holy Scripture speaks in this way—assigning in deeds, words, or names of this kind something to the individual persons that seems appropriate to them individually—Catholic faith should not be troubled but instructed. Through a property either of word or of work, the truth of the Trinity is suggested to us; yet understanding must not divide what hearing distinguishes. For this reason certain things are set forth under the designation of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, so that the confession of believers may not go astray concerning the Trinity. Since it is inseparable, the Trinity would never be understood [Col. 0422D] if it were always described as inseparable. Thus the difficulty of speech rightly draws our heart toward understanding; and through our weakness heavenly teaching helps us, so that—because neither singularity nor diversity is to be conceived in the deity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—true unity and true Trinity may in some measure be perceived by the mind, even if they cannot be expressed simultaneously by the mouth.

Let this suffice for the present concerning God’s essential names. Whatever we say of them is nothing, because whatever can be said of God is not adequate to him; for what is ineffable cannot be unfolded in words. Words fail; understanding grows dim. Yet because we are commanded always to seek the face of the Lord [Col. 0423A], and what is divinely commanded is in some fashion promised, we must not despair. Understanding must be disentangled and the effort of words raised as far as it can go; and where human capacity fails, the reality of God must be honoured by silence.

It must further be known that that supreme majesty called God, powerful, wise, and the like—names which are said essentially and in relation to himself—can also be said in relation to creation. For God, who in himself is he who is, is in relation to creation the God of all things that are, insofar as he is the Creator, ruler, and Lord of all things which are not what he is. He who has power in himself to be what he is is, in relation to every creature and in every respect, not only powerful but omnipotent. For him, to know or be wise concerning himself [Col. 0423B] is to be; his knowledge or wisdom concerning himself is not one thing concerning himself and another thing concerning creation. He who in himself is not so much good as the very essential good by which whatever is good in any manner is good, is the supreme good in relation to every creature of his, and supremely good—than whom nothing better can be conceived, and from whom comes every instance of well-being in whatever manner anyone fares well.

The same must be understood of almost all the divine names by which God is spoken of in relation to himself: namely, that he is also called by these names in relation to creation, not relatively in the sense of receiving from creation the being that is said of him in relation to it, but, if one may speak thus, communicatively, by granting being to the creature in relation to which he is so named. Thus God is called great in relation to creation by comparison with creation itself; great in himself without every comparison; just in relation to creation, by ordering all things justly. But in what he himself is, just as his being is just, so he is most just in himself; and similarly in all other cases. [Col. 0423C]

Whatever is understood of God in relation to creation by names of this sort, God is so in such a way that, as was said of his essential names, he is—not as though his being were constituted from these parts of himself, he who is not this and that in a partial sense, nor this or that in an individual sense. He is not present in part and absent in part; rather, he is what he is, who is all these things, and none of them is accidental in him. For he borrows none of them from elsewhere, but has them essentially, and has nothing in himself except what he himself is. And as all these things in him are not one thing and another, [Col. 0423D] but are a simple one, so they are not in him in one manner and another, but simply and in one manner, without any mode whatever.

Certainly, some of these names, when said of God, seem to display the character of relative accidents, as when he is called Creator, Lord, or principle in relation to creation. Yet they must by no means be understood in this way, since it belongs to every accident to change its subject, and none of them can happen to an unchangeable substance. Still, to be Creator, Lord, or principle is eternal for God, although there has not always been a creature of which he is Creator, Lord, and principle: this is difficult to understand. Human beings, trying somehow to speak of the ineffable and able to do so only in words, and finding no words better suited to expressing what must be said in this manner—where none are suitable—have called God Creator, Lord, and principle. These terms are manifest and entirely true in that God created all things and is Lord and principle of all things. Yet the temporal name “creature,” as was said, falling upon eternity, makes it difficult to understand how this is not accidental. [Col. 0424A]

But every accident, as was said, whether by coming or departing, must change its subject; this does not suit the unchangeable God. When such things and similar things are said of God, however, they must be understood in that unchangeable substance in a distinctively divine manner: they are said relatively to creation such that, although God may at some time begin to be called one of these things temporally, this must not be understood as something happening to the very substance of God, which is so named, but to that nature in relation to which he is named. Hence also, when we flee to him, no change occurs in him or in his nature; rather, we are changed when we are made better from worse. So too, when he begins to be our Father, he does not change; we are regenerated through his grace—he who gave us power to become children of God—and become children of God. When we become children of God, our substance is indeed changed for the better; but he begins to be our Father without any change in his substance. [Col. 0424B]

And when a righteous person begins to become a friend of God, that person changes; but far be it from God to change. He loves no one temporally as though with a new love not previously in him; he loved us before the foundation of the world, and with him neither have past things passed away nor are future things not already accomplished. Thus, when something begins to be said of God temporally which was not said before, it is clear that it is said relatively; yet not according to an accident of God which has happened to him, but plainly according to an accident of that in relation to which he begins to be so called. For when divine realities are spoken of in this way, they are by no means spoken of in their own manner, but in the manner in which what is said may somehow be grasped by human feeling. Therefore, when language is used about God, the principles governing words must be fitted to realities, not realities to those principles. [Col. 0424C]

For all the wordy reasoning of human reason ought to be nothing but an investigation of truth; wherever truth presents itself, reason is no longer reason if it does not immediately, abandoning concern for words, rest in truth. Nothing, however, is truer or more evident than that no creature, nor anything whatsoever originating from a creature, can happen accidentally to the unchangeable God. For in God, the Creator of all things—in whom all time and whatever belongs to time are eternity and life, and in whom whatever will occur at any time is already most present from eternity—a creature created in time does not act at any time so that God should begin at some point to be Creator, as though he had not been so before, even though this may begin to be said at a particular time.

Rather, the Creator, creating a creature, does this concerning it without time: that what was not may be at its own time. Nor does this so much happen to him as, if it is permissible to speak thus, he happens to it. Not that that substance in which whatever exists subsists can in any sense be called an accident; but words fail for expressing what can somehow be thought concerning matters of this kind. [Col. 0425A] In this sense, therefore, divine names which are in relation to creation must be understood relatively. Although they are in relation to temporal and mutable creation, they are nevertheless names of eternal and unchangeable essence, and must be judged in their proper manner.

For since in God, in whom what has been made is life and in whom whatever is, is God, there has been from eternity the principal essence of all things that exist temporally, all this external creation is only an image of that supreme exemplar and some likeness of inward truth: not an accident of him, but proceeding from him by natural origin, causal reason, and the order of providence. And since for the all-knowing God to be is to know, this whole external creation is not known there because it exists; rather, because it is known there, it exists. Though it may be mortal in itself in whatever manner, it is life in the unchangeable Word. [Col. 0425B]

Therefore, for him whose knowing himself is being what he is, he does not know himself in one way and creation in another, since he is not one thing in one way and another in another. The Creator knows time without time and orders all mutable things without any change in himself; whatever these things may be in themselves, all are life in him. And whatever is life in eternity neither at some time began to live nor can die.

Whatever that creature may be—living or non-living, intelligent or unintelligent—which is life in God, as every creature is, however it may change or decay in itself, begin and end: its first and principal essence and truth of existence, which is in God and is God, neither changes nor decays. His supreme wisdom unchangeably orders all its mutable things, just as it creates the mutable things themselves unchangeably. There, whatever is more like its principle is truer; what is less like it is less real. [Col. 0425C]

Accordingly, in this manner, according to the reasoning and rule of faith, the name “Creator,” in relation to the creature, is essential to God, insofar as God is the principal essence of every creature; and the name “creature” is relative to the Creator, insofar as the creature itself is from him. Everything we have said therefore tends to this: although the names of the creature are said relatively to the Creator, the names of the Creator in relation to the creature are to be understood not as relative accidents, but as signifying the creature’s principal essence in God. For this reason, according to the rule governing all essential names in God, these too are said when we say: the Father is Creator, the Son is Creator, the Holy Spirit is Creator; yet there are not three Creators, but one Creator. [Col. 0425D] The same must be understood concerning the name Lord or principle, and every name by which God is spoken of in relation to creation.

Accordingly, by this reasoning, having counted among the names by which God is spoken of in relation to creation those names by which he is said essentially and in relation to himself, let us pass to the relative names by which, in the Trinity which is God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said relatively to one another. First, however, it must be said that as essence contains unity, so relation proclaims Trinity.

No one who shares even to the slightest degree in human reason can err in the faith of that one of whom the Lord says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), or fail to hold the common judgment of all concerning him, namely that the Lord God is one God (Deut. 6). [Col. 0426A] For since our Lord Jesus Christ shone forth in the world, not only has the world—or humanity—been ashamed to worship the works of its own hands, but the worship of many gods and demons has fled from almost the whole earth. All agree in the worship of one God, not only Jew and Christian, but even pagan and barbarian. No one has ever dared openly to oppose this common judgment of all concerning God—not a Christian or Jewish heretic, nor a philosopher of the nations.

For this reason, the faith of the Trinity, together with the scandal of the cross—which had already begun to be revealed in the world to certain people from the time of the patriarchs and prophets—when it began to be preached to all in the times of grace, became a sign opposed by so many, as though it were a worship of three gods, along with the reproach of the Crucified One. For, leaving aside those who are outside, there are sometimes believers in the Church who, because they do not grasp what is said, ask: “Why is the Trinity preached to us? Let only one God, whoever or however he may be, be preached and worshipped.” Whoever says this errs and contradicts the grace of God. [Col. 0426B] For “no one has ever seen God; the Only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father has himself made him known” (John 1). For this purpose he came into the world and accomplished this: that God as Trinity might become known.

Nowhere in this life is deity better comprehended by human understanding than where it is understood to be more incomprehensible: that is, in the preaching of the Trinity. For this reason the Word became flesh and dwelt among us: so that, as the Lord Jesus Christ himself says in prayer to the Father, he might make the Father’s name known to human beings and pour the love of God into our hearts through the Holy Spirit whom he gave us (Rom. 5). Finally, this is the enigma of faith: terrible to the impious, to frighten and drive them from the face of the Lord; gracious to the devout, to awaken and urge them always to seek his face. [Col. 0426C–D] As has often been said already, we call God Father, God Son, God Holy Spirit—not three Gods, but one God.

Whoever, seeking some knowledge of the Trinity or of divine things through verbal signs, enters the labyrinth of divine revelation must know that there is one order of learning in human matters, for the signification of which all words whatsoever were devised, and another in divine matters, for signifying which no words whatever are adequate. Such a person is not a searcher of majesty to be overwhelmed by glory, but poor in spirit, to whom mercy is always near. [Col. 0427A] In human matters, the first object of study must be knowledge of words, by which one arrives at knowledge of things. In divine matters, however, the reverse is the case: not so much by the study of any discipline as by the devoutness of faith and the fervour of love must one first seek some understanding and apprehension of the realities; then knowledge of the words used concerning those realities will immediately offer itself to one who is advancing.

For example, to one inquiring about relative terms in God, there first present themselves those individual proper names or words, each belonging to one and relative to the others: “Father, Son, Holy Spirit; begetting, and proceeding.” These must be received by us as certain divine instruments for finding God, transmitted to us from God through men of God filled with God, but nevertheless not fully conveying knowledge of the realities of which they are signs. So long as they help us advance in the knowledge of God—as far as words can help us—they must be revered [Col. 0427B] and embraced. But where the words fail, they must be passed beyond as words, with the grace and blessing of him who is named.

For when “begetting,” “begotten,” “proceeding from both,” “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are said, these are words or names full of divine truth. Yet insofar as they also present some signification drawn from human things, they lift us little above earthly and human realities unless, when they are said, the inward things of faith are considered: namely, that in that generation, birth, and procession there is nothing active, nothing passive, nothing temporal, nothing local, nothing differentiated or separable, but the selfsame one God. For there, one being from another is for one birth and for another procession; being eternal from eternal is the co-eternity of the three; and one being from another is either eternal birth or eternal procession.

When the Son is begotten by being born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, one does not depart from another. For the Father is eternally and unchangeably in the Son, the Son in the Father, the Holy Spirit in the Father and Son, and they in him, by the truth of the one divine essence. The Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Father and Son, by the truth of the Trinity and the distinctness of the persons. [Col. 0427C] The Trinity there is the unity, and the unity the Trinity. No one person of that supreme Trinity is less than the whole Trinity, nor is the whole Trinity greater than one person in the Trinity.

The Father did not diminish himself in order to have a Son; rather, he begot from himself another self in such a manner that he remained whole, and was as great in the Son as in himself. Likewise the Son is whole from the whole, as great in the Father as from the Father; always in the Father and always from the Father; neither diminishing him by being born nor increasing him by adhering to him. And as the Son is from the Father and with the Father, so the Holy Spirit is from both and with both—except that the Son is from the Father by birth, while the Holy Spirit is from the Father and Son by procession. For just as, for the Son, to be from the Father and to be what the Father is is to be eternally begotten, so for the Holy Spirit, to be from the Father and the Son and to be what they are is eternal procession. [Col. 0427D]

In this way, then, God Trinity must be proclaimed—if indeed any mode exists in him from whom and under whom every mode exists—and they are disposed one toward another, if indeed there is any disposition there, where God has nothing except what he is. These are the things which, in order to be apprehended by human beings, are clothed, when set before human beings, in the name of Trinity or three persons or mutual relations, so that what is proclaimed almost ineffably concerning God may be grasped in whatever way by human beings. For understanding of the divine realities, of which these seem to be signs, is not given so much through these signs as we are shaped and nourished, for the purpose of understanding what we desire concerning God, by this form of words sound in faith.

To continue, then, what we began concerning relatives: the three persons are said relatively to one another, but outside the rule and order of relative terms, because not according to accident. For they are said in relation to something, as Father to Son and Son to Father. [Col. 0428A]

[Col. 0428B] This is by no means understood in God according to accident. The Father’s being called Father and the Son’s being called Son are eternal and unchangeable for them. For the Father is always Father and the Son always Son. This is not “always” merely from the point at which the Son was born, or in the sense that the Father will never cease to be Father and the Son will never cease to be Son; rather, it is because the Son has always been born, and neither the Father began at any point to be Father nor the Son began to be Son. If they had begun at some time to be so, or were to cease, they would be spoken of according to accident.

Yet not only are Father said relatively to Son and Son to Father; the Holy Spirit also is said relatively to Father and Son, and they to him, insofar as he is their Spirit. He proceeds from them, and they send him forth. What we have already touched upon briefly above should here be more fully explained, if anyone capable of judging such matters will judge how contrary to every principle and use of all relative terms is what we say. Every essence that is said relatively is also something apart from its relative, as a human being is a master and a horse a beast of burden. For “human being” and “horse” are said in relation to themselves and are essences; “master” and “beast of burden” are said relatively in relation to something. If human being and horse were not some substances, there would not be subjects to be relatively called master and beast of burden. [Col. 0428C]

Accordingly, if father is not something said in relation to himself, and likewise son, they do not exist at all as those said relatively to one another. But when “human master” and “human slave” are said in relation to one another, there are two human beings. God the Father and God the Son, however, are not two gods but one God. Yet because the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit—who is also called God’s gift—is neither Father nor Son, they are certainly three. Therefore it was said in the plural: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). He did not say, “One [person] am I,” as the Sabellians say, but “We are one.”

When, then, one asks what the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are—who they are; whether they are three someones or three somethings—what can we say apart from the relative terms by which they are related to one another? Apart from the relative terms, since no human names, either proper or common, for those three can be found, devout faith understands not without reason that this is so; recognizing that the matter at issue is ineffable, it is taught toward knowledge of deity more by reflecting on human ignorance. [Col. 0429A] Common names are such as when we say “three human beings”; proper names such as when we say “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

Here, however, nothing occurs except the nature or essence of the supreme good. If it is supreme, it is certainly not three things but one thing; and its name, “God,” is a name only of one, because God is only one. This is that one of which the Lord says: “I and the Father are one.” That solid and divine one is by no means composed of different things: it neither consists of parts nor can be dissolved into parts. For although the Trinity itself is the unity, and the unity the Trinity, the name of unity under the name of Trinity does not signify a numerical conjunction of threefoldness, but the inseparable simplicity of the divine essence. [Col. 0429B]

For this reason it is altogether impermissible to say that the three persons, spoken of in the inseparable Trinity, are in any way separable from one another, no more than the Trinity itself. The Trinity should not be called inseparable if those three persons can in some measure be separated. The three persons, although they cannot be spoken simultaneously, must nevertheless be understood only simultaneously. For that is truly called inseparable which admits no separation whatsoever. If anyone thinks that the three persons in the Trinity can be separated, it is not the Trinity but the unity that should be called separable. For the Trinity consists in the persons; unity, in the nature.

The nature of the Trinity, which alone is wholly everywhere, as it has its being everywhere one and whole, cannot admit a separation of persons. The persons themselves are indeed named individually there; but the Trinity has willed to show itself so inseparable in the persons that there is no name by which any person is named in such a way that it either does not belong to all three by natural unity—as when powerful, wise, good, and the like are said—or does not show, even in the name of its distinctness, one person to be referred to another—as when “Father, Son, Holy Spirit” are said. [Col. 0429C] For in relative names one person is not named individually in such a way that it is not referred to another by its very name. By a relative term, one person is named individually in itself in such a way that it is not named in relation to itself. Therefore the relation inherent in the personal term prevents the persons from being separated, because, while naming them together, it also indicates them together.

For when “Father” is said, the Son is understood with him, of whom he is Father; when “Son” is said, the Father is likewise understood, whose Son he is. When the Holy Spirit is called “gift,” just as the Son as “Word” is inseparably referred to the one speaking, so “gift” is inseparably referred to the giver. [Col. 0429D]

It must also be known concerning relatives that, although the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are their proper names, each individual name belonging to each individual person, and though certain operations are likewise proper to each—such as the Father’s begetting, the Son’s being begotten, and the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from both, and other similar things—yet in these proper characteristics there is no separation of that nature, but recognition of the persons. For the three persons are named individually so that they may be known, not so that they may be separated. In them there is no separation, just as no confusion can inhere in them.

Nor, I say, should anyone dare to call them separable in any respect, since one can find—or ought to conceive—none existing or acting before another, none after another, and none without another. Where no separability of operation can exist, unity remains naturally unchangeable. For example, the form which the only-begotten God assumed was made by the whole Trinity; yet it is certain that, although made by the whole Trinity, it pertains to the person of the Son alone. For the operation is of the whole Trinity, but the assumption is not found to be of the whole Trinity. [Col. 0430A]

Indeed, the property of the persons—that the Father is not the Son and the Holy Spirit is not Father or Son—shows that something made by the Father and Son is nevertheless found to have been assumed by the Son alone. The same is to be understood concerning the Father’s voice at the baptism, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3); likewise concerning the dove and fire, in the form of which the Holy Spirit was visibly manifested over the Lord and over the apostles. No example of this matter can be found among creatures, because, apart from the Trinity, which is Lord God by nature, there is no nature that can possess in itself three inseparable persons. [Col. 0430B]

Thus these two modes of predication, essential and relative, concerning God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit seem opposed to one another. One concerns what is in relation to itself, preserving unity everywhere; the other concerns what is in relation to one another, proclaiming Trinity. Yet precisely in this they agree more fully and embrace one another in the loving charity of that unity of peace which surpasses all understanding: essential predication declares one God and does not deny three persons; relation declares three persons relatively related to one another, yet entirely rejects the assertion of three gods. Thus each always declares what belongs to it without injury to the other: neither abandoning what belongs to it nor disrupting in any way what belongs to the other. From both is constituted what belongs to Catholic faith, namely the reasoning of faith, proclaiming the same unity that is Trinity, the same Trinity that is [Col. 0430C–D] unity—one God.

There are also other relative names by which God is spoken of relatively: for example, when God the Father is called the principle of deity, he is called principle relatively to the Son, who is from him; and, together with the Son, relatively to the Holy Spirit, who is from them.

For Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit, but principally the Father, because the Son too received from the Father, by being born, that he himself might be with the Father one principle of the Holy Spirit. But where the Father is said to be this principally, no priority of time, no precedence or rank of dignity, no greater or lesser majesty is to be understood; rather, it indicates who is from whom, or who is related to whom, and what is related to what, within that nature of the consubstantial Trinity. For the Father, deriving his origin from none, is the source of divinity. [Col. 0431A] The Son has from him what he received by being born from him: namely, that he is one with him in natural essence. From him also, and from the Son—but principally, as was said, from the Father—is the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from both, shares with both that he is what they are. The Son too is relatively called the “Word” of the speaking Father, and the Holy Spirit the “gift” of the giving God. Here, just as when “Father and Son” are spoken of, one must in no way imagine a derivative posterity of begetter and begotten, but the mystery of eternal birth; so too, when the “Word” of God is spoken of, one must not suppose a spoken-out word, but one consubstantial with and coeternal with the Speaker; and likewise, when the Holy Spirit is called the “gift” of Father and Son, one must not imagine a condition of one given and a domination of givers, but the concord of the given one and those who give.

[Col. 0431B] For the logic of that singular relation is such that, although the relations there may appear unequal—as those of Father to Son, speaker to Word, gift to giver—yet there is supreme equality there, since one are the other and he who is from the other, and one who is from two, and two from whom one is. Since, among those who know rightly and think devoutly about God, no first, middle, or last is found in that one of which the Lord says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), it is nevertheless necessary that three be distinctly named there. They must also be named in their order, so that it may be understood who is from whom. In the first place is set the Father who begot; in the second, the Son who was begotten; in the third, the Holy Spirit who proceeds from both.

[Col. 0431C] This must also be observed with the greatest care in the operation of the Godhead, or the cooperation of the Trinity, which seem to have a close affinity with the relation of the three persons. For example, the Apostle says: “From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things; to him be glory for ages of ages. Amen” (Rom. 11). Although here all things seem to be recalled as created from the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, yet in the differing use of the prepositions no difference of operation is to be understood, but a simple cooperation. For all things are equally from the Father and from the Holy Spirit, as from the nature that creates all things; equally through the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, as through God, the maker of all things; equally in the Father and Son and Holy Spirit, as in God who contains all things.

[Col. 0431D] In such arrangements of the three persons, or applications of prepositions, only the personal indication of the Trinity is to be understood; yet in such a way that all things are brought together for the understanding of the truth of divine unity in the Trinity. The Apostle immediately adds: “To him,” he says, “not to them.” Yet these individual expressions are apportioned to the individual persons: all things are said to be from the Father, from whom every creature is principally; through the Word by whom he spoke, and all things were made; and in the Holy Spirit, who is the goodness of Father and Son and contains all things. For those whose essence is one, and therefore whose operation is one, are said to cooperate insofar as they are three; and their operation is one insofar as they are one. [Col. 0432A] Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things that he does” (John 5). For the Son’s seeing the Father is to be what the Father is; seeing him at work is cooperating with him. Again: “All things were made through him”—that is, through the Word (John 1). Here cooperation is understood insofar as Father and Word are two; but a simple operation is understood insofar as God is said to have made all things through his Word—that is, through that by which he and his Word are one.

[Col. 0432B] This, however, must be understood of what is made or has been made: that is, of creation, which either is made by him so as to be what it previously was not, or undergoes some operation so that, having been made, it may endure. Whatever is not made in God, the Creator of all, but simply is, must be understood according to the apprehension of the creature. Thus the Father begot, which the Son does not do; the Son was begotten, which the Father who begot does not do. Yet this is not a making, but the essence of the Godhead that makes all things. For even when the Word became flesh, the whole Trinity cooperated in making that which the Word alone became: namely, flesh, which, having been made, was assumed by the Word alone into unity of person. Thus the Word, who is God with God, is said to have been made in time. Likewise, the whole Trinity made the voice of the Father heard over the Lord, saying, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3), though it sounded forth from the Father alone; and also the dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared over the Lord. For all these things were made in time and must be understood exactly as they are.

[Col. 0432C] We have said what we could concerning the divine names, whether spoken of God according to substance or relatively; and concerning the relation itself by which, according to the distinctive character of the names, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are spoken of in relation to one another. Whatever we have said, we have drawn not from springs of our own, but from the springs of the Savior: from the holy Scriptures and the most certain authorities of the holy Fathers, seeking some knowledge of realities from the indications provided by their names. These names themselves are indeed recent among human beings in the preaching of the faith—I mean the names, not the realities named. For the realities denoted by these names are not merely coeternal with God, but are God. Even the name “God” itself—what is it, or whence was it said? Who imposed this name upon God? A name is usually imposed upon an inferior by one who is above it. Why, then, is that highest majesty called “God” by absolutely all human beings, through common usage and the general judgment of all?

[Col. 0432D] There is in human beings a certain natural utterance of fear directed toward the highest essence: in some fashion it declares that this essence exists, willing but unable to declare what it is. For “God” is said to derive from the Greek θεός (*theos*), which signifies fear. [Col. 0433A] It signifies, as has been said, the human being’s natural fear before the highest essence: not daring to impose a name upon it, yet somehow indicating the reality—for which no name is fitting—rather by a customary use of human speech than by any proper act of naming. Hence, when we wish to speak of him and cannot, we call him “ineffable” in brief; and “invisible,” whom we cannot see. Thus, of him who is above every sense and understanding, we say more by saying less.

[Col. 0433B] Moreover, since, as has already been said above, all divine names are one, the name of the Lord our God must be understood as some knowledge of him, commended in some fashion to believers through all these names, and by which, whenever he wills, he makes himself known to whom he wills and in whatever manner he wills. This is the name which, instructed by saving precepts and formed by divine teaching, we daily pray our Father who is in heaven to sanctify in us. It is then sanctified in us when, from the experience of life contained in the name itself, he who is named makes himself known to us by sanctifying us; when, whether in speaking of God or praying to him, we name him in the Holy Spirit in that manner of naming of which the Apostle says: “Jesus is Lord, in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). For “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord in this manner shall be saved” (Rom. 10); and “all who know his name hope in him” (Ps. 9); “they glory in him who love his name” (Ps. 5); and “they desire to be judged according to the judgment of those who love his name” (Ps. 118).

[Col. 0433C] This happens when, for those who invoke the Lord’s name in this way, grace working inwardly makes the reality denoted by the name sweet in the heart, and the name tastes sweet upon the lips: when the Lord is invoked, who already rules in the affection of the one invoking him; when one cries to God in the Holy Spirit, “Abba, Father,” and one’s own conscience bears witness to the one crying out that he is a son of God. This is to be understood also of the Lord’s other names. For there is no name of God which does not breathe forth, according to its own character, a corresponding grace upon the person who invokes it. This is the new name promised in the Apocalypse to the conqueror of this world, written upon a new white stone, not with an iron stylus but with the finger of God (Rev. 2).

[Col. 0433D] For the wholly smooth and round stone is the Catholic faith: whoever wishes to gnaw at it finds nowhere to set his tooth. Upon it is inscribed the Lord’s new name—that is, the name that renews the faithful person who names him, when that person is formed by the knowledge of God according to the pattern of spiritual faith.
