This happens when faith, beginning to work through love, itself begins also to be formed into love; and through love into understanding; and through understanding into love—or rather, at once into understanding and love. For it is difficult for a person so disposed to distinguish what is from what, since in the heart of one who believes, understands, and loves, these three are already one, in a certain likeness of the supreme Trinity.

[Col. 0434A] But we have undertaken to investigate the outward account of faith concerning the Trinity and its public form. Later it will be ours to give life to this form once it has been formed in our inward person—of whom it is written that God first “formed man in his own image and likeness” (Gen. 1), and then “breathed into his face the breath of life, and he became a living soul” (Gen. 2). Therefore, having ventured upon and touched, a little, as far as we were able and as far as the Lord granted, what we could reach concerning the divine names—relying not on our own judgments but on those of the holy Fathers—we still proceed with fear and trembling, that we may fall down and weep before you, holy Trinity, O Lord our God, who made us and even now make us pray and entreat that you may not permit us in any degree to err in the contemplation or faith of that form to which we too long to be conformed, and to which you command us to be conformed in all the Scriptures that speak of you: so that, as you three are one, we too, through the power of faith by which we believe this, may become one in you (John 17).

[Col. 0434B] The form of faith, then, to which all that we have said above is directed, is this, as we have often said: Father God, Son God, Holy Spirit God; and yet not three gods, but one God. This form of Trinity and unity is not extended by outlines and spaces of bodily limbs. Nor does the Father receive the Son remaining in him locally, nor the Son the Father dwelling in him; nor are Father and Son emptied when they send forth the Holy Spirit to enlighten all their creation. For they are three, but not separately; they are one, but not confusedly. Being three, they are one; being one, they are three: three against Sabellius, one against Arius. Nor is the Trinity in one God; the Trinity itself is God. Nor is God in the Trinity; God is the Trinity itself. For God is not anything more than the Trinity itself is, nor is the Trinity anything other than the one God.

[Col. 0434C] Therefore, when we direct the mind’s gaze toward confessing Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let us drive far from the mind the forms of visible things and the ages of temporal natures; let us drive far away the places of bodies and bodies in places. Let that which is extended in space, enclosed by a boundary, and whatever is neither always everywhere nor wholly everywhere, depart from the soul. Finally, let a thought conceived of the Trinity’s Godhead understand nothing by distance and seek nothing by degrees; and if it perceives anything worthy of God, let it dare to deny this to no person there. For, once every degree of existence is excluded, the substance of divinity in the Trinity is one and immutable: undivided in operation, harmonious in will, equal in omnipotence, equal in glory, filling all things at once and containing the universe. [Col. 0434D] It must be confessed in three persons in such a way that the inseparable equality preserves the unity of one essence, and that the Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit admits no solitude. For God alone is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, besides whom there is no other God; yet God the Father is never alone, since he always exists in relation to the Son; the Son is never alone, since he always exists in relation to the Father; the Holy Spirit is never alone, since he always exists in relation to Father and Son.

[Col. 0435A] Yet God must not be called or regarded as threefold. Though he is one in three persons, he is nevertheless whole in each. For neither does plurality of three involve anything there, nor does unity cause confusion, because a certain divine number, altogether most remote from every merely numerical distinction, brings about there the Trinity which is there in such a way that the form of simple Godhead excludes from it every confused notion of triplicity. This form exists nowhere except where there is a number above number, by which three are one and one are three. Let no mortal seek by human reasoning to investigate the manner in which these things are said of God above human measure. For you, Lord our God, can by no reasoning and in no manner be conceived or believed subject to any manner; rather, beneath you and from you is every manner by which whatever is, or can be, exists. But you and your essence are yourselves to yourself both the cause and manner of existing.

[Col. 0435B] Therefore, being as you are, you are wholly an unfathomable and unsearchable depth—not wholly in such a way as to be defined by this term, but so that you may be understood, insofar as you can be understood, as immeasurable. In the life to come, those whom you have made worthy here through faith will see this by enjoying you. There they will see you face to face as you are, and by seeing will become as you are. For your beloved Apostle John promises us this: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Those who see you there will no longer lie or be deceived; their visions will no longer be uncertain, nor will their thoughts pass from one thing to another, going and returning. Rather, O God of truth, they will behold in one and the same gaze all their knowledge, which will be of you alone. [Col. 0435C] For the vision of that contemplation, or the contemplation of that vision, will not pass from Father to Son, from Son to Holy Spirit; it will not be divided into three or gathered into one. Rather, in blessed perpetuity and perpetual blessedness, no longer seeking but enjoying, they will contemplate you: one, true God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, living for ages of ages.

[Col. 0435D] The following appear to be said properly of God the Father: what the Lord says, “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18); and, “That they may know you, the only true God” (John 17); and what the Apostle says: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, to God alone, be honor and glory” (1 Tim. 1). Again: “The blessed and only mighty one, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6). Yet these and similar expressions are those properly said of God; they are not so proper to the Father as though they were in any respect less proper to the Son and Holy Spirit. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are consubstantially one; but the Father is principal—not principally as preeminent, or by some priority of time or dignity, but of origin.

[Col. 0436A] For God the Father is, as it were, a fountain and source of divinity, the principle of the Son and Holy Spirit, who are from him and have from him the being that they are. But although God the Father is the principle of the Son and principle of the Holy Spirit, and the three are the principle of every creature, far be it that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should be believed to be three or four principles. For they are one principle just as they are one God. Nor is the Father to be called the principle of a principle because the Son, of whom he is the principle, is with him the principle of the Holy Spirit. Rather, “principle from principle” must be understood there just as “God from God”: one God, one principle—the Father of the Son, and with him of the Holy Spirit; and, with Son and Holy Spirit, the principle of every creature.

We also pray to, worship, and always give thanks to God the Father, not without the Son and Holy Spirit; yet through the Son, as through our Lord Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, and in the Holy Spirit, our Paraclete and advocate of our prayers before God. Without him, we neither know how we ought to pray nor are heard when we pray. When we pray to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit—as one through another in another—we pray only one God, in no respect different from God; and we have confidence toward the God whom we pray to, not as coming from ourselves, but from the righteousness that is through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. We are made fit to be heard through the grace of the Holy Spirit, who inwardly consoles and gives us life.

[Col. 0436B] Of the Son it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Since it says, “was, was, was,” this must first be understood of him who always is. For it makes no difference how times are expressed in speaking of God, since no time can be found by which what is spoken—that is, eternity—can suitably be signified. [Col. 0436C] Where it says, “In the beginning was the Word,” the coeternity of Father and Son is indicated; where “the Word was with God,” the reality of the persons; where “the Word was God,” the consubstantiality of the Word with the Speaker. The Son is also said to be from the Father: this is divine birth. The Son is said to be everlasting from the everlasting Father: this is the eternity of divine birth.

[Col. 0436D] For the Son of God must be understood both as begotten and as always begotten: begotten, lest that birth be thought imperfect in any way; always begotten, so that the eternity of the birth itself may declare itself. “Begotten” pertains to perfection; “always” to eternity, so that by some temporal speech that timeless essence may, in whatever manner possible, be designated. He is Son because God was truly born from God, by a true birth, though divine, unsearchable, and ineffable. “For who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). Yet we do not shrink, like the Manichees or certain Arians who call the Son of God a creature, from proclaiming in God the true name of generation and birth. Rather, we believe and confess God born of God; and that he who begot and he who was begotten are one.

[Col. 0437A] As the Son is called Son of the begetter, so he is called Word of the Speaker, so that what cannot be expressed in any manner may somehow be spoken of in many ways. For the Word of God bears among human beings, in a great and hidden mystery, both the name and some likeness of a human word. Within the inner heart of a human being there is a word: a conception of truth concerning some matter, without voice, syllables, or any form.

Just as a human word, in order to be made manifest to human senses, in a certain manner becomes voice by assuming it, so the Word became flesh by assuming that in which he might be made manifest to human beings. And just as a human word becomes voice and is not changed into voice, so the Word of God became flesh; but far be it from the faith of all believers that he should be believed to have been changed into flesh. Having become flesh, the Word of God also became for us the word of doctrine—not human but divine—teaching us in brief to fulfill the whole law, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind; and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6). Then he says: “On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. 22).

[Col. 0437B] Moreover, his whole life on earth, through the human being whom he deigned to assume, was teaching and moral discipline. By lacking and by teaching, he made cheap riches, honors, pleasures, and everything which, while desiring to possess them, we had lived wrongly. By enduring them, he cast down poverty, insults, injuries, pains, bodily death, and everything which human beings commonly seek to avoid and thereby deviate from the pursuit of a good life. He also taught carnal persons, devoted to bodily senses and unable to behold truth with the mind, how exalted a place human nature holds among creatures: by assuming a human being, the Word of God became one person from two natures. Hence the Prophet says: “He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions” (Ps. 106).

[Col. 0437C] Yet in this sending there are two points to be considered more carefully: namely, lest the sending of the Son by the Father be understood as separable or temporal. Since Father and Son acted together in causing the Son to appear in flesh, the one who appeared in flesh was fittingly said to have been sent; while the one who did not appear in it was said to have sent him. For those things which occur outwardly before bodily eyes arise from the inward ordering of spiritual nature, and are therefore fittingly called sendings. But that form of the assumed human being belongs to the Son, not also to the Father.

[Col. 0437D] Accordingly, when the invisible Father, together with the Son invisible with him, made that same Son visible, he is said to have sent him. If the Son became visible in such a way that he ceased to be invisible with the Father—that is, if the invisible substance of the Word had changed by passing into visible creation—then the Son would be understood to have been sent by the Father so as to be found only sent and not also sending. But because the form of a servant was assumed in such a way that the form of God remained unchangeable, it is clear that Father invisible, Son invisible, and Holy Spirit invisible brought about what appeared in the Son: that is, that he himself was sent visibly by those invisible ones. For the whole Trinity made the servant-form which the only-begotten God assumed; but though the operation of the whole Trinity is in it, its assumption belongs to the Son alone, not to the whole Trinity.

[Col. 0438A] If one nature of divinity and flesh had been made in Christ, the incarnation of the whole Trinity would consequently be believed. But in Christ there is one nature which the only-begotten God is found to possess inseparably with Father and Holy Spirit; while he has his human nature as his own, and with this his divinity is found to have not one nature but one person. Nor should the mission of the Word be believed temporal, since in the Word himself, in the wisdom of God itself, there was eternally and without time the time at which he had to appear in flesh. When that fullness of time came, God is said for this reason to have sent his Son: that, being both God and human being, as he was born in both, so he might die in both, not compelled but willingly.

[Col. 0438B] For the divinity suffered in the flesh all things that belonged to flesh, because God assumed passible flesh with human affections; yet it did not suffer along with the flesh, because the divinity remained always impassible in its own nature. For he was the same God and the same human being. This too must be distinguished and held with most certain faith: as in the Trinity, which is God, we confess three persons and one nature, so in the Lord Jesus Christ we must understand two natures and one person.

[Col. 0438C] And as the three persons must be believed inseparable in the nature of divinity, so the two natures must be believed in the person of Christ. We therefore believe that the Son of God was begotten from the substance of the Father, without any beginning of his birth: God from God; not from nothing, because from the Father; not nominally so called, but possessing the name by the truth of his nature. For what benefit is it to the Son to be called by the name “only-begotten” if he is deprived of the truth of that name? He is called only-begotten in vain if in his generation not a natural truth from God who begets, but a bounty bestowed by a giver is proclaimed. For to as many as received him, power is given to become children of God. But in that mystery of everlasting birth, the everlasting and immutable Father begot another, not a different one; and however much he brought forth in begetting, he himself remained equally great. He distinguished personally from himself the one whom he possesses wholly in himself by nature.

[Col. 0438D] Therefore he who was ineffably born from the Father without beginning, when the fullness of time came (Gal. 4), so as to be sent by the Father from a woman, wholly reigning in the bosom of the Father, wholly forming himself in the womb of his mother, wholly came into the womb of the Virgin. No part of him remained in the Father and another part came into the Virgin: rather, he wholly remained in the Father what he was, and wholly became in the Virgin what he was not. Thus true and supreme God took the whole human being into himself; and thus the fullness of divinity, while the truth of both divine and human substance remained without confusion, joined itself wholly to the whole human being. Henceforth the unity of person remained, so that neither Christ the human being can be separated from his divinity nor Christ the same God from his humanity.

[Col. 0439A] This inseparable unity of person, in which Christ was born God and human being, brought it about that Christ as human being was born from God by grace, with the truth and fullness of human nature preserved; and that Christ the same God voluntarily suffered in flesh, with the impassible fullness of the divine substance preserved. Therefore we confess that Christ’s divinity, which holy Scripture commends as unchangeable, suffered in the flesh; yet we believe that it did not suffer along with the flesh. For God suffered in the flesh because he assumed passible flesh; but he did not suffer along with the flesh because, while suffering in the flesh, the divine nature remained impassible.

[Col. 0439B] “The Spirit is God,” says the Lord (John 4). The Father is Spirit, the Son is Spirit, and the one called the Holy Spirit is Spirit; yet they are not three Spirits but one Spirit, of whom the Lord says that “the Spirit is God,” just as there are not three gods but one God. Although each of them is Spirit, and certainly holy, the Holy Spirit, who is common to the two and is specifically designated by the name which is common to both, is—as he himself is common to both—whatever is common to them: their divinity, love, sweetness, blessedness, and the rest.

For as the Son is from the Father by being born, so the Holy Spirit is from Father and Son by proceeding; but principally from the Father, since the Son also received from the Father by being born that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him equally as from the Father. In being born from the Father, the Son received this: to be God from God and one God with the Father. Yet the logic of faith does not permit this to be reciprocated with respect to the Son—that, since Father and Holy Spirit are likewise one God, the Son should likewise be understood to be from the Holy Spirit equally as from the Father. For the birth of one Son from two sources would become a confusion of the Trinity, which is most remote from the logic of faith.

[Col. 0439C] Therefore, since the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Father and Son, proceeds from both, and is the love and unity of both, it is clear that he is not something belonging to either of the two by which the two are joined: by which the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter, so that they preserve unity of spirit in the bond of peace, not by participation in something alien but by their own essence, and not by another’s gift but by their own. In the procession by which the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from Father and Son, his divine coessentiality with them is understood. But insofar as he also proceeds into creation, he is declared to be God’s gift.

[Col. 0439D] For the Holy Spirit is God’s gift to such an extent that, among God’s gifts—which no one has all together—no one has any one of them who does not have the Holy Spirit; and whoever has any of them has it only in the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0440A] Many gifts besides love are given through the Holy Spirit; without love they are nothing and profit nothing. Nor indeed is the Holy Spirit properly called a gift except on account of love, of which it is said: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. IV). No gift is greater than this, which alone distinguishes the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition, and which alone, even if the other charisms are absent, leads to the kingdom. For faith itself can somehow exist without love, but cannot profit. Only that faith profits which works through love. The Holy Spirit is the love of Father and Son, by which they love one another, and the unity by which they are one. When he has been given to a human being, he kindles that person in love for God and neighbor. This love itself is that by which God is love; nor does a human being have the means of loving God except from God.

[Col. 0440B] Hence it is also said that God “first loved us” (1 John 4); and that we therefore love him because he first loved us. God first loved us not by an affection but by the effect of love: before the ages, he predestined us for adoption as children; and in the time of his good pleasure he poured out his love in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. For the eternal one does not love anyone temporally, nor does he who is immutable become something new. He is the Spirit of the Lord who fills the world (Wis. 1), through the goodness of his omnipotence bathing all things in the great abundance of overflowing grace, according to the capacity and measure of each, so that all things may retain their proper orders and willingly rest in their proper places. He bestows good things, orders what is beneficial, and grants distributions of graces to the devout and faithful. To the impious and unbelieving he often grants peace in their times, bodily health, prosperity in worldly matters, abundance from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, and similar things. Sometimes he withdraws these from the saints for the testing of holiness, and grants them to the wicked and sinful for the stirring up and building up of love.

[Col. 0440C] To the children of grace, poor in spirit, he is advocate and comforter in the exile of this present life; strength in adversity and helper in tribulations. Teaching how one ought to pray, disposing the human being toward God, and making that person pleasing and fit to be heard, he enlightens the understanding and forms the affection. [Col. 0440D] He acts, perfects, and alone—if he can be alone, or ought to be called alone—is sufficient; but he alone suffices because he cannot be separated from Father and Son, with whom he inseparably does all that he does.

[Col. 0441]

## A SHORT COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST TWO CHAPTERS OF THE SONG OF SONGS

Compiled from the sermons of St Bernard.

(It appears in volume III of the Works of St Bernard, *Patrologia* 184, col. 407.)

[Col. 0441]

## COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS

Collected from the writings of St Ambrose.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. 15, Works of St Ambrose, II, col. 1851.)

[Col. 0441]

## EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOKS OF ST GREGORY, POPE, ON THE SONG OF SONGS

(Galland, *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, XIV, 394.) These excerpts [Note: [Col. 0441B] Thus the autograph manuscript of the Abbey of Signy reads. It is clear that this exposition consists of the very words used by St Gregory when, on various occasions, he interpreted certain passages of the Song. Perhaps William knew no extended commentary by St Gregory on the Song.] were excerpted by Lord WILLIAM, Abbot of Saint-Thierry at Reims, later a monk of Signy.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0441A]

### CHAPTER I

**VERSE 1.—“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”** [Note: [Col. 0442B] *Morals*, book XXVII, chap. 10.] By the mouth of God the only-begotten Son may be signified, because, just as he is called God’s arm—since the Father works all things through him, of whom the prophet says, “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 51), and of whom John the Evangelist says, “All things were made through him” (John 1)—so also he is called the mouth, through whom God speaks all things to us. Hence he says through the prophet: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken this” (Isa. 1); as though the Word were plainly meant by the name “mouth.” We too commonly speak of a language in place of words, as when we say Greek or Latin language and mean Greek or Latin words. Thus, not without reason, we understand the Lord’s mouth to be his own Son. [Col. 0441B] Therefore the bride prays to the Father of the bridegroom and says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As if she said: “Let him touch me with the sweetness of the presence of the only-begotten Son, my Redeemer.”

[Note: [Col. 0442B] *Morals*, book XIV, chap. 20.] [Col. 0442A] As if it were said more openly: “He who before his incarnation had entrusted to me, through the mouths of the prophets, so many commandments to be performed—let him now, incarnate and coming to me in person, speak with his own mouth.” For holy Church, by coming to know his commandments through preaching, received as it were so many kisses of his mouth. Hence Matthew, when describing the commandments given by him on the mountain, says: “Opening his mouth, he said” (Matt. 5). It is as if he plainly said: “He then opened his own mouth in giving commandments, who had previously opened the mouths of the prophets.”

[Note: [Col. 0442B] Homily 33 on the Gospels.] Concerning the sinful woman who did not cease to kiss the Lord’s feet, which she wet with tears and wiped with her hair, the Lord said to the indignant Pharisee: “You gave me no kiss; but she, from the time I entered, has not ceased kissing my feet” (Luke 7). A kiss is a sign of love. [Col. 0442B] By the feet is understood the very mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, by which divinity touched the earth because he assumed flesh: “For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” [Col. 0443A] (John 1). Whom, then, does the Pharisee, presumptuously relying on false righteousness, signify but the Jewish people? And whom does the sinful woman signify, coming weeping to the Lord’s feet, but the converted Gentile world? That unbelieving people gave God no kiss, because it refused to love with charity him whom it served from fear. But the Gentile people, once called, do not cease to kiss their Redeemer’s feet, because they continually sigh for him in love and love the mystery of his incarnation with their whole heart. And because they prepare to obey their Creator through love, they rightly desire his kiss, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

**“Your breasts are better than wine.”** [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Morals*, book XXX, chap. 10.] The bridegroom’s breasts are the holy preachers; these are the breasts [Col. 0443B] which, fixed in the ark of the sinner, give us milk to drink, because, clinging to the hidden things of highest contemplation, they nourish us by subtle preaching.

**VERSE 2.—“The young maidens loved you.”** [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Morals*, book XIX, chap. 8.] Sacred Scripture often uses “young man” to indicate newness of life. All the churches which together form the one Catholic Church are called young maidens: no longer old through sin, but new through grace; not barren through old age, but, in the maturity of the mind, suited to spiritual fruitfulness.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] *Morals*, book XXIV, chap. 4.] Therefore the bridegroom, when he comes, is told: “The young maidens loved you,” that is, the souls of the saints renewed by the grace of baptism, who do not fail in the practice of the old life but are adorned by the conduct of the new human being.

**VERSE 3.—“We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.”** [Col. 0443C] [Note: [Col. 0443D] Homily 33 on the Gospels.] This the bride says in longing for the bridegroom. In sacred Scripture, the fragrances of ointments customarily signify the reputation of virtues. Thus the Apostle Paul, knowing that he was fragrant with the praise of virtues, says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. XV).

**VERSE 4.—“I am black, but beautiful.”** [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Morals*, book XVIII, chap. 19.] The more precious a person is in his own eyes, the more worthless he becomes to God; and the more worthless he is in his own eyes for God’s sake, the more precious he becomes to God, because “he regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137). The righteous do not become proud because of the light of righteousness; rather, through the grace of humility, they confess the blackness of sins within themselves. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (John 1).

**VERSE 5.—“They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.”** [Note: [Col. 0444D] Homily 17 on the Gospels.] There is something, dearest brothers, concerning the life of pastors that afflicts me greatly, and that accords with this saying. Yet lest what I affirm perhaps seem offensive to anyone, I accuse myself equally. For we have slipped away into outward affairs; we receive one thing through honour, and perform another through the duty of our activity. We abandon the ministry of preaching; and, as I see it, we are called bishops for our punishment, since we possess the title of honour but not its virtue. For those entrusted to us abandon God [Col. 0444A], and we are silent; they lie in wicked deeds, and we do not extend the hand of correction. Every day they perish through many evils, and we negligently watch them tending toward hell. But when can we correct another’s life, if we neglect our own? Intent upon worldly cares, we become the more insensible inwardly the more diligent we seem concerning outward things. For by the habitual practice of earthly care the mind becomes hardened toward heavenly desire; and, becoming hard through its very practice in worldly activity, it cannot be softened toward what pertains to the love of God.

Therefore holy Church rightly says concerning her weakening members: “They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” Our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate through the daily practice of labour; [Col. 0444B] but, set as keepers in vineyards, we by no means keep our own vineyard, because, while we become entangled in others’ affairs, we neglect the ministry of our own work.

**VERSE 6.—“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”** [Note: [Col. 0444D] Homily 33 on the Gospels, after the middle.] The Lord feeds when he delights in our good actions; he lies down at noon when, departing with ardent heart from the carnal desires of the reprobate, he finds in the breasts of his elect the refreshment of good thought. For the more intense heat burns at noon, and the Lord seeks a shady place, untouched by the fire of heat. Therefore the Lord rests in those hearts which the love of this present age does not kindle, which carnal desires do not consume, which do not wither, inflamed [Col. 0444C] by their own curiosities amid this world’s desires. Hence Mary is told: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). Therefore at noon the Lord seeks shady places in which to feed, because he feeds on minds which, tempered by the regard of grace, are not burned by bodily desires. Thus Mary the sinner, yet penitent, fed the Lord more inwardly than the Pharisee fed him outwardly, because our Redeemer had fled from the heat of carnal things to her mind, which the shade of penitence tempered after the fire of vices.

**VERSE 7.—“Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and follow the tracks of the flocks, and [Col. 0444D] pasture your kids.”** [Note: [Col. 0444D] *Morals*, book XVI, chap. 21.] All the elect carefully consider from whom and for what they were created; and, by a right consideration of the image bestowed upon them, they disdain to follow the multitude of the crowd. Hence the bridegroom addresses his bride, saying: “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women”—that is, unless by living well you recognize your dignity, in that you were created in the likeness of God—“go forth from the sight of my contemplation, and imitate the life of unlearned peoples.” For unlearned peoples are denoted by the name “flocks.”

She who is beautiful among women knows herself [Col. 0445A] when every elect soul, even placed among sinners, remembers that it was created in the image and likeness of its Creator and walks according to the order of the likeness it has received. If it does not know itself, it goes forth, because, expelled from the secret place of its heart, it is scattered among outward desires. Having gone forth, it follows the tracks of the flocks, because, forsaking its inward life, it is led onto the broad way and follows the examples of the peoples. Nor does it then pasture lambs, but kids, because it seeks not to nourish innocent thoughts of the mind, but the corrupt impulses of the flesh.

**VERSE 11.—“While the king is at his repose, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”** [Note: [Col. 0445D] *Morals*, book XXXV, chap. 13.] It is as though holy Church, perceiving in her elect a certain fragrance of sweetness, said more openly: “So long as the King is hidden from my sight [Col. 0445B] in the repose of his heavenly secrecy, the life of the elect is exercised in the wondrous fragrances of virtues, so that, because it does not yet see him whom it desires, it may become more fragrant through ardent longing.” For while the King rests in his repose, the nard gives forth fragrance: while the Lord rests in his blessedness, the virtue of the saints in the Church imparts to us the grace of great sweetness. The virtues of the advancing elect become known to other people as though they were fragrant with a sweet scent. Thus Paul says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2).

### CHAPTER II

**VERSE 2.—“As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.”** [Note: [Col. 0445D] Homily 38 on the Gospels, before the middle.] In holy Church neither can the evil exist without the good nor the good without the evil. For as long as we live here, we must travel intermingled [Col. 0445C] along the path of this present age; but we shall be separated when we arrive. The good are nowhere alone except in heaven, and the evil nowhere alone except in hell. This life, placed between heaven and hell, receives in common the citizens of both regions, just as it stands between them; yet holy Church receives them now without distinction and will distinguish them later at their departure.

If, therefore, you are good, bear the evil with equanimity for as long as you remain in this life; for whoever does not bear the evil gives testimony against himself through his own impatience that he is not good. He refuses to be Abel whom Cain’s malice does not test. Thus, by the nature of a threshing-floor, grain is pressed beneath chaff; flowers spring up among thorns; and the fragrant rose grows with the thorn that pricks. [Col. 0445D] The first human being had two sons: one was elect, the other reprobate. Noah’s ark contained three sons, but while two remained in humility, one fell into mockery of his father. Abraham had two sons: one innocent, the other the persecutor of his brother. Isaac had two sons: one preserved in humility; the other reprobated even before he was born. Jacob had twelve sons: one of them was sold because of his innocence, while the others, through malice, became sellers of their brother. Twelve apostles were chosen; but among them was one mingled with the reprobate [Col. 0446A], who persecuted them in order to test them, lest they should remain unproved. Seven deacons were ordained by the apostles; but while six remained in the right faith, one became the author of error.

Therefore, dearest brothers, call past times to mind and strengthen yourselves to endure the wicked. For if we are children of the elect, we must necessarily walk by their examples. He was not good who refused to bear the evil; nor is it especially praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the evil. For just as it is a graver fault not to be good among the good, so it is a matter of immense praise to be good even among the evil. Hence blessed Job declares of himself: “I was a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30). Hence Peter [Col. 0446B] extolled Lot with great praise because he found him good among the reprobate, saying: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the lawless conduct of the impious; for by sight and hearing he was righteous, dwelling among those who from day to day tormented the righteous soul by their wicked works” (2 Pet. 2). He could not indeed have been tormented unless he both heard and saw the evil works of those near him. Yet he is called righteous by sight and hearing because the life of the wicked touched the ears and eyes of the righteous not by delighting them, but by wounding them.

Thus blessed Job is described as having lived among the wicked in the land of the Gentiles, that the merit of his virtue might be expressed; and this contributes to his praise, that he was good among the evil and, according to the bridegroom’s commendation, grew as a lily among thorns. Hence Paul both praises and reproves the life of the disciples [Col. 0446C], saying: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world” (Phil. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0446D] Homily 9 on the Gospels, after the middle.] See, dearest brothers: in reviewing almost everything, we have learned that he was not good whom the depravity of the wicked did not test. Yet we complain that not all who live with us are good, because we refuse to bear the evils of our neighbours. We decide that everyone ought already to be holy, because we are unwilling to be what would enable us to bear our neighbours. In this matter it becomes clear, when we refuse to bear the evil, how much we ourselves still lack of goodness. For no one is perfectly good unless he is good even with the evil.

To speak in this way: the iron of our soul is not brought to the sharpness of its point [Col. 0446D] unless the file of depravity has rubbed it down. Often, when we are troubled by our neighbours’ way of life, we attempt to change our place and choose the seclusion of a more remote life, not knowing that, if the Spirit is absent, place does not help. Lot was holy in Sodom, but sinned on the mountain. That places do not fortify the mind is attested by the first parent of the human race, who fell in paradise. If place could save, Satan would not have fallen from heaven. Therefore the Psalmist, seeing that temptations are everywhere in this world, sought a place to which he might flee, but could find none fortified without God. For this reason he asked that God himself might become the place for which he was seeking, saying: “Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, that you may save me” [Col. 0447A] (Ps. 30).

Therefore neighbours must be endured everywhere, because no one can become Abel whom Cain’s malice does not test. There is, however, one reason why the company of the evil ought to be avoided: lest, if they cannot perhaps be corrected, they draw others into imitation of themselves; and, while they do not change from their own wickedness, they pervert those joined to them. Hence Paul says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). And Solomon says: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his paths and take a snare for your soul” (Prov. 22).

Thus, just as perfect persons ought not to flee their perverse neighbours, because they often draw them to uprightness and are themselves [Col. 0447B] never drawn into perversity, so also the weak must avoid the company of the evil, lest they take delight in imitating evils which they frequently see and are unable to correct. So, by hearing the words of our neighbours, we daily take them into our mind just as, by breathing in and out, we draw air into the body. And just as bad air, continually inhaled, infects the body, so perverse speech, continually heard, infects the mind of the weak, so that it wastes away in delight in a wicked deed through the continual iniquity of speech. But when a sinner is joined in malice to a righteous and perfect person, it is as when chaff is joined to gold with fire in a furnace: where the chaff burns, the gold is purified. Therefore they are truly good who can persist in goodness even among the evil.

[Col. 0447C] **VERSE 3.—“Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat.”** [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Morals*, book XXXIII, chap. 3.] In sacred speech, shadow sometimes denotes the Lord’s incarnation, or the refreshment of the mind from the heat of carnal thoughts. Thus, by the designation of shadow, this very refreshment of the heart is suggested as coming from heavenly protection; hence the Psalmist says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16). Therefore the bride, awaiting and foretelling the bridegroom’s coming, says: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat.” Here the shadow expresses refreshment of heart from heavenly protection. It is as though the bride said: “I rested from the heat of carnal desires under the protection of his coming.”

For that the Lord’s incarnation, while preserving the truth of the history, is signified by the designation of overshadowing [Col. 0447D] is testified by the angel’s words to blessed Mary: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). Since shadow is not produced except by light and a body, the power of the Most High overshadowed her because incorporeal light assumed a body in her womb; and from that overshadowing she received every refreshment of mind within herself.

**VERSE 5.—“Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”** [Note: [Col. 0447D] Homily 15 on the Gospels, near the beginning.] For a mind strongly loving its bridegroom, one devout consolation in this present life is customary: that, through its own delay from his vision, the souls of others may advance by his word and [Col. 0448A] burn with the torches of love for the heavenly Bridegroom. Rightly so; because it sees itself delayed, everything it sees is sad to it, since it does not yet see him whom it longs to see. But there is, as I said, no small consolation in this: while the fervent soul is delayed, many are gathered through it, so that it may see later with many the one whom it wished to see sooner alone.

Therefore the bride says here: “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” What are flowers except souls already beginning a good work and fragrant with heavenly desire? What are apples produced from flowers except the now-perfect minds of the good, which reach the fruit of good work from the beginning of their holy purpose? She who languishes with love therefore seeks to be supported with flowers and surrounded with apples, because, if she is not yet permitted to see him whom she desires, it is a great [Col. 0448B] consolation to rejoice in the progress of others. Thus the soul languishes with holy love and is supported by flowers and apples, so that it may rest in the good work of its neighbour, although it is not yet able to contemplate the face of God.

Let us then consider what manner of mind Paul had, who said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1). In how great a love had he joined himself to Almighty God, when he judged life to be Christ alone and death to be gain? Hence he says again: “I have the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is far better” (*ibid.*). But see: we perceive by what love he languishes, he who desires to be dissolved; yet, because he sees himself delayed meanwhile, he does not seek to be supported by flowers. Indeed, he does seek it, for he continues: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” [Col. 0448C] (*ibid.*). And he says to his advancing disciples: “For what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ?” (1 Thess. 2).

**IBID.—“I am wounded by love.”** [Note: [Col. 0448D] *Morals*, book VI, chap. 14.] Almighty God wounds in two ways those whom he seeks to restore to salvation. Sometimes he applies blows outwardly to their flesh, in order to cure the poison of their sins. At other times, even though outward scourges seem to cease, he inflicts inward wounds, striking the hardness of our mind with longing for himself. Yet in striking, he heals, because, piercing us with the arrow of terror, he recalls us to the sense of uprightness.

For our hearts are unsoundly healthy when they are wounded by no love of God, when they do not feel the misery of their pilgrimage, when they do not languish with even the slightest affection for a neighbour’s weakness [Col. 0448D]. But they are wounded in order to be healed, because God strikes insensitive minds with the arrows of his love and immediately makes them sensitive through the ardour of charity. Hence the bride says here: “I am wounded by love.”

For the soul, unsoundly healthy and cast down in blind security into the condition of this exile, neither saw God nor sought to see him. But, struck by the arrows of his love, it is wounded in its inmost affections by tenderness; it burns with desire for contemplation and is, in a wondrous way, brought to life by its wound, though it formerly lay dead in health. It burns, pants, and now desires to see him whom it fled; it burns [Col. 0449A] with desire for him; it no longer covets anything in the world; it regards the length of this present life as punishment; it hastens to depart and to rest in the embrace of love in the vision of the heavenly Bridegroom.

A mind already such as this receives no consolation from the present life, but sighs, burns, and is anxious from its depths for him whom it loves. It is the very health of the body that has been pierced by the wound of love; but the heart’s health is evil when it knows no pain from this wound. When the soul begins to pant for heavenly desire and feel love’s wound, it becomes healthier through the wound, though formerly it was sick through health. It is restored to health by the blow which the disturbance of inward love calls back from the security of repose. Whoever has been able to attain truth has burned with this love and longing.

Hence David says: “My soul thirsted for the strong, living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” [Col. 0449B] (Ps. 41). Hence he admonishes us: “Seek his face always” (Ps. 104). Hence Isaiah the prophet says: “My soul desired you in the night; indeed, with my spirit in my inmost parts I shall watch for you in the morning” (Isa. 26). Thus holy Church says to him: “I am wounded by love.” It is fitting that one who bears the wound of love in the breast through the heat of longing should attain health through the vision of the physician.

**VERSE 6.—“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.”** [Note: [Col. 0449D] *Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 27.] Let the things available to you outwardly serve you only so far that they do not bend your mind away from the pursuit of heavenly love; lest the aids granted to us while we are in exile temper the grief [Col. 0449C] of our inward pilgrimage, and we rejoice as though happy in transient things while we see ourselves meanwhile miserable because of our separation from inward things.

Hence the Church says here in the voice of the elect: “His left hand is under my head; his right hand will embrace me.” What is signified by the left hand except the present life? And what by the right hand except eternal life? She places God’s left hand—that is, the prosperity of this present life—under her head, pressing it down by the intensity of supreme love. But God’s right hand embraces her because she is held with complete devotion under his eternal blessedness. Hence Solomon says: “Length of days is in his right hand, but in his left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3). Thus he taught [Col. 0449D] how riches and glory should be held by mentioning that they are placed in the left hand. Hence the Psalmist says: “Save me by your right hand” (Ps. 59). He did not say merely “hand,” but “right hand,” so that, in saying “right hand,” he might show that he sought eternal salvation. Again it is written: “Your right hand, O Lord, has shattered the enemies” (Exod. 15). For although God’s enemies prosper in the left hand, they are shattered by the right hand: present life often exalts the wicked, but the advent of eternal blessedness condemns them.

**VERSE 8.—“Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.”** [Note: [Col. 0449D] Homily 29 on the Gospels, near the end.] In coming for our redemption [Col. 0450A], the Lord made, so to speak, certain leaps. Do you wish, dearest brothers, to recognize these leaps? From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb he came into the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross he came to the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven. Behold: that he might make us run after him, Truth manifested in the flesh made certain leaps for our sake, because “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18), so that we might say to him from the heart: “Draw me; after you we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1). Therefore, dearest brothers, we ought to follow the Lord in heart to that place where we believe he ascended in body.

**“My beloved is like a roe or a young stag.”** The Lord is called a young stag of the deer [Col. 0450B], according to the flesh he assumed: the son of the fathers of old. Hence the Apostle: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. V).

**VERSE 9.—“Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.”** [Note: [Col. 0450D] Homily 13 on Ezekiel, near the end.] Our Redeemer, mercifully incarnate for us, stood before human eyes as though behind a wall, because he appeared visible through his humanity while keeping himself invisible in his divinity. Therefore the Jews, who had awaited him on the basis of the prophets’ promise, were thrown into the confusion of their unbelief, because they saw as mortal the one whom they had believed would come for their deliverance. Seeing his miracles, they were drawn to believe; but then, considering his sufferings [Col. 0450C], they disdained to believe that he was the Lord, whom they saw mortal in flesh. Thus they came to doubt his identity.

They saw him hungry, thirsty, eating, drinking, becoming weary, and sleeping, and thought him merely human. They saw him raising the dead, cleansing lepers, giving sight to the blind, and casting out demons, and perceived that he was more than human. His humanity, contemplated in their hearts, disturbed them even amid his miracles. Therefore holy Church, speaking in the bride’s voice, openly desires to see his form in divinity but cannot yet do so, because the humanity he assumed concealed from her eyes the form of his eternity which she longed to behold. In sorrow she says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall.” It is as though she plainly said: “I now long to behold him in the form of his divinity, but I am still shut out from his vision by the wall of assumed flesh.”

For he who showed human eyes what he assumed from mortal nature and remained invisible in himself stood, as it were, behind a wall to those seeking to see him openly, because he did not offer himself to be seen in manifest majesty. He stood as though behind a wall because he showed the human nature he assumed and hid the nature of divinity from human eyes. Hence it continues: “Looking through the windows, gazing through [Col. 0451A] the lattice.” Whoever looks through windows or a lattice is neither wholly seen nor wholly unseen. Such indeed was our Redeemer before the eyes of those who doubted: if, while working miracles, he had shown nothing human, he would have appeared to them wholly as God; conversely, if, while suffering human things, he had done nothing as God, he would have been thought merely human. But because he both did divine things and endured human things, he looked upon humanity as though through windows or latticework, so that he appeared as God through miracles and was hidden through sufferings, while he was seen as human through sufferings—provided that he was recognized as more than human through miracles.

**VERSE 10.—“Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter has now passed; the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared on the earth; [Col. 0451B] the time of pruning has come.”** [Note: [Col. 0451D] *Morals*, book XXVII, chap. 14.] Winter is this present life, in which, though hope now raises us to heavenly things, the cold torpor of our mortality still binds us. For it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9). This winter has rains: unquestionably, the preaching of the righteous. Concerning these rains Moses says: “Let your utterance be awaited as rain, and let my words descend as dew” (Deut. 32). These rains suit winter; they will cease in summer, because now, while heavenly life is hidden from carnal eyes, it is necessary that we be watered by the preaching of the saints. But when the heat of eternal judgment has burned, no one will then need [Col. 0451C] the words of preachers.

Because holy preaching will cease with the present life—that is, rain with winter [Note: [Col. 0451D] *Morals*, book XXVII, chap. 14]—the bridegroom’s persuasive voice rightly says to holy Church, or to the soul departing and hastening toward eternal summer, while awaiting the day of true light as though the season of spring: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter has now passed; the rain has gone and departed.”

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Homily 17 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] Whether holy Church or each individual elect soul, she is the heavenly Bridegroom’s friend through love, dove through the Spirit, and beautiful through the beauty of her character. When she is taken from the corruption of the flesh, winter undoubtedly passes for her, because the torpor of present life departs. The rain too has gone and departed, because, when she is brought to contemplate Almighty God in his own substance [Col. 0451D], drops of words will no longer be needed, nor must the rain of preaching be poured out. For when winter passes, rain withdraws: when the present life is completed, in which the torpor of corruptible flesh had bound us under the cloud of ignorance, every ministry of preaching ceases. Then we shall see more clearly and more fully in ourselves what we now hear more obscurely and less fully through the voices of the saints.

Then flowers appear upon the earth, because, when the soul begins to taste certain first beginnings of sweetness from eternal blessedness, it smells their fragrance as though already among flowers while departing. After it has departed [Col. 0452A], it will have fruit more abundantly. Hence it continues: “The time of pruning has come.” In pruning, barren branches are cut away so that those which remain strong may bear fruit more abundantly. Therefore the time of our pruning now comes, when we leave behind this unfruitful corruption of the flesh, that we may attain the soul’s fruit; and this fruit will be most abundant for us: the vision of God.

### CHAPTER III

**VERSES 1–3.—“On my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him. I will rise and go about the city; through streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, and the watchmen who guard the city found me.”** [Note: [Col. 0452D] *Morals*, book VIII, chap. 13.] [Col. 0452B] Under the figure of each individual soul, the bride speaks this, animated by holy desires and stirred by the hidden impulses of holy love. It should be understood that in sacred discourse a bed, couch, or resting-place customarily signifies the secret place of the heart. Therefore the beloved is sought in bed and by night, because the form of the invisible Creator, stripped of every image of bodily vision, is found in the bedchamber of the heart, since he is desired in the inner chambers of the heart amid the Spirit’s tribulation.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Homily 25 on the Gospels, near the beginning.] We seek the Beloved in bed when, amid some slight repose of this present life, we sigh for our Redeemer. We seek by night because, although the mind is already awake in him, the eye is still darkened. Yet the bride, seeking him, does not find him, because every elect soul already longs to see [Col. 0452C] God, already desires to go out to him, already pants to be without the darkness of this present life; but, though it desires greatly in love, it is not yet granted to see him whom it loves, so that love, delayed, may increase through its very delay, and, as though denied, may grow through ardent longing, so that delayed desires may grow, and, growing, may receive what they find. Thus the bridegroom is first sought while not found, so that, when found later, he may be held more tightly; for holy desires grow through delay, but if they fail through delay, they were not desires.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] *Morals*, book V, chap. 4.] Therefore the bridegroom hides himself when he is sought, and the seeking bride is delayed from finding him, that, rendered more capable by the delay, she may at some point find more abundantly what she sought. But she who does not find her beloved must rise and go about the city [Col. 0452D]—that is, must traverse in mind and inquiry the holy Church of the elect. She must seek him through lanes and broad squares—that is, observe those walking by narrow and broad ways and seek his footprints, if she can find any among them—for there are some even in secular life who have something in their conduct of virtue worthy of imitation.

Therefore the bride, first seeking her beloved and not finding him at all, repeats her failure to find him, saying: “I sought him and did not find him.” But since finding is not long delayed if searching does not cease, she adds: “The watchmen who guard [Col. 0453A] the city found me.” [Note: [Col. 0453D] *Morals*, book XVIII, chap. 27, about the middle.] Whom should we understand as the watchmen who guard the city, except the holy Fathers, prophets, and teachers who strive, by the voice of holy preaching, to keep watch for our protection? Therefore the holy Fathers and diligent teachers, who guard the state of the Church, find every soul seeking the form of its Redeemer, because they meet its good efforts in order to instruct it either orally or in writing. But when the Church sought her Redeemer, she refused to fix her hope upon the Fathers and teachers themselves, and says:

VERS. 4.—“When I had passed by them a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” [Note: [Col. 0453D] In the same place.] For she could not have found him unless she had been willing to pass by these men. The unbelievers had fixed themselves upon these watchmen, believing that Christ, the Son of God [Col. 0453B], was one of them. But by Peter’s voice and faith holy Church passed beyond the watchmen she had found, for she scorned to believe that the Lord of the prophets was one of the prophets. [Note: [Col. 0453D] *Morals*, book XXVII, chapter 1, after the middle.] So too, unless the eager mind in its vision surpasses its estimate of the prophets, the height of the patriarchs, the measure of apostles, doctors, and all human beings, it will not come to him who is above humankind. For our Redeemer, though in humility a man among men, was in divinity above men. To pass by the watchmen, therefore, is also to set aside in comparison with him those whom the soul admires, and to refuse to fix one’s hope in them. When the watchmen are passed by, the beloved is found, because when we see prophets, apostles, and doctors to be beneath him, we consider that he who [Col. 0453C] is God by nature is above humanity—if indeed he is believed to be man, yet beyond the measures of men.

VERS. 6.—“Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke, from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” Here the bride’s excellence is praised by the bridegroom’s voice. Thus, when the holy Church of the elect raises itself from this world in holy prayers with ardent love, it ascends through the wilderness which it leaves. He adds how it ascends: “Like a slender column of smoke from perfumes.” Smoke arises from incense, and the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Psalm 140). Smoke commonly draws forth tears. Thus smoke from perfumes is the compunction of prayer [Col. 0453D] conceived from the virtues of love. Yet that prayer is called a slender column of smoke because, while it asks for heavenly things alone, it advances upright, so as not to bend down to ask for earthly and temporal things. [Note: [Col. 0453D] *Morals*, book I, chapter 19, near the end.] Therefore holy Church ascends like a slender column of smoke from perfumes, because from the virtues of its life it daily advances into the uprightness of inward incense; it does not dissolve itself by scattering among thoughts, but confines itself within the secret places of the heart by the rod of steadfastness. Notice that prayer is called not a rod but a little rod, because sometimes [Col. 0454A] in the fire of compunction the power of love is of such subtlety that even the mind which has merited, once enlightened, to possess it cannot comprehend it.

“From myrrh and frankincense” is well said. Frankincense is burned in sacrifice according to the law of the Lord; by myrrh dead bodies are preserved so that they are not corrupted by worms. They offer a sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense who both afflict the flesh lest the vices of corruption rule them, and burn the fragrant victim of their love before the Lord, presenting themselves to God in holy virtues. Therefore he adds: “And every powder of the perfumer.” The perfumer’s powder is the virtue of one who works well. Notice that the virtues of those who work well are called not perfumes but powder. When we do any good works [Col. 0454B], we offer perfumes; but when we reconsider the good works themselves and, by the judgment of reconsideration, attend lest anything crooked be in them, we make powder, as it were, from perfumes, so that through discernment and love we may kindle our prayer more subtly. [Note: [Col. 0454D] In the same place.] Thus, while we never cease to recollect and reconsider what we do, we have myrrh and frankincense in work, but powder in thought. Through the tears of compunction, dearest brethren, we ought to seek nothing earthly, nothing transitory: he alone who made all things should suffice us. Let us surpass all things by desire, that we may gather the mind into one—not now inflamed by fear of punishments or memory of vices, but by the flame of love—and burn in tears with the fragrance of virtues.


[Col. 0454C] VERS. 7.—“Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed, of the mightiest of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0454D] *Morals*, book VII, chapter 8.] For all the saints contemplate inward rest without any weakness of desire; to them the Psalmist says: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm 30). The righteous are strong to conquer the flesh, oppose their own pleasures, extinguish delight in this present life, love this world’s hardships for eternal rewards, scorn prosperity’s blandishments, overcome in heart the fear of adversity, strive not to be weak when they must bear the world’s dangers for the world, see their end, consider how transient this present life is [Col. 0454D], and refuse to undergo outward labours for its sake when they overcome its delight outwardly.

VERS. 8.—“All hold swords and are most skilled for battle.” [Note: [Col. 0454D] *Morals*, book XIX, chapter 16, toward the end.] Paul explained what the sword figures in divine Scripture when he said: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6). Therefore Solomon, describing the strong warriors of spiritual combat, did not say, “All having swords,” but “holding them,” because it is not wonderful merely to know the word of God but to do it. Those have, but [Col. 0455A] do not hold, the sword who know the divine utterance but neglect to live by it. Nor can one be learned for battle who does not exercise the spiritual sword he has. For one who postpones holding the sword of God’s word by living wickedly is wholly insufficient to resist temptations.

In the same place: “Each man’s sword upon his thigh, because of fears in the night.” [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 3.] This is said of the strong warriors of the heavenly country. The sword is placed upon the thigh when, by the sharpness of holy preaching, the perverse suggestion of the flesh is subdued. [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Morals*, book XX, chapter 5.] The sword upon the thigh is watchful guarding that restrains the enticements of the flesh. Nightly fears are the snares of hidden temptation. For by night the blindness of our weakness is expressed, because whatever adversity threatens in [Col. 0455B] the night is not seen. Therefore each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of fears in the night, since holy men, while fearing what they do not see, always stand ready in sure attentiveness. The holy are so certain of hope that they are nevertheless always suspicious of temptation; for it is said to them: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Psalm 2), so that exultation arises from hope and fear from suspicion. Lest nocturnal fear—that is, hidden and sudden temptation—creep in, it is always necessary that the sword of guarding placed above restrain our thigh.

VERS. 9–10.—“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. He made its columns of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved its midst with love [Col. 0455C] for the daughters of Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0456D] Homily XV on Ezekiel, in the middle.] We must not believe that Solomon, a king of such greatness, who so abounded in immeasurable riches that the weight of his gold could not be estimated and silver had no value in his days, made himself a wooden litter, as the bride says here. But there is our Solomon, our King and Peaceful One, who made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. The cedars of Lebanon are very incorruptible. Thus the litter of our King is holy Church, constructed from strong Fathers—that is, from incorruptible minds. It is rightly called a litter because it daily carries the soul to the eternal banquet of its Creator. The columns of this litter are silver because the preachers [Col. 0455D] of holy Church shine with the light of eloquence. With the silver columns there is a golden reclining-place, because through what the holy preachers speak clearly the minds of hearers find the brightness of inward clarity in which to recline. For through openly hearing hidden things, they rest in that which shines in the heart. Thus there are silver columns and a golden reclining-place because through the light of discourse a soul finds the brightness of rest. This inward splendour now illumines the mind so that it may rest there in intention, where the grace of preaching is no longer sought.

Of this same holy Church it is written: “The wings of the dove are silvered, [Col. 0456A] and the hinder parts of her back are in the colour of gold.” For she who here, filled with the spirit of gentleness, has as a dove silvered wings, holds in the hinder parts of her back the appearance of gold, because here she clothes her preachers with the light of discourse, but in the age to come displays in herself the splendour of brightness. But he adds what sort of ascent leads to that brightness shown within, when he immediately says of the same litter, “An ascent of purple.” True purple, because it is dyed in blood, is rightly seen in the colour of blood. And because a vast multitude of the faithful in the beginning of the rising Church came to the kingdom through martyrdom’s blood, our King made a purple ascent in his litter: through the tribulation of blood one comes to the brightness seen within.

What then shall we [Col. 0456B] miserable people, destitute of all strength, do? Behold, we cannot be columns in this litter, for in us neither strength of work nor the light of preaching shines. We have no golden reclining-place, for we do not yet, as we ought, behold by spiritual understanding the rest of inward brightness. We are not a purple ascent, because we cannot shed our blood for our Redeemer. What, then, is to be done with us? What hope is there if no one reaches the kingdom unless he has been marked by the highest virtues? But our consolation is present. Let us love God as far as we can, love our neighbour, and at the same time we too belong to God’s litter, because it is written there: “He paved its midst with love.” Have love, and [Col. 0456C] without doubt you arrive where the silver column rises and the purple ascent is held. That this is said for our weakness is openly shown when he immediately adds: “For the daughters of Jerusalem.” For when God’s word calls them daughters rather than sons, what does it signify through the female sex except the weakness of minds? Love is said to be in the midst among silver columns, the golden reclining-place, and the purple ascent, for the daughters of Jerusalem, because even those weak in virtues are not alien from God’s litter if they do not neglect to do with love the good things they can do.


CHAPTER IV.

VERS. 1.—“How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful! [Col. 0456D] Your eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which lies hidden within.” [Note: [Col. 0456D] *Morals*, book IX, chapter 6, near the end.] The bridegroom calls his bride beautiful and repeats “beautiful,” because she has one beauty of conduct in which she is seen now, and another beauty of rewards in which she will then be raised by beholding her Creator. All the elect are her members, because they go simply in all things. Her eyes are called doves’ eyes because they are irradiated with great light and shine with miracles of signs. But how great is every miracle that can be seen? More wonderful is the inward miracle which cannot now be seen, of which it is openly [Col. 0457A] added: “apart from that which lies hidden within.” Great is the glory of an outward work, but incomparably greater is that of hidden reward. Beautiful is all that by divine dispensation is seen, as it were, upon heaven’s face; but far more beautiful beyond comparison is that to which one comes invisibly.

VERS. 2.—“Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep coming up from the washing.” [Note: [Col. 0457D] *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 23; and book XI, chapter 15.] By the teeth of holy Church we understand holy preachers, who by their preaching crush the hardness of sinners. They are not undeservedly compared with shorn and washed sheep, because, taking on an innocent life in the washing of baptism, they have put off the old fleeces of their former manner of life.

VERS. 3.—“Your lips, bride, are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.” [Note: [Col. 0458D] *Morals*, book II, chapter 27, after the middle.] A ribbon binds the hairs of the head. [Col. 0457B] What do we understand by hairs except the flowing thoughts of the mind? The bride’s lips are therefore like a ribbon, because by the exhortation of holy Church all the thoughts spread abroad in hearers’ minds are bound, lest they flow loose, scatter themselves into unlawful things, and, once scattered, depress the eyes of the heart. Rather, they gather themselves, as it were, into one intention while the ribbon of holy preaching binds them. It is rightly called scarlet because the preaching of the saints burns only with the ardour of love.


VERS. 4.—“Your neck is like David’s tower, built with its bulwarks; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.” [Note: [Col. 0458D] Homily XV on Ezekiel, near the end.] In the neck is the throat, and in the throat the voice. What, then, does the bride’s neck signify, to whom these words are spoken by the bridegroom, except the sacred utterances [Col. 0457C] of holy Church? When a thousand shields are recorded as hanging upon it, this perfect number shows the number of universality, because all our defence is contained in sacred utterance. There are God’s commandments and the examples of the righteous. If the mind grows dull in desire for its Creator, let it hear: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your mind and all your strength” (Matthew 22). Does it perhaps fall into hatred of its neighbour? Let it hear: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (ibid.). Does it covet another’s property? Let it hear: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property” (Exodus 20). Is the mind inflamed to anger by injury done by a neighbour in word or deed? Let it hear: “You shall [Col. 0457D] not seek vengeance or remember the injury of your fellow citizens” (Leviticus 19). Is a mind badly stirred toward fleshly desire? Lest the eye follow the mind, let it hear what was said above: “Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). Does anyone propose to relax his mind into hatred against an enemy? Let him hear: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (ibid.).

But one who no longer steals another’s things perhaps still keeps his own inordinately. Let him hear: “Sell what you possess and give alms” [Col. 0458A] (Luke 12). Does the mind of one who is weak desire to enjoy God and the world at once? Let it hear: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6). Does another retain possessions not for need’s provision but for desire’s will? Let him hear: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). Some leave everything, but many renounce even while possessing, because they keep possessions for use in such a way that they do not submit to them from desire. Does anyone wish to be idle and, though able, shrink from undertaking labour for the Lord? Let him hear: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11). Thus upon the Church’s neck—that is, in the preaching of sacred utterance, which for its defence and height is called like David’s tower—[Col. 0458B] a thousand shields hang, because as many commandments as are there are so many defences for our breast.

Do we hasten, in order to preserve innocence, to persevere in humility even when injured by a neighbour? Let Abel come before our eyes; he is written to have been killed by his brother, but is not read to have resisted. Is purity of mind chosen even in marital union? Enoch must be imitated: though placed in marriage, he walked with God (Genesis 5), and was not found because God translated him (Hebrews 11). Do we hasten to set God’s commandments before our present advantage? Let Noah come before our eyes; setting domestic care aside, at the command of almighty God he lived occupied for a hundred years in building the ark. Do we strive to undertake obedience’s virtue? We ought to look upon Abraham [Col. 0458C], who left home, kindred, and country, obeying to go out into the place he was to receive for an inheritance: “And he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11). He stood ready to kill for eternal inheritance the beloved heir he had received; because he did not delay to offer his only son to God, he received in his seed the whole multitude of nations. Does simplicity of life please us? Let Isaac come to mind, whose life’s tranquillity adorned him in the eyes of almighty God. Is laborious strength sought? Let Jacob be recalled, who, after learning to serve a man strongly, was also brought to such virtue that he could not be overcome by the angel wrestling with him. Do we try to conquer fleshly enticements? Let Joseph [Col. 0458D] be recalled, who endeavoured to guard continence of the flesh even at the risk of life. Therefore, because he knew well how to rule his members, he was also set over the rule of all Egypt. Do we seek to be gentle? Let Moses be brought before our eyes; ruling six hundred thousand armed men besides children and women, he is described as meek above all people who lived upon the face of the earth. Are we kindled with zeal of righteousness against vices? Let Phinehas be set before us; piercing those who coupled with the sword, he restored chastity to the people and in anger appeased God’s anger.


Do we seek in doubtful matters to trust in hope of almighty God [Col. 0459A]? Let Joshua be recalled, who, entering doubtful battles with a firm mind, came to victory without doubt. Do we now desire to lay aside the hostilities of the mind and enlarge the soul in kindness? Let Samuel be brought to mind. When the people had deposed him from rule and yet asked him to pour out prayers to the Lord for them, he answered: “Far be this sin from me in the Lord, that I should cease to pray for you!” (1 Samuel 12). The holy man believed that he would commit a fault if he did not repay in prayer the kindness of grace to those whose hostility he had endured even to his deposition. Again, when the Lord commanded him to go and anoint David king, he answered: “How shall I go? Saul will find me and kill me” (1 Samuel 16). Yet [Col. 0459B] because he knew that God was angry with Saul, he afflicted himself with such mourning that the Lord said to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (ibid.). Let us weigh, then, how great a grief of love burned in his mind: he wept for the man by whom he feared to be killed. Do we wish to beware of one whom we fear? We must carefully consider lest, should we perhaps find the opportunity, we return evil for evil to the very person from whom we flee. Let David then be recalled: he found the king pursuing him and could have killed him, yet, placed in the very power of striking, chose the good he himself ought to do rather than the evil the other deserved to suffer, saying: “Far be it from me that I should stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed!” (1 Samuel 26). When Saul had later been slain by enemies, David mourned him who, while living, he had endured as persecutor. [Col. 0459C]

Do we resolve to speak freely to the powerful persons of this world when they err? Let John’s authority be recalled, who, rebuking Herod’s wickedness, did not fear to be killed for the truth of the word. Since Christ is truth, he laid down his life for Christ precisely because he laid it down for truth. Do we hasten to give our flesh to death for God? Let Peter come to mind, who rejoices among scourges, resists rulers when beaten, and despises his own life for life. Do we, with desire for death, intend to despise adversities? Let Paul be brought before our eyes; ready not only to be bound [Col. 0459D] but also to die for Christ, he does not make his soul more precious than himself. Do we seek to kindle our heart with love’s fire? Let us weigh John’s words, all of whose speech steams with the fire of love.
