Therefore, because whenever we seek it in the voice of sacred utterance we find a defence of virtue: “A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.” If we wish to fight against spiritual wickedness, let us seek in the Church’s neck, raised for us like David’s tower—that is, in divine utterance—the arms of protection, so that from discerning the commandment we may take the strength of help against vices. Behold, do we hasten to be strong against the powers of the air? [Col. 0460A] In this tower we find the armour of our mind: from it we take the commandments of the Creator, from it the examples of those who went before, by which we may be armed invincibly against our adversaries. Whatever virtue you desire to undertake for God, and see already fulfilled there by the Fathers, there you find your armour by which you are fortified for spiritual battles. A thousand shields hang upon it: whoever wishes to fight should take one, fortify his breast with that virtue, and send forth the arrows of words.

Notice that it is said to be built with its bulwarks. Bulwarks do the same work as shields, for both protect the fighter; yet they differ, because we move a shield wherever we wish for our protection, while we can be defended by a bulwark but cannot move it. [Col. 0460B] The shield is held in the hand; the bulwark is not. What is the difference, then, between bulwarks and shields except that in sacred utterance we read the miracles of the Fathers who went before and hear the virtues of good works? There we learn that one could divide the sea, another stop the sun, another raise the dead, another lift the paralytic by a word, another heal the sick by a shadow, another withstand fevers of the sick by his handkerchiefs. Yet all these were gentle in patience and long-suffering, fervent in zeal for righteousness, rich in preaching the word, and lavish in mercy. Their miracles witness that what they said about the Lord was true, for they would not have done such things through him unless they spoke truly concerning him. Their works witness how devout, humble, [Col. 0460C] and kind they were. If we are tempted concerning the faith received from their preaching, we see the miracles of those who spoke and are confirmed in the faith received from them. What, then, are their miracles but our bulwarks? We can be fortified by them, yet do not hold such things in the hand of our will, for we cannot do them. But the shield is in the hand and protects, because the virtue of patience and the virtue of mercy, grace going before, are both within the power of choice and protect from the danger of adversity. Thus our tower is built with its bulwarks, on which a thousand shields hang, because in sacred Scripture we are hidden from arrows beneath the miracles [Col. 0460D] of the Fathers, and also hold in the hand of work the defences of holy conduct. [Note: [Col. 0459D] In the same place, somewhat earlier.] Therefore, dearest brethren, do not despise the writings of our Redeemer sent to us. Through them the mind is greatly warmed, lest it grow numb in the cold of its iniquity. When we learn that the righteous who went before acted strongly, we too gird ourselves for strength in good work; the flame of holy examples sets the reader’s mind on fire. It sees what they did bravely and is greatly indignant with itself because it does not imitate such things.


VERS. 5.—“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe, feeding among lilies until the day breathes [Col. 0461A] and the shadows incline.” [Note: [Col. 0461D] *Morals*, book XXIV, chapter 6.] Dearest brethren, we ought always to consider the lives of the righteous, so that we may subtly discover our own condition. All the elect do not cease to do this: they consider the lives of their betters and amend the conduct of their own inferior way of life. What are the bride’s two breasts, to whom the bridegroom speaks, except the two peoples coming from Judea and the Gentiles, fastened in the secret of the heart by the intention of wisdom in the body of holy Church? The elect from these peoples are compared to fawns of a doe because, through humility, they understand themselves to be small and sinful; yet when they run in love, if obstacles from temporal encumbrance meet them, they pass them and climb upward by broad leaps of contemplation. [Col. 0461B] To do this, they look upon examples of the saints who went before; hence they are said to feed among lilies. What do lilies declare except the life of those who truly say: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God” (2 Corinthians 2)? Thus, that the elect may prevail to attain the heights, they are nourished by beholding the fragrant and white life of the righteous. They already thirst to see God and burn with the heats of love to be filled by his contemplation; but since they cannot yet while placed in this life, they meanwhile feed on the examples of the Fathers who went before. Therefore the time of this feeding among lilies is aptly defined when it says: “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” We need to be refreshed by righteous examples until, with the eternal day breathing, we pass beyond the shadows of this present mortality. When [Col. 0461C], after this mortality has passed, the shadow of temporality has inclined and we see the inward light of that day, we shall no longer desire to burn for love of it through others’ examples. But now, since we cannot yet behold him, it is supremely necessary that the seen actions of those who followed him perfectly incite us. Let us therefore look upon the beautiful agility of those who follow and see how ugly the lukewarmness of the slothful is. As soon as we behold the deeds of those who act well, inward shame avenges us by judging ourselves; shame shakes the mind, guilt raging justly condemns it, and even that which perhaps still basely pleases us displeases us strongly. Therefore all who desire to be led to the heights must always attend to the advances of the better, that they may judge their faults in themselves the more strictly as they see in the others more highly what they admire. [Col. 0461D]

VERS. 8.—“You shall be crowned from the top of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions.” [Note: [Col. 0461D] *Morals*, book XVII, chapter 20.] The coming bridegroom is told that he will be crowned from the dens of lions. What else is understood by lions except demons, raging against us with the most savage cruelty of wrath? The dens of demons were the hearts of the wicked, in which, because they drew them to their own perversity, [Col. 0462A] they rested as in their dwelling. But by the midwifing hand of the Lord, lions have been driven from their dens: while divine grace heals us, the ancient enemy who held us is cast out from us, as incarnate Truth says: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12). Because sinners are called to faith, whose hearts were once dens of lions, the Lord is crowned from lions’ dens when by their confession he is believed to have conquered death. The crown is the reward of victory; believers therefore offer him a crown as often as they confess from the resurrection that he conquered death.

VERS. 11.—“Honey and milk are under your tongue.” [Note: [Col. 0461D] *Morals*, book XV, chapter 5, near the end.] When many righteous persons see some acting perversely who must be struck with hard rebukes, [Col. 0462B] they take harshness upon the tongue but conceal kindness under the tongue of their mind. They do not wish to disclose the sweetness of their mind to the weak; speaking, they strike them with a certain harshness, yet amid harsh words they let slip certain hidden sweetnesses. Such people have sweetness not on the tongue but beneath it, because among the hard things they utter they send out some gentle and sweet things through which a saddened mind may be refreshed by kindness. But the perverse and hypocrites have evil not on the tongue but beneath it: they display sweet things in speech and contrive perverse things in thought.

VERS. 16.—“Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its perfumes shall flow.” [Note: [Col. 0462D] Homily II on Ezekiel, near the middle; *Morals*, book XXVII, chapter 23; and book IX, chapter 6, near the middle.] Since the north wind binds with cold, [Col. 0462C] the torpor of the malignant spirit is not unfittingly denoted by the north wind; the prophet Isaiah testifies that the devil declared he would sit in the sides of the north. He sits in the sides of the north because he possesses cold human minds. By the south wind, which is certainly warm, is rightly signified the fervour of the Holy Spirit: when one is touched by it, he is freed from the torpor of his iniquity; when filled by it, he burns for love of the spiritual homeland. The north wind is commanded by the bridegroom’s voice to arise, that the adversary spirit which holds mortal hearts in torpor may flee. When at God’s command the cold spirit departs, the warm spirit occupies believers’ minds and blows through God’s garden—[Col. 0462D] holy Church—so that its perfumes may flow. For when the Spirit of truth has filled holy Church with the virtues of his gifts, he scatters from her far and wide the fragrances of good work, so that the report of her virtues may flow like perfumes to the knowledge of many. When the north wind, that is, the malignant spirit, withdraws, the Holy Spirit fills the mind like the south wind; once he has blown by warming it, the perfumes of virtues immediately flow from believers’ hearts. Then the report of virtues is scattered from them, so that the tongue of saints, like a garden through which wind has blown, may rightly say: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God.”

CHAPTER V.

[Col. 0463A]

VERS. 2.—“I sleep, and my heart watches.” [Note: [Col. 0463D] *Morals*, book V, chapter 22.] In sacred Scripture, sleep or sleeping used figuratively is understood in three ways: it sometimes signifies death of the flesh, sometimes the torpor of negligence, and sometimes, when earthly desires have been trampled down, the rest of life. Sleep signifies death of the flesh, as Paul says: “I do not wish you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning those who sleep” (1 Thessalonians 4); and shortly afterwards: “So God will bring with him those who have slept through Jesus” (ibid.). Sleep again signifies the torpor of negligence, as the same Paul says: “Now is the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13), and again: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15). Sleep also signifies, after desires of flesh have been trampled down [Col. 0463B], the rest of life, as is said here in the bride’s voice: “I sleep, and my heart watches.” As though she said [Note: [Col. 0463D] *Morals*, book XXII, chapter 12, after the middle.]: While through outward senses I sleep from this life’s cares, with an unoccupied mind I know inward things more vividly. I sleep outwardly, but my heart watches inwardly; for while I scarcely perceive outward things, I attentively grasp inward things. [Note: [Col. 0463D] *Morals*, book V, chapter 22.] The holy mind knows inward things more truly the more it restrains itself from the noise of temporal desire, and watches toward inward things more eagerly as it hides itself from outward disturbance. The person sleeps with a watching heart who, through progress in inward contemplation, rests from restless outward work. Whoever desires to do worldly things watches, as it were; whoever, seeking inward rest, flees this life’s noise [Col. 0463C] falls asleep, as it were.


VERS. 4.—“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.” [Note: [Col. 0463D] Homily XIX on Ezekiel, before the middle.] The mercy of our Creator is generous, because the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is equally opened to the Jewish and Gentile peoples, and to the righteous and to sinners converted after their sins. The joys of the heavenly kingdom are opened not only to those who remain in innocence but also to sinners who condemn their sins by repentance, so that they may know the ineffable mysteries of the heavenly homeland, thirst as they know them, run as they thirst, and arrive as they run. The person who said, “My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm [Col. 0463D] 41), had known these secrets of inward joy. The preacher of the Gentiles longed for this entrance of the heavenly kingdom when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1). The bride had known these secrets of hidden exultation when she says here: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.” The beloved puts his hand through the opening when the Lord by his power touches our mind through subtle understanding. The belly trembles at his touch because our weakness, touched by understanding of heavenly joy, is disturbed by its very exultation. There comes to the mind [Col. 0464A] fear in joy, because it already feels what it loves of heaven’s joy, yet still fears that it may not receive what it scarcely feels in a small measure. What remains, therefore, except that all who know those joys of the heavenly homeland should direct themselves to the course of a more perfect life?

### Verse 5

“My hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of choicest myrrh.”  
[Note: Col. 0464D, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily X, near the end.]

Holy Church says this of her workers who strive for God even unto death. For by myrrh is signified the mortification of our flesh. Of the Magi who came from the East to Bethlehem to adore the Lord, the Evangelist writes: “And opening their treasures, they offered to the Lord gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matt. I). We too offer myrrh if we mortify the vices of the flesh through abstinence; for by myrrh, as we have said, it is brought about that dead flesh does not decay. But for dead flesh to decay is for this mortal body to rage in the flux of sensual indulgence, as it is said through the prophet concerning some: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). For beasts to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of sensuality. Therefore, we offer myrrh to God when we preserve this mortal body from the decay of sensuality by the seasoning of self-restraint.

### Verse 6

“My soul melted when my beloved spoke.”  
[Note: Col. 0464D, *Morals*, Book IV, chapter 30; and *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily XXV, after the beginning.]

The mind of a person who does not seek the vision of its Creator is miserably hard, because it remains cold within itself. But when it is touched by the breathing of a hidden utterance, weakened from the state of its strength, it melts in the very desire by which it is absorbed. And when it has begun to burn with desire to follow him whom it loves, melted by the fire of love it runs; and the more ardently it rises in the love of God, the more it grows cold toward worldly pursuit.

It becomes anxious with desire; all things that formerly pleased it in the world become worthless; nothing outside the Creator delights it; and things that once delighted the mind afterward become intensely burdensome. Nothing consoles its sorrow so long as he whom it desires is not yet seen. The mind grieves; even light itself is burdensome; and by such a fire the rust of sin is refined away in the mind. The kindled soul, like gold which has lost its beauty through use, shines brightly through the fire.

### Verse 7

“I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me. The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me, they wounded me. The keepers of the walls took my cloak from me.”  
[Note: Col. 0464D, *Morals*, Book XXVII, chapter 1.]

The bride seeking her beloved does not find him, because every chosen soul already burns with the torches of his love, yet is denied the sight of him whom it seeks, so that the desire of the lover may increase. Water is, as it were, withdrawn in thirst, so that the heat of that thirst may grow; and the longer she longs thirstily for it, the more eagerly she drinks when it finally comes.

But watchmen find her as she seeks, wound her, and take away her cloak, because when vigilant teachers find a soul already seeking the vision of her Redeemer, they wound it with the arrows of heavenly love through the word of preaching. And if they remove from it whatever covering of its former way of life still remains, this is done so that, the more it is stripped of the burden of this world, the sooner he whom it seeks may be found by it.

### Verse 11

“His head is the finest gold.”  
[Note: Col. 0465D, *Morals*, Book XXXIV, chapter 13.]

By the designation of gold is signified the innermost brightness of divinity, when the bride describes the beauty of the bridegroom. For since God is the head of Christ, and among metals nothing shines more brilliantly than gold, the bridegroom’s head is called gold because his humanity takes precedence for us from the brightness of his divinity.

## Chapter VI

### Verse 3

“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely, like Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered army.”  
[Note: Col. 0465D, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily VIII.]

The holy universal Church is described under the image of the beloved. Since Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace,” and by this name the heavenly homeland is expressed, holy Church is called sweet and lovely like Jerusalem: her life and desire are already likened to the vision of inward peace. In loving her Creator and longing to see his beauty—of whom it is written, “into which angels desire to look” (1 Pet. I)—she may already be called like the angels through the desires of her love. And the more lovable she becomes to God, the more she is made terrible to evil spirits.

How she is terrible is shown by the comparison added: “as an ordered army.” Why is holy Church to be feared by her enemies as an army? This comparison is not devoid of deep meaning and must therefore be considered carefully. We know and recognize that an army appears terrible to its enemies when it is so closely packed and dense that nowhere does it seem broken. For if it is arranged so that an empty place is left through which an enemy can enter, it is no longer terrible to its enemies.

Therefore, when we draw up the battle-line of spiritual warfare against evil spirits, it is utterly necessary that we always be found united and bound together through charity, never divided by discord. For whatever good works may be in us, if charity is absent, the evil of discord opens a place in the battle-line through which the enemy can enter to strike us.

The ancient enemy, when he finds chastity in us without charity, does not fear it, because he is not pressed by flesh so as to be dissolved in its sensuality. He does not fear abstinence, because he does not use food, being under no bodily necessity. He does not fear the distribution of earthly goods if charity is absent from that work, because he himself does not need the resources of riches. But he greatly fears true charity in us—that is, the humble love which we mutually show one another—and he fiercely envies our concord, because we possess on earth what he, unwilling to hold it, lost in heaven.

Thus it is rightly said: “Terrible as an ordered army,” because evil spirits fear the multitude of the elect to the extent that they see them united and massed against themselves by the concord of charity. The greatness of concord’s power is shown when, without it, the remaining virtues are shown not to be virtues.

Abstinence is indeed a great virtue. But if someone abstains from food in such a way as to judge others for eating, and even condemns among believers the same foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving, what has the virtue of abstinence become for that person except a snare of sin? Hence the Psalmist, signifying that there is no abstinence without concord, says: “Praise him with tambourine and choir” (Ps. CL). In a tambourine, dry curved skin resounds; but in a choir, voices sing in harmony. What, then, is signified by the tambourine except abstinence, and by the choir except the concord of charity? Therefore, one who observes abstinence in such a way as to abandon concord praises indeed with the tambourine, but does not praise with the choir.

There are some who, while striving to be wiser than is necessary, withdraw from peace with their neighbors, despising them as dull and foolish. Therefore Truth himself warns us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX). Whoever strives to possess the salt of wisdom must take care never to depart from the peace of concord.

What we have said about these two virtues must be understood of all the others. Hence Paul gives this fearful warning: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God.” And that nothing pleases God without concord, Truth himself shows when he says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, when you return, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23).

See: he does not wish to receive sacrifice from those who are at discord; he refuses to accept a burnt offering. Consider, then, how great an evil discord is, because of which even that is rejected through which sin is remitted. Holy Church, therefore, is rightly called terrible as an ordered army, because the elect, who are the camp of the spiritual army and have undertaken war against the powers of the air, are always joined together in charity; and this same charity of theirs strikes the evil spirits—that is, their ancient enemies—with the punishment of fear.

### Verse 6

“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your hidden things.”  
[Note: Col. 0466D, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily X, in the middle.]

The cheeks of holy Church are the spiritual Fathers, who, being full of charity, subdue the flesh through abstinence, enlighten the hearts of hearers by the light of preaching, perform signs, work miracles, and shine with wonders. Because their good works become known outwardly to us, they rightly appear venerable in the face of holy Church.

When we see many work wonders, foretell things to come, leave the world perfectly, and burn with heavenly desires, the cheeks of holy Church are regarded as like the rind of a pomegranate. But what is all that we admire in comparison with that of which it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II)? Thus, when he had admired the cheeks of the Church, he properly adds, “apart from your hidden things,” as though he were plainly saying: the things in her which are not hidden are indeed great, but the things which are hidden are utterly beyond estimation.

### Verse 9

“Who is this who comes forth like the dawn rising?”  
[Note: Col. 0467D, *Morals*, Book IV, chapter 14, in the middle; and Book XXIX, chapter 2.]

Holy Church, whom the bridegroom here admires, is plainly described as likened to the dawn. Leaving the darkness of sin, she has already broken forth into the light of eternity; through the knowledge of faith she is transformed from the darkness of her sins into the bright light of righteousness. For because dawn turns from darkness into light, the whole Church of the elect is rightly signified by the name dawn. As she is led from the night of unbelief to the light of faith, she is opened, after darkness, into the day by the splendor of heavenly brightness, as dawn does.

Holy Church, therefore, desiring the rewards of heavenly life, is called dawn because, as she leaves the darkness of sins, she shines with the light of righteousness. She rises like dawn because she leaves the darkness of former perversity and turns herself toward the brightness of new light.

Yet there is something more subtle which we should consider from the nature of dawn. Dawn announces that night has passed, but does not yet reveal the full brightness of day; while driving away the one, it receives the other, retaining light mingled with darkness. What, then, are all of us who follow truth in this life except dawn? For we already do some things which belong to light, yet we are not without certain remnants of darkness.

The prophet says to God: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII). Again it is written: “We all offend in many things” (Jas. III). Paul also says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. VII). Where the law of sin contends with the law of the mind, there is certainly still dawn, because the light which has already shone forth has not yet wholly overcome the passing darkness.

It is still dawn because, while the law of the flesh strikes against the law of the mind and the law of the mind against the law of the flesh, light and shadow struggle reciprocally with one another. Hence, when Paul said, “The night has passed” (Rom. XIII), he did not add, “The day has come,” but rather, “The day has drawn near.” For he who indicates that after night has departed the day has not already come but has drawn near clearly shows that, after darkness but before the sun, he is still in dawn.

But the day of the holy Church of the elect will be complete when she shines with the perfect fervor of inward light. The day will then be complete when, enduring no tempting recollection of her evils, she has hidden from herself even every remnant of darkness. But now, still enduring the troubles of temptations, Church rises like dawn and goes forward to her place, because through the intention of her heart she hastens toward something else.

For what is the place of dawn except the perfect charity of the vision of eternity? When dawn reaches it, it will have nothing left of the darkness of the night that has passed. If it did not behold that place in mind, it would remain in the darkness of this life. But while it daily sees its place increasing and seeks the sun to shine fully upon it, dawn considers its place when the holy soul burns to contemplate the vision of its Creator.

Dawn strove to reach its place when David said: “My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI). Dawn hastened to arrive at this place, which it had recognized, when Paul said that he desired “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). Again: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid.). And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. V).

Blessed Job speaks of this dawn, saying: “Let that night be solitary and unworthy of praise; let it wait for light and not see it, nor the rising of the dawn” (Job III).  
[Note: Col. 0467D, *Morals*, Book IV, chapter 4, in the middle.]

Therefore, in that light manifested at the coming of the strict Judge, the body of the condemned enemy does not see the rising of the dawn, because when the strict Judge comes for recompense, every wicked person, weighed down by the darkness of his own merits, does not know with what brightness holy Church rises into the inward light of the heart.

For then the mind of the elect is lifted on high to be illumined by the rays of divinity; and the more it is flooded by his regard, the more it is raised beyond itself by the shining grace. Then holy Church becomes full dawn, when she utterly loses the darkness of her mortality and ignorance. Thus, in judgment she is still dawn, but in the kingdom she is day: for although, with the restoration of bodies, she begins to see the light in judgment, she more fully completes the vision of it in the kingdom.

The rising of the dawn, therefore, is the beginning of the Church’s brightening, which the reprobate cannot see, because, pressed into darkness by the weight of their evils, they are drawn away from the sight of the strict Judge. Hence it is also rightly said through the prophet: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI).

## Chapter VII

### Verse 4

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.”  
[Note: Col. 0468D, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 33; and *Morals*, Book XXXI, chapter 17, after the middle. Also *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily XI, after the beginning.]

What praise is this, dearly beloved brothers, that the bride’s nose is compared by the bridegroom’s voice to a tower? But because we often foresee by smell something which we do not see with our eyes, and because through the nose we always distinguish fragrances and stenches, what is signified by the nose of the Church except the prudent discernment of saints and prelates?

A tower of watchfulness is set on high so that an approaching enemy may be seen from afar. The nose of the Church is therefore rightly said to be like the tower in Lebanon, because the prudent discernment of saints, while looking carefully in every direction, detects sin before it comes, being set on high; and the more watchfully it foreknows sin, the more strongly it avoids it.

The nose of the Church is rightly said to be like the tower in Lebanon because the discerning foresight of saints is so established on high that it stands fortified both against the assaults of temptations before they come and against them when they arrive. For things foreseen in the future become less powerful when they are present, because the more prepared one is made against a blow, the more the enemy who believed himself unexpected is weakened precisely because he was foreseen.

The nose of the Church is rightly said to be like the tower in Lebanon because the discernment of those set over others ought always to be fortified through watchfulness and established in the height of life—that is, not lying in the valley of weak conduct. For just as a tower is set on a mountain for observation, so that enemies who come may be seen at a greater distance, so the life of preachers must always remain fixed on high, that, in the manner of nostrils, it may distinguish the stenches of vices and the fragrances of virtues, perceive from afar the approaches of evil spirits, and by its prudence render pure the souls entrusted to it.

[Note: Col. 0469D, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily XI, shortly before the passage cited above.]

Thus, the life of a watchman must always be both elevated and watchful. Nor is it enough for a watchman to live on high unless, by speaking lofty things, he also draws his hearers upward and kindles their minds toward love of the heavenly homeland. So that it may not succumb to love of earthly things, it must be elevated; so that it may not be wounded by the darts of the hidden enemy, it must be watchful on every side.

### Verse 12

“Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit.”  
[Note: Col. 0469D, *Morals*, Book XII, chapter 24.]

Vineyards flower when the minds of believers propose good works, but they do not bring forth fruit if, overcome by some errors, they grow weak in what they have proposed. Therefore, we must not merely see whether the vineyards flower, but whether the flowers become strong enough for the bringing forth of fruit. For it is not wonderful if someone begins good things; it is very wonderful if someone perseveres in a good work with right intention.

Hence it often happens that, if right intention is not preserved in good work, even the good work itself which one believes one has may be lost. We must consider how a vineyard is harmed in its first flowering. If excessive cold, caused by the unevenness of the weather, touches a flowering vineyard, it immediately dries up all the moisture of its greenness.

[Note: Col. 0470D, ibid., somewhat earlier.]

There are some who, after perverse paths, desire to follow holy ways; but before their good desires, as we have said, are strengthened in them, some prosperity of the present age overtakes them. It entangles them in outward affairs and, by withdrawing their minds from the warmth of inward love, extinguishes them as if by cold; it kills whatever seemed to appear in them as the flowering of virtues.

For the mind grows very cold in earthly occupations if it has not yet been strengthened by inward gifts. Therefore it is necessary that greater positions or outward works which will benefit human necessities be undertaken by those who know how, through inward strength, to judge and keep these things beneath themselves. For when a weak person is drawn either to a position of governance or to outward activities, and is thus led, as it were, outside himself, he is uprooted. A tree which has not first sent down roots deeply is more quickly thrown down by the force of the winds if it raises itself to the height of its crown; and the higher it has grown in the air without roots, the more quickly it falls to the ground.

At times, however, it is not cold but heat that dries a flowering vineyard. When it is touched by excessive heat, the flower is scattered and the cluster withers. It often happens that those who do not come to good works with right intention, when they see that they please people, are inflamed more ardently to perform these same works. They anxiously strive to do things pleasing to human eyes, and seem to burn with holy zeal. What, then, has touched these people except heat in the flowering, when the desire for human praise has made them strangers to fruit? But it must be known that these things always happen to those who do not follow God with a pure and simple purpose.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 5

“Who is this who ascends from the wilderness, abounding in delights?”  
[Note: Col. 0470D, *Morals*, Book XVI, chapter 9.]

Surely holy Church could not ascend from the wilderness of the present life to higher things unless she abounded in the delights of God’s words. Therefore she abounds in delights and ascends, because, while fed by mystical understandings, she is daily raised to contemplate heavenly things.

To abound in delights is to be satisfied in the love of the Almighty by the delights of sacred Scripture. For in its words we find as many delights as the varieties of understanding we receive for our advancement: at one time bare history feeds us; at another, moral allegory, veiled beneath the texture of the letter, refreshes us in our inmost being; at another, contemplation raises us to higher things, already flashing in the darkness of this present life with the light of eternity.

It should be known that whoever abounds in delights is loosened in some part of himself and, as though through weariness, is relaxed from the pursuit of labor. For when the soul begins inwardly to abound in delights, it no longer consents to devote itself to earthly works. Captured by the love of its Creator, and now free by its captivity, it longs in faintness to contemplate his brightness; and, as though growing weary, it becomes strong, because, unable any longer to bear sordid burdens, it hastens in rest toward him whom it loves within.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “And night is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. CXXXVIII). For while the diligent mind is refreshed by mystical understanding, the darkness of the present life is already illumined within it by the brightness of the day to come. Thus, even amid the gloom of this corruption, the power of that future light breaks into understanding; and the mind, fed by the delights of words, learns by foretaste what it ought to hunger for from the food of truth.

“Who is this who ascends whitened?”  
[Note: Col. 0471D, *Morals*, Book XVIII, chapter 27, at the end.]

Since holy Church does not naturally possess heavenly life, but is adorned by the beauty of gifts when the Spirit comes upon her, she is described by the bridegroom’s voice not as white but as “whitened.” Thus also, when proud heretics in the Church were rebuked, all the truly humble faithful were called “most pure dyes,” when blessed Job said: “Not even the most pure dyes can be compared” (Job XXVIII).

Those are called most pure dyes who are truly humble and truly holy, who know that they have no beauty of virtues from themselves, but possess it from the gift of grace which comes upon them. For they would not be dyed if they possessed holiness naturally. But they are most pure dyes because they humbly preserve within themselves the grace of virtues which has come upon them and which they have received.

They are rightly called most pure dyes who had formerly been ugly through evil works, but when the Spirit comes upon them are clothed in the brightness of grace, so that they appear far other than they were. Hence baptism itself—namely, dyeing—is called our descent into water. For we are dyed; and we who were previously unattractive through the deformity of vices, having received faith, are made beautiful by the grace and adornment of virtues.

### Verse 6

“Set me as a seal upon your heart.”  
[Note: Col. 0471D, *Morals*, Book XXIX, chapter 4.]

Sacred Scripture commonly calls faith a seal. For the younger son who returned to his father after consuming his substance received a ring as a gift. The Gentile people, having lost immortality and returning to God in repentance, is fortified by the seal of faith. A seal is placed upon things so that they may not be violated by the reckless presumption of plunderers.

Therefore the bridegroom, who here speaks to the Church, places a seal upon the heart when the mystery of faith is impressed upon the keeping of our thought, so that the unbelieving servant—namely, our adversary—when he sees hearts sealed by faith, may not presume to break into them through temptation.

### Same verse

“Love is strong as death.”  
[Note: Col. 0471D, *Morals*, Book X, chapter 12, at the end.]

The true strength of charity is praised in the voice of holy Church, and love is compared with the power of death. For as death destroys the body, so the charity of eternal life utterly kills, in the mind which it has once begun to possess, love for bodily things and attachment to the world. For the one whom it has perfectly absorbed, it renders, as it were, insensible to outward earthly desires; and it establishes its mastery over him all the more forcefully as it makes him more insensible to terrors.

[Note: Col. 0471D, somewhat earlier.]

Whoever is fixed solely in the desire of eternity is neither exalted by prosperity nor shaken by adversity; since he has nothing in the world that he desires, there is nothing in the world that he fears. Did Paul not burn with the fire of this love when he said: “For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor power, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VIII)?

### Verse 8

“Our little sister has no breasts.”  
[Note: Col. 0472D, *Morals*, Book XIX, chapter 9.]

The age of holy Church, as that of each individual person, is described. She was little when, newly born, she could not preach the word, because before she advanced through growth in virtue, she could not offer the breasts of preaching to certain weak hearers. But Church is called mature when, united to the Word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, she becomes fruitful in the conception of children through the mystery of preaching, and those whom she brings forth by exhorting she bears by converting.

### Verse 13

“You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening: make me hear your voice.”  
[Note: Col. 0472D, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 26.]

The Church to whom these words are spoken in the bridegroom’s address dwells in gardens, since, cultivated unto inward greenness, she preserves the plantings of virtues. Holy Church is in gardens, and every soul dwells in gardens when it is filled with the greenness of hope and the fertility of good works.

The appearance of this world is dry, because everything loved here withers swiftly. The apostle Peter urges us to hasten, saying: “Into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Pet. I). Therefore, she who now dwells in gardens ought to make her bridegroom hear her voice: that is, she should utter such goodness in preaching as may delight him whom she desires.

The bridegroom desires to hear this voice because, through the souls of his elect, he longs for her preaching. For friends are listening—namely, all the elect—who desire to hear from her the word of life, the word of her preaching, so that they may come to life again for the heavenly homeland.

Whoever, therefore, advances in holy Church by seeing spiritual things ought also to share them with others by speaking. The one who advances in himself sees in order to proclaim; and by preaching he also cares for his neighbor’s advancement. Thus elsewhere it is written: “Let him who hears say: Come” (Rev. XXII). For once the voice of God calling has arisen in someone’s heart, it must break forth in the voice of preaching to a neighbor; and therefore that person calls another because he himself has already been called.

### Verse 14

“Flee, my beloved, flee.”  
[Note: Col. 0472D, *Morals*, Book XVII, chapter 15.]

We say that something “flees us” whenever that which we wish to remember does not come to our mind; we say that it “flees us” when we do not retain in memory what we desire. Therefore, after holy Church has described the death, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord, she cries out to him, full of prophetic spirit: “Flee, my beloved, flee.” As if she said: You who have been made comprehensible through the flesh, surpass the understanding of our sense by your divinity, and remain incomprehensible to us in yourself.

[Note: Col. 0472D, ibid., somewhat earlier.]

Hence it is rightly said through the Psalmist: “Darkness is under his feet; and he ascended above the Cherubim and flew; he flew above the wings of the winds, and made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. XVII). Darkness is beneath his feet because he is not seen by lower beings with the brightness in which he rules among higher beings.

“For he ascended above the Cherubim and flew.” *Cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore he is said to have ascended and flown above the fullness of knowledge because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. He flew because he carried himself far upward beyond our understanding. “He flew above the wings of the winds,” because he transcends the knowledge of souls. “And he made darkness his hiding-place,” because, while we are darkened by the obscurity of our minds, he is hidden from us through our ignorance, so that he may not yet be seen by us in eternal and inward brightness.

He hides from mortals the power of his majesty; in this life we do not know the glory of his kingdom as fully as it is possessed inwardly, and the glory of that heavenly kingdom is not seen as it is. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to follow the Lord with the heart to that place where we believe he ascended in the body.

Let us flee earthly desires; let nothing below delight us any longer, for we have a Father in heaven. And we must reflect carefully upon this: he who ascended gently will return terribly, and whatever he commanded us with gentleness, he will require of us with strictness. Therefore, let no one make light of the time granted for repentance; let no one neglect the care of himself while he is able to act, because our Redeemer will come to judgment with so much greater strictness as he has previously granted us great patience before judgment.

Do these things with us, brothers; turn them over in your minds with diligent reflection. Though the mind may still be tossed by waves of disturbance, fix the anchor of your hope in the eternal homeland, and establish the intention of your mind in the true light. Behold, we believe that the Lord has ascended to heaven; let us therefore preserve in meditation what we believe. Although we are still held here by bodily weakness, let us nevertheless follow him with the steps of love.

For he who gave our desire does not abandon it: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0473]

## Another Exposition on the Song of Songs

### Author’s Preface

[Col. 0473C] Lord our God, who created us in your image and likeness, namely to contemplate you and to enjoy you: no one contemplates you unto enjoyment except insofar as he is made like you. O beauty of the highest good, who draw every rational soul by desire for yourself—the more ardently toward you the purer it is within itself, and the purer the freer it is from bodily things toward spiritual things—free from the slavery of corruption that love in us which ought to serve you alone.

For it is love which, when free, makes us like you to the degree in which the sense of life, by which it perceives you, disposes us toward you. Whoever lives from the Spirit of life, who, as the Apostle says, “with unveiled face,” beholding your glory, “is transformed into the same image” “from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. III).

For when we love any creature not in order to use it for you, but to enjoy it in itself, love is no longer love but cupidity or lust, or something of that kind. With the loss of liberty it also loses the grace of its name, and the wretched human being is compared to irrational beasts and becomes like them.

This is the whole of such a person’s sin: to enjoy wrongly and to use wrongly, when he loves either any thing, or his neighbor, or himself, not in order to use it, as was said, for you, but to enjoy it in itself. Yet one ought to enjoy both one’s neighbor and oneself, but only in you; whereas you, O life of lives and good of all goods, are to be enjoyed both in you and in yourself.

And this is living and luminous love, free and freeing from corruption: the purer, the sweeter; the stronger in affection, the more constant in action. Through piety it grows sweet in the conscience; through justice it flourishes in the substance of works.

Free it, Lord, in us, so that your bride, the Christian soul—purchased by your blood, pledged by your Spirit—may love chastely; so that amid the grievous pressures of this life, in the weariness of her pilgrimage away from you and of her prolonged sojourn in a foreign land, she may sing to you her songs of love, breathe again, and find her pain made lighter; that she may be disposed toward you and meanwhile forget where she is; that she may receive something by which she may understand what she lacks.

Now is the time for showing mercy; now the time has come, when you have nourished her and led her into the wilderness, that there you might speak to her heart.

Speak, then, and say to her and to her heart: “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34); say it so that she may hear, breathe it into her so that she may feel it, grant it so that she may possess it, that all her inward parts may bless you and all her bones may say to you: “Lord, who is like you?” (ibid.), O her helper and defender; and that, by converse with you alone, many who say to her, “There is no salvation for her in her God” (Ps. 3), may be confounded in confusion. By your converse, let love come to be where it is not; where it is, let it grow and prevail, until your captive handmaid—won by right of war and by the lot of victory—finding favour in your eyes through fruits worthy of repentance, and, according to the law, having had all her superfluities cut away by you, may pass by everlasting charity and indissoluble union into the victor’s embrace.

For this reason, as we undertake to unfold and examine this epithalamium, this wedding-song, this song of bridegroom and bride—your work, O Holy Spirit—we invoke you, that we may be filled with your love, O Love, so as to understand the song of love; and that we too may in some measure become sharers in the converse of Bridegroom and Bride, so that what we read may be enacted in us. For where affections are in question, what is said is not easily grasped except by those similarly affected. Therefore dispose us toward yourself, Holy Spirit, holy Paraclete, holy Comforter; console the poverty of our solitude, which seeks no consolation outside you; enlighten and enliven the desire that strains toward you, so that it may become the love of one who enjoys. Be present, that we may truly love, and that whatever we feel or say may proceed from the fountain of your love. Let your song of love be so read by us that it kindles love itself within us; and let love itself disclose its own song to us through itself.

Yet we do not venture upon those deeper mysteries contained in it concerning Christ and the Church. Rather, restraining ourselves within ourselves, and measuring ourselves by ourselves, we shall briefly touch, concerning bridegroom and bride, Christ and the Christian soul, upon some moral sense in which everyone may venture according to the poverty of his understanding, seeking from our labour no other fruit than one suited to its subject: namely, love itself.

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0475]

[Col. 0475B] This book of Solomon, then, is entitled the *Song of Songs*, either because it seems to surpass all the ancient songs of patriarchs and prophets in the dignity of its meaning and the excellence of its subject, treating of bridegroom and bride, Christ and the rational soul; or because it is celebrated by the blessed people who know jubilation and walk in the light of God’s countenance, through the harmony of holy affections rather than through the vocal concord of differing sounds.

For it treats of the love of God: either that by which God is loved, or that by which God himself is called love. Whether it is called *amor*, *caritas*, or *dilectio* matters little, except that in the name *amor* there appears to be signified a certain tender affection of one loving, reaching toward or embracing; in the name *caritas*, a certain spiritual affection, or the joy of one enjoying; and in *dilectio*, the natural desire for a thing that delights. Yet the one and same Spirit works all these in the love of bridegroom and bride.

The affections of all holy virtues serve the love of bridegroom and bride in singing the New Song in such a manner that, if their advances proceed well and in their proper order, they all pass over into and terminate in its effects. The rest indeed are brought to nothing: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13). Or it is called the *Song of Songs* because it appears to contain four songs within itself. For it is distinguished by four divisions, each of which ends in its own reclining together—that is, in the union of bridegroom and bride. Because of reverence for the great sacrament in Christ and the Church, the Holy Spirit chose to honour this union with a more decent name, calling it rather a reclining together (*accubitus*) than a lying together (*concubitus*), as the bride says: “While the king was at his reclining, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1).

Each reclining together, moreover, has its own epithalamium preceding it—that is, a nuptial song—by which bridegroom and bride are, as it were, led to the bridal chamber. And it concludes in this: that peace and the security of rest may be ordered for the bride resting in the bridegroom’s embrace, the bridegroom himself acting and adjuring, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wills” (Song 2). The fourth, however, which is also the last, seems to conclude differently and with a higher mystery. For while the others seem to prelude a festal joy concerning the union of bridegroom and bride, this one ends with the bride urgently directing the bridegroom to flee, proclaiming and saying: “Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag” (Song 3). What this means shall be said in its place, if the bridegroom himself deigns to reveal it.

This Song is written in dramatic form and comic style, as though to be recited through characters and acts. Thus, as in the recitation of comedies there are different characters and different acts, so in this Song persons and affections seem to meet together in order to accomplish the undertaking of love and the mystical covenant of divine and human union. There are four characters: the Bridegroom and his companions, the Bride, and the chorus of young women. The bridegroom’s companions are angels, rejoicing with our good things and gladly serving in suitable ministries for this purpose. The young women, on the other hand, are tender and newly formed souls who, having enrolled themselves in the discipline and profession of spiritual love, delight to adhere, by the services of humility and by zeal for imitation, to the Bride—that is, to those more perfect. Yet the whole action of love is left to the lovers themselves; so that, while those who love with them are silent, standing, listening, and rejoicing with joy at the voice of bridegroom and bride, throughout this whole Song scarcely any voice is heard or speech inserted except that of the Bridegroom and Bride.

The plot of the historical drama, tale, or parable set before us may be this. King Solomon took as wife the daughter of Pharaoh of Egypt. To her he first granted some favour of betrothal, love, and kissing; afterward, when he had shown her in part his riches and in part his glory, he removed her from their mutual union and from the favour of the kiss, until, having laid aside Egyptian blackness and put off the custom of a barbarous nation, she should become worthy to be admitted to the royal bridal chamber.

Its spiritual meaning, however, is this. The soul converted to God and to be married to the Word of God is first taught to understand the riches of prevenient grace and permitted to taste that the Lord is sweet. Afterwards it is sent back into the house of its conscience, to be instructed, made chaste in the obedience of charity, perfectly cleansed from vices, and adorned with virtues, so that it may be judged worthy to be admitted to the spiritual grace of piety and to the affection of virtues, which is the bridegroom’s bridal chamber.

[Col. 0477B] These things ought to have been set forth at the beginning, so that henceforth we may run with an unobstructed course after the bridegroom’s fragrance—on the condition, however, that if at times the beauty of the way makes us somewhat overly curious observers, it may not offend our fellow traveller.

But before we undertake the intended journey, since all the parts of this Song are nothing other than differing states of those who pray, or forms, causes, or subjects of prayers, something ought to be said about the various modes of prayer. Thus the diligent and devout reader, as he runs through the reading of the Song itself, may always return to himself and, when he finds them in the holy Song, recognize them in his own heart.

It is clear, then, that there are three states of those who pray, or of prayers: the animal, the rational, and the spiritual. Each, according to his own mode, forms for himself or sets before himself his Lord God; for God appears to the one praying according as that person is who prays. For just as one who prays faithfully always strives to offer in prayer something solid and worthy of God, so he has an anxious and wary heart until he sees, at least in some measure, before whom he lays it down or to whom he entrusts it.

The animal man, however, praying to God but not knowing how he ought to pray, asks something of God apart from God himself, or in relation to God; and even if he makes great progress in his own order and is found wiser in his generation, he does not seek that his conscience be cleansed from evil works and his heart from perverse thoughts. He offers himself to God as he is: desiring and asking through God for something else, and requiring from God no other form than his own—that is, one granting things sought apart from himself. Even if he sometimes seems to direct his attention to him whom he prays to, it is enough for him to set before the eyes of his heart, as it were, or to think upon One who is unthinkable, invisible, incomprehensible. He does not find it enough to think of or look upon God in what God is, but only in that God is able to grant what is asked. Such a man sometimes prays in spirit but not in mind: his spirit, that is, his will, prays, but his mind is without fruit. For one never directs oneself toward God without the fruit of the mind whenever one truly does direct oneself, even though one rationally asks for something other than what God is.

Such a man, multiplying words in prayer, sometimes even without feeling, does not direct thoughts with understanding, or feeling or affection, toward God. Even if these are, as it were, brought before him unbidden, he turns them toward something else. Therefore, as once happened with carnal Israel, the God whom he prays to is always in darkness to him.

[Col. 0478A] But the Song of Love does not admit this mode of prayer, in which she who desires one thing, loves one thing, asks one thing only, and prays for one thing only.

There is also a certain animal prayer of the saints. Though it is at times also found among the good pleasures of people who work iniquity—for example, prayer for temporal peace, the fertility of the earth, or bodily health—yet in this they do not share the attitude of the elect. Although they ask for something else, they do not ask it for the sake of, or in relation to, anything other than the One. They ask devoutly and holily, entrusting everything to, and leaving everything to, the will of him whom they pray to: whether what they seek should or should not be given.

At times, indeed, one who is thus disposed sets before the eyes of his mind the Lord and Saviour in human form and, like one human being addressing another, assumes a certain human, almost bodily affection in prayer. He sets before himself him to whom he prays and the matter for which he prays as though placed in the middle; and according to the form of this arrangement he also fashions the manner of his prayer. Yet this manner of praying usually belongs more to a religious simplicity that has not yet perceived the things of God than to slothful animality or human prudence.

When such a person faithfully lays before Jesus, the merciful Judge, what he has, and places himself at his feet, washing his feet with tears and spiritually anointing them with the ointment of devout devotion, he nevertheless imagines this very thing more bodily. Yet from the sweetness of this animal imagining he often deserves to be enlightened and warmed into an affection of spiritual prayer or contemplation; in a manner unknown to himself, conceiving from these bodily imaginations certain sacraments of piety. In the simple heart, the surpassing grace at work does more than the effort of the one praying. For he loves much, and therefore much is granted or forgiven him; and even in things that are outward, he often deserves to obtain much.

Indeed, it is devout even to approach God in this way. As Job says, even thus, when a man visits his own likeness in God—that is, thinks upon his own resemblance—he does not sin (Job 5). And the Lord God of all is to be adored and worshipped through the faces of many persons. Yet Jesus still says to his disciples: “It is expedient for you that I go away” (John 16), that is, that I withdraw from your sight the person of my humanity; “for unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (ibid.). For as long as one praying thinks something bodily in him whom he prays to, prayer is indeed devout but not altogether spiritual. For “God is spirit” (John 4), and it is necessary that whoever worships him “worship in spirit and truth” (ibid.).

[Col. 0479A] This mode of praying is usually formed from the form of faith or the creed: when what is faithfully believed concerning the piety of the Christian faith is truly and simply loved, and the imagination of the bodily dispensations of the Lord Jesus Christ passes into affection.

Therefore the rational person, governed by reason, labours at this with the prompting of reason and strives until, victorious over himself, he transcends all these things and escapes into those things that are of the Spirit: until the good will passes into a good mind, and the desire of one stretching forward into the understanding of one seeing, or the love of one enjoying.

And when, with the Holy Spirit helping human weakness, a person’s own likeness begins to be renewed into the image of God, supervening grace makes reason, mind, life, conduct, and even the constitution of the body conform to one affection of piety, one image of charity, one countenance seeking God. A person then desires to know God, insofar as is permitted, and to be known by him; that the countenance of God’s grace may be revealed to him, and his own to the scrutiny of his conscience, so that, knowing God and known by him, he may pray to and worship him as he ought, in spirit and truth.

He is the Bridegroom and she is the Bride; this is their mutual converse. For when, according to the Lord’s promise, the divine condescension begins to come to one who loves him and to make its dwelling there (John 14), it makes itself known to that person in some measure. Since no human being can see God’s face and live—that is, apprehend the fullness of his knowledge in this life—it places within the loving sense and entrusts a certain likeness of its knowledge: not the likeness of a presumptuous phantasm, but of a certain devout affection, which a person still living in the flesh may receive or endure. These are the firstfruits of the Spirit, the pledge or bridal dowry of the bridal chamber, nobler and more abundant in proportion as the Bride becomes more fit or nearer to the Bridegroom’s chamber.

[Col. 0479C] The man of desires, having received this from God, entrusts it not so much to his own choice in memory as to the grace of God in his conscience, so that when he returns to prayer he may recover it; and, bringing before its author his own possession and the pledge of his grace, may appear more confidently before him. The more often it is restored to its source and the more devoutly and faithfully it is committed anew, the worthier it becomes of God and the more effectual and sweet to its possessor.

For even common knowledge of any things is accustomed to retain in mind or memory an impressed image of the thing known; and it possesses the known thing more familiarly in proportion as it retains a more distinct image of it. When this occurs concerning God in a human being, although at times a great likeness of divinity somehow known is formed in the mind, this happens without any fantastic imagination, through the purity of simple affection and the enlightened sense of love. This is what the imagination of things in the memory of the knower seems to do in ordinary knowledge of things.

Yet the loftiness of that nature makes a great difference here: that likeness is lower in proportion as it occurs in a lower nature, and more unlike in proportion as it occurs in more unlike matter—namely, the likeness of the Creator in the creature, of God in the soul. But again, that grace of divine knowledge which, as has been said, arises only in the sense or understanding of enlightened love, enriches its knower beyond all thoughts of things concerning itself and makes him blessed. It condescends to him and raises him to itself, transforming the majesties of its loftiness into certain familiar and friendly affections and experiences of divine sweetness and goodness, all the more sweetly in proportion as the blessed poor in spirit, humble, quiet, trembling at the Lord’s words, and simple soul—with whom the Holy Spirit is accustomed to converse—has, prior to the reverence of that knowledge or understanding, more truly and devoutly recognized the weaknesses of its own poverty, humility, and simplicity; and has brought to it perceptions that are subtler in proportion as they are simpler, not so much in learning as in the powers of the Lord and in his righteousness alone.

[Col. 0480A] This is the white stone of the Apocalypse, “having a name written upon it which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Rev. 19). This is the sweetness of which it is written in praise of Wisdom: “It is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28).

Therefore this rational or spiritual person—for as long as he strives toward this under the action of reason, he is rational; but after he has attained it, insofar as he has attained it, he is now spiritual—has, I say, a likeness and image of God in his mind, through creating grace. It is more like God and nearer to the knowledge of God in proportion as it is more capable of eternal things; and it is more capable of eternal things in proportion as, through illuminating grace, it is cleaner from the transitory things of this world.

For as long as God is seen only through a mirror and in an enigma, a human being passes to the contemplation of God only in an image. Whether that mirror or enigma is a clearer or a more obscure image, while one lives here, one passes there only in an image. Yet in proportion as the mind faithfully maintains within itself the dignity and truth of God’s image, it strives toward God by images more faithful and nearer to truth—not fashioning within itself concerning God or in God what is not there through fantastic or superstitious presumption, but approaching, in whatever form of affection it can and is granted, him who is.

To promise or hope for the perfection of the vision or knowledge of God in this life is the emptiest presumption. Reason admonishes, progress teaches, and affection forms such a person to pray to God as God. Conforming himself to God rather than God to himself, he asks nothing from God except God and for God; he consents to enjoy nothing except God or in God, and even to use nothing except for God.

This person, as has been said, is rational as long as he is being purified; once purified, he is spiritual. But as it is fitting that the rational state should always progress into the spiritual, so it is necessary that the spiritual person sometimes return to the rational. To be continually acted upon spiritually as a spiritual person does not belong to this life; nevertheless, a person of God ought always to be either rational in desire or spiritual in affection.

[Col. 0480D] In prayer, such a person sometimes seems, not without labour and struggle, to overcome and transcend every darkness of invading imagination. At other times, grace alone at work neither allows imagination to hinder nor darkness to envelop the devout endeavour of a good will. Instead, suddenly, where he had not prepared himself, he finds himself in the affection of one praying; and if imaginations occur, they serve and assist rather than hinder. For every use of passing imaginations is not always useless or harmful to weaker eyes. By their quasi-bodily vehicle, the spirit of one praying or contemplating—accustomed through the very practice of seeing and thinking bodies and bodily things—is carried where truth is. And though it is in an image, the person nevertheless passes by means of that imagined image into the very truth that moves his affection.

For this reason the Holy Spirit, intending to hand down the Song of spiritual love to human beings, clothed its entire inward spiritual or divine matter outwardly in images of carnal love, so that love of the flesh, to be led and transferred into love of the Spirit, might quickly seize upon what resembles it, since only love fully apprehends divine things. Since true love, hungry for truth, cannot remain or rest long in images, it might more quickly pass by a familiar path into that which it imagined. And, though spiritual, a person might embrace the natural delights of carnal love, belonging to him through participation in flesh, when they have been taken captive by the Holy Spirit into the service of spiritual love.

Thus here one bursts forth rather boldly, as though from some hidden place, declaring neither what she is, whence she comes, nor what she speaks: “Let him kiss me,” she says, “with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1).

O Love, from whom every love receives its name, even carnal and degenerate love—holy and sanctifying Love, chaste and making chaste, life-giving Life—open to us your holy Song; reveal the mystery of your kiss and the veins of your whisper by which you enchant the hearts of your children with the power and delights of your sweetness. Teach us your hidden signals, by which you make yourself known to your partakers. In order that they may deserve to be capable of you, you first cleanse them from the defilements of those things with whose desire or delight you neither deign nor ought to dwell; for you are from above and draw upward, while all those things are downward.

Teach us to enter that place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the sound of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting: into that state of mind from which came this sound of one feasting—or rather, of one hungering more vehemently for the feast—“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

[Col. 0481D] For one may infer from the order of the following events and the form of the words that, as that Egyptian woman once came to Solomon, so the converted sinful soul came to Christ: received ceremonially as Bride, endowed liberally, and introduced into the storehouses where the royal riches were contained; nourished there from the Bridegroom’s breasts and suffused with the fragrance of ointments; with the Bridegroom’s name and the mystery of that name revealed to her. Then the Bridegroom, as though the fire of love had been kindled in the Bride’s heart, suddenly departed and went away; and with him departed every grace and glory of the storehouses. And, as is said of the Jews, by withdrawing the presence of his grace and the joy of his countenance, he went away and hid himself from her (John 8).

Nor should it be passed over that the treasuries of the riches or delights of our King are contained in storehouses; their use is substantial and effectual, and their enjoyment life-giving. They are eaten and give life, drunk and give gladness, nourishing and strengthening; every use and enjoyment of them enters into the substance of the one using or enjoying them. They are not like gold, silver, and things of that sort, whose whole use lies merely in being seen or possessed.

Some of these riches are stored in the storehouses; for others there is a place only in the wine-cellar. But the storehouses and the wine-cellar differ from one another by a very great interval—not of location, but of merit, grace, and dignity. For these are the things of which the prophet says: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge” (Isa. 33). The abundance of knowledge is designated by the storehouses; and they are named in the plural for this reason also, because, as another prophet says, “Times pass, and knowledge becomes manifold” (Dan. 12).

But for wisdom, which is designated by the wine-cellar, there is only one thing necessary. This knowledge is that of Christian piety: not puffing up, but building up in charity; a learned prudence in the understanding of the Scriptures and in matters of faith, morals, and life. This is the rational part in the human soul, the proper workshop of faith and hope, though not altogether devoid of charity; even though the wine-cellar is charity’s proper dwelling.

[Col. 0482B] For just as it is impossible to love God if he is not believed, so, if he is truly believed, hoped for, or known, it is altogether impossible that he should not be loved. The wine-cellar, however, is wisdom; it is also piety, by which the worship of God is signified, and the raising of the soul from low things to higher—not by thinking lofty thoughts, but by loving devoutly. That is, when the human spirit raises itself toward those things that are higher in spiritual matters, so that, insofar as it is permitted to mutable humanity, it may know the eternal immutability of God immutably and apprehend his immutable principles for judging mutable things.

Although these are above humanity, they are recognized as not altogether alien to the nature of human reason from the fact that even those who, by living wickedly, attempt to act against them sometimes discern and judge truly and justly only by them. For whatever human reason rightly does or feels derives its form or knowledge only from those principles by which all things consist and in which they stand, and the return of all things that are is toward them.

Just as it belongs to knowledge and faith to act or think concerning Christ according to the things that belong to his human dispensation, so it belongs to wisdom and love to know and contemplate in him the glory of divine majesty, or even in human affairs the power of his divine operation. In morals, moreover, what knowledge or reason is in action, wisdom is also in affection.

Knowledge gathers, but not for itself; like bees, it makes honey, but for another, because some outward use of the things gathered is granted to it, while their inward savour is reserved for another and elsewhere. The study of this knowledge requires the discipline of social life; but the perfection of wisdom requires solitary seclusion, or a heart solitary even amid a multitude.

But when introduced into the storehouses, the Bride learned much concerning the Bridegroom and much concerning herself. Whatever was bestowed on her at her first approach to the Bridegroom was a stimulus of love and the grace of one drawing her: the milk of the breasts, the fragrance of the ointments, the knowledge of the Bridegroom’s name, and the pouring forth of his ointment. Then a purgative process receives her, to be exercised and purified, but not utterly abandoned.

For when the Bridegroom has gone out and departed, wounded by charity, burning with desire for the absent one, moved by the sweetness of holy newness, renewed by a good taste, and suddenly left bereft and abandoned to herself, she now loathes the storehouses themselves as empty and deserted—knowledge, that is, which, with the Bridegroom absent, only adds sorrow, as it is written: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1). Accompanied by the young women whom she had in some measure had as companions in the grace of the storehouses, she runs out after the fragrance of the fleeing one. And from the heat of her desire, beginning the holy Song, she cries and says:

## CHAPTER ONE

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” “I have seen,” she says, “his countenance shining over me; I have conceived the joy of his face; I have felt grace poured out upon his lips. Let no one intervene; let nothing come between. Let him himself kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for now I can no longer bear or receive the spirit of another’s kiss. Everything else smells to me of something perverse; the Bridegroom’s kiss breathes something divine.”

A kiss is a friendly and outward joining of bodies, a sign and incentive of inward union. It is offered by the ministry of the mouth, so that not only bodies, but spirits also, may be united through mutual contact.

Christ the Bridegroom, however, extended to his Bride the Church, as it were, a kiss from heaven when the Word became flesh and drew so near to her as to unite himself with her—united himself so completely that God became man and man became God. He also offers and impresses that very kiss upon the faithful soul, his Bride, when, from the remembrance of common goods, he commends to her a private and personal joy and pours into her the grace of his love, drawing her spirit to himself and pouring his own Spirit into her, so that they may mutually be one spirit.

[Col. 0483C] Having received in part this kiss of the departing Bridegroom in the storehouses, the Bride had been inflamed toward its perfection and full sweetness. Of this the Lord, praying to the Father for his disciples, says: “Father, I will that, as you and I are one, they also may be one in us” (John 17), “that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

What else does this mean than that she who had received from his fullness and “grace for grace” (John 1)—that is, the grace of love for the grace of faith—now desired the fullness itself: the fullness of the Holy Spirit, who is the unity and love of Father and Son, and full joy in him, which no one may take from her? She wished to be dissolved and to be with Christ, judging, after tasting the highest good, that it was no longer necessary for her to remain in the flesh (Phil. 1).

Let those who have not learned, learn. Let them turn to see; let them become eager to experience how these things are enacted in the conduct or conscience of those who, turned toward the Lord, walk in newness of life. Their affection and their entire life are shared between sorrow itself and this joy: sorrow at the Bridegroom’s absence, joy at his presence. Their sole expectation is everlasting joy from his vision.

For among them this does not happen once, or in one manner, but often and in many and various ways. All the labour of this holy exercise in the heart of one loving, or in the life of one making progress, is not the work of a single day, but of much time: manifold and varied according to the devotion of differing affections and the outcome of advances.

[Col. 0484A] As long as you say to the Bride, “I go and I come” (John 14), and do not remain with her eternally, O Bridegroom of chaste souls, so long, O Father of orphans, you allow your children, exiled in a land not their own, by the provident counsel of your wisdom, sometimes to be afflicted in the pain of their desire as though shut outside from you, and to waste away with love for your love. You cleanse them in the furnace of their poverty, drawing them more strongly to yourself by the very difficulty of receiving you.

At other times, from the sweetness of your grace, you freely open yourself to your little ones and do not repel those who come even to you. You allow them to lie down and weep in your bosom, where those who weep do not wish to be comforted so that they may cease weeping to you; for they regard it as the greatest gift that they weep to you, because they count it best and sweetest to weep before you, the Lord their God who made them. And in order that they may weep to you, you make them able to do this very thing.

When you deign to wipe away their flowing tears, the tears flow still more; because the very hand that wipes them becomes the cause of a certain sweet pain that moves and caresses them, and, in proportion as they grieve more intensely, consoles them more intensely through the consciousness of good hope.

For that rushing stream which makes glad plainly declares your presence to be near; and the sojourning of your children in a foreign land cannot forget its pilgrimage. While that joy and that sorrow are found together, they cause those sweet and delightful tears to flow: tears because of sorrow; sweet because of love—and of your love, O Love.
