To grieve for you is great joy; to weep for you is great consolation; to rejoice in you is supreme blessedness.

The whole course of this Song, both in words and in actions, contains this sweetness of one consoled and grieving, drawn and running, addressed and answering, caressed and loving. It takes place continually in the conscience and heart of the Bride, whoever she may be, pouring out her soul before the Lord her God and hearing with joy what the Lord God speaks within her.

[Col. 0484D] The conversation of Bridegroom and Bride is the testimony and devotion of a well-disposed conscience: when the Bridegroom bears witness in the Bride’s conscience to his own merit, and the Bride’s grateful devotion returns to the Bridegroom the due affection of piety.

Accordingly, the Bride, having gone out from the King’s storehouses, into which she had been brought to contemplate the Bridegroom’s loveliness, and from the taste and delightful experience of his good things, now desiring only that beloved one whom his loveliness commends, having received the pledge of the Spirit, languishes for the salvation of God. “I am weary,” she says, “of these empty storehouses in the Bridegroom’s absence: of these daily promises [Col. 0485A], these veiled sacraments, these parables and proverbs, this mirror and enigma. I desire the mystery of the kingdom of God; I ask that the Father be openly made known to me: face to face, eye to eye, kiss to kiss: ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.’ Why, however, ‘let him kiss,’ as though he were absent, rather than ‘kiss me’? It seems that in the storehouses she has striven greatly to see him face to face, and to behold and know him as he is, just as she herself is known by him: this is the kiss of perfection. But through the ministries of prophets, apostles, and other teachers, through knowledge of the Scriptures, the Bridegroom has offered her, as it were, various kisses of his grace; and, as though she had been satisfied, [Note: [Col. 0485D] That is, as though satisfaction had been given to her.] has withdrawn and departed. She, however, now complains as though he were absent [Col. 0485B], and impatiently cries after him, saying: ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.’ As though she said: How long will you add sorrow to me through the borrowed kisses of knowledge? Even if I do not deserve that kiss of perfection, let him at least grant me some kiss of his mouth before he departs from me. A transmitted kiss is indeed good, but, transferred from vessel to vessel, it does not seem to retain the full power of its grace. What his minister conveys becomes known; but what the spirit of his mouth or kiss inspires is savored—and it will then be savored fully, when joy itself is full in him.

Then, pursuing with her gaze as best she can the one who is leaving, and sweetly speaking to him though he now no longer hears, she says: ‘For your breasts are better than wine.’ As though asked whence came such hasty [Col. 0485C] boldness, such confident demand for a kiss, she says: “From the breasts, Lord, of your consolation” (Isa. 66), “for your breasts are better than wine.” They are sweeter to suck, more powerful to gladden, easier to intoxicate. I have been nourished by them so as to desire the kiss, intoxicated by them so as to dare to ask it. For as long as we live here, as long as we labor here, whatever gifts of charisms, whatever kinds of consolations are granted to the children of grace—in the distribution of graces, in the growth of progress or advance in virtues, in the splendors of divine illumination, in the affections of devout compunction, in the raptures of divine contemplation—these, O eternal Wisdom, are your breasts, nourishing the holy infancy of your little ones and testifying that your presence does not fail them until the consummation of the age.

But far be it that, in its own time, in the time of your good pleasure, their mouths should be judged unworthy to kiss your mouth in the fullness of your perfect knowledge—those to whom, in the time of patience and endurance, you offer your breast through these intermediary breasts, to be suckled for the nourishment of spiritual knowledge and progress toward perfection! For even if they have sometimes sucked some poison from elsewhere, they must be healed and cleansed by contact with these sacred breasts, and with the power and fragrance of your health-giving ointments.

Therefore, when the Bride fails, owing to the condition of human weakness, to attain that everlasting and blessed union and [Col. 0486A] kiss of eternity, she directs herself to these things; unable to reach your mouth, she turns her own mouth back toward your breasts and rests in them, saying, “For your breasts are better than wine.” Note also that, in her request for the kiss, she directed the highest reach of human capacity in prayer toward that light of God’s countenance; but, rebuffed by the brightness of that charity, she at once turns back toward more common things and exercises herself in them, saying: “For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments. Your name is oil poured out.” “As soon as I came to you,” she says, “you uncovered for me the breasts of your sweetness, the first nourishment of your grace; and from the sweetness of your delight and the good of conscience, they are better than every [Col. 0486B] wine of worldly wisdom or joy of fleshly pleasure, fragrant with the finest ointments, the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit.

“For when these gifts themselves came into me, in their proper order and through your working, first your fear seized me, urgently drawing me toward you with severity” (Job 28). “In second place came piety, gently receiving me into you. Since, as it is written, this is your worship—for Job says that piety is the worship of God—when it taught me to worship you, it taught me to say in the Holy Spirit, ‘Jesus is Lord’” (1 Cor. 12). “And immediately, for the fragrance of sweetness and the power of healing, the oil of your very name was poured out by you and infused into me, softening all my hardness, smoothing roughness, healing weakness. The yoke of my ancient captivity decayed away before the oil of this name; but your yoke, Lord, [Col. 0486C] became sweet to me, and your burden light. For when I heard your name—whether Lord, Jesus, or Christ—at once joy and gladness were given to my hearing” (Ps. 50). “For as soon as the name sounds in the ear, the mystery of the name shines also in the heart, and love in the affection, prompting devoted service toward the Lord; mercy and love toward the Savior, which is the meaning of Jesus; obedience and fear toward Christ the King.

“Rightly, Lord Jesus, at every one of your names every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2), “because you are named by no name except in some relation to us; nor is there any relation expressed by any one of your names which is not a bestowal upon us of some good belonging to you. For as Lord you rule by doing good; as Jesus you save; as Christ—that is, the Anointed—you rule as king or make propitiation as priest. Indeed, that relation of Son to Father, by which you were predestined and made Son of God in power, is known to those who have learned to cry in the Holy Spirit, ‘Abba, Father’; and who thereby understand that they have been made sons of God and your brothers. They know what an outpouring of oil has been made for us, and how great it is: you redeemed us for this very end, O good Brother—whereas, unless you redeemed, neither human being nor angel nor any creature would redeem. For when the only-begotten Son came, you did not will to remain alone; rather, you brought many sons into glory, whom you are not ashamed to call brothers, saying: ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers’” (Heb. 2).

[Col. 0487A] “Therefore,” says the Bride, “because of the sweetness of your breasts, because of the healing power of your name and oil, ‘the young maidens also loved you’ with me”: fresh plantings in your service, young souls renewed in the spirit of their minds, walking in newness of spirit, setting ascents in their hearts, going from strength to strength, advancing from glory to glory as from the Spirit of the Lord. Each says, “Draw me after you”; together they say, “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments.” For advancing young maidens, the fragrance of the ointments is the Bridegroom’s sweet renown for virtues; drawing is charity’s summons. But the anointing that teaches concerning all things remains with the Bride. There is, however, a great distance between that fragrance and this anointing. Yet, excluded from the storehouses [Col. 0487B] and deserted by the Bridegroom, she is now almost of equal condition with the young maidens, since she is fed only by the Bridegroom’s fragrance. Hence she too seems to say with them, “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments.”

She who is drawn runs because she is willingly summoned; and when grace breathes upon her the power of anointing through the fragrance, there is no delay or difficulty in the course of spiritual progress. She pursues the fugitive by confession and commemoration of his benefits—namely, his breasts and ointments, fragrance and poured-out oil—because grateful recollection of past benefits is an excellent and reasonable kind of prayer, pleasing to God and effective for obtaining benefits to come. Then the Bride says: “Draw me after you; we will run after the fragrance of your ointments.” See now one weary, failing, and in need to be drawn; except that his fragrance, though she no longer sees him, still draws her and makes her run. Hence she says, “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments.” As though she said: Even if for the present I do not deserve the joy of your countenance or the kiss of your mouth, at least do not withdraw from me the fragrance of your ointments.

For the Bridegroom’s presence is a well-disposed remembrance of him, a mind illumined in the light of his countenance, and the anointing of the Holy Spirit teaching concerning all things. The fragrance of the ointments when he departs is a certain lingering awareness in memory of departing sweetness, and, in the remnants of thought, a joyous recollection of consolation once received. “We will run, therefore,” she says, “after the fragrance of your ointments”: while it endures and draws [Col. 0487D] us, we endure in running; when it fails, we too must fail.

For this reason, recalling benefits received, she adds: “The King brought me into his storehouses.” First, she delights to call him King, by whom she desires to be ruled, just as she says in the Holy Spirit, “Jesus is Lord” (1 Cor. 12)—the one whom she delights to serve, while the sound of the spoken word declares the mind and will. Then, conceiving a more abundant hope from this very fact, growing warmer with greater love for him who has departed through hope itself, and, as it were, turning her eyes again after the departing one, she says: “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts,” by whose milk I was nourished, anointed with ointments, strengthened by fragrance. See her striving; [Col. 0488A] see her anxiety. Now she speaks to him, now about him. One way toward what is loved does not suffice for a lover. Thus, still more earnestly sighing toward contemplation of the now absent one, she says: “The upright love you.”

All animals are naturally bent toward the belly and the ground. The human being alone is raised upright toward heaven in bodily form, nature thereby showing that he has something in common with heavenly beings. “The upright,” therefore, she says, “love you”—that is, human beings; for whoever is not upright by loving you is not a human being but a beast. These three things, brought forth from the King’s storehouses, must be considered and distinguished, and are not fit to be concealed: remembrance of favors received, hope of things to come, and, for both these reasons, the uprightness of love in thanksgiving. “We shall exult,” she says, “and [Col. 0488B] rejoice in you”: this concerns the future. Of the past she says: “remembering your breasts.” The third is: “The upright love you.” By memory of past things we cling to the Lord our God; hope for the future restrains us from wishing to depart from him; upright love confirms us so that we cannot do so.

That when the Bridegroom departs she remembers the storehouses admonishes the Bridegroom’s children, when the grace of spiritual consolation is withdrawn from them, to take refuge in the consolation of the Scriptures. For just as she who is the Bride, when her mind passes beyond itself to God and, following the Lamb wherever he goes, gives her whole self in affection, so, when she returns soberly to herself, she ought to gather her whole self into understanding and feed her resting mind with the fruit of spiritual knowledge. She must return to the memory of the storehouses and breasts—that is, as has been said, take refuge in the consolation of the Scriptures—where the two Testaments are for her the Bridegroom’s two breasts, from which is sucked the milk of all the mysteries enacted in time for our eternal salvation, so that one may arrive at the food which is the Word of God, God with God.

For humble Christ is our milk, just as God, equal to God, is our food. Milk nourishes; food sustains. These breasts are sucked in the storehouses, because those mysteries are understood in the Scriptures. The Bride sucked the breasts when she first understood; she remembers the breasts when she meditates on what she has understood. There, her exultation is suited to her body and her joy to her mind: when incorruption from incorruption is promised to the body, but the vision of God to the mind, and her uprightness is ordered in the love [Col. 0488D] of God.

But as night must follow when the sun departs, so, when the Bridegroom departs and delays, the Bride begins to lose her former beauty and to grow dark in herself; all her works are deprived of their grace, so that there is no longer her former color in the heart or color in the work. For just as this outward light is, as it were, queen of all colors, without which they have neither beauty nor power, so illuminating grace is the power of all virtues and the light of good works. Without it, neither virtues can have their effects nor good works their fruits. Or, if they seem somehow to have them, they do not flourish, do not gladden, do not possess the oil of joy, the anointing that teaches, the taste of divine sweetness, the fragrance of eternity, or an effective [Col. 0489A] experience of spiritual perceptions.

Thus, ashamed of herself but fearing for those to whom she had been an example and an object of admiration, she says: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem; like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon”—things that seem to have more usefulness than beauty. As though she said: “My form is indeed whole, though my color has changed, because ‘the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’” (Matt. 26): faith is stable, but understanding darkened; the will is the same, but affection weakened. She confesses herself black because of the darkness of a troubled conscience, though she does not deny herself beautiful through the uprightness of faith. Having been nourished in the King’s storehouses, she knows that it belongs not to humility but to impiety to deny faith. For, just as it is deadly not to possess faith, hope, and good will, so it is culpable to deny them when possessed. The Bride always finds herself beautiful according to the right form of faith, purity of intention, and devotion of will, as long as she does not cease to be the Bride and never denies it; although she sometimes humbly confesses her blackness from consciousness of past sins, assaults of vices, or the blindness of human ignorance.

“Like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.” By Kedar, which is interpreted “darkness,” he means the darkness of conscience or of reason obscured; but by tents, or the skins of tents that are carried about, the instability of mind—how much these hinder contemplation of the inner light [Col. 0489C] is clear. Yet they are then Solomon’s—that is, the true Peaceful One’s—when they serve the warfare of the brethren or the peace of the Church. Nevertheless, devout charity always takes care lest its unwary humility injure anyone, lest confession of its guilt or weakness become an example or an occasion for a brother’s downfall. Therefore she adds: “Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.” I am not so dark that I am blind, as though I had no eyes of reason; but the Sun of righteousness has withdrawn from me the light of his grace. Without it every eye opens in vain, no color flourishes, every color grows cold. “I was,” she says, “a coal that laid waste; now I am laid waste. I glowed as long as I was in the fire, warming [Col. 0489D] and illumining; when the fire withdrew, I grew black. Yet I always offer you my form whole for imitation, although discolored; for though the beauty of love has departed from me, its substance remains.”

“Therefore do not wonder that, in the Bridegroom’s absence, I have become public prey. For ‘the sons of my mother fought against me.’ How? ‘They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.’ It is customary in Scripture for wine to signify joy, which gladdens the human heart. As the vine is the mother of wine, so worldly peace is the mother of worldly joy; spiritual peace, however, is the mother of spiritual joy. Thus whether the sons of my mother—namely, the original concupiscences of human nature—fighting against me, made me wish to preside over human beings; or whether the sons of my mother, the Church, took me away from myself and set me over them, and for fostering the joys of their flesh appointed me guardian of their outward peace—when I watch over it too attentively, I become negligent of my inward joys by neglecting my inward peace. Thus the sun discolored me: the concern of brotherly charity, through the obscuring haze of its occupations, darkened for me the appearance of inward purity.”

It must be understood that while the Bride is being guided and taught, and trained by various temptations, she has also entered upon the necessity of prelation. In it, divided among many things, she does not suffice for each; and while she watches more anxiously over the progress of others, she fails in her own; and over her private losses she is troubled in her conscience. See her abandoned to herself, wavering and tossed about. [Col. 0490B] She wishes to pray but does not suffice; she meditates with herself and fails. She speaks to the present as though absent, and to the absent as though present. Yet, as one nourished in royal storehouses, she does not neglect the Apostle’s counsel: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5). In the tribulations of her temptations she is not ashamed of the strength of confession, since she does not hesitate to disclose to her companions the hidden losses of conscience, saying: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” Hence after confession she returns more ardently to prayer, saying:

“Tell me, O you whom my soul loves, where you feed your flock, where you lie down at noon.” And see the most evident grace. When after confession she comes to prayer, she at once deserves to find the Bridegroom whom she seeks [Col. 0490C]; drawing him into her heart with the whole embrace of charity and, as it were, offering him her mouth for a kiss, she says: “O you whom my soul loves.” In the historical sense, indeed, the Bridegroom offered himself to the lover and seeker, but still as though turning away and shaking himself free from her, testing her in the hidden place of the storm, in the kiss of contradiction. Attacking him with burning love, she says: “O you whom my soul loves.”

First, this plainly shows that the Holy Spirit is already helping the weakness of the one praying, because the Holy Spirit is love itself, of which the Bride says, “O you whom my soul loves.” “Whom my soul loves,” she says. For nearly the whole human being is soul; the body is the smallest part of him. Therefore, when the soul of your Bride loves you, Lord Jesus, disregarding and as it were already casting off the body, she wholly follows you, desiring to be put to death all day long for your sake and loving to lose herself in this world, so that in eternal life she may possess herself in you. Certainly one must not doubt that the face of your beauty has at some time shone upon one who loves you thus, somewhat breathed upon by the spirit of your mouth; who thus sighs for you; who has experienced the sweetness of your embraces and is so familiarly dissolved in you.

For one loves you only from you, since you are that very love by which one loves you; and one loves you in oneself so greatly that one loves oneself in nothing except in you. For if beauty is loved, you are the beauty of all that is beautiful; if goodness, you are the good of every good; if usefulness, every person makes use of you, even one who hates you, while everyone who loves you enjoys you. Therefore she says: “Tell [Col. 0491A] me, O you whom my soul loves, where you feed your flock, where you lie down at noon.”

Notice to what the power and humility of confession advance the Bride: namely, to lying in Jesus’ bosom, where once lay that beloved disciple, receiving from it: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” “Tell me,” she says. “Tell me inwardly, in my heart, so that I may feel it within myself by the perception of most certain experience. Inspire me, that I may know by the experience of a conscience enjoying you: by what manner of life, by what state of soul, by what disposition of mind, by what gift of grace, in the affection of the person whom you make worthy—you who have mercy on whom you have mercy, for it is not of one who wills or runs, but of you who show mercy—you feed the loving understanding from the knowledge of your truth and the abundance of your sweetness, and dedicate that person’s memory to yourself, in which you may lie continually and delightfully; you yourself being to that person both the noonday heat of burning love and its refreshment.”

“The splendor of noonday light and its shade.” Or she asks that the end of her trial in tribulation be made known to her, so that she may know what is lacking to her. And, for consolation amid her changeableness, she prays that the day of eternity be revealed to her—not one that begins in morning and ends in evening, but one that ever remains at the noon of heat and light, wisdom and understanding, love and blessed enjoyment. There the Sabbath-rest is given to the people of God, so that they may lie down and rest from their works as God from his; there, in [Col. 0491C] eternal blessedness, he feeds from himself the company both of angels and of holy human beings, ever full because of the perfection of blessedness and ever desiring to look upon him because of the piety and sweetness of love.

Or: “O you whom my soul loves, tell my loving soul, through grace inspiring and experience inspired, what is that state of mind, what sweetness belongs to the one who perceives, what joy to the one who enjoys, when that very form is disclosed to faith that loves you—so far as faith can love, and as much as can be disclosed in this mortal life.” Then there comes to pass in the lover what you once said of him: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14). For when by loving thus a person has at some time gathered for himself the merit of somewhat worthier grace, the loving person begins also to be loved. Hence the Bride begins to experience more abundantly and sweetly, through the enlightened perception of love, the friendly sweetnesses of the Bridegroom’s love for her; and there comes to pass in her what the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

For she now begins to know as she was previously known, and, insofar as she knows herself to be loved, to love as she was previously loved. The Bridegroom’s prior knowing of the Bride was the gift of divine wisdom; his prior love was the free infusion of the Holy Spirit. But the Bride’s knowledge of the Bridegroom and her love are the same thing, because in this matter love itself is understanding. When this is brought about in the Bride’s heart, with more abundant grace, for an hour or a time, that is what the anxious Bride seeks so intensely in this life: [Col. 0492A] the Bridegroom’s noonday reclining—noonday light in knowledge, noonday ardor in love. As love returns to the place from which it comes, the Bridegroom both feeds and is fed. For this word “feeds” bears both meanings.

Or, she says: “If you judge me unworthy of your kiss, or your Word, or the Spirit of your mouth, at least show me one of your people in whom I may find not a morning and novice ardor, nor an evening and slackened one, but the noonday, steadfast, and luminous ardor of your love; one in whose heart you lie and rest, and from whom you may feed me when he teaches me what he has learned from you.” Or the Bride desires to be affected by the Bridegroom and fails; she wishes to gladden her heart in the light of his countenance and grows dark within herself. Since she cannot inwardly compose herself for the affection she desires, having no peace within herself, she longs to go out of herself into some outward action of that same affection, in which the good conscience of one loving may find the Bridegroom either feeding her or reclining with her. She who said, “Tell me, O you whom my soul loves, where you lie down, where you feed at noon,” desired one or all of these things.

“Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” She does not yet wander, but fears wandering. She still loves no one except the Bridegroom; for if she loved another, she would not be the Bride. For, as regards the soul, wherever we are moved, we are moved by love; therefore one who loves one thing is not moved about, does not wander. And one who travels by a single and straight [Col. 0492C] road toward the destination one desires does not wander or go astray, but sometime reaches the end. But for one leaving the road, the open field of error lies before him, and it has no end. Error is approving false things as true.

She is indeed still tossed in her thoughts, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon, which are customarily carried about; and she is assailed by her own desires, as she says: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” But while she still stands in her own place, love’s judgment is not moved; rather, she asks to be enlightened and desires to be strengthened. “I love,” she says—or rather, “I desire”—because, with the mind’s eye troubled by the pressure of desire and the phantasms of various thoughts, I do not see whom I love; with reason lulled to sleep, I do not understand what I desire. Thus I too waver and become unstable in my love, not by abandoning him, but by going out toward its end through diverse ways; and in this too I become unstable, not by unwillingness and willingness, but by seeking for myself a shorter and more suitable road to that which I steadily and singly will.

For I always have the same will; but until good will becomes a good mind, I always desire, though I do not always seem to myself to love, insofar as, as has been said, that which I desire is not always present to me in affection. For the love of one who desires is different from that of one who enjoys. The love of desire burns even in darkness, but does not shine; the love of enjoyment is wholly in light, because enjoyment itself is the lover’s light. Why say more? The Bride who longs to see God desires a pure heart, [Col. 0493A] a pure conscience, pure perception, pure understanding—everything pure. For fire, sword, or any danger cannot disturb the power of love; but enjoyment of its delights requires peace of heart and serenity of mind, “lest,” she says, “I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

Those who do not go astray know what great flocks error has made for itself in the world: people choosing death for life, embracing misery for blessedness, neglecting God, loving themselves, walking the beaten paths of this age, going in herds to hell, and leaving their tracks behind for many human beings and many peoples. For the prince of spiritual wickedness draws them after him; he works in the children of unbelief and, making himself the Bridegroom’s companion, said: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). He is the prince of this world and seems to divide the world or age with the Bridegroom as though on equal terms; yet he is found to make for himself far more numerous and densely packed flocks of those who wander.

But even in the heart of one who has already deserved to become the Bride, when the mind’s gaze fails in its search for the one truth, a manifold variety of thoughts at once takes its place. A soul divided among these begins to wander through so many paths of error and is drawn away from itself by as many phantasms of thought as dissipate it from the uprightness of its intention toward the good. Indeed, those diverse thoughts form from themselves great and varied flocks, and make themselves, as it were, companions of the Bridegroom when, sharing the Bride’s mind between themselves and him, they compel it in their turns and at their times to serve them.

[Col. 0493C] It follows: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and go after the tracks of the flocks.” As though he said: “What you ask me to tell you, you do not fail to know; rather, you do not know yourself. Therefore you seem to yourself not to know me, because you do not know yourself. You do not know yourself because you have gone out from yourself.” But first the loving endearments on both sides must be noted. The Bride says: “O you whom my soul loves.” The Bridegroom, however: “O beautiful among women, O my friend.” Wherever these reciprocal names of love and praise seem to sound in the fervor of intention and truth of conscience, they are not signs of one deserted or deserting.

Blessed is the conscience which, whatever it encounters or whatever befalls it, always says in the same spirit, “Jesus is Lord,” and confesses with the same piety, “O you whom my soul loves”; whose faith, whatever happens, suffers no loss in the beauty or praise of its truth. “Beautiful,” he says, “among women”: strong among the soft—for *mulier* (“woman”) is said to derive from softness; a virgin among pregnant women, to whom the Lord pronounces woe when he says: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Mark 13; Luke 21).

“Beautiful,” he says, because lovely; and lovely insofar as, through grace shaping you in this respect, your soul loves me—though somewhat black insofar as you are deprived of illuminating grace. “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out.” This mention of beauty may also be seen as a reproach for neglected beauty; likewise, when he says “go out,” it is not a friend’s counsel but, as it were, an angry permission. “If you do not know yourself, go out”—that is, you go out from yourself because you do not know yourself. But know yourself, because you are my image; thus you will be able to know me, whose image you are, and you will find me within yourself. In your mind, if you are with me, there I shall lie down with you, and from there I shall feed you.

Seek God, therefore, in simplicity; think of him in goodness; strive to keep him continually in memory; understand by loving and love by understanding. In the perception of his goodness you will receive a perception of his eternity, the manner of life, the condition of a good mind. “If you do not know yourself, go out.” “Where shall I go out, Lord? Whoever first finds me when I have gone out or been driven from your presence, as Cain was, will kill me” (Gen. 4). “Go out and go.” As though he said: “Go away from me, from my [Col. 0494B] likeness, to the place of unlikeness; and go out from yourself into the bypaths of desire or curiosity. Go, therefore,” he says, “and feed your kids,” which are assigned to the left hand—your wanton impulses, namely, among things outside yourself. “Go after the tracks of the flocks” of the perishing multitude, grazing in the pastures of self-feeders, self-lovers, around the tents of those whose tents are in generation after generation, who, as the Psalmist says, “called their names in their lands” (Ps. 48), and do not have them written in heaven.

But not so, O Bride of Christ. Rather, know yourself; be present to yourself, so as to discern yourself. If you wish the King, the Lord your God, to desire your beauty, then as you draw near him forget your people and your father’s house: the bodies to which you have become accustomed through bodily senses; their delights, to which you have clung through love; their images, which you have more deeply impressed upon memory through the desire of enjoyment. For through these you have gone out from yourself and departed from yourself in affection toward the tracks of your intentions, so impressing them on memory that even when bodies are absent, their images are not absent; when actions cease, their affections do not cease; when voices are silent, their meanings resound. Purify yourself; train yourself in piety, and within yourself you shall find the kingdom of God.

O image of God, recognize your dignity; let the likeness of your Maker shine again in you. You are of little value to yourself, but you are a precious thing. To the degree that you have fallen away from him whose image you are, you have been infected by alien images. But when you begin to breathe again toward that for which you were created, if you firmly lay hold of discipline, you will quickly shake off and escape the added cosmetics of adulterous images, which do not adhere firmly enough. Therefore be wholly present to yourself, and employ your whole self in knowing yourself and whose image you are; in discerning and understanding what you are and what you can do in him whose image you are. Stand in your rank, lest you fall or degenerate.

The strength of your standing is knowledge of grace—if you are not ungrateful that you were foreknown, predestined, pre-elected, and known. God’s foreknowledge concerning you is his goodness toward you; predestination is goodness already at work; election is the work itself; knowledge is the seal of grace, of which the Apostle says: “The foundation of God stands firm, having this seal: The Lord knows [Col. 0495A] those who are his” (2 Tim. 2). If you know, know that you have been foreknown; if you choose, know that you have been chosen; if you believe, you were created for this; if you love, you were formed for this.

And when the Bridegroom makes you thus, he lies down in you; when he affects you thus, you recline with him, and he feeds you. There experience teaches you of noonday light and ardor: when light is seen in God’s light; when the Holy Spirit bears witness to the human conscience, from the greatness and purity of love, that the human being is a child of God. “For no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom he wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11). Only the light of God’s countenance teaches this; the perception of life reveals it from the Spirit of life; grace for grace; great enjoyment of the highest good as the reward of great desire.

Nor does the soul ever know itself—what it is and what it can do—except when it finds itself in these things; nor does it wish to go out from itself in any respect while it is granted to enjoy itself in them. Blessed and happy is the man who has this glory and the riches of this grace in the house of his heart, in the treasury of his conscience. His heart is established; he shall not be moved—that is, he will not go out to alien things through desire or curious activity—rich at home, possessing peace and piety with sufficiency in a good conscience.

These riches belong to the poor in spirit: those who seek God in simplicity of heart, steadily do what is commanded, await with strong faith what is promised, already taste in the certainty of hope what they await, and therefore think of him in goodness; who are not high-minded but consent to the lowly, do not reject the Lord’s yoke, [Col. 0495C] and do not kick against the goad of his discipline. Far from this are the spirit of this world, its trifling, tale-bearing wisdom, the proud understanding of the Assyrians, and showy eloquence.

They are your cavalry, O you who rule Israel: not horses of pride and chariots of vanity, but, in the name of the Lord, the swiftness of the Spirit running forth and the strength of your love. For knowing that through you they have been rescued from the destroyer—which is the meaning of the name Pharaoh—and from the region of darkness, which is Egypt, through the shedding of blood and the sacrament of the paschal lamb, the Hebrews, that is, the “passers-over,” celebrate the *phase*, the “Passover of the Lord,” in haste: passing from vices to virtues, from temporal things to eternal, from earth to heaven, [Col. 0495D] from themselves to God; their pursuing sins and vices drowned in waters made red by the blood of the Lamb. In adversity, as though in the terror of night, they have light—the fire and strength of the Holy Spirit, like a pillar of fire; but in prosperity, as though in daylight, they have over them like a cloud the sheltering power of the Most High. Therefore he continues and says: “I have likened you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.”

Nor should it be passed over that at first he calls her beautiful among women, but afterwards his beloved; thereby making this point comprehensive: the measure of friendship is to correspond to the degree of beauty. Moreover, in saying, “I have likened you to my cavalry, my beloved,” the compassionate wisdom of the Bridegroom further seeks to call back to himself the Bride who is going out from him; and, where she seems to herself especially wise, reproves her for still greater folly, declaring to her the danger to her life and injury to her love. She desires its riches alone and avoids its exercise.

For this negligence of mind commonly entangles the tender, unwary souls of beginners and hinders them from the goal of perfection. Once they have begun even slightly to taste new sweetnesses of contemplation and more delightful experiences, they immediately suppose themselves to have escaped every necessity of contending with the vices of flesh and soul. And while they dream only of the delights of virtues, which naturally delight in themselves, they neglect their firm and sure possession by avoiding the exercises necessary to them. Trusting in the sweetness they have tasted—which belongs rather to God who shows mercy than to one who wills [Col. 0496A] or runs—they disregard the grave perils which wage war within them, from themselves and concerning themselves. Therefore, after the way of purity has been made known and the door of contemplative liberty opened, he adds and says: “I have likened you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” Though you are beloved—however greatly beloved—yet know that you still must ride, run, labour, and fight; and nevertheless you are no less beloved. You must indeed beware the vice of curiosity and the worldly or carnal desire which always accompanies it. Yet neither activity required for your own sake nor necessity arising from love for the brethren is to be refused. It follows:

“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” The Bride’s cheeks, and her face always unveiled before the Bridegroom, are a holy [Col. 0496C] conscience; the blush upon her face is affectionate repentance and reverent awe before one who reproves. For as long as the faithful soul labours amid temptations, it does not know what is being done within itself; often, while unaware, it advances, and is approved when it supposes itself rejected. For, being afflicted, it is humbled; being humbled, it is purified. And while assumed humility casts it down beneath itself amid a multitude of sorrows, that holy simplicity of which it is written, “Seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1), is fashioned—not by the soul, yet in the soul.

And when it judges itself worthy of rebuke and affliction, a devout conscience puts on, before its reprover, a certain holy and pleasing countenance of shame; through this, corrected from the boldness of its former confidence, it deserves to hear: [Col. 0496D] “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” Observe how, in that very moment—as if during a critical onset of temptation—the remedy of divine consolation is suddenly present; and according to the multitude of sorrows in her heart, the consolations of the Lord are present to make her soul glad.

For just as, in the time of estrangement, a mind inclined to the flesh and flesh inclined to sin formed in her the face of a vulture, so, in the hour of grace visiting her, a mind inclined to God and flesh inclined to the mind form in her the face of a turtledove, displaying humility, chastity, and the grace of holy simplicity. For just as conscience itself is the truest interpreter to itself of grace affecting it, so the outward face is commonly a witness before others of a well-disposed conscience; indeed, shame appearing in the face is commonly an indication of some good hidden in the heart.

For when the soul sees something which it judges either unworthy to be seen by it or itself unworthy to see, it withdraws inward, as physicians say, covered by the natural veil of blood. In the very moment of shame this blood seems to redden in the face, testifying to inward modesty: either its hatred of the disgrace presented to it, or its humility and reverence before an honour presented to it. And the Bride is quite suitably compared to a turtledove, since, grieving the loss of her mate and seeking no other, she consoles herself by lamentation alone.

Now, having been proved and found worthy, she is more generously raised by the Bridegroom’s praises through illuminating grace; that is, she is enriched by gifts worthy of the Bridegroom’s praise. Therefore he adds and says: “Your neck is like necklaces.” The Bride’s neck [Col. 0497B] is her holy intention, by which the whole body of action is joined to its head, which is Christ. Of this our Head himself says: “If your eye—that is, the intention of your work—be single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6). As necklaces are ornaments of the neck, so the marks of holy virtues belong to good intention. But the Bride’s neck is like necklaces because, although necklaces adorn a neck, conversely the Bride’s neck adorns all her virtues. Unless these depend upon a right intention, they are shown to possess neither their own grace nor beauty, nor even the name of virtues. Or the ornament of the Bride’s neck is love of the Bridegroom, without which every intention is foul and perverse. But when intention passes into affection, the Bride’s neck becomes like its necklace.

[Col. 0497C] Then, as if placing his own ornaments upon her: “We shall make,” he says, “for you golden little chains, inlaid with silver.” Gold signifies wisdom, because, as the Apostle says, “Christ was made wisdom for us” (1 Cor. 1): either in the time when he was made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man, and his weakness appeared stronger and his foolishness wiser than all men; or from the time when we began to cling to him, so that we might be wise in him. He therefore places golden ornaments upon the Bride’s neck when he adds the grace of wisdom to her holy intention, so that she may strive not only ardently but wisely.

They are inlaid with silver when, having received the grace of clear and resonant preaching in order to proclaim the Bridegroom’s glory, she orders her words with judgment. Little chains signify, as silver signifies the brilliance of eloquence, so also, in good works, the long-suffering of perseverance; their roundness signifies perfection. But why are they inlaid? So that eloquence, warned by the image of worms, may avoid the vice of boastfulness. For just as every material of wood or fruit has its own worm, as if a natural enemy of its soundness, so every virtue or good disposition of mind has some corresponding enemy among the vices. Hence it is written: “Pride is the worm of riches.” As pride is the particular worm of riches, so boastfulness is that of eloquence; unless guarded against, whatever virtue or usefulness it seems to possess must necessarily be corrupted.

Whether it is length [Col. 0498A] or roundness, all is founded in the substance of gold; for no perseverance in good, no perfection, no beauty or usefulness is made firm except in wisdom—that is, in love of God and spiritual understanding. But he says, “We shall make.” Who, or who are they? Certainly those of whom he said concerning his beloved: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14): namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, God the Father, and the Holy Spirit. Or: “I,” he says, “shall make them, with an angel serving me in this ministry.”

For angelic compassion rejoices with the good of human beings, and angels love to serve in the ministries of their salvation; they are always at hand in the holy and religious pursuits of those persons, though they do not always appear. Hence, when they are sometimes suddenly seen by someone, they are said to “appear,” a word properly used of something present but hidden, which suddenly makes itself visible. For the spiritual power of angels possesses a certain natural capacity to suggest or insinuate something both to one another and to human spirits. Of this the Prophet says: “The angel who spoke in me went out” (Zech. 2), and: “One angel said to another angel: Run and announce it to this boy” (ibid.).

The Apostle seems to call their hidden promptings—by which they insinuate what is to be suggested, whether good angels toward good by God’s will or evil angels toward evil by God’s permission—“tongues of angels,” where he says: “If I speak in the tongues of angels but have not love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Thus the angels of God are always present with the holy endeavours of those making progress, both exhorting and cooperating; and they rejoice all the more devoutly in the Bride’s spiritual ornaments because in them they more truly recognize the works of God’s fingers and the artistry of the Holy Spirit. Not only angels, however: holy teachers in the Church of God are also to be understood as cooperating with the Bridegroom in the Bride’s nuptial adornments. It follows:

“While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Those skilled in archery say that there is a certain perception in the archer’s hand by which he often knows, even without seeing, when the arrow released from his hand has not gone in vain. In the same way, it is established that there is sometimes in a faithful person praying faithfully a certain perception of devotion, by which the person knows when prayer has reached God; and from the answering grace that gives light and from the sense of a good conscience, no doubt of being heard remains. [Col. 0498D]

Thus the Bride, instructed by the discipline of reproof and glorified by wisdom’s gift, takes on this disposition and begins now more perfectly to know herself, and to understand and discern what is occurring within her. And now, as the Bridegroom indicates—that is, as grace gives light—she begins to find in herself what she seemed to seek elsewhere when she said: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you rest at noon”: namely, the kingdom of God within herself, a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob. She begins to contemplate it, not with the manner of contemplation upon which she had first rashly entered in the presumption of novice fervour, or in which she had expended what she received from gratuitous grace more ardently than wisely, [Col. 0499A] but with that devout contemplation which begins freely to disclose itself to a soul proved by temptations, instructed by corrective discipline, and enlightened by the merit of a purer conscience. Therefore he adds and says:

“While the king was in his reclining place, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Reclining takes place in two ways: either for sharing carnal pleasure or for receiving food. She sought both, but spiritually, when she above asked: “Tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon.” The Bridegroom’s and Bride’s place of rest or reclining is memory, understanding, and love. In these the Bridegroom and Bride recline: he, by infusing grace; she, by devoutly remembering, humbly understanding, and ardently loving.

The man who said, “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131), sought this place with anxious devotion. To the degree that his heart burned in this holy desire, it was already surely a place of God; but he desired to stand there in enjoyment, or to enjoy it steadfastly. Tormenting will, or desire—that is, vehement will—already filled and wholly possessed his memory. But because understanding lacked its light, love could in no way find its joy in enjoyment. Of this he later says: “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood” (ibid.). For one who does not perceive the God whom he prays to be present as he ought to be perceived prays anxiously; but one who holds him present enjoys his presence and worships with gratitude.

Therefore, when the Bride remembered the Bridegroom, or reflected in order to understand, she thought him absent so long as she did not understand in order to love. Yet good will is already the beginning of love. Vehement will, when directed as it were toward one absent, is desire; but when disposed toward one present, it is love, when that which the lover loves is present to the understanding. For love of God is itself his understanding: he is understood only when loved, loved only when understood; and certainly is understood as much as he is loved, and loved as much as he is understood.

The Bridegroom therefore reclines with the Bride when first, by gratuitous grace, he sanctifies in her free will its assent to him. But the Bride does not seem to recline with him so long as her understanding does not find its joy in love, [Col. 0499D] nor love its joy in the affection of enjoyment; so long as she sings with the spirit but not with the mind (1 Cor. 4): her spirit sings or prays, but the mind of the singer or pray-er is without fruit. Secret grace is already working powerfully in her, but until she is perfectly affected toward the One acting, she does not think herself to recline with the One reclining. Therefore she says: “While the king was in his reclining place, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” “In his reclining place,” she says, “not ours”: that is, in the place of reclining in which the Bride is made by the Bridegroom, but is not yet affected toward him as she wishes; as she later says concerning the bed, “Our bed is flowering.” “My nard gave forth its fragrance.”

Nard is a lowly herb, having abundant locks or spikes; it signifies humility fruitful in virtues. It is warm, signifying the heat of holy desire. It is suited for ointments, because without the virtue of humility no disposition of devotion whatsoever is acceptable to God. It has a distinctive fragrance, signifying confession of sins in humility. Hence she earlier said: “I am black, but beautiful.” Hence also comes the alabaster flask of costly pure or spiked nard ointment, which the humble devotion of the woman poured upon Jesus’ body, anticipating his anointing for burial (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Therefore, concerning the fragrance of humble nard—that is, devout confession—it is there added: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12).

“I sought outside myself,” says the Bride, “as though absent, him whom I already had within me reclining and feeding. His reclining in my heart was made manifest by the devotion of good [Col. 0500B] will; his feeding, by the outpouring of confession pleasing to God, wrought inwardly by grace. But I did not know where he fed or where he reclined, because, although all these things occurred in me through the good assent of my will and the judgment of reason, I did not possess the perception of spiritual affection by which the sweetness of his presence is felt.”

Then, describing more subtly the grace of spiritual reclining, and first adding her delights in thanksgiving so as to gather them into her memory, she says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts.” Opening the eye of spiritual understanding to the light of grace, she says: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus”; and, drawing its sweetness into the sense of love: “in the vineyards of Engaddi.” For a memory not ungrateful for God’s benefits soon merits the joy of spiritual understanding, which immediately dissolves into certain sweet experiences of love, delightfully rather than knowingly.

For when spiritual understanding begins to be illuminated by the more abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, it operates in the human soul as differently from human understanding as the nature of unbounded light differs more sublimely from the soul’s own nature. What the soul understands by natural understanding, it grasps; but by that understanding it is not so much grasping as grasped. What it naturally grasps by understanding, it distinguishes rationally; but what it does not suffice to perceive, it cannot distinguish.

For the Holy Spirit, just as he breathes where he wills, so acts when he wills, how he wills, and to whatever degree he wills. But a human being hears his voice—that is, feels the working grace—yet does not know whence it comes or whither it goes (John 3), because neither the beginning, nor end, nor manner of that operation is subject to human power or choice. The person does not know whence it comes or whither it goes: a certain experience of divine joy and of illuminating and beatifying grace is produced, which only love made luminous is permitted to feel; a sweetness which love merits and itself brings about, which ordinary understanding does not know but affection feels; the most solid substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen; the trustworthy testimony of the Lord of Christian faith, giving wisdom to the little ones.

For the sweetness of God which has been tasted is savoury to the one tasting it to such a degree that whatever belongs to the flesh, the world, or all creation becomes tasteless to the soul, so that it delights to die, provided it may be permitted to remain. And when it feels what it does not know, it prays what it does not know, because it is the Spirit who intercedes for it according to God, not according to man: the Spirit who makes it feel, ask, and desire precisely that which, in feeling, it does not know, and in not knowing, it feels. For he alone who searches the heart knows what the Spirit desires—that is, what he causes the desiring person to desire.

This happens with, or in, the soul which has deserved to be a Bride, when from those things of which the Lord said, “Indeed, those things which concern me are coming to an end” (Luke 22)—that is, from the dispensation of the Lord’s humanity and the many benefits which have flowed to us from it—it gathers the creed as a kind of [Col. 0501B] bundle of myrrh and makes a place for him between her breasts: in the heart, in the secure seat of memory and the tenderness of a well-disposed conscience. There hostile temptation cannot easily gain access, nor can that tenderness of love suffer even the least injury to faith.

For dead bodies are embalmed with myrrh; it is bitter in taste, according to the bitterness of the Passion which the Lord endured for us, and sweet in fragrance according to the sweetness of the love with which he loved us. Observe the pleasant delights of spiritual love. After necklaces and little chains, after the gift of wisdom and the grace of eloquence, there is added, as it were, a scent-container to be fastened to the breast, continually breathing the love of the Lord’s Passion and death, so that the Bride’s devoted memory may be affected by the unceasing sweetness of its fragrance. Indeed, according to myrrh’s physical property, its taste is said to strengthen the power of memory.

It is a little bundle, not a load, because no human strength could bear the whole burden of the Lord’s Passion. It is a bundle of delights: devout remembrance and sweet meditation upon the goodness and the cause of the One suffering, and upon the sweetness of his love, do not weigh down but raise the bearer up—the sacrament of redemption, the example of humility, the summons to love, and the power of resurrection. But if, as the Apostle says, “we neglect so great a salvation” (Heb. 2), and at judgment are called to account for the crucified One, for his cross, Passion, and blood trampled underfoot—Lord, Lord, who will endure? “That fearful expectation of judgment will consume the adversaries” [Col. 0501D] (Heb. 10).

Likewise, one who, trusting to penetrate the most exalted mystery of Christ’s twofold nature through the force of natural ingenuity, seeks or promises things too high for himself, has taken upon himself a heavy burden and must needs collapse under it. For that great sacrament of godliness in Christ, as the Apostle says, although manifested in the flesh, is not justified except in the spirit (1 Tim. 3): that is, no explanation sufficient to the dignity of the matter can be supplied to any human being, whether by himself or through another, of the righteousness which is through faith, unless the Holy Spirit has deigned to reveal it.

But the Bride does not labour under her bundle, because she loves. For one who loves does not labour. And the Bridegroom’s memory is said to be placed and dwell between the Bride’s breasts so that from there the Bridegroom’s children may draw the milk of sacred nourishment. These two breasts of the Bride are wisdom and knowledge, of which the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 12). From these the Bridegroom’s children draw the support of true life: that is, the love of God.

Created indeed in the image and likeness of the Creator, through sin we had fallen from God into ourselves, and from ourselves beneath ourselves, into such a depth of unlikeness that there was no hope. But the Son of God came, eternal Wisdom; he bowed his heavens and descended. He made something of himself in us that was like us, so that we might grasp it, and like himself, so that we might be raised by it. The continual remembrance of this mystery would be continual medicine. And [Col. 0502B] the bundle of myrrh is that which we grasp, but the cluster of Cyprus that by which we are raised. Of this he adds and says:

“My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus, in the vineyards of Engaddi.” Those whom the bitterness of myrrh makes sad are gladdened by wine. In myrrh is understood the bitterness of the Passion; in the wine of the cluster, the joy of the resurrection; in the bundle of myrrh, through faithful memory, all that in Christ belonged to human passibility and mortality; in the wine of the cluster, through hope and understanding, joy in the power of the resurrection; and in the vineyards of Engaddi and its balm, through love, the anointing from the Holy One and joy in the Holy Spirit.

Cyprus is an island in the sea, and Engaddi a place in Judaea; they are far removed from one another both by diversity of location and by the differing excellence of their noble fertility. Cyprus is distinguished by the fertility of its vineyards, Engaddi by the excellence of its balm. Yet they are joined into one sacrament of devotion: the cluster of Cyprus and its gladdening wine, because of the power and joy of the resurrection, temper the bitterness of myrrh arising from sorrow for the Passion; and the balm of Engaddi is joined to it, for the end of all consummation and perfection, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the bundle of myrrh and the cluster of Cyprus dwell between the Bride’s breasts when the memory, affected toward the Bridegroom, is humbled by the one—that is, myrrh—and raised by the other—that is, the cluster. Yet neither affects the memory, illuminates the understanding, or kindles love except in the balm of Engaddi—that is, except by the grace of the Holy Spirit visiting her. The cluster also signifies, in the Bride’s memory of the Bridegroom, a manifold matter of joys because of the multitude of grapes; Cyprus signifies a distinguished matter of joys. But the balm of Engaddi signifies something greater and worthier than every wine—that is, than every joy of this life: namely, the oil of gladness and the anointing of the Holy Spirit, with which God the Father himself anointed the Bridegroom, God, above his fellows.

Things belonging to faith and hope, memory and understanding, appear to possess some affection of love and joy. But joy in the Holy Spirit, in the fullness of love, advances into an effect of blessedness surpassing every joy; it is perfected in that which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, in that city of God of which the Psalm says: [Col. 0503A] “Like the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. 86). “Of those who rejoice,” he says, because they are not merely rejoicing, but rejoicing beyond rejoicing. That joy has no name, except “as joy” or “more than joy.”

This also seems to be supported by the fact that the vineyards of Cyprus and those of Engaddi seem to have a certain likeness, yet are widely distinguished, as has been said, by the unequal nobility of their fertility. For shrubs of balm seem similar to vine-shrubs in that they sometimes rise to the height of two cubits, in likeness to vines, but without external supports, which vines cannot do. Their seed also seems to imitate wine in taste or flavour. But they surpass vines by the perpetual glory of their foliage, presenting or signifying the joy of eternal blessedness, which needs no assistance in subsisting because it has no ground of being except from itself.

Moreover, Engaddi is interpreted “the spring of the kid,” that is, the spring of grace, in which the kid, passing from the left to the right, becomes a lamb. For lambs are set at the right hand and kids at the left (Matt. 25). The shrub is pierced and yields balm, signifying either the sacrament flowing from the piercing of the Lord’s side, or the remission of sins proceeding from compunction of heart, or what Solomon says: “Prick the eye and it brings forth a tear; prick the heart and it brings forth understanding” (Ecclus. 22). It follows:

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful.” “Behold”: that is, in this affection of devotion, in this [Col. 0503C] form of confession, in this aspect of perfection, in the image of God. For the human being was created in God’s image so that, devoutly remembering God—that is, remembering in order to understand—humbly understanding—that is, understanding in order to love—and ardently and wisely loving even unto the affection of enjoyment, the human being might be a rational animal. For this is to fear God and keep his commandments, which “is the whole human being” (Eccl. 12).

This is the image and likeness of God in the human being, such or so great as it can be in material so unlike him. For this likeness is reason, by which man differs from the beast. Not to remember God belongs to the beast; to remember, but not in order to understand, is something more than the beast yet less than man; to remember in order to understand belongs to man; to understand unto loving, or unto enjoying through love, belongs already to the perfected reason of man.

For devout memory quickly grows bright into a kind of understanding of God, or rational thought. Pure understanding or rational thought immediately grows warm into love; and love, through affection for the good, immediately assumes the image of the highest Good, such or so great as he himself is. This is present to good memory through assent, to pure understanding through thought, and to affected love through enjoyment: to love—that is, to the Bride loving—through a habitual disposition of mind; but to others through the desire of good will.

For the Bride’s memory of the Bridegroom is to seek the Bridegroom in simplicity of heart; understanding is to think of him in goodness; love is to be affected toward him, to enjoy him, [Col. 0504A] to be as he is. Thus, finding the Bride in this state or disposition of mind, the Bridegroom says: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful.” For in the Bride’s beauty, the sun of righteousness had restored colour to whatever had been discoloured: his presence restored colour to what his absence had discoloured.

For the Bride’s substance, of which the Apostle says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 10), has its own eminent colours, namely holy virtues. As was said above, these virtues are discoloured in her when they are deprived of illuminating grace, and recoloured when they are illumined by it. Therefore, beholding the Bride’s restored face, the Bridegroom is raised in praise of her and says: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful.” The repetition signifies confirmation or evidence of beauty making progress. Or: “You are beautiful,” he says, “in work; beautiful in affection. Beautiful because fair; beautiful because coloured.”

“Behold,” then, he says, “while you cleanse memory for me, humble understanding, and dispose love toward me, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful—my beloved in proportion to your beauty.” Since contemplative perfection consists in these things, he adds concerning it: “Your eyes are those of doves.” There are two eyes of contemplation: reason and love; and according to the prophet’s saying, “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge” (Isa. 33), one investigates human things according to knowledge, the other divine things according to wisdom.

When they are illuminated by grace, they assist one another greatly: love gives life to reason, and reason makes love clear. Thus the dovelike gaze becomes simple for contemplation and prudent for caution. These two eyes often become one eye when they cooperate faithfully; in the contemplation of God, where love works most fully, reason passes into love and is formed into a spiritual or divine understanding which surpasses and absorbs all reason. This is what the Bride later says to the Bridegroom: “You have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck” (Song 4). Then the Bride, receiving from the Bridegroom praise for beauty, returns a corresponding grace, saying:

[Col. 0504D] “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely.” An equal return is rendered to an equal: the Bride is called beautiful, beautiful, and beloved; but the Bridegroom beautiful, comely, and beloved. For once she has been instructed through temptations, cleansed by repentance, divinely illuminated, and begun to know herself and to find within herself the one whom she sought, Bridegroom and Bride, in friendly companionship and familiar conversation, mutually make themselves known to each other, please each other, praise each other, and taste beforehand the joy of their mutual union.

And so, while the business of love is being transacted, while they advance everywhere or gradually toward the measure of perfection to be bestowed by God, Bridegroom and Bride speak to one another: the Bride through the affection of devotion; the Bridegroom through the effect of working grace. Or the Bridegroom’s address is the work of grace that affects her; the Bride’s answer is the very joy of a well-disposed conscience. Or for the Bride to address the Bridegroom is for her to appear before his eyes as she is; but for the Bridegroom to address her is to order or dispose her, or matters concerning her, within her own understanding.

Whatever the Bridegroom here says in praise of the Bride is the testimony of a holy conscience; what the Bride says concerning the Bridegroom is the affection of devotion or the piety of contemplation. For no one is so perverse in himself or turned away from God, provided he is in some measure capable of reason, that God does not at some time speak within him. How much more does he speak in the Bride, who, as woman with man is one flesh, is herself one spirit with God.

Thus, called beautiful and beautiful beloved, she returns praise with grateful devotion, calling the Bridegroom beautiful, comely, and beloved. That is, she understands and firmly knows that whatever praiseworthy thing she has, she has from him who is the goodness of every good and the beauty of every beautiful thing, and whose praise consists in bestowing things worthy of praise.

The mutual resemblance of beauty and mutual enjoyment of Bridegroom and Bride produce this reciprocal grace toward one another of which we speak. For not only do we enjoy God, but God also enjoys our good, insofar as he delights in it and deigns to regard it as pleasing. And the measure of enjoyment corresponds to the measure of progress or resemblance; for resemblance cannot exist unless enjoyment affects it, nor enjoyment unless resemblance affects it.

For whatever grace a soul receives from God, granted for its benefit, it receives with the gift itself an understanding of the Giver, so that a person may not be ungrateful to God, but may always be turned toward the Giver. When humble love attends upon him more ardently, it is conformed to the one upon whom it attends, because by attending it is made by him into this very thing. And when it is made into the likeness of its Maker, the human being becomes affected toward God—that is, one spirit with God: beautiful in the Beautiful, good in the Good, existing in God by grace, according to the power of faith, the light of understanding, and the measure of love, as that One is by nature.

For when grace sometimes overflows into a certain and manifest experience of God, there suddenly becomes perceptible to the sense of illuminated love, in a new manner, something which no bodily sense can hope for, no reason conceive, and no understanding other than that of illuminated love comprehend. There, for that human being, to perceive God is nothing other than, through the affection of good experience, to receive his likeness according to the quality both of the form perceived and of the love perceiving it.

For, in things perceived through the body, sensation is a certain likeness of the perceived object, drawn by sensing into the mind through a mental image, according to the quality of the sensing faculty and the sensible object. Thus, for example, if the object perceived belongs to sight, it cannot be seen at all by the seer unless its visible form has first been fashioned through the likeness of an image in the seer’s soul, by which the perceiver is transformed into [Col. 0506A] what is perceived. So, and much more, the vision of God works the same thing in the sense of love by which God is seen.

Indeed, even in bodily perception of things, unless love also works together with sensation, sensation itself scarcely reaches any effect, because the perceiver immediately withdraws unless it clings to the object perceived through some desire of love. But in the vision of God, where love alone works and no other sense cooperates, the purity of love and divine affection act incomparably more worthily and subtly than every imagination of the senses: affecting more sweetly, drawing more strongly, and holding the perceiver more delightfully; faithfully transferring into God, both in mind and deed, the whole person who loves; strengthening, conforming, and giving life for enjoyment. Therefore he immediately adds concerning enjoyment and says:

[Col. 0506B] “Our bed is flowering.” The flowering bed is a delightful conscience, the joy of the Holy Spirit within it, and in its very source the unceasing enjoyment of truth. This is that of which the same Bridegroom says: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet man, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). It is pleasing to dwell upon the beauty of this flowering bed and to range about its delightful pleasures: flourishing in the beauty of chastity and charity, fragrant with the grace of spiritual perceptions or understandings, breathing forth the scent of divinity and the power of eternity. For in it occurs that wondrous union and mutual enjoyment of sweetness and incomprehensible joy—unthinkable even to those in whom it occurs—of human being with God, of created spirit with uncreated Spirit. They are called Bride and Bridegroom [Col. 0506C] when words are sought by which the tongue of man may in some fashion express the sweetness and delight of that union, which is none other than the unity of God the Father and the Son: their very kiss, their very embrace, their very love, their very goodness, and whatever in that utterly simple unity is common to both. All this is the Holy Spirit: God, charity, both the giver and the gift.

For there that embrace and that kiss conforms the Bride to itself, so that she begins to know even as she is known; and, as is customary in the kisses of lovers who in a sweet mutual contact pour their spirits into one another, the created spirit wholly pours itself out into the creating Spirit for this very end. The Creator Spirit, however, pours himself into the created spirit as he wills, and man becomes one spirit with God [Col. 0506D]. This is the sole refuge of the Bridegroom’s children from persecutions and afflictions amid the miseries of this life; their sole rest from labours and consolation in pains; the mirror of life, the strength of faith, the pledge of hope, the sweet nourishment of love or charity advancing toward God.

Thus also the Vessel of Election, when, as he himself says, he had at one time presented himself as God’s minister “in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in prisons, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering” (2 Cor. 6), as though fleeing after the exhaustion of such great labours to the flowering bed and its repose, adds immediately: “in kindness, in the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). Blessed is the conscience which, ever seeking the face [Col. 0507A] of the Lord, has always within itself, after the pressures of bodily labours and the tribulations of spiritual exercises, a ready dwelling-place of repose: that is, a flowering bed, the private joy of its own testimony. Of this the same Doctor of the Gentiles says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

Likewise blessed is the conscience which, whenever it goes forth from the joy of this inward sweetness to some work of necessity at charity’s command, always has a ready return thither. This is not always at hand for one who goes entirely out whenever he must go out. For when the delicate child of the flowering bed must sometimes go out among external things, he must never be wholly estranged from it. Rather, something of himself must always be left within to guard his own place faithfully; and that which is compelled to go out must always cling to it by a strong bond of love, lest it withdraw too far. Let the charity of truth always remain within, even when the necessity of charity compels it to go out among external things. Nor should the force of outward necessity ever prevail so greatly as wholly to tear the Bride’s mind from the power of inward sweetness.

But when, together with the fashion of this world, all iniquity has passed away, then all this necessity also will have passed away. Then the union of Bridegroom and Bride will become full and perpetual in the fullness of likeness: when not only will the Bridegroom be seen as he is, but whatever the Bride has deserved to be, she too will be as he is. Then the kiss will be complete, when there is full and perpetual enjoyment, eye to eye [Col. 0507C] and embrace to embrace. Then no one will any longer rouse the Bride or make her awaken until she herself wishes; and she will never again wish it.

Meanwhile, amid the afflictions of this life, a paradise is prepared for a good mind as aid in labour and solace in delay, and a flowering bed for a good conscience. In it there is not that eternal kiss and perfect union, but a longed-for imitation of the kiss itself and of perfection, and some likeness of that union and likeness. For by the Holy Spirit, to the spirit of man and to the sense of illuminated love, which sometimes swiftly reaches thither, that whatever-it-is becomes sweet and carries away the lover: loved rather than thought, tasted rather than understood. Thus for a time, [Col. 0507D] for an hour, it affects the lover and fixes the one who is pressing onward, so that he seems no longer to possess merely in hope but almost in reality the very substance of things hoped for; through a certain experiential proof of faith from the Word of life, he seems both to see with his eyes and to hold and touch with his hands.

For this is your consolation, O Father, to your children, to whom you promised, saying: “I will not leave you orphans; I go, and I come to you” (John 14). For, bending down your heavens, you descend to your children bound by hope in the prison of this exile; you dwell and walk in them. And upon their faith—which you first gave into their hearts—you gradually form your grace, grace for grace. Through the working of that grace, they conform their mind and life to it; and there comes to be that likeness which enjoyment immediately accompanies. For you are a good Father, a good [Col. 0508A] Lord, and good whatever you are; you present and reveal yourself as the good you are to their affections. Since power always goes out from you to heal our languors, you affect them as though by contact or perception of your goodness; from yourself you make them good, and thus, being good, you are loved by the good. You yourself are your love in them: you yourself mercifully and sweetly affect them from yourself, and most rightly, justly, and wisely love yourself from within them.

For that which has a taste of you is not alien from you, nor is that which receives you far from you—if indeed it receives him whom no place, whether sensible or intelligible, and no perception, whether through a bodily instrument or through the understanding of reason, can receive. Yet the expanded bosom of love, extending itself according to your greatness, while it loves you—or strives to love you—as great as you are, receives the unreceivable and comprehends the incomprehensible [Col. 0508B]. But why do we say, “receives”? Rather, love itself—that is, what you are—your Holy Spirit, O Father, who proceeds from you and the Son, with whom you and the Son are one: when the human spirit is worthy to be affected by him, spirit by Spirit, love by love, human love in some manner becomes divine.
