And now, in loving God, man indeed acts, but God is the one who acts. It is not Paul, but “the grace of God” with him (1 Cor. 15).

“Therefore,” she says, “our bed is flowering.” She offers the Bridegroom what she desires to receive from him. This offering is devout prayer. For love grows fresh again in remembrance of that which is singularly loved; and the great desire of one who remembers is devout prayer. This remembrance is nothing other than a holy conscience inviting its own Knower [Col. 0508C] within itself. It already has the flowers of the flowering bed—that is, the grace of holy virtues, bestowed by the Bridegroom in the assent of good will—but cannot enjoy their delight unless the Bridegroom is present to it and it to itself in him. Therefore it presents the bed, invites him to the bed, begs for his reclining there, and desires rest in peace together with him.

By the illuminating grace of his continual presence it wishes to have its memory fixed upon God and steadily disposed toward him; its understanding of him enlightened; charity surpassing knowledge toward him; and, in the practice of virtues, the continual sweetness of grace that affects it. “Our bed is flowering.” As a flower hastens to ripen into fruit, so good will hastens into affection. To this the Bride directs herself; for this she labours in travail; toward this she yearns. She wishes to love and desires to enjoy—not in the reclining of the will, but in the abiding disposition of the mind—when she longs for a flowering bed. For in the perception of a soul seeking God there cannot be a non-confident enjoyment of God where his likeness has gone before. Therefore she says, “Our bed.” “When it is ours,” she says, “common to me and you, it will breathe holy delights and be warm with mutual love. So long as it is mine—where through the night I seek him whom I love and do not find—it has no flowers and no fragrances: little grace, the smallest joy. It is a bed of night, not of day; it is wholly cold; and woe to one resting alone in it, for there is no one to warm him. Therefore, not my bed, but ‘our flowering bed.’”

Having at some time experienced some affection from the Bridegroom, [Col. 0509A] she sighs for the bed; having tasted for an hour that which is partial, she desires reclining or repose in that which is perfect. For in contemplation of the highest good, by the natural grace of that good itself, whatever delights the lover commonly at once becomes an object of confidence to the believer. And in the light of God’s countenance, just as love cannot ever be without reality, so understanding cannot be without hope. It follows:

“The beams of our houses are cedar.” Not only our bed, she says, but also our houses abhor solitude. For as in the bed, so too woe to one dwelling alone in a house. The Bride, however, has not only one house: she has as many houses in which to dwell, or in which the Bridegroom may dwell with her, as she has virtues. The Bride’s houses are holy virtues, of which one reads in the psalm: “God shall be known in [Col. 0509B] her houses”—that is, the Bride’s—“when he receives her” (Ps. 47). For the Bridegroom is known in the Bride’s houses when, having been received or accepted and become pleasing in his sight, they are illumined by the grace of his presence.

For chastity produced by charity is one thing; chastity produced by continence alone is another. Each and every virtue is one thing when it exists only in the desire of the will, according to reason’s judgment, and another when it exists in the affection of life-giving grace. For so long as their houses—the houses of virtues—are common to Bridegroom and Bride, they possess a remarkable defence: cedar beams and cypress panelling for inward beauty. The cedar beams, which do not decay, in the houses of virtues are faith and the hope of eternity, raised heavenward beneath the roof of God’s protection by the power of right intention [Col. 0509C]. The cypress panelling, moreover, signifies inward beauty, both through the beauty of ordered work and through fragrant efficacy. This beauty consists in the diligence of preserving the unity of the Spirit.

It is the mutual charity in God of the Bridegroom’s children: loving one another and receiving one another, just as timbers are interlaced with timbers in panelling to complete the inward beauty and inward protection, lest anything creep in or intrude to grieve those who dwell there. For a single mutual charity makes them both able to receive and receptive. Indeed, even some unbelievers seem to possess virtues of mind; but no virtues are proved to exist which are not raised to God through faith and hope, and which are not contained within the domestic unity of ecclesial devotion [Col. 0509D].

> [Note: [Col. 0509D] The fact that the author here appears, along with Augustine, to deny that those virtues can be found without faith and hope should be understood piously [Col. 0510D] of virtues capable of meriting the kingdom of heaven.]

For the natural nobility of virtues itself seems to invite or draw all human beings to it; but their charity receives few of them in God, and truth receives none. Therefore, as has been said, even those outside sometimes seem to have certain virtues in act, in will, even in love—so much so that one of them may be found declaring that only those people are good who hate to sin from love of virtue (Horace, *Epistles*, book 1, epistle 16, line 52). But for those to whom Christ is wisdom, he himself is every virtue. For in wisdom is contained the whole fullness of virtues. Nor is any virtue truly virtue unless it has savour for its possessor in him who is the wisdom of all virtues [Col. 0510A].

In him, just as true and solid virtue is not merely the zeal of labour or the aspiration of will, but an affection of the soul and an abiding disposition of a good mind, so love for him is true and living when he who is loved is present to the lover through understanding or through the perception of love itself. Then the bed is both ours and flowering. Thus, whatever is here said by the Bride to the Bridegroom concerning the flowering bed and the houses beamed and panelled is nothing other than a devout conscience inviting God, who knows its heart, into that heart. Or beneath the beams of faith and hope—that is, in the common life of believers—the Bride seeks a flowering bed; and beneath the panelling of social life, a sure dwelling-place of fixed station, to which the more secret business of mutual enjoyment with the Bridegroom and of love may be entrusted.

Yet these things seek a more suitable and more pleasant place for reclining; a more secluded place for enjoyment; a safer one for abiding. This is charity “out of a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned” (1 Tim. 1): whether in solitude or in a crowd, a heart solitary in God. It follows:

## CHAPTER II

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” The Spirit of wisdom is accustomed first to make poor in his own spirit the one whom he will enrich, and to humble the one whom he will raise up, so that he may establish the height of true perfection upon the foundation of true humility. But the loftiness of the wine-cellar, into which the Bridegroom prepares to introduce the Bride, admits no other heights except that of which it is said: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). For as every virtue is perfected in weakness, so every righteousness is perfected in humility [Col. 0510C]. Hence the Lord, when he was to be baptized in the Jordan, said to John: “Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3).

Therefore, approving rather than merely testing the virtue of humility as the fulfillment of righteousness in the Bride, the Bridegroom says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” It is as though he said: “If you are pressing on toward the fullness of enjoyment, act and strive to possess the fullness of my likeness: that is, in every perfection, the virtue of perfect humility. I am your example: the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

There is no small difference between the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. There is a certain humility, as it were open and level like a plain, from which none who shares the Christian name can excuse himself: namely, to be subject to a superior and not to prefer oneself to an equal. There is another, more exalted humility, awaiting the reward of perfection: namely, in God, to submit oneself to an inferior and prefer an equal to oneself, not merely by the judgment of reason but by the very affection of conscience. This is the lily of the valleys of lofty hearts, holy minds, and perfect people, who outdo one another in showing honour and regard one another as superior to themselves. For the height of a valley divides neighbouring mountains, but its depth unites them [Col. 0511A].

These indeed are those of whom the Apostle says: “There are divisions of gifts,” or “of graces,” “but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). These are those of whom the Psalmist says: “You send forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. 103); and elsewhere: “The valleys shall abound with grain” (Ps. 64). The exaltation of differing holiness separates them at the height of their differing merits; but a devout assessment of charity joins them together in the low places of a conscience humbling itself. In them, the more sublime the height of holiness, the deeper is found the valley of humility. There is the lily as a lily—that is, an example conformed and fitted to the exemplar of divine humility in Christ.

For the humility of an ordinary human being is one thing, when from awareness of his condition and knowledge of himself he becomes lowly in his own eyes before God or neighbour; the humility of God and man voluntarily lowering himself into the utmost condition of humanity in order to raise humanity up is another. In the Mediator between God and men, the divine condescension toward human beings, proceeding solely from the fountain of goodness, is humiliation rather than humility. Hence the Apostle says: “He humbled himself” (Phil. 2). But in a human being, self-knowledge is always humility: either, in one unwilling, the confusion of necessity; or, in one willing, the affection of virtue.

Therefore Christ appeared as the flower of the field—that is, as the common example of humility in man—of whom it is written that he “was subject” to his parents (Luke 2). Even in the lot of tax liability, both in payment and in the amount of the tax, he did not refuse Peter as his equal. To him he said, when ministers of earthly dominion demanded the tax: “Go to the sea, cast a hook, and open the mouth of the first fish that comes up; you will find a stater: give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matt. 17) [Col. 0511C].

He was also the lily of the valleys, either when, as man, preferring other human beings to himself, he willingly died for the ungodly that they might live; or when, as God-man, voluntarily subjecting himself to perverse people, he was unjustly judged by them. “Thus,” he says, “in me both the plainness of common life and the profession of a higher life have an example to imitate in the virtue of humility. For to some I appeared as the flower of the field; to others as the lily, surpassing all other flowers, as an example of perfection. Though I was in the form of God and did not count equality with God a thing to be seized, I emptied myself, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man.

“But you, attending to the beautiful one so that you might become beautiful from the beautiful one, perceived within yourself by the perception of love what you perceived in me by the perception of faith. Planted together with the lily, you became like a lily: not turning aside from the uprightness of my imitation either through feminine softness, which is suggested by the name ‘daughters,’ or through the pricking thorn, that is, the malice of those living with you. For to live well among the wicked is already the summit of a certain perfection.”

It must be understood, however, that although the highest example of humility for human beings always proceeds from Christ, humility in Christ is nevertheless different from humility in a Christian. In any merely human person, true humility is to judge of oneself what one is and, through self-knowledge, to become lowly in one’s own eyes. But Jesus Christ, the Truth, although he did or taught humble things beyond all other human beings, could judge of himself only what he was [Col. 0512A]. For although he was both God and man, that man was so worthy of God that there was nothing in him for which he could become lowly in his own estimation. Therefore his humility lay not in estimation but in action: he humbled himself by not merely teaching lowly things, but doing or enduring, beyond all human beings, things most lowly and most unworthy of his majesty.

Thus the Bridegroom is the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys; but the Bride is like a lily. Yet the Bride, embracing the humility of imitation and devout likeness but shrinking from the height of equality, does not reject the likeness of a humble but fruitless lily. She compares the Bridegroom to a lofty and fruitful apple tree, beneath whose shade she might hide and from whose fruit she might live, saying:

“As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shade, which I had desired, I sat down, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.” For there is nowhere a comparison of man with God, not even in the likeness of humility. For just as the power of almighty divinity is incomparable, majesty unsearchable, strength beyond estimation, and wisdom beyond conception, so, when we come to our own condition, his weakness is found stronger, his foolishness wiser, and his humility more exalted than all human beings.

Hence the Lord himself, speaking of John, said: “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist”—namely, in humility. “Yet he who is lesser,” that is, more humble, “in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 11) [Col. 0512C]. In what respect? In humility. For John’s humility shone greatly in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church; yet greater than he appeared the one who, being greater than all, showed himself least. The farther he descended from on high to our lowest state, the humbler than all humble people he appeared in the world.

Therefore the Bride, taught by the Bridegroom, trained by temptations, devout in imitation but fearful of equality, under the figure of a lofty apple tree recalls the Lord and his disciples reclining in the Pharisee’s house, herself as the sinner who came, and the Lord justifying her. She transforms that entire Gospel history of mercy into herself, saying: “As a fruitful apple tree among the steadfast trees of the woods,” making them beautiful by its beauty, gladdening them with fragrance, honouring them with fruit, “so is my beloved among the sons” of sweet affection and manly virtue—that is, reclining among the apostles, whom he illumines with virtues, strengthens by examples, establishes by deeds, and gladdens with teaching [Col. 0512D].

“Under the shade” of his protection, while the Pharisee condemned me, I anxiously desired to be protected and hidden; but, hearing from his mouth the judgment upon those who love the Lord’s name, I “sat down” secure. For he said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7).

“And his fruit was sweet to my throat”: namely, the taste of his love filling my desire with good things, when the fullness of his pardon gladdens my conscience, he himself saying: “Go in peace; your faith has saved you” (Luke 7). I desired when I sought by faith and hope; I sat down when the spirit rested in him through love; and his fruit was sweet to my throat when, through the power of illuminated love, I began to taste experiential knowledge of his sweetness. It follows:

“The king brought me into the wine-cellar.” For she who above, in native devotion, went out from the storehouses and yearned to contemplate, now, tested in all things, purified to cleanness, and fittingly humbled, begins to enter the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, in order to recline now in the enjoyment of what she had previously desired so impatiently, when she said: “Tell me, O you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you rest at noon.”

For, as has already been said, these are the things of which the Prophet speaks: “Wisdom and knowledge are the riches of salvation” (Isa. 33) [Col. 0513B]. In knowledge—that is, in the storehouses—reason and understanding are fed; in wisdom, which is the wine-cellar, love and affection are fed. Those things are known; these have savour. There is the labour of discriminating diligence; here there is only the joy of the experience of one who enjoys. For the things of knowledge do not belong to all, but are brought in by learners with labour, as though from without. The things of wisdom, however, are found by even the simple children of God, who perceive the Lord in goodness and seek God in simplicity of heart, as though grown together with nature within and acquired freely without labour.

The wine-cellar is a certain secret place of God’s wisdom, a state of mind more fully disposed toward God. Separated only by the intervening veil of this mortality—as God’s temple is separated from heavenly things, that is, from the Holy of Holies—it has a certain sure and familiar fellowship with heavenly things, according to the measure of its progress and the gift of illuminating grace [Col. 0513C]. There is the flowering bed, the bed of delights, which the Bride sought a little earlier: not to receive it beneath the beams of faith or hope, but in the fullness of charity, which is the wine-cellar. For charity, or the good conscience belonging to its perfection, is the wine-cellar; and the wine of this wine-cellar is joy in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore in the wine-cellar there is nothing except wine. Whatever enters or is brought into it either is wine or becomes wine, because the fire of God’s love takes everything to itself and consumes it; and, like ordinary fire, converts it into its own substance, since all things work together for good to one who loves God [Col. 0513D]. There, from the abundance and richness of the house of God and the torrent of delight, charity grows so fervent, overflows into its excesses, and is exhilarated in that toward which it tends, that it often seems to become disordered unless it is reordered by the King. Thus Paul wishes to be accursed from Christ for his brethren (Rom. 9), and Moses begs that he himself be blotted from the book of life unless the deadly sin of God’s people is forgiven (Exod. 32).

But even if a good conscience according to God is at times saddened in such matters of charity—if it sympathizes and grieves with another—this does not lessen but increases its joy. For the Lord’s joy in a good conscience, in which he has established his dwelling, is not broken off by any intervening worldly sadness or obscured by vain merriment. Rather, it is faithfully and firmly woven into one continuous tenor: always and everywhere tranquil, and unchanging, although it adapts itself to many things [Col. 0514A]. The disturbances of people and the contradictions of tongues accomplish nothing there. Far from here are vain merriment and every sadness, where the old human being has been utterly put to death and only the perception of sweetness and the affection of devotion live from the taste of the highest good.

Far away are the empty and trifling gaieties that commonly force their way in from without: painting the face but not filling the breast, bathing the skin but not penetrating the inward parts. These are the devastating joys of the world, bringing vain imaginings of pleasures, removing all vigour and strength from the soul, passing away and vanishing, and more harmful than every sadness. But the Lord’s joy is a serious reality; all the work of those who rejoice and exult in it is earnest—not only when they hear that their names are written in heaven and that their reward is abundant, but also when such people fall into various temptations, and when, for the sake of God whom they love, the world hates them, people cast them out, and reproach their name as evil [Col. 0514B].

For joy coming from without easily departs again. But a holy conscience, which does not rejoice in what belongs to another, always rejoices, because it has within itself the source of its joy. For a good conscience possesses a domestic possession and sure happiness. Of this the Prophet says, proclaiming blessed the man who fears the Lord: “Glory and riches are in his house” (Ps. 111). And the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). But what is a good conscience except one which, in the love of God, is pleasing to itself, and in faithful service of that love answers well to itself?

This joy does not lie in laughter of the mouth but in jubilation of the heart. Whoever thus rejoices, whatever may arise or rush upon him, is always cheerful and secure through the good of conscience; and whatever happens, he is always lifted up toward God. For joy is the good enjoyment of a beloved thing.

Accordingly, the measure or quality of joy accompanies the measure or quality of love: a more solid subject of love generally produces a more solid joy. Therefore the love of God has its own proper joy, joy in the Holy Spirit, which no one will take from the lover, because it is his own and the sure possession of that conscience. This is the wine of the wine-cellar [Col. 0514D]. He was drunk with it who said: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor virtues, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8). And the Psalmist: “My inebriating cup, how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22).

This indeed is that wine already breathing the power of the new covenant, which Jesus drinks with his disciples in the kingdom of his Father: wine, as the prophet says, “creating virgins” (Zech. 9); wine, as the Psalmist says, “of compunction,” or “making glad the heart of man” (Pss. 60, 103). Compunction in one who desires and joy in one who enjoys seem in some sense contrary; yet both belong to the wine-cellar and the good conscience, proceeding from the one fountain of love.

The Bride is therefore brought into the house of wine, into the joy of her Lord and Bridegroom. But at the first experiences of that good, impatient of measure or reason, she is disordered by the abundance of wine even to drunkenness from excessive fervour, even to the languor of human weakness failing in the salvation of God [Col. 0515A]. For one who loves, and loves greatly, would not languish unless she were disordered in love itself. If she loved prudently, temperately, courageously, and justly, she would not languish. For what produces languor even in bodies except disordered humours?

The natural order of holy love is to understand or have savour through prudence, but with sobriety—that is, temperance; and through courage to act upon what is understood, but according to justice. But when prudence has savour not unto sobriety and courage strives beyond justice, all things are disordered and languor results. For disordered love disorders everything; and while it follows without order, it does not attain, but fails and languishes. It sometimes strives more vehemently than is just; and, insofar as it is conscious of its own purity, it presumes to be its own law and order, impatient of one who orders it.

Yet, while the King orders and governs, the languor itself in the languishing person is so ordered that, however the languishing person may be agitated or sifted, the entire devout discipline of that languor and salutary exercise contains more joy than sorrow. For that joy and this pain greatly love one another and answer each other, as it were, with most harmonious antitheses: the devout affection of one enjoying, and the anxious desire of one longing [Col. 0515C]. Thus the one who languishes does not wish to be healed; the one who suffers does not wish to be consoled. For he rejoices to fail in love, when he feels love itself advance in that very failure.

Having tasted in some measure that the Lord is sweet, beginning to perceive the Lord in goodness, to perceive in some degree the highest good, to behold or contemplate the highest beauty, and to understand, with an understanding already in part enjoying, the blessedness and joy of incorruptibility and immutability—when a wholly corruptible and mutable human being strains toward escaping into that state but cannot do so, the corruption of his mortality becomes a grave weariness to him. And when he is told, “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33), he begins vehemently to hate whatever his life may be that delays or hinders the way of seeing God.

He desires, therefore, to die, but is not permitted; to die for Christ, but this is not granted to him; to die in Christ, but it is deferred. He resolves to live in Christ, but his understanding grows dim; to devote himself wholly to God, but his own fervour does not allow it; to work, but there is no place for his work. He wishes to expend himself, but has nothing from which to do so; to be spent and spent beyond measure, but finds no object upon which to be spent. He says and cries: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” (Acts 9), and no answer is given him; “What do you wish me to become?” and he is left to himself.

For he wants by reason to do what is just, and fails in discernment; he wants by affection to become just, and cannot except through God. His remedy is read to one who languishes, but he does not heed it; his law to one in love, but he does not comprehend it; his order to one disordered, but he does not notice it [Col. 0516A]. For he is commanded to love the Lord his God with all his heart, all his soul, all his mind, and all his strength, and his neighbour as himself. But because the impulse of love sometimes prevails everywhere, he does not know how to love either himself or his neighbour in preference to the love of God; sometimes God or neighbour in preference to self-love; sometimes God or himself in preference to love of neighbour. Yet, if love proceeds in its proper order and measure, true love either of self or neighbour is nothing other than love of God.

This is the languor of the Bride languishing from love: this love strong as death; this jealousy hard as hell; this drunkenness from the abundance of God’s house and the torrent of his delight.

There is also another languor of the Bride when she thinks of the Bridegroom: when, through the fault of a conscience at times neglected, while memory is defiled from another source, understanding grows dull and love languishes. For these are the three—memory, understanding, and love—which, according to their quality or quantity, shape one’s thought of God. If one’s memory of God intrudes from elsewhere or looks elsewhere; if it is slack, negligent, or faithless, then understanding follows as nonexistent, or rare, or thin, and prone to error; and love is either absent or corrupt—namely, when God is thought of for some purpose other than that He may be loved, or loved for some purpose other than Himself.

But if, in the thought of faith, memory burns fervently toward understanding, not setting its end there, but striving through understanding toward love: then, to one who loves and presses onward, that which is sought often becomes present through a certain blessed experience, when understanding passes into love, or love into understanding, according to the grace of the giver and the zeal or devotion of the receiver. There understanding sees something, but does not see through it completely. As added knowledge adds sorrow, so added wisdom adds love: rejoicing to see, languishing to see fully; not resting sufficiently in what it has received, which is partial, while it anxiously pants after what it has not yet received, which is perfect.

For what ought to be loved ought to be understood; and what ought to be understood ought to be thought upon. For unless that which ought to be loved is made present to the lover by memory and made known by understanding, love itself grows stale and languishes—especially in those things in which love’s enjoyment is prepared through memory and understanding alone, as among rational beings, and still more among spiritual things, but most especially among divine things.

Therefore the mind in which love of the homeland and of God the Father has taken root intensely hates its memory, wandering in foreign places, and its understanding, absorbed in alien occupations. Since love cannot wholly shake these off, ensnared by an unwilling inclination of the flesh, it languishes and suffers within itself. Thus it is said through the prophet: “As the Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI). For fire, naturally always striving upward, when shut up in a furnace burns the more fiercely within itself the more strongly it is held back by foreign obstacles.

Moreover, a torrent held back overflows more violently; fire confined burns more fiercely; and the Bride’s love, restrained, cannot contain itself. Impatient of law, since, while the bond of the flesh holds it, it cannot wholly escape to the place toward which it is wholly borne, it seizes upon whatever is nearest, like fire. The spirit of the lover pours out its whole self upon its neighbor, if perhaps by this way it may deserve to ascend more swiftly and more purely to God. For this reason the Bride turns to the maidens, to the daughters of Jerusalem—daughters of the heavenly peace, companions in desire and partners in her love:

“Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”

For she cannot fail to love in others that by which she herself singularly consoles her pain within herself; and the soul that truly loves God loves and embraces His love wherever it finds it. When it observes the likeness of this love in its neighbor, it often finds it more pleasing than in itself. For, seeing no conscience but its own, it sees in itself both what is evident to human beings and what is hidden; but in its neighbor it sees only what is evident—some fruits, that is, of the Spirit or of love—which it sees, and from which it infers and loves in that person the inward love which it does not see.

In itself it sees both what it lacks and what it possesses; but of its neighbor it can judge only from what it sees. Furthermore, it pursues its own things with strict justice, whereas it interprets all that belongs to its neighbor for the better with kindly charity. Therefore a little good in its neighbor, whose inward mixture it does not see, often pleases it more than much good in itself, whose mixture it alone suffers to be pierced by. Another who is beginning pleases it more than itself when it is progressing; another’s progress pleases it more than its own perfection.

Thus, through the kindly affection of fraternal charity, it enjoys in its neighbor what it cannot enjoy in itself, even when it possesses it—and more than in its neighbor. For, as has been said, where conscience is hidden in the other, only the appearance of good is visible; this it embraces in its neighbor through the rejoicing of fraternal charity. But in itself conscience dwells so much upon what offends that, even if there is perhaps something in it that could please, it does not dare appear before the face of one judging himself more strictly.

Therefore, when the very author of charity orders the Bride’s charity in this way, wearied by her own defects she wholly goes forth from herself and is dissolved into rejoicing at the progress of others. As was said, she approves another’s beginning more than her own end, and another’s progress more than her own perfection. For in flowers, in which there is hope of fruit, the good hope of beginners is signified; while in apples is signified the fruit of the perfect. By the former she is strengthened for delight; by the latter she is surrounded for strength. The flowers of a new creation in Christ breathe a sweeter fragrance to her in beginners than the fruit of her own perfection; another’s fruit of righteousness more than the consciousness of any holiness of her own. From the former, therefore, she receives an incentive to virtue; from the latter, a support.

Yet, in outward respects too, holy youth possesses in the discipline of devotion a certain prerogative of grace, and holy old age possesses its reverence because of the strength of a surer confidence. Tender age has a cheerful and adaptable material for all things; and, like soft wax, it readily receives whatever is impressed upon it and retains it more fittingly—especially when what is natural, that is, what belongs to virtue, is entrusted to it. And as virtue adds beauty to age, so the very flower of age adds a more excellent grace to virtue.

Age also, when advanced in goodness, commends itself to every conscience in which there is any love of good. A life already lived makes it praiseworthy in respect of the past; proven virtue renders it immune, in respect of the future, from every suspicion of changeableness; and old age, deserving through the very law of nature, claims reverence for itself. And as virtue appears more gracious in youth, so it is safer in old age and, as it were, more beautiful in its proper seat.

Accordingly, the Bride is strengthened by the flowers of the young and surrounded by the apples of the old. She delights in the former, is confirmed by the latter, and consoles her own defects by the progress of each. And when the man of God judges his neighbor better than himself, he not only loves him as himself, but also honors him more than himself.

For this is the order of charity and the lawful limit of languishing love. First, the Lord God is loved with the whole heart, that He may be continually thought upon by devout memory; with the whole soul, that one may always live in Him and for Him; with all human powers, that they may faithfully be spent in the work of His service; and with the whole mind, that He may be loved perfectly and intelligently.

Then, with every person according to God, there must be a covenant of nature and good will; while toward oneself and one’s neighbor there must be the affection of religious love, loving one’s neighbor as oneself. The neighbor is everyone who belongs to the household of faith; and among neighbors that person is loved more, as being nearer, who is found more closely joined to God—who is neighbor and beloved—by merit of life and the affection of piety.

A person who is beloved of God and loves God thus loves himself well and in due order, if he makes provision for his flesh not for its desires but for the sake of the spirit, and if he holds charity toward his own spirit in the Holy Spirit for God’s sake. For we do not live for the body; yet we cannot live without the body. We live in order that we may cling to God in spirit, and, by loving Him devoutly and sincerely, may live soberly in ourselves, justly toward our neighbor, and devoutly toward God; and thus, by living in this way, may sometime deserve to live blessedly and eternally in God.

Therefore, in accordance with the Apostle who said, “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V), it is enough not to hate the body. Care must indeed be taken of it, but short of servitude. Yet charity must be given to the spirit, and its proper worship rendered, even to the point of every service of the body. For the body is owed some care by the spirit, that the body may live; but the spirit is owed the body’s complete service, that the spirit may flourish; and God is owed both, that the whole person may serve God.

Thus one who possesses ordered charity loves the Lord his God, and himself in God, and his neighbor as himself, with the same quality and the same measure. For although the perfection of charity in his neighbor may perhaps be greater than in himself, he nevertheless desires it to be as great in that person as he embraces it in himself. But if he discovers or judges it to be greater in his neighbor, he enjoys God in that person more sweetly and, as was said, honors that person more than himself. This, then, is for a human being to love God as his Lord and God, and rightly to love himself and his neighbor as himself.

This is the order of charity: ordained by the law of the Spirit of life, declared by the Word of God in the Holy Spirit, inscribed by the finger of God in the heart of one who loves in order, and sketched by God in the very natural reason of the human being.

Hence the judgment of reason discerns it, and the sense of good will approves it; but the affection of a good mind does not possess it unless the grace of the Holy Spirit breathes upon it. Therefore the Bride is first brought into the wine-cellar, and then charity is ordered within her. At her first entrance, still disordered and intoxicated, she strives to do more than she can; in a single rush of love she undertakes to fulfill whatever God wills. But, failing in God’s salvation, she languishes until, through further advance and blessed progress, the King orders charity within her and she begins also to will what God wills.

Then, through likeness of will, she becomes one spirit with God. The intoxicated becomes sober, the languishing becomes whole, and the vehement becomes ordered. The intoxicated hastens to sleep; the languishing, to the flower-strewn bed; the vehement, to the embrace. Thus comes about the most delightful union of Bridegroom and Bride.

O Charity, God; O Holy Spirit, love of Father and Son, and substantial will: dwell in us and order us, that Your will may be done in us. Let Your will become our will, so that, when we do the will of the Lord our God, we may find His law and order in the midst of our heart. Grant us enlightened eyes of the heart, by which we may behold the light of Your unchangeable truth, so that from it the order of our changeableness and of our mutable, ever-changing will may be formed.

May our soul, Your Bride, loving You, understand in Your own love what it must do concerning itself. Or rather, You who dwell in her—God, who are Yourself Your love within her—cause her to love You from You, O her love; and Yourself, within her, to love Yourself from her, and from her within her to do and order all things according to Yourself.

For this reason You formerly said to Your servant Moses: “See that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV). On the mountain, indeed, the pattern of life and holiness was shown to Moses, when, in the height of contemplation, the order of supreme unchangeableness was revealed to him, so that he might order outward action in all things according to inward vision.

So too, when Your Bride, the soul devoted to You—whoever she may be—is brought into the Bridegroom’s secret chamber, a handmaid into the joy of her Lord, and tastes Your goodness, the very joy of Your charity orders and conforms her wholly to itself according to the pattern of Your goodness. It is not that one thing is commanded there and another forbidden; rather, in the affection of enlightened love, nothing is permitted and nothing desired that in the slightest degree offends either the fittingness of order or the conscience of that joy.

Blessed is the conscience which, whether it has prosperity or adversity in the world, draws its pattern of use and its manner of life from heaven; and wherever it turns, its judgment proceeds from Your countenance, O God. Thus it is always joined to You through likeness in willing the same thing; for one departs from You only through dissimilarity of will.

Therefore every soul that is a Bride desires and seeks this alone: that her face may be continually joined to Your face in the kiss of charity—that is, that she may become one spirit with You through unity of the same will; that the form of her life may be deeply impressed with the form of Your love through the force of great love, or even, if the material is harder, broken in by the power of ordering discipline.

When this has been brought to completion in Your Bride, Your friend, Your beautiful one, then, Lord, the light of Your countenance is marked upon her, and her joy is ordered in the devout soul. All things proceed rightly according to the order of charity; sleeping and resting together in peace, she rejoices in the Bridegroom’s embrace and says:

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.”

This embrace is exercised concerning the human being, but it is above the human being. For this embrace is the Holy Spirit. He who is the communion of God the Father and the Son, who is charity, friendship, and embrace—He Himself, in the love of Bridegroom and Bride, is all these things. There, however, He is the majesty of consubstantial nature; here, the gift of grace. There, dignity; here, condescension. Yet He is the same, wholly the same Spirit.

This embrace is begun here, but is to be completed elsewhere. This abyss calls upon another abyss; this ecstasy dreams of something far other than what it sees; this secret sighs for another secret. This joy imagines another joy; this sweetness foreshadows another sweetness. The matter of this good and of that is indeed the same, but their appearance differs; their nature is the same, but their dignity is other; their sensation is similar, but their majesty diverse. This belongs to mortality; that, to eternity. This belongs to the way; that, to the abiding place. This belongs to holy progress; that, to consummated perfection and perfect blessedness.

For when the face is fully revealed face to face, mutual knowledge is completed, and the Bride knows as she herself has been known, then there will be a full kiss and a full embrace. Then there will be no need of the left hand to support her; rather, the delights of the Bridegroom’s right hand will wholly embrace the Bride unto the end of infinite eternity.

Then, I say, there will be the full kiss and the full embrace, whose power is the wisdom of God, whose sweetness is the Holy Spirit, whose perfection is the full enjoyment of divinity, and in which God is all in all. There faith will not tremble, nor hope be afraid, because perfect charity, in the full vision of God, will transform all affections into the one effect of rejoicing and enjoyment, when everything that belonged to corruption or mortality has either died away or been raised into eternal life.

Meanwhile, however, she says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.” After the exercise of ordering charity, there follows the necessary and desired refreshment and consolation of sweetness, turning all the troubles of that exercise—sweet troubles indeed, yet troubles—into certain experiences and first-fruits of new grace, or into a taste of that future blessedness.

For, that the Bride may now begin to sleep and rest together in peace, she is at times received—not once only, but as often as ordering grace pleases—like that beloved disciple, into the bosom of Jesus, upon His breast; and she is admitted into the secrets of the Son, in whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God.

There the blessed conscience of the Bride rests sweetly: it is supported by the Bridegroom’s left hand, while His right hand wholly embraces it, when devotion is ordered within her together with sufficiency. Thus the grace of spiritual consolations takes possession of her whole being, and the Bridegroom’s compassion does not allow her head, which is the governing part of the mind, to cling to the earth because of want of bodily things.

For although she sometimes has need of certain things, she is not permitted to be in want of anything. For one necessarily succumbs to possessions when it is established that he has needed what he did not possess. Hence the Apostle says: “Having need of nothing, yet enriching many” (II Cor. VI). The one who desires is in need. But one who does not desire, or does not love, whether he has or does not have, confidently says with the Apostle: “For I have learned, in whatever condition I am, to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know also how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be full and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want” (Phil. IV).

This concerns the left hand which, as the Psalm says, the Lord places beneath the just person lest he meanwhile be dashed down (Ps. XXXVI). But concerning the embracing right hand, the Apostle immediately adds: “For I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV). For the embrace of the right hand—that is, of spiritual grace—strengthens the soul, lest it be in want of exterior things that it does not possess, or succumb to those it possesses.

As one who is needy succumbs to such things, so the person who knows how to use them subjects them: if he does not have them, he does not care; but if he has them, he does not keep them slavishly, but dispenses them generously. Therefore the Bride has the left hand beneath her head when sufficient temporal consolation, or contempt for things not possessed, is supplied to the mind devoted to God. But the right hand—that is, spiritual consolations—embraces her when she is both cherished by them in the present and confirmed, for the future, by certainty concerning eternal promises.

The left hand and right hand are bound to the Bridegroom’s heart when both the good use of temporal things and the devout enjoyment of eternal things work together for her love of God; and she sleeps between these portions when, because the Bridegroom delays, she acts patiently.

Ordered charity also has a left hand and a right hand in another sense. This embrace, indeed, is that of charity. It has a laboring right hand and a left hand friendly to rest: that is, the exercise of the active life, busy with much service, and the pursuit of contemplation, offering gentle support to the Bride’s head. And so, as though by two arms or two hands, the beloved Bride is bound, as was said, to the Bridegroom’s heart: by good action and holy contemplation, by reason and love, or by rational knowledge and effective wisdom.

For the contemplative love, or wisdom, is aptly signified by the left hand, which is less active: one thing is sufficient for it, and it has only one thing that is necessary. Hence it is said of Wisdom in the book bearing its name: “Those who are lessened in action shall apprehend her” (Ecclus. XXXVIII). The keenness of reason, or rational knowledge, is likewise well expressed by the right hand, concerning which it is also written: “Times shall pass, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII).

Thus reason draws, and love embraces, while that which is rationally chosen is loved. The Bride’s head—that is, the governing part of the heart—is cherished in the left hand when the rightly disposed mind enjoys, through understanding, that very love which it loves; and thus each works together with the other for good. Love strengthens reason to draw; reason strengthens love to embrace. Love is fortified by reason, and reason is illumined by love.

Or rather, grace that predestines, chooses, and calls goes before: reason affects love, and love affects reason, so that the spiritual mind judges all things while itself is judged by no one. The right hand also labors against tribulations, distresses, persecutions, famine, nakedness, peril, and swords; it is exercised in labor, hardship, and many vigils. But the left hand is patient and kind; it does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, and endures all things.

The works of the right hand are carried on only through many grave labors of exercise, both of mind and body; but those of the left hand can be observed in quiet and silence and do not require great bodily exertion. Yet by both, as has often been said, the Bride is bound to the Bridegroom—by the left as well as by the right—for both the patience of the right hand and the good conscience of the left hand are trained toward His love, toward peace, and toward the unceasing tranquility of a well-disposed mind. The right hand acts and protects; the left hand enjoys.

Whether in this way or that, or in both ways, the Bride, lulled in the Bridegroom’s embrace, is at times hidden in the hiding-place of His face from the contradiction of men; she is sheltered in His tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues. At one time her mind passes out of itself to God, at another she is sober for her neighbor; she is always ready both to remain hidden and to come forth, at the judgment of Him who hides and protects.

Finally, hear Him who hides and protects: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the young of hinds, that you do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wishes” (Cant. III, V). This adjuration declares necessity; that is, it is the effective operation of God’s power. The daughters of Jerusalem—souls newer and more tender in religion—are adjured, each by the virtues she has received, when the fear of losing the grace which she employs in practicing virtues is inspired in them, should they neglect to show due reverence and the fitting affection of rejoicing for the Bridegroom’s secret bridal chamber.

They are adjured by the roes, which are said to possess sharper sight and to love mountains; and by the young of hinds, enemies of serpents and swift in running. Thus they fear to lose the speedy and prosperous success which they seem to possess—the eye of purer contemplation, love of heavenly things, hatred of vices, and progress in virtues—if, through a lesser necessity or a greater importunity, they presume to profane or disturb the joy of the Bridegroom and Bride’s mutual union and enjoyment.

“That you do not awaken,” He says, “or rouse my beloved until she herself wishes.” The Bride is forced to wake when she is disturbed from the sleep of contemplation; she is roused when she is called to labor. Sometimes she wishes to wake from the quiet of her sleep, and sometimes she does not, because in the sleep of contemplation the charity of truth alone is sweet to her. Therefore she does not wish to be roused and called away unless the very truth of charity calls her away from contemplation of beloved truth; and then she does not refuse the work or office of necessity.

Then, in her excess or ecstasy, in the sleep of repose, the Bride hears the voice of Him adjuring—that is, she feels the grace that inspires and sees the power that acts—and sees those others yielding to this grace, yet progressing no less. “The voice,” she says, “of my beloved.” This adjuration, she says, this inspiration, this grace, is the voice of my beloved, who, loving in this manner, is greatly to be loved.

This peace, she says, this sweetness, this sleep of repose, is from the Lord; it is the Lord’s voice, preparing the young of hinds in the progress of the daughters, while revealing to me, His beloved, in the ecstasy of my mind, the dense mysteries and sacraments that are His own. “The voice of my beloved.” Few words, yet rich in grace.

For in this state of mind the matter is not conducted through words; rather, through the power of spiritual understanding and the devotion of affections, there is made one Word: the Word which is with God, God the Word, made in the Bride in that which He works in her. Yet it is called a voice rather than a word because it is not distinguished by syllables or formed by the tongue. It comes to be by pure affection in enlightened understanding, when every sense of body or reason is asleep or at leisure, and the entire business of the matter is wrought by the Holy Spirit in the sense of love.

The voice of this Word is the effective power of divinity, breaking the cedars of Lebanon—the arrogance of human wisdom and worldly height. This voice is heard only in the secret of silence and works only in a pure heart. Wherever it sounds or works, it works in no other way than according to what it itself is.

Our word, as if created in letters, distinguished into syllables, and formed into a word, when uttered by a speaker, produces something like itself and works similarly in the hearer: the same letters, the same syllables, the same word.

So too the Word of God, born of God in the form of God and inseparably, is made in the Bride in what He does in the Bride; and He is made without dissimilarity, because “whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in like manner” (John V). Therefore, when He speaks to the Bride or in the Bride, He speaks or works not something else or otherwise than what He Himself is and as He Himself is. He does not speak or work Himself so as to come into being; rather, working from Himself in her, He causes her to be in Him.

When He speaks to her, He speaks Himself to her; and so, in Himself, He makes known to the one to whom He speaks whatever He wills her to know. Having become wisdom for her, He does in her or through her whatever He wills; He Himself is her power; He Himself is righteousness, existing as the one who justifies her, and sanctification, sanctifying her.

The Word of God speaks to her who is the Bride—Himself and His Father—in the Spirit of His mouth, so fully that, from the fullness of illuminating grace, the whole conscience of one moved by love can scarcely breathe out the flame of its heart in these few words when it says: “The voice of my beloved.”

And the voice itself becomes both that of the Bridegroom to the Bride and that of the Bride to the Bridegroom, in the joy of their mutual union and enjoyment. There they continually speak and answer one another: the goodness of the giver and the love of the receiver. Thus, in the wine-cellar, in the fervor and joy of consummated charity, upon the flowering bed of conscience, that blessed reclining of Bridegroom and Bride is arranged and fitted together, of which the same Bridegroom promises, saying: “If anyone loves me, he shall be loved by my Father; and I shall love him and manifest myself to him; and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

O Love of loves, to whom the Song of Songs is devoted: anyone, however imperfectly, may take it upon his lips though he does not love; yet no one can sing it unless he loves, and loves truly. You know what my heart seeks in expounding Your song. Does the heart of Your servant seek anything else in this, O Spirit who searches all things and possesses knowledge of every voice? Does the intention of Your poor servant labor for anything else than that, by seeing Your brightness and sensing Your charity, my conscience may be enlightened in You; my soul purified by You; and, by treating of what properly belongs to You, may find You more sweet in taste and more fragrant in aroma? May Your savor be sweet to me; may Your fragrance breathe upon me; may my whole life be formed in You and from You.

Come, come, in the abundance of Your blessings, into me Your servant, into my heart, Your place. Unless You first find this place for me, I cannot find it for You—a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Until I find it for You, “I will not go up into the bed of my couch; I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids” (Ps. CXXXI).

Thanks be to You, because through the first-fruits of Your Spirit my former, hateful loves—which, being alien to You, estranged me from You—are now no more. With Your knowledge bearing witness in my conscience, I love You alone, uniquely: always, indeed, by the free judgment of reason; and whenever my mind can be free and master of itself, with the whole affection of my mind.

Yet certain remnants of former loves still bubble up in my memory, like a shadow without a body, a form without substance, a kind of sensation within the thought of vain and empty pleasure, without the assent of the will. Infected by these, conscience can scarcely at times deserve to be purely disposed toward You. Until You wholly turn back my captivity from them, I cannot fully breathe freely in Your liberty, purity, or steadfastness.

But when You come in the riches of Your fullness and the delights of Your goodness to Your poor one, and begin to show him through sure experience in his conscience how truly You are charity, O God; and how God and His love are one; how joy in the Holy Spirit and the Holy Spirit are the sweetness of loving and the beginning of enjoyment, love itself and its understanding—then, through charity praying and interceding for us from within us with unutterable groanings, and through enlightened affections—less by reason compelling toward desire than by contemplating You, O Love, for enjoyment—a sacrifice of praise from Your servant, in Your song, will honor You; and there is the way by which You will show him the salvation of God.

Meanwhile, may my needy and poor love, striving and feeling its way, follow where it is led and sigh for what it is called toward. Through figures of love and through its own imperfection, may it tend toward Your perfection; and, so long as it walks by faith and not by sight, may it devoutly and wisely use its elementary beginnings, until this outward parable of a drama becomes within it the history of truth.

Then in Your light it will become clear how far the devotion of the most simple lover surpasses, in Your understanding, the prudence of the most learned reasoner: when reason has been set behind, devout love itself will become its own understanding.

Now then, after the first reclining in the joy of the wedding feast has in some manner been treated, and after we have assigned to it its Song as best we could—a Song which seems to serve the elementary beginnings of novice fervor—let us, with God’s help, undertake the beginning of the second, in which, with wiser patience and more instructed prudence, the Bride prepares herself for the Bridegroom’s second embraces.

But first the historical sense of the following Song must briefly be tasted in advance and compared with its spiritual sense. As we have from the book of Chronicles, King Solomon, king of peace, having peace in his kingdom after enemies on every side had been subdued and the house of the Lord and the royal palace had been built in Jerusalem, said: “My wife shall not dwell in the house of David my father, king of Israel, because it has been sanctified, since the ark of the Lord entered into it” (II Chron. VIII).

Accordingly, a house was built in Lebanon for his Egyptian wife, Pharaoh’s daughter, outside Jerusalem and far from the royal palace. He commanded her to dwell there until she had completely laid aside her barbarian nature and all the Egyptian admixture. Yet there she might sometimes be visited by the king, and at times she herself might be summoned into the city, the royal house, and the king’s chamber—not to dwell there, but as one who might behold the king’s glory and partake in some measure of the grace of the royal chamber, and then return to her own place.

So too Christ, the King of eternal peace, Bridegroom of the Church gathered from the Gentiles and Bridegroom of the faithful soul set free from the darkness of sins—for Egypt is so interpreted—after the resurrection of His flesh, death having been swallowed up in victory, and after receiving for Himself His kingdom in the heavenly Jerusalem, commands His Bride, so long as she lives in the flesh, to rest in the place provided for her, separated by the condition of mortality from the glory of His heavenly dwelling. For, when ascending into heaven, He said to His disciples: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV).

What He then said to His disciples because of the Holy Spirit’s promised coming, He says even today to all the Bridegroom’s children because of His promise of perpetual dwelling with them unto the end of the age, and because of the grace of a visitation that is sometimes more present and more manifest (Matt. XXVIII).

This city is the Church in the pilgrimage of this life, built in Lebanon—that is, in the elevated and pleasant place of whitening grace. For *Libanus* is interpreted “whitening.” There the Egyptian Bride of Christ dwells: the faithful soul, to be cleansed into purity by the grace of God in the faith of the Church. In anxious devotion she continually directs her heart to the place where she has sent her treasure beforehand, daily awaiting and receiving the daily visitation of divine power clothing her from on high, until, some day released from the bond of flesh, she may deserve to be received into the Bridegroom’s eternal dwelling.

Therefore, there in the Church, in the unity of faith, the Bride is often illumined by the grace of inward visitation; often, by the power of contemplation, the Bride pursues the Bridegroom with devout love even to the vision of heavenly peace and the dignity of the royal chamber. But weighed down by earthly life, she is not permitted to remain there long. Having received the pledge of the Bridegroom’s Spirit and left with Him the pledge of her own spirit, she is quickly sent back from contemplating the Bridegroom’s riches to the house of her own poverty, knowing in some measure what she lacks.

From this point onward, therefore, until the end, this whole holy song of love is woven together. This is all its work and business; from this its parts are distinguished, and the divisions of its parts are brought into accord with one another: hope hastening, desire tormenting, wisdom ordering, love running, grace coming to meet it—until, at the end of the Song itself, the pain of one who desires, caused by the weariness of delay, is at last changed through mutual union into the joy of one who enjoys.

Restored to herself after the first rapture of that first repose, in which she had gone out of herself in mind to God, the Bride, having become sober again and ruminating upon the memory of the sweetness she had tasted, seeks, after the digestion of sacred affections, a secret place. Avoiding publicity, she loves to sit hidden in her cell, in the solitude of her heart, in the retreat of conscience, applying herself to cleansing the heart; anxious, amid mirror and enigma, to cleanse her face so as to see face to face. [Col. 0526C]

For there, she who is the Bride—who, as the Apostle says, cleaving to one, “is not divided, but is concerned only with those things which are the Lord’s, how she may please the Lord to whom she has proved herself” (I Cor. VII)—strives to become holy in body and spirit: without the stain of guilt, without the duplicity of pretence. She strives after what is honourable, and what affords opportunity to beseech the Lord. And, poised in expectation of the Bridegroom’s return—of his voice, of his face—she suddenly hears, as it were, a faint murmur from afar, as of one approaching and speaking with his companions: “The voice,” she says, “of my beloved.” What she says, “the voice of my beloved,” may be fitted both to what precedes and what follows; it may be both the end of the first repose and the beginning of the second. [Col. 0526D]

This also appears aptly suited to the matter at hand. Just as the morning of the following light takes its beginning from the evening of the preceding day, so the consummation of one inner day is often found to be the beginning and cause of another. “The voice,” then, she says, “of my beloved.” And, springing out to meet the one who comes, “Behold,” she says, “this one.”

The Bridegroom’s voice to the Bride is a sudden grace sweetly affecting the lover’s memory; his word is an affection shaped within her understanding. Therefore, at the voice of the Bridegroom who is coming, the Bride says, “Behold”; at the word of one now present and speaking, as though pointing with her finger to the one before her, she says, “This one.” The Bride goes out to meet the Word of God when devout affection hastens toward understanding. And she sees him coming when she mercifully feels him at work within herself. For what is his mercy upon us but his goodness, everywhere going before us?

But the Bride contemplates the Bridegroom’s coming to herself with a nearer and more intimate understanding of love, when she experiences in herself every manner of his coming, both effectively and affectively. She contemplates how the God of mountains comes to the hills; and what she contemplates in them, she experiences in herself, as has been said. She sees him coming to mountains by leaping upon the mountains; to hills, by passing over them. [Col. 0527A]

A mountain is earth raised above earth: that is, when, in some understanding, through love of heavenly things in contemplation of divinity, human nature rises above what is human. Among believers, the one in whom this operates more powerfully is a mountain; he in whom it operates more weakly is a hill. A mountain also is a conscience of righteousness rising from humility of heart into the height of hope. A hill likewise, according to its measure, stands in the same grace of hope, by the grace of God and by the consciousness of fruitful repentance. For the former has grown in the height of righteousness, yet is founded in humility; whereas the latter, although even his righteousness lifts him up before God, nonetheless restrains and humbles himself within himself from fear arising from a humble conscience.

The Bridegroom’s leaps are those of which the Prophet says: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his circuit unto its summit” (Ps. XVIII). Therefore, when the Bride contemplates the Bridegroom’s going forth from the summit of heaven and his circuit unto its summit—between these, his coming down from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb into heaven—what does she marvel at except certain wonderful leaps of his through the heights of so great works, as though across the ridges of the loftiest mountains? [Col. 0527B–C]

When, by the breathing of his love, he infuses faith in these leaps into the understandings of great persons, what does he do except leap upon the mountains? But, leaping upon the mountains, he passes over the hills when this understanding passes by many believers whom faith contains. Thus the Bridegroom comes to the Bride, leaping upon mountains and passing over hills: raising some by the grace of contemplation to higher things, while disposing others in the lower concerns of necessary action.

These leaps or crossings-over are those by which earthly people raise themselves to heavenly things, when from consideration of God’s works and of his great goodness toward us, “the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us” (Rom. V). The leaps of human endeavours indeed spring from the depths to the heights through love of the Spirit; but from above, from the Father of lights, they receive the power of their effect. Hence, when certain holy exultations occur in those who leap, they are, as it were, dances of human perception beyond human use and measure—more eager and higher in proportion as sweeter experiences draw the leaper onward. [Col. 0527D]

But these are leaps upon mountains, upon which the Bridegroom leaps, not upon hills which he passes over. Though the latter stand rooted and grounded in faith, they do not feel the feet of the one passing over; that is, they do not possess the sensible experience of grace affecting them. Yet as one who leaps from earth quickly falls back to earth, so the Bridegroom’s coming to the Bride is fleeting so long as he is still far away. Henceforth, however, having drawn nearer, he will change these leaps into illumined approaches, of which it is said: “Approach him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII); and into ordered ascents, of which the same Prophet says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from thee; he has disposed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, into the place which he has appointed. For the lawgiver will give blessing; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII). Meanwhile the Bridegroom comes, as was said, by leaping and passing over. [Col. 0528A]

These leaps and crossings-over may, however, be understood otherwise. Upon mountains—that is, in the saints—there are free leaps without the obstacle of sin; among hills—that is, among the less perfect—there are crossings-over not without a stumbling-block, although the one leaping does not stumble, but passes over them, forgiving all sins and bestowing grace. Even the just and perfect person leaps in the way of God, that is, proceeds freely; while one still less perfect does have something at which to stumble, yet bravely passes over whatever opposes him, whether from himself or from another.

It follows:

> “My beloved is like a roe or a young hart.”  

Now the Bridegroom coming becomes nearer to the Bride; and though not yet face to face, he nevertheless makes himself known to her through nearer figures. At one time he presents himself through certain affections sharing in divine power and goodness; at another through the effects of his human dispensation. [Col. 0528B–C]

No one doubts that the name *God*, as though peculiarly proper to that highest nature, is taken from Greek. It is derived either from the verb *theōrō* (θεωρῶ), “I behold,” or from *theō* (θέω), “I run”; or rather from both. For what runs more swiftly than that stable motion which, abiding immovably in itself, moves all things? What traverses all things so swiftly as he who spoke and all things were made? He also sees all things easily and at once—the one in whom are all things and who sees all things in himself. The divine nature in the Bridegroom, therefore, is signified by the roe, both because of the swiftness of its course and because of the keenness of its sight.

By the young hart, moreover, the human nature in the Bridegroom is fittingly expressed. For Christ the man appeared in the world like a young hart—that is, as a son of the Jews. He is indeed the beloved son of unicorns; he is also the son of many-horned harts. For a stag appears to possess many antlers in its single horn. The Jews are unicorns, that is, men presuming upon the singular righteousness of the Law; they are also many-horned, glorying in commandments, ceremonies, and the manifold observances of the Law. [Col. 0528D]

Christ, then, appeared in the world as the son of the Jews, like a young hart: the new man who came into the world without sin and lived in the world without sin. And, as it is written, “a most lovely hind and a most gracious young hart” (Prov. V), from the most gracious mother, the Virgin, appeared the most gracious Son, anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

He also comes daily to his Bride, the faithful soul, like a roe of keen sight and swift course, when he produces and cleanses in her the eye of contemplation, and perfects swift effects in the ministry of good action. For, by the wonderful condescension of grace, the wisdom of God, coming to her, subjects and conforms human understanding to itself. Thus, from illuminating grace and illumined intelligence, there arises in some ineffable manner a certain composite wisdom embracing all virtues: so that the human being of God is borne toward God through enlightened understanding, yet the mind of virtues does not deny the effects of its holiness in outward and lower things. [Col. 0529A]

There it sees; here it runs. For the unity of things so diverse could not be fulfilled in one person unless there arose from the Word of God and human intelligence, from the grace of God and human piety, a certain friendly and effective conformity.

He also comes to her as a young hart—that is, as the Son of Man—when, as he once came into the world to the Bride, the Church, bringing the mystery of assumed humanity as a pledge of love, so now he more effectively inspires the faithful soul with a faithful remembrance of that same grace, in the stirring of charity. Thus the Bridegroom is said to be like a roe and a young hart to the Bride when he feeds the hungry and refreshes the afflicted with certain such contemplations or manifestations of God (*theoriae* or *theophaniae*). She is filled with joy only through his countenance.

And when he comes, he does not always leap or pass over; sometimes he also draws near and stands still, when, granting himself to her with a somewhat fuller joy, he consoles by a more abundant grace the weariness of one who longs, the fatigue of one who strives, and the devotion of one who loves. Hence it is added:

> “Behold, he stands behind our wall.”  

Here it should be noted that, when she saw him coming, she said, “Behold, this one”; but when she sees him drawing near, she says, “Lo, he himself.” That is: this one is himself—he who is; not in prophet, angel, or apostle, but revealing himself to me, beyond mirror and enigma, in some measure in himself. [Col. 0529B–C]

For in calling him “this very one,” she confesses that he has drawn near to her not only in the sensible experience of grace but also in the sweetness of experience: so much so that, in that hour or season of divine visitation, only the wall of this mortality separates Bridegroom and Bride from the full kiss of mutual union and the full embrace of mutual enjoyment.

This is the very one to whom Moses said: “Show me thyself” (Exod. XXXIII); and again the Lord said to Moses: “No man shall see me and live” (ibid.). To see the Invisible behind the wall, therefore, is to see him only as much as he can be seen in this life.

“Behold,” she says, “he himself stands behind our wall.” “Behold” conveys awareness of presence; “he himself,” the joy of experience; “stands,” the sweetness of enjoyment. Or the wall separating Bridegroom and Bride is that of which the Prophet says: “In my God I shall pass beyond the wall” (Ps. XVII). What else is it than a mind, memory, and conscience infected by the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of life in outward things? So long as it is thus, it cannot be affected toward God. Hence the prophet says of such persons: “How long do they heap up against themselves thick clay?” (Hab. II). And elsewhere: “Your sins separate between you and God.” [Col. 0529D–0530A]

But when through this thick wall of clay no way of contemplation lies open from Bride to Bridegroom, yet you, O desire of her soul, make for yourself in it straight windows through which you look upon her directly, and slanting lattices through which you look upon her, as it were, from the side. The straight windows are your straight acts of justice, making upright hearts glad; the slanting lattices are the inventions of your goodness and mercy, coming, as it were, sideways from what is undeserved and unexpected.

Through the windows you look upon the Bride by approving what is good in her; through the lattices you look out for her with mercy in those matters in which she needs mercy. Thus, seeing her first, you make her see you; and standing firm for her, you make her stand firm for yourself, until the mutual drawing-near of one who has mercy and one who loves wholly dissolves the enmities of sin—the dividing middle wall—and there comes to be mutual sight, mutual embrace, mutual joy, one spirit. [Col. 0530B]

Meanwhile, too, at times she passes beyond the wall, not in herself but in you, the Lord her God. She is admitted to a clearer understanding, a more perfect knowledge, a sweeter love: not only to experience with you the fountain of life and light in your light, but also to be permitted for a while to stand and enjoy—with feeling so effective, affection so strong, and understanding so manifest—that, as was said above, she seems to be separated from the perfection of full vision only by the interval of human mortality.

This is what she says: “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall.” “He himself,” she says, “is he to whom Moses said: ‘Show me thyself’” (Exod. XXXIII), and of whom the Psalmist says: “But thou art the same” (Ps. CI). For at first she saw, not “himself,” but “this one,” leaping upon mountains and passing over hills; but now she sees “himself” standing. Great is the difference between “this one” and “himself.” “This one” is pointed out externally, as though with a finger; in “himself” the Bride glories and delights within herself. “This one” is in the movement of leaps or crossings-over; “himself” is in the steadiness of a good mind. [Col. 0530C]

Moreover, *en* (“lo”) signifies something nearer than *ecce* (“behold”). For *ecce* points out whatever is present to the senses, however far away; *en* what is at hand or held in the hand.

“Behind our wall.” “This wall of mortality,” says the Bride, “was mine, by reason of the common condition of sin, corruption, and suffering of nature; but the Bridegroom, approaching me, has made it his also by the condescension of his grace and the compassion of his goodness.” “Our wall,” therefore, she says: that wall in which mercy and truth met together. For after the first man’s sin, truth and the severity of truth wove that wall of common mortality for me; but in the time for mercy, mercy wove it for himself.

In it, as was said above, are windows and lattices: straight windows belonging to the righteous Lord who loves righteousness; slanting lattices belonging to one who forgives much to a sinner who loves much. The Bridegroom also, drawing near to the Bride, looks through the windows and looks out through the lattices, when, having drawn near to one who invokes him in truth, he affects her both in those things which belong to his divinity and in those which belong to his humanity. Displaying each aspect of himself to her in a manner fit for contemplation, he solemnly feeds the affection of the lover from both. [Col. 0530D–0531A]

For the soul seeking God, the window through which the eye of reason contemplates God is that through which, by illuminating grace, it beholds spiritual or divine things. It was made in humanity chiefly for this: that through it God might be seen by human beings. And just as, by the illumination of this sun’s light, the bodily eye, when it has an unobstructed gaze and a passage through clear air, advances in seeing wherever it directs itself until sight itself fails through its own weakness, so reason, acting and illumined by grace and aiming directly at divine contemplation, suffers no contradiction at any point in the simplicity and purity of the divine substance unless it gathers darkness of error from elsewhere—until, overwhelmed by itself, it grows weary and yields within itself. [Col. 0531B]
