The windows through which the Bride beholds the Bridegroom are piety, charity, and wisdom—the things called the worship of God. Through them, when she conceives something spiritual or divine by contemplating the Bridegroom’s joy, the Bridegroom sees her; that is, he makes her see.

But in the temporal dispensation of the Mediator, the lattice by which the Bride contemplates is faith in temporal things, through which she is raised to eternal things. In this contemplation the gaze of one beholding God must be turned obliquely, since in the one person of Christ she unhesitatingly marvels at the mystery of the twofold nature and worships both natures in the Mediator in unity of person. In the aspect of assumed humility, reason moving toward God seems to human beings especially to be made oblique, until, by faith illumined through grace, God who is man and man who is God begins not merely to be believed but also to be understood. Then the contemplative mind begins most delightfully to be fed in the one person. [Col. 0531C]

Then the Spirit speaks mysteries to understanding; the Word of God speaks himself; and his word swiftly runs into affection when, in the one to whom he speaks, the things intelligibly heard are effectively accomplished. For one rises and hastens, and whatever the ensuing word appears to command or teach to be done is done.

It follows:

> “Behold, my beloved speaks to me: Rise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song II.10).

He calls her friend when he makes her his friend, making known to her all things whatsoever he heard from his Father. He calls her dove when he makes her his own—that is, capable of the Holy Spirit, such as appeared over the Lord at his baptism. He exhorts her to take up the wings of spiritual understandings and flee into the solitude of the heart and the secret place of a simple conscience. He names her his beautiful one when he reforms her, according to the dignity of her ancient condition, to his image and likeness. He commands her not merely to rise and come but also to hasten: that is, not merely to love, but to love vehemently. [Col. 0531D–0532A]

He commands her to rise from earthly things when he inspires in her contempt for all earthly things; he commands her to come when he draws her; to hasten when he impels her. Thus, the Bride says, “My beloved speaks to me”: that is, the Word of God comes to be in the heart of one who hears and loves, when, as was said, the hearing of the almighty Word has now become affection for what is heard.

But he is heard through bodily senses, as through the sight gained in reading and the hearing of instruction, and at times through the grace of inward inspiration, calling the hearer from flesh to spirit and from the senses to inward understanding, so that the hearer may be not in the flesh but in the Spirit. This he does when he says, “Rise”; he shakes off torpor when he says, “Hasten”; he allures love when he says, “My friend”; he bestows grace when he says, “My dove”; he orders life and character when he says, “My beautiful one.” [Col. 0532B]

Then he says, “Winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed,” when he causes the winter of disturbances to pass and scatters the storms of vices, God making us for this very thing. First he exhorts her to rise; then, lest she who obeys should fail through fear of temptations, he tells her that winter and rains have departed with the softened storm of vices, and the pleasing temperateness of holy virtues, as it were, freely presents itself.

Until now, while she lay hidden and fearful amid winter’s temptations and the storms of vices, it was enough for her to remain safely within herself. She had no care or concern except for herself; no movement beyond herself; no flowers in the divine Scriptures; nowhere the grace of spiritual joys or the fruit of the Spirit, signified by the fragrance and blossoms of vineyards and the early figs; no retreat into the deeper things of more secret wisdom, signified by the turtle-dove, which speaks mysteries in places remote from the multitude—that is, among the perfect. Now she hears:

> “Rise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter has now passed; the rain has gone and departed. Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning is at hand; the voice of the turtle-dove has been heard in our land; as the fig tree has put forth its early figs, the flowering vines have yielded their fragrance” (Song II.11–13). [Col. 0532C]

Then, with the familiar names of grace repeated, she is again commanded to rise, hasten, and come. For first she is awakened by prevenient grace; then, by the subsequent judgment of reason and free choice. And, as conscience bears witness to her that we are children of God, the goodness which awakens her commends itself more sweetly and intimately.

This is what follows:

> “Rise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, and come; my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall” (Song II.13–14).

And what is said comes to pass: the Bride carries out what the Bridegroom exhorts. As winter recedes, tranquillity is granted; as the Bridegroom appears, the Bride exults. She delights to proceed and to follow wherever he goes the footprints of one promising happier things: outside the house, outside the city—that is, beyond the nature of the human condition and beyond the common manner of life—into the hidden places of the Son, which are the clefts of the rock; into the secrets of the Law, which are the hollows of the wall. [Col. 0532D]

For Christ the Rock is not closed on every side, but has clefts through which God is revealed. And the wall of the Law, by which two peoples are separated from one another, has penetrable hollows in the Word of God, which is more penetrating than any two-edged sword, through which things diverse and opposed are reconciled to one another. There also is the time of pruning, because when useful things are born, useless and harmful things are often wont to grow up within them unless they are more carefully cut away.

It follows: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face lovely.” The dove is wont to nest in the clefts of the rock and in the hollows of the wall, and thence to show her face and make her voice heard: a pleasing face and a groaning voice. What is this, except a conscience established in Christ and in faith in him, bearing the fruits of the Spirit, having a voice of confession pleasing to God, and sighing in hope because of the delay of future things? [Col. 0533A–B]

The Bride shows this face to the Bridegroom who desires it when, in the light of his countenance, a holy conscience loves to appear before its Creator. This voice of the Bride is sweet in the ears of the Bridegroom when it reaches him as it proceeds from her—namely, as love brings it forth.

Let us return a little to what went before and review the sequence of the matter according to the order of events and the rationale of the words. The Bride sat by herself, awaiting the Bridegroom’s return. Having the pledge of the Spirit, she trusted that he would return soon; she prayed, wept, and longed for his return. Suddenly she seems at first to hear what she does not see and to perceive by inward sense what she does not understand—the presence of divinity—and she says: “The voice of my beloved.” [Col. 0533B–C]

All the senses of the faithful soul are made joyful, and she hastens to meet him. Advancing a little, she sees him coming to her by leaping—that is, hastening—and passing over those who have little faith and cannot receive the coming of one who hastens; or rather, leaping over every understanding and passing beyond every reason. Seeing him coming to her, she recollects herself within herself in order to receive him, sensing him draw near and stand behind the wall.

And seeing him looking through the windows, looking out through the lattices, and offering himself to one who longs for him, she begins through experience itself to understand the mysteries of divine love: namely, that he often withdraws from her in order to be sought more ardently; and that he sometimes restores himself to one who loves, lest she be swallowed up by more vehement sorrow. [Col. 0533C]

When, at the voice of one calling and exhorting, she rises in order to see and hastens in order to hold him, suddenly he who appeared vanishes, and with him all that spiritual and divine loveliness of vineyards and flowers. For all his sweetness follows the Author of sweetness as he departs, together with all his delights: the joy of flowers, the fragrance of vineyards, the abundance of fruits. From the friend departs the confidence of friendship; from the dove, beauty of face and sweetness of voice; from the beautiful one, the grace of divine conformity.

There remains for the friend her solitude; for the dove, her groaning; for the beautiful one, her private condition. The clefts of the rock are closed and the hollows of the wall blocked, no longer receiving the dove, which has no heart. [Materially uncertain: the printed phrase *non habeatem cor* appears corrupt; perhaps “the dove that does not have a heart.”] Moreover, little foxes rush upon the flowering vineyards: that is, subtler insinuations of the enemy injure well-disposed minds, or deceptive introductions of scandals lay vineyards waste. [Col. 0533D–0534A]

For the following admits both readings: either, “Catch for us the little foxes which destroy the vineyards,” or, “Catch for us the foxes which destroy the little vineyards.” Foxes destroy little vineyards, which more mature vineyards do not fear. For only the little ones are scandalized, of whom the Lord says: “Whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones” (Matt. XVIII).

“Catch,” he says, “the foxes for us.” Whoever possesses discernment of spirits catches these foxes for himself: he quickly detects the deceitfulness of sin creeping in and subjects its desire to himself. Yet the wise Bride asks that they be caught for her—that is, for her benefit, by holy teachers or by her holy guardian angels—not trusting sufficiently in her own perception or strength to think herself able by herself to catch them.

For in this those who are tempted become manifest: one is tempted for approval, another for rejection. The one trusts himself less than anyone else in his temptations; the other trusts himself to no one except himself. But foxes are caught for the Bride herself because it most greatly advances her salvation that her vineyard be preserved undefiled for the Bridegroom. For, she says, “our vineyard has flowered.” She is not wholly forsaken whose vineyard is still in blossom—that is, whose mind remains in hope. [Col. 0534A–B]

For she who is the Bride is never so far forsaken by the Bridegroom that she forsakes him when he withdraws: enjoying him humbly when present and enduring him patiently when absent. She herself is the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, of whom the Lord says to the Prophet (Hos. III): “Dig her for me, and I said to her: For many days you shall wait for me; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man; and I too shall wait for you.”

For this reason the Bride, who is also the vineyard, continues and says:

> “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathe and the shadows incline” (Song II.16).

Happy is the mind, blessed the conscience, and truly the Bride of the Bridegroom, whose voice this is when she has been forsaken; whose failing in lower things is righteousness; whose deficiency is the perfection of the Bridegroom’s daughters. “Blessed is he whose Lord is his God” (Ps. CXLIII), and who is wholly his: in whom the grace of God, however it may at times affect the conscience, has already restored nature. [Col. 0534C–D]

For the state of a good mind is one thing, and affection another. The good constitution of a nature stably renewed in God through grace working is one thing; the temporary, momentary uplifting to God of that same good constitution by grace affecting it is another. The former belongs to one made a bride; the latter to one perfected.

“My beloved,” she says, “is mine, and I am his.” “Others,” she says, “belong to others; my beloved is mine. Other women belong to others; I belong to him alone.” This is not the voice of a conscience prostituted to alien loves; it is not the profession of trembling faith and doubtful love, or of a disturbed conscience and wavering intention.

Ever happy, I say, is the mind and blessed the conscience which, amid expectation of the Bridegroom who delays and the prolongation of its sojourn in this life, has this consolation. Amid the heat of worldly wickedness, it is a conscience of hope: a shade of refuge, consolation in pain, relief in labour, incentive to love, enlargement of heart amid this life’s pressures, and a certainty of faith and expectation concerning the future. [Col. 0535A]

He himself says: “In all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed; we are perplexed, but not driven to despair; we suffer persecution, but are not abandoned; we are cast down, but do not perish,” and so forth (I Cor. IV).

This stable condition of the good mind is piety, which according to Job is the “worship” of God (Job XXVIII); according to the Apostle it is “profitable for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (I Tim. IV). It is the form of faith and virtue, capable of spiritual graces, suited to sacred affections, and always near to divine understandings. To those established in this state the Apostle says: “So stand in the Lord, beloved” (Phil. IV); and again: “Nevertheless, to what we have attained, let us remain in it” (Phil. III). [Col. 0535A–B]

Yet here there are still only flowers of the flowering vineyard: hope of fruit, not fruit itself. But here, already to those ascending from the valley of tears, from the region of heavenly blessedness there begins to breathe upon the progressing soul, the loving Bride, a breeze of truth and a sweeter fragrance of the Bridegroom’s ointments, bringing richer first-fruits of the Spirit from the mystery of divine love, sweeter affections, and surer experiences. The more frequent and sweeter these become, the more the rewards of purity themselves render charity wondrous in a purer life.

For the disposition and settled state of an ordered life belongs to the soul as health belongs to a sound body; but all these experiences belong to a good mind as the acts of health belong to a healthy body, whether for a necessary use or at the pleasure of the will. Just as bodily health is in some sense unaware of itself and is not highly valued before the occasion of necessity or will, so that health of the soul is unaware of itself and is not highly valued while it remains in the blossom of hope, before the fruits of the Spirit. [Col. 0535B–C]

A prepared dwelling therefore requires its inhabitant; an empty bed, love’s counterpart; enduring faith, the joy of enjoyment. This is what she says: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” “He,” she says, “is mine, God making me for this very thing; I am his, made for this very thing. He is mine, granting grace beforehand; I am his, not ungrateful to the giver. He is mine, giving faith; I am his, preserving it.”

And the Bridegroom, even while the Bride does not know it, feeds upon that by which she is tormented, because without embrace and kiss, without the sweetness of mutual union, she accepts no consolation. Hence she continues and says: “Who feeds among the lilies.” [Col. 0535C–D]

The lily is the most beautiful among flowers, but sterile. Rising from the earth upward upon a straight, green stem, it is white outwardly but fiery in colour within. It is exceedingly pleasing to sight, sweet to smell, and possesses a natural power of softening hard things. Before sunrise, when the cold and night’s darkness are upon it, you may see the lily as though shrinking back and hiding within itself, keeping its tender delights closed within itself. But as soon as the more serene face of the rising sun shines upon it, it seems, as though smiling, to open its entire self to the sun and to return all its glory to its author.

This is the state of a good mind, produced by creating grace, but still sterile of the fruits of understanding and wisdom, which it awaits from illuminating grace. It is the conscience of a will and intention directed toward God, displaying before men the whiteness of chastity and outward works of faith, while presenting to God the inward fragrance of continual desire. It carries the good fragrance of Christ everywhere; in tribulations and pressures it possesses the virtue of patience to soften every hardness of human wickedness. It holds all its goods hidden in creating and giving grace, until its righteousness is brought forth like light and its judgment like noon in the manifestation of illuminating grace. [Col. 0536A]

But two meanings are understood in the word “feeds”: both the one who feeds another and the one who is fed. Therefore, among lilies of this kind the Bridegroom feeds—that is, is fed—when the fruitful will of the Bride solemnly delights him amid the mournful, sterile conscience of the lily. He also feeds the Bride, though she does not know it, when in the very delay of himself he nourishes her love of himself.

The Bride indeed knows what is done within her and what the Bridegroom does within her so long as they belong to one another; but she does not feel it while they are not mutually present to one another. They belong to one another by faith and are present by love; or they belong to one another by love and are present by affection. And things are well so long as they belong to one another; but best when they are present to one another. [Col. 0536B]

This is what follows: “Until the day breathe and the shadows incline.” For when the day breathes and the shadows incline, Bridegroom and Bride will no longer so much belong to one another in mutual assent as be present to one another in enjoyment; nor will the Bridegroom feed among the sterile loveliness of lilies, but amid the full abundance of the fruits of the Spirit.

For when, through the breathing of the Holy Spirit, even in this life our night is illuminated like day for an hour, for a time, and the shadows of worldly vanities incline, yielding to the light of truth—or rather, at the setting of this life, which is night and not light, and in the reception of the morning of the other life; or most properly in eternity’s morning, on the day of the general resurrection—then Bridegroom and Bride will begin not merely to belong to one another through faith, but to be present to one another through sight, face to face. Nor will the Bridegroom feed the Bride after the manner of sterile lilies in the blossom of hope, but in the fruit of reality. And then all the shadows of the vanity of this age will wholly incline: that is, they will be cast down from their assumed standing. [Col. 0536C]

[Col. 0536D] Then, just as once the new sacraments of grace put an end to the old sacraments, so the reality itself of all sacraments will put an end to every sacrament whatever. For in the sacraments of the New Testament the day of new grace began to breathe forth; but at that end when all things are consummated there will be noon, where there will be no mirror, no enigma, and no partial knowledge, but vision face to face and the fullness of the highest good. There the intellect will be fixed upon that sun around which reason was wont to range; there the affection will enjoy that for which love was wont to burn—not the intellect of reasoning, but of love illumined; not an affection in any way produced by what is loved, but effected by God in a divine manner, as the Apostle says: “God, who brings us to this very thing” (2 Cor. V).

For all the powers, virtues, wills, intentions, and affections of the soul of the human being glorified with God, [Col. 0537A] freed by the power of the resurrection from slavery to corruption and subjection to vanity, will be immutably established: fully to see what was gradually believed; most certainly to possess what was tremblingly hoped for; and securely to enjoy what was loved by faith. For this day of the present life, as it breathes forth, is changeable and does not possess an uninterrupted joy of its own light; rather, it has its hours—alternations in which illuminating grace dawns, drawing one nearer to God, in order to enlighten.

But the day of heaven, the day of eternity, the day above days, free from every shadow of this world, is wholly devoted to its own light and its own joy: without longing to will anything further, without fear of losing, without grief over what has been lost. Meanwhile “the expectation of creation, awaiting the revelation of the sons of God,” [Col. 0537B] groans and is in travail until now; and “we ourselves, who have the first-fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption as sons of God, the redemption of our body” (Rom. VIII). Preserve these things for those who possess them; bestow them on those who do not possess them, O Bridegroom of charity and chastity, so that your Bride—whatever faithful soul she may be—languishing after you and failing in herself, failing in your salvation but not away from your salvation, may meanwhile here taste a few hours of your day until she receives the full day. In this world she rejoices like faithful Abraham, that she may see your day, see it and rejoice, and that no one may take her joy from her (John VIII).

Breathe upon those who, from the depths of the night’s darkness of this life, hope in you, sighing and aspiring toward you: breathe, O day of days, day [Col. 0537C] of power, day above days, day who are and do not fail; who change all things within yourself but are not changed. Already, by some portion of your light which you have breathed upon us, O sun of righteousness, by the rays of your most manifest truth, these shadows of death, these shadows of the vanity of this world, are to some degree inclined for us; and the vanity of vanities becomes plain to us, and it becomes manifest to us, more clearly than light, that all things are vanity. And would that your truth shone forth to us in itself as this vanity appears to us in its light! For to those who attend prudently and assess these things by the light of your truth, they disclose themselves as vain and contemptible by their inseparable neediness, inherent misery, and unceasing failure.

Therefore all [Col. 0537D] the children of your light, and all who are not rebels against your light, give you thanks: those upon whom you have already shone so far that all these things are now known to them in you and do not deceive them, although they may still sometimes allure and impede them, since they are no longer loved from affection, though they may sometimes be attended to from necessity. For even if remembrance of the world sometimes steals into the mind, or enters thought with some pleasure, the will immediately meets it, reason awakening in memory; and, as the Holy Spirit aids human weakness and your light continually breathes upon it, those shadows are at once inclined through contemplation of that vanity and apprehension of your truth, the will being turned into love for you, so that it admits no pleasure outside you.

And immediately your light, O day of days, strikes the memory of the world [Col. 0538A] with horror of itself, and in place of the empty sweetness of worldly pleasure sprinkles a true and most bitter bitterness. Hence, O charity of chaste generation and Bridegroom of holy souls, your Bride, who keeps her will always devoted to you—at one time in tormenting desire, at another in enjoying love—cannot, during this time of alternation, attain in you and from you the stability of unbroken joy. Although by the testimony of a good conscience she continually possesses this in the state of good will, she does not possess it in feeling.

For, according to the counsel of your wisdom, the good pleasure of your will, and the judgment of your justice, you come and go. Sometimes, like a most pleasing doe and most pleasing fawn, you allow yourself to be apprehended by faith; often you even deign to be held in meditation; sometimes to be caressed by love. But when you are held more intensely and possessed more delightfully, you suddenly slip away, taking delight in the anxious weariness and fatigue of the love that runs after you, while it weeps and cries after you:

> “Return; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song II.17).

That is to say: If, so long as there is time and season, you do not grant me to possess you continually for enjoyment, at least be swifter to return, as you are swift to depart and abandon me. Let the alternation be more frequent, the flight slower, the return swifter, and your presence more familiar and more enduring. Your even momentary presence, or a small share of you, is of great value to me: some little liberty of understanding in beholding you; some whisper [Col. 0538C] of your voice; even a slight taste of your sweetness; the fragrance of your ointments; some condescension of your kiss and your embraces. For these are to me the pledge of the Spirit, the earnest of eternal blessedness, the foundation of faith, the strength of hope, and the incentive of love.

“Return,” then, she says: return. Return, though you are immediately to depart again; coming in, make glad; slipping away, make sad. Whatever comes to me from you is good, because you who are good do all things well; and whether you depart or return, this affection continually consoles me, whatever privations I suffer from you. For, as we said above, that we may gain some experiential sense, from the practice of carnal love, of the spiritual love and affection of Bridegroom and Bride, the Bridegroom often seems, as if in playful love, to mock the Bride [Col. 0538D] and frequently withdraw himself from her vehement love, then again give himself back to her desire. Sometimes he goes out and departs as though never to return, so that he may be sought more ardently; sometimes he returns and enters to her as though to remain forever, so that he may be more sweetly invited to kisses. Sometimes he stands behind the wall and looks through the windows, so that, to kindle the desire of the lover, he appears to flatter but not wholly; he is heard calling or inviting, but from afar. Then, as though a fire had been kindled in the heart of the lover, he goes away altogether and withdraws, so that he is neither seen nor heard nor felt.

But when the Bride cannot hold him as he departs, she at least sometimes asks him to return and says: “Return, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains [Col. 0539A] of Bethel.” Blessed is the Bride’s conscience, which so often calls upon the Bridegroom by this name, “my beloved.” For this is what he said: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI). When the beloved woman calls the beloved man by the name “beloved,” the name both displays and stirs the love of the caller; it commends the one who calls, and the conscience and devotion of the lover draw the one whom she calls.

Happy and well-omened is the prayer to God that, in the Holy Spirit, calls upon the one to whom it prays by this name; blessed is the soul whose prayer is commended by the confidence of this conscience. For what can one who prays thus not hope for? She prays him to return whom she possesses; she possesses the one whom she loves. Hence it is written: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. CXLIV). For the truth of calling upon him lies in the affection of the lover; and in the conscience of the one invoking him there is made a sure [Col. 0539B] proof of the most present presence of him who said: “I am the truth” (John XIV).

“Return,” therefore, she says, “my beloved.” For when you depart, all things are disturbed; when you turn your face away, holy affections collapse into failure; bitterness enters the conscience and irrational sorrow; among the brethren all things are full of scandals; in solitude there is tumult of mind. The inward light flees; crushing darkness wraps one round; faith languishes, hope trembles, charity grows weary; the mind becomes drunken and no longer master of itself; the body is a burden to the mind, and the mind to the body. Prayer totters, reading is sullied, meditation becomes barren; there is utter sterility of mind through hardness of heart, and the whole world fights against the wretched and senseless person.

But when you return, or turn [Col. 0539C] your face toward me, all things become serene and tranquil through the joy of your countenance and the sweetness of your presence. Holy joy arises from a holy conscience; understanding flourishes, zeal burns, affection is enlightened, the mind rejoices in God, the world grows cheap, the body serves. Strength increases, virtues are strengthened, faith is enlightened, hope is fortified, charity is set in order. There is frequent joy in the Holy Spirit, sweet fellowship with the brethren, and sweeter solitude with God; the mind is stable and fruitful in spiritual perceptions; prayer is eager, reading useful, meditation rational; and spiritual zeal prospers in everything. Action becomes earnest and leisure is sanctified; nowhere is there scandal, nowhere contradiction; humility in prosperity and courage in adversity. And so long as you, the strong armed man, guard your court, [Col. 0539D] all that you possess is in peace (Luke XI).

“Return,” therefore, “my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag.” What shall we say of the gazelle? It has sharper sight. “I do not wish,” she says, “to hide myself, like Adam (Gen. III), from the face of him who sees all things, whether approving or reproving; rather, Lord, I seek your countenance; my face seeks your face” (Ps. XXVI). You will also grant me the keenness of my inward eyes, that I may attend to you and provide for myself. And as the gazelle is swift, you will grant me also swiftness of spirit to understand concerning you, just as your word runs swiftly.

What of the young stag? It possesses a power from its father’s nature by which serpents flee from it and poisons do it no harm. So, wherever the Son of God turns himself, that ancient serpent flees; and at his power it loses all its strength, all its poison. “Upon the mountains of Bethel,” [Col. 0540A] or “Bether.” Bethel is interpreted “house of God”; Bether, “the house rising up” or “the house of watchfulness.” Bethel, therefore, consists in those in whom God dwells more familiarly: the simple children of God, humble and quiet, trembling at his words, upon whom the Holy Spirit rests. It is the house rising up, which always strives toward higher things; the house of watchfulness, in which those keep continual watch who await with devout and careful expectation the Bridegroom Lord’s return from the wedding.

The Bride therefore prays the Bridegroom to dwell more frequently over the house of Bethel or Bether: either enlightening it in contemplation of himself, or lifting it up in contempt for the world through love of God; or leading minds wakeful for him into the inward joys and silent places of a good conscience through enjoyment of himself. She also prays him to come more frequently upon the mountains, that is, upon the height of human perfection: namely, that the mountains may flow away before the face of the Lord, when all great persons judge themselves to be nothing in comparison with God and without his grace.

When, then, the Bride of Christ, the faithful soul, is sometimes admitted in some measure to contemplate her joy but cannot remain longer to enjoy it, and when that whatever-it-is slips in upon her unexpectedly and, just as suddenly, slips away from her grasp, then what follows occurs: “Be like a gazelle or a young stag.” In saying “be,” her well-disposed human will assents to the will [Col. 0540C] of God, most certainly believing that whether he deigns to visit one who desires him or seems, by withdrawing, to abandon her, whatever the best God does is good for the person to whom it is done. And when she anxiously seeks him as he slips away, though she had delightfully held him as he entered, what follows occurs:

## CHAPTER III

> “Upon my bed, through the night, I sought him whom my soul loves.”

First one must observe here that, just as night comes when day withdraws, and the eyes of the body are opened in vain in darkness when light is absent, so the Bride’s intention strives in vain, by the force of reason, to contemplate what she desires without the assistance of illuminating grace. Therefore she says: “Upon my bed, through the night, I sought him [Col. 0540D] whom my soul loves.”

But first we must see what is indicated to us here even according to the literal sense. The Bride, seeking the Bridegroom, can have neither day nor night free from occupation. Indeed, even literally, those who keep watch know how great an opportunity nocturnal vigils offer for the pursuits of spiritual exercise, and what fruits of the Spirit they bring to those watching for the Bridegroom’s return. For this is properly the time of the mind and of the things that belong to the mind. The senses are at rest, and nothing makes a clamor through them. First there is the privacy of the chamber, then the repose of the body through sleep. After the day’s labors and afflictions of this life, the bed consoles the person meditating upon God, as it consoled holy Job (Job VII). This is not the bed of a dead man’s grave or an inn of drunkenness, but the workshop of spiritual studies [Col. 0541A] and the place of sacred visions, where one is free to dream what one has wished to think, and where what was not disclosed to the wakeful person is often revealed to the sleeper.

Then, after yesterday’s food, cares, and thoughts have been digested, sobriety returns both to mind and body. Just as a fasting stomach more effectively cooks, more pleasantly digests, and more profitably assimilates the first food it receives to nature, so the fasting mind of one who wakes attends and clings more tenaciously to what first meets its thought—above all, to that with which it agrees. Therefore, for one who wakes and is the Bride, after sleep that is sober and only sufficient for nature, it is most important to take care that, still as it were undefiled and virgin, she may at once be united with the Bridegroom, cleave to God, and be affected wholly by him as far as she is able. Thus, throughout the night and throughout the day, remaining holy and immaculate in body and spirit, she may not be divided, but may belong wholly to him to whom she has proved herself, and receive no admixture of any base affection for another.

But in a higher sense, the Bride seeks within [Col. 0541B] the Bridegroom whom she lost without: in the chamber of the heart, in the secret place of the mind, in the conscience. For outwardly those things which concern action are performed: the Bridegroom commands, the Bride obeys. But inwardly the things of love are conducted—secret conversations and hidden mysteries—so long as the Bridegroom is present. For when the Bridegroom is absent, there is perpetual night there, a fearful solitude, a tedious dwelling, and no rest. Although he is always there by unfailing power, yet by the hidden counsel of his wisdom he is not continually there by grace presiding. For, as Solomon says: “There is a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces” (Eccl. III).

Therefore she adds: “I sought him, and did not find him.” When she does not find him, she calls him with a cry as great as the longing by which she pants for him; but he does not answer her call so long as he does not grant the desiring woman possession of himself according to her wish. She does this in the night—a night in which she does not begrudge spending the whole night again and again upon this task. The darkness of this life and the dense gloom of the world, the night of temptation or tribulation, may sometimes hinder her from the pursuit of seeking, but cannot deter her from it. Blessed is the person who fears “all [Col. 0541C] his works” (Job IX) and “is always afraid” (Prov. XXVIII): not as wickedness is always ordinarily cowardly, but because human blindness and weakness must always be suspect to itself.

Only she who loves and is the Bride knows these hardships of love in relation to the Bridegroom: the trials caused by his delay, the joy of possessing him, the fear of losing him, and the pain of having lost him. She seeks him best in the chamber who always labors for this end: always to have him with her in the chamber, preparing for him the chamber of her heart, that she may have him in conscience and meditation, in understanding and affection, in the service of devotion with the testimony of devoted action. “I sought him,” then, she says, “upon my bed,” where I was accustomed to find him more familiarly and frequently. I sought whether he was there in the truth of seeking, so that, as the order of charity advanced, I too might be present with him in the joy of seeing and sweetness of enjoying—the one who is always accustomed to be near to all who invoke him in truth. “I sought him and did not find him.” [Col. 0542A]

Why? Perhaps because it was night: the intention, wearied, had slightly slackened; the light was diminished for the seeker, and the fervor or heat for the desiring person. For if she had sought from affection, she would have found him in understanding, and would have been most happily in his embrace. But it seems more fitting that, just as the Bridegroom’s approach to the Bride occurs to console her weariness, so his withdrawal sometimes occurs to test her or even to increase her desire. For desires that fail because of delay are not true desires. Accordingly, the Bride reveals, by adding the following words, what she did in the Bridegroom’s absence:

> “I will rise and go round the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves.”

What is this city, these lanes, and these streets in which the Bridegroom seems to be sought and yet is not found? Surely it is the city of which the psalm says: “I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city; day and night iniquity will surround it upon its walls; labor and injustice are in its midst, and usury and deceit have not departed from its streets” (Ps. LIV). There the man of one mind, who takes sweet food together with the Bridegroom himself, extends treachery against him (Ps. XL); there the flesh lusts against the spirit (Gal. V), or neighbor against neighbor.

What is this city? The world. What is this city? To say it with grief: the worldly world, the Church in the world. I shall say more, and say it sorrowfully: every religious order, every religious habit. If the world—that which belongs to the world—conducts worldly affairs, custom and despair make us bear it more patiently and grieve over it less. But in [Col. 0542C] the Church of the living God, which, as the Apostle says, “is the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. III), above all in religious orders that profess the pursuits of a stricter life, who would not weep with tears of blood and heart that those perilous times have arrived which the Apostle foresaw would come in the last days—namely, “people loving themselves, having indeed a form of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. III)?

This city is now the whole world; and wherever Jerusalem seems to be, Syria and Damascus lawfully establish their garrisons there and reduce it to streets, without any opposition. For who today, while professing Christ’s poverty, does not endeavor and strive, with bosom swollen by riches and purses filled, to surpass even the rich of the world? The possession of religious persons is the greater part of the world. In deserts palaces are built; in solitudes and caves perfumed cells are constructed. No one entering religion now deigns to make even the smallest journey on his own feet; and though they rejoice to be called Christians or disciples of Christ, they do not, to put it somewhat mildly, sufficiently imitate in this respect either the example of Christ or that of Christ’s disciples. He who does not know how learns to ride; he who does know is ashamed to unlearn it.

What corner, moreover, is found today where that offense so notably marked by the Apostle is not abundant—namely, that “we have lawsuits among ourselves” (1 Cor. VI)? And would that the lawsuits themselves corresponded to their name, so that they were not unjust. Granted, we do not rob or defraud; but neither can we endure being robbed or defrauded, nor buy time at the cost of losing anything, so that, attending to our own business, we may eat our bread in silence. In the world’s covetousness we are enslaved to worldly people, flattering sinners and seeking not them but what belongs to them. Are not these the broad streets of the world by which one goes to death? Are not these the lanes of the world—various, indeed, but nonetheless worldly ways of living?

If we truly had wisdom, we would fear what the Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, one of those who have nothing and possess all things, says: “Those who desire,” he says, “to become rich fall into temptations and snares of the devil, and into many harmful desires which plunge people into the destruction of condemnation” (1 Tim. VI). [Col. 0543B] For by whatever occasion and under whatever appearance greed steals in, it is always “the root of all evils” (ibid.); and all who seek it “entangle themselves in many sorrows” (ibid.).

Yet amid so great a multitude of rich people in danger and laughing, there is sometimes found a poor-in-spirit man of God. As though rescued from the disturbance of a raging sea and set apart with himself in the harbor of most placid and peaceful charity, the same Apostle says to him: “Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life” (ibid.). For whatever has been said above, every man of God flees and escapes it, laboring courageously, but casting all his care upon God; avoiding negligence, placing his confidence in God, and always retaining a firm desire to please him. He has a good will to assist all, without the fault of covetousness; he prepares, with labor, whatever he can; what he has prepared he distributes prudently and generously; everywhere he prompts and seeks the affection of love, while execrating and fleeing the desire to please others.

For religion in which greed rules is the streets of Syria and Damascus in Jerusalem (3 Kings XX), and the lanes in which the Bridegroom is not found.

> “Through the lanes and streets I sought [variant: I will seek] him whom my soul loves.”

What does this mean? Is the Bridegroom in public? Is he in streets and lanes? Yet impatient love thinks he must be sought everywhere and, when it wishes to find him, that he cannot fail to be found anywhere. “He whom,” she says, “my soul loves.” Why not rather, “my spirit”? Because “the spiritual” does not come first, but “the animate,” and then the spiritual. By “soul,” which gives life, life itself is understood, by that manner of speaking in which the effect is understood through its cause. Therefore her soul loves and seeks the Bridegroom for whom Christ is life, in whose life Christ is glorified; for whom everything in him that lives serves, and who desires to live for this alone: that all which lives in him may serve Christ.

“I sought [variant: I will seek],” she says, “him whom my soul loves.” Grieving for him who had slipped away though she held him, she goes round everything: every place, every pursuit, every class of people, every way of life. Every beauty of sight, flavor of taste, sound of hearing, fragrance of smell, caressing touch, thing desirable to possess, and thing delightful to enjoy becomes nauseating to her. Steadfast love makes her unsteady; an immovable intention makes her mobile; an unchangeable affection makes her changeable. She delights to seek wherever he may be hoped to be found—he who is sometimes found even where he is not expected. But she finds some trace of the Bridegroom wherever and in whomever she finds some sign of virtue, example of devotion, mirror of integrity, ardor of religion, and love of purity.

“He whom my soul loves.” Again and again, and continually, blessed is the soul for whom “he whom my soul loves” is continually in the conscience and frequently on the tongue in relation to her Lord God: “I sought him and did not find him. The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves? A little while after I passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” [Col. 0544B]

Let us return a little to what preceded, in order to examine the historical sense and the order of the drama. The Bridegroom had already come to the Bride, leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills, looking through the windows and peering through the lattice. He had stirred her—while she rested in the leisurely business, or busy leisure, of the bed, doing or thinking only those things that belong to the bed—once, twice, and a third time. He had invited her to rise, to make haste, to come: to the more hidden mysteries of his love, to the face of a fuller vision of himself, to the pursuit of a clearer knowledge of himself, and to the higher rewards of eternal blessedness.

Then, departing and withdrawing into the secret place of his divinity, hiding from her that desirable countenance into which not only angels in heaven but also human beings on earth, rivals of angelic perfection, desire to look, he “made darkness his hiding place.” For the gratuitous visits of the Bridegroom had made her, delicately treated and nourished amid the delights of grace, more sluggish and lax in spiritual exercises, given only to prayers, spiritual leisure, and meditations, and caring for nothing else. Therefore, when called, she neither rose nor hurried nor came; instead she asked him more frequently to return to her, saying: “Return; be like a gazelle or a young stag.” And when he did not return as she prayed, she was like one unable to move her foot from delights and the warmth of the bed: she turned herself from side to side, seeking the accustomed kisses and embraces without spiritual labor, confident that she would continually find there the grace of accustomed delight without the burden of outward labor.

But when the Bridegroom delayed, she at last perceived that she had to rise, judging it more fitting to go out at the Bridegroom’s command than to remain alone in the bed of her leisure—not so much resting as being idle—with the Bridegroom absent. Indeed, leisure without him she considers not rest but rather the burial of a living person. “I will rise,” therefore, she says, “and go round the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loved.” That is: I shall seek the opportunity of good outward action to aid inward contemplation. “I shall seek,” she says, “him whom my soul loved.” For the more correct copies read thus: “whom my soul loved.” The Bride seems to herself no longer to love the Bridegroom so long as the flame of his divine goodness does not kindle her affection, and so long as neither her memory is affected by the remembrance of the abundance of that sweetness nor her understanding conformed to it. For when he departs, every consolation of the Bride suddenly disappears and flees; the mind is made barren of its former fruits; love becomes without affection, thought without understanding and without the fruit of devotion.

“I will rise,” therefore, she says, “and go,” wherever the heat of my love—or rather of my desire—carries me; I shall follow wherever it draws me. And although I am meanwhile unworthy for the Bridegroom to visit me with his accustomed grace, I shall seek some who are made by God for this very purpose, so that by enjoying God in them I may thus enjoy God through them. For they are sometimes found in the streets when, alas, they are not found in monasteries; they are found in lanes when they are not found in deserts. Not that they are not more frequently in monasteries and more familiarly in deserts; but when God is sought, just as he is found nowhere unless he first finds the one seeking him, so he is not found nowhere when he has gone before the seeker.

> “The watchmen who guard the city found me.”

The watchmen may be understood as the ministering spirits sent for those who receive the inheritance of salvation, or as holy teachers and preachers appointed, each in his own watch, to guard the city of the Church. For there are angels of the poor and little ones of God, always beholding the face of the Lord and, by the judgment of his countenance, helping and protecting the Bride. By certain hidden modes of suggestion they supply her with profitable admonitions and wholesome counsels. The Bride therefore says that she questioned them about the Bridegroom; but she does not say that they answered her, because answers from God are not always at hand for every question of ours, whether through hidden inspirations, angelic assistance, or a teaching human being—and especially in a time of temptation.

There are also holy teachers of the Church, shepherds who watch and keep the night watches over their flock. Through them—whether through the words of those living here or the writings of those now reigning with God—an answer from God concerning our secrets and necessities is often always at hand in a time of prosperity and illuminating grace. But in the time of tribulation, in days of removal, heaven becomes bronze and earth iron: there is no prophet or prophecy, no vision from the Lord; teaching has perished from the teacher, and counsel from the wise person. These men, whether by word, writing, or example, find the Bride who seeks, but do not assist her. And as commonly happens to the wretched, she has many counselors but no helper, because when God turns his face away all things are disturbed: words are only words, writings only letters. No one speaks to the heart of the grieving person, though many make noise in her ears; no one answers the questioner, no one gives a hand to the wanderer.

> “The watchmen who guard the city found me.” [Col. 0546A]

They found her seeking—the one whom grace had made loving. But they could not have found her even here unless grace had first gone before her. For just as no sensory perception can be imparted to one who does not perceive—for instance, sight to one who has never seen, hearing to one who has not heard, and so with the rest—so too, indeed far more, the inward perception of grace cannot be given when absent, or restored when lost, except by grace itself. Those who possess the joy of the Lord may preach and commend it to those who do not possess it; counsel may be given in seeking, some method may be indicated for recovering it; and even sometimes, if grace accompanies it, the will may be moved and desire implanted. But that joy belongs to no one except the person into whom it pours itself; no one ascends to that sublime state unless it condescends to that person; no one perceives that good unless it conforms that person to itself; no one lives that life unless it gives that person life.

The watchmen, then, are passed by. Just as they could not make her a seeker, so they could not complete her as one who finds. For “charity is poured forth in our hearts,” not through a teaching human being, but “through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us” (Rom. V). No word has effect, wherever it comes from, where the power of prevenient grace does not work. Therefore she says to them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loved?” The inward sound of sweetness in my soul, she says, sounds differently to me and speaks differently from the outward word of your preaching. My love possesses some perception of him whom I seek; and although you too possess it, neither your words nor those of anyone else express it.

Though you apprehend him whom I seek far better and more worthily, yet through your words neither do we find what we seek nor do you attain what you desire. For you tell us much, but do not bring us to the goal, because you do not make the reality known as it is. Certainly the consolations supplied to us through the study of readings, the occasions of spiritual meditations, the assiduous prayers prompted by imitation of your holy desire, and the other exercises, whether spiritual or bodily, contribute much. Yet in all these things you must be passed by and one must arrive where nothing is read except in the book of truth; where eternal wisdom is given instead of meditation, vision instead of consolation, and face to face instead of mirror and enigma.

But this lies far beyond you, because it is the state of the future life and eternal blessedness, surpassing and transcending every weakness. A little beyond you, however, is the state of devotion, in which the Bridegroom sometimes helps the weakness of his Bride—whoever she may be—to taste these things. Thus, just as the air above the moon and below heaven is said to have neither rain nor hail nor the storms of other winds, but to be perpetually serene, so by the progress of good will the effect is a state of good mind: it is freed from lower darkness and more nearly illuminated by higher light.

[Col. 0545]

Thus far Blessed William carried his exposition of the Song of Songs, and left it unfinished in order to declare war on Peter Abelard, who held and wrote erroneous views concerning the faith, as he himself states in the letter to the Carthusian Fathers prefixed to his book *On the Solitary Life*. He did not subsequently resume it, but undertook to write the life of Saint Bernard, who was still living; this too he was unable to complete, being overtaken by death. He also wrote another work on the Song of Songs, woven from the works of Blessed Ambrose, as he himself affirms in the aforementioned letter to the Carthusian Fathers. That work, however, is found wrongly attributed to Antonio Demochari among the works of Ambrose in the most recent edition.

[Col. 0547]

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

## PREFACE
[Col. 0547A] [Note: [Col. 0547] This exposition has been woven together from the writings of Augustine and of other Fathers.]

We have undertaken Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, entangled as it is with many varied and most difficult questions, not in order to expound what is above us, but, by gathering into this one small work certain opinions of the holy Fathers—and especially of blessed Augustine—upon it, or passages collected here and there from their books and shorter works, and by setting aside the troublesome questions contained in it, to weave one continuous explanation, not our own but theirs. This should be all the more welcome to readers because it was devised not by a presumption of novelty or vanity, but is commended by the great authority of great teachers: above all, as has been said, blessed Augustine; then Ambrose, Origen, and several other teachers; and also certain masters of our own time, of whom we are sure that in no respect they have overstepped the boundaries set by our Fathers.

Let no one, therefore, accuse us of theft: we ourselves disclose it. According to the poetic fable, we have ceremonially clothed our little bird with the feathers and colours of various birds; if they come and each takes away what it recognizes as its own, our little crow will remain naked—or nothing at all. What compelled me to this was the delight of contemplating God’s grace and the glory of proclaiming it to all: grace which, throughout this whole Epistle, its most steadfast champion, the Apostle, defends with apostolic authority and wisdom against the Jews, and which the holy Fathers everywhere defend against heretics. We desire it to be inscribed upon our hearts for the attainment of complete humility and pure devotion.

Those who have wholly devoted themselves to the worship of God ought to know that, as Scripture says, “Piety is the worship of God” (Job 23); yet there is no piety without thanksgiving, and no thanksgiving without recognition of grace. By frequently meditating upon this, they become “blessed poor in spirit” (Matt. 5), whose is the kingdom of God, whose whole spirit is entrusted to God. For grace, before we existed, when we were nothing, predestined us; when turned away, called us; when converted, justified us; and, if we are not ungrateful, will glorify us when justified. Grace itself works good in us, that we may will it; it cooperates when we will it, without which we can neither will nor accomplish any good.

For just as we were created by God from non-existent things, so that we might be something among his creatures, so by grace we have been created from no merits in good works. And thereafter, if we deserve anything, it is grace; and what we deserve is grace for grace. For to yield fruits from grace received is an increase of grace, just as first receiving grace is grace. Grace goes before us that we may pray; it helps us when we pray; it hears what we pray.

By this grace the Virgin was made full, so that she might become the Mother of God (Luke 1); by this grace he who was born of the Virgin was found full. Noah, Abraham, Moses, and the other holy Fathers are reported to have found this grace with God; and this grace is commanded to suffice for the Apostle Paul when he seeks something else (2 Cor. 12). For when you came, Lord Jesus, “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” grace was poured out upon your lips by a special prerogative; for this itself was the oil of gladness with which you appeared anointed above your companions (Ps. 44), and for this reason the young maidens loved you, running after the fragrance of your ointments (Song 1).

Indeed, those whom grace itself had gone before to this end saw it in your face: the tax collector, and, leaving the tax office, went after you (Matt. 9); Peter and Andrew, James and John, leaving nets and father, followed you. To this day, this grace, sounding something in your words to the ears of those whom it has preceded—something that does not reach the ears of others—calls things that are not as though they were, makes the lowly consent because they are brothers, and removes the reproach which they had imagined concerning you, gladdening the hearts of the humble and rendering their faces gracious, because they are as they were created and as they were led away into what belongs to another.

In this grace you freely bestow upon us whatever you bestow, receiving from us nothing that you have not given. Even when you wish to be loved by us freely, you reckon it to us as a free gift that we love you for your own sake, since, O Almighty One, you cannot give us anything greater as the reward of love for you than to love you itself. Moreover, redeeming our souls from the interest and iniquity of our shameful deeds and crimes, you make our name honourable before you, so that we may be called and may be children of your grace, as persons loving you freely; and, in order to make us worthy of that very love of you, you first grant remission of so many and such great sins.

But grace is yours, and comes to us from you; therefore, Lord our God, let glory be to you alone. If anyone glories, let him glory only in you. For even faith itself cannot exist in us unless it comes from you; without faith no good work is done in a human being, because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 11 [14:23]).

# BOOK I

[Col. 0549]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0549A]

**Verse 1.—“Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus.”** Great and exalted are you, Lord; you regard the lowly and know the lofty from afar. You knew Saul, fashioned after the proud king and persecutor, both in his persecution and in his name; yet you did not know him from afar. For you humbled him like a wounded proud man; and by the arm of your power and the spirit of your grace you made Paul out of Saul (Acts 9): a young Benjamin penetrating the heavens in an ecstasy of mind, hearing in the paradise of God secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter; once a ravening wolf, but in the evening dividing the spoil.

Yet he brought back for us some things which it was indeed lawful for a human being to utter, but which no one may fully understand unless that person possesses something more than human capacity. In Hebrew he was called *Saul*; in Latin, *Saulus*, as it were *Saülus*—just as Jacob becomes Jacobus, Joseph becomes Josephus, and similarly in other cases. But when you chose him as a vessel of election to preach your grace to the nations, he preferred to be called Paul rather than Saul—*Paulus*, as though *Paululus*, “little”: humble and quiet, upon whom the Holy Spirit rests—so that by his very name he might confound the pride of those who presumed to apply your grace to their own merits.

This pertains to his humility. But for your glory, when he had sent Paul, the proconsul of Asia, under your light yoke and made him a provincial subject of your kingdom, he too preferred to be called Paul rather than Saul, as a memorial of so great a victory (Acts 13). For the enemy is conquered more greatly in the one whom he possesses more greatly. The ancient enemy possesses more greatly those who are proud of nobility of name; and among these he possesses more people through the name of authority.

“Servant of Christ Jesus.” This servant’s profession is one of humility, glory, and exceptional authority, when he declares himself, almost exultingly, the servant of him who says, “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. 49), whom, as he himself says, Paul served in the Gospel of his Son.

“Christ Jesus.” Jesus is the proper name; Christ is the name of the mystery. For it is the same as Messiah. Thus in the name Christ Jesus is understood the power of the saving King, because salvation is to be hoped for only from the saving King.

“A called apostle.” Called by grace, because no one ought to take honour to himself unless called by God, as Aaron was.

“Apostle.” *Apostle* means “one sent,” or rather “one sent back,” that is, sent to call those who had hitherto been behind, concerning whom the prophet says, “You shall make them turn their back” (Ps. 20). For those are behind and at the back who are devoted to this world, which ought to be set behind.

“Set apart for the Gospel of God.” Notice that he preferred to indicate his separation by the very word used by him who set him apart, saying: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13). [Col. 0550A] The work to which he was called is the Gospel.

**Verse 2.—“Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets.”** It began through the prophets and was brought to completion through the apostles.

**Verse 3.—“In the holy Scriptures,”** that is, set forth by the Holy Spirit and held in a fixed and stable memorial for all. “Concerning his Son,” that is, eternally begotten of him before the morning star and before all time. He who, ever existing as the one God begotten from God, “by him”—that is, by his own willing and ordering, as his honour and goodness required—was made human in time.

The Son of God was made human because the one who was made was so assumed by the Son of God, who was not made but born, into unity of person that the same one is Son of God who is son of man: born of God the Father according to divinity, “made from the seed of David according to the flesh.” From the seed “of David,” namely, to whom the promise was made—more explicitly than it was to Abraham.

**Verse 4.—“Who was predestined Son of God in power.”** The Savior himself appeared as the most splendid light of predestination and grace to human beings, since by the working of that same grace every Christian is made a human being from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that man was made Christ from his beginning. Jesus, therefore, was predestined to be the future son of David according to the flesh, and yet Son of God in power.

In him the elevation of human nature to such supreme and exalted dignity was predestined, so that it had no higher point to which it might be raised; just as divinity itself had no lower point to which it might humble itself for our sake. For from the moment that man began to be, he also began to be the Son of God.

Or, according to the proper sense of the Greek translation, he was not “predestined” but “appointed”: he who was always God came in power, that is, in what he was. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Christ was also predestined, or appointed, for power—that is, without any obligation of sin, whether inherited by origin or committed by will. This predestination is his very glory, which the man born into the world had with the Father “before the world was made” (John 17). And just as he himself was predestined to be our head, so in him we were predestined to be his members.

“According to the spirit of sanctification.” For he was predestined to be born according to the spirit of sanctification, of whose mother it was said to Joseph: “For what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1); and to his mother herself: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). Although flesh was truly born from flesh, the conception of that flesh was altogether spiritual. In her, the love of God and the spirit of sanctification did what, in other human beings, the tinder of sin and love of the flesh—infecting all with the stain of original sin—ordinarily do.

Yet Christian piety must guard here against an offence to faith concerning Christ, lest it say or believe that the Son was conceived of the Holy Spirit as the Son of the Holy Spirit. Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit, not because she received from the substance of the Holy Spirit the seed of childbirth, but because, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, nature supplied its substance for the divine birth. For because love of the Holy Spirit burned uniquely in her holy soul, the power of that same Spirit worked wonders in her flesh.

It follows: “From the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.” This may be understood to mean that, from the resurrection of the dead whom Christ raised, or whom in his own resurrection he chose to have as witnesses and participants in that same resurrection, he made it manifest and evident that he was the Son of God.

But if what he says—“from the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord”—is again construed in this way, so that Paul is said to be one from among the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord, namely, those for whose life Jesus Christ our Lord died, in order to raise them from the death of the soul, this ought not to seem absurd, because it is not unusual in Scripture. So also: “Daniel, from the sons of the captivity of Judah” (Dan. 5).

But since a little earlier he had said, “Paul, servant of Christ Jesus,” why does he here again say, “Jesus Christ our Lord”? This manner of expression is commonly found in Scripture, especially in the older books, as in: “And Moses did as the Lord had commanded Moses” (Exod. 40). Or, what seems more likely: the name of him whose love burned in Paul’s heart had a certain sweet savour in his mouth; and it was pleasing to him to sprinkle his sayings, spoken or written, which concerned him, with frequent mention of his name. He likewise seems everywhere to use the pronouns of that name—“in whom,” “through whom,” “in him,” “through him”—so frequently and insistently that at times he may seem tiresome to a reader, unless the writer’s affection is considered.

**Verse 5.—“Through whom we received grace and apostleship.”** Through him, as reconciler for our sins, we received grace, that is, remission of those sins; through him, as wisdom producing contempt for present things, the grace of future things becomes sweet to us.

“Through whom,” he says, “we received grace and apostleship”: grace for enduring labours; apostleship for the authority of preaching; grace for persuading what ought to be persuaded; apostleship for restraining those who ought to be restrained.

“For obedience to the faith among all nations.” The apostles obtained such grace in this matter that the nations, formerly strangers to the covenant of God and to the commonwealth of Israel, not only believed the preachers in accepting the faith, but also obeyed by undertaking, out of reverence for Christ’s name, a new manner of life and order of religious conduct.

**Verse 7.—“To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called saints.”** They were not first called saints and then, as though on account of holiness, beloved; rather, they were first freely loved and afterward called saints—that is, called in order that they might be saints—so that grace may be grace.

“Called saints,” he says. In ordinary speech, the pupil of a craftsman, however recent a pupil, is already called a craftsman; and likewise in the disciplines of the other arts. So anyone who has been called and has now enrolled under the profession of holiness may rightly already be called holy. Hence the prophet also confidently says: “For I am holy” (Ps. 85).

Paul, called as an apostle, writes to disciples called saints, because just as Paul was called by grace to be Christ’s apostle, so each of them was called by the same grace to be a Christian, beloved and holy.

[Col. 0552B] “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” The grace of God is that by which our sins are forgiven so that we may be reconciled to God; peace is that by which we are reconciled—as in the phrase “the Law and the Prophets,” although the Prophets are contained in the Law. Both remission and peace belong to the general grace of God.

This apostolic blessing of grace and peace must be understood as given to the whole Church, and must not be judged of less power than those blessings pronounced by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob upon their children, since this same Apostle confidently proclaims of himself: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13). And again: “I think,” he says, “that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7).

From this apostolic blessing, the Churches must be believed to flourish to this day. And where the peace of God is found, grace too is undoubtedly present. But if it is not, the salvation of grace is far from sinners, while the preacher’s peace returns to him, as the Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel: “Into whatever house you enter, say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him; but if not, it shall return to you” (Luke 10).

**Verse 8.—“First indeed I give thanks to my God.”** The best preacher of grace took his beginning from grace, so that, just as God is first to be adored and afterward prayed to—as the Psalmist says, “Praising, I shall call upon the Lord” (Ps. 17)—so the preacher of grace first gives thanks to him from whom all grace is hoped for and received, and afterward preaches grace itself in due order.

For the supreme and good God is pleased, for our good, by a recipient’s mind that is not ungrateful in receiving his gifts, and by a humble and devout understanding of divine goodness. He is greatly pleased by the sacrifice of brotherly love in one who rejoices before God with heartfelt affection at a brother’s progress.

And just as before him no sin is counted greater than ingratitude toward his grace, so for a faithful soul accustomed faithfully to divine graces, nothing is sweeter or more delightful in one’s own progress or that of one’s neighbour than acts of thanksgiving themselves.

We give thanks for ourselves when we faithfully consider that the grace we receive is received freely from God, and by that consideration stir ourselves more devoutly and humbly to love the Giver; or when we thankfully return to God in action the capacity for a good work which we freely receive in affection—grace itself also working this in us. We give thanks for our neighbour when we rejoice that, in one whom we love in God, we receive grace.

Therefore, whoever strives always to appear grateful in these things before the Lord both deserves to receive ever greater gifts in himself and is worthy and fit also to intercede for others.

“First,” therefore, he says, “I give thanks to my God.” It is great human confidence and a great affection of piety to call the God of all one’s own Lord. Yet this is so. Whoever says “my God” with sweet and devout affection and with secure, trusting love says it securely, because that person has made his own the one whose own he is; and securely lays before him, to whom he offers it, whatever he offers, since that one is always most present to him, and he himself is always present before him.

One cannot say this if one’s god is the belly, or anything else loved as God or together with God, but not for God’s sake. For God alone is to be loved; nor does his love permit itself in any way to be defiled by alien loves, since he alone suffices for the one who loves him. The Lord, God of all, is properly the God of that person to whom God is pleasing in himself and for his own sake, and whose mind perseveres, in all God’s judgments, in this fixed disposition of will. For the satisfaction of the mind is a tranquil will.

This must properly and especially be understood in loving God: apart from him, beyond him, and outside him, nothing is to be loved unless it is loved for his sake and in him. For one who does not wish to fall with what falls must fix one’s step upon what is stable.

Moreover, the blessed person whose Lord is his God becomes in return a person of God when, just as the Apostle served God in his spirit in the Gospel of his Son, so each person, in his or her spirit and from the Holy Spirit, serves in the things of God. This is what the Bride says of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is mine, and I am his; he will dwell between my breasts” (Song 1).

“Therefore,” he says, “I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you.” Thus the Apostle, the supreme preacher of grace, understood that one must always return in everything, with thanksgiving, to the Lord God of one’s heart—and only through Jesus the High Priest and Mediator of God and human beings—so that through him, by whom the gifts of grace are brought to us from God, acts of thanksgiving for those same graces may always be rendered to him.

Here too it should be observed that, writing to different persons, the Apostle in some cases gives thanks for all; in others he gives thanks, but not for all; and in others he gives no thanks. Where he gives thanks for all, he neither alleges faults in them nor magnifies their reproaches. Where he gives thanks but not for all, as to the Corinthians and Colossians, he indicates that there is something reprehensible among them. But where he entirely omits to give thanks, he signifies that there is something serious in them, which he judges contrary to thanksgiving.

“Because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” Your faith, he says, is the same as the Catholic faith of all throughout the world, because the character and example of your faith are the instruction of the whole world. Perhaps the Apostle already foresaw in the Spirit that Rome, where the seat of the earthly empire stood, would become the first see of the Christian priesthood, from which, as from a fountain, that which would be preached and believed for salvation throughout the whole world might flow forth.

Therefore he not only gives thanks, but also prays concerning the future, as he says:

**Verse 9.—“For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, is my witness, that without ceasing I always make remembrance of you in my prayers.”** He was doing no evil who made good use of an oath. Although an oath is not itself good, since the Lord says, “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; what is more than this is from evil” (Matt. 5), it is nevertheless necessary in order that another may be persuaded of what it is beneficial to persuade, even though it comes from the evil of the person to whom the oath is made. For it arises from the weakness of that person—which is certainly evil—who either cannot otherwise be persuaded or is not expected to be so persuaded.

No oath should be thought greater than calling God as witness to what is said. In this every person who swears must most carefully guard against ever taking the name of God in vain, contrary to the commandment of the Law (Exod. 20).

“God,” therefore, he says, “whom I serve in my spirit, is my witness.” This service is free, because it is service of love and piety. “I serve in my spirit,” he says, because I do it willingly—not under the compulsion of fear, nor in hope of reward, but from the consciousness of righteousness and love of truth.

“In the Gospel,” he says, “of his Son.” And what could be more welcome, more delightful, or more joyful for a faithful servant chosen as this vessel of election than to serve God in the Gospel of his Son?

It follows:

**Verse 10.—“That without ceasing I make remembrance of you in my prayers.”** “I make remembrance of you,” he says, “in my prayers always and without ceasing”; that is, in my prayers, which I make always and without ceasing. For it is certain that he himself fulfilled what he commanded the disciples, saying: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5).

“Beseeching, if somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey, in the will of God, to come to you.” It should be considered that, setting out for the work of the Gospel, a holy work, he waits until by entreaties he has implored not merely that his journey may be made prosperous, but that it may be prosperous in the will of God; for the journey of one travelling always prospers in God’s will. The prosperity of a journey is then in God’s will when its cause corresponds to the cause which he adds, saying:

**Verses 11 and 12.—“For I desire to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace for your strengthening; that is, that I may be comforted together with you through the faith that is mutual between you and me.”** First of all, we ought to know that desiring or visiting brothers is an apostolic work, but only so that we may either impart some spiritual grace to them or receive it from them. Otherwise, it is not commendable to go about among brothers.

One grace is spiritual and another is not. For example, virginity is spiritual; marriage is not spiritual, though both are gifts of God. But especially spiritual grace consists in the charisms of spiritual understanding, whether moral or mystical, which are to be compared spiritually with spiritual things. Therefore, to those whom the Apostle urges toward the strength of perfection, he especially wishes to impart things that are of the Spirit.

When this happens, he himself also receives consolation, seeing his work firm and stable in the disciples’ progress; and they are comforted when they become participants in apostolic grace. For mutual edification of faith cannot be lacking when disciples see in their teacher what they may imitate, and the teacher is encouraged by the disciples’ progress toward greater labours for the Gospel. Nor does he wish them to be unaware of his concern for the brothers, so that, once the teacher’s goodwill is known, he may prepare a place in their hearts for teaching.

**Verse 13.—“And I was hindered until now.”** By whom was he hindered?
