If we say by God, it is certainly not unworthy of God to order the actions of his servants, since he knows over which city the rain of God’s word ought to fall and over which it ought not. Thus in the Acts of the Apostles: “We wished to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus prevented us” (Acts 16).

But if, as he says more plainly elsewhere, we say that he was prevented by Satan (1 Thess. 2), God sometimes permits this too, for testing the perseverance of his servants. Yet it must be understood that Satan can in no way know or disturb a holy intention and the holy plan which a person forms in the purpose of the heart, unless he detects it from some outward signs. What is displayed through outward action he can impede, if God permits it.

“That I might have some fruit among you also, as among the other nations.” Everywhere the Apostle dispensed the Lord’s talents and everywhere gathered gains for him. Everywhere he sowed and everywhere he reaped. “That I might have some fruit among you,” he says.

It should not be overlooked that he seems often to speak of “some fruit” of good things in the singular, but of the works of the flesh that he reproves in the plural. Thus elsewhere he says: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, and so forth” (Gal. 5). But concerning the fruits of the flesh he says: “They are manifest: fornication, uncleanness,” and so on (ibid.). This is because, as even the philosophers of the nations maintain, all virtues are one virtue: whoever possesses any one of them perfectly possesses them all. Vices, however, are mutually conflicting even with one another.

It follows:

**Verse 14.—“I am debtor both to Greeks and barbarians, both to wise and foolish.”** Love does not know how to be compelled; it does not know how to be confined. It owes itself to all; it gives itself to all. It does not shrink from Greek wisdom or from the foolishness of barbarians. It judges no one to be abandoned.

While to some, as wise persons, he speaks wisdom, to others, as foolish persons, he protests that he knows nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). He teaches some from the Law and the Prophets; others he persuades by signs and mighty works. Hence, in dealing with Timothy when he was ill, he used not the power of healing but medical counsel (1 Tim. 5); he also left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Tim. 4); but he healed the father of Publius, suffering from dysentery and fevers, by word and prayer alone (Acts 28), and restored Eutychus, who had fallen from the upper room, to life and health (Acts 20). For signs are owed not to believers but to unbelievers, not to the wise but to the foolish.

He adds most aptly:

**Verse 15.—“Thus, so far as it depends upon me, I am ready to preach the Gospel also to you who are at Rome.”** That is: I am debtor to preach the Gospel to you who are at Rome, insofar as it depends upon me—or, “so far as is in me.” As if he said: You who are at Rome are not among the foolish. For it was ready at hand for a wise person to speak to wise persons, although even concerning the foolish we must understand what he says elsewhere: “For if I do this unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me; and woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel” (1 Cor. 9).

For one preaching the Gospel must speak to all, wise and foolish alike; but he is ready to preach the Gospel to those of whom it is written: “Blessed is the one who speaks in the ear of a hearer.”

Therefore, to summarize briefly what has been said: after the Apostle had sufficiently commended to the Romans the business of the Gospel, received from God, not in learned and persuasive words of human wisdom but in simplicity, through the person of the evangelist, the authority of the sender, and the cause itself; after, as though entering the city of Rome through the Epistle in the abundance of Christ’s blessing, he had greeted it in peace, as the Lord himself instructed; and after he had prepared the goodwill of his hearers by the affection of pious concern and the service of prayers—then he begins to preach the Gospel itself to them.

Seeing, as though in support of his work, worldly wisdom from both Jews and Gentiles flocking together at Rome, and seeing his peace, with which he had greeted them, resting upon them, he began, saying:

**Verse 16.—“For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of God.”** At the very outset he knew the reproach of the Crucified would be cast against him: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles. But for him there could be neither shame in a conscience now healed nor embarrassment upon a countenance so free.

“For it is,” he says, “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.” Hence he also says to the Corinthians: “But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1).

Therefore he was not ashamed, as though unable to bear the reproach of Christ’s cross; not as though teaching one way and living another; nor as though deficient in the power of miracles. Rather, he says, it is “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes,” so that it may also be understood to be God’s power for the destruction of the one who does not believe. For there is also a power of God for destruction, concerning which it is written: “Destroy them in your power” (Ps. 58). And because of these differences of powers, right and left are spoken of in God.

“To the Jew first and also to the Greek.” To the Jew first and afterward to the Greek, that is, the Gentile, “because salvation is from the Jews” (John 4). The Greeks themselves first divided the whole human race under two names, calling every human being either Greek or barbarian; whoever was not Greek was barbarian. But Paul employs a far truer distinction, placing Jews first, then Greeks, and afterward barbarians. For since Greeks preferred themselves to all others because they used laws, the Jews were rightly placed before even the Greeks by the Apostle, because they received laws from God before all others.

He now proceeds first to discuss that power which is for salvation, saying:

**Verse 17.—“For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous shall live by faith.’”** This righteousness which justifies believers is faith. Veiled in the Old Testament, it is revealed in the Gospel. It is called righteousness because it makes righteous those whom it contains. It is God’s righteousness because faith itself is from grace.

This faith, this righteousness, advances or reaches from the faith of those who proclaim to the faith of those who obey; from the faith of the Old Testament to the faith of the New; from faith in which God is served to faith in which God is enjoyed; from the faith of the image here to faith in the reality then most immediately present; from faith in words, which we have believed here, to faith in the thing itself, which we shall possess eternally.

The righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel because no barbarian, no Scythian, nor anyone at all is now excluded from the kingdom of God.

[Note: [Col. 0557D] These words, and those which follow, affirming that the door of grace stands open to all—of which he frequently has similar statements elsewhere, as do Saint Bernard, *Sermon 1 on the Purification*, and others—show clearly, in the view of these Fathers, that God gives grace to all. I have noted this because below I intend to refute, by opposing these passages, the contrary opinion of an author of that age.]

Rather, the gate of grace stands equally open to all. “As it is written,” he says, “The righteous shall live by faith.” This is well written in the prophet Habakkuk [Col. 0557C]: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2), because faith itself causes us, by believing, to understand that not only our believing well but also our living well comes to us not from ourselves but from God. For even right living does not come from ourselves, unless he who gave us faith—by which we believe that we must be helped by him—helps us when we believe and pray.

Let heretical pride blush here: it claims for itself the first part in a good work when a human being arrogates to himself the beginning of a good will, as though it came to that person from that person alone.

VERS. 18.—“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.” Having commended the devotion of faith revealed in the Gospel, by which, once justified, we ought to be pleasing to God; and having also commended the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, he now turns from this point to its opposite, that is, to His power [Col. 0557D] in the condemnation of unbelievers, and seems to say: Not only are the righteousness and glorification of believers revealed in the Gospel, but also the unrighteousness of unbelievers, and wrath—that is, the just condemnation inflicted upon them. For wrath in a human being is an impulse of the mind toward vengeance; in God it is the just execution of vengeance. “Who,” moreover, “knows how, in fear of God, to reckon His wrath?” (Ps. LXXXIX). For God’s wrath consists in the vain and deceptive prosperity of the ungodly, bodily affliction through tribulation, inward blindness of mind, the sting of conscience in sin, and the sentence of eternal retribution; and sometimes, in those who misuse it—such as the philosophers of the Gentiles and the wise of this world—it consists in illumination of mind itself. Of these he adds: “Upon all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those men who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness.” For such persons it would have been far better to have been ignorant of God’s truth than to have held it in unrighteousness. “Upon all,” he says, “ungodliness and unrighteousness,” namely, alike of Jew and Greek, of the one who has the Law and of the one who does not. For whoever sins against the worship of God is ungodly, because, as is read in Job, “piety is the worship of God” (Job XXVIII). From ungodliness, moreover, unrighteousness proceeds, when what is due to God is paid to a creature. They too are unrighteous who sin against the faith by which [Col. 0558B] the righteous person lives. The Apostle also attentively calls them “men,” just as elsewhere he speaks, as though approving certain others, saying: “Are you not men?” (I Cor. III). But whence comes knowledge of truth to those to whom God gave no Law?

VERS. 19.—“Because that which is known of God is manifest in them.” It is manifest not only to them, but also in them: that is, it is manifest to them through the natural understanding which is in them. This is what follows: “For God has manifested it to them.” But how did He manifest it?

VERS. 20.—“For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made: His eternal power also and divinity.” Why did He manifest them? “So that they may be without excuse.” Whence, then, are they blameworthy?

VERS. 21–22.—“Because, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor give thanks.” But what did they do? “They became vain in their thoughts.” Nor was this without punishment: “For their foolish heart was darkened”; and by pride they lost what they had apprehended through curiosity. This blindness or darkness of heart is both sin, the punishment of preceding sin, and the cause of what follows. Of what? Pride. For they became proud, “saying that they were wise.” It is indeed customary for the proud to be close to folly. For although not every fool is proud, every proud person is shown to be a fool. Pride, in turn, is both the punishment of preceding sin and the cause of what follows. Of what? Folly. “For, saying [Col. 0558D] that they were wise, they became fools.” Folly too is the punishment of preceding sin and the cause of what follows. Of what? Idolatry. Hence it follows:

VERS. 23.—“And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible,” first, “man,” then “birds,” afterward “four-footed animals,” and finally even “serpents.” Idolatry in turn became the cause of ensuing impurity.

VERS. 24.—“Wherefore,” as he proceeds and [Col. 0559A] says, “God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, unto impurity.” Therefore, just as in the Gospel the advance of God’s righteousness is revealed by manifold grace “from faith unto faith,” so the decline of ungodliness and unrighteousness is revealed unto condemnation and death. “God gave them up,” he says, “to the desires of their hearts.” How did He give them up? “He let them go,” as the Psalm says, “according to the desires of their hearts,” that they might proceed “in their own devices” (Ps. LXXX). For to give up is to let go: that is, not to enlighten the blind, not to correct those who wander, not to help the weak. “He gave them up to the desires of their hearts.” Thus says the Apostle; thus says the Psalmist. Their heart was a heart abandoned to itself, blinded through itself, not illuminated by grace, in which at last the fool says: “There is no God” (Ps. XIII). [Col. 0559B] Their devices, moreover, came to be according to the desires of their hearts, desires which they were unwilling to overcome, but wished to fulfill. Therefore they are said to have been given up to the desires of their hearts. What, then, were the desires of their hearts? Impurity: in inclination, a desire to exceed the human measure; in action, to exceed human practice; so far as to subject their very bodies, contrary to what is fitting and opposed to nature, to outrages against nature in themselves, and by a kind of force to adapt them so as to make them more suitable for vice. But because these things have been said in passing, in order to set forth the sequence of the matter, we must return briefly to what went before.

“God’s wrath,” he says (v. 18), “is revealed against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those men who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because that which is known of God is manifest in them. For God has manifested it to them.” [Col. 0559C] Here he deals with the philosophers of this world: indeed, great men, of great diligence and distinguished talent, who were able to assess creation and, from creation, the Creator—certainly worthy of praise, had not that prophetic saying justly struck them: “I girded you, and you did not know Me” (Isa. XLV). For they were able to see that God is a certain eternal, immutable, intelligible, intelligent life; wisdom, which both is wise and makes wise; fixed, abiding, unchanging truth, where what has been made is life, and where all the principles of things and creatures, whether eternally ordered or temporally coming to be, are found. For those philosophers—whom renown not undeservedly preferred above others—saw that no body is God; and therefore, in seeking God, they transcended all bodies. They saw that whatever is mutable is not the supreme God; and therefore, seeking the supreme God, they transcended every soul and every mutable spirit. Next, they saw that every form in any mutable thing, by which that thing is whatever it is, whatever its mode of being and whatever its nature, cannot exist except from Him who truly is, because He is immutably; and consequently they saw that neither the body of the whole universe, from heaven down to earth, nor whatever bodies are in them, nor any life whatsoever, can exist except from Him who simply is: to whom to be is the same as to live, the same as to understand, the same as to be blessed. Because of this immutability and simplicity, they understood both that He made all these mutable things and that He Himself could have been made by no one. [Col. 0560A]

For they considered that everything which exists is either body or life, and that life is something better than body; that the form of body is sensible, while that of life is intelligible. Accordingly, they preferred intelligible form to sensible form. By “sensible” we mean what can be perceived by sight, touch, or any bodily sense; by “intelligible,” what can be understood by the gaze of the mind. For there is no bodily beauty, whether in a body’s state, as shape is, or in its movement, as melody is, concerning which the mind does not judge; and it certainly could not judge if it were not better than that beauty. But the mind is form without the swelling of bulk, without the sound of a voice, without extension in place or time. Yet even it, unless it were mutable, would not judge one thing better than another, nor judge sensible form now better and now less well. Hence intelligent and learned persons easily inferred that the primary form is not found in those things in which mutability is shown to exist. Therefore, since both body and mind appeared more or less beautiful to their view, and since, if they could lack every form, they would be altogether nothing, they saw that there is something in which first and immutable form exists, and which is therefore incomparable with these things; and they most rightly believed that there is another principle of things, which was not made, and from which all made things have their being.

Thus God Himself manifested to them “that which is known of God,” when “His invisible things are clearly seen by them, being understood through the things that are made: His eternal power also,” which governs and sustains all things, “and divinity,” which fills all things. The philosophers of the Gentiles [Col. 0560C] and the wise of this age saw these things concerning God, but they saw them from afar. They sought the way, but lost it because they were unwilling to be humble. They sought God with proud curiosity, though they ought to have sought Him with humble piety. They supposed that He was to be found in the realm of reason and the recess of more hidden knowledge; but He is found only in the kingdom of charity and the most luminous seat of wisdom—wisdom, moreover, not in windy verbosity, but in perfect charity “from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I). Although there were among them some who, with reason as guide, found life itself to some extent, yet, trusting in themselves, they failed in it. Thus their eminent Plato says: “We must flee to the most splendid fatherland, where God the Father is and luminous truth.” What is this fleet? What is this flight? Likeness. For we are made far from God insofar as we are unlike Him; insofar as we are made like Him, we draw near.

Therefore God’s wrath is revealed upon them, because, as Wisdom says, they ought not to be forgiven: for if they were able to know so much as to assess the world (Wis. XIII), how did they not more easily find its Lord in order to glorify Him? “Therefore the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all their ungodliness and unrighteousness,” when the preaching of the Gospel announces to them that a Judge is to come from heaven—the Judge of the ungodly and unrighteous—who, as the prophet says, changed God’s glory into an idol (Jer. II), worshipping the likeness of men, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents. [Col. 0561A] They would at least have worshipped these living things more fittingly, had they not, in saying that they were wise, become exceedingly foolish.

“Who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness.” God’s truth among human beings is the true and natural knowledge of divinity: namely, that God truly exists, that He cares for human affairs, governs and orders whatever He has created, and Himself created it. This cannot be doubtful to any person in whom human reason is present—especially to persons whose profession was philosophy, which is knowledge of human and divine things. Whoever hold this truth in idolatry hold it in unrighteousness. For idolatry is unrighteousness, wholly contrary to the righteousness of faith. Thus men who worship idols hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, as though it were resisting and unwilling, while human nature itself protests, contradicts, and rebukes the falsehood of religion in the conscience of human reason; “for that which is known of God is manifest in them. For God has manifested it to them” (v. 19).

That which is known of God—what human reason can attain concerning God through nature, not that to which charity is enabled to attain through grace—God manifested to them by giving them, from nature, reason capable of higher understanding, but the understanding itself from grace. For through the visible things of visible creation He manifested to them His invisible things: through visible creation, the invisible power of the Creator; through the visible order of things, invisible wisdom; through visible benefits, invisible goodness or charity of grace; or, as the Apostle says, His eternal [Col. 0561C] power and divinity. The eternal power and wisdom of God is Himself, of whom the Apostle elsewhere says: “But we preach Christ crucified: unto the Jews a stumbling block, and unto the Gentiles foolishness; but unto those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I). Divinity, however, is the Holy Spirit, the divinity of Father and Son; and just as He is understood to be their charity and their goodness, so divinity too is common to both, and absolutely everything which is common to them is common to both. This is what follows.

VERS. 20 and 21.—“For His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made: His eternal power also and divinity, [Col. 0561D] so that they are without excuse; because, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.” For God is an invisible substance, or intelligible essence: light illuminating and suffusing those who turn toward Him, striking and confounding those who turn away; splendor ready to hand for one who seeks Him; warmth from which no one hides himself; form drawing every soul that employs reason into contemplation of the love of truth, reproving the slothful and vain by the consciousness of vanity. Since the unstable motion of mutable things is not allowed to disturb His eternal and immutable laws, but is always recalled, by the bridles of recurring ages, to a likeness of stability, it shows that the natural kind of its origin is drawn from the state of immovable and immutable eternity, so far as the condition of a creature permits. [Col. 0562A]

There, things which occur solely by the condition of nature—such as all insensible or irrational things—are ordered in their place by the power, wisdom, and goodness of the Creator. But rational man is left to the choice of his own will and to the judgment of the reason granted him, so that, if by prevenient grace he wills it, he may cling with the affection of love to that place to which the power of reason leads him; may be conformed by the progress of piety to the beauty of righteousness and the eternity of blessedness; and, by the fullness of God’s righteousness, may attain the fullness of his own eternal blessedness, being grateful to God, his freely given illuminator and helper, and glorifying Him in himself. Such are those who, when they have known God, [Col. 0562B] give Him thanks and glorify Him.

But because the wise of this world did not do this, concerning whom the Apostle says, “They became vain in their thoughts, saying that they were wise” of themselves, they were abandoned by grace, cast away from the presence of the knowledge of God, and “their foolish heart was darkened.” As has already been said, they lost precisely what they had learned through curiosity. For they became so foolish and senseless that they said in their heart—in a foolish heart wholly abandoned by grace—“There is no God” (Ps. XI); and, as was said above, they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents. “Wherefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts.”

Augustine, in *On Grace and Free Will* [Col. 0562C] (ch. 21): “Here it is evident that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever He wills, whether toward good through His mercy, or toward evils according to their merits—by His judgment, indeed, sometimes open, sometimes hidden, but always just—by abandoning them.”

The question is raised whether it is rightly imputed to a person who is given up, though given up to desires on account of his sins, that he exists in those desires; just as no one ought properly to impute it to a person committed to prison for his crimes that, though justly, he is nevertheless unwillingly in darkness. But, as the same Apostle says, a human being is called spirit, soul, and body. Between spirit and flesh there is that familiar conflict, very well known to everyone. The one whom grace does not draw is joined to the flesh and becomes one flesh; and it is said of that person: “My spirit shall not remain in him, because he is flesh” (Gen. VI). [Col. 0562D] But the one whom grace draws is joined to the spirit and becomes one spirit with it; and it is said to him: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII). To be drawn or not drawn is to be given up or not given up. But why one person is drawn and another is not drawn—these are the hidden things of the Son; do not wish to inquire, if you do not wish to err. If you are not drawn, pray that you may be drawn; and if you already pray faithfully, you are already being drawn and are not being given up. In those who are drawn and not given up, there is God’s grace alone; but in those who are given up and not drawn, there is His irreproachable justice.

To whom, then, is the person who is given up given up? To unclean demons, who suggest unclean [Col. 0563A] desires, so that they may glory, as in the material of their work, both in their fulfillment and in the destruction of those who fulfill them. For it is evident that persons of this kind are, by God’s own judgment, wholly handed over to Satan for the destruction of flesh and spirit, unless they are anticipated by God’s swift mercy. Hence the ancient canons also judge that persons of this kind should be counted among the possessed, and that prayer should accordingly be made for them as for the demon-possessed. This entire passage, teeming with the filth of vices and displaying *kakemphaton* (κακέμφατον, “an indecent or obscene expression”), seems better neglected than read. Yet the Apostle most prudently was neither ashamed nor reluctant to write it, in order to humble the proud and to warn them what end contempt of God has. Avarice too brings its devotees to this end: avarice which serves the creature rather than the Creator, while it loves money more than God.

Therefore, the same judgment they used in the worship of divinity, preferring to it foul images of animals, they in turn exercise toward themselves, living in the manner of irrational beasts; and, having cast aside God’s image, they worship images of those creatures. This is the recompense which they received in themselves, as was fitting, through God’s just judgment. Why?

VERS. 25.—“Because they changed the truth of God [Col. 0563B] into a lie,” calling the work of their own hands God. “And as they showed by their conduct that they did not have God in their knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind,” so that those who had applied judgment to God might be proved reprobate in their own judgment. For those must be believed to retain God in their knowledge who, knowing that He is everywhere present, either do not wish or do not dare to sin before Him. Hence the repentant Prophet laments, saying: “Against You have I sinned” (Ps. L).

VERS. 29.—“Filled with all unrighteousness,” that is, with all these branches of unrighteousness. “Malice.” Malice is the fountain, cesspool, and, as it were, the womb of every evil. It is written: “Wisdom hates malice.” For wisdom is contrary to malice, because, just as good has a savor for the former in thought, so evil has a savor for the latter. “Wickedness.” A wicked person is one unable to do as much as the malice of his heart suggests. “Envy” is hatred of another’s prosperity when one cannot harm it. The things which are evident may be passed over, except that this must not be passed over: he joined whisperers [Col. 0563D] and slanderers, and declared both alike hateful to God. Finally, he placed the foolish and the disorderly, because all the things they begin will lead them to a certain foolishness of heart and a senseless disorderliness of conduct, so that, falling into a kind of stupor of nature, they have no affection at all for their neighbor, no loyalty to any bond or compact whatsoever, and no mercy in anyone’s need.

How contrary this is to the law of nature is made evident by nature itself. For three dispositions are found in the body: health, stupor, and immortality. Health has no illness; yet when it is afflicted, it feels pain. Stupor does not feel pain: it has lost the sense of pain, and is worse the more insensible it is. Again, immortality, when every corruption has been removed, does not feel pain. Thus there is no pain in an immortal body and none in a stuporous one; yet the health which feels pain is nearer to immortality than is stupor which feels nothing. [Col. 0564A] So a wise person’s soul, not being without affection, says from the feeling of health: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. II), and so forth.

From the fountain of pride, in which, saying that they were wise, they became fools, flowed the pestilential stream of all the evils that have been enumerated; its dreadful course must be turned aside and avoided. For through it all the reprobate, smoothly sailing to hell, make for the three harbors of their pleasures, and in each suffer a distinct giving-up. The word “giving-up,” with respect to God who gives up, denotes the sentence of a just Judge; with respect to the person given up, it denotes the deception of sin which deceives. First, therefore, embracing pride and idolatry, they are given up to the desires of their hearts unto impurity. Secondly, becoming as though wiser and advancing into worse things, judging that sacrifice should be offered not only to idols but also to the nature of things, they are given up to shameful passions and heaped with more grievous crimes. Thirdly, having now cast aside the knowledge of God, they are given up to a reprobate mind, plunged into the pit of every wickedness and of desperate destruction; and the pit, by the judgment of eternal death, presses its mouth over them—while the Apostle judges and says:

VERS. 32.—“That those who do such things are worthy [Col. 0564C] of death.” “Do,” he says, not “did.” For those who did them and no longer do them, but practice repentance, are worthy of life. Note that in the first and second stage pride is punished by such penalties that, if they had any sense, they ought no longer to be proud. In the third, however, they fully put on utter folly, so that the more the material for pride becomes diminished, the more they wish to be proud. Folly and pride are inseparable sisters, except that folly is the more tolerable because it is sometimes found without pride; but pride is never without folly.

“Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death.” They were an eye to themselves, and therefore they knew; but they could not be light to themselves, and therefore they did not understand. For they possessed from God the reason of nature; yet arrogantly claiming it for themselves, they did not care to seek the help of grace. Therefore they could not understand what it was most necessary for them to understand. “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.” To consent is to share the same mind with the sinner in affection toward the sin. Or consent is to foster error and remain silent when one is able to rebuke it.

## CHAPTER II

VERS. 1.—“Therefore you are inexcusable, O every man who judges.” The outstanding teacher, of marvelous prudence in the Gospel, the Apostle of the Gentiles—ever concerned to build up and honor his ministry, and knowing how to become all things to all—after sufficiently depressing and humbling the Gentile part according to its former condition, because this was expedient, now turns the scourge of correction upon the Jews, lest he add horns to their insolence. Thus those whom the censure of discipline made equal might more sweetly unite in the equal consolation of Christ’s peace. Although he could, as grievously as in the case of the Gentiles, have charged them with the filth of idolatry and impurity—for the books of the prophets are full of such accusations—he nevertheless spares them wisely, lest, when he came to questions concerning the Law, which he did not doubt would be most troublesome to them, their failing endurance collapse beneath the burden if it were too heavily laden. Indeed, moving from the specific case to the general, he here makes the correction of all of them public, with the modesty of one who corrects, so that others might profit from their correction [Col. 0565B] and they themselves, as has been said, might not fail in patience.

“Therefore,” he says, since all, both those who do these things and those who consent to them, are worthy of death, “you are inexcusable, O man.” A person is inexcusable when truth is not hidden from him and unrighteousness persists in him. “O man”: a person who is placed in honor, possesses God’s Law, judges according to God’s Law—and, with him, every sinful person, whether through the guilt of origin or the addition of his own will, whether he knows or does not know. For ignorance itself is undoubtedly sin in those who were unwilling to understand; in those who could not understand, it is the punishment of sin. Therefore, O person who judge from the Law, you are inexcusable; but you too, every person who neither knows the Law nor judges, are nevertheless inexcusable. For He admits no excuse who knows that He made man upright and in addition gave him the commandment of obedience: the testimony of conscience in the law of nature. Therefore in neither case is excuse just; but in both just condemnation applies. For if those who could not understand God’s invisible things from the creation of the world through the things made are inexcusable, how much more those who, instructed from His Law, are confident that they are guides of the blind and a light to those who are in darkness? This discourse is directed to them: “O man,” not “O spirit”; for it is with human pride that you strive to excuse yourself, being humanly wise and judging according to man. “For in that wherein you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things which you judge.” The world is full of people judging—or even punishing—in other people what they themselves do; when they judge others, they pronounce sentence upon themselves.

VERS. 2.—“For we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.” Since at times things which appear evil are done with a good intention, and good things with an evil intention, while there are other matters in which the intention of the agent corresponds either to good or to evil: true judgment belongs to Him alone who knows how to discern hearts.

VERS. 3.—“But do you suppose this, O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Let those who hate Him flee from before His face” (Ps. LXVII). Those who love God do not flee His judgments, but desire them, because they trust that they will be justified in them. But those who flee cannot escape. It follows.

VERS. 4.—“Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and patience and long-suffering?” He has now made the despiser anxious; therefore he adds the reason for patience, saying: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” God’s goodness is immeasurable riches, because, just as He makes His sun rise, so He does not cease to pour out His other good gifts upon good and evil alike. God’s patience is toward those who despise Him; His long-suffering is toward those who sin through weakness rather than intention. For while sinners persist in wickedness, God persists in patience, punishing a few things in this age lest divine providence be thought not to exist, and reserving many things for the final judgment, so that the judgment to come may be made known. But the mind conscious of its evil, already wholly given over to punishment, when it seems to suffer no punishment, believes that God does not judge. This is the reprobate mind, this the blindness and hardening of heart, these the inward darknesses by which the sinner is shut out from God’s inward light—yet not wholly so long as he is in this life. For there are outer darknesses, which are understood to pertain more to the Day of Judgment, so that one who refuses correction may be wholly outside God while he still has time. But what is it to be wholly outside God except to be in the utmost blindness? For God dwells in inaccessible light; into it enter those to whom it is said: “Enter into the joy [Col. 0566C] of your Lord” (Matt. XXV). “Do you not know,” he says, “that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” This is so while there is time for mercy. Would you hear of the time of judgment?

VERS. 5.—“According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God.” There are two kinds of those who sin stubbornly: one promises itself God’s mercy; the other despairs because of the enormity of its crimes. On account of those deceived by delay through hope of mercy, God made the final day uncertain; on account of those endangered by despair, He provided the harbor of pardon. Whether one belongs to the former or the latter, unless he quickly corrects himself, he treasures up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. A treasure is a place where riches of different kinds are stored up little by little, so that they may be found gathered together, as it were, in a single heap. Three treasures, therefore, are found in Scripture: treasure on earth, treasure in heaven, and this which is called the treasure of wrath. A person who stores his acts in the treasure of wrath with an impenitent heart is called hard; one who stores treasure on earth is called foolish. “Fool,” He says, “this night they require your soul of you” (Luke XI). But the wise person, rich toward God, makes whatever he does worthy of the kingdom of heaven. Thus the carnal person stores treasure on earth, the merely animate person in wrath, and the spiritual person in heaven. The day of wrath is the day of judgment, when it will be faithfully brought forth for each person what, how much, and where he has stored up. There the Judge will not so much take note of ability as crown the will. You willed it, and perhaps could not accomplish it: He will take note of you as though you had done what you willed, and it will also be said of you, “to each according to his works.” As great as is the diversity of merits here, so great there will be the diversity either of glory or of punishments.

Yet far be it that certain venial sins, without which this life is scarcely or never passed, should prevent a righteous person from eternal life; just as certain good works, without which the life of even the worst person is found only with great difficulty, will not benefit the ungodly. But wretched people, when they hear of eternal fire here, promise themselves purgatory there. “Many,” they say, “will be saved there, as through fire.” O hope of the despairing! First, it must be known that nothing in this life can be conceived harsher than that fire. Nevertheless, according to the Apostle’s testimony, the one who builds upon the foundation, Christ, not “gold, silver, precious stones,” but “wood, hay, stubble” (I Cor. III), will indeed be saved there through fire—provided, however, that he does not reject the foundation so as not to receive it, nor reject it once received, and that he sets it before all his carnal pleasures by which he is captivated or overcome, when the issue comes to this: either those pleasures must be abandoned, or Christ. Where Christ is not preferred, He is not that person’s foundation. For the foundation is placed before all the subsequent parts of a structure. Nor does ignorance of Christ or of any good excuse anyone there so that he does not burn in everlasting fire—except that if he did not believe because he had not heard, perhaps he will burn less.

Let these things for the present be said concerning the day of wrath, “in which God will render to every person according to his works: to those who, by patient continuance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life” (vv. 6–7). This is what he says, and this is the order of the following sense. To those, he says, who seek glory, honor, and incorruption through the patience of good work, eternal life will be given by God—not only to Jews, to whom the oracles of God appear to have been entrusted, but also to Greeks—because God’s judgment is just: God is not only the God of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles. But to those who, through contentiousness of mind and perversity of spirit, do not believe the truth but follow unrighteousness, there will be rendered wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish—not only to the Gentile, but also to the Jew—because there is no respect of persons with God.

These things concern the sequence of the discourse; but now let us examine what pertains to the inward meaning. “To those,” he says, “who by patient continuance in good work,” that is, who bear fruit in patience: “glory and honor.” This glory will be the blessed happiness of incorruption and immortality in the resurrection, both in body and soul. Honor, however, will be that which man possessed before he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them: when, abounding in the delights of God’s paradise, he continually enjoyed the vision of God and converse with Him. These things will be rendered in eternal life to those who seek eternal life, concerning which life itself He says: “And this is eternal life: that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (John XVII). Therefore, to those who seek God for God’s own sake, He Himself will be eternal life, [Col. 0568B] honor, and glory; He Himself will be all in all.

(V. 8.) “But to those who are contentious, and do not yield to truth but believe unrighteousness, wrath and indignation” (Rom. II), and so forth. Understand, prudent reader, the matters set before you, and observe that God is said to render glory, honor, and eternal life to those who do good; but wrath and indignation, anguish and tribulation await the reprobate, though these are not said to be rendered by God. For what is good we receive from God; evils, however, we inflict upon ourselves. “To those,” he says, “who are contentious.” Contentiousness is what produces heresies, schisms, and scandals; hence it comes about that truth is not obeyed and unrighteousness is believed. To such belong wrath, indignation, anguish, and tribulation. Wrath is the torment of the soul inflicted by the consciousness of sin. Indignation is understood as a kind of swelling of wrath itself, as of a wound, and as a disturbance in each particular part; as, for example, if we suppose wrath to be some grievous wound, whose swelling and distension are called the indignation of the wound. Tribulation, however, is not that which produces breadth, of which it is said, “In tribulation You have enlarged me” (Ps. IV), but rather that which produces the anguish opposed to such enlargement—that is, to the will made joyful by God’s grace in doing good. “To the Jew first,” who knew the Lord’s will and did not do what was worthy, and therefore will receive many stripes (Luke XII); “then to the Greek,” who, because he did not know, perhaps will receive few stripes (ibid.). For it differs whether one has known God or has known His will. A Gentile could know God from the creation of the world; but God’s will is known from the Law and the prophets.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0567]

THE SECOND CHAPTER CONTINUES.

[Col. 0567D]

VERS. 11–12.—“For with God there is no respect of persons.” Every rational soul, even when blinded by desire, nevertheless, when it thinks and reasons, must attribute whatever truth shines out to it in that reasoning not to itself but to the very light of truth, by which, even if only faintly illuminated, it perceives some truth while reasoning. [Col. 0568D] For there is no soul, however perverse, that is capable of reasoning and in whose conscience God does not speak. For the hand of our Maker has written in our very hearts: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV); and, “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII). [Col. 0569A] Even before the law was given, no one was allowed to be ignorant of this, so that those who had not received the written law would still have a basis on which to be judged. Yet lest people complain that anything was lacking to them, that which they were compelled to see in conscience was written down and set before their eyes. But the Jews alone received the written law; the natural law, however, was received both by Gentiles and Jews.

The works of the written law are twofold: some concern sacraments, others morals. Circumcision, the Sabbath, and other such things belong to sacraments. “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and the like, belong to morals. In observances, if they are observed without being understood, there is slavery alone. If they are understood and observed, they are beneficial, but in their proper time—as they were observed by Moses and the prophets, while such [Col. 0569B] slavery was still useful, so that people might be kept under a guardian and under fear. Yet nothing terrifies the soul so devoutly as a sacrament not understood. When understood, it produces joy; and, if the work is suitable to the time, it is freely celebrated. Otherwise it is merely read and discussed with spiritual sweetness. Every sacrament, when understood, is referred either to the contemplation of truth or to good morals. Contemplation of truth is founded on love of God alone; good morals, however, on love of God and neighbor, on which “the whole law and the prophets hang” (Matt. XXII).

As regards morals, the written law and the natural law are nearly the same, equally common to Jews and Gentiles—except that one has it written on tablets and in reason, while the other has it in reason alone. For that natural power is present in both, by which the rational creature recognizes and does what is lawful. Therefore, as is said here, “there is no respect of persons”; but “the one who sinned in the law” (v. 12), that is, while placed under the observance of the written law, will be judged according to that law, which forbids sins and assigns its own punishment to each sin. But one “who sinned without the law”—the written law—will be judged “without the law,” that is, not through the law he did not receive; for the law he did receive is sufficient for his judgment.

VERS. 13.—“For not the hearers of the law, but the doers,” whether of the written or natural law, “will be justified before God.” [Col. 0569D] His statement that only the doer of the law is justified before God requires sound understanding, lest it seem contrary to what is elsewhere said: “If it is from works, it is no longer from grace” (Rom. XI), and “grace is no longer grace” (ibid.). Far be it that righteousness should come to one who does the law as though from the works of the law itself. Rather, in order that one may do the law, he is justified by grace precisely in doing it. He is not first a doer of the law, so as to become righteous, as it were, in return for a law fulfilled. Rather, as a human being is created in order to be human, so one doing the law is justified in order to be righteous—or to be shown to be what he is in doing it, namely righteous.

It should be understood that here he speaks of Jews converted to the Lord and fulfilling the law spiritually. A converted Gentile also does naturally the things of the law and, in doing them, is justified; for the Spirit of grace restores in him the natural law inscribed by God upon his heart, but erased through vice. [Col. 0570A] For one converted to the Lord, this is to have the law of God written not on tablets but in the heart: to embrace the righteousness of the law with the inmost affection of the heart, where faith works through love. Hence there follows:

VERS. 14–16.—“For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, these, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another among themselves, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ.”

“Of thoughts accusing,” he says. The Latin translator seems to follow Greek usage: since the Greeks do not have the ablative case, they use the genitive in place of the ablative. He says “of thoughts,” moreover, because works are judged from the thought, and a person is judged innocent or guilty. Yet he says “of thoughts,” not of those which will then exist, but of those which now exist, because all our deeds and thoughts, although they perish from memory, do not perish from conscience. Before God the judge, these will all be brought into the light. A judgment indeed to be feared: nothing is introduced from outside, but everything is brought forth from conscience—the accuser, the witness, the judge, and the case.

VERS. 17.—“But if you are called a Jew and rest upon the law.” Here the Apostle enters upon a powerful and necessary argument concerning the law, not only against the Jews but also against the enemies [Col. 0570C] of grace and those whom he denounced a little above as acting “from contention.” The reader’s diligence will be greatly assisted if he keeps in mind four distinctions—whether of the law itself or of progress under the law.

When one lives according to the flesh in the deepest darkness of ignorance, with no reasoning resistance, this is the first stage of humanity. Next, once through the law knowledge of sin has come, if the divine Spirit does not yet help, a person who wishes to live according to the law is defeated and sins knowingly. Knowledge of sin thus causes sin to work every desire in a person; and, with the accumulation of transgression added, what is written is fulfilled: “The law entered in, that the offence might abound” (Rom. V). This is the second stage of humanity.

But if God looks upon a person so that he believes God himself helps him to fulfill his commands, and the person begins, by God’s Spirit, to desire against the flesh with the stronger strength of love—so that, although there is still something from the human being resisting the human being and the whole infirmity has not yet been healed, he nevertheless lives by faith as a righteous person, and lives righteously insofar as he does not yield to evil desire, the delight of righteousness prevailing—this is the third stage, of a person of good hope. If anyone progresses in these through devout perseverance, the final peace remains: it will be fulfilled after this life in the rest of the spirit, and then also in the resurrection of the flesh.

Of these four distinctions, the first is before the law; the second under the law; the third under grace; the fourth in full and perfect peace. Grace, however, was not absent even before then from those to whom it was fitting that it should be bestowed, though, according to the dispensation of the times, it was veiled and hidden. [Col. 0571A] According to these four distinctions, the whole body of this epistle treats now of the man of God individually, now of God’s people generally.

“But if,” he says, “you are called a Jew.” The skilled physician of souls, seeing one of two sick persons—namely his own people—more dangerously ill, becomes weak with the weak. He rebukes the Gentiles more harshly and without sparing them; but he identifies the same crimes among the Jews and touches upon them gently, in order to provoke these to patience through the obedience of the Gentiles, until, in the manner of physicians, he mitigates the cause of the disease—that is, pride—so that, as physicians commonly say, once the cause is mitigated, he may apply treatment more safely to the causative condition. Therefore, to console their weakness, he has not yet rebuked them separately, but together with the others.

But now, after the common admonition, seeking freer access to his sick person, he first begins to bind the madman with strong bonds of argument, so that, since he had the Gentiles readily compliant, he might also fit the hardness of the Jews to grace. For each, according to the distinctions stated above, was found under the law—whether written or natural.

VERS. 17–20.—“But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law, and boast in God, and know his will, and approve the more excellent things, being instructed by the law; and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having in the law the form of knowledge and truth.”

It should be understood that all the things here presented as though in praise of the false Jew are stated ironically. For everything he says here is like a plaster, by which he treats the swelling of pride, so that vanity may be compressed and emptiness may subside. What is emptier than to boast of what one does not possess, or to preach what one does not do? That people, indeed, was weak at the second stage of God’s people—that is, concerning the law. They were proud because they had received it, yet did not fulfill it even carnally; and, presuming upon themselves, they came more slowly to grace. For if they truly rested in the law and boasted in God, they would not do what they preached ought not to be done.

“If,” he says, “you are called a Jew”—which you are not, for the true Judaea is the Church, which the Lord God has clothed with the beauty of confession—and you seem to derive your name from the fathers from whom you have degenerated: they had circumcision of the flesh as a seal of faith, but circumcision of the heart by that faith itself. You also used to have kings from the tribe of Judah, for which reason you were all called Jews. But when you denied Christ the king from the tribe of Judah, you lost both kingdom and name together.

“You rest upon the law,” condemning and ridiculing the diverse errors of the Gentiles; or, resting in a carnal understanding of the law, you judge that nothing further need be sought. “And you boast in God,” as though you were God’s peculiar people, and because God was supposedly known only in Judaea. “And you know his will, because he has not done thus for every nation, nor made known his judgments to them” (Ps. CXLVII). “And, approving among useful things the more useful,” instructed by the law, “you are confident,” presumptuously, that “you yourself,” without the guidance of the Holy Spirit, “are a guide of the blind,” so that both of you may fall into the pit; “a light to those in darkness,” as though they were to be enlightened through you; “an instructor” of the Gentiles, supposedly “foolish” in the law; “a teacher of infants,” so that they may, as it were, learn to speak from the law the nursery tales of your fables; “having in the law the form of knowledge and truth,” that is, a formed and true knowledge of the law, to which no one would dare add anything further.

VERS. 21.—“Therefore, do you who teach another not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” The Jews, indeed, were thieves among themselves of their possessions; and, what is worse, they wished to steal from the law its sound understanding, from the Church grace, and from the world Christ’s advent. Thus they also committed adultery carnally, but still more spiritually, following their own desires. They likewise followed the idols of the Gentiles, but more so the idols of their own hearts; sacrilegious in both respects, not placing sacred things in what is sacred. They also dishonored the God of the law by transgression of that law, in which they thought they should boast. They dishonored him because they caused his name to be blasphemed among the Gentiles.

The name of Christ is “Christian”; when it is blasphemed, the blasphemy returns upon the author of the name. This is taken from the prophet Ezekiel. For the Jews rebuked here were already participants in the Christian name; but because they foolishly boasted of their former state, they preferred themselves to the Gentiles. By that very former state the Apostle wisely humbles them. [Col. 0572C] Therefore, what they considered made them especially conspicuous and glorious—namely, the law and circumcision—he proves is now useless and superfluous, and more a cause of shame to them than glory. He has spoken of the law; now of circumcision:

VERS. 25.—“Circumcision,” he says, “is beneficial if you observe the law”—namely, the law of circumcision. Circumcision is the cutting away of evils from oneself; the law of circumcision is persistence in good works, so that what is written may come to pass: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). True circumcision is also the circumcision of the heart, that is, a will pure from every desire. This is not accomplished by the letter teaching and threatening, but by the Spirit helping and healing.

“Circumcision, therefore, is beneficial if you observe the law. But if you are transgressors of the law,” so that you observe carnal circumcision rather, “your circumcision has become uncircumcision,” that is, it will be reckoned as unbelief. There follows:

VERS. 26–27.—“If, therefore, the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? And will not that which is by nature uncircumcision, fulfilling the law, judge you, who through letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law?”

“If uncircumcision,” he says—that is, those who came from uncircumcision. For he sets these, while keeping the righteous requirements of the law, in comparison with Jews who transgress the law through the letter and circumcision of the flesh. He does not say that they keep the law itself—that is, the law of works or of sacraments—but “the righteous requirements of the law,” that is, its moral discipline. By keeping this, uncircumcision is so far preferred to circumcision transgressing the law that it judges it. And appropriately he adds, “fulfilling the law.” For one who lives according to the letter observes the law; one who lives according to the Spirit fulfills it. Perfection belongs to the one who says: “I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V).

“Therefore, not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor that which is circumcision outwardly in the flesh; but the one who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision of the heart in the Spirit, not in the letter—whose praise is not from human beings but from God.”

The sense of the apostolic argument should be followed carefully, lest, because he seems from the variety of persons to address now these and now those, the order of the argument advancing directly should be confused as though the path had been lost, and the reader’s understanding be unable to reach the end to which the debater’s purpose leads. That end, to state it briefly, is grace, or the commendation of grace.

To return, then, a little above: Paul, cherishing both Jews and Gentiles with fatherly affection—embracing the Jews both in flesh and in spirit, but the Gentiles because of the grace of the Gospel and the honor of his ministry—threatens wrath and the things belonging to wrath upon those who were acting from contention, whether these or those; but promises to those doing good, whether these or those, the things belonging to glory and honor. Then, alternately lowering, raising, or equalizing now these and now those, he strives to order and direct everything so that he assigns neither greater glory nor greater odium to either party.

For he immediately adds concerning the Gentiles: “Whoever sinned without the law will perish without the law.” And at once concerning circumcision: “And whoever sinned in the law will be judged through the law.” Again raising the Gentiles, he says: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law,” and so forth. Then he turns his speech again to the Jews: “But if,” he says, “you are called a Jew,” and the things following. And lest he seem excessive in his rebuke of the Jews, he adds: “Circumcision is beneficial if you observe the law.” But immediately, setting limits to circumcision’s ground for boasting in favor of the Gentiles: “But if,” he says, “you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.” And raising the Gentiles a little: “If,” he says, “uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law,” and so forth. And still more strongly elevating their spirits: “That which is by nature uncircumcision,” he says, “fulfilling the law, will judge you, who through letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law.”

But because it was certain that there were many promises in the law and prophets which seemed to pertain to circumcision, in order to open to the Gentiles a way even toward hoping for those promises, he says:

VERS. 28–29.—“Not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor that which is circumcision outwardly in the flesh; but the one who is a Jew inwardly,” and so forth. Then follows what we now have in hand.

## CHAPTER III

VERS. 1.—“What advantage, then, has the Jew?” But let us proceed by clearing the way for ourselves, so that afterward we may walk more lightly to the conclusion concerning grace. “Much,” he says, “in every way.” For the Jew had many preparations and instructions for faith in Christ; the Gentile had none of these, apart from natural understanding alone.

“Do we, then, excel them? By no means,” because a greater preparation for faith, if you do not believe, is nothing to you but greater condemnation. But if you believe and the other believes, your faith does not precede theirs in merit. As regards merits, it has been shown by certain arguments from causes that all were under sin before grace. Through the law, however, comes knowledge of sin only, not remission. “But now”—that is, in the time of grace—“the righteousness” not of the law or merits but “of God in the blood of Christ has been manifested” (v. 21). This is grace. Hence, a little later, as though drawing a conclusion, he says: “We reckon that a human being is justified through faith apart from works of the law” (v. 23).

Let us return a little further upward. “There is no respect of persons with God” (above, ch. II, v. 11). What, then, is accepted with God? The endurance of a good work. But whence is this? Either from grace or from law. If from law, then it is not apart from law. Yet it is found apart from law, because Gentiles who do not have the law naturally do the things of the law—that is, they bear fruit in endurance. Then follows: “But if you are called a Jew” (ch. II, v. 17), and so forth. It is as though he said: O you who are called a Jew, whence comes the justification of the law—from the law or elsewhere? It is not from the law, because you who boast in the law dishonor God through transgression of the law. It is therefore from elsewhere: namely, from the Spirit, in whom the true and inward Jew is justified, whose praise is not from human beings but from God.

“What advantage, then,” he says, “has the Jew? Or what is the usefulness of circumcision? Much in every way,” because, whether spiritually or carnally, they received more preparations for justification by faith. The Gentiles, however, received more faith, as the Lord says: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII). Why did the Jews receive less faith? This is the depth of God’s wisdom. Therefore, if a good work is from grace and justification from the Spirit, both Jew and Gentile have open capacity and access to these things. But since, before grace, the Jew received more preparations toward this end—which were also temporal consolations to him—he received more in every way.

In the time of grace, however, the Jew does not excel the Gentile: because, insofar as the Gentile has now received more faith, grace found both equally under sin as regards the past. Therefore grace is equally necessary to both. But now, to return to the sequence of the reading:

VERS. 2–3.—“First,” he says, “because the oracles of God were entrusted to them,” namely in the law and the prophets, for the pattern of sacraments, instruction in morals, and preparations for receiving Christ’s advent. Among them there were indeed a few who believed; but the multitude who did not believe “will not annul the faithfulness of God,” that is, will not wholly estrange that people from faith in Christ. Since God’s promises to it are good, they cannot fail, because:

VERS. 4.—“God is true, but every human being a liar.” In this respect even that human being is a liar who either does not believe or does not say that the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. “For what,” he says, “if some of them did not believe? Will their unbelief annul the faithfulness of God?” “Far be it!” Far be it, he says, that the evil of any number of individuals should destroy the good of the whole; far be it that the truth of God who promises should be rendered void by the sin of an unbelieving human being! For “every human being is a liar, but God is true, as it is written: That you may be justified in your words and overcome when you are judged” (Ps. L).

Every human being is a liar; yet those to whom the word of God came are not liars, whom Scripture declares not human beings but gods, and whom the Lord confirms in the Gospel. But God is true, who is justified in his words. The sense of these words from the Psalm must be sought from what precedes: “Against you alone,” he says, “have I sinned” (Ps. L), because I am king and subject to no human judgment. “Against you alone have I sinned,” because I was not afraid to sin before you, who are present everywhere. Have mercy on me according to your great mercy—namely, so that you may be justified, that is, shown righteous in your words, in which you promised that a house would be built for me and that my seed would come after me, whose kingdom would be established forever.

In these promises you will appear righteous and true when you fulfill them for me, judging me according to the truth of the mercy you have loved, and restoring to me the spirit of prophecy, in which you revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom. You overcome the judgments of people who judge rashly and according to appearance, while they adjudge to me your forgiveness, my repentance, and the benefits of your promises. The Apostle, adopting this whole extended sense, takes what pertains to proving God’s truth: “That you may be justified,” he says, “in your words, and overcome when you are judged.”

The similarity in the example he introduces should be noted: just as, after David’s sin, so after the Lord’s passion, rash judgments of people denied all grace of pardon and promise to the whole Jewish people. That mercy, unjustly judged, prevailed when, from his unjust death, it brought about righteousness unto life even for his killers in great mercy. Thus, having heard blasphemy against God as though he were false, and a slander of universal destruction against his own people, the Apostle cries out almost impatiently: “Far be it! But every human being is a liar, and God is true!” Taking occasion from this blasphemy, and as though gathering his spirit against the blasphemers, he says that from this very proposition they argue as follows:

VERS. 5.—“But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath?” To show that he says this in the voice of blasphemers, he adds: “Far be it! I speak this according to man.” It is indeed according to man, but not even according to one sufficiently wise in human things. For God’s righteousness is commended by our unrighteousness not by the benefit of our sins, but by the consequence of reasoning itself: contraries are proved from contraries. For unrighteousness is, by every consequence, fittingly and deservedly the enemy and adversary of righteousness, just as light is of darkness and life of death; and it is just that God, in whom is highest righteousness, should inflict wrath upon human beings in whom is unrighteousness.

For this reason perhaps the Apostle does not say that unrighteous people commend God’s righteousness, but that our unrighteousness does, so as to show that it is not God who is contrary to human beings, but righteousness which is contrary to unrighteousness (v. 6). “Otherwise,” he says, “how will God judge this world?” For one who will judge the world justly cannot be unjust. This is another argument for God’s righteousness. Then he heightens the slander in order to repel it. For he says:

VERS. 7.—“If,” they say, “the truth of God has abounded through my lie unto his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?” But this, says the Apostle, we do not say—nor indeed what they imagine follows from it.

VERS. 8.—“And they say that we say: Let us do evil, that good things may come,” whereas we rather preach that good things should be done, lest evil things come. Those who say this sin knowingly, and therefore their condemnation is just.

VERS. 9–11.—“What then? Do we excel them? By no means.” Having repelled the slander, he returns to the sequence of his argument. What advantage, he says, do we retain? Since it is established that both parties were under sin before grace, and grace, when it comes, so far as it is concerned, makes both equal, no ground remains for contention or self-exaltation of one against the other. “For we have charged both Jews and Greeks with being under sin.” As is his custom, he confirms this from the Scriptures, thereby also giving an example to the teachers of the Church: they are to establish and fortify what they say from the testimonies of Scripture. “There is no righteous person, no one understanding, no one seeking God.” There is no righteous person because there is no one understanding; no one understands because no one seeks God. For if one sought, one would understand; if one understood, loving the one understood, one would surely be righteous.

VERS. 12.—“All have turned aside.” “Birds are deservedly caught,” says a certain wise person. “Those to whom the sky has been granted—what are they seeking on the ground, at snares?” We too, having abandoned heaven—toward which nature itself raised us even by the very posture of our bodies—all bend down to earthly things, useless, corrupting one another by the evil provocation of example. “There is no one who does good.” It is one thing to do good, another to do something well. To do something well is to do it by outcome, or as if in passing; to do good is to do it with purpose and affection. Conversely, regarding evil—for example, pride—it is one thing to be proud, another to make pride. Some suffer pride within themselves; others make and build it up. Of these the Prophet says: “The one who makes pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. C).

“There is none, not even one.” Count one and one: you will not find one perfectly good, until you come to the supremely good One, who says: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII).

VERS. 13.—“Their throat is an open grave,” namely when they speak. Because, according to the prophet, they are dead in heart, through unclean words they exhale the stench of the corpse rotting within. “The poison of asps is under their lips”: those who speak wickedly are more wickedly silent, when an incurable wickedness cannot accomplish what it wills and wastes away in their hearts.

VERS. 14.—“Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness,” because with a full mouth they curse where they dare, and with a full heart they are bitter where they do not dare.

VERS. 15.—“Their feet are swift to shed blood.” They are swift to every sin in the execution of action, because they are restrained and governed by no judgment of reason.

VERS. 16.—“Destruction and misery are in their ways,” because harsh necessity of bodily labor and affliction, and the misery of a tormenting conscience, are in all their actions.

VERS. 17–18.—“And they have not known the way of peace,” because “the fear of God is not before their eyes”—the fear which is the beginning of wisdom and of proceeding toward that peace of which it is said: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law” (Ps. CXVIII).

The evils which the Apostle here gathers together as one seem to have been introduced chiefly for the Jews, although at the beginning of the Psalm they seem to have been said concerning the Gentiles: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. XIII). But the pride of the Jews had especially to be broken by reminding them of the transgressions of the law in which they boasted. They also boasted of their father Abraham and the other fathers, as if they possessed righteousness by nature. Hence he adds:

VERS. 19.—“We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are in the law, so that every mouth may be stopped”—and may not be opened except in the praise of God. The Gentiles are most ready for humility from consciousness of their past error; the Jews, as stated, are humbled by transgression of the law in which they appeared to boast. The more special their reception and greater their knowledge of the law, the less excuse they have, the more evident their transgression, and the more certain their condemnation—even if they perform works of the law.

VERS. 20.—“By works of the law no one,” observing it carnally, “will be justified before God,” who sees the heart and the inmost will, where he sees that the one who fears the law would prefer to do otherwise if it were permitted. “So that the whole world may become subject to God,” understanding what each owes to whom and what each receives from whom. For from the law one has knowledge of sin, but from grace the manifestation of righteousness and justification itself. “For through the law comes knowledge of sin”: not because sin was unknown, but because it was thought it could be committed with impunity. But unless grace helps so that known sin may be overcome, the law works wrath instead.

VERS. 21.—“But now,” that is, under grace, “the righteousness of God has been manifested.” Although it justifies without the help of the law, it is nevertheless “witnessed by the law and the prophets,” so that, while the law announced it, faith might fulfill it and perfection result. For faith ought not to lack the testimony of the law, nor could the righteousness of the law be fulfilled except in faith. Thus the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from law, though witnessed by the law and prophets.

Those acquainted with Greek language or writings have observed that among the Greeks, because of the variety of laws, the law of Moses is marked in their Scriptures by the addition of a particular article. Since the word “law” occurs twice in this verse, they say that the article is added in the first occurrence, not the second. This gives us to understand that the law of Moses is that by which the righteousness of God is witnessed; but that it is aided by no law—whether given in Paradise, naturally implanted, or promulgated in writing.

It should also be noted that he says sin is “known,” but righteousness “manifested,” because everything manifested is light. Sin, however, is known rather than manifested, because it belongs to darkness. What then is this righteousness? “The righteousness of God,” he says, when faith obtains what the law commands: God’s righteousness, not that of human beings, works, or one’s own will. Not that it happens without our will, but because our will, shown weak by the law, has been healed through the grace which comes from faith and has fulfilled the law.

Here, too, the law is found useful: because, unable to heal, it sends those needing healing to grace by its free testimony and by the experience of its own weakness. One is sent to grace and to the life-giving Spirit, where all sins are erased and the love of doing good is inspired. This is the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, passing into all and over all who believe in him: into all, as regards the universality of believers; over all, because it surpasses every merit of those receiving it. For there is no distinction—whether of Jew or righteous person, as though one had less need; or of Gentile or repentant sinner, as though one received less.

VERS. 23.—“For all have sinned and need the glory of God.” God does not need to be glorified by anyone; rather, all without exception need God to be glorified in them. His glory consists in their being justified freely by his grace. Whose grace it is, his also is the glory.

VERS. 24–25.—“Through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” For those who had sold themselves needed to be redeemed. A person sells himself by consenting to sin, which is the death of the soul: accepting the pleasure of sin itself, he in some fashion gives away the hope of his present life and eternal life. There came the man who alone was born righteous; and, though he did not accept the pleasure of sin, he did not refuse sin’s penalty. He gave this righteousness to the person sold and having nothing in the substance of his nature by which to redeem himself, so that from Christ’s penalty he might pay the bond of his own debt.

This is the righteousness of God: by faith adhering to him who died for us, we possess from him what we cannot possess from ourselves. Because this has been bestowed upon us freely, it is grace. In order that all things might correspond to grace, he predestined him before the ages; but in this time he publicly set him forth as “a propitiator in his own blood,” when before the sight of the Gentiles he revealed his righteousness. By it he appeared righteous in not leaving sins unpunished, and justly justified the unrighteous by remitting sins expiated through the voluntary shedding of the propitiator’s blood.

When a sinner adheres to him by faith, that person may emerge justified in his righteousness, to the glory of the one who justifies: the blood of the propitiator expiating, love healing, righteousness justifying. Therefore, to display his righteousness, he long endured—or sustained—sinners; but in the time of grace he himself prepared and effected righteousness for the unrighteous. Thus he displayed his righteousness with regard to the past, by mercifully sustaining sinners; and with regard to the present time, by bestowing forgiveness through grace and justifying freely.

He did this once for all people; he continually does it individually for each person.
