He bears with and sustains the sinner; he inspires and prepares conversion; sometimes he even imposes necessity; he heals the will and aids weakness. And when he has done the whole work, he attributes all the merit of the work to the one for whom it was done. This is grace; this is God’s righteousness, of which the Prophet says: “Deliver me in your righteousness” (Ps. XXX).

The whole mass owed punishment; and if the penalty due for condemnation were rendered to all, it would undoubtedly be rendered not unjustly. Who, then, would be so utterly and madly insane as not to give unspeakable thanks to the mercy that delivers whom it wills—when such a person could in no way rightly blame the justice that condemns absolutely all? Since this has been concluded most justly, it is most plainly excluded that anyone should boast in himself, in the law, or in anyone but the Lord.

VERS. 27.—“Where, then, is your boasting? It is excluded. Through what law? That of works? No, but through the law of faith.” Whether he means commendable boasting, which is in the Lord, and says that it is “excluded,” that is, not driven away so as to depart, but pressed out so as to stand forth—whence certain silversmiths are called *exclusores* [embossers]. So too in the psalm: “That those tested by silver may stand forth” (Ps. 67); that is, that those tested by the utterance of the Lord may be conspicuous. Or whether he means the vicious boasting arising from pride: namely, the boasting of those who, when they seem to themselves to live rightly, boast as though they had not received it. This boasting, he says, is excluded—not through the law of works but through the law of faith—that is, cast out and rejected.

For through the law of faith each person recognizes that, if he lives well, he has this from God’s grace, and that he will attain perfection in the love of righteousness from no other source. This knowledge makes a person devout, because devotion is true wisdom. I mean that devotion which the Greeks call θεοσέβεια, “reverence for God.” It is precisely this which is commended in the book of Job, where it is said: “Behold, devotion is wisdom” (Job 28). For θεοσέβεια is the worship of God, chiefly consisting in this: that the soul should not be ungrateful to him.

For this is proud and, as it were, uncommon boasting—like boasting in eloquence or wealth—concerning those things which are peculiarly the proper goods of good persons, that is, concerning righteousness [Col. 0580A], when a person presumes to claim it as his own, whether a Jew on account of works of the law or any proud person on account of the merits of works. Although righteousness is possessed by no one except through faith, care must nevertheless be taken lest it be thought or said to be a wage for the merit of faith by those who pride themselves, as though wisely, upon righteousness.

For although faith obtains justification, as God apportions to each person a measure of faith, no human merit precedes God’s grace. Rather, grace itself earns an increase by this very means, so that it may also deserve to be perfected. For concerning faith itself: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4). Hence elsewhere the Apostle himself says: “I obtained mercy, that I might become faithful” (1 Tim. 1). He does not say, “because I am faithful,” but “that I might become faithful.” Faith, indeed, is not a matter of merits [Col. 0580B] or of one’s own choice. It is God’s free gift; and all good things begin from it.

Good works are indeed done by a human being; but faith is produced in a human being, without which no good works are done by any human being. “For everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14). Nor should anyone exalt himself on account of the merit even of prayer, even if he asks only for God or things belonging to God. When help is given to one praying, it is the faith given to one not praying that prays; if it had not been given, that person could not pray. In all these matters, O Jew, O proud one, “your boasting is excluded. Through what law? That of works? No, but through the law of faith.”

It must be understood how the law of works and the law of faith differ, although each alike says, “You shall not covet,” a prohibition containing all sins committed through desire [Col. 0580C], and although each has its own sacraments of works, though dissimilar. In the law of works is the righteousness of God commanding; in the law of faith, the mercy of God helping. What the law of works commands with threats, the law of faith obtains by believing. By the law of works God says, “Do what I command”; by the law of faith God is told, “Give what you command.”

For this reason the law commands: that it may admonish what faith is to do; that is, so that the one commanded, if still unable, may know what to ask for; but if immediately able and obediently does it, may know by whose gift he is able. This is that wisdom called devotion, by which the Father of lights is worshipped, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present (Jas. 1). He is worshipped by the sacrifice of praise and acts of thanksgiving, so that his worshipper may glory not in himself but in him [Col. 0580D]; and so that the good son of faith may know from whom he should hope for what he does not yet possess, and from whom he possesses what he already has.

The law of works, however, is holy law, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good; yet through its goodness sin works death, prohibiting and producing every desire, commanding but not helping, punishing but not delivering. The law of faith, however, has certain ordinances in the sacraments of the Church: easier in practice than the sacraments of the law of works, better in usefulness, greater in power, fewer in number—appropriate to righteousness revealed by faith, to children of God called into freedom, and to the yoke of slavery removed, which suited a harsh people devoted to the flesh.

Yet these sacraments too will cease in their own time; for, as Christ’s first coming imposed an end upon those earlier rites, so his second coming will impose an end upon these [Col. 0581A], namely, when the kingdom of manifest truth has dawned. It follows:

VERS. 28.—“For we judge that a human being is justified through faith without works of the law.” What then? Does faith not work through love? Certainly it does. But since there were some among the Jews who boasted of works of the law—which they did not perform through love but from fear—and who wished to appear righteous and superior to the Gentiles, as though the Gentiles had not performed the work of the law, the Apostle confidently declared that a person can be justified through faith without works of the law. Thus those who did what they did out of fear were not righteous to a greater degree than those whose faith works through love in the heart, even if it does not issue outwardly in a deed.

But far be it that the Apostle should be thought to have said that a human being can be justified without works in such a way that a believer, if given opportunity to act, need not do good! Rather, his meaning is that no one should suppose that he has come to justification, which is from faith, by the merits of preceding works. He therefore says that a person can be justified without preceding works; but he is justified through faith and grace, which cannot remain idle in him if he has opportunity to act. If not, however, the righteousness of faith remains with him.

On the other hand, he declares sterile faith, when it has opportunity to act, to be so completely useless that he says: “If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.” For faithful love always works; and in it, without doubt, one lives well, because love is the fulfilment of the law.

“But suppose,” says the Jew, “that a human being is justified only through faith, yet only a Jew; for faith belongs to the one to whom the law belonged.” To this Paul replies:

VERS. 29.—“Or is God,” he says, “God of the Jews only,” who received the law of works? “Is he not also God of the Gentiles,” to whom the law of faith alone has been delivered? “Yes, also of the Gentiles, because he who created both will save both.”

VERS. 30.—“Since indeed there is one God, who justifies the circumcision from faith and the uncircumcision through faith.” The phrases “from faith” and “through faith” appear to differ only in wording, not in meaning, since elsewhere he says that the uncircumcision is justified from faith and the circumcision through faith. Some, however [Col. 0581D], adhering to the letter, think this should be understood such that, when he says circumcision is justified from faith, they attribute the beginning of faith to circumcision, while they seek to establish that uncircumcision is justified through faith as in a second rank. Whether this sufficiently accords with the letter, we leave to the reader’s judgment. Meanwhile, let this stand: a human being is justified through faith without works of the law.

VERS. 31.—“Do we then overthrow the law through faith? Far from it! Rather, we establish the law.” For through the law comes knowledge of sin; through faith, the obtaining of grace against sin; through grace, the healing of the soul from the vice of sin; through the soul’s healing, freedom of choice; through freedom of choice, love of righteousness; through love of righteousness, fulfilment of the law. Thus the law is not overthrown [Col. 0582A] through faith, but established, because faith obtains the grace by which the law is fulfilled.

## Chapter IV

VERS. 1.—“What then shall we say that Abraham found according to the flesh?” The Apostle, commending the righteousness which is from faith against those who boast of righteousness from works, brings forward Abraham as an example, whose pleasing God is beyond doubt. This statement of Scripture intends to direct our attention to the following point: we believe, and the Apostle says, that Abraham has glory before God.

VERS. 2.—But “if he was justified from works, he has glory, but not before God.” Yet he has glory before God. Therefore he was not justified from works. From what, then? It follows:

[Col. 0582B] VERS. 3.—“For what does Scripture say?” That is: from what does Scripture say Abraham was justified? From what follows: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Therefore Abraham was justified from faith.

VERS. 4.—“But to the one who works”—that is, who relies upon works and boasts that God’s grace has been given to him as their merit—the wage is due to him, because it is not reckoned to him according to grace but according to merit. But woe to whatever righteousness a human being may possess, if it is judged with mercy set aside.

VERS. 5.—“But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness.” The act of believing itself is a work of grace. For this is what Christ works in us—not, to be sure, without us. “The works,” he says, “which I do, he also shall do” (John 14), because I bring it about that he may act, that a righteous person may be made from an ungodly one [Col. 0582C]. Then faithful love works, and then unquestionably one lives well.

It matters, however, how a person believes God, so as to believe in God. One believes God who believes him speaking or promising; or one believes God who entrusts himself to him. Hence the Prophet says of a certain people: “His spirit was not faithful to God” (Ps. 77). But to believe in God is, through believing and loving, to go into God, to become a member of his body, or to offer oneself to obedience to his good pleasure—whatever one is—as Abraham did. Because Abraham believed perfectly, his faith was therefore reckoned to him as righteousness.

For he believed God promising him offspring; he believed in God when, leaving his land and his kindred, he obeyed and went to a land he did not know (Gen. 12); or when he offered his son, in whom he had received the promises (Gen. 22); or when he rejoiced to see the Lord’s day, and saw it and was glad (John 8).

VERS. 5.—“According to the purpose of his grace.” For God thus decreed and arranged that, once the law had ceased, faith should justify.

VERS. 6.—“Just as David also declares the blessedness of the person to whom God, having made him acceptable”—that is, made acceptable freely—“reckons righteousness without works.”—“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Ps. 31). Since sins are found in everyone, it follows [Col. 0583A] that none are blessed unless their iniquities have been forgiven. And this is grace, where none of your merits is involved: forgiveness of your sins is freely given to you.

Therefore he did not say, “whose iniquities do not exist,” but “whose iniquities have been forgiven”; or, “whose sins have been covered”; or, “to whom sin is not imputed when it occurs.” Sins are not covered so that they may exist and live, but so that they may not be seen, noticed, or punished. Yet the difference in the order itself must be examined: he first said “iniquities forgiven,” then “sins covered,” and afterwards “sin not imputed.” For the beginning of conversion is to abandon evil, which merits forgiveness of past evils; then to cover individual evils with individual or greater goods; and, once the matter has reached perfection [Col. 0583B], through God’s grace and diligent good conduct, through love of virtue, to uproot from the innermost heart the very inclination toward sin. For then even sin committed is not imputed before God, when it has been cut away from a soul renewed by God’s justification.

“Iniquity,” which in Greek is ἀνομία, *anomia*, “lawlessness,” and “sin” seem to differ in this respect: iniquity is what is done against the law; sin is either what is committed against nature or against a reproving conscience.

Thus in what has been said, it has been found that our father Abraham obtained righteousness from faith, not from works; and blessedness from righteousness. Yet the understanding seems still to hesitate over what is said in verse 4: “To the one who works, the wage is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt; but to the one believing in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness.” For this seems to show that in faith there is indeed the grace of the one who justifies, whereas in work the righteousness of the one who repays seems to be implied.

But anyone who carefully considers the force of the words—when he says that a wage is reckoned to the worker according to debt—will find it difficult to persuade himself that any work can exist which claims God’s reward as a debt. For whatever good we are able to do, act, or think is God’s gift, and nothing can be offered to him which has not been the gift or grant of the Father of lights.

[Note: [Col. 0583] He denies that good works can claim recompense as a debt; but this should be understood with the divine promise and covenant set aside—a matter for theologians.]

Consider, then, whether “debt” ought rather to be understood as belonging to an evil work. For you frequently find debts of sin in the divine writings [Col. 0583D], as in: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6), and concerning the servant rendering an account: “Pay what you owe” (Matt. 18). Consider, then, whether perhaps in this passage also the Apostle refers the wage for work, which is paid according to debt, to this meaning: to those who work as Cain worked the ground, or to those addressed in the words, “Depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke 13).

Since, then, it is established that blessedness is from grace through faith:

VERS. 9.—“Does this blessedness remain only in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision?” For he had already said above that Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he had shown what blessedness such faith possesses. He now poses a question, from whose answer he teaches—also from the very sequence of times, which is most decisive against the Jews in favor of grace—that blessedness, namely the blessedness of justification, was bestowed through faith on Abraham not in circumcision but while he was still in uncircumcision, as Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15).

If Abraham was justified from faith while he was still in uncircumcision, everyone who believes God can likewise be justified through faith even if he is uncircumcised. The blessedness foretold in the psalm also applies to such a person, since faith too is reckoned to him as righteousness. For faith is reckoned as righteousness rather of those who were not righteous than of those who were righteous [Col. 0584B]: namely, of those who did not possess righteousness before they had this faith. Hence he says:

VERS. 10.—“How was it reckoned? In circumcision, or in uncircumcision?” And he himself answers that it was “not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.” For if Abraham had been found in circumcision at that time, uncircumcision would seem certainly to have been excluded from faith and grace. But now it is shown that faith was reckoned to him as righteousness while he was still in uncircumcision. Therefore it is declared that, since Abraham was justified through faith while in uncircumcision, he is without doubt rightly called the chief and father of all believers in uncircumcision—that is, while they are still uncircumcised.

That after the confession of faith made in uncircumcision he received circumcision, he subsequently explains as the reason why circumcision was received.

VERS. 11–12.—“That he might be,” he says, “a seal of the faith which he had” while in uncircumcision, so that through this he might become the father also of those born in circumcision, provided they belong to that faith which justified Abraham in uncircumcision. Thus he becomes father of both kinds: of those in uncircumcision through faith; and of those from circumcision through both faith and flesh. For from that point Abraham’s descendants begin under a twofold sacrament.

For Abraham’s faith itself is Abraham’s seed. Those who belong to the likeness of belief belong to the promise of heirs. Before moving on, however [Col. 0584D], we must investigate more closely how Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness, and whether everyone who believes God is immediately also righteous and has his faith reckoned as righteousness, since righteousness appears to embrace the fullness not of one virtue but of all virtues. For every unjust person is shown to be such in whatever respect he is proved to lack something of righteousness.

The ancient philosophers held that whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all. The Christian religion holds the same concerning those virtues proper to Christian devotion. For whoever believes, hopes, loves, and acts to the extent that he believes. Whoever hopes, hopes to the extent that he believes, loves, and acts. So also the one who loves; so also the one who acts. This is God’s full, perfect, and proportionate righteousness.

Therefore, when Abraham’s perfection was tested, a perfect work of faith was commanded of him, so that the believer’s faith might be tested through a father’s affection; and he was found perfect. He does not understand the perfection of Abraham’s work who does not observe the magnitude of the trial. The son whom he was commanded to offer had been born to him in old age from a barren wife; he was his only son, in whom he had also received the promises, and he could not hope for another. “Take,” said the Lord, “your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him to me as a burnt offering” (Gen. 22).

What did father Abraham do? [Col. 0585B] He did not weep, hesitate, or offer excuses. Rather, he openly showed whom he loved more, God or his son. And because he believed perfectly and loved perfectly, he undertook also the perfect work. Therefore he deserved both to receive his son back and to have his faith reckoned as righteousness.

He had heard words devised to break and tear apart a father’s heart; but clothed in the breastplate of faith, he securely passed through the trial. He did not disturb the sweetness of paternal affection, but increased it. Therefore it is fitting that it should often be said: his faith was reckoned to him as righteousness.

Likewise, whoever has Abraham’s faith, and offers to God on the altar of holy confession the laughter of his own heart—that is, the pleasures of the flesh and the desires of the soul—will hear from the Lord: “By myself I have sworn: because you have done this thing and have not spared your soul for my sake [Col. 0585C], blessing I shall bless you”; and that person’s faith too will be reckoned as righteousness.

The Jews, therefore, are compelled to confess that Abraham was justified through faith; and we too are compelled to understand that all the ancients who were justified were justified through this same faith. For what we believe partly as past and partly as future, they believed wholly as future, the Holy Spirit revealing it to them so that they might be saved.

It should be understood concerning Abraham’s circumcision and our baptism, each of which in its own time was a seal of faith, signifying circumcision of heart or purity of conscience. For the circumcised person begets an uncircumcised one, just as the baptized person begets one unbaptized, each transmitting the vice of origin from which he himself has already been freed. Therefore, as one then had to be circumcised, so everyone who wishes to be saved must now be baptized.

Yet each of these sacraments will pass away; but what these signs or seals signify will remain forever. For he used both terms, “sign” and “seal,” and they seem to possess some difference. A sign is that which, when seen or thought of, brings to mind the thing of which it is a sign. Jonah, in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, was a sign of the Lord Jesus Christ, who was to be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights (Matt. 12). Bodily circumcision too is a sign of spiritual circumcision.

A seal, however, is when a safeguarding is placed upon something to be kept for a time, which no one except the person who impressed it ought to unseal. This is the righteousness [Col. 0586A] of faith, by which Abraham is indicated to be the future father of many nations; and we believe that this will then be unsealed, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel then existing has been saved, so that Abraham’s holy posterity may appear as one.

It may also be understood that the mysteries foreshadowed in the law, the prophets, or the patriarchs were of such a kind that they were to be indicated by signs and closed under seals. Thus Abraham is said to have received a sign in those matters that were to be indicated by signs to believers and to the Gentiles; but he is said to have received a seal in matters that were to be kept and concealed for those who believed from circumcision. This seal will then be opened when, as stated, the fullness has entered and all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

Thus Abraham is father both of circumcision and of uncircumcision. His faith was reckoned to him as righteousness in uncircumcision, not circumcision; and he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith which is in uncircumcision—that is, which he possessed before being circumcised—“that he might be the father of all believers through uncircumcision,” that is, in uncircumcision, so that, as faith was reckoned to him, so “it may be reckoned to them also as righteousness, and that he may be father of circumcision, not only to those who are of circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith which is in the uncircumcision of our father” Abraham. “For the promise is not through the law”; if it were, it would belong only to those who serve the law.

VERS. 13.—“But now the promise to Abraham, or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, is not through the law” [Col. 0586C], so that his inheritance might be extended throughout the whole world, and all nations might be blessed in his seed. It is not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith; for keeping the law scarcely escapes punishment, while the merit of faith awaits the hope of promise. A command is imposed on slaves; faith, however, is required from friends.

VERS. 14, 15–21.—“For if those who are from the law are the only heirs, Abraham’s faith,” by which he deserved to be justified, “has been emptied” and made of no effect, and “the promise has been abolished,” so that there are now no heirs. For if it were so, Abraham would first have had to fulfil the law; yet he would strive vainly to fulfil it, because “the law works wrath” rather. But where there is wrath, there is no inheritance. Wrath, however, is in the law, for there is transgression. “But where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

Transgression is a twofold sin. What is without the law is simply sin; under the law it is both sin and transgression of the command. For where there is the transgression of one who despises, what remains except the wrath of the one commanding? Therefore inheritance is not from the law, because the law works wrath. It is from promise, because God himself does what he promises.

For whoever thinks that he fulfils the commands of the law by the choice of his own will without the Spirit of grace seeks to establish his own righteousness rather than receive God’s righteousness. This is not what God promised Abraham. God promised Abraham what he had himself to accomplish, not what human beings would accomplish, not by the power of our will but by the grace of his predestination. For even when human beings themselves do the good things belonging to God’s worship, he brings it about that they do what he commanded; they do not bring it about that he does what he promised [Col. 0587A].

Otherwise, the fulfilment of God’s promises would lie not in God’s power but in human power, and what the Lord promised would be rendered to Abraham by a human being. But Abraham did not believe in this way. Rather, “he believed, giving glory to God, because he is able also to do what he promised.” He says, “to do,” not “to foretell” or “to foreknow.” Therefore he promised acts that were his own, not another’s, when in the faith of the Gentiles he promised children to Abraham; for they cannot be such children if they do not have faith. Therefore he grants faith itself.

“But,” they say, “when it is said, ‘Whoever believes will be saved’ (Mark 16), one of these is required and the other offered. What is required from a human being lies in human power; what is offered belongs to God’s power.” Why then should not both be in God’s power—what he commands as well as what he offers? Indeed, what he commands should be asked from him, just as believing disciples ask that their faith may be increased (Luke 17).

“VERS. 16.—Therefore everything is from faith, so that the promise may be secure according to grace for all the seed, not only for the one who is from the law,” that is, who comes from the Old Testament to the New, “but also for the one who is of Abraham’s faith,” that is, an imitator of Abraham’s faith, claiming nothing for himself from the law promised to him, but a simple son of Abraham, who, with respect to faith, “is father of us all,” Jews and Gentiles alike.

VERS. 17.—“As it is written: I have made you father of many nations before God, whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they are” [Col. 0587C]. He calls them because he himself made the things that were to be. He predestined in us both nature and grace; and God makes both that we are human beings and that we are faithful, and he makes righteousness itself, if we are righteous. Those whom he chose for this purpose he has with himself—not in their own nature, but in his foreknowledge. This is what “before God” means. For what will be in God’s ordering has already been accomplished before God.

“And he calls the things that are not as though they are.” He does not call them in order that they may be; rather, he calls them as though they are. Those who were promised did not yet exist, lest anyone should boast of merits. Those to whom the promise was made were themselves also promised, so that Christ’s whole body might say: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

This is the grace which Noah, Moses, and the other saints are said to have found as a great treasure, Scripture saying: “He found grace in the sight of God” (Gen. 6). But further notice what he says: “Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be secure according to grace,” as though showing that if the promise were from the law, it would not be secure. Certainly, because things belonging to the law are written on tablets or little documents, whereas things belonging to grace are inscribed in our minds by God’s finger, that is, by the Holy Spirit.

For the faithful soul, unsealing to God the faith given by him, faithfully presents it to the Holy Spirit like prepared wax, so that he may inscribe what pleases him; and what is inscribed by him, the inward disposition holds eternally and inviolably through the Spirit’s love. This is the faith [Col. 0588A] reckoned as righteousness, which becomes capable of grace.

This happens to Abraham’s seed: not only to the one who is from the law—that is, who comes to grace from observance of the law—but also to the one who is from faith, that is, who is reckoned Abraham’s son by imitation of faith alone, in respect of the one in whom Abraham was made father of all believers, both from the Gentiles and from the Jews.

“Who gives life to the dead”: either those dead in the soul’s death of sin, or those who worshipped idols and, according to the Prophet, became like their images. “And who calls the things that are not as though they are”: whoever has no share in him who says, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3), must necessarily be called a non-being.

VERS. 18–19.—“Who believed against hope in hope.” Against hope, Abraham himself had reasons for despair: both his old age and that of his wife, together with her barrenness, denied him hope of begetting. Against all these things he believed in hope, because he believed God, who gave hope and whom he knew could easily fulfil what he promised.

He appropriately says that Abraham “believed in hope,” because through faith he advanced into hope. For hope is the advance of faith, while love is its perfection. “He was not weakened in faith,” although, as stated, many things seemed capable of weakening that faith. In believing, however, “he gave glory to God, fully knowing” that the one who had promised would neither deceive in promising nor fail in fulfilling.

“Nor did he consider his own body as dead, though he was nearly a hundred years old, or Sarah’s womb as dead.” For Abraham’s seed was no longer stirred by the dissolution of incontinence, nor was his holy wife stirred by feminine lust; in them the mortification of the members now had more vigor from religion than from nature [Col. 0588C]. But when they heard such a hope of offspring and descendants—that God promised their glory should be made equal to heaven and the stars—they no longer looked to their own goods and the grace of continence, but counted all things loss in order to gain Christ from their own seed.

For it was said to him: “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea.” By the stars are to be understood Abraham’s spiritual children, conspicuous in the light of virtues; by the sand of the sea, the innumerable multitude of carnal and unfruitful generation.

VERS. 20, 25.—“Even concerning God’s promise he did not waver in unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness. But it was not written only for his sake, that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned, if we believe in him who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, who was delivered up because of our offences and rose because of our justification.”

We must carefully inquire why, in this passage, the Apostle, naming the God in whom we believe and whom Abraham believed, does not say, “those believing in the exalted God,” or “in the God who made heaven and earth,” but only, “in him who raised the Lord Jesus from the dead.” Certainly because it is far more magnificent, to God’s praise, to raise the Lord Jesus Christ from the dead than to create heaven and earth [Col. 0589A]. The latter was making things that did not exist; the former is restoring things that had perished. The latter was establishing new things; the former was restoring things lost.

The mystery of this had already preceded in Abraham’s faith when, commanded to sacrifice his son, he believed—as Scripture says—that God was able even to raise from the dead (Heb. 11). Therefore he joyfully offered his only son, because in him he thought not of the extinction of his descendants, but of the restoration of the world and the renewal of the whole creation which was to come through the Lord’s resurrection.

Thus the comparison between Abraham’s faith and those who believe in God who raised the Lord Jesus Christ seems fittingly made: what Abraham believed would happen, we believe has happened. “Who was delivered up because of our sins and rose because of our justification.” Christ’s death both signifies and demands the mortification of our old human being and resurrection to righteousness. Therefore a person ought to hold his sin in implacable hatred, since he knows that his Lord was delivered up because of it.

No one, then, should suppose that the faith he has in Christ is reckoned to him as righteousness unless, having put off the old human being with its deeds and put on the new, he has made himself conformed to and a participant in Christ’s death and resurrection. Otherwise, there is no accord between unrighteousness and righteousness.

## Book Three

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589B] Now that in the two little books above we have in some fashion set forth the written states of the distinctions concerning the first and second things belonging to the human being of God, or the people of God, we proceed to what belongs to its third stage. We greet God’s grace and its wondrous light, and worship in that very light from which it begins to rise for us.

This does not mean that the progress of these distinctions takes place altogether according to the order of reading. Rather, they are marked in the writer’s sequence in various ways and places, just as they usually occur at various times in the heart of a person making progress. For there each person discovers the states of these distinctions according to the deficiencies or advances of his own inward condition.

At one time, a person, to be tested and shown to himself, is left by God to himself; and is thus found altogether lawless and without understanding, so that, as it is said, he does not know [Col. 0589C] how to distinguish his right hand from his left. These are the first things of the human being.

At another time, an eye is given to the blind person so that he may see what ought to be seen. Yet it does not help, nor does seeing delight the wretched person, since his sense—proper to natural sight—reports none of the things he sees to the mind. These are the second things of the human being.

At another time, a certain vision is infused into the eyes of reason, not so much by nature as by grace, so that it is not so much the seer seeing the thing shown to him as the thing seen drawing the seer to itself, conforming him and fitting him to itself. When this occurs without resistance, it is a pledge or earnest of approaching health; but when it occurs, yet not without the struggle of resistance, it is an admonition that weakness has not yet been exhausted. These are the third things of the human being of God.

But the people of God were first left to themselves under the natural law, so that they might understand what they were to themselves by themselves. Then written law was added even for some of them, so that there might be nothing by which a human being could excuse himself before God. Finally grace was sent to all, so that the human being might understand what he himself was to himself, what he was to God, and what God was to him; and might praise God while accusing himself.

The argument of the Apostle’s discussion seems to have reached this point, both concerning the human being of God and concerning the people of God; and from this point it now enters, in discussion, the kingdom [Col. 0590B] of grace, although it still often recalls and depicts to the reader’s eyes, in commending grace, that condition of the human being or human beings who are, or were, before the law and under the law.

“Therefore, having been justified from faith, let us have peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Thus far there has been discussion of the nature of faith reckoned as righteousness, and of the distinction between circumcision and uncircumcision. Let us now see how those justified from faith and not from works are instructed by the Apostle concerning grace.

Since, he says, it now plainly appears that neither the law of Moses prejudices the Gentile nor the law of faith prejudices the Jew, let all of us, both Jews and Gentiles, have peace toward God. Therefore, first, whoever understands and rejoices that he has been justified through faith should beware of being ungrateful for grace—that is, of having proud faith—and saying to himself: “If it is from faith, how is it freely given?” As though he himself gave faith and received justification. Let no faithful person say this, for it will be said to him: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4).

## Chapter V
VERS. 1.—“Having been justified by faith.” We are righteous because we have been made righteous. By whom were we made righteous? By him who gave the faith that made us righteous. “Let us have peace with God.” “In the world,” says the Lord, “you will have tribulation; but in me have peace” (John 16). For just as waves cannot be absent from the sea, so disturbances of whatever kind cannot be absent from the world, or from ourselves. Yet some neglect the peace that is with God in order to have peace with the world, although every peace ought to be set aside so that we may have peace with God. “Love truth,” says the prophet, “and peace” (Zech. 8). First truth, then peace—that is, peace according to truth. This peace is patient in truth; it is kind. It is not jealous; it does not act improperly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek what is its own; it is not provoked; it thinks no evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with truth (1 Cor. 13). This is peace with God.

But the reward of this peace is peace in God: that is, to will all things well and to possess all that one wills—the definition of true blessedness. Of this the children of God receive firstfruits in this age, and fullness in the age to come. And these are the fourth things belonging to the human being or to the people of God. This peace with God is through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is our peace, who makes both one: whether the two walls of circumcision and uncircumcision; or earthly and heavenly things; or humanity and God.

VERS. 2, 3.—“Through whom we also have access by faith,” because we cling to him, “into this grace in which we stand, and glory in hope of the glory of the children of God” (Eph. 2). For Christ’s teaching showed the way of this access to God; his example made it; his passion fortified it; grace draws us; truth receives us—and all these things are through faith. We stand in grace when we labor steadfastly for it; we stand in it when we hope for and love what we believe. “In hope of the glory of the children of God.” O to stand—how sweet it is to labor in you! “But stand here with me,” the Lord said to Moses, “and I will teach you” (Deut. 5). But the people were playing and worshipping the head of a calf. And David says: “In the morning I will stand before you and will see” (Ps. 5). He who stands before someone both sees and loves to be seen. Thus those who are proved to minister faithfully are said to stand before the faces of kings.

“Stand and serve me,” some petty ruler of this world says to you, “and I shall adopt you as a son and into the glory of my kingdom.” What disgraces, what hardships of labor, what delays of time will you not endure? “Stand with me,” God says to you, “and I shall adopt you as a son; all that is mine is yours; you shall be my kingdom, and I shall be your good.” You possess as a pledge my Son, who died for you while you were still ungodly; and, once justified, you hold the earnest of my Spirit. Give, Lord, give, O Father of lights, what you command; give what you promise—namely, to your servants the hope of the glory of your children: “and not only so, but let us also glory in tribulations” for your sake. Let them bring forth in us the disposition of patience, unto the result of testing and the advancement of holy hope.

VERS. 5.—“And hope does not put to shame,” because where faithful hope in you exists, the reality is immediately there also, “because the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit,” whom you give us. When he comes into us by your gift, he teaches us all truth, making known to us: in you, O Father, the author of supreme divinity; in you, O Son, the eternal birth of eternal consubstantiality; in you, O Holy Spirit, the holy communion of Father and Son; and in the three, one simple equality of holy consubstantiality.

And what is this glory, Lord, of your children? What is the hope of their pilgrimage? What consolation is there in their exile, however prolonged, when, Holy Father and Holy Son, you will us to have among ourselves and with you communion in that which is common to you, gathering us into one through that gift which you both possess as one? For in this we are reconciled to divinity; in this we are hidden in the secrecy of your face; in this we delight forever in the pleasures that are at your right hand [Col. 0592A]. For what would it profit us, whatever human beings we might be, unless by loving we also advanced in you, O God? Certainly, just as through truth we learn, so through love we love, in order both to know more fully by learning and, once we know, to enjoy more sweetly as blessed persons.

This is your prayer, Lord, which you made for us to the Father: “I will that, just as you and I are one, they also may be one in us” (John 17). For you will this, and strongly will it: that through your Spirit, your love, you may love us in yourself, and may love yourself from us and in us. For this precious substance by which we love you is not from ourselves, but from your Holy Spirit, whom you give us. Therefore give him to us; and, dwelling in us, O God, love yourself from us, moving and kindling us toward your love, enlightening and awakening us.

And because by our sins we were estranged from the possession of true goods, let your love cover the multitude of our sins. When you do this, O sweet and gracious one, your children, made from slaves, find it sweet and gracious to meditate or speak about you; and in speaking or meditating their heart becomes burning in you. Much more truly does this occur when, enlightened by the perception of love, they see you and address you; and most abundantly when you deign to speak to the heart of one who loves you. For you say to that person—as though adding oil to a furnace—that whoever loves may love more, and whoever burns may burn more. You speak inwardly in the conscience, through the illumination of your Holy Spirit, to one who understands, as Job says, “the vein of your whisper” (Job 4): “For why did Christ, when we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” Why, Lord?

VERS. 7–10.—“For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person. Yet perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person.” But God commends his love toward us, because, if Christ died for us at the appointed time while we were still sinners, much more now, having been justified in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, when you were enemies, you were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall you be saved in his life.

What? Is there no other escape for me from sin except through the death of Christ, your Son? None. For great love had to be set against great hatred: the love of the Son against the hatred of the enemy; your love, unto contempt of self, against the sin of love of self, by which you loved yourself unto contempt of God. By these realities and by the sacraments of realities, by mysteries and by the affections belonging to mysteries, the love by which one returns to God and clings to God had to be purified. Unless it is wholly cleansed and pure, one neither returns to God nor clings to God.

But once cleansed, seeing and enjoying, what does it say? “And not only so, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ”: no longer in the sacraments, but in the very reality of all sacraments; no longer in mysteries, but in the very light of manifest truth. For though it knew Jesus according to the flesh, now it knows him thus no longer. Yet through the flesh it passes to God, through our Lord Jesus Christ; through him we now receive reconciliation, and there shall dwell with him in the unity of blessedness [Col. 0593A].

God continually recalls this in the heart and conscience of the child of grace, commending his love toward us. For, with all the other sacraments of our salvation and faith intact, it was for this reason that he was born, suffered, and did all that God made man did upon earth: that, as a summons to our love for him, he might commend his love toward us. For love is drawn more strongly by love. He himself wished to be loved by those whose salvation he had undertaken; and he could not save them unless they loved him, since the measure of their salvation is in the measure of love. Therefore he died for the ungodly, for the weak, for sinners.

The Apostle wisely set down these three terms, designating through them every class of sinner: calling ungodly those who sin in worship toward God; weak those who offend through weakness or ignorance; and sinners those whom neither weakness nor ignorance excuses, but whose willing malice acts in sin. “For why did Christ, when we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” “At the appointed time,” he says: either according to the period of three days in which he rested in the tomb, or according to that which he possessed from time—that is, according to the flesh. “Because,” he says, “he commends his love toward us,” and so forth.

Suppose a physician undertook to cure a sick man but could not cure him except by the death of his only son. Would not that sick man be hateful and detestable to the physician instead? “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). The Son himself also “loved us and gave himself up for us” (Eph. 3). The more bitter the necessity of death was in saving him, the more sweetly, in the one saved, shone forth the joy of the life of the risen one in his resurrection.

We must consider how he assigns each thing to each. Sinners are justified; enemies are reconciled; they are reconciled through death; through life they are saved. The wrath of God, who judges all things with tranquility, is nothing other than just vengeance. Nor were we enemies of God except insofar as sins are enemies to justice; once these sins are forgiven, such enmities are ended. But if the just vengeance of God receives the name of wrath, what is God’s reconciliation more rightly understood to be than the ending of such wrath? Thus he is not moved by emotion even when he loves us, for he is always the same; but his love toward us is goodness, while our love toward him is the Holy Spirit, whom he gives us, through whom the love of God is poured out in our hearts.

Therefore he commended his love toward us by loving first. For we were loved first, so that we might become worthy to love and to be loved more fully. He did not begin to love us when we were reconciled through the death of his Son; rather, he loved us before the foundation of the world, so that with his Only-Begotten we also might be his children. Thus, indeed, it had to be shown to us how greatly he loved us, lest we despair; and what kind of people we were, lest we become proud.

The preceding statement, where he says, “When we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly,” is connected with the two following statements, in one of which he calls us sinners and in the other enemies of God—assigning each respectively: sinners to the weak, enemies of God to the ungodly.

“Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” Here the Apostle discusses at greater length two men: one, the first Adam, through whose sin and death his descendants have been bound as by hereditary evils; the other, the second Adam, who is not only human but also God. Since he paid for us what he did not owe, we have been freed from both ancestral debts and our own. Accordingly, because through that one man the devil held all who were generated through his corrupted flesh in concupiscence, it is just that through this one man he should release all who are spiritually regenerated through his immaculate grace [Col. 0594B].

Moreover, in this passage different persons hold different opinions because a certain obscurity seems to be present—not so much in the meaning as in the wording, perhaps arising from a translator’s carelessness. Without any loss of meaning, this seems to have an easy solution: “We received reconciliation through the one Lord Jesus Christ, just as sin entered into the world through one human being.” This is fitting because, as the former happened through one, so the latter too happens through one. Hence in what follows he compares and equates these two in many respects, as by contrast, though one surpasses the other.

Yet some wish the verse placed much lower down—“Therefore, just as through the trespass of one,” etc. (v. 18)—to answer this verse, so that everything between should be inserted as a supplement to the meaning. But while they avoid the obscurity arising from the complexity of the intervening arguments, they incur a greater entanglement of sense. Others say that, after teaching the difference between faith and law and opening the hidden things of the secret mystery—that, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son—he now goes on to explain the causes of enmity and reconciliation. For this reason he introduced the rationale of another secret, saying:

VERS. 12.—“Therefore, just as through one human being,” etc. When he says, “Just as through one human being sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all,” it remained for him to say: “So through one human being righteousness entered into this world, and through righteousness life; and thus life passed into all human beings, in whom all were made alive.” But Paul did not fail to say this through a deficiency of expression; rather, he perceived some usefulness in this. As a prudent steward of the word, when he comes to passages that seem to set forth something extraordinary concerning the goodness of God, he is accustomed either to state them more obscurely and briefly, or to conceal them altogether in silence, for the sake of the more lukewarm, lest through a relaxation of hope he make them more sluggish.

Therefore here too, when he had said, “Just as through one human being sin entered into this world,” and kept silent concerning what ought to be added, he left it openly to the wise to understand, while prudently withholding it from the unwise. At the same time he showed that, even if through one human being righteousness and life passed into all human beings, this does not immediately happen to the idle, but to those who can, with much labor and sweat, seek what is hidden, knock at what is closed, and desire what is concealed.

“Through one human being.” It is one thing to imitate Adam in sin; another to be born from Adam originally with sin. For Adam, even apart from the example of imitation, made equal with himself all who were to come from his stock. Conversely, whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him, even apart from the example of imitation, through the hidden communication and inspiration of spiritual grace.

“Through one human being.” Not through the deceiving serpent, nor through the woman seduced into transgression, of whom it is also written, “From a woman is the beginning of sin” (Ecclus. 25), but through one human being, because the woman conceives from the seed of generation received from the man. For from the man is the beginning of generation. He did not choose to be born in this manner who, born from a woman, alone appeared in the world without sin.

Those who maintain that not even one syllable in Paul’s writings is devoid of mysteries have observed that he did not say that sin entered “into all human beings,” but “into the world”; whereas he did not say that death entered “into the world,” but passed “into all human beings.” By “world” here may be designated those who are earthly and remain in earthly conduct; but “human beings” may be those who have begun to know themselves, because they were made in the image of God. Thus he says that sin entered those called “the world,” that is, the earthly, and he places no end to it there. But into those whom he wishes to understand as “human beings,” he says that sin passed: that is, it was indeed present, but through the conversion of repentance it was driven away and passed on, and did not remain in them any longer.

“And through sin, death.” Chaste marital intercourse is not blameworthy, but the origin of sin carries with it its due punishment. A husband is not mortal because he is a husband, nor is he mortal from any source other than sin. The Lord too was mortal, but not from sin. Yet he assumed our punishment in order to pay our punishment. For only that infant could be innocent who was not born from Adam’s sin—that is, from concupiscence. For after Adam’s sin of disobedience, concupiscence immediately appeared as both sin and punishment of sin, when the eyes of those first human beings were opened to mutual concupiscence. Through this, both original sin and concupiscence itself—which is called the law of sin in our members—pass into all [Col. 0595D].

“And sin, death.” This is undoubtedly the death of which the prophet says: “The soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18). One may rightly call this bodily death the shadow of that death, because wherever the former advances, the latter must necessarily follow, as a shadow follows a body. The Savior alone appeared without sin; yet death followed him also, because for our sins he himself was made sin. He willingly accepted death, who said: “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again” (John 10).

Through the baptism of him who came in the likeness of sinful flesh, the grace of God works so that sinful flesh may be emptied out. But it is emptied out not so that the concupiscence infused and innate in the still-living flesh should suddenly be consumed and cease to exist, but so that what was in the one born may not harm the one who has died. For if he lives after baptism, he has there that against which to struggle; and with the Lord’s help he conquers it, if he has not received his grace in vain and does not wish to be reprobate.

Therefore baptism does not grant this—except perhaps by an ineffable miracle of the almighty Creator—that the law of sin, which in the members resists the law of the mind, is utterly and completely extinguished and ceases to be. Rather, it grants that whatever evil a person has done, said, or thought while the mind served subject to that concupiscence may all be blotted out and regarded as though it had not been done. Concupiscence itself, however, remains for conflict once the bond of guilt by which the devil held the soul through it has been loosed, and the barrier by which it separated the human being from the Creator has been destroyed. By this conflict we chastise our body and bring it into servitude [Col. 0596B].

Meanwhile, temporal death remains even in those redeemed by Christ’s death, for the exercise of faith and the contest of the present struggle, in which the martyrs also fought. But it too will be consumed in the renewal of the body promised by the resurrection. Both death and sin pass into human beings. For if sin had not passed into them, not every human being would be born with the law of sin that is in the members. If death had not passed into them, not all human beings would die the death of the body.

“In whom all sinned.” Either in that sin of which he says, “Sin entered into this world,” in which all sinned; or “in whom,” that is, in that human being. Thus all also die in him, because it was just that punishment should pass to them together with guilt. Therefore, if Levi, who was born in the fourth generation after Abraham, is said to have been in Abraham’s loins (Heb. 7), much more were all human beings in Adam’s loins when he sinned; they sinned in him, were expelled from paradise with him, and through him death passed into all who were held in his loins.

VERS. 13.—“Until the law, sin was in the world.” What entered into the world through the first human being—both original sin and every other sin that could be contracted from the defect of a corrupted origin—was in the world until the law. That is, neither could the law take away sin, since it entered in so that it might abound still more: whether the natural law, under which anyone who uses reason begins to add personal sins to original sin; or the written law itself, given through Moses to the people.

“But it was not imputed, because there was no law”—no law whose rebuke might expose it, although before the Lord God it was not treated as though it did not exist. Yet “until the law” is so stated that the sentence also includes the law itself, so that there may be no law outside the continuance of the sin said to have been present up to that point. “The law [was] until John” (Luke 16), and sin until the coming of Christ, from which only the Savior’s grace frees.

“But it was not imputed,” as has been said, “when there was no law.” Those who accept this explanation remain silent and rest here. But some think it necessary to inquire which law is meant here. For human nature possessing reason has never been without natural law; even before the written law, this natural law not only noticed the sins of original concupiscence, but sometimes punished them most severely. Hence Cain said of himself: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve pardon for” (Gen. 4). And Noah said concerning his son: “Canaan the servant is cursed” (Gen. 5).

Therefore, from the curse of the earth in the act of the first human being, just as sin was always in the world, so the law that imputes sin was never lacking. Nor was original sin manifest to all or hidden from all: it was not hidden from Job, nor from Abraham and his household. For this reason Abraham also received circumcision, in faith in his seed, who is Christ; circumcision worked in them what baptism works in us. Thus David groaning said: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50).

There were also some who, thinking that the course of the argument ought to be pursued here, considered the whole sense of this passage worthy of investigation, so that they might derive the Apostle’s meaning in these matters not so much from their own judgment as from his words themselves. Later they found him saying, “For without law sin was dead; but I was once alive without law,” and they found him saying this concerning natural law. Thus the meaning is: until the natural law, which at a definite age begins to be capable of reason, when the distinction between the righteous and the unrighteous begins to exist, sin was inwardly dead in me because there was no law forbidding what ought not to be done, or reason showing what ought to be done. According to them, this cannot otherwise be understood of the Apostle on any rational ground, since he plainly seems to have said it of himself.

According to this interpretation, it does not seem wholly absurd if it is said here also that, until the understanding of the natural law, sin arising from the corruption of origin was in the world—understanding, however, that it was dead, because it was not imputed, natural weakness or ignorance providing excuse. As for his saying “in the world” rather than “in human beings,” the defenders of this view say that those who have become capable of reason and possess natural law should be called human beings; but the age that has not yet attained the capacity for natural law should be called not so much “human beings” as “the world,” because they seem to be a certain part of the world, but not yet as human beings worthy to put on the image of the Creator. But because this statement concerning law seems to others more properly applicable to the Mosaic law, let what is to be preferred be left to the reader’s judgment. What follows suits both views well enough.

VERS. 14.—“But death reigned from Adam to Moses,” that is, from the first human being to the very law divinely promulgated, because not even that law could remove the reign of death. By the reign of death he means the condition in which the guilt of sin so rules in human beings that it does not permit them to come to eternal life, which is true life, but draws them even to the second death, which is eternally punitive. The grace of the Savior alone destroys this reign of death in any person. It also worked in all the ancient saints who, before Christ came in the flesh, nevertheless belonged to his helping grace, not to the letter of the law, which could command but could not help. For this was hidden in the Old Testament, by the most just ordering of the times, which is now revealed in the New.

Therefore death reigned from Adam to Moses in all who were not helped by Christ’s grace so that the reign of death might be destroyed in them. But see over whom it reigned: “And,” he says, “over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” This is the better understanding of these words: when he had said, “Death reigned even over those who did not sin,” as though he moved us to ask why it reigned over those who had not sinned, he added, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”—that is, because the likeness of Adam’s transgression was present in their members.

It can also be understood thus: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” For after they were born they did not yet use reason, as Adam did when he sinned; they had not received the commandment that he transgressed; but they were held bound by original fault alone. Through this the reign of death drew them to condemnation. This reign of death is absent only in those who, reborn through Christ’s grace, belong to his kingdom; for although temporal death—also propagated from original sin—destroys their body, it does not draw their soul to punishment. Here he intended “the reign of death” to mean that the soul renewed by grace no longer dies in Gehenna—that is, is no longer alienated or separated from the life of God.

What he added concerning Adam, “who is a figure of the one to come,” is not understood in only one way. Either Adam is a figure of Christ by contrast, so that just as all die in Adam, so all are made alive in Christ, and just as many were made sinners through Adam’s disobedience, so many may be made righteous through Christ’s obedience; or he called Adam a figure of the one to come because he imposed the pattern of death upon his descendants. Yet the better interpretation is that he is believed to be a figure by contrast, which the Apostle strongly emphasizes. Finally, lest the same opposite things in this figure should be thought entirely equal in weight, he added and said:

VERS. 15.—“But the gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through the trespass of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound unto many.” “Much more” does not mean “many more”—that is, many more human beings; for more are not justified than condemned. Rather, it means that it abounded much more. Adam generated guilty persons from his one trespass; Christ, however, by his grace released and erased even the sins of personal will that human beings added to the original sin in which they were born. He says this more plainly in what follows.

But consider more carefully what he says: “Many died through the trespass of one.” For why through that one person’s trespass, rather than through their own personal sins, if imitation rather than propagation is to be understood in this passage? But attend to what follows.

VERS. 16.—“And the gift is not like that which came through one sin. For judgment indeed came from one unto condemnation; but grace from many trespasses unto justification.” “From one,” he says, “unto condemnation.” From one thing, unless it is a trespass? He explains this when he adds: “But grace from many trespasses unto justification.” Why, therefore, judgment from one trespass unto condemnation, but grace from many trespasses unto justification? Even if there were no original trespass, would not both grace lead human beings to justification and judgment lead them to condemnation through many trespasses? For grace forgives many trespasses; and does not judgment likewise condemn many trespasses?

Rather, let us understand the Apostle, and see why he says that judgment came from one trespass unto condemnation: because it would suffice for condemnation, even if there were no sin in human beings except original sin. Although the condemnation is more severe for those who have added their own sins to original sin—and more severe for each person in proportion as that person has sinned more grievously—nevertheless even that alone which has been inherited originally not only separates from the kingdom of God, into which even heretics themselves confess that little children dying without having received Christ’s grace cannot enter; it also makes them strangers to salvation and eternal life. There can be no other salvation and eternal life besides the kingdom of God, into which the fellowship of Christ alone introduces.

Accordingly, from Adam, in whom we all sinned, we have inherited not all our sins but only original sin; from Christ, in whom we are all justified, we receive forgiveness not only of that original sin but also of the other sins that we ourselves add.

“Therefore the gift is not like that which came through one sin. For judgment indeed from one trespass”—if it is not forgiven, namely, the original trespass—“can already lead unto condemnation; but grace from many trespasses,” once they are forgiven, that is, not only the original trespass but all the rest as well, “leads unto justification.”

[Col. 0599D] VERS. 17.—“For if death reigned through one by the trespass of one, much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of righteousness will reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.” Why did death reign through one by the trespass of one, unless because they were held in the bond of death in that one in whom all sinned, even if they added no personal sins? Otherwise death did not reign through one because of one person’s trespass, but because of the sins of many, through each individual sinner.

And what does “receive the abundance of grace and of righteousness” mean, unless that not only is the sin in which all sinned forgiven them, but also that grace of remission is given for the sins they have added? And righteousness so great is given to them all that, whereas Adam consented to the one persuading him to sin, these do not yield even to one compelling them. And what is meant by “they will reign much more in life,” when the reign of death draws many more into eternal punishment, unless we understand that the same persons are spoken of in each case—those who pass from Adam, that is, from death, into life? For they will reign without end in eternal life more truly than death reigned over them temporally and with an end.

VERS. 18.—“Therefore, just as through the trespass of one [the result came] unto condemnation for all human beings, so through the justification of one [the result came] unto justification of life for all human beings.” If we attend to imitation, this trespass of one could only be the devil’s.

> [Note: [Col. 0599] “The matter here is not sin of imitation, but of origin.”]

But because it is clear that Adam, not the devil, is being spoken of, we must understand not the imitation but the propagation of sin. For what he says of Christ—“through the justification of one”—he expressed more strongly than if he had said “through the righteousness of one.” He means that justification by which Christ justifies the ungodly, which he did not set forth to be imitated, but which he alone can perform. The Apostle could rightly say, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ”; but he would never say, “Be justified by me, as I have been justified by Christ.” Many righteous persons can be, are, and have been, worthy of imitation; but no one is righteous and justifying except Christ.

Hence it is said: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned” (Rom. 14). Whoever, therefore, has dared to say, “I justify you,” must consequently also say, “Believe in me.” No saint could rightly say this except the Holy One of holy ones, who said: “Believe in God, and believe also in me.” Thus, because he himself justifies the ungodly, faith in him is reckoned unto righteousness.

For if imitation alone made sinners through Adam, why does imitation alone not also make righteous persons through Christ? But if Christ is the one in whom all are justified because not his imitation alone makes people righteous but grace regenerates through the Spirit, then Adam likewise is the one in whom all sinned because not his imitation alone makes people sinners but punishment generates through the flesh. For this reason “all” and “all” are also said. Not all who are generated through Adam are themselves all regenerated through Christ; but this is rightly stated because, just as no one’s carnal generation is except through Adam, so no one’s spiritual generation is except through Christ. For if some could be generated in the flesh not through Adam, and some generated in the Spirit not through Christ, “all” could not plainly be said in either case.

But afterward he calls these same “all” “many.” For all can be few in some respect. Yet carnal generation has many, and spiritual generation also has many, although the latter spiritual generation does not have as many as the former carnal one. Nevertheless, just as the former has all human beings, so the latter has all righteous human beings; for just as no one is a human being apart from the former, so no one is a righteous human being apart from the latter—and in both there are many.

VERS. 19, 20.—“For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous. But the Law entered in, so that transgression might abound.” This now does not concern that offence which is derived from Adam [Note: [Col. 0601D] Here the discussion concerns actual sin.], of which he said above, “death reigned through one.” For the Law—whether we understand the natural law, which appears at the ages of those already able to use reason, or the written Law, given through Moses—could not itself give life or free anyone from the law of sin and death derived from Adam; rather, it added an increase of transgression. “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” [Col. 0601B]. Therefore, when the Law given in Paradise was transgressed, a human being is born from Adam with the law of sin and death, of which it is said: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind,” etc. Yet unless it is later strengthened by evil habit, it is more easily overcome—though never without God’s grace.

But when another law is transgressed, namely that which belongs to the exercise of reason in the rational soul at the age when a person is already using reason, all sinners of the earth become transgressors. And when even that Law which was given through Moses is transgressed, the offence abounds much more. “Therefore the Law entered in, so that transgression might abound”: either when people neglect what God commands, or when, presuming upon their own strength, they do not implore the aid of grace and add pride to weakness [Col. 0601C]. But when, through the divine calling, they understand for whom they ought to groan and call upon him in whom they believe, rightly saying: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy great mercy” (Ps. L); and: “I said: Lord, have mercy upon me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee” (Ps. XL)—when, therefore, a person stretches himself toward him and thus groans, what follows comes to pass: “But where transgression abounded, grace superabounded.” Many sins are forgiven, because she loved much; and the love of God is poured into his heart, by which the Law’s fullness may be accomplished, not through the powers of the will that is in us, but through the Holy Spirit given to us: “so that, just as sin reigned unto death, so also grace may reign [Col. 0601D] through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

But when he said, “just as sin reigned unto death,” he did not say, “through one man,” or “through the first man,” or “through Adam,” because he had already said, “The Law entered in, so that transgression might abound.” That abundance does not belong to the propagation of the first man, but to the transgression of human conduct; and in persons of more mature age it is added, through an abundance of wickedness, to that one offence by which infants alone are held bound. But because the Saviour’s grace is sufficient also to remove all this which does not belong to the origin of that one offence [Col. 0602A], he therefore added, after saying, “so also grace may reign through righteousness unto eternal life,” “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Then, raising an objection against himself:

## CHAPTER VI

VERS. 1.—“What then shall we say,” he says. “Shall we continue in sin, so that grace may abound? By no means!” For he saw that the perverse could perversely interpret what he had said, “where transgression abounded, grace superabounded,” as though he had said that sin profits on account of the abundance of grace. Refuting this, he answered, “By no means!” and added:

VERS. 2.—“We who died to sin, how shall we live in it?” That is: since grace has accomplished this, that we should die to sin, what else are we doing if we live in it except proving ungrateful to grace? For one who praises the benefit of medicine does not commend diseases and wounds from which it heals a person. Rather, the more highly medicine is praised, the more wounds and diseases are reproved and abhorred, from which that medicine so praised sets one free. Thus praise and proclamation of grace are reproval and condemnation of offences.

The ugliness of his sickness had to be shown to a person for whom, against his wickedness, not even the holy and good commandment had proved beneficial; by it wickedness was increased rather than diminished. For “the Law entered in, so that transgression might abound,” so that, convicted and confounded in this manner, he might see that he needed not merely a teacher, but also God as helper, by whom [Col. 0602C] his paths might be directed, lest every wickedness rule over them; and that, fleeing to the help of divine mercy, he might be healed. Thus, where transgression abounded, grace might superabound—not through the sinner’s merit, but through the aid of the one who comes to help.

Accordingly, the Apostle shows that this same remedy is mystically displayed in Christ’s passion and resurrection, saying:

VERS. 3, 4.—“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.” Surely it is sufficiently clear that the passing away of our old life and the arising of the new, the abolition of wickedness and the renewal of righteousness, are prefigured by the mystery of the Lord’s death and resurrection [Col. 0602D]. Whence comes so great a benefit to human beings, except through faith in Jesus Christ?

This holy reflection preserves the children of men who hope under the protection of God’s wings, so that they may be intoxicated with the abundance of his house and drink from the torrent of his delight, because with him is the fountain of life, and in his light we shall see light [Note: [Col. 0601] St Augustine, Letter 98 to Boniface, vol. XXXIII of the *Patrologia*.]. For Christ was sacrificed once in himself, and yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed to the peoples not only at every Paschal solemnity but every day. Nor does one lie who, when asked, answers that he is sacrificed [Col. 0603A]. For if sacraments did not possess some likeness of the realities whose sacraments they are, they would not be sacraments. Yet from this likeness they often receive the names of the realities themselves.

Thus, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; so also the sacrament of faith is faith. But to believe is nothing other than to have faith. Accordingly, when it is answered that an infant believes, though he does not yet have the disposition of faith, it is answered that he has faith on account of the sacrament of faith; and that he turns to God on account of the sacrament of conversion, because that answer itself belongs to the celebration of the sacrament. Thus the Apostle says concerning baptism itself:

VERS. 4.—“We were buried with Christ through baptism into death.” He did not say, “We signified burial,” but plainly says, “We were buried.” He therefore called the sacrament of so great a reality by the name of the reality itself. Thus, although an infant does not yet have that faith which consists in the will of believers, nevertheless the sacrament of that faith itself already makes him faithful. For just as he is said to believe, so he is also called faithful—not by assenting in his mind to the reality itself, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality [Col. 0603B].

When a person begins to understand, he will not repeat that sacrament, but will understand it; and he will adapt his will, in harmony with its truth, to it as well.
