So long as he cannot do this, the sacrament will avail for his protection against hostile powers; and it will avail so greatly that, if he departs this life before attaining the use of mature age, through the sacrament itself, commended by the Church’s love, he is freed by Christian aid from that condemnation which entered the world through one man. Whoever does not believe this and judges it impossible is surely an unbeliever, even if he possesses the sacrament of faith; and far better than he is that infant who, though he does not yet have faith in thought, nevertheless does not set the obstacle of a contrary thought against it.

“Therefore sin was not present in the Lord; and yet in a certain sense he died to sin, when he died to the flesh in which there was the likeness of sin. Thus, although according to the oldness of sin he himself had never lived, by his new resurrection he marked our life, reviving from the old death [Col. 0603D] in which we had been dead in sin. This is what is celebrated in us in the great sacrament of baptism: all who belong to this grace die to sin, just as he is said to have died to sin because he died to the flesh, that is, to the likeness of sin; and they live again by being reborn from the washing, just as he lives again by rising from the tomb, whatever age of body they bear.

“For from a newly born infant to a decrepit old man, just as no one is to be excluded from baptism, so there is no one who does not die to sin in baptism. Infants die only to original sin; adults, however, die to all those sins which, by living wickedly, they have added to what they derived by being born. Thus he closed this passage as he began it [Col. 0604A]: he set forth Christ’s death in such a way that he also called Christ himself dead to sin. To what sin, except to the flesh in which there was not sin, but the likeness of sin, and which was therefore called by the name of sin?”

Thus, speaking of those baptized into Christ’s death, in which not only adults but infants too are baptized, he says:

VERS. 11.—“So you also”—that is, just as Christ—“so you also reckon yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.” Whatever was done in Christ’s cross, burial, resurrection on the third day, ascension into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father, was so done that the Christian life now lived here might be conformed to these events—not merely mystically spoken, but also accomplished [Col. 0604B]. For the sake of his cross it was said: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. V). For the sake of the resurrection: “So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.” For the sake of the ascension into heaven and sitting at the Father’s right hand: “If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things upon earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

For that utterance was given by the sacrament of our inward person, pertaining to the signifying of our soul’s death, not only in the Psalm but also on the cross: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI) [Col. 0604C]. The Apostle’s words agree with this utterance:

VERS. 6.—“Knowing that our old man was crucified, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we might no longer serve sin.” By the crucifixion of the inward person are understood the pains of repentance and a certain salutary torment of continence. Through this death the death of ungodliness is put to death, and in it God has not abandoned us. Therefore through such a cross the body of sin is destroyed, so that we no longer present our members as weapons of wickedness to sin. For since the inward person is indeed renewed day by day, he is surely old before he is renewed. For inwardly is accomplished what the Apostle also says: “Put off the old man with his deeds” [Col. 0604D] (Col. III). He then explains this accordingly: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth.” But where is falsehood put away except inwardly, so that he may dwell upon God’s holy mountain who speaks truth in his heart?

Now, therefore, the form of Adam past and Adam to come has been described—a form not wholly uniform: alike indeed in genus, but contrary in species. In genus it is alike in this, that just as from one Adam it is diffused into many, so also from one Christ it is infused into many human beings. But in species it is contrary: through Adam’s transgression many were made sinners, but through Christ’s obedience many were made righteous. Thus, as has been said, the form of the first and second Adam is compared with itself through likenesses and unlikenesses [Col. 0605A]. Since we have followed the sequence of this reading at greater length, the order and sense of the words now seem to require condensation and more subtle examination.

For he compares the death which came through Adam with the life which is through Christ, and says: “The gift is not like the offence.” And again afterwards he says that the Law entered in so that sin might abound, and that, sin having abounded, grace superabounded. In these matters he resolves what appeared contrary and says (v. 2): “For we who died to sin, how shall we still live in it?” And wishing to show by the realities themselves what it is to be dead to sin, he says (v. 3): “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus,” etc. By these words he teaches that, if someone has first died to sins, that person is necessarily buried with Christ in baptism [Col. 0605B]. But if a person does not first die to sin, he cannot be buried with Christ. For no living person is ever buried. And if he is not buried with Christ, he is not lawfully baptized.

Then follows (v. 1): “What then? Shall we continue in sin, so that grace may abound?” First observe how measured his language is. For he says: “Shall we continue in sin?” To continue is not to cease from what has been begun. Whoever does this in relation to sin plainly has not yet received even the beginning of conversion. And since repentance from sin is the proper work of grace, where grace finds the obstinacy of impenitence, there it does not abound except unto judgment and condemnation. “For if we died to sin” (v. 2), “how shall we live in it?”

Consider more carefully the sequence of the mystical order [Col. 0605C]. One must first die to sin in order to be buried with Christ; burial is due to the dead. But one buried to sin ought in no way thereafter to live in it. Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ, buried in a new tomb and wrapped in a clean linen cloth, signifies in the one buried with him the newness of life and purity of conscience. “Do you not know” (v. 3) “that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” For this is signified also by the vessel of baptism, assigned to no other uses, and by the white garment. We must also know that no baptized person capable of reason may be ignorant of the faith and mystery of his baptism. Hence he seems to say, not without some movement of mind: “Do you not know,” [Col. 0605D] etc.

Therefore, whoever is baptized into Christ Jesus is baptized into his death: dying with him through renunciation of sin, buried with him through the profession of a holy purpose. But why are we said here to be baptized in Christ alone, when he who baptizes himself said, “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII)? The question of baptism was not under discussion here, but Christ’s death, to whose likeness he urged us to die to sin and be buried with Christ. Nor did it seem fitting that, where the remembrance of death was being discussed, the Father or the Holy Spirit should be named. Here the Apostle follows his custom: when he takes something from the Scriptures, he takes only what the proof of the present issue requires.

“So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory [Col. 0606A] of the Father” (v. 4), “so we too may walk in newness of life.” Christ rose, and the Father was glorified. If we, rising with him, walk in newness of life, people will see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven. We must walk and not cease, so that the last day may find us making progress.

VERS. 5.—“For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be [in the likeness] of his resurrection.” All these things answer that question, lest he seem to have given occasion for sinning when he said, “Where sin abounded, grace superabounded” (above, ch. V, v. 20). Therefore he says that we are baptized into Christ’s death, and have died with him, been buried with him, and been planted together with him, adding furthermore the hope of resurrection together with him [Col. 0606B].

For Christ’s death is, in the Church, the tree of life planted in the midst of Paradise. He is planted together with it who dies with it, so that, mortifying his members which are upon earth, he may, as the Prophet says, send roots downward and bear fruit upward (Isa. XXXVII): the fruit of flesh blossoming anew and of the spirit’s renewal, in the glory of resurrection and in the budding and fruitfulness of holy virtues.

VERS. 6.—“Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we may no longer serve sin.” For this is to die with him, be buried with him, and rise with him: that our old man—that is, the former life which we led in sins—should receive its end and destruction in faith in Christ’s cross, and that our members which served sin should be destroyed, so that they may no longer serve anything but God [Col. 0606C]. Thus our root is planted together with the root of the tree of life—that is, our love is conformed to Christ’s love—so that from the sap of his root it may produce branches of righteousness and fruits of life.

“So that the body of sin might be destroyed.” This body of sin is either the totality of sin, whose members are fornication, impurity, greed, and so forth; or it is our very body, infected from its origin by the poison of the ancient serpent. It is destroyed when a person dies to sin and begins to live to God: no longer his own, nor sin’s, but belonging to him who redeemed him at great price, to serve him. For one who has died to sin has been justified, since he serves not sin but the Lord his God, whom it is righteous to serve [Col. 0606D]. With what fruit, what recompense, what reward?

VERS. 8.—“But if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.” With what life—temporal or eternal?

VERS. 9.—“Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him.” For if he were still to die again, we too would have to die with him again. But when he inserted, “we believe that we shall also live with him,” he showed that although the certainty of resurrection follows, we shall nevertheless attain it only through the mediation of faith. Whoever dies with Christ and expects the glory of resurrection should know that he must undergo a burial of three days: faith in the heart and confession with the mouth unto salvation; then the mortification of the members [Col. 0607A]; and afterwards the resurrection of new life—or, alternatively, renunciation of the world, renunciation of vices, and then perfection in the light of wisdom.

VERS. 9, 10.—“Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God.” He who, for us, assumed the likeness of sinful flesh became sin, paying to sin and to the law of the flesh what belonged to it; he died once. But in that he lives, he belongs to God, because he is conformed to God’s incorruptibility.

VERS. 11.—“So you also reckon yourselves indeed dead to sin, but living to God.” The Greek has **λογέζεσθε** (*logízesthe*), that is, not “reckon,” but “consider,” which seems more fitting to certainty of understanding and faith [Col. 0607B]. For we must always consider and keep before our eyes what we vowed and established in baptism: namely, death to sin and life to God. For the addition, “in Christ Jesus our Lord,” expresses the manner of fulfilling the vow. It is the same as saying: living to God in wisdom, in peace, in righteousness, in sanctification—all of which Christ is. Thus to live in these things is to live in Christ Jesus our Lord.

VERS. 12.—“Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body.” For if sin reigns, it is a king. Sin is indeed a king, and has its own army serving it and obeying its laws, which are inscribed in the flesh and members of the body in which it has acquired royal right [Col. 0607C]. Its army consists of what the Apostle calls the works of the flesh: “fornication, impurity,” and so forth (Gal. V). Since these belong to sin’s kingdom, those who do them “will not inherit the kingdom of God” (ibid.). Heresies too are counted in that army, proceeding from the puffed-up mind of the flesh. This kingdom is the minding of the flesh, which the same Apostle declares to be death and hostile to God.

This utterly evil army is always ready for battle, attacking the camp of virtues so long as the flesh desires against the spirit. But unless it were within our power that the power of sin should not be in our body, the Apostle would not have given the command, saying: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body.” But he who gave the command did not leave us without counsel, saying elsewhere: “Put to death your members which are upon earth” (Col. III); and: “Always carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus” (2 Cor. IV) [Col. 0607D]. For sin hates the memory of Christ’s cross and flees the desire to imitate it. When the banner of the cross appears, that entire army of spiritual wickedness immediately vanishes; sin does not stand.

Nor is what the Apostle commanded impossible. For he did not say, “Let sin not exist,” but, “Let sin not reign in your body.” Sin is present while you take delight; it reigns when you consent. Never to take delight at all is wholly impossible; never to consent is not impossible, with grace’s aid. In one respect you are heir to God, in another to the world. Your portion—your flesh—rebels against you through the sickness of its own desire. That sickness is a tyrant [Col. 0608A]. Let the mind that cleaves to God not fail or abandon itself. It has great help; it will conquer if it perseveres in fighting. Often, when desire has been restrained, it will fail and begin not to exist.

“In your mortal body,” he says. He did not add “mortal” without cause, but either to suggest that the body is mortal—that is, capable of being mortified—or that it is mortal, so that one may remember what is written: “In all things remember your last end, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII). The seat of sin’s kingdom is the body; the law of its kingdom is the law of its members; its army is that described above; its power is desire; its reign is obedience to desires. The support of its kingdom is what follows: “Nor present your members as weapons of wickedness to sin.” To do this is to fight for sin’s kingdom. And it is most wicked to present as weapons to sin members created by God and dedicated to God [Col. 0608B].

VERS. 13.—“But present yourselves to God, as those alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God.” Consider Paul’s wisdom point by point. Where he says that weapons are not to be presented to sin or wickedness, he places not ourselves but our members. But where he urges us to present ourselves to God, he wills that not so much our members as we ourselves should be presented to God—that is, the soul or purpose of the heart. Once we have first presented ourselves and are cleaving to God, then finally we shall make even our members weapons of righteousness.

Again, if we mortify sin’s desire in our mortal body, we shall become as those alive from the dead: dead to sin and living to God, and our members weapons of righteousness, fighting for him whom it is most righteous that they should serve [Col. 0608C]. He fittingly develops the metaphor previously introduced: in sin’s kingdom he called our members weapons of wickedness, and again in God’s kingdom he called them weapons of righteousness. It follows:

VERS. 14.—“For sin shall not have dominion over you.” Here too observe the Apostle’s remarkable caution. When he speaks about us, he says, “Sin shall not have dominion over you”; when he speaks about the Saviour, he says, “Death shall not have dominion over him.” For death had a place in him, but sin none. Yet we should not have been told, “Death shall not have dominion over you,” since we cannot avoid it; but, “Sin shall not have dominion over you,” since we can undoubtedly avoid it [Col. 0608D].

“For you are not under Law, but under grace.” The Law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled. For the Law was not unfulfilled through its own fault, but through the fault of the minding of the flesh. That fault had to be revealed through the Law and healed through grace. Sin ruled those who were under Law and not under grace; from it a person is not freed through the Law but through grace. This is not because the Law is evil, but because, by commanding and not helping, it makes those who are under it guilty. Grace helps so that one may become a doer of the Law; without it, one placed under the Law will be only a hearer of the Law.

VERS. 15.—“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under Law but under grace?” The sense seems to be the same as that explained above where he says: “What then? Shall we continue in sin, so that grace may abound?” This alone seems to be the difference: there he seems to speak, as it were, to those who have not yet departed from sin, lest they remain in it; but here the question seems, as it were, to be asked by those who have already departed from sin [Col. 0609A]. There, grace not yet present was to abound; here, grace already present is assumed when he says that we are not under Law but under grace.

VERS. 16.—“By no means! Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey—whether of sin unto death or of obedience unto righteousness?” The expression, “whether of sin or of obedience unto righteousness,” perhaps seems less than fully regular; for one might rather have said, “whether of sin or of righteousness through obedience.” But since the sense is evident, it is superfluous to cling to the wording. This, therefore, is what he teaches: whichever side a person inclines his obedience toward, whether righteousness or sin, he commits himself as servant to it.

One must beware a voluntary fall into sin, or a rash leap; for what is committed once produces greater pleasure; pleasure demands repetition; repetition makes voluntary habit; habit produces the necessity of slavery [Col. 0609B]. It is therefore within our power, if we wish, to take up the yoke of slavery; but once it has been taken up, it is not within our power to cast it off whenever we wish.

VERS. 17.—“But thanks be to God that you were servants of sin, but have obeyed from the heart that form of teaching into which you were delivered.” Here he speaks to the perfect, for whom at the beginning of this Epistle he also gave thanks to his God, because their faith was proclaimed throughout the whole world. Yet he gives thanks not because they were servants of sin, but because, made servants of righteousness, they cast off the necessity of habit and the unworthy slavery of sin. For it is unfamiliar and difficult to change one’s disposition, and, as secular wisdom says, it is impossible to separate joined limbs without loss of blood.

“But you have obeyed that form into which you were delivered.” Behold the changed disposition, for which thanksgiving is truly due [Col. 0609C]. Some think that here the Apostle does not regard doctrine and the form of doctrine as one thing, but that “form of doctrine” signifies something less than doctrine itself: the form of doctrine being what we now see through a mirror and in an enigma, while doctrine itself is seeing face to face. Or the form of doctrine is the perfected and well-formed doctrine of righteousness.

Others explain differently. They propose three forms in the doctrine of faith: rational, spiritual, and intellectual. The rational form belongs to sacraments and conduct, suited to those persons to whom the Lord says that the kingdom of God is to be proclaimed in parables. The spiritual form belongs to study and meditation upon reading, and to the instruction of elders; it suits those to whom the Lord says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Luke VIII). The intellectual form belongs to the affection of illumined love; it is proper to pure hearts, which deserve to see God.

The rational form entails willing obedience and active perfection; the spiritual, sober discernment [Col. 0610A] and humble contemplation; the intellectual, peaceful and familiar experience. For this understanding, coming from above, is not formed by reason; rather, it itself conforms reason to itself—not that reason may comprehend it, but that, illumined by it, reason may at some time assent to it. The Apostle therefore speaks here of the first form of doctrine, into which those were delivered who obediently delivered themselves into it.

VERS. 18.—“But having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness.” Whether in sin or righteousness, wherever the will has been added, there is the necessity of slavery. It follows:

VERS. 19.—“I speak in human terms because of your weakness.” The prudent steward of speech, seeing that they had advanced in the first form of doctrine, judges that human things should be entrusted to human beings, although he would prefer divine things if he perceived that they had advanced somewhat beyond the human [Col. 0610B]. “I speak,” he says, “what you are able to bear.”

When you presented your members to wickedness to commit shameful acts, did fear lead you to sin, or sin’s sweetness? You will answer: sweetness. Thus sweetness leads to sin; but does fear impel toward righteousness? This is inhuman. Rather, it is human that, as the one was so too the other should be. As lust and the pleasure of sin have hitherto existed in you, so henceforth let there be delight and love of righteousness. This indeed does not yet appear to be perfect, but is in a certain way mature righteousness.

For more slavery is owed to righteousness than people customarily render to sin. Bodily punishment, although not proceeding from the will, nevertheless recalls one from the act of sin; but righteousness ought to be so loved that not even bodily punishment should restrain one from its works. Thus, just as that person is most wicked whom not even bodily punishments deter from the unclean works of foul pleasure, so that person is most righteous whom not even the terror of bodily punishments recalls from the holy works of radiant love [Col. 0610C].

But I speak humanly to you, O human being: love righteousness as you loved wickedness. In wickedness you followed pleasure; for righteousness endure persecution. You have come to things harsh, terrible, savage, threatening: tread them down, break them, and pass through. O to love, O to go, O to perish to oneself, O to arrive at God! “He who loves his life will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it unto eternal life” (John XII; Matt. X). Thus one who loves righteousness is to be loved; thus one who loves invisible beauty is to be loved.

VERS. 20.—“For when,” he says, “you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.” What freedom, I ask, can belong to an enslaved servant except when he delights in sinning? For he serves freely who willingly does his master’s will; and accordingly, he who is a servant of sin is free to sin. Hence he will not be free to do what is right unless, freed from sin, he has begun to be a servant of righteousness. This itself is true freedom: to possess joy in doing what is right; and at the same time pious slavery: to embrace obedience to the command [Col. 0610D]. But whence will this freedom for doing good belong to a person joined and sold over [to sin], unless he is redeemed by him whose saying is: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII)?

For people are free from righteousness only by the freedom of the will; but they are not free from sin except by the Saviour’s grace. For this reason the admirable teacher carefully distinguished even the words themselves.

VERS. 20, 21.—“For when,” he says, “you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit then did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?” There is indeed a certain useful temporal shame: a disturbance of mind looking back upon its sins, recoiling as it looks back; recoiling, blushing; blushing, correcting itself. Whoever does not have this shame will have eternal shame. Therefore it follows:

VERS. 21, 22.—“For their end is death. But now [Col. 0611B], having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life.” Here observe the distinction of the words. He said “free from righteousness,” not “freed,” lest they attribute this to themselves; but most carefully he preferred to say “freed,” referring this to the Lord’s saying: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.” But the will which is free in evils because it delights in evils is not free in good things because it has not been set free. Nor can a person will any good unless helped by him who cannot will evil.

But we call free for the performance of works of piety those to whom the Apostle says: “But now [Col. 0612A], having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life.” We could by no means possess this fruit unto sanctification—which fruit is unquestionably love and its works—from ourselves; rather, we possess it through the Holy Spirit given to us. For the divine Teacher was speaking of this very fruit when he said to the branches abiding in him: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). Therefore the Apostle also calls eternal life itself, which is certainly the reward of good works, the grace of God, adding and saying:

VERS. 23.—“The wages of sin are death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Wages are rendered for military service, not freely given. Thus “wages” is rightly said here, as though of diabolical military service, in which eternal death is rendered as a debt. Although he could have said—and correctly said—“the wages of righteousness are eternal life,” he preferred to say, “the grace of God is eternal life,” so that we might understand from this that God leads us to eternal life not on account of our merits but through his grace [Col. 0612B].

For eternal life is indeed the wages of righteousness, but to you, O human being, it is grace, just as righteousness itself is grace. Therefore, lest some way other than through the Mediator should be sought even for this, he added: “in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0611]

[Col. 0611C] Having already discussed at greater length above the righteousness of the law and of faith, the Apostle, with Jews and Gentiles in view, finally taught that both, once justified by faith, have peace with God. Then, by comparing the old Adam with the new, he showed them the surpassing excellence of the grace by which they had been reconciled; and, being established in it, he strongly encouraged them—through the mystery of the baptism they had received—toward what they call sinlessness and toward the works of faith; and toward passing from the slavery of the letter to the freedom of the spirit, in which consists the third state of the human being or of the people of God. Now, imitating Him whom he served in the Gospel of His Son—whose mercy fills the earth, and yet who fashions individually the hearts of each and understands all their works—our speaker, unskilled in speech though not in knowledge, [Col. 0611D] more plainly assumes the form of moral instruction. He reasonably demonstrates what meets the consciences of individuals; what any law works in them, what grace works, what faith, what the letter, and what that which is called freedom of the will. He also describes the conflict between the law of the mind and the law of the members, and declares that there is no liberation from the body of this death except through the grace of God by our Lord Jesus Christ. First, therefore, by an analogy from the law, he puts an end to the law, so that every mouth may be stopped; so that, once the Jews’ glory based on the law has been destroyed, the case of Jews and Gentiles alike may henceforth proceed on equal terms, and the grace of doctrine be similar. He therefore says:

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0612C]

**Verses 1–3.**—“Do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the law—that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives? For a woman who is under a husband is bound by law to her husband while he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.”

This is understood differently by different people. Some interpret the woman under a husband as a person under the law: just as a woman, if she attaches herself to another while her husband lives, is judged an adulteress, but when her husband has died is released from the law of her husband and has the power to marry whom she wishes; so, while the law lives—that is, while it retains its own standing—a person subject to the law has no right [Col. 0612D] to withdraw his neck from the yoke of the law. But if, by falling from its standing, the law has died, he is free to attach himself to another law. This is very easily understood of the law of Moses and the people of the circumcision, and contains no difficulty whatever. For when the Prophet appeared, of whom Moses said: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you hear me” (Deut. XVIII), the law became obsolete and aged, and came to destruction; a new song began to be sung, a new commandment to be preached, and all things to become new. Immediately the election from among the Jews became the Church, the new Bride of the Lamb, without spot or [Col. 0613A] wrinkle; and she cleaved to the new Bridegroom, having left her former dead husband, without any charge of adultery.

But in order that this analogy may embrace both Jews and Gentiles, others, examining it more subtly, observed three things in the analogy, and three things in the reality illustrated by the analogy, which are not unsuitably fitted to explain the analogy itself. For there are three things in the analogy: woman, husband, and law, since the woman is subjected to the husband through the bond of law. Such is the analogy. Likewise there are three things in the reality illustrated: person, sin, and law, because a person is under the law as long as he lives to sin, just as a woman is under the law of her husband as long as her husband lives. Yet, while in this analogy we find three things—the woman, the husband, and the law—in the reality [Col. 0613B] illustrated there are three: the soul, sin, and the law of sin. The sole difference here is that in the analogy the husband dies, so that the woman may be released from the law of her husband; whereas in the reality illustrated, the soul itself dies to sin, so that it may marry Christ. But when it dies to sin, it also dies to the law of sin.

Here sin must be understood as that which came in through the law, which he says becomes sinful beyond measure, because, once it already appears to be sin, it is further increased by the added transgression. “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” And this is what is called the sinner beyond measure, or sin through the commandment. These were passions—not passions at that time, but pleasures—which, increased through the law, worked in the members so as to bear fruit unto death. Under them the soul was held as under a ruling husband, before grace came through faith. But one dies to these passions who now serves the law of God with the mind, although the passions themselves have not yet died, so long as the law of sin is served in the flesh. For there still remains in one who is under grace something which does not conquer him but trains him, does not lead him captive but exercises him, until everything strengthened by evil habit is put to death.

The true Bride of Christ understands the difference between letter and spirit, which are also called, in another way, law and grace. Serving God no longer in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit, she is not under law but under grace. Thus letter with spirit, and law with grace, are no longer called letter and law in the same way as the letter and law considered in themselves, [Col. 0613D] when they kill through abounding transgression. For the law is called also the power of sin when, by severe prohibition, it increases sin’s harmful pleasure; and yet even then it is not evil, but sin, in order that it might appear as sin, works death through what is good. Thus many things are harmful to some persons although they are not evil.

Therefore this Bride of Christ has now died to the law—that is, to sin, which becomes more abundant through the law’s prohibition, when the law commands without grace but does not help. Dead to such a law, so as to belong to Another who rose from the dead, she makes this distinction without injury to the law, lest she commit sacrilege against its Author. For the same law which “was given through Moses,” while “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I), is transformed when the spirit is added to the letter, so that the righteousness of the law begins to be fulfilled—the righteousness whose non-fulfilment made persons guilty even by transgression. [Col. 0614A] For there is not one law which is holy, good, and just, and another through which sin works death, and to which we must die so that we may belong to Another who rose from the dead; it is the same law. Hence he continues:

**Verse 4.**—“Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ”: that is, to shadow through reality, to letter through spirit, to law through grace; so that you may no longer be the wife or bride of him who has died, but of Him who rose from the dead; so that you may no longer bear fruit to the dead one in dead works, but bear the fruits of life to God. For the law itself also foreshadowed something of this kind, commanding that when a woman’s first husband had died and she had received no seed from him, she should pass into the bed of the one who was the deceased’s brother and raise up seed for his brother, [Col. 0614B] which he had been unable to raise up. For spiritual understanding seems to be the more fruitful brother of the letter. He continues:

**Verse 5.**—“For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which are through the law were at work in our members, to bear fruit unto death.” When we were in the flesh—that is, when we lived amid the desires of the flesh and placed all our hope there—the passions of sins, which had been increased through the law rather than removed, were at work in our members in order to bear fruit unto death. For the law made the sinner who presumed upon himself a transgressor, because he did not have God as his helper. Your own desire conquered you, O human being, because it found you in a bad place, that is, in the flesh. Leave the flesh; though living in the flesh, do not be in the flesh. Be in the flesh [Col. 0614C] in the spirit. What does it mean, “Be in the spirit”? Place your hope in God. For if you place your hope in that spirit by which a human being is human, your spirit falls back again to earth, because you have not given it to Him from whom it may hang; for it does not sustain itself unless it is sustained. Do not place hope in yourself, but in Him who made you. He is your life; whatever you bring forth for Him is fruit borne for your life. He continues:

**Verse 6.**—“But now we have been released from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.” The law of death is the killing letter, from which those who die to sin are delivered. The law is letter alone for those who merely read it—this belongs to the Old Testament—but who do not fulfil it through charity, which belongs to the New Testament. It is not the helper of those who read, but the witness against those who sin; those renewed by the spirit are delivered from its condemnation, because the letter kills but the spirit gives life. In the oldness of the letter one serves through fear; in the newness of the spirit, through love, where slaves become sons. But so that we, who are sons by grace, may no longer be such slaves, we know that the Lord does this. That slave does not know this—the one who does not know what his master does, and who glories in himself rather than in the Lord.

**Verse 7.**—“What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known desire unless the law said: ‘You shall not desire.’” If the law is not sin but merely points out sin, it is nevertheless criticized in these words. For by its very disclosure of sin it makes guilty the human soul which had been secure, as it were, through ignorance. Thus, he says, “I did not know sin except through the law.” He did not say, “I did not commit it except through the law,” but “I did not know it except through the law.”

But the law was usefully given insofar as it revealed sin, because, since sin could not be conquered without God’s grace, the anxiety of guilt itself might turn the sinner toward receiving grace. Therefore guilt was not implanted by the law but made known; the law did not take it away, yet it showed by whom it might be taken away. It followed, however, that because desire could not yet be resisted before grace was received, it was even increased; for desire gains greater strength when the crime of transgression is added, since it acts also against the law, than it would have if no law had forbidden it. Therefore the Apostle chose desire as something comprehending everything, as though this were the voice of the law prohibiting every sin: “You shall not desire.” Whoever fulfils this commandment commits no sin at all. For no sin is committed except through desire.

Yet sometimes a sin happens to a person which he can be said neither to do nor to commit, because in that sin nothing is desired, but it is imposed through incapacity or ignorance. Even there, however, if there were no sin, the prophet would not pray: “Do not remember my ignorances” (Ps. XXIV). Good, then, is the law which commands, “You shall not desire.” But where the Spirit does not help—by inspiring a good desire in place of evil desire, that is, by pouring charity into our hearts—the law, though good, certainly increases evil desire by forbidding it. I do not know [Col. 0615C] how it is that what is desired becomes sweeter when it is forbidden; and this is what he says later, namely that sin deceives through the commandment and kills through it. Hence he continues:

**Verse 8.**—“But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, worked in me every desire.” Desire was already sin before the law, but it was not every desire. The river was checked by the law, not dried up. What carried you along when there were no barriers overwhelmed you when the barriers were broken. It was lesser when it stirred your lust; it is total when it transgresses the law. Do you wish to know how great it is? Consider what it broke: the commandment of God saying, “You shall not desire” (Exod. XX). For without the law sin was dead—that is, hidden, not apparent; it was altogether, as it were, buried in certain shadows of its own ignorance. “But I was once alive without the law”: that is, I was frightened by no death arising from sin, because sin did not appear when there was no law. I was alive—that is, I seemed to myself to be alive. “But when the commandment came, sin revived.” It stood out; it appeared; yet it did not begin to live but revived. For it had once lived in Paradise, when what had been committed contrary to the given commandment was plainly evident. But when it is drawn from those who are born, it lies hidden as though dead, until its evil, resisting righteousness, is felt through the law’s prohibition. For when one thing is commanded and approved, while another delights and rules, sin in some manner revived in the awareness of the person born, which had once lived in the awareness of the first-created human being. It revived: that is, it began to be felt; it began to rebel; it began to appear.

[Col. 0616A]

**Verse 10.**—“But I died”: that is, I became a transgressor; or, I came to know that I was dead; or, the guilt of transgression threatened the certain punishment of death—things of which I was ignorant when I followed my desires without knowledge, because without restraint.

**Verse 10.**—“And the commandment, which was for life,” if it were obeyed, “was found by me to be unto death,” when action is contrary to the commandment. Not only is sin committed, as before, but sin is now committed knowingly and in transgression. The commandment not to desire is rightly for life. For the one true life is not to desire. O life sweet and sweeter than the pleasure of desire! Happy the soul that delights in pleasures of this kind, where it is defiled by no shamefulness and purified by the serenity of truth—namely, when the law of God delights it, and delights it in such a way that all wanton pleasures are conquered. This does not happen immediately when a person comes to grace; rather, desire becomes slower in one who makes progress in proportion as, by progressing, he comes nearer to righteousness.

**Verse 11.**—“For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.” Sin, using the law unlawfully, made desire sweeter through its increase caused by prohibition, and therefore deceived me. For deceptive is the sweetness followed by more numerous and greater bitternesses of punishment. Therefore, because what is forbidden is accepted more sweetly by persons not yet spiritual, sin deceives through false sweetness; and because the guilt of transgression is added, it kills.

**Verse 12.**—“Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” For the law commands what ought to be commanded and forbids what ought to be forbidden. The fault lies in one who uses it badly, not in the commandment, which is good; for the law is good if anyone uses it lawfully. But a person uses the law badly if he does not subject himself to God in devout humility, so that the law may be fulfilled through grace. A little earlier (v. 7) the Apostle had defended the law against an accusation; now he raises it with its due praise. There, he said, “Is the law sin? By no means!” There truth is defended in one word, because the authority of its defender is great. Here, however, he says: “The law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.”

Receive, therefore, the commandment; know that it is your weapon—not one by which it kills you, but one by which the enemy is killed by you, if you are humble like little David. But if you are a great and proud Goliath, you will be killed by your own weapons. Goliath trusted in shield and spear, Pharaoh in chariots and horses; but you, in the name of the Lord. Thus, whether the law harms those empty of grace or benefits those full of grace, it is always good, as the sun is always good, whether it injures sore eyes or gently delights healthy ones. Accordingly, what health is to eyes for seeing the sun, grace is to minds for fulfilling the law. And just as healthy eyes are not killed by the sun’s delight but enlightened, while unhealthy eyes, struck back by the harsh blows of its rays, are driven into denser darkness; so the soul which has been made sound through the charity of the Spirit is not said to be dead to righteousness. Rather, the soul is dead which is subject to guilt and transgression, and which the law through the letter made so, so long as grace was absent.

[Col. 0617A]

**Verse 13.**—“Then has what is good become death to me? By no means! But sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.” Death is not the law; sin is death. But he had already said above (v. 8), “Without the law sin is dead,” where we said that “dead” means hidden: it lies concealed; it does not appear. Now observe how truly it was so said: “Sin,” he says, “in order that it might appear as sin.” He did not say “that it might be,” because it existed as sin even when it did not appear. What does “that it might appear as sin” mean? “I would not have known desire unless the law said: ‘You shall not desire.’” He did not say, “I did not have desire,” but “I did not know desire.” Likewise here he does not say “that sin might be,” but “that it might appear as sin; through what is good it worked death in me.”

What death? “That sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment.” Why beyond measure? Because transgression has now also been added. For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. “And the commandment which was for life was found by me to be unto death” (v. 10): for what is more relevant to life than “You shall not desire”? Yet it was found “to be unto death.” For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. It frightened desire; it did not extinguish it. It produced fear of punishment, not love of righteousness. What then? Why do we doubt that the law was given for this end: that a person might discover himself? For when God did not forbid evil, a person was hidden from himself. He does not discover the weakness of his own powers except when he receives the law of prohibition.

**Verse 14.**—“We know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. For what I do I do not know. For I do not do what I will, but what I hate, that I do.” These words adequately show that the law cannot be fulfilled except by spiritual persons, who become such only through God’s grace. For the more like the spiritual law anyone becomes—that is, the more he rises into a spiritual disposition—the more he fulfils it, because he delights in it more through the grace which forgives sins and pours in the spirit of charity, by which righteousness is not burdensome but sweet and pleasant.

When the whole context of this passage is carefully examined, it is rightly understood that the Apostle spoke these words and those that follow both in his own person and in the person of others faithfully established under grace, though not yet brought into that peace in which death will be swallowed up in victory, of which the Apostle says: “If the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, He will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit dwelling in you” (below, ch. VIII, v. 11). For when our mortal bodies have then been made alive, there will not only be no consent to sin, but even the fleshly desire to which consent could be given will remain no longer—the desire resisting the spirit, which no person could avoid having in mortal flesh except that one Man who alone did not come to humanity through it. For the body will be spiritual, and whoever is there will be wholly—that is, in both parts of which he consists—a spiritual person, when even the body is spiritual. Nor is it absurd that flesh also should be spiritual in that life, since even in this life the spirit itself can be carnal in those who still think according to the flesh.

These are the fourth things—or fourth stage—of the human being of God, which here begin through the sanctification of the Spirit and are perfected in that blessed portion of eternal blessedness. Thus the Apostle here says, and every spiritual person with him, “But I am carnal,” as though he did not yet have a spiritual body; just as he could say, “I am mortal,” since he was still living in a mortal body. So the other things said here must also be understood: though they are spoken, as has been said, in the person of spiritual people, they appear not to suit spiritual people; they will be discussed better in their places.

“We know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual.” Certainly the law is spiritual, because, as we have already said, “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” When the spirit is added to the letter, charity to the commandment, true freedom to the slave of sin, and free service to the freed servant of righteousness—because it is voluntary—the law is spiritual. “But I,” says the Apostle, “am carnal.” I am still in the flesh; daily dying, I put off the flesh; yet I have not perfectly attained the state in which I do not desire. I shall attain it perfectly when I have wholly departed from the flesh, when I, as spirit, have put on a spiritual body, and no part of me remains carnal, but in both parts of myself I shall be spiritual.

“Sold under sin.” Who sold you, O Paul? “I am human,” he says, “O human being.” A human being sold himself in order to be a slave under sin; I sold myself when I consented to the deceiver. I was able to sell myself; I cannot redeem myself. I sold myself when I gave consent to sin and received death. But again I give faith and receive righteousness from Him who gave faith also—the faith of His blood, which the devil unjustly shed. In that blood He justified me, He who alone was righteous without being justified, because He alone was born righteous. Therefore he says (below, ch. VIII, v. 23): “We who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.”

I know that I have been redeemed at a great price, but my body has not yet been freed from its corruption; and therefore, still corruptible and mortal, it has not yet received the hope of its redemption. Hence all of us who have received whatever firstfruits of the Spirit likewise groan daily within ourselves, knowing that we have been redeemed but not yet freed from the servile condition of the flesh. Therefore with anxious daily prayers we cry to our Redeemer: “Redeem me, Lord, and have mercy on me” (Ps. XXV). For You redeem us, Lord, when You fulfil in us the work of Your redemption.

For You had given humanity love and rejoicing in You; but miserable humanity gave them away, wishing to possess them in itself, and, delivered to death and corruption, attained neither the one nor the other—neither in You nor in itself. But You gave Yourself into servitude in order to redeem freedom for humanity. You gave Yourself to dishonour in order to redeem glory for humanity. The price of all these goods is Your blood. It is the fountain of David, open for the washing of the menstruous woman. Have patience with us, Lord Jesus, whom You deigned to value so highly that, in order to redeem us, You willed that nothing but Yourself should be our price. Yet we, though redeemed from vile bondage, have again sold ourselves for filthy pleasures—the truly most worthless slave-property of the flesh—and then bring You the stench of those very filths to be washed in the fountain of Your precious blood.

Yet, while washing all things, You are not defiled; indeed, the more You wash, the more healing You become, since the one to whom more is forgiven loves more. Spare us, Lord; and would that people would spare themselves, lest they bring things too filthy here—that is, lest they come here too filthy. Yet Your price is sufficient to redeem all; Your fountain is sufficient to wash all things. For even to those guilty of Your blood, when they sin against Your grace and return and weep before You, You know how most kindly to grant pardon. Yet You hand the guilty person over to the law for punishment, so that, as it is accustomed to demand eye for eye and tooth for tooth, so it may demand blood for blood from him: that the wicked pleasures of sin may sweat out in the bloody sweat of repentance and be searched out by the bloody tears of the heart. Yet since a person has none of these except as Your grace supplies them, the miserable human being, sold under sin, redeems himself for Your grace by the price received from You. And once restored to grace, he immediately finds battle and suffers the darkness of ignorance, which is customarily dangerous for those entering battle.

[Col. 0619C]

**Verse 15.**—“For what I do,” he says, “I do not understand. For I do not do what I will, but what I hate, that I do.” This does not mean that he did not understand sin, since sin appears as sin through the commandment. Rather, “I do not know” means, “I do not acknowledge; I do not approve,” as it is said: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII). Or: I think good what I do in order to satisfy lust; or I do not doubt that it is evil, and yet do it through blind desire; or I do not sufficiently perceive in myself the opposition between willing and unwilling.

But far be it that these words should be understood of the Apostle as meaning that, though he wished to be chaste, he was incestuous; though merciful, cruel; though devout, impious, when he says, “I do not do what I will.” Rather, he says: I will not to desire, and I desire; for the law said, “You shall not desire.” A human being heard the law, recognized the fault, declared war, and found captivity. Not all people apart from the Apostle, but the Apostle together with all, because he is human. For he has placed his own battle before your eyes, so that you may fear your own. If the blessed Apostle had not said this, then when you saw desire stirred in your members, though you did not consent to it, you might perhaps despair of yourself and say: “If I belonged to God, I would not be stirred in this way.” See the Apostle fighting, and do not despair.

“I do not,” he says, “do what I will,” because I do not will to desire, and yet I desire. This is that universal pestilence from Adam, that unavoidable contagion. For by doing in Paradise what was forbidden, he committed an act deserving punishment and found in himself a shameful movement, because their eyes were opened to something which they had never felt and never feared in the movement of their body. Their eyes were opened not for seeing but for gazing upon; hence they also took care to cover themselves. From this original sin is drawn, which no one escapes; from this the flesh desires against the spirit, which no one does not feel. This is sin, dwelling almost naturally in the body of every person born from that sin—the sin which produces every sin. Reason, therefore, hates desire; the son of grace does not will it. The flesh delights in desiring; the son of Adam also wills to fulfil what delights him. Therefore the Apostle does not do what he wills—that is, not to desire—because the human being acts in him what the Apostle hates: namely, to desire.

[Col. 0620B]

**Verse 16.**—“But if I do what I do not will, I agree with the law that it is good.” The transgression of the law would not be evil unless the law itself were good. For if it were not good, it would not be evil to transgress an evil law. But since it is evil to transgress it, the law is good. What is as good as “You shall not desire”? Therefore the Apostle says: My weakness does not fulfil the law, but my will praises the law. For I do not will what I do, and in what I do not will I agree with the law; though in what I do I am against the law. For my will is that of the law also: not to desire. Though I do not do this, I nevertheless approve it, both in myself and in the law, if I could do it. I agree with the law because it is good.

**Verses 17–18.**—“But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me.” Where in you? He continues: “For I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh.” This is the seed of Adam in our body, opposed to that seed of God in our spirit, of which John says in his epistle: “If anyone has been born of God, he does not sin; but His seed which is in him preserves him” (1 John III). For sin dwells in the body; but the person who calls upon God, fighting against sin, lives by faith by not consenting to it. For the willing is present, so that sin may not be; but it lies powerless—that is, it is impotent without the aid of grace, although willing itself is the work of grace. Therefore he adds: “But I do not find the power to accomplish the good.”

For in not consenting he does good; in hating his own desire he does good; yet he does not find the power to accomplish the good. He will find it then, when the desire which now dwells in our members no longer exists at all. At present the vice of the flesh is not good in a good thing; when it ceases to exist, there will still be flesh, but it will no longer be corrupted or vicious. Yet the same teacher shows that this flesh belongs to our nature when he says, “I know that no good dwells in me,” and, to explain this, adds, “that is, in my flesh.” He therefore calls his flesh himself; the flesh itself is not, then, an enemy. Even when one resists its vice, one loves the flesh itself, because it is being healed. “For no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V).

“For willing is present with me, but I do not find the power to accomplish the good.” Willing is present to both, to flesh and mind; but neither finds the power to accomplish, so long as the desire of the flesh cannot draw the will of the mind to consent to evil, nor can the will of the mind bring it about that desire does not exist at all. Hence he continues:

[Col. 0621A]

**Verse 19.**—“For I do not do the good which I will, but the evil which I do not will, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me.” For when I will the good, I will what the law wills, and I find, therefore, that the law is good for me who will to do good, because by commanding it sends me toward the good. But I do not find the power to accomplish it, because willing is present with me, is near me; sin dwells in my body, a domestic enemy. Everyone who progresses with a right intention departs, as he progresses, from every sin, and becomes farther from it in proportion as he becomes nearer to righteousness and perfection. For even desire itself, which is sin dwelling in our flesh, although it still remains in mortal members, does not cease to diminish in those who make progress.

For it is one thing to depart from every sin, which is now achieved in practice, and another thing to have departed, which belongs to that perfection. The guilt of original desire is forgiven in baptism, but weakness remains until the future life. There perpetual peace awaits those who fight well; until he is healed, everyone who makes good progress struggles most diligently against that weakness. For this is the hidden sin and the evil lying close at hand, of which it was said above: “It is not I who do it, but sin which dwells in me”; and again here, because evil lies close to me, like a serpent lying in wait for the heel.

When he says, “It is not I who do it, but sin which dwells in me,” this sin works in us and we do not work it when our will in no way consents to it and also restrains the members from obeying its desires. For what does sin work in us against our will except unlawful desires? If the consent of the will is not given to them, they are indeed stirred, but no result is yielded to them. Sin, then, works desires; if we obey them, we too work; but if we do not obey, we do not work it, but the sin which dwells in us does. [Col. 0621D] If we had no unlawful desires at all, neither we nor sin would work anything evil in us.

But we are said to do the movement of unlawful desire—even though, by not obeying it, we do not do that thing—because it is not a strength of an alien nature but a weakness of our own. We shall be saved from this weakness when we have become immortal in both soul and body. As has already been said, its guilt was forgiven in baptism together with all the deeds which we performed by obeying it; and it would no longer harm us if we were thereafter to give obedience to none of its desires.

**Verse 21.**—“I find, then, a law for myself when I will to do good”: that is, I find some law to be good. But when I will to do good, I find battle within myself, because evil lies close at hand—as he adds:

[Col. 0622A]

**Verse 22.**—“For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person. But I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members.” Does the fact that all iniquity has been blotted out in baptism mean that no weakness remains? If none remained, we would live here without sin. But in the part in which we have been liberated, we are free and serve God; in the part in which we are still slaves, we serve the law of sin. “I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inner person.” See: from that source we are free, and from it we delight in the law of God. For freedom delights. For as long as you do what is just through fear, God does not delight you. As long as He does not delight you, you still act as a slave; let Him delight you, and you are free. Do not fear punishment; love righteousness. Are you not yet able to love righteousness? At least fear punishment, so that you may arrive at loving righteousness.

Thus he already felt himself free in his higher part, whence he said: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” The law delights me; what the law commands delights me; righteousness itself delights me. “But I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members.” This is the weakness that remains. In this part he experiences captivity, where righteousness has not been fulfilled. For where he delights in the law of God, he is not captive but a friend of the law, and therefore free, because he is a friend. What, then, follows concerning what remains? “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII).

But this is the law resisting the law of the mind, which the first human beings deserved to have in the members of the death conceived within them after they transgressed the commandment. Marriage now orders it among the children of Adam, and continence restrains and checks it, so that, just as punishment was made from sin, so merit may be made from punishment. This is the law which takes me captive: captive, but in part; captive, but according to the flesh. For the mind resists and delights in the law of God, and does not consent to the sin which tickles, suggests, and flatters, because it possesses other inward delights, in no respect comparable with the pleasures of the flesh. There is, therefore, something dead in me. The mind does not consent, but death struggles. Yet just as what lives is in me, so [Col. 0622D] is also what is dead in me.

VERS. 24. — “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” What is it that he asks? If it is the dissolution of the body, it is not far off. Was the Apostle’s groaning so profound for that reason? Far from it! For not everyone who ends this life is delivered from this body of death, but only the one worthy to receive that life. He does not ask to be delivered from the substance of the body, which is good, but from carnal vices; and a human being is not delivered from these even in dying, except through the grace of the Savior. Death separates one from the body, but the vices contracted from it cling fast, and a just punishment is owed for them—a punishment which that rich man also found in hell. For he asks not merely that by pardon he may be unpunished for the past, but also that henceforth he may be strong and vigorous in not sinning. For he delights in the law of God, but sees another law in his members. He sees that it is present; he does not recall that it once was. He is pressed by present things, not remembering past ones; and he sees not only a law resisting him, but even taking him captive into the law of sin, which is—not which was—in his members. He might also have said, “from the mortal body.” What does “this body of death” mean?

For the bodies of the first human beings before sin, although animal and not yet spiritual, were nevertheless not such as had to die. This came about on the day when they touched the forbidden tree. Thus they possessed animal bodies indeed, but bodies that would not die unless they sinned, and that would receive an angelic form and heavenly quality. But as soon as they transgressed the commandment, death itself, like some lethal disease, was conceived in their members; and it changed that condition in which they ruled their body in such a way that they would not say, “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind.” For although their body was not yet spiritual but animal, it was not yet this body of death, concerning which and with which we are born.

Indeed, why should I say merely “born,” rather than “conceived”? We have begun wholly as a kind of disease, by which, after bodily diseases and many bodily deaths, captivities and afflictions of the soul, we must finally and necessarily die. For it is not as necessary that one who has become dropsical, consumptive, or elephantiasic should die of the disease itself, as that one who has begun to possess this body of death [Col. 0623C] should die—a body in which all human beings are by nature children of wrath, because it was produced only by the punishment of sin. Even the concupiscence with which we are born cannot end while we live. It can diminish daily; it cannot end. For this reason our body is called a body of death.

VERS. 24, 25. — “Who, therefore, will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God.” Grace, because it is given freely; grace, because it precedes all our good merits. It will deliver us from the body of death when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption. Through whom? “Through our Lord Jesus Christ.” For “as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15).

[Col. 0623D] Yet Paul is by no means to be blamed because, secure concerning the crown of righteousness laid up for him, he said: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit until that day” (2 Tim. 1). It is difficult for one who labors not to long for the end of labor. It was indeed good for him to remain still in the flesh for the sake of the brethren, but to be with Christ was much better.

O Lord, whose grace delivers us, the prophet who says, “You are my hope,” does not say without reason that you are also his patience (Ps. 70). But the body of death, the captivity of the soul under the law of sin, the world set in evil, and all the evils of this life press us toward you, the highest good, where there is no evil. You also promise yourself to us; but you do not disclose when we shall possess you. You create the evil which presses us hence [Col. 0624A] toward you; you prolong hope so that it torments the wretched. And amid all these things, if we say, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” your grace says to us, “I.” If we ask when, we are reproved for impatience; if we presume anything further, we are overwhelmed by ignorance of your judgments.

Therefore those dwelling at the boundaries of your grace are troubled by your signs; and the going forth of this morning and evening greatly delights them: there, concerning what they will be through your grace, they will no longer fear failure, nor beyond that desire further progress, holding that perfection in which you will be all in all to them. Lord, you will give them peace; meanwhile, give them patience.

“Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh.” The order of the preceding sense is this: because grace delivers, therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh. But if I serve the law of God with my mind, and if I also unwillingly serve the law of sin with my flesh, I am nevertheless now in Christ. If I am in Christ, there is no condemnation for me, because “there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” For whatever condemnation there is, we who flee to Christ escape, because we have found a deliverer.

## Chapter VIII

VERS. 1–3. — “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh.” — “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has delivered me from the law of sin and death.”

But in the law of the Spirit is fulfilled the righteousness which could not be fulfilled in the law [Col. 0624C] of the letter, because “wherein the law was weak, God sent his Son.” Therefore, he says, I myself serve the law of God with my mind. Up to this point the man of God, not discerning himself and not understanding what he does, begins to discern himself and to understand who works within him.

Therefore, he says, there is not one person in the flesh and another in the mind; but I am in the flesh, I am in the mind. There are not two contrary natures, but in both there is one human being, just as there is one God by whom the human being was made. I myself serve the law of God with my mind by not consenting; but with my flesh I serve the law of sin by desiring. Yet here I delight, and there I am not conquered.

For a new life is prescribed for you here, O old man. You are lifted up by joy in newness, but weighed down by the burden of oldness. A war against yourself begins for you. If, in the respect in which you displease yourself, you join yourself to God, then in the respect in which you are now joined to God you will be fit to conquer yourself, because he who conquers all things is with you.

But we grow weary of daily conflict. We would not always be conquering; we would at last like to find peace. For as far as our vows, our will, and our prayer extend, when we say, “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6), this is surely what we desire: that no evil desires at all should arise from our flesh. Yet while we live here, we cannot accomplish it. Human nature deserved this in itself: sickness comes from sin; it is healed, and it is no more. This discord labors toward peace.

The flesh pursues its own desires; pursue yours also. The desires of the flesh are not oppressed, extinguished, [Col. 0625A] or destroyed by you; do not let yours be extinguished, lest you fall in the contest. When the mind does not consent to evil desires, serve the law of God; but when the flesh desires, while you do not serve it, serve the law of sin. As long as you are thus, you are in Christ Jesus; and there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Though they are in the flesh, serving the law of sin with their flesh, nevertheless they do not walk according to the flesh, because with their mind they serve the law of God.

“Now,” that is, in this condition, there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Or “now,” that is, in the time of conflict: while we still fight, we have nevertheless already escaped the danger of condemnation. Peace will come when there will not even be that concupiscence against which we fight.

“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has delivered me from the law of sin and death.” The Apostle seems here to have set forth three laws, whose distinction is necessary for readers. The first is the law of the Spirit of life; the second, the law of sin and death; the third, the law which was unable to justify.

The law of the Spirit of life is itself the law of faith, the law of mercy, of which it is said: “Have mercy on me according to your law” (Ps. 113). For it is the law that grants remission of sins—the grace of God powerful to adopt. The second law is concupiscence. It is quite rightly called a law, because it was justly brought about that the flesh of the human being who refused obedience to the Lord his God should not obey him. It is the law of sin and the law of death. For sin is death, concerning which it is said: “On the day you eat, you shall die by death” (Gen. 21).

The third law is the law of the letter, powerless to accomplish what the law of the Spirit of life accomplished: namely, to deliver from the law of sin and death. It is the law of deeds, which knows how to threaten, not to assist; to command, not to help. One law shows sin; the other removes it. It was impossible for the law of the letter to remove sin, wherein it was weak through the flesh. For when the flesh rebelled and conquered, the human being heard the law and was stirred even more toward his own concupiscence. What could not be done through that law, therefore, was fulfilled through the law of grace.

VERS. 3, 4. — “When God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh on account of sin, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.”

Open, Lord, the Scriptures that speak of you, to those who seek none but you in them; and above all this Scripture, which you dictated to us through your Apostle, which is the work of your own finger and the stylus of your Spirit. In it, above all, disclose to us the seal of this mystery—a seal which no one worthy was found to open in heaven, on earth, or under the earth, except you, who possess the key of David (Rev. 5).

Open to us, therefore, what that is “which was impossible for the law, wherein it was weak through the flesh”: what could not be bestowed on the world unless your Only-Begotten came and appeared in the world in the likeness of sinful flesh. What is it but what follows: the destruction or condemnation of sin, and the fulfillment in us of the righteousness of the law?

Thus he also says to the Hebrews: “For if the blood of goats or calves, or the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself spotless to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (Heb. 9). What is here called condemnation of sin is there called cleansing from dead works; and service to God with a clean conscience is the perfect fulfillment of righteousness.

For under the law of the letter a human being sinned, and a goat paid the penalty; in this, not the spirit but the flesh seemed to be cleansed or sanctified, because the law, for the sake of awareness of its own weakness, demanded nothing further for cleansing than that external rite of purification. For the law seemed able to reach only as far as the flesh; but, being weak through the flesh, it failed to enter in order to cleanse the conscience.

It threatened that after sin, one who did not act as prescribed should be stoned or cut off from his people, doing nothing concerning the conscience—how it might be cleansed by the Lord its God. Yet this does not take place except in the fulfillment of the righteousness of the law.

We must therefore ask what that righteousness of the law is. It is plainly that which is called the righteousness of the law because the law was given in order that it might be fulfilled. What is it, except satisfaction for the past and security for the future? But there could be no satisfaction, from a nature corrupted by sin, for sin incorporated into nature; nor security for the future from one bereft of grace. Behold the weakness of the law through the flesh.

Therefore the Only-Begotten came from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1), so full of grace that it not only abounded in him but also overflowed from him into us, because from his fullness we all received, and grace for grace. First he grants us faith; then, as it were in return for the merit of faith, hope. But hope does not disappoint, because then the love of God is also poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5). When he is given to us, it is necessary that we hope as much as we believe, and love as much as we hope and believe; and this is the fulfillment of the law and of righteousness.

For when the Only-Begotten of God came into the world, the ruler of this world met him. Christ permitted himself to be killed for righteousness’ sake, although that ruler had nothing in him. But Christ, granting the righteousness of his innocent death to the repentant sinner, placed his faith and love in that sinner’s heart, confession unto salvation in the sinner’s mouth, and his body and blood in the sinner’s hand. Thus, presenting his guilty and redeemed one to God the Father, with the sin of the presumptuous man condemned and the sin of the penitent destroyed, he made him pleasing and acceptable in the sacrifice of his righteousness.

This is the redemption which you sent, Lord, to your people. This is your righteousness, concerning which your poor one cries to you daily from the ends of the earth: “Deliver me in your righteousness” (Ps. 70). This is your work, for which the prophet asks, saying: “Lord, let your work become true” (Hab. 3). For your work truly comes to be in us when we offer you this your sacrifice; when, remembering with the certain sacrament of faith and the devout affection of the heart what you did for us, faith receives with its mouth, hope chews over, and love [Col. 0627A] digests into salvation and life the blessed and beatifying food of your grace.

For there you present yourself to the desiring soul, accepting the embrace of its love and kissing it with the kiss of your mouth. As often happens in a kiss of love, it pours out its spirit to you and you pour yours into it, so that you become one body and one spirit, when it thus receives your body and blood. There conscience is not only cleansed from dead works, but is strengthened, filled with fruits of life and the Spirit, to serve the living God, when the righteousness of the law is fully fulfilled in it. Thus, as you presented yourself to us in some measure even to the contempt of yourself, so may your sons vow themselves to you even to the contempt of themselves.

But God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh: in true flesh, but not in sinful flesh. The first human being, created with no prior sin of any parent, was not created in sinful flesh; we, born after his preceding sin, are born in sinful flesh. Christ, in order to condemn sin on account of sin, appeared such—that is, in the likeness of sinful flesh.

The likeness of sinful flesh was in him because death exists only from sin, and that body was indeed mortal. For unless it were mortal, it would not die.
