Thus death is called sin, just as Greek speech or Latin speech is called “tongue,” not meaning the bodily member itself, but what is produced through that bodily member. Thus the Lord’s death is called sin, because it came about from sin: he assumed flesh from the very mass that had deserved death through sin.

For Mary too was dead through sin, being from that same mass; and the flesh of the Lord from Mary was dead for the destruction of sins. Mary was a virgin, without a man’s embrace and without the heat of concupiscence; and lest she experience that heat, it was said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). Therefore the Virgin Mary did not have intercourse and conceive, but believed and conceived; and the Lord was born mortal among mortals.

Why mortal? Because he was in the likeness of sinful flesh, not in sinful flesh. What does sinful flesh possess? Death and sin. What did the likeness of sinful flesh possess? Death without sin. For if it had sin, it would be sinful flesh; if it did not have death, it would not be the likeness of sinful flesh. Such was the Savior who came.

He was mortal and died, but he killed death; and on account of sin he condemned sin. Thus, as has been said, by the sin of the presumptuous sinner he condemned the sin of the repentant sinner; and by the death of his flesh he killed in us the death of the soul. Moreover, in the law the sacrificial offering for sin was itself called “sin.” Therefore, having himself become an offering for sin, he condemned and destroyed every sin in us. This is the righteousness of the law: fulfilled not through the law but through him who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Thus “the righteousness of the law” was fulfilled in us, “who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.” Not to walk according to the flesh is, through grace at work, not to obey concupiscences. For after grace has been received, conflict with the flesh remains: iniquity has been removed, but weakness remains.

## Book Five

[Col. 0627]

### Chapter VIII Continues

[Col. 0627C]

VERS. 5–7. — “For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.”

Wisdom hates evil. What is wisdom but a taste for good? What is evil but a taste for evil? Therefore, those for whom either good or evil tastes sweet and is delightful in the heart are the very persons who set their minds upon, or are mindful of, the things of the Spirit or the things of the flesh; they are likewise the persons who walk according to the Spirit or according to the flesh.

It follows: “For the prudence of the flesh is death.” Prudence is properly placed after taste, because just as taste distinguishes foods according to their flavor, so prudence weighs what is expedient. If someone seeks only what pleases the flesh, this is the prudence of the flesh, which is the death of the soul. For just as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; and whatever it desires beneath God is death to it.

But the prudence of the Spirit is to seek one’s life, which is God, and the peace which is in God. This peace cannot belong to one who relishes the things of the flesh; for, as has been said, wisdom hates evil, “and the prudence of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law of God; indeed, it cannot be.”

What does “indeed, it cannot be” mean? It is not that a human being, flesh, spirit, or any nature cannot be subject; rather, the prudence of the flesh cannot. A vice cannot; nature can. It is as if you said: “Lameness is not subject to walking straight; indeed, it cannot be.” A foot can, but lameness cannot. Remove the lameness and you will see straight walking. So long as lameness exists, it cannot; likewise, so long as prudence of the flesh exists, it cannot. Let there be no prudence of the flesh, and the human being can.

When he says, moreover, “the prudence of the flesh is hostile to God,” this must not be understood as though that hostility could injure God. It is hostile by resisting, not by harming. But it harms the person in whom the prudence of the flesh exists, because it is a vice and harms the nature in which it resides. Thus it cannot be subject to God’s law insofar as it is a vice; nevertheless, insofar as it is in a nature, it does not escape the ordering of God’s law. For God knows well how to order even the evils that lie outside his order in his creation. He orders not the vice, but the nature that has been corrupted. Hence it follows:

VERS. 8. — “For those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” Those who trust in the flesh, follow their concupiscences, dwell in them, delight in their pleasures, and locate a blessed and happy life in their delights—for these are the ones who are in the flesh—cannot please God.

This should not be understood as though “those who are in the flesh” meant those living in this flesh, in which many living persons have deserved to please God. They were not in the flesh, although they lived in the flesh. They carried the flesh; they were not carried by the flesh. Hence it is added: “But you are not in the flesh.” He says this to the people of God, to the Church of God; he wrote it to the Romans, but said it to the whole Church. He said it to the wheat, not the chaff; to the hidden grain, not the visible straw. Let each person know in his or her own heart whether it applies.

VERS. 9. — “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you”—if, according to the inner human being, you delight in the law of God. For this is what it means: “if the Spirit of God dwells in you.” For if you place confidence in your own spirit, you are still in the flesh. You are not in the flesh only if you are in the Spirit of God. If the Spirit of God withdraws, the human spirit, by its own weight, rolls back into the flesh; it returns to fleshly deeds, returns to fleshly concupiscences, and the last things of that person become worse than the first.

Thus have free will in such a way that you implore help. “You are not in the flesh.” And is this from your own powers? Far from it! From where, then? “If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his.” Therefore let needy and corrupted nature neither boast, exalt itself, nor attribute its own strength to itself; for if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his.

The Spirit of God is the Spirit of Christ: he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. But behold: assisted by his mercy, we have the Spirit of Christ; and from delight in righteousness and sound, catholic faith, we know that the Spirit of God is within us. But what of that mortal flesh? What of the law resisting the law of the mind? What of that groan, “Wretched man that I am”? Listen.

[Col. 0629D] VERS. 10, 11. — “But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.” The body, he says, is dead not because of earthly frailty, but because of sin. With the utmost care he did not say “it is mortal,” but “it is dead.”

For before it was changed into that incorruption promised in the incorruption of the saints, it could have been mortal without being destined to die, just as our body can, so to speak, be susceptible to sickness without being destined to fall sick. For whose flesh cannot become ill, even if, by some accident, it should perish before it becomes ill? Thus that body too was already mortal; but its transformation into eternal incorruption would have consumed that mortality if righteousness—that is, obedience—had remained in the human being.

[Col. 0630A] Yet that mortal body was not made dead except because of sin. The transformation to come in the resurrection will possess not only no death, which came about because of sin, but not even the mortality which the animal body possessed before sin. He does not say, “He will make your dead bodies alive,” after he had above called the body dead; but he says, “He will make your mortal bodies alive,” so that they may be not only no longer dead but no longer mortal, when the animal body rises as spiritual, this mortal puts on immortality, and this mortality is swallowed up by life.

For when he was defining the grace of the present time, he said that the body is dead because of sin, because in it, not yet renewed through resurrection, the consequence of sin remains—that is, the necessity of death. But he said that the spirit is life because of righteousness, because although we are still burdened with this body of death, we already breathe again, according to the inner human being, in the righteousness of faith through renewal begun in us. Nevertheless, lest human ignorance should hope nothing concerning the resurrection of the body, he says that the very body which in the present age he had called dead because of the consequence of sin will in the future be made alive because of the reward of righteousness; and not in such a way that it merely becomes alive from being dead, but that from being mortal it also remains immortal.

Attend to the light of apostolic teaching. Everything he says here he says so that people may not think that they have received no benefit, or only a small benefit, from the grace of Christ because they must necessarily die in body. They should observe that the body still bears the consequence of sin, contracted under the condition of death; but that their spirit has already begun to live through the righteousness of faith—a spirit which in the human being had itself been extinguished by a kind of death of unbelief.

Therefore, he says, do not consider the gift bestowed small, because Christ is in you: though the body is dead because of sin, your spirit already lives because of righteousness. Nor should you therefore despair even of the life of the body itself. “For if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he will also make your mortal bodies alive because of his indwelling Spirit in you.” He also explains how life, by putting death to death, turns death into life within itself.

VERS. 12, 13. — “Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live.” What else is this than: if you live according to death, the whole person will die; but if, living according to life, you make death live, the whole person will live?

Therefore, brethren, having received help—the arm of the Lord’s help stretched out to us from above, having received the Holy Spirit—“we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh,” but to possess love and through it be able to have good action. For faith cannot work except through love. “For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die.” This he said above already: the prudence of the flesh is death. Not because flesh is evil, but because living according to the flesh is evil.

“But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live.” This is our work in this life: to put to death by the Spirit the actions of the flesh; daily to afflict, diminish, restrain, and destroy them. The actions of the flesh are the concupiscences of the flesh. Not to consent to them is great praise; not to possess them is perfection. So that no one might presume upon the strength of his own spirit in this regard, he added:

VERS. 14. — “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God.” To be led is more than to be governed. For one who is governed does something, and is governed in order to do it rightly. But one who is led is scarcely understood to do anything personally. Yet the grace of the Savior grants so much to our wills that the Apostle does not hesitate to say: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God.”

The children of God are led so that they may do what must be done; and when they have done it, they may give thanks to the one by whom they are led, because they do what must be done as it must be done—that is, with delight in and love of righteousness—and may rejoice that they have received from him the sweetness which the Lord gave, so that his land might yield its fruit. For the designation “helper” implies one who acts, because the person himself also does something. Therefore all who are led by the Spirit—not by the letter, not by a law commanding, threatening, and promising, but by the Spirit awakening, enlightening, and helping—are children of God.

VERS. 15. — “For you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear,” as at Mount Sinai, “but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons,” so that in a wonderful yet true manner we who are servants may be able not to be servants: servants, that is, through chaste fear, to which belongs the servant entering into the joy of his Lord; but not servants through the fear that casts out, to which belongs the servant not remaining in the house forever.

For sons serve and are free; for this reason they are also counted under the name of the free. The Spirit of slavery and the Spirit of freedom are the same Spirit; but there he was on tablets of stone—that is, in hard hearts—unto fear, while here he is on tablets of the heart unto love.

What, then, is slavery in fear? No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good; for the spirit of fear profits nothing where the spirit of love is absent. If God’s command is done from fear of punishment and not from love of righteousness, it is done slavishly, and therefore is not done.

“But you have received the Spirit of adoption.” A father commonly rejoices in an only son, as one who alone will possess everything and has no one with whom to divide the inheritance. God the Father is not so. He had an Only-Begotten, but he did not wish to have only one. He sent him into the world so that he might have adopted brothers. The Only-Begotten came and took upon himself the sins by which we were entangled, lest the grace of adoption be hindered through them.

“In whom we cry, Abba, Father.” Of these two words, one comes from the law, the other from the uncircumcision. Those who cry out ask for something. What do they ask for, except what they hunger for—that is, righteousness? For the only Son of God gave his servants power to become children of God (John 1), and instructed them to ask, seek, and knock, so that they might receive, find, and have it opened to them. And we cry in him—that is, with him pouring love into our hearts; without that love, whoever cries out cries in vain.

VERS. 16. — “For the Spirit himself bears witness [Col. 0632A] to our spirit that we are children of God.” No soul is so perverse that God does not speak in its heart, provided that it can reason in some measure. Therefore question your inmost parts: are they full of love? Question your soul: is it moved by fear or by love?

He who pours love into your heart bears witness to your spirit about what is being done within it; the Spirit also bears witness concerning himself. How? Do you wish to hear how? Listen to him by whose gift, if you possess it, you receive the Spirit himself: “If anyone loves me,” he says, “that person will keep my commandments” (John 14). If love and delight in righteousness move you to keep God’s commandments, this is the testimony of the Spirit of God dwelling in you.

If you are thus, you are free; you are a child; all that belongs to the Father is yours. The Spirit of adoption inspires love for the Father in you, in whom you cry out as much as you love, because love itself is the cry in which you say, “Abba, Father.” If you invoke the Father with a child’s affection, the Holy Spirit, author of grace, making himself known to your spirit, testifies by that very effect that you are a child of God.

VERS. 17. — “And if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, but fellow-heirs with Christ.” When the Lord Jesus Christ died on the cross, we became his heirs, we who are his children, as he himself says: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Luke 5).

We are therefore called heirs because he left us the possession of ecclesial peace through the faith of the temporal dispensation, which we possess in this life, he himself saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14). But we shall become his fellow-heirs when, at the end of the age, death is swallowed up in victory. For then “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John 3).

We do not obtain this inheritance through the death of his Father, who cannot die, since he himself is our inheritance, as Scripture says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15). But because, when we were called, we were still little children and less fit to contemplate spiritual things, divine mercy extended itself even to our very lowliest thoughts, so that we might strive somehow to behold what we did not behold plainly and clearly. What we saw in a riddle will die when we begin to see face to face.

Accordingly, what is removed is aptly said to die. For “when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial shall be abolished” (1 Cor. 13). Thus, in a manner of speaking, the Father dies for us in the riddle; and that same Father becomes the inheritance when he is possessed face to face. Not because he dies, but because our imperfect vision of him is destroyed by perfect vision. Yet unless that earlier vision had nourished us, we would not become fit for the other, fullest and clearest vision.

If this understanding is also admitted concerning our Lord Jesus Christ—for we cannot be his fellow-heirs unless he himself is an heir—he is to be understood as heir in his body, that is, in the Church. We are her fellow-heirs, although she consists of us, just as we are called children of that mother although she consists of us.

More simply, we may understand that we are heirs of God insofar as we are made most secure possessors of his glory; fellow-heirs with Christ insofar as Christ glorified as man deigns to make us conformed to and sharers in his glory. For the whole Christ shall receive the inheritance. “Inheritance” (*haereditas*) is named from “adhering” (*inhaerendo*). We, who are members of his body, ought to hope for such an inheritance as will grant us a good that does not pass away and enable us to escape an evil that has no end.

“If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.” For since Christ obtained his inheritance for himself through his own blood and the suffering of death, it is necessary that those who wish to share in the inheritance should also share in the suffering. But because he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted. The remembrance of his passion alone can strengthen us to endure everything for his sake. For what will not those insults and scourges, that shameful garment, that beaten and spat-upon face, and that crown of thorns—not to mention much else—together with his cross and contemplated death, accomplish in us? And what of the greatness of the promised rewards? Hence it follows:

VERS. 18. — “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy”—they are not comparable—“to the glory to come”: these sufferings have an end, but the promised gifts have no end; these can be assessed, but that glory cannot. It is the great abundance of God’s sweetness, which he now hides for those who fear him but will perfect for those who hope in him; and he will so reveal it [Col. 0633C] to us that it will be fulfilled in us.

In this life, consolation is proportioned to the multitude of sorrows; there, however, no assessment is possible. For what is the glory we await, except to see God and to be joined to his holy angels?

VERS. 19.—“For the eager expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.” Whatever suffers within us when we mortify the deeds of the flesh—when we hunger or thirst through abstinence, when through charity we restrain the pleasure of concupiscence, when through patience we endure the wounds of injuries and the stings of insults, when, neglecting and rejecting our own pleasures, we labour for the fruitfulness of Mother Church—whatever in us suffers in this and [Col. 0633D] in such affliction is creation. For the body and the soul suffer, and they are certainly creation; and it awaits the revelation of the sons of God—that is, it awaits the manifestation of what it has been called to be in that glory to which it has been called. For the only-begotten Son of God cannot be called a creature, since through him all things whatsoever God made were made; whereas we are distinctly called “creation” before that manifestation of glory, and distinctly called sons of God, although we merit this by adoption. For he is Son by nature, the only-begotten. Therefore “the expectation of the creation,” that is, our expectation, “awaits the revelation of the sons of God”: that is, when what has been promised may appear; when what we now are in hope may be manifest in actuality. “For we are [Col. 0634A] sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John III). This is the revelation of the sons of God which the expectation of creation now awaits: not that creation awaits the revelation of another nature which is not creation, but that it itself, such as it now is, awaits when it shall be such as it shall be in the future. It is as though, while a painter works and colours are set beneath him and prepared for his work, one said: “The expectation of the colours awaits the manifestation of the image”—not because they will then be other things or cease to be colours, but because they will have another dignity.

VERS. 20.—“For creation,” he says, “has been subjected to vanity.” This is that saying: “Vanity of vanities, [Col. 0634B] and all is vanity” (Eccles. I). What abundance has a man in all his labour which he himself labours under the sun—to whom it was said: “In toil you shall eat bread”? “Therefore creation has been subjected to vanity, not willingly.” “Not willingly” is well added. For man sinned willingly, but was not condemned willingly. Sin, therefore, was the voluntary doing of what was contrary to the commandment of truth; but the punishment of sin was subjection to deceit. For creation was not subjected to vanity willingly, “but on account of him who subjected it in hope”: that is, on account of his justice and mercy, who neither left sin unpunished nor wished the sinner to be incurable.

In a higher sense we may understand that creation itself—that is, man himself—when, having lost through sin the seal of the image, he remained merely a creature, that same creation also, that is, that which is not yet called the perfect form of sonship but is called only creation, will be freed from the slavery of corruption. Therefore, when he says that “it also shall be freed,” he makes us understand: it also, as we are—that is, even those of whom there is no cause for despair, who are not yet called sons of God because they have not yet believed, but are merely creation—because they too will believe and will be freed from the slavery of corruption, just as we who are already sons of God, though it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

VERS. 21.—“Therefore it shall be freed from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God”: that is, they too will become free from being slaves, and glorious instead of dead, in the perfect life which the sons of God shall possess.

A further meaning may also be understood by “creation.” For all creation is reckoned in man: not because all angels and the eminent virtues and powers, or heaven and earth and sea and all things in them, are in him; but because every creature is partly spiritual, partly animate, and partly bodily. To consider this from the lower levels: bodily creation is extended through places; animate creation gives life to the bodily; spiritual creation governs the animate. And it governs rightly when it itself subjects what is to be governed to God. But when it transgresses his commandments, it becomes entangled in labours and miseries through those very things which it could have governed. Thus all creation is in man, because he understands by the spirit, feels by the soul, and moves locally by the body. “Therefore all creation” in man “groans and suffers.” He did not say “the whole,” but “all”; as if someone said that healthy human beings see the sun, but not the whole of them see. Thus all creation is in man, because he understands, lives, and has a body; but the whole creation is not in him, because besides him there are angels who understand and live; there are bodies which live and exist; and bodies which merely exist—since to live itself is more than not to live, and to understand itself is more than to live without understanding.

“And it travails.” Hence it is said: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow; but when she has borne, she no longer remembers the distress because of joy” (John XVI). Therefore, when [Col. 0635B] wretched man groans and suffers, all creation groans and suffers until now. He rightly said “until now”: for even if some are already in Abraham’s bosom, and that thief who was placed with the Lord in paradise ceased to suffer on the day when he believed, nevertheless until now all creation groans and suffers, because it is all in those who have not yet been freed, on account of spirit, soul, and body.

VERS. 23.—“Not only,” he says, does all creation groan and suffer, “but we ourselves”: that is, not only do body, soul, and spirit together suffer in man from the difficulties of the body, but we ourselves, apart from the bodies, groan within ourselves. And he rightly said, “having the first-fruits of the Spirit”: that is, those whose spirits have already been offered to God as a sacrifice and seized by the divine fire of charity. These are the first-fruits of man, because truth first takes possession of the spirit, so that through it the rest may be seized. Therefore he already has first-fruits offered to God who says, “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (above, ch. VII, v. 25); and who says of God, “Whom I serve in my spirit” (above, ch. I, v. 9); and of whom it is said, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI). But because he still says (above, v. 14), “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” and because such people are still told (above, ch. VIII, v. 14), “He will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of the Spirit dwelling in you,” it is not yet a whole burnt offering. [Col. 0635D] But it will be when death is swallowed up in victory, when it is said to death: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. XV).

“But now,” he says, not only all creation—that is, soul with body—“but also we ourselves, having the first-fruits of the Spirit”: that is, we souls, who have already offered to God our minds as first-fruits, groan within ourselves, that is, apart from the body, “awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (above, v. 13): that is, that the body itself too, receiving the benefit of adoption as sons of God, may show us wholly freed, all troubles having passed away, to be sons of God in every respect.

VERS. 24–25.—“For we have been saved in hope. But hope which is seen is not hope. For what a man sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience.” What does he await through patience? Salvation, that is, the redemption of his body. He rejoices that he has been redeemed, but not yet in actuality. He is secure in hope, but groans in hope, that he may come to reality. Therefore he awaited the salvation of the body, because the salvation which he had was not that salvation which hunger or thirst destroys if they are not relieved. We have indeed already been redeemed, but we have been saved in hope; because what we hope for we already await, but do not yet possess. Our flesh has already been saved, not in hope but in actuality, in our Head; what has not yet happened in us we mourn, what we hope for as promised we await through patience when it is delayed. Therefore this groaning is excusable: faith excuses it, hope produces it, and charity strengthens it. For the holier anyone is, and the fuller of holy desire, the more abundant is his weeping over this in prayer.

The first-fruits of the Spirit and the expectation of divine adoption produce this. For our coming into this misery is the punishment of sin; and the punishment lasts longer than the fault, lest the fault should be thought slight if punishment ended together with it. And thus, whether to demonstrate deserved misery, to correct a changeable life, or to exercise necessary patience, punishment holds man for a time, even the man whom guilt no longer holds liable to everlasting condemnation. It is a condition to be mourned, indeed, but not reproached. “Yet we have been saved in hope,” because the full adoption of sons will take place also in [Col. 0636C] the redemption of our body; nevertheless, we already possess the first-fruits of the Spirit, and thus have already become sons of God in actuality. But in other respects we are, in hope, as though saved, as though renewed, and likewise sons of God; yet in actuality, because we are not yet saved, we are not yet fully renewed, and not yet sons of God, but sons of the age.

Therefore we have already begun to be like God, having the first-fruits of the Spirit, and yet we remain unlike him through the remnants of oldness. The whole sinner will pass into adoption, so that if you seek his place you shall not find it. Meanwhile, we hope for what we do not see. Our lamp is our hope: as long as we do not see and yet hope, it is night, but the lamp shines; if we neither see nor hope, it is both night and the lamp does not shine. And what is more wretched than such darkness? [Col. 0636D] But the word of God, which speaks to us daily, is a continual pouring in of oil, lest the lamp be extinguished.

VERS. 26.—“Likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness. For we do not know what we ought to pray for.” Whatever prayer obtains, or endeavours to obtain, plainly shows that it is God’s gift; for if it were within our power, it would certainly not be asked for. Yet, lest even the merits of prayer should be thought to precede grace, so that grace would not be freely given but would no longer be grace because it was rendered as a debt, prayer itself is found among the gifts of grace. For the Apostle says that “we do not know what we ought to pray for,” unless we are helped by the Spirit. “But the Spirit intercedes for us and groans,” because he inspires in us the disposition to intercede and groan. But his help is expressed in such a way that he himself is said to do what he causes us to do.

For just as one does not believe without the spirit of faith, does not hope without the spirit of hope, and does not love without the spirit of love, so one does not pray as one ought without the spirit of prayer. For “one and the same Spirit works all these things” (1 Cor. XII): not yet dwelling in them, he helps them to become believers; already dwelling in them through faith, he helps them as believers. Therefore the Spirit himself, interceding for us, is the charity which he inspires in us. He who gave it does not know how to close his ears against it. Be confident: let charity pray; there are God’s ears. “What,” he says, “we ought to pray for, we do not know.” What, if not that we may be blessed? But although blessedness is defined differently by different persons, let our blessedness be that of which it is said: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God” (Ps. CXLIII). Let us therefore confidently ask that we may belong to that people and may attain to contemplate him and live with him without end.

But in our tribulations, which can both benefit and harm us, because they are burdensome contrary to the judgment of our weakness, we pray God that they may be removed from us. Yet we owe this devotion to our Lord God: if he does not take them away from us, we must not therefore suppose that we are neglected by him; rather, through the devout endurance of evils, we should hope for greater goods. When we pray for others, because we love them as ourselves, we ask for them as for ourselves; and the Lord God, knowing what ought to be done, grants us patiently and willingly to follow him in what he himself has chosen to do. [Col. 0637C] And in all that we pray for, we ought most firmly to believe that, if something happens otherwise than we pray, what God willed ought rather to have happened than what we willed. Thus “he asks for the saints”: that is, the Holy Spirit teaches them to ask.

There are also other spiritual forms of familiar prayer, by which they enjoy God, concerning whom he himself says, “My children are with me in the bedchamber” (Luke II); unknown to us who remain outside amid the senses of the flesh. For often a faithful and devout soul, while in prayer it attempts to direct the gaze of its mind toward him to whom it desires to offer in the Holy Spirit the first-fruits of the Spirit and the sacrifice of its prayer, strains to contemplate the invisible and to see with the trembling pupil of the inner eye. Wearied by the very difficulty, it returns to itself and makes of itself the steps of ascent: first, if it can, to consider itself; then to investigate, as far as it is able, that nature which is above itself.

But if our mind is dispersed among bodily images, it is wholly unable to consider either itself or the nature of the soul; for it is led through as many thoughts as through so many obstacles and is blinded. The first step, therefore, is that it gather itself to itself; the second, that it see what it is like when gathered; the third, that it rise above itself and subject itself in contemplation to its invisible Maker. But it cannot gather itself to itself at all unless it has first learned to restrain from the eyes of the mind the phantasms of earthly and heavenly images; to reject and trample underfoot whatever comes before its thought from sight, hearing, smell, bodily touch, and taste, so that it may seek itself within as it is without them. For when it thinks these things, it turns about inwardly certain shadows of bodies. Therefore all things must be cast from the eyes of the mind by the hand of discernment, so that the soul may consider itself such as it was created beneath God and above the body.

But once the soul, no longer distracted away from itself but gathered and raised to itself, understands its own measure, recognizes that it transcends all bodily things, and reaches from its own understanding toward the understanding of its Maker, then the understanding of God begins to operate in it more differently from its own understanding, in proportion as the nature of unbounded light differs from the nature of the soul. For whatever the soul understands, it comprehends; but by that understanding, in a certain unfamiliar manner, it does not comprehend but is comprehended. And there comes to be for it something perceptible, which only enlightened love is permitted to feel: a certain sweetness—not one which love has earned, but one which, when tasted, produces love; something which is not known and yet is felt; a most solid substance of things hoped for, a most certain proof of things not seen (Heb. XI); a testimony of the Christian faith—the Lord’s faithful testimony, “giving wisdom to little ones” (Ps. XVIII). For the little and quiet person, upon whom the Spirit of God rests, feels this, finds this sweet; so much so that all things of the flesh, of the world, or of any creature become tasteless to him, and he desires to die, provided he may be permitted to linger. [Col. 0638C] He prays for what he does not know, because he does not know what he feels. For it is the Spirit who desires and asks on his behalf and who, although he is for the present ignorant, nevertheless makes him feel, ask, and desire that very thing which he does not know while feeling it.

VERS. 27.—“But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires”: that is, what the Spirit causes to be desired, and will fulfil for him when what he promised is to be fulfilled, saying: “Then you shall know that I am” (John VIII). Therefore, asking one thing from the Lord, seeking one thing, seeking his face and seeking his face again, he casts away, rejects, and disapproves whatever comes to his mind. He knows that it is not what he seeks, although he does not yet know what that thing is like. And there is in him a certain learned ignorance, taught by the Spirit of God, who helps our weakness: humbling by exercise, and by humbling forming and conforming man to the face which he seeks, until, renewed according to the image of him who created him, through unity of likeness he begins to be a son who is always with the Father, to whom belong all things that are the Father’s, and to whom, while others depart and return, it is said: “But you, stand here with me” (Deut. V).

Meanwhile, let him who seeks, seek; let him walk in the light of God’s countenance, and let God’s judgment come forth from his countenance, so that for the present what follows may be fulfilled in him:

VERS. 28.—“We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to purpose.” For when the Apostle had said, “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God,” knowing that some love God but do not remain in that good unto the end, he immediately added, “to those who are called according to purpose.” For these remain in what they love—God—unto the end. Even if they turn aside from it for a time, they return, so that they carry through to the end what they began to be in goodness. Then, showing what it is to be called according to purpose, he immediately added:

VERS. 29–30.—“For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brethren; and those whom he predestined, he also called,” namely according to purpose; “and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.” All those things have already been done: “he foreknew, he predestined, [Col. 0639B] he called, he justified,” since all have already been foreknown and predestined, and many already called and justified. But what he set at the end, “he also glorified,” if that glory is to be understood here of which he himself says, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also shall appear with him in glory,” has not yet been done—although those two also, “he called” and “he justified,” have not been accomplished in all of those of whom they were said. For many are still to be called and justified until the end of the age (Col. III). Yet he used words in the past tense even of future things, as though God had already done what he had from eternity arranged should be done. Therefore the prophet Isaiah also says: “He who made the things that are to be” (Isa. XLI, XLIV).

Whoever, therefore, in God’s most provident ordering have been foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified—not only though they have not yet been reborn, but even though they have not yet been born—are already sons of God and cannot perish at all. For to such persons who love God all things work together for good, so completely all things that even if any of them wander and go astray, that very thing also makes them advance in good, because they return humbler and wiser. For by life itself they learn that they ought to rejoice with fear in righteousness, not arrogating to themselves confidence in their own strength to persevere, nor saying in their abundance, “I shall never be moved,” but rejoicing in God with fear lest they perish from the right way in which they have already begun to walk, while they ascribe to themselves the very fact that they are in it.

The Apostle used these words when he said: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II), and showed why with fear and trembling: “For it is God,” he says, “who works in you both to will and to work according to good will” (ibid.). Although even the death of the flesh came originally from the sin of the first man, its good use has made the martyrs most glorious. Therefore not only death itself, but all the evils, labours, and pains of this age, although they come from the deserts of sins, and especially of original sin—by which this very life was made bound by the chain of death—nevertheless had to remain even after sins were remitted, so that man might contend amid them for truth and the strength of the faithful might be exercised; so that the new man, through the New Testament, might be prepared amid the evils of this age for the new age, wisely enduring the misery deserved by this condemned life, prudently rejoicing because it will end, and faithfully and patiently awaiting the blessedness of the future life.

When it is said that God works together with us, this must be understood to mean that without God—either working so that we may will, or working together when we will—we can do nothing in works of piety. Of his working so that we will it was said: “It is God who works in us to will”; but of his working together: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God.” But how do all things? Even things thought adverse. For the enemies of the Church, even if they receive power to afflict it bodily, exercise its patience; if they oppose it only by evil thoughts, they exercise its wisdom, that enemies may be loved; they exercise its benevolence.

“For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.” Predestination is the preparation of grace, which cannot exist without foreknowledge; but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For in predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do. Hence it was said: “He made the things that are to be.” But he is able also to foreknow things which he does not himself do, such as all sins; although some things are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sins. Hence it was said: “He gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things which are not fitting.” There the sin is not God’s, [Col. 0640C] but the judgment. Therefore God’s predestination, which is directed toward good, is, as I said, preparation; grace, however, is the effect of that predestination.

This is the predestination of the saints, nothing else: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are freed are most certainly freed. But where are the rest left, if not in the mass of perdition by a just divine judgment? When, therefore, he says that the predestined are made conformed to the image of the Son of God, this may be understood according to the inward person. Hence he says to us elsewhere: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Rom. XII). Therefore, where we are transformed so as not to be conformed to this age, there we are conformed to God’s Son. It may also be understood thus: that as he became conformed to us in mortality, so we may become conformed to him in immortality; and this indeed pertains also to the resurrection itself.

“Those,” he says, “whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren”—firstborn, certainly, from the dead according to the same Apostle, because his flesh was sown in dishonour through death but rose in glory. “And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified.” This sanctification is granted to the righteous; but in order that they may be justified, calling precedes, and it is not of merits but of God’s grace. “For all have sinned and need the glory of God.” Those whom he called, “these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified.” Since calling is not from our merits but from God’s good will, the witness is he who says: “Lord, you have crowned us as with a shield of your good will” (Ps. V). For the good will of God precedes our good will, in order to call sinners to repentance; and these are the weapons by which the enemy is overcome, against whom it is said:

VERS. 33, 31, and 32.—“Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? And if God is for us, who is against us? He did not spare his only-begotten Son, but delivered him up for us all. For if, while we were still enemies, Christ died for us, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through him.” This is the most invincible shield by which the enemy is repelled when, amid a multitude of tribulations and temptations, he suggests despair of salvation. For we tend toward eternal and blessed life first by condemning our sins and then by living well, so that, after condemning the evil life and living the good, we may merit eternal life.

For according to the purpose of his most hidden justice and goodness, God predestined some, called them, justified them, and glorified them. Our predestination was not accomplished in us but secretly in him, in his foreknowledge; the remaining three take place in us: calling, justification, and glorification. We are called by the predestination of repentance; for thus the Lord began to preach the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. III). We are justified by the renewal of mercy and by fear of judgment. Hence it is said: “O God, save [Col. 0641C] me in your name, and judge me in your power” (Ps. LIII). For one who has first obtained salvation does not fear being judged. Called, we renounce the devil through repentance; justified, we are healed through mercy, so that we may not fear judgment; glorified, we pass into eternal life.

I think this is what the Lord meant when he said: “Behold, I cast out demons today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke XIII). He also displayed this in the three days of his passion and rising again. For he was crucified, buried, and rose again. On the cross he triumphed over principalities and powers; in the tomb he rested; in the resurrection he was exalted. Thus repentance torments, righteousness calms, and eternal life glorifies.

“What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?” It is as though he said: God is for us, to predestine us; God is for us, to call us; God is for us, to justify us; God is for us, to glorify us. If, therefore, God is for us, who is against us? He predestined us before we existed; he called us when we had turned away; he justified us when we were sinners; he glorified us when we were mortal. Therefore whoever wishes to oppose those predestined, called, and justified by God should prepare war against the Almighty.

How do you prove that God is for you? Most excellently, he says, because “he did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” Therefore let not the roar of the world terrify him for whom the Maker of the world was delivered up. “How,” he says, “did he not also give us all things with him?” What are all things? It will be known when [Col. 0642A] this promise is fulfilled, of which, when Christ died for us, we have already received so great a pledge.

Yet do you wish to know what all things are? The human spirit will be wholly without defect: there will be nothing beneath which it lies, nothing into which it falls, nothing against which it even fights praiseworthily; perfected in most peaceful strength, with ample and certain knowledge of all things, without any error or labour; there, from the very fountain of wisdom, it will drink in highest happiness without difficulty. The body will be wholly subject to the spirit and sufficiently quickened by it, so that it will need no food. For it will not be animal but spiritual, possessing the substance of flesh, though flesh without corruption. There all things will be possessed in such a way that each will possess all things and all persons will possess all things. For as desire possesses nothing without constriction, so charity possesses nothing with constriction. Therefore all things will be ours: the things above us for life, equals for companionship, and things below us for dominion.

VERS. 33–34.—“Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God who justifies—who is he that condemns?” And the rest. What is observed concerning ambiguous punctuation must also be observed concerning ambiguous delivery. For such ambiguities themselves, unless spoiled by the reader’s excessive carelessness, are either corrected by the rules of faith or by the connection of the preceding or following discourse. But if neither is applied as a correction, they will nevertheless remain doubtful, so that however the reader delivers them, he is not at fault.

For unless faith recalls us—by which we believe that God will not accuse his elect, nor Christ condemn his elect—the words may be delivered thus: “Who shall accuse God’s elect?” and then, as though an answer, “God who justifies.” Likewise, to the question, “Who is he that condemns?” the answer: “Christ Jesus, who died.” Since to believe this is utterly mad, the delivery must be such that inquiry comes first and a question follows. The ancients said that inquiry differs from a question in this: many answers can be made to an inquiry, but to a question the answer is either “no” or “yes.”

Therefore it should be delivered thus: after the inquiry, when we say, “Who shall accuse God’s elect?” what follows should be uttered with an interrogative tone: “God [Col. 0642D] who justifies?” so that “No” is answered silently. Likewise let us inquire: “Who is he that condemns?” and again ask: “Christ who died—indeed rather who rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us?” so that everywhere the answer may be: “No.”

When Christ is said to sit at God’s right hand, God’s power is shown through a human analogy; it is not that a throne is set up and God the Father sits on it, with the Son sitting beside him, but that we cannot understand him judging and reigning otherwise than through our own words. He intercedes for us by appearing before God the Father in the humanity which he assumed for us.

There follows, in the glad exultation of the spirit, a certain profession of great love, expressed by the greatness of the benefits just mentioned. “Who,” he says, “shall separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord?” For the Father is loved in the Son, in whose work his charity is commended. Hence elsewhere he is called “the Son of his charity” (Col. I). Therefore let one who has the sense of love understand the words of one who loves. Who, he says—of what power, knowledge, or cunning—shall separate us, predestined, called, justified, glorified, by counsel or by example, from the charity of God, from faith in the beloved, from love for the one believed? “Which is in Christ Jesus our Lord,” by whom we love to be ruled, rejoice to be saved, and whom we serve in our spirit. No one is found: the question is not “who?” but “what?”

VERS. 35–36.—“Tribulation, or distress” in the soul; [Col. 0643B] “hunger or nakedness” in the body; “peril” of death, or the slaying “sword? As it is written: Because for your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been accounted as sheep for slaughter.” We are not killed and do not die once only, but all day long: that is, without interruption we are put to death by afflictions and torments, ready to give for the law not merely what is ours, but ourselves, like a sheep for slaughter, from which not milk or wool but life is required.

What wonder, then, if a martyr suffers for his God what a miser suffers for his gold? For the miser exposes himself to the danger of the sea and says to his gold: “For your sake I am put to death all day long.” The martyr exposes himself to tortures and the sword and says to his God: “For your sake I am put to death all day long.” The utterance is similar, but the cause unlike: this man for Christ, that man for gold. Let Christ answer his martyr: “If you die for me, you will find me.” Let gold answer the miser: “If you die for me, you lose both yourself and me.”

“But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us.” Why not “through him whom we loved”? Because, as no one chooses unless chosen, so no one loves unless loved. Our love is an affection of the human mind; God’s love is an affection of grace. We are affected when we love God; but God is not affected when he is loved by us. Rather, his love is the Holy Spirit, whom, when he deigns to give him to us, he through him pours charity into our hearts, by which we love him. Therefore he loves us when he enriches us with the gift of his love; we love him when we are borne toward him with the whole weight of the soul. This is what we owe to God alone.

When the flesh and the concupiscence of this life strive to turn this away from God and toward themselves, the servant of God suffers the human temptations written above; but when the spiritual wickedness of iniquity attacks in him the love of God, he suffers the temptations which follow. For it continues:

VERS. 38–39.—“I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any creature, will be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Therefore let no one separate us from God by threatening death, because that very thing in us which loves God cannot die, except when it does not love God; and for it death itself is not to love God, which is nothing other than preferring something else to him in loving and following. Let no one separate us from him by promising life, because no one separates a person from a spring by promising water.

Let no angel separate us, because when we cleave to God, no angel is stronger in mind than our mind. Let no power separate us, because if “power” here means something which holds some authority in the world, the mind that cleaves to God is altogether above the whole world. But if that power means the most upright affection of our own mind, then if it is in someone else, it favours our being joined to God; if it is in us, it itself joins us. Let present troubles not separate us, because we feel them the lighter the more closely we cleave to him from whom they strive to separate us. Let not the promise of future things separate us, because God promises whatever good is future, and nothing is better than God himself, who is already certainly present to those who cleave to him.

“Neither strength, nor height, nor depth.” Among the philosophers of this world there are also those who dispute forcefully, think lofty thoughts, and investigate profound matters, often attempting to separate simpler persons from the charity of God which is in Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER IX
VERS. 1–5.—“I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that there is great sorrow for me and unceasing pain in my heart. For I was wishing that I myself might be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who [Col. 0644C] are Israelites; whose are the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever.”

See the great sweetness of a rightly disposed mind: through the greatness of its joy over the progress of the Gentiles it rises, as it were, up to heaven in the exultation of the Spirit; and suddenly, through grief of heart at the pitiable falling-away of its own people, it descends, as it were, to the abyss. Thus, leaving them as it were in heaven with God, he seems to return to earth, to die for his brothers. And just as it is written of Moses that his face appeared horned when he came forth from the presence of the Lord, and the fleshly people could not endure the brightness of his countenance (Exod. XXXIV): so he too, as though mad with love, [Col. 0644D] and wholly intoxicated with the Holy Spirit, does not know how to use sober words, but speaks as in an ecstasy of mind, saying that he wishes to be accursed from Christ for Christ—that is, for his brothers, that they might be in Christ.

He wished to be excluded from the blessedness of Christ while embracing the righteousness of Christ, judging it more just before God to desire the salvation of one whole people than that of his own single soul. But although this affection of love surpassing itself was admirable here, its effect was shaped very differently in the judgment of God’s righteousness. For when, for the glory of God and the salvation of his brothers, he offered the loss not of love but of his own salvation, he attained before the righteous Judge the highest increase of love: for the salvation of the elect from that people was granted to Paul, and he was not deprived of the reward of their universal salvation, since he offered himself with such steadfast love for the salvation of all [Col. 0645A] of them.

For love has affections and it has effects; and although this may not seem so to human beings, all its affections find their effects with him who discerns the disposition of the mind far more truly than human beings discern the outcome of an act. These words of the Apostle, therefore, are expressions of affection: for he does not desire to be accursed from Christ through transgression, but through devotion of love. It is the languor of a soul that loves and cannot accomplish what it desires. Hence she says in the Song of Songs: “I languish with love” (Cant. V).

“I speak,” he says, “the truth in Christ, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit.” Blessed is the soul whose truth is founded in Christ, whose conscience is made firm in the Holy Spirit, in whose conscience the truth of love burns, while in confession the love of truth shines forth.

VERS. 2.—“Great sorrow and unceasing pain.” Where there is such greatness and such continuance, what place can there be for joy? “In my heart.” For as he serves whom he serves in the Holy Spirit, so he grieves for whom he grieves in his own heart.

VERS. 3.—“For my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh.” These are names of natural relationship; for first comes that which is animate, then that which is spiritual. For he continues:

VERS. 4, 5.—“Who are Israelites,” made for the seeing of God; “whose is the adoption,” because the Son of God was sent properly to them; “and the glory,” because the oracles of God were entrusted to them; “and the covenant,” because the Old was given to them and the New was prefigured in the Old; [Col. 0645C] “and the giving of the law,” which they especially deserved to receive; “and the worship,” since the law and the prophets especially serve their salvation; “and the promises” concerning Christ; “whose are the fathers, from whom Christ” was born. For this is the chief cause of sorrow and pain: that the fathers were so great before Christ that he chose to be born from them, while the children were such that, leaving them, he passed over to the Gentiles.

VERS. 6.—“But it is not as though the word of God had failed.”—“I found tribulation and sorrow,” says the Prophet (Ps. CXIV). It belongs to the prudent person both to find sorrow where it is needed and to set a limit to sorrow when the time requires it. The Apostle has sufficiently disclosed the pain of his heart over the rejection of his people; and immediately, finding consolation for himself, he says: “It is not as though the word of God had failed”—that is, the promise made to them has not vanished. For whoever is a true Israelite will obtain God’s promises. But one who does not see God through faith—he who said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV)—cannot be called Israel. Therefore he says:

VERS. 6, 7.—“Not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children. But those who are children of the promise are reckoned as the seed”: that is, those who are children of that faith through which Abraham deserved to receive the promise of the future inheritance. This, indeed, was already signified in Abraham when, although he had many sons whom the Apostle calls children of the flesh, the posterity of his seed was placed in Isaac alone, [Col. 0646A] who was the son of promise, the Lord saying:

VERS. 8, 9.—“In Isaac shall your seed be called. For this is the word of promise: At this time I shall come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. XXI). Isaac, therefore, he says, is not born by the order of fleshly generation, since Abraham’s body was already dead and Sarah’s womb was dead; rather, he is born by the power of the one making the promise. Rightly, therefore, he is called a son not of flesh but of God, since he is born from the coming and word of God.

VERS. 10, 11.—“And not only she.” This principle, he says, is to be applied not only to Isaac but also to Jacob. For Rebecca too did not bring forth her offspring according to the order of fleshly generation. For when, after the long distress of prolonged sterility, she had conceived twins from a single union with Isaac, before they had been born and before either child had performed good or evil actions among human beings, divine election was exercised toward Jacob; and it was said: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV), and, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I).

Since these things were so spoken, he says, we are taught that God’s purpose according to election remains—not by works, but by the grace of him who calls. By the words, “The elder shall serve the younger,” and, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” we are taught that it is not the children of flesh but the children who are to be reckoned as the seed. For there Isaac was chosen from among many, and the younger from among two, to be adopted as a son of God. Thus it is true that God’s promises stand not in children of flesh but [Col. 0646C] in children of God; and that the purpose of God according to election remains not by works but by the grace of him who calls, not in children of flesh but in children of God.

For this reason he also took up, in support of this statement, the testimony of the much later prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” so that it might be understood that what was afterwards made manifest through the prophet was, before they were born, already in God’s predestination. For what did he love in Jacob before he had done anything good, except the free gift of his mercy? And what did he hate in Esau before, once born, he had done anything evil, except original sin? For he would not have loved in the former a righteousness which that former had performed in no way, nor would he have hated in the latter a nature which he himself had made good.

For, having proposed the astonishing matter of how it could rightly be said concerning persons not yet born and having done nothing good or evil that God loved one and hated the other, he himself expresses the agitation of the hearer, raising the objection to himself:

VERS. 14.—“What, then, shall we say? Is there unrighteousness with God? Far be it!” Here was the place to say: God foresaw their future works when he foretold that the elder would serve the younger. But the Apostle does not say this. Rather, lest anyone dare to glory in the merits of his own works, he intended what he says to serve the commending of God’s grace and glory. For after saying, “Far be it,” so that there might be no unrighteousness with God, as though we said to him, “How do you show this, when you maintain that ‘the elder shall serve the younger’ was spoken not on account of works but on account of him [Col. 0647A] who calls?” he says:

VERS. 15, 16.—“For Moses says” (Exod. XXXIII), “‘I shall have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I shall show mercy to whom I have shown mercy.’ Therefore it is not of one who wills, nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” Where now are merits? Where now are works, whether past or future, supposedly fulfilled or to be fulfilled by the powers of free choice? The Apostle has set forth a plain judgment commending gratuitous—that is, true—grace.

For the Apostle was sufficiently treating of this grace, and therefore he mentioned children of promise. What God promises, after all, no one performs except God. Thus, in commending the children of promise, he first showed this to be signified through Isaac, Abraham’s son. For God’s work is more clearly apparent in one whom the customary order of nature did not beget from a barren womb and persons exhausted by old age, so that it might be shown that the children of God, who were foretold as destined to be children of God, are the work not of humanity but of God; and so that vessels made from that same mass for honor might recognize, in the vessels fitted for destruction—for whom destruction is due from the condemned mass—what divine mercy has bestowed upon them.

VERS. 17.—“For Scripture says,” he says, “to Pharaoh” (Exod. IX): “‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.’” For God would create no angel or human being whom he foreknew would be evil unless he also knew at the same time what benefits to the good he would derive from them; and in this way he would adorn the order of the ages like a most beautiful poem, even [Col. 0647C] with certain antitheses.

For the proclamation of God’s name throughout all the earth was beneficial, of course, to the vessels of mercy. Pharaoh, therefore, was preserved for their benefit, as the outcome of the event taught. [Col. 0648A] Finally, he concludes both points: “Thus he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills.” He does this, though with him there is no unrighteousness. He has mercy, indeed, by a gratuitous gift; but he hardens by most just desert. Yet let the proud and unbelieving arrogance, or the culpable excuse of one who is punished, still speak:

VERS. 19.—“Why then is he still finding fault? For who resists his will?” Let it say this, and hear what befits a human being: “O man, who are you” to “answer back to God?” Let it hear this and not despise it. But if it despises it, let it know that even in despising it, it has been hardened; whereas if it does not despise it, let it believe that it has been helped—not hardened as it deserved, but helped freely. By what means will such persons excuse themselves? Surely by the means which the Apostle briefly raised as an objection to himself, as though from their own lips, so that they might say: “Why then is he still finding fault? For who resists his will?” And if they are not ashamed to contradict not us but the Apostle by this excuse, why should we be reluctant to say repeatedly what the Apostle says?

VERS. 20, 21.—“O man, who are you” to “answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same mass”—a mass of course rightly and deservedly condemned—“to make one vessel for honor,” not deserved, through the grace of mercy, “and another for dishonor,” deserved through the justice of wrath? So far as justice and grace are concerned, it may rightly be said both to the guilty person who is delivered and to the guilty person who is condemned: [Col. 0648C] “Take what is yours and go” (Matt. XX). “And to this one I will give what is due. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will?”

BOOK SIX.

[Col. 0647]

CHAPTER IX CONTINUES.

[Col. 0647C]

VERS. 22–24.—As for the words, “But if God, willing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order that he might make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, [Col. 0647D] which he prepared for glory, whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles,” the words to be understood are: “Who are you, to answer back to God?” Thus, by returning to the preceding words, the sense is this: If God, willing to show wrath, endured vessels of wrath, who are you to answer back to God?

Nor was he merely willing to show his power, but also, as follows, to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory. For what benefit is it to vessels fitted for destruction that God patiently endures them, in order to destroy them in due order and use them as an instrument for the salvation of those on whom he has mercy? Yet it benefits those for whose salvation he uses them in this way.

Behold, [Col. 0648C] a reason has been given to the human being, as much as ought to be given to a human being: as though he said, “Who are you, to answer back to God, if God, willing to show wrath and demonstrate his power—that he, being supremely good, can use even evil things well—endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction?” They are evil, to be sure, not by divine creation, but by [Col. 0648D] the iniquity of a corrupted will; their nature, created by God the Creator, is good. He endured them, not because angelic or human sins were necessary to him, to whom not even anyone’s righteousness is necessary, but in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, lest they exalt themselves in good works as though these arose from their own strength. Rather, they might humbly understand that, unless God’s grace—undeserved but freely given—came to their aid, what was due to their merits was what they saw rendered to others from the same mass.

The remaining human beings, not belonging to this fellowship, whose soul and body nevertheless have been made by God’s goodness, and whose nature possesses, apart from vice, whatever it possesses—the vice inflicted upon it by the rashness of [Col. 0649A] a proud will—were created by God, who foreknew this, so that in them he might show what the free choice of the deserter can accomplish without grace. And in their just and deserved punishments, the vessels of mercy, distinguished from that mass not by merits of their own works but by God’s gratuitous grace, might learn what had been bestowed upon themselves; so that every mouth might be stopped and whoever glories might glory in the Lord.

Why the Creator also willed some to belong to damnation rather than grace, the blessed Apostle states with all the more compressed brevity because he speaks with greater authority. For he says that God, willing to show wrath and demonstrate his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and did so in order to make known the riches of his glory in [Col. 0649B] vessels of mercy. Above he had spoken of him as a potter making from the same mass one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

It would rightly appear unjust that vessels of wrath are made for destruction, unless the entire mass from Adam itself stood condemned. Therefore, that vessels of wrath are made from it through birth belongs to deserved punishment; but that vessels of mercy are made through rebirth belongs to undeserved grace. God therefore shows wrath—not, certainly, an agitation of mind, such as is so called among human beings, but a just and fixed retribution—because from the stock of disobedience there is derived a progeny of sin and punishment. And a human being born of woman, as it is written in the book of Job, “is short-lived and full of wrath” (Job XIV). For he is a vessel of that thing of which he is full. Hence [Col. 0649C] they are called vessels of wrath.

He also shows his power, by which he uses even evils well: bestowing upon them many natural and temporal goods and employing their malice for the exercise of the good and to admonish the good by comparison with them, so that in them the good may learn to give thanks to God that they have been distinguished from them not by their own merits, which were equal in the same mass, but by his mercy. This is especially apparent in infants: when they are reborn through Christ’s grace and end this life at that tender age, passing into eternal blessedness, it cannot be said that they are distinguished by free choice from other infants, who die without this grace under the condemnation of that same mass.

But if only those were created from Adam who were to be [Col. 0649D] re-created by grace, and if no other human beings were born besides those adopted as children of God, the benefit bestowed upon the undeserving would remain hidden, because no deserved punishment would be rendered to anyone else descending from the same stock and liable to condemnation. But when he endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, he not only showed wrath and demonstrated his power by rendering punishment and using evils well, but also made known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy. For one justified freely thus learns what has been bestowed upon him, when he is distinguished, not by his own merit but by the glory of God’s most lavish mercy, from one condemned, with whom he too was, by the same justice, to have been condemned.

He willed that very many should be created and born whom he foreknew would not belong to his grace, so that their [Col. 0650A] incomparably greater multitude might exceed those whom he deigned to predestine as children of promise to the glory of his kingdom. Thus, by the very multitude of the rejected, it might be shown how insignificant before the just God is any numerical greatness, however vast, of those most justly condemned; and so that those redeemed from that condemnation might also understand from this that what they saw rendered to so great a part of the whole was due to the entire mass. This is so not only in those who, by the free choice of an evil will, add many evils to original sin, but also in so many infants, who, bound only by the chain of original sin, are snatched from this light without the grace of the Mediator.

For this whole mass would receive what is due under just condemnation, unless the potter, not only just but also merciful, made from it certain [Col. 0650B] vessels for honor according to grace, not according to debt—helping even infants, of whom no merits can be alleged, and preventing adults by grace so that they may be able to have some merits. Let the gathered person, therefore, compare himself with those left behind, and the chosen with the rejected. Let vessels of mercy compare themselves with vessels of wrath, and see that from the same mass some vessels were made for honor and others for dishonor; and let the one delivered learn from the one not delivered what would have befitted himself also, unless grace had come to his aid. For unless the debtor is held under suspension, the person whose debt is remitted gives less thanks.

A deep question has led us into the deep, yet it has not led us all the way to its bottom. For although a human being answering back to God, or clay answering its potter, is rebuked, the holy Apostle nevertheless does not prohibit inquiry for those of whom he says elsewhere: [Col. 0650C] “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. II); and especially, “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (ibid.). Rather, he prohibits such inquiry for those who are clay-like and earthly, who have not yet been inwardly regenerated or nourished, who bear the image of the one first made from the earth, earthly; and because he refused to obey him by whom he was made, he fell back into that from which he was made and deserved to hear: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III).

Such persons are rightly prohibited. For if an animal could speak and said to God, “Why did you make this man, but me an animal?” would you not justly be angry and say, “O animal, who are you to answer back to God?” God therefore prepared vessels of mercy and called them both from Jews and from Gentiles, because there is one mass from Adam, of sinners and ungodly persons, in which Jews and Gentiles alike, grace removed, belong to one mixture:

VERS. 25.—“As Hosea says” (Hos. II): “I shall call ‘not my people,’ ‘my people’; and ‘not having obtained mercy,’ ‘having obtained mercy.’ And it shall be: In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called children of the living God.” The apostles understood this prophetic covenant concerning the calling of the Gentiles, a people who previously did not belong to God. Recalling that the people of the Gentiles themselves are spiritually among the children of Abraham, and are therefore rightly called Israel, they also recalled the cornerstone and the two walls—one from the Jews and one from the Gentiles—meeting in him. [Col. 0651A]

The Apostle seems to return to the consolation for his sorrow: for as there is one mass of the lost among both Jews and Gentiles, so from both peoples one Church of the elect is made. The example he first adduced from Hosea therefore concerns the Gentiles; that which he subsequently adduces from Isaiah concerns the Jews. For the Gentiles were a people not God’s people and were made God’s people; they had not obtained mercy and obtained mercy.

VERS. 26.—“But it shall be,” he says, “in the place.” What is this place? Is it Judaea? Is it Rome? Far be it! Is Judaea a worthier, or Rome a more exalted, place in which it is fitting—or possible—for God to speak? The place here is the human mind, the faculty of reason, the governing part of the heart. There, when God acts, a condemning conscience says to the sinful people: “You are not my people.” But to those in whose hearts love is poured out through the Holy Spirit given to them, the Spirit himself bears witness “that they are children of God.”

But Isaiah cries out—that is, openly announces and proclaims—what takes place concerning Israel, and says:

VERS. 27.—“Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved.” For the prophet, foreseeing the future, saw that most Israelites, comparable to the sand of the sea because of the barrenness of righteousness, hardness of heart, and disordered and confused multitude, would be vessels of wrath fitted for destruction: not believing in their life, but crucifying the Lord of majesty. But the remnant, comparable to the stars of heaven, would become participants in heavenly glory. For both were declared to Abraham: “So,” he says, “shall your seed be” (Gen. XXII), like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven.
