VERS. 28.—“For he shall complete the word, and abbreviate it in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.” The word which completes and abbreviates in righteousness is that of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself: on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII). Or it is the compendium of faith through which believers are saved, with the innumerable observances omitted by which that multitude was oppressed in servile fashion.

That the salvation of the remnant is to be attributed to grace he teaches by the following testimony, speaking in the person of those who believed in grace:

[Col. 0651D] VERS. 29.—“Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have become like Sodom, and we should have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I). For they themselves were multiplied like seed, scattered over the earth. Or by “seed” is understood that grain of wheat which fell into the earth through the passion of death and, having died, produced much fruit. “We should have become,” they say, “like Sodom”—whose people deserved to perish through incest against guests—when, sacrilegiously acting against our brother, the Lord of majesty, we could not have escaped the danger of destruction except through the blessing of the holy seed sent into the earth.

Then, showing that the Gentiles had attained righteousness by faith, he adds:

[Col. 0652A] VERS. 30–33.—“What then shall we say? That the Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained righteousness, namely, the righteousness which is from faith; but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to a law of righteousness. Why? Because not from faith, but as though from works. For they stumbled at the stone of stumbling, as it is written: Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal; and everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame.”

Faith in Christ is believing in him who justifies the ungodly, believing in the Mediator without whom no one is reconciled to God, believing in him who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). But the person who, ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, the righteousness which God gives, he who justifies the ungodly—and wishing to establish his own righteousness as though made by the powers of his own will, for which God repays grace according to merits, does not wish God’s grace to precede and make him possess the righteousness which he believes he himself makes for himself, does not attain this faith.

Thus such people are said to pursue a righteousness which they suppose they are grasping by their own powers as though it were fleeing from them. This is characteristic of the Jews, who pursue the law of righteousness as though it justified by works. The Gentiles, however, do not pursue righteousness but attain it, finding it near at hand, grace of faith bestowing it upon them beforehand; they find it implanted in their hearts by the natural law.

“But the Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness”—the righteousness belonging to the law, which arises from fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness, which a human being performs and not God—“attained righteousness,” God’s righteousness, the righteousness of faith. “But Israel, pursuing the law” of the letter, which it thought or presumed to be “of righteousness, did not attain to the law of the Spirit,” which is truly a law of righteousness. “Because,” therefore, “not from faith, but as though from works,” as though by their own righteousness, they stumbled at the stone of stumbling.

The person who believes in this stone will not possess his own righteousness, which is from the law—although the law is good—but will fulfill that law, not by his own righteousness but by righteousness given by God; and thus he will not be put to shame. For love is the fulfillment of the law. And from where is this love poured out in our hearts? Certainly not from ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

It should be known, however, that in the prophet Isaiah this testimony is written thus: “Behold, I place in Zion a foundation stone, precious, chosen, [Col. 0652D] a cornerstone; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. XXVIII). But the Apostle inserted into this testimony the phrase “a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal” from another passage of the same prophet, where it is written: “And you shall not meet him as a stone of stumbling, nor as a stone of ruin” (Isa. VIII). Thus, drawing what appeared suitable to his argument from both passages, he fitted them together into one.

Why Christ the Lord, the way and the truth and the life, should be called here a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal ought to be an offense or scandal to no one. For those in Zion who were walking in bad ways were running swiftly along the path of destruction, encouraging one another in their evils, since, as the prophet says, “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed” (Ps. [Col. 0653A] IX). The Lord began to rebuke their crooked ways, saying, “Woe to you, Pharisees” (Matt. XXIII), and similar things. He became to them a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal because, not keeping silent concerning their evils, he began to obstruct their paths of destruction by rebuking them.

Christ is a stone of stumbling not only to them but to all evil persons. Whatever Christ says is bitter to them. But whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame; whereas one who glories in himself shall be put to shame, because he will not be found without sins—not merely for a day or an hour, but for eternity. Therefore, whoever does not wish to stumble, remove yourself: you are an obstacle to yourself. Remove your own righteousness; lay hold of that which is from God. Although you are called a Christian, if you deny his grace, you stumble against him. Yet it is less serious to stumble against Christ hanging on the cross than against him seated in heaven.

Let righteousness exist—but let it be from grace. Let it be from God for you; let it not be your own. “Let your priests,” he says, “be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI). A garment is received; it is not born with the hair. This is what the Apostle preaches to you; this is what God gives you. Groan, weep, believe, that you may obtain it.

CHAPTER X.

VERS. 1.—“Brothers, the desire indeed of my heart and my prayer to God is for them unto salvation.” The will, in order to be moved to believe true things, is not sufficient for itself unless it is helped by God’s grace. Therefore, although the Apostle persistently preached the Gospel to them, this was not sufficient for him unless he also prayed for them that they might believe. For otherwise they would not attain salvation. He prays, therefore, [Col. 0653C] for those unwilling to believe, that God may work in them both the willing.

VERS. 2.—“For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” “I have known; I know,” he says; “I was among them, and I myself was such.” Explaining what zeal, or ardor, not according to knowledge is, he adds:

VERS. 3.—“For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness.” He speaks of the Jews, who, presuming upon themselves, rejected grace and therefore did not believe in Christ. He says that they wished to establish their own righteousness, which is righteousness from the law, not because the law had been established by them, but because within the law that is from God they established their own righteousness when they believed that they could fulfill that same law by their own strength. They were ignorant of God’s righteousness—not the righteousness by which God is righteous, but that which a human being has from God.

And this is the whole great knowledge of a human being: to know that of himself he is nothing, and that whatever he is, is from God and through God.

VERS. 4.—“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” Faith is indeed distinguished from works, as is said elsewhere (above, ch. III, v. 28), that a human being can be justified by faith without works of the law. There are works which appear good without faith in Christ and are not good, because they are not referred to the end by which they are good. “For Christ is the end of the law.”

Therefore the Lord in the Gospel did not wish to distinguish faith from work; rather, he said that faith itself is a work. For faith is that which works through love. And he did not say, “This is your work,” but: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent” (John VI). A human being’s faith, therefore, is Christ’s, because it is from him; and every work of faith must be referred to him, because it is from him, because he is the end of the law and of all righteousness. For all perfection is in him, beyond whom there is nowhere for the hope of love and faith to extend.

VERS. 5.—“For Moses wrote that the person who has done the righteousness which is from the law shall live by it.” He does not say, “The person who has done it shall live by it,” so that you may understand that “law” is here used for the works themselves, in which those who perform them lived; otherwise ravens would feed upon them on the cross. The one who has done it, therefore, he says, will not be stoned, will not be killed: his reward will be not to die.

[Col. 0654B] VERS. 6, 7.—“But the righteousness which is from faith says thus: Do not say in your heart, ‘Who shall ascend into heaven?’ that is, to bring Christ down; or, ‘Who shall descend into the abyss?’ that is, to call Christ back from the dead.” The righteousness which is from the law of deeds consists in the deeds themselves; its reward or recompense is not to die, not to be punished. But concerning the righteousness which is from faith, the matter is very different. It requires only true faith of heart and free confession of mouth, received not by humanly elaborated reasoning but by a simple and voluntary assent of the mind.

For faith, in matters to be believed in religion, is the voluntary assent of the mind. The person who has in it a faithful and sober disposition does not investigate, through the perceptions of any divine wisdom or the arguments of any human knowledge, those things which in Christ are human, so as to demand that those things which belong to Christ’s divinity be brought down to his understanding from that heaven; nor does he demand that Christ be recalled for himself from that abyss, from the common lot of the dying. Rather, simply believing what divine authority commands to be believed and freely confessing what truth urges to be confessed, by the humility of belief he advances to an understanding of the faith he has received and to works performed through love.

For thus it is written in Deuteronomy, from which this example is taken: “This commandment which I command you today is not too high for you, nor far from you. It is not in heaven, that you should say, ‘Who will ascend into heaven for us and receive it for us, that, hearing it, we may do it?’ Nor is it beyond the sea, that you should say, ‘Who will cross over and receive it [Col. 0654D] for us?’” (Deut. XXX).

VERS. 8, 9.—“But the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. For this is the word which we preach: that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved.” Although in an unprecedented matter and one involving an unfamiliar miracle there may appear to be some difficulty in believing, nevertheless, when one faithfully confesses that Jesus is Lord and believes that he does not belong to the common lot of the dying, God—who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble—through the love of the Spirit illuminates the disposition of faith and supplies understanding. Thus what the person believes becomes sweet in his heart, and what he understands himself to believe most healthfully becomes glorious to confess.

By believing, moreover, he is made saved—not merely in order to live for the present, as that laborer of the law lives in his own righteousness or the righteousness of his works, but so that he may live here in God’s righteousness and live eternally with him; that he may live here the life of God by working through love, and hereafter receive perpetual glorification. For the true righteousness of faith has a twofold reward of blessedness: here it tastes, by the most certain evidence of experience, the substance of things hoped for; there it receives the manifest truth of eternal felicity which it believed.

For this reason it glories here in tribulations, in which the conscience of holy patience is already a kind of earnest and pledge of future blessedness. Therefore cause must be compared with cause, righteousness with righteousness, life with life: the life of the servant, as though shut up in the mill-house of harsh necessity, living only so long as he works servilely; and that of the son [Col. 0655B] of grace, for whom to serve is to live, to serve thankfully is a great grace, and to serve freely is great glory, while the reward is eternal life.

VERS. 10.—“For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Since the righteousness of faith, by which one believes with the heart unto righteousness, is established, it was not added without purpose: “but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Did not almost all those who denied Christ before persecutors retain in their hearts what they believed concerning him, yet perish by failing to confess with their mouths unto salvation—except those who came to life again through repentance? Who could be so empty-minded as to suppose that the apostle Peter held otherwise in his heart when he denied the Lord with his mouth? Why did he, speaking truth in his heart, punish by such bitter weeping the lie which he uttered with his mouth, unless [Col. 0655C] he saw how great a ruin it was that he believed indeed with his heart unto righteousness, but did not confess with his mouth unto salvation? For just as truth in the mouth is of no benefit if it is not also in the heart, so neither is it beneficial in the heart if, at the time when confession is necessary, it fails in the mouth.

VERS. 11.—“For Scripture says: Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame.” There are those who are not ashamed to confess Christ as the Word of God, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God; yet they are ashamed to confess that he was born, died, and was buried. And how will a sick person be cured who is ashamed of the medicine? But let him choose the time, for now is the time for choosing. For when that admirable one comes who was despised for our sake, he who was judged for our sake will judge, he who was slain will raise up, he who was dishonoured will honour; then, whether Jew or Greek—for there is no distinction—everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame.

VERS. 12.—“For the same Lord is Lord of all,” because he is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles, “rich in fulfilling the desires of all who call upon him.”

VERS. 13.—“For everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved.” He calls upon the name of the Lord who desires to be the Lord’s servant; whoever understands his name desires to be his servant. Those understand his name who experience his lordship within themselves. These are the people who know within themselves the grace of God and are not ungrateful; and therefore, calling upon the name of the Lord, they are saved. Thus faith in Jesus Christ [Col. 0656A] the Lord obtains salvation for us—both the salvation begun here for us in hope and that which will be granted in reality. When he says “shall be saved,” it is plainly as from a fever or from plague, since those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. Therefore, if salvation is promised to everyone who calls upon him, and there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, all must call upon him.

VERS. 14, 15.—“But how shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” Here the Teacher of the Gentiles seems to speak concerning the Gentiles, rejecting those who thought that the Gospel ought to be preached only to the Jewish nation and not also to the Gentiles. Wishing to show that it concerned not the Jews only but also the Gentiles, he put forward what had previously been announced through the prophet: “Everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved” (Joel [Col. 0656B] II); and then: “How,” he says, “shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? But how shall they preach unless they are sent?” Yet they were sent and preached, “as it is written” (Isa. LII): “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things!” For because God gives the increase, it does not follow that planting and watering ought not to be done; but by this path one returns to grace. Unless grace provides, and preachers truly make believers, there will be none who may be saved by calling upon him. Therefore beautiful are the feet of those proclaiming peace, those proclaiming good things: peace, by which, having received forgiveness of sins, we are reconciled to God; good things, which are promised to the children of grace; or beautiful feet, leaving us beautiful traces concerning the cultivation of the soul, love of God, and contempt for the world. Yet the evangelists were sent, but few were found obedient. Hence, under the prophet’s words (Isa. LIII), follows the voice of those lamenting:

VERS. 16.—“Lord, who has believed our report?” For what we heard from you, we announced to them; but few are those who obey us. The whole length of these words proceeds toward this: the Apostle continues his great sorrow and continual anguish of heart over the blinding of his own people, which he cannot conceal, acting on their behalf insofar as the truth and righteousness of God are found not to oppose his efforts; and he himself cannot resist that righteousness, while he is resisted by the hardening of stubborn wickedness. Therefore, joined to God, he indeed condemns the blind multitude of the hardened among them, but, as a remedy for grief, embraces the holy rarity of the elect from among them.

VERS. 17.—“Therefore,” he says, in them—that is, in the few among them—“faith comes from hearing, but hearing through the word of God.” He rejoices that the endeavor of the preachers has succeeded, even among a few of them. Then, removing every excuse from the rest:

VERS. 18.—“Have they not,” he says, “heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the inhabited world” (Ps. XVIII). If therefore all have heard, they too have heard. If the Gentiles dwelling at the ends of the earth [Col. 0657A] heard, how can the Jews, dwelling in the middle of the earth, where salvation was accomplished, excuse themselves?

VERS. 19.—“But I say: Has Israel not known?” As though he said: But I shall say why Israel did not know. Yet not I, but “first,” before me, “Moses”—and God in him—“says” (Deut. XXXII): “I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will move you to anger.” As though he said: By withdrawing from you my grace, which you yourselves also reject, I shall permit you to be brought into jealousy and envy toward a people which until now you did not deem worthy even of the name of nation; but which is now truly “not a nation,” that is, a nation ceasing to be what it was and changing, as it were, the natural birth of its error [Col. 0657B] into a new birth of faith. And I shall move you to anger—an anger from which envy is never absent—against a nation hitherto foolish and knowing nothing wisely concerning God, but now preceding you in the knowledge of God. Envy, therefore, is the chief reason why Israel did not know. For while the younger son feasted and rejoiced with his father, the elder refused to enter (Luke XV). Isaiah, although he knew that he would die for confessing God and for the truth of God’s word, nevertheless dared to preach the calling of the Gentiles in rejection of the Jews, saying:

VERS. 20.—“I was found by those who did not seek me; I openly appeared to those who did not ask for me” (Isa. LXV). Behold the most manifest grace. Yet we believe that the Lord God’s foreknowledge of future events, and his foretelling [Col. 0657C] the unbelief of the Jews, did not cause it—although the expression “bringing into jealousy” seems to suggest this. But God does not compel people to sin merely because he already knows their future sins. For he foreknew their sins, not his own; not those of someone else, but theirs. Accordingly, if the acts which he foreknew as theirs are not theirs, then what he foreknew was not true. But because his foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, without doubt it is not another but those very persons who sin, whom God foreknew would sin. Thus the Jews committed a sin which he who does not approve of sin did not compel them to commit; but he foretold that they would commit it, for nothing is hidden from him. And therefore, if they had wished to do good rather than evil, they would not have been prevented; and they would have been foreseen as doing this by him who knows what each person will do [Col. 0657D] and what he will render to each according to that person’s work. This much, for the moment, concerning the rejection of the Jews.

But regarding those by whom he was found when not sought, what shall we say? What, except what the man who had the Spirit of God says: “His mercy shall go before me” (Ps. LVIII)? If you, whoever you are, are one of those people and first brought something of your own, and first earned God’s mercy by some good thing of your own, then mercy did not go before you. But what did you do in order to exist? What did you do in order to become one who called upon God? For if you did something in order to exist, then you existed before you existed. But if you were entirely nothing before you existed, you did not earn the right to exist. God made you exist; and did you make yourself good? If God gave you existence, and someone else gave you goodness, surely he who gave you goodness is better [Col. 0658A] than he who gave you mere existence. But he was found by those who did not seek him, because his prevenient grace opened the understanding, and he openly appeared to those who did not seek him.

What then? People are given power to become children of God: let them give thanks because the power has been given; let them pray that weakness may not succumb. Let no one be lifted up into pride by excessive confidence in his own will, saying, “Why should I ask God not to be overcome by temptation, when this lies within my own power?” Let no one be cast down into negligence by excessive distrust of himself, saying, “Why do we strive to live rightly, when this lies in God’s power?” Rather, let the whole world be subject to God. Whoever is drawn, let him follow; whoever is not drawn, let him pray to be drawn. It follows.

VERS. 21.—“But concerning Israel he says:” The former concerns [Col. 0658B] the Gentiles; the latter, Israel. The former concerns the reception of the Gentiles; the latter, the rejection of the Jews: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe, but contradict me.” “Allow the children to be filled,” says the Lord. “For I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Therefore, all day long—that is, throughout the whole period of his life among human beings—the Lord stretched out his hands as though to embrace the Jewish people. He especially assigned to them both the works of his miracles, indicated by his hands, and the effort of his teaching; and thus, as it were, seeks to draw to himself with both hands those who do not believe but contradict him. And as though someone were to reply, “Where then are the promises made to Israel?” he immediately added:

## CHAPTER XI

VERS. 1, 2.—“I say then: Has God rejected his people? Far be it! For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” And in order to show that the remnant was left by God’s grace, not by the merits of their works, he next added:

VERS. 3–7.—“Do you not know, in the case of Elijah, what Scripture says—how he intercedes with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, dug down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.’ But what does the divine answer say to him? ‘I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal.’ [Col. 0658D] So also at this time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. What then? Israel has not obtained what it sought, but the election has obtained it; the rest, however, have been blinded.”

The Jewish nation was the people of God: theirs were adoption, glory, covenant, and legislation—the people, I say, among whom all the mysteries promising the Savior came beforehand. What then? Was all that condemned? Far be it! But when the threshing-floor was winnowed, the mass was set apart and the chaff lies outside. Everything you see among the rejected Jews is chaff. Those who were foreknown and predestined were not rejected. “I have reserved,” he says, “for myself.” What does “I have reserved for myself” mean? “I chose them because I saw minds not relying [Col. 0659A] upon themselves, not relying upon Baal. They have not changed; they are as I made them.” So also now a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. Beware of pride, Christian: even if you are an imitator of the saints, always ascribe everything to grace, because grace, not your merit, made it possible for something to remain in you. For the prophet speaks of this very remnant. If you rely on your own merits or works, grace is no longer rendered to you; a wage is owed instead. But if it is grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.

What, then, does “according to the election of grace” mean? We were evil, and we were chosen so that we might become good through the grace of the one choosing. For grace does not find merit; it produces it. “What then? Israel has not obtained what it sought.” What was it that Israel sought but did not obtain? Earlier he had said that, by pursuing a law of righteousness, it did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? “Because not by faith, but by works.” For it pursued a law of works and, seeking righteousness in it, did not obtain it; but the election, from both Jews and Gentiles, obtained it in the law of grace, the law of faith, the law of the Spirit of life. “The rest,” however, because they were unwilling to believe when they could have believed, “were blinded”: that is, they were made unable. Because they sinned voluntarily, they were punished also in their will; so that, because knowingly they declared truth to be false, afterward they could not even understand truth itself. For envy of this kind deserves not the ignorance of simplicity, but that of a perverse will.

[Col. 0659C] VERS. 8.—For this reason “God gave them a spirit of compunction.” This compunction is the penal affliction of a condemned conscience, of which he said above: “But for those who are contentious, wrath and indignation,” etc. For those condemned to the hell of Gehenna are first tormented here in the hell of conscience: not possessing the righteousness which is according to God, producing a steadfast repentance unto salvation, but a diabolical despair producing eternal death. It is not sufficiently apparent from where this testimony was taken, unless perhaps from Isaiah, where he says: “Go, and say to this people: ‘You shall hear with the ear and not understand; and seeing you shall see and not perceive. For their heart has grown fat’” (Isa. VI), continuing to the shutting of [Col. 0659D] the inner eyes and the stopping of the ears, so that they can now neither see nor hear, because when they could, they would not.

VERS. 9.—“And David says” (Ps. LXIII): “Let their table before them become a snare, a trap, a stumbling-block, and a recompense to them.” The table of the Jews is the Scripture of the Old Testament, upon which various dishes from Moses and the prophets are set forth. It becomes a snare to them when, caring nothing for spiritual matters, they suppose that only carnal things are promised to them in the Scriptures. But why “before them”? For they know their own iniquity and nevertheless persist in it most stubbornly; and such is the force of self-confidence that the snare lies before them, and yet they fall into it. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0660A] VERS. 10.—“Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see”: because they saw without cause, let it come about in them that they cannot see. What he says is prophetic, not wishful: not “let it happen,” but “it will happen.” “Let it become a stumbling-block to them,” because, seeing the Lord as capable of suffering, they were scandalized. “And bend their back,” so that those who refused to know heavenly things may now know how to think only of earthly things. Thus, from the place which they killed Christ in order not to lose, they were unhappily driven out and scattered throughout the lands; wherever the Church has spread, they are not absent, and from their own Scriptures they are a testimony to us that we have not fabricated the things proclaimed concerning Christ, but that they are found in their books. Therefore, when, blinded, they do not believe our Scriptures, their own Scriptures, which they read while blind, are fulfilled in them.

[Col. 0660B] VERS. 11.—“I say then: Have they stumbled so as to fall? Far be it.” There is a fall by which the righteous falls seven times and rises again (Prov. XXIV), and there is a fall in which one who falls does not add recovery by rising again (Isa. XXIV), as Lucifer fell from heaven in a fall of eternal despair. “Far be it,” he says, that Israel should have fallen by this fall, since among them there still remains meditation on the law and zeal for God, though not according to knowledge. For the fall of the Jews has resurrection, and their turning away has conversion. How? He follows and says: “But through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, in order to provoke them to jealousy.” Their fall was not found altogether useless, because where they fell, others rose. Hence he wished, as if more gently, to call their fall by the name of transgression. Their transgression, then, is salvation for the Gentiles, in order that they may provoke them to jealousy—that is, just as the Gentiles have now found among the Jews that by which they may be saved, so the Jews too may at some time, once truth is acknowledged, be moved by the Gentiles toward their own salvation.

VERS. 12.—“But if their transgression is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” The transgression of the Jews is the riches of the world, because in their transgression the whole world became the Lord’s portion, whereas at the first establishment of the boundaries of the world Jacob alone was appointed the cord of his inheritance (Deut. XXXII). “But if their diminution is the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” For what was diminished and taken away from the Jews was added [Col. 0660D] and granted to the Gentiles. And fullness is rightly set against diminution, because so long as Israel remains in unbelief, the fullness of God’s portion cannot yet be called complete; Israel itself will complete it by its conversion.

VERS. 13, 14.—“For I speak to you Gentiles: insofar as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I shall honour my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my own flesh to jealousy and save some of them.” For when the Apostle exercised watchful care and continual concern for the teaching of the Gentiles, and displayed their manner of life as commendable, this sight provoked Israelites to emulate those making progress. And this was the great glorification of his ministry: through one person’s progress, to arouse another to progress.

[Col. 0661A] VERS. 15.—“For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their reception be except life from the dead?” If the rejection of that nation brought reconciliation to the world, if such grace was among them that, taken away from them and given to the Gentiles, it filled the entire world, it cannot be estimated what the world will receive from its reconciliation. “What will their reception be except life from the dead?” For now, meanwhile, various advances are announced among those progressing toward life from the dead; but then there will be perfection itself. For then, namely at the end of the world, their general reception will take place, when that renowned resurrection will occur in all believers, by which mortality will put on immortality [Col. 0661B] and corruption incorruption.

VERS. 16.—“And if the first portion is holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.” God made the holy patriarchs an olive tree, from which the people of God flourished; this tree was pruned. For from it the proud branches were broken off: the blasphemous Jewish people. Yet good and useful branches remained there: the holy apostles. This is the first portion, a small part of any thing taken as a test of the whole mass. Hence he says: If the first portion has been found holy, the whole mass can be sanctified. As the root, so also the branches. For the nature of branches, as happens in every tree, corresponds to the holiness of the root; and a small sample of its fruits indicates the quality of the whole mass. Thus in the first portion and the branches there is the natural holiness of the root. But you, grafted in from elsewhere contrary to nature, have whatever holiness you possess from the benefit of the one who grafted you and from the richness of the root. Hence it follows:

VERS. 17.—“But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, though a wild olive tree, were grafted among them and made a partaker of the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches.” He speaks of certain branches broken off from the root of the patriarchs because of unbelief, and of the wild olive grafted in to partake of the richness of the olive tree—that is, the Church coming from the Gentiles. But who grafts a wild olive into an olive tree? An olive is usually grafted into a wild olive; we have never seen a wild olive grafted into an olive. For whoever does this will not find olive berries, but wild-olive fruit. For what you graft is what grows, and its fruit is produced. The fruit of the root does not grow, but that of the shoot. The Apostle shows that God, by his omnipotence, made the wild olive be grafted into the root of the olive, so that it might yield not wild berries but olives. Referring this to God’s omnipotence, he says: “But if some branches were broken off, and you, though a wild olive, were grafted among them and made a partaker of the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches.” Do not boast because you have been grafted in, but fear lest you be broken off through unbelief, as they were broken off. The proud olive was worthy to be broken off, which said: “We were not born of slavery; we have one father, Abraham” [Col. 0662A] (John VIII). Hear also the wild olive worthy to be grafted in: “I am not worthy,” he says, “that you should enter beneath my roof” (Matt. VIII). The centurion was a foreigner who said this, and concerning him the Lord also said: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (ibid.). I did not find in the olive tree what I found in the wild olive. Therefore let the proud olive be cut down, and the humble wild olive grafted in. Then see the one cutting off and grafting in: “Many shall come from East and West and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). Therefore let us not boast proudly against the broken branches; rather, let us consider by whose grace and by how great a mercy—and into what root—we have been grafted, so that we may not think lofty thoughts but may be in agreement with the humble.

VERS. 18.—“But if you boast, you do not bear the root, but the root bears you.” For you possess nothing that you have not received. And if you mock the breaking of the branches, you do not bear the root, but the root bears you—the root against which you mock. To such mockers he says:

VERS. 19, 20.—“You say then: ‘The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Well: they were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith.” Once the natural branches have been cut off because of the pride of unbelief, stand by faith, so that faith may be reckoned to you unto righteousness and there may be fulfilled in you not what your merit claims, but the benefit promised by the Lord. “Do not think lofty thoughts, but fear.” For grace has its own fear. This fear is commanded even to those who, living by faith, are heirs of the New Testament and called to freedom. To think lofty thoughts is to be proud. This fear does not delight in iniquity even if impunity is offered. It fears only losing the very grace [Col. 0662C] through which it has been brought about that it does not delight in sinning. For one who thinks lofty thoughts and therefore does not fear, certainly fails to fear ruinously. What good does a person love who perhaps loves even this very condition—of not fearing—for its own sake? Someone may persuade himself of this, not through soundness but through savagery. For precisely because he loves not to fear, he plots enormous crimes in order to practice what he loves. Therefore this must not be considered a great good merely because it may be found in a most wicked person.

Accordingly, let the Christian fear until perfect love casts fear out (1 John IV). Then, as one advances, let fear become smaller in proportion as one comes nearer to the homeland toward which one is journeying. For the fear of those travelling should be greater; that of those drawing near, smaller; that of those who have arrived, none. Yet fear leads to love, while perfect love casts fear out.

VERS. 20, 21.—“Therefore do not think lofty thoughts, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you.” For “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV).

VERS. 22, 24.—“See therefore the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness.” Scripture beneficially commends not only God’s goodness but also his severity, because God is both usefully loved and feared. Thus, while the holy patriarchs live in their root, the unbelieving pride of the natural branches is broken by the just severity of God, [Col. 0663A] and the faithful humility of the wild olive is grafted in by the grace of divine goodness. Therefore, whoever you are that have been grafted in, see, as has been said, God’s goodness and severity.

For just as all bodily matter, although unquestionably of one nature, produces different kinds of bodies through qualities incident to it—whether in human beings, animals, trees, or plants—so too, although all rational beings have one nature, endowed equally with freedom of their own choice, the movements proper to each, tested in the liberty of free choice and leading the soul subject to them either toward virtue or toward desire, either, through the preceding grace of God, form it into the kind of a good tree, or deform it through its own fault into an evil tree. Hence the Lord, in order to show that a good tree is made rather than born, says: [Col. 0663B] “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. XII). “Otherwise you also shall be cut off; but they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, shall be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in. For if you were cut from the natural wild olive and grafted, contrary to nature, into a good olive tree, how much more shall these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree?”

For just as, as was said, outwardly incident causes shape bodily nature into diverse forms, so God’s grace, as it were from the origin, forms the rational soul into an olive tree, or causes a wild olive to pass into it; conversely, the abuse of free choice does the opposite. For God is equally able to work in the olive tree of the Jews and in the wild olive of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0663C] VERS. 25.—“For I do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own eyes: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and thus all Israel should be saved.” To rejoice over another’s ruin is dangerous; but to mock it is a sign of one’s own impending ruin. Therefore, fearing this for the weaker disciples from among the Gentiles, the Apostle reveals to them this hidden mystery concerning the salvation of the Jews, lest they should suppose that the Jews had been wholly alienated from God—both because blindness had happened to them only in part and because the fullness of the Gentiles itself could not be completed without their general conversion.

Those are wise in themselves who, while judging others, neglect the fear of God’s hidden judgments and take on, as it were, a certainty of their own salvation from calculations of their own merits. For blindness came upon Israel through its sins, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter; once it has entered, the blindness among them must cease. How this will happen, he explains as follows:

VERS. 26.—“There shall come from Zion one who delivers and turns ungodliness away from Jacob; and this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their sins.” He shall come from Zion, of whom it is written: “From Zion comes the beauty of his splendour” (Ps. XLIX), to deliver the fullness of the Gentiles from the enemy’s possession and to turn ungodliness away from Jacob, so that they may no longer envy the Gentiles but emulate them in good.

VERS. 27.—“And this is my covenant with them.” [Col. 0664A] The Apostle adds on his own account what is not found in the prophet: “when I shall take away their sins.” For just as it is said concerning those Gentiles that the iniquity of the Amorites and Gomorrheans was not yet complete (Gen. XV), so until that time the iniquities of the Jews will not be complete or removed. What the number of the fullness of the Gentiles is, before the Jews’ iniquity is removed, and who this “all Israel” is that will be saved, are hidden matters of the mystery, which the Apostle wishes to be known in part and permits to remain unknown in part.

For from the Lord’s first, humble advent blindness came upon Israel. From the second, all Israel will be saved. For it is very widely held in the teaching and hearts of believers that, through Elijah, the great and wondrous prophet, the Jews, after the law has been expounded to them before judgment in the last time, will believe in the Lord Jesus. Indeed, he himself is expected to come before the Judge’s advent and is kept alive in the flesh until that time. He will expound spiritually the law which the Jews now observe carnally. “And he shall turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children” (Mal. IV): that is, so that the children may understand the law as their fathers, the prophets—among whom Moses also was—understood it. For the heart of the fathers is turned toward the children when the understanding of the fathers is brought to the understanding of the children; and the heart of the children toward their fathers, when these understand what those understood.

VERS. 28.—“According to the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, beloved [Col. 0664C] for the fathers’ sake.” What does “enemies according to the Gospel for your sake” mean, except that their hostility, by which they killed Christ, has, as we see, advanced the Gospel? And this shows that it comes from God’s ordering, for he knows well how to use even evil persons—not because vessels of wrath benefit him, but because, when he uses them well, they benefit vessels of mercy. For it is within the power of evil persons to sin; but it is not within their power, while sinning, to make their wickedness accomplish this or that. That belongs to God, who divides and orders darkness, so that even what they do against God’s will fulfills nothing but God’s will.

We read in the Acts of the Apostles that, while praying in persecution, they said, after some words: “For Herod and Pilate and the people of Israel assembled in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, [Col. 0664D] to do whatever your hand and counsel had predestined to happen” (Acts IV). Behold what was said: “Enemies according to the Gospel for their sake.” For God’s hand and counsel predestined such great things to be done by the hostile Jews as were necessary for the Gospel on our behalf. But what is the meaning of what follows: “But according to election, beloved for the fathers’ sake”? Are the same persons both enemies and beloved? Far be it! Rather, although the two things are contrary—enemies and beloved—and do not apply to the same persons, nevertheless they apply to the same Jewish nation and to the same carnal seed of Israel: some belonging to Jacob’s lameness, others to Israel’s blessing.

He explained this sense more plainly above (v. 7), where he says: “Israel has not obtained what it sought; but the election has obtained it; the rest, however, have been blinded.” Where we hear, “the election has obtained it,” there we should understand the beloved for the fathers’ sake, to whom these promises were made. For these were not called with that calling of which it was said, “Many are called, but few chosen” (Matt. XX); but with that calling by which the elect are called. Hence it is also added here: “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance,” that is, they are firmly fixed without change. All who belong to this calling are taught by God; nor can any one of them say, “I believed in order to be called in this way.” Rather, God’s grace goes before them all, because they are called in such a way that they may believe. For all who are taught by God come to the Son, because they have heard and learned from [Col. 0665B] the Father through the Son, who says most plainly: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John VI). None of these perishes, because of all that the Father gave him he loses nothing: “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” These are those to whom it is said: “that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John XV). By these words he shows that he has given them not only righteousness but also perseverance in it.

VERS. 30, 31.—“For just as you too once did not believe, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so these now have not believed in your mercy, in order that they too may obtain mercy.” He now explains the deeper causes of the unbelief of those who do not believe. [Col. 0665C] Namely, just as the Gentiles, formerly unbelieving, were nevertheless not wholly abandoned but, when occasion arose through the breaking of the natural branches, were themselves grafted into the olive tree from the wild olive contrary to nature, so, once the dispensation has been fulfilled by the fullness of the Gentiles, they too will obtain mercy. In this the Apostle wishes to show the goodness of God, by which he brings about the salvation of some through the unbelief of others.

VERS. 32.—“God,” he says, “has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.” Some flatter themselves by misunderstanding this, but the context of the passage shows whom he means by “all.” For he is dealing with Jews and Gentiles, from whom he has shut up in unbelief those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image [Col. 0665D] of his Son, in order that, confounded by repenting of the bitterness of their unbelief and turned by faith to the sweetness of God’s mercy, they might cry out that saying from the Psalm: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you. You have accomplished it for those who hope in you” (Ps. XXX)—not in themselves. Therefore he has mercy on all the vessels of mercy: on all whom? Namely, both those whom he predestined, called, justified, and glorified from the Gentiles, and those whom he predestined, called, justified, and glorified from the Jews. Not all human beings, but of all these he has left no one behind.

VERS. 33, 36.—“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor? Or who first gave to him, and will be repaid by him? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

Having set forth the most profound statement concerning the free grace of God, which is not unjust although no merits precede it, and which does not so much trouble us when it is bestowed on the undeserving as when it is denied to others equally undeserving, why election calls this person and not that one, the Apostle, as though knocking at the entrance to some secret of the Most High, since he was unable to gain admission to the inner things through knowledge, stood humbly before the door through humble confession; and what he could not comprehend inwardly by understanding, he praised outwardly in fear.

Therefore, insofar as God has deigned to make his judgments known to us, let us give thanks; insofar as he has hidden them, let us not murmur against his counsel, but believe that this too is most salutary for us. For it was not said without reason: “Your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. XXXV [36]). Alarmed by the depth of this abyss, the Apostle cried out in this way. Hence come the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, whom he calls to adoption; and he wills to make them known also through vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction.

His unsearchable ways are those of which the Psalm sings: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV [25]): mercy, because he has mercy on whom he wills, not by justice but by the grace of mercy; and he hardens whom he wills, not through iniquity but through the truth of retribution. Yet mercy and truth meet one another in such a manner that mercy does not impede the truth by which the deserving person is punished, nor truth impede the mercy by which the undeserving person is delivered.

Then are there no merits of the righteous? Certainly there are, because they are righteous; but there were no merits by which they became righteous. For they became righteous when they were justified. We therefore have very little understanding for examining the judgments of God and their justice—of him in whom, just as impossibility is not to be believed, so neither is iniquity to be believed—when he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas. IV [4]).

“O the depth!” This depth is not the distance between heaven and earth, for heaven and earth too are temporal and spatial; rather, it is the distance between God and every temporal and spatial creature—which all creatures are. Therefore the depth of God’s wisdom, in which all things were made, cannot be reached by the perception or comprehended by the understanding of any creature. Although all things come to be in it, sinful things do not defile it; nothing defiled enters into it, although it reaches all things because of its purity.

And since he himself is wise and begets wisdom from himself, the question is raised whether he is wise in himself, or through the wisdom that he begets from himself; whether he is wise in the way in which he is said to speak—for by the Word whom he begot, he is speaking. But if the Father who begot Wisdom is wise by that Wisdom, then being is not for him the same as being wise; wisdom is a quality of his, not the offspring, the Son. Nor would supreme simplicity be there. But far be it that this should be so, for there truly is a supremely simple essence! Thus, there, to be is to be wise. And if to be is there to be wise, the Father is not wise through the Wisdom whom he begot; otherwise it was not he who begot Wisdom, but Wisdom who begot him.

[Col. 0667A] For what else do we say when we say that for them to be is to be wise, except that he is wise by that whereby he is? Therefore, whatever is the cause of his being wise is itself the cause of his being. Accordingly, the Father too is Wisdom itself; and the Son is called the Wisdom of the Father as he is called the Light of the Father: that is, just as light from light, with both being one light, so Wisdom from Wisdom is to be understood, with both being one Wisdom. Thus there is also one essence, because there to be is to be wise. For wisdom’s being wise, power’s being able, and eternity’s being eternal, are what essence itself is: being. And because in that simplicity being wise is not different from being, Wisdom itself is essence.

Therefore Father and Son together are one essence, one greatness, one truth, and one wisdom. Yet no one has known these and similar things belonging to God except the Spirit of God, who is so in God through unity of nature that there is nothing in God which his Spirit cannot know by natural unity. This fullness of knowledge belongs to natural unity alone, through which his Spirit is so in God that he is naturally one God with him. Nevertheless, although he is so in God and is one God with him, the Holy Spirit does not form one person with him, as a human being’s spirit, which is in that human being, forms one person with that human being; yet he is one person in the Trinity.

For the Trinity is God of one and the same nature and substance: not less in each than in all, nor greater in all than in each; but as great in the Father alone or the Son alone as in Father and Son together, and as great in the Holy Spirit alone as in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together. For the Father does not diminish himself in order to have the Son from himself, but so begot another self from himself that he remained wholly in himself and was in the Son as great as he was in himself. Likewise the Holy Spirit, whole from the Whole, does not cut off that from which he proceeds; but is as great with him as from him. He neither diminishes him by proceeding nor increases him by abiding.

And these things are neither one confusedly nor three separately; but, though they are three, they are one; and though they are one, they are three. These are the riches of the wisdom of God, because to know God the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent is eternal life itself (John XVII [17]). But no one knows the Father except the Son; and no one knows the Son except the Father, and the one to whom he himself wills to reveal him (Matt. II [11:27]). He wills, certainly, through the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the will of Father and Son.

The providence, knowledge, or judgments of this Wisdom operate over one soul as over one city, over one nation as over the whole multitude of the human race; for the Lord attends to each individual as though he were free from all others, and at the same time attends to all as though he were free from each. This is the mind of which he says, “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” For he who fills all things by administering them governs them by filling them; and when he orders one thing, he is not absent from the whole, nor is he absent from one when he orders the whole. Certainly, in the repose of his natural power, he works all things.

The Son is from the Father, so as to be and so as to be coeternal with him. For if an image perfectly represents that of which it is the image, the image is made equal to it, not it to its image. There is already such complete correspondence, primary equality, and primary likeness: differing in no respect, unequal in no manner, and dissimilar in no part, but answering identically to that of which it is the image.

[Col. 0668A] There is the first and highest life, for which understanding is not one thing and living another; rather, to understand is to live, and this is to be. One, all things as a perfect Word lacking nothing; and a certain art of the almighty and wise God, full of all living and unchangeable reasons; and all are one in it, just as it itself is one from the One with whom it is one. There God knows through it all that he has made; and therefore, though times pass away and succeed one another, nothing passes away or succeeds in the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0668B] Things created are not known by God because they have been made; rather, they were made mutable because they are known unchangeably by God. This is that immeasurable depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God. That ineffable mutual embrace, as it were, of Father and Image is not without enjoyment, love, and joy. Therefore that love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if indeed it can worthily be named by any human word—is the Holy Spirit in the Trinity: not begotten, but the sweetness of the Begetter and the Begotten, pouring over all creatures, in abundant largeness and fullness, according to their capacity, so that they may keep their own order and rest in their proper places.

Let whoever sees this, whether in part or through a mirror and in an enigma, rejoice insofar as he sees it, and so, knowing the mind of the Lord to that extent, give thanks. But whoever does not see it should strive through piety to see and to love, not through blindness to slander—like a perverse counsellor wishing to correct the order of supreme equity according to the decision of his own will. All creatures either maintain that order or cannot escape it, if they do not rest in the places appointed by God.

It follows: “Who first gave to him, and will be repaid by him?” One says to a human being, “You owe me because you promised me,” in one sense; in another, “You owe me because I gave to you.” When you say, “You owe me because I gave to you,” the benefit came forth from you, but as a loan, not as a gift. But when you say, “You owe me because you promised me,” you gave nothing, and yet you demand. For the goodness of the one who promised will give, lest faithfulness be turned into wickedness.

[Col. 0668D] But one who deceives is wicked. Can we, however, say to God: “Repay me, because I gave to you”? What have we given to God, when we have from him everything that we are and every good thing that we possess? Therefore we have given him nothing. In this way, then, we may demand of the Lord our God, saying: “Repay what you promised, because we have done what you commanded”—and you did this yourself, for you helped us in our labours.

Consider what God first gave you, what he did for you when he predestined you, although you did not yet exist. Surely the Apostle says: “He calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. IV [4:17]). If you already existed, you would not be predestined; if you had not turned away, you would not be called; if you had not been ungodly, you would not be justified; if you had not been earthly and cast down, you would not be glorified. What, then, do we repay? “To him be glory,” because we did not exist when we were predestined; because we had turned away when we were called; because we were sinners when we were justified.

[Col. 0669A] For all these things let us give thanks to God, lest we be ungrateful. “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

Let religion bind us to the one almighty God. For between our mind, by which we understand him as Father, and truth—that is, the inner light through which we understand him—there is no creature interposed. Therefore let us venerate that very truth also, in no respect unlike him and with him: it is the form of all things made from the One and striving toward the One. Thus it appears to spiritual souls that all things have been made through this form, which alone fulfils what all things seek.

Yet all these things would neither be made by the Father through the Son nor remain sound within their appointed limits unless God were supremely good: he envied no nature which could be good from him; and in that good itself he granted to some what they willed, and to others what they were able, in order that they might endure. Therefore it is fitting for us to worship and hold fast the very gift of God, equally unchangeable with Father and Son: the Trinity of one substance, one God, from whom we are, through whom we are, and in whom we are; from whom we departed, to whom we became unlike, and by whom we were not permitted to perish.

[Col. 0670A] He is the beginning to which we return, the form which we follow, the grace by which we are reconciled: the One by whose authorship we were created, his likeness through which we are re-formed into unity, and the peace by which we cling to unity. This is the reality which alone we ought to enjoy: the holy Trinity—if it may be called a reality and not rather the cause of all realities; if indeed it may also be called a cause. For a name appropriate to such excellence is not easily found, unless it is better said that this Trinity is the one God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things.

Thus Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each God, and all together are one God; each is full substance, and all together are one substance. Yet the Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. The three have the same eternity, the same unchangeability, majesty, and power. In the Father is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the connection of unity and equality. These three are all one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, and connected through the Holy Spirit. Therefore “from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things” is not to be understood confusedly; nor is glory given to many gods, but “to him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0669]

# CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0669C]

VERS. 1–2.—“I beseech you therefore, brothers, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God: your rational service.”

Every good work done so that we may cleave to God in holy fellowship, and referred to that end of good by which we can truly be blessed, is a true sacrifice. Thus mercy itself, if it is not performed for God’s sake, is not a sacrifice; for sacrifice is a divine thing. Therefore the human being himself, consecrated in God’s name and vowed to God, insofar as he dies to the world in order to live to God, is a sacrifice.

Our body also, when we discipline it through temperance as we ought and do so for God’s sake, is a sacrifice—the sacrifice to which the Apostle here exhorts us. If, therefore, the body, which the soul uses as an inferior servant or instrument, is a sacrifice when its right and good use is directed toward God, how much more is the soul itself a sacrifice when it turns itself toward God, so that, set aflame by the fire of his love, it may lose the form of worldly desire and, subject to him as to an unchangeable form, be re-formed, becoming pleasing to him through that which it has received from his beauty?

The Apostle himself adds this immediately: “And do not be conformed to this age, but be re-formed in the newness of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

[Col. 0670C] Therefore, since true sacrifices are works of mercy, whether toward ourselves—for “Have mercy,” he says, “on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX [30:24])—or toward our neighbours, works which are referred to God; and since works of mercy are done for no other reason than that we may be delivered from misery and thereby become blessed, which does not happen except through that good of which it is said, “But for me, it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. LXXII [73]): it follows that the whole congregation and fellowship of the saints is offered to God as a universal sacrifice through the great priest, who also offered himself in his Passion for us, so that we might be the body of so great a head, according to the form of a servant. For he offered this form, was offered in this form, because in this form he is mediator, priest, and sacrifice.

“So that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” We are worthy to know God’s will in three ways: by being at leisure and living because he is God; by firmly believing that every word of God is true—for unless you believe, you will not understand—and by carrying out, according to our strength, the Word itself and God’s will.

Now one will of God is good, another pleasing, another perfect. The will of God is good when what is said is fulfilled: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI [6]); namely, when we show ourselves cheerful and ready in works of mercy and in bodily exercises directed toward God. It is pleasing in purity of heart; it is perfect when both in action and affection we are de-formed from the age and conformed to God.

[Col. 0671A] In bodily exercises, therefore, rational service is required; in purity of heart, the newness of spiritual understanding, serving in nothing the oldness of flesh or letter. Rational service is this: as we presented our members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now to present our members to serve righteousness unto sanctification (Rom. VI [6:19]). Through this we become worthy of newness of mind and receive the grace of the Spirit’s understanding; through this we advance toward the likeness of God and recover his image, which by doing contrary things we have partly lost—not wholly. For if we had lost it altogether, nothing would remain from which it could be said: “Although man passes through in an image, nevertheless he is troubled in vain” (Ps. XXXVIII [39]). But if we had lost nothing of it at all, there would be no basis for saying: “Be re-formed in the newness of your mind.”

Yet the soul cannot re-form itself, as it was able to de-form itself. For no one can be continent unless God grants it (Wis. VIII [8:21]). This re-formation consists of two things: prohibition and command. The general prohibition is, “You shall not desire”; the general command is, “You shall love.” This is precisely not being conformed to the age and being conformed to God. The former belongs to not desiring, the latter to loving; the former to self-restraint, the latter to justice; the former to turning away from evil, the latter to doing good. By not desiring, we are stripped of oldness; by loving, we are clothed with newness.

This the love of God will accomplish in us, which will be poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit given to us. Therefore, when our affections have been restrained from love of the age and “not being conformed to the age” has been fulfilled in us, renewal in the newness of our mind will immediately follow. We shall no longer be according to kind, as though imitating our neighbour and living by the authority of a better human being. For God did not say concerning human beings, “Let man be made according to kind,” but “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I [1:26]). Rather, we ourselves may at last begin to prove “what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

[Col. 0671D] For the mind, renewed and beholding the understood will of God, does not need a human guide in order to imitate its own kind; but, with God himself showing it, it proves for itself what is God’s will, his good pleasure.

“For I say through the grace that has been given to me.” What I say to you, he says, I do not say through human wisdom, but through the grace given to me. For “to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. XII [12:8]). The word of knowledge makes what is said clear and pleasing; the word of wisdom makes it savoury and moving. “Even if,” he says, “I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.” Thus it is clear that the Apostle received the grace of the word of wisdom and knowledge, but in the ornament of words he confesses himself unskilled.

For the proclamation of truth, where it deals in truth and grace, shapes the entire bearing of the speaker—face, voice, and words—into certain proper and manifest instruments, so that what the Lord says may become plain: “For you are not the ones speaking, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Luke XII). There is a great difference between one who speaks through wisdom of speech and one who speaks through grace, and their efficacy is far from equal. Therefore, here too, restraining his hearers from the vanity of worldly wisdom:

[Col. 0672A]

VERS. 3.—“Not,” he says, “to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think unto sobriety.”

For he speaks to the proud branches of the wild olive, to whom he had said above: “Do not think highly, but fear” (Rom. XI [11:20]). Regarding the word of doctrine and the deeper rationale of knowledge, whoever has not received grace and seeks self-display, though understanding less, wishes to understand more than he ought.

“But to think unto sobriety.” The Greek does not here have “sobriety,” but “temperance” (*sōphronein*, σωφρονεῖν), so that in all that we do, say, or think, we may preserve moderation. “And to each according as God has divided a measure of faith.” Here is an explicit confession of that grace which the Apostle strongly commends. He says that God has apportioned to each person even the measure of faith—without which it is impossible to please God, from which the righteous live, which works through love, before which and without which no works whatsoever of anyone are to be considered good, since everything not from faith is sin.

For “there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. XII [12:4]). It is certain that without the Holy Spirit we cannot love Christ and keep his commandments; and that we can do or perform this in proportion as we receive him—less insofar as we receive him less, more insofar as we receive him more. Therefore he is promised not only to one who does not have him but also to one who has him. The Only-begotten alone did not receive him by measure, for in him dwells all the fullness of divinity. That the Only-begotten Son is equal to the Father is a matter not of grace but of nature; but that a human being was assumed into unity of the person of the Only-begotten is of grace, not of nature.

[Col. 0672C] To all others he is given by measure, to each as God apportions the measure of faith. For the Spirit himself is not divided, but gifts are given through the Spirit. Hence it follows:

VERS. 4–5.—“For just as we have many members in one body, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.”

One strives to exceed the measures assigned to oneself when one attempts to be capable of more than one has received. But one stretches out one’s foot over a precipice when one does not observe the boundary of one’s measure. We are instructed by the very arrangement of the body, and it is utterly shameful not to imitate what we are. For the foot sees through the eye, and the eyes walk by means of the foot; and thus all the members support one another, becoming one by their mutual correspondence. Hence it follows: “Individually, however, members of one another.” In order that this may happen, different gifts are possessed for this purpose.

VERS. 6.—“Having gifts differing according to the grace given to us.”

These gifts are gifts of the Gift, that is, of the Holy Spirit, by whom they are given; and gifts once given are added until each person’s proper measure is completed according to the degree of that person’s perfection. They differ among those who differ, so that the unity of the body may be built up from the diversity of members.

“Whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith.” This prophecy is the very thing taught by Paul the Apostle, not that which says, “Thus says the Lord.” For “the law and the prophets were until John” (Luke XVI [16:16]). This does not mean that after him there were no prophets who foretold future things, revealed secrets, or declared things absent, wherever and whenever it pleased him to whom these gifts belong. But in the time of grace, after everything prophesied by the prophets had shone forth, that prophecy belongs to the order of miracles and, unless a just cause requires it, is not to be sought—though it is to be bestowed by the Giver of gifts when and where he himself judges it necessary.

[Col. 0673B] This, however, is the prophecy of which the same Apostle says: “The one who prophesies speaks to people for edification” (1 Cor. XIV [14:3]), for exhortation and consolation. And surely is it not prophecy when contempt for present things and desire for future things are preached? Hence among Elijah and Elisha the sons of the prophets were said to lead a prophetic life (III–IV Kings), which we now call the eremitic life. Whether in the Church or in the wilderness, if rightly conducted, whether in teaching or in manner of life, this stands among the chief gifts if it is genuinely exercised according to the analogy of faith—for this is what the Greek translation has.

But plagues have often been found in the chairs of churches, and dens of asps in the wilderness, while people seek to understand something more than they ought to understand and do not walk according to analogy, that is, according to the right rule of faith and the devout moderation of the Church. Prophecy is also discernment of spirits, knowledge in the Scriptures of hidden meanings, and having the means to bring forth from the good treasure of the heart things new and old at the proper time. In teaching, which follows, simple edification is to be understood; in exhortation, moral and kindly instruction.

VERS. 7 and following.—After prophecy, ministry is placed, because, just as prophecy is necessary in spiritual matters, so ministry is necessary in temporal matters. “The one who gives, in simplicity”: that is, let one give in simple love, seeking nothing beyond it. “The one who presides,” let that one preside “with diligence,” not worldly diligence, but that of which the Apostle likewise says: “My daily concern for all the churches” (2 Cor. XI [11:28]). Explaining what that concern is, he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (ibid.).

“The one who shows mercy” should adorn the work of mercy with the grace of cheerfulness. Teaching and exhorting seem to belong to prophecy; but giving in simplicity, presiding with diligence, and showing mercy with cheerfulness belong to ministry. What follows is common to all.

“Love without pretence. Hating evil, cleaving to good.” Yet one must note in these things the purity of holy instruction. In love a simple affection is required; nor is it enough to turn aside from evil and do good unless there is also hatred of evil and love of good.

[Col. 0674A] In what follows, “loving one another with brotherly charity,” attend to the Apostle’s thought as he instructs others from his own understanding. For what is brotherly charity except charity for charity? What is it to love brotherly charity except to love the love of love? This is exactly so. If we truly love brothers, we love both the brothers and brotherly love itself within us.

The following two statements concern the discipline of this love: honour, forestalling one another, should call forth mutual charity; and they should be diligent in heart, not lazy in work. In the services of this same charity, “fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,” that is, serving the Lord with fervour of spirit; “rejoicing in hope,” and therefore “patient in tribulation,” and for that very reason “continuing steadfastly in prayer.” For one must persist in prayer lest either the enemy snatch it away or negligence cause it to be lost.

Helping the necessities of all, but also “sharing with the saints,” so that, if necessary, you may even suffer need together with them. Not merely showing “hospitality,” but “pursuing” it, because guests must even be urged and drawn in. “Bless those who persecute you”: bless with the mouth, “and do not curse” in the heart. “Rejoice with those who rejoice,” over the good progress of those who rightly rejoice; “weep with those who weep,” through the compassion of brotherly charity unto repentance for sins. “Think the same thing toward one another,” and therefore “consent to the lowly.” Not conversing with them, but consenting to them, because the very disposition of humility must be put on; and this cannot happen if you are “thinking high things.”

Notice that in matters common to all he said “thinking,” but in matters lofty and above others, “being wise,” because whatever a proud heart can devise for the display of singular exaltation is usually savoury to it. This commonly happens to those who are great in their own eyes, concerning whom he adds:

VERS. 16.—“Do not be wise in your own estimation.”

In all these matters, or on account of them, if anyone brings any evil upon you, “repay no one evil for evil. Provide what is good not only before God but also before all people.” For we owe conscience to God and reputation to our neighbour. By saying “all,” he signifies that we owe a good example also to those outside.

[Col. 0674D]

VERS. 18.—“If possible, insofar as it depends on you, live peaceably with all people.”

For it was difficult that, if they corrected everything that ought to be corrected, they should have peace with all people. Yet sometimes, by overlooking certain things, peace must be sought outwardly in such a way that inwardly one does not depart from the peace of God.

VERS. 19.—“Do not defend yourselves, beloved.”

He calls them “beloved” as though tenderly encouraging them when he more earnestly invites them to humility and patience. For the holy simplicity of the soul finds it sweet to reserve vengeance for God, lest, if it undertakes to defend itself, it lose the exercise of patience and at times be found to act against God’s chastening rod.

[Col. 0675A] “But give place to wrath.” To give place to anger is not to resist the angry person, but to expose oneself and all one’s possessions to one who is raging. “For it is written: Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord.” We ought to wish our persecutors to be corrected rather than punished. If judgment is inflicted upon them in this age, we should not delight in the punishment of an enemy whom we do not hate, but in the justice of God whom we love.

VERS. 20.—“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; and if he thirsts, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.”
