Some say regarding enemies that it is enough not to hate them; but we are obliged also to love them, because they benefit us, as the Lord says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” (Matt. V [5:10]). But anyone who does good to an enemy merely in order to heap coals of fire upon that person’s head—that is, merely in order to shame the person—is himself an enemy. Rather, let us simply and with good intention do what belongs to us; then it will follow that they may be ashamed and perhaps converted. And even if this does not occur in the heart of the one for whom it is done, it ought nevertheless to be the intention of the one who does it. If that person perseveres in so acting, that person will not be overcome by evil by becoming evil through an evil intention, so that there are two evil persons; rather, that person will overcome evil with good, and there will be two good persons.

# CHAPTER XIII

VERS. 1.—“Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.”

Those in authority, if they are good, are our nourishers; if evil, our tempters. Let us both love to be nourished and not refuse to be tested. For both are from God. Therefore let us be subject to God, not as to human beings. This subjection is through love; but just as those who fear powers that inspire fear ought to render them love, so those who inspire fear should know themselves to be debtors in love to those who fear them.

“Therefore whatever powers exist have been ordained by God.” Human malice can have its own desire to harm, but it cannot have power to harm unless that power has been given from above. At times power is given to wicked people, but by God’s ordering, so that the patience of the righteous may be tested and the iniquity of the wicked punished.

VERS. 2.—“Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. But those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves.”

Provided, however, that authority commands what God forbids, then, Christian, despise authority. For this authority threatens punishment; that one threatens Gehenna.

VERS. 3.—“For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God’s minister to you for good.”

If you do good and the authority is good, you will receive praise from it as it judges; if it is evil, even when afflicted, even when killed, you will receive praise from it as it rages.

VERS. 4.—“But if you do evil, fear; for it does not bear the sword without cause.”

For at times one must fear, namely when an evil conscience deserves punishment. It is evil to sin, but worst of all is not to fear punishment in sin. For the judge of the world fulfils a very great part of God’s law, serving in this respect: crimes which God does not wish to be punished through bishops and leaders of the Church are punished through the judge’s ministry. Hence he says:

[Col. 0676A]

VERS. 5.—“For it is God’s minister. Therefore be subject by necessity,” because he who so orders so wills it. “Not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience.” Not merely in order that we may avoid offending human beings, but also in order that we may have a good conscience before God, who so ordained it. For just as being angry is not without sin, so provoking anger is not without sin.

VERS. 6.—“Therefore,” by the Lord himself as author, although you are children and free, you also pay “tributes,” but you “render” them, to receive from him whose command and example you observe in this matter. “For they are ministers of God, attending continually to this very thing,” and those who serve are owed their wages. Hence the Lord also commanded that ministers of the Gospel should live by the Gospel.

VERS. 7.—“Render therefore to all their due.”

To whom does the Apostle say this? Certainly to those who, through confidence in Christian holiness and liberty, considered that they had escaped slavery to public vanity, to which creation is subject both willingly and unwillingly. Unwillingly, because it groans for the glory of the children of God and in expectation of its blessed freedom; willingly, however, on account of him who subjected it in hope. Therefore, according to the Apostle’s counsel, even if one can become free, one rather makes use of one’s condition.

[Col. 0676C] “Render therefore,” he says, “what is due,” as you render debts faithfully, since you make a debtor of him to whom you do not refuse to be debtors for the sake of obedience. “To whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax.” Whoever is a child of the kingdom, so long as he is in the world, is a resident upon the earth, dwelling in a foreign land. To wish to violate the laws of the land in which one is a guest is to wish to violate the laws of hospitality. “To whom fear, fear; to whom honour, honour.” It is stupid madness, under the arrogance of supposed holiness, to be unwilling to fear anyone; and it is most vain pride to be unwilling to honour anyone. Fear is owed to the sublimity of authority, honour to usefulness, and the love of goodwill to humility—or, perhaps, humanity (*humanitati*).

### Verse 8

“**Owe no one anything, except to love one another.**” Passing from the higher authorities to the grace of social life, just as, under the law of the world, he commands that whatever is owed be paid [Col. 0676D], so under the law of charity the learned interpreter of God’s law decrees that nothing be owed except the single debt of charity—a debt which is owed all the more the more it is repaid, and which is possessed more abundantly by being repaid. For one who loves makes the person whom he loves his debtor. Love itself also exacts this debt: that, serving fraternal charity, we should help, insofar as we can, the person who rightly wishes to be helped, remaining always debtors to charity. For it is owed even when it has been paid, because there is no time at which it ought not to be bestowed. And when faithfully repaid, it itself brings it about that we owe nothing besides it.

See how through charity he reduces all things to unity. For in the faith of Christ there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, slave and free, ruler and subject, insofar as all believers are one in Christ Jesus [Col. 0677A]. And if faith, by which one walks justly in this life, does this, how much more perfectly and abundantly will the vision itself accomplish it when we see face to face? For now, although we have the firstfruits of the Spirit, who is life because of the righteousness of faith, yet because the body is still dead because of sin, this distinction of nations, status, and sex—already removed from the unity of faith—remains in mortal life. The apostles therefore command that its order be maintained on the journey of this life. They also hand down most salutary rules for how persons should live together according to their differences of peoples and conditions; and the Lord himself earlier commanded: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” [Col. 0677B] (Matt. 22).

Then he comes to the common and reciprocal love of social life, which he so highly praises and approves that he says the whole law is fulfilled in love of neighbour alone. Thus he says:

### Verses 8–9

“**Owe no one anything, except to love one another. For the one who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law. For, You shall not commit adultery; You shall not kill; You shall not steal; You shall not bear false witness; You shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself.**”

It may be asked why the Apostle mentioned only love of neighbour, by which he said that the law is fulfilled. Why, unless because people can falsely claim love of God, since fewer trials test it? But in love of neighbour they are more easily proved [Col. 0677C] not to possess it when they act unjustly toward others. It follows that one who loves God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind loves his neighbour as himself, because this is commanded by the one whom he so loves.

But if a person loves himself for his own sake, he does not refer himself to God. Turned toward himself so as not to be turned toward something immutable, he thus enjoys himself with a certain deficiency; for he is better when he wholly clings and is bound to the immutable good than when he is loosened from it even toward himself. Therefore, if you ought to love yourself not for your own sake but for him in whom the most upright end of your love lies, let no other person resent it if you also love that person for God’s sake. For this rule of love has been divinely established [Col. 0677D]: “You shall love,” he says, “your neighbour as yourself” (Lev. 19).

But we must love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind, so that we direct all our thoughts, our whole life, and our whole understanding toward him from whom we have the very things that we direct toward him. When he says “with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind,” he leaves no part of our life that ought to remain vacant, as though giving room to enjoy some other thing. Rather, whatever else presents itself as worthy of love must be drawn there with the whole mind, where the entire impulse of love runs.

Whoever therefore rightly loves his neighbour ought to work with him toward this: that he too may love God in this manner. For by loving him as himself, he directs the whole love of himself and of the other toward that love of God which permits no stream [Col. 0678A] to be drawn away from itself, by whose diversion it might be diminished.

### Verse 10

“**Love does no evil to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law.**” Every human being must be understood as one’s neighbour, since there is no one against whom evil ought to be done. But who does evil to one whom he loves? Love, and it cannot happen that you do not do good to the one whom you love. Perhaps you rebuke: love does this, not cruelty. Perhaps you strike: you do it for discipline, because the love of charity itself does not allow you to neglect one who lacks discipline. Thus there arises, in a sense, a differing and contrary result: hatred sometimes flatters, while love is severe.

Therefore charity works no evil; rather, it works every good, “because charity is the fulfilment of the law,” by which God and neighbour are loved [Col. 0678B]. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets (Matt. 22). Rightly, then, the one who acts against that upon which all things hang becomes guilty of all; and no one sins except by acting against it.

“Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law”—not that love by which people love themselves, but that love which the Lord distinguished from other loves when he said: “As I have loved you” (John 15). For why did Christ the Lord love us, except that we might be able to reign with him? Therefore, if we are to fulfil the law, let us distinguish our love from that of others, who do not love themselves for this end, because indeed they do not love themselves. But those who love themselves for the sake of possessing God truly love themselves. Therefore, in order to love themselves, let them love God. This love is not shared by all: few [Col. 0678C] are those who love themselves so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

“And knowing this, that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For our salvation is nearer now than when we believed.” Up to this point he has been occupied with moral instruction; now he hastens and presses the matter, reproving the sluggish and rousing those who are, as it were, asleep, introducing the consideration of time, which is of highest importance in every undertaking. For no one is so drowsy and lazy that the brightness of the approaching day does not awaken him, or that the splendour of the rising sun does not rebuke his sloth if it finds him sleeping.

Understanding and love are the faculties of the rational soul. Those are awake in whose hearts these faculties are devoted to the Lord their God. They sleep or doze when they grow dull and languid in the desire or delight of temporal things [Col. 0678D]. Therefore, since those who sleep sleep by night, when the day has now appeared he knocks upon those who are drowsing, that they may awake, and says:

### Verse 11

“**It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.**” What hour? Surely the morning of grace, when the night and darkness of unbelief have passed, and that illumination is awaited in which the thoughts of hearts will be revealed, and then each person will receive praise from God.

Therefore, placed in this pilgrimage, in this light of faith—which, compared with the darkness of unbelievers, is day, but compared with the light in which we shall see face to face is night—we must rise from sleep. Our life must be conformed to the life to come, which is now nearer than when we believed, just as the Lord says: “When you see these things happening, know that the kingdom [Col. 0679A] of God is near.” Therefore, because we ought to be lovers of eternity and unity, desiring to cling to the one Lord our God, we must turn our mind away from the multitude of things that are born and die.

### Verse 12

“**Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light, that we may walk honourably, as one ought to walk in the day.**” For when we walk honourably, we are in the day in comparison with unbelievers. He then explains in sequence what are the works of darkness that must be cast off, what ought not to be done in the light of faith, and what the manifested light of truth reproves:

### Verse 13

“**Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies.**” For most shameful intoxication commonly accompanies luxurious banquets. And what else do these in turn demand but indecent [Col. 0679B] and foul beds? What but strife and jealousy?

But those who walk honourably as in the day do what follows. Avoiding care for the flesh in its desires, and doing nothing through strife and jealousy, they hasten to put on the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and the other virtues. Whoever has admitted these into his affections is believed to have put on the Lord Jesus. For this follows:

### Verse 14

“**And make no provision for the flesh in its desires.**” Care for the flesh must indeed be taken, but not in its desires. Hunger and thirst are certain diseases, and, like fevers, they kill unless the remedy of food comes to their aid. When this is at hand, heaven, water, and earth serve our weakness through the consolation of God’s gifts [Col. 0679C]; misery is called pleasure.

Temperance teaches us to approach food as we would medicines. But while we pass from the distress of need to the repose of satiety, the snare of desire lies in wait for us in the very passage. For that passage itself is pleasure, and there is no other route by which one may pass where necessity compels one to pass. Although health is the reason for eating, a dangerous pleasantness attaches itself as though an attendant, and often tries to go before, so that what was thought to be done for health may be done for its own sake. Nor is the same measure sufficient for both. What is enough for health is too little for pleasure.

And often it becomes uncertain whether necessary care of the body is still seeking assistance, or whether voluntary desire is supplying the service of deception [Col. 0679D]. At this uncertainty the unhappy soul rejoices, preparing in it a defence of excuse and delighting that what is sufficient for moderation of health does not appear. Under the pretext of health, it casts a shadow over the business of pleasure.

For we are not forbidden to take care of the flesh, except in its desires; those who yield to these live miserably. But those who have undertaken war against them will have no peace so long as the flesh lusts against the spirit.

## Chapter XIV

### Verse 1

It follows: “**Receive the one who is weak in faith.**” After restraining the wantonness of desire in care for the flesh, he also prescribes a necessary measure of continence for those who, gathered from Jews and Gentiles into one Church, seemed to be creating division [Col. 0680A] because of the diversity of foods. Accordingly, restraining the scandals arising among them and their rash judgments against one another, he restores them to the unity of peace.

For the Jews, because even after the Gospel had begun to shine they abstained from foods prohibited in the law and could not so quickly be torn away from the ancient custom of the law, were thought by the Gentiles to be Judaizing. But the Gentiles, confidently receiving all things with thanksgiving in the freedom of faith and not even abstaining from things sacrificed to idols out of regard for the conscience of faith, were thought by the weaker believers—and especially by the Jews—to eat such things in awareness of the idol. Thus, creating divisions and judging one another, they seemed to divide unity.

For the sake of peace he teaches that each should for the present be left to his own understanding, because something by which conscience is injured little or not at all must sometimes be endured, lest one fall into that by which salvation is endangered [Col. 0680B]. He therefore commands that one weak in faith, and failing in discernment concerning foods, be received rather than rejected—that is, be invited to better things by word, example, and patience. He also forbids disputes concerning other people’s thoughts, so long as, because of the blindness of this mortal life, the intention with which something is done remains hidden.

### Verse 2

“**For one person**”—that is, one stronger in faith—“**believes that he may eat all things**”; another, not yet having attained this measure of faith, does not judge it lawful for himself. Let him therefore be left for the time being: “**let him eat vegetables**”; let him receive ordinary foods, until through practice and growth in faith he may be strengthened for better things.

### Verse 3

“**And let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat**” [Col. 0680C], as though he were Judaizing; “**and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats**,” as though he ate things sacrificed to idols with awareness of the idol, or things forbidden by the law through the vice of intemperance. For whether he eats or does not eat, “**God has received him**,” since God himself is the reason for either his eating or not eating.

It should be understood that righteousness concerning the use of foods lies neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in even-mindedly bearing want and in not corrupting oneself through abundance by lack of restraint; also in taking or not taking, at the proper time, those things whose use, not desire, must be restrained. For it makes no difference whatsoever what kinds of food you take to meet the body’s need [Col. 0680D], provided you conform in the kinds of food to those with whom you must live. Nor does the quantity you take matter, since we see that some people’s stomachs are more quickly filled, yet they avidly, intolerably, and altogether shamefully crave even the little by which they are filled. Others, however, are satisfied by rather more, but bear want more tolerably and can look calmly, without touching them, even upon dishes placed before their eyes, if the time, duty, or necessity requires it.

What matters more, then, is not what or how much food someone takes, according to what befits his station and the needs of his health, but with how much ease and serenity of mind he can lack it when he ought, or even must, lack it. Thus may be fulfilled in the Christian mind what the Apostle says: “I know how to abound [Col. 0681A], and I know how to endure want” (Phil. 4).

Not so those who had desired to eat meat, while manna rained upon them from heaven (Num. 11). They despised what they had and shamelessly demanded what they lacked, as though they ought rather to have asked—not that the food they lacked might be supplied to their unbecoming desire, but that their distaste for the food present might be healed. For when evils delight us and goods do not delight us, we should rather ask God that goods may delight us than that evils may be granted. Not because eating meat is evil, since every creature of God is good; but because it was no slight offense to reject what wisdom gave and seek what desire craved, although they did not even ask for it but murmured because it was lacking.

But so that we might know that God’s creature is not blameworthy, but rather stubborn disobedience [Col. 0681B] and disordered desire, the first human being found death not because of a pig but because of an apple (Gen. 3). Nor did Esau lose his birthright because of a chicken but because of lentils (Gen. 25). Therefore one must beware rash judgment in such matters. Hence it continues:

### Verse 4

“**Who are you, that you judge another’s servant?**” Here “to judge” is used for condemning or thinking ill of someone. This does not mean that the Apostle forbids believers every judgment, since elsewhere he says through them that the world, and even angels, will be judged. Rather, he declares that it is dangerous to judge hidden things.

For everyone who judges in such matters must beware two things: when either the reason is hidden, or it is not known what the person judged will become, though perhaps at present he seems to deserve judgment [Col. 0681C]. Those who do not love to correct their brother but to criticize him do not consider this. “**He stands or falls before his own master. And he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand.**” Lest the person who stands claim perseverance for himself, it is added: “God is able to make him stand.” Therefore, he who gives perseverance is able both to establish those who stand, so that they stand most steadfastly, and to restore those who have fallen.

### Verse 5

“**For one judges one day above another; another judges every day.**” “Who are you,” he says, “who judge another’s servant? Are you a human being or God? For one”—that is, a human being—“judges a day” set between the day past and the day to come; that is, he has power to judge only the present. Another is God [Col. 0681D], who judges every day: who knows, concerning the person who sins, what his zeal and will were before the fall into sin, what his intention is in sin, and what his conversion will be after sin.

To the one who has this knowledge concerning the sin of the sinner must be left judgment concerning the sinner. Yet it must be understood that in matters which ought to be subject to each person’s own discretion, and in matters unknown to us, rash judgment must be feared. But in acts in which God is manifestly offended, it is dangerous to defer judgment—unless perhaps a person doing the same things has lost the confidence to rebuke, and it is said to him [Col. 0682A]: “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will be able to cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Luke 16).

Therefore let neither be judged by the other; but let the one who is mindful of God in his work abound in his own understanding, that is, in God.

### Verse 6

“**For the one who regards the day**”—that is, who appreciates the work of a conscience active by day—“**regards it for the Lord**”; that is, his continence is sweet to him in the Lord. “**And the one who eats, eats for the Lord,**” when, in eating from faith, he glorifies God, the author of his faith. “Therefore both the one who eats and the one who does not eat either eat or do not eat for the Lord,” because each gives thanks to God.

Each acts for the Lord in what he does, because he acts in praise of him. For a good work is then done devoutly, rightly, and justly when it is done in praise of him from whom it is given that it may be done. In this disposition, everyone who advances does whatever he does for the Lord—that is, in praise of the one from whom he received the ability to do it. Hence comes thanksgiving, which is celebrated in the inward ministry of the faithful [Col. 0682B].

### Verses 7–9

“**For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.**” Whether we live or die, no one ought to live or die for himself, but for the glory of him whose we are. We serve him while living, and in dying we shall not cease to be his.

For if you will never cease to be his, and will never cease from his praise, could you fear that while you live here you are his, but after you have died you will not be his? Yet the Apostle says that “whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” [Col. 0682C], because he redeemed us at the price of his blood. And how does one who died lose a dead servant, when his own death is your price? Therefore, after saying, “whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s,” in order to show that price, he adds: “For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead.” Therefore the kingdom of death cannot hold the one for whom he died free among the dead.

### Verse 10

“**But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother?**” As though he said: Since we have the Lord as our judge, why do we judge one another? Those actions whose intention is uncertain ought to be interpreted in the better sense.

> **Note:** [Col. 0681D] Bede, on Luke, chapter 6.

For what is written, “You shall know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7), was said of manifest things [Col. 0682D] which cannot be done with a good intention, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and the like. We are permitted to judge these, as the Apostle says: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do we not judge those who are within?” (1 Cor. 5).

But concerning kinds of food, because any human foods may be taken indiscriminately with a good intention and a simple heart, without the fault of desire, the same Apostle forbids those who ate meat and drank wine to be judged by those who abstained from such foods. For concerning such matters, which can be done with a good and simple intention [Col. 0683A], although they can also be done with an evil intention, those people, being human, wished to pronounce judgment upon the hidden things of the heart, concerning which God alone judges.

Therefore it is rash, especially with a view to condemnation, to judge actions whose intention we do not know, since they can be done with either a good or an evil intention. The time will come when these matters shall be judged, when the Lord “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of hearts” (1 Cor. 4). Hence it follows: “For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.”

### Verse 11

“**For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to the Lord.**” The judgment seat of Christ is the divine power of his wisdom, by which, seated in himself, he orders and judges all things. To stand before it is for nothing to be able to remain hidden from the subtle judgment of his examination [Col. 0683B].

“**As I live, says the Lord.**” This is not an oath but a testimony to truth, as though he said: As truly as I live—whose living is identical with being, and from whom is all life—so truly do I speak, whose true speaking is true being, and from whom is all truth. This testimony of life or truth belongs to no one except him who lives so from himself that every life is also from him, and who so is that whatever truly is comes from him.

In saying “I,” the propriety of the divine essence is understood; in saying “I live,” the truth of essential life. Every knee bends to him because the force of his power will appear worthy of worship to all, when there will be no one who hides himself from his heat (Ps. 18), when it will be manifest to all that they themselves are manifest, and that no one can hide from the sight of the truth that penetrates all things [Col. 0683C]. For before him who alone truly is, confession will consist in its becoming apparent that the person is not, insofar as by sinning he has ceased to be, the more gravely because he has fallen away from him from whom everything has whatever being it has.

Therefore, he says, since we must be presented before so fearful a judge, let us no longer judge one another rashly.

### Verse 13

“**But judge this rather**”—that is, discern and observe by judicial reasoning—“**that you do not place before a brother**,” whether Jew or Gentile, “**a stumbling-block**” of evil example, “**or an occasion of offence**” causing grief. *Skandalon* in Greek, or *scandalum* in Latin, means a striking of the foot. Our way is evangelical teaching, whose end is Christ; the foot carrying us on this way is the affection of the mind, which naturally tends forward but, when corrupted by fault, quickly stumbles [Col. 0683D].

There are travellers on this road: blind pride; enviousness that sees; humility that does not see; charity that sees. For the road contains both evil and good persons, but the end distinguishes them. Blind pride does not see where it is going and disdains to be led. Envy, supposing that it sees for itself, judges all whom it has not led—though it wishes to lead no one—to be wandering. Such persons often give scandal to one another and are scandalized by one another. They often stumble so as to fall; and once fallen, they rarely and with difficulty add the further step of rising again.

Humility that does not see holds out its hand to be led; concerning it it is said: “Cursed is he who places a stumbling-block before the blind” (Deut. 27). Charity that sees chooses, in making progress, to go as though more slowly, so that the other may not be abandoned [Col. 0684A]. The Apostle wished them to be such persons, to whom he preached righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Such people take every care not to cause scandal and are not easily scandalized.

### Verse 14

“**I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him, except for the one who considers something to be common: for that person it is common.**” “Nothing is common through him,” that is, through faith in him, except for the person who, lacking faith, considers something common; for that person it is common—not in its nature, which God certainly created good, but insofar as it becomes common, that is, unclean, for one who eats without faith.

For just as things sacrificed to idols, which were unclean, were made clean by the conscience of those who received them faithfully, so things that were clean were made unclean by the judgment of those who received them without faith [Col. 0684B]. This concerns the Jews, who sinned by refusing to eat foods forbidden by the law. It next concerns the Gentiles, who sinned by eating without asking questions and receiving all things, even at the cost of scandalizing the weak.

For Jews ought to avoid the sins and vices which they were commanded symbolically to avoid in kinds of food by the law; but they ought to receive with grace and faith the foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving. Gentiles, however, ought to abstain from foods lawful by faith when these caused scandal to brothers weaker in faith. For in hope of correction, what had become deeply embedded in the Jews through the long custom of the law had to be endured for the present, because it could not quickly or easily be torn away from them [Col. 0684C]. But the Gentiles had for the present to forgo what was allowed by freedom of faith and yielded no, or no great, benefit, yet was not expedient because it endangered a brother’s salvation. Hence it follows:

### Verse 15

“**For if your brother is grieved because of your food, you no longer walk according to charity. Do not destroy by your food one for whom Christ died.**” Accordingly, for a fitting necessity we ought sometimes to forgo lawful things; but we are commanded to commit unlawful things under no necessity.

### Verse 16

“**Therefore let not our good be blasphemed.**” What is this “our good”? It is the gift peculiar to Christ’s disciples, of which he himself says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” [Col. 0684D] (John 13). For just as Christ’s disciples are recognized by the sign of mutual charity, so through the neglect of charity the whole splendour of Christian religion is at first sight obscured.

Then the remarkable teacher, restraining the faults of the present time by the authority of the future mystery, and disclosing the mystery of the kingdom of heaven in order to establish the pattern of the Church, says:

### Verse 17

“**For the kingdom of God is not food and drink.**” As though he said: Why do we concern ourselves so greatly with foods, when we hasten toward the kingdom of heaven? There, just as they neither marry nor are given in marriage, so neither do they eat or drink; rather, they are like the angels of God.

Therefore, by the Apostle’s most complete doctrine and evident declaration, it has been determined that in the kingdom of heaven there is no necessity either for food [Col. 0685A] or drink, but there are righteousness and peace. And because joy of the flesh commonly accompanies food and drink, he adds here “joy,” but “in the Holy Spirit.” These things work the kingdom of heaven in us here; in the future they bring us to where these same things are possessed more surely and firmly. Righteousness is in action; peace is in the heart or conscience; joy is in the Lord. Whoever has these already has the kingdom of God within himself.

### Verses 18–19

“**For the one who in this serves Christ is pleasing to God and approved by men**”—in righteousness, while in peace he dwells well with himself. Therefore, from the affection of peace, which we enjoy inwardly, let us outwardly “pursue the things of peace”; and from the affection of righteousness, “let us preserve the things of edification.” What does righteousness demand more clearly [Col. 0685B] than that, on account of food, we should not destroy in our brothers the work of Christ’s redemption?

### Verse 20

“**For all things are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through an occasion of offence,**” because he wounds the conscience of inward righteousness while, through that by which he himself is refreshed, his brother’s soul is endangered.

### Verse 21

“**It is good, therefore, for a person not to eat meat, nor drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened.**” God permitted meat to human desire; human curiosity itself devised wine for desire. Neither, indeed, is natural. Thus, when the Lord fed those people in the wilderness, no mention was made of drink, since what is natural was available [Col. 0685C] near the Sea of Tiberias (John 6).

Therefore it is good to abstain, especially from things required not so much by the necessity of life as by fleshly desire, and from things by which a brother is offended: disturbed as though he wished to depart from faith, not knowing what to hold; or scandalized and grieved; or weakened in faith, not indeed departing from it, but beginning to doubt.

### Verse 22

“**Do you have faith? Have it within yourself,**” where no one may take it from you; have it also before God, who approves it, not before the weak person who is scandalized. In this way we pursue the things of peace. For children of this age, while each seeks his own interests, pursue peace; but children of the kingdom of heaven pursue it even when it flees, with danger, labour, loss of possessions, and sometimes even loss of reputation [Col. 0685D].

For where true and certain faith cleanses all peoples from contamination through the acknowledgment of faith, every food also is purified by word and prayer. Yet because what is good becomes evil to one who eats through an occasion of offence, one should abstain from what is lawful but not expedient. It follows:

### Verse 23

“**Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves.**” This is the same as saying: Blessed is the person who so conducts his good that it does not become a scandal to others. For the person who, while embracing what he approves, neglects the salvation of a weak brother, judges himself in what he approves and makes himself liable to judgment and condemnation.

This cannot be avoided here. For if a person strong in faith believes that he may eat all things, but the weak person, following the strong person’s example, eats all things without attaining the faith whose act he imitates [Col. 0686A], the one who eats not from faith is condemned; and the one who compelled him to this by his example is judged in his own action.

### Verse 24

“**For everything that is not from faith is sin.**” For not merely every act, but the entire life of unbelievers, is sin. Where knowledge of immutable truth is absent, virtue is false even in the best moral conduct. For, as has already been said, and must often be said and firmly believed, the best works are done by a human being, but faith is wrought in a human being. Without faith no good works are done by anyone, because whatever is not from faith is sin.

Therefore the one who eats without faith sins; but the one by whose example the weak person sins judges himself. In its own kind, what cannot yet be led to something better must be cared for [Col. 0686B].

## Chapter XV

### Verse 1

“**We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak,**” not so that they may remain so forever, but so that they may be healed in their proper order. For it is better first to soothe a harmful wound with ointment and gentle handling than rashly to inflame it, until the patient wisdom of the physician brings matters to the point at which it may be opened without danger.

“**And not please ourselves.**” The reward of those who please themselves, says a certain man of God, is the very fact of pleasing themselves, when, neglecting the charity of their brothers, they seek not to please them for their good but to please themselves according to the choice of their own will. Hence follows:

### Verses 2–3

“**Let each of us please his neighbour [Col. 0686C] for good, unto edification. For Christ also,**” when he saw the time had come for the building up of universal salvation, did not wish, for the public good, to please himself by private self-love. He said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26).

Then also the “reproaches of those reproaching” God the Father concerning his Passion, when they said, “Let him deliver him now, if he will; for he said: I am the Son of God” (Matt. 27), fell upon him when they did to him whatever they wished.

### Verse 4

“**For whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.**” Therefore, for the recollection of our faith, the consolation of hope, and the exhortation of charity, we read the prophetic and apostolic books. Their meanings harmonize with one another, and by that harmony, like a heavenly trumpet, they awaken us from the torpor of mortal life and call us to the prizes of the heavenly calling [Col. 0686D].

Finally, considering that every good which we can possess, whether in nature, institutions, moral conduct, or virtues, comes from God’s gift and not from ourselves, he concludes in prayer:

### Verse 5

“**May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ, that with one mind and one mouth you may glorify God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.**” For just as he himself is our salvation because he gives salvation, and our refuge because we flee to him, so he is the God of patience and consolation [Col. 0687A], because we are patient from him and await consolation only from him.

For patience or consolation does not come from the Scriptures, though it sometimes comes through the Scriptures. For not only does patience come from him, but, as the Prophet says, he himself is our patience (Ps. 70), he himself is consolation, consoling the one who loves him only from himself. For when does he console that person except when he grants him to perceive him? And when we perceive the same thing toward one another, what is so good, what so delightful? Is this not for brothers to dwell together as one?

And this is according to Jesus Christ, who said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15). He also pours the sap of the good root into the grafted branches: “As,” he says, “I have loved you.” Far be it from Christ’s disciples that there should be fleshly affection [Col. 0687B], or any love that does not tend toward the same thing. All this is so that, “with one mind,” believing in the heart unto righteousness, and “with one mouth,” confessing unto salvation, “you may glorify God,” who creates all things and through the Son renews and restores what has grown old. “Let your good works shine before people,” he says, “that they may see them and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

This is the honour by which God is to be honoured by us. He himself, however, is our honour, to whom the Prophet says: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured” (Ps. 138).

### Verse 7

“**Therefore receive one another, as Christ also received you, unto the glory of God.**” For we shall not love one another unless we receive one another. We receive one another when we see our brother suffering need and do not close our hearts against him, but receive him into the bosom of charity. We receive one another when the Jew does not judge the Gentile, nor the Gentile the Jew, but we become one body and one spirit to the glory of God, just as Christ also received us—rejecting neither, reproving neither because of the mark of his origin [Col. 0687C].

He shows that Christ received both when he says:

VERS. 8–9.—“For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision, for the truth of God, in order to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy.” For one wall came from the circumcision, joining itself to the cornerstone; but that stone would not make a corner unless it received another wall from the Gentiles. The wall [Col. 0687D] from the Jews properly pertains to truth; hence he says, “for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.” But this other wall, from the Gentiles, pertains to mercy, concerning which he likewise says, “that the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy.” Thus in Christ mercy and truth have met one another.

Yet it was not fitting to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs, unless the dogs, humbled to gather the crumbs falling from their Lord’s table, should through that very humility be exalted, become human beings, and deserve to approach the table itself (Matt. XV). Moreover, he granted the Jewish people this singular honor: that the glory of his presence should dwell in their land. There he was born; there he lived; and from there he began to preach, because from Zion comes the beauty of his splendor. From there too the apostles were first sent to [Col. 0688A] them. There were the patriarchs; from there came the prophets. There, coming from the seed of Abraham, he was manifested; to them he was sent, their apostle, as he himself said: “I am not sent except to the sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XIX). For this reason the Apostle calls him “a minister of the circumcision,” that is, of the Jews.

“But that the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy, as it is written: Therefore I shall confess you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.” Through me, says the Son to the Father, the Gentiles shall confess you, and through their good conduct you will become more widely known. This confession is one of praise. And when he says, “I shall sing,” it is the new song which he himself sings in us, by whose grace we sing. Hence elsewhere he says, “singing in your hearts to the Lord” (Col. III). For this joy is inward, [Col. 0688B] where the voice of love both sings and is heard by him who is praised by that very voice. For this song is to love freely, with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength. And again the Holy Spirit says in the song of Deuteronomy:

VERS. 10–12.—“Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people. And again: Praise the Lord, all Gentiles, and magnify him, all peoples. And again Isaiah says: There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises up to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope.” Jesse is interpreted “he is mine.” For at Christ’s coming, the believer says: “He is mine,” because he who says to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. III), is present as God to the believer. He shall rise up, moreover, so that he may be both man and above man: having no sin, neither coming through sin by the common law of birth, and taking away the sin of the world. Therefore, because [Col. 0688C] the Gentiles will deservedly hope in him, he adds in prayer:

VERS. 13.—“May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.” This prayer seems to contain the power of faith, hope, and charity, when it prays for the believer the joy of a well-pacified conscience, full joy, and abundance in hope and charity, which is the particular power of the Holy Spirit. Our God is properly the God of hope, in whom the hope of believers is not put to shame; but all the gods of the Gentiles are demons and the works of their hands.

VERS. 14.—“But I myself also am certain concerning you, my brethren, that you yourselves are full of love, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able [Col. 0688D] to admonish one another.” Here the sails are now loosed, as it were, in the harbor of silence; after so great an ocean of profound meanings and the transport of foreign merchandise, he first commends to them his own goodwill, which he brought among those whom he knew to abound in it. Then he also proclaims the fullness among them of knowledge and love, which is sufficient rather to admonish than to need admonition.

VERS. 15–17.—“But I have written to you somewhat boldly, brethren, as one bringing you to remembrance, because of the grace given to me by God, that I may be a minister of Christ Jesus among the Gentiles, consecrating the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.” Boldly indeed. For unless this proceeded from confidence in the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, it was great boldness in a man still abiding amid the darkness of this murky ignorance to venture, as though investigating them, upon such high and deep recesses of God’s wisdom: concerning law and grace, the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and very many other matters which he says he wrote “in part,” because, so long as we are thus situated—where we know in part and prophesy in part—complete understanding of such meanings is granted to no one.

But in this way he consecrated—or rather, as the Greek more correctly has it, “sacrificed”—the Gospel of God, in which a certain high-priestly ministry is also displayed, so that “the offering of the Gentiles might become acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.” For the goodwill and teaching of a teacher, when understood by hearers and dispensed in its proper time and manner, contributes greatly to them. [Col. 0689B] Hence he adds further, as though commending the merchandise which he conveys: “He has,” he says, “glory toward God.” And qualifying what he had said, he says, “in Christ our Lord.” For although every good of ours is the glory of him whose grace it is, yet the one who glories in the Lord does glory. But in what does he glory?

VERS. 18.—“For I dare not speak of anything except what Christ accomplishes through me.” Again, a commendation of grace: not what I do, but what Christ accomplishes through me. For Christ acts, but acts through me. Christ acts in me, but through me causes his action to appear outwardly; for this seems to be the force of the word “accomplishes.” At the same time one must understand that, for preaching, the consciousness of holy love builds up more than practice in speech, when the one who teaches reads inwardly what he says.

VERS. 18–19.—“For the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deeds; by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit.” Though about to speak of deeds and of the powers of signs and wonders, he placed before all else, even before the word of his preaching, the obedience of the Gentiles, ascribing all that follows more to their merit than to his own labor. At the end, however, he devoutly assigns both the obedience of the Gentiles itself and everything accomplished through their merit and his labor to the power of the Holy Spirit. The prudent preacher of grace makes all things return to the place from which they proceed. Then, commending his own diligence in the Gospel, he adds:

VERS. 19–21.—“So that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have filled all the intervening region with the Gospel of God. But I have preached it in such a way not where Christ had been named, lest I should build upon another’s foundation, but as it is written: Those to whom no announcement was made concerning him shall see; and those who have not heard shall understand.” For I did not wish to invade the labors of others; rather, by casting the seed of the word everywhere, I was preparing the lands for harvesters who would follow. “For this reason my long circuit greatly hindered me from coming to you,” although willingness was not lacking.

VERS. 23–24.—“But now, having no further place in these regions, and having had for many years a desire to come to you, when I begin my journey into Spain, I hope, as I pass through, to see you, and to be sent forward by you there, if I have first in some measure [Col. 0690A] enjoyed your company.” Admirable is the foresight of the teacher of the Gentiles. Though he desired to labor among the Romans and had the opportunity at hand, he neither made a promise nor pressed himself upon them. Yet he offered them his presence, saying that he would come to Rome not for Rome’s sake but for Spain’s, lest the word of the Gospel in his mouth become less precious if he came upon unwilling hearers as though shameless and importunate. Yet, announcing that he would first enjoy their company only in part and, as it were, in passing, he commends his affection for them; then, saying that he was to be sent onward by them, he also wins their love for himself. For a teacher of the Church must take every precaution not to frighten hearers away by any appearance of pride, but likewise not to make the word of God in his mouth cheap through excessive self-abasement. [Col. 0690B] Thus it is said of Samuel, when he was sought by all, that “the word of the Lord was precious” (1 Sam. III).

VERS. 25–28.—“Now therefore I shall depart for Jerusalem, ministering to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have resolved to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem. For it pleased them, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things. Therefore, when I have completed this and assigned to them this fruit, I shall depart through you into Spain.”

For the believers from among the Jews, having recognized the truth and been converted to him whom they had crucified, partly through envy and partly through error, mortifying the desires of the old man and burning with the newness of spiritual life, sold, as the Lord had commanded in the Gospel, all that they possessed and laid the prices of their goods at the apostles’ feet, so that the apostles might distribute to each according to need. Living harmoniously in Christian love, they called nothing their own; rather, all things were common to them, and they were one soul and one heart in the Lord (Acts IV). [Col. 0690C] Then they themselves suffered persecution from their fellow citizens, the carnal Jews, so that Christ might be preached more widely through their dispersion.

Therefore the Apostle, while establishing churches among all the Gentiles to whom he sowed the Gospel, earnestly commanded that, since they had come from the worship of idols and were inexperienced in worshipping one God, and thus could not easily attain the summit of this perfection, they should make offerings for the poor among the saints [Col. 0690D] in Judaea. He regarded the latter as soldiers, the former as provincial suppliers of pay.

It follows:

VERS. 29.—“But I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing.” The whole world shares in the abundance of Christ’s blessing which the Apostle brought to the Romans when he came.

VERS. 30–32.—“I beseech you therefore, brethren, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit, that you assist me in your prayers to God, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judaea, and that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, so that I may come to you with joy, by the will of God, and be refreshed together with you.” In saying “in prayers,” [Col. 0691A] the Greek seems rather to convey the struggle of prayer, so that we too may know that the assaults both of our vices and of spiritual wickedness must never be absent from our prayers. Who, indeed, can be secure concerning himself when the Apostle seeks from his disciples the assistance of their prayers?

At the same time observe how great is his concern for the saints and how great his reverence for them: secure concerning himself and his salvation, he is anxious only that the offering of his service should be conveyed in such a way as to be acceptable to the saints. And so it happened. For once he had completed the service of his offering in Jerusalem, he was seized by the Jews and, bound, was handed over to the Gentiles. Thus the necessity of appealing to Caesar arose, and he was brought to Rome.

VERS. 33.—“Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.” He concludes with peace, having begun with peace, saying: “Grace to you and peace.”

## CHAPTER XVI

VERS. 1–5.—“I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry of the Church at Cenchreae, that you receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever matter she may need of you. For she herself has also assisted many, including me. Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life; to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the Churches of the Gentiles; and greet the Church in their house. Greet Epaenetus, beloved to me, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ Jesus. Greet Mary, [Col. 0691C] who has labored greatly among you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow captives, who are notable among the apostles and who were in Christ Jesus before me.”

Perhaps these persons were joined to the Apostle by a closer bond of spiritual love, and for this reason he calls them kinsmen; and they were of higher merit, for which reason he calls them fellow captives. He knew that they bore painfully the exile and hardships of this life through love for their heavenly homeland; and therefore, for their consolation, he calls himself their fellow captive.

VERS. 8–16.—“Greet Ampliatus, most beloved to me in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker, and Stachys, my beloved. Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. Greet those of the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet [Col. 0691D] those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who have labored in the Lord. Greet Persis, most beloved, who has labored greatly in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother—his in the flesh, but mine in the spirit. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegontia, Hermas, Patrocla, Hermes, and those with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympias, and all the saints who are with them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the Churches of Christ greet you.”

It is as though he said: Why do I separately divide those who send greetings and those who receive them? Everyone who is in the Church of Christ is greeted by all the Churches of Christ.

VERS. 17.—“But I urge you, brethren, to watch those who cause dissensions and stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and turn away from them.” It is plain that dissensions arise from stumbling-blocks, divisions from dissensions, and from these come heresies and schisms. But if the Apostle commands that those who cause stumbling-blocks be avoided, how much more those who divide the Church through dissensions!

VERS. 18.—“For such persons do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly,” caring not whose heart they may empty, provided they can fill their own belly. He seems here to touch upon certain plagues of heresy already springing up in the Church, deceiving innocent hearts through sweet, as he says, speeches and blessings; making, according to the prophet, darkness light and light darkness, bitter sweet [Col. 0692B] and sweet bitter (Isa. V); speaking agreeable sweetness, flattering vices, and in all these things seeking nothing except what belongs to the belly.

VERS. 19.—“For your obedience has been made known in every place.” This is what teachers of the Church must most earnestly fear and guard against: lest the craftiness of the wicked misuse the goodness of the simple for evil. For behold, if the praiseworthy obedience of the Romans should fall among preachers of this sort—secret in deceiving, cunning in persuading, smooth in suggesting the things of the flesh—what could be more dangerous? Therefore he adds: “I rejoice in you.” I rejoice in you because of your obedience, but I fear for you because of the enemy’s cunning. “But I want you to be wise in what is good [Col. 0692C] and simple in what is evil.” Wise in good is the one who immediately, as though naturally, relishes a good purpose; simple in evil is the one whom the duplicity of evils does not deceive while he holds in his mind the very form of the good, because however evil’s form may be adapted, it cannot be fitted to the form which he bears in his mind.

VERS. 20.—“But may the God of peace swiftly crush Satan beneath your feet.” It was said to the woman—or rather, to the serpent—when God punished the sin of the first human being: “She shall watch your head, but you shall watch her heel” (Gen. III). The twisting serpent, then—Satan—watches your heel when you slip from the Lord’s path, so that you may fall and he may possess you when fallen. But watch his first suggestion, that is, his head. If you have despised promised gain because of the harm to your soul, [Col. 0692D] you have trampled the serpent’s head. If you act thus often, the God of peace, who makes peace, will be with you; and the harmful serpent’s head, often trampled, will begin to be unable to rise. But you will crush all Satan beneath your feet when you gain complete victory over desire, so as fully to fulfill the commandment of the law: “You shall not covet.” Happy, but rare, is the conscience which deserves to receive this fully in the present life. He then adds the source from which this may come: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

VERS. 20–27.—“Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I, Tertius, who wrote this epistle in the Lord, greet you. Gaius, my host, and the whole [Col. 0693A] Church greet you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and Quartus the brother greet you. The grace of God be with you all. Amen. To him who is able to establish you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages, but now disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures, according to the command of the eternal God, made known among all the Gentiles for obedience to faith—to God alone wise, through Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.”

That is: To him who is able to establish you—to God alone wise—be glory for ages of ages. But the phrase inserted, “through Jesus Christ,” is ambiguous: should it be taken with “to God alone wise through Jesus Christ,” so that God the Father alone is understood to be wise through Jesus Christ, being wise not by participation but by begetting Wisdom, which is Christ Jesus? Or is it not God’s wisdom, but rather glory that is through Jesus Christ—to God alone wise?

But who would dare say that God the Father comes to be wise through Jesus Christ, when there can be no doubt that he is wise according to his own substance, and when it is rather the substance of the Son which is from the begetting Father than the substance of the Father which is from the begotten Son? It remains, then, that glory is through Jesus Christ to God alone wise: that is, the clear knowledge accompanied by praise through which God, the Trinity, became known among the Gentiles. [Col. 0693B] And this is through Jesus Christ because, not to mention other things, he himself commanded all nations to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and there especially the glory of the indivisible Trinity was commended.

God, therefore, who is the Trinity itself, is rightly called alone wise because he alone is wise according to his substance, not according to an accidental or additional participation in wisdom, as every rational creature is wise. But the addition of “to whom,” so that “to whom be glory” is said, when it would have sufficed to say simply, “but to him be glory,” indicates an unusual idiom of our language; it does not suggest a meaning that we should seek out or about which we should be uncertain. For what would be lacking in the meaning if it were said, “to him be glory,” to whom through Jesus Christ be glory? For “to him through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory” is the same as “to whom through Jesus Christ be glory”; but the former is an unusual and the latter a customary order of words.

“He who is able,” he says, “to establish you [Col. 0694A] according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ.” Paul’s Gospel and Christ’s preaching contain nothing discordant or different, since one proceeds from the other. “According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages.” What is this mystery except that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us? For his humiliation became our exaltation; through his weakness we were made strong.

But one must inquire what eternal times he means. For if he intended eternity to be understood, then surely Christ’s mystery was not hidden from eternity: its reason and manner always existed in eternity, which is God, even before any time existed. For there was no time before creation; indeed, times would never exist unless there were a creature altered by some change. From the motion or change of such a creature, when one thing that cannot exist at the same time as another yields and another succeeds, time follows in shorter or longer intervals of duration.

But he says that the mystery was silent to some in those eternal times, yet known to God alone wise; now, however, it has been disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures according to the command of the eternal God, for the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles. But what is the force here of adding “eternal” to the name “God”? Perhaps the eternal God commanded—that is, God commanded from eternity—that what had been hidden from the other generations of the ages should now, that is, in the time of grace, be disclosed through the Scriptures of the prophets, when the Lord opened the disciples’ understanding so that [Col. 0694C] they might understand them (Luke XXIV).

Moreover, it would not be absurd to call “eternal times,” during which Christ’s mystery was hidden from humankind, all that long stretch of time before Christ’s coming. Although it was disclosed in part to certain patriarchs and prophets, as though in riddles and figures, it was disclosed to no one as it now has been. Especially since elsewhere the Apostle says that even angels advanced through the Gospel in the knowledge of truth, and that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God was made known to principalities and powers in the heavens (Eph. III). What was known to God alone wise was disclosed in the time of grace through the preaching of the apostles, so that, as they preached among all nations, faith might be obeyed.

[Col. 0695]

# TWO BOOKS ON THE NATURE OF BODY AND SOUL

Written under the name of Theophilus, that is, “one who loves God.”

*(Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium, through the labor and study of Brother Bertrand Tissier, doctor of theology of Bonfont in Therascia, prior of the same order. Bonfont, 1660, folio, vol. IV, p. 65.)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0695] A famous response of Delphic Apollo is reported among the Greeks: “Man, know yourself.” Solomon also says this—or rather, Christ in the Song of Songs: “Unless,” he says, “you have known yourself, go out” (Song I). For the person who does not dwell upon what belongs to himself through contemplation of wisdom necessarily enters what belongs to others through the vanity of curiosity. Therefore, since scarcely even his own understanding suffices for any person capable of reason, unless aided by grace, to know himself—and since this knowledge benefits him only if, from what he himself is, he ascends to him from whom he is and who is above him—he errs and acts most foolishly who disperses his understanding outside himself among things foreign to him, when nature—or rather God, the author of nature—has assigned him so great a task of activity within himself.

Therefore, in order that we may investigate, in some degree, our microcosm—that is, the lesser world, namely the human being—both inwardly and outwardly, that is, in soul and body, so that through the visible or sensible things understood in ourselves we may rise to the author of all visible and invisible things, let us first examine certain matters concerning the nature of the body, then those concerning the soul. Know, however, that what you read is not my own, but in part belongs to philosophers or physicians, and in part to ecclesiastical teachers; nor have I collected merely their opinions, but their very words, spoken or written as they published them, excerpts from their books which I have assembled here into one work.

# BOOK ONE: THE PHYSICS OF THE HUMAN BODY

[Col. 0695]

[Col. 0695A] Every living body is formed from earth, that is, composed of four things. For being formed from earth is one thing; the things of which it consists are another. The things of which it consists are the four elements. Each of the elements, however, contains only one quality: fire, heat; air, moisture; water, coldness; earth, dryness. But fire, since it is mobile, acquires dryness from motion and is hot and dry. Air, because it is beneath fire, receives from it what is proper and natural to fire, namely heat; and it is hot from fire, moist from itself. Water is placed beneath air, and therefore receives moisture from it, while it is cold of itself. Earth is beneath water, and therefore cold from it, but dry in itself.

Accordingly, according to Hippocrates, if a living body consisted of one element, it would never suffer pain, because, being one, it would have nothing from which to suffer. But earth becomes mud through water; water, rarefied, heated, and evaporated, becomes air; air, condensed and gathered, becomes water; and so with the remaining elements. This is how corruption comes about. From these same four elements four humors are also generated in the living body; for this reason they are called the elements’ children. As the elements supply to the world, so these supply to the living body the material and order of life and health—if they are administered in their own manner and order and are not corrupted through defect or neglect. Otherwise, just as water, when thickened, changes into earth, and earth, when made muddy, changes into water, so the humors, when corrupted into one another or by one another, corrupt and destroy their own body, which they ought to vivify and order.

Thus, in the living body there is its own primary and natural complexion, the conjunction of the elements within it. If this is balanced and well composed, so that contraries are not attacked or destroyed by contraries, but hot things are tempered by cold, cold by hot, and so with the rest, a good complexion results; and, with nature in agreement, there arises *eucrasia*, that is, the good tempering of the four qualities. For while natural things remain in due balance, it is impossible for a human body to be afflicted by any disease, if, as has been said, it is *eucratic*, that is, of good complexion. But when these are out of balance, the body must be altered. More on these matters elsewhere.

Now we must see whence the four humors themselves arise or are nourished. Every food, wherever it is obtained, consists of the four elements, as was shown above concerning the living body. But the many and differing ways in which the nature of the elements is disposed in edible things according to heat and coldness, dryness and moisture, are set forth in the *Book of Degrees*. When food is taken, the mouth first prepares it into fine and minute portions by means of teeth and tongue. The tongue indeed serves; the teeth break and grind. Thus prepared, the food is conveyed to the stomach through the throat and the *meris*, scarcely extending the power of taste to the measure of a palm.

The *meris* is a long, round, hollow, and internally shaggy organ. It has within it long hairs, some crosswise and others directed upward toward the mouth. The upward-directed hairs naturally draw in food; those that run crosswise in the stomach constrict it and, through constriction, transform it into juice, gradually sending it down into the mouth of the stomach. The stomach [Col. 0697C] has two mouths, one upper and the other lower; these are also called gates because they close and open at times. The upper mouth of the stomach closes after receiving food until it is digested. Then, retaining from that digestion what it finds suitable for its nourishment, it expels the rest downward when the lower gate has opened.

The stomach performs these functions through four natural powers: appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive. Certain other parts of the body also possess these, but especially the four parts called the foundations of the body: the brain, because of the animal or sensory power; the heart, because of the spiritual power; the liver, because of the natural power; and the genitals, because of the generative power. The appetitive and digestive powers produce desire; the intermediate retentive power serves digestion by holding the food so that it does not return whence it descended, constricting it and gradually conveying it downward in portions, and arranging digestion as is appropriate.

The appetite, retention, and expulsion of the stomach, as was said concerning the *meris*, occur through the agency of certain hairs extending lengthwise and crosswise through the stomach; certain lower intestines beneath the stomach also possess them. These processes belong to the first digestion, which is carried out in the stomach. Digestion of anything is boiling through natural heat. What is expelled through the lower gate is received by the intestine called the duodenum, so named because it measures twelve fingers. [Col. 0698A] As soon as digestion has occurred, and the thing digested has been altered through digestion, the evacuation of feculent matter follows.

Other intestines also receive what is expelled: three thin ones above, around the mouth of the stomach, and three large ones below. There is, moreover, one lower intestine called the thin intestine. After the digestion which we have said occurs in the stomach, when that which is expelled descends into it, it remains there for some time, until by a certain second digestion that juice is more thoroughly purified and refined; then, through the veins called mesaraic, it sends what is fine and pure to the liver.

It should be known that, in digestion, some foods alter but are not altered, such as scammony (*diagridium*); others are altered and alter, such as onions and garlic, which are both foods and medicines. The aforementioned liver, receiving the juice through the aforesaid veins and through what is called the portal vein, transforms it into its own nature, to be digested again. For whatever in it is fiery is taken up by red choler for its nourishment; whatever is airy, by blood; whatever is watery or moist, by phlegm; whatever is coarse and earthy, by black bile (*melancholia*).

Thus the four humors, generated in the liver and distributed from the liver through the whole body, if they proceed according to nature’s proper rule, produce one condition of health despite their differing qualities, cooperating with and helping one another. Red choler, being hot and dry, refines the blood by its heat and accompanies it without sharpness, once refined, so that the blood may provide suitable nourishment to those members which are fine and require fine food. Blood, being hot and moist, tempers choler’s dryness by its moisture. Phlegm, being cold and moist, serves the blood’s heat by its coldness and relieves the dryness of black bile by its moisture, agreeing with it in coldness.

And note that the children of the elements proceed according to the way of their fathers. For the elements act in the greater world in the same manner as the four humours act in the lesser world, which is man—that is, the microcosm—as was said above: harmonizing through their very diversity, and through harmonious diversity producing the most beautiful unity of their order.

From this digestion likewise a gentle and sweet vapour rises, softly touches the brain, and oppresses its ventricles [Col. 0698D], so greatly that it lulls all its activities: this is sleep. In sleep, while all the powers of the soul cease, the natural power alone remains active; and it works then all the more intensely because the whole of nature is free for it. But the soul, resting within, with all the offices of the senses excluded, turns over within itself things past, present, and future: and these are dreams.

When these four humours are produced and formed in the liver, nevertheless not each one is separated into its own distinct form; rather, according to the form of the liver itself, which appears sanguine, all appear confusedly as of the sanguine kind. Thus generated, each is distributed for nourishing and governing the whole body through its proper channels, namely veins and arteries, in this manner. First, foods become white in the middle of the stomach [Col. 0699A], that is, phlegmatic; near the lower regions, close to the liver, they become like watery blood; when cooked in the liver, blood; more thoroughly cooked, red bile; excessively cooked, black bile.

But red bile, issuing from the liver and pouring itself in many ways into the body, descends through a certain vein toward the lower parts with a kind of corrosive action, and provokes the evacuation through excretion of the sediment which remained. Whoever compels nature before its prompting acts against health. He also harms health who, when the prompting comes, postpones nature’s necessity. Red bile, entering the stomach through another branch of a vein, produces digestion and appetite there. It is also divided among other parts of the body, and the gall bladder receives its residues. For it is the office of the gall bladder to cleanse the blood of red bile, lest, remaining with the blood [Col. 0699B], it inflame it. When red bile predominates excessively by itself, setting everything ablaze, it produces the worst diseases.

Blood, issuing from the liver through two veins, one of which is called the hollow vein and the other the portal vein, diffuses itself into innumerable parts through veins and branches of veins. One enters the stomach and, if it finds any food there, carries it thence to the liver. Another enters the breadth of the stomach, carrying food there from the liver, so that the stomach, digesting food, may take nourishment for itself. Another proceeds as far as the spleen and draws from the liver the dregs of the blood. But before it arrives there, it is divided into many parts and is sent to nourish the flesh. Physicians call this vein *panagras* [uncertain reading]; for it is blood’s particular function [Col. 0699C] to nourish the body.

It is also proper to blood to imitate the quality of air, whose nature, as has already been said, it possesses, insofar as it undergoes very many changes in itself, like air. For if it is thick and turbid, it signifies excessive heat and moisture; if thin and watery, it signifies coldness of the liver; if red and fetid, it signifies infection by red bile and its own putrefaction; if foamy, windiness; if clotted and watery, it signifies excessive phlegm and a failure of the expulsive faculty. For that which ought to have been expelled through urine, sweat, or other means has remained in the blood.

Phlegm is half-digested food; therefore it is cold and moist. Phlegm sometimes serves as nourishment for the body when blood is lacking, and, once digested, it is changed into blood. [Col. 0699D] If phlegm is emitted liquid and without taste, it is natural; if sweet, it is infected with blood; if salty, infected with red bile; if acrid, with melancholy; if glassy and clotted, it arises from coldness. It will be recognized from its effects in this way. If natural phlegm abounds, it diminishes the appetite for food and drink because of the abundance of moisture in the stomach; it lessens the flavour of food and drink, just as water mixed with any food is accustomed to lessen its flavour. If sweet phlegm predominates, every food tastes sweet and is quickly digested. If salty phlegm predominates, diminution of food follows, together with a bitter mouth and desire for drink. Acrid phlegm, however, weakens appetite, or rather provokes appetite for food when food has not been digested and has collected in the lower part of the stomach, leaving the upper part empty and craving food. [Col. 0700A] Glassy phlegm destroys food and drink and produces chills because of excessive coldness.

These four humours, therefore, seeking the upper regions, are cleansed there by a certain natural purification: bile through the ears, melancholy through the eyes, phlegm through the nostrils and mouth. Urine, however, is the filtering and cleansing of the blood. Since blood and phlegm, because of their moisture and abundance, are more readily conveyed and expel their superfluities, they discharge them through the kidneys and bladder. They have no vessels of their own, as red bile has the gall bladder and melancholy the spleen. For melancholy has its seat in the spleen, where it is strained from the blood of the liver, and is then sent back to the mouth of the stomach in order to strengthen appetite.

This is the distribution of the humours proceeding from the digestion of the liver [Col. 0700B].
