Then, from the heat of this digestion, a certain vapour proceeding from it generates the spirit called the natural spirit, vivifying the liver itself for the service of nature, in whatever direction the natural faculty requires. For there are three faculties governing the body. A faculty is an operative disposition in a member, directed toward that which is accomplished. One faculty is natural, in the liver; another spiritual, in the heart; another animal, in the brain.

All governance of the body arises either from soul and nature, or from nature alone. What is governed by nature and soul is animate; what is governed by nature alone is inanimate. At present, inanimate things are irrelevant. But in things that are animate, it is necessary that soul and nature possess some faculty by which they can fulfil [Col. 0700C] their action. This faculty is understood from its actions. In our desiring, retaining, digesting, and expelling, the natural faculty is exercised; in our sensing and moving ourselves by voluntary motion, the animal faculty; and in drawing in and sending out air, the spiritual faculty.

The natural faculty is common to trees, beasts, and human beings; the spiritual faculty to beasts and human beings; the animal faculty likewise belongs to animals in some respects but not in others. For no being except a rational animal can possess imagination and memory perfectly. The natural faculty has three powers—that is, three faculties: generative, pascitive (feeding), and nutritive. The generative is in semen, the pascitive in vegetation, the nutritive in growth from small to large. These are chiefly performed by blood [Col. 0700D], which possesses the nutritive and augmentative faculty. Its cleansing superfluities serve it in this: the gall bladder, spleen, and kidneys. The gall bladder draws red bile to itself lest it burn the blood; the spleen receives its superfluities into itself; and the kidneys discharge the watery superfluities from the blood into the bladder for evacuation, just as the intestines receive from the stomach coarse foods for evacuation.

And the natural spirit accomplishes all these things. Born in the liver, it increases and governs the natural faculty, preserving its actions; just as the spiritual spirit does in the heart and the animal spirit in the brain. For there are three spirits, governing and vivifying three faculties. And just as the natural spirit has its origin and seat in the liver, so the spiritual spirit has them in the heart. For the heart is the foundation of spiritual heat [Col. 0701A]. Its means of nourishment are the lung, membranes, and muscles of the chest. For muscles are nerves mingled with flesh; by their movement air is drawn in for cooling, and heat is expelled as vapour through a kind of digestion of the spirit.

Spirit is the power of the faculties for carrying out their actions. For spirit is a certain power of the soul through which the faculties perform their acts: the natural in the liver, the spiritual in the heart, the animal in the brain. These three faculties, or three spirits, are founded in these three principal members—the liver, heart, and brain—and from them are diffused through the whole body.

The spiritual spirit, therefore, or its faculty, founded in the heart, produces expansion and contraction. Expansion occurs when the heart expands and the artery expands in order to draw in air—[Col. 0701B] sometimes in a suitable amount, sometimes excessively—and the most refined blood from the veins. For unless the heart’s heat were thus tempered, it would burn its own seat and all adjacent things. Hence the heart is also said to rest in the bosom of the lung, as though in the bosom of a nurse, which continually draws air for its nourishment. If the passage of this drawing-in is obstructed in any way, the heart always returns to it so long as it finds in it some air by which it may be nourished. If this entirely fails, the heart dies. Hence physicians say that a human being cannot live more than seven days without food, nor more than seven hours without air. The spiritual faculty, therefore, is that which vivifies all things, and through which whatever lives in the body lives. And this is the spiritual spirit. [Col. 0701C]

This spirit, as has often already been said, born in the heart, goes through the arteries to the members of the whole body, increasing and governing the spiritual faculty and preserving its actions. The arteries proceeding from the heart and serving it by carrying vital spirit everywhere are hairy, having hairs both within and without. Those on the outside extend lengthwise, in order to draw heat or spirit from the depths of the heart; then the arteries themselves expand. But other, inner hairs, arranged crosswise, constrict the spirit and expel vaporous superfluities. This is the first digestion of the spiritual spirit.

Then the spirit itself ascends into the brain through the arteries called “youthful,” which rise through the right and left sides of the neck. For these “youthful” arteries enter the skull [Col. 0701D]. The skull is the seat of the brain: that is, the shell of the head in which the brain itself is contained. It is composed of many bones, both because of vapour, so that through pores between the joints of the bones the spirit may have a way of escape, and in order to admit veins and arteries within.

The youthful arteries, carrying vital spirit, penetrate the skull and spread in many ways beneath the brain itself, at the seat of the brain, in the form of a net, so that under the fostering protection of this net the spirit may be digested again. For while the spiritual spirit remains there, it is purified through digestion. From this digestion the animal spirit is produced. It then comes out through two arteries twisted above the net and flows down to the ventricle of the prow of the brain, where, again refined and purified, it expels its impurities [Col. 0702A] through the passage of the palate and nostrils. This is its third digestion.

The spirit itself passes to the ventricles of the stern through the middle passage between prow and stern, and there produces memory and motion, just as in the prow it produces imagination and sensation. The prow is the anterior part of the brain, situated in the front part of the head; the stern is the posterior part of the brain, situated in the back part of the head. Each has, as it were, a proper dwelling-place, a particular ventricle in which its faculty is contained; between them, the middle ventricle contains reason and understanding.

It must be known that the brain does some things by itself and some through its officials. By itself it produces reason, situated in the middle like a queen and mistress, through which we differ from beasts; imagination in the prow; and memory in the stern [Col. 0702B]. But it produces the animal faculty, that is, sensation, in the prow through the five senses, and motion in the stern through the nerves proceeding from the stern.

When we say that it produces reason, memory, and imagination by itself, although imagination and memory seem also to exist in brute animals, as do sensation and motion—for otherwise a dog would not recognize its master, nor would a bird return to its nest—it must be understood that they possess neither memory nor imagination. Rather, they possess a correspondingly greater power of the senses, or exercise of sensory activities, because their soul is alien from reason, wholly given and attached to its body, and wholly occupied only with senses and motions. Hence they also have livelier movements [Col. 0702C] and a readier use of their members for their motions.

Some philosophers said that this spiritual spirit was the soul, because they wished the soul to be bodily. But this is false. For the soul is a spiritual substance, made in the image of God and most like God; and it is in its body, in a certain manner, as God is in His world: namely, existing everywhere in the body and wholly everywhere—wholly in natural, wholly in spiritual, and wholly in animal operations. It acts subtly in natural operations, more subtly in animal operations, and most subtly in spiritual operations. For it does some things naturally; some actually and passively, that is, animalically; and some through itself and according to itself, that is, spiritually. Therefore neither the natural, animal, nor spiritual faculty [Col. 0702D] is the soul; they are instruments of the soul.

But let us return to our subject. All these principles of spiritual actions are founded in the heart and issue from the heart. Since it burns with natural heat, as has been said, by that heat it draws to itself whatever can temper its heat. And since its form is such that it seems to have two little ears, it receives through the right auricle a vein from the liver, through which it draws blood to itself; while through the left it sends out a great artery which, through its many divisions, administers vital spirit everywhere.

It must also be known concerning the arteries that throughout the body they are joined to veins by a certain kinship, and through pores, which provident nature has created in them and with which they abound, they communicate with one another: the arteries communicate vital spirit to the veins [Col. 0703A], and the veins natural nourishment to the arteries. Nourishing blood is never lacking in the arteries, nor animal spirit in the veins. But let us return to spirit.

We have said that the spiritual spirit, passing into the posterior stern of the brain, produces memory and motion there: memory by itself, motion through its officials, the nerves; just as in the anterior prow it produces imagination by itself and sensation through its officials, which are the five senses. It is difficult to dispute concerning the spiritual actions of the spirit; but something may readily be said of what it does through officials in the body or about the body—namely, sensation and motion.

Therefore, to speak first of motion: the motive faculty established in the brain moves by itself those things which are nearby. For provident nature established in the brain itself seven pairs of nerves. Passing out through suitable channels, they move what is around and below the head and neck, down to the diaphragm—that is, to the middle of the viscera [Col. 0703B]—both by themselves and through other nerves proceeding and branching from them; they move what must be moved and administer what must be administered. For they furnish to the five senses, each in its own way, the power of motion and sensation; likewise to the brain, tongue, throat, and the others, as was said, down to the diaphragm.

But because this faculty founded in the brain—that is, the motive force proceeding from the brain—would make an animal exceedingly slow and sluggish in moving if the power of voluntary motion were distributed through the force of nerves issuing from the summit of the brain, and through their courses and returns throughout all parts of the body down to the soles of the feet, nature provided the brain with a suitable auxiliary, descending even to the lower parts, to which it might lend the power of motive operation and sensation for conveyance everywhere below.

Nerves naturally produce motion; muscles, together with nerves, sensation. Delicate members tremble at foreign humours, and nothing in the body suffers sensation of pain unless it is governed by these. For the pain which we feel in injury to bones, nails, or the like is not in the bone or nail, but in their junctions with flesh and nerves. Therefore, because if nerves were stretched from the summit to the bottom, as has been said, they could easily break because of their very length, and sensation and motion [Col. 0703D] would become dulled, there was provided a nerve called in the Arabic tongue *nucha*, descending from the brain and from the end of the stern, through the vertebrae of the back—that is, the bones of the spine—to the lower parts. Hence it is also called the brain of the back or spine.

For this reason it is clothed and covered, in imitation of the brain, with certain coverings and nourishments. For since the brain is enclosed with the skull, it has between itself and the skull’s hardness two interposed membranes: one very soft and gentle, by which it is kept warm, and therefore called by physicians the *pia mater*; the other stronger, by which it is defended from the skull’s hardness, and therefore called the *dura mater*. So too the spinal brain, or *nucha*, has a pia mater and a dura mater; in addition, it has two further membranes composed of ligaments, by which it is defended [Col. 0704A] and covered.

For if all the coverings are injured by some accident as far as the pia mater, provided that the *nucha* remains uninjured, there will be no danger. But if the *nucha* suffers injury or is cut, all the lower parts lose sensation and motion while the upper parts remain in their condition; so much so that, if it is cut in the first vertebra after the skull, all adjacent and subjacent parts are deprived of sensation and motion. From this *nucha*, therefore, sensation and motion are administered to all members below or around it through nerves proceeding on either side. In this manner voluntary motion proceeds from the brain into the whole body.

The stern, from which motion proceeds, is smaller than the prow, because the operation of the prow is more important and more extensive, and it contains more instruments of operation than the stern. The prow is also softer than the stern [Col. 0704B], because the stern had to be harder in order to endure motion more readily, whereas the prow had to be softer, so that the sensory nerves proceeding from it might quickly receive sensation. These are seven pairs, while only a few proceed from the stern and produce motion and sensation. Indeed, to these and to all that proceed from the brain nature has given both motion and sensation: motion more agile, and sensation sharper and more excellent. But because that universal motion and sensation of the body proceed from the nerves of the stern and of its intermediary, called the *nucha*, motion and sensation have been specially assigned to the stern.

We must now pass to the animal faculty, or animal spirit. Since it displays itself most fully in the five well-known senses of the body [Col. 0704C] and in their actions, it seems proper to examine the senses themselves somewhat more closely. Let us speak first of sight, whose small but wondrous workshop, the eye, could scarcely ever be investigated or comprehended by the minds of some philosophers or physicians.

Nature itself shows how great is the dignity of the eyes above the other senses, since it placed them nearest in front of the seat of reason, as the sense more akin to it in likeness of power and more necessary for discerning those things that are beneath and around it. The organs or instruments conveying sight from the brain are the optic nerve, the humours, and the coats, of which we shall speak later.

The optic nerve proceeds from the brain beneath the pia mater, and is born and nourished there. Lest, because of its tenderness [Col. 0704D], it be injured in passing out through the bones of the skull, it is brought forth wrapped in a film of the pia mater. Proceeding to the eyes and administering to them the visible power, it is fixed in the middle of the crystalline humour. The humours and coats that produce or assist sight are as follows. There are three humours and seven coats.

The middle humour is called the crystalline, in which, as has been said, sight is founded. Its form is round, so that it may not easily suffer injury; yet it is flat on one side, so that sight may be directed firmly and steadily. Beneath or behind it—that is, to the rear—is situated the vitreous humour, in this order. First, the retinal coat is placed beneath it or around it, so called because it is composed from veins and arteries in the manner of a net. Its office is to refine the incoming blood [Col. 0705A], so that the thicker substance of the blood may not harm the crystalline humour. The crystalline is the proper instrument of sight, so named from crystal because of its brightness.

From this retina—not through veins or arteries, of which there is no connection there, but naturally—the vitreous humour draws off blood, transforming nourishment into its own nature; and therefore supplies nourishment to the crystalline humour. Between the retina and the vitreous humour, however, there are still two coats: the secondina, so called because it occupies the second place; and the *seliros*, that is, the hard coat, in order to protect the eyes on the inner side from incoming superfluous humours and other superfluities.

Above these three coats is placed the vitreous humour, that is, one like glass. The optic nerve joins it not singly but in pairs, so that each eye may have its own spirit administering to it visible power. After the vitreous humour is the fourth coat, called the spider’s web because of its thinness: so that it may easily draw the humour and, by its lightness, soothe both humours. For the crystalline is placed above it, and after the crystalline is the *evagaidos*, that is, the albuminous humour, like the white of an egg. It nourishes the crystalline outwardly with its moisture and protects it from the air, lest the air dry it out. After it is placed the uveal coat, made in the form of a grape and receptive of tears. After it comes the corneal coat [Col. 0705B], hard like horn, in order to protect the *evagaidon* from external assaults. It also holds the crystalline humour in place, lest, if the gaze of the eyes were constantly directed outward, sight should be dried up or dulled, as in fish, which never close their eyes and therefore run into nets. The seventh coat, the conjunctiva, is placed around all the rest, containing and joining them. It is the white which appears in the eyes. It does not cover the uveal coat but surrounds it.

Moreover, the optic nerve coming from the brain is hollow, in order to supply sufficient spirit to sight. When it comes to the eyes, it expands so as to surround the whole vitreous coat. The spirit of vision, issuing from the brain and striking this same coat, irradiates the eye. It follows that the crystalline humour, which is most shining and clear and is the first instrument of seeing, quickly adapts itself to colours. For the visible spirit, clarified in the hollowness of the nerves, goes out and reaches the brightness of the crystalline humour [Col. 0705D], and then, going forth from it, mingles with the air of day. When these two are incorporated with one another, both are easily and very swiftly changed. For air and spirit readily mingle with the colours of things seen. But the spirit issuing from the crystalline humour and carrying a change to it quickly changes it.

When the mind, which is in the ventricle of the brain, perceives this change, it distinguishes external things by their colours; and through colours it also understands the body’s form, size, and motion. For the most brilliant daylight gives the spirit as much assistance as the brain gives the nerve. The nerve carries sensation and motion from the brain and conveys them to its members. Likewise, the external air bears changes in visible colours, and the spirit brings the same change to the mind. For every sense in some manner changes the perceiver into that which is perceived; otherwise there is no sensation. This occurs in the eye when outward brightness is united with the inward spirit, and it occurs without any intervening delay. Thus sight is formed in the eye.

Sight itself, if it is subtle and abundant, sees both distant and near things perfectly. Abundant sight sees distant things; subtle sight distinguishes visible things well. Sight that is abundant and gross sees distant things because it is abundant, but not perfectly because it is gross. Sight that is scanty and subtle sees what is near, and sees it perfectly: not far away because it is scanty, but perfectly because it is subtle. Sight that is scanty and gross does not see far because of its scantiness, nor perfectly because of its grossness. This is concerning sight or the eye.

As for the nostrils, the two nasal passages are necessary for two reasons [Col. 0706B]. The larger one is for drawing in spirit and smell; the other for sending out gross superfluities coming from the brain. These passages admit smell to the prow of the brain but do not themselves produce it. For two little pieces, very like udders, are the instruments of smell. Set against the dura mater, passing through it where it is perforated as far as the brain, and descending below almost to the nostrils, they produce smell in this way. Vapour from fragrant bodies, dispersed and mixed with air, is drawn through the nostrils by those udders and transmitted as far as the brain. The ventricles of the brain draw it in and change it into their own nature. The mind perceives this change, and thus smell occurs.

The drawing-in of air is necessary to the brain because it does for the brain what breathing does for the heart. When the brain expands, air is drawn in to cool it. But when it contracts, superfluous vapour is expelled. When it expands, air is drawn in from the lungs, nostrils, and throat, and smell occurs. For odours are smelled in this manner: the vapour dispersed from a fragrant body and mixed with air is drawn to the brain through the aforesaid little breasts, as has been said.

Hearing is produced by a pair of nerves proceeding from the brain and spreading into the ears, where the opening of the ears is covered with cartilages for two reasons: lest something fall in that would impede hearing, and to assist the voice, which, coming to the cartilage, is collected there in order to enter the openings strongly. Moreover, the two nerves spread into the opening of the ears [Col. 0706D], as has been said, and cover it completely. This covering contributes as much to hearing as the crystalline humour does to sight.

Voice is struck air. Thus the touch or impact of air comes to the ears and, entering, is gradually passed along. For the impact upon nearer air strikes air still nearer, and that strikes what follows it. Thus, passing successively, it penetrates to the ears until it reaches the covering of the nerves already mentioned. There the covering itself is naturally changed into the nature of the struck air. For they are alike, since both are airy. This transformation is conveyed to the mind through the nerves; the mind discerns the nature of the voice received, and thus hearing occurs.

The tongue is the instrument of taste and speech. It has certain neighbouring veins which continually supply it with saliva [Col. 0707A]. These begin at the root of the tongue in the manner of arteries, from which a phlegmatic moisture flows, called salivary moisture. A nerve comes from the brain and is divided through the tongue, in order to give it the sense of taste. Taste occurs in this way. When a thing to be tasted comes to the tongue and touches its substance, nature operates in it so that the tongue is changed into the nature of the thing tasted. This change, touching the nerve, transmits taste through it to the mind for discernment and judgment: and this is taste.

Touch resembles the other senses, because it is changed into the substance of the thing touched. This change is conveyed to the mind through the nerves, and in this way the mind perceives that change. All senses have a proper member except touch. For touch belongs to the whole body, excepting those parts which lack nerves, such as hairs, nails, and the like; these sense only where they are connected, since this cannot occur without nerves. To conclude concerning the senses: nothing suffers in the body without sensing, and nothing senses that is not governed by nerves. [Col. 0707B]

It must also be understood that the senses correspond to the four humours, of which much has been said above. Sight is of an igneous nature; hearing, of an airy nature; smell, of a vaporous nature; taste, of a watery nature; touch, of an earthly nature. What wonder is it, since the individual ages of human life also correspond to individual humours?

Adolescence, up to the twenty-fifth or thirtieth year, resembles blood, which nourishes through moisture and heat. For whatever grows grows through what is moist [Col. 0707C] and warm. Up to this point a person increases in strength, height, length, and breadth. Then follows youth, like red bile because of dryness and heat. Its heat consumes the moisture of adolescence; hence it is dry, because dryness follows upon diminished moisture. Youth, which preserves the body in perfection without diminution of strength, ends in the thirty-fifth or fortieth year.

Then old age, cold and dry, resembles black bile: cold because the moisture of youth, which is nourishment for heat, has dried up. This ends at the fifty-fifth or sixtieth year. There succeeds senility, naturally most dry and cold, but accidentally moist because of indigestion and an abundance of phlegm.

[Col. 0708A] We have spoken of the outward human being—not, however, wholly of the outward human being, but of certain things which are in human bodies and yet are not wholly subject to human senses, but are discerned by reason and experience among physicians and philosophers who have been able to reach this point in investigating the dignity of human nature. Yet they degenerated most absurdly in this: that they thought that the part of the human being by which a person is the incorruptible image of God and surpasses other living creatures—namely, the rational soul—ought to be included among these things. They commended and celebrated only this ornament of humanity: how, namely, a human being, naturally erect toward heaven above all living creatures, testifies that he has something in common with heaven; how throughout the whole body, in its length [Col. 0708B], a central unity flourishes in the differentiation of the members, while on this side and that a beautiful equality of members corresponds across its breadth; and how the whole body is found composed in weight, measure, and number.

Let us pass to the soul. The equality of weight in the human body is attested by the symmetry of the members, while careful experience in measuring can demonstrate measure. For physicians say that if a person lies supine with hands and limbs outstretched, and a compass placed at the centre of the navel is turned in every direction, that person is found equal and proportionate to himself in all his parts, with the course of the measure encountering no hindrance. Concerning number, the matter is sufficiently clear. To omit the external members, whose number no one can fail to know, there is no doubt that all internal things also consist in fixed numbers. For even the bones have been counted by those whose concern this was, and they were found to number two hundred and forty-one in the whole human body. Likewise with the nerves: those proceeding from the brain were found to be seven pairs; those from the *nucha*, thirty-two pairs and one unpaired nerve. Why say more? It is certain that veins, muscles, and all things in the body consist in determinate numbers. But now, as has been said, let us pass to the soul. Let us briefly set forth, not what the philosophers or physicians of the world think or suppose about it, but what the Catholic Fathers learned from God and taught human beings.

## BOOK II. THE PHYSICS OF THE SOUL

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707D] The soul, as the philosophers of this world say, is a simple substance, a natural form, distinct from the matter of its body, the instrument of its members, and possessing the power of life. But according to our teachers—that is, ecclesiastical doctors—the soul is a spiritual and proper [Col. 0708D] substance, created by God, life-giving, rational, immortal, yet capable of turning toward good and evil. It is called a proper substance because no other spirit takes on flesh or a body so as to suffer with, or rejoice in, its afflictions.

[Col. 0709A] It is understood to vivify its body in wondrous and ineffable ways. For we understand that there are three things concerning bodily nature, for whose sake the individual things in us are constituted. Some things exist merely for living; others for living well; and others are fitted for the succession of future goods. Whatever things in us are such that human life cannot be maintained without them, we understand to exist in three parts, as was set forth in the previous little book: namely, the brain, heart, and liver.

All other things are additions of goods which nature has bestowed upon human beings for living well, such as the organs of the senses and many other things which indeed constitute life in us, since, if very many of them fail through any accident, a person nevertheless continues to live. Yet some things have been added by nature to the constituents of life and serve the workshops of life, and without their assistance those constituents cannot fulfil their office: such as the stomach and the lung, and certain others. For the lung cools the fire in the heart by blowing through the drawing-in of air; if it did not do this, the heart’s fire would burn both itself and everything nearby. The stomach introduces food to the viscera, without which nature would immediately fail.

Very many things serve and assist these, each in its own way. For the power by which we live is not conveyed uniformly from some single source; rather, with the soul given by God as its author, nature inspires into many parts their own occasions and efficacies for the constitution of life, and from all of them makes one necessary and almost inscrutable [Col. 0709C] contribution to living.

Whatever nature has contrived for the protection or beauty of life—omitting the many things which differ among themselves and have their own mutual distinctions—let us separate out the primary principles upon which the constitution of life is founded: namely, the brain, heart, and liver. Let us first consider the brain, whose powerful efficacy in the administration of life is shown, by contrast, from the fact that it suffers not even the slightest injury without death immediately following the wound. That sinewy or membranous covering in which the brain itself is contained, which the Greeks call *hymen*, is known to be the source and cause of all voluntary motions. From it a kind of voluntary spirit descends through the nerves proceeding from it and diffuses itself through the whole body by those nerves; and thus there arises a varied and manifold administration of movement, exceedingly swift, flexible, and suited to every motion.

Hence come the turning of the neck, the lowering and raising of the head, agility about the jaws, the very rapid movements of the eyelids and eyes, and the varied use of the hands. Hence, in walking, come the alternating movements of legs and feet, and the motions of all the other limbs: through nerves either relaxed or contracted, these move themselves by a kind of natural mechanism and by a voluntary spirit of life. The power itself, however, in the seat of the brain possesses a certain proper commanding motion, which by a ready spirit, according to a certain administration of nature, performs in each member its particular operation.

The same is true of the heart: if its natural heat is extinguished, death immediately follows when the body grows cold. This clearly shows that a certain source and cause of life is also situated in the heart. From it proceed tubular channels and the manifold branching of arteries, arising one from another, which distribute fire and vital spirit throughout the whole body. Since, moreover, it was altogether necessary that some nourishment should be supplied by nature to the heat of the heart—for fire cannot maintain itself from itself unless it is nourished by suitable food or material—therefore streams of blood, rising as if from a fountain in the liver, run everywhere through the body by the service of the veins along with warm spirit, lest one affection, separated from the other, should corrupt nature. [Col. 0710B] For every excess is a corrupting affection.

Thus, for the nourishment of life and the strengthening of natural growth, a power joined from the outset to the rational soul is displayed through this artificial and disciplined formation—more obscurely indeed in its first manifestation, but afterwards more clearly through the development of nature and the practice of good pursuits. For just as one who carves the image of a human being in stone first cuts out the form of the figure, and then gives that form distinction and beauty according to its features, so God, the author of nature and creator of body and soul, forms humankind in his own image and likeness: more obscurely at first, but more evidently and perfectly after the work has been completed.

[Col. 0710C] Thus, in the fashioned instrument of the soul, its form is prefigured according to the analogy of its subject: imperfect in what is imperfect, destined to be perfect in what is perfect. It too would have been perfect from the beginning, had nature not been corrupted in its origin through wickedness. Therefore we are born like cattle; nor can the image of the Maker immediately shine forth in us, or indeed except through great and prolonged labours. Rather, by a long path through the material and animal properties of the soul, a human being is led to his own perfection.

Yet let the whole human being render thanks to the Creator—not as much as is owed, but as much as can be rendered—who, in humanity’s very beginnings, confers upon it the perfection of every creature: granting it existence with stones; granting it vegetative life with herbs and trees; granting it sentient or animal life with cattle; and intending also to grant rational life with angels. But however herbs and trees may appear to live, and brute creatures and all animals to have a soul, it is nevertheless certain that all these things, however they live, do not possess a soul and do not rise thereby to the dignity of the human condition. For in seeds there appears a certain animal operation; yet it does not proceed as far as motions effected through sensation. There is life there, though there is no soul.

To bring that life about, observe and see how the seeds of all the elements have come together, each in its own portion. For there is earth in solidity, water in moisture, air in growth, and fire in sprouting. Since, in the ordered sequence of things, lower things are rarely affected except by higher things, after winter cold has passed, through the revolution of heaven and the return of the stars, heat coming from above first affects the air, which is nearest to it both in place and in nature. And because air yields to fire by as much as it surpasses water, it draws waters from the depths of the earth through the roots of trees or of whatever plants spring up. Fire, naturally drawing all the elements to itself, compels the warmed air toward itself; and through the pith of the tree, just as fire draws air, so air draws water, and water earth—just as we, when we wish, draw water up from below through a straw.

[Col. 0711A] From these four elements, which harmonize together in measure and musical concord for the life of a tree, if anything either diminishes or becomes excessive contrary to measure, the tree first sickens and then dies, as though overcome by weakness. Brute animals, however, seem in some way to live more nobly than herbs or trees through voluntary motion and the addition of the senses; yet not as far as the perfection which consists in the grace of reason and understanding. Therefore we say that the true and perfect soul belongs to human beings alone, because it is capable in every kind of action. If anything else participates in life, we call it “animate” only improperly, because in such things there is not a perfect soul, but only certain operations of animal activity—operations which are plainly innate even in human beings at their beginnings.

For brute creatures are wholly devoted to their senses and capable only to that extent; hence they exert these senses even more strongly than human beings, who transcend them by reason. It is like a river flowing gently: wherever it is blocked by any obstacle and prevented from advancing, there it presses onward with greater force. But the human spirit is very different. It rules the senses and judges concerning them. Reason sits, as it were, like a queen in the central citadel of its city; the gates of the senses stand open on every side, bringing in domestic things to their domestic places and foreign things to foreign places. It distinguishes and receives each thing by its own appearance and character, assigns each to its proper place in knowledge, distinguishes individuals also by kind, kinship, and nation, and distributes to each its own dwelling-place in memory.

[Col. 0711C] Thus the mind, in accordance with its nature, is something wonderful: it distributes itself through the powers of the individual senses, and through each power suitably receives the knowledge belonging to those senses. For no wise person can doubt that it is something other than the senses. If it were one with sensation, it would have one undivided fellowship of operations according to sensation. But now, though simple and uncompounded, and though divided into a sensibility apportioned in many ways, it is nevertheless found manifold in its unity and one amid variety. Rather, because nothing manifold can be considered in what is simple, it is not one thing when it touches, another when it smells, another when it tastes, and so with the rest.

See then how far the sensibility of the rational human being differs from that of the brute animal. Let every conjectural and vain reasoning of those also fall silent who confine the intellectual power within certain parts of the body. Some of them assign primacy to the heart; others maintain that the mind is ordered in the brain; and each brings forward his own physical conjectures on these matters. But conjectures about bodies should be referred to whatever bodily constitutions may be concerned. The mind, however, must be judged to occupy every individual part through an ineffable principle of union or power.

If those who argue for the heart appeal to Scripture, in which God is said to be “searching hearts” (Jeremiah 17), we too shall add that God also “searches the kidneys” (Psalm 7). Whoever therefore mentions the heart has also remembered the kidneys; he locates the intellectual substance either in both or in neither. For the author of nature willed the relation and a certain union of intellectual substance with bodily existence to be ineffable and incomprehensible: [Col. 0712B] namely, so that it is neither within—for what is incorporeal is not enclosed in a body, nor comprehended by a body—nor found outside according to the same law of nature.

For in a certain suprarational and incomprehensible manner the mind approaches nature; fitted into nature itself and about it, it is apprehended insofar as it can be apprehended neither as placed within or enclosed, nor as placed outside or as though enclosing it. Rather, in a way that can neither be stated nor understood, it wholly permeates nature and is effective for its operations. That intellectual nature is wholly present in the whole, not in some part; it is neither placed inside in the hollows of bodies nor driven out by an abundance of flesh or of any other thing. Rather, it makes the whole body, like a musical instrument, serve its own effects.

And just as those skilled in musical performance, when they find an instrument fitted to their art, properly exercise the office of that art, but if it has been worn away by decay or age or disturbed by any occurrence, the artist loses nothing of the art while the instrument remains inactive and discordant: so too the mind, possessing the whole instrument and touching the individual parts with intellectual operations as it is accustomed to do, performs its own work in those things that are arranged according to nature; but in those that are weakened it has a sluggish and inactive exercise of its art. Hence nature composes and adapts the bodily instrument in every respect for the use of reason.

For example, consider hands joined to the body, which you will find in no irrational animal. From this observe what great harmony follows in the instrument of the human body. First, all beasts have feet in the front part, whereas human beings have hands. Then, although there are many uses in this life for which nature has contrived the functions of hands, whether in peace or in war, nevertheless above all nature added hands to the body out of a definite necessity of reason. For if a human being had lacked hands, the form of the mouth would have been shaped for the use of food, after the manner of four-footed creatures: the neck would have been extended to take food from the ground; the nostrils would have been narrowed like those of brute animals; before the mouth would protrude callous, heavy, thick lips suited to cutting fodder; and the fleshy part around the teeth would be hard and rough, as in dogs and other flesh-eating creatures.

[Col. 0713A] Thus, if hands were lacking to the body, formed, articulate speech would be lacking to the mouth. Since the structure of the mouth would not be conformed for the use of sound, a human being would necessarily bleat, bellow, bark, or utter some other animal cry. But now, because the hand serves the mouth, the mouth serves reason, and thereby the mind, a spiritual and incorporeal thing. A grace not shared with irrational animals has been added: when the mouth touches with something like a plectrum the parts fitted for speech, it interprets its inward motion by speaking through such formation of sounds. This is as though someone skilled in music lacked a voice of his own because of some ailment, but, wishing to make music manifest, played upon other voices, displaying his art through pipes or lyres.

Thus the mind, inventor of various thoughts, though itself incorporeal and not possessing bodily words in itself, is able to make the impulses of understanding known through bodily senses. The hands also have another prerogative worthy of reason. It is a great gift of rational grace that we speak by writing with our hands, and that through the hands we in some fashion utter the voices of letters, joined together in their characters. Both hands and mouth, therefore, serve reason: the hands by writing to those in the future or absent; the mouth by readily and promptly speaking whatever reason suggests within.

For spirit, driven through the windpipe from bellows that receive breath, strikes the air and by a certain force of itself strengthens the windpipe into voice. Then, according to the form of a pipe instrument, through certain circular motions of membranes, modulating in a circle by the vehicles of those membranes, it rises upward. There the jaws, teeth, and tongue, imitating as it were the form of a plectrum, adapt sounds for use with manifold and extremely rapid variation. The lips too, by a certain distinct opening and closing of themselves, do the same thing as the fingers of a player upon a pipe: by their varied action in the pipe’s holes, they form the contained breath into one melody.

[Col. 0713C] Thus nature articulates its human words, while reason orders them. If, then, as has been said, the heavy and laborious office of servitude in connection with food had been assigned to the lips, the soul would remain inwardly mute and would not exercise its reason by this organic distinction of speech; nor could we, as rational beings, converse with one another. But now the hands, taking such service upon themselves, have left the mouth suited and free for the service of reason.

The mind, exercising its motions through speech, receives into itself the motions of others through the aid of ears, eyes, and other senses. It possesses so great an inward capacity that everything poured in from any source may flow into it; and it has its own styli by which to inscribe these things in memory—some more attentively, and therefore more firmly adhering; others more negligently, and therefore more quickly erased.

Thus, after the image of him who created it, who, remaining stable in himself, causes all things to move, the indwelling mind is one power; going out through each instrument of the senses, it traverses whatever it encounters—hearing itself through the ears, seeing itself through the eyes, and so with the rest. Yet in this it is far unlike him whose image it is: God does not apprehend existing things by differing powers, since it is absurd to conceive, in the simplicity of the Godhead, reception and the manifoldness of a receptive operation. But an image is not required to fail in none of the things [add: *of those things*] understood in its archetype. For then it would be identity, not image.

[Col. 0714B] Therefore it is not necessary that one who receives the image should possess in every respect an imitation corresponding to the archetype in those things considered concerning the divine nature and the incomprehensibility of its essence. For if the nature of the image comprehended its archetype, it would without doubt be above that which it comprehended. Indeed, in this very fact—that the rational mind does not attain perfect knowledge even of itself—it seems, by a certain likeness, to represent the nature of divine incomprehensibility.

Further, what does the uprightness of bodily form itself signify? The erect figure of the human being, stretched out toward heaven and looking upward, signifies the imperial and royal dignity of the rational soul. It shows that the Creator has committed to it dominion over all things that look downward, and that it has much in common with things above, provided it preserves the dignity of its inborn image: that is, provided the mind rules by reason and does not fail to choose what is useful.

Those are deprived of this dignity who make reason, naturally the mistress, serve the desires of nature and slavishly flatter the lust that operates through the senses. For their mind follows the natural affections of flesh or sense, becoming the servant of those things of which it ought to have been ruler and judge. Thus bodily nature imposes upon the mind at will both the feeling of sorrow and the desire of joy. Such people, having put off the image of the Creator, have put on another image—one looking toward the earth, animal-like, bestial.

For the likeness to God does not lie in human rage, nor is it imitated from pleasure exceeding nature. Fear too, ferocity, desire for some things, and hatred for others are far from the pattern of divine beauty. These and similar things human nature has drawn to itself from the irrational life. In irrational creatures they are natural defenses for self-preservation; transferred to human beings, they are passions of the soul. And they are truly passions, by which a human being made in the image of God permits himself to be humbled into the image of beasts. They are truly passions because they are contrary to nature.

Hence David says: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and made like them” (Psalm 48). For, as has been said, what is nature in beasts is vice in human beings. Flesh-eating creatures are driven by rage; love of pleasure preserves the fertility of animals; fear preserves the weak; fear [preserves] the weaker from the stronger; gluttony preserves the corpulent. No passions arise in cattle or beasts from any of these things, because in irrational creatures none of the things belonging to desire furnishes material for sorrow.

[Col. 0715A] Human wretchedness, admitting these passions into itself with an open heart and, through the cooperation of deliberations, increasing within itself their beginnings into a kind of multitude and strength, produces from them a most turbulent and uncertain generation of consequent vices. Thus the love of pleasure indeed has its beginning from this very resemblance to irrational creatures; but, enlarged in human offences, it has produced through lust as many kinds of sins as no one can find among irrational creatures. Reason casts these things away into what is kindred to them among irrational creatures, but they are enlarged by the aid of thoughts. From anger arise madness, envy, lying, and plots. All these are malicious operations of a mind that has degenerated.

For if passion were stripped of the aid of thoughts, it would quickly fail and perish like a bubble. And all these things, as has been said, entered into the constitution of humanity from animal generation, when the author of nature had assigned them to its service. For he who established for reason occasions of a twofold form—joining mind to body and mingling the earthly with the divine—willed that through the kinship and fellowship by which the human being possessed both, one should be enjoyed and the other used: God should be enjoyed through the more divine nature, while earthly goods should be used through the related sense.

For the best craftsman made our nature convenient and fitted for the operation of kingship. Both in the dispositions of the soul and also, as has already been sufficiently said, in the very form of the body, he prepared such a living creature as would have fitness for kingship: namely, one not bent toward earth, but erect toward heaven. The rational soul, understanding and preserving its own honour, is something royal and exalted; it thereby shows itself by nature to be far removed from rustic lowliness and degeneration. Being free and self-governing, it rules all things, makes them serve its own wills, and administers them by its own powers—which is proper to royal dignity.

[Col. 0715D] For this reason, human beings are born naked of natural protections and unarmed, so much so that while nature appears a joyful mother at the beginnings of other living creatures, in human beings alone she seems a sorrowful stepmother. To other animals she has assigned coverings of many kinds: shells, bark, spines, hides, fleece, bristles, hair, down, feathers, scales, and wool. She has even protected trunks or trees, sometimes with double bark, against cold and heat. But the human being alone, as we have said, she casts naked upon bare ground on the day of birth, immediately to crying and weeping; nor has she brought any other of so many animals into the light in tears, and those at once.

Indeed, in all ancient and recent histories only Zoroaster, the inventor of the magical art, is recorded as having been born laughing—evidently so that one who was destined to assail common natures by ill-omened arts might appear conspicuous by an ill-omened and unnatural birth. Then, so that wretched humanity may understand itself to have been given into prison, bonds immediately receive it, along with the fastening of all its limbs, except for the use of eyes and mouth alone, which is left free only for tears and cries. And this is so even for one who is happily reared, the son of an emperor or king.

[Col. 0716A] Thus there lies bound hand and foot, weeping, a creature that begins life from punishments, guilty of one thing only: having been born. Alas for the madness of those who think that from such beginnings a human being is born for pride! Then the first hope of strength and the first gift of time make him like a quadruped. And when does a human gait follow? When are voice and tongue formed into words? When does the taking of food occur? When does the crown of the head, long throbbing, become firm? Add that, beyond all animals, wretched humanity alone knows nothing of itself except how to cry; whatever ought or can naturally belong to a human being must be learned through the great labour of mothers, nurses, or the person himself.

But when at last the whole condition of human dignity seems somehow settled and established, diseases and medicines immediately follow, and at the end the care of burial. No life or health is more fragile; no life or health calls forth more assiduous care. A person is suddenly cut off by some accident—crushed by a collapse, killed by the poison of some plant or tiny worm, or suffocated by some beast. Hardly even through watchful care or flight can one protect oneself from everything that has power to harm in any way. Exposed to all things through bodily frailty, though reason has subjected them beneath human feet, the poor human being, destitute of everything useful, is brought into this life [Col. 0716C] rather to seem miserable than blessed, according to outward form.

For a human being is armed neither with the thrust of horns, nor with sharpened claws, hooves, or teeth, nor with deadly fang or sting as many animals are; nor is the body covered in a garment of hair. Humanity alone is slower than creatures that run swiftly, shorter than enormous creatures, and more vulnerable than creatures fortified with natural weapons.

“But how,” someone will say, “can one who is such possess dominion over all things?” In every way well. First, human reason holds under its control the power to harm possessed by subject things: it prudently avoids that power, powerfully destroys it, and reduces it to its own service. What appears to be a lack in our nature is an occasion for dominion over things subjected to it. Perhaps a human being would disdain rule if no service from subjects were needed. But now, for this very reason, the advantages of life have been distributed through every thing brought under us, so that rule is necessary to us—the rule by which God has exalted human nature above them.

[Col. 0716D] The slowness of our body and its difficulty in moving have commanded and tamed the horse into service. Again, humanity has subjected other animals to burdens as carriers. Nakedness of flesh has made the dominion of sheep necessary. So as not to eat grass like an ox, humanity has subjected the ox itself to the cultivation of the earth. It also has the dog, like a living sword against fierce and harmful beasts and a guardian of nocturnal sleep. It has iron, sharper and stronger than the point of horns or the sharpness of claws, providing human beings with weapons—not beastly, savage weapons that always burden them by nature, but weapons to be taken up and laid aside with reason. From iron itself it also has defenses for the body stronger than the scales of a crocodile: namely, helmets and breastplates.

Why say more? Every creature serves and does military service for humanity as for a king. Therefore see and embrace, O human being, the dignity of your nature. Do not consider yourself only cheap in bodily matters, in which you are surpassed by animals; consider how precious you are in your inward self, in which you surpass everything that lives or does not live. For according to inward dignity you were born into a royal condition. What else is it to be made in the image of omnipotent nature than that one’s nature was created royal from the beginning?

[Col. 0717B] To speak according to human custom: those who make images of kings or powerful persons reproduce the form of their figure and portray royal dignity in a purple garment; and, according to human usage, the image too is called “king.” Thus human nature, because it has been constituted to rule others, has been chosen as a kind of living image according to the likeness of the King of the universe, sharing with God the archetypal likeness, dignity, and name. It does not indicate its dignity by being clothed in purple or by a sceptre or diadem—for the archetype is not in such things—but instead of purple it is clothed with virtue, surpassing all royal insignia; instead of a sceptre it is marked by the blessedness of immortality; instead of a royal diadem it is adorned with the crown of righteousness. Thus in every respect it is shown in the dignity of kingship carefully to resemble the form of its archetype.

For in saying that the human being is made in the image of God, it is as though one said that God made human nature a participant in every good. For God is the fullness of all goods, and the human being is the image of God. Therefore, because humanity is capable of the fullness of every good, the image possesses likeness to its archetype. For God is for us the form of every good: of virtue, wisdom, and all things that can be understood as better. Likewise, because the mind is free from every necessity and is subjected to no natural power, but possesses through itself a will capable of attaining what it desires, it expresses its dignity through the power of free choice. For virtue is a thing without domination and voluntary; what is compelled and suffers violence is not virtue.

[Col. 0717D] This mind, or soul, is given by God; from the soul comes our natural life.

Given the soul, one must inquire what it is, why it is, and how it is. When we ask what it is, this belongs to natural philosophy; why it is belongs to rational inquiry; how it is belongs to ethics. What it is, no one comprehends, because it has no material, because it is a spiritual, intellectual thing and most like God. Whoever does not wish to know why it is does not deserve to live: namely, that one may live according to reason. How it is requires the very manner of living according to reason.

For this, just as the body consists of four elements in order to live, so the rational soul has four elements, as it were, of virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. From these four elements, therefore, the rationality of the soul is formed—that rationality which is the manner of living according to reason. For these four elements of virtues, divided through their own elements as it were into many parts, produce manifold and varied shoots of virtues in the soul.

Just as the soul, in administering material life, employs four powers in the principal parts of the bodily instrument—namely, appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive—so it exercises rational administration through four passions: hope, joy, fear, and sorrow. And just as the whole nature of bodily life operates through three powers—natural power in the liver, spiritual power in the heart, and animal power in the brain—so spiritual or rational practice exerts itself through three powers: rationality, concupiscibility, and irascibility.

[Col. 0718B] And just as those three powers generate three effects from themselves without which human life cannot subsist—the natural power in the liver producing nourishment, the spiritual power in the heart producing life, and the animal power in the brain producing sensation—so, for ordering or bringing to completion spiritual or rational life, faith is founded in rationality, hope in concupiscibility, and charity in irascibility. For although faith has no merit when human reason furnishes proof, nevertheless, because it is founded in rationality, it is naturally always eager for reason; for scarcely can it be brought to believe what neither fitting authority nor reason itself in some manner shows to be reasonable.

> **Note:** [Col. 0717D] Faith does not reject reason as a companion; yet those are rightly criticized who refuse to believe anything except what [Col. 0718D] human reason proves. This is the author’s point.

But how closely concupiscibility and hope are joined is not difficult to demonstrate—indeed, it is idle labour to labour at demonstrating it. Irascibility and charity, on the other hand, appear so opposed to one another that either seems destructive of the other. Yet a certain ardour of spirit gathers this diversity into unity, because there is ardour in anger and ardour in charity. I do not mean, however, this bestial anger, but human, rational anger. There is rational anger and there is bestial anger.

Rational anger is divided into two: zeal and discipline. Its disposition of mind is nothing other than love of God and neighbour and hatred of vices. It is hatred of vices precisely because it is love of God and of human beings. Bestial anger, however, is divided into three: into fury, where there is no measure in intensity; into that called *manis* [perhaps “mania”], where there is no limit; and into that called *coitus* (“intercourse”; the term is uncertain), for which vengeance alone provides an end, just as intercourse provides an end to the ardour of flesh.

[Col. 0718D] Rational anger, therefore, burns from charity; and charity likewise burns in the anger on which it is founded, because unless anger came first, charity would not follow. For justice cannot be loved unless injustice is hated. Therefore, just as the powers already mentioned in the liver, heart, and brain, together with the effects of those powers, administer and preserve bodily life, so these administer and preserve spiritual life.

And just as the former suffer various impediments to their operations through either the relaxation of their deficiencies or the intensification of excess—impediments which are bodily passions or infirmities—so do the latter. For corrupted rationality often produces presumption, heresies, and similar things from itself; concupiscibility produces the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life; irascibility produces bestial anger, savagery, and hatred.

Now let us consider the senses.

The soul has animal senses; nevertheless, it also has spiritual ones. In both sets it operates so powerfully, so wonderfully, that human understanding can scarcely comprehend it. For the soul is something invisible and incorporeal, [Col. 0719B] and yet through the senses it produces, from a visible body, something invisible and corporeal. Each one of the five senses stands between the invisible incorporeal soul and the visible body as something invisible yet corporeal, since it is in the same body. The soul is invisible and incorporeal; and that invisible yet corporeal thing which the soul wonderfully performs by means of the visible body is sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. For sight is one thing and the eye another; the ear one thing and hearing another; and so with the rest.

The soul’s inward sight is brightened by prudence and darkened by folly; its hearing is offended by falsehood and soothed by truth. Equity is fragrant to the rational soul; injustice or impurity stinks. It wastes away through vanity and grows fat through virtue; it is wretched [Col. 0719C] in companionship with folly and blessed in the embrace of wisdom. It is wholly an eye, because it sees wholly, and sees the whole of whatever it beholds. The outward human being, however, neither sees wholly, because he sees only with the eye, nor sees the whole of what he sees, because he sees not all parts of any visible body. Moreover, there, seeing is the same as hearing, and smelling as tasting or touching, since such unity or power cannot exist in the body.

But when we have called the soul something invisible or incorporeal, and therefore non-local—for nothing incorporeal is local—we must inquire, in order to investigate something more clearly concerning the soul itself, whether it may truly be shown to be non-local; whether it is wholly separated, like the Godhead, from those categories which belong properly to bodies or bodily things. To none of these is the divine essence subject, although it is itself the first and highest [Col. 0719D] substance. For one cannot say “of what quality” is he who is incomparable; nor “of what quantity” is he who is great by no bulk; nor “what has he?” who lacks nothing; nor “how is he?” who is himself the measure. Nor should one seek a disposition in him who has all things; nor a place for him who is non-local and wholly everywhere; nor time for the eternal; nor action in one at rest and possessing all things in rest; nor passion in the impassible.

The human soul, however, because it has no bulk, has no quantity; because it is subject to the mutability of affections, it does not escape quality; because it is not enclosed locally in a place, it does not receive locality. For just as God is in the world, so in some manner the soul is in its body: namely, everywhere and wholly everywhere; wholly in each sense, so that it may wholly perceive in each; wholly in every part, so that it may wholly animate and make the whole sentient. [Col. 0720A] How then shall it be called local? So too with the remaining categories. Therefore the Godhead is subject to no category, the soul to some, the body to all.

For the soul is acted upon not by places but pleasantly or painfully according to the diversity of its affections. Though it may be soothed or afflicted by affections incorporeally and without the body, nevertheless the whole body without the soul feels neither pain nor pleasure. For in its actions the soul has a wider and swifter power than the body. Hence, even while it administers and makes the body sentient, if at any time it raises itself by the inward gaze of the mind toward heavenly and eternal things, it in some manner abandons bodily senses and departs from them non-locally, so that it does not see things placed before it, does not hear sounds occurring near it, does not understand a page which it has read through. [Col. 0720B] By a wonderful power, in some sense like the divine, at the same hour it is wholly in the intellect contemplating heavenly things, wholly in sense or action doing things; yet it does not perceive what it does, while it is wholly in the body which it gives life.

It is the same soul which perceives; the same which does not understand what it perceives; the same which, neither perceiving nor understanding, animates and gives life to the body, through which it perceives what it does not understand through itself. The soul itself is also its own power. For what it thinks is an accident of it; but it itself is its substance, by which it thinks. The same applies to the will. To will something is an accident to it; but willing itself is its substance. Therefore it thinks wholly, because it is wholly thought; and it wills wholly, because it is wholly will.

[Col. 0720C] See, I beg you, how we advance toward the image of him who created us. For if the soul, thinking, is wholly thought, and if it is wholly will, then surely, loving wholly, it is wholly love. God too is called—and is—love. But that love is such that it can neither itself love except what is good, nor be loved through except rightly. This love, however, which is the human soul, according to the mutability of its affections can burn upward toward him who alone is above it, God, with heavenly charity, and can flow downward toward lower things with condemnable love.

The soul, created with such majesty and dignity in the image of its Creator, contemplating itself and him, pauses somewhat within itself. It beholds its own power not without awe; and, considering whether there is something above it which it must pass beyond from itself, it finds that all changeable or movable things can be moved only by what is unmoved. [Col. 0720D] Understanding concerning itself that, even if it is not moved through place, it is nevertheless moved through affection, and that above it there is another, more stable foundation, which is moved neither by place nor by time—for, as has been said, nothing is moved except by what is unmoved—it sees that it must stand still in order to move the body through place and time alike, just as God, standing within himself, moves the soul through time. It finds itself midway between God and body, because it is like none of the bodies, being an image of God; yet it cannot be equalled with God, because although it began from him, it is not from him or out of him.

It sees incorporeal things through itself and bodily things through the body; it also sees that it sees bodily things through itself without the body. For, to omit other examples, it sees the internal parts of its own body: namely, the threefold structure of the brain, the mass of the liver lying joined together and adhering to alien ligaments; the weight hanging from the stomach, striking without cessation the plectrum of the heart; the courses of the veins, the interweavings and origins of the nerves, the joints of the bones, the hollows of the lungs, and innumerable other things. [Col. 0721A]

Wherever it thinks—whether of places or regions—it is there, although by nature it cannot contemplate them; and it contemplates the situations of places, the courses of rivers, human faces, and other such things. Although it does not see these things, since they are bodily and can be seen only by bodily eyes, nevertheless it is present wherever it thinks, so that it does not see by bodily vision the places of which it thinks; just as it is present where it gives life, where it does not see the internal parts of its own body which it animates. [Col. 0721B] In this too it recognizes in itself some measure of the image of its Creator: it sees him as illuminating light, but itself as light capable of illumination.

More than this: it sees that those things which are present to it within itself somehow correspond to the image of the highest Trinity: namely, mind, thought, and will. For when it thinks something, the whole thing which it thinks is in the mind; and whatever it remembers wholly at once, it thinks wholly at once, and wills to think and remember it—that is, it loves to possess mind and thought. When it remembers that it thinks, it certainly comprehends the whole thought with the whole mind; and it thinks its whole love or its whole mind with its whole thought, when it thinks that it loves or remembers itself. With its whole love it wholly loves that same whole mind and that same thought, when it loves to remember and think and love itself. [Col. 0721C] And if the individual three wholly and simultaneously either love, think, or remember themselves, the three taken wholly together will not be greater than either the whole mind remembering at once, the whole thought knowing, or the whole love loving.

Seeing this to be in itself—indeed, seeing that it itself is this—and hearing God in some manner speaking to it, the soul sees truth shining forth and fixes its attention on Christ preaching and saying: “I and the Father, and my charity, are not three, but ‘we are one’ (John 10): we are one God. But you, rational mind, thought, and your love, are one human being, made in the likeness of your Maker, not created in equality with him. For you were not begotten; you were formed, not yourself the former. Depart from the things below you, less formed and less beautiful than you are; draw near to the forming Form, so that you may become more beautiful and ever be joined to it. For the more deeply you impress yourself upon it with the weight of greater charity, the more you will receive from that Form. From it you will obtain the unchangeable stability of this image, from which you received your beginning.”

[Col. 0721D] These and other things does Truth speak to the ear of the heart, inwardly admonishing us. Whatever the soul hears, since human misery is always ready for envy, it has no ground for envying an angel; for such a human being, angel, and God are now one spirit, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 6), or are one in God, according to the Gospel (John 17). This is especially so because Christ the man, the head of humanity, truly and perfectly assumed into unity of person [Col. 0722A] by Truth itself, the Son of God, deserved long ago to hear what no angel could ever hear. For he heard from God the Father: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

Let holy humanity therefore rejoice, glorified in its head, Christ, and exult in itself, exalted above the angels, when it hears the angel, refusing worship from a human being, say with devout humility and sweetest charity: “See that you do not do this; for I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren” (Revelation 22). Let even the least pilgrim of the kingdom of God, still in this age, presume upon this, because, as the same Truth testifies, “his angel always sees the face of the Father” (Matthew 18).

But let us return again to the image of the Trinity. Just as nothing exists without God the Creator, namely the holy Trinity itself, so nothing at all can exist which is not both one and constituted threefold. Every soul, as has been said, subsists in three indivisible elements: memory, counsel, and will. Every body, however, is one, measurable, countable, and weighable. Through its three elements the soul becomes capable of these three things, since by them it judges measurable, countable, and weighable things—that is, all bodies. [Col. 0722B] For there flows from the highest, which is God, through the middle, which is the soul, to the lowest, which are bodies, an image of the united Trinity, impressing signs of itself upon bodies and granting knowledge to souls.

The soul, beholding all these things with the intellect, now takes delight not so much in its own beauty as in the forming Form, [Col. 0722C] and by attending to it is always made more beautiful. For to attend to it is to be formed. Whatever is directed toward God is not its own, but belongs to him by whom it is directed. O blessed soul, truly blessed: if it prays, as the Apostle says (Romans 8), it is not itself, but “the Holy Spirit” who prays for it “with groanings too deep for words”; if it speaks, “the Spirit” speaks mysteries through it; whatever it finally accomplishes, it is not itself, but “the Spirit” who “works all things” in it “in all,” “apportioning to each” particular gifts “as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

For as the body lives from the soul, so that soul lives from God, sighing for him alone, continually breathing him alone as a living body breathes air; remaining wholly in God through faithful affection, and having him whom it loves remaining in itself through omnipotent operation, being one spirit with him. [Col. 0722D] For the will of Father and Son, the Holy Spirit, by inconceivable grace, ineffable joy, most secret inspiration, and most manifest operation, conforming its will to himself and uniting its love to himself by spiritual omnipotence, becomes so one with it that, as has been said, while it intercedes with unutterable groanings, he is rather said to intercede.

And this is the Son’s prayer to the Father: “I will”—that is, by the power of my will, which is the Holy Spirit, I effect—“that as I and you are one” in substance, “so they also may be one in us” by grace (John 17). One in love, one in blessedness, one in immortality and incorruption, and in some manner one even in Godhead itself. For “as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1).

But let us consider the steps from the lowest to the highest by which the soul, striving for perfection, ascends through progress to its Maker. On the first step, the soul gives life by its presence to this earthly and mortal body; [Col. 0723A] gathers it into one and holds it in unity; does not allow it to flow away and decay; causes nourishment to be distributed through the limbs, giving to each its due portion and preserving its proportion and measure, not only in beauty but also in growth and generation. But all these things may seem common to human beings even with shrubs. For we say that these also live; and we see and acknowledge that each is preserved in its own kind, nourished, grows, and generates.

[Col. 0723B] Ascend then to the second step and see what the soul can do in the senses, where life is understood more clearly and manifestly, and in which we can have no fellowship with things fixed by roots. The soul applies itself to touch and feels and distinguishes hot, rough, smooth, hard, soft, light, and heavy things. Then, by tasting, smelling, hearing, and seeing, it judges innumerable differences of flavors, smells, shapes, and sounds. In all these things it takes to itself and desires those things which suit the nature of its body; it rejects and flees their contraries. It withdraws itself from these senses at fixed intervals of time and, as though restoring their movements by certain holidays, turns over within itself in crowds and in many ways the images of things which it has received through them; and this whole process is sleep and dreams.

It often delights in leaping and wandering through ease of movement, and without labor orders the harmony of the limbs. For sexual union it does what it can, and in the union and love of the twofold nature it strives to make one body. But no one denies that the soul can again do all these things even in beasts. Raise yourself then to the third step, which now belongs properly to human beings. Consider memory: not merely memory of countless things brought into the soul through the senses by habit, which belongs to beasts, but of things commended and retained through attention and signs; the many arts of craftsmen, cultivation of fields, construction of diverse cities, the manifold wonders of buildings and great works; [Col. 0723D] the inventions of so many signs in letters, words, gesture, this sort of sound, paintings, and pigments; the languages of so many nations, torrents of eloquence, varieties of poems, a thousandfold representations for play and amusement, skill in musical modulation, subtlety in measuring, skill in counting, and conjecture from present things concerning past and future things.

These are great things and wholly human; but this faculty is still common in part to learned and unlearned souls, in part to good and evil souls. In these three steps you see what the soul can do in the body. Look upward, then, and leap to the fourth step, where goodness and all true praise begin. From here the soul dares to set itself not merely above its own body, insofar as it acts as a part of the universe, but even above the whole bodily universe; it does not reckon the universe’s goods to be its own goods, and, comparing them with its own power and beauty, discerns and despises them. [Col. 0724A] Thus, the more it delights in God, the more it withdraws itself from defilements; it wills nothing for another which it would not wish to happen to itself; it follows the authority and precepts of the wise, and through these believes that God speaks to it.

In this most illustrious activity of the soul there is still labor, and a great and keen conflict against such troubles and allurements. For in the very work of purification there remains a movement of death. When this has been accomplished—that is, when the soul has been freed from every stain and washed clean of blemishes—then at last it rests most joyfully in itself and fears no misfortune for itself, nor is it troubled for any cause of its own. This, then, is the fifth step. [Col. 0724B] For it is one thing to achieve purity, another to retain it; and it is altogether another activity by which the soul, restoring itself when defiled, does not allow itself to be defiled again.

At this step the soul conceives in every way how great it is. Once it has conceived this, it proceeds to God with a certain immense and incredible confidence—that is, to the contemplation of truth and to that highest and most secret reward for which it has labored so greatly.
