But this activity, namely the desire to understand those things which truly and supremely are, is the highest vision of the soul; it has none more perfect, better, or more upright. This will be the sixth step of activity. For it is one thing to cleanse the very eye of the soul, lest it look vainly and rashly and see wrongly; another to preserve and strengthen its health; another to direct a serene and upright gaze toward that which must be seen.

[Col. 0724C] In these two steps you see what the soul can do in itself. But consider that those who wish first to possess a serene and upright gaze before they have been cleansed and healed are so dazzled by that light of truth that they think there is not only no good but even much evil in it, deny it the name of truth, and, with a certain miserable lust and pleasure, flee back into their own darkness—which their sickness can endure—while reviling the remedy. Therefore, by divine inspiration and in the most orderly manner, the Prophet says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; renew a right spirit within my inward parts” (Psalm 50). For the right spirit is, I believe, that by which the soul cannot [Col. 0724D] wander or err in seeking truth. It is certainly not renewed unless the heart has first been made clean; that is, unless thought itself has first restrained and purified itself from every desire and dregs of mortal things.

But in the very vision and contemplation of truth, which is the seventh and final step of the soul—indeed no longer a step, but a certain dwelling reached by those steps—what joys there are, what enjoyment of the true and highest good, what breath of serenity, only the one who enjoys it understands.

Through these steps, therefore, the faithful soul, burning with desire and with diligent, unwearied care, makes an *anabathmon*, that is, an ascent, and orders ascents in its heart until it comes to the place which God has proposed or appointed for it. It lives, as the Apostle says [Col. 0725A] (2 Corinthians 4), the life of God: namely, spiritual life in the joy of the Holy Spirit, in the hope of the children of God, and in contemplation of the exemplar of highest justice. It also lives, while it lives here, while it sees here in part through a mirror and in an enigma, using its natural passions in such a way that, though placed in flesh, it does not live according to the flesh and almost becomes impassible, since the passions themselves are not passions for it but virtues: while it fears only with chaste fear; while it grieves only because the kingdom is delayed; while, rejoicing in the breadth of charity, it runs gladly in the way of God’s commandments, believing all things, hoping all things, enduring all things, and lovingly contemplating its end; sweetly resting in hope in him alike in what it enjoys, suffers, and awaits, so long as these three remain: faith, hope, and charity.

[Col. 0725B] But when death has been swallowed up in victory and that which is in part has been abolished, there will no longer be faith or hope, but the reality alone. In that reality, the greatest of all, charity, will reign and exult, fear and sorrow having been destroyed and hope and faith having passed away. Then entry will be made into the joy of the Lord, into which the blessed soul will enter happily, to live eternally in him, and will wonderfully rise again into its own proper body, so that what was a participant in labor may also be a participant in glory in eternal life.

By contrast, the unhappy and degenerate soul—if indeed it ought to be called a soul—which kills itself and is dead within itself, makes a *catabathmon*, that is, a downward descent; indeed not a descent but a fall, so that the one who is in filth may become still filthier. [Col. 0725C] It acts and suffers everything in the contrary way, alienated from the life of God. Created for the image and vision of God, where it ought to begin to savor God, there it begins to lose wisdom; and, going out from the face of the Lord like Cain (Genesis 4), it dwells in the region of unlikeness, in the land of Naim, that is, of commotion. Banished from virtue, it is subjected to vices; alienated from the peace of the children of God, it is tumultuous within itself. Corrupting natural art into wickedness and cunning, it becomes malicious; shamefully immersing itself in the enticements of animality or of the senses, it gives itself to lust.

[Col. 0726A] It becomes like horse and mule, which have no understanding: prudent only to do evil, but unable to do good. It has no care for itself, no remembrance of God. Therefore it is foully tormented by its passions, which it miserably abuses: it fears only things troublesome to the senses; rejoices only when things which flatter are present; grieves only when they are taken away. In all things it is like a beast or a brute animal, except that, as was said above, what is nature in them is vice in the human soul.

Yet, by continual practice of malice, it is sometimes so stupefied by the excess of its sickness that it itself in some manner becomes impassible or insensible. Through excessive devotion to wickedness it does not recoil from even the hardest and roughest things to the flesh, in order to serve its own—that is, the soul’s—corruptions: [Col. 0726B] namely avarice, the desire of the flesh, desire of the eyes, or worldly ambition. Thus it lives while it is enclosed in the tomb of the body. But when it has been torn away from it, it dies almost wholly with the whole body, as do brute animals to which it feels itself similar.

For when its true essential power has wholly perished within it, of which Wisdom says, “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole human being” (Ecclesiastes 12), nevertheless, by the most just judgment of God, it is not allowed to die wholly. Rather, it is kept capable of suffering only for pain, excluded from all joy, alienated from all hope, having no fear except pain, but wholly enslaved to pain itself. [Col. 0726C] For something living and life-giving remains in it, because it lives only in order to suffer: capable of suffering, in order to be punished or tormented; life-giving, in order to give life again to the body, so that it may be tormented with it forever, with which it would have sinned forever, if it had been possible. Alas, how much better it would have been for it, if, like the soul of a beast, it had died wholly with the body, lest it be punished eternally!

But the dissimilarity between the blessed soul and the wretched soul is produced solely by the dissimilarity of love. In the one, love preserves the tenor of natural dignity; in the other, it degenerates into the bestial animality of the flesh.

## Before the middle of the twelfth century. Saint Alger, Canon and Scholastic of Liège

### Three Books of Saint Alger on the Sacraments of the Body and Blood of the Lord

There is added a short treatise on the sacrifice of the Mass attributed to the same Saint Alger. Newly and more accurately brought to publication, with notes and a preface added, by J. B. Malou, Canon of Bruges, Doctor of Sacred Theology in the Catholic University of Louvain, Professor in the Faculty of Sacred Theology and Prefect of the Academic Library, now Bishop of Bruges.

(Louvain: at the expense of C. Fonteyn, 1847, 32mo.)

To the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord Cornelius Richard Anthony van Bommel, Bishop of Liège, most vigilant, learned, and devout pastor: the editor dedicates, gives, and consecrates this new edition of the three books on the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord by Saint Alger, twelfth-century writer, Canon and Scholastic of Liège, in commemoration of the sixth centenary festival of the instituted solemnity of the Body of Christ.

[Col. 0727]

## To the Devout and Learned Reader: Greetings

[Col. 0727] As soon as news reached me that the sixth centenary of the feast instituted for the solemnity of the Lord’s Body was to be celebrated in the Church of Liège, I immediately resolved to prepare for the press that illustrious work on the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, which Saint Alger, a twelfth-century writer and likewise Canon and Scholastic of Liège, had formerly written in order to refute the heretic Berengar. Indeed, it was my intention to publish sufficiently early the new edition I was preparing of that most celebrated work, so that it might serve as a kind of herald of that centenary feast. But because the printer caused delays, it happened that the solemn festival of the Church of Liège was completed before my Alger had been printed. Let my edition, then, of Alger’s work be a memorial of that Liège festival, since it could not, as I had wished, be its herald.

You, Christian reader, receive this truly golden little book, composed by a man commended to posterity no less than to his contemporaries for piety as well as learning. Concerning his life, and also the subject of the book which we offer you, these preliminary observations seemed appropriate.

Alger was born at Liège toward the end of the eleventh century. From childhood he devoted himself to literary study “under the most distinguished men, by whose learning and upright morals the Church of Liège then shone and France was made illustrious,” as Nicholas, Canon of Liège, recorded in his encomium of Alger. [Note: [Col. 0729] In Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 129, ed. 1723; and below, p. XXXV.]

As a young man he first served God in the church of St Bartholomew, a cleric by religious profession and habit, a deacon by rank, and scholastic by office. Later, enrolled in the churches of St Mary and St Lambert by Bishop Otbert, who died in 1119, he directed ecclesiastical affairs with the highest praise for nearly twenty years, until the death of Bishop Frederick, who departed this life in 1121; and he issued various writings through which he acquired a far from ordinary reputation.

After Frederick’s death, though he abounded in wealth and still possessed a strong body and unimpaired senses, he renounced his possessions and offices and professed a stricter rule of life under the Rule of St Benedict in the monastery of Cluny. He did so in such a way that to the end of his life he spread everywhere the good fragrance of Christ.

He had so bound all hearts to himself that Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, could scarcely ever refrain from praising him. Writing to Alberon, Bishop of Liège, after Alger’s death, he says:

> “Cluny received gifts from the Church of Liège far more precious than gold and topaz, when it joined to the humble company of its own members illustrious men coming from you, men to be remembered with the highest praise and affection. For, not to mention others who came before our time and whose faces were unknown to us, when can the memory of the Church of Liège perish at Cluny, which made Hezelo, Tozelin, and Alger—canons and great teachers in their time—disciples of humility and, as we who saw them testify, true monks? . . . . The third, Alger, whose memory I can scarcely mention without tears, surpassing by his humility, the sincerity of his entire life, and his purity those who went before, lived among us in my time and conducted himself so kindly and holy that, although he has departed from us in the flesh, he cannot fail to remain always with us in spirit and singular remembrance while we live. He also left us a book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, invincibly fortified by the authorities of the holy Fathers: an outstanding testimony to his faith and a singular defence against the ignorance or error of certain modern people.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0729] In D. M. Marrier, *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 794, Paris, 1614.]

“Now an old man,” writes the author of the *Chronicle of Cluny*, “Alger was ordained priest; and, having lived religiously for nearly ten years, he ended in a blessed death the good life which he had also led while a cleric.” [Note: [Col. 0729] In the notes to the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 138.]

From these facts we infer that Alger was born around 1070 or 1075, since he was appointed by Otbert to ecclesiastical affairs in 1101, when he was, as may be conjectured, twenty-five or thirty years old. It also follows that he remained in the rank of deacon for the twenty years during which he managed the Church’s affairs. Likewise it is clear that he was not invested with priestly dignity before he had reached old age as a monk. [Note: [Col. 0729] Peter the Venerable entitles chapter 17 of Book I of *On Miracles*: “On Alger, an Old Religious”; *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 1247.] This occurred in the monastery of Cluny, as Peter the Venerable—Alger’s companion and friend—writes, not at Corbie in Saxony, as Trithemius wrote while inattentive. Hence it is finally evident that Alger died at about the age of sixty around 1132 or 1135, after spending some twenty years in the clerical state, another twenty in administering the affairs of the Church of Liège, and finally about ten years in the monastery. [Note: [Col. 0729] I do not know upon what documents the opinion rests of J. A. Fabricius, or of the most learned Mansi, who writes in *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 70, Luc. ed. 1754, that Alger died in 1152; or of His Eminence Cardinal Mai, who thinks in *Scriptores veteres, Nova Collectio*, vol. IX, p. 371, that he died in 1151.]

Many outstanding writings of his survive. The chief of these is the three-book work *On the Sacraments of the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which Peter the Venerable greatly prefers to the writings composed by Lanfranc and Guitmund against Berengar. [Note: [Col. 0729] In the *Treatise on the Sacrifice of the Mass and Transubstantiation against Peter of Bruys and Henry, Masters of New Impieties*, p. 197, Vlimmerius ed., Louvain, 1561; and here, p. XLI.] Closely following this work is the short work *On Mercy and Justice*, whose preface was first published by Mabillon, [Note: [Col. 0729] In *Analecta*, p. 130.] and which shortly afterward appeared, through the care of Fathers Martène and Durand, from a Clairvaux manuscript in the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*. [Note: [Col. 0729] *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, p. 1019, Paris, 1717.]

The little book *On Free Will*, which Dom Cellier conjectures from one of Alger’s letters to be by the same author, [Note: [Col. 0729] *Histoire générale des écrivains ecclésiastiques*, vol. XXII, p. 267.] was published by Dom Pez from a manuscript belonging to the distinguished Ab Uffenbach. [Note: [Col. 0729] *Thesaurus novissimus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, part II, p. 111, Augsburg, 1723.] Trithemius entitles this small work of Alger *On Grace and Free Will*. [Note: [Col. 0729] Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 328.]

The Most Eminent Cardinal A. Mai, well known throughout the learned world, recently published under Alger’s name a little work *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*. Its copy had been transcribed by the distinguished Augustin Theiner from a certain Paris manuscript. Mai indicates in the following words that this little book is a genuine offspring of our author:

> “Our Alger’s treatise *On the Sacrifice of the Mass* is found in Latin manuscript no. 812 of the Royal Library of Paris, and is appended to his treatise *On Grace and Free Will*, which is found in the same excellent parchment manuscript of the middle thirteenth century. [Col. 0731] It does not give Alger’s name, but it was written by the same hand as the treatise *On Grace and Free Will*, with the copyist’s added note: ‘There follows *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*.’ Thus no doubt whatever can be raised concerning the author of our treatise.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0731] A. Mai, *Scriptores veteres, nova collectio*, vol. IX, p. 371, Rome, 1837.]

Let the learned judge for themselves concerning this conjecture of the most learned Theiner. For our part, we are certainly convinced that the little book *On the Sacrifice of the Mass* is most worthy of being attributed to Alger and should henceforth not be separated from his books *On the Sacraments of the Body and Blood of the Lord*. We have therefore judged that it should be added to this volume.

These are Saint Alger’s works which the passing age has not grudged us. The rest have lamentably perished. For Alger also wrote a *History of the Church of Liège*, concerning which Nicholas says: “He had so carefully learned the ancient dignity of the Church of Liège from the testimony and writings of the elders that Alger left it all written down for posterity’s study and remembrance.”

It is certain from the testimony of the same Nicholas that he published many letters. “For ecclesiastical business,” he says, “he wrote many notable letters to various persons and churches, which many preserve and read with the greatest eagerness.”

Trithemius writes that he excelled in poetry and prose; hence it is probable that he also published certain poems.

Pagi, under the year 1132, no. 13, [Note: [Col. 0731] In Baronius, vol. XVIII, p. 485, Luc. ed. 1746.] observes that Alger wrote those *Deeds of St Lambert* published by Dom Chapeauville in vol. I of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège*. But Pagi is mistaken. In the appendix to that volume are published the four principal authors who separately wrote the deeds of St Lambert; Alger is not counted among them, nor is mention made elsewhere of any writing by him. I conjecture that the most learned Pagi did not distinguish our Alger from Hariger, Abbot of Lobbes, who carefully wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* and is the first author listed by the most learned Chapeauville in the volume cited.

It is now established that the book *On Spirit and Soul*, formerly attributed to Alger, was written by Alcher, monk of Clairvaux.

These are the observations I had to make concerning Alger’s life and writings. It remains for me to add some remarks concerning his outstanding work entitled *On the Sacraments of the Body and Blood of the Lord* and concerning this new edition of that work.

Alger, in his Prologue, reviews the heresies and errors by which Catholic teaching concerning the most holy sacrament had repeatedly been corrupted; he then discusses excellently the goodness of the Savior and the omnipotence of God as manifested in the Eucharist. “Although the mystery,” he says, “is incomprehensible, it is not unbelievable; for, though we are incapable of understanding it, God is certainly not unable to accomplish it” (p. 6). He next employs this very beautiful comparison: if sight were to declare to hearing the variety of colors, or hearing to sight the variety of sounds, each would have to believe the other concerning what it did not perceive at all. By the same reasoning, although we perceive neither by the senses nor by the intellect the presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, we must believe God who asserts things that surpass the power of the senses and the grasp of the intellect.

In the first book he proves and, by examination, confirms the truth of the real and substantial presence of Christ’s body in the most holy sacrament. He teaches that the universal and perpetual tradition of the Catholic Church concerning this dogma is such that, if it is false, the Christian faith itself is entirely abolished. “Since,” he says, “believers past and present throughout the whole world believe and maintain this, if this universal faith of the Church has not been true unto salvation, then either the Catholic Church has never existed, or it has perished. . . . Since all nations glory that they thus believe, if they lack the blessing of salvation, the truth of God is endangered alike in prophecy and in the Gospel. . . . Therefore let him be anathema, maranatha, who has presumed to contradict divine authority in this sacrament and has not believed that Christ’s body—the true bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world—truly exists as it is” (Book I, ch. 13, p. 124).

He establishes the nature of the sacrifice of the new law in its representation of the immolation of the sacrifice of the Cross, and carefully explains how our daily offering is the same as that which Christ the Lord performed once upon Mount Calvary (p. 143).

From chapter XX (p. 178) onward, he discusses the manner of receiving Christ’s body, and with this concludes the first book.

In the second book he is wholly occupied in resolving the questions customarily raised concerning the matter, form, accidents, and effects of the most holy sacrament—questions which everyone will gladly examine with Alger.

In the third book Alger especially attacks the then-growing Waldensian error that the uprightness and holiness of the minister are altogether required for the validity of the sacraments. From the teaching of St. Augustine and other Fathers, he demonstrates at length that the divine sacraments derive their efficacy from God their author, not from the ministers to whom their dispensation has been entrusted, and that they far exceed human merits.

In the little work *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, he explains individually the prayers customarily recited in the holy sacrifice and the sacred rites.

[Col. 0733] Alger’s teaching accords with the Catholic faith. Indeed, those points of his teaching which certain authors denounce as erroneous or to be understood cautiously, I judge to deserve either no censure at all, or certainly not such great censure.

The Cologne editor observes that Alger did not speak with sufficient precision when, following Paschasius (*On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, ch. 4, p. 1563, Paris ed. 1618), he wrote (Book I, ch. 16, p. 149) that Christ’s body is created potentially in the most holy sacrament. But many passages of our author, in which he describes transubstantiation with the utmost precision, clearly explain what “potential creation” means in Alger. “The bread,” he says, “becomes the same flesh [of Christ]; flesh is not born, nor does [the bread] assume flesh, but it is changed into flesh: thus becoming what it was not, so that it ceases to be what it had been” (Book I, ch. 6, p. 49). Chapter VII (p. 53) bears this title: “THAT, WHILE ITS QUALITIES REMAIN, THE SUBSTANCE OF BREAD AND WINE IS CHANGED INTO THE TRUE BODY OF CHRIST.” Moreover, Alger never taught that the Lord’s flesh and blood are potentially created *from* bread and wine, but that bread and wine are truly, through the consecration of the Holy Spirit, potentially created as flesh and blood; as though he meant that the substance of bread and wine is transformed by a divine operation—a transformation which may indeed be likened to a kind of creation. What theologian, then, would disagree with Alger here?

The same Cologne editor also feared where there was no cause for fear when, as if correcting Alger, he remarked that Christ’s body while he dwelt on earth is called immortal and impassible only insofar as it exists in the sacramental state; for Alger himself believed this. He asks there (p. 89) whether, before the Passion, the Lord gave his body in the sacrament incorruptible and immortal, as now after his resurrection he gives it to us daily. . . . Although the Master of the Sentences, St. Thomas, St. Bonaventure, and the greater part of theologians followed the negative opinion, not a few theologians, without any injury to faith or Catholic doctrine, have defended the affirmative position with Alger. What, then, is there in his opinion to be counted against him?

Bellarmin himself is more unjust to our Alger than is fair when he writes:

> [Note: [Col. 0733] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1130, p. 246, Brussels ed. 1719.] “Alger seems to maintain that it is of divine law that the sacrifice of the Mass be celebrated with unleavened bread; but this is not true. . . .”

For Alger means nothing of the sort, since he expressly writes (Book II, ch. 10, p. 270) that many good Catholics consider it not contrary to the Christian faith whether the divine sacrifice is performed with unleavened or leavened bread, both because each is bread and because Christ’s example, who consecrated with unleavened bread, does not have the force of divine law. The Cologne editor therefore needlessly observes that Christ’s example, by which Alger confirms the practice of the Latin Church, must by no means be treated as a command. Alger himself had already noted this at the beginning of that chapter.

I would also wish that no one had falsely attributed the error of the Callixtines to Alger. For he teaches that bread is consecrated in itself into the body and wine in itself into the blood, yet so that neither a bloodless body nor blood separated from the body is conceived in the sacrament (Book II, ch. 8, p. 266). From this it follows of itself that under one species the whole is received which is contained under both species. When he writes that body and blood are received by the faithful (p. 267), he does not teach that this is done by command or from a necessary cause. Therefore he must be freed from every suspicion of error in this matter as well.

Alger indeed labors greatly to explain the corruption of the sacramental species, which had furnished heretics of that age with an occasion for blaspheming Catholic doctrine. Indeed, he becomes entangled in resolving difficulties from which neither Lanfranc nor Guitmund could extricate themselves. Alger maintains, namely, that the species of the sacrament can never decay, be gnawed by mice, or be dissolved by putrefaction, and so forth; rather, that they vanish. Thus, if they seem to rot or to be eaten by brute animals, they rot or are eaten not truly and really, but only in appearance: namely, God permits this apparent corruption as a punishment for those who have treated the sacrament unworthily. Hence he vehemently attacks the heresy of the Stercoranists, who, as he reports, maintained that bodies are expanded and nourished by the sacrament as by food, while the species pass away as ordinary food in excrement, and so forth. Accordingly, he most rightly denies that the matter stands as the Stercoranists were thought to imagine and represent it.

Alger therefore held the doctrine held by all theologians, indeed by the Church herself: that no injury is inflicted upon Christ’s body through corruption of the sacramental species. But he falsely and unnecessarily asserted that those species never decay. Falsely, indeed, because experience contradicted his opinion; unnecessarily, because, having taught that the accidents of the sacrament do not adhere to Christ’s body but are preserved in a wondrous way without a subject, he could certainly, without injury to the Savior, have granted that the species themselves behave no differently than if they adhered to their own proper substance, and consequently that bodies are nourished by them and discharge them as excrement just as other foods. For, since they do not adhere to the substance of Christ’s body, the Savior’s body cannot be said to suffer what happens to the species. Moreover, as soon as through any external cause the accidents of the sacrament lose the appearance of bread, both the sacrament itself and the presence of Christ’s body under that species simultaneously cease. . . . From this you may conclude that Alger, if he defended his opinion against the cavils of heretics with less than complete skill, nevertheless departed not even a finger’s breadth from the true doctrine of Catholic theologians.

[Col. 0735] There are serious men who think that the heresy of the Stercoranists never really existed, but was first, as it were, invented when Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, in the celebrated disputation he held at Constantinople in 1054 with Nicetas Pectoratus, charged it against his opponent. Nicetas reproached the Latins, namely, that during Lent they broke their fast by receiving the Eucharist at the third hour—which for us is nine in the morning. Cardinal Humbert replied:

> “O faithless Stercoranist,” he said, “you who think that the Lenten and ecclesiastical fasts are dissolved by the faithful partaking of the body and blood of the Lord, utterly believing that the heavenly food, like earthly food, is discharged as excrement through the foul and filthy evacuation of the belly; you plainly think with Arius!”

> [Note: [Col. 0735] F. Humbert, *Reply to the Booklet of Nicetas Pectoratus*, no. 22, in Galland, *Library of the Fathers*, XIV, 219.]

Learned writers derive the origin of the fictitious heresy from this, and say that it was never espoused by the Greeks. Yet I should suppose that Berengar, and whatever disciples he had, attacked the Catholic dogma of Christ’s bodily substantial presence in the Eucharist through the absurd arguments attributed to the Stercoranists, and thereby moved the defenders of the Catholic faith to refute this filthy heresy.

Whatever judgment is made concerning this, Alger defended sincerely, if not very skillfully, the opinion by which both the sacrament’s due honor and the highest reverence are maintained.

I admit that our author, though deservedly praised for his learning, nevertheless here and there cited apocryphal writings of the Fathers, or genuine books under false names. Thus, for example, he frequently cites Paschasius under Augustine’s name. He once and again praises under the name of St. Basil the books *On the Priesthood*, whose eminent authorship by St. John Chrysostom no one fails to know (p. 117). Under the name of Eusebius of Emesa he adduces homilies falsely attributed to the Greek writer Eusebius of Emesa and assigned by more expert critics to St. Eucherius of Lyons, Faustus of Riez, some Gallic Eusebius, or anonymous writers. He also uses the book entitled *Sentences of Prosper*, which has no affinity with the work now preserved under that title among the writings of St. Prosper. But these faults are readily forgiven Alger, not only because of the extreme scarcity of books under which his age suffered, but also because he never adduces apocryphal testimonies without abundantly proving his position by genuine and clear ones.

Wherever I could conveniently do so, I carefully noted the genuine books of the holy Fathers according to the order in which they now stand in the best editions, so that anyone wishing to consult them might find them without difficulty. I made this my chief effort after vainly searching for manuscript codices by which I might correct the old editions of Alger. For that codex listed under Alger’s name in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Burgundy at Brussels is not Alger’s, but consists of certain patched-together scraps from the holy Fathers. Our edition therefore proceeds from that prepared at Louvain two hundred and eighty-five years ago by the most learned Vlimmerius, a regular canon of St. Augustine. I was sometimes able fortunately to correct the reading from the text provided by the Cologne *Library of the Fathers* (1618, vol. XII, p. 410 ff.); on p. 69 I supplied one word from my own conjecture; I left the rest intact, lest perhaps I add errors to errors.

Do not doubt, Christian reader, that this volume presents you with a book whose praise has been celebrated by ancient and more recent theologians. Peter the Venerable, a man most renowned for learning and wisdom, praises it.

> [Note: [Col. 0735] In the passages cited above.—Erasmus, in his letter to Balthasar, bishop of Hildesheim, prefixed to his edition of 1530 and retained by Vlimmerius in the Louvain edition, greatly extols Alger. But because Erasmus discusses Catholic doctrine skeptically or playfully in that letter, I judged that it should be passed over.]

Bellarmin, the terror of heretics, writes that he is very good.

> [Note: [Col. 0735] After noting certain blemishes in Alger, he adds: “I wished to note these things, not in order to diminish the glory of Alger, who defended the truth in his age with great zeal, but lest the reader encounter a stumbling block in reading this work, otherwise very good. . . .” *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1130, p. 246, Brussels ed. 1719.]

All who have written against Protestants in our age proclaim him most useful. Cardinal Du Perron uses his authority and teaching to refute heretics, and set him before heretics as a witness of the faith and an eminent theologian.

> [Note: [Col. 0735] *Treatise on the Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist*, pp. 697, 698, 713, etc., Paris, 1633.]

Alger, says the most learned Pierre de Marca,

> [Note: [Col. 0735] *Treatise on the Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist*, p. 141, vol. V of the minor works, Bamberg ed. 1789.]

was the first to teach that accidents subsist without a subject in the most holy Eucharist, and corrected in many respects the opinions of preceding writers. The authors of the work entitled *The Perpetuity of the Faith of the Catholic Church concerning the Eucharist* not only reckon Alger among the principal defenders of the Catholic faith, but assert that no one explained more clearly St. Augustine’s doctrine concerning the venerable sacrament.

> [Note: [Col. 0735] *Perpetuity of the Faith*, vol. VI, historical and chronological table, p. 42. See ibid., “Tradition of the Church,” p. 195, where Alger’s arguments are enumerated. See also *Literary History of France*, vol. XI, p. 158, and Dom Cellier, *General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. XXII, p. 254.]

Therefore, Christian reader, make use of this outstanding little work and of this whatever-it-may-be labor of ours. You will not meditate upon it in vain if you wish more deeply to understand that infinite love which our Savior has displayed to us in the most holy sacrament. And if you derive any fruit from reading Alger, that will be our reward; for what we most desire is that this little book concerning Christ’s true body may serve for the edification of Christ’s mystical body. Let it also stand as a token of the love with which our Catholic university is borne toward the sacrament to be adored, and likewise as a kind of memorial of its devout affection for the Church of Liège.

Written at Louvain on the feast day of Saints Jude and Simon, 1846.

J. B. MALOU.

[Col. 0737]

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING ALGER

[Col. 0737A] I. Eulogy of Alger the Scholastic, by NICHOLAS, canon of Liège, his contemporary.

> [Note: [Col. 0737] From Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, p. 129, ed. 1723.]

Alger of Liège, devoting himself wholly from earliest infancy to the study of letters, flourished nobly under the most distinguished men whose learning and honorable morals then made the Church of Liège shine and gave lustre to France. Thus no rule of the Christian faith seemed unknown to him, and no liberal art foreign to him.

And, to commit something concerning his character to memory: first he served God in the church of St. Bartholomew the Apostle, which lies in the suburb of Liège—by profession and habit a cleric, in rank a deacon, and in office a scholasticus [schoolmaster]. Later, honorably transferred by Bishop Otbert to the greater church of Holy Mary and St. Lambert, and gladly received by his predecessors, he wrote for twenty years, until the death of Bishop Frederick of blessed memory, many distinguished letters on ecclesiastical affairs to various persons and churches; these are preserved and read by many with the greatest zeal.

Because the golden mean was familiar to him throughout his life, he showed himself wholly free from every ambition in seeking the exaltation of riches. For when certain bishops of Saxony or Germany sought him because of his outstanding reputation in both philosophy and sacred letters, and invited him with rich revenues from possessions and great ecclesiastical dignities, he preferred the private position which he held to a higher one, saying with Solomon: “He who loves riches shall not receive fruit from them” (Eccles. 5:9).

He was subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, prudent in counsel, diligent in managing his household, faithful in what was entrusted to him, steadfast in purpose; and, what is more precious than all these, he was considered—and was—Catholic both in faith and in doctrine.

He had so carefully acquired knowledge of the ancient dignity of the Church through the accounts and writings of the elders that he left it all committed to writing for posterity, as an aid to memory, lest it should someday be shaken by the factions of certain clerics who seek innovations, or lest there should come into doubt what belongs to the privilege of the greater church for the good of common concord.

[Col. 0738A] Accordingly, after the death of Bishop Frederick, when he possessed abundant resources and was very vigorous in body and sound in mind, he put his affairs in order and, naked, followed the naked Christ. He undertook a stricter and therefore happier life under the Rule of St. Benedict in the monastery of Cluny, where he is said even now to survive, not without great renown for holy conduct and learning.

Among the other memorials of his talent, while still a cleric he produced two treatises certainly very useful for ecclesiastical affairs and the Catholic faith. He entitled the first, suppressing the author’s name for humility’s sake, *On Mercy and Justice*. He divided it into three parts: the first, tempering justice with mercy, treats sufficiently of the toleration of evildoers; the second, of ecclesiastical sinners and their canonical correction; the third, of those outside the Church and their sacrilegious communion. These are of four kinds: excommunicated persons, condemned persons, schismatics, and heretics. The beginning of its Prologue runs as follows: “Whoever I may be, [I consider] neither the weight nor the amount of time which Jethro [assigned] to Moses, according to his measure, [nor] to all Catholics.” [The quotation is incomplete or corrupt as printed.]

He produced another work, so much nobler as it was more sublime, namely on a wonderful and necessary subject: the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, concerning which various errors and various heresies had arisen. As is found in the preface to that work, although this mystery is incomprehensible, it nevertheless does not seem unbelievable to believers; not by human reason, which is insufficient for this, but by the testimonies of Christ himself and of his saints, by which the Church is strengthened, it is affirmed and maintained. This work is divided into three parts. The first treats directly of the truth and efficacy of Christ’s body and contains twenty-two chapters; the second, divided into ten chapters, treats of various questions concerning the sacrament itself; the third, which seems more difficult to investigate, treats in fourteen chapters of sinful ministers outside the Church—that is, heretics or schismatics—whether the sacraments which they appear to celebrate are true and valid, or should rather be called, and are, sacrileges.

Let us therefore embrace with the greatest desire this praiseworthy work of a distinguished intellect, in which nothing is found discordant with the sayings of the saints, nothing contrary to the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0739A] II. From the treatise of PETER THE VENERABLE, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass and Transubstantiation against Peter of Bruys and Henry, Teachers of New Impieties*.

You have rejected Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, the ancient and holy doctors of the Church. I would send to you learned and Catholic men of modern times—Lanfranc, Guitmund, Alger—if only you would deign either to read even these, not because of their greater authority but because of their nearness in time and familiar acquaintance, or to permit yourselves to hear them. One of these was Archbishop of Canterbury, another Bishop of Aversa, the third formerly canon and master at Liège, afterward in our time a monk and priest in the monastery of Cluny, where his book is also kept; he was a man of pure and devout life. The first of these discussed well, fully, and perfectly the truth of Christ’s body and blood, which is veiled beneath the covering of the sacraments; the next, better, more fully, and more perfectly; the last—Alger—best, most fully, and most perfectly, so that he left nothing for even the most scrupulous reader to seek.

III. TRITHEMIUS, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 328.

Alger, formerly a scholasticus and afterward a monk of Corbie in Saxony, German by nation, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man continually exercised in the study of the holy Scriptures, rich in reading the ancients, and magnificently learned in secular letters, cautious in intellect and sufficiently eloquent in speech, powerful in verse and prose, wrote in a highly polished style the notable work *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, three books. “Because the saints [write] concerning the body . . .” — *On Grace and Free Will*, one book: “It should be known that free . . .” — and certain letters. He is also said to have written several other works which have not reached our hands.

[Col. 0739]

## [ON THE SACRAMENTS]

### PROLOGUE OF THE DIVINE ALGER TO THE BOOK *ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE LORD’S BODY AND BLOOD*

[Col. 0739C] Because the saints, writing variously about the Lord’s body and blood, sometimes speak of the whole Christ, namely head and members; sometimes not of the whole, but either of the head or of the members; sometimes with reference to the sacrament and sometimes without it—errors are generated among the simple, as concerning an ineffable matter not understood, and heresies among those wishing to be wise beyond what is fitting. Thus the simple, unless more perfectly instructed, perish by erring; while those wise beyond what is fitting, unless corrected, destroy themselves and others by teaching and defending what they do not know. For some attribute to the head what is said of the members; others impose upon the members what is said of the head; and they think so confusedly of both, or of either, that they either abase the head too much or glorify the members too highly, and thus judge neither what is true nor what is fitting in either case.

And not only concerning the truth of Christ’s body, but also concerning its sacrament, various errors and various heresies arise. Some say that bread and wine, unchanged, are called Christ’s body not truly but figuratively, merely as a sacrament, like the water of baptism or the oil of chrism; as when it is said, “Receive the white garment which you shall bear before the tribunal of Christ,” though it does not mean the garment itself but that which is signified by it. Others say that the bread is not merely a sacrament, but that Christ is, as it were, “breaded” (*impanatus*) in the bread, just as God was personally incarnate in flesh. Others say that bread and wine are changed into flesh and blood, but not into those of Christ: rather, into those of any holy son of man acceptable to God, so that what Christ said may be fulfilled: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Others, detracting from God’s grace, say that the evil merits of priests so nullify the invocation of the divine name that through their unworthy consecration the bread ought not to be changed into Christ’s flesh. Others say that it is indeed changed into Christ’s flesh, but that because of the evil merits of those receiving it, it does not remain Christ’s flesh but returns again to the bare sacrament of bread and wine. Others, worse still, say that through eating it is changed into the corruption of foul digestion.

Therefore, because so many heresies—and any others that may arise—spring up concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, I shall, with the aid of divine grace, explain as faithfully as I can its truth and efficacy. I shall do so not by human reason, which is insufficient for this, but by the testimonies of Christ himself and of his saints, by which the Church stands strengthened. The more firmly she holds the true faith from these witnesses, the more certainly she obtains eternal salvation. For, as the Apostle says, it pleased God to save believers not through persuasive words of human wisdom but through the folly of preaching; because “the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 2:4). It seems foolish—but to fools—that Christ becomes bodily present to us under the appearance of bread and wine, that is, of a brute material thing, and that so great a majesty is contained in so small a form of bread. But who should blame in God what is pious in him and necessary to us? It does not indeed seem fitting to his dignity that the corruptible substance of bread should become his incorruptible body; yet it is fitting to our salvation that he should refresh us with such a sacrament, the bread of angels. It is most wise, indeed, that faith may be exercised for merit through a hidden mystery; and most powerful, that the mind strengthened by such food, after overcoming the enemy, may strive more strongly toward the kingdom. Most wisely, I say, and most powerfully, so that neither the power nor the workmanship of so great a work, accomplished from a thing at once least and greatest, can be comprehended. For above all it is wonderful to change the existing substance of bread into the coexisting substance of his flesh: that what is seen should not be what it appears to be; and that this flesh itself, though localized, should truly and substantially be present in heaven and on earth; and that, though his flesh is truly eaten and his blood drunk by the people, Christ himself nevertheless remains alive and whole in his kingdom. But these things are hidden to blind reason and manifest to faith.

Therefore what Christ deigns to work for us of himself, so wondrously and so beneficially, must not be lightly esteemed, but continually revered and worshipped by us. For he who is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matt. 3:9), and who changes the brute elements of bread and wine into his own substance, will much more transform his faithful people, under the image and power of such great hope, into the glory of his body, giving grace not according to merit but from grace. Hence Augustine (vol. V, ch. 1104): “You receive your mystery from the table of the Lord: be what you see, and receive what you are.”

[Col. 0741C] Since I am about to speak of so wondrous and necessary a mystery, I think that believers must first be admonished that, although it is incomprehensible, it ought not therefore to seem unbelievable. For though we are not capable of understanding, God is certainly not incapable of accomplishing, he who, as the Psalmist says, “has done all things whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 113:3). Human littleness ought to consider its own measure: because it has not received the power to comprehend the great works of God, it should not therefore believe them to exist any less. For since man is a creature, though an excellent one, just as he rules certain creatures over whom he has been placed, so too, not yet made equal to certain others, he is subject—far more unlike them—to him by whom he was made. For just as a stone has not been granted perception, nor a beast understanding, so man has not yet been granted to see God as he is with the angels. Since, therefore, man is neither perceived by the stone nor understood by the beast over which he rules, does he understand himself to exist any less because he is not known to his inferiors?

Thus, then, God, who does not ordinarily make his incomprehensible majesty perceptible to beastly senses or human intellects as he does earthly things—should he be thought to exist any less by us, who are far his inferiors, because we cannot grasp his truth, which is far, far more beyond us than we are unable to grasp our inferiors? For by as much as the things made beneath us are far from us in sense or understanding, by so much—and incomparably more—are we far from him who made us. For since “man, when he was in honor, did not understand, and was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13), he received in his body beastly senses, by which he perceives only bodily things, and not even those truly and perfectly; while in his mind he has an intellect so dull that he distinguishes bodily things only a little, spiritual things less.

It is not fitting, therefore, that with our beastly sense or limited intellect—by which we are insufficient even to know these earthly things—we should wish to comprehend the immensity of divine majesty, when the angels themselves, who are still superior to us, “desire to look into” him (1 Pet. 1:12) but are unable to penetrate the immensity of his majesty, although they contemplate him as he is, face to face, and are filled with his manifest glory. For what creature, being circumscribed, can comprehend the immeasurable? If it can in any measure be comprehended, it is not immeasurable. Therefore, as the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think unto sobriety”; and let each do so “according as God has divided to each a measure of faith” (Rom. 12:3). For he does not give all things to all, but each has his own gift from God.

To show this by an appropriate likeness of our body’s members in the Church, different senses are distributed to different members, through which color is perceived by the eyes and sound by the ears in different ways, and so with the rest. To speak figuratively, then: if sight were to declare to hearing the variety of colors, and hearing were to declare to sight the variety of sounds, would not each have to believe the other concerning those things which it did not perceive at all? A thing ought not to be unbelievable because it is incomprehensible to that faculty. Are things seen any less real than things heard, or conversely? Behold: the eye sees the movement of a wagon, but the ear does not perceive its creaking because of its slowness. Since movement and creaking do not exist without one another, are they any less together because sight and hearing do not perceive them together? Is not the whole world together because it is not all visible at once to anyone, as it was to blessed Benedict?

> [Note: [Col. 0741] St. Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book II, ch. 35, col. 269, vol. II of the 1705 edition.]

Since, then, one sense ought not prejudice its equal so as to believe less that something exists because it is perceptible not to itself but to another sense, how should it prejudice its superior, the intellect, so as to believe less that something exists because it is not intelligible to itself? For just as sound is invisible to the eye and color inaudible to the ear, so the intellect of the soul is imperceptible to all bodily senses. Is that by which the soul distinguishes bodily and spiritual things through its intellect any less real? By it the soul detects in shrubs or herbs the nature of heat or cold, moisture or dryness; checks thoughts that depart from it by its imperceptible discernment; applies itself imperceptibly even to governing bodily senses; and in all these things it alone understands itself and understands. To what end are these observations? So that, just as things incomprehensible to the senses are believed to exist nonetheless, so things incomprehensible to human intellects may likewise be believed to exist nonetheless. Therefore, while, as the Apostle says, we contemplate God now “through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12), we know much of him if we believe him incomprehensible to us and more wonderful in himself than he is wonderful in the things which he made from nothing.

[Col. 0744A] In exhorting and persuading toward faith, I seem to have exceeded the bounds of a prologue; but I have done so because I saw faith to be especially necessary for apprehending the truth of the sacrament of which I am to treat. Now, therefore, with God’s consent, I shall set forth the first little portion of this work concerning the truth of the Lord’s body, and the second concerning various lesser questions of the sacrament itself.

## FIRST BOOK OF THE DIVINE ALGER, *ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE LORD’S BODY AND BLOOD*

[Col. 0743]

### CHAPTER I. That God exalted above all things the Lordly man assumed for us.

[Col. 0743B]

Because, blinded by original sin from the true knowledge of faith, we had fallen into various errors and, at the devil’s instigation, served idolatry and the passions of sins, tending with obstinate mind toward death, the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14): so that he who was incomprehensible to us from what was his own might become knowable to us from what is ours, and from what is ours might become, as it were, desirable to us at close range. For we saw in him the glory of our kindred flesh, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father; and, drawn by the visible signs of the glory of one now, as it were, of the same origin as ourselves into love of invisible things, we might be brought back to the homeland of eternal life.

Thus the work of the Lord’s Incarnation, as it was peculiarly proper to God himself beyond all his other works, so he made it especially preeminent beyond all his works: namely, he glorified the man assumed into the unity of his person and, as it were, deified by the divinity joined to him, so that, setting him forth to be adored not only by human beings but also by all angelic spirits, he placed him at the right hand of God the Father. Hence Augustine, in the book *Against Maximinus* (Book III, ch. 2, vol. VIII, col. 693):

> The Apostle says: “Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings” (Phil. 2:4). And you do not ask to whom he gave it—whether to man or to God. For how he gave it is plainly apparent. “He humbled himself,” he says, “unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (ibid.).

Was the Son of God, the Word who is God with God, not exalted before this took place? Or did he only begin to be the exalted Son of God, the only God of God, and to have the name above every name after he was exalted for becoming obedient unto death, even death on the cross? Who could say anything more foolish? Therefore this was given to him as man, [Col. 0744B] according to which he became obedient unto death on the cross—what he, the same Son of God, God born of God and equal [to the Father], already possessed. Again St Augustine, in the same work (book II, ch. 2, vol. VIII, col. 693): “He gave these things, therefore, to the man, not to God.” For when he was in the form of God, was he not exalted, and did not the heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bend the knee to him? But when it is said, “Therefore God exalted him,” the reason for which he exalted him is sufficiently apparent. Thus the form in which he was crucified was itself exalted; to it was given the name above every name, so that, when that form of a servant is named, the only-begotten Son of God may be understood. Again Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 8 (II.2, vol. IV, col. 43): “And thou hast set him over the works of thy hands. Since [Col. 0744C] the angels too are works of God’s hands, we understand that the only-begotten Son was set even over the angels—he whom we hear and believe to have been made a little lower than the angels through the humility of his carnal birth and passion. ‘Thou hast subjected all things,’ he says, ‘under his feet.’ He excludes nothing when he says ‘all things.’” And lest this be understood otherwise, the Apostle commands us to believe it thus when he says: “Except him who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:27).

Nor is it surprising that the Son of Man, united in one person to the Son of God, should attain not only a share in the divine name but also in divine glory: so that, exalted above every creature, he is worshipped by all through the bending of the knee, and the Only-begotten of God is named through the one to whom he is united. [Col. 0744D] For why should God do less for the man personally united to himself than the soul does, through him, for the body united to it? For the soul grants a participation in the name and nature which it has, so that what did not possess this of itself may live and feel as animated by the soul. Fire too, when it penetrates iron, makes it incandescent; imparting its own brightness and heat, it makes the iron sparkle, blaze, and burn contrary to its own nature. Therefore, when fire makes incandescent and the soul gives life, what does God do but deify the man united to himself and, exalting him above every creature, glorify him with himself by the prerogative also of purity, omnipotence, and Deity?

## CHAPTER II. Since Christ has been exalted above all things, and in him all things have been given to us, we too ought to hope for a like glory.

[Col. 0745A]

Moreover, so that we may hope more confidently for glory in our like nature through Christ’s grace, he made us his brothers and gave us both him and, with him, all things (Rom. 8:7); so that, when we believe that the Lord’s man, in the unity of God’s person, has been deified, it may not be doubtful that, through his grace, what John testifies has been given to us. For he says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12), who are born of God. Hence Augustine, in the second sermon on John (no. 15, vol. III, part II, col. 303): “That human beings might be born from [Col. 0745B] God, God was first born from them. Do not marvel, then, O man, that through grace you are made a son, because you are born of God according to his Word. That same Word first willed to be born from man, so that you might securely be born from God.”

Indeed, so that we might be more secure in him concerning the conformity and unity of so great a grace [Note: [Col. 0745D] Elsewhere: “glory.”], God united to himself in the same person, within our lowly nature, the nature of our flesh; so that, seeing it so wonderfully glorified, we might not despair of the glorification of our own true flesh. Therefore, since he willed to adopt us into this grace, so that he might make children of God those who had not even been worthy servants, and appoint us co-heirs with Christ, he endowed with the privilege of every grace—not by measure but above every creature—the very one whom he willed to be firstborn among [Col. 0745C] many brothers and his own only-begotten, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. Thus he, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born as the Son of God—not reborn, but born—might cause us, conceived in iniquities and born servants of the devil, to be reborn through grace as children of God; and, gathering and transforming them by a second birth, might advance to his glory those whom he surpassed in every respect by his first birth.

So that the power of Christ’s deifying body might become evident: just as the sun penetrates glass without injury either to itself or to the glass, so he himself, not phantom but true, whole passing through the intact virginity of his virgin mother, is neither dispersed by it nor disperses it. The matter is indeed astonishing and ineffable, but not unbelievable to us, because it is not impossible for the Almighty. Hence Augustine, on John (tractate 91, no. 3, vol. III, part II, col. 719): “What he was born of a virgin surpasses indeed all other miracles; he alone could neither violate his mother’s integrity when conceived nor when born.”

That God should thus be born befitted him and profited us: born pure, that he might cleanse us; born mighty, that he might strengthen the weak. For he willed that his purity should be ours, so that through that conformity we might please him, being united to him. But lest we should fail through our weakness against the most savage enemy, he made his power [Col. 0746A] ours, so that, since his strength is more readily available to us than our own, we might through his grace be more devoted to him; and, since he is stronger, might through his omnipotence be stronger against the enemy. For by nature we could be created powerful, yet not almighty; but now, because the Almighty is our strength, we are made almost almighty through grace. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:31). If, then, because all things are possible to us, we are made almighty, what harm does our weakness do us, with God’s help? It both increases the merit of humility and suffers no diminution of strength. For what strength would a rustic lose if, in his cause against some powerful opponent, the king supported him where he himself could not act? Hence also the Apostle: “If God [Col. 0746B] is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:7). Again, in the Psalm: “In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing” (Ps. 59:20). Again the Lord in the Gospel: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John 16:18). Why would he say this unless that victory of his were ours? Hence Augustine, in his sermon on the birthday of martyrs (334, no. 2, vol. V, col. 1298): “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. How then did he not also give us all things with him?” (Rom. 8:32). “When he gave us himself, he gave us all things with him. Does the roaring of the world terrify you—to whom the maker of the world has been given?” Let us rejoice that Christ has been given to us, and fear no enemies in this age. Whatever power he displayed—whether in being born, healing the weak, raising the dead, [Col. 0746C] rising himself from the dead, or ascending into heaven—he did for us, so that he might be believed and be mighty for strengthening our weakness and bestowing salvation, and so that flesh might not despair of arriving there where it had known flesh to have ascended. Hence Augustine, in the eleventh sermon on the words of the Gospel: “The serpent’s cunning malice, so as to turn you away from Christ by praise of Christ, craftily proclaims him whom it does not dare to disparage. It magnifies his majesty so as to make him unique, lest you hope for anything such as was shown in him when he rose. Stir up faith, therefore; and to one saying, ‘Christ alone could do this; we cannot,’ answer and say: ‘Christ could do it because he is God.’ He will answer: ‘Certainly, because he is God.’ And you say: ‘And because he is God, because he is almighty, why should I despair that he will be able to do in me what he showed in himself for my sake?’”

For indeed, because, as Isaiah says, “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6), and with him, as has been said, all things: whatever he accomplished in humanity, he accomplished for us, so that when he who possesses all things was given to us, nothing pertaining to salvation might be lacking to us in so abundant a gift; but even in this life, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 15:28), God might be all in all. Therefore, that this might be plainly certain to us, lest we in any way distrust his grace, commending his love to us and stirring up ours by teachings, examples, sacraments, promises, and benefits, [Col. 0747A] and strengthening our frailty, he willed through an affection of fatherly love to be called and to be our Father. He promised that he would give whatever we asked in his name; and because we were by origin and misery slaves of our enemy—and enemies of God our Father in the same nature by which we had perished—restoring us with greater honour and to the greater shame of the enemy, he who owed nothing of himself became our substitute in order to pay Adam’s debt for us. And, to render us free and secure from the enemy, he repaid with the surrender of his own blood to the enemy’s will the gratification Adam had offered for forbidden food. By this price he redeemed us in such a way that, because the Lord had unjustly been stripped of life by his wicked servant, he justly stripped that servant of all that was his—namely, us—and, having been taken captive by him, took him captive; [Col. 0747B] by his single death he took away our double death, the three-day and the eternal. By bearing in himself the undeserved penalty of that death, he paid for Adam’s sin, which could not remain unpunished; by satisfying the Father’s wrath for us, he appeased it and remitted the endless penalty owed by us. And because, by preserving for the Father alone from the world’s beginning a full obedience unto death, he triumphed over his enemy, by this singular merit he was, in that same humanity in which he suffered death, exalted above all things, as has been said. He made us, reconciled to the Father’s grace, children of God from slaves of the devil, regenerating us by the sacrament of baptism and cleansing, enlightening, strengthening, and adorning with various charisms the hearts of believers by the Spirit of adoption as sons.

## CHAPTER III. For greater certainty of so great a grace, God so constituted Christ himself as our head and us as his members that we are called Christ—his body together with the head—uniting and incorporating us to himself through the sacrament and reality of his body.

[Col. 0747C]

Finally, lest anything in him seem foreign or difficult to us, he communicated himself to us so truly and perfectly that, visibly also, by the wondrous sacrament of his body and blood, he united and made the Church one body with himself, honouring it with so great a grace that he himself was its head and it his body—not in name only, but truly incorporated with him in the reality of his body. Thus there might be no separation for us from any grace in him, with whom the sacrament of so unique a unity binds us firmly; and it might be certain [Col. 0747D] that by this covenant we shall, with him and through him, attain in eternal life a like glory of dignity, if with him and through him we are willing in this life to preserve a like grace of innocence. This is especially so since, when he was about to die, under the New Testament of his own most holy blood—upon which, as the Apostle says (Gal. 3:15), it is unlawful to impose further provisions or make changes—he assigned to us the covenant of eternal life; and, by rising from the dead in himself as our head, showed how he ought to glorify his body. For it would not be worthy of God’s mercy and justice if he rejected from partnership in his kingdom those whom he deigns to unite with himself so intimately in the exile of this world, and did not repay with reciprocal honour in the manifest vision of his majesty those by whom he has been worthily received and worshipped in the hidden and pilgrim figures of his sacraments. How, moreover, could what has here been made one become different there? Hence Hilary, in book VIII *On the Trinity* (no. 13, col. 222): “If the Word truly became flesh, and if we truly receive the Word made flesh in the Lord’s food, how is he not to be thought to remain naturally in us, he who, being born man, assumed to himself the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated to us?” For we are all one in this way: because the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in these things. If, therefore, we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body, and thereby are one because the Father [Col. 0748B] is in him and he in us, this natural possession through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity.

Accordingly the saints called Christ the head of the Church and the Church the members or body of Christ, and called it, together with its head, Christ. Hence Augustine, in *On the Trinity* (book IV, no. 12, vol. VIII, col. 818): “Just as the body is one,” he says, “and has many members, so also is Christ. He did not say, ‘so also are Christ’s members,’ but ‘so also is Christ,’ showing that the whole is rightly called Christ as well—that is, the head together with its body, which is the Church.” And in many places of Scripture we find Christ called in this sense too, so as to be understood together with all the members to whom it was said: “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Cor. 12:7). Hence Augustine himself, marveling in sermon 26 on [Col. 0748C] John (no. 13, vol. III, part II, col. 499), says: “Be in Christ’s body.” The body of Christ cannot live except by Christ’s Spirit. This is why the Apostle, explaining this bread to us, says: “We, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). O sacrament of piety! O sign of unity! O bond of charity! Whoever wishes to live has where to live and whence to live. Let him approach, believe, and live in God. Let him be incorporated into God, that he may be made alive. Let him not shrink from the joining of the members; let him not be a rotten member deserving to be cut off; let him cleave to the body and live to God from God.

Again Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 130: “Speaking of Christ’s members, the Apostle did not say, ‘so also are the members of Christ,’ but called all that he had said ‘Christ.’ Many members, one body: Christ.” Therefore all of us together with our head are Christ, powerless apart from our head. Again he says, in sermon 111 on John (no. 6, vol. III, part II, col. 783): “How is the love with which the Father loved the Son in us, unless because we are his members and are loved in him, when he is loved as the whole—that is, head and body? Therefore he adds: ‘And I in them,’ as if he said: ‘Because I am also in them.’ For he is in us in one way, as in his temple; but we are in him in another way, because we too are himself, since according to that by which he was made man to be our head, we are his body.” Again, in his exposition of Psalm 142 (no. 3, vol. IV, col. 1590): “All the members of the body, though many, are one body; [Col. 0749A] so also is Christ. He does not say, ‘so also are Christ and the body,’ but, ‘one body, many members, so also is Christ.’ Therefore Christ is the whole. And because Christ is the whole, the head says from heaven: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4). Again in the same place: “Hold this, and commit it firmly to memory, so that you may recognize Christ as head and body; and from this see how great a grace belongs to you in relation to God: he who is one with the Father willed to be one with us. How is he one with the Father? ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). How is he one with us? ‘He does not say, “and to seeds,” as though of many, but as of one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ.’ But someone says: ‘If Christ is Abraham’s seed, are we also?’ (Gal. 3:16). Remember that Christ is Abraham’s seed; and therefore, if we too are Abraham’s seed, then we too are Christ.” And shortly afterward: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 5:24). The Apostle says: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Christ and the Church: two in one flesh.” This unity of our head and the body of the Church is strengthened and confirmed, in communicating in the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, through the twofold love of God and neighbour, as he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:55).

Hence St Augustine, in sermon 27 on John (no. 1, vol. III, part II, col. 502): “The sign that he has eaten and drunk is this: if he abides and is abided in, if he dwells and is dwelt in, if he clings and is not forsaken.” [Col. 0749C] Therefore he taught and admonished us in mystical words that we should be in his body under himself as head, among his members, eating his flesh and not abandoning his unity. This unity is preserved by true love of God, so that his body may be united to his body—that is, to us. Hence Augustine, in sermon 229, *On the Sacraments of the Faithful*, Monday of Easter Week (vol. V, col. 976): “Because he suffered for us, he commended to us in this sacrament his body and blood, which he also made us ourselves. For we too have been made his body; and by his mercy, what we receive, we are.” Therefore, because we are Christ’s body and receive Christ’s body, we ought to be united not only to the head through love but also mutually with our members. [Col. 0749D] Hence he says in sermon 26 on John (no. 12, col. 499): “The rock was Christ in a sign; the true Christ was in flesh and Word.” Therefore this is the bread descending from heaven, “so that if anyone eats of it he may not die” (ibid., 50). But this pertains to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; who eats with the heart, not the one who presses it with the tooth.

Accordingly, he wishes this food and drink to be understood as the fellowship of his body and members, which is the holy Church. The sacrament of this reality—that is, the unity of Christ’s body—is received from the Lord’s table by some unto life and by others unto ruin. But the reality itself of which it is the sacrament is unto life for every person and unto ruin for no one who shares in it. For the power and reality of the sacrament are that all who partake in it should, by loving one another, belong to the unity of the Church’s body; this is ruinous to no one but salvific to every believer, whoever may truly be able to participate in so great a fellowship, Christ conforming and uniting him [Note: [Col. 0749D] Elsewhere: “may be willing.”]. Hence Augustine himself, in the sermon *On the Sacraments of the Faithful* (vol. V, col. 976): “You came to the water; you were sprinkled; you were made the Lord’s bread. As you see that what has been made is one, so be one by loving one another. Heretics seek division, whereas this bread signifies nothing but unity. So too wine was in many clusters, and now is one. Therefore, because we are Christ’s body [Col. 0750B] and are Christ, so that we are even marked at the altar by the same sacrament: since the Lord’s bread is in itself Christ’s body, and Christ willed by the wondrous grace of unity that we, Christ’s body in the Church, should belong to him; and since he granted that we should receive our mystery, just as his own, in the sacrament of the altar lest we die: so too his mystery, received in the reality of his body, benefits no one unless he has received, in the same sacrament, our mystery—that is, ecclesiastical fellowship. For just as the head is not living without the body, so Christ bestows life on no one apart from the unity of the Church’s body.” Yet let not our mystery in any way exist in the sacrament of Christ’s body without his own, so that, just as through love we are one with one another, so we may be still more one with him; so that, [Col. 0750C] as he abides in us, so we may abide in him. For since he is inseparable from his body, Christ is not truly said to be received even in his sacrament unless he is received whole, incorporating us into himself with his mystery and ours. Hence Augustine, in sermon *On the Sacrament* (272, vol. V, col. 1104): “Hear the Apostle saying: ‘You are the body of Christ and members’ (1 Cor. 12:7). Therefore, if you are Christ’s body and members, your mystery has been placed on the Lord’s table; you receive your mystery. You answer ‘Amen’ to what you are. Be a member of Christ’s body, so that your ‘Amen’ may be true. Why, then, in bread? Recall that bread is not made from one grain, but from many. When you were exorcised, you were as it were ground. [Col. 0750D] When you were baptized, you were as it were moistened. When you received the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, you were as it were baked. Be what you see, and receive what you are. Likewise, brothers, recall this concerning wine. Many grapes hang on the cluster, but the liquid of the grapes is blended into one. Thus the Lord Jesus Christ signified us and willed us to belong to him; he consecrated the mystery of our peace and unity on his table. Whoever receives the mystery of unity and does not keep the bond of peace receives not a mystery for himself but testimony against himself.”

Therefore, because through spiritual unity we are so made one body with Christ and sharers in the same sacrament that, by the analogy just mentioned, we are called the Lord’s bread, and are also called food of Christ’s body and drink of his blood—because, namely, just as food and drink sustain temporal life, so the unity of the Church confers eternal life—the saints call that same unity the power and reality of the sacrament: its reality, because it is signified by it; its power, because through the effect of divine grace it operates especially with Christ. Nevertheless Christ, as our head, is the principal power and reality of the sacrament substantially and truly; ecclesiastical fellowship and unity are so only figuratively.

Let no error, therefore, arise because the saints sometimes speak of Christ’s body and sometimes separately of the body of the Church in the same sacrament. For although in the unity and saving effect of both bodies there is [Col. 0751B] likeness, in the preeminence of dignity and in the truth of substance a supreme distinction, belonging to our head Christ alone in his singularity, must be maintained. For although by this sacrament he refashions the body of our humility, even in this life conformed to the body of his glory, we nevertheless ought not to extend ourselves so far that, however much he exalts us by his humanity or likeness, we presume to attain to his dignity. Rather, let us receive his mercy in the midst of his temple, so that his praise may reach to the ends of the earth according to his name. For he is the head of the Church’s body, not by unity of person but by grace.

## CHAPTER IV. What a sacrament is, and in how many senses it is understood.

[Col. 0751C]

Since, then, by this sacrament Christ unites and incorporates his Church with himself, let us discuss, so far as God grants, its truth and power, as matters that are almost ineffable—provided first that, examining what a sacrament is, we show how a figure is to be distinguished from the truth of the reality it signifies. Augustine, in book X of *The City of God* (ch. 5, vol. VII, col. 241): “A visible sacrament is the sacrament of an invisible thing—that is, a sacred sign.” Again Augustine, in book II, ch. 1, of *On Christian Doctrine* (vol. III, col. 19): “A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into knowledge from itself.” Again elsewhere (*Questions on Leviticus*, 84, vol. III, col. 524): “A sacrament is the visible form of invisible grace.”

It should be understood, however, that sacrament and mystery differ in this: a sacrament is a visible sign signifying something, whereas a mystery is something hidden signified by it. Yet one is used for the other, as was said above: “You receive your mystery,” so that *mystery* is both what conceals and what is concealed, while *sacrament* is both what signifies and what is signified. Hence Maximus, in a certain homily on the Epiphany (homily 10, p. 77, ed. 1784): “His mystical birth gladdened both earth and heaven with everlasting joy. Therefore impious Herod trembles before this king of heaven and ruler of human beings, coming under the mystery of flesh.” Nor is sacrament found only for either one, that is, either sign or thing signified, but [Col. 0752A] also for both together. Thus when it is said, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:15), “flesh” stands for flesh and soul. Likewise: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13:1): “soul” is understood as flesh and soul.
