Nor is it surprising if sacrament is often used for both the sacrament and its reality, because the body of Christ too is found used for both the sacrament and Christ’s body. Augustine, *On the Sacraments of the Altar*: “Christ’s body is both reality and figure. It is reality when Christ’s body and blood are made, by the power of the Spirit in his word, from the substance of bread and wine. It is figure in that which is outwardly perceived.”

It should also be understood that in the sacred books *sacrament* is not always used for a sacred sign, but is sometimes understood as an oath and sometimes as a consecrated thing. Hence Ambrose, in his book addressed to Gratian, says that the Father’s only-begotten appeared to human beings through the sacrament of assumed manhood—as though he said: through the man whom he consecrated to himself, since man was not a sign but rather a concealment of divinity.

## CHAPTER V. The visible sacrament of bread and wine is called Christ’s body only by denomination.

Since, then, the saints use *sacrament* indifferently for the sacrament and its reality, and *body of Christ* for reality and figure, let us distinguish, lest error arise, what in the Lord’s bread is sacrament and what is truly and properly Christ’s body. Augustine testifies in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*, distinguishing them thus, that the form [Col. 0752C] of bread and wine and the other remaining visible qualities of the elements are truly called and are only the sacrament; but that invisible substance which is covered by the sacrament, and into which the substance of bread and wine has been transformed, is truly and properly called and is Christ’s body: “This is what we say, what we strive by every means to establish: the sacrifice of the Church is made from two things and consists of two things—the visible species of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. It is like Christ’s person, which consists and is made from God and man, although Christ himself is true God and true man, because every thing contains in itself the nature and reality of the things from which it is made. But the Church’s sacrifice is made of two things: the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body.” Therefore the two things which he demonstrates—the visible sacrament and the invisible reality of the sacrament—are not one and the same but different things. Hence again Augustine, in the sermon *On the Words of the Lord* (272, vol. V, col. 1104): “What you see on the altar is bread and a cup, as your own eyes report to you; but what faith, needing instruction, requires is this: the bread is body; the cup is blood.” And shortly afterward: “These, brothers, are called sacraments because one thing is seen in them and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has spiritual fruit.” Therefore, since what is seen bodily is one thing [Col. 0753A] and what is understood spiritually another, the sacrament is another thing than the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Again Augustine, in Prosper’s *Sentences*: “It is his flesh which we receive, brought about in the sacrament under the form of bread.” He does not therefore say that the form of bread is Christ’s flesh or form, but that it is the covering of Christ’s flesh. Hence also at the end of a certain Mass it is prayed and said: “Bring about in us, O Lord, we beseech you, what your sacraments contain, so that what we now celebrate under a species we may receive in the reality of things” [Note: [Col. 0753D] Saturday of the Four Ember Days in September.]. The priest indeed asks that Christ’s body, now celebrated under the species of bread and wine, may sometime be received in manifest vision as it truly is. Of this vision the Lord says in the Gospel according to John: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21). And concerning this same sacrament there is a reading in the Passion of blessed Dionysius: while he was celebrating the sacred mystery in prison, the Lord appeared to him and, giving him the holy gifts, said: “Receive this, my dear one, which I shall soon complete for you together with my Father.” As if he said: What I now give you as provision for the journey, I shall not exchange for a reward by giving something else; rather, I shall complete this very thing by manifesting myself.

Since, therefore, the priest says that the sacraments are not Christ’s body but contain it, nor even the true form of that body, but only a likeness-bearing species and figurative form of that which he desires to receive in the reality of things—that is, in the true species of Christ’s glory—and since the Lord also assures blessed Dionysius that this is not complete in the present life but is to be completed in the next: how can sacraments, which are visible and mutable, be his true body or the true form of that body in which Christ after the resurrection is invisible and immutable? Hence Augustine, against Faustus (book XIX, ch. 16, vol. VIII, p. 321): “For what else are bodily sacraments except certain visible words—indeed most holy, yet mutable and temporal?” Far be it, therefore, that the transient species of bread and wine should be the true substance or true species of Christ’s immutable body. But if it is ever called Christ’s body, it must be understood denominatively and not truly. Hence Augustine, to Boniface (letter 23, no. 2, vol. II, col. [Col. 0753D] 150): “If sacraments had no likeness whatever to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. But from this likeness they commonly take the names of those very things. Thus, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body; the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; and the sacrament of faith is faith. Therefore an infant, who does not have the affection of faith, is said to believe and to have faith on account of the sacrament of faith.”

Here it should be noted that the sacrament of Christ’s body is called Christ’s body “in a certain manner”—that is, by likeness and denomination, not properly—in respect of the species and form of the elements. Yet it is truly and properly called and believed Christ’s body in respect of the substance it contains and into which the substance of bread and wine has been changed. Hence Eusebius of Emesa: “The one and perfect sacrifice is to be judged truly by faith, not by appearance nor by outward sight, but by inward disposition. For although outwardly nothing is seen except the species of bread, inwardly the truth of the Lord’s body is believed.” And, as Augustine says in Prosper’s *Sentences*, it is Christ’s blood which we drink under the species and taste of wine.

## CHAPTER VI. Christ is not personally “enbreaded” in the sacramental bread as God is personally incarnate in flesh.

Although the sacrament has above been sufficiently distinguished from the reality of the sacrament, as figure from truth, certain persons erring from some sayings of the saints nevertheless maintain that Christ is personally “enbreaded” in bread just as God is personally incarnate in human flesh [Note: [Col. 0754D] The heresy of Luther and the Lutherans is censured.]. Since this heresy is new and absurd, it must, so far as God inspires, be uprooted by arguments and authorities. For they derive and defend their heresy from a certain comparison by blessed Augustine in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*, where he says: “The sacrifice of the Church is made from two things and consists of two things, just as Christ’s person consists and is made from God and man.” For by a mistaken unexpressed addition they say that the sacrifice of the Church—that is, Christ sacrificed on the altar—consists personally of two things in the same person, just as Christ’s person consists [Col. 0754C] of God and man. If it is objected to them that the species of the elements is not one person with Christ, but only his sacrament, mystery, and figure, they still do not desist, saying that blessed Ambrose says to Gratian that, just as the sacrament of assumed manhood is spoken of, so the sacrament of the Lord’s body is spoken of. And blessed Maximus speaks of God coming under the mystery of flesh; likewise in many Scriptures God is said to be covered by human form or figure, just as Christ is [covered] on the altar by the form or figure of bread. This error is supported by no authority of the saints, but seems to arise from an indiscriminate and improper use of names or comparisons, by which they speak of the sacrament and its reality as though they were to be taken as one thing by those who understand wrongly. [Col. 0754D] But when it is said, “Christ’s body is reality and figure,” should it be understood as one person, as when it is said, “A human being is body and soul”? The grammar is similar, certainly, but the meaning is not similar. For it is not said that these two things have been made personally one in Christ’s body; rather, Christ’s body is called reality and figure equivocally, as if, speaking of a real man and a painted one, one said that “man” is used of both a true man and a painting. Yet the figure of bread is more closely associated with the reality of Christ’s body than a painting with a human being, since it not only represents it as a sacrament but also contains it, and has been substantially [Col. 0755A] changed into it. Again, one must not take the comparison in every respect when Augustine says that the Church’s sacrifice consists of two things as Christ’s person consists of two; for he did not make the comparison of personal unity in both cases, but only compared the way in which each consists of two things.

But they further object that Christ is said to assume the species or form of bread on the altar just as the Word of God assumed the species or form of flesh in the Virgin’s womb; and that, just as the Word becomes flesh, so bread becomes that same flesh. But will those who seek to overthrow God’s truth through a confusion of analogies prevail even thus? For truly the Word becomes flesh, and bread becomes that same flesh; but in a very different manner. The Word becomes [Col. 0755B] flesh, and flesh is born from flesh, by assuming flesh, not by being changed into flesh: becoming what it had not been, without ceasing to be what it was. Bread, however, becomes that same flesh: flesh is not born, nor does it assume flesh, but it is changed into flesh; becoming what it was not, so as to cease to be what it had been [Note: [Col. 0755D] Behold the doctrine of transubstantiation.]. This is our fair hope and fair mystery: that rational nature may not despair of being transformed into Christ’s body, into which even brute nature is transformed—if it ceases to be what it had wrongly been of itself, and becomes in Christ what it had not rightly been.

That bread is not born Augustine testifies against Faustus: “Bread and the cup become mystical for us not by any sort of consecration, but by a definite consecration; they are not born.” Accordingly, insofar as it is not so consecrated, although it is bread and cup, it is food for refreshment, not a sacrament of [Col. 0755C] religion—except that we bless it and give thanks to the Lord for every one of his gifts, not only spiritual but bodily as well. Since, then, mystical bread is not born, nor is it created in this sacrament of divine grace through any origin or condition of earthly nature, but becomes Christ’s body in such a way that it ceases to be bread, how can a thing which no longer exists either be impersonated to another, or have something impersonated to it?

But how can Christ be said to be “impanated” in bread which no longer exists, when Christ is neither converted into bread nor in any way becomes bread? On the contrary, bread is converted into Christ’s body and becomes Christ’s body, so that bread does not remain. He is not, therefore, to be said to assume on the altar the species or form of bread as he assumed in the Virgin’s womb the species or form [Col. 0755D] of flesh. In the womb he assumed the species or form together with the substance; but on the altar there is the species or form of bread, its substance having been changed and no longer remaining. For when “the species or form of bread and wine” is spoken of, these are terms belonging to those things which previously existed—namely, bread and wine. For bread and wine are no longer in the sacrament; they were there before. What new person, therefore, can they create in Christ’s sacrament, when they do not retain even their former substance? Hence it must be noted that when Holy Scripture calls the Lord’s body “bread,” it is not said substantially but mystically and figuratively: either because it is made from bread [Col. 0756A] and retains certain of bread’s qualities; or because it feeds the soul and supplies it with the substance of eternal life; or because it is the bread of angels. Scripture is accustomed to call things by the names of those things from which they are made: as when a man is told, “Why do you, earth and ashes, boast?” although man is not ashes but was made from ashes. Or it calls things by names of what they are thought to be, though they are not: as when Abraham is read to have seen three men, though they were angels (Gen. 18:2). Or it calls things by names of what they resemble in some respect: as when God is called a lion because of strength. Thus the Lord’s body is called bread either because, as has been said, it is made from bread; or because, although it is flesh, it appears as bread to the eyes of those who behold it; or by the analogy that, as material bread nourishes the flesh, so this spiritual bread nourishes the mind.

[Col. 0756B] But they object that, just as the Word assumed the true species of flesh together with its substance, so Christ assumes on the altar the true species of bread together with its substance. For when Augustine says in his sermon *On the Words of the Lord*, “What you see on the altar is cup and bread, as your very eyes report to you,” they attempt, by the testimony of the eyes, to establish the truth of bread. Yet when he subsequently says, “The bread is the body; the cup is the blood,” they falsely infer personal unity. Nevertheless, one must not believe the bodily senses in every respect: for the eyes think a branch in water broken; or, overcome by distance, report as small what is large; or, through darkness, report something other than what it is—just as Mary in the darkness thought Jesus a gardener, and the disciples at night thought him, walking upon the sea, a phantom. But [Col. 0756C] what perfection can human sight possess, when it does not equal lynx-eyed vision even in penetrating those things which it sees only at the surface? Who, therefore, can doubt the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, which is believed spiritually, whatever bodily senses may falsely report of it outwardly in form, smell, or taste? Christ was no less truly Christ when Mary thought him a gardener than when she recognized him.

## CHAPTER VII. That, while their qualities remain, the substance of bread and wine is changed into the true body of Christ.

But again, on the testimony of blessed Ambrose, where he says that Christ’s word is effectual so that bread and wine may be what they were and be changed for the better, they appear [Col. 0756D] to maintain that they remain substantially what they were and are changed into something else. Yet this was tolerably said, unless it is intolerably expounded by a perverse interpreter. For if it is understood that bread and wine are what they were, not according to substance but according to their form and their other qualities remaining there, while in substance they are changed into something else, then, although somewhat improperly expressed, it will nevertheless have been said tolerably and truly. Indeed, lest Ambrose contradict his own authorities and those of the other saints, it must necessarily be expounded thus. For whatever is changed into something else ceases in some respect to be what it was, whether substantially or accidentally. But when bread and [Col. 0757A] wine are changed into Christ’s body, their accidents do not cease to exist, but all remain; therefore the substance of bread and wine ceases to exist.

Since, therefore, the statement is soundly expounded to mean that they remain what they were according to the visible species that remains, and are ineffably changed according to their inward essence—so that the true species of the elements may be shown to remain what it was in the invisible sacrament, while inwardly their substance is changed for the better into what it had not formerly been—let us set forth blessed Ambrose’s words in their order, that we may see that he is not contrary to himself or to the other saints. For he says in *On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 4:

> “Perhaps you say: ‘My bread is ordinary bread.’ But this bread is bread before the words of the sacraments; when consecration has been added, from bread it becomes Christ’s body. [Col. 0757B] By what words, then, and by whose utterances does consecration take place? By those of the Lord Jesus. Therefore Christ’s utterance makes this body. What utterance of Christ? Surely that by which all things were made. If, then, there is such power in the Lord Jesus’ utterance that things which were not began to exist, how much more effectual is it so that things may remain what they were and be changed for the better? Therefore, to answer you: before consecration it was not Christ’s body; after consecration it is now Christ’s body. He himself spoke, and it was done; he himself commanded, and it was created.”

Therefore you have learned that Christ’s body is made from bread, and that wine and water are put into the cup, but become blood by consecration through the heavenly word. Here it should be noted that blessed Ambrose uses an argument from the greater: since God made both substance [Col. 0757C] and form from nothing, he can much more change one for the better while the other remains. Thus he says in the same work, book IV, chapter 5:

> “Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added, it is Christ’s body. And before Christ’s words, the cup is full of wine and water; but when Christ’s words have worked, there the blood of Christ is brought about, which redeemed the people.”

Therefore see in how many ways Christ’s word has power to convert all things. Then the Lord Jesus himself testifies to us that we receive his body and blood. Must we doubt his faithfulness and testimony?

Likewise Eusebius of Emesa (*Homily 5 on Easter*):

> “Let no one doubt that the primary creatures can, at the nod [Col. 0757D] of power and through the presence of majesty, pass into the nature of the Lord’s body, when he sees that man himself, by the workmanship of Christ’s heavenly mercy, has become Christ’s body. For just as anyone coming to faith is still under the bond of the old debt before the words of baptism, but, once these words have been spoken, is immediately stripped of every dreg of sin, so the creatures to be blessed are placed upon the sacred altars, and before they are consecrated by invocation of the highest name, the substance there is bread and wine; but after Christ’s words, it is Christ’s body and blood. What wonder, moreover, if he who was able to create them by a word is able to convert what has been created by a word? Indeed, [Col. 0758A] it now appears a lesser miracle if he who is acknowledged to have made something from nothing is able, once it has been made, to change it for the better. Ask what can be difficult for him for whom it was easy, by the command of his will, to bring visible and invisible things into being; for whom it was easy to clothe with the image of his own divinity man formed from the material of clay, and to render the human body conformed to the body of his glory.”

Likewise Augustine in the homilies [Note: [Col. 0757] This is Sermon 84 of the Appendix to the works of St Augustine, vol. V, col. 152, copied from St Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V, chapter 4.]:

> “Before the words, when bread is offered, it is called bread; when Christ’s words have been uttered, it is no longer bread, but is called Christ’s body.”

Because the saints say that after consecration it is no longer bread but Christ’s body, some maintain that nothing whatsoever of bread remains in the sacrament. They compare it to a rod changed into [Col. 0758B] a serpent, which is no longer called a rod but a serpent—although in the serpent they believe not the substance of the rod from which it was made, but only its form, to have perished. So in the sacrament bread is not bread, although they believe that not the form of bread but its substance is changed. For why could God, who created both from nothing, not change the substance equally, or even reduce it to nothing, just as he changes the form? Thus blessed Ambrose says:

> “See in how many ways Christ’s word has power to convert all things: either into a different form, as a rod into a serpent; or into a different glory, as man from mortality into immortality; or into a different substance, as bread into Christ’s body; or into something other than what they are, whether better or worse, in many other ways known [Col. 0758C] only to himself.”

Thus divine Augustine says in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*:

> “But in the species of bread and wine which we see, we honour invisible things, namely Christ’s flesh and blood; and we do not weigh these two species in the same manner as we weighed them before consecration, since we faithfully confess that before consecration they are bread and wine, formed by nature, but after consecration Christ’s flesh and blood, consecrated by blessing.”

Although he says this in order that no one may suppose that, because the visible species of the elements remains, their substance too—which has now become Christ’s body—remains, he nevertheless clearly maintains that before and after consecration the species are the same; and because of the change of substance he says that he does not weigh them in the same manner before and after. Yet because many err from the visible species of the elements themselves, although it is sufficiently established that Christ’s body is made from their substance—for, as Augustine says, Christ’s body and blood are brought about from the substance of bread and wine—let us consider the species themselves.

For if bread is so completely changed into Christ’s body that nothing of it remains or appears, or if what appears is not real but becomes phantasmal, this seems contrary to reason. For if, with the bread changed, nothing visible were retained, the merit of faith would be diminished: either because, through an evident miracle, bread would completely vanish at the consecration [Col. 0759A] of the sacrament; or because, with faith lulled into forgetfulness, devotion would grow dull when no sign remained in so great a mystery to prompt remembrance. No visible thing would remain around which the mystical signs of Christ’s passion and crucifixion could be celebrated in the Mass; nor would there be anything through which, in receiving his body and blood, the mysteries of his incorporation and ours could be fulfilled, or viaticum given to the sick; nor could the other things which are visibly and beneficially administered through it in holy Church be performed. For the Lord did not say in vain, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19), presenting the sacrament as truly visible for the stirring of remembrance, just as it is true to faith: so that what is certain to faith may feed the mind, and what is certain to sight may strengthen devotion. Since it was fitting that he should penetrate the heavens according to the flesh, so that we might tend there with greater confidence, he left us, who are fleshly, the visible figure and imprint of his flesh and blood in this sacrament, so that, stirred by remembrance of his passion, we might do this more steadfastly.

Likewise, if the elements were entirely changed into Christ’s flesh, Christ’s flesh would be no more than it is now. Yet, even if the proper species of human flesh visibly appeared in bodily form, it would nevertheless be believed to be spiritual, as it now is believed and is. What benefit would there be in seeing him under the proper species of human flesh, when one would nevertheless have to believe that he truly possesses the spiritual species of resurrection? Moreover, as will be established below, [Col. 0759C] the merit of faith would be diminished by so manifest an experience of truth; or the convenience of receiving it would be impeded by the horror aroused at eating a human body.

But in the sacrament the form of bread, its solidity, colour, and taste are perceived; and this is said to be either real or phantasmal. Far be it from us that the deceit of phantasy should be asserted of perfect truth, especially when it is maintained that the angels themselves, and the Holy Spirit himself in the form of a dove or tongues of fire, whenever they are recorded to have appeared, assumed not phantasmal but real bodies in the air; and when in all the other sacraments of the New and Old Testaments nothing phantasmal but all things real are found. For it is truly absurd that what is not real should attest truth, and that what deceives judgment about itself should convey true faith about another. Phantasmal illusion befits magical and diabolical deceits; the affirmation of truth, divine ordinances. Therefore, lest a phantasmal species—wholly alien and unworthy to Christ’s sacrament, and more apt to deceive than to establish truth—be thought superimposed, let us see how this is contrary not only to reason but also to authority.

As Augustine says: “It is his flesh which we receive in the sacrament, covered by the form of bread; it is his blood which we drink under the species and taste of wine.” But because, as stated above, at the end of Mass prayer is made that the body of Christ which is now borne under the species of bread and wine may be received in the truth of things, no one should suppose that the species of bread and wine itself—which Augustine says is not true or proper [Col. 0760A] to Christ’s body—is likewise not real in itself but phantasmal, like the phantasmal appearances of things commonly seen in dreams or in magicians’ tricks. Why is it that St Augustine strives by every means to establish that the sacrifice of the Church is made from two things and consists of two things: the visible species of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of Christ? If this were false and empty, that great man would vainly strive by every means to establish it; vainly, to demonstrate a true sacramental making from real things, would he introduce by analogy Christ’s personal constitution from true God and true man. In vain, too, would he add the universal proposition by which he establishes that each constitution—the sacrament’s and Christ’s person’s—consists of real things, saying: “For every thing contains within itself the nature and truth of those things from which it is made.” Far be this! For the sacrifice of the Church truly contains in itself the truth and nature of the things from which it is made, because it truly and naturally contains Christ’s body and blood, and no less truly and naturally the same species of the elements that was there before. Otherwise, how can Ambrose’s statement concerning the sacramental elements be true—that they remain what they were and are changed into something else—unless something of them is retained in the sacrament, so that one thing remains what it was and another is changed so that it may become better?

Likewise, how can it be true that, in the presence of Pope Nicholas and 113 bishops, the holy Roman synod delivered in writing to Berengar the heretic concerning the Catholic faith in this matter, and he confirmed by oath: namely, that bread and wine after consecration are not only a sacrament but also Christ’s body and blood? If bread after consecration is both—a sacrament and Christ’s body—it must be sacrament in species, and Christ’s body must be made by a change of substance. Hence Augustine says: “What you see on the altar is bread and cup, as your eyes also report,” approving, by the testimony of the eyes, not a phantasy but the truth of the species. And he added: “But what faith requires is this: the bread is the body, and the cup the blood”—namely, by a change of substance. Otherwise, if Christ’s sacrament is believed to be made from phantasy and truth, it will no longer be a making, since no making can consist of some thing and no thing. The sacrament, therefore, is made from Christ’s true body and blood and from the true species of bread and wine.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the sacrament of Christ’s body differs from, or agrees with, the other sacraments.

But since we have spoken of the making of the sacrament, let us see how the sacrament of Christ’s body differs from the other sacraments, or in what respects it agrees with them.

The other sacraments of the New and Old Testaments were only figures; nor were any of their species, in order that they might become what they signified, changed in any respect from what they had been—as manna or the rock. The water of baptism and the oil of chrism are not changed in the sacrament from what they are; nor is it believed that they contain essentially the Holy Spirit whom they signify—the water as cleansing and purifying, the oil as strengthening and illuminating—although through their mystery they bestow him on believers. Rather, they are believed to contain him only figuratively. The sacrament of bread and wine alone is changed in such a manner that substantially it is not what it had been before; its substance becomes Christ’s body, while its remaining form signifies and contains it.

Christ did not will the substance of this bread and wine to remain in his sacrament, lest, if two substantial realities—our ordinary bread and he himself, the living and true bread—were in the same sacrament, they should generate error concerning the truth. For there would be there both the true bread, because he is eternal life, and ordinary bread, true in its own way because it is the sustenance of temporal life. Christ’s body is more easily and certainly believed to be made and present in that sacrament in which it had not bodily been before, not only because of the sacrament but also because of the miracle, while the bread there ceases to be what it was. And perhaps he willed it to be pure from every contamination of corruptible nature or matter, lest heresies of impanation and vile digestion could be ascribed to this unique sacrament of his.

It must nevertheless be known that blessed Augustine compares this sacrament with the others in signifying Christ, although it surpasses them all, both new and old, by the great privilege already mentioned. For he says in book III of *On the Trinity* (chapter 4, no. 10, vol. VIII, col. 798):

> “If the apostle Paul, although he still saw only in part and in a riddle (1 Cor. 13:12), could nevertheless preach Christ by signifying him—one way through his tongue, another through his letter, another through the sacrament of his body and blood—while we do not call the sounds uttered by his speaking tongue, nor the signs of letters written upon skins, Christ’s body and blood, but only that which, received from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystical prayer, we duly receive for salvation: what wonder, if God also makes, in the creature of heaven and earth, sea and air, visible and perceptible things through which he signifies and displays himself, as he knows to be fitting?”

Since, therefore, Christ is said to be signified through the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and it is numbered among the things signifying him, while other significant species are shown capable of being made by God after its example, it is evident that this sacrament, like the others, is significant.

Likewise Augustine, in Sermon 26 on John:

> “We too today receive visible food; but the sacrament is one thing, the power of the sacrament another.”

And shortly afterwards: “This is the bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:33). Manna signified this bread; God’s altar signifies this bread. Those were sacraments; in their signs they differ, in the thing signified they are equal. Hear the Apostle: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, [Col. 0762A] and all passed through the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food” (1 Cor. 10:1). The same, certainly, spiritually; but bodily a different food, because they had manna and we something else, while spiritually they had the same food as we do. “And all drank the same spiritual drink.” They had one thing and we another, but in visible species; yet the same thing was signified by spiritual power. How the same drink? “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (ibid., v. 4). From there came the bread; from there the drink. The rock was Christ in the sign; the true Christ was in the Word and flesh.

He calls manna and the visible species of bread and wine bodily food, different for them and for us; but what is signified through this diverse food to both them and us who believe is the same, namely Christ. Thus he says that manna and bread are different in signs, but equal in the thing—that is, in Christ, who is signified through them. Yet the sacrament of bread signifies Christ more directly than manna, because manna signifies him as future, while bread signifies him as present; manna only externally, but bread so that it is substantially changed into Christ’s body and formally signifies Christ’s body. Those before Christ were saved by the same faith in Christ by which those now living are saved, because they believed that he would come whom we believe to have come. Hence Augustine says in *On Penance* (*Tractates on John*, XXV, no. 12, vol. III, part 2, col. 489): “Why prepare teeth and stomach? To believe in him is to eat the living bread. Whoever believes in him eats him.” Likewise Augustine on Psalm 104: “The bread of heaven is the assumed body [Col. 0762C] of the Lamb, by which we are refreshed in the Church, just as they were refreshed by manna.”

The sacrament of Christ’s body is compared with the other sacraments not only in jointly signifying Christ, but also in not remaining eternally in Christ’s body. For although, as has been said, the substance of bread is believed miraculously to be changed into Christ’s body, the form which remains in the sacrament is believed not to remain perpetually in Christ’s body, but to cease completely after this life, like the other sacraments. For Scripture says, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25). Humanity is refreshed on its journey by believing in the same Christ by whom angels in their homeland are satisfied when they see him as he is; they enjoy him that they may live without a sacrament, whereas we enjoy him with a sacrament lest we die. When we are like God’s angels, shall we be able to see with unveiled face, as he is, the one whom the angels see without a sacrament, unless the shadow of the sacrament is removed? How can his face or ours be unveiled unless every shadow of the veil is cast off, and we appear as the children of God that we are, while he appears to us as what he is—as God? We would pray in vain that what is now borne under species may be received in the truth of things, if we also had the shadow of this sacrament there, where we hope to see Christ’s glory face to face as it is. What reward would there be for us in the other life if, while the shadow of the sacrament covered us, the truth of Christ’s glory were never made manifest to us? Thus Ambrose says in *On Duties*, book I, chapter 48, vol. II, col. 63:

> “We must therefore seek those things in which perfection and truth are found. Here is shadow; here is image; there is truth. Shadow is in the Law, image in the Gospel, truth in heaven. Formerly a lamb and a calf were offered; now Christ is offered, as though receiving passion, and offers himself as priest, in order to forgive sins. Here it is in an image; there it is in truth, where with the Father he intercedes for us as advocate.”

It should be noted that in the Old Testament God gave only the shadow of a figure; in the New, truth together with a figure; in the future he will give truth not with a figure but manifestly. Thus, through this progress of the ages, he showed us ever nearer to perfect truth: after shadowed truth, nothing remained to be given except that same truth made manifest. For the Old Testament promised truth but did not give it; the New gave it but did not show it. What remains except that the same truth should be manifested in the other life? Thus the venerable presbyter Bede says in his exposition of the Gospel passage, “A good tree is not one that bears bad fruit” (Luke 6:43): In this life we need the light of holy Scriptures and refreshment from the heavenly sacraments; but in the future we shall not need such aids, where, according to the Psalmist’s words, all who appear with righteousness will be satisfied by the unveiled glory of Christ. For how shall we need refreshment where there will be eternal satisfaction? Or how shall we need a sacrament, which the bodily eye indeed sees, when God, as the Apostle testifies (1 Cor. 2:9), has prepared for those who love him what eye [Col. 0763C] has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived?

Likewise, since the Lord himself commanded us, whenever we do this, to do it in remembrance of him, when we see him as he is, how will such remembrance be necessary, since in the vision of his presence no forgetfulness can intervene? Hence St Jerome, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “He left us this final memorial, as though someone setting out on a journey were to leave some pledge with one whom he loves, so that whenever he sees it he may remember both that person’s benefits and friendship. If he loves him perfectly, he cannot see it without great longing or tears.”

[Col. 0763D] Therefore the Saviour handed down this sacrament so that through it we might always be reminded that he died for us. For when we receive it, the priests remind us that it is Christ’s body and blood, lest we be ungrateful for such great benefits. Since, then, remembrance of death will not be necessary to stir longing or tears where eternal life and joy will not have departed on a journey but will always be present, the Apostle, declaring an end to this sacrament so that it may not appear eternal, says: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:26). Augustine, explaining this in *Against Faustus* (XII, chapter 20, vol. VIII, col. 236), says:

> “It signifies the end of the age, when the saints will have rest—not yet in the sacrament of hope through which the Church is united in this time, when that which flowed from Christ’s side is drunk, but already in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, so that in that clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we may need no bodily mysteries.”

Since, therefore, Christ’s death is not to be proclaimed in this sacrament eternally, but only until he comes, because afterwards we shall need no mysteries, it is evident that it is a transitory and temporal sign, which we need only now, while we see in a mirror and in a riddle. Thus Augustine says again in his sermon on the Lord’s Prayer (67, no. 7, vol. V, col. 333):

> “When this life has passed, shall we ask for daily bread? Then it will not be called ‘daily,’ but ‘today.’ Now it is called daily when one day passes and another comes. Shall it be called daily when there is one eternal day? Certainly this petition for daily bread is to be understood in two ways: either concerning the necessity of bodily food or concerning the necessity of spiritual nourishment. The faithful know the spiritual nourishment which you too, if you are pure, are going to receive from God’s altar. It will be bread, and daily bread necessary for this life. Shall we receive the Eucharist when we have come to Christ himself and have begun to reign with him forever? Therefore the Eucharist is daily bread; but let us receive it so that we may be refreshed not only in the stomach but also in the mind.”

And shortly afterward:

> “When we come there, we shall eat and drink the Word himself, as the angels do now. For they see truth itself and are satisfied from the very fountain from which we are sprinkled.”

Since, then, the Eucharist is daily bread necessary for this life, which we shall not receive when we come to Christ himself, when we shall eat the Word himself as the angels do now, it is evident that it is not eternal with respect to its species, although we believe it eternal in the truth that it itself is.

Since, therefore, mystical bread is made for us and is not born, and is not held to be eternal even in its mystery but temporal and daily—qualities which agree with Christ neither in origin nor eternity—how can it be believed to be of one person [Col. 0764D] with him, when the Lord even said of our own person, “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21:18)? We should therefore judge the form of this sacrament as we have learned that blessed Augustine distinguished an impersonated form from a mystical form in the first book *Against Maximinus* (chapter 17, vol. VIII, col. 690). For he says:

> “The Son is still in the human form which he raised into heaven and which will be eternal in the kingdom—this same form immortal. But the Holy Spirit, who assumed no form into the unity of his person, although he deigned visibly to show himself through a subject creature, whether in the form of a dove or in tongues of fire, was never called less than the Father. For those things appeared for a time [Col. 0765A] which visibly displayed the invisible Holy Spirit by signifying him: the dove because of holy love, the fire because of the light and ardour of charity. When their office of signification had been fulfilled, those bodily species passed away and ceased to exist, like the cloudy pillar of fire by day and luminous one by night. But Christ did not assume a human appearance for a time, in which he might appear to humans and then that species perish. Rather, while the invisible form of God remained, he assumed into the unity of his person the visible form of a human being. Not only was he born in it from a human mother; he also grew in it, ate, drank, slept, was killed in it, rose again, ascended into heaven, sits in it at the Father’s right hand, and in his kingdom will be subject in it to him who subjected all things to him.”

Thus, in the sacrament of Christ’s body, we should not call the form of bread impersonated to Christ [Note: [Col. 0765D] Bellarmine attributes this opinion to Rupert; Gerberon refutes him in *Apology for Rupert*, p. 156, vol. IV of Rupert’s Works, Venice edition, 1751.]. Although the substance of bread itself is miraculously changed into Christ’s body, the form of bread which remains in the sacrament should not be thought to remain perpetually in Christ’s body; rather, like the other sacraments, it should be believed to cease entirely after this life, lest some heresy of impanation arise. For if Christ is impanated, then either he is converted into bread—which is wicked, since he is immutable—or he becomes bread as the Word became flesh—which is frivolous, since neither evangelical nor prophetic authority establishes it, whereas, on the contrary, bread itself becomes Christ’s flesh so that bread does not remain. It would not be a great matter [Col. 0765C] that the Apostle, in commending God’s love for humanity and the dignity of human nature, says that the Son of God did not take hold of angels but took hold of Abraham’s seed, if he who disdained to be personally united to angelic nature, impersonated to the brute substance of bread, were willing to become bread. For his impersonation would no longer be unique to human beings but, having also been made common to breads, would diminish the dignity of human nature and render less commendable God’s love for humanity.

Nor, therefore, should anyone be disturbed by his saying of himself, “I am the living bread” (John 6:51), figuratively; for if he is believed truly to become bread, how will he be able also to effect [Col. 0765D] daily upon the altar the same redemption that he effected once upon the cross? For he who, once incarnate, “was made a little lower than the angels,” because he was made passible, if thus made bread as often as he is consecrated upon the altar, would be made far lower even than human beings, because he would be made irrational. For just as, by the right of assuming an impersonal nature, in order to be true man in man he took a soul with its reason and flesh with its senses, so that he might suffer in it, so he would take bread with its irrationality. Thus, because he would become lower than those redeemed by him, he would not appear to be an adequate and sufficient price of redemption. For if neither in heaven nor on earth nor beneath the earth was found worthy [Col. 0766A] to open the book of our redemption (Rev. 5:3), neither angel nor living man nor dead man, much less could anyone made lower than man do so. It is therefore absurd to think so foolishly concerning the wisdom of God, and to bend certain Scriptures toward such a meaning. For why should God become something other than that which he became once for our salvation—namely, man—when in the sacrament he performs nothing other than what he once performed for us in himself, namely our redemption, on the cross and at the altar? For its worthy reception he always wished to stir up our devotion by the sign of his presence, through the remembrance of so great a benefit, present and past. Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit is believed to have appeared in the form of a dove or tongues of fire without a unity of person, so Christ is affirmed to be effected bodily in the sacrament of bread and wine, but not to be personally united to it.

## CHAPTER IX. That the new bread and wine, changed into Christ’s body, do not generate new flesh or blood.

But again, some draw an excessively simple analogy for this change from common nature. [Note: [Col. 0766D] This opinion is attributed to St John Damascene and Paschasius by the illustrious de Marca, *Opuscula*, vol. V, p. 141, Bamberg edition, 1789.] They argue that, just as bread and wine are transformed into our living flesh and blood, or even into the living and life-giving flesh of Christ himself, so long as he lived among us through the natural process of eating, so they are likewise transformed into the living and life-giving flesh and blood of Christ through the grace of priestly blessing.

[Col. 0766C] But bread and wine become Christ’s flesh and blood in the sacrament through grace in a manner very different from that in which they become flesh and blood in anyone’s stomach, even Christ’s, through nature. In Christ’s stomach bread and wine, while their substance was neither changed nor destroyed but their form was changed, generated new flesh and new blood, to some extent subject to corruption, as in other human beings. In the sacrament, however, with the substance changed and not the form, bread and wine do not become new flesh and new blood; rather, the existing substance of bread and wine is changed into the coexisting substance of Christ’s body, so that by its newness it introduces no novelty into him, and by its change it alters nothing in him. For if he is mutable, he is changed either for increase or for loss. But [Col. 0766D] if he needs increase, he did not rise as a perfect man; if he is subject to loss, he has not yet escaped corruption. But Augustine, on the contrary, says in Letter 205, to Consentius, concerning the Lord’s body after the resurrection (*Works*, II, col. 767):

> It is established, therefore, and must in no way be doubted, that Christ’s body, although it did not see the decay of corruption in the tomb—whence it is written, “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10)—could nevertheless be pierced by nails and lance; but now it abides altogether in incorruption.

If, then, you ask how a corruptible thing is changed into [Col. 0767A] an incorruptible one, an existing thing into a coexisting one, a new thing into an ancient one, without the latter’s renewal or alteration, Augustine answers you in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences* (X, 223):

> If you ask how this can take place, I answer briefly for the present: it is a mystery of faith; it can be believed unto salvation, but cannot usefully be investigated.

Likewise, against Felicianus: [Note: [Col. 0767] Chapter 8. This book is by Vigilius and is falsely ascribed to St Augustine. See the Appendix to the Works of St Augustine, vol. VIII, p. 43.]

> Let us set aside in God the rule of bodily understanding, lest we say that the maker is like his works.

And shortly afterward:

> Let faith believe this; let understanding not inquire into it, lest it judge what it has not found to be incredible, or, having found it, fail to believe it unique.

Likewise Ambrose, in *On the Mysteries of Initiation* (ch. 9, *Works*, II, col. 338), excluding from this singular sacrament of divine [Col. 0767B] grace every origin or condition of earthly nature, says:

> Perhaps you say: “I see something else. How do you maintain to me that I receive Christ’s body?” And it remains for us to prove this. How many examples do we employ in order to prove that this is not what nature formed, but what the blessing consecrated; and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is changed! Moses held a rod; he cast it down, and it became a serpent.

And shortly afterward:

> Moses struck the rock, and water flowed from the rock. Did not grace act contrary to nature, causing the rock to pour forth water which it did not naturally possess? We observe, therefore, that grace is greater than nature. But if human blessing had such power as to change nature, what shall we say of the divine consecration itself, [Col. 0767C] where the words of the Lord and Saviour are at work? For this sacrament which you receive is effected by Christ’s word. Therefore, can Christ’s word—which was able to make from nothing what did not exist—not change things that exist into what they were not? Is it not greater to give new existence to things than to change natures? Why do we employ arguments? Let us employ his own examples, and let us establish the truth of the mystery by the example of the Incarnation. Did the course of nature precede when Christ the Lord was born of Mary? It is clear, therefore, that a virgin gave birth apart from nature’s order. And this body which we effect is from the Virgin. Why do you seek nature’s order here in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born of a virgin beyond nature? Truly [Col. 0767D] it is Christ’s flesh that was crucified and buried. Therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh. The Lord Jesus himself cries: “This is my body” (Luke 22:19). Before the blessing of the heavenly words, another kind is named; after consecration, Christ’s body is signified. He himself calls it his blood. Before consecration it is called something else; after consecration it is named blood.

In this passage it must be noted that blessed Ambrose, in proving the third miracle of this singular mystery, first set forth two wonderful works of God: one of creation, by which he made things exist that did not exist; the other of change, by which he caused things that existed to become what [Col. 0768A] they were not. Since he ceased from the former, so as no longer to create substances and forms from nothing, he communicated the latter to nature, whereby things that are are changed in form into what they are not: miraculously, as a rod into a serpent; and naturally, as every seed into the fruit of its kind. Assigning the third to the privilege of the divine word, he added: “And this body which we effect is from the Virgin.” For in saying, “we effect,” he affirmed the newness of the bread in the present act; while in “the body which is from the Virgin” he affirmed the immutability of the ancient reality. Thus, while bread, its form remaining, is changed into what it was not—namely, Christ’s body, which was from the Virgin beyond nature’s order—Christ’s body is neither believed to be created in the sacrament from nothing, according to the origin of primary nature, nor the bread’s form [Col. 0768B] to be changed according to nature’s customary operation. Rather, in a new and unheard-of manner, the substance of bread is so changed into the substance of Christ’s body that the bread is no longer bread, though it appears to be what it had been, and Christ’s body does not cease to be what it was. It was fitting, indeed, that because this belonged uniquely and properly to himself, he should make the miracle of so great a mystery incommunicable to his other works.

It is asked, however: since before the Passion the Lord gave his disciples the sacrament of his body, while it was subject to the sufferings of nature, did he give it in the sacrament incorruptible and immortal, as it is now given to us? Especially since he said, “This is my body, which shall be given for you; this is the blood which shall be shed for you” (Luke 21:19). But it is not [Col. 0768C] strange if he who before the Passion transfigured himself into such a body as he would have after the resurrection, and after the resurrection showed his body wounded and tangible, such as he had possessed before the Passion, thus gave in the sacrament his immortal body which was to die, just as after the resurrection he showed as wounded the same body which was invulnerable. Let both the one and the other be ascribed to divine power. For divine operation, as blessed Gregory says (*Homilies on the Gospels*, 26.1, col. 1552), if it is comprehended by reason, is not admirable; nor does faith have merit when human reason furnishes proof.

[Col. 0768D] He, therefore, who presented himself, in two forms—human and sacramental—as though another, though he was altogether the same, and distributed himself to be eaten while remaining living and whole, must be believed to have presented himself incorruptible and immortal in that sacrament, in which he could neither be corrupted by being worn away with bites nor be killed by being devoured in the eating of so many people. Therefore, just as, though about to die in himself, he became immortal in the sacrament beyond nature, so likewise, although at that time his flesh and blood could be renewed by foods and drinks and changed through nature in himself, his same flesh and blood must not be believed capable of being renewed or changed by new wine and new bread in the sacrament. That he [Col. 0769A] distributed himself to the disciples is attested by Augustine in the heading of Psalm 33 (*Exposition*, II.10, *Works*, IV, col. 214), concerning David’s flight from Saul the persecutor:

> “And he was carried in his own hands.” How can this take place in a man? Who can understand it? For who is carried in his own hands? We do not find how this is to be understood literally in David; but we find it in Christ. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his body, he said, “This is my body.” For he carried that body in his own hands.

Since, therefore, it is established that while about to die he gave himself immortal, visible yet invisible, in the sacrament, it is established that his body, such as we now receive it, was then such: one and wholly the same in substance [Col. 0769B] both then and now. Yet then it differed in mortality and immortality, in the forms of man and sacrament; now it differs only in the forms of man and sacrament. Augustine, distinguishing this identity of substance and diversity of form, says concerning the identity of substance, so as to exclude every novelty or diversity, in his sermon to the newly baptized:

> Receive in the bread what hung upon the cross; receive in the cup what flowed from Christ’s side. For death, not life, will be his lot who judges Life to be false.

He who so truthfully affirmed concerning the substance that this same thing is here which was there, says concerning the diversity of form in the Letter to Irenaeus:

> You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed. It is indeed the same, and not the same: the same invisibly, not the same visibly.

That is, as though he said: the same indeed according to invisible substance, and not the same according to visible form.

## CHAPTER X. That “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” is to be understood not of any son of man whatsoever, but of Christ himself.

But from this statement of blessed Augustine, in which he says, “You are not going to eat this body which you see,” and from the Lord’s own words, there arose a heresy in the time of Pope Celestine and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria. [Col. 0769D] Through their efforts the Council of Ephesus was held, and the heresy was destroyed. It maintained that the bread and wine of the altar could be changed in the world not into the proper flesh and blood of Christ, which was already in heaven, but into the flesh and blood of any righteous and holy son of man, who was God’s temple and, by his merit, Christ’s body; concerning this person Christ himself had said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Therefore, the 150 bishops gathered at Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0769D] Labbe, *Councils*, vol. III, col. 415, in the fifth letter of Cyril of Alexandria, read at the Council of Ephesus in 431; nearly two hundred bishops attended that council, as Vincent of Lérins writes in the *Commonitorium*, ch. 29.], wrote thus against Nestorius, bishop of the heretics:

> We are sanctified by becoming participants in the holy [Col. 0770A] body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not by receiving common flesh, far be it! nor the flesh of a man sanctified and united to the Word by a unity of dignity, or as one possessing a divine indwelling; but flesh truly life-giving and made proper to the Word himself. For he, existing by nature as life because he is God, and united to his own flesh, professed it to be life-giving. Therefore, although he says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” we must not suppose it to be the flesh of one man from among us. For how could the flesh of a man be life-giving according to its own nature? But we profess it truly made proper to him who for our sake both became and was called Son of Man.

[Col. 0770B] Since, therefore, this council has sufficiently established that it is not the flesh and blood of some ordinary human being that is received in the mystery, but life-giving flesh made proper to the Word himself, let us nevertheless establish that only Christ’s body is truly there. This is necessary lest from blessed Augustine’s words—when he said in the person of the Lord, “You are not going to eat this body which you see,” as though removing it from himself, and again, “Your mystery is placed upon the Lord’s table: be what you see, and receive what you are”—someone may, through this apparent familiarity of unity, surreptitiously presume to aspire to this dignity and suppose that his own body, or the body of some ordinary person, is received in the sacrament. Augustine says in Book IV of *On the Trinity* (ch. 14, *Works*, VII, col. 823):

> What priest is as holy and just as the only Son [Col. 0770C] of God? And what could be offered and received as acceptably as the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our Priest? Thus, since four things are considered in every sacrifice—to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—the one and true mediator himself, reconciling us to God by the sacrifice of peace, remained one with him to whom he offered; made one in himself those for whom he offered; was himself the one who offered; and was himself what he offered.

Likewise Pope Leo, in a letter sent to Bishop Anatolius (80.2, *Works*, I, col. 1040, Ballerini edition):

> Otherwise, in the Church of God, which is Christ’s body, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true High Priest reconciles us in the property of our [Col. 0770D] nature, and the true blood of the spotless Lamb cleanses us. Though he is established at the Father’s right hand, nevertheless in the same flesh which he took from the Virgin he carries out the sacrament of propitiation.

Likewise Leo: [Note: [Col. 0770D] In the sixth sermon *On the Fast of the Seventh Month*, which is Sermon XCI, col. 386, cited edition.]

> Since the Lord says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” you must communicate at the sacred table in such a way that you do not entertain the slightest doubt concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood. For what is received by the mouth is what is believed by faith; and those who dispute against what they receive answer “Amen” in vain.

[Col. 0771A] Likewise Eusebius of Emesa (*Homily 5 on Easter*):

> The invisible priest, by his word and hidden power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “Take and drink, for this is my body” (Matt. 26:26); and, after the sanctification has been repeated: “Take and drink, this is my blood” (ibid., 27). Therefore, just as at the command of the one who gave the order the heights of heaven, the depths of the waters, and the vast regions of earth suddenly subsisted from nothing, by equal power in spiritual sacraments, where power commands, the effect serves the reality.

Who, then, among ordinary people is such as the only Son of God, who, seated at God’s right hand, carries out for us the sacrament of propitiation in that same flesh which he took from the Virgin, and who as invisible priest changes visible [Col. 0771B] creatures into the substance of his body? Eusebius wholly restrains us from such presumption when he says:

> When you approach the venerable altar to be fed with food, behold with faith the sacred body and blood of your God; touch it with your mind; honour it; marvel at it; receive it with the hand of your heart; and above all take it by an inward draught.

And shortly afterward:

> May the very power of the consecrator strengthen you for recognizing and receiving the sacrifice of the true body. He who then lay hidden, prefigured in manna, has been manifested to you in grace. The Prophet also shows that he himself was prefigured in that form of manna, saying: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25). And who is the bread of angels but Christ, who satisfies them with the food of his love [Col. 0771C] and the light of his brightness?

## CHAPTER XI. That Christ’s body in the visible sacrament is spiritual and invisible.

But see: from Eusebius’s words, in which he affirms that the invisible priest changes visible creatures into the substance of his body, and urges us to receive the body and blood of God himself spiritually—by faith, mind, the hand of the heart, and inward draught—it seems necessary to ask: if the priest is invisible, how are body and blood his substance when they are visible? But it must be understood that after the resurrection Christ’s body was invisible just as it was incorruptible; for, as the Apostle says, it rose not animal but spiritual [Col. 0771D] (1 Cor. 15:44). And such as it came forth from the tomb, such it is in the sacrament of bread and wine. What is written, that after the resurrection he showed his hands and side to the disciples (John 20:20), blessed Gregory distinguishes thus in his Easter homily (*Homilies on the Gospels*, 26.2, *Works*, I, col. 1553):

> What is touched must be capable of corruption, and what is incapable of corruption cannot be touched. Yet in a wondrous and inestimable manner our Redeemer, after the resurrection, showed his body both incorruptible and tangible: by showing it incorruptible he invited us to the reward; by offering it as tangible he formed us to faith. Thus he showed himself both incorruptible and tangible, in order to demonstrate that his body [Col. 0772A] after the resurrection was of the same nature but of another glory.

That Christ’s body is spiritual, incorruptible, and invisible, yet no less substantial in the sacrament, the saints testify together with Eusebius. Thus Ambrose says in *On the Sacraments* (*On the Mysteries of Initiation*, ch. 9, no. 55, *Works*, II, col. 340):

> By these sacraments Christ feeds his Church, by which the substance of the soul is strengthened. What we eat and drink the Holy Spirit expressed through the Prophet, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). Christ is in that sacrament, because it is Christ’s body. Therefore it is not bodily food but spiritual food. For the body [Note: [Col. 0771D] Elsewhere: “the Lord’s.”] of God is a spiritual body; Christ’s body is the body of the divine Spirit.

Likewise Augustine:

> This is what we call the sacrifice of the Church: it consists of two things, the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise the same writer:

> In the appearance of bread and wine which we see, we honour invisible things, namely Christ’s flesh and blood. But let the human mind conceive nothing bloody or corruptible in this flesh and blood, but a life-giving and saving substance, made proper to the Word himself, bestowed to us in bread and wine; if they are worthily received, remission of sins is granted to us through them. [Note: [Col. 0771D] Thus Cassiodorus, *Commentary on Psalm 109*, vol. [Col. 0772D] col. 379, Rouen edition, 1679, nearly word for word.]

Likewise Augustine to Irenaeus:

> You are not going to eat this body which you see. It is indeed the same, and not the same: the same invisibly, and not [Col. 0772C] the same visibly.

Whence it is also added:

> If it must be celebrated visibly, it must be understood invisibly.

Since, therefore, the Lord’s body is spiritual, it is not bodily food but spiritual; and it must be understood invisibly. Accordingly Augustine says in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine* (ch. 16, no. 24, *Works*, III, col. 52):

> A statement which seems to command a disgraceful or criminal act, or to forbid usefulness and beneficence, is figurative. “Unless,” he says, “you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” seems to command a criminal or disgraceful act. Therefore it is a figure commanding that one share in the Lord’s Passion and usefully store in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

This too the Lord himself commands: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Likewise Jerome says in a homily on Leviticus:

> Not only in the Old Testament is the killing letter found; in the New Testament too there is a letter which kills the person who does not attend spiritually. For if you follow the letter, the very thing which is written—“Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood”—kills: this letter kills. But if you understand it spiritually, it does not kill; rather, the spirit in it gives life.

Augustine explains this more openly in his exposition of Psalm 54 (no. 23, vol. IV, col. 514):

> The first heresy among Christ’s disciples arose, as it were, from the harshness of his [Col. 0773A] saying. For when he said, “Unless anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have eternal life” (John 6:54), they, not understanding, said to one another, “This saying is hard” (ibid., 61), and separated themselves from him. When they had gone away, he instructed those who remained: “It is the Spirit,” he said, “who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (ibid., 64). You have understood spiritually: they are spirit and life. You have understood carnally: and they are still spirit and life, but not to you. Understand spiritually what I have spoken. [Note: [Col. 0773D] St Augustine, Tractate XXVII on John, vol. III, part 2, col. 503.] You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed. I have commended to you a sacrament; understood spiritually, [Col. 0773B] it will give you life. “The flesh profits nothing” (ibid.)—but in what manner did they understand it? They understood flesh as it is torn in a corpse or sold in a butcher’s shop. But Jesus, knowing this, said: “Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” (ibid., 62). What does this mean? They thought that he was going to distribute his body; he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole. “When you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before,” then surely you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose; then surely you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites.

For Christ’s body, being spiritual and invisible, must not truly be believed capable of being torn apart and consumed by our teeth and bites after the manner of common foods. Yet although in his sacrament it is truly present and truly received as regards substance, it is received more truly and more perfectly by faith and devotion as regards the grace of salvation. Hence Augustine says in the second book *On Penance* (*Tractate XXV on John*, no. 12, col. 489):

> Why do you prepare teeth and stomach? To believe in him, that is to eat the living bread. Whoever believes in him eats him.

Likewise the same writer in *On the Words of the Lord*:

> Christ’s body and blood will then be life to each person if what is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually drunk in the reality itself.

Gregory explains this more clearly in his Easter homily (*Homilies on the Gospels*, 22.7, *Works*, I, col. 1533):

> What the Lamb’s blood is, you have learned not merely by hearing but by drinking. That blood is put [Col. 0773D] upon both doorposts when it is drunk not only with the mouth of the body, but also with the mouth of the heart. For the Lamb’s blood is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his Passion, received with the mouth for redemption, is also contemplated with attentive mind for imitation.

It should be noted here that Augustine and Gregory say the same thing: what is visibly received in the sacrament by the mouth of the body is drunk in the reality itself spiritually by the mouth of the heart. They do not mean that something is believed more truly in substance by the heart than it is received by the mouth. Rather, if truth is said to be received in pure truth when that which is [Col. 0774A] spiritual is received spiritually, what is invisible invisibly, and what is salutary savingly—that is, when what is as it is, is received inwardly through love—then the same thing is not said to be received outwardly in the sacrament in the reality itself. For in the sacrament, as regards its extraneous and visible form, what is does not there get received as it is; nor, as regards grace, does what is as it is act in those who receive unworthily. Though one manner of tasting does not profit apart from the other if the other is neglected, yet the spiritual is in this respect truer, because it always works salvation in the good, whereas the bodily sometimes brings death even to the wicked. Therefore, because Christ’s spiritual body and blood are not fleshly but spiritual food and drink, by which Christ spiritually unites and incorporates the Church, which is his own, to himself as the body to its head, Augustine said that the figurative expression commanding Christ’s flesh to be eaten must be understood allegorically.

[Col. 0774B] Likewise Jerome called it a killing letter unless it were understood spiritually, so that one might not suppose that Christ’s body ought to be eaten limb by limb, cooked or raw; but rather that Christ’s body should be believed to be spiritually, as stated, incorporated and united with the faithful.

Nevertheless, although Christ’s body and blood are spiritual food and drink and are commanded to be received spiritually, they are not to be understood as spiritual in every respect in such a way that they effect eternal salvation only for our soul and not for our body also. For Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0774D] Understand Ambrosiaster. See the Appendix to the Works of St Ambrose, vol. II, p. 149.] in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> We receive the mystical cup for the preservation of soul and body. [Col. 0774C] The Saviour’s flesh was given for the salvation of the body, and his blood was shed for our soul, in order that he might make the whole human being whole.

Likewise Augustine, in Sermon 26 on John (no. 16, col. 500):

> When he had said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” he immediately added: “And I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid., 55), so that in the meantime he may have eternal life according to the Spirit, in the rest which receives the spirits of the saints.

As regards the body, however, it too is not deprived of eternal life, but receives it in the resurrection of the dead on the last day. Hence we are said to be members of Christ our head even according to the body. Augustine says in the sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*:

> If our Lord Jesus Christ had assumed only a human soul, our souls alone would be his members. But because he also assumed a body, through which he is also our head—we who consist of soul and body—certainly our bodies too are his members.

Since, therefore, we consist of body and soul, while Christ consists of body, soul, and divinity, let us see whether, in this most singular sacrament of unity, by which he incorporates his body into the Church as his body, we are worthy to have communion not only in the Lord’s body and soul but also in his divinity itself. Ambrose says in *On the Sacraments* (Book VI, ch. 1, no. 4, *Works*, II, col. 381):

> Because our same Lord Jesus [Col. 0775A] Christ shares both in divinity and in body, you who receive his flesh participate in his divine substance in that food.

## CHAPTER XII. That Christ’s body, though spiritual and invisible in the sacrament, is nevertheless no less substantial and true.

Since, therefore, we have established that Christ’s body is spiritual and invisible, yet through it we participate not only spiritually but also bodily in his humanity and divinity, having in the viaticum, for our protection, the same one whom we shall have for glorification in reward, he must be believed to be substantially and truly present in his sacrament, by which he and we are united to one another. [Col. 0775B] Although the truth of his body has been stated clearly above, we shall nevertheless discuss it yet more fully.

Since Augustine says, “Death, not life, will be his lot who judges Life to be false,” who would not believe him whom God the Father, commending him to the world and setting him forth as supreme priest, declared: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3:17; Luke 9:35)? We shall be disobedient to God the Father if we do not hear the Son as he commanded—by ears of hearing, that is, ears of faith. The Son himself testified to the world: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). And because all flesh is in his own power, lest a flesh other than his own could be understood, he added: “Whoever eats [Col. 0775C] me will live because of me” (ibid., 58). But because eating a human being was contrary to human custom and law, his disciples were scandalized, said, “This saying is hard,” and withdrew from him. Thus Augustine says on Psalm 33 (*Works*, IV, col. 212):

> To the ignorant, these words of the Lord seemed childish: “Unless anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have eternal life in himself” (ibid., 54). But these words concealed his power. The Lord was thought mad when he said these things; but the faithful know that he was proclaiming sacraments.

Likewise the same writer in *On the Words of the Lord*: [Note: [Col. 0775D] Sermon 131, no. 1, *On the Words of the Gospel*, vol. V, col. 640.]

> We have heard the truthful teacher, the divine Redeemer, the human Saviour, commending to us our price, his [Col. 0775D] blood. He spoke to us of his body and blood: he called his body food and his blood drink. The faithful recognize the sacrament of the faithful.

Therefore, when, commending such food and such drink, he said, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (ibid.), and said this concerning life, who was speaking but Life itself? But death, not life, will be the lot of that person who judges Life to be false. His disciples had been scandalized. Therefore, lest, as those disciples supposed, the supreme priest, offering himself to the Father for us, should be eaten torn into pieces and raw or cooked, he instituted the sacrament by which he could truly and savingly [Col. 0776A] be eaten and drunk. Handing it to the disciples, lest he might be thought to speak of the mystery mystically and not properly and truly, he said: “I do not predict something future, I do not announce something absent; but what I give at present is my body—not figurative but true—the very body which shall be given for you. This is my blood, the very same blood which shall be shed for us.” He further added the properly distinctive effect of his flesh and blood: namely, the remission of sins. Since it belongs to God alone to forgive sins, to whom alone remission of sins is due, whose blood but that of God himself could effect the remission of sins? In order that this privilege be removed from every son of man, even if he were a son of a virgin without union with God, how could he bring about the remission of sins for the world, when Adam, [Col. 0776B] formed from virgin earth without father or mother, not only did not accomplish this but also propagated sin to all, because he was not God and would not be ruled by God’s Word?

Since, therefore, by the most certain privilege of his blood he established in the mystery the truth of his flesh and blood, it remains only that we avoid the folly of the scandalized disciples, hear him as the Father commanded from heaven, and, because he is Truth and Life, believe him to be truthful, as he truly is. In order that this may be more certain and more true, let us see what Peter, the prince of the apostles, answered—speaking for himself and the others—when Christ asked him and the others, after the scandalized disciples had withdrawn, whether he too wished to depart. For he said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words [Col. 0776C] of eternal life” (John 6:69).

Lest I seem to interpret his answer by my own judgment, Augustine explains it thus in Sermon 27 on John (no. 9, col. 505):

> See how Peter understood, God granting it.
