From what source, unless because he believed? “You have the words of eternal life.” For you possess eternal life through the ministry of your body and blood. “And we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (ibid.); that is, you are eternal life itself, and in your flesh and blood you give nothing other than what you are. Behold: Peter testifies the same thing as Christ concerning the truth of his body; and because he spoke also for the others, the other apostles testify with him.

Let us see, then, whether, together with Peter and the other apostles, the rest of the saints also bear witness to Christ’s testimony. Ambrose says in *On the Sacraments* (bk. IV, ch. 5, no. 23, vol. II, col. 371): “The Lord Jesus testifies to us that we receive his body and blood. Must we doubt his faithfulness and testimony?” Likewise Hilary, in book VIII of *On the Trinity* (no. 14, vol. II, col. 223): “He himself says: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him’ (John 6:56). No room for doubt has been left concerning the truth of the flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and when received and drunk, these bring about this result: that we are in Christ and Christ is in us. Is this not truth?” [Col. 0777A] “Therefore he himself is in us through the flesh, and we are in him, while that which we are is with him in God.” And shortly afterward: “This, then, is the cause of our life: that we, who are fleshly, have Christ abiding in us through the flesh, and that we shall live through him, on the condition on which he lives through the Father.”

Likewise Eusebius of Emesa: “Heavenly authority confirms: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.’ Let every uncertainty of unbelief therefore depart; since he who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness of its truth.” Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Hedibia (question 2, vol. I, col. 824, Venice ed., 1766): “But let us hear that the bread which the Lord broke and gave to the disciples is the body of the Lord and Saviour, he himself saying to them: ‘This is my body’; [Col. 0777B] and that cup is that of which he again spoke: ‘This is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins.’ If therefore the bread which came down from heaven is the body of the Lord, and the wine which he gave to the disciples is the blood of that new covenant which was poured out for the remission of sins, then Moses did not give us the true bread, but the Lord Jesus did. He is himself the guest, himself the banquet; himself eating, and himself eaten. We drink his blood; without him we cannot drink. And daily, in his sacrifices, from the fruit of the true vine and of the vine Sorech, interpreted ‘chosen,’ we drink new wine in the kingdom of the Father—that is, in the kingdom of the Church—not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit.”

I have presumed to introduce other witnesses to Christ’s testimony; [Col. 0777C] but since he indeed always speaks truly, though at times properly and at times figuratively, and since he so distinguished his hearers that to some it was given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, while to others it was given in parables, knowing of what spirit they were (Matt. 13:3), I have judged it necessary to repeat what the saints themselves did not consider burdensome to write. Thus this understanding may appear not to be my own presumptuous assertion of truth, but the authority of the Catholic Church: of those who believed in this manner and deserved in this manner to be saved. For the more certain Christian faith becomes, the more beneficial it is. Therefore, that it may be more certain, let the authority of further saints be set forth.

Augustine says in his exposition of Psalm 98 (vol. IV, col. 1065): “I find how the earth may be adored without impiety, how the footstool of his feet may be adored without impiety. For Christ received earth from the earth, since flesh is from earth; and he received flesh from the flesh of Mary. And because he walked here in that flesh, and gave us that same flesh to eat for salvation, while no one eats that flesh unless he has first adored it, it has been found how we may adore such a footstool of the Lord’s feet—and not merely not sin by adoring, but indeed sin by not adoring.” [Col. 0777D]

Saint Basil, marvelling at this flesh of the Son of God which is truly to be adored, says in his dialogue *On the Dignity of the Priesthood* (John Chrysostom, *On the Priesthood*, bk. III, ch. 4): “O miracle! O God’s benevolence toward us! He who sits above at the right hand of the Father is nevertheless held by human hands at the time of sacrifice, and is handed over [Col. 0778A] to those desiring to lick him and embrace him with a blessing; and all this takes place beneath human eyes.” Likewise the same author (bk. VI, ch. 4): “When the priest has invoked the Holy Spirit, offered that venerable victim, and thereafter touched the common Lord of all, where, tell me, shall we place him in our estimation? What purity shall we require of him? What reverence? Consider what hands must be, which minister such things; what tongue must be, which pours forth those words; and how much purer and holier than all others must be the soul which receives such a Spirit. Then angels stand around the priest, and the tribunal and place of the altar are filled with heavenly powers, in honour of him who is sacrificed, etc.”

Likewise Gregory, in book IV of the *Dialogues* [Col. 0778B] (ch. 58, vol. II, col. 472): “What believer can doubt that, at the very hour of the immolation, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that choirs of angels are present in this mystery of Jesus Christ; that the lowest are joined to the highest, earthly things united to heavenly, and one thing made out of visible and invisible? But it is necessary, when we do these things, that we sacrifice ourselves to God in contrition of heart; and, as we celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, we ought to imitate what we do.” Therefore, then, he will truly be a victim to God for us when we have made ourselves a victim to God. Hence Augustine, in book X of *The City of God* (ch. 20, col. 256): “In the form of a servant God preferred to be sacrifice rather than to receive sacrifice, lest anyone suppose, even on this ground, that sacrifice should be made to any creature. For this reason he is both the priest who offers and the offering itself; and he willed the daily sacrifice of the Church to be the sacrament of this reality, so that the Church, being the body of its Head, may learn to offer itself through him.” [Col. 0778C] In this it must be noted that the flesh of God is truly present in the sacrament: of such dignity that angelic powers honour it by ministering, and human beings by adoring and offering themselves as victims.

With this certainty the saints affirm that Christ is eaten. Augustine, in Sermon 26 on John (no. 20, vol. III, pt. II, col. 501): “Those who eat Christ certainly die temporally, but they live eternally, because Christ is eternal life.” Likewise in the second homily on Psalm 33 (no. 10, vol. IV, col. 220): “The Jews approached Christ in order to crucify him; [Col. 0778D] let us approach him in order to receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the Crucified One; we are enlightened by eating the Crucified One and drinking.” And somewhat later: “Truly great is the Lord, and truly great is his mercy, who gave us his body to eat, in which he endured such great things, and his blood to drink.”

Likewise Ambrose, *On the Mysteries of Initiation* (ch. 8, no. 47, vol. II, col. 337): “This food which you receive, this living bread which descended from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats it shall not die eternally, and it is the body of Christ.” Likewise the same author (*On the Sacraments*, bk. VI, ch. 1, vol. II, col. 379): “As our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God—not as other human beings are sons by grace, [Col. 0779A] but as Son by nature, that is, from the substance of the Father—so his flesh, which we receive, is true flesh, as he himself said, and his blood, which we drink, is true blood.”

Likewise Augustine, in a homily on Psalm 65 (no. 5, vol. IV, col. 645): “Now the shed blood of the Innocent One has been granted to murderers, and by grace they drank the very blood which in madness they had shed.” Likewise the same author, on Psalm 45, addressed to the Jews (no. 4, vol. IV, col. 401): “Be baptized in the name of him whom you killed; your sins are forgiven you. Once you have recognized the physician, now safely drink the blood which you shed.” Likewise, in Sermon 38 on John (no. 7, vol. III, col. 558): “Many believed from among them; Christ’s blood was granted them, so that they might drink it for their deliverance rather than be held guilty concerning its shedding.” [Col. 0779B] Likewise, in the sermon *On Wednesday*: “If you receive Christ’s blood with all reverence, you will know that through it your sins are forgiven you.” Likewise, in Sermon 31 on John (no. 9, col. 523): “They saw Christ dying through their crime, and believed in Christ forgiving their crimes. Until they drank the blood which they had shed, they despaired of their salvation.” Likewise Pope Leo, in his sermon *On the Lord’s Passion* (11, col. 239): “His own malice deceived him: he inflicted punishment upon the Son of God which would be turned into both remedy for all the children of men and, in reconciling the world, both a price and a cup.”

## Chapter XIII. That the truth of Christ’s body has also often been shown by visible signs

[Col. 0779C]

What, then, can be said more certainly concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament, unless perhaps we wish to see that very body with our eyes? Yet in this matter the Lord himself did not wish to fail us, but made provision in every way for our weak faith. For although it has been sufficiently established by the testimonies of Christ himself, of so many saints, and even by the faith of the universal Catholic Church—which, from the beginning of its conversion, believed thus and was saved thus—that the true flesh of Christ and his true blood are immolated on the Lord’s table, nevertheless, lest any corruptor should understand or explain this otherwise, God performed miracles suited to this faith of ours, whenever, wherever, and to whomsoever he deigned to reveal the secrets of this mystery. [Col. 0779D] Anyone who has read more carefully the deeds of the holy Fathers will not be unaware that such things occurred. They testify that, once the appearance of bread and wine had been removed, the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood displayed flesh and blood in their natural appearance, as they ordinarily are.

For, as Augustine says against Felicianus (ch. 2, vol. VIII, col. 40, Appendix): “If the rationale is incomprehensible and the truth is evident, in matters of faith testimony is more readily believed than reason is investigated.” Therefore, although these writings do not possess the same height of authority as prophetic and apostolic writings, they sufficiently prove that we hold the same faith as our faithful and holy predecessors; and they claim complete authority for themselves in this proof, because, unless matters stood as they teach, they would have been condemned in the sacred canons or in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs as heretical or apocryphal writings, and Catholic men would neither read nor recite them in the Church. [Col. 0780A]

Since, therefore, believers past and present throughout the world believe and maintain this, if this universal faith of the Church has not proved true unto salvation, then either there never was a Catholic Church, or it has perished. But no Catholic will agree either that the Church has not existed or that it has perished. For since the Church was founded by prophecies and Gospels, where is that which Truth promised Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 17:18)? Likewise, where is that which the same Truth said to the apostles: “Teach all nations. Whoever believes shall be saved” (Mark 16:16)? For since all nations glory that they believe thus, if they lack the blessing of salvation, God’s truth is imperilled in both prophecy and Gospel. [Col. 0780B]

Likewise, since he deigned to reveal his flesh and blood to his faithful in their natural appearance, if he did this to satisfy their longing and the thing is not so, he did not fulfil but deceived the devotion of his servants; if he did it to heal doubt and the thing is not so, he did not remove but increased the error of the weak. To entertain even lightly such a suspicion concerning divine goodness and truth is not only sacrilegious but impious. Therefore let him be anathema—maranatha (“Our Lord, come!”)—who has presumed to contradict divine authority in this sacrament and has not believed Christ’s body truly to be what it is: the true bread which descended from heaven and gives life to the world. Ambrose and Augustine call it *epiousion*, that is, “supersubstantial,” because Christ’s flesh rightly surpasses every created substance. [Col. 0780C]

## Chapter XIV. That Christ’s body, though local, is in heaven and on earth

Since, therefore, it has been plainly established by the testimonies of Christ himself and of so many saints that Christ’s spiritual body and blood are truly and substantially in the sacrament of bread and wine, let us examine, concerning what is established as truth, its power also. For although every body and every creature is local, we must nevertheless believe of this supersubstantial body that, at one and the same time, it is truly in its sacrament on earth and truly sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father. [Col. 0780D] For at the time of his immolation we would say in vain, “You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy upon us,” if we were falsely saying that he whom we adore in the sacrament is in heaven.

Since, then, the matter has been established concerning the sacrament, where his presence seemed less evident, let it also be established concerning heaven, where, ascending, he raised his body before his apostolic witnesses; and where, as the Creed of our faith also testifies, he sits at the right hand of God the Father, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead. Since he is believed to sit there until the day of judgment, no doubt remains that he is there also at the hour of his immolation. Hence, as was said, Augustine in book II against Maximinus: “The Son is still in the human form which he raised into heaven, and this same immortal form shall be everlasting in the kingdom.” And shortly afterward: “Christ [Col. 0781A] received the visible form of humanity; not only was he born in it, but he also ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father in it.”

Likewise, in Psalm 75 (no. 17, vol. IV, col. 803): “If you think of the Father and Son according to divinity, he is present everywhere. But if you understand the Son as he was seen in the flesh among human beings, crucified and risen, we know that he ascended into heaven and angels are around him.” Likewise, in Psalm 54: “Until the age is ended, the Lord is above; yet the Lord as Truth is also here with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place; but his truth is spread everywhere.” Likewise, in Sermon 27 on John (no. 4, col. 503): “According to the unity of person, Christ was in heaven while he spoke on earth. The Son of Man was in heaven in the same way in which the Son of God was on earth: the Son of God on earth in the flesh assumed; the Son of Man in heaven in the unity of person.” [Col. 0781B]

In this it must be noted that that human form in which Christ, dining with his disciples, delivered himself to them in the sacrament as though another, yet the same, is whole in one place in heaven at the right hand of the Father—just as it was whole at the supper when it was eaten by the disciples in the sacrament. Yet both in human and in sacramental form, the same true Christ is in each place, both in heaven and on earth.

Hence Pope Leo, in a letter sent to Bishop Anatolius: “Although he has been established at the Father’s right hand, nevertheless in the same flesh which he took from the Virgin he performs the sacrament of propitiation.” Likewise Basil, in his dialogue (John Chrysostom, *On the Priesthood*, bk. III, ch. 4): “He who sits above at the Father’s right hand is nevertheless held by human hands at the time of sacrifice.” Hence also the priest, acting in Christ’s place, consecrates the Lord’s body upon an earthly altar; yet ascribing nothing to his own merits but everything to divine power and grace, he prays in the Canon to God the Father, saying: “Command these offerings to be borne to you through the hands and power of your angel, who is the Angel of Great Counsel, your Son—not to this lowly and visible altar where he is now, but to your sublime altar, that is, your Son, whom you have exalted to your right hand in the presence of your majesty—so that they may become for us the body and blood of your beloved Son.” [Col. 0781C] This shows that the Son himself, by the Father’s command, is in heaven both offering, and victim, and that upon which the offering is made; for we rely wholly upon his faith and grace in believing that earthly bodies are changed into Christ, that he himself sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us, and that he is consecrated and present in the sacrament of the altar. [Col. 0781D]

Since, then, it has been said that we receive Christ’s body in the sacrament such as it is in itself after the resurrection, let us see what glory and power our bodies will have after the resurrection, so that, once the members are seen, we may more readily recognize in the Head the prerogative of such great dignity.

Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* (ch. 91, [Col. 0782A] vol. VI, col. 230): “The bodies of the saints shall rise without any defect, without any corruption, without the difficulty of burden. In them there shall be as much ease as happiness; for this reason they are called spiritual, though beyond doubt they will be bodies, not spirits.” Likewise Augustine, in book XIII of *The City of God* (ch. 20, vol. VII, col. 340): “The body shall rise spiritual, because it shall be subjected to the spirit with the highest and wonderful ease of obedience, so as to fulfil the most assured will of indissoluble immortality, all sense of trouble, all corruptibility, and all slowness being removed.” And shortly afterward: “The bodies will possess the substance of flesh, but, under the life-giving spirit, will suffer no slowness or corruptibility of the flesh.”

If the bodies of the saints will possess such ease [Col. 0782B] that they are hindered by no slowness of their own from fulfilling the spirit’s will, what must be believed concerning the body of Christ, our Head? To it belongs not merely an ease by which it is not delayed in doing whatever it wills, but also—as he himself says—“all power in heaven and on earth,” so that it can do all things with God in the unity of person. If our bodies will become spiritual because they are bodily joined to the spirit—

> [Note: Col. 0781D. Elsewhere: “personally.”]

—what is God’s body except divine, because it is united to God? We do not, then, call the divine flesh substantially identical with God; but certainly, since the Apostle says that all things are subject to him, except him who subjected all things to him (1 Cor. 15:27), and since the Son of God himself testifies that all power has been given to him, we believe it to be joined to God in the unity of person in such a manner that what God has by nature, the flesh itself has by grace. [Col. 0782C]

Therefore, although we shall have—and angels now have—the ability to cross intervals of place, however great, with almost no interval of time through their extraordinary swiftness, they nevertheless do not have the ability to remain where they depart from. By this privilege alone the flesh of Christ, exalted by God above every creature, is distinguished above and beyond every nature: that, through the omnipotence given to it in heaven and on earth, wherever and however it pleases, it may be wholly, entire, and substantially both in heaven and on earth—not by passing from place to place, but by remaining where it is and existing elsewhere wherever it wills. For what omnipotence would it receive from him who is wholly everywhere [Col. 0782D] if it could not itself be wholly and substantially wherever it willed? Or how would it differ from the angels, above whom it has been exalted, if it could be in heaven and on earth only by departing from one place for another?

The rotating millstone, by the excessive speed of its circuit, gives the false impression of standing still. Human nature, flying in the twinkling of an eye across all the spaces of land, sea, and air from west to east in seeing the sun, seems to equal an atom of a moment; and since the swiftness of angels is faster, in what respect will Christ’s flesh be exalted above these creatures if its presence in heaven and on earth is ascribed not to power but to speed?

> [Note: Col. 0782D. The perceptive author wisely rejects the opinion proposed by Dr. Statler in *Theologia dogmatica: De sacramento eucharistiae*, p. 217: namely, that Christ’s body is made present in the most holy sacrament by an exceedingly rapid motion.]

## Chapter XV. That Christ’s body, divided and received by the faithful, remains incorrupt and whole

[Col. 0783A]

Therefore, in order to show that he possesses omnipotence both in heaven and on earth, Christ, about to bring his deified body into heaven and give it to the world, withdrew from us in respect of its human form, yet nevertheless offered us no less substantially and truly in the sacrament of his body and blood. Thus, being bodily present here and there—as befits one who is of one person with him who is nowhere absent—he may work reconciliation with the Father there, and redemption and remission of sins for us here at the altar, as he did once upon the cross. His own body, given into the mouths of the faithful, is divided among individuals, yet is possessed as one whole, undivided and entire, by all collectively: received but not consumed, so that, just as it remains undivided when divided, it may be believed incorrupt when received. [Col. 0783B]

For how would he grant us incorruption if, having risen, he suffered corruption in himself? Or how would he incorporate us into himself through his sacrament, making us one—as body to head, or as members to members—if in himself he were not united but divided and crushed by the teeth of those receiving him? Yet reason is astonished and faith itself marvels at how Christ’s body can be present in heaven and in the world, divided without division, and received without consumption. But, not doubting, faith reveres the possibility that this is done by the power of the associated divinity, which is wholly present everywhere in his spiritual body—or rather by the omnipotence bestowed upon it, now made divine.

For if we wish perfectly to investigate the deeds, miracles, or words by which the Son of God disclosed his majesty to the world, we shall find that the humanity which he united to himself in one person is separated from no grace, so that even with respect to the flesh, as was said, all things are subject to him, except him who subjected all things to him. [Col. 0783C] But let us see whether the saints agree with this faith which marvels and is marvellous.

Augustine, in a sermon *On the Words of the Lord*: “The Lord invites his servants and has prepared himself as food. Who would dare eat his own Lord? Yet he says: ‘He who eats me shall live because of me’ (John 6:58). For while Christ is eaten, life is eaten; he is not killed in order to be eaten, but gives life to the dead when he is eaten, because he rose after being killed. Nor, when he is eaten, do we make parts of him. And indeed this is so in the sacrament. The faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh. Each receives his own part; he is eaten in parts and remains whole: wholly in heaven, wholly in your heart.” [Col. 0783D]

Likewise Eusebius of Emesa: “Concerning this bread the ancient history relates: ‘He who gathered more had nothing over, and he who prepared less found nothing less,’ because the sacred reception of the Eucharist consists not in quantity but in power. That body, when distributed by the priest, is as great in a small portion as it is known to be in the whole.

> [Note: Col. 0784D. Saint Thomas, employing nearly the same words, wrote: “There is as much under a fragment as is contained under the whole.”]

When the Church of the faithful receives it, it is proved to be as full in all collectively as it is whole in each individual. Concerning this bread, when it is received, individuals have no less than all collectively. One receives all, two receive all, many receive all without diminution, because the blessing of this sacrament knows how to be distributed and does not know how to be consumed by distribution.” [Col. 0784A]

Likewise Augustine, in a sermon *On the Words of the Lord*: “Do you think that I shall make parts of this body which you see, cut up my members, and give them to you? What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? Certainly, he who could ascend whole could not be consumed. Therefore he gave us health-giving refreshment from his body and blood, and in few words resolved so great a question concerning his wholeness. Therefore let them eat and drink; let them eat life and drink life. To eat that is to be refreshed. But you are refreshed in such a way that that by which you are refreshed does not fail. Eat life; drink life; and life remains whole.” [Col. 0784B]

Likewise Ambrose, *On the Mysteries of Initiation* (ch. 8, col. 337): “Consider now whether the bread of angels is more excellent, or the flesh of Christ, which certainly is the body of life. That manna is from heaven; this is above heaven. That is of heaven; this is of the Lord of heaven. That was subject to corruption if kept for another day; this is free from every corruption. Whoever tastes it reverently cannot experience corruption.” Likewise Ambrose, Fifth Sunday after Epiphany:

> [Note: Col. 0784D. Preface of the Mass.]

“Each receives Christ the Lord, and he is whole in each portion; he is not diminished by individual portions, but offers himself entire in each.” [Col. 0784C]

But why should it seem impossible that the flesh of the Word of God, much more spiritual and powerful than our word, should be whole and entire in the mouths of all who receive it, when our one and same word is whole and entire in the ears of all who hear it? Christ himself made this clearer in his own person: at the supper he distributed his body and blood to his disciples; and although he himself was eaten and drunk by each one in the sacrament, he nevertheless remained alive and whole in himself.

But what wonder is it if Christ is eaten and remains whole, when the widow of Sarepta ate no less oil? For, as sacred history testifies, the jar of oil was not diminished, although the same Scripture says that she went and did according to Elijah’s word, and he and her household ate (3 Kings 17:15). [Col. 0784D] Hence Ambrose (John Chrysostom), in the homily on Hebrews (Homily 17, vol. XII, p. 168): “In Christ the victim was offered once, powerful for eternal salvation. What, then, of us? Do we not offer every day? We offer, but for remembrance of his death; and there is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because Christ was offered once; but this sacrifice is an image of that one: the same thing, always the same thing. Thus this very sacrifice is one alone. Otherwise, since it is offered in many places, are there many Christs? By no means. Rather, Christ is one everywhere: whole here and whole there, one body. For as that which is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so too it is one sacrifice. But that high priest is he who offered the victim cleansing us. We offer it even now, the very victim which, having then been offered, cannot be consumed.” [Col. 0785A]

What, as the saints testify, is sacrificed in different places and at different times is therefore not many bodies, but everywhere one body of Christ. It is received by different persons, and the one and same body remains whole. This must be attributed to the omnipotence bestowed upon Christ even in respect of his flesh: by which, as stated above, he can be present bodily in heaven and on earth, wherever and however he wills. Therefore Christ’s flesh is whole and present wherever he wills, contrary to the nature of flesh—

> [Note: Col. 0785. Contrary to the nature of flesh which has not yet been made spiritual through resurrection, as Algerus explained in chapter 14.]

—because it has been made omnipotent in heaven and on earth. [Col. 0785B]

But Augustine’s statement, “And indeed this is so in the sacrament: each receives his own part, and he is eaten in parts,” does not in any respect hinder his wholeness. For he says that this occurs in the sacrament—that is, in what is seen—not in the reality of the sacrament, which is not seen: namely, Christ’s body. For, as the same Augustine says, bodily sacraments are like certain words, because these, like words, are signs of things. Thus Cephas, Simon, and Peter are different names for the same Peter; likewise Christ is not another, though represented by different sacraments. For although the appearances of bread and wine are two sacraments, there are not two different Christs in them; in each is the one Christ. He is neither divided in himself by the distribution of the sacrament, nor received more or less according to the size of a portion; for in his spiritual power he is always believed to be whole. Thus one who receives more sacrament does not have an excess, nor does one who receives less suffer deficiency. He is always the same whole: whole in the great quantity, whole in the small, whole in the whole, whole in the broken; for however the signs vary, he always remains the same in himself. [Col. 0785C]

Hence Eusebius rightly says: “Truly a single and perfect victim, to be judged by faith, not by appearance; not assessed by outward sight, but by inward disposition.” It is single because it is not many through variety of places or times, but always one victim; perfect because it can neither be increased nor diminished. And because the appearances of the elements—that is, bread and wine—are Christ’s figure, not his truth, it is therefore to be judged not by appearance or assessed by outward sight, but by the inward disposition of faith. For although the sacramental appearance of the elements seems to vary as a sign, Christ’s body is believed unchangeable in itself. [Col. 0786A]

Therefore, just as manna was uniform merely in appearance, but inwardly seasoned with various flavours according to the will or pleasure of those using it, so that in one appearance there was the flavour of many foods; so, conversely, the complete reality of Christ’s body is inwardly present in the varying quantity of the sacraments. Thus, as is read of manna, “he who gathered more had nothing over, and he who prepared less found nothing less.” So in the sacrament of Christ’s body there is no deficiency in the lesser amount nor abundance in the greater, because grace lies not in the appearance or quantity of the sacrament but in Christ’s power.

## Chapter XVI. That Christ’s immolation on the altar is not said to mean that he is killed again, but that his true immolation is represented, and that what he then worked on the cross he now works on the altar

[Col. 0786B]

Now, since Ambrose (John Chrysostom) said shortly before that the victim offered once in Christ is powerful for eternal salvation, we must consider why he asked whether our apparently daily offering, after that true offering made once, would not be true, or whether, after that offering powerful and sufficient for salvation, it would be superfluous: “What, then, of us? Do we not offer every day?”

But it must be understood that if our daily offering were other than that once offered in Christ, it would not be true but superfluous. For since that offering once made in Christ is truly real, because it is truly eternal life and sufficient to confer it upon us, what other life could our offering promise [Col. 0786C] or confer, if it were another? For another offering would have to confer another salvation; or, if it were directed to conferring the same salvation for whose bestowal Christ’s offering alone suffices, it would be superfluous and vain. Since, therefore, it is impossible for another salvation to be conferred, that offering made once and our daily offering must be the same, so that the same offering may not be superfluous to itself, but may always be the same, always sufficient, and always necessary.

First, then, let us see whether ours and that offering are the same; next, whether the same effect of salvation always follows the same offering. But Ambrose (John Chrysostom), as if answering his own question, says: “We offer, but for remembrance of his death; and there is one victim, not many, because Christ was offered once. But this sacrifice is an image of that one: the same thing, always the same thing.” [Col. 0786D]

It must therefore be observed that he calls our daily sacrifice “the very same” as that in which Christ was offered once on the cross, with respect to the same true substance of Christ’s body here and there. But when he calls our daily sacrifice an image—that is, a figure or form—of the one offered once, he does not mean that another Christ is essentially established here or there. Rather, he shows that the same Christ is immolated and offered in one way once on the cross and in another way daily on the altar: there in the reality of the Passion, in which he was killed for us; here in a figure and imitation of that Passion, in which Christ does not truly suffer again, [Col. 0787A] but the true memorial of his Passion is daily renewed for us.

Ambrose himself (John Chrysostom) observes this and adds: “What we do takes place in remembrance of what was done. For he says, ‘Do this in remembrance of me.’ We do not offer another sacrifice, but always offer the same; rather, we perform the remembrance of the sacrifice.” Thus there is no diversity in the reality of Christ himself, but in the action of his immolation. Insofar as this action represents, by a certain likeness of its own, the true Passion and death of Christ, it invites and kindles us to imitate that Passion, strengthens and fortifies us against the enemy, purifies us from vices, adorns us with virtues, and renders us fit and worthy for eternal life.

For although his offering on the cross, once made, sufficed for the salvation and redemption of all, [Col. 0787B] it is nevertheless daily necessary also for strengthening and cleansing human weakness, which is daily tempted and falls into either mortal or at least venial sins, without which this life cannot be lived. For through this unique victim we obtain not merely absolution of sins from God, but are also fortified against temptations. For when the adversary sees, through reception of Christ’s body, that our dwelling is occupied by the splendour of heavenly presence, he understands that Christ has closed the place against his temptations, and he will flee and withdraw.

It must therefore be understood that, although Christ’s offering once on the cross is true and the daily offering on the altar is figurative, nevertheless the grace of our salvation is exactly the same here and there: here and there true, sufficient, and always [Col. 0787C] necessary, because here and there the same true Christ is powerful for all things.

That the saints attest this so plainly, let us see from the authorities cited below, both concerning the essential truth of Christ here and there, and concerning the true and equal benefit for our salvation here and there. Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*:

> “Christ was offered once in himself, and yet is daily immolated in the sacrament. This must be understood thus: in the manifestation of his body, in the distinctness of all the members belonging to him, true God and true man hung only once upon the cross, offering himself to the Father—a living sacrifice, capable of suffering, mortal, effectual for the redemption of the living and the dead: namely, of those whom the depth of the divine counsel judged, foreknew, and predestined to be redeemed, in the ways and at the times in which this fittingly came to pass.” [Col. 0787D]

He therefore says that Christ suffered once upon the cross in his manifest body and in the distinct members of his humanity; whereas he is daily in the sacrament, not manifestly but invisibly, not suffering, but represented as though suffering. For it was altogether unfitting that Christ should be immolated again in a real passion: both because it was impossible for one who is immortal to be killed, and because it would be cruel that, in the Church’s sacrifice, a human being should be torn apart as beasts are sacrificed and devoured with teeth. Since, therefore, we could not at once be cruel toward God and devout toward him, it was fitting that what was pious for Christ’s faithful should be unbloody: that the offering should not be fulfilled by them through Christ’s actual passion and death, [Col. 0788A] in which Christ deigned to accomplish his propitiation for all. For how should we be better than those who crucified him, unless we differed in piety and devotion from those who presumed to destroy him?

Hence Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Hebrews (John Chrysostom):

> “But in this flesh and blood let the human mind conceive nothing bloody, nothing corruptible; rather, let it believe that the life-giving and saving substance, made proper to the Word himself, is present in bread and wine; through these, if they are worthily received, remission of sins is bestowed upon us.”

Hence Augustine, in the book *On the Sacraments of the Altar*:

> “Truth says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’ (John 6:56). Otherwise, how will this be true: ‘The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,’ unless the flesh be true?” [Col. 0788B]

But since it is not lawful for Christ to be devoured with teeth, he willed that this bread and wine should, in the mystery, truly be made his flesh and blood potentially through the consecration of the Holy Spirit, and should be mystically immolated daily for the life of the world. Thus, as true flesh is created from the Virgin through the Spirit without sexual union, so through that same Spirit the same body of Christ is mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine.

This offering is repeated daily, although Christ suffered once, because we sin daily—at least with those sins without which mortal weakness cannot live. And therefore, because we fall daily, Christ is daily mystically immolated for us. That this immolation [Col. 0788C] occurs not by a real act but by an imaginal representation of passion and death, yet works true salvation, Gregory testifies in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (chap. 58, col. 472):

> “This singular sacrifice saves the soul from eternal destruction, because it renews for us, through mystery, the death of the Only-begotten. Though, having risen from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9), yet, living immortally and incorruptibly in himself, he is again immolated for us in this mystery of sacred offering. For there his body is received, his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people, and his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of believers. Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us: one which always imitates, for our absolution, the passion of the only-begotten Son.” [Col. 0788D]

Although he does not say that it truly effects the passion of the Only-begotten, but that it imitates it imaginally, he nevertheless testifies that this sacrifice truly saves us from eternal destruction. Hence the Venerable Bede, in his homilies:

> “He not only washed us from our sins in his blood when he shed his blood on the cross, but he also washes us daily from our sins in his blood, when the memorial of that blessed passion is repeated at the altar, when the creature of bread and wine is transferred by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit into the sacrament of his flesh and blood. Thus his body and blood are not poured out and slain by unbelieving hands to their destruction, but are received by the mouth of believers for their salvation.”

Likewise Eusebius of Emesa:

> “Because he was about [Col. 0789A] to remove his assumed body from our eyes and carry it to the stars, it was necessary that on this day he should consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that what was offered once as a price might continually be worshipped through mystery. Thus, because unceasing and tireless redemption was being enacted daily for human salvation, the offering of redemption also might be perpetual; that perpetual sacrifice might live in remembrance and always be present in grace.”

Likewise Augustine, in the sermon *On Wednesday* (chap. 4):

> “If you receive the blood of Christ with all reverence, you will know that through it your sins are forgiven you.”

Again, in the same work (chap. 6):

> “You, Christian soul, see that you do not forsake the table of your bridegroom, if you would remain beautiful. You shall eat his flesh daily, that you may have eternal life, and you shall drink his blood.”

We have therefore established that Christ’s daily immolation is necessary and sufficient for us for the remission of sins and the attainment of eternal life. We have also shown that it is not burdensome to Christ himself through the punishment of passion or killing, but is useful to us through a certain representation of his passion, to stir remembrance, increase devotion, and invite imitation. For why would blessed Ambrose (John Chrysostom) say that Christ’s sacrifice is offered daily in remembrance of his death, and that our sacrifice is an example of that sacrifice, unless he wished us not to be ungrateful for such benefits, but rather to be bound to so great a grace by our devotion and imitation?

Yet because we are joined with Christ in sacrament and body, although he is immolated in himself not by a real but by an imaginal passion, he is nevertheless immolated in his members by a real and not imaginal passion, when we—who, in remembrance of his passion, celebrate the sacrament of such great mercy by offering it—announce the death of so pious and beloved a Lord and Father by weeping and crushing our hearts with true compunction. [Col. 0789C] For just as, when Peter said, “Lord, where are you going?” Christ answered, “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again”; or as Paul says, “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24): so he suffers with all his members, so that those who suffer with him may more readily be believed to reign with him also. For in truth he will deign to make them partakers of his glory whose share in affliction he does not disdain to be. Since wine is sacrificed for Christ and water for the people, and both become one blood, what does this signify except the unity of head and members in compassion and death?

Hence Augustine, in Book X of *The City of God* (chap. 20, vol. VII, col. 256):

> “He willed that the sacrament of this thing should be the Church’s daily sacrifice; and since the Church is the body of that head, she learns through him to offer herself.”

For one cannot be the body of the Crucified who has not been crucified. Hence the Apostle: “Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Hence Gregory, in Book IV of the *Dialogues* (chap. 59, col. 472):

> “We who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion ought to imitate what we do. Then, therefore, the sacrifice will truly be offered to God for us when we have made ourselves a sacrifice.”

Likewise Ambrose, [Col. 0790A] in the book *On the Sacraments*:

> “Because you have been marked with the form of his cross, you have received from his passion its seal and likeness, so that you may rise again into his form, live as his image—he who was crucified to sin and lives to God.”

Since, then, the sacrament of Christ’s body is so excellent and so beneficial to us in its benefits and examples, let us see that no error deprives us of so great a grace; rather, let the truth of faith itself make us as certain concerning the things it presents as it makes us strong concerning the things it exhorts us to do. For weak people, carried about by every wind of doctrine, immediately doubt the truth of faith when they hear what they do not know. Let us endeavor, so far as we can, with God’s assent, to heal them.

For since the sacrament is a figure of Christ’s truth, [Col. 0790B] and in the sacramental figure there is enacted a figure of the imaginal action of sacrifice, they hesitate that truth lies concealed amid so many figures. This is especially so since Christ is said to be immolated once in himself and daily in the sacrament, as though he should be understood as real when said to be in himself, but not real—rather, imaginal—in the sacrament. But it must be known that Christ is said to be immolated in himself, that is, in human form, and in the sacrament, that is, in the form of bread and wine; not because he is not here immolated in himself as truly in substance as there, but in order to indicate here and there a different form of the same substance.

## Chapter XVII. That the body of Christ is spoken of in a twofold or threefold manner

For this reason too the saints speak variously, but not contrariwise, concerning the body and blood [Col. 0790C] of the Lord. Thus blessed Jerome maintains that it should be understood in two ways, while Augustine maintains that it should be understood in three. Lest they appear to disagree with themselves or with other saints in this matter, let us see how Christ’s body should be believed to be twofold.

Jerome says in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians (Book I, chap. 1, vol. VII, col. 553, ed. 1769):

> “The blood and flesh of Christ are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’; and, ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have eternal life’; or as that flesh which was crucified, and that blood which was poured out by the soldier’s lance.”

He must be understood not to have said this with respect to a twofold substance, [Col. 0790D] but with respect to a twofold form of the same substance, which is now understood in human form and now in the form of bread and wine. Augustine makes this clearer. Having called the Church a third mode of Christ’s body, he discusses the same twofold body of which Jerome speaks thus (same place, col. 608):

> “The body of Christ is also that mystical body which is consecrated from the substance of bread and wine through the Holy Spirit.”

And he adds:

> “But that body which was born from the Virgin Mary, into which this is transferred,” etc.

In saying that this is transferred and converted into that through the consecration of the altar, he indicates the same substance. But in distinguishing it by saying “this” or “that,” he does so, as stated, according to a diversity of form. Perfectly implying this identity of substance, he says of the third body of Christ, which is the Church: “To this, if we communicate rightly, we direct our minds, that we, who are his body, may receive his flesh from himself and through himself, while he remains whole.” Since he bids us receive his flesh from himself, what does he signify except that giver and gift are the same? He adds:

> “This flesh is indeed itself, and the fruit of his flesh, so that he may always remain the same and feed all who are in the body.” [Col. 0791A]

Eusebius says that this body, carried to the stars, is continually worshipped by us through mystery. Of this the priest prays at the end of a certain Mass, that what we bear in outward appearance we may receive in the reality of things—indicating that it is the same in substance, though different in form. Christ himself displayed this twofoldness at supper, when present himself in human form, he gave himself to the disciples in the sacrament. The saints marked this twofoldness not of substance but of form whenever they said, concerning Christ’s body, that it is itself and not itself: itself according to substance, not itself according to form.

Since, therefore, Christ’s body in human form, Christ’s body in the sacrament, and Christ’s body as the Church are spoken of in three ways, great confusion arises among those who cannot distinguish this in Holy Scripture, so that what is said of one body of Christ is believed to have been said of another.

There is also another confusion. Since Christ’s body is spoken of in three ways, they attribute the sacrament of bread and wine to Christ’s body on the altar, and make that body of Christ on the altar itself the sacrament of Christ’s body in human form. Thus, because the form of bread and wine is called the sacrament of Christ’s body on the altar, and Christ’s body on the altar itself is called the sacrament of Christ’s human body, they contend that what is itself is not the same itself, but establish the one as though different from the other. [Col. 0791C] For someone says: “That which is on the altar, which you assert to be Christ’s true body, is called in Holy Writ appearance, likeness, figure, sign, mystery, sacrament. But these words are relative terms; and no relative terms can be the things to which they refer. Therefore the sacrament is not Christ’s body.” And so concerning the other terms.

But no prejudice is done by these terms either to the faith which we believe or to the truth which we maintain. For, as was said above, as regards the visible sacrament, *appearance* and *likeness* are names of those things which existed before—namely bread and wine—not of Christ’s body; yet they are called Christ’s body and blood by denomination, according to that manner of speech in which a signifying thing is customarily called by the name of the thing signified. Hence Augustine, in the book *Expressions in Genesis*, chap. 59 (CXLIII, vol. III, col. 334):

> “The expression is to be noted in which certain signs are called by the names of the things which they signify. Thus the Apostle says: ‘And the rock was Christ’ (1 Cor. 10:4); he does not say: ‘The rock signified Christ.’” [Col. 0791D]

## Chapter XVIII. That Christ’s invisible body in the sacrament is the sacrament of his visible body in human form: true of true, the same of the same

And this sacrament or figure is indeed different from its thing, as a visible thing is from an invisible one, as was said above. Yet no one should rightly be troubled if the same true flesh and the same blood of Christ are also held to be sacraments of themselves, when received according to different respects: by the imaginal breaking of bread and pouring of blood from the cup, thus representing the true breaking of his body and the pouring out of his blood in the passion. For example: if I, as an old man, by stammering, crawling, and imitating my other childish actions, represented myself as a child, I would nevertheless be not another person but myself; I myself would be both figure and thing figured. Yet the action by which I represented myself in my old age would be an imaginal one of that which, in me as a child, had been real. [Col. 0792B]

So too, after his resurrection, Christ bore the type and figure of himself through a different action and under a different relation of times. For, as Augustine says, when he appeared to the two disciples and pretended to be going farther, he signified that after a few days he would ascend into heaven, a journey farther removed from ordinary human life. Christ, therefore, pretending to go farther is the sacrament of Christ ascending into heaven: the same of the same, but not in every respect the same. For the same true Christ both pretends and ascends; yet the pretence of an earthly journey is one thing, the reality of ascending into heaven another. [Col. 0792C]

Nor is anyone so foolish as to deny that the one pretending to go farther is the true Christ because, by the pretence of a longer journey, he signifies that he, the true Christ, will ascend into heaven. Therefore, lest those inexperienced in faith should waver in so great a matter, the authorities of the saints will show, by the inspiration of divine grace, what is to be thought about this: namely, that they may believe Christ’s body in the sacrament—both sacrament signifying and thing signified—to be substantially and truly one and the same Christ, in the form of bread and wine and likewise in human form.

Concerning the sacrament of bread and wine—how it signifies and is called Christ’s body—enough has been said above. But that the invisible true body of Christ after the resurrection is the sacrament of his visible body, that is, of himself in his passion, Augustine testifies in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*:

> “His flesh is that which we receive in the sacrament, veiled by the form of bread; and his blood is that which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine: flesh, the sacrament of flesh; blood, the sacrament of blood. By flesh and blood, both invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, is signified the visible and tangible body of our Lord Jesus Christ, full of the grace of all virtues and of divine majesty.” [Col. 0792D]

Likewise in the same work:

> “Thus the heavenly bread, which is truly Christ’s flesh, is in its own manner called Christ’s body, although it is in reality the sacrament of Christ’s body—namely, of that body which was visible, tangible, mortal, and placed upon the cross. And the very offering of flesh which is performed by the hands of the priest is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion, not in the truth of the thing but in the signifying mystery. Thus too the sacrament of faith, which is understood as baptism, is faith.”

Hence likewise blessed Augustine, in the letter to Boniface (98, no. 9, vol. II, col. 267):

> “Was Christ not once immolated in himself? And yet in the sacrament he is immolated for the peoples not only at every Paschal solemnity but every day; nor does one certainly lie who, when asked, answers that he is immolated. For if sacraments did not have some likeness of the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they often even receive the names of the things themselves. For as, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood, so the sacrament of faith is faith.” [Col. 0793B]

Here it should be noted that the immolation which he says occurs not in the truth of the thing must be understood as occurring by the likeness of the sacrament alone, representing Christ’s true immolation, death, passion, and crucifixion, with the mystery itself signifying them. Thus baptism, which is the sacrament of faith, is called faith not in the truth of the thing but by likeness alone.

But when he said that Christ’s true flesh is called Christ’s body “in its own manner,” although in reality it is the sacrament of itself, this should not be understood as though it were not truly called Christ’s body. Rather, “in its own manner” means in a way singularly proper to itself: because, although every body is visible and tangible, Christ’s body alone after the resurrection, with nature changed but not substance, is not bodily but spiritual and invisible, as stated above. [Col. 0793C]

But what he says to Boniface—“As in a certain manner the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, so the sacrament of faith is faith”—must be understood of the form of bread and wine, which is called Christ’s body not truly but figuratively and by denomination. Therefore Augustine gave two likenesses to prove that the sacrament of faith is called faith: one of an actual sacrament, namely imaginal immolation; the other of a real thing, namely the form of bread and wine. Thus, as imaginal immolation is figuratively called Christ’s death and crucifixion, and as the form of bread and wine is figuratively called Christ’s body, so the sacrament of faith, namely baptism, is figuratively called faith.

It should be noted that in one of these two likenesses he said that the heavenly bread, which is truly Christ’s flesh, is called Christ’s body not in the common manner but in its own and, as it were, proper manner, because he saw that body to be singularly, above all bodies, not bodily but spiritual and divine. In the other likeness, however, he said absolutely that the sacrament of Christ’s body—that is, the form of bread—is in a certain manner Christ’s body, because he indicated that it is called Christ’s body by the common figure of speech through which things are called what they are not. [Col. 0793D] But when he called Christ’s invisible body the sacrament of his visible body, this is to be understood intelligibly only through some outward action concerning it, not sensibly.

For how, after the manner of other visible sacraments, can that which cannot be seen be the sign of a visible thing except through the representation of some outward action concerning itself? [Col. 0794A]

## Chapter XIX. That a sacrament signifies in two ways: either by its own inherent likeness, or by some action performed upon it

Since enough has been said above concerning the third body of Christ, which is the Church—namely, that it shares sacramental union with Christ its head, and that, as head and members, it is one body with him by grace though another by substance—let us see in how many ways sacraments resemble their things and signify them in the threefold body of Christ.

They seem to do this in two ways: namely, [Col. 0794B] either through their own inherent likeness, or through some outward action directed toward them. A sacrament signifies by its own inherent likeness, as when the Lord says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink”; and, “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:55). For just as food and drink sustain temporal life, so he gives eternal life. Hence he says: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (ibid.). And rightly so. For if food which does not live or endure has such power as to nourish and preserve the fleeting life of this present age for as long as God pleases, how much more ought Christ, living food immortally, be believed to bestow eternal life upon those whom he pleases? For he who has life in himself and is life ought more readily to be believed to confer life than one who does not have it.

Since he is the way, the truth, and the life, his body is our provision for the journey, lest we die and fail on the way, but may be brought to life; he is truth, lest we be deceived by his promises; he is life, that we may enjoy it happily in its fruition. Thus in this mortal life he feeds us with the immortal food of life, lest we die eternally. [Col. 0794C]

Nor did he will to signify himself as eternal life only by the inherent likeness, name, and appearance of food and drink; he also willed, through the likeness of bread and wine, to signify his other body, namely the Church. Hence Augustine, in the sermon *On the Sacraments of the Faithful*, Monday in Easter Week (vol. V, col. 976):

> “Because he suffered for us, he entrusted to us in this sacrament his body and blood; and he also made us ourselves this. For we too have become his body, and through his mercy what we receive, we are.”

And shortly afterward:

> “You came to the water; you were sprinkled; you were made the Lord’s bread. As you see that what has been made is one, so be one yourselves, by loving one another.”

Likewise, in Sermon 26 on John (vol. III, col. 500):

> “He wishes this food and drink to be understood as the fellowship of his body and members, which is the Church.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The sacrament of this thing—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is received from the Lord’s table: by some unto life, by others unto destruction. But the thing itself, of which it is the sacrament, is unto life for every person, unto destruction for none, whoever shares in it.”

For because people seek food and drink in order not to hunger or thirst, this food and drink alone truly grants this: it makes those by whom it is received immortal, namely the fellowship of the saints itself, where peace and complete, perfect unity will be. For this reason the Lord entrusted his body and blood in things which are brought together into one thing from many. One thing is made into one from many grains; another flows together into one from many grapes. [Col. 0795A] He called the fellowship of the Church food, drink, and the Lord’s bread, both because it truly satisfies in eternal blessedness and because it brings many into one through true charity. Whoever truly receives that fellowship cannot be deprived of eternal salvation.

Since, therefore, the sacrament of Christ’s body signifies Christ himself, or his Church, through its inherent likeness, let us see whether it does the same by the likeness of some outward action performed with it.

Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*:

> “While the sacrifice is broken, while the blood from the cup is poured into the mouths of the faithful, what else is designated but the immolation of the Lord’s body upon the cross and the pouring out of his blood from his side? Therefore he himself broke and delivered his body, to signify that of his own will he would be broken and delivered to passion for us—he who alone had the power to lay down his life. The priests also imitate this in his stead at the altar, so that they may represent the same thing: that is, Christ’s body, the sacrament of Christ and the Church, through an outward action.”

Pope Sergius says [Note: [Col. 0795D] In Gratian, Distinction II, canon 22, vol. I, p. 455, Pithoeus edition, Paris, 1687. It is apocryphal.]:

> “The Lord’s body is threefold. The portion of the offering put into the cup signifies the body of Christ [Col. 0795C] which has already risen; the portion eaten, that which is still walking on earth; the portion remaining on the altar until the end of Mass, the body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in their graves.”

Likewise Pope Julius, in decrees sent to bishops throughout Egypt [Note: [Col. 0795D] Falsely ascribed to Julius; in Gratian, canon [Col. 0796D] 7, *On Consecration*, Distinction II. It should be referred to the Council of Braga, A.D. 675.]:

> “The Lord’s cup, according to the precept of the canons, must be offered mixed with wine and water, because we see that the people are understood in the water, while Christ’s blood is shown in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and bound to him in whom it believes. This union and conjunction of water and wine are so mixed in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated. [Col. 0795D] For if anyone offers wine alone, Christ’s blood begins to be without us; but if water alone, the people begin to be without Christ.”

Nevertheless, it should be known that although wine and water are first mystically mixed, after consecration nothing but blood is drunk; because, having first been reborn through the water of baptism, we subsequently become spiritually not only fellow-members but also blood-relations of Christ. Wine is mixed to signify Christ and water to signify the people because, although wine comes from water, it is nevertheless more noble by means of the vine; and Christ is generated from our flesh through Mary. Wine is also found more powerful than water for refreshing and inebriating, because “how excellent is the Lord’s cup that makes drunk” (Ps. 22:5), when the mind, intoxicated by the fervor of his love, forgets all earthly things.

Hence too, by an unprecedented and astonishing miracle, after he gave up his spirit, blood and water flowed from Christ’s side contrary to nature, mystically signifying that regeneration and redemption are one work of our salvation, while through this twofold sacrament the one body of Christ and the Church was conformed by the Holy Spirit. Hence too there are three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit, water, and blood (1 John 5:7). For it was wondrous that mortals should receive the Holy Spirit from heaven according to Christ’s promise, and that one dead should, after the manner of one living, pour forth not pus but blood; indeed, beyond the manner of either living or dead, should pour water with blood from the wound in his side. Yet it is established that this was a mystery as well as a miracle. [Col. 0796B]

But why should I run through each detail? Whatever is done in the office of the Mass is a sacrament of Christ and the Church. Hence Augustine, in the book *On the Trinity*:

> “Because we have been set free by the Lord’s death, mindful of this fact, in eating and drinking we signify the flesh and blood which were offered for us. For the fact that Christ’s body in the sacrament is held in the hands of the faithful, broken, ground by teeth, and incorporated into them signifies that in the passion he was held by the hands of the ungodly, broken even unto death, and crushed because of our crimes; and it signifies the Church—his body—incorporated and conformed to him through imitation of this his passion. [Col. 0796C] Let no one think it unworthy of Christ himself, now made immortal and incorruptible, that the devotion of the faithful represents this to him in the sacrament, in imitation of the Lord’s passion: that which the Lord, about to suffer, commanded to be done in remembrance of himself. Thus, when the memory of so great a thing has been aroused and strengthened by the aid and example of the divine presence, one may will and be able, through his grace, to do what one in no way presumes by the nature of one’s own frailty.

> “For what was permitted to evil persons in Christ’s body for their own condemnation, and was not deemed dishonorable by God the Father because of our salvation, is much more pleasing and glorious to Christ himself: namely, that it should devoutly be broken in the sacrament by the hands of his faithful, ground by their teeth, as he commanded, in remembrance of himself—not indeed in the truth of passion, crucifixion, and death, as was said above, but in the signifying mystery. Thus he himself, though broken and ground, remains whole, and the grace of his redemption, divided among all, is effectual.”

That this may be known more certainly by the faithful, let the confession of Berengar of Angers, the heretic—written by him concerning the Catholic faith of this matter and affirmed on oath at Rome, in the presence of Pope Nicholas II, before 113 bishops (A.D. 1059; Labbe, IX, 1050)—be set forth here:

> “I, Berengar, unworthy deacon of the Church of Saint Maurice of Angers, acknowledging the true, Catholic, and apostolic faith, anathematize every heresy, especially that by which I have hitherto been defamed, which endeavors to maintain that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, after consecration, only a sacrament and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor can be handled by the hands of priests, broken, or ground by the teeth of the faithful sensibly except in the sacrament alone. [Col. 0797A] But I assent to the holy Roman Church and Apostolic See, and with mouth and heart profess that concerning the sacraments of the Lord’s table I hold the same faith which the lord and venerable Pope Nicholas and this holy synod have, by evangelical and apostolic authority, delivered to be held and confirmed to me: namely, that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, after consecration, not only a sacrament but also the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that they are sensibly handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful, not only sacramentally but also in truth. I swear by the holy *homoousion* Trinity and by these most sacred Gospels of Christ,” etc. [Col. 0797B]

## Chapter XX. That in the sacrifice there is a bodily sacrament and a spiritual body; therefore there are also two eatings of it, one bodily and the other spiritual; and the good receive Christ’s body by both eatings, the evil by one only

Since, then, in the declaration of Berengar the heretic in the holy synod, bread and wine after consecration are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of the Lord—and Augustine also strives in every way to affirm this—the Church’s sacrifice is accomplished from and consists in two things: the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of Christ, namely the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament. Corresponding to these two are also two eatings of Christ’s body in the Church, one bodily and one spiritual; one takes place with the mouth, the other with the heart. The bodily eating is common to good and evil alike: to the former unto salvation, to the latter unto judgment; but the spiritual is for the good alone.

We eat and drink bodily with the bodily mouth whenever, from the Lord’s altar, we receive the Lord’s body itself substantially, through the priest’s hand, in the sacrament of bread and wine. But we eat and drink spiritually with the heart whenever, as blessed Augustine says, we store in memory that the Son of God hung upon the cross for our salvation; and, not only in remembrance of this but also in imitation, we kindle ourselves by crucifying our flesh with its vices and desires. Of bodily eating the Lord himself says: “Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be delivered for you. Drink: this is my blood, which shall be poured out for you” (Matt. 26:26). Likewise the Apostle: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). [Col. 0797D]

But of spiritual eating Augustine says in Sermon 26 on John (col. 498):

> “Eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar.”

And shortly afterward, distinguishing both eatings, he adds:

> “This is the bread which came down from heaven, so that if anyone eat of it he may not die” (John 6:50). “But this concerns the power of the sacrament, not the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats with the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth.” [Col. 0798A]

Likewise the same writer, in the book *On the Words of the Lord*:

> “Then the body and blood of the Lord will be life for each person if what is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually eaten and spiritually drunk in the truth itself.”

Likewise Gregory, in the Paschal Homily (Book II, no. 7, vol. I, col. 1533):

> “The blood of the lamb is put upon both doorposts when it is drawn not only with the mouth of the body but also with the mouth of the heart. For the lamb’s blood is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his passion is received with the mouth unto redemption and is also considered with an attentive mind unto imitation.” [Col. 0798B]

## Chapter XXI. That, as the reality of Christ’s body is consecrated neither less by an evil priest nor more by a good priest, so it is received in substance neither less by an evil person nor more by any good person.

Although, therefore, the spiritual eating of Christ’s body is prior and more worthy than the bodily eating, because the former belongs only to the good whereas the latter is shared alike by good and bad; yet, since both are necessary for salvation and are true with respect to the substance of the Lord’s body, [Col. 0798C] it seems necessary to ask why blessed Augustine said that Christ’s body will then be life to each person if it is eaten spiritually in the truth itself—as though it were not received bodily in the truth itself, and as though the wicked, who receive Christ’s body only sacramentally, do not receive that true body because they do not receive it spiritually. Hence certain persons in error maintain that Christ is separated from his sacrament, asserting that the wicked receive the bare sacrament and not Christ’s body; and, by certain authorities of the saints, they contend that Judas the traitor was not present at the communion of Christ’s body in the Lord’s Supper, as though none but one truly incorporated into Christ could receive Christ’s body.

Having therefore set forth the matters by which they seem to conceive their error, we shall, God willing, subsequently establish the truth more freely: namely, that the good truly receive Christ’s body in every respect, while the wicked receive it truly indeed with respect to its substance, but not truly with respect to the efficacy of grace.

Augustine says in Sermon 27 on John (no. 10, col. 506): “Let us not eat the flesh of Christ and drink the blood merely in the sacrament, as many wicked persons do, but unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members and be enlivened by his Spirit.” Again, the same author in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*: “He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who remains in Christ and in whom [Col. 0799A] Christ dwells. For one who is at discord with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even though he daily receives without distinction, unto the judgment of his presumption, the sacrament of so great a thing.” Behold: he seems to assert that the wicked receive Christ’s flesh merely in the sacrament, as though not truly but merely figuratively; and likewise that, even though they receive the sacrament, they do not eat Christ’s flesh. Yet he does not say this with respect to the substantial reality of Christ’s body, which, though unworthy persons receive it to their judgment, they nevertheless truly receive; rather, he says it with respect to the power of the sacrament’s grace, which they neglect.

But again they adduce blessed Hilary of Poitiers, in his exposition of Matthew (ch. 30, vol. I, col. 799), as though he were a witness for this position. He seems plainly to affirm that Judas was excluded by the Lord from communion in so great a sacrament because he was unworthy, and therefore could not drink Christ’s blood in the mystery because he was not going to drink it in the kingdom. For he says:

> “After these things Judas the traitor is identified; without him the Passover is celebrated, the cup having been received and the bread broken. For he was not worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments, because he was unworthy of eternal life. For he is understood to have departed immediately, since he is shown to have returned with the crowds. Nor indeed could he drink with him in the mystery who was not going to drink in the kingdom, when he then promised that all who drank of this fruit of the vine would afterward drink it with him.”

If, therefore, we show that Augustine thus removed the wicked from the sacrament both truly and not truly, and that Hilary thus excluded Judas himself from communion, without contradicting either themselves or other saints, it will be evident, God willing, that the wicked receive Christ’s body truly with respect to substance, but not truly with respect to grace. First, then, let blessed Hilary’s words be explained in harmony with the other saints.

For he says that the Passover—that is, the passage into life—was celebrated without Judas, because Judas was not its spiritual participant. Thus he added: “For he was not worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments, because he was unworthy of eternal life.” He confirms this from the inclination of Judas’s deed, because he went out to destruction immediately after the morsel. That he did not say this according to bodily and temporal communion, but according to spiritual [Col. 0799D] and eternal communion, in which only the good share, he shows when he adds: “Nor indeed could he drink with him in the mystery who was not going to drink in the kingdom.” For how could he have been unable bodily to drink the bodily sacrament with him, when he had not yet been removed from the apostolic order and Christ’s fellowship? The Apostle testifies, and with the other saints we see daily, that the wicked receive the Lord’s body indiscriminately—not unto salvation, but unto judgment. Unless, then, that impossibility of receiving the Lord’s body spiritually is attributed to Judas, while other wicked persons can and customarily do receive it bodily, it does not seem consistent that he alone could not do what the others can do.

Since, therefore, it has been acceptably explained that Judas was spiritually absent, as unworthy, from the consecration of Christ’s body, let us see whether, according to the testimony of other saints, he was bodily present and received the sacrament from the Lord himself.

Pope Leo says in his sermon *On the Passion of the Lord* (ch. 3, col. 220), which begins, “I know indeed, dearly beloved”:

> “While the disciples reclined to eat the mystical supper, and it was being planned in Caiaphas’s courtyard how Christ might be killed, he who was instituting the sacrament of his body and blood taught what sort of victim ought to be offered to God. Nor was even the traitor removed from this mystery, so that it might be shown that he was not exasperated by any injury, though the voluntary impiety was foreknown to him.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Why, unhappy Judas, do you not avail yourself of such kindness? Neither the honor of the apostolic order nor communion [Col. 0800B] in the sacraments is denied you.”

Likewise Augustine, in Sermon 26 on John:

> “Not, as certain careless readers suppose, did Judas then receive Christ’s body. For it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed the sacrament of his body and blood to all of them, among whom Judas himself was, as Saint Luke narrates most clearly; and afterward they came to that point where, according to John’s narrative, the Lord most plainly identifies his traitor by a dipped and offered morsel.”

Therefore, since Leo says that the traitor was not removed from the mystery of Christ’s body and that communion in the sacraments was not denied him; and since Augustine likewise affirms, on the testimony of Luke the Evangelist, that Judas himself was present when the Lord had distributed the sacrament of his body and blood to all [Col. 0800C] the disciples, we must see how Judas and other wicked persons are understood both to receive and not to receive Christ’s body, lest such great Fathers—in whom there was one spirit, not of discord but of peace—appear to disagree with one another.

Augustine himself, discussing this question in his sermon *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, says (Sermon 71, no. 17, vol. V, col. 391):

> “How shall we understand also what he says: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ [John 6:57]?
