Shall we be able to understand this also of those of whom the Apostle says that they eat and drink judgment upon themselves, although they eat that very flesh and drink that very blood? Did Judas, seller and betrayer of his Master, although he ate and drank with the other disciples the sacrament of his flesh and blood made by the Master’s own hands, as Luke the Evangelist more plainly declares, remain in Christ, and Christ in him? But surely there is a certain manner of eating Christ’s flesh and drinking his blood, in which manner whoever eats and drinks remains in Christ, and Christ in him.”

Again, the same author in a sermon *On the Words of the Gospel*:

> “What is it to eat Christ? It is not merely to receive his body in the sacrament. For many receive unworthily, of whom the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats and drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ [1 Cor. 11:29]. But how must Christ be eaten? As he himself says: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ If he remains in me and I in him, then he eats and drinks. But one who does not remain in me and in whom I do not remain, even if he receives the sacrament, gains a great torment.”

This is not said as though Christ were separated from his sacrament, with respect to the reality of his substance, because of the wickedness of someone receiving it, but with respect to the effect of his grace. For when he gives his body in the sacrament so that, by perfect unity, a person may be incorporated into his body and remain in him as in his head, and he in that person as in his member, so clean a head cannot be united to a foul and rotten member.

For Augustine says in Sermon 26 on John (place cited):

> “He who eats me, he too shall live because of me. Participation in the Son through the unity of his body and blood, which that eating and drinking signify, makes us better. Therefore we live because of him, eating him—that is, receiving him as eternal life, which we did not have from ourselves.”

Although this signification of unity is not fulfilled in the wicked, so that they are made better and live because of God, what they receive is nevertheless no less substantially and truly his body. Hence Augustine says in Book V *On Baptism* (ch. 8, vol. IX, col. 146):

> “Just as Judas, to whom the Lord gave the morsel, made room for the devil within himself not by receiving something evil, but by receiving something good evilly, so every person who receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not make it the case that, because he himself is evil, it is evil, or that, because he does not receive it unto salvation, he has received nothing. For the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood were nevertheless present even for those of whom the Apostle said: ‘Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’”

Since, therefore, it has been sufficiently established above that even the wicked can eat Christ’s body in the truth of its substance, while only the good can eat it in the truth of spiritual grace; and since it has also been said above that bodily sacraments are, as it were, certain words, let us see whether there is some likeness in words also, by which this matter may be made clear through the sacraments.

For just as a word is a sound signifying and containing an understanding, so a sacrament is the species of bread signifying and containing Christ. And just as a word is heard and understood by some, and is thus received in every way, while by others it is heard but not understood—and then it is received outwardly by the ear with respect to sound, but not inwardly by the heart with respect to understanding—yet it contains understanding no less when it is not understood than it has sound when it is not heard; so the unbelieving or unworthy person receives the sacrament outwardly by the mouth under the species of bread, but does not receive Christ’s body inwardly by the heart in the truth of unity and conformity. Nevertheless, the sacrament is no less Christ’s body in the truth of its substance, in which it is received even by the wicked, than when it is received in every way by the good, both in the truth of substance and in the truth of spiritual grace.

Hence Augustine says also on Psalm 54 (*Tractate 27 on John*, no. 6, col. 504):

> “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life. You have understood them spiritually: they are spirit and life. You have understood them carnally: even so they are spirit and life, but they are not so for you. Understand spiritually the things I have spoken.”

Therefore, just as words understood spiritually and words not understood are always spirit and life, so Christ’s body, received spiritually or not spiritually, is no less so in the truth of substance, although it is not so for you, whoever you are that receive unworthily, in the truth of grace. For in a certain manner you perceive Christ’s body by bodily taste, but you do not taste it by spiritual affection. And insofar as you do not perceive the savor of its sweetness and pleasantness, Christ’s body is not yours; yet insofar as you presume outwardly to receive it, it is no less Christ’s body—just as a word is not a word to one who hears but does not understand, but only a sound, and yet it is no less a word.

Since, then, the saints testify that the wicked truly receive Christ’s body, and that Judas himself received it from Christ the high priest with the other apostles, it also seems established that it does us no harm if wicked persons wickedly receive the sacraments from us or together with us. Judas received them from Christ himself with the other apostles. Nor are the sacraments themselves consecrated any less truly by wicked persons, since the traitor himself, receiving the ministry of so great an office from the supreme pontiff with the others, heard: “Do this in remembrance of me.” For if, as had been commanded him by the Lord, [Col. 0802C] Judas had consecrated the Lord’s body, would it truly have been made any less by that wicked man than by any good person?

Because Judas had not been accused and condemned, Christ was unwilling to condemn his perverse conscience, though known to himself, in order to instruct us that the depravity of certain persons can in no way harm the good, whether by association, by consecration of the sacraments, or by sharing in them. Hence Augustine says in the book [Note: [Col. 0801D] “Sermon.”] *On the Body of the Lord*:

> “Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery of Christ’s body, nothing greater is accomplished by a good priest, nothing less by an evil priest, because it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator and by the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it were by the priest’s merit, it would not belong to [Col. 0802D] Christ at all.”

Again Augustine, *To Parmenian*, Book II (ch. 10, vol. IX, col. 37):

> “In all questions we admonish that it must be understood that, although all sacraments harm those who handle them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons.”

Again Augustine, *Against the Donatists*:

> “Communion with wicked persons does not stain anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds.”

Again, the same author in his homilies:

> “That you may endure even one whom you know to be evil, attend to the Apostle saying: ‘Each one shall bear his own burden’ [Gal. 6:5]. For you do not share with him in avarice, but in Christ’s table. And what harm is it if you share Christ’s table with him? ‘He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’: upon himself, he says, not upon you.”

Therefore, as Leo says, the Lord neither denied Judas the honor of the apostolic order in consecrating the sacraments nor communion in receiving them. He made great provision for his Church, showing by this [Note: [Col. 0803D] “Otherwise, this.”] alone that the preeminence or companionship of wicked persons would be harmless to it. Unless in this point the cause of so great a schism had been cut off, many would, more proudly than religiously, drive away even with kicks those whom they saw among themselves to be of lesser estimation.

Hence Augustine says in Sermon 49 on John (no. 10, col. 632):

> “What did the Lord intend to admonish his Church, when he willed to have one lost person among the twelve, except that we should tolerate wicked persons lest we divide Christ’s body? [Col. 0803B] Behold Judas among the saints; behold a thief and a sacrilegious man. Such a one approached the Lord’s supper with the disciples; he could associate with them, but could not defile them.”

## CHAPTER XXII. How Christ’s body may be received truly and beneficially

We have shown that the wicked receive the sacraments wickedly, but nevertheless truly. Let us now see how the good may receive them not only truly, but beneficially.

Pope Clement says in his letter:

> “In receiving the Lord’s body and blood, great discernment must be employed. For care must be taken lest, if it is delayed too long, it result in the destruction of the soul, the Lord saying: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son [Col. 0803C] of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.’ But if a person receives indiscriminately, that saying of the Apostle must be feared: ‘He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’ Therefore, according to the words of that same Apostle, ‘Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup’ [1 Cor. 11:28], so that, cleansing body and soul from the works of the flesh, he may prepare himself to receive so great a sacrament.”

Again blessed Hilary [Note: [Col. 0803D] Hilary, pope, in Gratian, *On Consecration*, dist. II, canon 15, p. 455; [Col. 0804D]]:

> “If a person’s sins are not such that he must be excommunicated, he ought not withdraw himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body. Therefore it must be feared lest, if long separated from Christ’s body, he remain estranged from salvation. Let one who has ceased to sin not cease to communicate.”

Again Ambrose (*On the Sacraments*, Book IV, ch. 6, vol. II, col. 372):

> “If Christ’s blood is poured out for the remission of sins whenever it is poured out, then I, who sin continually, ought continually to receive it; I ought continually to have the medicine.”

Again blessed Cyprian (*On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 209, ed. 1726):

> “We receive the Eucharist daily as the food of salvation.”

Distinguishing this, Augustine writes to Januarius (Letter 54, ch. 3, vol. II, col. 125):

> “One person may say that the Eucharist should not be received daily; another may affirm that it should be received daily. Let each do what he piously believes should be done according to his faith. For Zacchaeus and that centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either set himself above the other, when one joyfully received the Lord into his house and the other said: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’ [Matt. 8:8; Luke 19:6]. Both honoring the Savior, though not in one manner; both miserable because of sins; both having obtained mercy.”

Again elsewhere:

> “I neither praise nor blame receiving Eucharistic communion daily; nevertheless, I urge and exhort communion on every Lord’s Day, provided the mind is without an intention to sin. For one who still has a will to sin is, I say, made heavier rather than purified by receiving the Eucharist. Therefore, although a person is wounded by sin, let him not have the will to sin henceforth; and when about to communicate, let him make satisfaction by tears and prayers; trusting in the Lord’s mercy, let him approach the Eucharist fearless and secure. But I say this concerning one who is not burdened by mortal sins.”

By these words of the saints, a great necessity of acting well is enjoined upon us, lest by receiving the Lord’s body unworthily we receive judgment, or by ceasing to receive it we likewise, being thus alienated from life, incur the danger of death. For the Lamb must necessarily be received, so that we may be protected from the destroying angel. But if there is danger in receiving or not receiving so great a medicine, how shall we escape?

Yet lest human weakness, hemmed in by these straits, despair, Augustine leaves to each person’s own discernment the choice of receiving or not receiving; although it is certain that to withdraw from so great a medicine, either through obstinacy in sin or through neglect of the sacrament itself, is a great loss to salvation. For it is not without a great privilege of grace that God deigns to use even the human body and heart as his lodging; and not merely to lodge there, as in his temple, but to incorporate that person into himself as a member to his head. For what can be lacking to our salvation when he who is the salvation of all is united to us?

Therefore God’s invincible grace must not be despaired of, however much we consider the enemy’s deceit or our own frailty. For we make God’s grace narrower through the enemy’s deceit or through our own fault if we believe the enemy more powerful to harm than God to deliver, and ourselves more able to fall than he to establish us. What else does the Apostle mean when he says, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” [Rom. 5:20], except that grace is more powerful to save than sin [Note: [Col. 0804D] “Otherwise: to destroy.”] is to destroy? Therefore the necessity of doing good need not be feared by those in whom there is, in God, such power for that very necessity that whatever good we wish, we may accomplish through him who can do all things.

Hence blessed Hilary, condescending to beginners and the imperfect lest anyone distrust God’s grace, gave the counsel that one who has ceased to sin should not cease to communicate. Yet authority forbids those who remain in the intention of sin, or have not worthily repented of grave sins, or are known to those ministers who are outside the Church, to receive.

Since, therefore, Christ’s body must be received with great hope and also great discernment, and since enough has been said above concerning the perfect—that they are Christ’s body and receive his body, because Christ remains in them and they in him—let us see how the imperfect, who wish to become Christ’s body and receive it, may do this fittingly.

Therefore, that those who sin criminally may observe their decrees: just as a lamb was given to the Israelites in Egypt (Exod. 12:3), but to those who were immediately going to depart from it, so likewise the Lamb of God must be given to sinners, that they may be protected from the destroying angel, but to those who will thereafter renounce sins.

Since we have drawn our analogy from the very figure of the Lamb, let us likewise take from it the discernment required for receiving. The lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house, and nothing of it is to be carried out. For since outside the Church there is no place for the true sacrifice, however excellent someone may be in morals, no one rightly gives or receives the Lamb unless he is Catholic—that is, preserving the Church’s unity both in faith, so as not to be a heretic, and in obedience, so as not to be a schismatic.

Hence Jerome on Isaiah (*Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, Book III, ch. 6, vol. VII, col. 679):

> “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed [1 Cor. 5:7]; he is eaten not outside but within, and in one house.”

We are commanded to eat the lamb with our loins girded, our feet shod, holding staffs, and in haste with wild lettuces: so that, girded with chastity; securing the steps of our deeds by the examples of the holy Fathers, lest we be bitten by serpents on the way of this age; chastising the intemperance of the flesh by the rod of discipline; we may eat the lamb with wild lettuces—that is, full of bitter compunction—while hastening with the fervor of desire toward our homeland.

For it is *phase*, that is, the Lord’s passage, by which he passed from this world to the Father. Whoever is slow through idleness and lingers beside the flesh-pots in the Egypt of this world cannot pass over with him so as to arrive where Christ sits at God’s right hand. But, as has been said, he unites himself to us in the sacrament so that what is impossible for us may become possible in him.

Accordingly, lest what he gave should appear empty [Col. 0805D] and frivolous, he gave the sacrament of his body and blood neither before nor afterward but at the very hour of his passion and passage: so that, in that from which he gave an example, he might also give the beginning of the mystery; that he might imprint more closely upon our memory the mark of his passion, appoint more securely to our hope the pledge of his passage and our provision for the way, giving it, as the first of all things, at the end of his temporal life, under the institution of the New Testament.

For by the testament of his blood, redemption and remission of sins having been given, he annulled the compact which we had with death; he made with us a covenant of eternal life; and he left the sacrament of so great a testament in common to all, in order to bind the holy Church to himself. Thus, from that of which we have a taste on the way, we may seek satiety in [Col. 0806A] the homeland, and find him through himself when he appears in the manifestation of his glory. For when we have received Christ’s body and have become his body, he will pass in us to the Father, and we shall pass in him; so that, having become one with him in the labor of so great a passage, we may always be one in the joy of arrival.

It must be understood, moreover, that the Lord’s body is to be received not only spiritually but also bodily, because the blood that protected from the destroying angel was sprinkled on both doorposts. This signified that the true Lamb must be received no less by the mouth of the body than by the mouth of the heart; for he who came to redeem both body and soul willed to communicate himself to both in his sacrament, so that while the soul believed what the body tasted, one hope of salvation might arise equally for both in Christ.

But we must consider why, when the law gave, for eating the Lamb, the footwear as a safeguard lest we be deceived by vices; the staff as discipline by which to correct deeds already committed; the lettuces as compunction, so that we may repent not only outwardly but inwardly; and haste as the ardor of desire by which we may yearn for heavenly things—it commanded abstinence from lust more expressly by girded loins, whereas it named none of the other vices individually, but figuratively represented the safeguard or discipline common to them all.

It must therefore be understood that the lustful and incestuous receive the spotless Lamb of God, who is the Virgin’s Son, more dangerously. For since in Christ’s sacrament we ought to be united to him through conformity in suffering and purity, nothing so opposes the passion of the cross as pleasure; nothing so opposes purity as foulness; nothing so opposes union with him as union in a fornicator’s fellowship.

For lust entices and inflames by its appetite; it defiles and weakens by its act; it renders slippery and ensnares by its use. Thus, while displeasing by pleasing and pleasing by displeasing, it admits difficult or no repentance for itself; and unless aid is given by the strong hand of God’s mercy, it destroys its lovers by its miserable end without end.

For, passing over that which is abominable and unspeakable outside nature, and detestable within nature in incest and adultery, or deadly in fornication and sexual defilement, even that which is lawful within marriages, although it does not take away life, so diminishes the crown that, while virginity receives the hundredfold fruit, widowhood the sixtyfold, and marital union the last and thirtyfold fruit. If, therefore, it humbles so greatly where indulgence heals what is not expedient, how much harm does that do over which the judgment of divine indignation hangs?

For this plague, the more familiar to nature it is than other vices, the more difficult it is to avoid. When repelled, it importunately intrudes upon the unwilling; when admitted, it presses upon the willing with a gently burdensome weight; and while it thus gradually pours in its love, it wholly uproots the love of heavenly things.

But what, on the other hand, must be done that we may not perish? Since life is reached only by a narrow and difficult way, yet—with God’s cooperation—not an impossible path, let us enter the way, so that, because we do not advance in merely human life, [Col. 0807A] we may lead an angelic life on earth. Thus, conforming through the purity of chastity, in heart and body, to Christ’s purity, we may not be refreshed unworthily with heavenly nourishment. Let us be heavenly in hope and manner of life, because the bread of angels is the provision only of an angelic life.

Hence, when the wicked presume to communicate, they are made weak, and many sleep, through food incompatible with wickedness, as the Apostle says, because they do not discern the Lord’s body (1 Cor. 11:30): [Col. 0808A] so that either they may be corrected by God’s mercy through the affliction of bodily sickness, or by the sleep of bodily death lose temporal and eternal life. Advising how to avoid this danger, the Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup” (1 Cor. 11:28), because one who desires to become a participant in so great a communion ought truly to weigh carefully what his conduct is, or at least what his intention is.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0807]

## CHAPTER ONE. That the sacrament of Christ’s body is in no way dissolved by digestion or any foul corruption

[Col. 0807B]

Since in the preceding little book, by the inspiration of his grace, we have explained somewhat concerning the truth and power of Christ’s body, let us consider, insofar as God grants it, certain questions concerning the sacrament itself. We said above that the Lord’s body must be received no less by the mouth of the body than by the mouth of the heart. But from this visible and bodily eating, which occurs merely sacramentally, arises the most foul heresy of the stercoranists.

For they say that the sacrament itself is subject, just as to bodily eating, so also to evacuation. They seek to establish this by many arguments, including Christ’s own testimony, when he says in the Gospel: “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the belly and is cast out into the privy” (Matt. 15:11). Yet it is clear that he said this not about spiritual food but about common and carnal food.

It would therefore be dangerous to answer these obscene heretics about this matter, and more fitting to stop our ears, unless it were more dangerous for them to set such things forth to the scandal of the Church and for us not to strike down their great falsehood by any arguments of the Catholic faith.

Against them we first set that saying of blessed Hilary (*On the Trinity*, Book VIII, no. 14, vol. II, col. 223), by which he warns that matters concerning God must not be discussed according to human or worldly judgment. Then comes that pronouncement of Wisdom itself: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not investigate things stronger than yourself; but always think upon what God has commanded, and do not be curious about his many works” (Ecclus. 3:22).

For in what manner bread becomes flesh, wine is changed into Christ’s blood, the nature of either essence being altered, or whether they pass into evacuation after the manner of common foods—these things the righteous person who lives by faith does not seek to investigate or comprehend by reason. Hence Gregory says in his Paschal Homily (*Homily 22 on the Gospels*, no. 8, vol. I, col. 1535): “What remains from the Lamb we burn with fire: whenever we cannot understand something concerning the mystery of his Incarnation, we humbly reserve it to the power of the Holy Spirit.”

For we know that this sacrament must be separated from common foods with every reverence. [Col. 0808A] [Col. 0808B] For, as the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily, not discerning the Lord’s body”—that is, not distinguishing it from other foods—and so forth. Although it is sent by the mouth into the stomach in a similar manner with respect to eating, far be it that so great a sacrament should be believed subject to evacuation. If in it such an order of nature were completed, the mystery of faith would be degraded by excessive indignity.

For if, as Eusebius says, this victim must be valued by faith, not by appearance, nor judged by outward sight, since the substance of this victim is believed to be Christ, why is it judged liable to the indignity of evacuation on account of the appearance of bread under which it is hidden, when it must not be judged by outward appearance or sight? This is contrary not only to faith but also to reason grounded in nature.

For in those appearances of bread and [Col. 0808C] wine there is either no substance except that of Christ’s body, or our faith is futile. For when the substance of bread and wine has been changed into Christ’s body and blood, in becoming what it was not, it ceases to be what it had been. If, therefore, the substance of bread is not there, what can be [Note: [Col. 0807D] “Otherwise: be defiled.”] befouled and corrupted unto evacuation? For Christ’s substance, which is truly there and into which the substance of bread and wine has been changed, must in no way be believed corruptible, because it is incorruptible.

Hence Ambrose says: “Christ’s body is free from every corruption; whoever religiously tastes it cannot experience corruption.” And rightly so. What glory of incorruption would he bestow upon us if he himself suffered so great an ignominy of corruption? And he who, although he seemed to owe this to the laws of death, could not see corruption in the tomb—how can he be believed to be corrupted in a human stomach?

The bodily foods offered to angels for eating, which are recorded as having been wholly consumed through divine power, escaped the evacuation due to their nature; and shall spiritual food, which gives eternal life to the world, incur an evacuation due to its nature—an obligation unworthy of majesty and altogether contrary to power?

Hence Ambrose says in the book *On the Sacraments* (*On the Initiation into the Mysteries*, ch. 9, vol. II, col. 341): “Christ feeds his Church with these sacraments, by which he strengthens the substance of the soul.” And shortly afterward: [Col. 0809A] “The Holy Spirit has expressed through the Prophet what we eat and drink, saying: ‘Taste and see that the Lord is sweet’ [Ps. 33:9]. In that sacrament Christ is present, because it is Christ’s body. Therefore it is not bodily food, but spiritual.”

If, then, it is spiritual and not bodily food, how is it subject to bodily evacuation? For spiritual food is shared by us with angels, because “man ate the bread of angels”; carnal food is shared by us with beasts. Bestial food undergoes the failure of digestion; angelic food preserves the glory of incorruption.

But it should be noted that the food which Ambrose declares not bodily, Augustine calls bodily. To prevent disagreement between them, it must be understood that Augustine calls it bodily because it is bodily received merely sacramentally; Ambrose denies that it is bodily because, being substantially spiritual, it nourishes not the body but the soul. Since, therefore, Augustine calls this food bodily according to the species of the sacrament, let us see how bodily evacuation cannot occur even in those sacramental species.

In every substance, the qualities of forms, colors, and flavors are grounded; when any alteration supervenes, they do not remain in it, and their being thus changed does not occur through the corruption of an excretion, but solely through the failure involved in their own alteration. For example, when whiteness is changed into blackness, does it suffer the digestion of some excretion through its failure? So too, if any deterioration is observed in the forms and qualities [Col. 0809C] of Christ’s body and blood, it must not be degraded as far as excretion; for since they perish without filth from the bodies in which they naturally inhere, how could those which, after their substances have failed, are wondrously preserved in Christ’s sacrament, incur through their own failure the indignity of an excretion contrary to their nature? Moreover, since Augustine says against Maximinus, concerning the other sacramental appearances—namely the dove and the fire in which the Holy Spirit appeared—that those bodily appearances, once their office of signification had been completed, passed away and ceased further to exist, nothing more unworthy ought to be thought of these bodily appearances which cover Christ’s body. For the office [Col. 0809D] of this visible sacrament is, by bodily eating and drinking, to show that Christ is incorporated into his Church. What thereafter becomes of it, if the foregoing arguments do not seem sufficient, should faithfully and honestly be entrusted to God, whose it is. For it is better humbly to entrust to God what we cannot know than perversely to invent and maintain against him what we nevertheless do not know.

But the dialecticians ask: since the substance of bread, having been converted into Christ’s body, is now no longer bread, on what foundation do the qualities remain, so that the color and flavor belonging to what had been bread may be grounded and exist, when the substance of the sacrament itself—that is, Christ’s body—[Col. 0810A] is neither colored with bread’s color nor savory with bread’s flavor? The answer is that, as God is wonderful in all things, so he is in these also. For in his sacrament he causes accidental qualities to exist by themselves, which is impossible in other cases. But he who gave fertility to a virgin without seed—what wonder if he causes qualities to exist without the foundation of a substance? Therefore, since in so great a sacrament there is no substance of bread and wine capable of corruption, but only the form of bread and wine with their qualities—which can indeed fail, but cannot thus be defiled [Note: [Col. 0809D] Elsewhere: “be purified.”]—and beneath which Christ’s body is believed to be hidden, an incorruptible substance, you should not suspect excrement where there is no nature of such foulness, but only the miracle of divine [Col. 0810B] power.

Therefore the ravings of the Greek heretics, who are rightly called Stercoranists (“Excrementarians”), are not to be heeded. They say that participation in Christ’s body and blood breaks ecclesiastical fasts even to the point of gluttony, drunkenness, and distension of the belly; they suppose that heavenly food is received indiscriminately like earthly food and emitted into the filthy excretion of the belly. But let it be far from the hearts of believers that they should think a fast broken, on days of fasting, at whatever hour Mass is celebrated; for since this food is not bodily but spiritual, bodily abstinence is not broken by it.

Nor should one observe what is decreed in certain apocryphal writings: namely, that ordinary [Col. 0810C] food should not be taken until the received sacraments have been digested by themselves, lest they be corrupted by mixture with other food. For the Lord would not have given his disciples the sacraments of his body at supper after the eating of the Paschal lamb, if he had seen that his sacraments incurred corruption from the admixture of ordinary foods—although the Church does not decree that this be imitated in him, for certain reasons, but for entirely different ones. For it was fitting that he, the mediator of God and men, the end of the law and beginning of grace, after eating the Paschal lamb, after the completion of the old law, should institute at evening the new testament of grace by a new sacrament, so as to declare that he would do both at the end of the world. It was no less fitting that the Church, to which no such reason for an office [Col. 0810D] belongs—that it should institute truth after shadow—should not imitate such an order in Christ, but should decree, out of reverence for so great a sacrament, that with the body fasting, while sobriety prevails, the ardor of the flesh is quiet, and the mind is more serene for understanding, the inner person should first be refreshed with spiritual food. Thus he who is pre-eminent in us, strengthened by the power of heavenly food, may more easily rule the body subject to him, lest it be relaxed toward superfluous or harmful things. Hence Augustine, in his letter to Januarius (54, no. 8, vol. II, col. 126): “It pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the Christian’s mouth before other foods.” Nor, because the Lord gave food first, [Col. 0811A] should the brethren therefore come, after breakfast or supper, to receive that sacrament, or—as those whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects used to do—mix these things with their own meals. Yet if anyone, spiritually refreshed, fasts for some time out of the same reverence for the sacrament, so as to delight in sober joy with Christ his guest, that is good; although, with every suspicion of excrement removed, it is permitted, if necessary, to give it to those in danger of death both before food and after food.

But the heretics object: if many loaves and much wine are consecrated, a person can live from them for a long time, so that they maintain that in the meantime he has an excretion, not from past food, but from this present and prolonged nourishment. They also say that some have experienced this over long periods, desiring even in this life to be nourished with angelic food; and, lest they should seem to have had an excretion through the failure of their own flesh, as normally happens in illnesses, they maintain that such persons were sustained and fattened in their flesh by these foods as by ordinary foods, so that, when the failure of the flesh is denied, it may be proved that the excretion was from sacred communion.

But, God permitting, the heretics will not prevail even thus. For it must indeed be believed that the heavenly food which confers eternal life can confer temporal life upon those whom it pleases; but if one who produces an excretion in the sick through the failure of his flesh is not believed to discharge indigestion, cannot that same person produce an excretion from the flesh itself—though it does not fail—in one who is healthy? The jar of the widow of Zarephath was being used up and yet was not diminished; and what wonder [Col. 0811C] if, through the power of so great a food, the flesh of one who eats should be sustained, grow, and digest, yet not fail? Five barley loaves, after five thousand persons had been satisfied, increased until twelve baskets were filled; and since, at God’s command, they received increase while being consumed, what wonder if, by the will of the same God, human flesh suffers no failure in its digestion? We read indeed of certain holy Fathers, taking no other food, who lived for many years refreshed only by the Lord’s communion on Sundays; just as Elijah fasted forty days in the strength of the food ministered by an angel (3 Kings 19). But by whose power, except his who “did all that he willed in heaven and on earth”? He who made all things from nothing, just as he can nourish flesh without fleshly food, can also give it excretion without fleshly failure.

Yet again the heretics object, to the indignity of so great a sacrament, that bread and wine in the sacrament become moldy or rotten; that the bread is gnawed by mice and found in their bellies; and that it is even burned by fires.

But because, as Augustine says, sacraments are so called because one thing is seen in them and another understood, what occurs in them is likewise seen in one way and understood in another. For just as, in any body, without detriment to its substance, whiteness is driven away by blackness, or any quality by a contrary quality that supervenes, so in [Col. 0812A] Christ’s sacrament, whatever seems to occur merely in appearance through a change of form or other qualities, whether through the gnawing of mice, the mold of age, or any other means, does not concern the substance of the sacrament, namely Christ, whom we know with complete certainty to remain incorrupt in heaven, whatever may seem to happen in his sacrament on earth. For just as in his own body he appeared now as a gardener, now as a traveler, now as a phantom, according to the faith of those looking at him, while outwardly he endured slaps, spittle, and scourges, so also, until the end of the age, he will permit such things to occur in his sacrament for the testing of believers and the scandal of unbelievers: that the elect may be exercised and the reprobate hardened. For while Christ is hidden in the sacrament and so obscured by its great [Col. 0812B] indignity, he is nevertheless believed to be no less present there and is worshiped by believers with no less reverence. Faith, thus tested, earns greater things because it thinks of God contrary to what it sees; unbelief, hardened by its greater scandal, is condemned, because there it despises Christ’s substance, which it ought to revere, when it sees no display of his power in repelling the indignity of his sacrament. But if Christ there made himself known either by the manifest evidence of his presence or by miracles displaying his power, what merit would faith have, to which he gave so evident an experience of knowing him?

Such indignity also sometimes occurs in order to punish or correct the negligence of ministers, [Col. 0812C] because they have handled the Lord’s body unworthily, less attentively than they ought, contrary to ecclesiastical rules, or have kept it longer than they should. For was not manna, if kept until the next day, made rotten because the Lord had forbidden it? Yet if it was gathered on the day before the Sabbath and kept until the Sabbath, it remained incorrupt because he had so ordained.

Therefore whatever deformity may occur, merely in appearance, in Christ’s sacrament ought not to wrench from us faith in its truth; because he who, though true God, endured many unworthy things in his body, endures them no less in his sacrament, although he is truly present there. For, as Gregory says in his Dialogue (Homily 39 on the Gospels, vol. I, col. 1651), Christ appeared in the form [Col. 0812D] of a leper to the monk Martyrius; after he had been carried away from Martyrius’s neck and vanished, he said afterward: “Because you were not ashamed of me, O Martyrius, on earth, neither ought I to be ashamed of you in heaven.” Who, then, should be ashamed of any indignities in Christ’s sacrament, when for its worthy reverence he ought to obtain a heavenly reward? The old man Simeon, not attending to the Savior’s seemingly brutish and insensible infancy, to the small and weak form which he held in his arms, or to the person wrapped in poor cloths, recognized and believed the majesty of the Godhead in that tiny body. He called him Lord, professed himself his servant, prayed to be dismissed by him in peace, declared that he had seen God’s salvation, and prophesied that he would be a light for the revelation of all nations and the glory of [Col. 0813A] his people Israel. Therefore, lest true faith be ashamed of any indignities in Christ’s sacrament, it must be known that, just as many things occur in Christ’s sacrament which are not seen, many things are seen to occur in it which are ordered otherwise. Gregory says that at the very hour of the offering the heavens are opened and choirs of angels are present, and so forth; though these things truly occur, they are nevertheless not seen (Dialogues IV, ch. 58, col. 472). The same author also says: “His flesh is divided for the salvation of the people, and his blood is poured out; and it occurs otherwise than it appears, while he himself remains whole and living.” But what is surprising in these things? Christ’s very body appears to be bread, and is not bread. Therefore in that which appears to be what it is not, many things appear to occur which do not occur; just as, because Christ appeared as a leper to Martyrius, was Christ—more beautiful than the sun—really covered with leprosy? In the Lives of the Fathers it is read that a most holy Father saw an angel of the Lord withdraw the Lord’s body from certain persons communicating unworthily and offer coals in its place. Thus one thing appeared to them and another occurred. Likewise, it is read that the martyr Tarsicius, carrying the Lord’s body, was seized by pagans and asked what he was carrying; because he refused to give the holy thing to dogs, he obtained martyrdom. When, after his death, they searched carefully for what he had carried, Christ’s body having been removed by heavenly agency, only the linen cloths . . . in which it had been contained were found. So too many other things must be believed to occur invisibly in this spiritual sacrament through angelic ministry.

Therefore whatever may appear to occur, even monstrously, in Christ’s sacrament merely in appearance [Col. 0813C]—whether for punishing or correcting some persons’ negligence, for testing and instructing faith, or for the scandal and ruin of the faithless—does not nullify faith in Christ. For, since God disposes otherwise, it must in no way be believed to concern an indignity to his body. Nor do we deny mold and decay to the visible sacrament itself any more than to Christ’s body, for the same reason by which we above denied digestion. Since those appearances exist without the substance of bread and wine, it is not readily evident how they could become moldy and rotten any more than they could be digested. Yet we cannot deny failure to the appearances themselves, since they are not eternal; but we say that this failure is so simple that it admits no corruption involving foulness. They may, however, appear moldy and rotten although they are not so, just as Christ appeared as a gardener or traveler according to the minds of those who saw him; but through this vision wrath is exercised against those to whom it occurs, so that the foregoing purposes may be fulfilled in them.

As for the claim that they distend the belly or intoxicate, we do not grant that this belongs to them either; but when they appear [Note: [Col. 0813D] Elsewhere: “thus.”] to do these things, we believe this occurs for the same reasons mentioned above. If an appearance of this kind is found in the vomit of drunkards or sick persons, or if something else is displayed even in the bellies of beasts, what else is shown except that it disdained, as was fitting, to remain with drunkards or impenitent sick persons; [Col. 0814A] or that it showed those by whom it ought to have been preserved and received to be worse than beasts? For, apart from sin, all things are clean to the Creator, who is everywhere; how, then, can it seem more unclean to be in a mouse’s belly than in that of an impenitent adulterer?

As for the claim that the sacramental appearances themselves are entrusted to fire by religious persons and disappear there, this does not occur to Christ’s indignity, as though he were handed over to be burned by flames—which is impossible, since he is God of all the elements. Rather, whenever some such indignity has carelessly befallen the sacrament itself, so that the sensible appearances themselves, which God in his highest counsel willed to remain there after the change of their substance, inspire horror at receiving them, they are consigned to flames in order to show what belongs to them: failing [Col. 0814B] and disappearing without any foulness in that most pure element of fire.

Accordingly, just as it must be received with the highest reverence, so it must also be kept with the highest care; for a thing of such dignity and such salvation ought not to be subject to negligence or forgetfulness. Rather, what is accomplished by God’s great grace ought fittingly and necessarily to be honored, above all things, with the Church’s great care, devoutly and without ceasing.

## CHAPTER II. Why a visible sacrifice is offered to the invisible God

The question is raised: since the Church’s sacrifice consists in a visible appearance of elements, why did God will it to be visible, since he himself is invisible and said that the Father ought to be worshiped in spirit and truth by true worshipers [Col. 0814C] (John 4:24), while the Psalmist declared that a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God (Psalm 50:19)? But it must be understood that in the visible sacrament he willed the presence of his invisible body to be presented to us, in order thereby to stir our memory more strongly to recall the grace of such great mercy. For just as, though he could do all things, he willed our temporal life to be sustained not by ourselves but by external provisions, lest we seem to owe our existence to ourselves rather than to him from whom come the gifts by which we live, so also by his visible sacrament, through which we receive the pledge of eternal life, he willed us to be reminded that we must ascribe to his grace the fact that we receive eternal life from him—a life which we did not possess in ourselves, indeed which we had lost through ourselves. Therefore, as the Apostle testifies, his invisible things, [Col. 0814D] understood through the things made, are perceived from the creation of the world (Romans 1:20); so he willed his sacrament to be a sign of his invisible presence, so that by making our understanding more certain of his grace, he might make our affection toward him more fervent. And lest it be thought that, because he is invisible, the sacrifices of visible sacraments are unsuitable to him, Augustine says in Book X of *The City of God* (ch. 19, vol. VII, col. 235): “Those who think that these visible sacrifices are fitting for other gods, but that invisible sacrifices are fitting for the invisible God, greater sacrifices for the greater, and better sacrifices for the better—such as the offices of a pure mind and good will—certainly do not know that these things are signs of those things in the same way as spoken words are signs of things.” Accordingly, just as when praying and praising we direct to God meaningful words, while offering in our heart the things themselves which those words signify, so when sacrificing we should know that visible sacrifice is to be offered to no other than him whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts. For it must be understood that we, who are not only spirits but also bodies, ought also to offer bodily sacrifices, so that, since we consist of both, and lest either remain idle, we may serve God through both body and spirit.

## CHAPTER III. Why the Church’s sacrifice does not consist in the sacrament alone, or in Christ’s body and blood without the sacrament, and why it consists in both

[Col. 0815B]

The question is raised, then, why the Church’s sacrifice does not consist in the sacrament alone, or solely in Christ’s body and blood without the sacrament, or why it consists in both.

The answer is this: if it consisted in the sacrament alone—that is, consecrated but unchanged bread and wine—there would be no reason why the sacrifice of the New Testament should be set above the Old Testament. For just as the latter was only a shadow and figure of things to come, so the former would only be a commemoration of things past. Since Christ said, “Do this in remembrance of me,” what would it do except represent and recall Christ’s past passion? Let us therefore compare the new shadow with the old ones, the simple with the simple, so that we may see in what respects the former surpass them, both bodily [Col. 0815C] and spiritually.

For if the present sacrament is only a sacrament, it is bodily food, as the former was. Was not the manna which God rained from heaven, containing in itself every delight of flavor, worthier and better? Likewise the loaves of presentation, fine flour offerings, calves, and the other things that people sacrificed—were they not better for refreshment than a small amount of bread and wine, scarcely enough to taste? For in the new sacrament, if faith in inward grace is removed, the external appearance in a crumb of bread or drop of wine has no value; indeed, its outward elements were made of no value precisely so that the fullness of all devotion might be bestowed upon the grace believed to be within. For the venerable diligence of so many persons standing by, ministering to, or worshiping this sacrament would appear vain unless the sacrament itself were believed to possess truth and benefit far greater than it appears to have. Therefore, since those outward things are almost nothing, though such offices of reverence are bestowed upon them, either we are senseless or we are directed to profound mysteries of great salvation.

Nor does the new surpass the old in sacramental office. Since it is merely a memorial and figure of Christ’s passion, the new is so much more unworthy in proclaiming past things—something belonging to the memory of any human being—as the old is better and more divine in foretelling the same things to come, something belonging only to divine prophecy. For if we say that the bread is not truly Christ’s flesh but only shadowingly a memorial of his crucified flesh, will not the new sacrament, like the old, be merely a shadow and figure? Indeed it would be inferior, because the old was spiritually a shadow of future things, while the new would be bodily a shadow of past things. Nor would it surpass it in effect, because it would neither remit sins nor open heaven’s gate. For since the old covenant, consisting only in foods and drinks, various washings, and ordinances of the flesh, could not, as the Apostle says, make the worshiper perfect in conscience because it possessed only a shadow of good things to come (Hebrews 10:1), not the very image of the realities, how could the new, similarly a shadow, make the worshiper perfect through remission of sins, growth in virtues, and purity of conscience? Therefore, because the old could not confer in this life perfect grace of merits, it did not, while the gate of paradise remained unopened, confer the perfect reward immediately after this life; it deferred the crown, granting rest from labor to holy souls, but not granting rest with glory as recompense for labor. Since, then, the new does not surpass the old in fullness of the belly, sacramental prophecy, or the effect of spiritual grace, temporal and eternal, how could it profit more than the old? Unless it confers fullness of grace in this life, it will not confer fullness of rest and glory after this life. Therefore, if the new sacrament were neither bodily nor spiritually better than the old, there would be no reason why it should be set above it. What, then, would Christ have conferred more worthily than Moses—the Son in his own house than the servant in another’s? And if he changed shadow for shadow and did not fulfill it, when and by whom would the truth figured and promised by the old sacraments be fulfilled, if he who is the Truth gave not truth but shadow in exchange for shadow? Therefore Truth gave his Church truth: Christ gave his body and blood, so that what the old shadow could not do, he himself might do—namely, the redemption and remission of sins which he had once accomplished on the cross, likewise on the altar daily; and that he might more beneficially meet the daily contagion of sins with a daily remedy. He who would be life and reward for the elect in the future might himself be medicine and provision for the journey in the present. For unless the priest who penetrated the heavens became our way [Col. 0816D] to himself, heaven’s gate would have remained closed to us forever. It was opened to believers after Christ’s passion because he who is priest, having become sacrifice, is united to those dying with him; so that, when they become one with him, they may be in him where he is [Note: [Col. 0815D] Elsewhere: “there.”]. Thus, too, in Christ’s passion, to the great hope of righteous persons and sinners alike, the thief was made righteous and taken with Christ into paradise on that same day, the first before all righteous persons; so that it might be clear not only that paradise’s gate was opened to human beings on that day, but also that God’s grace is not restricted by an instant of time or overcome by the quantity of sins, since scarcely one hour’s repentance after so many crimes sufficed for him immediately to confer the rewards of eternal life. Who, then, could doubt that Christ’s passion is truly a remedy for all sins, when it justified and saved, so late and so swiftly, as if the firstfruits of all sins, the most criminal man?

Blessed Ambrose, considering such a prerogative of grace in Christ’s sacrament, says in his sermon *On the Sacraments to the Neophytes* (*On the Mysteries*, ch. 8, vol. II, col. 337), preferring the new sacraments to the old: “With the utmost care we wish to prove both that the Church’s sacraments are older than those of the Synagogue and that they are more excellent than manna.” And shortly afterward: “It has been proved that the Church’s sacraments are older; now recognize that they are more powerful. Truly it was marvelous that God rained manna upon the fathers; yet all who ate that bread died in the wilderness. But this food which you receive, this living bread which descended from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life and is Christ’s body. Consider now whether the bread of angels or Christ’s flesh is more excellent, for it is surely the body of life. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. That was of heaven; this is of the Lord of heaven. That was subject to corruption; this is free from every corruption. For them water flowed from the rock; for you blood flows from Christ. Water satisfied them for an hour; blood washes you for eternity. The Jew drinks and thirsts; when you drink, you cannot thirst. That was in shadow; this is in truth. If what you marvel at is a shadow, how great is this, whose shadow too you marvel at? You have recognized the greater things. For light is greater than shadow, truth than figure, and the body of the author than manna from heaven.” And shortly afterward: “Receive what I say: the sacraments of Christians are more divine than those of Jews.” Therefore the new sacraments have rightly been set above the old, surpassing them so greatly in truth, dignity, power, and grace that they fulfill everything which had been impossible for them. For as truly as Christ will give himself to the saints for glory in the future, so truly does he now give himself to his Church for every grace, although not so manifestly but under the sacrament. For if he gave his body and blood without the sacramental veil, who would not recoil from receiving them?

For, as Augustine and Jerome say above, for human beings to eat a human being would be a shameful deed or crime, [Col. 0817D] because it is forbidden by divine and human laws. Hence, when the disciples heard that he would give his flesh to be eaten and blood to be drunk, they supposed that he would visibly give himself raw, boiled in water, or roasted on a spit; and they withdrew from him, saying, “This saying is hard.” “Therefore,” as Ambrose says (*On the Sacraments*, VI.1, col. 380), “lest more should say this, as though there were some horror of bloodshed, while the grace of redemption might remain, you receive the sacrament indeed in a likeness, but attain the grace and power of the true nature.”

And to prove that Christ is more beneficially received with the sacrament than without it, let us consider in every way what would follow. We would receive him either living or dead. But it is impossible to receive him dead, since he is immortal: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more” (Romans 6:9). Besides, what life could we hope for from one whom we received dead? Therefore we cannot receive him cut into pieces, boiled, or roasted, as they imagined. But if living, then either in the state in which he was before his passion, or in that in which he was after his resurrection. If in the state before his passion, who could swallow a living and whole man of thirty years? Even if this could occur by the same power through which he passed his whole body through the intact virginity of his mother, faith would have no merit, since such an evident experience of him would furnish proof of his presence. [Col. 0818B] But if in the state in which he is after the resurrection, displaying his glorified body as it is in heaven, he would offer his unbearable brightness to the eyes of observers, and human frailty could not endure it. Hence Augustine, in the book *To Orosius*: “Christ indeed rose with glorified flesh, but he did not wish to appear to the disciples in that glorification (Matthew 17), because their eyes could not look upon such brightness.” If, before he died and rose again, when he was transfigured on the mountain, the disciples could not look upon him, how much less could they look upon the Lord when his flesh had been glorified? But if by his power he adjusted our sight to his brightness, he would take away merit, granting us beforehand the reward of contemplating his glory neither in its proper place nor time; for it would no longer be desirable to labor, as Peter also said at the Transfiguration: “It is good for us to be here; let us make three tents here” (Matthew 17:4). As Leo says, this was not wicked, but disordered. Accordingly, Christ himself, when the sons of Zebedee asked for a seat at his right or left (Matthew 20:20), sent them to labor before rest, saying: “You shall drink my cup,” because he saw that it was more expedient for them to reach rewards more worthily and fruitfully through the order of merits.

Therefore, because it was not expedient in his sacrifice to give either the sacrament by itself or his body by itself, he set above all legal sacraments one sacrament more worthy than them all. By it he concealed his body from us, removing the stated disadvantages of horror or brightness; by the truth of his body, he fulfilled the shadows and figures of the old sacrifices and dismissed them as superfluous; and by the very figure of his sacrament, because it is more than a figure, he surpassed them. For although Augustine says that sacraments differ in signs but are equal in the thing signified, this unique sacrament, because it is both a figure and Christ’s body, is like John, who was a prophet and more than a prophet because he showed what he foretold (Matthew 11:9). Thus this sacrament too is a figure and more than a figure: equal to things signifying together with it insofar as it signifies, but surpassing things that merely signify because it both signifies and is the thing signified. Nor [Col. 0819A] did the gracious Lord merely dismiss the old shadows and figures as superfluous when the novelty and truth of his sacrifice came; by reducing the multiplicity of old sacrifices to the singleness of his sacrifice, he diminished our outward occupation and multiplied for us the grace of his benefits. By his one, unique sacrifice he accomplishes redemption and remission of sins, and through growth in faith and the other virtues brings us to eternal life. For it must be understood that God gave so many sacrifices in the law in order to show that none of them was sufficient. For the others would have been superfluous if one could suffice; thus his one sufficient sacrifice might be desired the more. Meanwhile, even if they perceived a little help in those sacrifices, they were occupied with greater exercise in their multitude, so that they might learn to worship God, depart from the worship of idols, and be instructed by the more certain testimony of so many figures, in order not to doubt that the truth to come was to be hoped for.

Therefore God provided for us in his sacrifice an excellent sacrament, surpassing all others: for good reason he concealed the truth of his body and blood beneath the qualities of bread and wine, lest it be exposed to unbelievers and become cheap through their blasphemies, or lest they judge us inhuman and cruel as eaters of human flesh and drinkers of blood. But for believers, whom he prepared for salvation, he made it fit to receive in the appearance and flavor of bread and wine, lest—as stated above—if one saw the color or tasted the flavor of human flesh and blood, human compassion recoil; [Col. 0819C] lest, if one were struck by its intolerable brightness, one fall into mental stupor; or lest, if one were charmed by its glory, one become dull in the torpor of good works. For just as he removed our bodily occupation by uprooting the multitude of old sacrifices, in order to free the mind for spiritual things, so he did not wish to impede us with any unfamiliar circumstances of his sacrifice, so that he might unite us to himself more spiritually and freely in his sacrament. Therefore, lest the mind be disturbed by an unfamiliar sight, he retained a familiar appearance in his sacrament, so that we might direct the purer gaze of faith toward contemplating inward things. For through reception of this sacrament we ought to be perfectly united and incorporated into Christ: in this life, as far as we can, by conformity of innocence; [Col. 0819D] and after this life, by like blessedness, as far as we are worthy. Nor is it fitting that those who must be gathered back from all things in order to be one with Christ should be stretched out toward externals or scattered among many things.

Yet, although God willed this to be so fruitful for his Church, he did not will it to be altogether effortless. For while in the mystery that which is not is apparent and that which is is hidden, a struggle of faith is presented so that merit may increase. While the believer, contrary to what is seen, believes what is not seen, he obtains a double grace: from the truth believed inwardly and from the outward falsehood overcome. For Christ’s other miracles are signs for unbelievers, so that they may be converted; this alone is given to believers as a means of merit, so that they may be instructed by it. In those things which God did in external matter, faith is strengthened; [Col. 0820A] but in this one thing, which he does from himself, faith is exercised, so that, defeated yet unconquered, it may be crowned more happily—defeated, I say, lest it comprehend; unconquered, lest it distrust. For the external senses, confronted with the appearance, color, smell, and flavor of bread and wine, falsely strive to maintain that it is what it had been, namely bread and wine—which it is not—while the inward understanding, contemplating what it is, namely Christ’s body, though incapable of comprehending it, nevertheless does not cease to believe.

Attentive to and wary of this difficulty of belief, the saints laboured long and earnestly to establish this sacramental consecration. For they saw that it was not merely invisible, but also unfamiliar and wonderful: that the invisible priest invisibly converts visible creatures [Col. 0820B] into the substance of his flesh, and makes heavenly that which is earthly, so that he who works such great things in himself for us may promise us, from ourselves, things yet greater. For he who changes water figuratively offered for us, just as he changes wine offered for himself, into the reality and unity of his blood in his sacrament and ours, will much more make us one with himself in the reward of his eternity. Yet, in the faith of so great a mystery, Augustine, hinting at the struggle between inward understanding and the outward senses, says in his sermon *On the Words of the Lord*: “What you see upon the altar is bread and a cup, as even your eyes report; but what faith, having been instructed, demands is this: the bread is the body, the cup is the blood.”

[Col. 0820C] But such a thought may arise in someone’s mind: We know whence the Lord Jesus Christ received flesh—namely, from the Virgin Mary. He was nourished, grew, was buried, rose again, and ascended into heaven; he lifted his body there, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead. There he now sits at the right hand of the Father. How then is bread his body? Or how is what the cup contains his blood? These, brothers, are called sacraments precisely because in them one thing is seen and another understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit. In this it seems to be implied—as though the question were being asked—since Christ conducted himself reasonably in human form, whether by human nature or divine power, and is to remain bodily in heaven until the day of judgment [Col. 0820D], who has brought Christ’s body down here, or who has lifted our bread up there, so that it can so suddenly be changed into Christ’s body?

Because it is ineffable how Christ’s body is made here and remains there, he recalls those who think such things to spiritual understanding and faith. Though it cannot be known, it can be believed; for what is seen is not the material body of bread, but a bodily appearance; whereas what is understood is Christ, who can do whatsoever he wills in heaven and on earth. Thus, while faith does not yield to the testimony of the outward senses and does not comprehend by inward inquiry, it nevertheless does not waver from the truth. By God’s grace our faith is exercised in such a contest: through exercise it is increased, through increase perfected, and, once perfected, crowned. Hence Augustine [Col. 0821A], in his sixty-eighth sermon on John (no. 3, col. 680): “Faith is that by which the hearts of those who are to see God are cleansed while they are pilgrims. It believes what it does not see. For if you see, it is not faith. Merit is gathered for the believer; reward is rendered to the seer. Therefore let the Lord go; let him go so that he may not be seen; let him be hidden so that he may be believed; let him be desired when believed, so that he may be possessed when desired. Therefore, in this our pilgrimage it is expedient that Christ should be hidden so that he may be believed,” etc.

Christ therefore rightly gave himself to us under a sacrament, so that through it he might increase for us both the merit of faith and the benefit of his grace. In an earthly and altogether lowly form of bread and wine, we do not blush to believe and venerate [Col. 0821B] the majesty of the wisdom of the Word of God, substantially contained yet incomprehensible. By its quantity and quality this form seems so unworthy of his excellence that it ought not to be considered at all—except that he is God, who has done whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth; and except that his flesh itself is that to which all power in heaven and on earth has been given, so that by such power, in the unity of his person, it may be in heaven and on earth whenever and however it pleases him. With this faith we adore the sacrament itself as something divine; we address and entreat it as something living and rational: “Lamb of God, who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us”; because we believe that there is Christ—not what appears, but what truly is.

## Chapter IV. Why faith is so greatly required in this sacrament of Christ’s body

[Col. 0821C]

It is asked why faith is so greatly required in this sacrament. Clearly, because the world perished through false faith when Adam presumed to believe the devil more than God. In the forbidden tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he hoped more to attain the divinity promised by the enemy than to incur the death threatened by God. Therefore, just as the devil, presenting not a shadow in the tree of disobedience but the real and visible fruit itself, promised what was not seen—namely, “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3:5)—so also God, presenting in his visible sacrament not a shadow but him who hung upon the tree of obedience itself, [Col. 0821D] promises eternal life, which is not seen. Thus, since now he is believed more than the enemy in this matter, as is fitting, that faithless faith by which in former times the devil was unjustly believed more than God may be healed by this true faith.

Therefore, as judgment ought not to have been based upon sight or taste in the forbidden tree, so neither ought it be in Christ’s sacrament. For just as the fruit, beautiful to look at and pleasant to eat, seemed life-giving food and brought death, so, conversely, the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood appears to be food belonging to our mortality, although it is truly eternal life. Accordingly, true faith seems necessary as the means between both things: for Adam, that he might believe death to be in the fruit and thus avoid it; for us, that we may believe life to be in Christ’s sacrament and thus attain it. Each [Note: [Col. 0821D] Elsewhere: “both.”] produces an effect contrary to what it appears to sight: the former, while seeming food of pleasure and life, brings death; the latter, while seeming food of mortality, bestows eternal life. Therefore, just as Peter was required to make a threefold confession after his threefold denial, so true faith must be required of a human being if he is to be saved, in place of the faithless faith through which he perished. For so great a sacrament can neither be understood without faith, nor can we be saved through it without faith.

## Chapter V. Why Christ’s body and blood are consecrated in bread, wine, and water rather than in other bodily forms

[Col. 0822B]

It is further asked why Christ’s body is consecrated in bread and wine rather than in other bodily forms, when eternal life does not seem fittingly signified by food belonging to mortality. But it must be understood that in this sacrament Christ did not will to be signified in the manner in which he is related to the Father by nature, but in that in which he is related to us by grace: namely, not as the Father’s wisdom, but as the life of all human beings, so that he might commend his love more strongly to us and more greatly kindle ours toward him.

Although eternal life could not be expressed by any bodily form in a perfect likeness, no form was more fitting than that which is in some manner life, since it serves to nourish and sustain human life. Because [Col. 0822C] our temporal food and drink could not and ought not to be eternal life, Christ willed to signify himself as eternal life by their name and outward form. Thus he would correspond not only to the familiar likeness of food in receiving it, but would also benefit us through that same likeness in our hope: namely, as food and drink are our temporal life as long as God wills, so that heavenly bread is, much more, eternal life for those whom he wills.

And what wonder if the Creator can bestow eternal life upon a creature, when even a creature can preserve that life eternally for a creature? Just as the tree of life was placed in paradise, by which a human being might live eternally in the body, so Christ placed himself, the tree of life, in the Church, so that eternal life might be in those who believe in him [Col. 0822D]. This was not only Christ’s own mystery, but also a great support for our faith. For if it was natural to a non-living creature to preserve life eternally for the body, how much more is it wholly possible for the true and living tree of life, Christ the Creator, to confer eternal life more gloriously and eternally upon body and soul?

Moreover, since we live by food and drink in such a way that we cannot do without either, he willed both to be present in his sacrament, lest, if either were absent, he himself should seem to be signified as not full but imperfect life, through an apparently imperfect sign of life.

It was also fitting that by the same forms through which flesh and blood are naturally nourished and produced in any human being [Col. 0823A], they should be spiritually consecrated also in the man who is the Lord. This was fitting not only because it makes sacramental reception more suitable, but also so that faith might be helped by some evident likeness: for if bread is naturally transformed into the flesh and wine into the blood of any person, how much more, if God wills it, are they transformed omnipotently into his own flesh and blood?

Nor could the unity of his incorporation into us be more fittingly signified by other forms than by those which are more familiarly and truly incorporated into us in common food and drink. Likewise, the mutual unity of the ecclesiastical body is more fittingly signified, because, as bread is gathered from many grains and wine from many grapes, so the Church is gathered from diverse persons. Likewise [Col. 0823B], because bread and wine are properly the food and drink of human beings, not of beasts, Christ willed, through the mystery of both uses, to be believed to be the singular and proper refreshment of human beings. Yet afterward, through the apostles, he willed water to be mingled with it. Water is the common drink of beasts and human beings, in order to signify that the fellowship belonging to the unity of so great a mystery includes not only the righteous but also sinners, if they are willing to repent; so that he himself might first perform, at the beginning of the sacrament, that which was his own, while we might afterward add what belonged to our mystery.

Moreover, he willed that this sacrament should outwardly appear to be food of mortality, although inwardly it is truly eternal life, conforming it to our own mystery. For inwardly we are renewed by the same [Col. 0823C] sacrament unto life, yet outwardly we are not changed into the glory of immortality. Thus nothing outwardly would be changed in his sacrament, just as nothing outwardly is renewed in us; although inwardly we find in ourselves the very thing we believe concerning him, because we receive life from life. Therefore, because we do not yet appear to be what we are, Christ did not will to appear as what he is, that he might be more desired. He will indeed then appear as what he is when we shall appear as what we are, that he may be more glorious. Hence St John says in his Epistle: “We are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3:2). And Paul says: “When Christ, our life, shall appear, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

Therefore, just as at Emmaus he appeared, in outward form, as a stranger to those who were strangers to faith (Luke 24:13), so [Col. 0823D] to us, strangers in the world’s exile, he appears in the sacrament under a form alien and foreign to himself. Thus, because what appears outwardly of us is mortal, he himself outwardly appears as food of mortality, although through him, who is the nourishment of immortality, eternal death is truly and invisibly healed within.

## Chapter VI. Why, after receiving Christ’s body, we do not immediately live eternally also in the flesh, although he himself is eternal life

It is also asked: since so great a sacrament is life, and Christ says, “Whoever eats [Col. 0824A] my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55), why do we not immediately live eternally also in the body by the power of so great a sacrament, when he did not say in the future tense, “will have eternal life,” but in the present, “has”?

But it must be understood that just as it was said to Adam, “On whatever day you eat the forbidden thing, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17), and yet on that same day he died not in body but in soul, so Christ says, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” not because he immediately lives eternally in the body, but in order to affirm that the soul—which died before the body in Adam—is raised again through union with so great a sacrament. That is, in proper order, the soul which, by sinning, was separated from God, who is eternal life [Col. 0824B], and was first dead, is believed through communion in so great a sacrament to be joined again and united to God, and to live again as before.

Because Adam was separated from God by sinning, God afterward, in bodily death, made him divided from himself, so that in the division of body and soul he might recognize that his soul had not clung to God, who is true life. Since outward death was both a figure and a punishment of inward death, it was therefore in one respect a terror and in another an admonition—a medicine for the fault itself. If God had first removed the medicinal punishment before the deadly fault, he would not make people incurable, because, once punishment had been removed, we would take greater delight in sin; and thus, while fault remained active and obstructive, no place would remain for divine grace.

Since fault is the death [Col. 0824C] of the soul, it was meanwhile to be punished through the distress of temporal death and thereby healed through grace, so that, during the reign of death, the bitterness of sufferings and labours might purge sins by burning them away; and so that heavenly grace, implanting the seeds of virtues all the more abundantly as it did so more freely, might restore us to eternal life.

Therefore, for the burning away and purging of sins, temporal death was not meanwhile to be removed, but eternal death was; lest we should either, unclean and impure, obtain unlawful rest, or, weak and undeserving, receive the reward of justice that was not due to us. For it would not be fitting to the equity of divine discernment either to stain its own purity by joining to itself the uncleanness of the perverse, or, by rewarding the idleness of the undeserving, to grant to a human being no more deserving than a stone [Col. 0824D] the dignity of so great a glory.

Therefore, lest we become incurable through the stubbornness of sin, in his great grace God did not remove temporal death, lest we should die eternally; he deferred eternal life, so that we might receive it with greater merit and greater fruit. For certainly, if it were otherwise, all would rush to Christ’s faith merely for the eternity of the present life; and thus, while they were not trained unto good by the torpor of such great security, they would forfeit the greater gain of Christ’s future glory.

For this reason also God mercifully prohibited Adam from the tree of life, saying: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life.” For if he who had perished in [Col. 0825A] soul through the tree of disobedience were also to live eternally in flesh through the tree of life permitted to him, he would perish utterly: while living eternally in flesh and dying eternally in soul through sin, he would be incurable like the demons—or like evil human beings who, after this life, will live eternally with their bodies. For the wicked too will have eternal life in the body, though I would call it death rather, because they will not please God, who is truly life. Therefore, without divine grace eternity will be miserable for them, because it is eternal misery.

## Chapter VII. Why eternal recompense is made for temporal merits

It is asked again why eternity of happiness or punishment is rendered for temporal merits of sin or [Col. 0825B] righteousness.

The answer is that God rewards or condemns not a temporal action but a perpetual will toward good or evil.
