If that will lived eternally, it would remain eternally in its purpose; and therefore he justly weighs eternity of recompense against eternity of will. Hence, as the Apostle says, the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us; for even if from the beginning of the world to its end (Rom. 8:18) someone were not only to labour for God but also to suffer, it would still not be worthy that he should purchase eternity by this temporal exchange.

Yet, lest the wicked be allowed to sin longer, to their greater punishment, and lest the good grow weary of living in the world’s exile if the delay before reaching their homeland were too long [Col. 0825C], God shortened the days of human life for the sake of the elect, lest they fail under the affliction of the wicked or their excessive labour. But lest the reduction of temporal labour should seem to diminish eternal reward, he willed the life of his own forerunner—than whom, according to his own testimony, no greater had arisen—to be thirty-two and a half years long; and he completed his own life, he who is above all, in the same number of years. Thus he showed that, because God considers not how long but with how great a heart one serves him, perfection of merit is to be ascribed not to time but to virtue.

For behold: in so very short a time he rendered complete obedience to God the Father, which no one had been able to do from the world’s beginning. Who would have lived longer than he, if he had seen duration of time, rather than virtue, sufficient for the perfection of merits? [Col. 0825D] And how could no one greater than John have arisen, when Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and very many others are known to have laboured longer in divine service? But it is certainly evident that, though many laboured longer than he, none did so more fervently and purely—he who in the time of his youth was found faithful and strong in temptation, when the flesh is always more rebellious against the spirit—so much so that even when he was to be killed, he did not fear to rebuke Herod in prison because he had presumed to take his brother’s wife.

## Chapter VIII. Why bread is consecrated separately into flesh, and wine separately into blood

It is also asked why bread is consecrated separately into flesh and wine [Col. 0826A] separately into blood, and why the former is separately called flesh and the latter separately blood, when the whole Christ is believed to be received in the flesh and the whole Christ in the blood; yet not two divided Christs, but one Christ alone in each.

The answer is that this practice became established in the Church from Christ himself, who consecrated and gave his body and blood separately—not to divide his substance, as though recipients received two Christs when they receive one Christ in each, but to distinguish the figure: so that bread, when it is ground by teeth, may signify Christ’s flesh bruised in the Passion, and wine, when it is poured into the mouths of the faithful, may signify the blood poured out from Christ’s side.

[Col. 0826B] Nor are body and blood spoken of separately as though the body were to be believed lifeless, and the blood poured out and separated from the body, since both are the one Christ, immortal and undivided. Rather, they are so named in remembrance of his Passion, because in the sacrament itself we ought to proclaim the Lord’s death. Thus water is also mingled in the sacrament, not only to signify that the ecclesiastical people are united to Christ their head, but also to represent the water that flowed from Christ’s side with the blood.

Bread and wine are called two distinct sacraments with respect to their distinct appearances; yet they are one with respect to their one and the same meaning. Hence Augustine says that the Church’s sacrifice is made of two things and consists of two: namely, one sacrament, because bread and wine signify the same thing; and one reality of the sacrament [Col. 0826C], because body and blood are the one Christ. Otherwise the Church’s sacrifice would consist not of two but of four: as bread and wine are two sacraments, so body and blood would be two distinct realities of the sacrament. This is impossible, since Christ’s body is not bloodless and dead.

Body and blood also appear separately in the sacrament so that, because Christ died for us, it may be signified that we, who perished in body and soul, were redeemed by body through body and soul through soul, and that his body and soul were divided in death for our redemption. His body lay in the tomb, while his soul descended to the underworld to free the souls of the saints. Since, therefore, in such a mystery Christ’s body was to be signified by body and his soul [Col. 0826D] by some visible appearance, nothing was found among creatures by which it could be represented more nearly and fittingly than blood, which is the seat of the soul.

By this too it is signified that our souls and bodies ought to be united and conformed to Christ’s soul and body. The faithful therefore receive body and blood together, so that, having received Christ’s body and soul, the whole human being may be given life by the whole Christ in soul and body—while Christ’s flesh itself, as has been said, is believed not to be bloodless and dead but living and life-giving. Hence, as Augustine says, flesh is rightly communicated not without blood, nor blood without flesh.

Likewise Gelasius to the bishops Majoricus and John: “We have learned that certain persons, having received only a portion of the sacred body, [Col. 0827A] refrain from the cup of the sacred blood. Such persons must without doubt either receive the sacraments entire or be excluded from their entirety, because a division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without great sacrilege.” [Note: [Col. 0827D] In Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction II, chapter 12, p. 454.]

## Chapter IX. Why Christ’s body is consecrated more especially in white bread than in black or bread of any colour, while blood is consecrated in wine of any colour

It is asked why Christ’s body is consecrated more especially in white bread than in black bread or bread of any colour, while blood is consecrated in white or red wine, or wine of any colour.

Indeed, Christ’s body is not forbidden to be made from bread of any grain or colour if necessity requires it [Col. 0827B]. Yet, if resources do not fail, it is certainly fitting that it should be as white and clean as possible when it is to be transformed into the most splendid body of the spotless Lamb. For just as mould and staleness are forbidden in such a sacrament lest they cause disgust to recipients, so there ought to be nothing in it that diminishes the desire to receive it.

## Chapter X. Why Christ’s body is consecrated more especially in unleavened than in leavened bread

Likewise, it is asked why Christ’s flesh is consecrated more especially in unleavened bread than in leavened or sediment-laden bread, while blood is consecrated in wine either clarified and pure or with sediment, as in must freshly pressed from grapes. Why then is sediment or leaven rejected in bread [Col. 0827C] when it is accepted in the wine by which the same sacrament is made?

As was said above, bread and wine are one sacrament, because in each there is one Christ. Whether Christ’s body ought to be made from unleavened or leavened bread is therefore a matter of great dispute between Latins and Greeks—so much so that the latter call the former “Azymites,” and the former the latter “Fermentarians,” branding one another as though by the name of some heresy. Yet, as it seems to many good Catholics, it is not contrary to Christian faith whether the sacrifice is offered with unleavened or leavened bread [Note: [Col. 0828D] This is the true opinion]. This is so both because each is bread, and as both sustain transitory life, so Christ’s body gives eternal life; and because, although Christ made his body from unleavened bread [Col. 0827D]—perhaps not because the thing being done required this, but because the supper in which it was done provided no other bread—he nevertheless did not forbid leavened bread.

For although the Old Law commanded unleavened bread to be eaten at Passover, so that Christ’s future sincerity and purity might be figured by it, and so that we, who were to eat his body, might likewise be warned to cleanse ourselves from all leaven of malice and wickedness, we do not need such a figure in the bread from which we make Christ’s flesh. For we who have passed from the old figure to the truth receive Christ’s unleavened and pure flesh in bread consecrated of whatever kind.

[Col. 0828A] They further maintain that just as, at the invocation of the divine name—which is believed to be nullified in no sacrament but by God’s grace alone works all things in all—the merits of priests neither hinder nor assist the greater or lesser reality of ecclesiastical sacraments, so neither colour nor any form of bread or wine hinders or assists the lesser or greater making of Christ’s body, provided only that it is bread and wine, whose substance, as Christ commands, passes into the substance of Christ’s body and blood.

The Greeks nevertheless say that the Latins unlawfully offer unleavened bread, since unleavened bread belongs to the Old Testament, and Christ, having removed all antiquity as superfluous to human salvation because the truth was now present, instituted the New Testament not in unleavened but in leavened bread. They contend [Col. 0828B] that he would not have instituted the New Testament perfectly unless he had wholly abandoned the old, both in unleavened bread and in all its other rites. They therefore detest Latin sacrifices because they consider the Latins to be Judaizing by offering unleavened bread.

The Latins reply that Christ instituted the New Testament in unleavened bread because, after the Old Testament had been fulfilled and the New instituted on the evening of the sixteenth moon, leavened bread could not be found throughout all Israel. Therefore, since the supper itself in which this was done offered only unleavened bread, he instituted the New Testament in unleavened bread. If Christ did this without Judaizing, who would say that we Judaize by imitating him? But the Greeks object that Christ miraculously supplied himself with leavened bread, just as it is written that he fed thousands of people with five loaves.

[Col. 0828C] The Latins answer: It is not written that he performed this miracle, though he could have; and no authority establishes that he did so, especially since he had up to that point observed the Law so fully that he would not dissolve even one iota of it. Since he was born of a woman and made under the Law, he stood obligated by the Law. If he had set aside the Law up to that point, he would have become a sinner by transgressing it, and the cause of our salvation would have perished. Unless one wholly innocent and pure died for us, who were impure and unjust, he would by dying pay the debt not of another’s fault but of his own; and thus, unless Adam’s sin were removed, the kingdom of eternal death would not cease.

[Col. 0828D] For, since the Law says concerning the observance of unleavened bread, “Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from Israel” (Exod. 12:15), the Jews would have found a just cause for putting him to death if they had punished him as a transgressor of the Law. Those who so zealously suborned many false witnesses against him would not have kept silent concerning such a just cause, especially when the traitor himself, who had been present at the supper, denounced him.

The Greeks object: Although before the Passion he was obligated by the Law, after the Resurrection he owed the Law nothing. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he lives, he lives unto God.” Therefore, since after the Resurrection he lives not to the Law but to God, [Col. 0829A] he himself, now owing nothing to the Law, instituted that the baptism of new grace—which he had not previously done—should be preached and administered for the remission of sins not only to Jews but to all nations.

They consequently maintain that, even if Christ consecrated unleavened bread, this should not be imitated in him, just as we do not adopt circumcision along with baptism or the celebration of the old Passover together with the new. Yet Christ, as mediator of the New and Old Testaments, deigned to perform both: fulfilling the old, and instituting the new. Before the Passion, indeed, he duly performed certain things of the New Testament and of the Old according to his office; but after the Resurrection, having removed all shadowy superfluity of legal antiquity, he established for all only the truth of grace.

[Col. 0829B] The Latins reply that it is indeed salutary to imitate in him what he handed down to his Church to be done by example, testimony, and command. For after he had said, “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,” he blessed, broke, and gave unleavened bread, saying, “This is my body, which shall be given for you.” And he added: “Do this in remembrance of me.” Since therefore he testified that unleavened bread had become his body and commanded, without exception, that this be done in remembrance of him, who, with God himself bearing witness, would not believe that unleavened bread becomes Christ’s body? Who would not obey the one commanding this same act to be done, under the example of doing the same?

If Christ had known that it would be deadly for his faithful to make his body from unleavened bread, he would have forbidden us to do so as he forbade other sins, or at least would not have commanded it. [Col. 0829C] But now, since he said, “Do this,” and did not except unleavened bread, who dares except what he did not except? Or who dares forbid what he did not forbid in his sacrament? He himself did it and commanded us to do this very thing. When he says, “Do this,” it is fittingly understood, “what I do.” Who would dare as fittingly to understand, “but not from that from which I do”?

Likewise, if unleavened bread is to be changed for leavened bread, then wine should also be changed for any other liquid. For if wine is received, why is unleavened bread rejected? Just as he ended the old Passover and began the new with unleavened bread, so he did with wine, and he handed down both to us as equally to be celebrated in his sacrament. The Jews use wine in their ceremonies just as they use unleavened bread. Therefore, in doing this, Christ did it not merely [Col. 0829D] to observe the Passover command concerning unleavened bread, but also in order, by rejecting the Fermentarians whom he foresaw, to approve the Azymites; or at least, if Fermentarians too were to be approved, he, being an Azymite, preferred Azymites.

For if we ought to celebrate divine sacraments through those species of elements which are more worthy, what bread shall we consider [Note: [Col. 0829D] Elsewhere: “judge.”] more worthy than that which both the Old Law chose to signify, and the Gospel chose to present, the reality of the Lord’s body? In the Law unleavened bread is called bread of affliction, so that by it we too, who recall the memory of Christ’s Passion in the sacrament, may be taught [Col. 0830A] to afflict our souls. For in grace, as the Apostle says, we are admonished to keep the feast “not with the old leaven, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:8), so that unleavened bread may signify that we ought to be sincere and pure.

What, then, is worthier for making Christ’s sacrament than that which in every way works salvation both by truth and by figure? Yet we should not be thought to Judaize by using figures, because although we do the same thing as the Jews in this matter, we do not do it for the same reason as they do: we do not do it in order to preserve Judaism. And while they, by their figures, foretell things still future, we do not signify by the figure of unleavened bread that Christ is in any respect still to come; rather, we represent that he whose body is offered was without leaven—that is, without the infection of sin. And we admonish ourselves, according to the Apostle, to keep the feast not with the leaven of malice and wickedness but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. [Col. 0830B]

Therefore, since we Christians signify not, as Jews do who figure and await future things, that Christ will be pure, but that he has been pure, and exhort ourselves to become such as he is: the Greeks rebuke us in vain concerning unleavened bread—unless perhaps they wish Christians to use no figures at all because the old things have passed away, in which shadows of future things were necessary. Where then is what the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:4), if baptism is not for us a figure of Christ’s death and burial? But perhaps they do not wish us to use the same figures [Col. 0830C] which the Jews use in their ceremonies? Yet if unleavened bread is forbidden because Jews use it in their rites, then leavened bread should likewise be forbidden, because Jews also use it in their sacrifices. Hence in Leviticus: “He shall offer leavened loaves with the sacrifice of thanksgiving, which is offered for peace offerings” (Lev. 7:13). Likewise in the same book: “At Pentecost you shall offer first-fruit loaves of two tenths of leavened fine flour” (Lev. 23:17).

Since, then, no reasoning compels unleavened bread to be excluded from Christ’s sacrifice, it is fitting that what Christ instituted, and what every Church except the Greek has celebrated without interruption from its beginning by the tradition of the chief Apostles, namely Peter and Paul, should continue to preserve until Christ comes for judgment [Col. 0830D], as he himself instituted it.

For if, because the Apostle says, “Old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17), all things are believed to have passed away and the institutions of the Old Testament to have perished: where are love of God and neighbour, the commandments of the Decalogue, the order of Levites and priesthood, the dedication of altar and temple? All these have passed from them to us, not by failing but by advancing. We do not cease to celebrate the Dedication, Passover, Pentecost, and Lent because they were instituted in the Old Law. We establish bishops, priests, Levites, and the remaining ecclesiastical orders after the example of the ancients, and many other things in the same manner.

# Book Three

[Col. 0831]

## Chapter I. That certain authorities of the saints seem to establish that the sacraments of heretics are invalid and harmful

[Col. 0831A]

Having established that sinful ministers who nonetheless belong to the Church celebrate true and valid sacraments, let us now consider sinners outside the Church—namely heretics and schismatics—and whether the sacraments they celebrate, though not valid, are at least true. This is especially necessary because, in some passages, the saints deny that these are sacraments and call them rather sacrileges.

And because concerning the body and blood of the Lord, which is the present subject, the doubt is greater, let the present discussion, with his help, address this matter itself and the other sacraments as well. Having therefore set forth the authorities by which the saints detest the sacraments of heretics as invalid and, so far as the heretics themselves are concerned, harmful, let us append the authorities and reasons by which they are established to be, so far as God is concerned, true and holy.

Augustine says: “Outside the Catholic Church there is no place for the true sacrifice.” Pope Pelagius, among other things, to Viator and Pancratius: “You ought to abstain from the sacrifices—or rather the sacrileges—of schismatics.” Again, he writes to the same persons: “What a schismatic consecrates is not the body of Christ.” Again Augustine, in the *Enchiridion* (ch. 5, vol. VI, col. 196): “If matters pertaining to Christ are considered, Christ is found among any heretics in name only; but in the reality itself [Col. 0831C] he is not among them.” Again Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0831] Thus it is read in the statement of the eighty-seven bishops concerning the baptism of heretics (among the works of St Cyprian, p. 330), which the Apostolic See condemned.]: “It is evident that they cannot sanctify the oil with which the baptized are anointed, nor can the Eucharist be performed among them: where there is no hope, and faith is false, where everything is carried on through falsehood.” Again Ambrose, in the book *On Initiating the Uninstructed* (*On the Mysteries*, ch. 4, vol. II, col. 330): “The baptism of the faithless does not heal; it does not cleanse but pollutes, because in this flood of waters one does not draw near to God.” Again Jerome, on the prophet Haggai (ch. 2, vol. VI, col. 764): “Everything that heretics do, or offer to me—whether vows or other things—shall be defiled in my sight. For although what is offered appears holy in its outward form, yet, because it has been handled by one who is defiled in soul, everything is defiled.” Again Blessed Gregory, in the [Col. 0831D] *Dialogues* (book III, ch. 31, vol. II, col. 345):

> When the day of the Paschal festival came, the faithless father sent an Arian bishop to Hermenegild, that he might receive from his hand communion of a sacrilegious consecration and thereby deserve to return to his father’s favour. But the man beloved by God drove that faithlessness from himself with fitting rebukes.

Again the same author: “Why is it not considered that a blessing is turned into a curse for one who is advanced in order that he may become a heretic?” [Col. 0832A] Again: “I do not think that the priesthood subsists there.” Again Cyprian:

> To all these evils is added this further evil: that a bishop of the devil should dare to make the Eucharist, when the offering cannot even be sanctified there where the Holy Spirit is not present.

And a little later:

> Those who fabricate false altars, unlawful priesthoods, sacrilegious sacrifices, and adulterated things of every kind, all those known to have withdrawn from the charity and unity of the Catholic Church, are to be counted among pagans and tax collectors. Therefore everything that heretics do is carnal, empty, and false. Things that are vaunted in Christ’s name are not to be immediately received and accepted, but those which are performed in Christ’s truth. For how can those who attempt against God what is not permitted them accomplish what they do, or obtain [Col. 0832B] anything from God?

Again Gregory, in the *Morals* (book XXIII, ch. 1, col. 733): “The sacrifices of heretics cannot be acceptable to God unless they are offered for them by the hands of the universal Church.” Again the same author (book XV, ch. 3, no. 13, col. 1148): “For the lamb is eaten in one house, because the true victim of the Redeemer is immolated in the one Catholic Church.”

By all these authorities the saints seem to maintain that outside the Church the body of Christ cannot be consecrated by heretics or schismatics, since neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit—through whom all things are sanctified—is among them; nor is there among them a place of sacrifice, nor does priesthood subsist among them. Therefore they offer sacrifices that are sacrilegious, empty, and false. To this [Col. 0832C] is added that the other sacraments are only a form and figure of holy effects, not the reality itself. Among heretics they may indeed be called true with respect to their form, but empty and false with respect to the effect of grace, which they do not confer among them. But since the sacrament of Christ’s body can in no way exist without Christ’s body, if it is true among heretics, it is in no way empty and false among them; for wherever the sacrament of Christ’s body is, there also is Christ, who is not empty and false but always true. Therefore, if their sacrifice is sacrilegious, since Christ is the sacrifice, then Christ is sacrilegious. If it is not acceptable to God, then the Son in whom the Father was well pleased is not [Col. 0832D] acceptable to the Father. If it is not to be received and accepted by human beings, then he whom angels must adore is to be rejected and spurned by human beings.

To hold this concerning Christ, who is the spotless Lamb, is impious: to believe that he can in any way be defiled by another’s crime, though he alone bore and took away all the sins of the world. Therefore, lest [Col. 0833A] this incongruity be believed of him in any respect, they agree with Pelagius that what a schismatic consecrates is not Christ’s body, and with Cyprian that the Eucharist cannot be performed among heretics. They wish the invocation of the divine name—which Gregory calls a sacrilegious consecration—to be judged ineffectual in this sense; and Cyprian says that what is vaunted in Christ’s name is not immediately to be received, but what is performed in Christ’s truth. Thus, by maintaining that there is absolutely nothing which heretics appear to consecrate, they remove from Christ that dishonour which the saints attest concerning the sacrifices and other sacraments of heretics.

## CHAPTER II. That it belongs to God alone to make all sacraments always true and holy in relation to himself.

[Col. 0833B]

But if this is to be believed, let us see how far-reaching the absurdity is. First, it is impious to believe that the invocation of the divine name is annulled in their sacraments. For Augustine says to Parmenian (book II, ch. 6, vol. IX, col. 32): “The sacrifices of the ungodly are an abomination to the Lord, for they offer them wickedly.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore the sacrifices of the ungodly harm those very persons who offer them wickedly. For one and the same sacrifice, on account of the Lord’s name which is invoked, is always holy; yet it becomes such for each person as is the heart with which he approaches to receive it.” Again the same author, in Homily 80 on John (no. 3, vol. III, col. 703): “Whence has water such great power that it touches the body and washes the heart, unless the word accomplishes this? Not because it is spoken, [Col. 0833C] but because it is believed.” Again, to the Donatists: “If God is present in his sacraments and words, through whomever they are administered, then God’s sacraments are everywhere right, and evil people, to whom they do no good, are everywhere perverse, that is, both inside and outside.” Again: “Therefore no one who belongs to the devil’s party, whether outside or even inside, can defile in himself or in anyone else the sacrament which is Christ’s.”

For how could an evil person defile what a good person cannot consecrate or improve, what Christ alone accomplishes and no other? If someone else accomplished it, it would no longer belong to Christ. But what good could exist without the supreme Good? Although, therefore, all sacraments are said to be Christ’s and the Church’s, this is not so as though the Church were made equal to Christ in them, but [Col. 0833D] because she is shown to participate in Christ’s grace: they are Christ’s alone with regard to the power by which they are performed, and the Church’s with regard to the benefit by which they are conferred. Thus in them he displays his own grace, and she supplies her own need. For Christ, knowing that human sins may hinder and human merits may be insufficient for life, provided the grace of his sacraments, so that the Church, believing that what she lacks in merits is supplied by divine sacraments, might become more perfect in the superabundance of his benefits in proportion as she was more humble before God in her own imperfection.

What Christ reserved to the prerogatives of his own grace, therefore, he willed to owe nothing to the merits or offices of ministers. What was his own he made freely his own, so that it is neither better through their [Col. 0834A] worthiness nor worse through their unworthiness—lest good people seem to have added something to the divine work, as though better than God; or evil people to diminish it, as though stronger than God; or to claim altogether as their own, as though they themselves were God, what is altogether divine. Therefore, so that the Church’s sacraments may be shown to belong not to good or evil human beings but to God alone, they are believed to be true and holy in themselves without distinction among all persons. Since among all they are always the same from the same source, just as God, who is unchangeable, is never worse or better than himself, so his sacraments among all persons are unchangeably always the same, never worse or better than themselves.

## CHAPTER III. That Christ’s sacraments must not be believed to vary according to the merits of their ministers, lest the unity of the sacraments and of the Church perish.

[Col. 0834B]

For if they were thought to be better or worse among these or those according to the merits of those who administer them, they would be attributed no longer to Christ’s grace but to their merits. And since whatever is now worse, now better, is not the same but different, the unity of baptism and of Christ’s body would no longer stand; because his baptism, being better or worse among these or those, would be different, and likewise Christ’s body would be different. For if evil sacraments came from an evil person, good sacraments from a good one, and better sacraments from a better person, would there not be different baptisms and bodies of Christ according to the varying merits of human beings? And if there were many bodies of Christ, then there would be not one Christ but many Christs; and not one Church but many—which is impious. Since it is evident that there are not [Col. 0834C] many Christs, let us consider the unity of baptism and of the Church, so that what will be demonstrated concerning the lesser sacrament may be still more evident from the greater.

Augustine says in Homily 6 on John (no. 6, col. 332):

> Through this power, which Christ retained for himself alone and poured into none of his ministers, though he deigned to baptize through ministers—through this the unity of the Church stands, signified by the dove of which it was said: “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6:8), “one to her mother.” For if that power were transferred from the Lord to our ministers, there would be as many baptisms as ministers, and the unity of baptism would not stand. Therefore, although both the just and the unjust baptize, the holiness of baptism is attributed only to him upon whom the dove descended, of whom it was said: “This is he [Col. 0834D] who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). Let Peter baptize: it is he who baptizes. Let Paul baptize: it is he who baptizes. Let Judas baptize: it is he who baptizes. For if baptism is holy according to the diversity of merits, then, because merits are diverse, baptisms will be diverse. But just as, when a good and a better person baptize, the one does not receive something good for that reason and the other something better, but what they receive is one and equal, so also when an evil person baptizes: what is given is one, not unequal because the ministers are unequal, but equal and the same, because it is he who baptizes.

But lest this be thought spoken only of evil persons who are either unknown or tolerated within the Church itself, Augustine says to Cresconius the grammarian [Col. 0835A] (book II, ch. 21, vol. IX, col. 422): “If you ask how those condemned by the Church baptize, I answer: they baptize in the same way as those condemned by God baptize, before the Church has pronounced any judgment about them.” Again (book III, ch. 5, no. 6, col. 438): “If, among good ministers, when one is better than another, the baptism given through the better is not better, then the baptism given even through an evil person is by no means evil, because the same baptism is given. Thus through unequal ministers God’s gift is equal, because it is not theirs but his.” Again the same author in book VI of *On Baptism* (ch. 1, vol. IX, col. 161): “Even those slower in understanding perceive that Christ’s baptism cannot be violated by any perversity of giver or receiver.” Again, in book VI: “That which is in a just person and in an unjust person [Col. 0835B] is always holy, because it is neither increased by anyone’s righteousness nor diminished by anyone’s unrighteousness.” Again the same author in book III of *On Baptism* (ch. 2, col. 113):

> For this reason the Catholic Church ought not to repeat baptism which has been administered among heretics: lest she seem to judge that what is Christ’s belongs to them, or that they do not possess what, once received within the Church, they cannot lose by going outside. Therefore one and the same baptism of Christ exists among all—good and evil, condemned and uncondemned, heretics and non-heretics—so that through unequal ministers God’s gift is always equal, because it is not theirs but his: neither better nor worse with respect to holiness, neither greater nor less with respect to truth; not violated by giver [Col. 0835C] or receiver, not lost by one withdrawing from the Church, not to be repeated for one returning. Thus, in a matter where all human merits are judged of no account, God’s grace alone is believed to have force.

For if, through their own merits, they could lose it by withdrawing from the Church and retain it by remaining, then what they themselves could confer or remove would seem to be theirs, not God’s. Again, if it were lost by one withdrawing, it would have to be repeated for one returning; and there would be two baptisms, by which one born once carnally would be spiritually reborn twice. Again, if what exists among heretics is not a sacrament, then what is rejected with them is judged to be theirs rather than Christ’s. Again, the invocation of the divine name is annulled among them and must be repeated by Catholics in order to become valid; and so God’s grace, as though powerless in itself [Col. 0835D], would owe to human merits what it has power to do. Where it is no longer gratuitous but subject to human merits—doing nothing among heretics apart from merits, and among Catholics operating only on account of merits—grace is no longer grace.

Therefore baptism must be believed to be one and the same among all in its truth, just as the Catholic Church is one and the same in its unity. For just as our Father in heaven is one, so also his bride, our mother the Church who gives birth, is one; and so also is the one baptism by which she gives birth. Although waters differ in diverse places and times, she nevertheless confesses only one baptism for the remission of sins, because, as the Apostle testifies, “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). Likewise, though baptizers differ, [Col. 0836A] baptism is always one.

For if as many fathers were believed to regenerate as there are baptizers, spiritual regeneration would be worse than natural generation. Natural generation began from one human being, lest the human race rise up against itself and be divided from itself through pride, if it had its first origin not from one but from this person and that person, better or worse. How much worse would spiritual regeneration be if it came not from one God but from this person and that person, better or worse—if it had as many fathers as baptizers. The second generation, conferring nothing more than the first, would be called earthly, not heavenly, just like the first. The children of the Church, reborn from earthly fathers, would not become children of God, heirs of God, or fellow heirs of Christ, because in their regeneration they would be deprived of the nobility and [Col. 0836B] inheritance of so great a Father.

The Church also, divided among so many fathers, would be endangered by the confusion of various schisms, while all her adulterous children cried out as though for the division of Christ: “I belong to Apollos; I belong to Cephas; I belong to Paul” (1 Corinthians 1:12). And what charity would there be where unity did not exist? Since love is the root of all goods, the Church without the unity of love would be deprived of every good, both in merit and in reward.

## CHAPTER IV. That God placed precious sacraments in unprecious outward forms, not so that they might be cheap and contemptible, but gratuitous.

Therefore, lest the Church seem to have as many fathers as would dissipate her unity and cause her to decline from heavenly nobility, all sacraments are believed [Col. 0836C] to belong to God alone. Let us consider how gratuitous, useful, and magnificent he has made them. When we see how great gifts he confers on his Church through such small things, it will become most evident that they belong to God alone and that he works through them.

All sacramental outward forms, by their nature or quantity, are of so little monetary value that they seem to attain no sacramental dignity through any privilege of their own. They have only this: by their natural resemblance they display a shadow or image of sacramental effect, and thus stir up and strengthen faith for receiving the corresponding grace of the Holy Spirit. For example, the Church’s sacraments chiefly consist in four forms: water, oil, bread, and wine. Water, [Col. 0836D] although necessary for everyone, is not precious because of any commercial value of its own. Oil, bread, and wine likewise, in the sacrament, are so slight in quantity that they escape valuation in price, and seem to claim usefulness only in spiritual grace.

Yet God did not do this in order that his sacraments, because their outward forms have no value for sale, might seem cheaper and more contemptible, but rather more gratuitous. For, since nothing appears to have force in them except what is his, all grace for them is ascribed to him alone. In his benefits he removed our expense, lest we be burdened, and bestowed his incomparable grace, that we might be helped more gladly. If God had instituted his sacraments in more precious forms, which by their nature and quantity were so valuable that the whole world [Col. 0837A] could not suffice to purchase them, their purchase would indeed not be worthy of the sacraments; access to them would become difficult and burdensome for the poor. Therefore, in order that God’s grace might be altogether gratuitous, he sought not dignity but suitability in sacramental forms.

Because water extinguishes, cleanses, and whitens beyond other liquids, it also extinguishes the incentives of the flesh in baptism, washes away the stain of sins—both original and actual—and restores the brightness of innocence; and, thus restoring the image of the heavenly Father, regenerates children of adoption. Oil, because it is suitable for athletes and is receptive to fire and light, is used in chrism, baptism, and confirmation, so that human frailty may be more strongly fortified against spiritual evils. Thus the Spirit given in twofold love may enlighten the soul [Col. 0837B] by faith, set it aflame by love, and fortify and strengthen it with heavenly hope. Because bread and wine, incorporated into a human being, are temporal life, Christ, incorporated into us through this sacrament as the head into his members, becomes eternal life for believers.

By these three sacraments baptism is duly completed: because it is celebrated in the name of the Trinity and testifies by its ministry to faith in the Trinity. Through water it regenerates us to God the Father; through communion in Christ’s body and blood it incorporates us into the Son of God for life; through the anointing of oil it confirms us by the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus, having been undeservedly forestalled at the beginning of regeneration by so great a grace of God, we may not despair of being led to the prize of life, if we are willing to strive with that same grace.

## CHAPTER V. That God’s sacraments are so great that they surpass the merits of all human beings.

[Col. 0837C]

To whom, then, belongs the conferral of such great grace except to God alone? In the excellence of his sacraments he so surpasses all merits that they are altogether judged unworthy to aspire to their dignity or power. For who can regenerate the children of the devil as children of God, except God the Father? Who can justify sinners except Christ, who died for our sins? And since everything performed in baptism is spiritual, who can accomplish this except the Holy Spirit? It would be pointless to perform it in the name of the Trinity if it passed from the Trinity’s power to someone else. Therefore no human being should presume to claim for himself [Col. 0837D] what belongs to God alone to do.

For the Apostle says: “There are diversities of graces; but one Lord, who works all things in all, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:4). Therefore also, when Christ said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:5), he was altogether silent concerning ministers, because he saw that nothing of so great a grace belonged to them. Hence Blessed Augustine, on John (Tractate V, no. 15, col. 327):

> But the heretic says to me: “You do not have baptism, because an evil person gave it to you.” If he is evil, I reply, then Christ is evil, and it was an evil one who gave it to me. I do not dispute about the official. Let human beings be whatever they may be: I received from Christ; I was baptized by Christ. I know that the dove, which John saw, taught me this. Let ministers be just, if they wish; but if not, my master makes me secure, he of whom his Spirit said: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33). If the minister is just, I count him with Paul, who does not seek his own glory, saying: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase.”

If a minister is proud, he is reckoned with the devil (*Zabulus*), but Christ’s gift is not defiled. For the spiritual power of the sacrament is like light: it is received pure by those illuminated, and if it passes through unclean things, it is not defiled. Since, therefore, according to the Apostle, ministers are nothing, but God works all things in all, [Col. 0838B] what do they accomplish in God’s sacraments, when they are nothing and God alone accomplishes everything? Hence Augustine again, on John: “Baptism is such as he is in whose power it is given, not such as he is through whose ministry it is given.”

## CHAPTER VI. That a layperson or a pagan is permitted to baptize.

Thus, in order that the boast of merit might be removed from ministers, the saints allow a layperson to baptize in necessity and do not deny baptismal grace even to a pagan. Without office and without merit, such persons would not be permitted to do so if human merits or offices were considered necessary for baptism. Hence Pope Gelasius, ch. 7: “Deacons must not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless those aforesaid officeholders are perhaps far away and extreme necessity compels it; this is also [Col. 0838C] often permitted to Christian laypersons.” Again Isidore:

> If someone is ordained through negligence before being baptized, those baptized by him must be baptized again, and he himself must not thereafter be ordained. For the Roman pontiff judges not the person who baptizes, but that the Spirit of God supplies the grace of baptism, even though the person baptizing is a pagan.

Again Pope Nicholas, in his replies to the Bulgarians, ch. 104:

> You state that many in your country have been baptized by someone whom, as I hear, you do not know to be a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what should be done about this. If they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, or even in the name of Christ alone, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles—for, as St Ambrose explains, the two are one and the same—it is established that they are not to be baptized again.

But lest [Col. 0838D] such baptism be thought imperfect, Augustine says conversely in book IV of *On Baptism*: “One person can be called more learned than another; no one can be called more or less baptized than another.”

## CHAPTER VII. That baptism is completed by the shedding of blood or by faith alone.

But lest officeholders also attribute something to themselves, let them observe that even a layperson or pagan has at least performed their function, and recognize God’s grace to be so free, bound by no human merits or offices, that it pours itself out whenever it wills, however it wills, and upon whomever it wills. Since it is evident that saints are baptized either by their own blood or by faith alone, what can officeholders here attribute to their merits, [Col. 0839A] where they exercise no ministry? Therefore, since God baptizes without them, it is clear that here he alone is the one who baptizes.

Hence Augustine, *On Baptism*, book IV (ch. 22, vol. IX, col. 139):

> Blessed Cyprian adduces no slight evidence from that thief to whom, though unbaptized, it was said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), that suffering sometimes fulfils the place of baptism. And, considering this again and again, I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name can supply what is lacking from baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if assistance cannot be obtained in the straits of time for celebrating the mystery of baptism. For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name, but for the deserts of his crimes; [Col. 0839B] nor did he suffer because he believed, but, while suffering, he believed. Thus in that thief was demonstrated how much force the Apostle’s statement has even without the visible sacrament of baptism: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). But this is invisibly fulfilled when not contempt for religion but a circumstance of necessity excludes the mystery of baptism.

> And just as the kindness of the Almighty supplied in that thief what was lacking of the sacrament of baptism, because it was lacking not through pride or contempt but necessity, so the same grace of the Almighty must be believed to supply it in infants who die baptized: because through the need of their age, not through an impious will, they cannot either believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation [Col. 0839C] (ch. 24, col. 140). Baptism can indeed be present where conversion of heart is absent; but conversion of heart can indeed be present without baptism received, though not where baptism has been despised. Conversion of heart to God must in no way be said to exist when God’s sacrament is despised. [Ch. 25, col. 141.]

Again, in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*:

> True baptism consists not so much in washing the body as in faith of heart, as apostolic teaching hands down when it says: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Ephesians 5:26). And elsewhere: “Baptism saves—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God” (1 Peter 3:21). Behold: although the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16), human beings are saved by faith alone [Col. 0839D] without baptism, as was the thief, and by baptism alone without faith, as are infants—but only when not contempt for religion but a circumstance of necessity excludes one or the other.

Hence Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices* (book II, ch. 25, vol. VI, p. 467, ed. Arevalo): “Infants are baptized while another professes on their behalf, because they do not yet know how to speak or believe; similarly the sick, mute, or deaf, for whom another professes in their stead, answering for them while they are baptized.” Again Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will* (book III, ch. 23, vol. I, col. 637):

> People commonly inquire what benefit the sacrament of Christ’s baptism brings to infants, since, after receiving it, they often die before being able to know anything from it. In this matter it is sufficiently devoutly and [Col. 0840A] rightly believed that the faith of those by whom the child is presented for consecration benefits the infant. The Church’s most salutary authority commends this, so that each person may understand from it how his own faith benefits him, since another’s faith can be lent for the benefit of those who do not yet possess their own. O ineffable grace of God, which, where one of the two is lacking by a circumstance of necessity, both anticipates faith by the mystery of the sacrament and fulfils the place of the sacrament by the merit of faith, so that, bound by no laws, we may not suffer in any degree—so far as depends on you—the loss of eternal salvation!

But lest it seem strange that God works by himself, without ministers, what is his own, let us see what he did at the beginning under both law and grace. The Lord says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men, and lead [Col. 0840B] them to the tabernacle of the covenant, and I will take from your spirit and give it to them” (Numbers 11:16). He did not say, “You will take and give,” but “I will take and give.” And lest this perhaps be attributed to Moses’ leadership, two of those who had been enrolled did not come to the tabernacle and yet received the Spirit, as the others did, without Moses leading them. Likewise under the new grace, though the Spirit was ordinarily given only through laying on of hands, while Peter was still speaking the Holy Spirit fell upon them all (Acts 10:44). Who then can attribute divine grace to his merits or office, when in the lawgiver and in the prince of the apostles God employed neither of these in distributing it as he wills?

## CHAPTER VIII. That, as in baptism, so in consecrating Christ’s body, nothing is done more by a good minister or less by an evil one.

[Col. 0840C]

Since it has therefore been established that the grace of baptism does not belong to the merits of officeholders, let us also consider the consecration of Christ’s body and blood. Indeed, when the matter is established concerning the lesser sacrament, it seems sufficiently established concerning the greater. For Christ’s body and blood are not only equal to baptism but its foundation and completion. Just as Eve is believed to have been brought forth from the side of Adam while he slept, so the Church is believed to have been brought forth from the side of Christ resting in death; for as she was generated from that side, so this Church was regenerated from it. From it his sacraments wonderfully flowed: water for regeneration, blood for redemption.

Hence John says [Col. 0840D] in his Epistle: “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood” (1 John 5:6). And he rightly repeated this, because water would have profited nothing without blood, which not only washes but also redeems—and because it redeems, it washes. Hence in the Apocalypse: “These are those who have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). Therefore, lest the arrogance of ministers appropriate something to itself even in this greater sacrament, let us attend to what the saints think about it.

Augustine says in the book *On the Lord’s Body*:

> Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing is accomplished more by a good priest or less by an evil one, because it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator [Col. 0841A] but by the word of the Creator and by the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it were accomplished by the priest’s merit, it would not belong to Christ. But now, as he himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself, through the Holy Spirit, makes this his creature flesh and transforms it into blood. For it must be believed that the sacraments are consecrated in Christ’s words. By the power of him through whom they were first created, they are surely recreated for the better through his word.

Since Augustine says that things first created are created again in the sacrament, if human beings could do this, it would follow that they are makers of Christ’s body and thus, as it were, creators of their Creator—which is impossible. For Eusebius of Emesa says: “The invisible priest, by his word and hidden power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and [Col. 0841B] blood.” Again Blessed Ambrose: “When consecration takes place, bread becomes Christ’s body. By what words, then, and by whose speech is the consecration performed? By those of the Lord Jesus. Therefore Christ’s speech makes this body.” Again Augustine, in the homilies: “Before the words, when bread is offered, it is called bread; when Christ’s words have been uttered, it is no longer called bread but Christ’s body.”

Therefore, if the invisible priest makes his body by his word, how can it be the work either of the word or merit of any visible priest? Since it belongs in no respect to the visible priest, how can it be made better by a good priest or worse by an evil one, by whom it is not made at all? This being so, there are no longer diverse bodies of Christ according to diverse merits, but always one [Col. 0841C] Christ, who, while ministers of whatever sort offer sacrifice, alone both offers for us and is offered. Hence Augustine, in *On the Trinity* (book IV, vol. VIII, col. 823): “What could be offered and received more gratefully than the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our priest, so that the one and same true mediator might be both the one who offered and that which he offered?” Again the same author, to Parmenian (book II, ch. 6, vol. IX, col. 32): “The sacrifices of the ungodly are an abomination to the Lord, for they offer them wickedly.” The answer has already been given: Christ, who offered himself for us and is our mediator in heaven, is not wicked. While he governs his Church, evil people do not harm the good, whether they are unknown or tolerated for peace.

## CHAPTER IX. That the sacraments of heretics are from the Church and are performed in the Church.

[Col. 0841D]

But they object that outside the Church there is no place of sacrifice, and that Christ and the Holy Spirit are not among heretics. On the contrary, Augustine says to Vincentius the Donatist (Letter 93, no. 45, vol. II, col. 249): “All the Lord’s sacraments which you possess and give are from the Catholic Church, just as they were possessed and given before you went out from it. Yet you do not for that reason fail to possess them because you are not in the place from which you gave them.” Again, to Emeritus (Letter 87, no. 9, vol. II, col. 212): “The sacraments which you have not changed are approved by us as you possess them, lest, perhaps, while we seek to correct your perversity [Col. 0842A], we commit a sacrilegious injury against those mysteries which have not been corrupted by your perversity.” Again Augustine, in book I of *On Baptism* (ch. 8, vol. IX, col. 85):

> Those who separate themselves from fellowship with the rest, violate charity, and break the bond of unity: if they perform none of the things which they received in unity, they are separated in all things, and therefore anyone whom they join to themselves, if he returns to the Church, must receive everything which he did not receive. But if they perform some of the same things, they have not separated themselves in those things and are connected with the Church in that respect. In the holiness of the sacrament, in which they are not against us, they are for us; in the wound of schism, by which they do not gather with Christ, they scatter.

Since, therefore, all the Lord’s sacraments without exception [Col. 0842B] are from the Catholic Church—even among heretics, who are connected with the Church in this respect because they celebrate them rightly—who can doubt that wherever the sacrament of divine sacrifice is performed, it is within the Church, since it is from the Church? Nevertheless, it must be understood that, although among them even Christ’s sacrifice is from the Church with regard to its own truth, its place is not for those outside the Church with regard to their benefit. For, since the Son of Man finds among them nowhere to lay his head, neither Christ himself nor the Holy Spirit is among them through grace—though he is among all and absent nowhere through the presence of his majesty.

## CHAPTER X. That priesthood remains altogether intact among heretics in respect of the sacrament alone.

[Col. 0842C] But they object again that the priesthood does not subsist among them. And what can be consecrated by persons who act neither by merit nor by office? For Ambrose says in the book *On the Mysteries of Initiation* (ch. 5, col. 332): “Since Scripture testifies that, at Jeroboal’s prayer, fire came down from heaven, and again, when Elijah prayed, fire was sent which consumed the sacrifice (Judg. VI, 21), do not consider the merits of the persons, but the offices of the priests.” But among heretics there are neither merits nor offices. St Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old Testament* (III Kings XVIII, 38): “By this it is shown that the Holy Spirit follows not the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the order of transmission, [Col. 0842D] so that, though someone may possess good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he has been ordained, in order to perform the office of ministry.”

Therefore, since merits are not to be considered but at least offices, because no one can bless unless he has been ordained so as to exercise the office of ministry, how can heretics bless where the office of ministry does not subsist—an office which, by withdrawing from the Church, they have lost in the Lord’s sight? But, conversely, Augustine says in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* (vol. III): “Even if someone is removed from office because of some fault, he will not lack the sacrament of the Lord once conferred, although it remains unto judgment.” Likewise, in his work against Parmenianus (bk. II, ch. 13, vol. IX, col. 45):

“What some say—that one who withdraws from the Church does not lose the baptism he received, but loses the right to give what he received—is plainly said in vain and without reason in many ways. First, because no cause is shown why one who cannot lose baptism itself should be able to lose the right to give it. For each is a sacrament, and each is given to a person through a certain consecration: the former when he is baptized, the latter when he is ordained. Therefore neither may lawfully be repeated for a Catholic. For when persons coming from that very party, even leaders, were received for the sake of peace after the error of schism had been corrected, and it was judged necessary for them to exercise the same offices which they had exercised, they were not ordained again. Rather, just as baptism remained intact in them, so too did ordination; for the defect had been in the severance, which was corrected by the unity of peace, not in the sacraments, which, wherever they are, are themselves.”

Likewise, against the Donatists [Col. 0843B] (*On Baptism*, bk. IV, ch. 4, vol. IX, col. 124):

“Just as I seem to be pressed when someone says to me, ‘Then a heretic remits sins when he baptizes according to you,’ so I press in turn when I say, ‘Then an avaricious pretender to religion remits sins.’ If this is by the power of God’s sacrament, then both the one and the other do so; if by their own merit, then neither the one nor the other does so. For that sacrament is acknowledged to be Christ’s even in evil persons; but in the body of the one dove—incorrupt, holy, chaste, having neither spot nor wrinkle—neither the one nor the other is found.”

Likewise he says: “Since baptism given through a contemptible man has as much force as baptism given through an Apostle, it is recognized to belong neither to the one nor to the other, but to Christ.”

But because the right to give baptism is so broad a sacrament [Note: [Col. 0843D] Another reading: “wide.”] that it is granted even to laypersons if necessity requires, [Col. 0843C] let us see whether the ordination of heretics, intact as stated in giving baptism, is likewise intact in consecrating the body of Christ.

Jerome says in his dialogue *Against the Luciferians*: “As Christ is the one who baptizes here, so he is the one who sanctifies here.” And shortly afterwards: “I ask you,” he says, “either grant permission to offer sacrifice to one whose baptism you approve, or reject the baptism of one whom you do not consider a priest. For it cannot happen that one who is holy in baptism should be a sinner at the altar.”

Therefore, since one who withdraws from the Church through heresy or schism does not lose the sacraments of holy orders—which, wherever they are found, he administers, like an ecclesiastical sinner, not through his own [Col. 0843D] merit, since neither is found in the body of the one dove, but through the power of the sacraments themselves—the priesthood remains wholly intact among heretics, although unto judgment; since, as Jerome says, they must be granted permission to offer sacrifice equally with permission to baptize.

Likewise, since Augustine maintains that one withdrawing from the Church can no more lose the order to give baptism than baptism itself, because each sacrament is given to a person through a certain consecration and may not be repeated for a Catholic; and since he confirms this by ecclesiastical practice, saying that those coming from that party were not ordained again in order to exercise the same offices that they had exercised, [Col. 0844A] but that, as baptism, so ordination remained intact in them: who can doubt that heretics possess an intact administration of the sacrifice? If it is believed to be lost, it must be repeated—which is impious—and the priesthood itself can be intact in no other way than by being unimpaired both in baptizing and in offering sacrifice.

Hence Leo, to the bishops of the Moors (12, no. 6, col. 665): “Even Maximus, although he was improperly ordained from the laity, nevertheless, if he is no longer a Donatist, we do not exclude him from the episcopal dignity which he acquired in whatever manner.” Likewise, to the same persons: “Donatus Seiacensis, who, as we have learned, has converted from the Novatians together with his people, we wish to preside over the Lord’s flock on the condition that he condemn the error of Novatus’s doctrine.” Behold: for these heretics, with Leo’s approval, ordination was not repeated upon their return [Col. 0844B] but remained intact. Since it was episcopal ordination, who would deny that it remained intact for offering sacrifice, when it was regarded as intact even for consecrating priests?

## CHAPTER XI. That the sacrifice of heretics is also salutary if Catholics communicate in it with purity.

Augustine himself plainly approves this, testifying that among heretics the sacrifice is not merely true and holy, but also salutary. Thus he writes in his dialogue against Petilianus (bk. II, ch. 30, vol. IX, col. 237):

“Petilianus said: ‘If anyone has memorized the words of a priest’s chant, is he therefore a priest because with a sacrilegious mouth he publicly utters the priest’s chant?’ Augustine: [Col. 0844C] You say this as though we were asking who is a true priest, rather than what is true baptism. For, in order that someone be a true priest, he must be clothed not only with the sacrament but also with righteousness, as it is written: ‘Let your priests be clothed with righteousness’ (Ps. CXXXI, 9). But one who is a priest by the sacrament alone, although he himself is not truthful, nevertheless gives what is true, provided that he gives not his own but God’s. If the Apostle himself bore witness to the testimony of some unknown foreigner because he found it true, why, when we find anything that is Christ’s and true in anyone—although the person in whom it is found is perverse and deceitful—should we not distinguish the defect which the person has from the truth which he possesses, not as his own but as God’s, [Col. 0844D] and say: ‘This sacrament is true,’ just as the Apostle said, ‘This testimony is true’?”

Likewise: “But you must inevitably remain always in error as long as, because of human faults, you violate God’s sacraments; or you suppose that, because of God’s sacraments—which we do not wish to violate even in you—we ourselves assume the sacrilege of your schism.” Likewise (ch. 48, col. 253): “Saul did not possess innocence, yet he possessed holiness—not the holiness of his own life, but that of God’s sacrament, which is holy even in evil persons.” Likewise (ch. 52, col. 255):

“We say that the sacrifice is to each person such as is the person who approaches to offer it, and such as is the person who approaches to receive it; and that those eat from the sacrifices of such persons who approach them in the same condition as those persons. Thus, if an evil person offers to God and a good person receives from it, it is to each such as each person is; for that too is written: ‘All things are clean to the clean’ (Titus I, 15). By this truthful and Catholic judgment, neither were you defiled by Optatus’s sacrifice if his deeds displeased you. Certainly his bread was bread of mourning, beneath whose injustices all Africa mourned; but your common bread of mourning is made so by the evil of schism shared by you all.”

Likewise, against Parmenianus (bk. II, ch. 10, col. 39): “In all questions we advise that it be understood that, although all sacraments harm those who administer them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons, just as does the word of God. Hence it was said: ‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do’ [Col. 0845B] (Matt. XXIII, 3).”

Therefore, since the saints maintain that all sacraments, because they are Christ’s, are true and holy both among heretics and Catholics, and further testify that the same sacraments are salutary for those who use them with purity, because all things are clean to the clean; while they nevertheless also declare them defiled because they are handled by one whose soul is defiled: careful attention must be given to the discernment by which Catholics are to receive them, lest heresy obtain a wicked authority in the Church if no principle of choosing or rejecting distinguishes heretics from Catholics in their sacraments.

The Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a person sins, being self-condemned” (Titus III, [Col. 0845C] 10). Though this must always be observed spiritually with respect to every heretic, and sometimes bodily as well, a more discerning course must be taken with prelates and with those who can disturb the peace of the Church. For when it is canonically established that, if a pastor deviates from the faith, he must first be corrected secretly by his subjects, and if, God forbid, he proves incorrigible, he is to be accused: how meanwhile is he to be avoided by his subjects, although the Apostle commands that one not even eat with such a person, when canonical order directs that not even an accused person be prohibited from communion unless he delays appearing for judgment?

Accordingly, it must be understood that, if not bodily, they ought at least spiritually to avoid consenting to him, just as Augustine said a little above: “You were not defiled by Optatus’s sacrifice if his deeds [Col. 0845D] displeased you.” Behold, these persons knew that Optatus was schismatic; but because [Note: [Col. 0845D] Another reading: “they.”] they did not consent to his communion, they remained undefiled. Concerning him, moreover, because he could disturb the peace of the Church, Augustine says to Emeritus (87, no. 4, vol. II, col. 209): “We do not blame you if, at that time, you did not wish to excommunicate Optatus, lest, once excommunicated, he should draw many away with him and sever your communion in the madness of schism.”

Why, then, does Augustine not blame the temporary toleration of Optatus’s communion, unless because he judged it more useful to avert the worse scandal that Optatus would inflict upon the Church? Hence Augustine again says:

“Those to whom evil persons are pleasing in unity themselves share fellowship with evil persons; but those to whom they are displeasing, and who cannot correct them, do not root up the wheat together with the tares. They communicate not in their deeds but at the altar; so that not only are they not defiled by them, but they deserve praise by divine words, because for the good of unity they tolerate what they hate for the good of unity.”

This must be observed with the greatest caution, especially in the sacraments of heretics and schismatics. For although it belongs to the perfect to tolerate evil persons without blemish in their conduct, it is difficult for others, if they act without caution, not to be corrupted by their example. Eleazar, refusing even under threat of death to feign eating swine’s flesh (II Macc. VI, 18), feared that, though the act would not harm him by sin, it might harm others by the example of suspicion. Hence Ambrose, giving sound counsel, says: [Col. 0846B] “If there is any Church which does not possess the foundations of apostolic truth, it must be abandoned, lest it be able to bring some stain upon you.”

Thus, in avoiding the wickedness of the depraved, one must consider the necessity of one’s own salvation and that of one’s brethren: so that good persons may tolerate the depraved lest they destroy the Church’s unity, and may also flee them bodily lest, through either consent or public impression, they neglect their own salvation or that of their brethren.

## CHAPTER XII. How the statements of the saints concerning the disapproval of heretical sacrifices are to be resolved.

It has been established that the sacraments of heretics, because they are Christ’s, are beneficial to Catholics if they use them discerningly; yet it must certainly be known that they are harmful and deadly to the heretics themselves [Col. 0846C] and to their accomplices. For, as Augustine says to Peter the subdeacon, fellowship in ecclesiastical society is so powerful for salvation that even baptism does not save the person to whom it is not given where it ought to be given.

Hence the African Council, ch. 24: “In the Church all sacraments are received healthfully and life-givingly; but for those persisting in heresy they acquire a great penalty of condemnation, so that what would be more luminous for them unto life in truth may be darker and more ruinous in error. The same sacraments, true and holy everywhere, are received healthfully in the Church and damnably outside the Church.”

Hence blessed Augustine calls Optatus’s sacrifice—which he had declared clean for the clean—bread of mourning [Col. 0846D] because it defiled those for whom, outside the Church, there was no place for the true sacrifice. It is also called by the saints abominable to the Lord, not with respect to that which is holy in it, but with respect to those who are equally condemned by unlawfully offering and receiving it, as though they were perpetrating something abominable to God. The saints also call it sacrilegious, defiled, void, and false.

It is sacrilegious because, just as gold is genuine in a thief’s chest as in a king’s treasury, yet sacrilegious because unlawfully appropriated by a thief, so too is this sacrifice when appropriated by heretics. It is defiled, not because it is so in itself, but just as a day is called joyful because it makes people joyful, so the sacrifice is called defiled because it defiles more—making [Col. 0847A] its offerer guilty—than it cleanses by justifying. It is void and false because it does not confer the effect of salvation which it appears to promise, though it would confer it if it were properly performed. Hence God also says: “I will curse your blessings” (Mal. II, 2), depriving them of the fruit of salvation.

When it is said that the body of Christ is not that which a schismatic makes, because the Eucharist cannot be made among such persons, this must not be understood as though he does not make the essentially true body of Christ in the sacrament. Rather, because at the altar the Church is made one body with Christ and shares in his sacrament, the schismatic does not make the whole body of Christ—that is, the head together with its members—because, being outside the Church, he does not unite himself to Christ and the Church in the sacrament of each. For since the altar-sacrifice, signifying [Col. 0847B] the unity of the Church herself and of Christ, is the sacrament of Christ’s whole body, Christ is not made there where the whole is not made. Thus the Eucharist does not take place there where the grace of unity of the whole Lord’s body is not administered.

Hence Augustine: “Heretics seek division, whereas this bread signifies unity.” And elsewhere: “Whoever receives the mystery of unity and does not maintain the bond of peace receives the mystery not for himself but as testimony against himself. Therefore neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit is among them by grace, though he is everywhere by essence.” Hence Jerome, on the prophet Amos (vol. VI, col. 303): “God hates the sacrifices of heretics, casts them away from himself, and whenever they assemble in his name, he detests their stench and closes his nostrils. He says this in a human manner of speaking: not because God disapproves his holy things, but because he does not receive their propitiation.”

These statements, therefore, and any others found spoken by the saints against the sacraments of heretics in condemnatory terms, are not to be expounded as disapproving their truth or holiness, since all are wholly Christ’s; rather, they redound to the wickedness and condemnation of those who unlawfully appropriate them.

## CHAPTER XIII. Whether sacraments are properly performed if, in their solemn words, something contrary to the faith is inserted through carelessness or heresy.

The question is raised whether, since solemn words and invocation of the divine name possess such power that they accomplish all the Church’s sacraments, the sacraments are still properly accomplished if some flaw of error sounds forth in them through the deliberate intention or negligence of the speaker. It must therefore be understood that the Church so condemns the sacraments of those who sin faithlessly by remaining silent or by uttering incorrectly what they ought to say in the solemn words that it either repeats them as reckoning them null, or completes them as imperfect; yet in such a way as to acknowledge and approve what is true in them.

Hence Augustine, in *On Baptism* (bk. I, ch. 8, vol. IX, col. 85):

“Those who separate themselves from the society of others, violate charity, and break the bond of unity, are separated in all things if they do none of those things which they received in unity. Therefore, if one whom they associate with themselves returns to the Church, he must receive all that he has not received. But if they do some of the same things, they have not separated themselves in those things, and in that respect they remain joined to the Church. Therefore, if anyone associated with them wishes to come to the Church, he is healed in that point in which he wandered while torn apart; but where he was soundly joined, he is not cured but acknowledged. Thus the Church baptizes outright laypersons coming from the Paulianists, who reject the name of the Trinity—not, I would say, as baptized, but as merely washed with water. But it does not repeat the baptism of Arians and other heretics, because they invoke the name of the Trinity; rather, it completes it with repentance and the laying on of hands. For it must be known that all sacraments are completed by faith, since, as the Apostle says, ‘with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ [Col. 0848A] (Rom. X, 10).”

Likewise Augustine: “Whence does water have such power, that it touches the body and cleanses the heart, except because the word works it? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.”

It is therefore clear that, since in performing sacraments one must both speak and believe, both must be done sincerely; above all, lest the mind waver in faith, even if the tongue errs carelessly in speech. For the Lord weighs our outward things less than the inward things of the heart; in every action he examines more closely not what is done, but with what intention or faith it is done.

Hence Augustine, in his exposition of the First Epistle of John, ch. 7 (*Tractate* VII, vol. III, col. 875): “If the Father handed over the Son, and the Son handed over himself, what did Judas do? The handing over was done by the Father, by the Son, and by Judas. One deed was done; but what distinguishes them? [Col. 0848C] The Father and the Son did this in love, but Judas in betrayal. You see that one must consider not what a person does, but with what mind and will he does it.”

Likewise, in his homilies: “‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (Matt. XVI, 16). Peter said this and heard: ‘You are Simon Bar-Jonah.’ The demons also said it and heard: ‘Be silent’ (Luke IV, 35). The utterance is one, but the Lord questions the root, not the flower.”

Likewise Jerome, on Hosea, vol. VI, col. 93: “They offer sacrilegious bread, etc. If these are truly performed, I interpret them as burnt offerings; but when they have abandoned the knowledge of God, they boast in vain that they retain the remaining members after the head of faith has been cut off.”

It is therefore evident that, if by silence or by mingling heresy into the solemn words [Col. 0848D] they introduce error, their sacrament is mutilated either in truth or in usefulness, as Ambrose testifies in the book *On the Initiation of Catechumens*. For, according to the Apostle, “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23); and it benefits neither those who perform it nor those for whom they perform it, but is unto judgment.

But if words of error are inserted through carelessness, negligence, or ignorance, the sacrament is not thereby to be believed less effective. For, as was said above, God questions the root of true faith, not the flower of speech. Hence Augustine, *On Baptism*, bk. VI, ch. 25, no. 47, vol. IX, col. 175:

“If water is not sanctified when an unskilled sinner pours out some words of error, then many not only evil but even good brethren in the Church itself do not sanctify [Col. 0849A] water. For the prayers of many are corrected daily if they are recited to more learned persons, and many things contrary to the Catholic faith are found in them. If it becomes known that some were baptized when those prayers were said, are they ordered to be baptized anew? Why not? Because the disposition of the person praying commonly outweighs the defect of the prayer; and because all [Note: [Col. 0849D] Another reading: “certain.”] those Gospel words, without which baptism cannot be consecrated, have such force that by them whatever is said in the faulty prayer against the rule of faith is so nullified as a demon is expelled by the name of Christ.
