Thus, if anyone produces prayers contrary to the rule of faith, believing them to be good, what is perverse in them does not nullify what is correct there; rather, it is nullified by the correct things.”

[Col. 0849B] Likewise Pope Zachary to Bishop Boniface:

“Your messengers reported that there was in that province a priest who was entirely ignorant of the Latin language; and, while baptizing, not knowing how to speak Latin and corrupting the language, he said: ‘I baptize you in the name of the fatherland [*patria*], and of the daughter [*filia*], and of the holy spirit [*spiritua sancta*].’ On this account your reverend brotherhood considered rebaptizing. But, most holy brother, if the one who baptized did not introduce error or heresy, but said this solely through ignorance of Roman speech, corrupting the language as we stated above, we cannot agree that they should be baptized anew.”

Behold: Augustine does not permit persons baptized with prayers spoken contrary to the faith to be baptized again, because the disposition of the one praying outweighs the defect of the prayer; and Zachary, though the very words without which baptism cannot properly be performed were corrupted, forbids rebaptism because the baptizer did not introduce heresy. Yet, if heresy had been introduced, they surely would have needed to be baptized again, because the name of the Trinity would not have been truly uttered.

Hence also, as was said above, although Pope Nicholas, in reply to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, maintains—Ambrose also testifying—that baptism in the name of the Trinity or only in the name of Christ is one and the same, Pope Pelagius, conversely, prohibits it because he saw heresy introduced by this practice. Writing to Bishop Gaudentius, he says:

“Many assert that they are baptized only in the name of Christ, and with a single immersion. But the Gospel command, handed down by the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ himself, admonishes us to give holy baptism to each person in the name of the Trinity, with a threefold immersion, our Lord Jesus Christ saying to his disciples: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ [Col. 0849D] (Matt. XXVIII, 19). If perhaps they truly confess that the aforementioned heretics, said to dwell in places neighboring your jurisdiction, were baptized only in the name of Christ, then, without any ambiguity of doubt, you shall baptize them in the name of the holy Trinity when they come to the Catholic faith.”

He says this because perhaps these heretics, like the Paulianists, rejected the name of the Trinity. He therefore ordered them to be baptized again in the name of the Trinity, lest they think they could be baptized in the Lord’s name as though in the name of a single person only [Col. 0850A]—something Pope Nicholas permitted where it could be done without danger of heresy.

But Augustine, conversely, says in *On the One Baptism*: “We have sufficiently shown that, for baptism consecrated by Gospel words, the error of the one giving or receiving it is irrelevant, whether he thinks otherwise concerning the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit than heavenly doctrine teaches.” Behold: these heretics, because they thought otherwise, were ordered to be baptized again after their previous baptism had been nullified, because, though they were baptized in the Lord’s name, they were not baptized in the name of the Trinity.

Hence Gregory, to Bishop Quirinus in Ireland (bk. XI, ep. 67, vol. II, col. 1167): “Heretics who are not baptized at all in the name of the Trinity, such as the Bonosiacs and Cataphrygians, are baptized when they come to the holy Church, because what they did not receive in the name of the holy Trinity while established in error was not baptism. Nor can the baptism be said to be repeated when it was not given in the name of the Trinity.”

Likewise Pope Innocent, in chapter fifty, when ordering those coming from the Paulianists to be baptized again, added the reason: “Because,” he says, “the Paulianists do not baptize at all in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” But an objection is raised: if baptism consecrated in God’s name without the name of the Trinity is judged invalid, then invocation of the divine name is nullified, and the wickedness of evil persons violates Christ’s sacrament—something prohibited by many holy authorities.

But, conversely, it must be understood that what those established in error do contrary to Christ’s institution is not Christ’s sacrament, nor is it a true invocation of the divine name; because the fullness of the Christian faith is endangered contrary to Christ’s command. Nor is the very name “Lord” or “God” true when adulterated by the infidelity of the speaker: it indeed sounds the word “God,” but means something else according to the heresy. That is, the heretic who rejects faith in the Trinity restricts the name “God” or “Lord” to the singularity of one person only, or presumes to fashion for himself a god according to some various heresy. Therefore, just as the saints do not say that those petition in the Saviour’s name who petition contrary to salvation, so those do not invoke the Lord’s name who do this contrary to the faith by changing the Church’s rite.

Therefore, when ecclesiastical words are changed [Col. 0850D] and error or heresy is introduced, where there is neither faith nor words of faith, how can the truth of the sacrament be thought to subsist? Hence Augustine, to Emeritus (vol. II, col. 212): “The sacraments which you have not changed are approved by us as you possess them.” And shortly afterwards: “Those things which schismatics and heretics possess and perform no differently from the true Church, when they come to us we do not correct but approve.” Likewise, to Vincentius (ep. 87, vol. II, col. 212): “All the Lord’s sacraments come from the Catholic Church, which you possess and give as they were possessed and given before you went out from it.”

In this connection it should be noted that, if the sacraments of heretics are changed from the rite which the Church established and maintains, Catholics must not approve them; for once changed, they are no longer ecclesiastical but heretical. Thus Innocent, Pelagius, and Gregory rejected the baptism of heretics performed in any name of God whatever, because they saw that it was altered from ecclesiastical institution and not celebrated in the name of the Trinity. But if the solemn words are not changed and are properly uttered, and the sacrament itself is properly carried out, then the perfidy of heretics does not obstruct the sacrament’s truth; for what heretics possess and do no differently from the true Church is not corrected by Catholics but approved.

Hence Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Rules*: “If any have been baptized among those heretics who baptize in confession of the holy Trinity [Col. 0851B] and come to the Catholic Church, let them be received as baptized, lest invocation or confession of the holy Trinity be nullified in the sacraments.”

Thus error of heart harms the performance of sacraments when words contrary to faith are uttered in the prayer, because the disposition of the one praying is not then superior to those words in faith; but it does not harm when the words themselves are uttered without any change from the Church’s use. But if error of heart is absent, a variation in the utterance of the words or execution of the sacraments does not harm; for the disposition of the person praying outweighs the words even if they are contrary to faith, and, where faith is one, diverse Church custom does no harm.

Hence, though Pelagius orders heretics baptized in Christ’s name with one immersion to be baptized again with three immersions, blessed Gregory nonetheless approves one immersion as well as three. [Col. 0851C] Yet he commends this differing Church custom where the faith is one, indicating that, where faith is one, a differing administration of the sacrament does not obstruct it. For he says to Bishop Leander (bk. I, ep. 43, vol. II, col. 532):

“Concerning the threefold immersion in baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have judged: in one faith, a differing custom of the Church does no harm. But because we immerse three times, we signify the sacrament of the three days’ burial, so that when the infant is brought up from the water for the third time, the resurrection after three days may be expressed. If anyone should think that this is also done for reverence toward the supreme Trinity, neither does anything oppose immersing the baptized person once in water, because in three persons there is one substance. It can in no way be blameworthy to immerse an infant either three times or once in baptism, since in three immersions the persons of the Trinity may be designated, while in one immersion the singularity of the Godhead may be designated.”

Therefore, since Pelagius prescribes only threefold immersion for heretics, while holy Gregory approves both threefold and single immersion where there is one faith; since Nicholas allows baptism in Christ’s name to be valid, while Pelagius commands that it be repeated for heretics: it is evident that a change in sacramental words or acts which is granted as valid among the faithful is judged invalid among heretics.

For one who baptized “in the name of the fatherland [*patria*], and of the daughter [*filia*], and of the holy spirit [*spiritua sancta*],” if he had believed as those words sound, would undoubtedly have erred; and by thus erring he would have nullified the truth of the sacrament by the name. For if he believed that the holiness and saving effect of baptism consisted in the dwelling-place of some fatherland—as the Donatists believed that only the African [Col. 0852A] Church was Catholic, and the Jews regarded Judea as the place of sanctification—or in the marriage of some daughter, or in some female saint, who would not judge this to be heresy? Who would believe baptism to be consecrated by words so profane? Yet because the simplicity and faith of the speaker excused these words uttered contrary to faith, the truth of baptism remained valid, Zachary permitting it.

It must therefore be understood that, although in all sacraments all that has been solemnly instituted ought to be said and done faithfully and attentively, yet if, God forbid, something happens differently through carelessness among the faithful, it is not to be judged invalid. For, as was said, the disposition of the person praying prevails, and the sequence of Gospel words properly uttered nullifies even the other matters mingled in contrary to faith.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why baptism was instituted to be performed in the name of the Trinity.

The question is raised why Christ wished baptism, above other names of God, to be consecrated especially in the name of the Trinity, so that baptism performed in other names of God apart from the faith is invalid, while baptism consecrated in the name of the Trinity is valid even apart from faith in the Trinity.

But, conversely, it must be understood that what is consecrated in his name without faith or any merit is valid; this is so, as said above, in order that all sacraments may be reckoned as belonging to his grace. But he especially willed this to occur in the name of the Trinity because therein lies the perfection and summit of the Christian faith: it contains the mystery of the Son’s generation from the Father and of the Holy Spirit’s procession from both; and it belongs so properly to the true God that from the beginning of time it has not been communicated to any false god.

For, as the Apostle says, “Though there are indeed many gods and many lords” (I Cor. VIII, 5), nevertheless in none besides him could one be found who might be called three and one. This name, concealed from the beginning of time under varied figures of mysteries, is marvelous not merely because it is new, but unspeakable also because of the mystery of the divine majesty: for in it what is three does not exceed unity, and what is one does not remove trinity.

Therefore, so that he might call us back and distinguish us from the error of false gods, he granted to reveal the fullness of this faith as well as the fullness of grace for washing away every sin in baptism—not through a name shared with false gods, but through the proper name of the Trinity, belonging to the true God alone. Because he gave it new for renewing human beings and perfect for bringing them to completion, he willed it also to be valid and certain against the subtleties of heretics.

Therefore, by the new name of the Trinity he instituted that the new faith of Christianity be given in baptism: so that from that from which it receives the beginning of regeneration, it may obtain the effect of renewal; and so that it might hold more certainly and strongly against all heresies that faith without which it would know that entrance is open to none, whether into the Church or the heavenly country. He also willed that Christian regeneration be initiated and consecrated by the new name of the Trinity [Col. 0853A] so that, through what had not been revealed in any earlier age, the faith of the nascent Church might shine with so much greater merit and reward as it was instructed in a mystery of greater divine knowledge—a mystery whose revelation to humankind had been reserved by privilege for the Son of God alone.

Hence the prophet himself says: “Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I who spoke—behold, I am present” (Isa. LII, 6). Likewise in the Gospel: “Father, I have manifested your name to humankind” (John XVII, 6). Although the saints in earlier ages believed in the Trinity, without faith in which they could not be saved, they did not believe it so manifestly as in the fullness of grace; for, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke [Col. 0853B] X, 24), because it had not been revealed to them.

Thus Christ, foreshadowing that baptism was to be proclaimed and consecrated by faith in and the name of the Trinity, when he was baptized, the voice of the Father was heard testifying that the Son was pleasing to him; the Holy Spirit was seen above him in the form of a dove (Matt. III, 17). Thus the Church might believe that the Trinity is not absent from her own baptism, since she had recognized the Trinity as bodily present also at the baptism of Christ, her head: hearing the Father in the sound, seeing the Son present in the flesh, and seeing the Holy Spirit present in the form of a dove.

Upon the firmness of this faith Christ, intending to found his Church, replied to Peter, the shepherd of his Church, when he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16)—because in this he had perfectly understood the Trinity—“And I say to you: you are Peter, and upon this rock,” that is, upon the firmness of this faith, “I will build my Church” (ibid.) [Col. 0853C]. Hence also God the Father says through the prophet: “I will place in Zion a precious cornerstone, firmly founded in the foundation; whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 28:16) [Col. 0854A]. Likewise Paul: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation; but no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:10). For in Christ the whole Trinity is understood, as Bede testifies in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles.

Since the rule of the Church is that the faithful be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, how is it that Luke, throughout the text of this little book, testifies that baptism is given only in the name of Jesus Christ? Ambrose resolves this by saying that the mystery has been fulfilled through the comprehensiveness of the Name: for whether you say “Christ,” you have designated God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed; the Son himself, who was anointed; and the Spirit by whom he was anointed. For it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth—how God anointed him with his Spirit” (Acts 10:38) [Col. 0854B]. Or, whether you say “the Father,” you have indicated the Father, his Son, and the Holy Spirit together, provided that you also grasp this in your heart. Or, whether you say “the Spirit,” you have named God the Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, and the Son also, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well. Therefore, since Christ ordains that his Church be founded in faith in and in the name of the Trinity, who, by acting otherwise against this institution—an institution authorized both prophetically and evangelically, and apart from which the Apostle declares that no one can lay another foundation—can accomplish anything valid or true?

Therefore, in celebrating Christ’s sacraments, let us strive not to introduce the novelties or heresies of sects, but faithfully to serve his institutions, so that what we do in them may be true through his power, valid through his authority, and experienced by us as saving through his grace [Col. 0854C]. He who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0853]

# Of the Blessed Alger, Scholastic of Liège, On the Sacrifice of the Mass

[Note: [Col. 0853] From the Most Eminent and Reverend A. Mai, *New Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. IX, p. 371, and Paris, Royal Library, Latin manuscript no. 812.]

[Col. 0853D] The solemn celebration of the whole Mass was instituted in order to express the remembrance of Christ’s coming in the flesh and to represent anew his Passion in mystery. Thus, those elements first set forth—from the entrance of the Mass until the secret prayers which the priest, speaking to himself, pours forth—represent the coming of the Lord and the times of evangelical preaching. First, the secret prayers offered over the gifts represent the threefold prayer which, before his Passion, the Saviour poured out to the Father, saying: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39).

[Col. 0854D] There also it is read that the Lord sweated blood and, being in agony, prayed more earnestly, plainly indicating how great must be the contrition of heart and anxiety of spirit with which a sinful priest ought to offer to God the sacrifice of prayer, since the priest of righteousness, about to offer himself, sent forth prayers to the Father not without the shedding of blood, and thereby clearly displayed the compassion he bears toward us. The priest under the Law did the same, entering the Holy of Holies never without blood, since, according to the Apostle, without shedding of blood there is no remission.

[Col. 0855A] Afterwards our priest greets the people in a raised voice; he exhorts them to lift up their hearts and give thanks to the Lord, expressing what the Lord, returning to his disciples, said: “Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation” (Matt. 26). There follows that heavenly hymn: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” which the living creatures are said to have sung in the Old Testament. This shows that, at the hour of sacrifice, the angelic spirits are present, rendering due reverence to the divine mysteries.

Next our priest begins the *Te igitur*; and, as though entering the Holy of Holies, he first pours out a general prayer for the whole Church, making the sign of the cross and sprinkling that offering with Christ’s blood. For as often as he places the likeness of the cross upon the heavenly sacrifice [Col. 0855B], so often he sprinkles the offering set forth with Christ’s blood. He calls the things offered first *gifts* (*dona*), because they are given to us by the Father of lights; second, *offerings* (*munera*), because by those gifts we make an offering to the one who prays; third, *sacrifices* (*sacrificia*), because through them we are both washed from sins and, reconciled, have peace with God.

The second prayer in the Canon is made for those who have either offered bread for the sacrifice or stand around the sacred mysteries. In the third prayer he humbly implores the suffrages of the saints and, as though bringing in coals of fire according to the Law, lays upon them the incense of heartfelt prayer, so that, in the manner of the heavenly high priest, a cloud of compunction may overshadow the offering set forth. In the fourth place the priest prays that the offering may be made, first, blessed, so that through it we may be filled with every heavenly blessing [Col. 0855C]; second, enrolled, so that through its efficacy we may be enrolled in the book of the living; third, ratified, so that through its effect, rooted or grounded in faith, we may never be torn away from the love of God.

He then recites the words of the Lord, which Christ is reported to have spoken at supper, by whose power and grace the Catholic faith confesses that bread is changed into flesh and wine transformed into blood. Why, however, is the cup said to be the cup of the blood of the new and eternal covenant? It is so called because by faith in the blood of Jesus Christ we are promised both the washing away of sins and the attainment of the heavenly kingdom. Each is called new and eternal because, while it cleanses us from sins, it renews us; and while it grants us the kingdom, it transfers us, the corruptible mutability having been removed, to eternal incorruptibility [Col. 0855D].

Moreover, it is a mystery of faith because Christian faith holds that under the appearance of bread and wine there is the reality of flesh and blood. For that mystery is at once both sacrament and the thing of the sacrament: outwardly it presents indeed the color and taste of bread and wine, but inwardly it supplies to the eyes of faith the substance of flesh and blood. Subsequently the priest says that this visible victim is pure, because it cleanses from vices; holy, because it bestows upon the elect the grace of virtues; undefiled [Col. 0856A], because it grants to the righteous the glory of incorruptibility.

The priest prays that the sacrifice may be accepted as was Abel’s gift, whose innocence and life signify Christ’s innocence; as was Abraham’s sacrifice, which intimates the holiness of the Lord’s Passion; and as was Melchizedek’s offering, which in bread and wine prefigures the Church’s daily sacrifice. Meanwhile the priest humbly prays the Lord to command these things to be carried by the hands of his holy angel to his sublime altar, so that the mystery may be evident at that hour: that this bread is united to the Lord’s body and joined to it in the communion of one substance. Then he also kisses the altar, to show that he wishes to become a participant in the same sacrament; and, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he prepares himself to receive the mystery. He prays for the departed [Col. 0856B], then also for himself; and at the end, inserting the names of the saints, he represents, like another Aaron, the names of the twelve patriarchs engraved upon his breast.

There follows: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things”: by bringing forth from bread the substance of flesh; you sanctify them, by filling them with the spiritual abundance of virtues; you bless them, by granting the efficacy of every grace. Next he removes the corporal, and, making a cross from that consecrated bread over the chalice, shows Christ’s crucifixion; then, laying it again upon the altar and covering it with the corporal, he represents the Lord’s burial for three days. There he also says that this sacrament of power is accomplished for us through him who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach; with him who rules and orders all things; and in him in whom we live, move [Col. 0856C], and have our being.

The Lord’s Prayer follows, but “deliver us”; at its end the priest divides the Lord’s bread into three portions. The first he places in the chalice; the middle portion he keeps for himself; the last he offers to those who are to communicate. The breaking of the bread signifies Christ’s Passion, in which the temple of his body was broken and dissolved, and which divine power raised up after three days. The chalice signifies the Lord’s tomb, in which Christ, swallowed by death as Jonah was in the belly of the whale, lay for three days in the heart of the earth.

The first portion, which is mingled with the blood, prays for those who have already put off their bodies but, being bound by the vices of their bodies, have within themselves something that ought to be examined and purified by purgatorial punishment. The middle portion prays for those [Col. 0856D] who are still alive in the flesh and, as it were, placed in the middle, can by freedom of their will turn wherever they wish, to the right or to the left. The third portion gives thanks for the saints who, established in glory, have no need for prayer to be poured out for them. Thus Christ’s Passion, set before all, benefits the departed unto forgiveness, the living unto grace, and the saints unto glory. The same sacrament works for the good of each: it purifies the dead, justifies the living, and crowns the righteous, through the same one who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0857]

# Of the Blessed Alger, Canon of Liège: Book on Mercy and Justice

(Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, V, 1019, from a Clairvaux manuscript.)

## Preliminary Notice

We have found the book *On Mercy and Justice* by Alger, a scholastic and a man most learned in his time, in three very ancient handwritten codices: one belonging to the most celebrated Cistercian monastery of Clairvaux; another to the monastery of Villers in Brabant; and a third to the distinguished monastery of Aulne, on the river Sambre, in the diocese of Liège. Our Mabillon had formerly seen this same book in one or the other of these monasteries and intended to publish it in the second volume of his *Analecta*, had he been able to obtain a copy, as he himself attests in the preface to that volume. We, more fortunate in this respect, have received it through the kindness of the most reverend Lord Peter Bouchu, highly deserving abbot of Clairvaux, a man especially commendable for his zeal for regular observance. In his great courtesy he had it copied for us and sent it to us; we now make it public.

Alger divided this book into three parts. In the first he treats of mercy: namely, how and for how long it should be shown to the wicked. In the second, he treats of justice: namely, at what time, in what order, or with what discrimination it should be exercised against those same persons. In the third, he treats of various heresies: namely, how, in the condemnation of themselves or of their sacraments, they differ in some way from Catholics, and in some way from themselves. Whatever subject he undertakes to treat, he strives to prove and confirm by the authority of the holy Fathers or of councils. At times he quotes their words in excerpted form, not always entire, but only those passages which appear relevant to his purpose. We consider it altogether superfluous to discuss Alger at greater length, since the preface of Nicholas of Liège, which is prefixed to his works in the manuscript codices, commends him more than sufficiently.

## Here Begins the Preface of Lord Nicholas of Liège to the Books of Master Alger

(It appears above at col. 737, prefixed to the books *On the Sacrament of the Altar*.)

## Here Begins the Epistle of Master Alger of Liège

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857A] Whoever I may be, [the opening is syntactically defective: “not the burden or import of the time which Jethro [did something] to Moses, according to his measure, [to] all Catholics”], I perceive the state of the holy Church to be shaken by various errors and various schisms, because the precepts of the canons are either unknown or neglected by the wicked, while by the more simple they are understood either not according to their proper meaning or not with proper discrimination. Therefore, as almighty grace has breathed upon my desires, I have brought all these matters into view, so that devotion to what is good might be aided by discrimination of the truth, and the contentiousness of the perverse might be overcome by the clarity of canonical authority.

For canonical precepts are some of mercy and some of justice, so distinguished according to various orders, persons, and times that at one time mercy entirely remits justice, and at another justice entirely passes over mercy. Those who do not know how to temper such different things by discernment think that they oppose one another discordantly through contradiction. They fail to observe that the method of ecclesiastical government, whether it pardons or punishes, preserves the same intention of charity and the same work of salvation [Col. 0858A]. Consequently, using canonical rules uncanonically, they batter and attack precept with precept, so as at times, through undue leniency, to deprive justice of its place, and at other times, through unrestrained justice, to deprive grace of its place.

Therefore, since canonical precepts must be adapted to various persons, changing times, different orders, and varying degrees of discernment—so that a heretic, a sinner, a subject, and a prelate, and indeed anyone distinguished by differing intention, action, or condition, must each be reproved differently—I have laboured, insofar as God has granted, to distinguish these matters, so that in the canons such a unity of intention, usefulness, and truth might shine forth that none of their diversity should produce any discord of contradiction. For since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth—because pardon is due to the penitent and punishment to the hardened—I have endeavoured, by the very authorities of the sacred canons, to explain, as I could, how one should not by its own proper discrimination prejudice the other. I have shown that what is merciful must be administered only justly, and what is just only mercifully; I have distinguished, not one rule for the other nor the other for this one, but for each its own measure, according to heresy or crime, person or time, without confusing right or order, whether for judgment or for grace [Col. 0859A].

For clarity in so great a matter, I have set down, with equal authority, the deeds of the saints as well as their enactments; for, just as their precepts must be obeyed, so their deeds must be imitated. Since even the Lord Jesus began first to do and then to teach, who can believe that they taught otherwise than they acted? I have therefore divided the work into three sections: in the first [Col. 0859B] I treat of grace, namely, how and for how long it should be extended to evils that must be tolerated; in the second, of justice, namely, at what time, in what order, or with what discernment it should be exercised against those same persons; and in the third, of various heresies, namely, how in the condemnation of themselves or of their sacraments they differ—indeed in some way from Catholics, but in some way from themselves.

“But because,” as Augustine says to Jerome, “it can happen that something other than the truth may seem right to you, provided that nothing other than charity is done by you,” if I should appear perhaps to have distorted the sayings of the saints with insufficient discernment, so that I defend no authority for my error, if it is an error, I nevertheless ask charity for a reciprocal return: since I composed this little work for the sake of fraternal benefit, if what is done negligently is neglected, let not at least whatever I, however insignificant, have been able beneficially to establish from the decrees of the saints be neglected [Col. 0860A].

For, as Augustine says in his letter to Boniface, we ought not to regard the disputations of just anyone, even of Catholic and praiseworthy men, as though they were canonical Scriptures, “so that, while preserving the honour due to them, we may not be permitted to disapprove or reject something in their writings, if perhaps we find that they have thought otherwise than truth has it, either as understood through divine help by others or by ourselves. Such am I in the writings of others; such do I desire interpreters of my own to be.” Likewise Isidore, to Bishop Mason, chapter 10.

At the end of this epistle I thought it should be added that whenever a discordant opinion is found in the acts of councils, the opinion of that council should be preferred whose authority is both older and less numerous [Col. 0860B]. Therefore, when such great and distinguished men have left their own writings, the writings of others, and even the opinions of any councils to the discernment of others for examination or correction, who am I that I should dare to be angry with those who correct me—lest, by rejecting whatever good things of mine there may be, not on account of me but for themselves, they harm themselves? I have therefore taken care to mark every opinion with its own titles, so that they might be more readily found by the diligent and more plainly understood by the slow. Among them I have also inserted certain passages, as though in addition, which might aid these as if from the side and openly defend their own cause.

# Book on Mercy and Justice, Part One

[Col. 0859]

## Chapter I. That mercy is to be preferred to all precepts

[Col. 0859C]

“I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1), because the Lord himself, with ineffable discernment, either mercifully remits sins to the penitent in this life, or judges them both in this life and in the other, condemning them eternally. But because the Lord says in the Gospel, “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36); and, “Do not judge, lest you be judged” (Matt. 7:1); and James says in his epistle, “Mercy exalts itself over judgment” (Jas. 2:13): therefore the Psalmist placed mercy before judgment as that which is to be sung to God. For he saw that mercy was more necessary for all: that they might receive it from God and that all might extend it to all their fellow servants; for even the prince of the apostles fell, that he might forgive the faults of the fallen.

## Chapter II. That mercy is to be preferred even to divine observances

[Col. 0860C]

Hence Pope Callixtus, epistle 2, chapter 6, chapter 101: “Avoid not merely holding but even hearing any opinion that prohibits mercy, because mercy is preferable to all holocausts and sacrifices.”

## Chapter III. That Christ in the Gospels mercifully added indulgence and counsel to precept

Therefore, in his most merciful ordering of the Church, so that no one might find difficulty in attaining life, the Lord has established for us a threefold way, according to our various capacities and conditions: indulgence, counsel, and precept. In matters without which life cannot be attained, he imposes a general precept, that we may be saved. In matters to which human frailty is prone, and which, if they do not benefit, nevertheless do not harm, he grants indulgence, lest we perish. In matters which are not necessary for life but invite us to a greater crown, he gives counsel, that we may attain progress toward perfection.

For he gave indulgence to the frail and imperfect in the Gospel when, speaking of three kinds of eunuchs, he added at last concerning those who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven: “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19:12) [Col. 0861A]. He established both precept and counsel in the Gospel when, in answer to the young man asking what he should do to possess eternal life, he first proposed to him the precepts necessary for life. When the young man answered that he had observed all these from youth, Christ, preserving the proper order, added counsel, leaving it to his choice: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have” (Matt. 21), etc.

## Chapter IV. Likewise Paul in his Epistles

[Col. 0861B] Paul, agreeing with this view, permitted each man to have his own husband or wife as a concession; after lawful union, he commanded that neither depart from the other. But concerning virgins, regarding whom he had no precept, he gave counsel: it was good if they should be as he himself was. Therefore, of these three, indulgence and counsel are left to the choice of those who use them.

## Chapter V. That precept was relaxed with discernment even for the prophets and apostles themselves

Although precept is necessary for all, nevertheless for various reasonable causes it must very often be relaxed by canonical authority, as it has with remarkable mercy been adopted by very many saints for the salvation of their brethren. For when Nathan the prophet had commanded David to build a temple for the Lord [Col. 0861C] (1 Chron. 17:1), because he had seen him devoted to this undertaking, he afterwards forbade it; for, since David was a man of blood, he saw through revelation of the Spirit that he was not suited for it.

Likewise Paul, although he had prohibited circumcision in every respect (Acts 16:3), as a figure rendered wholly superfluous by the advent of the truth of faith, nevertheless afterwards performed it himself in Timothy. He did not do so to show that circumcision could cooperate with faith in any respect, but to destroy the error of the simple, lest anyone reckon circumcision an idolatry equally sacrilegious, when the Lord in its own time had commanded it, with great benefit, as a shadow of things to come. For though the Apostle avoided each alike, he did so for a different reason: circumcision as superfluous, idolatry [Col. 0861D] as sacrilegious.

Hence Augustine, from his letter to Jerome (Letter 82): “Paul circumcised Timothy, paid a vow at Cenchreae, and, at James’s admonition, undertook to observe the legal rites with those who knew them. He did this not because he thought Christian salvation was given through those sacraments, but to show that they ought not to be condemned as sacrilegious, although he forbade them to be sought as necessary. Since this was sufficiently shown in Timothy, Titus also, being a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised.”

## Chapter VI. That canonical precepts are, according to time, person, and varied circumstances, either partly moderated or wholly omitted

Canonical precepts are also found to be, according to time, person, and varied circumstances, either partly moderated [Col. 0862A] or wholly omitted.

## Chapter VII. A precept omitted solely out of regard for mercy because of circumstances

For although Leo says in his decrees, chapter 49 (Letter 87), that what is contained in general statutes must not be passed over in the case of any person, he nevertheless later says in the same place concerning laymen suddenly ordained bishops contrary to canonical decrees:

“The circumstances demand that fitting punishment be pronounced not only against such prelates but also against those who ordained them. But on one side the gentleness of mercy surrounds us, and on the other the severity of justice, so that we judge certain offences to be tolerable in some measure and others to be cut off altogether. Therefore we permit those whose advancement incurs only this reproach—that they were chosen from the laity for the episcopal office—to retain their position. We do not thereby prejudice the statutes of the Apostolic See or dissolve the rules of the blessed Fathers, because remission does not give licence to sin. Nor may what could be allowed for some reason be committed henceforth with impunity, lest what we have conceded for a time in merciful leniency be punished later by just retribution” [Col. 0862B].

Here Leo (ibid.), because of the circumstances—“because they had been chosen and consecrated as bishops from the laity”—spared, mercy intervening, the electors, the consecrators themselves, and those consecrated.

## Chapter VIII. Likewise, with regard to the person

Likewise Gregory, in accordance with the person’s condition, with mercy intervening, says to Bishop Januarius in his letter (Book IX, Letter 4):

“So great an evil concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still took human considerations into account, we should already strike it with a fixed curse. Indeed, a sentence was almost to be cast against you; but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, we are silent for the present.”

Yet while sparing him, he excommunicated the counsellors of this crime, saying to Bishop Januarius [Col. 0862C]: “Henceforth be more cautious concerning their counsels, lest, if you are their disciple in evil when you ought to have been their teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any longer.”

## Chapter IX. Likewise, with regard to necessity and time

Likewise Pope Innocent, when he received persons ordained by the heretic Bonosus because of the necessity of the time, lest there should be too great a scandal in the Church, says in his decrees, chapter 5 (Letter 22, no. 5):

“What has been established as a remedy and because of the necessity of the time is manifestly not the original arrangement. Therefore, what necessity discovered as a remedy ought certainly, when necessity ceases, to cease together with that which compelled it; for legitimate order is one thing, and another is the usurpation which the exigency of the present time forces” [Col. 0862D].

## Chapter X. Likewise, with regard to time

Likewise Pope Gelasius, because of the necessity of the time—seeing that the Italian Church, owing to the invasion of war and famine, had been deprived of almost every clerical office, so that many peoples lacked assistance for the redemption of souls—permitted clerics to be chosen from monks and even from laymen. He says in his decrees [Col. 0863A], chapter 1 (Letter 9 to Bishop Lucius):

“We are constrained by the necessary ordering of affairs and summoned by the moderation of the Apostolic See so to relax the decrees of the canons of the Fathers that, when the necessity of present times demands concessions for restoring churches, we may temper them by careful consideration as far as may be possible.”

Later, in chapter 2, he says:

“Therefore, while ancient institutions remain in force out of reverence for themselves—institutions which, where no hardship of circumstances or times presses, it is fitting to keep according to rule—we grant this much to churches deprived either of all ministers or of sufficient ministers, so that they cannot supply divine offices to the many people belonging to them: if anyone comes from monastic discipline to clerical office, especially from the laity, his previous life must be examined, lest he be stained by some grave crime, illiterate, a bigamist, one who has taken a woman abandoned by another, physically impaired, of servile or native condition, bound by the obligations of a municipal council or public affairs, marked by public penance, or examined without waiting the fitting period of time” [Col. 0863B].

## Chapter XI. Likewise, a precept partly moderated out of regard for mercy because of circumstances

Yet later in the same decrees, chapter 6, concerning illiterate and physically impaired persons, he says: “If any such persons have been admitted through their own rashness or through the negligence of their superiors, let them receive no further promotion, and let them consider sufficient what has been granted them through excessive mercy.”

Likewise, from the decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 15 (Letter 1 to Himerius), concerning a penitent, a twice-married man, or a husband of a widow who has become a cleric:

“We must meanwhile, solely out of regard for mercy, grant lenient pardon to anyone who as a penitent, anyone who as a twice-married man, or anyone who as the husband of a widow has improperly and incompetently intruded into sacred service. Let him understand that this pardon is granted by us on the condition that he ought to count it a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion removed from him, he remains with permanent stability in the rank in which he is found” [Col. 0863C].

## Chapter XII. Likewise, omitted out of regard for necessity

The same pope, when a serious scandal arose among fellow bishops concerning a bishop ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge, says in his letter, chapter 2:

“Since we see that whatever has been alleged by either party is confused by every kind of perversity [Col. 0863D], having regard to the necessity of the times, we decree on this ground that what has been done belongs to pardon, provided that henceforth no bishop be ordained without the knowledge and consent of the metropolitan.”

## Chapter XIII. Likewise, moderated by mercy

Likewise Pope Leo, in his decrees, chapter 15 (Letter 92, response 1):

“No reason permits persons to be accounted among bishops who have neither been elected by clerics, nor requested by the people, nor consecrated by provincial bishops with the metropolitan’s judgment. Yet if any clerics have been ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination has been performed with the consent and judgment of their superiors, it may be held valid, provided they remain in those same churches [Col. 0864A]. Otherwise such an ordination must be considered void.”

Nevertheless, the Council of Constantinople (canon 3) decrees thus concerning the unlawful ordination of Maximus: “It has seemed good that Maximus neither is nor was a bishop, nor are those whom he ordained as clerics in any rank, since all things perpetrated by him appear to have been rendered void.”

## Chapter XIV. That decrees must be curtailed by necessity or utility

Likewise Pope Gelasius, in his decrees, chapter 9 (Letter 9):

“Some things must for a time be passed over in silence, although they do not manifestly disgrace the Church; and even if such things must sometimes be passed over in silence, when the integrity of the rest is assured, they cannot by themselves be capable of causing harm. Those things, however, which cannot be received without manifest exposure must be very carefully guarded against. And if even those things which are sometimes believed allowable without any harm are excused either by regard for circumstances and times or by the need to expedite provision, how much more must those things never be curtailed which neither any necessity, nor evangelical utility, nor any utility whatever can compel?” [Col. 0864B]

For at times canonical precepts are curtailed and relaxed for the necessity or utility of the Church.

## Chapter XV. Likewise, by necessity

By necessity, as Pope Innocent testifies in his decrees, chapter 56: “Whenever sin is committed by peoples or a multitude, because punishment cannot be imposed on all on account of their number, it is accustomed to pass unpunished. I therefore say that past matters are to be left to God’s judgment and that, in what remains, the greatest care is to be taken” [Col. 0864C].

## Chapter XVI. Likewise, by utility

By utility: “Thus the Council of Meaux prohibits that children born of virgins forcibly abducted and thereby joined in marriage to their abductors be admitted to ecclesiastical orders, unless perhaps the Church’s very great utility or necessity requires them, or an evident pre-eminence of merits recommends them. With this Peter also agrees, saying: ‘In truth I have discovered that God is no respecter of persons’” (Acts 10:34), etc.

## Chapter XVII. Likewise, although absolutely no sin ought to be committed, a canonical precept is curtailed so that, in the difficulty of a greater and a lesser crime, the lesser is to be chosen

[Col. 0864D] Since, therefore, canonical precepts have been moderated by mercy, necessity, and utility in different persons by so many holy men, let us see whether the same should likewise be done in a single person beset by various difficulties. Gregory says in the *Moralia*, Book XXVI:

“When the mind is constrained between greater and lesser sins, if no way of escape wholly free from sin is open, the lesser must always be chosen. For one enclosed by a circuit of walls so that he cannot flee throws himself into flight where the wall is lower.”

## Chapter XVIII. That a shameful promise should not be performed

Hence Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book III (chapter 12): “Promise nothing dishonourable; or, if you have promised it, it is more tolerable not to perform promises than to perform what is shameful” [Col. 0865A]. Likewise in the same work: “It is, however, sometimes contrary to ecclesiastical duty to fulfil a promise or keep an oath, as Herod swore that he would give the daughter of Herod whatever she asked, and gave John’s head.”

## Chapter XIX. That a pledged word should be broken

Hence Isidore, in the *Synonyma* (Book II, chapter 10): “Break faith in evil promises, so that you may not do the shameful vow and decree which you rashly vowed. A promise fulfilled by a crime is impious.”

## Chapter XX. That an oath should not be fulfilled

Likewise Isidore elsewhere (*Sentences*, Book II, chapter 31): “It is more tolerable not to fulfil an oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication. Behold: although God commands that one not commit perjury, the saints mercifully command that one not fulfil it—not because this is excusable, but because it is more tolerable” [Col. 0865B].

## Chapter XXI. That, in order to avoid lust, vainglory may be tolerated

Hence Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 62 [38]:

“Often, when the affliction of two vices attacks, one presses more lightly and the other perhaps more grievously; aid is rightly brought with greater speed to that vice through which one hastens more quickly to destruction. Often someone oppressed by the goads of lust, frightened by fear of this struggle, tries to restrain himself through abstinence and is harassed by the temptation of vainglory. In this case one vice cannot at all be extinguished unless the other is nourished. It must therefore be tolerated that arrogance grows for the time being in a young man through the virtue of abstinence, lest lust utterly destroy him from life through gluttony [Col. 0865C].

“This is why Paul, when he saw that his hearer was weak, either still wishing to do small things or taking pleasure in the reward of human praise for right action, said: ‘Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it’ (Rom. 13:3). Good deeds are not to be done in order that the authority of this world may not be feared, or that through them the glory of passing praise may be obtained. But when Paul saw that a weak mind could not simultaneously avoid depravity and praise, he offered one and tolerated the other, so that, while the mind is left familiarly in something of its own, it may without pain endure being deprived of something else of its own.”

## Chapter XXII. Likewise, that in order to avoid pride it is expedient to fall into lust

[Col. 0865D] Likewise, if pride weighs heavily upon someone, it is better that he fall into lust. Hence Augustine, in his homilies: “Finally, my brethren, I dare say to proud persons who are continent: it is expedient for them to fall, so that they may be humbled in the very matter in which they exalt themselves. What profit is continence to one in whom pride rules? He despises that from which man was born and desires that from which the devil fell. It is better to limp on the road than to walk strongly off the road.”

Hence Augustine, in the literal exposition of Genesis, concerning the good of marriage: “It is better to possess all goods, even lesser ones, than a great evil together with a great good; for among bodily goods it is better to have Zacchaeus’s stature with health than Goliath’s with fever.”

## Chapter XXIII. Likewise, that every sin is to be admitted in order to avoid a worse one

[Col. 0866A]

Hence Augustine: “There is no sin which should not be admitted in order to avoid a worse one. For it is better to have lame children than to mourn the dead.”

## Chapter XXIV. How the remedy of pastors ought to be tempered for persons placed amid diverse difficulties
Gregory, in agreement with this discretion, says in his *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, ch. 61 [37]):

> Often a grievous illness oppresses a weak body, and it must be met with strong remedies. But a weak body cannot bear a strong remedy. Therefore the physician must compound the remedy with such discretion that he both counters the illness and does not cause life to fail.

Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0866B] “I gave you milk to drink, as little children in Christ, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). Thus Moses, coming out from the secret place of God, veils his shining face before the people, because he does not disclose the mysteries of inward brightness to the base.

And, so that we may observe how great a discretion must be applied in administering divine commands, the same Gregory in his *Pastoral Rule* describes so many persons to be admonished in different ways that the work cannot be read by one unskilled in the care of souls—which is truly the art of arts—without great astonishment. For not everything is to be preached to everyone, nor the same things to different people, but different things in different ways to different persons. Hence he says in the same work, ch. 40:

> Paul, bestowing different commands on two disciples who were not endowed with different love, says to Timothy: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort, in all patience” (1 Tim. 4:22). But to Titus: “Exhort [Col. 0866C] and rebuke with all authority” (Titus 2:15): tempering the more fervent, inflaming the gentler. And different provisions must be made not only for different persons but also for different times; for it is written: “A time to speak, a time to pluck up” (Eccl. 3:7).

As Leo says in his letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne:

> Just as there are certain things which cannot be removed on any grounds, so there are many which ought to be moderated either in view of ages or because of the necessity of circumstances.

## CHAPTER XXV. That discretion in God’s commandments must be administered through the love of God.

How great this discretion must be, and with how great a love it must be administered, the same Leo says to Athanasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Ep. 84):

> In correcting persons, [Col. 0866D] let goodwill accomplish more than severity; exhortation more than agitation; love more than authority.

Since, therefore, love ought to accomplish more than authority, the Psalmist rightly said that mercy must be sung before judgment. Yet judgment, in its proper order, must sometimes be carried out against offenders as authoritatively as it is severely. For Paul would not give patience to one person but authority in rebuking to another, unless, for the correction of the perverse, endurance sometimes prevailed even more than judgment.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That justice ought to punish those whom mercy does not correct; and that those who sin openly must be rebuked openly.

It is fitting that justice should punish those whom mercy does not correct: justice commands that the wicked be avoided, reproved, rebuked, [Col. 0867A] and accused. Distinguishing its order, method, and cause, Isidore says:

> One who is not corrected through gentle words must necessarily be rebuked more sharply when chastised. Things which cannot be healed gently must be cut away with pain.

One who, when secretly warned, neglects to amend his sin must be rebuked publicly. Those who do harm openly must likewise be reproved openly, so that, while they are healed by an open rebuke, those who had sinned by imitating them may be corrected. For it is better that one person be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through one person’s licence.

Hence Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, ch. 17 [6]):

> Let the ruler stand erect against the vices of offenders through zeal for justice, so that, when the fault of the wicked requires it, he may not fear to enforce the claims of righteousness. [Col. 0867B] For it is necessary that subjects fear him when he finds that they do not at all fear him, so that those who do not dread divine judgments may at least fear to sin through human dread.

And shortly afterward:

> Sometimes a more grievous offence is committed when, among the perverse, equality is maintained more than discipline. For Eli, overcome by false piety, would not strike his offending sons; and before the strict Judge he struck himself together with his sons by a cruel condemnation.

Hence he says in the same work, ch. 21 [10]:

> Some things must be rebuked vehemently, so that, when the offender does not recognize his fault, he may feel from the rebuker’s voice how weighty it is.

Augustine says in his homilies:

> “By their fruits you shall know them.” We are commanded to judge concerning these fruits of evil conduct—that is, manifest sins—such as fornications, blasphemies, [Col. 0867C] thefts, drunkenness, and whatever other sins there may be. But when it is said, “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” (Matt. 7:11); and, “Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Luke 6:37); and, “Do not judge before the time, until he comes who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5), we understand this to be said about matters in which it is uncertain with what intention they are done.

Likewise Augustine, in his homilies (*Sermon* 82, *On Scripture*):

> Those things which are sinned before all must themselves be rebuked before all; those which are sinned secretly must themselves be rebuked more secretly.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That some canonical decrees belong to mercy, others to justice, and that a balance must be made from both.

[Col. 0867D] Since, therefore, the Church must be governed by the discretion of mercy and justice, as Gregory says in his *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, ch. 17 [6]):

> A certain balance must be made from both, so that subjects are neither wounded by excessive harshness nor relaxed by excessive leniency.

For this reason, under the teaching of Truth, the half-dead man is brought by the Samaritan’s care into an inn, and wine and oil are applied to his wounds: the wounds are bitten by the wine and soothed by the oil. Observing this discreetly in their decrees, the saints have sometimes laid down differing rules, so that the commands of this most holy balance appear to the ignorant not balanced but wholly conflicting and contrary. For at times they bite [Col. 0868A] without soothing in any way; at times they soothe without biting in any way.

But suppose three men commit one and the same vice: one from malice, one from ignorance, one from weakness; and let one be obstinate, another broken by despair, another pierced by repentance. Must judgment be made upon all in one and the same manner? Certainly, the penitent must be assisted, the despairing raised up, and the obstinate either refuted or endured.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That, if the wicked cannot be corrected, they must be endured.

Thus Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule*, ch. 21 [10], after stating that the vices of subjects must sometimes be prudently overlooked, though made known because they are overlooked; that those openly known must sometimes be patiently endured; that hidden matters must sometimes be investigated subtly; that some faults must sometimes be reproved gently and others vehemently rebuked: [Col. 0868B] afterward he says of the obstinate:

> Those whom I cannot correct I bear like a burden laid upon me, as the Psalmist says: “Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 128:3).

Thus one lightly chastised in both discipline and imprecation shows reverence toward the one chastising him; but one offended by the harshness of rebuke receives neither the rebuke nor healing. Therefore the saints patiently endure as weak those whom they could not amend by chastisement. Those who cannot be rebuked because of their weakness must be tolerated with gentle mercy.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the wicked must be avoided.

But, on the other hand, Ambrose says elsewhere:

> Sin [Col. 0868C] which, though known, is not rebuked contaminates many—indeed, all who know of it and do not avoid it, and who, though able to rebuke it, overlook it. For a person does not think that he sins when no one reproves or avoids him.

This must be understood thus: we must never consent in mind; and sometimes we must also withdraw bodily, lest we supply counsel, help, or authority to wickedness. For, as was said above (Book IX, Epistle 1), Gregory excommunicated the counsellors of Januarius, bishop, by whose authority and counsel the crime had been committed. Likewise Pope-bishop Eleutherius says in his letter:

> To neglect, when you are able, to disturb the wicked is nothing other than to foster them; nor is one free from the stain of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.

## CHAPTER XXX. That the wicked must not be defended.

[Col. 0868D]

Hence in the exposition of Proverbs:

> “The mouth of the wicked conceals iniquity” (Prov. 10:6). The wicked are those who, by defending and concealing either their own errors or those of their neighbours, prevent them from coming to healing.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That the wicked must not be flattered with adulation.

Thus Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, ch. 19 [8]):

> Woe to you who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand, and make pillows beneath the head of every age, to capture souls (Ezek. 13:18). An elbow is received upon a cushion, or the head of one lying down upon pillows, when the hardness of correction is withheld from a sinner and the softness of favour is applied, so that he may lie softly in error—[Col. 0869A] he whom no harshness of contradiction strikes. But rulers who love themselves undoubtedly offer these things to those from whom they fear that they may become known in their pursuit of temporal glory.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That flattery must not be given to wicked prelates, but contradiction.

But concerning the same flattery which is here discussed in rulers toward their subjects, he shows elsewhere, in ch. 17 [6], that subjects ought to rebuke rulers:

> Often a ruler swells precisely because he stands above others; and while all things lie subject to his use, while his commands are swiftly performed as he wishes, while all his subjects extol with praises whatever has been well done, but oppose wickedly done things with no authority—while they often praise even what they ought to have reproved—he is deceived by those who minister beneath him [Col. 0869B] and raises his mind above himself; and while he is surrounded outwardly by favour, he is emptied inwardly of truth.

See how the wicked, both prelates and subjects, must be avoided bodily, lest through the authority of favour, the aid of defence, or counsel promoting their advancement, we heap up both their evil and our own. Hence he says elsewhere (*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, ch. 31 [17]), warning subjects not to be so subject to wicked prelates as to consent to and favour them:

> The humble must be admonished not to be subject more than is fitting, lest, while they strive to be subject to men more than is necessary, they be compelled also to revere vices through flattery.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That one must not obey in evil.

Thus Ambrose says in the book *On Paradise*:

> It is not always evil not to obey a command. If the command [Col. 0869C] is good, obedience is honourable; but if it is wicked, not to obey is beneficial.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That wicked prelates must be rebuked and corrected by their subjects.

Indeed, unless subjects sometimes avoid wicked prelates, so as not to fulfil wicked commands according to their wish, and unless they reject those evils with authority so as to resist their deception, they should know themselves guilty. For if Balaam’s ass had carried its rider onward up to the angel’s sword, would not both have undergone the sentence? But instead it resisted him, struck its feet, rebuked him with words contrary to nature, and thus saved itself as well as him.

So too Paul resisted Peter to his face, because he was blameworthy. Hence it is written in Letter 82 to Jerome: [Col. 0869D]

> Peter accepted what Paul did with the useful freedom of holy love and the kindness of humility’s mercy; and thus he provided for posterity a rarer and holier example, so that elders might not disdain, whenever they had perhaps left the path of rectitude, to be corrected even by their juniors; and so that those who were lesser might dare more confidently, like Paul, to resist even their superiors in defence of evangelical truth, while preserving brotherly love. For although it is better never in any respect to turn aside from the path one is following than to turn aside in some respect, it is nevertheless far more wonderful and praiseworthy to accept gladly one who corrects than boldly to turn aside from one who goes astray.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That a prelate ought gladly to embrace correction from subjects.

Likewise Gregory in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part II), ch. [Col. 0870A] 19 [8]:

> A prelate who strives to do wrong and nevertheless sees his subjects silent concerning it is himself a witness against himself that he wishes to be loved more than truth, because he does not wish to be defended against himself. Thus Peter gladly accepted Paul’s rebuke (Gal. 2:11); thus David gladly heard a subject’s correction (2 Sam. 12:7), because good rulers, since they do not know how to love themselves with private self-love, regard the word of free purity from their subjects as an act of humble service.

But although above he seemed to say that subjects should freely and fraternally oppose and rebuke prelates, and that prelates should kindly and humbly receive this from subjects—saying that “it is praiseworthy for subjects to correct, but more praiseworthy for prelates to hear correction”—what follows seems to contradict this, because such action is now said to be done rashly and indiscreetly. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That subjects ought not rashly or bitterly, but humbly and discreetly, to reprove prelates.

> (Ibid.) But amid these matters it is necessary that, even when the mind of subjects can rightly perceive, it should come forth into freedom of speech in such a way that freedom does not burst into pride; lest, perhaps, when an excessive freedom of tongue is granted them, humility of life may be lost by them.

Here he retracts nothing from what was said concerning superiors, except that this must be done humbly.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That subjects, although they reprove prelates’ vices, must nevertheless show them the reverence of subjection.

Likewise, in Part III, the same chapter 28 [4]:

> Subjects must be admonished [Col. 0870C] not rashly—that is, not in the proper order, or not at the proper time, or in other unsuitable ways—to judge the lives of their superiors if they see them doing anything blameworthy; lest, where they rightly condemn evils, they be plunged more deeply through an impulse of pride. Rather, they should judge wrongful acts within themselves in such a way that, nevertheless, bound by divine fear and love, they do not refuse beneath their superiors the yoke of reverence.

The deeds of superiors must not be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they appear rightly blameworthy; for they are to be reproved neither vehemently nor bitterly, but gently and secretly, at the proper time. If a prelate sins secretly, he must be secretly rebuked by a subject, just as was also said above concerning subjects. But if the subject makes the secret [Col. 0870D] public, he will be condemned like Ham, because he uncovered his father’s shame.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That subjects must not publish the hidden vices of prelates, but rather endure them, lest, when a ruler of the people is appointed deservedly, their own guilt be punished in him.

Hence Pope Anacletus, in his third letter to all bishops, ch. 5:

> The sentence of Ham, Noah’s son, condemns those who reveal the fault of their teachers or superiors: he did not cover his father’s nakedness but displayed it for mockery. But a teacher or shepherd of the Church, if he departs from the faith, must be corrected by the faithful without reservation; yet for reprobate conduct he must rather be endured. For the rulers of the Church are to be judged by God, as the Prophet says: “God stood in the assembly [Col. 0871A] of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81:1). Therefore every believer, if he sees or learns that the people are swelling against their shepherd, or that the clergy are engaged in detractions, ought to strive, according to his power, to root out and prudently correct this vice; and if they appear incorrigible, he should not presume to join them in any undertakings before they have been reconciled to their teacher.

This is to be understood either of shepherds’ hidden faults, as of others’ hidden faults, or of their manifest faults as being reserved to God more especially than are those of others. For if the sins of prelates are altogether reserved to God’s judgment, why do ecclesiastical judgments command that they be deposed and condemned for their various faults?

But here he retracts nothing from what was said above, where he forbids detraction and the publication of paternal secrets—not correction, but mockery. Even in these matters he does not command absolute endurance, but rather endurance; and in the same chapter he adds why such a person should be endured: perhaps that ruler sins because of the merit of his subjects. For he says that the shepherds of the Church are often corrupted because of the merits of the people, so that those who follow may fall more readily. When the head is sick, the rest of the body is more easily infected, as it is written: “The whole head is sick” (Isa. 1:5), etc. They ought, therefore, to endure one whom they see weakened through their own fault.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That a prelate, unless he has departed from the faith, must rather be endured by subjects than accused or defamed.

Likewise, in ch. 2 of his second letter, Fabian, bishop, to all bishops:

> Establishing this by apostolic authority, we command that the sheep entrusted to a shepherd should not dare to rebuke their shepherd unless he has erred in faith. If he has departed from the faith, he must first be corrected secretly by his subjects. If, God forbid, he appears incorrigible, then he must be accused before his primates or before the Apostolic See. But for his other acts he must rather be endured by his sheep than accused or publicly defamed; because when subjects abandon him in these matters, they oppose the appointment of him who set him over them, as the Apostle says: “He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:2).

Since this decree is almost the same as that above, it must be understood in the same way: he is not to be endured absolutely, but rather endured; nor is he truly to be publicly defamed, lest this conflict with other decrees. And that matters hidden in prelates must not be publicly revealed, after the manner of Noah’s son Ham, Pope Alexander testifies to all bishops, ch. 1 of his first letter:

> Establishing this, we decree that all who persecute their fathers, or openly strive to remove or tear them apart, are infamous and are to be made strangers to the thresholds of the Church until satisfaction has been made. They are made infamous for this reason: because they persecute fathers; for persecution belongs to those who are hateful and enemies.

Hence Anacletus says in his third letter, ch. 5:

> Worse are those who corrupt the life and morals of teachers than those who plunder the possessions and estates of others. The latter take from us things which are outside us, although they are ours; but our detractors, corrupters of our morals, and those who arm themselves against us properly deceive us ourselves. Therefore they are justly infamous and deservedly become outsiders to the Church. For losses of morals differ greatly from losses of temporal things, since the latter are outside us, whereas the former are within us.

See how it was permitted above that prelates be charitably rebuked by subjects; here it is forbidden that they be maliciously defamed or disgraced. Hence Jerome to Rusticus (formerly Ep. 5, now 95):

> One must not assume that one has attained perfect maturity merely because past life defends it and the title of rank honours it. Yet because we are human, and sometimes, contrary to the maturity of our years, slip into the vices of children: if you do not wish to correct an offender, rebuke him openly; but do not bite in secret. [Col. 0872B]

Likewise he says:

> What advantage is it if you report my evils to others and wound me, who do not know it, by your detractions—so that, while eagerly recounting them to everyone, you speak to each person as though you had told no one? This is not to amend me but to satisfy your own vice.

## CHAPTER XL. That tolerance of the wicked must not be extended so far that they sin more through hope of continual impunity.

Yet because the opinion of Anacletus, Fabian, and many other saints inclines strongly to the view that a prelate should rather be endured than rebuked, we must consider with what distinction this tolerance is to be maintained, since Pope Vigilius says, on the contrary:

> It is indeed a thing consonant with the divine command to show patience toward sinners; yet it ought not to be extended so far that, through hope of continual impunity, sin is committed continually without correction.

For Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part I, ch. 1 [2]):

> No one sins more in the Church than one who, while acting perversely, holds the name or order of holiness. For no one presumes to rebuke such an offender, and the fault spreads greatly by example when, out of reverence for his office, the sinner is honoured.

As the Lord says in the Gospel: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14). Hence the Psalmist: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their back continually” (Ps. 68:24). For when the eyes are darkened, the back [Col. 0872D] is bent: because, when those who sin are blind, their followers bend down to carry the burdens of sinners. Since, then, the fault of prelates is poured out upon their subjects, tolerance appears difficult when they are made worse even by others’ faults. Nevertheless, it does no harm if it is shown to both prelates and equals with the discretion demanded by necessity or just compassion.

## CHAPTER XLI. That the wicked are tolerated because they cannot be accused with certain proofs.

For Augustine says in the book *On Penance*, Sermon 351, no. 10:

> Many good Christians are silent and bear the sins of others which they know, because they often lack proofs and cannot establish before ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know. Although all these things may be true, they must not easily be believed by a judge unless they are demonstrated by certain indications. [Col. 0873A]

## CHAPTER XLII. That tolerance of the wicked does not harm the good, if correction is applied, as far as is possible without violating peace, according to each person’s rank and condition.

Likewise Augustine, in *On the Words of the Lord*, ch. 28 (Sermon 88, no. 23), concerning the words, “Be gone, depart from there, and touch no unclean thing” (Isa. 52:11), says:

> “How, then, shall we bear the wicked for the sake of peace, from whom we are commanded to depart?” We understand this spiritually. What is it to touch the unclean thing, except to consent to sins? What is it to depart from there, except to do whatever belongs to the correction of the wicked, as far as can be done, without violation of peace, according to the rank and condition of each person? You have reproved; you have rebuked; and, if the matter requires it, you apply suitable discipline which does not violate unity: you have departed from there. A person is free before God when God imputes to him neither his own sins, because he did not commit them; nor those of another, because he did not approve them; nor negligence, because he was not silent; nor pride, because he remained in unity.

> Therefore, my brothers, as many as have among you the greedy, perjurers, adulterers, and other wicked persons, rebuke them as far as you can, and do not consent to them.

## CHAPTER XLIII. That the wicked must be endured in order to preserve the unity of peace.

Augustine teaches against the Donatists that unity must be retained:

> The Lord confirmed the tolerance of his servants, lest, while the good think themselves defiled by association with the wicked, they should through human and rash dissensions either lose the little ones or cause the little ones to perish. The heavenly Master warned against this so carefully that he even made the people secure concerning wicked superiors, lest the chair of saving doctrine be abandoned because of them—a chair in which the wicked are compelled to learn good things.

Likewise Augustine to Eleusius (Ep. 43):

> The crimes of wicked persons are charged against us—not our own, but others’, and some of them unknown. If, even when we saw them truly present, we were to tolerate their impunity, sparing the tares for the sake of the wheat, anyone who heard the holy Scriptures without a deaf heart would pronounce us worthy not merely of no blame, but even of considerable praise.

[Col. 0873D] Hence Augustine on John, ch. 49:

> What did the Lord intend to warn his Church when he chose to have one lost man among the twelve, except that we should tolerate the wicked lest we divide Christ’s body? See: Judas is among the saints; see: he is a thief—and do not despise this. He is a thief and sacrilegious, not an ordinary thief, but keeper of the Lord’s money-bags, keeper of sacred funds. Such a Judas came with the disciples to the Lord’s Supper; he could associate with them, but could not defile them.

Likewise Augustine, in the second book, in the passage *On Shepherds*:

> The harvest will come, and the tares will be separated from the wheat. This is not now the time for separation, but for tolerance. God is now silent—do you wish to speak? He is silent from the vengeance of judgment, not from the word of correction. He does not yet separate—do you wish to separate? If you wish the grain to be cleansed before the winnowing, you will be winnowed by your own evil wind. [Col. 0874A]

Hence Augustine, *The City of God*, Book II:

> But because this person listens and that person despises, and because more are friendly to vices which wickedly flatter them than to the usefulness of virtues, Christ’s servants are commanded to endure—even if necessary—a most wicked and disgraceful commonwealth, whether they are kings, princes, judges, soldiers, provincials, rich, poor, free persons, slaves, of either sex. In that heavenly commonwealth of holy angels, where God’s will is law, this tolerance will prepare for itself a most glorious place.

Likewise, in the book *Questions on the Gospels*:

> The firm weight of grain is not proved except by the disturbances of chaff.

If someone cannot restrain these disturbances while defending truth, let him yield while preserving unity.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That the wicked must sometimes be endured solely out of regard for piety.

Thus the wicked are sometimes to be endured lest the Church’s unity and peace be disturbed; sometimes solely out of regard for piety and love. Hence Augustine, in Book II of *The Harmony of the Gospels* (ch. 30):
