> The Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens,” and again: “Each one shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5). But some burdens involve sharing weakness; others involve rendering an account of our acts. The former are shared with brothers; the latter are borne personally by each individual. Who bear one another’s burdens except those who have love? Those who do not have love are burdensome to themselves. Let no one fear that he is weighed down by such burdens; rather, let each one take care not to be weighed down by his own sins. For when you bear your brother’s weakness, his sins do not burden you. But if you consent, your own sins then burden you, not another’s. You saw a thief and ran with him: what belonged to him has become your deed alone, because it pleased you. But if it displeased you and you prayed for him, you bear another’s burdens, so that another may bear yours, and you have fulfilled Christ’s law.

Hence in the book *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*:

> Paul says that through love we are to serve one another. This cannot happen unless each person takes another’s weakness as his own, so as to bear it patiently.

Hence Augustine, in Letter 40 (formerly 9) to Jerome:

> “I became weak to the weak,” that is, through the compassion of mercy, not through the pretence of deceit. For one who ministers to a sick person becomes, as it were, sick: not because he falsely claims to have fevers, but because, with the mind of one who sympathizes, he considers how he would wish to be served if he himself were sick.

Hence Augustine, in the book *Questions*, ch. 83:

> Let us therefore render to one whose weakness we wish to bear what would be rendered to us by him if we happened to be in that weakness.

Hence Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, ch. 21 [10]):

> “Considering yourself, lest you too be tempted.” It is as though he said: When what you see in another’s weakness displeases you, weigh what it is, so that the spirit may restrain itself from zeal in rebuking while it fears in itself also what it rebukes.

Likewise, from the Letter of the Council to the Donatists:

> Whoever lives well in the Church is not prejudiced by the sins of others. [Col. 0875A]

For each person shall bear his own burden in it, and whoever eats Christ’s body unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself (1 Cor. 11:29). When he says “to himself,” he sufficiently shows that it is not to another but to himself. For the wicked person bears his own case, and does not prejudice another who has no share in the guilt through consenting to the wicked deed.

## CHAPTER XLV. That the perfect ought not to abandon cohabitation with the wicked.

Hence Ambrose—or rather Gregory, *Morals*, Book I, ch. 1—says:

> It is not greatly praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked. For just as it is a more grievous fault not to be good among the good, so it is a matter of immense praise to have been good even among the wicked.

[Col. 0875B] These things seem sufficient to prove that cohabitation with the wicked is harmless, provided one is strong enough to show them patience and not consent.

## CHAPTER XLVI. That persons of every kind who are weak must even physically avoid the company of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0875D] Something seems to be missing here, e.g. “companionships”], lest they be corrupted by them.

But if someone is unable not to be enticed toward evil by their suggestions or examples, let him hear Isidore:

> Those who desire the heavenly homeland flee not only the morals but also the associations of the wicked. If you are a companion in the way of life of the good, you will also share their virtues; for like is accustomed to be joined with like. It is dangerous to live with the wicked. It is ruinous to associate with those of perverse will. It is better to hate the wicked than to have fellowship with them. As the common life of saints possesses many goods, so the associations of the wicked bring still more evils.

Hence Jerome, to a mother and daughter living in Gaul:

> Why need you dwell in a house in which you must daily either perish or conquer? What mortal ever takes secure sleep beside a viper? Even if it does not strike, it certainly causes anxiety. It is safer to be unable to perish than not to have perished beside danger. In the one there is tranquillity; in the other, navigation. There we rejoice; here we escape. It is difficult to keep a fast among feasts.

Thus Gregory, ch. 46:

> When we carelessly join ourselves to friendships with the wicked, we are bound by faults. We already differ from him who is supremely righteous precisely insofar as our life agrees with the friendships of the perverse. [Col. 0875D]

## CHAPTER XLVII. That an elder must be sternly rebuked when he gives bad example to younger persons.

Therefore one whose wickedness goes so far that others are corrupted through him must indeed be greatly reproved. Hence Gregory, in his letter (Book IX) to Bishop Januarius:

> Paul says: “Do not rebuke an elder” (1 Tim. 5:1). But this rule of his must be observed when the fault of an elder does not, through his example, draw the hearts of younger persons to destruction. But where an elder gives younger persons an example leading to destruction, there he must be struck by stern rebuke. For it is written: [Col. 0876A] “A snare of young men are all of you” (Isa. 42:22). And again: “The child a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa. 65:20).

See: in order that we may have authority to restrict the rule and commands of the saints to the appropriate understanding of particular circumstances, Paul says this absolutely and, as it were, universally. Gregory restricts this not to all faults of elders, but only to certain faults which are not to be rebuked.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. That it does not harm the good if they communicate in sacraments even with wicked persons whom they know.

But if these things have been said concerning enduring or avoiding cohabitation with the wicked, what should be held concerning participation in the sacraments with them? Augustine says against the Donatists:

> Those whom we are unable to correct, even when necessity compels us, we should tolerate for the salvation of others [Col. 0876B] so that they may share God’s sacraments with us. Yet we must not share in their sins; and this occurs only by consenting and showing favour. Fellowship with the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in sacraments, but through consent to their deeds.

Likewise Augustine to Emeritus (Ep. 87, no. 2):

> It must not be left unsaid that even wicked persons known to be such do no harm to the good in the Church, if either the power to exclude them from communion is lacking, or some consideration of preserving peace prevents it.

Likewise, to Emeritus (no. 3):

> It is clear that a person is not defiled because someone with whom he approaches the altar is wicked, even if that person is known to be wicked, provided that he is not approved and is separated from him by a good conscience which disapproves.

Likewise, in his homilies:

> In order that you may endure even one whom you know to be wicked, attend to the Apostle saying: “Each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5). Do not share his greed, but share Christ’s table. And what harm is it if you share Christ’s table? “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:24). “To himself,” he says—not to you. But if you are a judge, if you have received authority to judge, if he is accused before you according to ecclesiastical rule, if he is convicted by true proofs and witnesses: restrain, rebuke, excommunicate, depose.

## CHAPTER XLIX. That receiving sacraments from wicked prelates who consecrate and administer them does no harm, although the saints seem to intimate this in certain of their statements.

[Col. 0876D] But what is to be said of receiving the sacraments from the very prelates who consecrate and administer them? For Jerome says of such men in his commentary on Zephaniah: “The priests who serve the Eucharist, who distribute the Lord’s blood to his people, act impiously against the law of Christ, thinking that it is not the life but the words of one pronouncing the prayer that make the Eucharist; and that the necessary thing is the solemn prayer, not the merits of the priests.” Hence Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part I), chapter 10: “We all know plainly that, when one who displeases us is sent to intercede for us, the offended mind is provoked to worse anger. Therefore, one who is still bound by earthly desires must take care lest, by more grievously kindling against himself the wrath of the strict Judge, while he delights in the glory of his office, he become for his subjects [Col. 0877A] the author of ruin.” Likewise Leo, in his decrees, chapter 48, *On Evil Prelates*: “This is not to take counsel for peoples, but to harm them; not to render governance, but to increase danger.” For the integrity of those who preside is the safety of those subject to them.

Is it not therefore dangerous to be subject to such persons, or for any sacraments to be consecrated or received by such persons, since according to these authorities they appear not only not to benefit, but even to harm? This must be understood in fullest harmony with the other holy Fathers, and resolved piously and catholicly. For as regards the truth of the sacrament, it is not made better by a good priest or worse by a bad one. But as regards the power and effect of the sacrament, it is given, according to the faith and merits of those who receive it, to some [Col. 0877B] for salvation and to others for judgment.

This is also what blessed Jerome himself establishes. Although his words, by which he exhorted priests to purity of life, seem to sound otherwise, nevertheless by those same words he both attests the truth of the sacrament in the case of evil priests and threatens that, according to their merits, it will be evil for them unto judgment. For he said that they serve the Eucharist by priestly ministry; if there were no Eucharist, either for themselves or for another, he would not say that they serve a thing that did not exist at all. He also says that they distribute the Lord’s blood to his people. Unless he were attending to the truth of the sacrament, he would neither call blood of the Lord that which was not blood, nor call them his people; but, from that communion, he speaks of those who think that the words of one pronouncing the prayer, rather than his life, make the Eucharist.

He does not say that they perform Christ’s sacrament falsely, but that they act impiously and irreligiously against Christ’s law. For, while they offend in one point, they are guilty of all, receiving for judgment when they receive badly what is good. They err in thinking that the sacrament itself of the Lord’s body and blood makes the Eucharist for them—that is, not judgment, but good grace and salvation—through the words alone of the one pronouncing the prayer, rather than through his life. Yet the solemn words of the one pronouncing the prayer effect the truth of the sacrament, not salvation; the merits obtain only the effect and salvation of the sacrament, not the words.

For although that sacrament is wholly one and the same in its truth, it is nevertheless varied toward a twofold effect: for the good it is a Eucharist of salvation, but for the evil it is judgment [Col. 0877D] unto condemnation. Thus he further says that they act impiously by thinking that, for making and obtaining the Eucharist, only the solemn prayer is necessary and not the merits of the priests. The solemn prayer makes the truth of the sacrament for the priest; but his merits obtain its effect and power unto salvation. Hence Gregory, at the end of the *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 60), says: “For then we offer a true sacrifice to God for ourselves, if we have made ourselves a sacrifice to him.” For then, namely, it will accomplish the effect of salvation which it promises.

Thus Christ too, when in his own country he displayed the truth of his presence, nevertheless could exercise no power, and wondered because of their unbelief [Col. 0878A]. For just as the sun shines in itself, yet by its presence cannot illuminate one who is blind, so, because of their evil merits, he could not give them Christ’s signs of salvation. Therefore Jerome himself subsequently added concerning evil priests:

“Of them it is said: ‘And a priest in whatever blemish he may have shall not approach to offer oblations to the Lord.’”

Although priests do this, nevertheless the Lord is merciful and just: merciful, because he does not withdraw from his Church, displaying through such ministers the presence and truth of his sacraments for the salvation of believers; just, because he renders to each one what he deserves, so that his sacraments are for the depraved unto judgment. He adds that the manifestation of this judgment will be revealed not in the present but in the future. For after the morning has come and the night of this age has passed, he will give his judgment in the light, and the proud rulers, whom God resists because they refuse to be subject to him, from their thrones and from the height which they held—[Note: [Col. 0877] *It seems that “will overthrow,” or some similar verb, is missing.*]

In this it should be noted that evil prelates are to be believed to hold the thrones and eminence of the sacraments while they live, although God resists them in respect of their evil merits, until at last God removes them from the thrones which they meanwhile hold—unless they are first corrected or, having been deposed, punished. This must indeed be maintained concerning those who administer the Eucharist to their own judgment.

But when Gregory says, “Because, when one who displeases us is sent to intercede, the offended mind is provoked to worse anger, and [Col. 0878C] in this way such an intercessor becomes for his subjects the author of ruin,” he speaks of those subjects who, by deliberately electing evil prelates, consenting evilly to them, or even imitating them, have as authors of ruin those whom they ought to have had as guides of life. By them they do not appease the Judge, and with them they also share their sins. This too is indicated when it is said, “one who is sent to intercede.” Indeed, if we preside for the peace of the Church, we must avoid sending such persons to intercede. Hence the Apostle says: “There will be perilous times, when they will not endure sound teaching, but, with itching ears, will heap up teachers for themselves” (II Tim. III, 1).

But if sometimes we do this because of necessity or toleration, we should do so not by consenting to that person’s wickedness [Col. 0878D], but in this faith: knowing that the truth of each sacrament is in itself administered even by evil persons, we should believe that salvation comes to the devout and worthy, in the grace of the Holy Spirit, not through those persons but through the sacrament itself.

## CHAPTER L. That in the holy Church the Holy Spirit gathers the upright through the ministry of the wicked, and not outside the Church, where the excommunicated and heretics are.

Hence Augustine, *On Blasphemy against the Spirit* (Sermon 71, no. 37): “The Spirit works in the holy Church even in this present time, when she is threshed like a threshing-floor with chaff, in such a way that he despises no one’s true confession, is deceived by no one’s pretence, and so avoids the reprobate that even through their ministry he gathers the upright [Col. 0879A].”

## CHAPTER LI. That good preaching is to be heard even from evil preachers.

Augustine says of evil preachers in Homily 44 (Tractate 46, no. 6) on John: “Many in the Church, pursuing earthly advantages, nevertheless preach Christ; and through them the voice of Christ is heard, and the sheep follow not the hireling but the voice of the shepherd through the hireling. Hear the hirelings identified by the Lord himself. ‘The scribes and Pharisees,’ he says, ‘sit on Moses’ seat: do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matt. XXIII, 2). What else did he say except: through the hirelings hear the shepherd’s voice? What the hireling does wickedly, he does not preach from Christ’s seat. He harms by the evil that he does, not by the good that he says. Carefully gather grapes (*botros*) among thorns, lest while you seek fruit you tear your hand. When you hear one saying good things, do not imitate him in doing evil.”

Likewise in the same place (*ibid.*, no. 6): “Truth is Christ. Let truth be proclaimed by hirelings from ulterior motive; let truth be proclaimed by sons in truth. For through the tongues of hirelings and sons Christ’s glory is spread abroad, whether Christ is proclaimed from ulterior motive or in truth.”

Augustine likewise says in a homily on the three raised dead: “If I should wish to defend myself before the Lord by saying: ‘Lord, I saw that cleric of yours living wickedly, and therefore I lived wickedly,’ will he not say: ‘Wicked servant, did you not hear from me: Do what they say, but do not do what they do?’ (Matt. XXIII, 3). He who follows evil should not seek for himself a patron for an evil cause.”

Likewise in the same work: “Whatever sort of man I may be, I defend the Lord’s threshing-floor; for it I cry aloud. I do not want you to concern yourself with what I am in it; wait for the winnowing-fan. Or, if you wish to concern yourself, do not concern yourself contentiously, so that you may be able to care for your brother.”

Likewise Gregory: “Let no one despise me in this matter because of myself. For it often happens that a powerful person holds a servant in contempt, and yet, when he sends some answer through him, perhaps to his own people or to strangers, the person of the speaking servant is not despised, because reverence for the sending master is preserved in the heart. Those who hear do not consider through whom, but what and from whom, they hear.”

## CHAPTER LII. That baptism, even if given by a pagan, is not to be repeated.

[Col. 0879D]

And, having said enough about accepting the good preaching of evil persons, let us consider baptism: whether, when it is administered by an evil person, it is true and fruitful even if the persons are known to be sinners or heretics. For this sacrament, because it is more necessary, has been extended more broadly than the others, even to laypeople; and, if it happens or is necessary, even to pagans.

For, as is found in ecclesiastical history, when Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, was celebrating the feast-day of Peter the martyr, after the solemn rites had been completed he saw on the seashore children at play, imitating, as often happens, a bishop and the things customarily done in the Church [Col. 0880A]. At once he ordered them to be brought before him and asked what they had done. They disclosed the order of events and admitted that certain catechumens had been baptized by the boy Athanasius, who had played the bishop. But when from their answers he saw that everything conformed to the rite of our religion, he decreed that baptism should not be repeated for those upon whom water had been poured with the prescribed questions and answers intact, but that those things customarily performed by priests should be completed.

But because ecclesiastical history is regarded as less authoritative, it seems still less authoritative that the baptism of this pagan boy, who played the bishop, should appear to have been accepted as valid by the Alexandrian bishop—except that blessed Isidore seems to establish the same thing in his sayings as follows:

[Col. 0880B] “[Note: [Col. 0879] This passage is also cited under Isidore’s name by Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian in Part II of the *Decretum*, cause 1, question 1, chapter 59.] If anyone is ordained through ignorance before being baptized, those baptized by him ought to be baptized again, and he himself should not thereafter be ordained. But the Roman pontiff judges not the man who baptizes, but that the Spirit of God supplies the grace of baptism, even though the one baptizing is a pagan.”

For this reason rebaptism is forbidden by canonical authority: lest the name of the Holy Trinity, in which the baptism was performed, should seem to be annulled.

## CHAPTER LIII. That baptism is rightly celebrated even through evil ministers who are known to be such.

But let us return to ministers who are even known to be evil. Augustine says in Homily 6 (Tractate 6, nos. 6, 7, 8) on John: “By this power, which Christ [Col. 0880C] alone retained for himself and transferred to none of his ministers, although he deigned that baptism should be administered through ministers—by this power the unity of the Church stands, signified in the dove of which it is said: ‘My dove is one; she is one to her mother’ (Song VI, 8). For if that power were transferred from the Lord to ministers, there would be as many baptisms as ministers, and the unity of baptism would not stand.

“Therefore, although baptism is administered by either righteous or unrighteous persons, the holiness of baptism is bestowed by none but him upon whom the dove descended, of whom it was said: ‘This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’ (John I, 33). Peter baptizes: this is he who baptizes. Judas baptizes: this is he who baptizes. For if baptism is holy in proportion to diversity of merits, then, because merits differ, baptisms will differ. But just as, when a good and a better man baptize, the one recipient does not receive something good and the other something better, but what they receive is one and equal; so too, when an evil person baptizes through some ignorance or toleration of the Church—for evil people are either unknown or tolerated—that which is given is one, not unequal because of unequal ministers, but equal and nearly the same. This is he who baptizes.

## CHAPTER LIV. That with wicked persons who have been condemned we ought not only not share divine sacraments, but not even take bodily food.

Yet Augustine himself seems contrary to this opinion of his in a homily: “If he is evil, and it happens that he has the ministry, and people do not know him [Col. 0881A], though God knows him, God permits baptism to be administered through him—he who reserved the power to himself.” In this he seems to suggest that, if evil persons are known, baptism cannot be administered through them.

But lest he be contrary to himself or to the other saints, this must not be understood of persons known in every manner, who are often tolerated in the Church for reasonable causes. Rather, it concerns those known as though openly confessed or judicially convicted, to whom divine ministry is not entrusted because of scandal to the Church, and with whom the Apostle wills that we should share not only no sacraments but not even bodily food.

Hence Augustine says in *On Penance* (Sermon 351, no. 10): “The Apostle says: ‘But now I have written to you not to associate with anyone called a brother if he is a fornicator, an idolater, covetous, abusive, a drunkard, or a robber—not even to eat with such a one. For what have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those within? But God will judge those outside. Remove the evil person from among yourselves’ (I Cor. V, 11). By these words it is clear that evil persons must be removed from the communion of the Church. Nor is what the Apostle says elsewhere contrary to this passage: ‘Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls’ (Rom. XIV, 4).

“For he did not wish one person to be judged by another on the arbitrary basis of suspicion or by a judgment usurped outside due order. Rather, he wished judgment according to the law of God and the order of the Church—whether the person had confessed voluntarily, or was accused and convicted. Otherwise, why did he say, ‘if anyone called a brother is a fornicator,’ unless he intended by such designation that which is made concerning someone when a sentence is pronounced with judicial procedure and integrity?”

Therefore it must be said as follows: if people do not know a person to be evil as confessed or convicted after canonical examination—that is, if they do not know him notoriously and in a condemnable manner—God permits baptism to be administered through him before he is condemned, because, although unworthily, he nevertheless exercises his ministry catholicly. But one who has been condemned administers unworthily for himself and uselessly for others, because thereafter no one ought to communicate with him.

Otherwise, if known evil persons could not baptize rightly in the Church, why would Augustine elsewhere testify that John knew the mystery of baptism would pass to both good and evil persons? What John knew would happen, I see as present reality [Col. 0881D]. Hence Augustine (Tractate 5, no. 11 and following):

“John the Baptist knew that the power would pass from the Lord to no one, but that the ministry would pass to good and evil persons. Let not the dove be horrified at the ministry of evil persons; let it look to the Lord’s power. What can an evil minister do to you where the Lord is good? But the heretic says: ‘You do not have baptism, because an evil person gave it.’ I reply: ‘If Christ is evil, then an evil person gave it to me.’ I see who the minister was; I do not dispute about the official, I do not wish to investigate the official’s case. Let the men have been whatever they were; I received from Christ.

“‘No,’ he says, ‘but that evil bishop baptized you.’ I was baptized by Christ. I know it, because the dove which John saw taught me. Let ministers be righteous if they wish; but if those sitting upon Moses’ seat do not wish to be righteous, my Master made me secure, he of whom his Spirit said: ‘This is he who baptizes’ (John I, 33). ‘The scribes and Pharisees,’ he says, ‘sit upon Moses’ seat.’ If the minister is righteous, I count him with Paul, who does not seek his own glory, saying: ‘I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase’ (I Cor. III, 6).

“But if the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil (*Zabulus*); yet Christ’s gift is not defiled, because it flows pure through him, passes clear through him, and comes to fruitful ground. I know that a stone cannot bear fruit from water, yet water passes through a stony channel to the garden-beds. The stony channel produces nothing, but the garden bears abundant fruit. For the spiritual power of the sacrament is like light: it is received pure by those illuminated, so that, passing through unclean persons, it is not defiled.”

Likewise in the same work (Tractate 5, no. 18): “Judas gave baptism, and no one was baptized after Judas. John gave baptism, and baptism was administered after John, because the baptism given by Judas was Christ’s baptism, whereas that given by John was John’s. We rightly place Christ’s baptism, given even through Judas’s hands, above John’s baptism” (*ibid.*).

Likewise: “When Judas baptizes, Christ baptizes; therefore, when a drunkard, murderer, or adulterer baptizes, Christ baptizes. I do not fear those evil persons, because I look to the dove through which I am told: ‘This is he who baptizes.’”

Likewise: “The sacrament of the Church is so great that it is not defiled even when a murderer administers it; and this is granted not only to evil ministers but also, if necessity requires, to laypersons.”

## CHAPTER LV. That baptism given even by laypersons in some necessity is valid.

Hence Gelasius, chapter 17 (Letter to the bishops of Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily): “Deacons should not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, except perhaps when the aforesaid officeholders are far away and extreme necessity compels it—a concession often made even to Christian laypersons.”

## CHAPTER LVI. That sacraments may be administered and consecrated by any Catholic, even a sinner; nor are they effected more greatly by a good person or less greatly by an evil person.

[Col. 0882D] But since we have spoken of the sacrament of baptism, let us consider the Eucharist: whether it can truly and profitably be consecrated or administered by any sinner who is nevertheless a Catholic. Hence Augustine:

“Concerning the Lord’s body, within the Catholic Church in the ministry of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing is effected more greatly by a good priest or less greatly by an evil one; for it is not effected by the merit of the consecrator, but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it were by the priest’s merit, it would not belong to Christ. But now, just as he himself baptizes, so he himself, through the Holy Spirit, makes this his flesh and transforms it into blood. For it must be believed that the sacraments are effected by Christ’s words [Col. 0883A]. For by whose power they are first created, by his word they are surely recreated unto something better.”

## CHAPTER LVII. That in the divine mysteries the merits of priests are not to be considered, but their offices.

Likewise Ambrose, *On the Sacraments* (*On the Mysteries*, chapter 5): “When Scripture testifies that headlong fire came down from heaven upon Jeroboam, and again, at Elijah’s prayer, fire was sent which consumed the sacrifice, do not consider the merits of the persons but the offices of the priests. That visible fire was sent in order that they might believe; for us, who believe, invisible fire works. Therefore believe that the Lord Jesus is present when invoked by the prayers of priests, he who said: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am also’ (Matt. XVIII, 20). How much more, where the Church is, where [Col. 0883B] his mysteries are, does he deign to show his presence.

“If Elijah’s word had such power as to bring down fire, will Christ’s word not have power to change the species of the elements? Christ’s word, which could make from nothing what did not exist—because he himself spoke and they were made (Ps. XXXII, 9)—cannot change the things which exist into what they were not?”

Here it should be noted that within the unity of the Church, it is not through the merit but through the office of priests, for the faith of those standing by, that Christ’s word effects the true sacrifice; whereas, as Augustine says, outside the Catholic Church, that is, among heretics, there is no place for sacrifice, because their sacrifice is altogether void.

## CHAPTER LVIII. How, in his judgment, God does not deny that even those who lack a prophet’s merit possess the spirit of prophecy.

[Col. 0883C]

Hence Augustine, in his treatise on the Epistle of John, chapter 103, *On Evil but Catholic Priests*: “Even Saul, an evil king, prophesied while he was persecuting holy David. Therefore let those who perhaps possess God’s holy gift without charity, such as holy baptism, not boast. Instead, let them consider what account they will render to God, who do not use holy things holily. They will be among those who say: ‘In your name we prophesied’ (Matt. VII, 22). They are not told, ‘You lie’; rather, they are told: ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity’ (*ibid.*). Therefore they must be said both to have possessed the spirit of prophecy and not to have possessed the merit of a prophet.”

## CHAPTER LIX. That those who offer sacrifices unworthily upon the altar, although the sacrifices are holy, are not sanctified by them.

[Col. 0883D]

Hence Jerome on the prophet Haggai: “O people, who, though only the altar has been built and my house lies in ruins, offer me sacrifices upon the altar and suppose yourselves to be sanctified by its victims: know that what is offered on the altar is indeed holy, but you are not so much sanctified by the sacrifices as you are meanwhile defiled by dead works.”

## CHAPTER LX. That the body and blood of Christ, who redeemed us, are effected by the Creator’s word alone.

Thus the saints too, knowing that the merits of believing priests neither benefit nor harm the sacraments, often make no mention of those priests, but only of him [Col. 0884A] to whom belongs all that is best. Hence Ambrose, *On the Sacraments* (Book IV, chapter 5):

“So great is the power in the Lord’s word that things which were not began to be. The earth did not exist; he himself spoke and they were made (Ps. XXXII, 9). Therefore, to answer you: Christ’s body did not exist before the consecration. The chalice is full of wine and water; where Christ’s words have worked, there blood is made which redeemed the people. But perhaps you say: ‘I do not see the appearance of blood.’ Yet it has the likeness. For just as you received the likeness of death, so too you drink the likeness of the precious blood, so that there may be no horror at bloodshed, while the price of redemption works.”

## CHAPTER LXI. That the flesh which we receive in the sacrament is true flesh.

[Col. 0884B] Likewise Augustine in his homilies: “Before Christ’s words are spoken, what is offered is called bread; once Christ’s words have been uttered, it is no longer called bread, but Christ’s body.”

Hence Ambrose, in *On the Sacraments*: “Just as Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is true—not in the way human beings are sons through grace, but because he is Son from the Father’s substance—so the flesh which we receive, as he himself said, is true flesh, and the drink is true drink. And because our same Lord Jesus Christ shares in divinity and body, you who receive this food participate in his divine substance.”

## CHAPTER LXII. That in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, the species is seen and ground by the teeth in one way, but the reality is eaten by faith in another.

Hence Augustine, in Homily 26 (Tractate 26 on [Col. 0884C] John, no. 12): “This is the living bread which came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it he shall not die. But he who eats inwardly, not outwardly; who eats with the heart, not by grinding with the tooth, belongs to the power of the sacrament, not merely to the visible sacrament itself. Manna came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth. The sacrament and unity of Christ’s body and blood are received from the Lord’s table, by some unto life and by others unto destruction. But the reality itself, of which it is the sacrament, is unto life for every person and unto destruction for none who partakes of it” (no. 18).

“For he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. Therefore to eat that food and drink that drink is to abide in Christ and to have him abiding in oneself. Accordingly, whoever does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, undoubtedly does not eat his flesh or drink his blood, even though he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment.”

In this it should be noted and believed that, whereas other sacraments contain only two things in themselves—the sacrament and the effect of the sacrament—this one alone contains three: the sacrament, namely the species that is seen; the reality of the sacrament, that is, the truth of the Lord’s substance, which is believed to be true in it, just as he was truly born of the Virgin; and the effect of the sacrament, inasmuch as it is received by some unto life and by others unto judgment.

For just as in baptism water is not changed from being water, and in chrism [Col. 0885A] oil is not changed from being oil, but that which was substantially before the sacrament remains unchanged in the sacrament, so it must not be believed concerning bread and wine. Before consecration they are indeed bread and wine in substance; after consecration they are changed into the Lord’s flesh and blood, in the same substance in which he was born of the Virgin, suffered in the flesh, and sits at the right hand of the Father.

Thus, after the office of baptism, water is poured back into the remaining water, and oil is burned with the rest. But Christ’s body alone, just as it appears to be what it is not—for it seems to be bread when it is true flesh—so, although it seems to be ground by teeth and broken by hands, nevertheless Christ himself is received wholly and entire, essentially and truly, by all; and he remains wholly and entire in heaven with the Father [Col. 0885B].

How this can be, since it exceeds human understanding, must be consigned to the fire; for where reason fails, faith makes progress, and faith has no merit where human reason furnishes proof by experience.

But when blessed Augustine said above (Tractate 26 on John, no. 18) that an evil person, even if he eats and drinks the sacrament to judgment, nevertheless does not receive the Lord’s body and blood unless he abides in Christ, he does not thereby say that the substance can be separated from its sacrament. Rather, just as the Jews crucified him only bodily, though he was the true Christ, so Christians truly receive sacramentally, as regards Christ’s true essence; but they do not truly receive as regards the efficaciousness of their own salvation, so as to be one with him. For it is far different to be received or seen essentially from being received or seen spiritually.

Hence in the Gospel: “Many kings desired to see what you see” (Luke X, 24)—not, that is, what Judas saw and betrayed, but that of which he said: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he should see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII, 56). For both Abraham and Judas saw Christ truly; but the one corporeally, the other spiritually; the one unto condemnation, the other unto salvation.

## CHAPTER LXIII. That the sacrament is to be received not only in its species but also in its reality, so that we may be, as it were, one with Christ.

Augustine also makes this distinction in a homily [Col. 0885D] (Tractate 27 on John, no. 1): “Let us not eat Christ’s flesh and blood only sacramentally, as many evil persons do, but unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members and be made alive by his Spirit.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. That it does not harm if evil persons receive the sacraments with us, when they are either unknown or tolerated.

And because we are forbidden to give what is holy to dogs, lest we suppose that all evil persons whom we either do not know or tolerate are to be excluded from so great a sacrament, he adds (*ibid.*): “And let us not be scandalized even if many eat and drink the sacraments with us temporarily, who at the end will have eternal torments; for the threshing does not consume what the winnowing is to cleanse. In this age we must live among evil persons until the end [Col. 0886A].”

Hence the same author, against the Donatists: “Communion with evil persons does not defile anyone by participation in the sacraments, but by consent to their deeds.”

## CHAPTER LXV. That forgiveness of sins is given through a reprobate but Catholic minister.

To show sufficiently that even evil priests consecrate Christ’s true body and blood, not by their merit but by their office, and that all evil persons—both they themselves and others—eat the true body and blood of the Lord, though unto judgment, let us also consider whether evil persons can give forgiveness of sins.

Hence Augustine, in *On the Words of the Lord* (Sermon 71, no. 37): “Thus blasphemy against the Holy Spirit comes about: one never comes from dispersion to the gathering [Col. 0886B], which receives the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins. Yet someone may come to that gathering through an evil cleric, a reprobate and pretended minister, but nevertheless a Catholic, with a heart that is not pretended. In that same Holy Spirit he receives remission of sins—the Spirit who gathers the upright through a reprobate ministry.”

This indicates that forgiveness of sins is given not by a heretic, but by any Catholic, although a sinner, whether in baptism or in confession, through the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER LXVI. That sins are loosed or bound by God not through ministers’ merit, but through the grace and justice of the Holy Spirit, so that neither is a person unjustly admitted within the Church nor unjustly kept outside it.

[Col. 0886C] Hence Augustine, *On the Forgiveness of Sins*, wishing to show clearly that sins are forgiven by the Holy Spirit whom the Lord gave to his faithful, not by human merits, says in one place: “‘Receive the Holy Spirit’;” immediately adding: “‘If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven him.’ This means: the Spirit forgives, not you.”

Accordingly, just as someone whom a priest admits into the Church may nevertheless be outside the Church and not belong to the body, so someone is within the Church and belongs to the body if, through a shepherd’s prejudicial judgment, he is compelled to be outside. This shows that sins are loosed or bound not by the will or merit of a good or evil person, but by the grace or justice of the Holy Spirit alone.

## CHAPTER LXVII. That an unjust excommunication harms the excommunicator more than the excommunicated person.

[Col. 0886D]

Hence the same author, to Cassius [to Classicianus]: “I would certainly not say rashly that, if anyone has been excommunicated unjustly, it harms rather the person who commits the wrong.” Hence the same author, in *On the Highest Good*: “The nature of God cannot harm anything; nor can it harm unjustly; nor does it permit anyone to cause harm.”

Likewise, to the clergy of Hippo (Letter 78, no. 4): “What harm does it do a man if, from that tablet [in Augustine: ‘human ignorance wishes to remove him from it’], human ignorance wishes to take him away, provided that an [in Augustine: ‘unjust’] human conscience does not blot him out from the book of the living?”

## CHAPTER LXVIII. That not only guilt but also due order must be observed in judgment.

Hence the same author, in *On Penance*, lest anyone be condemned through the ignorance of a judge, says (Sermon 351, no. 10): “God did not wish one person to be judged by another on the arbitrary basis of suspicion or by a judgment usurped outside due order, but rather according to God’s law and the order of the Church—whether he has confessed voluntarily, been accused, or even been convicted.”

In all these matters it is evident that a person is bound or loosed not through a priest’s merit but through his office, according to the order of justice.

## CHAPTER LXIX. That ordination performed by pseudo-bishops may be regarded as valid.

Concerning orders, it has been sufficiently said above that they can be administered by evil priests; for the present, a little said may suffice. For Leo says, chapter 25: “If any clerics of the presiding clergy have been ordained by pseudo-bishops, such ordination may be regarded as valid.”

## CHAPTER LXX. That all sacraments are rightly administered by a sinner who is nevertheless a Catholic.

[Col. 0887B]

And, to conclude well that all sacraments can be rightly administered by evil priests who are nevertheless Catholics, Augustine says against the Donatists in Book V (chapter 20, no. 28): “How does God hear a murderer when he prays either over the water of baptism, or over oil, or over the Eucharist, or over the heads of those upon whom they lay hands? Yet all these things are done and are valid even through murderers—that is, through those who hate their brothers—and within the Church itself.”

And he makes the distinction well. For outside the Church there is neither faith nor merit: what power can a sacrament have?

## CHAPTER LXXI. That in Christian unity an evil priest harms neither his good colleagues nor the people subject to him.

[Col. 0887C]

Hence Augustine, *Against Parmenian*, Book II (chap. 5, no. 10):

> “God renders to each according to his heart. For if, in the earliest times, bad priests did not harm either their good fellow-ministers—as was Zechariah—or the people—as was Nathanael, in whom there was no deceit—how much more does a bad bishop in Christian unity harm neither good fellow-bishops nor good laypersons, now that that priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and our high priest seated at the right hand of the Father, intercedes for us—he who was delivered up for our offences and rose again for our justification? Nor does that saying harm the good, but those who make the offerings:  
> 
> [Col. 0887D]  
> 
> ‘The Most High does not approve the gifts of the ungodly’ (Ecclus. 34:23). For he did not say: ‘The Lord does not approve the gifts of those who, for peace, endure the wicked. … The sacrifices of the ungodly are an abomination to the Lord; for they offer them unjustly’ (Prov. 21). The answer has already been given: Christ, who offered himself for us and is our mediator in heaven, is not unjust. While he governs his Church, the wicked do not harm the good, whether they are unknown or endured for the sake of peace. The crimes of such persons would do no harm to the charity of the good, which endures all things in unity, even if those crimes were known and could not be proved to ecclesiastical judges. Therefore the sacrifices of the ungodly harm those very persons who offer them ungodly. For [Col. 0888A] one and the same sacrifice, because of the name of the Lord invoked in it—which is always holy—is such for each person as is the heart with which he approaches to receive it.”

And a little later (chap. 7, no. 12):

> “Let them tell me, then, what saint, whether placed among the priests or among the people, has been harmed in respect of spiritual salvation by a bad and defiled priest. Where Moses and Aaron were, there were sacrilegious murmurers; where Caiaphas was, there were Simeon and the other good persons. But each shall bear his own burden.”

And a little later (chap. 8, no. 15):

> “They say that it is written in the Gospel: ‘God does not hear sinners; but if anyone worships God and does his will, him he hears’ (John 9:31). Do they say this in order that a bad bishop may be understood not to be heard when he prays for the people? But even if that were so, the people, if good and faithful, ought not therefore [Col. 0888B] to be anxious. For Scripture makes them secure when it says: ‘My brethren, I write these things to you, that you may not sin; and if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2:1). It did not say: ‘You have me as your mediator with the Father,’ but: ‘You have Jesus Christ as your advocate.’”

And a little later (chap. 8, nos. 16–17):

> “The one mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, in whom we are one: thus let us preserve unity in the bond of peace; and let us not abandon the good on account of the bad, but endure the bad on account of the good. For it is also certain that God hears sinners. Balaam, a prophet not from the people of Israel but a foreigner hired by a friend (Num. 24:1) to curse God’s people, [Col. 0888C] was turned by God to blessing; and we hear and read all his words as those of one invoking good. Although he had another purpose in his intention, the words of his prayer were good and were heard by the Lord for the people. Hence it is no wonder if good words spoken in prayers for the people, although uttered by bad bishops, are nevertheless heard—not because of the necessity of their rulers, but because of the devotion of the people.
>
> “But the saying written in the Gospel, ‘God does not hear sinners’ (John 9:31), was not spoken by the Lord, but by the man whose bodily eyes had indeed been restored, while the eyes of his heart had not yet been opened. Therefore he still regarded the Lord as a prophet; afterwards, however, when he recognized the Son of God, he worshipped him. The Lord himself, when the tax collector and the Pharisee were praying in the temple, declared the sinner who confessed [Col. 0888D] his sins more justified than the Pharisee who boasted of his merits. Although, once justified, he ceased to be a sinner, nevertheless he prayed in order to be justified and confessed his sins. He was heard and justified. He would not have ceased to be a sinner unless the sinner had first been heard.
>
> “For this reason Truth itself testifies both that every sinner is heard and yet that not every sinner is unheard. But they object that the Psalm says: ‘But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous ordinances and take my covenant into your mouth?’ (Ps. 49:16 [Vulgate]). They do not understand that this means that the sinner should know that the words he utters do not benefit himself, because he does not do what he says; nevertheless, the Lord himself teaches in the Gospel that the things which others hear through bad persons and do are beneficial to them: ‘The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat; therefore do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matt. 23:3).”

## CHAPTER LXXII. That, in hearing the commands of the Lord, one must attend not to the person through whom they are spoken, but to what is spoken and by whom.

Hence Gregory:

> “Let no one despise me in this matter on account of myself. For it often happens that a powerful person has a despised servant; and when he sends through that servant some answer to his own people or to strangers, the person of the speaking servant is not despised, because reverence for the sender is preserved in the heart. Those who hear do not consider through whom they hear, but what they hear or from whom they hear it.”

## CHAPTER LXXIII. That all sacraments, although harmful to those who handle them unworthily, nevertheless benefit those who receive through them worthily.

[Col. 0889B]

In all questions we admonish readers to understand that all sacraments, although harmful to those who handle them unworthily, nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such ministers, just as the word of God. Hence it was said: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do.” Indeed, bad ministers in the Church cannot prejudice divine grace. For the Holy Spirit, being omnipotent, is free in all things: he breathes where he wills (John 3:8), when he wills, and how he wills—now through himself, now through ministers both good and bad.

Hence the Apostle says: “There are diversities of graces. But there is one Lord, who works all things in all, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12: [Col. 0889C] 9). Therefore, if he himself works all things in all, no one does anything apart from him. Hence the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men, and lead them to the tabernacle of the covenant; and I shall take from your spirit and give it to them” (Num. 11:16). He did not say, “You shall take and give,” but, “I shall take and give.”

And lest this should be attributed even to Moses’ merit in gathering or leading them, two of those who had been enrolled did not come to the tabernacle; yet, without being led by Moses, they received the Spirit just as the others did. Although it is said that the Spirit was taken from the spirit of Moses, this happened with no diminution of his own possession, just as if a hundred other lamps were lit from a burning candle. Yet it was said thus in order that one and the same Spirit might be believed to be poured out upon rulers and subjects.

Likewise, under the new grace [Col. 0889D], although the Spirit was ordinarily given only through the laying on of hands, while Peter was still speaking the Holy Spirit fell upon all. Likewise, as is read in Gregory’s *Dialogues*:

> “Not a bishop ordaining him, but an angel bleeding his tongue, an unlearned man became an outstanding preacher.”

## CHAPTER LXXIV. That evil is given beneficially to the good, as Satan’s angel was given to Paul for his protection; and good is given harmfully to the wicked, as the spirit of prophecy was given to Caiaphas for his ruin.

But why should this be surprising concerning good persons, when the Holy Spirit, by inspiring even wicked persons, made them his instrument? Balaam, although a diviner, prophesied that a star would arise from Jacob. Nebuchadnezzar, with the three boys in the furnace, recognized a fourth like the Son. Saul, while pursuing David, was a prophet among the prophets with Samuel at Ramah [Col. 0890A] (1 Sam. 19:24). Caiaphas, because he was high priest that year, prophesied rightly concerning the salvation of the world.

And why should these cases surprise us, when God even placed his own words in the mouth of an ass in order to rebuke Balaam? As the serpent spoke to the human being, so the ass spoke to Balaam. The former deed was diabolical; this one angelic. Thus God put into Balaam’s mouth the bit of his power and compelled him to bless the people whom he wished to curse.

What is the point of all this, except that we should believe that the Holy Spirit does not always breathe where it is worthy, but where he wills and how he wills? In order to show that he comes to the wicked but does not remain with them, he declares that he comes to the good and makes his dwelling with them. Therefore no merits can prejudice his grace or power, since the Lord says to [Col. 0890B] Moses concerning the sons of Aaron: “They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I shall bless them” (Num. 6:27). Likewise in Exodus: “I am the Lord who sanctifies you.”

Hence Augustine says:

> “Let the ministers be righteous, if they wish. But if they do not wish it, the Master makes me secure, saying: ‘Keep and do what they say’ (Matt. 23:3)—not they, but I, who sanctify you.”

For what harm did it do Samuel that he was Heli’s disciple and was brought up with Hophni and Phinehas, who perished under Heli? What benefit did it give Judas that he was chosen by the Lord with the other apostles? What benefit did it give Nicholas that he was received by the apostles into the Levitical rank? An angel of Satan was given to Paul for his protection; the spirit of prophecy was given to Balaam and Caiaphas for their ruin.

[Col. 0890C]

Hence Augustine, Homily 62 (*Tractate 62 on Job*, no. 1):

> “It matters greatly not what is received, but who receives it; nor what sort of thing is given, but what sort of person receives it. For good things harm, and evil things bene[.....]fit, according to the character of those to whom they are given. Why, then, are you surprised that Christ’s bread was given to Judas, through which he was handed over to the devil, when conversely you see that an angel of the devil was given to Paul, through whom he was perfected in Christ? Thus good harmed the wicked and evil benefited the good, because the good person does not consent to evil.”

## CHAPTER LXXV. That evils are committed through consent alone, because no sin exists unless it is voluntary.

Hence Jerome, to Rusticus (Epistle 95, alternatively 4):

> “The vessel of election disciplines his body and subjects it to servitude; yet he sees the natural ardour [Col. 0890D] of his flesh resisting the judgment of his mind, so that he is compelled to do what he does not wish to do, and, as though suffering violence, cries: ‘Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?’” (Rom. 7:24).

Hence Augustine, in the *Retractations*:

> “Sin is so completely a voluntary evil that it is in no way sin unless it is voluntary.”

This definition may seem false; but if it is carefully examined, it is found to be entirely true. For the sin in question must be understood as that which is sin only, not that which is the punishment of sin.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. That even carnal intercourse is not sin without consent of the will.

Hence, although in carnal intercourse consent can most difficultly be excused, Jerome nevertheless says [Col. 0891A] in Book II:

> “Imagine that in some persecution a virgin is prostituted. Since she does not sin voluntarily, she is received as a virgin under the Gospel, though under the Law she is rejected as though defiled.”

The same writer, in the *Hebrew Questions*:

> “It is not a man who defiles a woman’s body, but her will.”

Hence Augustine, *The City of God*, Book I (chap. 18):

> “When the purpose remains, by which the body itself deserved to be sanctified, even the body does not lose its holiness through the violence of another’s lust; it preserves that holiness through the perseverance of its own continence.”

Likewise, we admonish from this passage that:

> “The holiness of the body is not lost while the holiness of the mind remains, even when the body is violated; just as bodily holiness is lost when the holiness of the mind has been violated.”

Hence the same author, in *On Free Choice*:

> “Who could doubt that chastity is established in the mind, [Col. 0891B] since it is a virtue? Therefore it cannot itself be taken away by a violent ravisher.”

And why should it be surprising that, where there is no consent, there is no guilt, when even where consent exists, if there is nevertheless an intention of rational discernment, the fault is venial or none at all?

## CHAPTER LXXVII. That even where there is consent to carnal intercourse, if reason is applied, guilt is either removed or diminished.

Hence Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (chap. 6):

> “Marital intercourse for the sake of begetting has no fault; intercourse to satisfy concupiscence nevertheless has venial fault when it is with one’s spouse for the sake of fidelity to the marriage-bed; but adultery or fornication has mortal fault.”

[Col. 0891C]

Therefore, in that singular unity in which two are one flesh … Hence Augustine says a little later:

> “Since they abstain far more easily, so as not to engage in intercourse, than they moderate themselves so as to engage well, sin is either avoided or moderated by refusing consent or by consenting with discernment. Much more in the Church, where wills and actions differ, can any persons, by not consenting or by enduring with discernment, remain free from the faults of prelates and brethren, and nevertheless participate with them unto salvation in the heavenly sacraments.”

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. That only those to whom evil persons are pleasing communicate with evil persons; those to whom they are displeasing do not communicate with them.

Hence Augustine:

> “Those to whom wicked people are pleasing in [Col. 0891D] unity themselves communicate with the wicked. But those to whom they are displeasing, even though they cannot amend them lest they uproot the wheat together with the tares, communicate not in their deeds but at the altar. Thus they are not merely unstained by them, but deserve praise in the divine words because, for the good of unity, they endure what they hate for the good of unity.”

## CHAPTER LXXIX. That correction must sometimes be withheld from the wicked, lest they themselves become worse or, provoked, harm others.

Likewise Augustine, *The City of God*, Book I, chap. 60:

> “If anyone spares those acting wrongly from rebuke and correction because he seeks a suitable time, or lest they themselves become worse as a result, or lest they impede or oppress [Col. 0892A] weaker persons who are to be instructed in a good and devout life, this does not appear to be an occasion of cupidity, but a counsel of charity.”

## CHAPTER LXXX. That there is no harm in associating with pseudo-bishops and presbyters without consenting to them.

Hence Pope Zacharias, to Boniface, in the letter beginning, “Blessed are you, O God and Father”:

> “Because you have associated with pseudo-bishops and presbyters without consenting to their wickedness, you suffer no harm before God.”

## CHAPTER LXXXI. That those who give any consent to the faults of prelates are implicated in them.

On the contrary, Cyprian the martyr says in his letter:

> “Let not the people flatter themselves as though they could be immune from the contagion of sin while communicating with a sinful priest [Col. 0892B] and lending assent to the unlawful crime of their superior. For it is certain that all who have been polluted by the sacrifice of an unjust and profane priest are bound by the same crime.”

Was it not because Jonah, in disobedience, was in the ship that the ship was in danger of being broken up? Because Achan, with the accursed golden plate, was in Israel, the army was struck down and driven from the city of Ai. If those unaware of the fault were punished thus, what will happen to those who know and consent?

## CHAPTER LXXXII. That the wicked must be carefully avoided, lest we become implicated in their faults; and cast out of the Church, lest we perish with them.

Hence Ambrose, in his homilies:

> “By the offence of one person [Col. 0892C] the merits of all are shaken. For Christ slept for Peter, lest he should remain awake for Judas. Therefore, if all the apostles are endangered by the sin of one person, let us by this example beware of the faithless, beware of the traitor, lest through one person many of us be tossed upon the waves. Indeed, let us cast such a person out of our little boat, so that the Lord may not sleep but keep watch for us. For the Lord sleeps or keeps watch according to our deeds.”

And a little later:

> “Through the fault of one person cowardice is imparted to all, and through the offence of one person weakness is produced in all.”

But the Lord punished these persons, though ignorant, for another’s guilt in order that we might not, through any simplicity or negligence, become implicated in the evils of others. Rather, we must watch carefully that we offer them no assent.

[Col. 0892D]

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15). Behold: the Lord commands that wickedness veiled under any appearance of virtue be carefully watched for. Hence the Apostle: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1); and again: “Do not believe every spirit” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. By what discernment so great a diversity of Scriptures is to be fulfilled: since the wicked are at one time commanded to be excommunicated, while at another time they are to be moderately corrected in order that they may be healed.

Since, then, it has been said that the wicked, even when known, are to be endured for the peace of the Church whenever they do us no harm either by their association or by participation in the sacraments—but rather benefit the faithful [Col. 0893A] by their preaching, prayer, and all other ecclesiastical mysteries, whether they celebrate these from self-interested motive or, as the Apostle says, in truth—Augustine asserts that we deserve praise for enduring them; the Lord in the Gospel admonishes us to beware of them; Ambrose commands that they be cast out of the Church’s vessel lest we perish with them, teaching that the fault of one person brings cowardice upon all. From this variety of commands no contradiction may be imputed to the saints, whose Spirit is one not of dissension but of peace.

But since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, the greatest discernment must be exercised, so that with the Psalmist we may sing mercy and judgment to God (Ps. 100:1), showing that both must be carried out not discordantly but harmoniously and concordantly, [Col. 0893B] each in its proper order and with its proper discernment. Thus, that must be done and this must not be omitted; there is a proper time for endurance and likewise a proper time for discipline. For, as Solomon says: “There is a time to plant and a time to uproot” (Eccl. 3:2).

So long as the wicked cannot be accused—either because we lack the evidence for accusation, because there is no accuser, no sufficient number of witnesses, no credibility, or no such manifest proof of guilt as can be testified to; or because, even if accused, they would not be heard by wicked judges of the Church; or because accusers could not correct them but would be forsworn; or because they are persons who, by themselves or through their supporters, can stir up throughout the Church the scandal either of schism or oppression—so long they must be endured, [Col. 0893C] though by no consent embraced. Yet it must be diligently considered whether they act from intention, frailty, or necessity.

Thus, in order that mercy may be sung and harmonize with judgment, Augustine describes the balance and discernment of each in *On Faith and Works* (chap. 3, no. 4):

> “The Lord forbids the holy thing to be given to dogs; nor is the Apostle contrary to the Lord when he says: ‘Rebuke those who sin before all, so that the rest also may fear’ (1 Tim. 5:20), while the Lord says: ‘Rebuke him between yourself and him alone’ (Matt. 18:15). For both must be done, as the diverse weakness of those whom we have undertaken not to destroy but to correct and heal requires; one person is to be healed in this way, another in that way.
>
> [Col. 0893D]
>
> “Likewise, there is a rationale for overlooking and enduring evil persons in the Church; and, again, a rationale for punishing, rebuking, refusing admission, or removing from communion. But people err by not observing the proper measure; and once they begin to incline toward one side, they do not look to the other testimonies of divine authority by which they could be recalled from that tendency and stand in the balanced diversity and moderation arising from both.
>
> “Some, looking at the commands of severity by which we are admonished to rebuke the unruly, not to give the holy thing to dogs, to regard a despiser of the Church as a heathen, and to remove from the body’s structure the member that causes scandal, so disturb the peace of the Church that they attempt to separate the tares before the time; blinded by this error, they themselves are rather separated [Col. 0894A] from the unity of Christ.
>
> “Others, by contrast, fall into danger when they see that the mingling of good and bad persons in the Church has been demonstrated or foretold, and when they receive commands of patience—which make us steadfast, so that even if tares appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity may not be hindered, lest, because we see tares, we ourselves withdraw from the Church. They think that ecclesiastical discipline must be abandoned and grant the rulers a most perverse security, as though their task were only to say what should be avoided or done, while caring nothing whatever for what anyone does.
>
> “But we judge that sound doctrine requires life and judgment to be moderated by both sets of testimonies: that we endure dogs in the Church [Col. 0894B] for the peace of the Church, but do not give the holy thing to dogs where the Church’s peace is secure.
>
> “Therefore, when, whether through the negligence of rulers, some excusable necessity, or secret intrusions, we find in the Church evil persons whom we cannot correct through ecclesiastical discipline, then let not that impious and destructive presumption rise in our heart whereby we suppose ourselves obliged to separate from them lest we be defiled by their sins. Let those Scriptural comparisons, divine oracles, and most certain examples come to mind by which it has been shown that evil persons will remain mingled with the good in the Church until the end of the age and the time of judgment, and that they will do no harm to good persons in unity and participation in the sacraments who do not consent to their deeds.
>
> [Col. 0894C]
>
> “But when those through whom the Church is governed possess, while peace is preserved, the power to exercise discipline against the wicked, then, lest we sleep in sloth and indolence, we must again be roused by other spurs of precepts concerning the severity of correction. Guided and aided by him, we must direct our steps in the Lord’s way from both sets of testimonies, neither becoming sluggish under the name of patience nor becoming cruel under the pretext of diligence.”

[Col. 0894D]

And a little later:

> “If, in the aforesaid accommodation, anyone accuses you of some kind of dissembling or feigning, we read that useful dissimulation is to be employed at the proper time. Thus Cephas withdrew and separated himself, fearing those persons; and the vessel of election shaved his head and circumcised Timothy. The Son of God himself also pretended to be going farther and pretended not to know what he knew.”

Likewise, in the same chapter 180:

> “We must beware of thinking that these parables of wheat and tares have been proposed so that ecclesiastical discipline may sleep—discipline of which, under the figure of that woman, it was said: ‘Her house is of severe conduct.’ Rather, I warn that the rashness of what is more madness than severity of discipline must not advance so far as to presume to separate, through wicked schisms, the good from the bad. For these parables and pronouncements do not give the good counsel of indolence, so that they neglect what they ought to prevent; rather, they give counsel of patience, so that, without injury to the doctrine of truth, they endure what they cannot amend.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. That some persons are not to be excommunicated, lest they contaminate others by their excommunication.

[Col. 0895A]

Hence Augustine also, to Emeritus the Donatist (Epistle 87, no. 4):

> “We do not blame you if at that time you did not wish to excommunicate Optatus, lest, once excommunicated, he should draw many people with him and your communion should collapse through the fury of schism.”

## CHAPTER LXXXV. That correction must not be delayed.

Hence Augustine also, *Against Parmenian*, Book II (chap. 11, no. 25):

> “Since it is clear that nothing is more serious than schism, there is no just necessity for breaking unity apart; since the good endure the wicked in order not to be spiritually separated from the good, although the wicked can in no way harm them spiritually; since consideration [Col. 0895B] for preserving peace restrains or defers the severity of discipline, which security nevertheless exercises; since it is clear that they can be punished by ecclesiastical judgment for a more salutary correction without the wound of schism.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. That one must sometimes assist a sinner—not in what he does wrongly, but in what he does rightly, even if his intention is wrong.

Even if good persons meanwhile support or rejoice with bad persons, not in evil but in any good thing they may happen to accomplish, even with an evil intention, this does no harm. Hence Augustine says a little later—the book appears to be missing—in the same work (*Against Parmenian*, Book II, chap. 18, no. 37):

> “Who says that a sinner is to be helped in that in which he does not wish to sin? Thus [Col. 0895C] Jehoshaphat assisted Ahab by going to battle with him, although Ahab despised the words of the prophet Micaiah (2 Kings 22:18); nevertheless, his other good deeds prevailed so that they were delivered from the danger of war.
>
> [Col. 0895C]
>
> “But one who lives in the Church of God, where there are also those who seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, who proclaim Christ through envy and contention and not sincerely, and who says, ‘Whether in truth or from self-interested motive, Christ is proclaimed’ (Phil. 1:15), ‘in this I rejoice, and shall rejoice’—such a person remains unstained among them, because he does not consent to them in seeking their own interests, but blames and rebukes this. Nor does he help them toward sin, but toward that by which Christ may be more widely preached: so that through those who hear and do, Christ may be believed through what such persons say, not what they do; Christ may be hoped in; [Col. 0895D] Christ may be loved.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. That the correction of sinners must be exercised charitably, mercifully, and with discernment.

And a little later in the same work (ibid., chap. 21, no. 41):

> “Certainly, someone associates with evil persons if he commits some evil with them or favors those committing it. But if he does neither, he is in no way associated with them. Further, if he adds a third thing—that he is not sluggish in judging, but either rebukes and reproves, as a righteous person, in mercy; or, if he holds such an office and the consideration of peace allows it, rebukes sinners before all so that the rest may fear; even removes them from some rank of honor or from communion in the sacraments themselves—and does all this with [Col. 0896A] love for correction, not hatred for persecution, he has fulfilled the fullest office not merely of most chaste innocence but of most diligent severity. But where the other measures are impeded, those first two, always retained, preserve him uncorrupted: that he neither does evil nor approves what has been done.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. That it is a sin to defer correction if it can be carried out without impediment.

And a little later (ibid., chap. 22, no. 42):

> “By ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0895D] In Augustine: ‘ecclesiastical discipline.’] rule, correction must be made lest, through persuasion, it spread to many. Where the condition of peace permits this to be done and it is not done, negligence itself incurs guilt and brings danger of consenting, either by neglecting correction or through sloth.”

And a little later, Book III (chap. 1, no. 12):

> “Whoever despises the discipline of the Church of God, so as to [Col. 0896B] cease admonishing, correcting, and reproving evil persons with whom he does not sin and whom he does not favor—if he also holds such an office and the peace of the Church permits it, even to separate them from participation in the sacraments—does not sin in another person’s manner, but in his own. Negligence itself in so great a matter is a grave evil. Therefore the Apostle admonishes a person to remove evil from himself: namely, not only the boldness to commit evil, but also the slowness to correct and the negligence to punish.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. That, when many are infected with the same disease, correction ought rather to be delayed than exercised, because it is better for some persons not to be corrected in the Church than for the Church itself to be torn apart.

And a little later, explaining this, he says (Book III, chap. 2, [Col. 0896C] no. 13):

> “When firm security remains concerning the stable condition of the grain—that is, when each person’s crime is so well known and appears so detestable to all that it has either no defenders at all or none such through whom schism could occur—then let the severity of discipline not sleep. In it the correction of wickedness is more effective in proportion as the preservation of charity is more diligent.
>
> “But this can be done without injury to peace and unity and without damage to the grain when the multitude of the Church’s congregation is free from the crime for which the person is anathematized. Then it assists the ruler in rebuking rather than the criminal in resisting; then it beneficially withdraws from association with him, so as not even to eat with him. Then he is struck by fear and healed by shame, [Col. 0896D] seeing himself anathematized by the whole Church.”

And a little later (ibid., no. 14):

> “The Apostle says of such a remedy: ‘Sufficient for such a person is the rebuke imposed by many’—that is, when the person rebuked has no allied multitude. But when the same disease has seized many, nothing remains for the good except grief and groaning, and the stern mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For counsels of separation are empty, harmful, and sacrilegious: they destroy more weak good persons than they correct resolute bad ones.”

The first part of the book ends.

# SECOND PART

[Col. 0897]

## CHAPTER I. That in the discipline of the Church, measure and proper times must be observed.

[Col. 0897A]

Since enough seems to have been said above concerning the endurance of the wicked, let us explain what measure of discernment and order ought to be observed in the canonical exercise of discipline upon them. Hence Augustine, *Against Parmenian*, Book III (chap. 2, no. 15), says:

> “When someone must be removed from the congregation of brethren through the correction of separation, this must be done with the aim of healing, not with the hatred of destroying. A proper measure must be applied and the appropriate times observed, lest the peace of the Church be violated; in that peace the wheat must especially be spared, lest it be uprooted together with the tares. Let every person carefully consider this, lest in preserving unity he neglect the severity of discipline, or by excessive coercion break the bond [Col. 0897B] of fellowship.”

## CHAPTER II. That discipline must be exercised with good intention and great discernment.

For the accomplishment of this, good intention is especially effective. Hence Leo, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Epistle 92):

> “Justice must be held firmly and clemency bestowed kindly. Let sins be hated and proud persons rebuked; let the weak be endured; and what must be more severely punished should be punished not in the temper of one raging, but of one healing.”

Hence Augustine, in *On True Religion*:

> “Let them do nothing weakly, nothing rashly, regarding the sins of others. Either let them wholly banish anger, or restrain it so that it resembles anger already banished. Let them observe most carefully, when judging, that they do not do too much; when forgiving, that they do not do too little. Let them punish nothing [Col. 0897C] that cannot conduce to improvement; indulge nothing that may turn to worse. Let them avoid enmities most cautiously, bear them most fairly, and end them most swiftly. In all human intercourse it is enough to keep this one common proverb: let them do to no one what they would not wish to suffer.”

Likewise Augustine, in the *Soliloquies*:

> “Just as those who fear are commanded to owe love to those who terrify them, so those who terrify others are commanded to fear those whom they terrify. Let nothing be done from a desire to harm, but let all things be done through the charity of concern; then nothing will be done vainly, nothing inhumanely.”

## CHAPTER III. That in discipline mercy must be maintained more than severity.

Hence Ambrose, Book I of *On Penance against Novatian* (chap. 1):

> “Moderation ought to temper [Col. 0897D] justice. For how can one whom you regard with disgust offer himself to you for healing, when he thinks his physician will treat him with contempt rather than compassion? Therefore the Lord Jesus suffered for us in order to call us to himself, not frighten us away; he is gentle and humble. Accordingly he says: ‘Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you’ (Matt. 11:28). The Lord refreshes; he does not exclude or reject. Rightly, therefore, he chose disciples who, as interpreters of the Lord’s will, gathered the Lord’s people rather than cast them off.

[Col. 0898A]

> “Hence it is clear that those are not to be reckoned among Christ’s disciples who believe that harshness rather than gentleness, pride rather than humility, ought to be followed; and who, though they seek mercy for themselves, deny it to others.”

And a little later (ibid., chap. 3):

> “He makes no distinction, who promised his mercy to all and granted his priests authority to remit without qualification.”

And a little later:

> “That we may recognize that the Lord is more inclined to mercy than insistent upon severity, he himself says: ‘I desire mercy more than sacrifice’ (Matt. 9:13).”

Likewise (ibid., chap. 4, no. 16):

> “Where the Lord confesses, he confesses for all; he embraces all. Where he denies, he does not deny all. ‘Everyone who confesses me, I too shall confess him’ (Matt. 10:32): that is, every [Col. 0898B] person.
