It would have followed that he should likewise say below, ‘Everyone, however, who denies’; but, lest all should appear to deny, he instead added: ‘But whoever denies me before human beings, I too shall deny’ (ibid.). He promises grace to all; he does not threaten injury to all. He amplifies what belongs to mercy; he qualifies what belongs to vengeance.”

## CHAPTER IV. That both in forgiving the wicked and in punishing them, one must always act with the intention of love and correction.

Likewise Augustine:

> “Discipline must not be extended unto death, so that there may remain someone to whom it can be beneficial; for both in punishing and in forgiving, the only good purpose is the correction of human life. But if impiety is so great that neither discipline nor pardon can benefit its correction, nevertheless the duty of love, as God discerns the intention, is fulfilled if, in acting against him [Latin uncertain: *in senem agendo*], [Col. 0898C] integrity is preserved so that humanity is not lost.”

## CHAPTER V. In how many ways consent is given to the wicked: by praise, imitation, and silence.

But because assent must not be given to evil prelates, so that it may be guarded against more carefully, observe in how many ways it occurs: it occurs by imitation, or also by failing to rebuke what is evil. Gregory forbids us to assent by imitation in the *Moralia* (book XXV, ch. 16, no. 31):

> “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34:30). “If,” he says, “through the anger of God on account of our deserts, we receive bad rulers, we may gather from their conduct what we ought to think of our own estimation. But we must beware lest we reverence them to the point of being compelled to imitate them, since Peter says that we ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Augustine forbids us to assent by praise, saying:

> “If you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Ps. 49 [50]:18). “Perhaps you would say: ‘I did not commit theft; I did not commit adultery.’ But what if the person who did it pleased you? Did you not run with him by that very pleasure? Did you not assign your share with him who acted, by praising him? For even if you do not do it, yet praise what is done, you are an accomplice in the deed. You do not commit evils; you praise evils—is this a small evil?”

Leo forbids us to assent by not rebuking:

> “He who does not recall others from error shows himself to be in error.”

And Gregory (book X, ch. 6):

> “He seems to assent to one who errs who does not intervene to cut away vices, so that he may be corrected.”

Likewise Innocent:

> “An error that is not resisted is approved; and truth, when it is not defended at all, is crushed.”

And Pius, pope, forbids us to offer any assent to one who errs:

> “What profit is it that a man is not polluted by his own error when he gives assent to one who errs?”

## CHAPTER VI. That truth must not be concealed either from love or from fear.

Likewise Fabian:

> “He who fears almighty God in no way consents to act contrary to the Gospel, the apostles, the prophets, or the institutions of his fathers.” [Col. 0899B]

Augustine says that truth must not be abandoned even through fear of some authority or of offending carnal affection, if need requires:

> “Whoever conceals the truth through fear of some authority provokes the wrath of God against himself, because he feared man more than God.”

Likewise:

> “It is most certain that neither friendship, nor kinship, nor the height of royal power ought to be more precious than truth.”

Hence Gregory, chapter 48:

> “When Moses saw God angry with the people, and ordered swords to be drawn for vengeance, he declared those to be on God’s side who would without delay strike the crimes of the guilty, saying: ‘Whoever is for the Lord, let him join me; let every man put his sword upon his thigh. Go to and fro from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother,’ etc.” (Exod. 32:26).
>
> “To go from gate to gate is, by rebuking, to range from vice to vice through which death enters into the mind. But to go through the midst of the camp is to live within the Church with such impartiality that one who reproves the faults of the guilty ought not to turn aside through favor toward anyone. Therefore, if he is called God’s who is stirred by zeal for divine love to strike vices, then he plainly denies that he is God’s who, insofar as he is able, refuses to rebuke the life of the carnal.” [Col. 0899C]

## CHAPTER VII. That truth must not be kept silent either through fear of scandal or through false compassion.

[Col. 0899D]

But this is sometimes kept silent, not from a desire for favor, but through fear of scandal or compassion arising from false mercy, as Gregory says in his homilies on Ezekiel (Homily 7, no. 5):

> “So far as we can without sin, we ought to avoid causing scandal to our neighbors. But if scandal is taken from truth, it is more useful to permit scandal to arise than to abandon truth.”

## CHAPTER VIII. That, although outward peace is disturbed by rebuke, inward peace must nevertheless be maintained through love.

Hence Gregory in the *Pastoral Rule* (part III), chapter 46 [22]:

> “Present peace must be so maintained that it ought both to be loved and despised, lest, if it is loved without moderation, the mind of the one who loves it be taken captive in punishment. Therefore peaceful persons must be warned lest, while they desire human peace too greatly, they fail altogether to rebuke the depraved morals of men and, by consenting to the perverse, become separated from the peace of their Creator; lest, while they fear outward human quarrels, they be wounded by the rupture of the inward covenant.
>
> “For what is transitory peace except a trace of eternal peace? What, then, is more foolish than to love footprints impressed in dust, but not to love that from which they were impressed? Hence David testifies that he maintains no concord with the wicked, saying: ‘Do I not hate those who hate thee, O God, and pine away over thine enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred, and they became enemies to me’ (Ps. 138 [139]:21). To hate God’s enemies with perfect hatred is to love what they have become and to rebuke what they have not become.
>
> “It must therefore be considered, when rebuke is withheld, how great is the fault in maintaining peace even with the worst persons, if so great a Prophet offered to God, as it were, this sacrifice: that for the Lord’s sake he stirred up against himself the enmities of wicked men. Hence the tribe of Levi, because it was unwilling to spare sinners, was said to have consecrated its hand to God (Exod. 32:27). Hence Phinehas struck the man coupling with the Midianites and, being angry, appeased the Lord’s anger (Num. 25:9). Hence Truth says: ‘Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace on earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword’ (Matt. 10:34).
>
> “Hence Jehoshaphat, who is extolled by so many praises for his former life, is rebuked for friendship with King Ahab: ‘You give aid to the ungodly,’ he says, ‘and join in friendship with those who hate the Lord’ (2 Chron. 19:2). Therefore peaceful persons must be warned, when they leap forth with words of correction, not to fear disturbing their temporal peace; and again they must be warned to maintain inwardly, by undiminished love, that same peace which they outwardly disturb by the attack of their speech.” [Col. 0900C]
>
> “Hence the Psalmist says: ‘With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause’ (Ps. CIX, 7). Behold: while speaking, he was attacked; when attacked, he remained peaceable, because he neither ceased to rebuke those who raged nor neglected to love those whom he rebuked. Hence Paul says: ‘If it be possible, as far as depends on you, live at peace with all men’ (Rom. 12:18). It is as though he said: If peace is driven away by those who are rebuked, nevertheless let it remain in your mind.
>
> “Hence the same Apostle says to his disciples: ‘If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark that man and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed’ (2 Thess. 3:14). But, lest he be hated even when avoided, he added: ‘Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother’ (ibid., 15). It is as though he said: Let your disagreement strike the sinner in such a way that peace does not depart from your hearts.”

## CHAPTER IX. That mercy is unjust when bestowed upon the wicked and impenitent.

But because the undiscerning fall from this commanded peace of charity into false mercy, Ambrose says on Psalm 118 [119] (sermon 8, no. 25):

> “To wish to forgive before repentance for sin is unjust mercy. For it is written in the Law: ‘You shall not spare him’ (Deut. 19:13); and in the book of Kings, Saul incurred offense precisely because he spared Agag, king of the enemies (1 Sam. 15:8), whom the divine judgment forbade to be preserved. Thus, if someone, moved by the entreaties of a robber’s children and bent by the tears of his wife, thinks that he should be absolved while he still desires to commit robbery, does he not hand over the innocent to destruction when he frees one who is plotting the destruction of many?” [Col. 0901A]

## CHAPTER X. That it is true mercy to correct the wicked.

Hence Pelagius, to all bishops and to all who spiritually serve the Lord throughout Campania and Italy:

> “Strictness exercised toward persecutors and criminals is mercy.”

Likewise:

> “Remedies must be foreseen before the disease grows.”

Likewise:

> “The conduct of the world is restrained by fear of laws; but ecclesiastical guardianship is preserved and governed by the reins of rules.” [Col. 0901B]

## CHAPTER XI. That sometimes failure to correct is attributable not to simplicity but to sloth.

Hence Augustine, Homily 6:

> “There are some who are called simple but are slothful. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, was not such a man: he was simple because he harmed no one; he was fervent because he rebuked the ungodly.”

## CHAPTER XII. That we must forgive, for God’s sake, what is committed against us; but canonically punish what is committed against God.

And because Stephen himself prayed for his stoners, whom he rebuked as transgressors against God, Augustine says:

> “Let us therefore forgive, for God’s sake, what has been perpetrated against us; and what has been committed against God—which we cannot forgive—let us punish according to canonical authority.” [Col. 0901C]

## CHAPTER XIII. That prelates ought not only to be rebuked but also accused and convicted by their subjects.

Therefore, since transgressors must not be left unreproved because of favor, fear, mercy, or simplicity, and since this is established with respect to others, it must be considered at what time, with what discrimination of intention, and in what order prelates are to be rebuked by subjects, and by whom; and, if they refuse correction, accused, and afterward condemned by prelates.

We find that ecclesiastical practice has observed, and the authority of the canons has sanctioned, that prelates are not merely rebuked but accused and convicted by their subjects. For, as we read in the books *On Illustrious Men*:

> “Pope Damasus, accused of adultery by his subjects, was cleared together with forty-two bishops.” [Col. 0901D]

Likewise:

> “Pope Symmachus, stripped of his rank in the Roman synod, was first decreed to be restored to his former position, so that he might then come to trial and, if it seemed right, make answer. The matter seemed worthy to the great number of priests, so that it obtained effect. And afterward, when it was arranged how the aforesaid pope should be accused so as to plead his case, this came to pass, unless it was hindered by his enemies.”

Likewise Paul:

> “The bishop of the city of Deaclina, accused by his subjects of a lapse of the flesh, was convicted and deposed; another was appointed in his place.”

Let us see how Gregory approved this in his register, to Bishop John (book XII, epistle 31), chapter 217:

> “The bearer Nemezion, coming to us, reported that Paul, bishop of the city of Deaclina, had been accused by his own clerics of falling into a bodily crime, and, after an inquiry had been held, convicted. Therefore, after he had been deposed by episcopal sentence, another bishop was ordained in his place.” [Col. 0902A]

Having said this, he does not take vengeance on the accusers or those who deposed him, but proceeds further against the deposed man:

> “If he should hereafter aspire to the episcopate, let him be shut up in a monastery to perform perpetual penance.”

## CHAPTER XIV. That bishops ought to accuse their metropolitan.

That this is not merely practiced but sanctioned by canonical authority, and that punishment was imposed upon those who refused to rebuke or accuse prelates, let us see by what authority bishops may accuse the faults of their metropolitans. Gregory says to Innocent and the other bishops of Sardinia (book IX, epistle 8):

> “Do not presume to set aside your metropolitan in any matter, except if—as we do not wish—it should happen that you have some case against him, so that for this reason you ought to seek the judgment of the Apostolic See.” [Col. 0902B]

Likewise Gregory to all the bishops of the Council of Vizacium (book XII, epistle 32):

> “Just as it is praiseworthy and discerning to show reverence and honor to one’s superiors, so it is a matter of rectitude and fear of God, if they need correction in any respect, to pass nothing over through dissimulation, lest—God forbid—the disease invade the whole body if the sickness in the head is not cut away.
>
> “For certain matters concerning your primate Clementius have been brought to us; and, because they are so grave that they ought in no way to be passed over without investigation, we exhort your brotherhood to investigate their substance in many ways, with every care and vigor for truth. And if they are as they have been reported, let them be cut away by canonical punishment. We warn you, moreover, that no regard for any person, no favor, no flattery whatsoever, soften any one of you toward the matters reported to us or shake him from the truth; but gird yourselves priestly, for God’s sake, to investigate the truth. For if anyone should presume to be slothful or negligent in this matter, let him know that before God he shares in the crimes spoken of, whose zeal is not moved to search out carefully the causes of the abominable offense.” [Col. 0902C]

## CHAPTER XV. That clerics may accuse anyone of a superior rank, even a bishop; and that the bishop himself ought not to rebuke.

Likewise Gelasius, chapter 28, commands all clerics of every rank generally, with respect to their prelates:

> “Therefore, let none of the clerics trust that he will be free from this offense if, in matters which we have declared ought salutarily to be followed, he sees a bishop, priest, or deacon exceed the bounds and does not promptly take care to report it to us, provided suitable proofs are presented, so that punishment may be imposed on the transgressor and others may be forbidden to offend.” [Col. 0902D]

Every pontiff will himself be a violator of his rank and honor if he judges that these matters should be suppressed from the hearing of any clerics or of the whole Church.

And so that it may be clear that it is a sin to assent to evil and not to accuse prelates, Lucillus, bishop of the city of Miletus, is accused before Gregory (book IX, epistle 63). Gregory, recognizing through the testimony of fellow bishops that the charges brought were true, orders him deposed; and, as is found in his writings, he likewise condemns the priests and deacons who had known of or participated in his crime. [Col. 0903A]

## CHAPTER XVI. With what discrimination one should understand the fact that the saints forbid prelates to be rebuked or accused by subjects, yet again command that they be accused and rebuked by them.

Since, then, this has both been practiced and canonically commanded, and punished if not done, what does it mean that the saints forbid prelates to be defamed, rebuked, or accused by subjects? Especially since Sylvester, with the consent and subscription of all in a synod, expressly decreed that no layman should dare bring an accusation against a cleric, nor a cleric of lower rank against anyone of higher rank; moreover, other saints command that such defamers of prelates be deemed infamous, deprived of their own rank, or marked with some stigma of dishonor.

In all these matters, the greatest discrimination must be made concerning the persons who accuse and those accused; and attention must be given to the intention and order in which they act. Augustine, distinguishing this in the *Soliloquies*, says:

> “It is one thing to rebuke or disapprove; another thing to accuse anyone. For prelates presume that they ought not to be rebuked because the canons do not establish that they may be accused indiscriminately. Yet this is denied only to criminal persons, since Truth itself establishes, by rebuking: ‘If I have spoken evil, bear witness concerning the evil’” (John 18:23). [Col. 0903C]

## CHAPTER XVII. That even good laymen are to be admitted to accuse bishops.

Hence the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 21, provides that clerics or laymen who accuse bishops and clerics indiscriminately and without proof ought not to be admitted to accusation, unless the reputation of their character is first examined.

In this, not only clerics but laymen also are admitted to accuse bishops, provided that they accuse not indiscriminately and disorderly, but with proof of another’s fault and with a good reputation for their own intention and life. Hence the Council of Carthage, chapter 8: Numidius, bishop of Affulita, said:

> “There are very many men of bad conduct who think that elders or bishops ought to be assailed in accusation indiscriminately and at random. Ought they to be admitted so easily or not?”

Bishop Aurelius said:

> “It pleases your charity, then, that one entangled in certain crimes should not have a voice to accuse elders.” [Col. 0903D]

## CHAPTER XVIII. That good young men ought by strict rebuke to strike evil old men.

But what is forbidden to these evil persons is elsewhere permitted to good younger men against evil elders. Hence Gregory (book IX, epistle 1) to Bishop Januarius:

> “Paul says: ‘Do not rebuke an elder’ (1 Tim. 5:1); but this rule of his is to be observed when an elder’s fault does not by its example draw the hearts of the younger to destruction. But where an elder offers the younger an example leading to destruction, there he must be struck by strict rebuke. For it is written: ‘A snare of youths are all of you’ [reading uncertain] (Isa. 42:22); and again: ‘The child a hundred years old shall be accursed’ (Isa. 65:20).” [Col. 0904A]

Behold: so that we may have authority from the saints to restrict rules to their true meaning according to different persons, Gregory has restricted to certain faults of elders that are not to be rebuked what Paul stated absolutely and, as it were, universally—not to all elders.

## CHAPTER XIX. That not all bishops are bishops.

For there are elders who are not elders; there are bishops who are not bishops. Hence Jerome to Heliodorus (epistle 5, otherwise 1):

> “Not all bishops are bishops. You look to Peter, but consider Judas. You admire Stephen, but look also at Nicholas. Ecclesiastical dignity does not make a man a Christian. Cornelius the centurion, still a heathen, is cleansed by the gift of the Holy Spirit; Daniel, a boy, judges priests. It is not easy to stand in the place of Peter and Paul, to hold the rank of those now reigning with Christ. Salt that has lost its savor is good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled by swine. If a monk falls, a priest will pray for him; for the fall of a priest, who will pray?” [Col. 0904B]

Likewise Augustine, Homily 6 (*Tractates on John*, tractate 6, no. 4):

> “Not everyone who says, ‘Peace be with you,’ is to be heard as a dove.”

Immediately distinguishing the raven from the dove, he says:

> “Ravens feed on death; the dove does not do this, but lives on the fruits of the earth; its food is innocent. This truly, brothers, is remarkable in the dove; but even the very smallest sparrows kill flies. The dove does none of these things; it does not feed on death.” [Col. 0904C]

Therefore, because bishops are not bishops, priests are judged by Daniel, a boy; salt loses its savor and is trampled by swine; and he who says, “Peace be with you,” is not regarded as a dove but as a raven. Thus one must not always act against younger persons on account of a person’s office or authority, since every person sinning criminally is, so to speak, altered and is deemed by the laws to have suffered a diminution of civil status. For “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34), both in punishment and in guilt.

## CHAPTER XX. That a bad or shameless bishop should be called a dog rather than a bishop.

[Col. 0904D]

Hence Gregory:

> “He who neither exercised the reason of governance in himself, nor wiped away his own offenses, nor corrected the crime of his children, ought to be called a dog rather than a bishop.”

Therefore, from those to whom Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory take away the name of dove or bishop, ought not the privilege also to be taken away, so that they may be rebuked by a subject? Hence Scripture, disregarding the privilege of depraved old age, says: “Accursed—not an elder, but a child a hundred years old” (Isa. 65:20).

## CHAPTER XXI. That correction from inferiors must not be shunned.

Therefore, because the Church maintains in practice and authority that subjects rebuke and accuse prelates, it also commands that prelates not disdain or shun the rebukes of subjects. Hence Augustine to Jerome:

> “Although, according to the terms established by usage, a bishop is greater than a presbyter, Augustine is less than Jerome; for correction, even if it comes from one inferior, must not be shunned or despised if it is made without injury to charity.” [Col. 0905A]

## CHAPTER XXII. That, even if subjects rebuke prelates with an evil intention, prelates ought nevertheless to defend themselves in order to avoid a greater scandal.

But even if something is done by subjects through a perverse intention or importunity, the prelate ought humbly to endure it and reasonably defend himself, lest a greater scandal arise in the Church and he become an author of ruin to others. Hence Gregory to Theotista, patrician lady (book II, epistle 45):

> “Consider, I beg you: where will patience be if there is nothing to be endured? He cannot be Abel whom Cain’s malice does not test.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0905] In Gregory: “I do not suppose that he is Abel who has not Cain as a brother.”]
>
> “For the very abundance of the wicked is the purification of the good.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But because the murmuring of foolish people can be stilled by calm reasoning, I believe it is a sin if a good thing which can be done is neglected. For when we presume to appease insane minds and lead them back to salvation, we ought by no means to scandalize them. There are some scandals which ought wholly to be despised; but others, when they can be avoided without fault, ought not to be despised, lest they be preserved with fault.
>
> “We have learned this from the preaching of the holy Gospel: when Truth said, ‘What enters the mouth does not defile a man,’ and the disciples said, ‘Do you know that the Pharisees were scandalized when they heard this saying?’ he immediately answered: ‘Leave them; they are blind leaders of the blind’ (Matt. 15:11). Yet when the tax was demanded, he first gave a reason why he ought not to pay the tax, and immediately added: ‘Nevertheless, lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast in a hook, take the fish, and, when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Give it to them for me and for yourself’ (Matt. 17:26).
>
> “What, then, is meant by the fact that concerning some who were scandalized it is said, ‘Leave them’; while for others, lest they be scandalized by the Lord, a tax not owed is paid? Why did he permit one scandal to occur but prohibit another, except to teach us both to disregard those scandals which entangle us in sins and, by every means, to mitigate those which we may presume to appease without sin? Your Excellency, therefore, can calmly avoid the scandals of perverse men.” [Col. 0905D]

And shortly afterward:

> “Let it not seem unworthy to us to satisfy the people, by anathema, concerning the perverse propositions by which they speak against us.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Certainly Peter had received the power of the kingdom of heaven, so that whatever he bound and loosed on earth should be bound and loosed in heaven; he walked upon the sea, healed the sick by his shadow, killed sinners by a word, and raised the dead. Yet because, at the prompting of the Spirit, he had entered the house of Cornelius, a Gentile, the faithful raised a question against him: why had he gone in to Gentiles and eaten with them; why had he received them in baptism?” [Col. 0906A]

And shortly afterward:

> “If, when he was blamed by the faithful, he had considered the authority that he had received in the holy Church, he could have answered that the sheep entrusted to him ought not to dare rebuke their shepherd. But if he had said anything concerning his power in the complaint of the faithful, he would certainly not have been a teacher of gentleness. Therefore he appeased them with humble reasoning, and in the matter for which he was reproved he even produced witnesses, saying: ‘These six brothers also came with me’ (Acts 11:12).
>
> “If, therefore, the shepherd of the Church, the prince of the apostles, uniquely performing signs and miracles, did not disdain humbly to give an account in a matter for which he was reproved, how much more ought we sinners, when we are rebuked concerning some matter, to appease our reprovers with humble reasoning?” [Col. 0906B]

Likewise Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*:

> “Did not God speak with Moses? Yet he accepted, being both very prudent and least proud, counsel for governing so great a people from his father-in-law—namely, a man who was a foreigner. For that man knew that, from whatever soul true counsel proceeded, it ought to be attributed not to that person but to him who is Truth, the unchangeable God.”

In this it should be noted that superiors ought to comply with the corrections and counsels of inferiors, just as it is salutary and necessary for inferiors to offer such things to superiors, or conversely for superiors to offer them to inferiors.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That prelates are to be rebuked by subjects, and subjects by prelates, in turn.

Hence Isidore to Saint Cyril:

> “The examples of the divine Scriptures terrify me, and I am compelled to say what is necessary. For whether I am a father, as you say, I fear the condemnation of Eli, because he did not restrain his sinful sons; or whether I am your son, as I know more truly, I dread the punishment of Jonathan, who, because he did not prevent his father when he was able, died in battle.” [Col. 0906C]

Hence Ambrose in his homilies:

> “He who does not rebuke a brother who sins in some way encourages him to sin.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. That prelates are to be accused not by everyone, but only by good persons wholly unstained and not even suspected.

But although, by canonical authority, prelates are to be rebuked and accused by subjects, it must be understood that this is not by everyone, but only by good persons, wholly unstained by any present or past blot, and not even suspected. Hence Anacletus in the second epistle (no. 2):

> “An accusation against priests ought to be made only by suitable and thoroughly approved men, free from suspicions and crimes; because the Lord did not wish the ministers of his sacred body to be defamed or calumniated by base and reprobate persons, but himself drove out the priests with his own whip.”

And a little later:

> “A priest is commanded to be chosen without crime; he is by no means permitted to be accused or calumniated by persons entangled in crimes, nor by any except those who are without crime and who, if necessity requires, may themselves be made or ordained priests according to the rule of election.” [Col. 0907A]

Hence Pope Damasus to Stephen, from the Council of Africa:

> “The accusers and witnesses of bishops about whom you have asked must be free from every infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain, fully instructed in the true faith, and such persons as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For priests, as ancient authority hands down, may not be accused or testified against by persons who neither ought nor can be advanced to the same honor.”

This indicates that those who ought and can be advanced, although they are not themselves priests, may nevertheless accuse priests and testify against them, provided they are not infamous.

## CHAPTER XXV. Which persons are to be called infamous.

Describing them, Pope Stephen says to his most beloved brother and familiar friend Hilary, in the first epistle (no. 1):

> “We call infamous those persons who are marked with infamy because of some fault: that is, those who reject the rule of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical statutes; likewise thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators of tombs; all who take arms against fathers; likewise incestuous persons, murderers, perjurers, sorcerers, kidnappers, poisoners, adulterers, deserters from wars, and those who seek to hold offices unworthy of them, or take away the goods of the Church, or provoke the minds of rulers to anger against the innocent; all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes; and all whom ecclesiastical or secular laws pronounce infamous. None of these, indeed—nor slaves before lawful freedom, penitents, persons twice married, those serving in the municipal curia, persons physically impaired, those without sound mind or understanding, the disobedient to holy decrees, or the insane—ought to be advanced to sacred orders; neither freedmen nor suspected persons.” [Col. 0907C]

## CHAPTER XXVI. That those who were enemies yesterday or the day before yesterday cannot be accusers or witnesses.

Hence Anacletus, chapter 2 (epistle 3, no. 5):

> “Those who were enemies before yesterday or the day before yesterday cannot be accusers or witnesses, lest in anger they desire to harm, or, having been injured, wish to avenge themselves.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. That blood relatives and household associates ought not to be accusers or witnesses.

[Col. 0907D]

Hence Pope Callixtus, chapter 2 (epistle 2, no. 5):

> “Blood relatives shall not give testimony as accusers against strangers; nor household associates, nor those proceeding from one household. And if they wish and agree among themselves, relatives may testify only among themselves and not against others. Neither suspected accusers nor suspected witnesses shall be admitted, because affection arising from kinship, familiarity, and domination commonly impedes truth. Carnal love, fear, and greed often dull human understanding, so that they regard profit as piety and money as the reward of prudence.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That not only the life and reputation of accusers and witnesses, but also their intention, must be investigated.

Hence in the decrees of Evaristus, chapter 11 (epistle 2):

> “We have heard that certain bishops have been defamed and torn to pieces, driven from their own sees, and that others have been established in them while they themselves were still alive. Therefore we write this to you, that you may know it is not lawful for this to be done.” [Col. 0908A]

And shortly afterward:

> “If there are detractors or accusers of priests, they ought not to be heard by the judges of the Church before the reputation of their character has been examined: with what rashness, with what intention, with what faith, with what life, with what conscience, and with what merit they act; whether for God, or vain glory, or from enmity, hatred, or greed. All these matters must be faithfully investigated and carefully considered. For there are some who persecute and rebuke their superiors if those superiors have caused them even a little inconvenience. Therefore the primates of the Churches must beneficially take care with a sound eye that none of them be vexed or scandalized while innocent.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the saints intended accusations of priests to be either impossible or difficult, lest they be harassed by evil persons of any kind.

[Col. 0908B]

Hence Pope Fabian, in his Decrees sent to eastern bishops (epistle I, no. 2):

> “Considering such matters, the holy apostles and their successors, filled with the Holy Spirit, foreseeing evil persons and considering the simple, intended accusations against priests to be difficult or impossible, lest they might be removed or driven away by evil persons. For if this were easily allowed to secular and evil people, either no priests, or scarcely a very few, would remain. For it always has been, is, and—what is worse—always flourishes, that evil persons persecute good people and carnal persons harass spiritual persons.
>
> “Therefore, as has been stated, they decreed that priests should not be accused; and if it could not be otherwise, that their accusation should become exceedingly difficult, and that it should not be presumed by those persons mentioned above; nor should bishops be driven from their own sees or churches.” [Col. 0908C]

Behold: Fabian most openly explains why the saints forbade priests to be accused indiscriminately and rashly by common and base persons: namely, lest through the undiscerning folly or reckless malice of ignorant or evil sheep the shepherds be burdened. Yet they allowed it to good subjects, lest prelates appear able to commit any evils with impunity.

And indeed, the shepherds whom the Lord left to us as his vicars, he willed to be his eyes and his tongue; and those whom he chose especially and willed to be specially reserved to his own judgment—since a ruler is appointed according to the deserts of the people, and again the shepherds of the Church are condemned according to the deserts of the people—unless their sins are very great, manifest, and incorrigible, ought for the Lord’s name to be tolerated rather than judged, lest, while we persecute them in a perverse order, we make them pay for our own sins, by which they themselves are corrupted, before we make ourselves pay for them. [Col. 0908D]

## CHAPTER XXX. In what order discipline must be carried out.

Since, therefore, it has been said at what time, with what discrimination of intention, and by what accusers and witnesses discipline is to be exercised, let us now see in what order it is to be carried out. For order is so powerful in the Church that, whether deeds or words are concerned, unless they are done in an orderly manner, they are also invalid.

Hence Pope Zephyrinus, chapter 1 (epistle I):

> “In a doubtful matter, no definite judgment is to be pronounced; nor is any judgment to be held valid unless it has been conducted in due order.” [Col. 0909A]

Likewise Pope Leo, chapter 49:

> “If in secular matters each person’s right and proper order must be preserved, how much more ought no confusion to be prescribed in ecclesiastical arrangements?”

## CHAPTER XXXI. That before a bishop is accused he must be approached not once but very often, not in bitter but in familiar conversation, so that he may correct whatever he recognizes needs correction in himself.

Therefore, in order that discipline be carried out in due order, before he is accused the bishop must be approached not once but often; and, for the sake of the Church’s scandal, he must be urged either to clear himself or to correct himself—humbly and gently, first privately and afterward publicly.

If he is unwilling to do either—that is, to clear himself or to be corrected by the counsel of his subjects—then at last the matter must be made known to his primate by letters that are not clandestine or preliminary, but canonical; sent not through conspiracy but through charity; and by these letters a day of accusation and judgment must be sought from him.

Hence Anacletus, chapter 11 (epistle II, no. 2):

> “If anyone is moved against shepherds and their Churches, or has charges against them, let him first have recourse to them in a spirit of charity, so that, being warned in familiar conversation, they may heal what needs healing and correct in charity what they recognize must rightly be corrected. But if any persons presume, before doing this, to tear them apart, accuse them, or harass them, let them be excommunicated and by no means absolved until they have made worthy satisfaction; for injury to them pertains to Christ, whose embassy they fulfill.” [Col. 0909C]

Likewise Alexander, chapter 1 (epistle I, no. 3):

> “If anyone believes that he has any just complaint against a bishop or the authorities of the Church, let him not first approach primates or other judges before he has approached in familiar conversation those by whom he considers himself injured—not once, but very often—so that he may receive from them either his justice or their defense. But if he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion both by them and by others, as one who despises the apostles and other Fathers.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. That metropolitans ought not to be proud or burdensome toward their suffragans, nor transact anything without their counsel except what belongs to their own diocese.

[Col. 0909D] Hence Pope Anicius, chapter 1: “If any metropolitan should become puffed up and, without the presence or counsel of all the bishops of his province, should wish to handle either their causes or other causes—except only those that pertain to his own diocese—or to oppress them, let him be strictly corrected by all, lest he dare henceforth to presume such things. But if he should appear incorrigible and disobedient to them, let his contumacy be referred to the Apostolic See, so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the rest may be afraid.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. If a bishop proves incorrigible after admonition by his subjects, his case is then to be referred canonically to the primate, who is to summon him to a council.

Hence Felix, chapter 11 (Epistle 2): “If any bishop [Col. 0910A] is accused by accusers who are admissible, after he has first been approached by them in a spirit of charity, so that he ought to amend and correct the matter itself, and refuses to do so, then—rather than previously—his case is to be referred canonically to the chief primates. They shall regularly hold a council in a suitable place within that province and at a suitable time, that is, in autumn or summer, so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of that province. Having been regularly summoned, he must attend unless prevented by illness or another grave necessity; for no permission exists to bring an accusation beyond the boundaries of the province before a higher hearing has been requested.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Subjects should rebuke their prelates humbly, and should venerate them when rebuked.

[Col. 0910B]

Therefore, since a prelate must first be approached before being accused, Gregory explains in Book V of the *Moralia* how this is to be done: “When certain actions of better men or prelates displease those who are inferior, what moves the mind must by no means be kept silent; but it must be expressed with great humility, so that the intention of one who thinks piously may preserve the form of uprightness all the more because it proceeds by the path of humility. Thus what we think must be stated freely, and what we say must be uttered very humbly, lest perhaps, through an improper manner of expressing what we intend, we fail to act rightly.”

Likewise, in Book XXX of the same work: “While the matter remains unharmed, it is the merit of virtue if what belongs to a superior is endured. Yet it ought to be suggested humbly, if perhaps what displeases may be amended.” And shortly afterward: “If the life of teachers is rightly rebuked, subjects must nevertheless venerate them even when they displease. But this must be carefully considered: do not despise to venerate those whom you disdain to imitate.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. Prelates rebuked by their subjects ought either to clear themselves, if innocent, or to amend themselves, if guilty.

Since, therefore, prelates ought to be approached and rebuked by their subjects, they in turn ought either to clear themselves, if innocent, or to amend themselves, if guilty. Let both points be explained by certain authorities. For it is exceedingly dangerous for a prelate to be, or to appear, blameworthy. Since the Lord calls them [Col. 0910D] the salt of the earth and the light of the world (Matt. 5:13), who will be wise if the salt becomes tasteless? Who will not stumble if the light is darkened? Hence Paul says: “See that you place neither a stumbling-block nor an occasion of scandal before your brethren” (Rom. 14:13). And elsewhere: “Provide things good not only before God, but also before all people” (Rom. 12:17). And Augustine (*Sermon* 355, no. 1): “Whoever neglects his reputation is cruel.” And in the Gospel: “Woe to that person through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7). Again: “If anyone causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths” (ibid., 6).

It is therefore no slight matter for any prelate, by his own fault or by an occasion arising from him, to destroy those committed to him, for whom Christ died and for whom he himself will render an account [Col. 0911A] at God’s severe judgment. Thus Samuel also, when Israel asked the Lord for a king, being himself a judge and so far-sighted that he would suffer no harm to his reputation through prejudicial suspicions, disclosed his innocence, with divine adjuration and even the people’s testimony: namely, that he had injured no one, but had resisted their gifts.

Gregory has likewise testified above that Peter, the prince of the apostles, cleared himself regarding fellowship with Cornelius the Gentile through the testimony of six brethren (Acts 11:12). Many saints also, lest they should in any way become a scandal to the Church, solemnly cleared themselves even of mere suspicion. For in Gregory’s *Register*, addressed to Emperor Justinian, chapter 107, it is read “that Bishop Leo cleared himself by an oath upon the altar of Saint Peter.” Likewise, in the *Register* addressed to Queen Brunichild, chapter 232, Bishop Menas did so by a similar examination; likewise Briccius, bishop of Tours, for the purpose of calming popular scandal, by carrying burning coals and by conversing with a month-old infant.

Hence Gregory also wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English, in the letter beginning, “It is desirable to me from you” [Note: [Col. 0911] This letter is not extant today among Gregory’s works.], and so forth: “A presbyter, or any priest whatsoever, accused by the people, if there are no certain witnesses who establish the truth of the accusation brought, shall take an oath publicly; and let him bring forth as witness to the purity of his innocence Him to whom all things are known and open, and thus remain in his own rank.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The sin known by all ought to have a penance known by all.

[Col. 0911C] But if he cannot clear himself before a council, or even by the testimony of his subjects, then, in order to allay scandal, it is necessary that he make satisfaction. For Genebald, bishop of Laon, after a lapse of the flesh, was placed by Saint Remigius in an underground crypt and performed seven years’ penance at Laon, on water and ash-bread, before those very persons among whom he had been defamed. For it is indeed fitting that those whom the foul odor of guilt has infected should be refreshed by the good odor [read: “odor”] of repentance.

Hence Augustine says in his homilies: “Those sins which are committed publicly should themselves be rebuked publicly; those committed more secretly should themselves be rebuked more secretly. Thus the Lord raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house; but Lazarus, before the Jews who saw, he called from the tomb [Col. 0911D] with a loud cry.”

Hence Augustine, in the book *On Penance*: “When the wound of sin and the force of the disease are so great that the remedies of the Lord’s body and blood must be deferred, each person ought, by the authority of the bishop, to withdraw from the altar in order to perform penance, and by the same authority to be reconciled. For this is to receive the Lord’s body and blood unworthily: to receive them at the time when one ought to perform penance.”

Likewise, in the same work (*Sermon* 351, no. 9): “Let one who seeks the judgment of medicine come to the bishops, through whom the keys of heaven are administered to him in the Church; and, as a good son now beginning to be such, preserving the proper order of the maternal members, let him receive from those set over the sacraments the measure of his satisfaction, devout and suppliant in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart. Yet let him do what benefits not only himself for the recovery of health, but also others by way of example: so that, if his sin is not only a grave evil to himself, but also a scandal to many others, and if it appears expedient to the bishop for the Church’s welfare, he may not refuse or resist performing penance in the knowledge of many people, or even of the whole congregation, lest he add swelling to a deadly and fatal wound.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Although any light fault is believed to be remitted by the brethren’s daily confession, grave sins are nevertheless relaxed only by the absolution of prelates.

But some object that the imposition of satisfaction for grave sins [Col. 0912B] can be made by inferiors and equals. Yet the venerable priest Bede explains this passage thus: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5:16). “In this statement,” he says, “there ought to be this distinction: daily and lighter sins should be confessed to one another and to equals, and we should believe that they are forgiven through their daily prayer. But the uncleanness of a more serious leprosy we should reveal, according to the Law, to a priest, and take care to be cleansed according to his judgment, in whatever manner and for however long he commands.”

Hence Augustine, after distinguishing grave sins, says: “But for daily and slight sins, without which this life cannot be lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Although a priest’s penance ought to be known, it should not be seen by everyone.

[Col. 0912C] But although a priest performs penance in such a way that everyone knows it, he should not do so in such a way that everyone sees every aspect of his penance, as they would that of any layperson. For the laying on of hands in placing ashes upon his head should not be performed for him by any priest as it is for laypeople; nor should he be expelled publicly from the Church like a layperson. Rather, he must perform penance in a private place—either in his own cloister or in some monastery—whether temporarily or permanently, as he is ordered. So Genebald also performed penance for seven years in an underground crypt, where he neither saw people nor was seen by them.

Hence Leo, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, chapter 16 (Epistle 92, no. 2): “It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those consecrated in the honor of the presbyterate or in the rank of deacon should receive, for some crime, the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands. This without doubt derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: ‘If a priest sins, who shall pray for him?’ (1 Sam. 2:25.) Therefore those who have fallen in this manner must seek private withdrawal in order to obtain God’s mercy, where their satisfaction, if worthy, may be fruitful.”

This was said as a warning, so that a priest may pray to God more familiarly and more earnestly, the fewer or rarer mediators he has between himself and God; and more readily and freely, since in his private withdrawal he is neither hindered nor offended by any importunate intrusion of secular persons. And if [Col. 0913A] his satisfaction is worthy in this manner, it will also be fruitful in two ways: for salvation and for the recovery of ecclesiastical honor.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. If a priest has performed worthy penance, he should be restored to his former dignity.

Hence Jerome, on Micah: “When they are proved to have been diviners rather than prophets, they will be mocked for their dreams; and the people previously deceived by them will speak against them. Then those teachers themselves will perform penance; and because I am merciful and do not will the death of the sinner, when I have heard them I shall give them the power of my Spirit and fill them with my judgment and strength, so that those who previously deceived the people by flatteries may afterward frighten them by announcing the truth and call them back to the right way; and those who were the cause of error may begin to heal the wounds they inflicted and become an occasion of health.”

And after saying this in the person of the Lord, he subsequently shows what he had understood from these words: “Observe,” he says, “in the present passage that someone may teach after sin, provided that he has expiated his former vices by worthy penance.”

Thus David, after adultery and homicide, says in the Psalm: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:9). Nor is he already content with his own cleansing; rather, he adds: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (ibid., 14). “And when you have done this, I shall teach transgressors your ways, and the impious shall be converted to you.”

Hence Pope Calixtus, chapter 199: “Those err who think that priests, after a fall, cannot minister to the Lord and enjoy their honors, if they have performed worthy penance, afterwards led a good life, and worthily maintained their priesthood. Those who think this not only err, but also appear to spurn the keys entrusted to the Church, of which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven’ (Matt. 18:18). Otherwise this judgment of the Lord is not true. But we unquestionably believe that both the Lord’s priests and the rest of the faithful can return to their honors after worthy satisfaction, the Lord testifying through the prophet: ‘Will not one who falls rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?’ (Jer. 8:4). And elsewhere: ‘I do not will,’ says the Lord, ‘the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live’” (Ezek. [Col. 0913D] 33:11).

“And David the prophet, performing penance, said: ‘Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit’ (Ps. 50:14). For he himself, after penance, both taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to teachers of the Church that, if they have fallen and performed worthy penance, they can do both. For he taught when he said: ‘I shall teach transgressors your ways, and the impious shall be converted to you’ (ibid., 15); and he offered sacrifice for himself when he said: ‘A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.’ For, seeing his crimes cleansed through repentance, he did not hesitate, by preaching and offering sacrifice to the Lord, to heal the sins of others.”

And immediately afterward, chapter 200, to show that this is done through mercy, he adds: “Reject the judgment that forbids mercy not only to be maintained but even to be heard,” and so forth, as above.

## CHAPTER XL. How it should be resolved that some saints prohibit restoration to dignity after penance, while others permit it.

But saints who say that after a fall or penance no one can come to the clergy, return to it, or remain in it appear to oppose this judgment, whereas others say conversely that all these things can be done. Hence Gregory, to Constantius, bishop of Milan, chapter 61 (Book V, Epistle 4): “If permission is granted to the fallen to return to their rank, the vigor of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken, since, through the prospect of return, no one fears to conceive desires for wrongful conduct. Your Fraternity has in fact consulted us whether Amandinus, who, while presbyter and abbot, was deposed by your predecessor as his fault required, ought to be recalled to the rank he held. We decree that this is neither permitted nor to be done for any reason. Yet if perhaps his manner of life has merited it, appoint him, as a private person, to sacred service in every respect in a monastery before the other monks, as you shall judge fit. Above all, therefore, take care that no petition ever persuade you in any way to restore persons fallen in sacred orders, lest punishment in such cases be believed not to have been established but merely delayed for a time.”

Likewise Gregory, to Bishop Fabian: “Let him know that the presbyter concerning whom your Fraternity consulted us, through the report presented in the presence of the messenger, can neither remain in sacred order after his fall nor be restored to it for any reason. Yet he is to be treated more leniently, because he is said to have confessed the crime committed by an easy admission.”

Likewise, to John, bishop of Syracuse (Book IX, Epistle 63): “The page of the records you sent us makes clear what accusation has been raised against Lucillus, bishop of the city of Muclenia [Note: [Col. 0913D] In Gregory: ‘of the city of Malta.’]. Therefore, because punishment for so great a crime ought not be delayed at all, let your Fraternity associate with itself three or four of your fellow bishops and priests, so that, in their presence also, when the truth has been disclosed and satisfaction made, it may strive without hesitation to depose the aforesaid Lucillus from the episcopal rank, which the contamination of this crime has stained.”

[Col. 0914D] Here it should be observed that this ruling is not to be understood of all who have fallen. For some fall concerning whom suspicion is either absent or uncertain. Of these Gregory himself says: “Those fallen in ecclesiastical rank, but not deposed, we entrust to God’s judgment, concerning whose mercy, as Leo says, we presume neither to set measures nor to determine times; for with him a pure confession suffers no delay in forgiveness, as the Spirit of God says through the prophet: ‘When you groan, you shall be saved’” (Ezek. 33:12). Thus he says that they are to be purified by a true confession.

Others fall concerning whom there is not merely suspicion but certain evidence; yet subjects lack the proof needed to accuse them, or the aforesaid troubles of the times or ecclesiastical judges obstruct them. Therefore, as has been said, they are tolerated; or they are even approached by their subjects in accordance with canonical order, so that they ought to be rebuked and corrected by them. They are moved to compunction and cleansed through satisfaction for the penance of their subjects, and are not deposed. For why would the saints canonically prescribe such an order to subjects, that before accusation they should approach their prelates for rebuke and should accuse them only if they were incorrigible, except so that correction might forestall deposition? One who has been corrected ought not to be accused; one not accused cannot be deposed. How, then, if canonical order is to remain intact, can someone known, however evidently, to be evil be deposed if he is willing to be corrected upon admonition?

Hence Gelasius, chapter 5: “Those found to have committed forbidden acts, or who do not rather correct their misdeeds of their own accord, will incur danger to their own rank.” Hence Isidore: “One who is not corrected by gentle rebuke must necessarily be corrected more sharply. Those things that cannot be healed gently must be cut away with pain.” Likewise Symmachus: “Wounds that do not respond to poultices must be cut away with iron.”

## CHAPTER XLI. With respect to grave and deadly sins, if a prelate is willing to be corrected, he is not to be accused by his subjects; and, since one who has been corrected ought not to be accused, he is not to be condemned.

But some object that this ought not to be so in grave and deadly sins, such as homicide, [Col. 0915C] perjury, and the like, but only in lighter sins, such as a simple lapse of the flesh and the like. Yet truly, as Gregory says: “The greater the fault that follows someone, the greater the punishment to be imposed; nevertheless, where sin has abounded, let grace be shown to abound still more.”

No offense is found greater than departing from the faith through heresy, because it is not mortal bodies but souls destined to live eternally that are destroyed. By it, the whole Church is shaken from its foundations. Concerning this great sin, the same order was canonically instituted by the holy Fathers Anacletus, Fabian, and the others: if a pastor has departed from the faith, he must first be corrected secretly by his subjects. But if, God forbid, he proves incorrigible, then he is to be accused. How, moreover, is a heretic to be condemned if he is willing to be corrected by his subjects, when he is not to be accused unless he proves incorrigible, and unless accused, as Gregory says, he is not to be judged by an irregularly usurped judgment—unless, that is, he has been accused, or has voluntarily confessed, or has been convicted?

Therefore, lest we despair even of God’s grace concerning grave sins, Jerome, as was said above, testifies that the prophet David—whose authority he used to strengthen his judgment—repented of adultery and homicide and afterward taught. We must certainly believe that the kindness of the unchangeable God has not changed toward us, if he finds in us a like satisfaction of repentance.

## CHAPTER XLII. Gregory’s words that the fallen ought not to be restored must be interpreted with discrimination, lest he be contrary to the other saints and to himself in what follows.

[Col. 0916A]

Since this is so, the words of blessed Gregory must be interpreted with discrimination, so as not to disturb the order of the canons. For what he said concerning the deposed presbyter and abbot, the presbyter who confessed in court by an easy admission, and Lucillus already accused by an ecclesiastical complaint—namely, that all these should neither remain in ecclesiastical rank after their fall nor be recalled—was intended to prevent scandal in the Church.

For truly, after someone has shown himself incorrigible and contumacious up to the point of accusation, as was said above, he must be punished more severely; nor should he be restored, either because of the infamy he had cruelly neglected up to the hearing of the case, or because of the hostilities he would carry on against the Church by which he had been corrected, or also because he is useless for other purposes. Yet none of these reasons prevents us from conceding that he could have been corrected if he had been willing before accusation or deposition.

But we must take care that through us God’s name is not blasphemed and that our ministry is not reproached. Therefore, whoever neglects his reputation is cruel, because many matters are judged severely not on account of despair of forgiveness but on account of scandal to the Church. For, as Isidore says, “It is better that one person be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through the license of one.”

Hence Martin also, in the letter beginning, “By the zeal of your Fraternity”: “Whoever after his ordination has fallen once is already deposed and can attain no rank of the priesthood; but it should suffice for him to remain in the same penance for as long as he lives, with continual lamentations and tears, so that he may be able to extinguish the committed offense by divine grace.” Likewise: “If anyone after his ordination has fallen and is found liable to the sin of transgression, he must altogether be forbidden to handle the mysteries of our salvation with muddy and defiled hands.”

When, therefore, lifelong penance with continual lamentations and tears is imposed upon one who has fallen once, where is that very ready grace of pardon by which, at the hour when the sinner groans, he shall be saved? If one hour suffices, why are all the periods of a life said scarcely to suffice? Where is what Augustine says in *On the Christian Conflict* (chapter 30): that the bowels of mercy ought nowhere to be so vigorous as in the Catholic Church, so that, like a mother, she may neither cruelly mock her sinful children nor be slow to forgive those corrected?

Where is what Augustine says in Homily 38: “What is not forgiven to one converted, if the blood of Christ poured out is acknowledged? What murderer should despair, if he is restored to hope by him by whom even Christ was killed? Many believed from among those; Christ’s blood was given them so that they might drink it for their liberation rather than remain guilty of having shed it. Who should despair when the thief upon the cross was saved—shortly before a murderer, shortly afterward accused, convicted, condemned, hanged, and liberated? Do not wonder: where he was convicted, there he was condemned; but where he was changed, there he was liberated. Who then should despair of the grace of him who penetrated the heavens and intercedes with the Father, who looks upon the face of his Christ, that he may obtain for himself, when convicted and condemned but changed, the same grace that he granted even at the hour of death to a thief like him or his equal?”

But, as has been said, the loss of pardon is not because pardon is despaired of, but because of scandal and injury to others. “For if,” as blessed Gregory said above, “the penance of removal from office seemed not established but postponed, men would lay snares for their accusers or plot vengeance during those penances. Others too, seeing vice corrected in them mildly or badly, would be endangered by their evil example. And if Christ, who did no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, stretched out his hands upon the cross all day until death to an unbelieving people, to show that the world is to be despised, should not also the sinner perform penance all his days, to show that the vice for which he was condemned must be avoided?”

## CHAPTER XLIII. Even one who has been condemned may be restored if he truly repents, because one who practices justice does not sin.

Yet if he has truly repented and has been changed so perfectly that the aforesaid difficulties do not appear, and if some discriminating consideration of necessity or usefulness intervenes, the rigor of discipline ought to be relaxed. For in their proper places grace does not prejudice justice, nor justice grace.

Hence Augustine, to the judge Donatus: “‘Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.’ It is as though he said: If the Law commands it, if Moses commands it, I also command it; but I require ministers of the Law suited to the task. You consider the woman whom you bring; consider also who you are. Jesus ordered her to be stoned; he did not act against the Law, yet he also pardoned her. He did not act against the Law, just as an emperor is not said to act against the Law when he pardons certain defendants who have confessed. For both could be dispensed by him: the one as just, the other as merciful.”

Hence Augustine, to Boniface, concerning Donatist heretics, on receiving them into ecclesiastical honors even after penance, lest they provoke a greater scandal in the Church (Epistle 185, no. 44): “‘If, then,’ they say, ‘we must repent of having been outside the Church and against the Church in order to be saved, how shall we remain among you as clerics or bishops after this penance?’ This would not be done, because what ought to be done should not be done unless it were healed by the compensation of peace.”

And shortly afterward (ibid.): “There is a manner of grafting in which he who is outside is grafted in without cutting off any branch that is between, though not without any wound to the tree, but with the lightest wound. Thus when these people come to the Catholic root, the honor of clerical office or the episcopate is not taken from them, even after repentance for their error. Something is indeed done, as it were, against the integrity of severity in the bark of the tree.”

And shortly afterward (ibid., no. 43): “The establishment in the Church that no one may receive clerical office after penance for any crime, or remain in the clergy, was made not because forgiveness is despaired of, but through the rigor of discipline. Otherwise there would be dispute against the keys given to the Church, of which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven’ (Matt. 16:19). But lest perhaps, even when crimes had been exposed, a mind puffed up by hope of ecclesiastical honor might perform penance proudly, it was most strictly decreed that after penance performed for a condemnable crime no one should be a cleric, so that, through despair of temporal elevation, the medicine of humility might be greater and truer.

“For Saint David performed penance for grave, deadly sins, and nevertheless remained in honor. And blessed Peter, when he shed bitter tears, surely repented of denying the Lord, and yet remained an apostle. But for this reason the care of later generations should not be considered superfluous. Where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, so that salvation might be more safely fortified—having learned, I believe, through the pretended penance of some people who coveted powers of honor. Many experiences of diseases compel the discovery of many remedies.

“In such cases, where grievous ruptures of dissension lie before us, and not the danger of this or that individual but the slaughter of peoples, something must be taken away from severity so that sincere charity may come to the aid of healing greater evils. Let these people, therefore, feel bitter grief over their former detestable error, as Peter did over his deceitful fear; let them come to the Church of Christ, the true Catholic mother; let them be bishops and clerics in her usefully, though they were her enemies hostilely. We do not begrudge it; indeed, we embrace it, desire it, urge it, and compel to enter those whom we find in the roads and hedges.

“The apostle Peter, who denied the Savior, both wept and remained an apostle; he had not yet received the promised Holy Spirit. But these people received him still less when, divided from the body which the Holy Spirit alone makes alive, they held the Church’s sacraments outside the Church and against the Church, and fought against us with standards and weapons erected from ours against us.”

And shortly afterward (ibid., no. 47): “Thus the Church is accustomed to come to the aid of multitudes perishing through schisms and heresies.”

It should be noted here that Augustine resolves what was said above: that peace is not to be disturbed in the execution of justice when the scandal stirred is not that of this or that person but of the whole Church; and conversely, that it is to be disturbed firmly where the perversity shaken is not that of this or that person but of a few wicked persons. According to this distinction, justice must either be pursued without reserve, so that the wicked may be punished severely not for the disturbance but for the correction of others; or it must be moderated through charity and grace, lest the rest of the good be endangered by the scandal of one evil person.

Yet this must be so ordered that, when wicked persons are received through grace, they do not lay snares or cause trouble for those who corrected them, nor repent proudly and falsely, but furnish others with examples [Col. 0919A] of true humility and repentance.

Hence Isidore, to Bishop Masanus, chapter 10: “When your servant, the religious man Nicetius, came to us, your venerable Fraternity made known in its letters what followed: no difference is to be understood in judgments of this kind. For elsewhere it is read in the same canon of Ancyra, chapter 19, that after a bodily fall a rank of honor is to be restored through penance. But elsewhere it is read that, through such an offense, the distinction of the former order is by no means to be restored. This diversity is distinguished in the following way.

“The canon commanded those to return to the first ranks of office whose penance had been preceded by satisfaction or by a worthy confession of sins. But those who are not amended from the vice of corruption, and who strive with a certain superstitious rashness even to defend the very carnal offense they commit, receive neither rank of honor nor the grace of communion. Therefore each judgment must be decided thus: those who have been reconciled to divine mercy through penance must necessarily be restored to a place of honor. And those who are known to have received the remedy of life through amendment rightly attain the standing of the dignity they had acquired.

“For the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of faithless Jerusalem, shows that former honor is restored through penance. ‘Be ashamed, O Judah, and bear your disgrace’ (Ezek. 16:52). And shortly afterward: ‘You and your daughters shall return to your former state’ (ibid., 55). Therefore, while anyone is ashamed through the work of his own shame, bears his disgrace, and mourns his deposition with humility, he may according to the prophet be recalled to his former condition.

“Likewise John the Evangelist writes among other things to the angel of the Church of Ephesus: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and perform penance, and do the first works; otherwise I shall come to you and remove your lampstand from its place’ (Rev. 2:5).”

And shortly afterward: “The priest’s lampstand, understood as the chrism of honor, is wholly removed according to John when, after the fall into sin, admitted crimes are not erased because penance is neglected. For he did not say, ‘Because you have fallen, I shall remove your lampstand’; but, ‘Unless you perform penance, I shall remove your lampstand.’ Therefore, if penance for his fault comes first in the case of any sinful superior, restoration of his merit will certainly follow.

“As it is said in Proverbs: ‘He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper; but he who confesses and abandons them shall obtain mercy’ (Prov. 2:13).” And shortly afterward: “For the fact that canonical censure decreed that a person should return after seven years, through penance, to his former state was established by the holy Fathers not according to their own judgment, but rather according to the sentence of divine judgment.

“For it is read that Miriam, Aaron’s sister, was struck with leprosy for the sin of detraction. And so that she might be cleansed, God commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after cleansing, to be admitted again to the camp. Miriam, Aaron’s sister, therefore signifies the flesh of the priest. When it is infected by the contagion of corruptions, it is cast outside the camp for seven days—that is, outside [Col. 0920A] the fellowship of the Church for seven years—and through cleansing from vices receives again the merit of its place or former dignity.”

And shortly afterward: “But one who does not mourn what he has done, but commits acts that ought to be mourned, cannot be restored to his former rank.”

When blessed Isidore had authoritatively and reasonably distinguished two opinions of the saints, in order to show that both these and the rest must be discerned justly and usefully according to person and time, he added: “I thought that this should be added at the end of this letter: Whenever conflicting opinions are found, the opinion of that council is to be maintained more strongly whose authority is the more ancient and weighty.” He said “more ancient” with reference to truth, “weightier” with reference to usefulness. Therefore, since blessed Isidore observes that the angel’s lampstand is to be removed not because he sinned, but unless he has done penance [Col. 0920B], it accords well with canonical order that a prelate should first be approached and admonished by his subjects; and, if he appears incorrigible, then he should be accused and condemned, so that his lampstand may be removed from its place, because God so commands and threatens. For, since to sin is human and to persist is diabolical, it is fitting that, unless what is human is corrected, what is diabolical should be punished.

Blessed Gregory also, agreeing with Isidore in distinguishing diverse opinions, says to Secundinus, the servant of God and recluse, chapter 222 (book IX, letter 52): “You say that you have read differing judgments of the canons concerning the priestly office: some allowing recovery after a fall, others allowing it in no way. We therefore venerate the most general councils beginning with Nicaea together with the remaining four [general councils], because through them we agree unanimously with those that follow. Beginning, then, with the head and continuing down to the fourth minister of the altar, this rule must be observed: as the greater precedes the lesser in honor, so also in guilt; and the greater the fault that follows a person, the greater the punishment in which he is involved, so that after penance it may be believed to be fruitful. For what profit is there in sowing wheat and not gathering its fruit? Or in building a house and not inhabiting it? Therefore, after worthy satisfaction, we believe that one can return to honor, the Lord saying: ‘Will not he who falls add [that he may rise again]?’ (Ps. XL, 9), and ‘Will he who has turned away not return?’ (Jer. VIII, 4). Again: ‘On whatever day he groans, he shall be saved’ (Isa. XXX, 15). Hence the Psalmist also says: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts. Cast me not away from thy face, and take not thy Holy Spirit from me’ (Ps. L, 12). For while, doing penance for the fall of his sin, he asked not to be cast away by the Lord, he added: ‘Restore to me the joy of thy salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit’ (ibid., 14). For if he had not performed penance worthy of God, he would by no means have preached to others. For he says: ‘I will teach the wicked thy ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to thee’ (ibid., 15). Since he perceived that his own sins had been cleansed through penance, he did not hesitate to heal the sins of others by preaching; and he strove to offer to God a sacrifice from himself, when he said: ‘A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God’ (ibid., 19).” [Col. 0920C–D]

Therefore, although Jerome, Calixtus, Augustine, Gregory, and Isidore sufficiently approve the judgment of severity, they embrace more fully that which belongs to grace and charity: so that, whether in order to avoid a greater scandal heretics may be received with their rank, or because of the fruit of true penance sinners may be restored to their honors, it accords better with discernment that the prelate be approached and admonished by his subjects with canonical honor; then he may be corrected and thus enjoy his honor. In this way there will also be less scandal of disgrace, nor will there arise a suspicion of personal hatred such as might result from the injury of accusation. Yet, lest this happen, and lest evil example should also spring up among others from his impunity, the holy Fathers decreed that any accused person, if either confessing or convicted, should without doubt be deposed and another substituted in his place. But if thereafter he presumed to aspire to the same honor, he should be shut up in a monastery to perform perpetual penance.

Thus Gregory, without contradicting his own judgment, gave a stern and fixed sentence of deposition for the fall of a deposed abbot, of a presbyter, or of Lucillus, an accused bishop; although, because of the fruit of true penance, he granted all who truly repent a general return to honor. No one doubts that he established this not inconsistently with himself, but with discernment, each provision in its own place and time. For he who gave so severe and fixed a sentence concerning the accused bishop Lucillus relaxed it in the case of the accused primate of Byzacena, in order to avoid scandal, so that it may be shown that he acted discerningly in whatever he either pursued justly or remitted mercifully. Thus the same Gregory writes to John, bishop of Syracuse (book IX, letter 59):

“The primate of Byzacena had been accused of a certain crime, and the most pious emperor wished him to be judged according to the ordinances of the canons. But Theodore, then master of the soldiers, having received pounds of gold, opposed its being done. Then the most pious emperor admonished us to do whatever was canonical; but, seeing the opposition of men, we were unwilling to undertake the same case.” [Col. 0921A–C]

Behold: the same Gregory gave judgment concerning the accused Lucillus, but was unwilling to execute the same judgment against the similarly accused man of Byzacena. Why? Because he was not contrary to himself, but contrary to the deed.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That after a prelate, often admonished, has remained incorrigible, his case is then to be referred to the primate.

[Col. 0921D]

Since, then, all things must be done with discernment and order, after a prelate who has been approached and admonished by his subjects has refused correction, his case is then first to be referred canonically, not treacherously, to the primate. Thus Eleutherius, chapter 1 (no. 3): “Neither the calumny nor the voice of a traitor is to be heard; nor, still less, is an accusation by inferiors against bishops readily to be received.” Thus Anacletus, chapter 4 (letter 5, no. 5): “Those who disclose the fault of their own teachers or superiors are condemned by the judgment upon Ham, the son of Noah: like Ham, who did not cover his father’s nakedness but displayed it for ridicule.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore every faithful person ought, if he learns that the people are swelling up against their shepherd and that the clergy are occupied with detractions, to strive according to his ability to root out and prudently correct this vice. For it is wholly unworthy that the sins of fathers be disclosed not for correction but for ridicule, and that they be torn apart by detractions.”

## CHAPTER XLV. That betrayers and slanderers of bishops ought to be declared infamous, deposed, and handed over to the curia.
