Thus Alexander, chapter 1 (letter 1, no. 1): “We decree and establish that all who persecute their own fathers, or endeavor to remove and tear them down, be openly declared infamous and excluded from the thresholds of the Church until satisfaction is made.” Thus Fabian, chapter 11 (letter 2, no. 2), after warning that those who cannot lawfully become priests neither ought nor can accuse priests, added shortly afterward: “It is established that, if anyone is hostile to or has laid snares for his bishop, and attempts to accuse him, or is a conspirator, he shall immediately, before trial and examination, be removed from the clergy and handed over to the curia, which he shall serve for the days of his life, remaining infamous without any hope of restoration.” Behold: the same authority did not forbid those subjects who can lawfully become priests to accuse priests, but imposed punishment upon one who lies in wait, accuses maliciously, or conspires.

Thus from the Council of Carthage: “A cleric found to be occupied with flatteries and betrayals shall be degraded from office.” Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 14 (canon 18): “The crime of conspiracy or plotting is forbidden even by civil laws; much more ought it to be admonished that this should not occur in the Church of God. Therefore, if any clerics or monks are found plotting, conspiring, or laying snares against bishops and clerics, let them be deposed from their proper rank.” [Col. 0922A–C]

## CHAPTER XLVI. That one who publicly fabricates written or spoken insults against another is to be scourged.

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Adrian: “Whoever fabricates in public a writing or insulting words against another’s reputation, and, when discovered, does not prove what he has written, shall be scourged; and whoever first finds such things shall tear them up, if he does not wish to incur liability for the author’s deed.”

## CHAPTER XLVII. That an insult is not to be treated as an accusation.

[Col. 0922D]

Likewise Fabian, chapter 3 (letter 3, no. 4): “If anyone, in anger, rashly casts some accusation against another, the insult is not to be treated as an accusation. Rather, after time has been allowed for deliberation, he must declare in writing that he will prove what he said in anger; so that, if upon coming to his senses he is unwilling to repeat or write what he said through anger, he may himself be held guilty of the crime. Therefore everyone who alleges a crime shall write that he will prove it; and he who does not prove what he alleged shall suffer the penalty which he himself sought to impose.”

## CHAPTER XLVIII. That a bishop is not to be harassed if the accusers are not legitimate.

Therefore, since a prelate ought not to be assailed by traitors, abusive persons, or any such people, Pope Eutychianus says, chapter 11: “Accusations of priests or of the remaining shepherds ought not to be made indiscriminately and at random. For if they were readily admitted, exceedingly few would be found, because all who wish to live devoutly suffer persecution.” Likewise Pope Felix II, chapter 11 (letter 1, chapter 17): “Whenever a shepherd of the Church is accused of certain crimes, if the accusers are such as ought canonically to be received, he shall be canonically heard by all the bishops in the province in a lawful synod gathered at its proper time. But if the accusers are not legitimate, the accused shall not be troubled; because priests ought to devote themselves to sacrifice, not to litigation, and those who are called thrones of God ought not to be disturbed by the snares of wicked persons.” [Col. 0923A]

## CHAPTER XLIX. That an accused bishop is to be convicted by seventy-two suitable witnesses.

[Col. 0923B]

Likewise Pope Zephyrinus, chapter 1 (letter 1), showing how many and what kind of witnesses are required, says: “Patriarchs or primates examining an accused bishop shall not pronounce a final judgment before they have been supported by apostolic authority, and unless he either confesses himself guilty or is convicted through innocent witnesses regularly examined. These witnesses, indeed, must not be fewer in number than those disciples whom the Lord chose to assist the apostles—that is, seventy-two.”

## CHAPTER L. That Pope Sylvester does not forbid subjects to accuse prelates, but forbids them to do so presumptuously.

[Col. 0923C]

Pope Sylvester also, chapter 1, distinguishing a fixed number of witnesses for each order, says: “A bishop shall not be condemned except by seventy-two witnesses; a cardinal presbyter, except by sixty-two witnesses; a cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, by twenty-six; a subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or doorkeeper shall be condemned by seven witnesses. Let witnesses and accusers be free from every infamy.” Yet he forbade the lower ranks from proceeding against the higher, not that they should bring no accusation—for in that case he would be contrary to the other saints—but that they should not presume, that is, should not do so presumptuously.

## CHAPTER LI. That when the cause for accusation has been canonically brought to the primate, the primate ought rather to restore peace than to proceed to judgment.

[Col. 0923D]

Therefore, after one suitable accuser, or several if desired, has been chosen, and after a definite number of witnesses has also been assembled, the cause for accusing anyone should publicly and canonically be referred to the primate. Before he fixes a day for the accusation, if the matter perhaps admits of reconciliation or pardon, he ought to reconcile the accusers with the accused. If this cannot be done, he should canonically appoint a synodal day. Thus Felix II in his first letter (chapter 13): “If anyone chooses to accuse a bishop, let him make known his case to the highest primates of bishops, and not to secular persons; for they should bring them back more toward peace than judgment.”

Thus Innocent also, chapter 57, when through the intervention of the subjects of Bishop Photinus he rescinded a condemnation which the Roman see had aimed at him through the deceit of a false report, himself became an intercessor and reconciler, rather than an agent of condemnation, in the matter of Deacon Eustachius, whom they wished to accuse and condemn. He says (letter 22, chapter 7): “Receive Eustachius, who has been approved by me; do not wait for him to be stripped of the grace of the diaconate. I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation. To the one to whom you extend a hand, I extend one with you; to the one to whom I extend one, extend yours with me. For this apostolic kindness was declared to the Corinthians: that, in one spirit, they should always follow without distinction a judgment carried out and reconsidered for good.”

For it is not a sin sometimes to pardon, for some reasonable reason and through grace, one whom we see may be condemned by justice. Thus Augustine, Homily 115 (Tractate 115 on John, no. 5): “‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber. We do not rebuke you, O Jews, because at Passover you set a guilty man free, but because you put an innocent man to death.” Likewise Leo (letter 92), speaking to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, concerning certain persons to be corrected, says: “In applying spiritual medicine to the sick who must be healed, act more gently with them, as Scripture says: ‘Do not be overly just.’” [Col. 0924A–B]

## CHAPTER LII. That if he cannot restore peace, then the accused, having received a truce of at least six months, must summon for his defense a synod gathered within the province at a suitable time by apostolic authority.

If, however, the primate cannot reconcile them, he shall canonically appoint a synod or council within the province, in a place and at a time—spring or autumn—not without apostolic authority and consent, granting the accused a truce of at least six months so that he may be ready to answer. Thus Pope Cornelius writes to Rufus, his fellow bishop (letter 2, no. 1): “No priest shall commit his case to an alien judgment unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic see; but each shall have as judges his fellow provincials and those known to him, unless he fears there the violence of a reckless crowd or has enemies or suspects there. For these reasons it is permitted to appeal and go to judges of greater utility and to other provinces.” Likewise Pope Stephen (letter 2, no. 8): “The license of accusation shall not proceed beyond the boundaries of the province, but every accusation shall be heard within the province and concluded by fellow provincials, unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic see.” Innocent, Pelagius, and the rest agree with this.

Concerning the autumnal and summer times, sufficient has been said above by Pope Felix, chapter 2. Let us consider apostolic authority. Pope Marcellus II (letter 1): “No bishop, when charged with whatever crimes, shall be heard or judged except in a lawful synod gathered at its proper time by apostolic authority, lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.” Concerning the granting of truces, Felix, chapter 1, says: “Concerning the truces for bishops about which you consulted us, we find different rules established by the Fathers. Some commanded that a year and six months be granted in order to repel the machinations of emperors, prepare their responses, confirm witnesses, and seek councils of bishops and friends; others a year, with which most agree. But less than six months I do not find. For truces are not to be granted in a narrow period of time but over a long interval, so that the accused may be able fully to arm and prepare themselves against those who lie in wait.” [Col. 0924C–0925A]

## CHAPTER LIII. That Pope Damasus briefly and clearly describes the entire synodal order.

Pope Damasus also, briefly and clearly setting forth all these matters, says to Archbishop Stephen, chapter 4 (letter 4, chapter 2): “Metropolitans, together with all their fellow provincials, so that none of these is absent and all agree in the cases of individuals, may examine bishops and the highest ecclesiastical cases. But it is by no means lawful to determine their principal complaints and those of the Churches, or to condemn bishops, without the authority of the see of this Church, since all ought, if necessary, to appeal and be supported by its aid. For, as you know, it is not Catholic for a synod to be held without its authority; nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a lawful synod, at his proper time, assembled by apostolic summons; nor are any councils ever found valid which are not supported by apostolic authority” (ibid., chapter 4).

“The summons of one who is charged to a synod must be made over a suitable and canonical period; because unless he has been canonically summoned at his proper time and in canonical order, even if he comes to the assembly under whatever necessity, he will in no way answer those who lie in wait for him unless he chooses voluntarily. Concerning those driven out and stripped of their possessions, I can signify nothing more truly to you than what the holy Fathers decreed. For their decree reads thus: ‘The holy canons decree that bishops who have been expelled and stripped of their possessions shall first be restored to their own churches, and that all their goods shall be legally restored to them.’” [Col. 0925B–C]

And afterward (ibid., chapter 5): “If anyone should wish to accuse them, they decreed, with equal risk, that the judges must be rightly wise and willing to act justly, whether those whom their primates give them or those whom they themselves choose by consent” (ibid., chapter 7). “A suitable time must indeed be provided, when the case of every accused person may most rightly be brought forward, and all may duly attend to it, so that they may answer it rationally in every respect and clearly show their will to act justly. But no one shall be introduced in person; rather, accused and accusers shall be heard on equal terms, as the order of the proceedings requires. Accusers and judges shall not be the same persons; but accusers by themselves, judges by themselves, witnesses by themselves, and accused persons by themselves—each in his own proper order. A written accusation must always first be filed, so that the false accuser may suffer retaliation; for before the filing no one ought to be judged or condemned, since even the laws of the secular world maintain these same provisions. In criminal cases, truces of six months for the accused, and longer if necessary, must be granted” (ibid., chapter 8).

“It is also established in the decrees of the Fathers that it shall not be canonical for any priest to be judged or condemned before he has canonically examined accusers present and has an opportunity to defend himself—that is, ecclesiastical truces for washing away sins” (ibid., chapter 9); “nor shall the first accusation for investigation be made outside his own province without apostolic authority, to which apostolic reverence is due in all causes; because investigation of the crime must take place where the crime was committed.” And the canons command that all matters be concluded in the places where they arose, while apostolic authority is nevertheless preserved in all things.

Behold: Damasus, setting out almost the whole synodal order, grants accused bishops, at the first summons to the synod, at least six months’ truce; and likewise, after they have come to judgment, at least six months’ truce to defend themselves. Those stripped of their possessions, even when they have come to judgment, are not to be accused until all their goods have been restored to them in full. Then afterward they are again to come upon a canonical summons to the synod, and only then are they first to be accused. [Col. 0925D–0926B]

## CHAPTER LIV. That the accused ought not to be suspended from communion before conviction, unless he withdraws himself from judgment. But one stripped of possessions is to be restored to them for as long as he was despoiled before he answers.

To see how other saints distinguish these matters more plainly, consider Pope Felix II, chapter 11 (letter 1, chapter 6): “If any bishop is lawfully accused and canonically summoned to a council, he ought to go without any fear; and if he cannot go, let him send an envoy to the synod in his place. But an accused man shall not be barred from communion, unless, after canonical summons to the judgment of the elect, he delays coming within three, six, or more months to render an account of his alleged offenses. If he can prove that he wished to come but could not, it shall harm him in no way. But one who has been driven out by force or fear, or stripped of his possessions, shall not be summoned to a synod until both he and all his possessions have been restored to their legal entirety; and he shall remain established in his own position, disposing by his own authority of all things belonging to his own peace, for as long as he appears to have been deprived of his possessions.” [Col. 0926B–C]

“But when he comes to judgment, if he wishes and if it is necessary, the truces established by the Fathers shall be granted without hindrance to one requesting them, and judges chosen by him shall be assigned—either in the place from which the accused comes, or, if there he fears the violence of a reckless crowd, let him choose a suitable place where he may have his witnesses without fear and can canonically bring his case to conclusion without impediment.” [Col. 0926D]

## CHAPTER LV. That an accused bishop must choose twelve judges for himself.

Concerning how many judges there should be, Pope Zephyrinus says, chapter 1 (letter 1): “Every accused bishop, if necessary, shall choose twelve judges by whom his case may be judged justly; nor shall he be heard or excommunicated before they themselves have been separately chosen, so that his case may first be heard justly and rationally distinguished by them in a regular assembly of his own bishops.” It has been said above that he is to be heard by all the bishops of the province, so that no bishop is absent; but necessity sometimes ordains otherwise. Thus Sylvester, chapter 2: “If a bishop is under such great necessity that he cannot assemble many [bishops], lest he remain under accusation, [he shall be judged] by twelve bishops; and a presbyter by six bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.” [Col. 0927A]

## CHAPTER LVI. That the primate must investigate what faith and manner of life characterize the accusers and the accused, so that by this he may give more or less credence to the accusers and show more or less leniency to the accused.

Therefore, when every difficulty has been removed, as was said above, and the bishop to be accused has come to the council, as Calixtus says, chapter 2 (letter 2, no. 5), “the primate must inquire in judgment what manner of life and what faith characterize both the accuser and the accused, lest persons of whatever faith, life, and free condition, and persons of low standing, be received to accuse their elders.” Since it has been set forth above what sort of persons the accusers must be, and likewise the witnesses—since no further inquiry about them is needed beyond whether they are such as have been described above—let us consider why inquiry must be made into the manner of life and faith of the accused. For he may in the rest of his conduct be so harmful, useless, or incorrigible that the accusers will more readily be believed concerning the alleged crime, and the accused will receive less leniency in the punishment of judgment.

For Judas, because he was a thief and kept the money-boxes, and maliciously betrayed his Master, did not obtain pardon. But Peter, because he denied the Lord not maliciously but through the weakness of fear, returned to the prerogative of his honor. The devil also, because he sinned maliciously and proudly, was not restored; but man, because deceived, fell through his weakness and was redeemed by God. [Col. 0927B–C]

## CHAPTER LVII. That accusers and witnesses must be present and accuse or testify orally, that the accused must be judged in person, and that they must not defame or calumniate one another except concerning the present case.

Likewise Pope Calixtus in the same place (letter 2, no. 5): “The persons of accusers must be investigated thoroughly. They are scarcely to be received without a written document, but never by a written document [alone], because no one can be accused by writing; rather, every accuser must be believed by his own voice and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse. Similarly, witnesses shall not give testimony by any writing, but, being present, shall truthfully testify to what they saw; nor shall they testify of matters other than those known to have been done in their presence.” [Col. 0927C–D]

It should be understood that witnesses or accusers ought not to accuse or defame a bishop concerning anything other than that for which they accuse him. Nevertheless, apart from the crime for which he is accused, the primate must inquire concerning his other faith and conduct—but from others, not from the accusers themselves. Thus Gaius in his letter (no. 3): “Therefore, if anyone brings forward an unprovable charge against persons of this sort, let him understand that by authority of this sanction he will suffer the loss of reputation.” Just as accusers ought not to defame the accused except for the matter on which they accuse him, so the accused ought not to defame or discredit them before he has cleared himself of the crime. Thus Stephen, chapter 11: “Accused persons are denied license to make accusations before they have freed themselves from the crime under which they are pressed; for their assertion against others is not to be believed while they are implicated in crimes, unless they have first proved themselves innocent, because the declaration of a defendant against anyone is dangerous and ought not to be admitted.” [Col. 0928A]

But what Sixtus says—that one present ought not to be accused except by one present—the saints testify not only concerning accusation but also concerning judgment. Stephen, chapter 11 (letter 2, no. 5): “No absent person can either accuse or be accused.” Likewise Pope Cornelius, chapter 2 (letter 2, no. 2): “Everything that is either done or judged against absent persons in any matter shall be wholly void, because no one awards judgment against an absent person and no law condemns him.” Likewise Eleutherius, chapter 1 (letter, no. 3): “Let the judges of the Church beware of pronouncing sentence while the person whose case is under discussion is absent; for it will be wholly invalid, and they will give an account for the case in the synod.” Likewise Zephyrinus, chapter 1 (letter 2): “Let no one be judged in absence, because both divine and human laws forbid this.” [Col. 0928A–B]

## CHAPTER LVIII. That if one evades judgment, the accuser and the accused alike are to be condemned as absent just as if present.

Yet if either evades judgment, the accuser and accused alike shall be judged guilty, whether absent or present. Thus from the Council of Carthage, chapter 19: “A person against whom a crime is alleged shall not be suspended from communion unless, summoned by letter on an appointed day to plead his case before the judgment of the elect, he entirely fails to appear—that is, within the space of a month from the day on which he received the letter. But if he proves some true causes of necessity by which it is evident that he could not appear, let him have the full opportunity of a second month to plead his case. Yet after the second month he shall not communicate until he has cleared himself. But if he refuses to attend a universal council within the space of a year so that his case may be determined there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the first sentence of condemnation against himself, during the time when he does not communicate either in his church or parish.” [Col. 0928C]

“But if the accuser has never failed to attend on the days appointed for pleading the case, he shall not be removed from communion. But if at any time he is absent, withdrawing himself, once the bishop has been restored to communion the accuser shall be removed from communion; provided, however, that the opportunity to plead his case is not taken away from him either, if he proves that he wished to appear on the day but could not. But it shall be for the judgment of the bishops to determine that, if the person of the accuser is blameworthy, he is not to be admitted to make an accusation unless he wishes to assert his own causes, though not ecclesiastical ones.” [Col. 0928D]

Likewise Pope Boniface I to the bishops of Gaul (letter 2): “If the chief bishop wishes to be present, let him, being present if he has confidence, answer the charges; if he does not wish or neglects to be present, let him not profit by a delay of sentence resulting from his absence. For it is clear that he confesses the crime who, although so often granted and assigned an opportunity for judgment in which to clear himself, does not use it; for it makes no difference whether all that has been said is established in a hearing at which he is present, since it is equally certain that he himself, having repeatedly been summoned, has made a declaration by his absence.” Likewise Pope Julius, chapter 11: “No one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment just as the innocent person seeks it in order to be acquitted; nor is he free from suspicion who alleges that calumnies are false, when he himself, summoned to judgment in order to prove what he alleged, delays coming.” And shortly afterward: “It is indeed clear that those confess their own crime who, repeatedly summoned, delay coming without unavoidable cause and do not avail themselves of the will to clear themselves.” [Col. 0929A]

## CHAPTER LIX. That four persons must be present in every judgment.

[Col. 0929B]

In so grave a crisis, in which either the accuser with his witnesses or the accused must be condemned, there must be no confusion of persons or indiscriminate handling of complaints; rather, everything must be done in order and with discernment. Thus Fabian, chapter 11 (letter 2, no. 2): “No accuser shall ever at the same time be judge or witness, because in every judgment four persons are necessary: elected judges, suitable accusers, appropriate defenders, and lawful witnesses. Judges ought to employ equity, witnesses truth, and accusers intention, to develop the case.”

## CHAPTER LX. That judgment must not be rendered until the question has been fully examined.

[Col. 0929C]

Likewise Pope Eleutherius (letter, no. 2): “A judge ought to investigate everything and examine the order of events by full inquiry, having afforded patience for questioning, presenting, and adding matters, so that there the pleading of both sides may be fully refined. Nor should the judge wish to anticipate the litigants with his sentence before, once everything has been completed, they have nothing left to propose in the question; and the action should be examined until the truth of the matter is reached. For it is often necessary to question, lest something perhaps remain omitted which ought to be added. Likewise, no short truces must be granted for inquiry, lest anything appear to have been done hastily by either party, because many things occur through deceit.” [Col. 0929C–D]

Thus Augustine answers so great a person as Jerome, who was reproving him, with this moderation: “It may be that something appears otherwise to you than truth has it, provided that nothing other than what charity has is done by you. But if even charity may be deceived in the darkness of this world, what then of hostility and dissension?”

## CHAPTER LXI. That the accused can clear himself in three ways: namely, by more suitable witnesses, by the supreme ordeal, or by confession and penance before any public disclosure.

If the accused can produce witnesses for his innocence, not indeed of unequal integrity but of greater dignity, as Pope Damasus cleared himself of adultery with forty-two bishops, the accusers and their witnesses being joined, let him solemnly clear himself. But if he cannot have this, let him invoke as his witness, in the sacred examination of the very body and blood of the Lord, him whom he will have as judge. Thus in the body of canons the following authority is found:

“If a criminal charge—homicide, adultery, or sorcery—has been alleged against a bishop or presbyter, he must celebrate Mass separately in each case, publicly say the secret prayer, receive communion, and thus show himself innocent of each allegation made against him.”

There is also a third way of excusing himself and escaping deposition: if he shows and proves that, before every public disclosure of that sin, he forestalled it by confession and worthy penance. For God will not judge twice for the same thing. [Col. 0930A]

## CHAPTER LXII. That if the accused refuses to clear himself, he will then either be convicted or voluntarily confess his sin and be condemned.

[Col. 0930B]

If he cannot clear himself by these three methods, then, if upon seeing his difficulties he voluntarily confesses, he shall be treated more leniently, as was said above. But if he refuses, he shall be convicted by the accuser and the latter’s witnesses in this manner: they shall swear that they saw or heard, if the matter is suited to sight or hearing, such as homicide or perjury; or, if it is not, such as adultery or sorcery, they shall assert that they know by certain signs—for example, that the two were often found alone at night in a chamber, or that the adulteress thereafter gave birth; and similarly concerning the remaining sins, according as they can establish them more truthfully and clearly.

## CHAPTER LXIII. That if judgment has not been conducted in due order, or has been overturned through fear of some power, the accused is to appeal to the apostolic see either before or after condemnation.

[Col. 0930C]

Gregory, to John the defensor (Book XIII, Epistle 45): “Since therefore Bishop Stephen maintains that he has been unjustly condemned, it must first be carefully investigated whether the judgment was duly conducted, whether the accusers were different persons from the witnesses; then the nature of the charges, whether they deserved exile or deposition; whether testimony against him was given in his presence under oath, or whether proceedings were conducted in writing, so that he had freedom to reply. Careful inquiry must also be made into the persons of the accusers and witnesses: of what rank and reputation they are; whether they are poor, or have harboured enmities against the bishop; whether they have given testimony from hearsay, or have testified that they know the matter specifically; and, if judgment was rendered in writing, whether the decisions were read aloud with the parties present. If these things were not solemnly done, he is by every means to be restored to his church. Those who unjustly condemned him are to be excommunicated and sent to a monastery to perform penance for six months. But the man who, while he was alive, rashly sought his place is to be excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry and handed over to that same bishop of ours for custody. The bishops who presumed to ordain him, or to consent to his ordination, having been deprived of communion, are to be assigned to a monastery for six months to perform penance. But if they freely confess that they did such things through fear of the judge, the measure of their penance is to be moderated. But if the man who seized the place of the aforesaid Stephen has died, and another bishop has been ordained after him, because the offence appears lighter—for he succeeded not the living man, but the deceased—the office of bishop is adjudged to him only in that church; so that, in another church which is vacant of a priest, if he is elected, he may be bishop.”

Therefore, since, as Gregory says, a judgment is subverted through fear of a judge, Pope Calixtus says, chapter 1 (Epistle I, no. 2): “An unjust judgment and an unjust decision ordered or carried out through fear or at the command of any bishop or powerful person whatsoever is invalid.”

Hence Fabian, chapter 3 (Epistle 3, no. 2): “If anyone considers that a judge is hostile to him, let him lodge an appeal. No affliction or confinement in custody should wrong an appellant; rather, an appellant must be allowed to remedy a defective case by the remedy of appeal; in criminal cases appeal must be allowed, nor may the voice of appeal be denied to one whom a sentence has assigned to punishment. Let an accused person state his case before his own judge; but an accused person brought before someone who is not his own judge may, if he wishes, remain silent. Whenever an accused person appeals, a postponement is to be granted, and no sentence pronounced by a judge who is not his own may bind anyone.”

Likewise Pope Victor, chapter 1 (Epistle 1, no. 3): “It has pleased us that a bishop accused or judged by fellow-provincials in any matter may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange that his case be reconsidered either personally or through his vicars. While the pontiff is conducting his case at the renewed trial, no bishop is to be placed or ordained in his position. For although fellow-provincial bishops may investigate the case of an accused pontiff, they are nevertheless not permitted to determine it without consulting the Roman pontiff.” Hence Pope Zephyrinus, chapter 1: “The final determination of the same case is to be referred to the apostolic see, that it may there be concluded; nor is it to be concluded before it is supported by that authority.”

*Here ends the second part.*

# PART THREE

[Col. 0931]

## CHAPTER I. That there are four classes of those outside the Church, whose sacraments are not valid.

[Col. 0931B]

Since above we have briefly treated, insofar as divine mercy has granted, the mercy or justice to be shown to ecclesiastical sinners, let us now deal with those who are outside the Church. There are four classes of these: the excommunicated, the condemned, schismatics, and heretics. To participate at times in their sacraments is damnable. Hence Gregory, in his *Register*, concerning excommunicated persons (Book IV, Epistle 21): “We can in no way call that a consecration which is celebrated by excommunicated persons.” Likewise Innocent, concerning the condemned Bonosus, chapter 55: “Those who went over to the condemned Bonosus and allowed themselves, or desired, to be ordained by him received nothing from him and are guilty of usurped rank.”

## CHAPTER II. How schismatics differ from heretics.

Therefore, having said enough concerning the avoidance of the sacraments of the excommunicated and the condemned, let us consider schismatics and heretics: how they differ from one another, and how they cause harm through their sacraments.

Hence Jerome, on the Epistles: “We judge the difference between heresy and schism to be this: heresy holds a perverse doctrine; schism separates itself from the Church by a severance. Yet no schism fails to devise for itself some heresy, so that it may seem to have rightly departed from the Church.”

Likewise Augustine: “A heretic is one who does not follow Catholic truth; a schismatic is one who does not embrace Catholic peace.”

It is written: “The place of true sacrifice is not outside the Church.” Hence Pelagius, among other things, to Victor and Pancratius: “You ought to abstain from the sacrifices of schismatics—or rather, from their sacrileges.” This is to be understood in a holy and Catholic sense alike concerning schismatics and heretics. All sacraments consecrated by anyone in the name of the Trinity are, in themselves, true and holy, as will appear below; but in respect of their effects they are neither true nor holy, but defiled and sacrilegious, because they confer not salvation but condemnation. Let us first consider this concerning schismatics, and afterwards concerning heretics.

## CHAPTER III. That schismatics possess the holiness of the sacrament on our side, but not the wound of schism.

Hence Augustine, in the book *On Baptism*, chapter 237: “Those who separate themselves from the fellowship of the rest and break the bond of unity, if they perform none of the things which they received within unity, are separated in all things; and therefore one whom they associate with themselves, if he returns to the Church, must receive everything that he had not received. But if they perform some of the same things, they have not separated themselves in those things, and in that respect they remain joined to the Church. Therefore, if anyone joined to them wishes to come to the Church, he is healed in that in which he erred.

“But where he was joined to the saints, he is not cured but acknowledged, lest, while we seek to cure what is sound, we inflict a wound. In the holiness of the sacrament, in which they are not against us, they are for us; in the wound of schism, they who do not gather with Christ scatter.”

## CHAPTER IV. That the baptism of schismatics is indeed true, but profits nothing as long as they remain in schism.

Likewise in the same work, chapter 278: “The objection of the Donatists: They seem to themselves to ask with great subtlety whether Christ’s baptism begets children in the party of Donatus or does not beget them. If we agree that it does beget them, they will assert that their church is a mother, since it could beget children through Christ’s baptism; and because there must be a Church, they will then accuse ours of not being the Church. But if we say that it does not beget them, they ask: why then are those who pass from us to you not born again among you through baptism, when they had been baptized among us, if they have not yet been born? As though it begets from that in which it is separated, rather than from that in which it is joined. For it is separated from the bond of charity and peace, but joined by the unity of baptism. Thus the Church is one, and it alone is called Catholic; and whatever of its own it possesses among those separated from its unity by the changing fortunes of different persons, it itself surely begets through what it possesses in them, not they; their separation does not beget, but rather that which they have retained from it with themselves. But if they relinquish even this, then it does not beget at all.”

Likewise in the book of *Sentences*, chapter 191: “They also ask whether sins are forgiven through baptism in the party of Donatus. If we say that they are forgiven, they reply: ‘Then the Holy Spirit is there; for when he was given by the Lord’s breathing, he then said to the disciples: “Baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven; if you retain them, they shall be retained”’ (Matt. 28:19). ‘And if this is so,’ they say, ‘our communion is Christ’s Church. For the Holy Spirit does not work forgiveness of sins outside the Church. And if our communion is Christ’s Church, your communion is not Christ’s Church; for there is one Church. “My dove is one” (Song 6:8); there cannot be as many Churches as there are schisms.’ But if we say that sins cannot be forgiven there, then, they say, baptism there is not true; and therefore you ought to baptize those whom you receive from us. Since you do not do so, you acknowledge that you are not in the Church.

“We oppose them by asking: Are sins forgiven where charity is absent? For sins are darkness, and whoever hates his brother is still in darkness. If sins are forgiven, how then is anyone born again among schismatics? For what is it to be born again except to be renewed from oldness? And how is he renewed whose past sins are not forgiven? But if he is not reborn, neither has he put on Christ. From this it appears that he should be baptized anew, because, as the Apostle says, ‘As many of you as were baptized have put on Christ’ (Gal. 3:27). Yet because we say that he was baptized in Christ, we confess that he has put on Christ; therefore that he has been regenerated, therefore that his sins have been forgiven. How then does John say, ‘Whoever hates his brother is still in darkness’ (1 John 2:11), if sins are forgiven in the hatred of schism?

“They resolve this by saying that baptism does not exist among schismatics. But we, acknowledging that it does exist even among them, resolve it thus: if any hypocrite approaches baptism, are his sins forgiven or not? Let them choose what they wish. If they say that they are forgiven, how shall the Holy Spirit of discipline flee the hypocrite if it works forgiveness of sins in that hypocrisy? If they say that they are not forgiven, ask whether, if such persons ever confess their hypocrisy through true repentance, they are judged to require baptism anew. Since it is utterly mad to say this, let us acknowledge that John may be baptized with true baptism, yet his heart, persevering in malice, may prevent the abolition of sins. Thus let me understand that baptism may be given and received against the Church of Christ with the same celebration of the sacrament, but that it profits for the forgiveness of sins only when someone, reconciled to unity, puts off the sacrilege of dissension, through which his sins were held and could not be forgiven.

“Just as this hypocrite is not baptized anew but purified by the correction of confession—which cannot occur without baptism, yet what was given before then begins to avail when the hypocrisy has departed through true confession—so one baptized in heresy or schism, through whose crime his sins were not forgiven, is not to be baptized again when he comes to the unity of the Church. For reconciliation itself and peace ensure that the sacrament, which could not profit when received in schism, now begins to profit in unity for the forgiveness of his sins.

“Or baptism did not profit because the Holy Spirit came in order that sins might be forgiven for a moment and depart, and immediately departed so that they might return: just as one who passes from darkness through light into darkness is illumined by the light only in passing. Thus it would be both true that hypocrites put on Christ for a moment through the power of the sacrament, and that they immediately drive away the Holy Spirit, as it is written that he comes to some but does not make his dwelling. Yet the saints agree more with the former view; and it is more probable that heretics neither give nor receive the Holy Spirit in their heresy. For how is the Holy Spirit given so as to be ineffectual?”

The same author confirms this elsewhere also, in Book V of *On Baptism*, chapter 204: “Even those slower in heart understand that Christ’s baptism cannot be violated by any perversity of the giver or receiver. But since the sacrament is one thing and the effect of the sacrament another, and since those who live ruinously even within the unity of the Church plainly can neither grant nor possess forgiveness of sins—because it was said not to the wicked but to the righteous, ‘If you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven; if you retain them, they shall be retained’ (John 20:23)—it is clear that they only give or receive the sacrament of baptism. Hence it has also been established by conciliar authority that a wandering sheep which had received the Lord’s character outside from false preachers, when it comes to the salvation of Christian truth, is to be corrected from error, freed from captivity, and healed from its wound; yet the Lord’s character in it is to be acknowledged rather than rejected.”

Likewise Augustine against the Donatists: “Just as I seem to be pressed [by the fact] that sins [are forgiven] when he baptizes beside you, so I too am pressed when I say: ‘Therefore even a covetous simulator of religion forgives sins.’ If by the power of the sacrament, so does this man and that man; if by his own merit, neither this man nor that. For that sacrament is recognized as Christ’s even in evil persons; but in the body of the one spotless dove neither this man nor that is found.”

Likewise Augustine, in Book VI of *On Baptism*: “If anyone converted from the perversity or separation of heresy or schism comes to Catholic peace, his sins shall be forgiven under the same baptism which he had received, because of the bond of charity, under which his sins had been held because of the sacrilege of division. For that baptism is always holy in a righteous or an unrighteous person: it is neither increased by anyone’s righteousness nor diminished by anyone’s wickedness.”

## CHAPTER V. That ordained schismatics who convert are also received.

Hence Augustine, to Count Boniface (Epistle 185, no. 44): “If, therefore, they say, it is necessary that we repent of having been outside the Church and against the Church, if we are to be saved, how do we remain clergy or bishops among you after this repentance? This would not happen, because what truly must be done ought not to be done unless it were healed by the compensation of peace itself.”

And a little later (ibid.): “There is a manner of grafting in which no branch that is within is cut off, but the one that is outside is grafted in; yet it is not without a wound to the tree, but with a very slight wound. So too, when these men come to the Catholic root, in order that the honour of clerical office may not be taken from them even after repentance for their error, something is indeed done, as it were, in the bark of the tree, contrary to the integrity of strictness.”

## CHAPTER VI. That, as a withered hand is a true but ineffective member, so the same words or deeds are useless or harmful according to intention or faith.

For if someone’s hand were withered, it would indeed be his true member, though bloodless, ineffective, and dead; and just as faith, though true, is dead without works, so the same words or deeds are judged useful or dead according to intention.

[Col. 0935C]

Hence Augustine, in the *Epistle of John*, chapter 7, no. 9: “If the Father delivered up the Son, and the Son delivered himself, what did Judas do? There was a delivering-up by the Father, a delivering-up by the Son, and a delivering-up by Judas. One thing was done. But what distinguishes them? The Father and the Son did this in charity; Judas, however, in betrayal. You see that what a person does is not what must be considered, but with what mind and will he does it.”

Likewise Augustine in his homilies: “‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God’: Peter said this and heard, ‘You are Simon Bar-Jonah.’ The demons said the same thing and heard, ‘Be silent.’ The utterance is one, but the Lord asks after the root and the flower.”

Likewise Augustine, in the book *On the Trinity*, chapter 22: “Faith can indeed exist without charity, but cannot profit. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Faith works through love’ (Gal. 5:6), thereby distinguishing it from that by which demons believe and tremble. Accordingly, the devil is better than a heretic; for though he has faith, however transgressive he is, he is nevertheless not a heretic. Thus, when persons baptized among ecclesiastical sinners are received without a mark, because even in such evil persons perfect faith confers a perfect sacrament, corrupted faith among heretics confers an imperfect sacrament. The Church altogether baptizes those from the Paulianists—not to say baptized persons, but persons washed with water; but those baptized by Arians and other heretics it reconciles to itself only through imposition of hands under the form of penance.”

## CHAPTER VII. That faith is necessary for those performing sacraments or miracles.

[Col. 0936A]

For all the sacraments of the Church are fulfilled by faith, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, and say to the mountain, ‘Move yourself and cast yourself into the sea,’ it shall happen for you” (Matt. 17:19). Thus he rebuked Peter concerning faith when he was sinking: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31).

It must therefore be noted that faith is necessary for those who perform sacraments or miracles, and no less for those for whom they are performed; for the Lord could not perform a sign in his own country because of their unbelief. Hence Augustine, Homily 80, no. 3: “Take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element, and a sacrament results: itself also, as it were, a visible word. Whence comes this great power of water, that it touches the body and washes the heart, unless through the working of the word—not because it is spoken, but because it is believed? For even in the word itself one thing is the passing sound, another the abiding power.”

## CHAPTER VIII. That the sacraments of heretics are condemned or approved according to their faith.

The saints, clearly attentive to this, either condemn or complete even the sacraments of heretics; and so approve them according as they see their faith in those sacraments to be imperfect, corrupt, or annulled.

Because the Paulianists reject even the name of the Trinity, the Church so condemns all their sacraments that it receives none of their laity unless they are baptized afresh in the name of the Trinity. Arians and the rest, however, because they invoke the name of the Trinity, though they believe faithlessly, are not baptized again; rather, their baptism is completed with penance and imposition of hands.

But the Donatists are more schismatics than heretics, though nevertheless heretics also, because they believe that they are saved apart from the unity of the Church. The Novatians too, whom they call Cathars—that is, “the pure”—otherwise hold the orthodox faith, except that they despair of the Holy Spirit’s forgiveness for persons married twice and for those who fell in persecution, even after repentance. The Church receives not only their laity with penance, but even their clergy by imposition of hands alone. For although they in no way deny the faith of the Trinity, they nevertheless faithlessly disparage the grace of the Holy Spirit in some respect: whereas Donatists believe and hope that they have the grace of the Holy Spirit outside the unity of the Church, which is impossible, Novatians despair that he is willing, after repentance, to forgive the sins of the fallen. It is impious to think so cruelly concerning true grace.

## CHAPTER IX. That the baptism of Paulianists is void, but the orders of Novatians are valid with imposition of hands.

This is evident from the clearest authorities of the saints. For when Pope Innocent I, chapter 55 (Epistle 22, chapter 5), discussed jointly the two heresies of the Paulianists and the Novatians, and decreed that those coming from the Paulianists were to be baptized, but wholly prohibited this in the case of those coming from Novatians and other heresies, he gave the reason, saying: “Because the Paulianists do not baptize at all in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Since he said that this reason alone required the rejection of their baptism, he said that not only the laity but also the clergy of the Novatians were to be received with imposition of hands; because among those Novatians no question was ever raised concerning the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore, out of all the separated groups, this heresy alone was chosen as one to which this concession was thought applicable—that its clergy should be received—because it sinned in no respect against the sacrament of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But this was commanded in a particular way only concerning these two heresies, and not concerning the rest: namely, that even the baptism of the Paulianists should be rejected, while even the ordination of the Novatians should be received. Pope Innocent himself distinguishes this plainly a little earlier, saying (Epistle 22, chapter 5): “As for the decision of the Nicene synod, that, after receiving imposition of hands, they should remain in the clergy: we can truly say to your charity that this was prescribed concerning the Novatians alone and does not concern the clergy of other heresies. For if they had intended to determine this concerning all, they would have added that those coming from the Novatians and other heretics ought to be received in their own rank. If it were so, that too which was said concerning the Paulianists could be weakened, namely that those coming from them are to be baptized. For when they give orders concerning the Paulianists, are all who return from heretics to be baptized by this example? Since no one dares to do this, reason itself demonstrates that the rule concerns them alone.”

## CHAPTER X. That the clergy of no heresy except the Novatian are lawfully to be received.

Therefore, since the command concerns the clergy of the Novatians alone, what is to be said concerning the reception in the Church of the sacraments or orders of Donatists and Bonosiacs, except that these were not lawfully celebrated, but were usurped and permitted through some ignorance or necessity of the Church? But what, after this, of Arians, Patripassians, and Simoniacs, whose ordination appears to be prohibited along with these, is found to be usurped or permitted by no authority?

## CHAPTER XI. That Bonosiacs were received from necessity.

[Col. 0937D]

But let us deal first with those who are in some manner permitted, and afterwards with those who are entirely prohibited. Bonosiacs are Photinians, who, like the Jews, deny that Christ was begotten of the Father before the ages.

Concerning them the same Innocent says, chapter 5 (Epistle 22): “The careful deliberation of Annisius, our former brother, and of other fellow-priests was that those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received as ordained, lest they remain with him and no small scandal arise.” Therefore what necessity discovered as a remedy ought, when necessity ceases, likewise to cease along with the pressure that occasioned it. This, indeed, applied before his condemnation.

For concerning those ordained afterwards, he added subsequently: “Those who passed from Catholicism to the condemned Bonosus and allowed themselves, or desired, to be ordained by him, are plainly not to receive the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination.” And a little later: “At the very most, even those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of usurped rank, since they believed themselves to be what had not been granted by any regular procedure.”

## CHAPTER XII. That Donatists were received for the sake of expediency.

The Donatists, however, deviate from the faith in no other way than by making a schism from the unity of the Church, angered because Caecilian had been made bishop against their wishes. It seemed good to the Council of Carthage that, when any one of them intended to come to Catholic unity, if this appeared advantageous to Christian peace—which they vigorously attacked—he should be received in his own rank, whether a layman in baptism or a cleric in his order.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Leo receives Maximus, who was ordained bishop from being a layman and a Donatist.

Likewise Pope Leo, among other things, in his letter to the bishops of the Moors (Epistle 87, no. 3): “We do not deprive Maximus of episcopal rank, although he was reprehensibly ordained from being a layman, provided that he is no longer a Donatist and is free from the spirit of schismatic perversity, even though he obtained that dignity in whatever manner he did; provided that he himself, by a written petition submitted to us, makes manifest that he is Catholic.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Likewise, Novatians according to Innocent.

And because Novatians similarly do not depart from the faith, authority agrees concerning the reception of their laity and clergy. Hence Innocent I, to Victor, bishop of Rouen, chapter 15 (Epistle 2, chapter 8): “Those coming from Novatians or Montanists are to be received by imposition of hands alone, since, though they come from heretics, they have been baptized in Christ’s name.”

## CHAPTER XV. Likewise Donatus the Novatian according to Leo.

And Leo, to the bishops of the Moors (Epistle 87, no. 3): “Donatus of Sejac, a convert, as we have learned, from Novatianism together with his people, we wish to preside over the Lord’s flock, provided that he remembers to send us a written statement of his faith; in it he must condemn the error of Novatus’s doctrine and fully confess Catholic truth.”

To show that this concession concerning the Donatist and the Novatian was not regular but made with a certain discretion, he subsequently excuses himself, saying: “What we have relaxed in consideration of particular causes must henceforth be observed according to the ancient rules, so that what we have conceded for a time in pious leniency we may thereafter punish with just severity.”

From these authorities it is gathered that sacraments which heretics possess and perform no differently from the Church—having and administering them, that is, with the same faith and order in which they possessed and administered them before departing from it, while holding faithless opinions elsewhere than in the sacraments themselves—are completed and approved by imposition of hands when they return to the Church. Yet this has sometimes been done in view of necessity and mercy, but not often, as Leo says, lest heresy acquire a wicked authority in the Church if no principle for approving or rejecting distinguishes heretics from Catholics in their sacraments.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the sacraments of heretics, though true, are nevertheless unprofitable.

For Augustine says to Emeritus (Epistle 87, no. 9): “The sacraments which you have not altered are approved by us as you possess them, lest perhaps, while we desire to correct your perversity, we commit a sacrilegious injury against those ministries which have not been corrupted in your perversity. Nor had Saul corrupted the anointing which he had received; to that anointing King David, though afterwards God’s servant, showed such honour.”

Likewise Augustine to the Donatists: “Just as hypocrites who become truly converted are received without their baptism being rejected, so too, when schismatics and heretics come to us, we do not correct but rather approve those things which they possess and perform no differently from the true Church.”

Likewise, to Vincent the Donatist (Epistle 93, no. 46): “All the Lord’s sacraments are from the Catholic Church; although you possessed them before you departed from it, you nevertheless do not possess them for that reason because you are not the source from which you administered them.”

Likewise, to the Donatists: “If God is present in his sacraments and words through whomever they are administered, and God’s sacraments are everywhere, then the perverse are within and without.”

Likewise: “Therefore neither outside nor inside can anyone who belongs to the devil defile in himself or in anyone else the sacrament which belongs to Christ.” This was said concerning the truth that ought to be approved in the sacrament, not concerning its usefulness; for in fact what is given by heretics does not profit unless the recipient is united to the holy Church and reconciled by imposition of hands or also by penance, according to the nature of the heresy.

Hence Augustine—

> **[Note: Col. 0939D]** This book is not by St Augustine but by St Fulgentius, as ancient manuscripts written a thousand years ago, as well as the style, demonstrate. It was therefore relegated to the end of volume VI in the new edition of the works of St Augustine [Col. 0940D].

—to Peter the subdeacon, *On Faith* (St Fulgentius, chapter 56): “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that those baptized outside the Church, if they do not return to the Church, accumulate destruction through baptism.”

For communion in the ecclesiastical society has such force for salvation that one is not saved by baptism if it is not given where it ought to be given. Concerning such persons the prophet says: “Go out from their midst, and do not be defiled by them” (Isa. 52:11).

But in receiving or rejecting the sacraments of heretics, the distinction between heresies is of greatest weight, as has been said: the baptism of Paulianists is rejected; the baptism and ordination of Novatians and Donatists are received through imposition of hands; while the baptism of Arians and of the rest is purified also with penance.

## CHAPTER XVII. That they are also harmful.

Concerning these Ambrose says specifically, in the book *On Initiating the Uninstructed*: “The baptism of unbelievers does not heal; it does not cleanse, but defiles. For in the flood of these waters one does not draw near to God, because, according to the Apostle, ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin’ (Rom. 14:23); and for both those who perform it and those for whom they perform it, it is not only unprofitable but tends to judgment.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That those baptized by heretics are to be received through imposition of hands.

Hence Leo, chapter 29 (Epistle 37, no. 2): “Since those baptized by heretics have received in whatever manner the form of baptism, they are not to be baptized; but by imposition of hands they are to be joined to Catholics through the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics.”

Likewise Leo, to Leonicetus, bishop, chapter 19 (Epistle 79, no. 7): “Those who received baptism from heretics, having not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone through imposition of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification. We proclaim that this rule must be observed in all churches, and that the washing once begun is not to be violated under any pretext, as the Apostle says: ‘One Lord, one faith, one baptism’ (Eph. 4:5). This washing is not to be violated under any pretext; rather, the sanctification of the Spirit alone is to be invoked, so that what no one received from heretics he may obtain from Catholic priests.”

## CHAPTER XIX. That no sacraments of heretics are valid.

That their sacraments are not valid is everywhere attested by authority. Hence Jerome, on the prophet Haggai: “‘Such is the people of all heretics in my sight,’ says the Lord: ‘whatever they do, whatever they offer to me—whether vows, offerings for salvation, peace-offerings, sin-offerings, burnt-offerings, alms, fasts, or bodily chastity—shall be defiled in my sight.’ For although what is offered may seem holy in its outward appearance, yet because it is handled by one defiled in soul, all things shall be defiled.”

Likewise, on the prophet Amos: “God hates the sacrifices of heretics and casts them away from himself; and whenever they gather in his name, he detests their stench and closes his nostrils.”

## CHAPTER XX. That the sacraments of heretics are true in form, but not in spiritual grace.

Likewise Augustine, in the Lord’s words concerning blasphemies against the Spirit: “The bodily sacraments which persons separated from the unity of Christ’s body carry and celebrate may have an appearance of godliness; but true invisible and spiritual power cannot be in them, just as sensation does not follow a member when it is amputated from the body.”

Hence Leo, in his letter to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 40, no. 2): “Let those who condemn their evil deeds by full satisfactions, and choose rather to accuse themselves than to defend themselves, rejoice in the unity of our peace and communion, provided that what has been prescribed against the Catholic faith is first condemned by a fitting anathema. For otherwise in the Church of God, which is Christ’s body, neither are priesthoods valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true high priest reconciles us to the proper condition of his nature.”

But having stated these things universally, let us now consider them jointly in particular instances.

## CHAPTER XXI. That the Lord’s body consecrated by Arians is called a sacrilegious consecration.

For concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood consecrated by Arians, Gregory says in Book III, chapter 31, of the *Dialogues*, concerning Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild: “When the day of the Paschal festival came, in the silence of the dead of night his faithless father sent an Arian bishop to him, so that he might receive from his hand communion of sacrilegious consecration and thereby deserve to return to his father’s favour. But the man devoted to God reproached the Arian bishop who came to him, as he ought, and rejected his faithlessness with fitting rebukes.”

## CHAPTER XXII. That without faith the remaining ecclesiastical things appear to be possessed in vain.

Hence Jerome, on Hosea: “They offer sacrilegious bread, give alms, and appear to practise humility; if these things are truly done, I interpret them as burnt-offerings. But once they have abandoned the knowledge of God, they boast in vain of possessing the remaining members after the head of faith has been cut off.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. That those baptized by heretics are to be received with penance and imposition of hands, but their clergy are not.

Of the sacrament of orders, Innocent I says, [Col. 0941C] ch. 47 (Epistle 18, ch. 3):

> “Moreover, concerning Arians and the other plagues of this kind: because we receive their laypersons who have converted to the Lord under the form of penitence and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands, it does not seem fitting that their clerics should be received with the rank of priesthood or of any ministry. For we allow only their baptism to be valid, since it is indeed performed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet we judge that they do not possess the Holy Spirit from that baptism or from those ministries, since, when their founders departed from the catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received. Nor can they give others that fullness which operates especially in ordinations, a fullness which, through the faithlessness of their impiety rather than through faith, [Col. 0941D] I would say they lost. How, then, can it happen that we should judge their profane priests worthy of Christ’s honours, when, as I have said, we receive their laypersons as imperfect persons, under the form of penitence, in order that they may receive the grace of the Holy Spirit?”

Likewise, the same author, ch. 53 (Epistle 22, ch. 3):

> “We come to the third question. Since we say that those ordained by heretics have their head wounded by that laying on of hands, medicine must be applied where the wound was inflicted, so that it may recover health. But health following a wound cannot be without a scar; and where the remedy of penitence is necessary, the honour of ordination cannot have a place. For if, as it is written, ‘Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean’ (Num. 19:22), how can that be bestowed upon him [Col. 0942A] which purity and cleanness customarily receive?
>
> “But, conversely, it is asserted that he who has lost an honour cannot give that honour, and that the recipient received nothing, because there was nothing in the giver which he could receive. We agree, and this is certainly true: one who did not have it could not give it. He did, however, give condemnation, because he possessed it, through a perverse laying on of hands; and how one who has become a participant in one condemned ought to receive honour, we cannot discover.”

But since Innocent says that heretics are permitted to retain as valid only baptism, and not the other sacraments—while Gregory calls their communion sacrilegious and Innocent calls their ordination condemnation—he seems opposed to Jerome, who says in *Against the Luciferians*:

> “As Christ is the one who baptizes, so he is the one who sanctifies.” [Col. 0942B]

Likewise, to the same person:

> “I ask you,” he says, “either grant permission to offer sacrifice to him whose baptism you approve, or disapprove his baptism if you do not think him a priest. For it cannot be that one who is holy in baptism should be a sinner at the altar.”

This must be understood of a sinful ecclesiastic, not a heretic: whatever such a person does in faith in the performance of his office, though unworthy, is believed to be valid through the cooperation of divine grace. Otherwise, if it is said of heretics, Jerome contradicts himself when he says in Hosea: “Their sacrifices are the bread of mourning; all who eat of it shall be defiled” (Hos. 9:4). And elsewhere, in the person of the Lord: “I will curse your blessings” (Mal. 2:2), that is, whatever is blessed by you through me shall be cursed. Therefore this [Col. 0942C] is to be understood, as Jerome says, of a sinful ecclesiastic; the other statement concerns a heretic.

## Chapter XXIV. That the various ordinances of the Church must be referred to different matters

The Church’s ordinances are diverse, and are directed to different matters; yet in both cases they accord with truth and justice and suit the order of the cases. Otherwise, if they must be maintained immutably and without discrimination, the greatest confusion of contradiction arises. Did not the Lord say to Abraham, “Sacrifice your son”? And conversely, “Do not stretch out your hand over him” (Gen. 22:12). Moses likewise says in the law, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13); and conversely, “Whoever does this or that shall be put to death.” Solomon says, “Answer a fool” (Prov. 26:5); [Col. 0942D] and conversely, “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” (Ecclus. 22:14). Paul says, “Rebuke with all authority” (Tit. 1:13); and conversely, “Rebuke with all patience” (1 Tim. 4:2).

Therefore, because only baptism is allowed to heretics as valid and true—yet, being without the sanctification of the Spirit, it is useless and harmful—all their sacraments, both those deemed valid and those not deemed valid, must truly be avoided. For, as it is written: “To the pure all things are pure; but to those who are defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Tit. 1:15).

## Chapter XXV. That all sacraments are received beneficially from Catholics in the Church, but damnably from heretics

Thus the African Council, ch. 24 (under Celestine, ch. 14), states:

> “In the Church all sacraments are received beneficially [Col. 0943A] and life-givingly; but for those who persevere in heresy, those things procure a great punishment of condemnation which, in truth, would have been more luminous for their life.”

Thus Leo, ch. 14:

> “It concerns the peril of the soul if anyone among those who, having fallen away from you into the error of heretics and schismatics, has in any manner stained himself by the contagion of heretical communion, is received upon returning to catholic communion without the profession of lawful satisfaction.”

## Chapter XXVI. That those baptized by heretics, whether by consent or awareness, are to be deprived of clerical rank

Hence Innocent I, ch. 54 (Epistle 22, no. 4):

> “Concerning the communion of baptism, which sacrament is judged more valid among heretics, the Church’s rule is to grant only lay communion through the laying on of hands to those [Col. 0943B] baptized by heretics, and not to appoint any of them, even to the least clerical rank. Yet if we did not fall into their communion knowingly, but either through ignorance or under violent compulsion, we may be excused.”

## Chapter XXVII. That those ignorantly baptized by heretics ought not to be excluded from orders

Hence in the African Council, ch. 14 (under Pope Celestine, chs. 14, 24):

> “It has been resolved concerning infants alone who are baptized by heretics: because they did not act by their own judgment, the error of their parents must not prevent them, once they have returned to the Church of God with a saving purpose, from being promoted to the ministry of the sacred altar.”

The same council, ch. 24:

> “Those baptized as little children among the Donatists, being still unable to know the ruinous character of their error, and who, after reaching an age capable of reason, have recognized the truth, abhorred their falsehood, and been received into the Church according to the ancient order through the laying on of hands: the name of that error ought not to impede their entering the clergy.” [Col. 0943C]

## Chapter XXVIII. That those forcibly ordained by heretics have some appearance of excuse

Likewise Innocent I, *On Those Compelled by Force*, ch. 55 (Epistle 22, ch. 5):

> “It is established that many have suffered violence and have been dragged away against their will and, though resisting, ordained by heretics. But if such a person, after such an ordination, was not present when they performed the sacraments; if he did not participate in their communion; [Col. 0943D] if, as soon as they departed from their most wicked assembly, he returned to the Church: such a person may have some appearance of excuse. Otherwise, let those who returned further consider that they were ordained by heretics. Certainly those who received nothing from them are guilty of usurped rank.”

This particularly indicates that consenting to any communion of heretics is highly condemnable.

## Chapter XXIX. That heretics are to be avoided even in bodily association

Thus Ambrose:

> “If there is any church which does not possess the foundations of apostolic truth, it must be abandoned, lest it be able to bring some stain upon you.”

Thus Gregory to Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera (Book VIII, Epistle 10):

> “Therefore,” he says, “because your Fraternity, after you had formerly, through negligence, brought yourself into Maximus’s association and communion, later recalled to your senses by priestly seriousness, suspended yourself from it, so that you would by no means endure to be content merely with separation from him unless, entering the enclosure of a monastery, you bewailed your former offences: therefore do not doubt that you have been received into communion with my favour.” [Col. 0944A]

Likewise the blessed martyr Cyprian, in his letters against heretics:

> “If anyone,” he says, “has departed from the Church through heretical presumption, he has condemned himself. With such persons, according to the Apostle, we ought not even to take food. This is made clear in the Book of Kings, where the man of God was sent to Jeroboam to reproach him with his sins and foretell the coming vengeance. He was forbidden to eat bread or drink water there. [Col. 0944B] Because he did not observe this, as he was returning, divine judgment caused him to perish on the road through a lion’s bite.
>
> “And does anyone dare say that the saving sacrament and heavenly grace can be shared with heretics, with whom neither earthly food nor secular drink ought to be shared? It is established that the oil with which the baptized are anointed is sanctified; and that the eucharist cannot at all be performed among them, where there is no hope and faith is false, where everything is done through falsehood. For heretics, like apes, though not human beings, imitate the human form; they claim for themselves the appearance, authority, and truth of the catholic Church, although they themselves are not in the Church. One cursed by God blesses; one dead promises life; a blasphemer invokes God; a profane person administers the priesthood; a sacrilegious person sets up an altar. [Col. 0944C]
>
> “To all this evil is added that a bishop of the devil dares to perform the eucharist, though an offering cannot be sanctified there where the Holy Spirit is absent, nor can the Lord benefit anyone through the prayers and petitions of one who has violated God himself. For if those who violate the Church are reckoned heathens and tax collectors, much more should rebels and enemies who fabricate false altars, unlawful priesthoods, sacrilegious sacrifices, and every kind of adulteration be counted among heathens and tax collectors—namely, all who are known to have departed from the charity and unity of the catholic Church.
>
> “Therefore whatever heretics do is carnal, empty, and false, so that none of the things they have done ought to be approved by you. Not everything claimed in Christ’s name is immediately [Col. 0944D] to be received and accepted, but what is done in Christ’s truth. For how can those who attempt against God what is not lawful for them accomplish what they do, or obtain anything from God by their unlawful undertakings?
>
> “Therefore those who support heretics and schismatics are shown by divine judgment to share in their crime; and not only leaders and instigators, but participants also, are destined for a worse fate unless they separate themselves from communion with the wicked. For the Lord commanded through Moses: ‘Separate yourselves from the tents of these most stubborn men,’ and, ‘Touch nothing of all that is theirs, lest you perish together with their sins’ (Num. 16:26). What the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled: whoever did not separate himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalty for impious communion. [Col. 0945A]
>
> “So too, through the prophet Hosea, the Holy Spirit testifies: ‘Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them shall be defiled’ (Hos. 9:4), plainly teaching and showing that all who have been defiled by their sin are altogether joined with its authors in punishment. Therefore, brothers, we exhort your reverent concern for integrity and faith as far as we can: do not mingle yourselves, by sacrilegious communion, with profane and polluted priests.”

But since blessed Cyprian—whose little works Augustine teaches should be accepted; whom he praises in the book *On Predestination* as a most lucid teacher; whose tongue, he declares, pierced heretics as with an invincible weapon; and whom he further affirms to be everywhere laudably renowned in Christian faith and doctrine—since, I say, so great a man agrees with the other saints that heretics’ sacraments must be avoided lest people be contaminated by their sacrilegious sacrifices, let us see, then, how the saints agree once more: how grave they judge the crime of simony to be as heresy, and how they either detest or approve its sacraments. [Col. 0945B]

## Chapter XXX. That a simoniac departs from the faith

That one who commits simony departs from the faith and imputes blasphemy to the Holy Spirit by assigning a monetary valuation to the grace of the Holy Spirit is attested by Ambrose in the first book *On Penance*, addressed to Novatian:

> “When Simon, corrupted by his habitual practice of magic, thought that he could purchase the grace of Christ by money through the laying on of hands and the imparting of the Spirit, Peter said: ‘You have neither lot nor part in this faith, because your heart is not right before God’ (Acts 8:21). You see that, by apostolic authority, he condemns this man who blasphemes the Holy Spirit through magical vanity—and all the more because he did not possess the pure conscience of faith.”

Thus Gregory, in the *Register*, ch. 4:

> “Since all avarice is the service of idols, whoever does not vigilantly guard against it—especially in conferring ecclesiastical honours—is subjected to the perdition of unbelief, even though he appears to retain the faith which he neglects.” [Col. 0945C]

## Chapter XXXI. That selling and buying the Holy Spirit is indeed a capital crime

Thus Gregory to Queen Brunhild (Book IX, [Col. 0945D] Epistle 109):

> “It is altogether a grave crime, beyond what can be spoken, to sell the Holy Spirit, who redeemed all things.”

Likewise Gregory Nazianzen, *On Purchase*:

> “Concerning one who strives to buy God’s gift at a price, there can be no doubt that he can thereafter neither remain in nor be restored to sacred order in any way; and he must by all means be cut off from communion.”

But the remedy of penitence must be considered very carefully. For what is it to purchase the gift of the Holy Spirit with money except a capital crime and the heresy of simony?

## Chapter XXXII. How the heresy of simony was punished in both Testaments

Let us see how detestably it was condemned in both Testaments. Gehazi sold to Naaman the Syrian [Col. 0946A] the grace of healing; but, judged by Elisha, he lost that very grace of healing when he became leprous. Judas sold the Redeemer of all; immediately, hanging by a noose, he did not obtain that same grace of redemption. And rightly so, because no one can retain what he sells.

When Simon Magus sought to buy that same grace of the Spirit, he heard from Peter the sentence of his condemnation: “May your money perish with you, because you thought to possess God’s gift by money” (Acts 8:20). Therefore the Lord also, in order to show that sellers and buyers of this grace are deprived of it, while he forgave other sinners in the Temple through grace, singled out sellers and buyers for rebuke and drove them from the Temple with a whip. It is clear that his grace of the Holy Spirit left his own sellers and buyers destitute and empty. For those whom [Col. 0946B] Christ expelled from the Temple—will the Spirit of Christ make them his temple?

From this it must be understood and believed that in this heresy too is fulfilled what Innocent I decreed above concerning other heresies (Epistle 22, ch. 3):
