> “Those who lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received cannot give others that fullness, which works especially in orders, and which they lost through their own faithlessness.”

And again:

> “One who did not possess the honour could not give the honour, and the recipient received nothing because there was nothing in the giver; but through a perverse laying on of hands he gave the condemnation that he possessed.”

This, indeed, is true in the case of those whom a simoniac ordains simoniacs, just as an Arian ordains Arians and a Donatist ordains Donatists: both truth proves it and authority agrees. For if a blind person offers a lamp to a blind person, neither can see any better for it.

But concerning those whom a heretic ordains not as heretics but freely, and who do not consent to him but either are weak or unwilling, and endure such an ordainer for some reasonable toleration of the Church: let us see what reason and authority allow, and first concerning those whom a simoniac ordains simoniacs through sale. [Col. 0946C]

## Chapter XXXIII. That the priesthood does not subsist in those who obtain it by payments

Gregory to Queen Brunhild, ch. 24 (Book IX, Epistle 109):

> “We utterly execrate and most gravely detest the conferring of sacred orders through the heresy of simony, which first arose against the Church and was condemned by a severe curse. The result is that the dignity of priesthood is held in contempt and holy honour becomes criminal. Reverence has consequently perished and discipline is taken away. For who, after all, will revere what is sold? Or who can fail to regard as cheap what is bought?
>
> “Therefore I am deeply saddened and grieve for them in my heart, because they despise the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God deigns to bestow by divine gift through the laying on of hands, and obtain him instead by payments. I do not judge that priesthood subsists there.” [Col. 0946D]

## Chapter XXXIV. That blessing is turned into a curse for one promoted by purchasing spiritual things, so as to become a heretic

Likewise Gregory to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, ch. 129 (Book IX, Epistle 106):

> “A report reaching us [Col. 0947A] and spreading abroad has declared that sacred orders are conferred through the heresy of simony in the regions of Gaul. We are afflicted by an overwhelming and sorrowful grief if money has any place in ecclesiastical offices and what is sacred becomes secular. Whoever strives to obtain this by paying a price desires not to be a priest, but only vainly to be called one.
>
> “For what is accomplished by this, except that there is no examination of conduct, no concern for morals, no inquiry about life, but only the person able to supply money is thought worthy? Therefore, dearest brother, let sincerity prevail in ordaining priests; let agreement be straightforward and without sale; let a pure election be preferred, so that one may be believed to have been advanced to the highest priesthood not by the support of sellers but by God’s judgment.
>
> “For evangelical authority bears witness how altogether grave a crime it is [Col. 0947B] either to buy or to sell God’s gift for a price. When our Lord and Redeemer entered the Temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21:12). What else is it to sell doves than to receive payment for the laying on of hands and to sell the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God grants to human beings? That their priesthood falls before God’s eyes was plainly signified by the overturning of the seats. Yet the perversity of wickedness still exerts its power. For it compels those whom it deceived into buying to sell; and, while the command of the divine voice, ‘Freely you have received; freely give’ (Matt. 10:8), is disregarded, the condition of seller and buyer is doubled in one and the same offence. Since it is clear that this heresy crept in before all others with a pestilential root, and was condemned by apostolic detestation at its very origin, why is it not avoided? Why is it not considered that blessing is turned into a curse for one promoted in order to become a heretic?” [Col. 0947C]

## Chapter XXXV. In how many ways a payment is expended in simony

How payment is given in this heresy in various ways, the same Gregory explains in his homily on the Gospels:

> “There are indeed some who receive monetary payments in connection with ordination, yet confer sacred orders for human favour and seek from that very generosity only the recompense of praise. [Col. 0947D] Such persons plainly do not give freely what they received freely, because, in discharging an office bestowed by God, they seek the coin of popular favour under the appearance of holiness.
>
> “Therefore, when the prophet described a holy man, he rightly said: ‘Who shakes his hands free from every gift’ (Isa. 33:15). He did not merely add ‘from a gift,’ but ‘from every gift,’ because one kind of gift is from the hand, another from the tongue, and another from service. A gift from the hand is money; a gift from service is improperly rendered submission; a gift from the tongue is favour. Therefore one who confers sacred orders then shakes his hands free of every gift, when in divine matters he seeks not only no money but no human favour.”

Thus Gregory also to John, bishop of Corinth, ch. 220:

> “By a strict prohibition we have forbidden receiving anything for orders. Therefore you must neither consent nor permit anyone to be brought to sacred orders through advantage, favour, or the entreaties of certain persons.” [Col. 0948A]

## Chapter XXXVI. That a simoniac, both seller and buyer, must be punished by the reproach of anathema, loss of acquired honour, and confinement in a monastery

Likewise Ambrose in the *Pastoral Book*, ch. 10:

> “What cannot be said without great sorrow is that very many persons are found wishing, by the business of payment, to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit. One gives a price so that he may receive the eminence of pontifical rank, forgetting Peter’s words to Simon: ‘May your money perish with you, because you thought to possess God’s gift by money’ (Acts 8:20).
>
> “Therefore, since this evil is customary and has often been cut down by the sword of our forebears, [Col. 0948B] we too apply the remaining iron to this cancerous wound. We decree absolutely that whoever hereafter is discovered to have offered any payment in order to receive the dignity of a divine gift shall know himself condemned from that moment under the reproach of anathema and separated from participation in Christ’s body and blood, since he is known to have committed an abominable crime against Christ.
>
> “If anyone accuses such a person, the man who obtained this order through acceptance of payment shall be deprived of the rank he has assumed and thrust into a monastery for perpetual penitence. Those, however, who have received payments for this purpose, if clerics, shall be punished by loss of rank; but if laypersons, they shall be condemned by perpetual anathema.” [Col. 0948C]

## Chapter XXXVII. That anyone who sells or buys, not merely orders, but the administration of any ecclesiastical property, is liable to the danger of losing his own rank

Likewise, from the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 2 (canon 2):

> “If any bishop performs an ordination for money and reduces to a price the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be sold; if he ordains for money a presbyter, deacon, or any person among those named in the clergy; or promotes for money a steward, advocate, or any person subject to the rule, for the sake of his own most shameful gain: the person against whom this is proved shall be liable to the loss of his own rank. And the person ordained [Col. 0948D] shall derive no benefit from the ordination or promotion transacted by commerce, but shall be excluded from the dignity or administration which he acquired by money. If anyone has served as intermediary in such shameful and impious giving or receiving, then, if he is a cleric, he shall fall from his own rank; but if a layperson, he shall be anathematized.”

## Chapter XXXVIII. That selling or buying a church or tithes is the heresy of simony

Likewise Gregory in the *Register*:

> “If a presbyter obtains a church through money, he shall not only be deprived of the church but stripped of the honour of priesthood; for no believer is ignorant that selling an altar, tithes, and the Holy Spirit is the heresy of simony.”

[Col. 0949A] Likewise Jerome:

> “The Church’s possessions are the vows of deceased believers, the price of sinners, the patrimonies of the poor. Whoever diverts them to his own uses is like Judas the traitor and the Pharisees who sold and bought Christ’s blood.”

Pope Gelasius, ch. 24 (Epistle 9):

> “Those who are found, unworthy by their merits, to have purchased sacred dignity for a price must, once convicted, be excluded without danger while committing such a crime; for the condemnation of Simon, to which Sacred Scripture bears witness, envelops giver and receiver alike.”

Therefore, since according to Gregory priesthood does not subsist among simoniacs and blessing is turned into a curse; according to Ambrose they are condemned under the reproach of anathema and excluded from participation in the Lord’s body and blood; [Col. 0949B] according to the Council of Chalcedon they appear to derive no benefit from such an ordination; according to Gelasius they are enveloped in Simon’s condemnation; and by Christ they are expelled from the Temple—what else can a simoniac confer upon a simoniac in his ordination except what Innocent testifies concerning other heretics: namely, the condemnation which he possessed, given through a perverse laying on of hands? Consequently, one may not be a priest, but only vainly be called one.

## Chapter XXXIX. That modern simoniacs strive to purchase the Holy Spirit in sacraments as Simon did in miracles

“But Peter Damian objects that simoniacs of the modern age are sound with respect to faith, because, [Col. 0949C] since they despair of becoming illustrious through miracles, they are simoniacs not because they wish to buy the Holy Spirit or his gifts, but because they are ambitious and aspire to the summit of earthly dignity.”

But do not our simoniacs buy in sacraments the same Spirit whom Simon wished to buy in miracles? For who wishes to be called a bishop unless in order to exercise episcopally the remission of sins through the laying on of hands and the other spiritual acts? The same applies to the offices of every other order.

But Pope Paschal testifies that they do not thereby escape the heresy of simony, even if in spiritual dignities they seek only earthly things:

> “If anyone objects that consecrations are not bought, but the very things that result from consecration, he is proved utterly foolish.”

For since a corporeal Church—such as a bishopric, abbacy, or something of that sort—accomplishes nothing at all without corporeal goods, just as the soul does not live bodily without the body, whoever sells one of these, without which the other cannot be attained, leaves neither unsold. Therefore let no one buy a church, prebend, or anything ecclesiastical; nor pay a cake (*pastellum*) or a meal for such things. [Col. 0949D]

## Chapter XL. That simoniacs have no authority from the Old Testament for selling or buying, although this may appear to be suggested somewhere

But simoniacs seem to possess at least a little authority, as though this had been practiced even by holy men in the Old Testament, because Saul did not dare go to Samuel to seek an oracle unless he brought a gift. Blessed Jerome suitably resolves this in his commentary on Micah, declaring that only wicked persons accepted such things, not good persons:

> “Its rulers judged for gifts, its priests gave answers for payment, and its prophets practiced divination for money; yet they leaned upon the Lord, saying: ‘Is not the Lord among us? No evils shall come upon us.’ Therefore because of you Zion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a watchman’s hut in an orchard. Let no one doubt that Jerusalem was overthrown because of the crimes which are recounted in this chapter.” [Col. 0950A]

And a little later:

> “Peter could have sold Simon Magus what he sought; indeed, he could have pretended to be selling it. For the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought; rather, he condemned the money offered along with the offerer. Nor should anyone be troubled by what we read [Col. 0950B] in the First Book of Kings: Saul, wishing to go to Samuel, said to his servant that he did not wish to go to him because he had no payment to offer for an oracle; and the servant replied: ‘Behold, a quarter-shekel of silver has been found in my hand; I shall give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.’
>
> “For it is not written that Samuel accepted it, or that they offered it to him; rather, they are fed by the prophet. But who makes him out to have accepted it? The supports of the tabernacle are more to be valued than the gifts of a prophet. A shekel contains twenty obols, and a quarter of a shekel is five obols. Therefore our priests too, if they wish to sell prophecy and set up doves on their seats—the doves which the Lord overturned with a whip—should be content with only five obols as their fee. Would that they received not the price of estates, but five obols.” [Col. 0950C]

The same sense is expressed in the Book of Kings concerning Jeroboam’s wife going to Ahijah, the man of God, although those accustomed to go to soothsayers may, because of their evil custom, have thought the same thing about prophets and wished to offer holy men what they customarily offered to diviners.

## Chapter XLI. That no good fruit can arise from the beginning of simony

“But Peter Damian objects that, although buying ecclesiastical things is evil, adverse beginnings often reach happy outcomes: Jacob attained blessing through supplanting; a crop sown by a leprous hand is nevertheless harvested clean; beautiful offspring is born from adulterous [Col. 0950D] intercourse; and many similar things which do not operate for this purpose, according to the testimony of sacred authority.”

Thus Leo to the bishops of Mauretania, ch. 49 (Epistle 37, no. 1):

> “A primacy which sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if it does not offend in conduct and actions, is nevertheless pernicious by the example of its own fault; and it is difficult for things begun from an evil principle to reach a good outcome.”

Likewise Gregory to the bishop of Antioch:

> “We give thanks to Jesus Christ our Lord, who declares himself to be the door for shepherds entering lawfully into the sheepfold, and the Holy Spirit to be the doorkeeper. But one who enters through the door and does not climb up another way as a thief and robber expresses in himself the ways of his Creator both by example and word, and receives the height of governance in order to bear all as a duty, not from desire for a transient honour. For since Paul says, ‘No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ,’ it consequently follows that where Christ is not the foundation, no building of good work follows.” [Col. 0951A]

Likewise Gregory to John, bishop of Corinth, and to all established throughout Greece (Book V, Epistle 57):

> “I have heard from certain reports that some persons in your regions obtain sacred orders for a price. If this is so, I say it weeping and announce it groaning: when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it cannot long remain standing outwardly. We know also what our Redeemer himself did in the Gospel, when he entered the Temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves.”

## Chapter XLII. That the Holy Spirit does not shine in simoniacal sacraments

[Col. 0951B]

And, that we may see that no good fruit whatsoever springs from the root of simony, Augustine’s authority establishes it:

> “Just as the eunuch who bought Joseph was a eunuch, so one who purchases grace has no living seed, because his genitals are dry. Likewise the sacrificial fire which had lived under water for seventy years during the Babylonian captivity was extinguished when Antiochus sold the priesthood to Jason. This signified that the fire of the Holy Spirit does not shine in simoniacal sacraments.”

What did blessed Augustine intend to indicate by these comparisons except that the sacraments of simoniacs, like those of other heretics, though true in form, are nevertheless empty and false in effect, since they cannot beget or kindle heavenly grace in human minds? Peter Damian therefore approves sacraments in which Augustine testifies that the fire of the Holy Spirit does not shine.

For he says that, just as Christ when sold restored Malchus’s ear and performed miracles, so the Holy Spirit can be sold and can work his grace in the very act of his sale. But the comparison is not valid for the Holy Spirit to work spiritually in faithless commercial dealings of avarice what Christ did bodily for a definite mystical purpose, as an example of patience. For if the comparison is universal, and the Spirit is believed able to be sold as Christ was sold, then the Holy Spirit must also be believed capable of being crucified—which is impossible. [Col. 0951C]

## Chapter XLIII. That the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought

[Col. 0951D]

Thus Jerome on Micah:

> “Can divination be taken in a good sense? They indeed seemed to themselves to be prophets; but because they took money, their prophecy became divination. Peter certainly could have sold to Simon Magus what he sought; indeed, he could have pretended to sell it.”

For the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought; if prophecy, which seemed to be of God, is turned into divination, which is diabolical, by those who sell it—what else follows except that, as said above, no spiritual grace cooperates with simoniacs? For in the sacraments, if neither the planter nor the waterer is anything, who works in them if God, who ought to give the increase, does not shine in them but is inactive?

And although beautiful offspring is born from adulterous intercourse, none can be born from a eunuch whose genitals are dry. Gregory’s authority further establishes that a simoniac is liable both for himself and for others: he cannot redeem even his own sins by alms made from the price of simony, but by the evil merit of that act rather renders the Judge angry with himself. [Col. 0952A]

## Chapter XLIV. That almsgiving cannot be made even from the price of simony

Thus Gregory to Bishop Syagrius, ch. 29 (Book IX, Epistle 106):

> “It must not be thought almsgiving if that which is received from unlawful sources is distributed to the poor; for the person who receives wickedly with the intention of distributing well is burdened rather than helped. Hence it is also certain that if monasteries, hospices, or anything else are built with money given for sacred orders, it does not profit one’s reward.
>
> “Therefore, lest under the pretext of almsgiving we strive to receive anything with sin, Scripture forbids it, saying: ‘The sacrifices of the ungodly are an abomination to God, offered from crime’ (Prov. 21:27). Therefore the sins of the heresy of simony must be avoided most carefully under the pretext of almsgiving. If it harms when almsgiving is the motive, what when avarice is the motive?” [Col. 0952B]

## Chapter XLV. That simony harms those who know of it and consent to it
Likewise Gregory, to Theodoric and Theudebert, kings of the Franks, chapter 26 (Book V, Epistle 110):

> “It is reported that the Simoniacal heresy prevails within the bounds of your kingdom, although in priests faith must be chosen together with life. If life is lacking, faith has no merit, because faith without works is dead (James 2:18). For what works can a priest have, when he is proved to obtain the honor of so great a sacrament by payment? The result is that those who seek holy orders strive not to reform their lives, but to amass the riches by which sacred honor is bought. And where gold is pleasing, vice is pleasing too. Thus a mortal wound is inflicted not only upon the soul of the ordainer and of the ordained; your royal eminence also is weighed down by the fault of bishops, by whose intercessions it ought rather to have been helped. For if one is believed worthy of the priesthood not because merits but payments commend him, it follows that in ecclesiastical honors neither moral seriousness nor diligence will preserve anything for itself, but the profane love of gold will possess all; and while those vices are rewarded with honor, the priesthood is judged not to profit such a man, but to perish. For when the shepherd is wounded, who will apply medicine to the sheep that need healing? Or how shall he protect the people with the shield of prayer, who exposes himself to be struck by darts? Or what fruit will he produce from himself, whose root is infected by a grievous plague? Greater calamity, therefore, is to be feared in places where such intercessors are brought to the office of government: men who provoke God’s wrath against themselves rather than appease it through themselves. We therefore ask you to strive to prohibit so detestable an evil from the bounds of your kingdom, and to allow no excuse, no suggestion against your soul, to find place with you; for beyond doubt, he who neglects to amend what he can correct shares the fault of the one who does it.”

Therefore, since according to Leo Simony does not end well, and according to Gregory no good work follows from it; and again, since a priesthood which has fallen inwardly cannot stand for long, nor is almsgiving to be considered when made from the price of Simony; and again, royal eminence is burdened, no medicine is applied to the sheep needing cure when their shepherd is wounded, evil fruit is produced from an infected root, and even greater calamity is feared in the future—what happy outcome can anyone expect from a sinister beginning?

But if someone, with the consent or approval of his own heresy, is ordained by such a man even without payment, will he be free from sin? Will he have any semblance of excuse either from ignorance or from the violence by which he was compelled? For, as Augustine said above, those who are eunuchs—that is, barren of every good—and in whose sacraments the Holy Spirit does not shine, could not give what, as was said above, they did not possess. How then can one who agrees with a heretic validly receive orders? For he who approves the seller is like the buyer. He receives the sacrament only in its outward form, not in the reality and substance of its effect. For if a blind man offers guidance to a blind man, do not both fall into a pit? (Matthew 15:14). How, then, can those who are anathematized by God himself and by all the saints, and judged not to be priests but merely to be called so in vain, be approved as truly administering priestly acts?

## CHAPTER XLVI. That he is to be deposed who permits himself to be ordained by one whom he does not doubt to be Simoniacal.

Hence Pope Alexander says among other things:

> “If anyone permits himself to be consecrated by one whom he does not doubt to be Simoniacal, both consecrator and consecrated alike shall incur a sentence of condemnation; both shall be deposed, shall do penance, and shall remain deprived of their own rank.”

And what wonder if anyone is judged incapable of ordaining because of Simony, when the same judgment is made if someone presumes through negligence to ordain men who are unworthy? Hence Leo, chapter 49, says among other things:

> “If any bishops have ordained such a priest as it was not lawful for him to be, even if somehow they escape loss of their own honor, they shall thereafter have no right of ordination; nor shall they ever take part in that sacrament which, neglecting divine judgment, they conferred upon an unworthy person.”

If those who negligently gave so great a gift as the Holy Spirit are prohibited thereafter from that sacrament, how much more those who hand it over greedily and treacherously? If anyone consents to communicate with them in any sacrament, though Sacred Scripture commands that they be avoided, opposed, accused, and cut off from communion by every means?

## CHAPTER XLVII. That one must burn fiercely against Simony.

Hence Gregory, to Bishop Victor (Book XII, Epistle 29):

> “Whoever, in consideration of his office, does not burn fiercely for the correction of this crime, namely the Simoniacal heresy, should not doubt that he shares the lot of him from whom this particular outrage first took its beginning.”

Therefore, if one who does not burn with zeal shares a lot with Simon, what condemnation does one not incur who consents, approves, and submits himself to him in consecration? Therefore they must altogether be avoided.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. That Simoniacs are to be persecuted or avoided.

Hence Gregory:

> “Who is chosen for morals, who for uprightness, who for integrity of life? Therefore wolves are to be pursued; all who are promoted in order to become heretics are to be avoided. They possess the leprosy of Gehazi together with his riches, and by their ill-gotten reward they have amassed not so much an inheritance of resources as a treasure of crimes.”

Therefore, since they are judged to be pursued and avoided, who will mingle himself with their leprosy unless he wishes to be leprous?

## CHAPTER XLIX. That Simony must also be opposed.

Likewise Gregory, to Virgil, bishop of Arles (Book XI, Epistle 55):

> “Since, by the testimony of divine Scripture, the service of idols is called covetousness, it is evident with what zeal it ought to be opposed; and yet, as we say with grief, it is not avoided by certain priests.”

For while they themselves creep into the Church through idolatry, lest they perish alone they bestow ecclesiastical grace for payment; and, for the scattering of the sheep, they bring wolves into the Lord’s sheepfold. Therefore Simony, together with its handmaid idolatry, is worshipped in God’s temple; and though the Lord himself overturned its seats and cast it out of the temple, and Gregory together with the other saints commands it to be opposed, we revere it contrary to canonical precepts and indiscriminately bow our necks beneath the blessings of that whose curses have been stated above.

## CHAPTER L. That, although the sacrament is in truth a good thing for the good, it becomes a great evil for the wicked.

Let those who commend the sacraments of Simoniacs, then, go to Peter Damian and have him as their advocate on the Day of Judgment. We indeed approve those sacraments as he does: true in respect of their form, but empty in respect of spiritual grace. For although things celebrated at the invocation of the divine name are good in themselves, they nevertheless become evil for those by whom they are administered unworthily or treacherously; and evil also for those who, by consent or approval—and thus unworthily or treacherously—communicate in them.

And what wonder if sacraments, though good in themselves, have no good effect in those who either handle them badly or communicate badly? Our very Salvation gave the morsel to Judas, and immediately with the morsel there entered, not a good spirit, but an evil one. Why? Not because one who is good did not give a good thing, but because an evil man received a good thing evilly; and so the good thing did not produce its good effect, because it found no place in which to produce it.

Likewise, the Lord was present and true in his own country, not through an evil minister but by himself, yet he could do nothing because he found no faith. He did not lack his own truth because of others’ unbelief, but he lacked the power of a good effect.

## CHAPTER LI. That the Lord was transfigured twice in the flesh.

In order to show this plainly in all his sacraments, he was transfigured twice while in the flesh. In one transfiguration he appeared wondrously shining like the sun, so that faith, raised above itself to contemplate heavenly grace, might advance. In the other, as an unrecognizable stranger, he pretended to be going farther from those who doubted about him; and, lest he be recognized, he held their eyes fast.

For what other reason than that, because he was not in their minds through faith, he might show himself as withdrawing farther from them; and because they did not believe him to be what he was, they might see him as other than he was? Behold: in each vision his presence and truth were there; but in the one faith was exercised, so that it might believe more than it believed in the other; in the other unbelief was restrained so that it might not even recognize what it saw.

Thus the sacrament of his body and blood is for some unto salvation, for others unto judgment. Thus it is the great sacrament of faith; yet faith, though true, is dead without works (James 2:20). Thus all ten virgins were equally virgins; yet five of them were foolish and five prudent (Matthew 25:3). The reality of virginity was present, but because of the intention accompanying that virginity, the worthiness of merit was not equal for all.

Thus martyrdom, or almsgiving, is sounding brass and a clanging cymbal, as the Apostle says, when charity is absent (1 Corinthians 13:1). But if a blind man administers the truth of the lamp to a blind man, neither thereby illuminates his own blindness any more. So too an evil man gives true sacraments to an evil man, but not thereby spiritual gifts; because, through the evil merits of both, the Holy Spirit is hindered from working in them what belongs to him.

## CHAPTER LII. That in the baptism of heretics, although it is allowed to be valid, one must not believe that the Holy Spirit is possessed unless imposition of hands follows.

Hence Innocent, although he grants that the baptism of heretics is valid, does not grant that the Holy Spirit is possessed through that baptism. And Leo does not permit those who received the form of baptism from heretics to be rebaptized [perhaps: “does not permit them to be rebaptized”]; rather, he commands that they receive from Catholic priests, through invocation and imposition of hands, the Holy Spirit whom no one received from heretics.

Hence it is evident, as Innocent says, that those who received that perverse Simoniacal imposition of hands have a wounded head—unless ignorance excuses them, or the violence of coercion, or perhaps an intention of piety. Thus, as with certain other heresies, Catholic imposition of hands, together with satisfaction and penance, restores them.

Yet this remedy does not prejudice any authoritative judgment . . . for I find the condemnation of Simoniacs and of those who consented to them and did not burn against them; but I have not read of an authoritative remedy expressly named for this heresy. Only because such a practice has been adopted among Novatians and Donatists—lesser heretics, indeed—not by canonical rule but from an intention of piety, I have inferred from these cases that the same may also be done here. And this also because in every other respect they have the orthodox faith, except that they believe the Holy Spirit to be for sale. And, as blessed Augustine says, when heretics return, they are to be cured in the respect in which they separate themselves from the Church, while in the respect in which they adhere to it they are to be acknowledged.

## CHAPTER LIII. That whoever defiles himself by heretical communion ought not thereafter to be promoted.

Likewise Leo, chapter 14, to Bishop Januarius:

> “Every cleric of whatever rank who, abandoning the Catholic faith, has defiled himself by the contagion of heretical or schismatic communion, if he returns to the Church with lawful satisfaction and condemnation of his error, shall count it a great benefit if, all hope of promotion having been removed, he remains in the rank in which he is found.”

Although Peter Damian defends his own by this chapter, it sufficiently shows that no communion is due to heretics: for it is to be accounted a great benefit if, even after satisfaction, not merely the rank in which one stands but any promotion within that rank is denied to a person. For communion with heresy stains its adherents with a fine mark, taking from them promotion to every dignity. They may indeed retain their station with satisfaction; it permits this to be imputed not to justice but to conditional grace.

## CHAPTER LIV. How the sacraments of heretics are called void and untrue, although they are true and holy.

It should be noted that sacraments are called void, even condemnable, or untrue not in themselves—for they are true and holy even when celebrated by a heretic—but because, being administered by faithless persons unlawfully, they are unto judgment, and because, when unlawfully received from them, they do not confer the Holy Spirit. They are therefore called void and untrue because they do not accomplish what they promise and ought to accomplish; and they are called condemnable so that their being given and received from heretics may not be approved but forbidden.

For they are not polluted in themselves, although they are said to be polluted by heretics. Hence Gregory calls Arius’s consecration an “execration,” and Innocent calls the ordination of Bonosus a “condemnation,” not as regards what these things are in themselves, but because of what they effect for those who give or receive them wickedly. Hence Jerome also, in Hosea, calls their sacrifice “bread of mourning.” Showing that he says this not of the sacrifice in itself but of its effect, he adds:

> “Whoever eats of it shall be defiled, because they take judgment upon themselves.”

## CHAPTER LV. That some sacraments are of necessity and others of dignity.

It should also be noted that some sacraments are sacraments of necessity and others of dignity. Since necessity has no law but itself makes a law for itself, those sacraments which are necessary for salvation are allowed to be valid when accompanied by penance. But those sacraments which pertain to dignity, unless they are administered worthily—so that they proceed worthily from worthy persons to worthy persons—cease to be sacraments of dignity: not because the truth of the sacrament is diminished, but because the office of administering it ceases, whether through place, time, or promotion.

## CHAPTER LVI. That one who is unlawfully ordained is to be condemned in respect of place, time, or promotion.

[Col. 0957A]

In respect of place, as Leo says:

> “If any have been ordained by pseudo-bishops, such an ordination may be considered valid, provided that they remain in those same places.”

Otherwise such an ordination is to be regarded as void. Behold: someone ordained by a pseudo-bishop, if he changes the place of his ordination, will have a void—that is, non-ministering—ordination.

In respect of time, Innocent says of those ordained by Bonosus:

> “What was established from the necessity of the time ought, when the necessity has ceased, likewise to cease, together with that which it compelled; for one thing is lawful order, another is usurpation.”

Therefore, one ordained at another time by someone like Bonosus will cease from the administration which was permitted because of the necessity of that time.

Likewise in respect of promotion, as Leo says:

> “If anyone has defiled himself by the contagion of heretical communion, let him count it a great benefit if, all hope of promotion having been removed, he remains in the rank in which he is found.”

Behold: if a cleric communicates with heretics either by ordination or by any sacrament, he ceases from promotion and scarcely remains even in his own rank. For this sacrament is not like the others. The others are either given to wash away sins, as baptism or penance; or, because of sins, denied not forever but for a time, as the Eucharist—which nevertheless is granted at the point of death to a penitent even for heinous sins. This one alone is forbidden not only because of guilt but because of disgrace, because its prerogative of outward or inward purity and perfection has been diminished; thus it is denied to bigamists, to husbands of widows, to the illiterate, or to those impaired in any part of the body. To which bigamist, illiterate person, or bodily impaired person is baptism or the Eucharist denied?

## CHAPTER LVII. That such a bishop is permitted to administer the other sacraments, although he is forbidden to make ordinations.

Yet such a bishop may administer the other sacraments, although he is incapable of conferring this one alone. For Leo says (Epistle 87, no. 1):

> “If any bishops have consecrated such a priest as it was not lawful for him to be, even if somehow they escape loss of their own honor, they shall thereafter have no right of ordination; nor shall they ever take part in that sacrament which they conferred upon an unworthy person.”

Behold: although they escape danger to their rank, so that they are permitted to administer the other sacraments priestly, they are removed from this one alone—not only for heresy or any greater fault, but for negligence alone.

## CHAPTER LVIII. That he who surpasses others in dignity ought to surpass them in holiness.

In all these matters it should be carefully noted that the sacrament of priestly promotion must be given or received more carefully and worthily than all others; because, unless it has been conferred rightly, it ceases to be valid in the respect in which it has not been perfectly accomplished.

For the other sacraments are given to each person for that person’s own sake; and for each person they are such as they are received with the heart or conscience. This sacrament alone is given not only for one’s own sake but for others; and therefore it is necessary that they receive it, as regards themselves, with a true heart and clean conscience, and, as regards others, not only without every fault but also without every disgrace, because of scandal to the brethren. It is given for their benefit, not only that they themselves may be helped, but that the priesthood may be beneficial.

Hence Jerome, on Micah:

> “Those who ordain any persons out of personal favoritism, and expose their lives as a scandal to the people, are guilty of the faithlessness of those who are scandalized.”

Indeed, those chosen to preside over others ought, just as they are set above them in dignity, to surpass them in holiness. Otherwise, why are they preferred to others when no grace of merits distinguishes them from others? Hence Symmachus, to Lawrence, bishop of Milan:

> “He who is superior in honor is to be compared with the basest man unless he excels in knowledge.”

## CHAPTER LIX. That Pope Anastasius was condemned, together with his decree, by which he attempted contrary to the authority of the saints to absolve those ordained by the condemned Acacius.

Peter Damian nevertheless adds, in excuse or defense of those ordained by Simoniacs, the case of Acacius, the heretical bishop of Constantinople, and those ordained by him. His chief ground is that Pope Anastasius, writing to Emperor Anastasius, approved the ordination of that heretic as so valid that he asserted the guilty person had harmed in no respect even those whom Acacius had baptized or ordained after his own condemnation.

But Gelasius proves that he did this unlawfully and uncanonically . . . and contrary to the decrees of his predecessors and successors: Felix and Gelasius, who excommunicated Acacius before Anastasius, and Hormisdas, who, third after Anastasius, later condemned the same Acacius. Therefore the same Anastasius is recorded in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* to have been rejected by the Roman Church and struck by God, as follows:

> “Anastasius II was a Roman by nation; he lived in the time of King Theodoric. At the same time many clerics and presbyters withdrew themselves from his communion, because, without a council of bishops, presbyters, and clerics of the whole Catholic Church, he had communicated with the deacon of Thessalonica named Fautinus, who had communicated with Acacius; and because he secretly wished to restore Acacius, but could not. He was struck by a divine nod.”

## CHAPTER LX. The decree by which Pope Felix condemns Acacius.

[Col. 0958D]

And so that it may be evident that in this decree Anastasius was opposed to his predecessors and successors, Felix III says, chapter 82 (Epistle 6):

> “Felix, bishop of the city of Rome, to Acacius. You are found liable for many transgressions and repeatedly engaged in contempt of the venerable Council of Nicaea. You have rashly claimed for yourself the rights of other provinces. You thought that heretics, usurpers, those ordained by heretics, and those whom you yourself had condemned and asked the Apostolic See to condemn, should not only be received into your communion; you even caused them to preside over other churches—something that could not have been done even in the case of Catholics—and increased them in honors which they did not deserve. Therefore have willingly your portion with those whom you embrace. By this present sentence, which we have sent to you through the defender of your Church, recognize that you are separated from priestly honor and Catholic communion, and likewise from the number of the faithful; recognize that the name and office of priestly ministry have been taken from you, condemned through us by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and apostolic authority, and that you are no longer to be released from the bonds of anathema.”

## CHAPTER LXI. Likewise Gelasius condemns him.

> “After Acacius had become alien to communion, we could not fail to cut him off from Catholic and Apostolic fellowship, lest, if we delayed even briefly because of him, we too might seem to have contracted the contagion of the impious.”

## CHAPTER LXII. Likewise Hormisdas.

Likewise, concerning Hormisdas, the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* states [Col. 0959B]:

> “This Pope Hormisdas went to King Theodoric at Ravenna and, with his counsel, sent an authoritative document to Justin; with the bond of a written undertaking and the text of a document, he restored [them] to the unity of the Apostolic See by condemning Peter and Acacius and every heresy.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. That Anastasius’s decree was contrary to Innocent’s decree.

Accordingly, even that decree of Anastasius, by which he attempted canonically to restore Acacius, is found condemned in writing. For Gelasius says in his *Tome*:

> “Things proved contrary to the privileges of the universal Church cannot stand for any reason.”

Likewise Gregory, among other things, says to Anastasius of Antioch:

> “How can those chapters be received whose authors are condemned?”

And Alexander likewise says:

> “It is written: ‘Do not transgress the boundaries of the ancients which your fathers set.’ He unquestionably transgresses the boundaries who sets aside and confounds the ordinances of the Fathers.”

How could Anastasius have declared the ordination of Acacius, a condemned heretic, canonically valid, when on the contrary Innocent calls those ordained by Bonosus, a condemned heretic, guilty of usurped dignity? Innocent asserts that they received nothing from him when they permitted or desired to be ordained by him, and allows no appearance of excuse except for those compelled and immediately withdrawing from him. Herein it is clear that to give any assent to the sacraments of heretics is a great crime.

## CHAPTER LXIV. That Acacius was condemned.

[Col. 0959D]

To make clear how Acacius was condemned, let us bring the matter forward. Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, the imperial city, had at first most vigorously pursued schismatics or heretics with the authority of the Roman See and caused them to be condemned. At length, however, whether through error or presumption, he dared to prejudice the privilege of the Apostolic See. He believed that the see of Constantinople was universal and first in the Church just as it was in the Empire. To such an extent did this go that he absolved Peter of Alexandria and the other pseudo-bishops—not by apostolic authority but by royal and his own authority—although they had been tyrannically imposed over certain bishops not condemned or expelled, and had therefore been excommunicated by the Roman See; and he communicated indiscriminately in their sacraments.

When he had confessed in his letters to the Roman pontiff that he had done this, he would not permit a universal synod to be summoned or himself to be accused in person. Instead, though absent, he was condemned by anathema through letters, as though present and confessing in his own voice.

Therefore, because Acacius was condemned in absentia by Felix solely on the confession in his letters, in which he declared that he had communicated with heretics, a very great disagreement arose among people of differing opinions. Some said that the emperor had absolved Peter and the other pseudo-bishops by royal power, and that Acacius had merely assented. Others said that Acacius had acted, and could act, by the privilege of his own see. Others said that he had truly sinned. Others said that, even if he had truly sinned, he was not justly condemned by the Roman See: because he had not been convicted, had not confessed in his own voice—though he confessed in letters—had not been present, since no one ought to be judged while absent, and had not been condemned in the proper judicial order in a universal council, but by the Roman See alone.

Accordingly, amid so many doubts, and under pressure from the royal power that favored him, he ought to have been tolerated for the sake of ecclesiastical peace; especially since some thought that, for so many and such great reasons, he ought lawfully to be absolved. Certain authority concerning all these matters follows.

## CHAPTER LXV. That although before Christ’s coming persons in the Church were kings and priests, yet after the coming of the same King and Priest the kingdom was separated from the priesthood.

As to the assertion that the emperor had absolved the pseudo-bishops and Acacius had assented, or that Acacius had acted on his own authority, Gelasius testifies against both claims as follows. He says in his *Tome* (Treatise 1, *On the Bond of Anathema*):

> “Before the coming of Christ it was so, that certain persons, still established only figuratively in carnal acts, were both kings and priests. But when the reality came—the same person being King and Pontiff—thereafter neither did the emperor assume the pontifical name for himself nor did the pontiff usurp royal exaltation. Yet the members of that true King and Pontiff, through participation in his magnificent nature, are said to have received both in sacred regeneration, so that they may be at once a royal race and a priestly people. For Christ, mindful of what suited the salvation of his own, so distinguished the offices of the two powers by their dignities that Christian emperors might use pontifical dispositions for eternal life, and pontiffs imperial dispositions for the course of temporal affairs. Thus spiritual action would remain separate from carnal incursions; one serving God would not entangle himself in secular affairs, nor in turn would one engrossed in secular affairs preside over divine matters. In this way the moderation of both might be preserved and neither power exalted itself.”

By all this it is sufficiently clearly shown that a pontiff can neither be bound nor loosed at all by secular power. It is thereby more clearly proved that Peter of Alexandria could in no way be absolved by imperial sentence alone. If one asks whether the associated assent of pontiffs preceded or followed: if it followed, it was flattery rather than lawful sanction.

## CHAPTER LXVI. That no one ought to absolve except the same person who binds, unless perhaps by consent.

(Treatise 1, *On the Bond of Anathema*.)

> “If it preceded, let it be shown by whom and in what manner the proceeding was conducted; whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church; whether it proceeded from paternal tradition; whether it was celebrated by a synodal assembly; whether it was regularly referred to the First See, to whose judgment belonged the sentence by which Peter was bound; whether the same authority that bound him absolved him; or whether, without the authority that had bound him loosing him—or even knowing of it—he could be absolved. If these things were not done, by what custom or rite is Peter of Alexandria alleged to have been absolved, when he could in no way be absolved either lawfully by pontiffs or by secular power apart from the path of the Church?”

## CHAPTER LXVII. That an inferior cannot absolve a superior.

But perhaps it is said (ibid.):

> “The emperor did not absolve him, but requested that he be absolved by the pontiffs.”

So much the more ought it to have been explained to the emperor requesting this from the pontiffs that, if he wished him to be lawfully absolved, absolution ought lawfully to proceed according to the ecclesiastical order; and especially because the case concerned the bishop of the second see, he could rightfully be absolved not by any inferior or arbitrary see, but by the First See. For an inferior cannot absolve a superior; the superior alone absolves.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. That persons guilty of prevarication do not absolve an accused person by a prevaricating absolution.

Thus Peter’s absolution is not established from either source (ibid.):

> “For persons who are themselves guilty could not absolve a guilty man by a prevaricating absolution.”

## CHAPTER LXIX. That secular power ought not to judge concerning divine matters.

Likewise Gelasius, to Euphemius of Constantinople (Epistle 4) [Note: [Col. 0961D] This passage is not found in Gelasius’s letter to Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, but in the letter [Col. 0962D], or memorandum, to Faustus, holding the office of envoy at Constantinople.]: 

> “But they say: ‘The emperor did this.’ In what canons was this itself commanded? Why did Acacius consent to so perverse a course? By what canons, by what rules, was Calendion expelled, or the Catholic priests of different cities who, by the tradition of the elders, call the Apostolic See to judgment? The emperor ought to learn from pontiffs—and especially from the vicar of blessed Peter—what divine things are; he ought not himself also to judge them. A Christian, indeed, does not presume this for himself unless perhaps he is persecuting religion.”

## CHAPTER LXX. That although the two chief powers are kingdom and priesthood, nevertheless, just as priests are subject to kings in temporal affairs, so kings ought still more to be subject to priests in divine matters.

Likewise the same writer, to Emperor Anastasius (Epistle 8):

> “There are two powers, most august Emperor, by which this world is chiefly ruled: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Of these the burden of priests is so much weightier because they will render an account in the divine judgment even for kings themselves. Do not, dearest son, though you preside over humankind in the dignity of kings, fail devoutly to submit your neck to the bishops of souls and to seek from them the means of your salvation. In receiving the heavenly sacraments and arranging them as is fitting, you know that by the order of religion you ought to be subject rather than to preside. Therefore in these matters you depend upon their judgment; you should not wish them to be reduced to your will. But with regard to the order that pertains to public discipline, recognizing that empire has been entrusted to you by divine disposition, the bishops of religion themselves obey your laws, lest in worldly matters they seem to oppose the heavenly decree. With what voice and effect ought you to obey those to whom, because of the dignity of their rank, venerable mysteries have been entrusted?”

## CHAPTER LXXI. That the Apostolic See is set above all priests and churches.

[Col. 0962B]

(Ibid.)

> “If it is fitting that one faithfully submit one’s neck to all priests generally, how much more ought assent to be given to the bishop of that See whom the highest Divinity willed to surpass all priests, and whose primacy the succeeding piety of the universal Church has continually celebrated? There your Piety recognizes that no one whatsoever can be elevated by any merely human council above the privilege or confession of him whom the true voice of Christ set above all, whom the venerable Church has always confessed and devoutly holds as primate. Things established by divine judgment cannot be assailed by human presumption.”

The same writer says:

> “I beg you, let certain persons in your time cease rashly to seek, through the occasion of ecclesiastical disturbance, things which are not lawful; lest they fail altogether to obtain what they wickedly seek and fail to retain their proper measure before God and men.”

And a little later (ibid.):

> “The authority of the Apostolic See—that it has been set above the whole Christian Church in every age—is established both by the sequence of the canons of the Fathers and by manifold reasoning.”

## CHAPTER LXXII. That the power of the imperial city cannot alter the prerogative of ecclesiastical dignity.

Likewise the same writer, to all the bishops of Dardania (Epistle 13):

> “As for Acacius being called bishop of the imperial city: one thing is the power of a secular kingdom, another the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities. Just as even a small city does not diminish the prerogative of royal power, so the imperial presence does not alter the measure of religious ordering.”

## CHAPTER LXXIII. That a king must be publicly rebuked by priests if he sins.

(Ibid.)

> “Likewise, it was fitting for a priest to advise the Christian ruler to allow the churches to be guarded by the Church.”

Likewise:

> “Nathan the prophet openly and publicly rebuked King David to his face for his committed error, and afterwards absolved him upon his confession. But Acacius showed that he both could have given such counsel and did not wish to do so; indeed, he disclosed that he had favored the course, so that even the emperor did not conceal that he had done everything on Acacius’s advice.”

In this Gelasius sufficiently shows that neither the king by his own power nor Acacius by the authority of his see could have absolved him.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. That every heretic is to be rebuked according to the rule governing that heresy itself.

As for the assertion that, even if Acacius had sinned, he was nevertheless not justly condemned by the Roman See because he had not been convicted or confessed in his own voice, although he confessed by letters; because he had not been present; because he had not been condemned in a general council but by the Roman See alone: Gelasius likewise refutes this as follows. He says to Euphemius (Epistle 4):

> “I wonder whether the man who says that Acacius could not be condemned by one person fails to perceive his ignorance. Does he not see that Acacius was condemned according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, in which it is clear that the authors of this error were condemned by the numerous judgment of priests? Manifest reason shows that this has both been done and is done in every heresy from the beginning of the Christian religion. My predecessor was an executor of an old institution, not an author of a new constitution. This is lawful not only for the apostolic bishop but for every pontiff: namely, to separate from Catholic communion any persons, or any place, according to the rule of the heresy itself already condemned. Thus, because new opinions had arisen, he joined himself by his communion to another’s crime. Thus it was necessary that he should fall back, by the just balance, into the synodal sentence which the author of the error had incurred.”

## CHAPTER LXXV. That the Apostolic See ought to be appealed to by all churches; but it ought neither to appeal nor to be judged by any church.

[Col. 0963C]

Likewise (ibid.): “These are the canons which ordained that appeals from the whole Church should be referred to the examination of this See; but that from it there should absolutely nowhere be an appeal. They decreed that through this See judgment should be rendered concerning the whole Church, but that it should itself be subject to no one’s judgment; nor did they ever command that judgment be passed upon its judgment, nor that its sentence be annulled; rather, they commanded that its decrees be followed.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI. That heretics are to be deposed by the authority of the Apostolic See alone

Likewise (ibid.): “For this very reason Timothy and the others—not one, but certainly several, bearing the title of priest—were deposed by the authority of the Apostolic See alone.”

## CHAPTER LXXVII. That a heretic condemns himself by his own judgment

(Ibid.) “It is not lawful for us to enter into controversy with persons outside communion, since divine Scripture has already decided the matter: ‘Avoid a heretical man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man sins, being condemned by his own judgment’ [Tit. 3:10]. Thus they may know that the heretic is condemned not only by another but also by himself; nor should a contest be entered into with those who do not correct themselves, just as conflict with the adherents of other heresies must be refused.”

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. That fault cannot be forgiven without correction

[Col. 0964A]

Likewise (ibid.): “A fault of the past can be forgiven, provided correction undoubtedly follows. For if perversity is feigned to remain thereafter, it is not the kindness of one forgiving, but a renewal [assent] of one consenting. Nor is it surprising that these men presume to blaspheme the See of blessed Peter, when they either harbour such monstrosities in their hearts or defend them with their mouths.”

## CHAPTER LXXIX. That the judgment upon each heresy is not to be reconsidered, but action is to be taken without any further debate according to the tenor of the ancient determination

Likewise Gelasius, to all the bishops of Dardania, chapter 32 (Epistle 13): “Our Catholic fathers and learned pontiffs wished that, in every heresy arising at any time, whatever they had decreed once a council had been held, for Catholic faith and truth in accordance with the course of the Scriptures, should thereafter remain unshaken; nor did they permit, by any presumption, that matters already settled should be reconsidered in the same case. For if it were lawful for anyone to reopen decisions healthfully made, no ordinance of the Church could remain firm against any individual errors. For what would happen if, after controversies had been resumed, the faithless were continually permitted to devise counsels? Whenever any truth has been made manifest, there is nevertheless never lacking something that destructive falsehood may put forward, even though it fails in authority or reason, yet does not yield in mere obstinacy.

[Col. 0964B]

“A council condemned Sabellius; it was not necessary that his followers should afterwards be condemned anew. Rather, in accordance with the tenor of the ancient determination, the universal Church judged that all who were participants either in that perversity or in its communion were to be rejected.”

Likewise: “When the First See had learned by certain evidence that Acacius had departed from the truth—though it knew that he had often acted in carrying out its policy against heretics—it did not cease for nearly three years to admonish him through letters.”

The same author: “The error which has once been condemned together with its author bears within every person made a participant in its wicked communion both its own curse and its penalty. In this way Timothy and Peter are shown to have been condemned, not by a council convened anew, but solely by the authority of the Apostolic See,

[Col. 0964C]

with Acacius himself also requesting or executing it.”

## CHAPTER LXXX. That, without any debate in a synod, the Apostolic See can both condemn and restore those whom it ought, inasmuch as it may judge concerning all, while none may judge concerning it

(Ibid.) “The whole Church throughout the world knows that the Apostolic See possesses the right of releasing, since it is lawful for it to judge concerning all, while no one is permitted to judge concerning its judgment. For appeals from every part of the world are to be made to it; but it ought itself to appeal nowhere. Nor do we omit this: that the Apostolic See has had authority, without any preceding synod, both to release those whom an unjust synod had condemned and to condemn,

[Col. 0965A]

when no synod existed, those whom it ought.”

## CHAPTER LXXXI. That those are heretics who are set over living Catholic priests in any place, or who communicate with persons so set over them

It should be observed that he calls Peter and the others heretics for this reason only: because they were unjustly placed over bishops who were still living; and Acacius also, because he consented to them or communicated with them. Thus Gelasius again (Epistle 13): “Acacius proved a transgressor in regard to all those whom he caused to be set over the Catholic pontiffs after these had been expelled, like a tyrant, in the several churches; or with persons set over them in this way he mingled himself in a perverse communion. For on this very account they ought, according to the canons, to have been removed from ecclesiastical communion,

[Col. 0965B]

because they allowed themselves to be appointed successors while priests were still alive.”

Likewise: “What Christian does not see that, once Catholic pontiffs have been driven from their own sees, none but heretics could have been introduced? Acacius was either the instigator of installing all of them, or joined in communion with them after they had been installed.”

## CHAPTER LXXXII. That one who has confessed his crime both in writing and orally ought no longer to be heard

Likewise (ibid.): “Every person is summoned to judgment for one of two purposes: either to confess the accusations, or to be convicted by them.”

Likewise: “After his confession had been produced in the tenor of his letters, why was Acacius to be summoned to judgment? In it he confessed that he had associated himself in communion with Peter, whom he had requested should be condemned by command of the Apostolic See. Nor, once he had become a participant in an external communion, could he any longer be believed in defense either of himself, or of those men, or of Peter—he whom he had previously joined in an accursed fellowship, entering into communion with him before he had been lawfully examined and cleared. Since he had joined himself to one still accused, why had he no longer confidence to speak for that same person?”

[Col. 0965C]

Likewise: “Does Acacius now again complain that he was not refuted by a special synod, when he himself disclosed his own crime in his letters and, having confessed voluntarily, ought no longer to have been heard?”

From all these answers of Gelasius it is clear that there was great confusion or disagreement concerning the condemnation of Peter of Alexandria or Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, which, as was said above, was regarded by many in many ways as unjust.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. That the sacraments of every evil priest, heretic, or condemned person are true

[Col. 0965D]

How the sacraments of any evil priest, heretic, or condemned person can be true, though not ratified, Augustine testifies in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*: “Even if someone is removed from office because of some fault, he will not lose the sacrament of the Lord once conferred, although he remains subject to judgment.”

The same, against Parmenianus, concerning even condemned heretics (ibid., Book II, chapter 13): “What some say—that one who departs from the Church does not lose the baptism he has received, but does lose the right to confer what he has received—is plainly said in vain and without reason in many respects. First, no reason is shown why someone who cannot lose baptism itself can lose the right of conferring it;

[Col. 0966A]

for both are sacraments, and are given to a human being by a certain consecration: the one when he is baptized, the other when he is ordained. Therefore a Catholic may not repeat the former.

“For if persons coming from that party, even their superiors, have been received for the good of peace once the error of schism was corrected, and if it seemed advisable that they should exercise the same offices which they had exercised before, they were not ordained again. Rather, just as baptism remained intact in them, so did ordination: for the defect was in the separation, corrected by the peace of unity, not in the sacraments, which are themselves what they are wherever they are.

“And when it seems beneficial to the Church that their superiors, coming into Catholic fellowship, should not administer their offices there, the sacraments of ordination themselves are nevertheless not taken away from them, but remain

[Col. 0966B]

upon them. Therefore hands are not laid upon them, lest an injury be done not to a human being but to the sacrament itself.

“Now, just as in baptism there is that which can be conferred by all persons, so in ordination there is the right of conferring it. Both may be possessed to one’s destruction so long as persons lack the charity of unity. Yet it is one thing not to possess something, another to possess it destructively, and another to possess it beneficially. Whatever is not possessed must be given to one who needs it to be given. But where something is possessed destructively, correction must be undertaken so that it may be possessed beneficially.

“Even if a layperson, compelled by necessity, has given something to one who is perishing—something which he learned, when he received it, had to be given—I do not know whether anyone would say that it ought piously to be repeated. For when no necessity compels, it is an usurpation of another’s office. But if necessity presses, it is either no sin or a venial one. Yet even if it is usurped without any necessity, and what has been conferred is given by anyone to anyone else, it cannot be said not to have been given, although it may rightly be said to have been given unlawfully.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. That one who unlawfully confers or receives sacraments must be punished unless he repents

Illicit usurpation is therefore corrected by the disposition of one who remembers and repents. (Augustine, ibid.) “But if he does not correct it, what has been conferred will remain for the punishment of the usurper—whether the one who conferred it unlawfully or the one who received it unlawfully—yet it will not be regarded as not conferred. For if they should at some time secretly or irregularly strike and stamp gold or silver, not in the public mints, when this has been discovered, would not the royal stamp, once recognized, be compelled into the royal treasuries after those persons had either been punished or released by pardon?”

And shortly afterwards: “If perhaps a non-serving soldier, in fear, had recoiled from the military mark upon his body and fled to the emperor’s clemency, and, pardon having been obtained, had begun again to serve as a soldier, would that mark be repeated after the man had been freed and corrected, rather than recognized and approved? Or do Christian sacraments perhaps possess less than this bodily mark, when we see that not even apostates lack baptism? Baptism is certainly not restored to them when they return through repentance, and is therefore judged incapable of being lost.”

[Col. 0966D]

From these words of blessed Augustine and the other saints it is evident that Christ’s sacraments remain among all apostates, heretics, and condemned persons: true and holy in themselves; but unless repentance or pardon comes to their aid, they result in the condemnation of the usurper, whether the possessor, the giver, or the receiver. What advantage, then, is there in their being true and holy, if they destroy wicked usurpers just as much as if they were evil and harmful? Crassus thirsted for gold and perished through gold just as Nero through poison.

Likewise: Gold is just as real in a thief’s chest as in a king’s treasury; but it is possessed lawfully by the king, given unlawfully by the thief, and received unlawfully. Therefore both the thief himself and one sharing in the theft, unless perhaps he has cleared himself in conscience of the theft, as Gelasius also attests to Emperor Anastasius, shall each deservedly and justly be condemned.

Thus it is truly dangerous to communicate with heretics by approval,

[Col. 0967A]

consent, or even merely knowingly; for although this has sometimes, as is clear above, been permitted at the discretion of judgment or piety, it is nevertheless clearly condemnable according to the just and true judgment of God.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. That avarice alone commends simony

Since heresies together with those who communicate with them are condemned, they have therefore been utterly rooted out by the holy Church—with the sole exception of simony, which avarice alone commends amid inextricable misery. The other heresies which were rending the Church by their irrevocable pronouncements have been put to sleep; this one alone, powerful through countless sums of money, incessantly produces scandal in the Church. The others seemed to derive authority for themselves

[Col. 0967C]

from prophets and evangelists, and yet fell; this one is condemned by God himself, the prophets, and all the saints, and yet, like the head of the Hydra of Lerna, grows from its very cutting-off.

Thus, as is clear, neither arguments nor riches overthrow the Christian faith. For what heresies, eloquent but poor, cannot compel people to do, this one, mute but rich, can entice them to do. Royal estates and coinage, once they have passed as an endowment to the Church, are not sold; but royal words, once they have passed into the Church’s jurisdiction, are to be sold. The whole bishopric is bestowed freely by the prince in a body, and is the ban or jurisdiction of a deanery to be sold by a bishop?

Therefore God commanded in vain, “Freely you have received, freely give” [Matt. 10:8], if what is freely received as a gift is to be sold in its administration, whereas the Lord requires from a priest not monetary gains but the profit of souls. Hence Jerome also complains in his commentary on Micah, when it is said to the apostles, “Do not possess gold or silver or copper in your belts” [cf. Matt. 10:9], and when even money earned by labour is shaken from the hands of a holy man: they hawk the Lord’s words and buy and sell doves in the temple.

[Col. 0968A]

For things once offered to God are truly not to be sold. For how should one sell what was not sold by the one to whom it belonged? Christ, who was poor, redeemed his Church with his own blood, and established not rich people but poor ones; he chose not the things that are of the world, but the things that are not; he wished his successors to be enemies, not friends, of the world. From his Church he removed not only moneylending and every commercial dealing for profit, but uprooted also the hindrances of desire, pleasure, and anxious care; he enjoined contempt for earthly things and love for heavenly things alone.

Since, then, from the succession originating with him, the Church neither possessed nor ought to possess anything which it had not obtained from the world by plunder—except perhaps through the free offering of some faithful persons, and only for the support of itself and its own—it is sufficiently absurd that those who are commanded to leave their own possessions should sell those of others. Worse still, those forbidden even earthly profit from earthly goods dare to trade in heavenly things, so that not even the alms of deceased believers, nor even the grace of divine ministration, can be safe from the avarice of their venality.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. That no one may remain silent concerning the condemnation of simony

[Col. 0968C]

I may indeed seem to have spoken harshly about simoniacs; but Almighty God knows, beneficially and truly, that I have not done so presumptuously from my own opinion, but on the authority of the Lord himself and of all the saints, who, in word and example, while striving to love or possess nothing in this world, exposed as utterly base commerce the exchange of heavenly things for earthly ones.

I did not presume to remain silent, nor indeed should anyone remain silent. For, as Ambrose says, you may be silent in a monetary lawsuit; but in God’s cause, where there is danger in communion, even concealment is no light sin. And Gregory says: “Whoever is not violently inflamed against simony will have a share with him from whom this crime originated.”

[Col. 0968D]

[Col. 0967]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK

(D. B. Pez, Preface to vol. IV of the *Anecdota*, p. X.)

The most distinguished Father Dom Edmund Martène very recently published the *Book on Mercy and Justice* by Alger, a Cluniac monk formerly scholastic of Liège, in volume V of the *New Treasury of Anecdota*, beginning at column 1019. In its preface Dom Nicholas of Liège, writing about all Alger’s little works, records a few things about Alger’s life and writings—few indeed, but weighty and trustworthy.

“Alger of Liège,” Nicholas says, “a contemporary writer, devoted himself wholly from earliest childhood to literary study under the most distinguished men, by whose learning and upright morals the Church of Liège then shone and France was adorned. He flourished nobly, so that no rule of the Christian faith seemed unknown to him and no liberal art foreign to him. And, to preserve something of his character in memory: at first he served God in the church of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, situated in the suburb of Liège, as a cleric by profession and habit, a deacon by rank, and scholasticus by office. Later he was honourably transferred by Bishop Obert to the greater church of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, and was gratefully received by its elders. Until the death of Bishop Frederick of happy memory, for nearly twenty years, he wrote many distinguished letters concerning ecclesiastical affairs to various persons and churches; these are preserved and read with the greatest zeal by very many,” etc.

Perhaps not the least of these letters was the little work which we have entitled the *Booklet or Treatise on Free Will*, following the testimony of an old manuscript belonging to the distinguished and very friendly Zacharias von Uffenbach, and of Johannes Trithemius. In chapter 328 of his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Trithemius expressly lists among Alger’s works one book *On Grace and Free Will*, whose beginning is: “It must be known that free…”

Although the work as it now stands bears no form of a letter, it may nevertheless be that copyists, for the sake of brevity, cut off and omitted what according to custom is prefixed and appended to letters. This could easily be demonstrated by many examples. Moreover, it is remarkable how clearly and Catholicly Alger resolved, in this very brief work, the most serious and intricate questions concerning grace, predestination, and free will. One may confidently declare that more light may be sought in this single work on controversies of this kind than in several volumes even of recent scholastics. Let anyone who thinks we have praised it too highly merely run through the little writing.

[Col. 0969]

# THE BOOKLET ON FREE WILL OF BLESSED ALGER, CANON OF LIÈGE

(Edited by Dom Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, part II, col. 111, from the celebrated manuscript library of the distinguished Zacharias Conrad von Uffenbach.)

## CHAPTER ONE. The nature of Adam’s free will before and after the Fall

[Col. 0969A]

It must be known that the first man is said to have possessed free will before, by tasting the fruit, he became a slave of sin. But, although he possessed free will, we must consider what freedom belonged to his will.

The will was certainly free so long as it remained under its own power, so that, with no force compelling it either from God or from the devil, it did whatever good or evil it wished. Yet though it was free in this respect, because no dominion and no force could compel it to will or not will anything, it was nevertheless weak in itself, so that through its own weakness it could fall if it consented to the devil, who did not compel but persuaded. But it could in no way stand through its own strength, even if it wished, unless, trusting God’s counsel, it might by the help of that same God accomplish the good which it willed well.

[Col. 0969B]

Thus, although Adam possessed a free and self-determining will, he did not possess a self-derived ability, but one derived from another: so that there might be in humanity something which God could justly reward—namely, a free will serving God without compulsion—and something in God for which he might be glorified when he strengthened humanity by his own power.

Therefore, since Adam was free and weak, after he had trusted himself too greatly, he consented to the enemy through free will and fell through his own frailty. Had he trusted in the Lord alone, he certainly would never have fallen, with the Lord’s help.

[Col. 0969C]

But after the fall of the first father, when the whole world was enslaved to sin, the Lord came and restored us to our former condition, restoring the first man’s will to freedom from external force as before, but not from its own weakness,

[Col. 0970A]

so that no one may presume upon himself, but may always trust in God alone.

## CHAPTER II. Neither the predestination of the good to reward nor the foreknowledge of the evil to punishment harms free will

But free will appears contrary to this: that the Lord predestined eternal life from eternity for the saints, and likewise preordained the cause of eternal life, namely merit; whereas for the reprobate he ordained eternal death, but not the cause of eternal death, because God predestined no one’s sins. For it does not belong to God to determine how a sinner is to sin; nevertheless, knowing that he will sin, God ordains death for him as a true judge. [The copy: “would ordain.”]

If, then, he preordains and predestines life for the good and death

[Col. 0970B]

for the evil, he appears to impose force upon free will. For since his predestination cannot fail, it is necessary that the one whom he predestined for death should be evil, and the one whom he predestined for life should be good. And if it is necessary that this person be good and that one evil, free will perishes, being compelled by necessity.

But if the will is not free and is compelled by necessity, the person who sins, whether willing or unwilling, is not blameworthy; nor is the person who acts well, whether willing or unwilling, praiseworthy. Rather, praise and blame must be assigned to the one who compels. Why then is there punishment for the evil and glory for the righteous? What the righteous receive is therefore not a reward, but grace alone from God; nor is what the unjust suffer vengeance, but an injustice—far be it!

For God’s predestination compels us by no force toward good

[Col. 0970C]
