or evil. Rather, God, with whom there is “no change nor shadow of turning” [Jas. 1:17], held from eternity before his sight as present the things which would be future to us. He saw us, such as we would be, face to face as though present; and, such as we presented ourselves to him either through our own perversity or through righteousness, he judged us as though present.

For things that are past or future to us never pass from the sight of God, but are always present. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” [Matt. 24:35]. If words which pass away among us in a moment remain always with God, who can doubt that in God’s sight all things remain which are transient among us? Just as sight sees the whole circumference of a circle at once, while touch perceives it only bit by bit through feeling, so God sees all things at once, whereas we see some things only in parts and at different times.

[Col. 0971A]

If, therefore, we have always been in his sight and he has seen us as present—such as, through him, we would become in good, or such as, not through him but through ourselves, we would become in evil—then, seeing diverse merits, he did nothing inappropriate in also appointing diverse rewards for us. Our perversity presented itself from eternity as evil before God’s sight through its own wickedness; God destined it to death.

## CHAPTER III. God’s eternal vision, by which he has always held all our actions present, imposes no necessity upon them, but leaves them entirely free

What then? Did God compel us to appear evil to him from eternity? Far from it! Rather, we offered ourselves to him so that he might see us as evil. For example, if I see someone lying down, it is certainly necessary that the person whom I see lying down is lying down, or else it is false that I see him lying down. But does this necessity arise from the person lying down, or from the one seeing? Clearly, the one seeing does not impose necessity upon him to lie down; it arises from the person who placed himself so as to lie down.

[Col. 0971C]

Thus the Lord, for whom nothing is past or future, always saw us present to himself as evil, not so that this vision might impose the necessity of perversity, but because that perversity could not remain hidden from the foreknowledge of the Judge. Did Peter deny the Lord because the Lord said, “You will deny me three times” [Matt. 26:34]? Or did Judas betray him because the Lord said, “You will betray me”? Or did Lazarus die because the Lord said, “Lazarus sleeps” [John 11:11]?

[Col. 0971D]

Certainly, before he said this of them, Lazarus was already dead; Judas had already arranged the betrayal with the Jews; Peter alone, when he heard of the denial, swore that he would not deny him. Yet Peter was no more compelled by the Lord’s words to do what he did not wish than Judas was compelled to do what he wished. For it would have been impious that one who knows all things should not know what would happen to them.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether predestination can be obtained through our merits and prayers

Therefore, just as predestination to death does not compel the evil to perish, so predestination to life does not compel the good to be saved. But when the Lord predestines the good to life, he predestines them in such a way that his own predestination is obtained through our merits and prayers.

Did not the Lord say to Abraham, “In Isaac shall your seed be called” [Gen. 21:12]? Yet, although the Lord promised fruitfulness of offspring in Isaac, Isaac’s wife was barren. Isaac prayed, however, and God granted Rebecca conception. Therefore, if God promised him fruitfulness and gave barrenness, while Isaac prayed and obtained fruitfulness, what else does this mean except that prayer obtained predestination? From this it may be inferred that God promises us his goods in such a way that they are nevertheless acquired through our labour; and if we are willing to labour, he will cooperate with us in all the good that we do.

## CHAPTER V. Our will is now free in such a way that it can will evil from itself alone, but can will good only through grace

[Col. 0972C]

It must be observed, however, that though our will is, as stated, free from external violence, it is not therefore in itself absolutely free, so that, just as it has of itself simply the capacity to will evil, it also has of itself the capacity to will good without grace breathing upon it. For although we possess from ourselves the incapacity to see when we close our eyes, we do not simply possess from ourselves the capacity to see even when we open them, unless we are illuminated by some brightness. And just as brightness cannot fail to illuminate if the eyes are opened while it is present, so the grace of God cannot fail to breathe upon our good will when it is joined to it, since grace is set before all.

[Col. 0972D]

## HENRY OF SALTRY, ABOUT THE YEAR 1150

[Col. 0971]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 227.)

Henry of Saltry, an Irish monk, wrote about the year 1150 to Henry, abbot of Sartis, *On Saint Patrick’s Purgatory*—whether of the ancient Patrick or rather of Abbot Patrick about the year 850 is uncertain—or concerning the cave which, when any truly penitent person enters it and remains there for the space of one day and night, cleanses him of every sin by which he offended God throughout his whole life.

Thomas Messingham published not only the prologue but Henry’s whole treatise in the *Florilegium of the Island of Saints of Ireland*, Paris, 1624, quarto, pp. 89–109; accordingly Oudinus, vol. II, p. 1440, must be corrected. It is also extant in John Colgan’s *Trias Thaumaturga*, Louvain, 1645, folio. Compare also what is noted on Saint Patrick’s Purgatory in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. II for March 17, p. 587 ff.

The *Visions of Saint Oenus, the knight*, do not differ from Henry’s narrative of Saint Patrick’s Purgatory, though Carolus Vischius distinguishes them from it, p. 145 of his *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. See Messingham, p. 99 ff. Vischius and Pitseus, p. 207, make Henry a Cistercian; others, such as Bale, II.77, call him Benedictine. Indeed, the Cistercians themselves are a kind of Benedictines.

[Col. 0973]

# TREATISE ON THE PURGATORY OF SAINT PATRICK, APOSTLE OF THE IRISH

## PREFACE TO THE READER

(Thomas Messingham, *Florilegium Insulae Sanctorum, or Lives and Acts of the Saints of Ireland*, etc., Paris, 1624, quarto.)

John the Evangelist, that sublime eagle who raised himself above the whole constitution of visible and invisible creatures, the contemplator with fixed eyes of inward and eternal light, and the special herald of the divine generation, does not blush to conclude the streams of his most lofty Gospel, which he drank from the sacred fountain of the Lord’s breast, with this period: “There are also many other things which Jesus did; if they were written one by one, I suppose that not even the world itself could contain the books that would be written” [John 21:25]. Thus he showed that he had not written for favour because he was Christ’s friend.

For those who write to win someone’s favour are accustomed to omit nothing done by him that is worthy of mention; whereas John omitted very many things, more numerous than what he wrote and highly memorable. Or, what appears more probable, he did so lest anyone should suppose that Christ had performed no more miracles than those which he and the other Evangelists recorded, and should set the limit of faith there, believing nothing further that he might either read elsewhere or hear from another source to have been done by Christ.

By this single Achillean spear, or stone hurled from David’s sling, that proud Goliath and uncircumcised Philistine in heart, Luther, is struck down and put to flight with his camps of heterodox followers, since he rejects apostolic and other ecclesiastical traditions as human inventions and asserts that nothing is to be believed unless it is expressly contained in the written Word of God. If anything opposed to his most shameful pleasure or his cloaked liberty—such as the canonical Epistle of Saint James, and so forth—were contained there, he would assert that it was nothing but empty and straw-like, and with equal madness would see to its removal from the Bible.

Who, then, could reasonably wonder if some ordinary writer, far inferior to any Evangelist, in describing the life of so great a saint as our Saint Patrick—whose infancy, youth, mature age, and old age appear to be nothing but an unbroken outpouring of virtues, performance of mighty deeds, and accomplishment of miracles, to which death itself set no limit—either entirely fails to know some, indeed many, memorable deeds performed by such a saint, or omits them despite knowing them?

Since, therefore, it is absolutely certain, as will become manifest from what follows, that an extraordinary Purgatory was discovered in Ireland by Saint Patrick; and since it is likewise certain that Jocelin in his *Life* of Patrick either passes it over in complete silence or leaves it after the slightest mention, we do not therefore believe that the common domestic tradition and foreign testimony concerning this Purgatory are weakened, or that Jocelin should be called the author of an incomplete work. For we may sufficiently excuse him and fittingly apply to the servant of God Patrick the above-cited saying of John about the Lord, saying thus: “There are also many other things which Patrick did, which are not written in this book composed by Jocelin,” for the reasons mentioned above in the explanation of the Gospel text.

Further, not without strong probability, we maintain that Jocelin did not treat Saint Patrick’s Purgatory in the book of his *Life* because, deceived by the opinion of some persons, he thought that the discoverer of this Purgatory had been not Patrick the Apostle but another Patrick, distinct from him in both age and rank. You will see below that this view is refuted as false. And indeed, if we were not eager to investigate the truth, there would be no reason to argue so strenuously concerning the author of this Purgatory. Would it not be enough for us that it was discovered by someone, whoever he may finally have been, that our country enjoys such a singular privilege of God and that our people enjoy so salutary a benefit?

Therefore, friendly reader, do not wonder at the diversity of style in this treatise on Purgatory. Since we could find no one who had treated it exactly, but one had touched upon this point and another upon that, we judged it better to gather into one work what we found among different writers than to leave the work in some respect incomplete. But lest anyone be deprived of the reward of his labour, or of the merit due to his work, or lest the works of different writers be confused as the writings of one author rather than another, you shall recognize them in this way.

We have arranged for the first four letters of the alphabet to be placed in brackets. Thus, whatever you find written under the letter A, up to the next following letter, attribute to the Most Reverend Lord David Roth, Bishop of Ossory and Vice-Primate of all Ireland: a man most learned in every branch of knowledge, an eloquent rhetorician, subtle philosopher, profound theologian, highly celebrated historian, a most vigorous reprover of men, defender of ecclesiastical liberty, champion of his country’s privileges, a most devoted champion in Ireland’s calamities, and finally a most diligent promoter of peace and unity among ecclesiastics. For that reason he began in Ireland, in the year 1640, the congregation commonly called the Peaceful Congregation, which with great benefit to ecclesiastics spreads ever more widely each day throughout that kingdom. He left various monuments of his talent to posterity; we refrain, not without reason, from inserting their catalogue here, and hope shortly for greater works from him.

[Col. 0975]

Whatever is then written under the letter B, attribute to Henry of Saltry, an English monk of the Cistercian Order. He learned liberal learning and excellent precepts for right living from Florentianus, an Irish bishop, and Gilbert of Luda, abbot of Cistercian monks. Himself now instructed, he was accustomed to teach others that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. And because he saw that people are generally deterred from vices more by fear of punishment than by love of virtue, he used to impress upon the people that nothing defiled can enter the kingdom of heaven, and consequently that every sin has its own due punishment and that satisfaction for offenses must first be made according to divine justice, either in this age by doing good or in Purgatory by suffering punishments, before access to the everlasting refreshment of heavenly blessedness may lie open to anyone who has ever contracted the stain of sin.

Accordingly, he wrote to Henry, abbot of Sartis, one book on Saint Patrick’s Purgatory: one book *On the Punishments of Purgatory*. He flourished in the year of grace 1140.

Those finally found under the letter C were written by Matthew Paris, an English Benedictine monk, who, having been committed from his very youth to monastic discipline, refined the excellent natural ability granted him through every most commendable branch of learning and adorned it with every virtue: a very notable writer, no ordinary painter, an elegant poet, a keen dialectician, a sound theologian, and—what is chief among all—pure in integrity of character, distinguished by innocence of life, simple, candid. Pits has much more concerning him, which I omit for brevity’s sake, under the year 1259, when this same Matthew died.

Both this Matthew and the aforesaid Henry contain the history of Owen, the Irish knight; but the former more briefly, and, as we suppose, copied from Henry; the latter more fully.

Accordingly, we shall construct the complete history from both, supplying from one what is lacking in the other. Yet we shall report the whole in their own words; and, except where the additions are few, we shall mark in the margin, by a different letter, what we add from one to the other.

What is finally found under the letter D we have either added ourselves or gathered from others, as the completion of the Treatise required. Use all these things devoutly, reader, and pray God for us, that we may either never feel the burning of Purgatory’s fire or, if we do feel it, be delivered from it as swiftly as possible. Farewell.

## THE PROLOGUE OF HENRY OF SALTRY TO ST. PATRICK’S PURGATORY BEGINS

[Col. 0975A] To his most dearly beloved father in Christ, HENRY, abbot of Sartis, brother HENRY of Saltry, least of monks, offers his father continual welfare and, as a son, the duty of obedience.

You have commanded, venerable Father, that I should send you in writing what I have related that I heard concerning Purgatory in your presence. I undertake this all the more willingly because I am more urgently compelled to accomplish it by the command of your fatherhood. For although I desired that its benefit might reach many through me, your fatherhood is by no means unaware that I have never read anything from which I might make so great progress in the fear and love of God.

And since we read that blessed Pope Gregory said many things concerning what happens to souls stripped of their earthly bodies—so as both to terrify the minds of the negligent by sorrowful matters and to inflame the righteous in devotion by joyful ones [Col. 0975B]—I shall more confidently carry out your command for the advancement of the simple. For in many examples which he sets forth, he says that at the departure of souls there are present angels, whether good or evil, who, according to their deserts, either drag souls away to torments or lead them to rest.

He also acknowledges that souls still placed in bodies sometimes know beforehand, before their departure, much concerning what is to come upon them, whether through the inward testimony of conscience or through revelations made outwardly. He says likewise that souls carried away and afterward restored to their bodies relate certain visions and revelations made to them, whether concerning the torments of the wicked or the joys of the just. Yet in these accounts they relate nothing except what is bodily or like bodily things [Col. 0975C]: rivers, flames, bridges, ships, houses, groves, meadows, flowers, black and white people, and other things such as are commonly in this world either loved for delight or feared for torment. He also relates that souls, once released from their bodies [Col. 0976A], are dragged by the hands, led by the feet, suspended by the neck, scourged, hurled down, and suffer many such things, which in no way conflict with nature.

It is well known that many people have often asked how souls leave their bodies, whither they go, what they find, what they experience, and what they endure. Since these things are hidden from us, they are more to be feared than investigated. Yet this is held certain: an evil death does not follow a good life. And although merit remains until death and reward is rendered after death, there is nevertheless said to be a punishment after death called purgatorial, in which those who in this life have lived with certain faults, though righteous and predestined to eternal life, are tormented for a time in order to be purified.

Hence, just as bodily punishments are said to have been prepared by God, so bodily places in which those punishments occur are said to be assigned to the punishments themselves. It is nevertheless believed that the greatest torments, to which guilt presses souls downward, are in the lowest place; that the greatest joys, to which one ascends upward through righteousness, are in the highest; and that good and evil things are in the middle. This also seems to accord with the present account of St. Patrick’s Purgatory. This narrative likewise asserts that the lowest region beneath the earth, or within the hollow of the earth, is commonly believed to be, as it were, a prison and dungeon of darkness; and it shows that Paradise is in the East, in the land of Sur, where the souls of the faithful, delivered from purgatorial punishments, are said to remain pleasantly for a while.

What blessed Augustine and blessed Gregory say—that a spirit is tormented by the punishment [Col. 0976C] of corporeal fire—also seems to be affirmed by this narrative. But in purgatorial punishment, by which the elect are cleansed after their departure, it is certain that some are tormented more and some less according to their merits. Such matters cannot be determined by human beings [Col. 0977A], because they cannot be known by them. Yet certain signs resembling bodily things are related, for the manifestation of spiritual realities, by those whose souls leave their bodies and, at God’s command, return again to their bodies. Unless such things were seen by souls stripped of animate bodies in and through such things, they could in no way be made known, upon their return to bodies, to those living in bodies and knowing only bodily things. Thus in this narrative spiritual things are said to be seen by a bodily and mortal man as though in bodily form and appearance.

But who related it to me, and how he came to know it, I shall indicate at the end of the narrative.

The prologue ends.

## ST. PATRICK’S PURGATORY BEGINS

[Col. 0977]

## CHAPTER I. On the Name, Existence, and Location of Purgatory

[Col. 0977A]

[A] 1. This place is distinguished by various names among ecclesiastical writers. Besides being called Purgatory by its common name [Col. 0977B], it is also very often called St. Patrick’s Well and a cavern or cave. It is called Purgatory from its effect of cleansing and purifying souls; a well and cavern from its deep situation and subterranean passage, into which those to be purified are enclosed.

2. It has not yet happened to me to visit the place itself, although I greatly desired to do so. But either the dangers of the journey or the occupations by which I was continually detained prevented me. Therefore, concerning the site of Purgatory itself, the time of purification, the manner of purifying oneself or undertaking the pilgrimage itself, and the remarkable occurrences and examples of those entering it which are usually commemorated, I have received my information from the reports of others—such persons, however, that I had no reason to doubt their trustworthiness.

[Col. 0977C] 3. For I had inquired of various ecclesiastical and secular persons of proven faith and authority, antiquarians as well as others, who had visited the place; and some of those whom I consulted had completed that expiatory course more than once. I shall briefly set down here such things as, from their accounts compared with what is contained in written records, I found to be more certain or more probable.

4. Before all else, it must be observed that foreign writers mention two Purgatories in Ireland. One is that of St. Patrick, situated in the northern part of the kingdom; the other is that of St. Brendan, which Ralph asserts to be in the western parts of the same kingdom.

5. Next it must be recalled from the same [Col. 0977D] Ralph that he distinguishes two Patricks, separated from one another by a long interval in age as well as rank. One, the first, was an archbishop; the other, the second, an abbot. “The first Patrick,” he says, “is said to have performed, among other signs of his works, two deeds: first, that with his staff he expelled from the land every venomous creature; second, that no Irishman will await the coming of Antichrist. Yet the memorable matter which is read concerning his Purgatory is more ascribed to the second Patrick, the younger, who was not a bishop but an abbot. He flourished about the year of the Lord 850. The Martyrology mentions him, saying that, because he found the people rebellious, he withdrew from Ireland and ended his last day at the monastery of Glastonbury [Col. 0978A] on the very feast-day of St. Bartholomew.” So he writes.

6. That this Purgatory was discovered by Patrick, whether the first or the second—of which more suitably elsewhere—is the common opinion and tradition of the Irish, which they seem to have sucked in with their nurse’s milk; and their very popular tongue is almost a saving doctrine, as the great Doctor of the Church and teacher of morals, Augustine, once said in a similar case. Here we seek certain supports for that conviction and devout belief, which has so persuaded this whole Catholic people that, should you endeavor to press upon them a contrary opinion, you would be discredited and driven out by high and low alike, and by all, as an innovator and sower of novel opinions. By these supports may the Tantalus-like thirst of the curious be quenched and the intolerable impudence of heretics blunted.

7. The first support of the received tradition, then, is its own constant and harmonious acceptance from every age and throughout human memory among this entire nation [Col. 0978C]. For not without reason is that said which is borne on the lips of all, especially when it is established by the lips of devout, learned, prudent people, with no one opposing it.

8. The second is that domestic testimonies are supported by the attestations of foreigners: namely, Henry of Saltry and Matthew Paris in the vision of Owen the knight, to be described at length below; Dionysius the Carthusian, in *On the Four Last Things*, part three, article XIV; James of Janua, otherwise Genoa, a Dominican, in the Life of St. Patrick in the *Legend of the Saints*; Ralph Higden, the Cistercian, in the *Polychronicon*; Caesarius of Heisterbach in his *Dialogues*; Mombrizio, vol. II, *On the Lives of the Saints*; Marko Marulić [Col. 0978D], book III, chapter 4; the Sicilian Maurolycus in the *Martyrology*; and others.

[D] 9. To these it is pleasing to add John Camers, in chapter 35 of Solinus, who, guided by the conjecture of others, suspects that the poet Claudian, book X, *Against Rufinus*, adapted the following verses to this pit:

> There is a place where Gaul reveals its furthest shore,  
> stretched out before the waters of Ocean, where Ulysses,  
> it is said, after pouring blood, stirred the silent people.  
> There, amid the faint whistling of flying shades,  
> a mournful lament is heard; pale apparitions of the inhabitant,  
> and the forms of the departed are seen to wander.

If this comes near the truth, so that we grant the place to have existed before Patrick’s birth—as the history of the knight to be described below also not obscurely suggests, in these words [Col. 0979A]:

> “[C] Therefore, while Patrick, intent upon fasts, vigils, and prayers for the salvation of the people, was praying more earnestly to the Lord, the devout Son of God appeared to him, led him to a desert place, and showed him a round cavern [Note: [Col. 0979D] Therefore made earlier.] dark within, and said: ‘Whoever, truly repentant and steadfast in faith, enters this cavern and remains there for the space of one day and night shall be cleansed from all the sins by which he offended God throughout his entire life,’”

and so forth. Yet it was not adapted to a celebrated religious use before Patrick.

Therefore, if every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses, as Truth itself says in the Gospel (Matthew XVIII), who but a person of brazen face would dare to contradict the authority of the number three, tripled—especially of historians who are religious and of approved faith [Col. 0979B]?

[A] 10. A third proof is drawn from the ecclesiastical office itself and the unanimous agreement of ecclesiastics and of the saints of the Church who flourished there for many centuries. Whoever he might be who did not fear to despise the authority and mutual agreement of all these, sufficiently expressed in the ancient manuscript Breviaries and Antiphonaries of every province, I certainly would not excuse his rashness and audacity.

11. This tradition is found both in ancient parchments and in printed books handed down to us by the earliest infancy of typography. Thus it appears to have been the unanimous opinion of clergy and people alike, retained privately and publicly acknowledged in those duties and rites of divine and ecclesiastical worship which they observed with the greatest holiness and reverence [Col. 0979C]. Who would dare to object to a usage so accepted, so ancient, so approved, so celebrated in the speech and hearts of the faithful, unless one avid for novelty and a despiser alike of antiquity and piety?

[D] 12. But against all these supports some clever person will object that Giraldus Cambrensis, the most diligent investigator of Irish antiquity, describes with the utmost care every tiny and narrow corner of Ireland, yet nowhere makes mention of this Purgatory. And although, if you direct the reasoning to the exacting form of logical topics [Col. 0979D], this does not follow necessarily and dialectically, nevertheless, since Giraldus had proposed to bring into sight and light all notable places of Ireland out of obscurity, it seems scarcely probable that such a remarkable monument would have been passed over by him if at that time it had been either known or made famous by miracles.

13. Yet, so that nothing of controversy may remain in this matter, I assure the reader that St. Patrick’s Purgatory was known and widely publicized in the age of Gerald of Wales. Indeed, Gerald’s own writings not only suggest this but declare it. It is worthwhile to append his words. For in the second distinction of his *Topography of Ireland* he writes:

> “There is a place in the parts of Ulster containing an island divided in two. One part, having a church of approved religion, is remarkable and pleasant through the visitation of English people and incomparably illuminated by the visible frequenting of the saints of that place. The other part is exceedingly rough and dreadful, said to be assigned to demons alone; it is almost always exposed to visible throngs and processions of evil demons. This part contains nine pits, in any one of which, should anyone perhaps presume to spend the night—something never known to have been proved by rash persons—he is then seized by malignant spirits and tormented throughout the night as though by grievous punishments. He is unceasingly afflicted with such numerous, great, and ineffable torments of fire, water, and varied kinds [Col. 0980B] that when morning comes, scarcely, if at all, does any recognizable form survive; only remnants are found in the wretched body. These torments, they assert, if anyone has endured them once as an imposed penance, he shall thereafter not undergo infernal punishments unless he commits graver sins. This place is called Patrick’s Purgatory by the inhabitants. For when the holy man disputed with an unbelieving people concerning the infernal punishments of the reprobate and the true and everlasting life of the elect after death, in order that so great, unusual, and unexpected a novelty might be impressed more certainly on the uncultivated minds of unbelievers by the evidence of sight, he obtained on earth, through the effective urgency of his prayers, a great and marvelous knowledge of both matters, beneficial for a stiff-necked people.”

[Col. 0980C] Thus Gerald, who expresses both the place and its author sufficiently clearly. This is not the place to discuss the bitterness of style habitual to him, or his censure of the rashness of those who go to those penitential pits. His exceedingly harsh judgment is sufficiently and more than sufficiently refuted by the multitude and frequency of penitents who, from his age onward, customarily undertake those sacred observances every year with great fruit of devotion and a sense of compunction. They are therefore not to be condemned for rash presumptions.

14. But perhaps someone may still wonder that we maintain this Purgatory when Jocelin, who described the Life of St. Patrick from infancy to death with the greatest exactness, speaks not even one word anywhere [Col. 0980D] about it. Yet I think that anyone who has attentively read what we said above in the little preface to the Purgatory will cease to wonder. To this, for the reader’s enjoyment through variety, we have chosen to add the answer of our Stanihurst in book II of the *Life of St. Patrick*. He says:

> “The same Patrick, who was the apostle of Ireland, is called abbot by certain ancient writers. From this opinion, insufficiently understood and disseminated, I judge that those are led into error who ascribe that punitive cave to Patrick the abbot and deny it to the apostle.”

After proving by various testimonies that Patrick the apostle was also an abbot, he finally concludes as follows [Col. 0981A]:

> “Therefore, this title of abbot, bestowed upon our Patrick of Armagh by some ancient historians, led certain persons into the error of distinguishing Patrick the abbot from Patrick, apostle of the Irish, and of making the abbot the founder of this Purgatory of which we are treating. But this is otherwise, as has been sufficiently proved.”

We may therefore say, not implausibly, that Jocelin was among those whom the title “abbot” had led astray. These points having been established:

[A] 15. Thirdly, it should be noted that some think the cavern or well itself—the opening which appeared when St. Patrick prayed, and which Christ the Lord showed him—is unknown and invisible; or at least that it is not the same as that which pilgrims enter when they are shut up in the cave for twenty-four hours, but that it either lies hidden beneath or is situated a few paces away. Thus the Reverend John Gamhneus, abbot of Leathra, and John Fursus Hac Kegan, a seventy-year-old priest, related to us from ancient tradition. Others have thought that its location is wholly unknown and will not appear to human beings except at the end of the age; that concerning this well one should think as ancient Hebrews thought concerning Moses’ tomb and the ark of the covenant before the return from Babylon. Tornius Mulchonrius, officially devoted to antiquarian matters and himself very old, attributed this opinion, in my hearing, to Father Eugene Duffy of the Order of St. Francis, a man of popular piety.

6. But James of Vitry, in chapter 92 of his *Oriental History*, speaks thus of this well:

> “In [Col. 0981C] Ireland there is a certain place called St. Patrick’s Purgatory. If anyone enters it without being truly penitent and contrite, he is immediately seized and killed by demons and never afterward returns. But one who enters truly contrite and confessed is seized there by demons and purified through fire, water, and a thousand kinds of torments. Whoever has sinned more is punished more bitterly in the same place. But whoever returns purified from the aforesaid place can never thereafter laugh, play, or love any of the things that are in the world; but, always mourning and groaning, forgetting what lies behind, he stretches himself forward toward what lies ahead.”

17. We learn by daily experience that most of these things are not founded in truth, if the reference is to the cave now known and frequented. For many have entered the cavern of Purgatory repeatedly, yet, when returned, play, laugh, burst into laughter, associate in the world with secular people, and conduct the business of this world no differently than if they had never entered that place [Col. 0981D]. Otherwise, we should have countless philosophers in Ireland from the school of Heraclitus, whereas there are far more of Democritus’ family, more inclined to unrestrained laughter than to tears.

There still survives a person of the highest credibility who, on his priestly word, assured us that he had seen fifteen hundred people all at once performing barefoot circuits and other customary penances on the island, while awaiting admission to the well in groups of nine; except that some, by exchange, lodged in one of the seven penitential beds of other saints situated near St. Patrick’s well. If at one time the number of pilgrims was so great, what should we think concerning any single age, especially when access was freer than we now experience because of the Protestant settlements in the surrounding district [Col. 0982A]?

18. But if Vitry speaks, not of the present and visible Purgatory, but of that other hidden and concealed one; if the report of Duffy, Gamhneus, Conrius, Kegan, and others concerning this is true—though their opinion is less received—I determine nothing now concerning the matter itself in either direction. Nor do grave men think that one should rashly depart from the more common opinion and conviction which appears to have prevailed among most people without distinction: namely, that in the island of Darrig, that cavern still visible, vaulted with its low and depressed arch, is the true site in which the well we seek is contained.

19. Moreover, from the teaching of St. Thomas there occurs this observation concerning the place of Purgatory: where nothing is found expressly determined, one must speak according to what agrees better with the sayings of the saints and with revelation granted to many. Thus the place of Purgatory is twofold: one according to the common law, and in this sense the place of Purgatory is a lower place joined to hell; the other according to dispensation, and in this sense some are recorded as punished in various places, either for the instruction of the living or for the aid of the dead [Col. 0982C], so that, when their punishment becomes known to the living, it may be mitigated through the suffrages of the Church.

20. Certainly, both parts of the distinction just given—both that according to the common law and that according to dispensation—belong to the posthumous place of Purgatory and to punishments to be paid after this life by enduring them sufficiently. But we are now discussing satisfactive punishments, which may also be meritorious in this present life, in the course of this age through which we travel toward the appointed goal of our fatal departure from the life and society of humankind.

Thus we distinguish a twofold Purgatory: one living or wayfaring, in this present life of those journeying and living as pilgrims away from the Lord; the other posthumous and preliminary [Col. 0982D], when the soul, after death, having laid down the burden of mortal flesh and completed its worldly battle and conflict, is punished and purified in the vestibule, so that, cleansed from every wrinkle and stain and expiated from every liability of punishment and venial fault, it may be admitted to the courts of the Lord and recline at the supper of the Lamb, at the table of the heavenly Bridegroom. He prepared and adorned it by grace on the way, that in the homeland he might set it in its place and clothe it with the robe of immortality.

21. Therefore, in treating of this wayfaring cleansing, it seems more consonant with the sayings of the saints handed down in writing and with the revelations to be cited below, and it agrees better with the office of St. Patrick, if we say that in that little building on the island of Darrig, mentioned above, is located the Purgatory, or place of cleansing [Col. 0983A], in which this holy preacher of the divine word opened the understanding of unbelievers so that they might believe in the punishment to follow after their departure from here and conceive what it is like; so that, while life remained, both those then living and those to be born afterward, and the children of those born, might escape the posthumous punishments of eternal burning by the present purification which they underwent in this cleansing arena. There they could expiate themselves while living, in order to forestall God’s severity in the future.

22. The ancient antiphon to which the Irish Church sang in remembrance of this event, with grateful and joyful heart in praise of God and St. Patrick, appears to refer to this:

> Wonderful are the merits of Patrick, the great father,  
> [Col. 0983B] to whom the Lord showed the place of Purgatory,  
> where living children who have sinned may cleanse themselves.

Therefore, although that Purgatorial place is sometimes called a well or a cavern, this designation does not adequately denote the whole purification, but only a part of it—and the more arduous part of the penitence or punishment undertaken in this pilgrimage.

## CHAPTER II. On the Manner and Rite of Completing the Pilgrimage of This Purgatory in These Later Centuries

23. The order for completing the whole journey is as follows.

A period of nine days is spent in performing the prescribed circuits on the island itself. The entire island is surrounded [Col. 0983C] by stagnant and very deep water, like an estuary, scattered here and there with other islands. But this island of Purgatory, together with the adjacent island of St. Avogus [otherwise Virbius, or Fintan], where the monastery of the Regular Canons of St. Augustine is situated, two or three stadia to the west, is the most famous and celebrated of all. Pilgrims are conveyed to it by rowing in a hollowed-out single-log boat prepared for this purpose.

During the entire time they remain on the island, namely those nine days, they must fast on bread and water—not in any fashion whatever, but with one meal of unleavened bread baked in ashes or cooked on a griddle, or at least uncooked oat flour; and lake-water, boiled or at least heated in a pot, without salt or any other seasoning. This food, so raw and meager, however much their intestines may grumble, is to be tasted only once in twenty-four hours, except that it is permitted to refresh parched throats more often when thirst presses. The power of this water, although stagnant, is such that however much one wishes to drink of it, one feels no discomfort from it, just as if it flowed from a mineral spring. This is said of the Spa water flowing from an acidic little spring by those who have drunk it without burden or heaviness of stomach [Col. 0983D].

24. During the day pilgrims must make the sacred stations three times—morning, noon, and evening. Wearied at nightfall, they lie down on hay or straw, without blanket, pillow, or mattress, unless they wrap themselves in their cloaks or put their breeches beneath their heads.

[Col. 0984A] 25. The stations themselves are performed in this order. Having been admitted by the spiritual Father, who presides over the Purgatory by the institution of the canons, to undertake the pilgrimage, they remove shoes and stockings and enter barefoot, devoutly, the church dedicated to St. Patrick. There, after prayer, they make sacred circuits seven times inside the church itself and as many times outside in the cemetery.

Having completed these, they withdraw to the penal dwellings or beds, which they call the penitential cells of the saints, arranged in a circle. They go round each one seven times: on the outside barefoot, on the inside with knees bent. Likewise they make their rounds both of the cross in the cemetery and of another cross fixed in a heap of stones. After completing all these circuits, they come by a rough and often rocky path [Col. 0984B] to a place where they plant the soles of their feet upon submerged marble, sometimes tearing them, but always wearying them. For a quarter of an hour less than half an hour, while they recite the Lord’s Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, and the Apostles’ Creed, they experience such refreshment and strength from the stone beneath their feet—upon which St. Patrick himself is said to have prayed and to have left the imprint of his feet—that they would be ready immediately to make a second circuit. This, however, is not permitted except after some interval of time.

26. After this austerity has been repeated for seven days, on the eighth day they double the stations or circuits, to make satisfaction for the same on the following day, when they are to enter the well. For on that day of the well it is not permitted [Col. 0984C] to make the circuits, nor even to leave the cavern which they must enter, observing the following ceremony.

27. The group of nine whose turn it is to enter the cave gathers before the spiritual Father. Having delivered a word of exhortation, he warns them of the danger should they enter with defiled minds, and of the reward should they enter with cleansed consciences. In set words he recalls examples of horrors capable of moving the dullest person and terrifying the most hardened. He awakens in them the remembrance of penitence and steadfastness, so that, after sacramental confession and reception of Holy Communion, they may prepare and arm themselves against the principalities and powers of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Now contrite and absolved, with [Col. 0984D] the banner of the cross going before them, he leads them to penitential obsequies, that they may now pay the due rites for their former life negligently lived, offer funeral honors to the old Adam with his deeds in the burial of sins, and provide through the interest of a better purpose. As they are about to enter, sprinkled with lustral water at the mouth of the cavern, as though passing into another world and hastening from the road to the end, they stand in their agony groaning and sighing, offering pardon and peace to all and asking it for themselves. Forgiving the whole world whatever it has done against them, most enter the cavern with sobbing, weeping, and tears; and when the door has been shut from outside, those who accompanied this funeral depart.

28. The cavern itself is a stone chamber, with walls so narrow and vault so low that a person of tall stature could not straighten himself enough even to sit except with bent neck. The nine, sitting and leaning close against one another, are tightly compressed; nor can a tenth remain with the others except with the greatest difficulty [Col. 0985A]. The cavern has a little side-window through which a faint ray shines during the day. The length and width of the well are sufficient to contain comfortably a man of normal stature lying flat upon his back. The far part of the floor is covered by a great stone, beneath which some report that there lies that chasm and pit which God opened—or showed already opened—when the saint prayed and the earth gaped, to terrify the obstinate.

Although in our own days, and from the furthest memory of human beings, the floor of the cavern has been leveled and made even with the rest of the ground, the tradition of certain elders is that it was deeper at the first establishment of the place and was gradually raised by decree of bishops and with the assent of the Apostolic See [Col. 0985B].

29. And just as the well itself lies north of the island church, so north of the well are arranged those dwellings or cells of the saints which we have mentioned. To the west are certain huts or cottages of brushwood and turf, serving as pilgrims’ lodgings.

30. Therefore, after they have remained fasting in this cave for twenty-four hours, having taken absolutely no food since the preceding noon—for it is not permitted to taste anything at all in the well itself, except perhaps a little water to rinse the palate—they are visited by the overseer of pilgrims and led to the edge of the lake [Col. 0985C]. There they immerse themselves naked in the waters of the lake; and, cleansed by this expiation, they proceed to the church as new soldiers of Christ, reborn and purified from the bath of penitence. There, according to custom, after giving thanks to God for their completed penitence, they are renewed for fearlessly pursuing Christian warfare and courageously bearing Christ’s cross.

For they ought not to promise themselves security or cessation from the Christian conflict, even though they have run this penitential contest; nor freedom from wrestling with the ancient serpent, even though St. Patrick expelled serpents from Ireland. In remembrance of this expulsion there is customarily shown on the island a large bony knot, said to be a fragment of serpent-bone from the poisonous brood which the saint expelled. But while this journey lasts, the vigilance of those on the way must endure against hidden plotters and open enemies, with whom devout people can have neither peace nor trustworthy truce [Col. 0985D].

Indeed, just as right living belongs to the whole body, so bearing the cross belongs to the whole course of time. This is especially recognized as true when faith itself is attacked and all those supports of integrity and innocence are forbidden us which serve to increase and strengthen it. Such, among many others, are works of satisfaction and penitential exertions, by which punishment is exacted for things past and healing and protection are obtained for the future.

31. And since this place, by its institution, serves this purpose, experience itself has proved that the visitation, satisfaction, and purification customarily practised in it have always been of great efficacy in every age. For, if it takes place in summer, who does not know how painful is so narrow, so dark, so prolonged a confinement, from the heat of the sun outside and from the steaming breath of those crowding and stifling one another within the cave? Or if it takes place in winter, how difficult it is to be immersed in water so as to emerge for penance? And at whatever time it takes place, how severe are the going barefoot for so many days, the ulceration of the feet, the raw walking over rough ground and the stations in rocky cells, frequent genuflection in penal cells, fasting, sleeping on the ground, wakefulness, and the other things which stimulate contrition, provoke weeping, and draw forth tears. Thus, during the brief time of the nine-day exile and pilgrimage, scarcely any thought arises except of mourning, sorrow, penance, sins, fasting, lamentation, prayer, meditation upon heavenly things, and the renunciation of every earthly consolation.

Accordingly, if James of Vitry were speaking of the place itself and of pilgrims’ stay in it when he declares that, always weeping and groaning, they forget what lies behind and stretch themselves toward what lies ahead, he would not think absurdly, nor speak incongruously with their usage and practice while they remain there. But insofar as he extends this to their whole remaining life and to the time outside the island, it is certain that not all are Drithelms or Heracliteans, nor are those tears perpetual beyond the borders of the Red Lake. Yet I do not therefore think that the pious island should be despised, but rather that it ought to be visited at a fitting time by those into whose minds God has put the resolve, and to whom He has supplied strength suitable for completing the journey. [Col. 0986A–C]

32. It should also be observed that, although very many persons of both sexes customarily frequent the place, they are not admitted together indiscriminately into the pit; rather, the men enter separately and the women in turn. If a great multitude of pilgrims should gather—as, on one occasion, we have said that fifteen hundred persons appeared to have assembled—the visitation of the pit is not fixed to a certain stated day, but is arranged at the discretion of the superintendent, so that so numerous a company may be dealt with more conveniently. [Col. 0986C]

33. As for what popular report circulates concerning monstrous apparitions which confront those shut up in the cave, omitting the rest, let us relate one instance only, which I received from a learned man and venerable prelate. A certain pilgrim from Tirconnell, while undertaking the pilgrimage and already shut up in the cave, had a draught-horse stolen by a fellow-countryman. Though absent on this island—and indeed enclosed in the pit—he nevertheless, as though present and accompanying the thief, saw all his turnings and paths: the track by which he came, the halter which he put around the horse’s neck, the place to which he led it, the means of escape which he sought, and the entire circuit he made while taking away the stolen animal. He also reported this in the pit to a fellow pilgrim sitting beside him.

When he emerged and returned home, and learned that the animal had been taken, he at once exposed the thief and summoned the denier before Hugh O’Donnell, lord of the region. Although the latter at first denied the theft, he was convicted by the pilgrim, the owner of the animal, through certain indications of time, place, implement, manner of concealment, escape route, and so forth; he yielded and restored what he had stolen. [Col. 0986D–0987A]

34. Although the truth of this and other things of the same kind has been attested by many, I determine nothing rashly. For it is certain that guardian angels have been assigned to watch over us, and that the powers of darkness, lying in wait for our salvation, could know such matters and insinuate them at the critical moment to persons absent. If, however, these things were disclosed by an evil demon, they must be understood to have been revealed only for ruin, disturbance, and deception. But if by a good angel, let us understand that they were disclosed as an exercise toward virtue, an admonition to piety toward God, repentance for sins, and greater trust in divine providence, to which all things are subject, and which has even the hairs of its servants’ heads numbered. [Col. 0987A–B]

35. Let these things, then, have been said somewhat cursorily concerning this Purgatory of Saint Patrick—not in every respect, but as it is now customarily visited in its present manner and rite: concerning the cave which is entered, the time spent there, the penitential cells and stations that are undertaken, and the fasting that is performed. We do not now inquire whether some alteration in these things has arisen in the course of time, but consider the matter itself—its origin, institution, and continuance. [Col. 0987B]

36. By what method a visitation of Purgatory was celebrated by a certain penitent five hundred and fifty years ago, you will learn from the following history. You have it transcribed in Matthew Paris under the year of the Lord 1152; he seems to have taken the entire account from Henry of Saltry, who was almost a full century older than Matthew and possessed the same narrative in its entirety. And although the account of the event is somewhat lengthy, nevertheless, because the authors from whom it is taken are not available to everyone, receive it here entire in their own words. I mention it all the more willingly because you may find the same narrative briefly set down and accepted as a true history by Denis the Carthusian, both in Book IV of *On the Four Last Things*, article 48, and in the dialogue *On the Particular Judgment of the Soul after Death*, article 24 and the following articles through article 29. [Col. 0987C]

## CHAPTER III. On the discovery of Purgatory and the rite formerly observed in pilgrimage to it

[Col. 0987D]

[C] While the great Patrick was preaching the word of God in Ireland and shining there with many miraculous signs, he endeavoured to call back the unbelieving people of that country from evil through fear of infernal torments, and to strengthen them in good through the promise of the joys of paradise. But they asserted that they would not be converted to Christ by plain preaching unless some among them should see those torments of the wicked, so that, by things seen, they might be made more certain than by promises.

But blessed Patrick, devoted to God, became then still more devoted on behalf of the people’s salvation in vigils, fasts, prayers, and good works. And while he was intent upon such things for the people’s salvation, the merciful Lord Jesus Christ visibly appeared to him, led him into a desert place, showed him a cave, round and dark within, and said: “Whoever, truly penitent and steadfast in faith, enters this cave and remains in it for the space of one day and one night, shall be cleansed from all the sins by which he has offended God throughout his whole life. And, passing through it, he shall see not only the torments of the wicked but also, if he perseveres steadfastly in faith, the joys of the blessed.” [Col. 0987D–0988A]

[B] 37. Thus, when the Lord had vanished from his sight, blessed Patrick was filled with spiritual joy, both because of his Lord’s appearance and because of the showing of the cave, through which he hoped to convert the unhappy people of Ireland to the Catholic faith. At once he built a church in that place and introduced into it Regular Canons of the blessed Father Augustine, following the apostolic life. He enclosed the aforesaid cave, which lies in the cemetery beyond the eastern front of the church, with a wall, furnished it with bolts and doors, lest anyone should presume to enter it rashly and without permission, and entrusted its key to the prior of that church for safekeeping.

In the time of blessed Patrick himself, many persons, moved by penance, entered this pit. Some perished in it; others returned and testified that they had endured torments and had seen joys. Blessed Patrick ordered their accounts to be recorded in the same church. By their testimony, therefore, others began to accept blessed Patrick’s preaching; and because people are cleansed there from sins, the place itself is called Saint Patrick’s Purgatory. The place of the church, however, is called Reglis. [Col. 0988A–C]

38. Here, moreover, it must be understood that there is a custom, established both by Saint Patrick and by his successors, that no one enters that Purgatory unless he has permission from the bishop in whose diocese it lies and chooses of his own will to enter it for his sins. When such a person comes to the bishop and reveals his intention, the bishop first urges him to desist from this purpose, saying that many have entered it who never returned. But if he persists, having received the bishop’s letters, he hastens to the place.

When the prior of that place has read these letters, he immediately dissuades the man from entering Purgatory and carefully warns him to choose another penance, showing him the danger in which many have perished there. If he still persists, the prior brings him into the church, that he may devote himself there for fifteen days to fasting and prayer. When these have been completed, the prior gathers the clergy together; and, after Mass has been celebrated in the morning, the penitent is strengthened by Holy Communion and sprinkled with water blessed for the same office. Thus he is finally led with procession and litanies to the door of Purgatory.

Opening the door before all, the prior announces to him the assault and destruction of many in that pit. If he remains steadfast in his purpose, having received the blessing of all the priests, commending himself to the prayers of all, and making the sign of the cross upon his forehead with his own hand, he enters. At once the prior bars the door behind him, and the procession returns to the church. On the following day, again in the morning, it proceeds from the church to the pit; the prior opens the door, and, if the man is found to have returned, he is led joyfully into the church, where he remains for another fifteen days, devoting himself to vigils and prayers. But if he has not appeared again at that same hour on the following day, all, certain of his destruction, depart after the prior has barred the door. [Col. 0988C–0989A]

## CHAPTER IV. On the knight’s penance, his entry into Purgatory, and the messengers sent to him by God

[B] 39. A certain knight named Oenus, who had served for many years under King Stephen, having obtained leave from the king, set out for Ireland, his native land, in order to visit his parents. After he had remained for some time in that region, he began to recall his exceedingly wicked life: how, from his very cradle, he had always occupied himself with arson and robbery; and, what grieved him more, how he had violated churches and seized ecclesiastical property, besides many enormous sins hidden within. Moved by repentance, the knight approached a certain bishop of that region, in whose diocese Purgatory lies. When he had devoutly laid out his sins before him in order, the bishop severely rebuked him, declaring that he had grievously offended the divine mercy. The knight was therefore greatly distressed and resolved to offer God worthy penance.

[B] For the knights of that country have this almost by nature: just as they are, through ignorance, more ready for evil than persons of another nation, so, when they recognize that they have erred, they are more ready and steadfast in repenting. [Col. 0989B–C]

[C] 40. When the bishop wished to impose upon him such penance as seemed just, the knight replied: “Since, as you assert, I have so grievously offended my Maker, I will undertake a penance more severe than all penances; and, that I may deserve to receive forgiveness for my sins, I wish to enter Saint Patrick’s Purgatory.” [Col. 0989C]

[C] 41. The bishop recounted the destruction of very many in it, in order to turn him away from this intention; but the knight, a man of resolute spirit, did not consent to the bishop’s dissuasion. The bishop advised him to take the habit of a canon or monk; but the knight replied that on no account would he do so until he had entered the aforesaid Purgatory.

When, therefore, the bishop recognized that he was truly penitent and unyielding, he gave him letters to the prior of the place, commanding him to deal with him as was customary with those who requested entrance into Purgatory. When the prior had seen the letters and performed the other ceremonies described above, he brought the knight into the church, where, according to custom, he continued fifteen days in fasting and prayer. When these were completed, Mass having been celebrated in the morning by the prior, he fortified the knight with Holy Communion. Having summoned the brothers and the neighbouring clergy, he led him to the entrance of the cave, sprinkled him with blessed water, opened the door, and said:

“Behold, you shall now enter in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. You shall walk through the hollow of the cave until, emerging into a plain, you find a most artfully constructed hall. When you have entered it, you will immediately have messengers from God, who will carefully explain to you what you are to do and what you are to suffer. When they depart and you remain alone in it, tempters will at once come; for this is known to have happened to those who entered before you. But remain steadfast in faith.”

The knight, however, showing a manly spirit, did not fear the danger which he had heard had swallowed up others. Once armed with iron, he had taken part in battles among men; now, harder than iron, armed with faith, hope, and righteousness, trusting in God’s mercy, he boldly rushed into battle against the demons. Commending himself to the prayers of all, he fortified his forehead with the sign of the life-giving cross and fearlessly entered the gate. The prior, locking it from outside, returned with the procession to the church. [Col. 0989D–0990B]

42. Thus the knight, desirous of undertaking a new and unfamiliar knighthood, went boldly through the cave, though alone. As the darkness grew heavier and heavier, he soon lost all light. At length, opposite him, a small light began faintly to shine through an opening; and before long he reached the aforesaid plain and hall. Yet no light appeared there except such as is found here in winter after sunset.

The hall had no walls, but was supported all around by columns and small arches, like a monks’ cloister. After he had walked for some time around the hall, marvelling at its wonderful construction, he saw within its enclosure something far more wonderful. He therefore entered it and sat inside for some time, turning his eyes here and there and admiring its beauty and construction. When he had sat alone for a little while, behold, fifteen men, as if religious, recently shaven and dressed in white garments, entered the house. Greeting him in the name of the Lord, they sat down.

Then, while the others kept silence, one who appeared to be their prior and leader spoke with him, saying: “Blessed be almighty God, who inspired you with the good purpose of entering this Purgatory for your sins. But unless you conduct yourself manfully, you will perish in body and soul. For as soon as we have left this house, a multitude of unclean spirits will be present. Inflicting severe torments upon you, they will threaten to inflict severer ones. They will promise to lead you to the gate by which you entered, attempting, if possible, to deceive you in this way, so that you may return.

“But if, overcome by the affliction of torments, frightened by threats, or deceived by promise, you give them assent, you will perish alike in body and soul. If, however, you are strong in faith and place your hope in the Lord, so that you yield neither to their torments, nor threats, nor promises, but despise them with an undivided heart, you shall not only be cleansed from all sins, but you shall also see the torments prepared for sinners and the repose in which the righteous rejoice. Keep God always in your remembrance; and whenever they torture you, invoke our Lord Jesus Christ. By the invocation of this name you shall immediately be delivered from whatever torment you are undergoing. We cannot remain here with you any longer; but we commend you to almighty God.”

And so, after giving the man their blessing, they departed from him. [Col. 0990B–0991A]

## CHAPTER V. On the demons’ approach and the first torment suffered by the knight

43. Left alone by those men, the knight began to prepare himself for a warfare of a new kind. Armed with Christ’s weapons, he fearlessly waited to see which demon would first challenge him to battle. He put on the breastplate of righteousness; his mind, as his head, was encircled with the helmet of hope, victory, and eternal salvation; his breast was protected by the shield of faith; and he also had the sword, the word of God. He devoutly invoked Jesus Christ, that he might be protected by that royal defence and not overcome by hostile adversaries. Nor did divine mercy disappoint him, for it does not know how to disappoint those who trust in it.

Thus, as has been said, while the knight sat alone in the house, awaiting with fearless spirit the demons’ battle, suddenly a tumult began to be heard around the house, as though the whole world were being convulsed. For even if all human beings and all living creatures of earth, sea, and air had made a noise together with all their strength, they would not, as it seemed to him, have produced a greater tumult. Therefore, unless he had been protected by divine power and more suitably instructed by the aforesaid men, that tumult itself would have driven him mad.

And behold, after the horrible sound followed the more terrible visible appearance of the demons. An innumerable multitude of deformed demons began to rush into the hall from every side, laughing as they greeted him and saying, as if in mockery: “Other people who serve us come to us only after death. But you wished to honour our company, to which you have diligently devoted yourself, so greatly that, unlike others, you would not wait for the day of death, but while living would deliver both your soul and body to us, so that you might receive greater recompense from us. This you have done; therefore you will receive abundantly from us what you have deserved. You have come here to suffer torments for your sins; therefore with us you shall have what you seek—namely, afflictions and pains.

“Nevertheless, because you have served us until now, if, submitting to our counsels, you are willing to return, we will do this for you as your reward: we will bring you unharmed back to the gate through which you entered, so that you may still enjoy life in the world and not lose everything pleasant to the body.”

They promised him these things because they wished to deceive him either by terror or by flattery. But Christ’s valiant knight was neither shaken by terror nor seduced by blandishment. With the same spirit he condemned both those who threatened and those who flattered, giving no answer whatever. [Col. 0991A–D]

44. Seeing themselves despised by the knight, the demons raged horribly against him. They kindled in the hall a pyre of immense fire and, binding his hands and feet, threw the knight into the flames. Shouting, they dragged him here and there through the blaze with iron hooks. But when he had been thrown into the fire and first felt the grievous torment, protected by the defence of the true God and recently instructed by the aforesaid men, he did not forget the weapons of spiritual warfare. Instead, invoking the name of his most merciful Saviour Jesus, he said, “Jesus Christ, have mercy on me,” and was so delivered from that blaze that not one spark of the entire pyre was visible.

Seeing this, the knight became more ashamed, firmly resolving thereafter not to fear those whom, upon invoking Christ’s help, he saw could easily be overcome. [Col. 0991D–0992A]

## CHAPTER VI. On the four penal fields to which the knight was dragged

45. Leaving that hall with wailing and horrible tumult, the demons went out and, separating from one another, some of them dragged the knight for a long time through a vast region. The earth was black and the region dark, and he saw nothing in it except the demons who dragged him. A burning wind blew there, scarcely perceptible to hearing, yet its violence seemed to pierce his body.

They dragged him toward those regions where the sun rises at midsummer; and when they had come there, as though to the end of the world, they began to turn to the right and proceed through a very broad valley toward that quarter where the sun rises in midwinter. As they turned aside, the knight began to hear the most miserable wailings and weeping of what seemed the whole populace of the earth; and the nearer he approached, the more distinctly he heard their cries and tears.

At last, dragged by the demons, he reached a field of vast width and length, entirely full of misery and pain; because of its excessive extent, the knight could not see its boundaries. This field was full of naked people of both sexes and of various ages, lying on the ground face downward. Their hands and feet were transfixed to the ground with iron nails made red-hot, and they were miserably tormented. At times, in the extremity of pain, they seemed to eat the earth, crying and wailing, “Spare us, spare us! Have mercy, have mercy!” But no one who knew how to spare or have mercy was present. The demons ran over the wretched people and beat them with exceedingly harsh scourges, saying to the knight: “Unless you submit to us and return to the gate through which you entered, you will experience these torments which you see. If you are willing, you will be led peacefully to it.”

But recalling how God had delivered him elsewhere, he utterly scorned to believe them. Then the demons threw him down upon the ground and attempted to afflict him in the manner of the others. But when he invoked the name of Jesus Christ, they failed in their attempt. [Col. 0992A–D]

46. Leaving that field, they dragged the knight to another field, full of greater misery. Between it and the preceding field he observed this difference: in the upper field the afflicted people lay with their bellies turned downward, but in this field their backs clung to the ground. Fiery dragons sat upon some of them and, as though devouring them, miserably tore them with fiery teeth. Fiery serpents encircled the necks, arms, or whole bodies of others; pressing their heads into the breasts of the wretched, they fixed the fiery sting of their mouths in their hearts. Toads also, of astonishing size and seemingly fiery, appeared to sit upon some persons’ breasts, fixing their hideous beaks into them, as if trying to draw out their hearts.

Moreover, demons ran among and over them and, beating them with very cruel scourges, grievously tortured the miserable. The people, thus fastened and afflicted, never ceased their weeping and wailing. Likewise, because of its length, he could not see the end of this field, but only its breadth where he entered and left; for he crossed the fields transversely.

“These are the torments,” said the demons, “which you see and shall suffer unless you consent to us and return.” When he scorned them, they tried, as above, to fasten him with nails, but at the sound of Christ’s name they could do nothing further. [Col. 0992D–0993A]

47. Passing from there, the demons led the knight into a third penal field. This field too was crowded with people of both sexes and of various ages, lying fastened to the earth with iron nails made red-hot, so densely that, because of the multitude of bodies, from the crown of the head to the tips of the feet no vacant place could be found large enough to be covered by the tip of a single finger. They could form a voice to cry out, but uttered it as do persons near death. They were naked, like the others, and were tortured by a cold and burning wind and by the demons’ scourges. When the demons wished to torture the knight here as in the other punishments, he invoked Christ’s name and remained unharmed. [Col. 0993B]

48. Then, dragging the knight, they came to a fourth field, full of many fires, in which every kind of torment was found. Some were suspended by fiery chains from their feet, others from their hands, others by their hair, others by their arms, while others hung head downward and were immersed in sulphurous flames. Some hung by their nails, with iron hooks fixed in their eyes, ears, throats, nostrils, breasts, or genitals. Others were being burned as though upon frying-pans. Others, pierced with fiery spits, were roasted over the fire; some demons turned them, while others poured upon them various molten metals.

Nor, amid the wretched weeping and wailing of all, were the lashes of the demons running about absent. There also he saw and recognized certain persons who had once been his companions. Every kind of torment that can be imagined was seen there; no tongue is sufficient to express the cries and wailings that he heard. These fields were full not only of tortured people but also of demons torturing them.

“These are the torments,” said the demons, “which you shall suffer unless you are willing to return to the gate through which you entered.” He despised their threats and, invoking Christ’s name, escaped free. [Col. 0993C–D]

## CHAPTER VII. On the fiery wheel, the smoking house, the lofty mountain, and the most frigid river to which the demons dragged the knight

49. Therefore, as the demons drove the knight away from that penal place, there appeared before them a wheel of marvellous size, made of iron and burning, whose spokes and rim were everywhere surrounded by iron hooks made red-hot, from which people hung transfixed. One half of the wheel stood aloft in the air, while the other was plunged downward into the earth. A flame of black and sulphurous fire rose from the ground around the wheel and most miserably tormented those hanging from it.

“These things,” said the demons, “which these people suffer, you shall suffer unless you are willing to return. But first you shall see what they endure.”

Then the Tartarean ministers, some on each side opposing the others, thrust iron bars between the spokes of the wheel and spun it with such speed that no person hanging upon it could be distinguished from another; for, because of the excessive swiftness of its motion, it appeared like a circle of fire. When they had cast him upon the wheel and raised him into the air by its rotation, he invoked Jesus’ name and came down unharmed. [Col. 0993D–0994B]

50. Proceeding from there, they dragged him toward a great house emitting smoke horribly. Its breadth was immense, and its length so great that he could not see its end. While they were still a little way from it, he halted, terrified to go farther because of the excessive heat issuing from it. The demons said to him: “These are baths which you see. Whether you wish it or not, when you have gone in there, you shall bathe in them with the others.”

From that house began to be heard most miserable weeping and lamentation. Brought into the house, he saw a harsh and dreadful sight. The floor of the house was full of round pits, joined so closely to one another that one could scarcely, or not at all, pass between them. Each pit was full of different molten metals and boiling liquids, in which a considerable multitude of people of both sexes and various ages were immersed. Some were submerged entirely; others to the eyebrows, others to the eyes, others to the lips, others to the neck, breast, navel, thighs, knees, or shins; others were held in the cauldrons by one foot only, by both hands, or by one hand alone. And all, in the extremity of pain, cried aloud and wept miserably.

“Behold,” said the demons, “you shall bathe with these.” Raising the knight, they tried to throw him into one of the pits. But at the sound of Christ’s name, they could prevail no further. [Col. 0994B–C]

51. Departing from that house, they went on to a lofty mountain and showed him an abundant multitude of people of both sexes and various ages. In comparison with them, all those whom he had seen before appeared few. All sat naked, bent over upon their toes. As though seeking death with trembling, they proceeded toward the north.

When the knight wondered what this wretched multitude was awaiting, one of the demons said to him: “Perhaps you wonder what the people here await with so great fear. Unless, agreeing with us, you are willing to return, you shall know what that trembling multitude awaits.”

The demon had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, a whirlwind came from the north. It seized both the demons and the knight with them, and all that people, and cast them, weeping and wailing miserably, into a foul and most frigid river on the other side of the mountain, where they were afflicted by immeasurable cold. When they tried to rise from the freezing water, the demons ran over the surface of the water and continually forced them under. But the knight, not forgetful of his helper, cried aloud the name of Christ and immediately found himself upon the opposite bank. [Col. 0994D–0995A]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the flame-vomiting pit and the most lofty bridge to which the demons led the knight

52. The demons, not yet satiated with their injury to Christ’s knight, approached and dragged him southward. There he saw before him a most hideous flame, full of sulphurous stench, rising from a certain pit; and naked people, as though fiery, driven up into the air like sparks of fire, and, when the force of the flames failed, falling back again into the pit and fire.

As they approached, the demons said to the knight: “This flame-vomiting pit is the entrance to hell; here is our dwelling. And because you have diligently served us until now, you shall remain here with us without end. For all who serve us shall remain here forever; if you enter this place even once, you shall perish eternally in both soul and body. Yet, if you are still willing to agree with us and return to the gate through which you entered, you may return unharmed to your own country.”

But he, trusting in God’s assistance, who had delivered him so often, despised their exhortations and promises. Then the angry demons hurled themselves into the pit and thrust the knight in with them. The deeper the knight descended into it, the wider he saw the pit and the more grievous a punishment he felt within it. In that pit the knight endured such distress and intolerable miseries that for a long time he forgot his Saviour’s name. But at last, God inspiring him, he came to himself and cried out the name of Jesus Christ as best he could. Immediately the force of the flame lifted him upward into the air.

Descending beside the pit, he stood for some time stunned, not knowing where to turn. But behold, new and seemingly unknown demons burst forth from the mouth of the pit and said to him: “Why do you stand there? Our companions told you that this is hell. They lied; know that it is not so. For it is always our custom to lie, so that those whom we cannot deceive by truth we may deceive by falsehood. This is not hell; but now we shall lead you to hell.” [Col. 0995A–D]

53. Thus the new enemies, dragging the knight with great and horrisonous tumult, came to a very broad and foul river, wholly covered as though with the flame of sulphurous fire and filled with a multitude of demons. They said to him, “Know that hell lies beneath this river.”

A bridge extended across the river, and it displayed three things which seemed almost impossible and very terrifying to those crossing it. First, it was so slippery that, even if it had been broad, no one—or scarcely anyone—could set a foot firmly on it. Second, it was so narrow and thin that no one could stand or walk upon it. Third, it was so high and so remote from the river that it was dreadful to look down.

“You must cross this bridge,” said the demons. “We will stir up winds and whirlwinds and cast you from the bridge into the river; and our companions who are in it will seize you and plunge you into hell.
