For we wish to test how safe it is for you to walk upon this bridge. Yet if you are still willing to agree with us and return, you may return unharmed to your homeland even from this peril.”

But Christ’s faithful knight, considering within himself from how many evils his most merciful advocate, Jesus, had delivered him, again invoked His name, boldly entered the bridge, and began to walk slowly. Feeling nothing slippery beneath his feet, he walked steadily upon the bridge, trusting in the Lord. The higher he ascended, the broader he found the bridge. And behold, after a little while, its width increased so greatly that it resembled the breadth of a public road and could receive eleven carts coming toward it.

The demons who had brought the knight there, holding his hand, rubbed it against the bridge; unable to go farther, they stood at the foot of the bridge as if awaiting the knight’s fall. But, seeing him cross freely, they struck the air with cries so horrisonous and profane that, stunned by the shrieking, he thought this horror of clamour more unbearable than any of the former punishments he had suffered from others. Yet, seeing that they had stopped and could proceed no farther, and remembering his pious guide, he went on securely. Other enemies ran below over the river and hurled their iron hooks, made red-hot, at him, but could not touch the knight. At last, proceeding safely and finding nothing adverse, he saw the bridge’s breadth grow so great that he could scarcely see its boundaries on either side. [Col. 0995D–0996C]

## CHAPTER IX. On the heavenly glory and earthly paradise shown to the knight, and the bishops’ conversation with him

54. The unconquered knight, now freed from the assaults of unclean spirits, saw before him a high wall rising into the air. It was a wall of marvellous and incomparable beauty and of inestimable workmanship. In it he saw a single gate, yet closed, ornamented with various metals and precious stones and gleaming with wonderful splendour. When the knight had approached it, though he was still about half a mile away, the gate opened toward him. Such a sweet fragrance came forth through it that, as it seemed to him, if the whole world were transformed into spices, it could not surpass the abundance of this sweetness. From it he received such strength that he thought he could now endure without distress the torments he had suffered. Looking through the gate, he saw a brightness surpassing the splendour of the sun. [Col. 0996C–D]

55. When he had gone a little farther, there came out to meet him, with crosses, candles, banners, and as it were branches of golden palms, such a great and splendid and well-ordered procession as, he thought, had never been seen in this world. [Col. 0997A] Those aforesaid followed: people of both sexes, of different ages, and of every rank—some like archbishops, others like bishops, others like abbots, monks, canons, priests, and ministers of every ecclesiastical grade—clothed in sacred garments appropriate to their rank. Clerics and laypeople alike appeared there dressed in the same manner of clothing in which they had served God in the world. All received the knight with great reverence and joyful gladness, and with a harmony unheard of in the world happily led him with them within the gate.

56. When the music had ended and the procession dispersed, two who seemed to be archbishops, withdrawing apart, received the knight into their company and led him on, as though intending to show him their country and its loveliness. [Col. 0997B] Speaking with him, they first blessed God, who had strengthened his soul with such constancy amid the torments through which he had passed and which he had endured. As they led the knight through the pleasant places of that country, he passed here and there and beheld delights and joys far more numerous than he, or any person most skilled, could express by tongue or pen.

That country was illuminated with such brightness of light that, just as the light of a lamp is obscured by the brilliance of the sun, so the brightness of the midday sun seemed capable of being darkened by the wondrous radiance of that land’s light. Night never cast its shadow over it, because the splendor of the most pure heaven illumined it with perpetual brightness. The whole country was like pleasant green meadows, adorned with varied flowers, [Col. 0997C] fruits, and many kinds of herbs and trees. “By their fragrance,” he said, “I could have lived without end, if I had been permitted to live there.” Because of its immense size, he could not discover the limit of that country, except on the side by which he had entered through the gate.

He saw there so great a multitude of men and women as he thought no one in this life had seen, nor believed the remainder of the world could contain. Some remained in one place, some in another, distinguished by their companies; yet, as they wished, some passed joyfully from these groups to those, and others from those to these. Thus they rejoiced in visiting one another. Choirs stood in their places facing choirs, and with a concert of sweet harmony they resounded praises to God. As star differs from star in [Col. 0997D] brightness, so there was a harmonious diversity in the beauty and brilliance of their garments and faces.

Some appeared clothed in gold; others in green, purple, violet-blue, azure, or white. Yet the form of each person’s dress was the same as that which he had used in the world; and thus it showed the knight what merit or rank each person had possessed. Their garments’ varied colors seemed to have varied splendor. Some walked like crowned kings; others carried golden palms in their hands. So delightful to the knight was the sight of such and so great a company in that rest of the righteous; nor was the sweet and ineffable delight of their harmony less great. From every side he heard the harmonious singing of saints proclaiming the praises of God. Each rejoiced in his own blessedness, and each also exulted in the joy of the others.

All who looked upon the knight blessed the Lord for his arrival and rejoiced with him at his escape from the demons; at his arrival, something like a new exultation seemed to arise there. He felt neither heat nor cold there, nor saw anything that could in any way offend or harm him. For all was peaceful, all tranquil, all pleasing. He saw in that repose vastly more than any person could adequately speak or write. [Col. 0998A]

57. When these things had been completed, the bishops said to the knight: “Behold, brother, with God’s help you have seen what you desired to see. In coming here, you have seen the torments of sinners, and here the rest of the righteous. Blessed be the Creator and Redeemer of all, who gave you such a purpose, by whose grace you acted steadfastly while passing through the torments. Now we wish you to know what were those places of torment which you saw, and what is this country of such great blessedness.

58. “This country is the earthly paradise, from which Adam, the first-created man, was expelled because of the fault of disobedience. For after he disdained to submit in obedience to God, he could no longer see what you see, indeed joys incomparably greater by far. Here he had diligently heard the very words of God; he could enjoy purity of heart, the height of inward vision, and the sight of the blessed angels. But when by disobedience he had fallen from such blessedness, he lost the light of mind by which he was illumined; for, when he was in honor, he did not understand, and therefore was compared to senseless beasts and made like them. [Col. 0998C] All his posterity, moreover, on account of his fault, received, like him, knowledge of death. O detestable crime of disobedience!

59. “At last, moved by compassion for the misery of the human race, the most merciful God ordained that his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, should be incarnate. Looking to faith in him, through baptism we have deserved to return to this country, freed both from actual sin and from original sin. Yet because we stained the robe received in baptism when we sinned through the frailty of the flesh, it was necessary that through repentance we should obtain pardon for actual sins.

“The repentance which we undertook before death, [Col. 0998D] or while lying at the point of death, but did not complete during life, we discharge after the body’s dissolution in the punitive places which you saw: some enduring torments for a longer, others for a shorter time, according to the measure and quantity of their offenses. For all who are here in this repose passed through those places; and all whom you saw in each of the punitive places, except those detained below the mouth of the infernal pit, will, once purified, come to this repose and be saved. Every day, moreover, some arrive purified; receiving them as we received you, we joyfully bring them in here.

“No one among those in punishments knows how long he will be tormented there. But through Masses, psalms, prayers, and alms, whenever these are performed for them, either their torments are mitigated or they are transferred to lesser and more tolerable ones, until at last they are completely freed through such benefits. When they have come to this place of rest, they are wholly ignorant how long they will remain here. For none of us can know this concerning himself. Just as, in the punitive places, they are detained according to the quantity of their offenses, so we who are here will remain in this repose for a greater or lesser time according to our good merits. [Col. 0999A]

“Behold: as you see, we are free from punishments and enjoy great repose; nevertheless, we are not yet worthy to ascend to the heavenly joy of the saints, and none of us knows the day or term of his advancement to a better state. But after the appointed term for each, we shall pass into a greater repose. Every day our company in some manner both increases and decreases, since each day some ascend to us from punishments, and some ascend from us into the heavenly paradise.” [Col. 0999B]

60. Having said this, the venerable bishops took the knight with them onto a mountain and ordered him, looking upward, to say what color the heaven seemed to him in comparison with the place where he stood. He answered: “It seems to me like gold glowing in a furnace.”

“This which you now see,” they said, “is the gate of paradise. Through it enter those who are taken up from us into heaven. Nor should it escape you that, while we remain here, God feeds us once each day with heavenly food. What this food is and how delightful it is, you shall now experience with us by tasting it, God granting it.”

Hardly had they finished speaking when, behold, something like a flame of fire descended from heaven [Col. 0999C] and covered the whole country. Divided, as it were, into rays, the flame settled over the head of each person and finally entered wholly into them. It descended also upon the knight among the others and entered him; and he felt in heart and body together such sweetness of delight that he could scarcely tell whether he was alive or dead. But that hour passed in an instant.

“This,” they said, “is that food with which God feeds us once each day. But those who are taken up from us into heaven enjoy it without end.”

The knight would gladly have remained there if he had been permitted to enjoy these delights; but after such and so great joys, sad things were told him.

61. “Therefore, brother, since you have in part seen what you desired to see—namely, both the repose of the blessed and the torments of sinners—you must now return by the same [Col. 0999D] way by which you entered. If henceforth you live soberly and holily, you may be secure not only of this repose but also of a dwelling in heaven. But if—may it never be—you live wickedly and defile your life with the enticements of the flesh, behold, you yourself have seen what torments await you.

“Return, therefore, without fear. For whatever terror the demons inflicted upon you as you came here, do not fear anything like it as you return. The demons will not dare approach you; indeed, they will be afraid even to appear to you. Nor can the torments which you saw harm you in any way.”

At these words the astonished knight, weeping and wailing, began humbly to beg the bishops [Col. 1000A] that he might not be compelled to return from so great a blessedness to the miseries of the world. He said: “I cannot leave here, because I greatly fear that, through the frailty of human life, I may commit something that will prevent my returning here.”

“It shall not be as you ask,” they said; “but it shall happen as he who made both us and you has ordained. For he alone knows what is expedient for all.”

## CHAPTER X. How the Knight Departed from Purgatory, Went to Jerusalem, and Spent the Rest of His Life

The knight Oenus, having received a blessing, departed sorrowfully; deeply sad, he returned by the same way by which he had come. The bishops led him back to the gate of paradise, and when he had gone out, the gate was shut behind him. Leaving paradise, grieving and mourning because his blessedness had been changed and he had been compelled to return to the misery [Col. 1000B] of this world, he returned by the way he had come and reached the hall in which the demons had first attacked him.

He saw the demons on his return, but at the sight of him they fled through the air as though afraid; and the torments through which he passed could not harm him. When he fearlessly entered the aforesaid hall, behold, the fifteen men who had first appeared there and instructed him immediately came to meet him, glorifying God, who had granted him such constancy amid the torments. Rejoicing in his victory, they said: “Come, our brother. We know that through the torments which you courageously endured, you have conquered and have been purified from all your sins. Behold, the dawn of light is already shining in your homeland. [Col. 1000C] Ascend as quickly as possible; for if the prior, after the solemnities of the Masses, comes with the procession to the gate and does not find you returned, he will despair of your return, shut the gate, and go back to the church.”

The knight, having received a blessing, immediately ascended; and at the very hour when the prior opened the gate, the knight appeared coming out from within. The prior received him joyfully and with praises of Christ, led him into the church, and had him devote himself to prayer there for fifteen days. Then, taking upon his shoulder the badge of the Lord’s cross, he set out devoutly for the Holy Land and sought the Lord’s sepulcher at Jerusalem, together with other venerable places, in holy contemplation.

Thereafter, having laudably fulfilled the vow of his pilgrimage, he returned and went to consult Stephen, king of the English, his lord, to whom he had formerly been attached, so that, by the counsel of this industrious and prudent man, he might spend the remainder of his life in a holy religious order and henceforth serve the King of kings. [Col. 1000D]

It happened at that time that Gervase, abbot of the monastery of Louth, obtained from King Stephen a place in Ireland for building an abbey. He sent his monk named Gilbert—[Note: This Gilbert was abbot of Besmagroeirt.]—with certain others to the same king, that he might receive a site from him and found a monastery there. But when Gilbert came to the king and was graciously received by him, he complained greatly that he did not know the language of that country. Hearing this, the king said: “With God’s help, I shall find you an excellent interpreter.” Calling the knight Oenus, the king ordered him to go with Gilbert and remain with him in Ireland.

The knight most willingly accepted this command and said to the king: “I ought gladly to serve a monk; and you also, O king, ought with thanksgiving to receive monks . . . [lacuna] . . . in your kingdom, because, to confess the truth, in the repose of the saints I saw no people endowed with so great glory as the men of this religious order.”

Crossing into Ireland, they began a monastery and remained together there for two and a half years. Gilbert was cellarer of that monastery; the knight, however, acted outside it as general steward and devoted servant, [Col. 1001B] and as a most faithful interpreter. Having then received the monastic habit, he lived holily and religiously, as Gilbert himself testified.

[C.] Whenever Gilbert was alone anywhere with the knight, he eagerly questioned him concerning the state of purgatory and the marvelous punishments which the knight had seen and learned by experience. But the knight, who could never hear purgatory mentioned without bursting into the most bitter tears, began, under the seal of secrecy, to recount to his friend for edification what he had heard and seen and learned by experience, affirming that he had beheld all things with bodily eyes.

Through the industry and diligence of this monk, the experience of this knight was committed to writing, together with the report of the bishops of the region and of other religious persons who, for the sake of justice, bore testimony [Col. 1001C] to the truth.

## CHAPTER XI. Examination and Manifold Proof of This History

[B.] 63. “When the often-mentioned Gilbert,” these are the words of Henry of Saltrey, “had frequently recounted the foregoing narrative before many people, with myself also listening, as he had often heard it from the knight himself, one among the others was present who said that he doubted whether these things had happened thus. Gilbert replied to him:

“‘There are some who say that, after entering the hall, he had been carried off into ecstasy and had seen all these things in the spirit. But the knight most certainly affirms that this did not happen to him; rather, he steadfastly testifies that he saw all things with bodily eyes and suffered them bodily.

“‘Moreover, I was in charge of a monastery, and with my own eyes I saw something not very unlike these things; many also saw it with me. There was in the monastery a certain monk of very great religious devotion, whose holiness the demons envied. While he slept, they bodily carried him away from the dormitory by some death-like condition. He was held by them for three days and three nights, while the brothers did not know what had happened to him. But after the third day he was found by the brothers in his bed, almost beaten to death and horribly scourged by the demons. He also confessed to me that he had seen dreadful torments. [Col. 1001D]

“‘He lived afterward for fifteen years, but no medicine could heal his wounds. They always appeared open and as though fresh; some were as deep as the length of one finger. Whenever this monk saw some younger man laughing or joking too immoderately, or behaving in any way disorderly, he would say: “O, if you knew how great a punishment awaits this dissipation, perhaps you would reform your unrestrained gestures and conduct for the better.” I saw this monk’s wounds and touched them with my own hands, and I myself buried him after his death. Therefore the account of this man, so holy, so religious, and so familiar to me, entirely removed whatever doubt I had concerning the foregoing account.’ Thus far Gilbert.”

64. “But I,” Saltrey continues, “after hearing all these things, consulted two abbots from Ireland in order to be still more certain about them. One of them affirmed that all was true, and also testified that many who entered did not return.” [Col. 1002B]

65. “More recently I spoke with a certain bishop, nephew of the third Saint Patrick, namely a companion of Saint Malachy, named Florentianus. In his bishopric, as he himself said, is this same purgatory. When I inquired rather closely concerning it, the bishop replied: ‘Certainly, brother, it is true. That place is in my bishopric, and many perish in that purgatory; and if perhaps they return, because of the enormity of the torments which they have suffered, they waste away through lasting weakness or pallor. But if afterward they live soberly and justly, they are certain that they will not suffer further punishments for their sins.’”

[Col. 1002C] [D.] 66. We have taken this history of the knight Oenus, insofar as it belongs to Henry of Saltrey, from an ancient manuscript of the Library of Saint Victor in Paris—in which it was formerly written in three different places and is still found in two. Insofar as it belongs to Matthew Paris, we have transcribed it from his printed works. If anyone, as we suppose, should refuse to believe it, or wish to attack it, more rashly than soundly and piously, let him consult the most holy Fathers: St Gregory (*Dialogues*, book IV), the Venerable Bede (*Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 19), and Denis the Carthusian (*On the Particular Judgment of the Soul*, where he resolves various objections to the contrary); and let him attentively read the various revelations, visions, and narratives not unlike this one which they report, to which they themselves do not hesitate to give credence as probable, nor presume to deny them. [Col. 1002D]

## CHAPTER XII. On the Time and Matter of Purification, and the Subject Capable of Being Purified in This Purgatory

67. To complete this treatise on purgatory, it remains to speak briefly concerning the time and matter of purification, in order to satisfy a subtle objection concerning the adequate matter of expiation, or the subject capable of expiation in this purgatory.

It must therefore be noted that this purgatory has the distinctive feature that it properly concerns persons still living and surviving, not the dead. In this there is a broad difference between this privileged and vital purgatory, as I call it here, and that other universal and posthumous one—so named for the sake of distinction: in order to separate the former, which is undergone in this life, from the latter, which is not suffered except after death. The former may be called the wayfaring or preliminary purgatory; the latter, terminal or post-vital, or, more meaningfully, posthumous. [Col. 1003A] This is a fuller distinction than calling one extraordinary—namely this one, which concerns the living—and the other ordinary, which concerns the dead.

For after death too there is an ordinary and an extraordinary purgatory, as has been brought forward above from other authorities. When the purification of souls released from their bodies is performed in a proper and determinate place near the limbus and edge of the abyss of the damned, beside the navel of the earth, it is said to take place in ordinary purgatory. But when, outside those limits, in baths, caverns, corners, or other recesses, where souls undergoing expiation can be heard or approached by mortals, that purification is said to take place in an extraordinary location. [Col. 1003B]

68. But if we refer these terms “ordinary” and “extraordinary” not to place but to time—so that the purification occurring after death is said to occur at the ordained time, according to the ordinary course and measure of time, in which all who die in grace and have anything to expiate after this life can and must share—while that other purification, granted extraordinarily as though by privilege in this life to those who bind themselves to undergo that penitential cavern which, by the prerogative and prayers of St Patrick, has been designated and fixed within definite limits: then there seems nothing absurd in saying that this expiation is extraordinary with respect to time. [Col. 1003C]

69. The adequate matter to be purified in this purgatory, extraordinary in respect to time, as has been said, may be every liability to punishment and all stains or bonds whatsoever that can be erased or dissolved in the wayfarer’s state through the power of penance and an act of contrition. For those who are thus extraordinarily purified are not the blessed who have attained their end, nor are they confirmed in grace or charity; rather, they are wayfarers placed in the course of the journey and of mortal life, absolutely in a state in which they can merit and demerit.

Nevertheless, through the intercession and singular patronage of that titular saint of whom we spoke, they may conceive a pious hope that, if they fulfill their part and practice repentance for sins with the diligence proper and possible to them, they will be supported and strengthened by greater helps of grace, so that they may neither fall during life into mortal sin [Col. 1004B] nor after life into damnation; or at least, should they fall through human frailty, they will not depart this life unrepentant.

This view concerning St Patrick’s purgatory may be greatly illustrated by the opinion of certain doctors concerning the cemetery of St Andrew, consecrated and privileged by St Gregory, and likewise concerning the soul of Trajan, liberated by the same saint’s prayers—an opinion which St Thomas appears to follow, although both claims are attacked by others. There is no need to discuss this matter at present. We shall be content piously and modestly to defend our own assertion and that of our elders, leaving others meanwhile their own opinion and judgment. For if we should wish to dispute too fervently, thrusting forward reasons and probable conjectures as demonstrations—which the subject permits—or, at least, pressing and introducing demonstrations *quia* (“that”), as demonstrations *propter quid* (“why”), we risk being reproved by people of more moderate disposition as immoderate and overly self-confident. [Col. 1004C]

[Note: [Col. 1003] See the story of the Spanish viscount concerning this purgatory in Philip O. Sullevanus, *Compendium of the Ecclesiastical History of Ireland*.]

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1145–1153: EUGENIUS III, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1003]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 621)

Eugenius, a native of Pisa, a man distinguished for religion and holiness, was made pope in the year of the Lord 1145, in the time of Emperor Conrad. “At the beginning of the dignity which he received,” says Otto of Freising, book VII, chapter 31, “because the people, at Arnold’s instigation, wished to urge him, as they had his predecessors, to surrender the regalian rights to the City, he departed from Rome with the bishops and cardinals. On the following Sunday, in the monastery of Farfa, changing the customary practice because of the violence of persecution, he was elevated by pontifical consecration.

“To this Pope Eugenius the venerable Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, wrote the book *On Consideration*, arranged in four divisions, in which he demonstrated most clearly the insight of a perfect life and of a most subtle intellect. For this same apostolic man, formerly called Bernard, first vice-lord of Pisa, and afterward at Clairvaux, having despised all worldly things for Christ, became a disciple of the same venerable Abbot Bernard. Later he was appointed by him abbot of the monastery of Blessed Anastasius, of the Cistercian Order, in the city of Rome, and, as we have said, was made supreme pontiff. [Col. 1005]

“After his consecration, avoiding the fury of the Roman people, he withdrew to fortified places and then came to Viterbo, where he remained for some time. But the Roman people, together with their patrician Jordan, having become enraged, abolished the dignity of the prefecture and compelled all princes and nobles among the citizens into subjection to the patrician. They demolished not only the towers of certain distinguished laymen but also the houses of cardinals and clerics, and carried off an immense quantity of plunder. They did not fear sacrilegiously and most profanely to fortify as a castle the church of St Peter, head of all churches. Pilgrims arriving for prayer they compelled, for the sake of profit, to make offerings by blows and beatings; and they did not shrink from killing some who refused to offer, in the very portico and vestibule of the church, with wicked audacity.

“The venerable pontiff, having first struck Jordan and certain of his supporters with the sword of anathema, restrained them with the military aid of the people of Tivoli, the ancient enemies of the Romans, and finally forced them to seek peace. He granted that peace on the condition that they should renounce the dignity of the patriciate and restore the prefect to his former dignity, while they should retain senators by his authority. Thus, returning to the City, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.”

Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, came from England to the newly created Pope Eugenius. He was kindly received by Pope Eugenius, whose kindness and affability are wonderfully commended by Roger in the *Annals*, where he writes: “In the same year Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, again making for Rome, was honorably received by the new Pope Eugenius, a man worthy of the highest dignity, whose mind was always gracious, whose judgment always equitable, whose expression always not merely cheerful but also pleasant.” These are Roger’s words about Eugenius—Roger being a most accurate writer of this period.

At that time also, while Eugenius was staying at Viterbo, he received embassies from the East, from Armenia and Syria, as is reported in these words by Otto, who was present and who most faithfully wrote down what he saw (*Chronicle*, book VII, chapters 32–33):

“At that time the envoys of the Armenian bishops and of their metropolitan—the one whom they call the Catholicos, that is, universal, because he has beneath him an innumerable number, that is, more than a thousand bishops—came from the farthest East almost to the supreme pontiff at Viterbo, having completed a laborious journey of one year and six months. Offering him, in greeting, complete submission on behalf of that church, they explained before us and many others present at the old hall the reasons for their journey. These were as follows.

“Between themselves and the Greeks there is agreement in some matters concerning the rite of sacrifice, but disagreement in others. For they use leavened bread, like the Greeks; but they do not mix water with wine, as we and the Greeks do. Moreover, joining the Nativity of the Lord to Epiphany, they make those two feasts one. On account of these matters and others, while they disagreed among themselves, they chose the Roman Church as judge, came to seek counsel, and requested that the form of sacrifice according to its custom be given to them.

“The Roman bishop received them graciously, admitted them to the solemnities of the Mass and to the secrets of the sacrifice, and instructed them carefully to observe what was being done there. While they did so and stood attentively before the sacred altar, one of them invested with episcopal rank, as he afterward related in full assembly, saw, on the octave of St Martin—when the dedication of the church of St Peter is customarily celebrated—as the supreme pontiff was performing the divine mysteries, a ray of sunlight shining in splendid radiance over his head, and two doves ascending and descending in it. Looking more carefully in every direction, and finding no opening through which that light could have entered, he recognized this as divine and was further inflamed toward obedience to the Roman See. He made known to all what he had seen.

“But the venerable Father attributed this not to his own merits, but affirmed that it had been shown him from heaven rather on account of that man’s faith: namely, so that the church from which he had been sent might recognize the power of the sacraments flooded with the light of truth and might henceforth learn with what reverence and in what form it ought to administer them.

“The aforesaid bishop also reported that, on the border of Armenia, there were certain peoples who bore children emitting a stench, and immediately sent them to the waters of the Armenians to be washed. When the Armenians immersed them in the water of baptism and drove away their innate stench, they nevertheless, once sent back, immediately returned to the rite and filth of paganism. They likewise consulted the Roman Church whether this ought to be done.

“We also then saw there the aforesaid bishop of Gabala from Syria, by whose particular efforts Antioch began fully to be subject to the Roman See. He made complaint both about his patriarch of Antioch and about the mother of Prince Baldwin, daughter of the former king of Jerusalem; and, claiming tithes by right of antiquity from spoils taken from the Saracens, according to Abraham’s example—for he, acknowledging God’s victory, gave Melchizedek tithes from his spoils—he sought the authority of the Apostolic See in this matter. We heard him lament tearfully the peril of the overseas Church after the capture of Edessa, and say that for this reason he wished to cross the Alps to the king of the Romans and of the French, to demand assistance.”

Having heard these things, Pope Eugenius, caring not for what was his own but for what he knew to be God’s, judged that the arms of the Christian princes of the West ought not to be turned against the Romans for the purpose of freeing him from exile, but should be stirred with every effort, under pontifical authority, against the Saracens who were attacking and occupying Christian lands in the East. He was the first of all to write to Louis, king of the Franks. For it was very easy to urge him toward the religious undertaking, since he had already resolved to make a pilgrimage to the holy places. Otto of Freising says the following about this (*Deeds of Frederick*, I, 34):

“Louis, secretly desiring to go to Jerusalem because his brother Philip, bound by the same vow, had been prevented by death, did not wish to delay his purpose longer. He summoned some of his princes and revealed what he was considering. At that time there was in Gaul an abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux, called Bernard, venerable in life and character, distinguished in religious observance, endowed with wisdom and literary learning, and renowned for signs and miracles. The princes decided that this man should be summoned and consulted, as though a divine oracle, concerning what ought to be done in this matter.

“The aforesaid abbot was summoned, and his advice was requested concerning the will of the aforesaid prince. Thinking it frivolous to give an answer on so great a matter by the judgment of his own authority, he replied that it would be best for the matter to be referred to the hearing and examination of the Roman pontiff. Accordingly, an embassy was sent to Eugenius and the whole matter was laid before him.

“Reviewing the examples of his predecessors—namely, that Urban, on such an occasion, had received into the unity of peace the overseas Church and the two patriarchal sees, Antioch and Jerusalem, which had been severed from obedience to the Roman See—he approved the vows of the aforesaid king for the enlargement of the practice of the Christian religion. He granted to the aforementioned abbot authority to preach and to move the minds of all toward this end, since among all the peoples of Gaul and [Col. 1007] Germany he was regarded as a prophet or apostle. Accordingly, a letter of his directed to the king and his princes is found in the following form.” Thus Otto.

That letter of Eugenius appears below.

But what happened to the pope? Surely what Christ had promised when he said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matthew 6). While Eugenius labored for the liberation of the Holy Land, God subdued his enemies, the Romans themselves. The same author says of them (*Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 31): “The venerable pontiff, having first struck Jordan, created by them patrician, and certain of his supporters with the sword of anathema, restrained them with the military aid of the people of Tivoli, the ancient enemies of the Romans, and finally compelled them to seek peace.” So it was that Eugenius returned to the City and solemnly celebrated there the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

The same author says further below concerning Eugenius’s return and entry into the City: “But Eugenius at this time made peace with the Romans, on condition that they should renounce—that is, abolish—the dignity of the patriciate; that they should restore the prefect, who was to hold that office by the pontiff’s decision, to his former dignity; and that they should retain senators by his authority. Thus, returning to the City, he celebrated there the Nativity of the Lord, as the year 1146 from the Lord’s Incarnation began.”

In a Vatican manuscript, however, Eugenius’s entry into the City is narrated thus:

“Thus, by God’s working, there was great joy throughout the City at the unexpected arrival of the pontiff himself. A vast and dense multitude of people came to meet him with branches; running continually to his footsteps, after kissing his feet they were raised to kiss his face. Standard-bearers advanced with banners; archivists and judges followed. Nor were the Jews absent from so great a joy, carrying the Mosaic Law on their shoulders. For the whole Roman choir sang together, saying: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Matthew 23). Thus, amid great joy of the people, that pontiff was able to ascend the Lateran palace.” Thus there.

Coming to Paris, Matthew Paris relates, he consecrated a certain Peter, nephew of Aimeric, chancellor of the Roman Church, as archbishop of Bourges, against the will of King Louis of France. The king, violently angered that this had been done to the injury of his dignity, publicly displayed the most sacred relics and, in the presence of many, swore that the aforesaid archbishop would not enter the city of Bourges so long as he lived. Thus for three years the king’s person lay under interdict. In whatever city, town, or castle he entered, the celebration of divine offices was suspended. At length, through the persuasion of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the king’s heart was inclined to receive the archbishop and to promise that, in atonement for the breach of his oath, he would set out for Jerusalem. Therefore a general levy was made throughout all France; neither sex nor rank nor dignity excused anyone from contributing aid to the king. At the urging of Saint Bernard, he condemned William, the usurper of the Church of York, who had been protected through fraud upon Celestine, and ordered him banished.

“Adalbert, archbishop of that place, most generously maintained at his own expense for three months the pontiff who came to Trier with eighteen cardinals for a synod” (*Chronicle of Hirsau*).—“Through Saint Bernard he obtained from Emperor Conrad and King Louis of the Franks that they should bring aid to the Christians in Asia against the followers of the Koran, undertake an expedition against the Saracens, and take the cross” (TYRE, bk. XVI, ch. 18).

And when he had withdrawn to Tivoli for a pleasant retreat, the just man, distinguished for religion, died in the year of the Lord 1152, in the month of July, as Matthew Paris says, about the beginning of the reign of Frederick I, having held the pontificate for eight years, four months, and twenty days.

Concerning his death, Baronius says the following in volume XII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*:

> “On the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July], Pope Eugenius died at Tivoli, after sitting eight years, four months, and thirteen days. The following is written concerning him in an old Vatican Library codex of the Roman pontiffs: ‘He recovered Terracina, Sezze, Narni, and the fortress of Fumone, which had long been alienated from the lordship of Saint Peter. He united the bishopric of Velletri with those of Ostia and Saint Rufina. He performed ordinations during the month of December, in which he created ten deacons, eleven priests, and sixty-one bishops. He died at Tivoli on the said eighth day before the Ides of July; from there he was borne along the public road and through the middle of the City to the Vatican, amid a very great throng of all the Roman clergy and people, with the deepest mourning and the immense shared grief of all, and was buried in the church of Saint Peter itself before the high altar.’”

So far there concerning Pope Eugenius, whom Godfrey, a writer of this period, attests at the end of the *Life of Saint Bernard* to have been distinguished by many miracles.

“Moreover, among other things, this same Eugenius earned great praise because he was most abstinent from gifts. Besides what Saint Bernard asserts, John of Salisbury says the following of him in the *Polycraticus*:

> ‘Pope Eugenius, of memory to be cherished and holiness to be imitated, whom you saw, accepted absolutely no gift from a litigant, or from anyone whom he believed was likely to have litigation. Hence, when at his arrival a certain prior of modest means, whose case he had not yet heard, urgently offered him a mark of gold with great devotion, he said: “You have not yet entered the house, and already you wish to corrupt the master?” For the holy man called that which was offered to a judge while a suit was pending corruption.’

Thus John of Salisbury concerning Eugenius.

“An outstanding memorial of these matters still survives at Terracina in the fortress, in the middle tower, on the wall facing south, in these words:

> **POPE EUGENIUS III ORDERED THIS WORK, REPRESENTING THE MEMORY OF HIS GLORY, TO BE MADE. ENDOWED WITH REMARKABLE … OF SPIRIT AND A ZEAL FOR HONOUR, HE RESTORED TO BLESSED PETER MANY ROYAL RIGHTS LOST FOR A LONG TIME. HE REDUCED THE VICES OF CERTAIN MEN TO A STANDARD OF HONOUR. [HE ORDERED] THAT THEY SHOULD ASK NOTHING FROM ANYONE, NOR RECEIVE ANYTHING FROM ANYONE BEFORE A CASE HAD BEEN DECIDED; BUT, AFTER IT HAD BEEN DECIDED, SHOULD ACCEPT WHAT WAS OFFERED MODESTLY AND WITH THANKSGIVING.**”

[Col. 1009]

# LITTLE BOOK ON THE MIRACLES OF POPE EUGENIUS III

(Dom MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, col. 1139, from a manuscript of Blessed Mary of the Mercy of God.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

Pope Eugenius III, whose miracles we here present from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Blessed Mary of the Mercy of God in the diocese of Poitiers, was called Bernard before he was raised to the supreme pontificate. Born in a town in the territory of Pisa called Montemagno, he was first a canon and vice-lord of the Church of Pisa. Then, moved by the preaching and miracles of Saint Bernard the abbot, he bade farewell to the world and withdrew to Clairvaux. There he became a monk, performed all the humble offices of the monastery, and was then sent as abbot to administer the Roman monastery of Saint Anastasius at Acquae Salviae. When he governed it vigorously, he was proclaimed supreme pontiff after the death of Pope Lucius II in 1145. Distinguished by holiness, he died in 1153.

Robert of Torigni, in his appendix to Sigebert, says the following of him:

> “In June, on the seventh day before the Ides of that month [7 June], Eugenius III, pope of venerable memory, entered upon the way of all flesh: a man exceedingly devout, generous in almsgiving, just in judgment, yet gracious and pleasant to all, poor and rich alike. At his tomb, honourably made for him in the church of Saint Peter, miracles appeared immediately after his passing.”

His epitaph in a manuscript codex of the monastery of Pont-Otrant, in the diocese of Angers, is as follows:

> Here lies Eugenius, dead in the flesh,  
> Whose holy life was lived with Christ.  
> Pisa bore the man; Clairvaux showed him forth  
> As the fruit of sacred religion.  
>   
> Thence he was transferred to the shrine of the martyr Anastasius;  
> From abbot he became the supreme father of the world.  
> July, as it bore the eighth day, snatched away  
> The solemn light and ornament of the world.  
>   
> The years from the conception of the sacred Virgin  
> Were two thousand, two hundred, and forty.

# HERE BEGINS THE MIRACLES AT THE TOMB OF LORD EUGENIUS III, ROMAN POPE

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009A]

1. Of the many things that in these days we have seen accomplished by God’s working and power, and have proved by sight to be true, we judge a few worthy both of remembrance and of writing. For we cannot refrain from speaking of the mighty works of God which we have heard and seen, since to his mighty works we owe praise, and to praise confession.

2. A certain man named John, surnamed Ritius, by nation and city a man of Castellana, had contracted hands and arms, feet and legs. Full of faith and devotion, he came to the tomb of Lord Eugenius III, that is, the pope, and with many tears and sighs prayed to the Lord for his infirmity. Suddenly the compunction of tears was followed by joy, and the health sought in prayer followed his sicknesses. This was publicly done, while the canons were singing Vespers, [Col. 1009B] and was seen by all. He had suffered thus for three years.

3. Another man, Peter by name, from the castle of Formello, had his left hand so rigidly outstretched that he could not bend or flex it for any use. His right arm too was so contracted that he could neither raise nor move it [Col. 1010A] for any purpose. On that same day and at that same hour—namely, while the praise of Vespers was being performed—before the tomb of the aforesaid Lord Eugenius, God’s mercy completely restored his weakened limbs. He had suffered for five months and was healed on the vigil of Blessed Apollinaris.

4. On the second day after this, a girl named Romana, about twelve years old, whose father was called Peter and her mother Clara, lay at the tomb of Eugenius of blessed memory, weeping, wailing, and praying for health: for the curing of her contracted arm and wholly useless right hand, and also of her legs—especially her shins, which she had lost—and likewise of her feet. She was not disappointed in her desire. At Matins, on the feast of Saint Apollinaris, through the working [Col. 1010B] and power of the Holy Spirit, she was cured of her infirmity, and her limbs were restored to their functions, so that she walked and did everything necessary. She was by birth from Reniano.

5. On the same day, a boy named Romanus, son of Saxo and his mother Gatta, from the region called the Bridge of Saint Peter, lying before the tomb of the aforesaid father, [Col. 1011A] was healed. The infirmity by which he was held was this: he had lost the use especially of his left side and left hand, which had become almost withered, and he limped with his left foot. He was entirely freed from it a little before the hour of Matins.

6. On a certain day, a Roman by birth named Stabilis lay in our choir. Lord Eugenius appeared to him in a dream and said, “Stabilis.” He answered, “Lord.” Blessed Eugenius said to him, “Do you know me?” He replied, “Very well, lord: you are my lord Eugenius.” He said to him, “Why have you not visited me?” He answered, “Where can I visit you, when it is said that you are dead?” Taking him by the hand, Eugenius led him to his own tomb and said, “If you seek me here, you will not return without grace.” [Col. 1011B] Immediately, when the bell was rung for None, he rose hastily and came to the tomb. Seeking with many tears and sighs the grace promised him by the aforesaid Lord Eugenius, he deserved to obtain it at once through God’s mercy. For his left arm and hand, which he had had so withered for many years [Col. 1012A] that he could move them for no use or service, were, by God’s mercy and the merits of our lord Eugenius, completely restored to health; they could be moved for every use and service as though he had never suffered any infirmity in arm or hand. What he had been unable to obtain from physicians through great expense, he obtained from the Lord Jesus Christ through the merits of our lord.

7. A Roman named Todinus suffered severely from tertian fevers. Fearing death, he approached the tomb of the aforesaid pontiff with the greatest confidence and was restored to complete health by God’s mercy and the merits of our lord Eugenius.

8. A man from a castle called Casamamanii, cruelly tormented by a demon [Col. 1012B] for twenty years, could not enter any church at all without the greatest injury and suffering to his most wretched body. When he entered the church of the chief of the apostles, he began to cry out, “Where are you taking me?” At last he was brought, though unwillingly, to Eugenius’s tomb and was immediately freed.

[Col. 1011]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF EUGENIUS III, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Note: [Col. 1013] For the books used, see the index prefixed to volume CLXXIX.]

(There survive three letters of Eugenius III written while he was still an abbot: the first addressed to Innocent II, and the second and third to Saint Bernard. They are printed among the letters of Saint Bernard, nos. 343, 344, and 478 [formerly 428], in *Patrologia* vol. CLXXXII, cols. 547, 548, 686.)

## [LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES]

### I. He informs P., prior of the church of Saint Frigdianus at Lucca, that, after the death of Lucius II on 15 February, he was elected pope in the church of Blessed Caesarius. He asks for prayers for himself. (2 March 1145.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchese ed., IV, 593.]

[Col. 1013A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons P., prior of Saint Frigdianus, [Col. 1014A] health and apostolic blessing.

Because we have great confidence in your religious devotion and integrity, we have taken care briefly to inform your charity of what has recently occurred concerning us. When our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Lucius, had entered the way of all flesh on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February] and had been honourably buried [Col. 1015A] in the Lateran church, our brethren—the cardinal priests and deacons, together with the bishops and subdeacons of the Holy Roman Church—assembled in the church of Blessed Caesarius. There, although unwilling and resisting, and suspecting no such thing whatsoever, I was, by a judgment of God unknown to us, elected Roman pontiff by unanimous vote and equal agreement.

Recognizing myself therefore to be burdened by so great a weight, we have thought it fitting to visit your charity by apostolic letters, asking that you offer special prayers to the Lord for me and strive to have them offered by the communities of religious brethren in those parts. We, following the custom of our predecessors, desire to love and support your persons and places, and to help you in your needs.

[Col. 1015B] Given at Narni, on 2 March.

### II. At the request of Bishop Dodo, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Huesca. (14 March 1145.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, XLVI, 289.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DODO, bishop of Huesca, and to his successors canonically appointed in his place, in perpetuity.

Matters decided by the truth of judgment ought to be entrusted to the record of letters, lest in the future they can be disturbed by the opposition of wicked men. … In the dispute between you and our brother William, bishop of Roda, concerning the churches of Belsa, Gestau, [Col. 1015C] and Alquézar, our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Innocent, had ordered restitution to be made to you. In this matter of restitution, he alleged the illness and death of his predecessor, along with certain other excuses not sufficiently reasonable; he demanded that Barbastro be restored by you to him, asserting also a certain document in the name of his predecessor which contained a determination that Urban himself had established the episcopal see to remain at Barbastro. He furthermore produced two privileges of Pope Paschal of blessed memory, derived from that same document of Urban, which likewise stated that the episcopal see was to be held at Barbastro.

You, on the other hand, produced privileges of Gregory VII and of that same Urban, [Col. 1015D] in which both Barbastro and the aforesaid churches—Belsa, Gestau, and Alquézar—had been confirmed to García and Peter, your predecessors. Having therefore heard the arguments of both parties and carefully examined the documents, we discovered that the earlier document of the said Urban, from which the other privileges of Paschal had issued, was altogether false. Having consulted our brethren on this matter, in the strictness of justice we condemned that document and the aforesaid privileges, and ordered them cut up before us. We also punished with due severity both that bishop of Roda and the persons of his church, because they had presumed to present false documents to us.

Therefore we adjudge to you and your successors in perpetuity the possession and ownership of the aforesaid Barbastro and of the other churches, namely Belsa, Gestau, and [Col. 1016A] Alquézar, with all their appurtenances; and we wholly release you from the claim of the same bishop of Roda and his successors concerning these matters. Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See, the boundaries of the bishopric of Huesca on its eastern side: namely, as the River Cinca, descending from the Pyrenean mountains, runs through hills and plains as far as the valley of Lupera—boundaries confirmed to your predecessors García and Peter by our predecessors of blessed memory, Gregory VII and the aforementioned Urban.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should not make amends by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to stern vengeance. But for all who observe these provisions, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

### III. To the Premonstratensian abbots and provosts: that they are to assemble once a year at Prémontré for the general chapter. (14 March 1145.)

[LEPAIGE, *Bibliothèque Prémontrée*, 626.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all abbots and provosts of the Premonstratensian Order: health and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1017B] For the stability of the Order and observance of religious life, it has been decreed that all abbots and provosts of the Premonstratensian Order shall gather once yearly at the chapter of Prémontré. There, by the common counsel of the brethren, they shall correct what needs correction and, with the Lord as author, establish what must be established. But now, as we have learned, some among you, alleging prohibitions from their bishops, disdain to attend so holy an assembly. Therefore, by these apostolic letters, we command and direct you in no way to neglect this most holy institution. Rather, as ordained, assemble once a year and observe without contradiction whatever shall there, as we have said, be established for the stability of the Order. Otherwise, the sentence which the abbot of Prémontré, [Col. 1017C] by the counsel of his brethren—that is, the abbots who have assembled—shall regularly pronounce upon the contemners, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, hold valid.

Given at Narni, on the eleventh day before the Ides [Note: [Col. 1017D] For “XI Id.” read “II Id.” The words “in the second year of our pontificate” were added by another hand. Read “in the first year.”] of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

### IV. He receives the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Curba-fossa (in the diocese of Luçon) under protection and confirms its possessions. (16 March 1145.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, III, p. 61.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons TESCELLINUS, abbot of Curba-fossa, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular [Col. 1017D] life.

It is fitting that we willingly grant a request shown to concern the purpose of religion and the salvation of souls, and afford suitable support to petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the church of the Holy Trinity of Curbafossa, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gift [Col. 1018A] of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: all the land of the demesne of Turgis de Tracy; at Luçon, his mill, with all the milling from all his land in that village; two sheaves of tithe from all his demesne; the tithe of woodland, whether from the sale of timber or from pasture; the share of woodland in the canons’ demesne; all the land of the demesne of Gilbert son of Adam at Luçon; six acres of land beside Richard de Rochelle’s fishpond, which he himself gave; the whole tithe from Gripon of all revenues belonging to the lord of the castle; two field-strips of vineyard at Suligneio; [Col. 1018B] one acre of land at Marceio; one fishery at Bollion; and the tithe of William of Sunilleio’s mill at Burri.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should presume to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should not make correction by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final judgment to stern vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Parma [Note: [Col. 1018D] Read: Narni.] through the hand of Robert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April [16 March], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III.

### V. Privilege for the monastery of Saint John at Kaltenborn. (20 March 1145.)

[SCHÖTTGEN and KREYSIG, *Diplomata*, II, 697.]

[Col. 1018D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GODESCHALCUS, provost, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life in the Church of Saint John the Evangelist of Kaldenborn, in perpetuity.

It accords with the clemency of apostolic governance to cherish religious persons and strengthen their places with the protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. Following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Calixtus, Honorius, and Innocent, Roman pontiffs, we confirm by apostolic authority the order of canonical life according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine which you profess. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Saint John, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings, bounty of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm [Col. 1019B] and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names:

At Nyenburgk and Gravesdorff, ten and a half *mansi* and a vineyard; at Haldenstell, eight *mansi* and a vineyard; at Helpede, one *mansus* and a vineyard; at Erardesdorff, eleven *mansi*; at Suithardesdorff, two; at Roweckesdorff, one; at Panukendorff, three; at Seburk, one half; at Aseckendorff, one; at Dielnice, one half; at Lieffdegersdorff, one half; at Deussene, thirty-seven; at Ludeslene, thirty-three, apart from other remaining *jugera* and one mill; at Storquice, seven *mansi*; at Zceulice, fourteen; at Namelickesdorff, thirty; at Czeckendorff, one half; and at Querenvorde, one half. These are situated in the bishopric of Halberstadt [Col. 1019C] and in the county of Count Palatine Frederick.

At Constebolde, eight *mansi*; at Modelwice, five; in the new village beside it, six; at Dhretis, one; at Droganice, four; at Bittine, fourteen; and at Rureschezeze, twelve. These fifty *mansi* lie in the district of Orlon.

At Sengenfeld, seven; at Durnoefeld, nine; in the other Durnefeld, one; at Rothorff, eight; at Urthern, one; at Teubecke, ten, and one mill; at Suegrestede, five; and at Vranchenhusen, two *panstadel* [uncertain tenure-unit].

When you, the present provost of that place, or any of your successors die, no one shall be placed over it through any craft of deceit or force, except the person whom the brethren, in the fear of God, shall duly provide to be elected. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should not make correction by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be alienated from the most sacred [Col. 1020A] body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final judgment to stern vengeance. But for all who observe the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Pavia [Note: [Col. 1019D] Perhaps read: Narni.] through the hand of Robert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April [20 March], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### VI. To Alvisus, bishop of Arras. (1 April 1145.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, II, 169.]

[Col. 1020B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALVISUS, bishop of Arras: health and apostolic blessing.

We have carefully considered, both from the testimony contained in the letters of your chapter and from the oral account of that priest and of your messengers, the dispute between you and the priest Hermarus concerning money which his brother had stolen from you and which you demanded of him. Having heard the arguments of both parties and diligently examined the documents, we have, with the counsel of our brethren, judged that the priest shall restore to you the same money, as he swore, without prejudice to his honour and rank. You, however, because you summoned that priest to the Apostolic See without [Col. 1020C] burdening him, shall repay him the reasonable expenses of the journey.

Given at the city of Castellana, on the Kalends of April [1 April].

### VII. He confirms the privilege of the brethren of Saint Frigdianus at Lucca, that cardinal deacons of Saint Mary the New are to be taken from their number. (5 April 1145.)

[Bullarium Latinum, 28.]

### VIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of the Prison. (8 April 1145.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, III, appendix 418, from copies of Saint Michael of Murano.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1020D] sons DOMINIC, prior of Saint Mary of Carcere, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Whenever something is requested of us which is shown to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable support to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to the prayers of our venerable brother Bellinus, bishop of Padua, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the church of Blessed Mary of Carcere, in which you are devoted to the service of God. [Col. 1021A] We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God permitting, acquire through the grant of popes, the liberality of kings, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought it proper to specify expressly:

The tithes of all newly cultivated lands which have already been made, and which shall henceforth be made, in the place called Caracetulum and at Aguciano; likewise throughout all Scudasia and Fracta. Whatever goods have also been canonically granted you by the aforesaid bishop and by his predecessor of blessed memory, Senebald, we likewise confirm. Moreover, we confirm and judge to remain valid the sentence which the aforesaid bishop Bellinus [Col. 1021B] lawfully pronounced concerning the dispute between you and the clerics of Saint Thecla of Este regarding the person of Hugh Balistarius, his son, and his property. We further decree that the canonical order established there according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the observance of the brethren of Porto shall, by God’s grace, be preserved inviolate for all time.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole for the use and complete benefit of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop [Col. 1021C] and the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 1021D] Amen.

**“Make for me, O Lord, a sign for good.”**

## IX. To William of Montpellier.  
*(9 April 1145.)*

[GARIEL, *Series episcoporum Magalonensium*, I, 122.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ WILLIAM of Montpellier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1022C] No lawful authority has ever been granted to any layman, however religious, to dispose of or exercise jurisdiction over churches or their revenues; for these must remain within the power and ordering of the bishop and other ecclesiastical persons, and must accrue to their use. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command you to permit the churches of Montpellier—namely, Holy Cross, Saint Nicholas, and others already established or to be established—to remain, as is just, in the free disposal of the bishop and clergy of the church of Maguelonne, since they are recognized as belonging by right to that church. You are not to interfere in the deposition or removal of priests therein. You are to restore in full to the church of Maguelonne the rights which the burgesses of Montpellier had forcibly withheld from that church. [Col. 1022D]

Given at the city of Castellana, on the fifth day before the Ides of April [9 April], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

[Note: [Col. 1021] The words “in the sixth year of our pontificate” have been added erroneously to the closing formula.]

## X. Privilege confirming the liberty and all the goods of the Church of Marmoutier.  
*(9 April 1145.)*

[BOCHELLUS, *Opera of Gregory of Tours*. Paris, 1610, 18mo. Appendix, p. 130.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GARNER, abbot of the Greater Monastery of Blessed Martin, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in Christ.

[Col. 1023A] Although, by the office of the apostolate laid upon us by God, we are debtors to all the children of the Catholic Church, it is especially fitting that we devote a more earnest care of charity to those known to belong more particularly to the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, granting our favourable assent with due kindness to your just petitions, both because of devotion and reverence for blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, and because of the pre-eminence of true religion, we have received under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See, for special care, the aforesaid monastery built by that glorious confessor of Christ, Martin, following the example of our predecessors of holy memory, Urban, Paschal, and Callixtus II, Roman pontiffs. We decree that [Col. 1023B] whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God permitting, acquire through the grant of popes, the benefactions of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought it proper to specify expressly:

In the district of Chartres, the church of Saint Martin of the Valley, with its churches, tithes, and all appurtenances.

In the district of Soissons, the church of Saint Mary of Châtillon, with its appurtenances; and the church of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius, with all appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Troyes, [Col. 1023C] the church of Saint Mary of Ramerenc, with its churches, tithes, and all appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen of Arcis, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Rassermis, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Susanna and the church of Saint Nabor, with their appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Coutances, the church of Saint German of Healville; the church of Saint Peter of Bueville; the church of Saint Peter of Hereville; and the portion of tithe which you possess in the parish of Guasteville; likewise the churches on the island of Greneliac: Saint Peter of Port, Saint Mary of Toreville, Saint Samson, the Holy Trinity, Saint Andrew, and Saint Martin of Laberlussa, with their appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Exeter, Harpeford and Wella. In the bishopric of Lincoln, [Col. 1023D] Vuingla. In the bishopric of Bordeaux, the church of Saint Dionysius, with its appurtenances. In the bishopric of Bazas, the church of Saint Mary Magdalene, with its appurtenances. In the bishopric of Paris, the church of Saint Nicholas of Gonesse, with its appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Alet, the church of Saint Martin of the Castle of Goscelin, with all its appurtenances, and what you possess in the church of Saint Mary of that same castle; the church of Miniac of Podrohoit [lacuna], with all that belongs to it; the church of Saint Peter of Imphintic, with its appurtenances; the church of Talenceac, with its appurtenances; and the church which you possess in the castle of Ploasmel.

In the bishopric of Le Mans, the church of Saint Hippolytus [Col. 1024A] of Vivoin, with its churches, tithes, and all appurtenances; the church of Saint Albin of the Vines; and the church of Saint Mary of Noyon, with their appurtenances. In the bishopric of Poitiers, the churches of Quidmicheriis, with their appurtenances; saving the canonical right of the bishops in whose parishes the aforesaid churches are situated.

[Col. 1024B] In the parish churches which you hold, you shall choose priests to whom, if they are suitable, the bishop of the parish shall commit the cure of souls; such priests are to render to the bishop an account concerning the people, but to you the due subjection regarding temporal matters.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any craft of deception or violence, unless he whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel from among your community, shall, until a suitable person is found there, provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall go for consecration either to the Roman pontiff or to whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, according to the constitution of our aforesaid lord Pope Paschal; and, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he shall grant what is requested.

The chrism, holy oil, and ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders are to be received from the bishops of the places in whose dioceses your brethren dwell, provided that they enjoy the favour and communion of the Apostolic See. If they refuse to provide that favour without improper exaction, they may receive the sacraments of consecration from whatever Catholic bishop they prefer.

[Col. 1024C] We strictly forbid public Masses to be celebrated in the aforesaid monastery, or a station to be held there, by any archbishop or bishop, lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of the servants of God. We also forbid anyone to compel the monks of that place, against their own will and that of the abbot, to go to any church for a station or for the celebration of funerals. [Col. 1024D] Adding further, and desiring that no archbishop or bishop henceforth presume, for any cause and in any place, to excommunicate the Greater Monastery of Blessed Martin or the monks of that Greater Monastery: every more serious case concerning them shall depend upon the judgment of the Apostolic See.

Nor are the brethren of your cells, wherever situated, to suffer suspension of the divine offices on account of any interdict or excommunication. Rather, both the monks and their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to the monastic profession, shall, with the doors of the churches closed and diocesan officials not admitted, celebrate the offices of divine service and perform the rites due at burial. [Col. 1024D]

Furthermore, we add that the same monastery of Blessed Martin shall remain, God permitting, free from the subjection of all mortals, subject only to the Roman Church, and shall enjoy such liberty and authority. We also confirm to you all that has been confirmed by the authentic privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs.

[Col. 1025A] Therefore let no person whatsoever rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all be preserved whole for the complete benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; [Col. 1025B] and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.
