We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass by unjust vexations the altars belonging to it or their ministers; but that all things shall be kept intact [Col. 1159A] for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly disregarding this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1159B] so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Julius, cardinal priest of St. Marcellus. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo. [Col. 1159C] I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Bavo, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1146 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CXXXI. To the Abbot and Monks of Bec.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 10.)*

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 682.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1159D] sons LEARD, abbot of Bec, and his brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office exhorts us to cherish more earnestly those whom we know to be more devoted toward the holy Roman Church and toward ourselves, and to confirm their right to them by the protection of the Apostolic See. For this reason, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Rotrod, Bishop of Évreux, we willingly grant assent to your just petitions. We confirm to you by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, possession of the church of the Holy Trinity of Bellomonte, with all its appurtenances, canonically adjudged to you by our venerable brother H., Archbishop of Rouen—provided always that the prebends of the surviving [Col. 1160A] canons remain intact. If anyone, knowingly disregarding this page of our confirmation, should attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Viterbo, on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

### CXXXII. Privilege for the Monastery of Peterborough.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 17.)*

[Hugh Candidus, *History of the Monastery of Peterborough*, p. 78, in Sparke, *Histories of English Writers*.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MARTIN, abbot of Peterborough, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1160B] It is fitting that we willingly grant a request recognized as pertaining to the purpose of religious life and the salvation of souls, and give appropriate assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Martin, since through many labors you have visited the thresholds of the apostles and our presence with due devotion, we graciously assent to your and your brothers’ just petitions. We take under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of Peterborough, of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions and goods the same church now [Col. 1160C] justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the benefactions of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or by other lawful means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

In Northamptonshire, Burch, formerly called Medeshamstede, where the monastery itself is situated, with chapels, market, toll, mint, marshes, woodland, and its other appurtenances. In Farseta, two fishermen with two holdings of land, and two boats on Whitlesmere; the castles with the church and chapels adjacent to that church, with mills and all their appurtenances; Witherington [Col. 1160D] and Walton with their appurtenances; Glinton and Peakirk, with church and chapels, with the toll of Deeping and Peakirk, fishing rights, and other appurtenances; Pilesgate with its appurtenances. In the church of Barnack, ten shillings; in Stamford, fifty-nine holdings of land, with lands, mills, churches, toll, and mint. In that same town in Lincolnshire, seven holdings; Tinguellam, with church, mill, and other appurtenances; Oundle, with church and chapels, and with all the right adjoining that town which is called Etehundred, with mill, market, toll, woods, and appurtenances. Eisetuna, with its mills and appurtenances. Wermingtune, with churches, mills, and its other appurtenances. Heteringe [Col. 1161A] with church, mill, and its appurtenances. In Hirtlingburch, ten hides, with church, mill, and appurtenances. In Stanwiggat, three hides, with church, mill, and appurtenances. In Haldewincla, three hides, with church and appurtenances. Coringham, with church, mills, and other appurtenances—namely, Beinfield, Driffeld, and Middletum—with the forest; Pithesle, with church, mills, and appurtenances. In Northampton, sixteen holdings. In Lincolnshire, Scotere, with church, mills, and appurtenances—namely, Nortorps, Scaltorp, and Fhiskertun, with church and its appurtenances. In Hoylande, three carucates of land, with saltworks. In Walecote, seven carucates of land. In Turlebi, one carucate and three bovates of land, with church and appurtenances. [Col. 1161B] In the city of Lincoln, four holdings. In Graham (*mansuras*, S. W.), a holding and land which Colgrim gave to the church of Burch. In Torkeseies, eighteen leagues of meadow, one fishery, and one holding. In Nottinghamshire, Colingham, with churches, mills, fisheries, and appurtenances. In Huntingdonshire, Alwoltum, with church, mills, toll on ships, and appurtenances. Flettona, with church and appurtenances. In the borough of Huntingdon, the land of Godric Lefled. In Leicestershire, Estun, with the church of Brynehirst, with mill and other appurtenances. In Lenna, one holding. In Wella, four thousand eels annually. In Cloptuna, one virgate of land.

We have likewise thought fit to record the following properties held in fief from the monastery itself: [Col. 1161C] the fief of Viz Ansketilly of St. Medard—Thornawe (*Thornehage*, S.), Witeringa, Sibertune, Estune, and Angostebi, with their appurtenances; the fief of Roger the younger, of Torpel, Ufferwrthe (*Ufforde*, S. W., as it is now incorrectly called), Pilktune with its appurtenances, and the land which he holds in Mokeseie; the fief of Ascelin of Waterville—Torp, Marham, and Uptun, with their appurtenances; the fief of Ralph son of William—Ludintun and Messingham, with their appurtenances; the fief of Geoffrey the younger—Gunnetorp, Suttorp, and the land which he holds in Stokes, with their appurtenances; the fief of Geoffrey de la Mare—Makeseie and Turlebi, with their appurtenances; the fief of Ralph of Neuville—Scotuna and Malmintun, with their appurtenances; [Col. 1161D] the fief of Roger Malfet (*Malfe*, W.)—Wodeford, with its appurtenances; the fief of Robert Frehlle—Dalmtun, with its appurtenances; the fief of William de Lwetot—Cloptuna, with its appurtenances; the fief of Robert Marmion—Langetun and Pokebroc, with their appurtenances; the fief of Geoffrey of Winchester—Armestun and Burchle (*Burgelai*, S. and W.); the fief of Gilbert Fawele and Robert de Fisi—Subtuna (*Suttona*, S. W.), with its appurtenances; the fief of Roger of Miletuna, with its appurtenances; the fief of Ralph de Tot, in Pastona; the fief of Walon in the same town, with its appurtenances; the fief of Isenbard—Paple (*Pappelai*, S.), with its appurtenances; the fief of Wirmund—Stokes, with its appurtenances; the fief of Ingelram, in the same town; the fief of Robert de Oili—Craneford; [Col. 1162A] the fief of Richard Engaine—Benigfeld; the fief of William Engaine—Haregrave, with its appurtenances; the fief of Theobald—Brinighirst (*Brenehirst*, S.), with its appurtenances; the fief of Godfrey of Cambrai—Plumbetere (*Plumbetre*, S. W.) and Berham, with their appurtenances; the fief of Robert de Guineges—Careby, with its appurtenances; the fief of Geoffrey of Neuville—Walecote, with its appurtenances; the fief of Eylsi—Helpetune, with its appurtenances. At Winewich, the holding of Brithwold (*Brutwaldi*, S. W.); the fief of Pancewolt in Estona; the fief of Ansered (*Ansredii*, S. W.) in Overtona and in Torp. In Ermestun, the holding of Turiei. In Kirkefeld (*Chirchefeld*, S. W.), Wermingtun, and Oundle, the holding of Vivian; in Wodecroft, the holding of Osbern; in Muscam, the holding of Gerold.

[Col. 1162B] We likewise confirm to you the liberties granted to that same monastery by the kings of England in pious devotion and confirmed by their charters, as well as the monastery’s ancient and reasonable customs. Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brothers, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall provide to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

Furthermore, following in the footsteps of our most holy predecessor Pope Gregory, we absolutely forbid public masses to be celebrated by a bishop in your monastery, lest, in the retreats and dwelling-places of the servants of God, any occasion be afforded for popular [Col. 1162C] gatherings or for a new admission of women—something wholly harmful to their souls. Nor may a bishop dare to exercise authority to command, or to perform any ordination, however slight, unless invited by the abbot of the place, so that the monks may always remain under the authority of their abbots; and no one may retain a monk in any church, or promote him to any order, without the testimony or permission of his abbot.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations whatever; but that all things shall be kept intact, for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance [Col. 1162D] and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly disregarding this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards [Col. 1163A] of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest, have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of St. Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal priest, have subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon, have subscribed. I, Damian, deacon, have subscribed. I, . . . . . . . of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1163B] on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and forty-six of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CXXXIII. Privilege for the Same Monastery.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 20.)*

[Hugh Candidus, *History of the Monastery of Peterborough*, p. 82, in Sparke, *Histories of English Writers*, p. 82.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MARTIN, abbot of Peterborough, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever a matter is requested of us which is recognized as consistent with religion and propriety, it is fitting that we willingly [Col. 1163C] grant it and give fitting assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Martin, since through many labors you have visited the thresholds of the apostles and our presence with due devotion, we graciously assent to your and your brothers’ just petitions. What, from your right, you have granted to the sacristy of your monastery through devotion and reasonable foresight, we also grant and confirm by the page of this present writing.

Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the chapels of the parishes of Burch, Torp, Pastun, and Oxneya; the churches of Kateringa (*Castere*, W.; *Catere*, C.; but correctly *Keterniga*, S.), Wermingtun (here S. adds “of Peikircha”), and, from the church of [Col. 1163D] Oundle, one mark of silver. From the church of Bernak, ten shillings; from Marham, ten shillings; from the land of Groham, one mark; from Hirtlingburch, Aldewincle, and Stanwigge, two parts of the demesne tithe; from Thornhage and Witering, two parts of the demesne tithe of Geoffrey of St. Medard; two parts of the tithe of Roger of Torpel, Ivo of Gunnetorp, Geoffrey Fawel, Ascelin de Tot, Robert Peverel, Turold of Miltun, Hugh of Gimiges, Guido Malfet, William of Cloptune, Martin of Pappele, Roger of Wodecroft, Gilbert of Bernoke, Geoffrey son of Sucin, Ralph of Glinton, Richard Salide of Badinton (*et Selide de Badingtona*, S., fol. 100), Robert of Wauton, and Robert of Wodecroft; from the Soke of Glinton, and the entire demesne tithe [Col. 1164A] of Gilbert the clerk of Uffewrte. From Aluric of Witherington, two shillings; from Ansfrid of Turlebi, twelve pence; from Odo of Witheringtun, twelve pence; Pilergate with the soke; the church of Castre, with chapels, tithes, lands, and all things belonging to it; the land of Alsuart of Burch; and fifteen acres next to the granges of the abbot of Burch; the marshes of Wodehithe (*Wudehyda*, S.) as far as Lawe; the land of Godric Lefled in Huntingdon (*Huntendone*); the service of Aluric the mason; of Aelred the shoemaker (*Egelredi*, S.); Walter the Englishman; Lefwin (*Leawini*, S.) the carpenter; Godwinicarlet Sinodi foci [“Godwinicarlet of Sinod’s hearth,” apparently uncertain; *Coci S. Sinothi Coci*, W.]; Alaric; and Norman the secretary. From Robert of Wodecroft, seven shillings for one holding in Burch, and two shillings for the land [Col. 1164B] which he holds in the soke of Glintun and for the land which Bonde holds in Peikirke; the land which belonged to Litlebrand in Burch, and two houses held by Ulric (*Alfricus*, S.), priest. From Ralph (all as far as “therefore no king” is lacking in S.) de la Mare, ten shillings each year—five on Palm Sunday, for celebrating the anniversary of Lord Abbot Turold, and five at the feast of St. Michael for the soul of his wife. From Guido of Miltun, five shillings.

Abbot Martin acquired these privileges and protections at Rome. And since our writing still deals with these matters, no king, prince, or any powerful person, ecclesiastical or secular, may dare rashly to remove, take away, retain, diminish, or harass with any molestations these same goods from the office of the sacristy. But if anything there must be altered, increased, or diminished, it shall be done by the counsel and assent of the abbot and of the brothers collectively, or of their sounder part. If anyone knowingly presumes rashly to act against this page of our constitution, let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. Amen, amen, amen.  
*(Eugenius and the others named above in the preceding bull subscribing.)*

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction, [Col. 1164D] in the year one thousand one hundred and forty-six of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CXXXIV. To T[heobald], Bishop of Verona.—He admonishes him to order the observance of the excommunication pronounced against the enemies of the canons by the priests of Runcho and others.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 23.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 785.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother T., Bishop of Verona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you remember that we confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See the excommunication against the persecutors of the Church of Verona and the interdict of the city canonically proclaimed by you, [Col. 1165A] and ordered that they be firmly observed. But, as we have learned, neither the priests of Runcho nor many others observe that interdict and excommunication. Since it will therefore profit little to place sacrilegious persons under interdict or excommunicate them if the sentence is not observed, we command and order you by apostolic letters to ensure its firm observance until worthy satisfaction is made; and likewise to ensure observance of that sentence which you canonically pronounced against the priests of Runcho for contempt and disobedience. Concerning the other priests who have scorned to observe it, administer justice nevertheless according to the ordinance of the canons; and restrain Odel, Saccetus, and Eleazamur by ecclesiastical censure from harassing the canons. You also, in accordance with the obligation of your office, shall diligently provide for the peace and tranquillity of these your brothers.

Given at Viterbo, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CXXXV. To L[othair], Bishop of Vicenza.—That he punish the archpriest of St. Boniface, who has communicated with excommunicated persons.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 23.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, p. 786.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother L., Bishop of Vicenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

A complaint has reached our ears that the archpriest of St. Boniface presumes to communicate with certain wrongdoers excommunicated [Col. 1165C] for injuries and wrongs inflicted upon the Church of Verona, and has even, in rash boldness, imposed a cross upon one of them. We do not believe that your brotherhood is unaware of the gravity of his offence in this matter. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and order you to administer such justice concerning that archpriest that he may suffer punishment worthy of his presumption, and that others, through the example of his correction, may fear to perpetrate similar acts.

Given at Viterbo, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CXXXVI. Privilege for the Monastery of St. George in the Diocese of Prüfening.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 23.)*

[Hund, *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, III, 132.]

[Col. 1165D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ERBO, abbot of the monastery of St. George of Brufening, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, for this purpose: that we may cherish religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever acceptably rendered unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved from perversity. Therefore, all lovers of the Christian faith ought to cherish religion and to foster more attentively venerable places [Col. 1166A] together with the persons devoted to divine service therein, so that they may not be troubled by any molestations of wicked people or wearied by oppressive and burdensome demands.

For this reason, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We take under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Blessed George of Brufening, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions and places have been canonically bestowed upon your monastery by Otto, bishop of Bamberg of good memory, and by his successor Engilbert, or may hereafter be conferred upon that place by their successors or other faithful people of God in the same manner, or by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the benefactions [Col. 1166B] of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or by other reasonable means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the church of Schambach; Homburch with its appurtenances; Gebenpach with its appurtenances; Oberdorf with adjacent vineyards; the church of Neunkirchen; Irenreut; Dietpurgreut with its appurtenances; Avve, Achebach, Buche, and Bruckedorf.

No one whatsoever may presume to demand tithes from you for the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. We further add that, in churches which are on the land of your monastery, you may choose honorable priests, who are to be presented by you to the bishop; and, if they are suitable, are to receive the care of souls from that bishop and render account to him in spiritual matters but to you in temporal matters. [Col. 1166C] If a general interdict is imposed in that land, you may, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded from your church, and with the doors closed, celebrate divine offices in a low voice. We also grant that the burial-place of the same monastery shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the right of the mother church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations whatever; but that all things shall be kept intact [Col. 1166D] for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly disregarding this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last [Col. 1167A] judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of St. Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of St. Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. [Col. 1167B] I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of the title of St. George at the Velum Aureum, have subscribed. I, Guido, minister of the altar in the Roman Church, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1146 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CXXXVII. Privilege for the Monastery of St. Margaret at Osterhofen.  
*(A.D. 1146, December 23.)*

[Monumenta Boica, XII, 334.]

[Col. 1167C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons TRUTHMAR, provost of the church of St. Margaret at Osterhofen, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Since the unity of charity cannot endure without the worship of true religion, nor can an office pleasing to God be offered, it befits apostolic authority to love religious persons and to fortify their places with pious protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, [Col. 1167D] decreeing that whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter be able to acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the benefactions of princes, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Certainly, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. We also decree that the canonical Order, according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institutions of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, we prohibit anyone of your profession, prompted by frivolity or under the pretext of a stricter religion, from leaving the cloister without permission of the provost or of your congregation; [Col. 1168A] and, if he leaves, no bishop, abbot, or any person whatsoever shall dare to retain him without the security of letters shared by the parties. If, however, when summoned a second or third time, he scorns to return, the provost of that place may pronounce canonical sentence against him.

Likewise, during a general interdict of that land, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, you may celebrate the offices in a subdued voice. You shall receive ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them to you freely and without any improper condition; otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. Furthermore, we prohibit any advocate from harassing your place, its people, or its goods with unjust or undue exactions. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the right of the mother church being preserved.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but [Col. 1168C] that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop being preserved. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall hereafter rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place, [Col. 1168D] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Viterbo, the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December], indiction 10, in the year of the Lord 1146, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CXXXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Windberg. (23 December 1146.)

[HUND., *Metropol. Salisb.*, III, 490.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GEBEHARD, provost of the church of Windberg, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1169A] It is fitting that we readily grant a desire known to pertain to the purpose of religion and the salvation of souls, and afford suitable support to the wishes of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter be able to acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the benefaction of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

[Col. 1169B] Among these, we have judged that the following should be expressly named: namely, the church of Saizcovia, with the adjoining allod and all its appurtenances; likewise the wood adjoining your mountain on the road to Mulbach; Virlebach with all its appurtenances; Embra with its appurtenances; Syrinchke with its appurtenances; Mainckoven with its appurtenances; and Vennebach with its appurtenances. We also decree, in accordance with the devotion of Count Albert of blessed memory, founder of your church, that the eldest person of his lineage shall defend your place and its goods from the assaults of evil persons for the salvation of his soul, and that no one shall impose exactions upon them. If he proves unfit, you may, with the counsel of the bishop of Bamberg, remove him from that defense and appoint another suitable person.

Certainly, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you [Col. 1169C] on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. We also decree that the canonical Order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institutions of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Moreover, we prohibit anyone of your profession, prompted by frivolity or under the pretext of a stricter religion, from leaving the cloister without permission of the provost or of your congregation. If he leaves, no bishop, abbot, or monk shall dare to retain him without the security of letters shared by the parties. If, when summoned a second or third time, he scorns to return, the provost of that [Col. 1169D] place may pronounce canonical sentence against him.

Likewise, during a general interdict of that land, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, you may celebrate the divine offices in a subdued voice. You shall receive ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them to you freely and without improper condition; otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or [Col. 1170A] under interdict; the right of the mother church being preserved.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop being preserved. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall hereafter rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; [Col. 1170B] let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guy, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December], indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CXXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary at Abingdon. (23 December 1146.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 107.]

[Col. 1170C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons INGULF, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Abingdon, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity: greeting.

A petition of pious intention ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding result, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, [Col. 1170D] receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of the holy Mother of God, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter be able to acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these, we have judged that the following should be expressly named: the place itself in which your monastery is founded; the hundred of Hornimere; Abingdon; and the market, with all its liberties and customs, as the kings of England [Col. 1171A] have granted them to you; together with Cumnor and Bertuna, and all appendages of the hundred; Marcham, Middleton, Drayton, Saringeford, Wlachenesfeld, with all their appendages; the church of Saint Mary of Colum with its appurtenances; the church of Cinsentuna and two hides, with their adjacent lands; the church of the Holy Innocents and our hospices beside the church in London, on the Westminster road; the church of Saint Martin and the church of Saint Aldad, and whatever land and right you have at Drenford; the church of Miuneham; the church of Sustuna; Lating; Garing; Ferneberg; Witteham; Apesford with its appurtenances; Offenton; Gost; Urdeham; Cerm; Wuelteford; Chivelaun; Vuinekefeto; and Visselea, with their appurtenances; [Col. 1171B] Chuleham, Chutesdon, Leonechenora, Thademerton, Bereden, Lechamsterdam, Lemvartona, Tubbeneia, Linford, and Fageflor, with all adjacent lands.

In the shire of Gloucester: Dulueltuna and Cirne, with their appurtenances. In Chilton: five hides. In Pesth: two hides. In Dencheswrdea: seven hides. In Bocland: five hides. In Chadeleswrda: four hides which belonged to Ralph Basset. In Gersendon: twenty hides. In Cestreton: one hide. In Hulla: two hides. In Bereford: five hides. In Hernicota: two hides. In Sultuna: one hide and the mill of Henovara. In Fencota: one hide. In Benneham: two hides, by the gift of Humphrey de Bohun. In Niweham: [Col. 1171C] one fishery with its appurtenances. In Colebroch: whatever land and right you possess by the gift of Milo Crispin and Robert Geruum. In Dumeltuna: one hide by the gift of William Guizemboez, and half a hide by the gift of King Henry. In Stretona: one hide and three virgates by the gift of Henry de Albenneio.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, provide to be elected. Furthermore, we prohibit anyone who has made profession there from daring to depart from that monastery without the permission [Col. 1171D] of the abbot and his brethren; and no one shall dare to retain one who departs.

We also decree that no one whatsoever may alter the order established there according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict in your monastery, where brethren live professing the regular life; nor shall any bishop in future times dare to expel from your monastery brethren of that religious profession when the abbot and brethren do not consent. We also grant that burial in the monastery shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Moreover, we confirm to you forever all liberties and reasonable customs of your monastery granted to you by the kings of England and your bishops, and confirmed in their writings, [Col. 1172A] as you have hitherto possessed and held them in peace.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishops being preserved. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall hereafter rashly attempt to act [Col. 1172B] against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve that place’s rights, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. [Col. 1172C] I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Ubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Manfred, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Velum Aureum, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary Nova, have subscribed. I, Cithius, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 1172D] Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guy, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December], indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CXL. The regular order of the Canons of Saint Augustine established at Klosterneuburg, together with its other privileges and immunities, both temporal and spiritual, is confirmed by apostolic authority. (27 December 1146.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, I, 338, from the original.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MARQUARD, provost, and the brethren in the monastery of Saint Mary of Neuburg, situated in the diocese of Passau, [Col. 1173A] professing the canonical life, both present and future: in perpetuity.

Although, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by the Lord, we are debtors to all churches and ecclesiastical persons, it is nevertheless fitting for us to devote more earnest care to those whom we know to strive especially after the service of almighty God and observance of the regular order. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the guardianship and protection of the same prince of the apostles the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, offered to blessed Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of the Apostolic See.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order [Col. 1173B] known to have been instituted in that place according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be preserved there perpetually in future times. Likewise, the goods and possessions which the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of emperors, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these, we judge that the following should be expressly named: namely, the estate and people of Neuburg on both sides of the river, with the tithe and parochial right, and the chapels with their appurtenances. Likewise, the villages of Altentoe, Struphigrn, Rugestorff, Haselbac, Seweindorf, Tattendorff, Haduartesdorff, Vezendorff, [Col. 1173C] Pirinbom, Eberhartesdorff, Pruche, Wilantesdorff, and Miverlingen, with the other estates and vineyards belonging to your right.

We also decree that in chapels founded or to be founded on your possessions, no one shall minister without your permission. A sentence canonically pronounced upon your parishioners by you, the provost, or any of your successors, shall be held valid by apostolic authority. Certainly, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You shall receive ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing [Col. 1173D] to administer them to you freely and without any improper condition; otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

We also grant that burial in your place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the right of the mother church being preserved. Upon the death of you, the present provost of the same place, upon your transfer to the rule of another church, or upon the death of any of your successors, no one shall be placed or substituted there by any artifice of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part [Col. 1174A] of the brethren, shall canonically provide to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

Moreover, we prohibit anyone of your profession, prompted by frivolity or under the pretext of a stricter religion, from leaving the cloister without permission of the provost or congregation. If he leaves, no bishop, abbot, or monk shall receive him without the security of letters shared by the parties, so long, namely, as the pattern of canonical order in your church, by the Lord’s favor, remains in force. If, when summoned a second or third time, he scorns to return, the provost of that place may pronounce canonical sentence against him.

Also assenting to the devout petition of your congregation, we decree by the present ordinance that no advocate [Col. 1174B] of the aforesaid church shall be appointed except from the house and lineage of Liupald, margrave of blessed memory, and then only by your own choice, provided that no burden or exaction is inflicted upon that place in return for his protection. If he proves unfit for the aforesaid church and, after being warned a second or third time, does not amend, you and your successors may remove him from such administration and substitute another suitable person for him.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way [Col. 1174C] of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop being preserved. As a sign of this freedom received from the Roman Church, moreover, you shall pay to us and our successors one bezant annually.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall hereafter rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that [Col. 1174D] place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, in the future, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Velum Aureum, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Saint Rufina, have subscribed. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy minister of the altar in the Roman Church, have subscribed. [Col. 1175A] I, Ubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy deacon of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary Nova, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guy, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [27 December], indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CXLI. He grants Bishop Eberhard of Bamberg the right of the pallium and other privileges. (31 December 1146.)

[USSERMAN, *Episcopatus Bambergensis, Probationes*, 103.]

[Col. 1175B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, . . . to EBERHARD, bishop of Bamberg, and to his successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Although, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, we are debtors to all children of the holy Church, it is nevertheless fitting for us to devote a more earnest zeal of charity to those places and persons known to have a more special connection with the Apostolic See.

For this reason, venerable brother Bishop Eberhard, whom . . . concerning the ordinations of clerics, etc., as in the privilege of Innocent II, given 20 October 1139 (*Patrologia*, CLXXIX, no. 420). On the feast of blessed King Henry, whose body is believed to rest in that church. Of which pallium indeed . . . to ride, [Col. 1175C] as in the passage cited.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guy, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, the second day before the Kalends of January [31 December], indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CXLII. He sends back and commends Henry, bishop of Moravia, to Conrad, king of the Romans. (31 December 1146.)

[BOCZEK, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, I, 238.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ CONRAD, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1175D] On behalf of our beloved son C. [Eberhard], bishop-elect of Bamberg, we have received and carefully considered letters and petitions from Your Nobility and from many religious and discerning men. Although we greatly love the Church of Bamberg as a special daughter of the Apostolic See, and the man himself because of his learning and integrity, yet, moved by your petitions and recommendations of his person, and having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, we consecrated him as bishop of that church with our own hands, as it were the hands of blessed Peter. Having renewed the provisions made by our predecessors concerning the dignity of his church, we have sent him back to his church with the favor of the Apostolic See and under the protection of our letters.

Concerning the duke of Poland, regarding whom we likewise received your requests, [Col. 1176A] we wish Your Affection to know that we await his envoys during the coming Lent. If they come then, after more diligently investigating the truth of the matter, we shall willingly do, for love of you, whatever we can do with God’s honor—since we love your person with true charity in the Lord as a special soldier of blessed Peter, and wish to grant your requests in accordance with God.

Moreover, we receive with paternal kindness our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Moravia, because of his religious character and integrity and also because of his own recommendation. Although we should most gladly retain him with us for some time in the highest honor and affection, as a religious man beloved by God, nevertheless, because we know that he is necessary to you, we have thought fit to send him back to Your Nobility. [Col. 1176B] In return, therefore, we commend him to your affection all the more earnestly. We ask that for love of us you hold him dearer than dear, and humbly comply with his salutary admonitions.

Given at Viterbo, the second day before the Kalends of January [31 December].

### CXLIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Sept-Fontaines. (1146.)

[HUGO, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, II, 1189.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BESCELIN, abbot of Sept-Fontaines, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1176C] The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, in order that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For service is never rendered acceptable to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved by the purity of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, subject to a rent of twelve Châlons denarii payable to the church of Saint Peter of the Mount, we receive the church of Saint Nicholas under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now [Col. 1176D] justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the benefactions of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these, we have judged that the following should be expressly named: by the gift of Count Theobald, the place called Novus, with its appurtenances, with the consent of Bishop Bartholomew and Bartholomew, treasurer of Laon; by the gift of Archbishop Raynald and of the Church of Rheims, the site of a mill in the place called Wandra; whatever Bartholomew and his son, also Bartholomew, conferred upon you as alms; the field of Bovo, granted to you with the consent of his son Walter and of Hugh of Fixa, with his wife’s assent. By the gift [Col. 1177A] of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres: the church of Andelo and the church of Saint Aper with its appurtenances. By the gift of Henry, bishop of Toul: the allod of Boanivilla and the church of Geburvat. By the gift of Geoffrey of Jovilla: the place called Sept-Fontaines with its appurtenances, and the tithes of that place from the chapter of Molesme, subject to an annual payment of two solidi in Toul currency. By the gift of Haimo and Odo: the place called Radun. By the gift of Gosbert: the place called Bonus.

We confirm by the page of this present writing the agreement reasonably made between you and the church of Crista concerning pastures and other matters, and likewise the agreement between you and the monks of Saxifontaine concerning the land of Saint Mary. Certainly, no cleric or layman whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you [Col. 1177B] on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. We also decree that the canonical Order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the reasonable institutions of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. No lay brother, after making profession, may leave that cloister without the permission of the abbot and chapter; and no one shall dare to retain one who leaves.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact [Col. 1177C] for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop being preserved. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall hereafter rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights in that place, [Col. 1177D] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given in the year 1146, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III, etc.

### CXLIV. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury. (1146.)

[Only a notice of this privilege survives in the chronicles of W. Thorn, in TWISDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, II, 1807.]

### CXLV. To Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. (1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 653.]

[Col. 1178A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren HUGH, bishop of Auxerre, and G., bishop of Langres, and to his dearest son B., abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The administration of the Apostolic See, in whose service we labor though unworthy, makes us debtors to all churches. And just as we rejoice in their peace and tranquility, so, if anyone disturbs them with undue troubles [Col. 1178B] and vexations, we grieve with paternal affection and are earnestly concerned to provide for them kindly, both through ourselves and through our brethren.

We have learned that our son W., count of Nevers, is endeavoring, contrary to justice and ancient custom, to burden the venerable monastery of Saint Mary of Vézelay, by compelling our beloved sons Pons, its abbot, and the brethren of that place, together with their burgesses, to leave the town of Vézelay for the purpose of rendering or receiving justice, contrary to the provisions of the privileges of the Apostolic See. Since that monastery belongs to blessed Peter and stands under the patronage and protection of the holy Roman Church, we can neither fail it nor ought to fail it in the maintenance of its rights. [Col. 1178C] Therefore, by this present writing we command you to take care earnestly to admonish the same count on our behalf that henceforth he shall not compel either the abbot, the monks, or the burgesses to leave the aforesaid town in matters of this kind. If he attempts this, we shall not be able to refrain from taking severe vengeance for the injury done to blessed Peter.

### CXLVI. To William, count of Nevers.—That he shall not compel the monks and burgesses of Vézelay to leave Vézelay in order to render or receive justice. (1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 649.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1178D] son WILLIAM, count of Nevers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Venerable places and religious persons who have fixed their purpose upon God’s service ought not to be shaken by any burdens or harassed by any vexations. We have learned, to our great astonishment, that you are compelling our beloved sons Pons, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Vézelay, together with their burgesses, contrary to the provisions of the privileges of the Apostolic See, to leave Vézelay in order to render or receive justice. We bear this all the more gravely because that monastery has a particularly close connection with the Apostolic See and appears properly to belong to its defense and patronage.

It is therefore unworthy of you, and wholly foreign to the conduct of Catholic princes, [Col. 1179A] that the ordinances of the most holy Roman Church should be rashly set aside by anyone—its privileges, divinely rooted, can in no way be uprooted. By this present writing we command Your Nobility that henceforth you shall not compel either the abbot, the monks of the aforesaid monastery, or their burgesses to leave Vézelay in the above-mentioned matters. If you neglect to obey our admonitions and commands, we shall not be able to refrain from vindicating the injury done to blessed Peter, as the duty of our office requires.

### CXLVII. To the same.—That he cease from harassing the people of Vézelay. (1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 650.]

[Col. 1179B] **EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman WILLIAM, count of Nevers: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

You cannot be unaware with what devotion your father always clung to the Apostolic See, how zealously he loved what he knew belonged to it, and how carefully he sought to foster and uphold it. Therefore blessed Peter honored him while he lived, advanced him, and enlarged his lands; and, at the end of this fleeting life, received him into the fellowship of holy men, opened to him the gates of the heavenly kingdom, and, as we believe, happily placed him among the holy companies in the eternal palace. Our predecessors also loved him with due affection and effectively assisted him in his necessities. We too, in our time, have loved and honored your person and household with paternal kindness, as a special household of blessed Peter; and, God guiding us, we always desire to do the same, if you, adhering to the footsteps of your parents, love with devotion your mother, the holy Roman Church, and strive to foster and uphold what belongs to her.

But we are astonished that, as we have learned from the complaint of our beloved son Pontius, abbot of Vézelay, you are attempting to infringe the ancient liberty of that monastery—which from the very beginning of its foundation is undoubtedly known to belong by special right to blessed Peter—and to impose new customs and unlawful exactions upon that same son of ours, the abbot. You do not consider [Col. 1179D] the sentence of anathema pronounced by so many and such holy popes, which, as is declared in their privileges, is known to have been issued against the disturbers of that monastery.

Therefore, since that place is manifestly under the special guardianship of blessed Peter and our protection, and since we neither can nor ought to permit any diminution of its liberty or immunity, we command your nobility by these present letters to leave the monastery in its liberty and to abstain entirely, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, from harassing our aforesaid son Pontius, abbot of that place. But if you refuse to desist from your attack, we offer you whatever the rule of equity requires; and we wish our aforementioned son, Abbot Pontius, to stand with you in judgment concerning this matter in the presence of our beloved son I., legate of the Apostolic See, who, by God’s favor, will shortly return to [Col. 1180A] those regions. Or, should that legate—something we scarcely believe—delay his return too long, we wish the matter to be examined and settled through justice in the presence of our venerable brothers S. [Samson], archbishop of Reims, G. [Guillencius], bishop of Langres, and our most dear son B. [Bernard], abbot of Clairvaux. But if you are unwilling either to do this or to desist from harassing that abbot and the brethren serving the Lord there, we cannot tolerate it without defending the patrimony of blessed Peter and freeing the aforesaid monastery from your unlawful oppression, both through ourselves and through the faithful of the Church.

### CXLVIII. To Louis, king of the Franks.—On the same matter. (A.D. 1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 651.]

**EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

The highest good in kings is to cultivate justice, to preserve and love God’s churches in their due right with fitting devotion, and not to allow their subjects to do whatever power permits, but to maintain what is equitable. The present unimpaired condition of the monastery of Vézelay clearly demonstrates—and both those nearby and those far away acknowledge—how properly and specially it has belonged to the Apostolic See from the beginning of its foundation, and with what care the liberty and immunity granted to that place have been preserved in their integrity down to our times, through the zeal and exact diligence of our predecessors, of Roman pontiffs and kings and other princes, and of your own forebears. [Col. 1180C]

Now, however, the nobleman G. [William], count of Nevers, departing from the footsteps of his ancestors, is attempting to infringe its liberty and to impose new customs and unlawful exactions upon our beloved son Pontius, abbot of that place. He gives no heed to the sentence of anathema known to have been pronounced against the disturbers or harassers of that monastery by so many and such holy Roman pontiffs, as is declared in their privileges. Since, therefore, that place is undoubtedly known to be the right of blessed Peter and to stand under his guardianship and our protection, and since we neither can nor ought to endure a diminution of its rights, we command your nobility by apostolic letters to cause the aforesaid count to desist from troubling that monastery and to leave it in its liberty.

If he refuses to cease from his attack, we offer him whatever the rule of equity requires, and we wish our aforementioned son Abbot Pontius to stand in judgment with him concerning this case in the presence of our beloved son I., legate of the Apostolic See, who, by God’s favor, is shortly to return to those regions. [Col. 1181A] Or, if that legate should, as we scarcely believe, delay his return too long, we wish this business to be examined and settled through justice in the presence of our venerable brothers S. [Samson], archbishop of Reims, G. [Guillencius], bishop of Langres, and our most dear son B. [Bernard], abbot of Clairvaux. But if the aforesaid count is unwilling either to do this or to desist from harassing that abbot and the brethren serving God there, necessity will compel us to defend the patrimony of blessed Peter and to free the aforesaid monastery from the unlawful oppression of that count, both through ourselves and through the faithful of the Church.

Accordingly, because we cannot exhort a more eminent and devoted faithful servant and defender of the Church, we earnestly urge your diligence by our entreaties to recall that count firmly from so great a presumption and forbid him altogether.

### CXLIX. To the same.—On the same matter. (A.D. 1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 651.]

**EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

By reason of the prerogative of sincere love and paternal affection which we have frequently shown you in letters and in speech, if it should sometimes happen that we ask your prowess concerning certain matters, you ought to heed more attentively our prayers—or rather, those of blessed Peter, made through us. Yet although we wrote to your nobility concerning the vexation which the count of Nevers is known, in tyrannical presumption, to inflict upon the monastery of Vézelay against God and all justice, he has afterward oppressed and afflicted that monastery more violently and cruelly than before. Nor has he ceased, together with the faithless townsmen of that place, to assail it and, though in vain, to attempt to take away the very allod and patrimony of the prince of the apostles.

We do not know why this has occurred: whether because you have been unwilling, according to our command, to restrain the aforesaid count from such presumption, or have neglected to do so; or because the count himself has made little of your admonition and lordly authority. [Col. 1181D] Since we neither can nor ought to overlook such unrestrained wickedness without punishment, we command and earnestly entreat your nobility by repeated letters to admonish the aforesaid count strictly to make full restitution for the losses which he is known to have inflicted upon the said monastery and to leave that place in its peace and liberty. If he believes that he has any right in that monastery, we shall afterward cause what is just to be rendered to him.

But if, hardened in his obstinacy, he scorns to carry this into effect, we have ordered that a sentence of excommunication be pronounced, without remedy of appeal, against him and the townsmen of Vézelay, and that throughout all his land every divine office be forbidden, except the baptism of children and the penances of the dying. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we command that from that time you abstain from him as from an excommunicate; and that you utterly forbid those townsmen, under your ban, from all fairs in your kingdom, and order, in zeal for justice, that wherever they may be found they be seized and stripped of their goods, as perjurers and disturbers of the Church. [Col. 1182A]

### CL. To the same.—On the same matter. (A.D. 1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 652.]

By other letters we commanded your nobility diligently to restrain the count of Nevers from harassing the Church of Vézelay, which belongs by special right to blessed Peter. And behold—what we cannot say without great grief of mind—we do not know whether your magnificence neglected to address him about this matter, or whether he himself refused to obey your command. After we sent you our letters on this account, that same count pursued the same Church more harshly; and now in person, now through those subject to his authority, he does not cease to frighten with threats and weary with injuries the brethren dwelling there in God’s service.

Indeed, apart from every admonition of ours, you ought to be a protection both to them and to all the churches established in the land entrusted to you by God, and you ought zealously to defend them from the attacks of wicked men—especially those who obey your commands. [Col. 1182C] Yet now, though our petitions and prayers have been added, we do not see that Church freed from his disturbances. Therefore, by apostolic letters and prayers, we admonish your magnificence that, as you are confident of our affection, so you should strictly restrain that count from harassing the Church of Vézelay and its possessions, and cause his men diligently to admonish him.

Moreover, if he believes that anything is justly due to him against that Church or its goods, we, to whom the care and governance of that Church especially belong, shall, if he asks, ensure that justice is rendered to him, through ourselves or delegated judges, with equity as mediator.

### CLI. To Odo, duke of Burgundy.—On the same matter. (A.D. 1145–47.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 653.]

[Col. 1182D]

**EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, the nobleman ODO, duke of Burgundy: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It is recognized as belonging to the diligence of Catholic princes to foster venerable places dedicated to God with due affection and to defend them from the attacks of wicked men. Both those nearby and those far away acknowledge how properly and specially the monastery of Blessed Mary Magdalene at Vézelay belongs to the right of blessed Peter, and that from the beginning of its foundation it has been entrusted to the guardianship of the Apostolic See. Therefore, placing great confidence in your nobility, we have thought fit diligently to commend to your prowess that monastery [Col. 1183A] and what belongs to it, requesting by these present letters that, out of devotion, you love and protect that place, and, in reverence for blessed Peter and for us, uphold and defend it from the attacks of those who strive to infringe or disturb its ancient liberty.

We write the same to Archambault of Bourbon and to Count Theobald.

### CLII. He confirms Hugh, archbishop of Tours, as metropolitan both of Dol and of the other bishops of Lesser Brittany. (A.D. 1147, January 3.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus*, III, 892.]

**EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Tours, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.**

The order of justice and reason counsels that one who wishes his own commands to be observed by successors should preserve the will and enactments of his predecessors. For our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Innocent, committed for examination and settlement to our venerable brother Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, then legate of the Apostolic See, the controversy long disputed between their pastors concerning the primacy of the Church of Tours and the subjection of Dol. When the matter had been treated in his presence in several places in Gaul but had not yet been brought to its due conclusion, the archbishop of Dol came into the presence of that predecessor of ours, complaining that he had often been burdened by delay in the case and had incurred many expenses on that account. He therefore humbly requested that our predecessor recall the case to his own presence and impose a due conclusion.

Granting his petition, he commanded you by apostolic letters to present yourself before the Apostolic See, prepared to demonstrate your church’s right in this matter. Meanwhile, by divine judgment, he entered upon the way of all flesh; and both you, brother archbishop, and the archbishop of Dol appeared before our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Lucius, for the determination of the same controversy. When you had produced many arguments, writings, and proofs concerning your church’s right, there was at last produced in the midst a privilege of our predecessor of good memory, Pope Urban. It explicitly stated that, after many discussions and reconsiderations of this matter in his own presence and also in that of legates of the Apostolic See, Pope Urban had carefully examined the writings of the Roman pontiffs Nicholas, John, Leo IX, and Gregory VII, and, after all matters on both sides had been thoroughly examined, had decreed by the common counsel of his brother bishops and many clerics of the Roman Church, and confirmed by the protection of his written instrument, that both Dol and all other bishops of the Bretons thereafter should acknowledge the Church of Tours as their metropolitan, render it due reverence always, and that, after the death of Roland, who then presided over the Church of Dol, no bishop of Dol should at any future time aspire to use the pallium. [Col. 1184A] To these points the archbishop of Dol answered nothing supported by reason; nor could he defend his side by the authority of any Roman pontiff.

Accordingly, after hearing the allegations of both sides and carefully examining the writings of the Roman pontiffs produced on behalf of the Church of Tours, our aforesaid predecessor Pope Lucius, having taken counsel in the assembly of his brother cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons, and of many other noble Roman citizens, confirmed the same judgment by apostolic authority. With his own hand, by the staff, he invested both you and the Church of Tours with the obedience of those bishops. He commanded, in accordance with the tenor of that judgment, that both the bishop of Dol and all bishops of Lesser Brittany thereafter should be subject to the Church of Tours as their proper metropolitan and humbly render it due reverence; and that no bishop of Dol thereafter presume to aspire to the use of the pallium, but, as already stated, should acknowledge the Church of Tours as his proper metropolitan and reverently obey it. [Col. 1184B]

We, therefore, although unworthy, having by the Lord’s disposition been placed in the seat of justice and neither wishing nor being bound to depart from the way of truth, adhere to the footsteps of those same predecessors and confirm the same judgment by the authority of the Apostolic See granted us by God, strengthening it by the safeguard of this present writing. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our confirmation, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But upon those who observe these provisions, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 1184D] **Saint Peter. Saint Paul. Pope Eugenius III. Place of the monogram. “Work for me, O Lord, a sign for good.”**
