[Col. 1213A] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this charter of our confirmation, after being warned a second and third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. [Col. 1213B] I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Humbald, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Gillibert, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Jordamio, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Gregory at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. [Col. 1213C] I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège

*(Year 1147, 11 May.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, IV, 1177.]

[Col. 1213D] EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Wazelin, abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish to establish in lasting stability those measures which our brother bishops have reasonably ordained for the peace of churches, lest they may hereafter be disturbed by the opposition of evil men. Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we confirm and decree to remain valid the ordinance prudently made by our venerable brother Henry, Bishop of Liège, and confirmed by his written instrument, concerning parish churches bestowed upon your monastery and the benefices of the priests serving those churches: namely, that henceforth the parish churches granted to that monastery shall not pass to the use of others, but, with the usufruct retained by the monks, priests [Col. 1214A] shall be canonically appointed in them. Those priests, however, shall have from their revenues the means to live—namely, the offerings of solemn and daily Masses, the offerings from visits to the sick, and from burials and funeral offices for the dead. Moreover, from the grain-rent in mother churches which have other churches under them, they shall have twenty-four *modii* of grain; in churches which are independent, twelve *modii*. Henceforth no one may bestow those benefices upon other persons; rather, they shall remain with the monks to whom they were granted, saving the synodal right and obedience due to the Bishop of Liège.

Given at Paris, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

## CLXXVI–CLXXVII. Bull in favour of Galther, Abbot of Saint Mary of the Chapel at Plancas

*(Year 1147, 15 May.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, XII, 267.]

[Col. 1214B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Galther, abbot of Saint Mary of the Chapel at Plancas, and to his brethren, etc.

Beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring you, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other [Col. 1214C] lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The territory upon which the church itself is built, given by Simon, lord of Belfort, and his mother Emeline, with the right of use in the whole wood as far as the castle of Merchericourt, with its appurtenances; and the land around that estate, given by Ralph of Saint Margaret; the mill on Mount Suzanno, with the land adjoining the mill—likewise given by the said Ralph, with the consent of his brothers and of the lords from whose fief it was held, namely Count Theobald, Giles with his brother Lebald, and Macarius of Magnicourt. The estate of Saint Petronilla with its appurtenances; the land of [Col. 1214D] Altignis; the new house situated above the Maxenna. One third of the tithe of the village of Saint-Ouen, which you hold from the church of Saint Quentin of Beauvais, and whatever that church of Saint Quentin lawfully possessed there. The entire tithe of Curcelles, excepting the priest’s share; half of one third of the tithe of Junchery, saving the right of the monks of Rosnay. A portion of the tithe of Longueville in the church of Chacericourt; the free election of a priest granted to you by Atto, Bishop of Troyes.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand from you a tithe of the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions [Col. 1215A] retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest, acting in the place of Guido, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate.

## CLXXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Bellelocus

*(Year 1147, 15 May.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, Preface, p. 256.]

[Col. 1215B] EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Ralph of Bellelocus and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a speedy result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid place, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring you, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the territory in which the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, is situated above the Aube, and the water from the village of Gessena as far as the elm of Givanzey, with the ban-right granted to the aforesaid church by Airard, formerly Count of Brienne, together with land which he held within the boundaries of that village. Moreover, throughout the entire county of Brienne, as was ordained by the said Airard and Walter his son, and in the dependencies of the town of Bellefort, the livestock of the brethren of that place shall have free pasturage both in woodland and open country.

Further, in the place called [Col. 1215C] the Chapel in the Forest of Der, there is the gift made to the aforesaid church by Simon, lord of the castle of Bellefort, and his mother Ameline: the right of use in the woods belonging to that castle, for making fires and other necessities; Rosteria with its appurtenances, given by the knight Warner and his brother Mainard; Vendolium; and the house of Trailbaosco, given by Philip of Valentiniac, Angelbert of Brienne, the knight Herbert of Bar, and his brother Ancher, with as much land there as one plough-team shall at all times require, and the right of use within the boundaries of Valentiniac, both in pasture for the feeding of livestock and in woodland for making fires and for everything necessary to that house. Also, whatever Hangelbert of Brienne held within the boundaries of Saint Remigius of Bosamont, given by him and his sons; the whole land of Pont Mainard falling to Mainard, given by him and his son Peter; in the boundaries of Darzeicourt, [Col. 1216A] twenty *jugera* of land given by Odo son of Fulbert; and more than half of the whole land there, given by Walter and his mother called the Countess; that place’s court with its appurtenances and mill; the estate of Farnerol with its appurtenances and mill; and the estate within the boundaries of Beurreville with its appurtenances.

Also the whole tithe of Berville, given by Philip, Bishop of Troyes; two parts of the greater and lesser tithes of Ferrières and Casa Salefridi, saving the share of Hugh the monk in the greater tithe; one third of [Col. 1216B] the tithe of Hauncourt; in the tithe of Junscherio, half of one third, saving the share of the church of Rosnay; and, in one third of the greater tithe of Sommeverae, five houses out of twelve. Also the entire tithe of Blegnicourt, together with its church and the free power to choose therein a suitable priest, whether from your clerics or from others, as this was canonically granted to you by Atto, Bishop of Troyes. We also confirm to the same church one third of one third of the greater tithe of Saint Remigius of Bosemont.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand from you tithes of the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the [Col. 1216C] aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this charter of our ordinance, after being warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable amendment, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and [Col. 1216D] blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New. I, Ignatius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

[Col. 1217A] Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Prémontré

*(Year 1147, 16 May.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, Preface, p. 15.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Hugh, Abbot of Prémontré, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1217B] Although we ought generally to provide for all ecclesiastical persons, it is fitting that we should be solicitous with more earnest care for those who are known to pursue the service of almighty God with greater zeal, and to shine by a stricter religious life and upright conduct. Therefore, from this concern of charity, beloved sons in the Lord, we grant the petition of your devotion with due kindness. Following the example of our predecessor Pope Celestine II of blessed memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the church of Prémontré, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all its appurtenances, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods the same venerable place now justly [Col. 1217C] and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring it, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the precinct of the valley of Prémontré itself, as contained in your documents and defined by fixed boundaries, free from every exaction, whether land-tax, tithe, or rent; the estate of Fontenelles, with its fishpond, two parts of the mills below it, and its other appurtenances; the estate of Penencourt, with vineyards and other appurtenances; the estate of Merliu with its vineyards; the estate of Roseries with its dependencies and appurtenances; the estate of Vercigny with its appurtenances; the estate of Souppy, [Col. 1217D] with the mills below it on the river called the Aisne and its other appurtenances and dependencies; two parts of the tithe of Crépy; one third of the tithe of Chavus; at Valavergni, ten *modii* of wine from the tithe of that village; the tithe with land-tax of Vrevin; and the land-taxes of Concivilla, excepting two *modii* which must be paid from them to the Church of Blessed Mary at Nogent; likewise, the fishpond and mill near that same village, as Ingelrannus son of Thomas of Marle had held them in his own lordship in the aforesaid two villages; the rent of Poilly; the mill of Rochis, the mill of Proisel, the mill of Achery, the mill of Cortun, and the mill of Cenceny.

[Col. 1218A] The wine-rents of Bourguignon; the land of Carenni; two parts of the mill of Aquila; vineyards of Broiencourt; Ursignicourt, Brummont, Lizy, Valavrigny, Montarcenne, and Monthavin; vineyards at Coucy-le-Château and Coucivilla; the wine-rents and vineyards of Novavilla; in the diocese of Soissons, in the suburb of the city, an estate and site, winepress, and vineyards. At Pommeraye, wine-rents; the money-rent of the castle of Brane and the village of Branella; the estate of Bucy with vineyards and its other dependencies; the mill of Rupibus beneath that village; the estate of Clamecy, with winepress, vineyards, and other dependencies; at Sorny, two winepresses, vineyards, and other revenues; the estate of Tenselva with its dependencies; the estate of Luilly, and half a mill with its other dependencies; [Col. 1218B] at Bethencourt, wine-rents and other revenues; at Pinon, a certain rent, one third of the small tithe from the court, one sixth of a certain mill, and the tithe which Josbert held there; the chapel and estate of Rosel, with mill, fishpond, winepress, vineyards, and all appurtenances; on the hill of Trosly, one estate with mill, fishpond, winepress, vineyards, and all appurtenances.

On the hill of Trosly, one estate, and another in the valley, with lands, vineyards, and other dependencies; and that part of the village with its appurtenances which Andrew of Baldimento bestowed upon you, as he held it in his own lordship; together with certain other things offered by other faithful people of God. The estate of Biucy with its dependencies; the estate of Attechi, two parts of the tithe, vineyards [Col. 1218C] with other appurtenances. At Cauny, a rent and wine-rents. In the village called Pont-Saint-Médard, a certain portion of the tithe. At Margival, half a mill; half the chestnut-groves of Vausaillon.

In the diocese of Noyon: the altar and estate of Benolio with its dependencies; the estate of Bolmont; the estate of Calveni; the allod of Germainnes; the estate of Montisel; the estate of Thory; and the estate of Landricourt. In the suburb of Noyon, land, vineyards, and meadows; an estate with its appurtenances; the mills of Despeville and half the tithe of that same village; two parts of the tithe of Destoily; one sixth of the tithe of Duri; the mills of Offois and two parts of the tithe of that village; one third of the tithe of Grecy; half the site of a certain mill [Col. 1218D] at Dinisa, and half the tithe of that village; two parts of the tithe of Calveni; one third of the tithe of Caullaincourt; two parts of the tithe of Gricourt; three parts of half the tithe of Leherwes; one third of the tithe of Lancy; the tithe of Kivres; land at Omencourt; land of Liencourt and Curcy; three *jugera* at Greum; the free chapel of Saint Nicholas at Saint-Quentin; the estate of the allods with its appurtenances; the estate of Voiana with its appurtenances; the estate of Hanapiis, held in allod, with its tithe; two parts of the tithe of Bechincourt; two parts of the tithe of Cartigny; the entire tithe of Falvi, except the small tithe; one fourth of Aldeni; the mills of Escauly with their appurtenances; the mills of Hamel; and the site of a certain mill at Pieton.

[Col. 1219A] We have also recognized, in accordance with the principle of humanity, and by this present decree valid in perpetuity enact, that the sisters who, through the labour of our brother Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg of blessed memory, and through your exhortation, entered the service of almighty God and offered themselves to God, shall, from your goods—of which no small part is known to have come to that place through them—receive, now and always, without anyone’s opposition, the necessities for their maintenance.

Likewise, we decree that you shall not be compelled to give tithes to anyone from the produce which you gather by your own hands and at your own expense; nor may any bishop, on any [Col. 1219B] pretext, prohibit the divine offices in your church. If a general interdict is imposed in the diocese, you shall nevertheless celebrate divine offices, excluding the excommunicated and with the doors closed. You shall receive the ordination of canons, the consecration of altars or churches, and the remaining ecclesiastical sacraments from the Bishop of Laon, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See; otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. If any nobleman should decide to be buried there, no one may oppose his gift and final will, unless he is excommunicated or under interdict, saving the right of the mother Church.

[Col. 1219C] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this charter of our ordinance, after being warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable amendment by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and [Col. 1219D] blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

[Col. 1220A]

## CLXXX. Privilege for the monastery of Calvimont, of the Premonstratensian order

*(Year 1147, 17 May.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, Preface, p. 340.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons John of Calvomont and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a speedy result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid [Col. 1220B] place, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord favouring you, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The altar of Adon, with the village itself and mill, and the land of Pontius; the altar of Roseico with land and meadows; the altar of Rubeniac; the altar of Saint Neuntius; the altar of Saint Ferreolus; the altar of Parniac, with the lands belonging to those altars; the altar of [Col. 1220C] Membercis; the mill of Ronna; Campiniolas with the other villages; and half of Remoldicourt, which Count Roger and Count Hezelin gave, with its male and female serfs, free from every customary due; the land of Hermanfrid and part of the allod of Adeliac; the allod of Justinia, given by Hugh the Scot; the allod of Cerisiac; the allod of Saint Ferreolus; the allod of Buriniacimont; the land of Persoir; the land at Rubiniac of Woderic son of Valerius; one ninth of Guistreio; one ninth of the count’s revenues belonging to Calmont; one ninth of the oven of that same castle; one ninth of the mills of the Tower; five homesteads of Fusamimont with the lands pertaining to them; the land of Bus, the land of Eselci, the land of Scon, the land of Altavilla with meadows, the land of Scipsis with meadows, the land of Vasineio, the land of Eunicebus, the land of Abilo of Ruba; [Col. 1220D] the land of Ohard of Mont-Outre; land at Mambertiac; the allod of Intersisola upon the stream Vob, granted by Count Henry and the other heirs; likewise, the village formerly called Trion, with altar, tithe, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands belonging to that village, and everything which Ralph and Warner acquired there; the land of Walter of the Castle; the land of Mont-Proveri with all its appurtenances; the land of Mont-Outre with its appurtenances; the land of the powers of Saint Mary; the land of Mandencio; the land of Nantuel; the land of Fin; [Col. 1221A] the mill of Fannion with land; the mill of Treinel; the land of Curcinis with its appurtenances; land with woodland at Luchiac; the land of the spring of Viriguandano; the tithe of your cultivation in the territory of Saint Ferreolus; and the portion of tithe which Gilbert held from Ralph of the Tower, as these were granted to you and confirmed by the written instrument of our venerable brother Samson, Archbishop of Reims. Likewise, whatever has been or shall be lawfully acquired from the fiefs of Count Henry, the Countess of Calmont, and the aforesaid Ralph of the Tower, as granted to you by them.

We also enact that the canonical order which, by God’s grace, is known to have been [Col. 1221B] established in the same church of Calmont according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the institution of the brethren of Prémontré, shall be inviolably maintained for all time. Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand from you tithes of the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against [Col. 1221C] this charter of our ordinance, after being warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable amendment by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our God Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Emarus, bishop of Tusculum.

[Col. 1221D] Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest, acting in the place of Guido, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXXI. Privilege for the church of Saint Nicholas of Theles (at the March of Ralph)

*(Year 1147, 18 May.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, II, Preface, p. 73.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Ulric, abbot of the church of Saint Nicholas of Theles, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1222A] A desire shown to concern the purpose of religious life and the salvation of souls must, God being its author, be fulfilled without delay. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it with the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord providing, through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The land of the March of Ralph, given to you by [Col. 1222B] Ansculph of Senooz, with half the tithe of that same land, granted to you by the nuns of Saint Paul (Order of Saint Benedict, near Beauvais), and the other two parts granted by Amalric of Fresnaulx and Osbert, his sons; the land in the valley of Dompierre (Dompierre, a village half an hour distant from the March of Ralph), given by Ralph of Poelly; the garden of Frenels, with the share of the mill granted to you by the same Ralph, and a small amount of neighbouring land; another mill, granted to you in full ownership by the same Ansculph, with a fishpond and a small adjoining piece of land; the land of Goi (Joui, a village dependent on Bellimont); land beside Budencourt; dwelling-sites upon the water with a fishpond in the land of [Col. 1222C] Warin; and the chapel of Saint Genevieve with adjoining land.

Moreover, we prohibit any one of your brethren, after making profession there, from daring to depart that cloister without the permission of the abbot and chapter; nor may anyone dare to retain one who has departed. Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand from you a tithe of the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit, in every respect, [Col. 1222D] of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should presume rashly to act against this charter of our ordinance, after being warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1223A] and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Guido, cardinal of Blessed Mary in Portico. I, Ocumanius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tusculan Prison.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest, holding the place of Lord Guido, deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXXII. He confirms all the goods and possessions of the convent of Saint Mary at Soissons

*(Year 1147, 25 May.)*

[GERMAIN, *History of Notre-Dame of Soissons*, p. 438.]

[Col. 1223B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, Mathilda, abbess of the convent of Saint Mary at Soissons, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Religious desires deserve readily to receive assent, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document; [Col. 1223C] decreeing that whatever possessions and goods the aforesaid church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favour acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the estate of Patriniacum and Morcinctum, with their hamlets; Molnicatum, Cavinionum, Esiacum, Nantoilum, Laffoce, Trosliacum, Colesiacum, Ressontium, Morcinum, and Saconia, with their appurtenances; the tithe which you hold at Altrepia; Caudunum and Colomella, with their appurtenances; Billiacum, Asiacum, and Carcrisia, [Col. 1223D] with their appurtenances; Corciacum, Choy, Gehennae, and Carliacum, with their appurtenances; Bachevel, with its appurtenances; Ulliacum and what you possess at Guni; Nigella and Nugaredum, with their appurtenances. In the territory of Cologne, Caldelaich with its appurtenances; in the territory of Mainz, Chrocam with its appurtenances; Edumhum; likewise the altar-right of Troisli, of Colysi, of Corcy, of Flori, of Mansi, also of Colomella, of Nantolium, of Chacrisia, of Patriniacum, and of Morcinctum, with the liberties and conditions canonically granted to you by Bishops Hugh and Simon and confirmed by their written instruments; likewise the altar-right of Fresnicii and that of Bruelium. Outside the town of Saint-Quentin, the monastery [Col. 1224A] dedicated in honour of Saint Mary, in the district of Troyes; land at the village called [lacuna], and also in the hamlets of that same village; Arnulf’s fief; the advocatial right over the villages of Cavinionum, namely Esiacum, Fillenias, and Paremniacum. Likewise another advocatial right over the same Esiacum; the village near Bestisi called Mesnil, with its appurtenances; a right of way at Charliacum; a tithe at Cavinionum of twenty shillings; at the bridge of Soissons, Sauvalon’s fief and Roger of Thorota’s fief; at Bucyvinaticum, eight modii; at Charliacum, two modii of wine and half a modius of oats, and certain other things; at the village, two modii of wine; at Bruelium, the land which the nun Elizabeth possessed; the tithe of the cultivated lands of Hugh, provost of Charliacum; [Col. 1224B] at Bursona, the tithe which Paganus Delbuisson held; at Gehennae, the fourth part of the advocatial right which the nun Adelais possessed.

Moreover, by the present document we confirm the agreement reasonably made between you and Ralph, lord of Nigella, concerning the mark of silver which he had been accustomed to receive from you every year, and concerning the village called Fresneices and the wood pertaining to that village: namely, that henceforth your church shall not pay that mark, and that the aforesaid Ralph, in compensation for it, shall henceforth hold the said village and render to you the service due and customary; while to your church shall remain for ever the church and churchyard of that village, the tenants of the churchyard, and all jurisdiction. Further, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce [Col. 1224C] which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Albertus, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. [Col. 1225A] I, Humbaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Jordanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, John Paparo, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Jacinthus, cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

[Col. 1225B] Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXXIII. To Letard, abbot, and the monks of Bec. (A.D. 1147, 27 May.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 683.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LETARD, abbot, and the monks of Bec: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When a dispute concerning temporal matters [Col. 1225C] arises among religious persons, it must be ended with such priestly care that contention cannot continue to grow in the customary manner. Understanding this, we have settled in the following manner the controversy long conducted between you and Robert, prior, and the canons of Saint Frideswide of Oxford, concerning the Church of Beaumont and all its appurtenances; and by this settlement we have entirely cut off the litigation. For the aforesaid Robert and the canons have altogether renounced to you in perpetuity every claim and right which they maintained that they had in the same Church of Beaumont and its appurtenances, and have freely surrendered them into our hands. Accordingly, through our hand, they have in like manner received from you, as their perpetual lordship, the village called Edivetona, with every tithe of the demesne of that village, to be received from the peasants only from [Col. 1225D] that land itself, together with all its appurtenances in pastures and meadows, wood and plain, and mills; saving to you all the remaining parochial right and the third sheaf of the peasants’ tithe of the same village, which properly belongs to the church of Hundrefort, in whose parish the village itself lies. This is on the express condition that the canons shall never hereafter be able to build a church or chapel in that village. Since it is our office to establish firmly in permanence those matters which we ourselves have particularly ordained for the peace of religious persons, we confirm the same decision or agreement by the authority of the Apostolic See and command that it be firmly observed by both parties.

Given at Paris, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

## CLXXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Waverley. (A.D. 1147, 28 May.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, II, 912.]

[Col. 1226A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GILBERT, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Waverley, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: greeting in Christ.

It accords with the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious persons and to fortify their places by pious protection. For it is recognized as worthy and befitting honour that we, who have been raised to the government of the Churches, should both protect them from the wickedness of evil persons and cherish them under the patronage of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests [Col. 1226B] and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s assistance acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the place itself in which the abbey was founded, with all its appurtenances; from the gift of Stephen, king of the English, Nieta and Fermeham, [Col. 1226C] with all their appurtenances; from the gift of Queen Adeliza, the wood of Nolholte and the cultivated land beside that wood; from the gift of Alan of Vilers, the land of Bochilld; from Faramuz of Boulogne, Wenebergia; from the gift of Richer of Laigle, Oxeneford; from Ralph the sheriff, Riheulla; from the gift of Soworli, Acserugia; from the gift of Robert of the Manor, Nutescheolva; from the gift of Richard of Sifrewalt, half a hide of land at Polementona; from the gift of Ingelrannus Piscis, a virgate of land and pasture beside the Winchester road, from the manor of Stiventona. Further, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you upon the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the sustenance of your animals.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1226D] rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to correct his or her offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord, our Redeemer Jesus [Col. 1227A] Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXXV. To Peter, abbot of Cluny.—He reduces the abbey of Baume to a priory because of the heinousness of a certain crime committed against Master Osbert and contempt for the Roman Church, and entrusts it to Peter’s governance in order to restore religious observance there. (A.D. 1147, 29 May.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 443.]

[Col. 1227B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Nearly the whole world recognizes how properly and especially the monastery of Cluny pertains to the holy Roman Church, how greatly it has advanced in religious observance through God’s grace, and how many persons it has instructed in upright living by the example of its good way of life. Taking this more carefully into account, because of the execrable and horrible crime and the unprecedented contempt of the holy Roman Church which the monks of Baume, with sacrilegious audacity, committed against our beloved [Col. 1227C] son Master Osbert, to the dishonour of blessed Peter and ourselves, we have for ever removed from that place the name and dignity of an abbey, and, with the counsel of our brethren, entrust it through apostolic benevolence to you and your successors, to be ordered and administered as a priory. It is therefore for you to apply yourself to the restoration of that place and the reform of religious observance, so that under your rule the place itself may receive growth pleasing to the Lord in both spiritual and temporal matters.

> [Note: [Col. 1227D] Mabillon calls Osbert a legate of the Roman Church, vol. VI of the *Annals*, p. 43. Concerning the crime committed, Peter the Venerable says the following in the same work, p. 500: “I pass over an occurrence far too well known to people of our time, and one which, because of its indignity, ought not to be transmitted to posterity in writing.”]

Given at Paris, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

## CLXXXVI. To William, count of Mâcon.—That he assign the church of Baume to the Cluniacs and render assistance. (A.D. 1147, 29 May.)

[Same work, p. 444.]

[Col. 1227D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the nobleman G[UILLELMUS], count of Mâcon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Nearly the whole world recognizes how properly and especially the monastery of Cluny pertains to the holy Roman Church, how greatly it has advanced in religious observance through God’s grace, and how many persons it has instructed by the example of its good way of life [Col. 1228A] to live uprightly. Taking this more carefully into account, because of the execrable and horrible crime and the unprecedented contempt of the holy Roman Church which the monks of Baume, with sacrilegious audacity, committed against our beloved son Osbert, to the dishonour of blessed Peter and ourselves, we have for ever removed from that place the name and dignity of an abbey and, with the counsel of our brethren, entrust it to Peter, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and his successors, to be ordered and administered as a priory. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your nobility, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: assign the place itself, with its treasury, all its goods, and all its appurtenances, intact to the brethren of Cluny; recall the monks expelled from it to their obedience; and, by every means by which you can according to God, provide for the peace and tranquillity [Col. 1228B] of the brethren of Cluny.

> [Note: [Col. 1228D] William obeyed; indeed, not only with his assent but also at his instigation were all these things done. “This is shown,” says Peter in the same place, “by the charter preserved in the Cluniac archive, sealed with the impression of his seal”; it may be seen in the history of the town of Poligny, book II, p. 683 ff.]

Given at Paris, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

## CLXXXVII. To Humbert, archbishop of Besançon.—That he render the Cluniacs assistance in reforming the church of Baume. (A.D. 1147, 29 May.)

[BOUQUET, same work, p. 444.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H[UMBERT], archbishop of Besançon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish you to know that, because of the execrable and horrible [Col. 1228C] crime and the unprecedented contempt of the holy Roman Church which the monks of Baume, with sacrilegious audacity, committed against our beloved son Master Osbert, to the dishonour of blessed Peter and ourselves, we have for ever removed from that place the name and dignity of an abbey and, with the counsel of our brethren, through apostolic benevolence entrusted it to our beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, and his successors, to be ordered and administered as a priory. Therefore, by these present letters we command and direct you to provide the brethren of Cluny with aid and counsel for the restoration of that place and the reform of religious observance.

Given at Paris, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

## CLXXXVIII. Bull in favour of the monastery of Tiron. (A.D. 1147, 30 May.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VIII, 328.]

[Col. 1228D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of Tiron, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Religious desires deserve readily to receive assent, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. [Col. 1229A] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Tiron, in which you are devoted to divine service; and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favour acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have appended the following, to be recorded by their proper names.

In the kingdom of England, in the diocese of Saint David, the church of Saint Mary of Chatmeis, with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Saint Andrew [Col. 1229B] of Scotland, the abbey of Saint Mary of Roxburgh, with its appurtenances; the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul of Ogra, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Giles of Castenariis; the church of Saint Leonard of Ferreries; the church of Saint Mary of Asneriis; the church of Saint Michael of Lucezio; the church of Saint Mary of Telio; the church of Saint Lawrence of Brigia; the church of Saint Peter of Audita; the church of Saint Martin of Hildrevilla; the church of Saint Mary of Jarzia; the church of Saint Mary of Aguille; the church of Saint John the Baptist of Murgeriis; the church of Saint Andrew of Anglia, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Mapedroella; the church of Saint Mary of Titileia; [Col. 1229C] the church of the Holy Cross of Insula.

In the archdiocese of Rouen, the church of Saint Sulpicius of Germunvilla; the church of Saint Martin of Crasvilla; the church of Saint Lawrence of Calcia; the church of Saint Mary of Baschevilla; the church of Saint Silvester of Clara; the church of Saint Mary of Turneio; the church of Saint John of Monteursino; the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene upon the Seine. In the district of Évreux, the church of Saint Cecilia of Guest; the church of Saint Anastasia; the church of Saint Martin of Busseium; the chapel of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Lupus of Chavigneium; the church of Saint Bartholomew; and the church of Saint Maurice of Cherenthaio. In the diocese of Chartres, the church of Saint Mary Magdalene near Briheriivalis; the church of Saint Remigius of Neronius; the church of Saint Spanus of Abluis; [Col. 1229D] the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Oisemum; the church of Saint Michael of Climart; the church of Saint Mary of Ledum; the church of Saint Mary of Cumbris; the church of Saint Lawrence of Gastina; the church of Saint Vincent of Maierolii; the church of Saint Martin of Brenella; the church of Saint Vincent of Arseciae; the church of Saint Germanus of Colungis; the church of Saint Peter of Hargenvilla; the church of Saint Leobinus of Quinque Fontes; the church of Saint Mary of Planis; the church of Saint Nicholas of Foetellae; the church of Saint Mary of Hironius; the church of Saint Andrew of Silvelonia; the church of Saint Mary of Molendinum Novum; the church of Saint Mary of Monterium; the church of Risubovis; [Col. 1230A] also the granges of Tiron: Saintes Vallées, Cintreium, Vallarium Maffredi, Gimigneium and another Gimigneium, Childreium, Spesovilla, Cultura, Pertas, Ogeriivilla, Leporisvilla, and Villadunum.

In the diocese of Séez, the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene of Resno; Runcheria; the church of Corgehot; Mesnilbertre; the church of Saint Jovinus; the church of Montechevrel; the church of Martigneium; and the church of Nuileium. In the diocese of Bayeux, the church of Saint Antoninus of Montehargis; the church of Saint Mary of Strata; the chapel of William of Crévecœur; the church of Saint Mary of Rensiacum; the church of Budunellum; and the chapel of Tigerium. In the diocese of Meaux, the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Montegihellum, with its appurtenances and tithes, and the place of Dormant with its possessions. [Col. 1230B] In the diocese of Poitiers, the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Rusaium; the place of Puteoli; the place of Trusseia; the place of Megum; and the place of Tiliatum. In the diocese of Nantes, the place of Septem Fagi; the place of Trapa; and the place of Oiseleria. In the diocese of Angers, the place of Sauceia. In the diocese of Le Mans, the church of Saint Michael of Planities; the church of Saint John of Grandirivus; the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Crucisvallis; the church of Saint Mary of Passubovis; the place of Vabobrunetum; the church of Mary Magdalene of Montetallarium; the church of Saint Mary of Bellolocus; the church of Saint Mary of Cohardum; the church of Saint Mary of Vallibus; the church of Saint Sulpicius of Pail; the church of Saint Maurice near Cortpoltrain; the church [Col. 1230C] of Saint George of Blimart; the church of Saint Silvester of Montelusellum; the church of Saint John the Baptist of Jarreia; the church of Saint Audoenus of Turnemium; and the abbey of Saint Mary of Jugo-Dei, together with the tithes, revenues, and possessions of the aforesaid places.

And so that you may be able to celebrate the divine office more honourably among yourselves and possess your places more securely, we grant that you may have oratories and cemeteries on your lands, provided that this causes no detriment to the surrounding parishes. Further, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals, nor parochial dues from your servants. We also grant you free burial in [Col. 1230D] your places, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while nevertheless preserving the rights of the mother church.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any disturbances or vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 1231A] person hereafter, knowing this page of our institution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the reward of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. [Col. 1231B] I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, have subscribed. I, Jordanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Jacinthus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary [Col. 1231C] in Cosmedin.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor, on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CLXXXIX. Privilege for the church of Saint Mary of Braine. (A.D. 1147, May.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, 322.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary and Saint Evodius of Braine, and his brethren, both present [Col. 1231D] and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Religious desires deserve readily to receive assent, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favour [Col. 1232A] acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, chief tenants (*homines capitales*), vineyards, wine-cellars, wine-dues, wine taxes, rents, and land-rents, and whatever you possess in the castle of Braine; the entire village of Vassenis, except the land of Saint Médard; the land of Espretelle; at Couvrelles, a rent of ten shillings and a certain cultivated tract; the whole tithe of the court of the Monks; four sextarii of grain from the mill of Hugh son of Ralph at Mont-Notre-Dame; four sextarii of grain from the mina and rent; at Quincy, rents; at Joagne, ten shillings of rent and seven from tenants, [Col. 1232B] together with an oat-render and land-rent. At Cerseuil: the altar-right and the whole tithe on the doves belonging to the lord of that village, vineyards, arable lands, and a mill. At Lymé: vineyards and wine-dues. At Luy: rents and land-rent. From the tithe of Cuiry: one modius of grain. At Cramaille: rents; at Villers: rents and land-rent; at Betisi: rents; at Villers-sur-Ayne: wine-dues, rents, and land-rent. At Pontarcy: wine-dues and rents; at Duisels: rents, land-rent, and wine-dues; at Courcelles: rents, land-rent, wine-dues, and a meadow; at Brenel: wine-dues, rents, land-rent, [Col. 1232C] meadows, and a winepress; at Ay: rents and an ash tree; four sextarii of grain; in a certain mill, the re-tithe (*redecimatio*) of the lordship of the castle of Braine—of its wine, vineyards, winepresses, and wine-dues, and of all grain in ovens, mills, its own cultivated lands, land-rents, returns of oats and hay—and the re-tithe of all the grain of three villages, namely Villers and Ville-Moyenne, and of the oats owed to it for use of the wood; provided that wherever the possession of the lordship is transferred, the aforesaid church’s re-tithe shall be reserved; and whatever it held in the fishing-rights of the mills of Braine. The court of Bruyères, with its appurtenances; the mill of Jouy; the tithe, land-rents, and rents of certain cultivated lands [Col. 1232D] belonging to the church of Saint Peter of Hasnon, at a rent of five shillings. The same lord also granted you that all his vassals might freely make alms to you from the fiefs which they held from him. A fourth part of the pastures of Granges; three arable lands at Port d’Ancy; one mill; two parts of the great tithe of Blansy; arable lands, vineyards, a mill, a meadow, and a wood. The whole court of Sertiaux and everything pertaining to that court; a fourth part of the tithe of Vaissy. At Vergely: rents; the court of Curtiaux; and everything pertaining to that court in the city of Soissons: one modius of salt, [Col. 1233A] one modius of wine, and ten shillings of rent. In the diocese of Laon, two mills and arable land which Bishop Bartholomew gave you at a rent of twelve denarii. At Bergues, five thousand herrings and ten weights of cheese. Further, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way [Col. 1233B] of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 1233C] Amen.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CXC. Privilege for the monastery of Jandure. (A.D. 1147, 3 June.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, p. 651.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEOBALD, abbot of the church of Jandure, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular [Col. 1233D] life: in perpetuity.

Religious desires deserve readily to receive assent, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid place, in which you are devoted to divine service; and fortify it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favour acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper [Col. 1234A] names: the place of Jandure, marked out by fixed boundaries; the two parts of the tithe which you receive there from the other inhabitants; the third part of the tithe of Wacincort; the place of Graveriae and of Wacincort, marked out by fixed boundaries, as confirmed by the bishop of Toul; the meadow which Vivianus and his brothers gave you; the place of Walt which Rudolph of Burrei and Anscherus of Lord Martin gave you; and the site of a mill which those who possessed it by hereditary right gave you below Roseries. Further, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1234B] rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any exactions; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body [Col. 1234C] and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal priest, acting in the place of Lord Guido, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CXCI. Privilege concerning the churches subject to the bishop of Paris, the agreement concluded between Bishop Stephen and King Louis, the prebends of canons who become bishops, and, moreover, the *tallia*—the levy which the king had customarily imposed upon the bishop’s lands—remitted by King Louis. (A.D. 1147, 5 June.)

[*Cartulary of the Church of Paris*, I, p. 25.]

[Col. 1234D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEOBALD, bishop of Paris, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The more famous the noble and glorious Church of Paris is because it is the seat of the king of the Franks, and the more devoted you show yourself, venerable brother Stephen, bishop, by manifest proofs in love and reverence for blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, the more readily do we grant the desired assistance in matters known to concern the honor and advantage of both. [Col. 1235A] Therefore, dearest brother Stephen, assenting to your reasonable petitions, whatever the Church of Paris presently possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings, the benefaction of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just titles, by God’s favor acquire, we confirm to you and your successors, and through you to the Church of Paris, by the privilege of apostolic protection. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the church of Saint Marcel; the church of Saint Cloud, with its estate and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Germanus of Auxerre; the church of Saint Eligius; likewise the church of Campelles, with its prebends and three parishes—namely, those of Saint Merri, La Chapelle, [Col. 1235B] and Kerris—belonging to that church, while preserving the annual payment to the Church of Sens of a rent of two solidi in the currency of that land, namely the currency current in those regions; all of which aforesaid churches are known to belong by right and property to the bishop of Paris. We also confirm episcopal jurisdiction in the following abbeys and in all their parishes and parishioners: namely, in the abbey of Lagny; in the abbey of Val-Sainte-Marie; in the abbey of Sarneia; in the abbey of nuns, that is, of Montmartre [de Edera] and of Kala; and furthermore in the church of Argenteuil.

Wishing also to provide for the peace and tranquillity of the Church of Paris, we apostolically prohibit anyone henceforth from exacting the levy and tallage which, [Col. 1235C] after the death of your predecessor Stephen, bishop of Paris of good memory, our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks, imposed upon the lands of that bishopric. Rather, as it was remitted in perpetuity to you and your successors by the same king and confirmed by his written charter, we confirm it by the present document.

Moreover, we likewise confirm to you the pact and agreement made between you and our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks of illustrious memory, concerning the place in the suburb of Paris called Campellus: namely, that one third of the entire income from the ditch of that land—whether arising from rents, purchases, sales, profits, [Col. 1235D] or any other manner whatsoever—shall be paid to you and your successors without any diminution; while the remaining two thirds shall be rendered to the royal fisc. Whoever is the king’s provost shall, concerning this matter, swear fealty to you and your successors; and yours shall swear fealty to the king and his heirs; and neither shall receive or dispose of anything from that land without the other.

We further enact that if any canon of the Church of Paris is promoted to the dignity of a bishopric, his prebend shall freely revert to the Church of Paris.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb you or your successors on account of this our confirmation, or take away the possessions of the Church [Col. 1236A] of Paris, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the tenor of this our constitution, should rashly act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, fails to amend that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But may all who preserve their rights for that same Church have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict [Col. 1236B] judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hugh, cardinal priest, acting in place of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CXCII. He confirms the agreement made between Stephen, formerly bishop of Paris, and Theobald the archdeacon through Matthew, bishop of Albano, John, cardinal priest of Saint Chrysogonus, and Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Callistus. (Year 1147, June 5.)

[Collection of Cartularies, IV, 27.]

CXCIII. Bull for the nunnery of Saint Dionysius at Montmartre. (Year 1147, June 7.)

[FÉLIBIEN, *History of Paris*, Proofs, III, 62.]

[Col. 1236C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, Christina, abbess of the monastery of Saint Dionysius at Montmartre, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions; and we receive, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves as our own daughters, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid monastery, built and endowed, with the consent of Louis, king of illustrious memory, and Adelaide [Col. 1236D] his queen and wife, for the salvation of their souls and remission of their sins, in which you are devoted to divine service. First, indeed, we enact that monastic order according to the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity; that henceforth in that place the almighty Lord shall be served by nuns of honorable conduct and praiseworthy life; and that the aforesaid nuns shall have free power to elect an abbess, so that no person may be placed over them by force. Nor shall their abbess, or the nuns themselves, ever be expelled entirely from their monastery for any negligence unless they have first been judged by the lawful judgment of their holy mother, the Roman Church, whose protection supports them; rather, they shall be corrected by the admonition and counsel of the bishop of Paris and of other religious persons. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods you presently possess justly and canonically from that king or queen, or from other faithful servants of God, or may hereafter, by grant of popes, benefaction of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favor acquire, shall remain firm and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the church of Saint Dionysius on Montmartre, and the tithe belonging to that church with its appurtenances; [Col. 1237B] the church of Saint-Martyr, with the vineyards of Aden and Morel’s cultivated land; the cultivated land which Prior Matthew bought from Warnerius of Portus; likewise the estate called Mansionillus, with all its appurtenances; two mills at Clichy, with the water-enclosure and the milling of the entire estate; one oven at Paris, with all its customary dues. In the forest of Vincennes, one cartload daily of dead wood; the house of Gerricus, with the butchers’ stalls and the vicariate of that house; Bernard’s land, called Puncta, free and quit; fishing rights and land on the island of Berelliis, free from every customary due; at Chelles, ten arpents of meadowland. In the district of Senlis [Col. 1237C] at Bray, one house, vineyards, and sufficient land for one plough-team, free from every exaction and customary due, so that for that plough-team—or for others, if, by God’s gift, you should have more plough-teams there—you shall pay no share of the open field and no customary due, as was granted to you by the illustrious king of the Franks and confirmed in his charter. In the district of Étampes, the estate called Tolforium with all its appurtenances. In the district of Melun, woodland and a boat for conveying wood down the Seine, free from every customary due. One tenant, free from every exaction, riding-service, and the like, to bring your grain down the Seine from Melun to Paris. If he does not serve well or dies, another person suitable for this work shall be supplied to you by the king. In the district of Gâtinais, three small estates with land, a mill, and all their other appurtenances. At Étampes, one oven with all its customary dues. At Pratellum Holdeum, an entirely free estate with all its appurtenances. Whatever you may acquire from the king’s fief, we likewise confirm to you this and the other things granted to you by the king and confirmed in his charter; likewise twenty pounds from the Cambitum at Paris, which Louis, son of King Louis, gave you; and at Bestesiacum, ten arpents of meadowland and forty arpents of arable land. Likewise his orchard of Saint Leodegarius, and the pond with its mill; the fishmongers’ street between the butchers’ house and the king’s small castle; one chapel [Col. 1238A] at Bestesiacum; and at Boulogne, five thousand herrings annually; the entire share in the fief of the royal huntsmen which had belonged to Matthias on this side of the Seine; and at Vetreacum, land that had belonged to Galon the priest from the king’s fief. At Paris, one house near the Petit-Pont; another near the butchers’ stalls. On Mont Savies, Burgard’s vineyard, and there also a winepress with one vineyard-guardianship. At Brumille, five solidi of rent with jurisdiction; half of one vineyard; and what Walter of Booron gave you at Montmartre, namely one vineyard-guardianship, together with all the vineyards he had there, and four solidi and two denarii of rent; and what you have in the village of Pomponia; one chapel at Calvo Monticulo with the fief of Paganus Trencebise, [Col. 1238B] and with the fief of Garsilia; and the allod of your brother Eustace and of your sisters Cecilia and Hildeburg, beloved daughter in Christ Christina, abbess. Also Gozon, their man, and what he held from them; eleven arpents of meadows commonly called *Mareis*. Certainly, from the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals, no one may presume to exact tithes from you.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance [Col. 1238C] and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the tenor of this our constitution, should rashly act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, fails to amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But may all who preserve justice for that same place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict judge, the rewards of eternal peace [Col. 1238D]. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Hugh, priest of the title in Lucina. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 1239A] I, John Paparo, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Paris through the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.
