We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God willing, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings and princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the place in which the monastery itself is situated, Gumprechtingen. [Col. 1265D] Certainly, let no one presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with wanton vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the full benefit of those for whose support and governance they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly [Col. 1266A] attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But for all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Auxerre, by the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of August, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1266B], and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CCXVIII. Privilege for the convent of Saint Mary of Huntingdon. (1147, August 15.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, II, 26, from the autograph in the Cottonian Library.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, prior of Saint Mary of Hunduni, and his brethren, present and future: greeting.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as befitting religion and honour, it is proper for us to grant it with willing mind. [lacuna] [Col. 1266C] [lacuna] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God willing, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: outside the town of Huntingdon, two hides of land; and within the town, the church of Saint Mary [Col. 1266D], the church of Saint John, the church of Saint Martin, the church of Saint Benedict, the church of Saint Edmund, and whatever right you possess in the church of All Saints; the castle chapel with its appurtenances; the church of St Ives with its appurtenances; the church of Godmanchester with its appurtenances; the church of Sudwic with its appurtenances; and the church of Evenley with its appurtenances. Whatever you possess in Sudhem, Perry, Cattewrida, Calikcota, Hisham, Ristona, Cloptona, Pouhebroc, Turninga, Winewic, Soltreia, Papperwrde, Dpvefort, and Hemmingeford; the tithe of Ralph Tesard, of Wansingelai, of Sticheltona, Overtona and the other Overtona, Chestretona, and Sibetorp.

[Col. 1267A] Moreover, the manor of Herford with its church and mill; the land which belonged to Ingelran of Auco in the town of Huntingdon; the land of the Old Castellan [*Veteri Castellario*], and other lands and holdings which you possess there; one third of the mills of that town; and two meadows beneath the castle. At Stiveclai, one hide and twenty acres between woodland and open country, and one *losta* and one virgate. Gunild in that same village; at Lolintona, one virgate; at Westona, one hide. At Dena, two hides, one and a half virgates. At Saltreia, one virgate. At Sudham, half a virgate. At Gratham, one virgate. At Hargrawe, one virgate, and whatever right you possess in the tithe of Roger Moin. At Cunintona, one virgate; at Stottona, land assessed at twenty solidi. At Leia, land assessed at twelve solidi; at Pappewrda, one hide of land, given by Alfred [Col. 1267B] of Coldintona; at Stochas, land assessed at sixty solidi: half of Hedure. At Sproxtona, a mill given by Oger; the tithe of the mills of Stanford. At Crochestona, one hide; at Bedford, certain land given by Ralph the knight. In the diocese of Norwich, the church of Wetinges with its appurtenances. At Fletwello, land assessed at six solidi, given by Hugh de Plaic. At Rechesham, the tithe of the mills; at Wella, one thousand eels annually, given by William son of Roger; and another thousand at Paccelade, given by William de Lovetot; at London, land assessed at four solidi, given by Goie.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1267C] rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment [Col. 1267D] let him be subject to strict vengeance. But for all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberius, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Gillebert, unworthy priest of Saint Mark, etc.

Given at Auxerre, by the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CCXIX. Bull confirming the possessions of the abbey of Saint Mary of Bertinia-curtis, or Moncel. (1147, August 22.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, II, Preface, p. 192.]

[Col. 1268A]

EUGENIUS, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GISLEBERT, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Bertinia-curtis, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as befitting religion and honour, it is proper for us to grant it with willing mind and give fitting support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 1268B], and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary, of the holy martyrs Maurice and his companions, of Blessed Nicholas, and of All Saints, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God willing, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: at Bertinia-curtis, two ploughlands, two mills [Col. 1268C], meadows, fishing rights, and woodland, from [lacuna] of your own and of the illustrious Count Theobald, and Helvidis; Aviniacum, where your sisters dwell, with the lands and meadows which you possess there; a field on the boundary of the bridge of Novae-villae; half the mill of Ingny, given by Guy of Dampetra, with the consent of his wife and sons; the tithe-assessment of its ploughlands and of the land-rents; a part of the allod of Escalon; two mills below Aviniacum, which you hold for an annual rent of twenty-four sextaries of grain from certain persons; a part of the allods [lacuna] which Guy his son, your canon, gave you near the castle called Dampetra; an acre and arable lands, and a share of a certain mill, which Robert, your canon, gave you with the consent of the aforesaid Guy; in [Col. 1268D] the village called Mallis; and in another village called Piper, the tithe which you possess by grant of Atto, bishop of Troyes; the tithe which you possess in the village called Dampetra; whatever right you possess from the share of Milo the knight or of others in lands, rents, men, tithes, and meadows; the land of Saint Mary of Wanno, which you hold from the church of Saint Paul of Verdun for a rent of four [units] of Châlons currency.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any other vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishops [Col. 1269A]. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But for all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1269B] I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Hugh, cardinal priest in Lucina. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.

Given at Auxerre, by the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## CCXX. Privilege for the monastery of Rigny. (1147, August 23.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, XII, documentary appendix 119.]

[Col. 1269C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Stephen, abbot of Regniac, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

A desire shown to pertain to the religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore, beloved sons in God, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Regniac, in which you are devoted to divine service, [Col. 1269D] decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses in tithes, fields, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, pastures, and other things, or may in the future acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

Namely, the land called Carbonaria in the parish of Coves. The land and meadows which Milo of Noeriis and Ansericus of Mont-Réal gave you, within these boundaries: namely, the rock of Ogerius and the village of [Col. 1270A] Tormentiac. The territory of the grange of Carbonaria which Ansericus of Mont-Réal and Theobald of Scutignei gave you. The land of Cavannis which the sons of Niard and the sons of Erard of Mongalei, and Fromund of Rufiaco, gave you. The meadows which you hold from the canons of Saint Lazarus of Avalon. The meadows and whatever right you possess in the wood of Carbonaria from Ansericus of Mont-Réal. From the gift of Landricus of Praiac, the cultivated and uncultivated land of Uldinus. From the gift of the son of Gualterius of the Tower, the wood called Fagineus on one side and Sagitta on the other. From the gift of Ansericus of Tarel and Guido of Curte, the cultivated and uncultivated land of Fortumenserium. From the gift of Ascelinus of Château-Censurii, the land of Porliac and the cultivated and uncultivated land of Exsard. From the gift of Uldoerus and Gerard, his brother, the cultivated and uncultivated land of Leiserium, [Col. 1270B] as it is known to be divided by boundaries and markers. The land which Joscelin of Arserium gave you. In the territory of Rainac, land from the gift of Josbert Capelli, Hugh of Château-Censurii, and Gibaldu. From the gift of William, count of Nevers, the water from Fonte-roboris to the Perreria of Bellimont. From the gift of Geoffrey of Dunziac, the land of Lescheriis. The land of Chaillo which you bought from the free persons who held it.

Moreover, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labor which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, [Col. 1270C] or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly available for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place [Col. 1270D] may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Eugenius, Pope III. I, Humbaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, have subscribed. I, Aribatius, cardinal-priest of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. [Col. 1271A] I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Jacintus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

Given at Auxerre, through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CCXXI. To the bishops of Mâcon and Chalon.—That they should compel Jocerannus Grossus, lord of Brancidunum, to make satisfaction for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Cluny, according to the judgment of the archbishop of Lyons. (A.D. 1147, August 23.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 445.]

[Col. 1271B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren P[ontius], bishop of Mâcon, and G[ualterius], bishop of Chalon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, appearing before us, lodged the complaint that G[ocerannus Grossus, lord of Brancidunum], contrary to what he had confirmed by the solemn obligation of an oath, and in contempt of the Christian faith, refused to obey the judgment of our brother A[medeus], [Note: [Col. 1271C] Guichenon recounts the judgment delivered by Amadeus, archbishop of Lyons, in his *Bibliotheca Sebusiana*, p. 365, in the following terms: “Let it be known to all into whose hands this charter may come that I, Amadeus, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, at the pressing command of the lord pope, summoned before me the venerable brethren of Cluny and Josserannus Grossus, in order to settle the controversy that had long been disputed between them.

“Both parties having therefore appeared before us, the men of Cluny alleged that the aforesaid Josserannus had inflicted grave injuries and exactions in the lands of the Church of Cluny which were under his power; that he had forcibly exacted lodging rights which his predecessors had not possessed in those lands; and that, by plundering, tallages, and diverse harassments, he had severely oppressed their men. Josserannus, on the contrary, maintained that he had received nothing in their lands except those things which his predecessors had customarily received there.

“Having heard the arguments of both parties, and after taking counsel with religious men—Archbishop Eraclius, William of Marzellis, Master Otmar, and Gilbert the archpriest—the witnesses produced by the men of Cluny, having carefully given oath, testified [Col. 1272C] that Josserannus ought by no means to inflict any force or exactions as a matter of custom in the aforesaid lands of the Church; and Josserannus’s witnesses did not contest their testimony.

“Furthermore, the Church’s witnesses asserted that, in their presence and hearing, Bernard, father of the aforesaid Josserannus, when he was preparing to go to Jerusalem, to the house of the Hospital to which he had given himself, declared in the presence of the brethren of Cluny and many others not only that he possessed no customary rights whatever in the aforesaid lands of the Church, but also expressly commanded his sons Josserannus and Henry, who were present, not thereafter to presume to inflict any injuries or exactions in the aforesaid lands of the Church. Should they fail to obey his command, he forbade them their paternal inheritance.

“Having heard these matters and taken counsel with those who were there with us, we rendered the judgment that Josserannus should make satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren for the injuries inflicted and should henceforth restrain himself from such exactions; for he possessed no such authority in their lands.”] archbishop of Lyons. Since, therefore, restraining lay transgressors is not acting against the laws but bringing aid to the law, we command you by these present letters to warn the said G[ocerannus] diligently and earnestly that, in accordance with the judgment of our aforesaid brother, he make satisfaction to the abbot and brethren of Cluny for the injuries inflicted and abstain from unlawful exactions. If he refuses to do this, pronounce against him a sentence of excommunication and against his land a sentence of interdict.

Given at Auxerre, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.

CCXXII. He confirms to the monastery of Cluny Baerna Monteria, granted by William, count of Mâcon. (A.D. 1147, August 25.)

[*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, 1409.]

[Col. 1272A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Peter, abbot of Cluny, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

We desire that those things which the faithful of the Church of God establish by reasonable provision, for the salvation of their souls and the support of religious persons, should remain in their stability; and it is fitting for us to provide with suitable care lest in the future they be disturbed by the opposition of wicked people. As we have learned from the charter of the nobleman William, count of Mâcon, which you presented before us bearing his seal, the same Count W., partly as a gift for the salvation of his own soul and those of his parents, partly by sale, granted to you and your successors to possess freely in perpetuity a certain holding with its appurtenances in the borough of Lons, commonly called Baerna Monteria, which had belonged to Aymo, provost of Lons, together with a burgess, custodian of that possession; in exchange, another Baerna Monteria was given to him by common agreement. [Col. 1272B] For so great a benefit, you gave him sixteen thousand and four solidi of Cluniac coinage.

To this gift and sale, Pontia, countess and wife of the said count, [Col. 1272C] Stephen and Gerard, their sons, the aforesaid provost Aymo, his mother and brothers, Gualterius, viscount of Frotoniac, and all others who seemed to have any right in that possession, gave their common consent. That this might stand established with firmer stability, Count William himself, his aforesaid wife and sons, and all the others mentioned above confirmed it by oath, on these terms: that they should forever be, in good faith, guarantors and defenders of this grant. If anyone should attempt to bring a claim or inflict damage, they themselves would defend the said grant in every respect, to the best of their power.

The leading men of the land of the same count—namely Hugh of Berziac, Henry Grossus and his brother Jocerandus, William of Neblens, Pagan of Classiac, Bernard Paganus, Majolus Tabutinus, and Stephen of Basenens—also swore that, if the aforesaid agreement were not maintained or were broken by any occurrence, then, when summoned by the brethren of Cluny, they would come to Mâcon and remain there as hostages until the matter had been settled peacefully and, with permission of the abbot of Cluny, they returned. Moreover, Guido of Munet, William Joret, G. of Loiseac, and many others named in the aforesaid charter of the count likewise swore that they would come as hostages to the borough of Lons, as did the other persons mentioned above.

[Col. 1273B] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, by apostolic authority we confirm this gift or sale to you and your successors, and through you to the monastery of Cluny, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we decree that it shall remain valid for all future time. We prohibit anyone whatsoever from rashly disturbing the monastery of Cluny regarding that possession or harassing it with any molestations; rather, it shall be preserved intact and free from every claim, wholly available for the use of those for whose governance and support it was granted.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our confirmation, [Col. 1273C] should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon those who observe it may the peace of our Lord Jesus rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Albericus, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and [Col. 1273D] Damasus, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Aribertus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd, have subscribed. I, Jordanus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal-priest of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. [Col. 1274A] I, John Paparo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Jacintus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

Given at Auxerre, through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CCXXIII. Bull confirming the possessions and immunities of the Church of Stivagium. (A.D. 1147, September 6.)

[Hugo, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, II, Preface, p. 543.]

[Col. 1274B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gillibertus, abbot of the Church of Stivagium, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life.

Whenever a request is made of us which is fitting for religion and uprightness, it becomes us gladly to grant it and to give suitable assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive the aforesaid Church of Stivagium, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the order [Col. 1274C] of canons which is known to have been established in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren shall there be observed inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now possesses or may in future acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, through the Lord’s assistance, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place of Stivagium [Note: [Col. 1273] The Church of Stivagium was subject to Andelac through Saint Richard, who from the beginning subjected his monastery of Andelac to the Roman Church.] where the abbey is founded, which, by an ordinance of Charles, formerly emperor of the Romans, after the death of Rechardis, his wife, who had held it as her own possession, is known to remain perpetually subject to the monastery of Andelac. That monastery had been built from its foundations by the same empress, [Col. 1274D] and, in the presence of the emperor just mentioned, had already been assigned to the Roman Church. Thus it owed no service by right to any ecclesiastical or secular person, or to any church whatsoever, except only to Andelac, to which it is subject.

Matilda, abbess of the same Church of Andelac, with the counsel and consent of the chapter of her nuns and canons, of Count Hugh, advocate of the same [Col. 1275A] church, and of the ministeriales, as well as at the request of the secular canons who had long inhabited the same Church of Stivagium, graciously granted it in perpetuity to the Premonstratensian order and to your brethren serving God there, together with one third of the ban of Stivagium: its lands, meadows, woods, waters, fisheries, and the pastures for all animals of the entire ban; the head-rent of residents within or outside the ban, namely two Deodatian denarii from a man and one from a woman; and the remaining possessions which, by the ancient institution of popes and emperors, are known to belong to the prebend of those serving God in that church.

Namely, the fifteen measures of wine which you receive as rent from the Church of Salwamunt, which your church has held from ancient days; the tithe of fifty-two *hobae*, of both wine and grain wherever they are situated, held from the fief of Count Hugh of Dasborc; your court and allodial estate of Salwamunt; your court and allodial estate of Tambac; the allodial estate which Count Hugh of Dasborc gave you; the allodial estate which Kertrudis of Tambac gave you; the allodial estate which Holricus Grossus of the same village gave you; the allodial estate which Hesso of Berchemel gave you; the vineyard plot which Countess Kertrudis gave you at an annual rent of eight denarii; the liberty of harvesting grapes which the same countess gave you on the day when the count harvested; the allodial estate which you hold at Rothseim; the church of Donceres and the chapel of Xasteviler, with their tithes and all [Col. 1275C] appurtenances; your court of Donceres with its allodial estate in lands, meadows, and woods, and with the tithes of all cultivation belonging to the same court, which the Church of Stivagium has possessed from ancient days; the court of Heibermeis (Sabemey), with the allodial estate you have there in lands, meadows, woods, and the common pastures of neighboring villages.

The allodial estate of Envas and the grange situated in that place, with its ban and other appurtenances—lands, meadows, woods, male and female serfs; tithes of croadors and *anzaugiae*, and of the cultivation carried on by four oxen ploughing in that same allodial estate, and of the *brolia*—all of which you have held from ancient times. The land which you possess at Saint Paul, with one household and a wood. The four quarter-units of land which you hold at Frevilla. The twelve Toul denarii which you hold in the allodial estate of Bervilla; the twelve which you hold in the allodial estate of Bassumpunt; the two quarter-units of land which you hold at Regnervilla; the allodial estate of Sendrouviller, with its ban and other appurtenances—lands, meadows, woods, male and female serfs—and with the pannage of pigs feeding in the wood, without any share for the advocates; the allodial estate of Mosteriol, in lands, meadows, and woods, together with the land of three ploughs in the territory of Nohegenis, which you hold from the abbess of Andelac at an annual rent of twelve [Col. 1276A] Metz denarii; the tithes of Cretumviller; the two denarii which you hold in the allodial estate of Persomme; your allodial estate of Juncheris, in lands, meadows, and woods, with the site of a mill; and the two quarter-units of land which you hold at Gundresum.

Furthermore, the parish church of Stivagium with all its appurtenances, tithes, chapels, and their rents—namely, for each individual, according to ancient custom, thirty-two denarii of Deodatian coinage; the chapel of Belmunt; the chapel of Burguntia; the chapel of the church of Norprad; the chapel of Saint Remigius; and the parish church of Mosteriol with the chapel of Nohegenis, together with their tithes, rents, and all appurtenances.

Likewise, the governance of souls, both of clerics and of laypeople, in the above-mentioned [Col. 1276B] parishes, since the same Church of Stivagium has always possessed this from ancient times. The abbot of that place and his successors, because such an office is appropriate to religious persons, shall hold it perpetually from the bishop of Toul by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves. [Note: [Col. 1275D] Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter and the Apostolic See, the abbot of Stivagium holds the governance of souls and parishes not from the bishops of Toul. You might suppose them to be the conferrers of such jurisdiction merely because, in that age, they invested the abbots in the pope’s name and by papal delegation; but they have for centuries fallen away from that delegation, and after confirmation the new abbots voluntarily approach this governance and do not pay the four solidi to the Church of Toul which they had been obliged to pay by reason of investiture.]

We also grant you the synodal pleas in which the parishioners of Stivagium must pay, one year, pennies, and the next, halfpennies; while those of Mosteriol must pay a penny, one loaf, and a *bicatum* of oats; and we grant you all jurisdiction over the same residents within the boundaries of the aforesaid churches. We also grant that the appointment of priests to be installed in those churches, whether from among your canons or from secular clergy, shall be made by you without consulting bishop, archdeacon, or dean, so that [Col. 1276C] they receive from you both the care of souls and their prebend, and need answer neither bishop, archdeacon, nor dean for their actions. We likewise confirm that the Church of Stivagium shall annually pay four Toul solidi to the dean of the archdeaconry of Fluns at the next synod after the feast of Saint Remigius, of which two parts shall be the bishop’s and the third the archdeacon’s.

Since you ought to attend upon almighty God, devote yourselves to prayer, and lead a peaceful life from your own labor and from the benefactions and offerings of the faithful, we decree that no one shall presume to exact from you any tithes on your newly cleared lands and cultivated fields which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. [Col. 1276D] You may also receive into conversion clerics or laypersons fleeing the world who are free and absolved, and retain them without opposition.

When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may, after excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, celebrate the divine mysteries in a low voice and without ringing bells. We further prohibit anyone from giving churches, lands, or any benefice of your church personally to another, or alienating them in any other way, without the consent of the whole chapter [Col. 1277A] or its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than stated, we judge them void.

Furthermore, none of your brethren may stand surety for anyone without the consent and permission of the abbot and the sounder part of your chapter, or borrow money from anyone beyond the amount provided by the prudent arrangement of the chapter, unless perhaps for a manifest benefit to your church. If they presume to do so, the community—without whose permission and consent they acted—shall in no respect be bound to answer for those acts.

Moreover, in your causes it shall be lawful for you to bring forward suitable brethren as witnesses and, by their testimony, if it is right, both to repel violence and to claim justice. [Col. 1277B] To avoid the crowds of secular people, you may freely construct oratories and cemeteries in your courts, and there celebrate divine offices and burial, when necessary, for yourselves and your households.

We also grant you by apostolic authority that you may receive chrism and holy oil, sacred orders, and the consecration of your abbot or churches from whichever bishop you choose. [Note: [Col. 1277] From this, conclude that Stivagium is not, and never has been, in or of the diocese of Toul, as follows from the constant discipline of the canons.] No one may presume, under pretext of custom or in any other manner, to demand anything from you for bringing the abbot to the episcopal see or for any other ecclesiastical sacraments. If anyone attempts to act against these provisions, let him know that he will have a share with Gehazi, whose deed he imitates by demanding a shameful payment. [Col. 1277C]

It shall also be lawful for your abbot to bless and consecrate clerical tonsures, altar linens, and priestly vestments. You may lawfully anathematize your wrongdoers and robbers and, by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves, prohibit the celebration of divine offices in churches, parishes, and every place whatsoever where they or their household may be, or wherever your stolen property is retained; those who repent, however, you may absolve from the bond of excommunication. We also decree that burial at that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion of those who ask to be buried there—even if they are excommunicated—provided that their relatives and friends have piously promised to undertake penance on their behalf and to make suitable satisfaction according to ecclesiastical [Col. 1277D] discipline.

Wishing also to provide with paternal care for your peace and tranquility, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your places or granges, from daring to commit violence, robbery, or theft; set fire; seize or kill a person.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any other vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact, wholly available for the use of those for whose governance [Col. 1278A] and support they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, [Col. 1278B] amen.

Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Pope Eugenius III. “Make for me, O Lord, a sign for good.”

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albericus, bishop of Ostia. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title in Lucina. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, John Paparo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Jacintus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Auxerre, through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 1278C] in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CCXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Yergua. (A.D. 1147, September 17.)

[Oihenart, *Notitia utriusque Vasconiae*, 101.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Raymond, abbot of Yergua, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

Whenever a request is made of us which is known to be fitting for religion and uprightness, it becomes us freely to grant it and give suitable assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests [Col. 1278D] and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid place of Yergua, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may in the future acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names: namely, the land of Yergua with its tithes, pastures, and appurtenances; the place of Fiterio [Col. 1279A] with its tithes, pastures, and appurtenances; and the place of Oliva with its lands, granges, tithes, pastures, and appurtenances.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact, wholly available for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine [Col. 1279B] judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albericus, bishop of Ostia. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New. I, Sanctius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in [Col. 1279C] Cosmedin. I, Humbaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Aribertus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd.

Given at Cîteaux, through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest acting in place of the lord Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1147 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CCXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Nienzabas. (A.D. 1147, September 17.)

[Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, I, 416.]

[Col. 1279D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Raimundus, abbot of Saint Mary of Nienzabas, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

Whenever a request is made of us which is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it becomes us freely to grant it and give suitable assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons of the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and receive under the power of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid place of Nienzabas, in which you are devoted to divine service; [Col. 1280A] and we strengthen it by the document of this present writing, decreeing that whatever goods and whatever possessions the aforesaid monastery possesses, or may in the future acquire through grants of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact, wholly available for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our enactment, [Col. 1280B] should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Cîteaux, through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-priest acting in place of the lord Guido, [Col. 1280C] cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, 9, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CCXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Vitus of Prül. (A.D. 1147, September 17.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XV, 156.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Wernherus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vitus, martyr, at the place called Prül, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

[Col. 1280D] It is fitting to grant ready consent to religious desires, so that faithful and devout devotion may swiftly attain its effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vitus, in which you are devoted to the Lord’s service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree first that the monastic order established in your church according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the observance of the brethren of Monti [Note: [Col. 1279D] This observance Werner, the abbot, had doubtless brought with him from that same monastery, from which he had been summoned, as is clear [Col. 1280D] from Pusch and Fraelich, *Diplomatarium sacrae Styriae*, II, 240.] shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with God’s favor acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, three mansi at Schalckaim, and one mill with the serfs belonging to it; a vineyard at Hoffdorf; two mansi at Tollmaissing, with the serfs belonging to them; and the other things which our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Regensburg, lawfully conferred upon you out of devotion and confirmed by his written instrument.

Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any crafty intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, provide to be elected.

[Col. 1281B] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, [Col. 1281C] unless he or she makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe. I, Albert, bishop of Ostia, subscribe. I, Hunibald, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, subscribe. [Col. 1281D] I, John, deacon of Saint Mary the New, subscribe. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, subscribe. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, subscribe.

Given at Cîteaux through the hand of Hugh, cardinal priest acting in the place of Lord Pinder, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III, pope.

### CCXXVII. Bull to the brethren of Savigny.—It confirms their union with the Cistercian order. (1147, September 19.)

[Marten, *Amplissima collectio*, I, 807.]

[Col. 1282A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the convent of Savigny and the abbots of the monasteries belonging to that abbey, and to their brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The peace of the Church, concord among brethren, the vigor of religious life, and the condition of monasteries are preserved by the bond of unity. With this purpose in view, our beloved sons Serlo, abbot of Savigny, and Hosmund, abbot of Beaubec, coming to the chapter at Cîteaux, humbly requested in our presence, through our dearest son Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, that both they and your whole community [Col. 1282B] might be received into the unity of the Cistercian congregation and order. Commending their religious devotion in the Lord, we have rejoiced in fulfillment of the duty of paternal charity, knowing that it is written: “A brother helping a brother: both shall be comforted.” Therefore, according to their desire, pleasing to God and praiseworthy, joining both them and you to that holy fellowship, we establish by apostolic authority that this beloved and joyful association shall be observed inviolate in times to come. Accordingly, we have commanded you to render filial obedience to the aforesaid our son, the abbot of Saint Savigny, in accordance with the observances of the same order, all the more devotedly [Col. 1282C] because he is known to labor more diligently for your salvation. But if anyone knowingly attempts to act against this page of our confirmation, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Saint-Seine, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October.

### CCXXVIII. Charter concerning the acknowledgment of the right of Saint Mammes in the territory of Dijon. (1147, September 25.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, IV, Instruments, 171.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Humbert, dean, and the canons of the church of Langres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the authority of the Apostolic See and by duty we are compelled [Col. 1282D] to concern ourselves with the welfare of all churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace and tranquility. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, solicitous for the welfare of your church, we have thought fit to assent to your just petitions. We have inspected the letters of Hugh, duke of Burgundy, of illustrious memory, confirmed by his own seal and by those of his son Odo and our venerable brother Geoffrey, bishop of Langres. They show that the aforesaid Duke Hugh, having received from you five hundred solidi, made an agreement and settlement with you concerning the injuries and unlawful exactions which his father and he himself had imposed upon your lands in the territory of Dijon. The duke acknowledged that he had no right in [Col. 1283A] the village called Gibriacus, in the village called Fiscinis, or in the holdings, one of which is at Cocheio and the other at Cavenniaco; and he wholly relinquished whatever he or his officials had been accustomed to receive in those places. He also wholly relinquished the toll which was collected from your common or private carts as they passed through the gate of Dijon. In the village called Neronis, however, he retained for himself nothing except the *marischachia*, the *brennaria*, and jurisdiction—yet only if your mayor should not wish to exercise it. We confirm this agreement or settlement by the protection of our favor and decree that it shall remain valid. But if anyone, having learned the tenor of this confirmation of ours—God forbid!—should attempt to oppose it, let that person suffer the loss of rank and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction.

Given at Auxerre, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October.

### CCXXIX. To Abbot Suger.—He asks which bishops refuse to assist him in defending the kingdom; a definite place for the council is appointed; concerning the excommunicated duke of Lorraine; concerning the church of Buxis. (1147, October 6.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 636.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1283C] blessing.

We have kindly received your messenger and letter, and have carefully considered what they contained. We are grateful that you are concerned for the church of Paris; and if anything is wrongly done there, we grieve over it in accordance with the duty of our office, and, with the Lord’s help, shall take care to exert ourselves so that such matters may be recalled to the path of rectitude. As for those bishops who refuse to bring you aid and be present for the defense of the kingdom, lest we seem to charge them all together with blame, inform us by name concerning some of them, so that we may rebuke and exhort them by apostolic words to be more ready to preserve the state of the kingdom and to furnish strength and counsel for those things which are expedient for the honor [Col. 1283D] and advantage of the kingdom. Moreover, since you have offered places in the kingdom entrusted to you, at our disposal, for holding a council, we praise your devotion in the Lord; but because we had fixed our decision, we have not thought fit to alter our purpose. Further, concerning the duke of Lorraine, whom we have excommunicated for other offenses: when place and time allow, we shall do you more fully and carefully the justice which we deny to no one. Finally, concerning the church of Buxis, for which your belovedness has petitioned, if opportunity permits, it may, with the Lord’s help, be accomplished upon our return.

Given at Auxerre, on the second day before the Nones of October.

### CCXXX. Fragment of a bull by which he confirms the goods and possessions of the monastery of Saint Lambert of Laetia. (1147, October 10.)

[Reiffenberg, *Monuments pour servir à l'histoire des provinces de Namur, de Hainaut, etc.*, vol. VII, p. 642.]

[Col. 1284A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gerric [Wedric?], abbot of Saint Lambert of Laetia, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

A pious petition ought to be fulfilled through the ensuing effect of the will, etc.

Given at Auxerre through the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1284B] on the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III, pope.

### CCXXXI. He summons Henry, bishop of Moravia, to the council of Trier and commends to him his legate John. (1147, October 11.)

[Boczek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, I, 259.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, bishop of Moravia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have great confidence in your love and fidelity, which we have already come to know by experience in the affairs of the Roman Church. Since, in order to drive back the many [Col. 1284C] enormities that have increased and to confirm those things which will please God, we have resolved, in reliance on the Holy Spirit, to celebrate a council at Trier on the next Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, we have thought fit to summon our brothers the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches from various parts of the world. Therefore, by apostolic letters and through our beloved son John, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, we command your brotherhood, under obedience, to come thither at the same time, setting aside every other matter, into our presence, so that, relying upon your help and counsel, we may correct errors and, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, establish what ought to be established. Moreover, we earnestly commend to you the said our son John, requesting [Col. 1284D] that you diligently assist him in negotiating and, if possible, arranging peace between the expelled duke and his brothers, and that you provide help and counsel.

Given at Auxerre, on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

### CCXXXII. To Archbishop H. [Eberhard], the bishops, and abbots established throughout the province of Salzburg.—Of the same subject. (1147, October 12.)

[Edited by Jaffé from Vienna Library MS no. 2192, *Regesta Romanorum pontificum*, p. 629.]

To the venerable brothers H. [Eberhard], archbishop, and the bishops, and to the beloved sons the abbots established throughout the province of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1285A] It is beyond doubt, and all Christendom throughout the world acknowledges, that the holy mother and apostolic Roman Church was founded and willed to be established upon the firm and immovable rock of faith by him alone who entrusted to blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, the rights of both earthly and heavenly rule. For it enjoys the privilege not of any earthly sentence, but of that Word by which heaven and earth were made; it is supported by his authority. Thus the height of the divine counsel ordained that the holy Roman Church of which we have spoken, rising as a marvelous structure upon our head, the Lord Jesus Christ, as its most solid foundation, should surpass in perpetual preeminence all churches throughout the world, and should diligently apply itself, on its own initiative, to cutting off emerging heresies and other evils and vices that spring up; and, as the circumstances of cases and times require, should stir up the efforts of others to accomplish this end. Therefore, impelled by this duty of apostolic authority, we have thought fit to summon our brothers, the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches, from various parts of the world; and we have decreed, in reliance upon him, to celebrate a council at Troyes on the next Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung (21 March 1148), with you and our other brothers and sons present, for driving back the many [Col. 1285B] enormities that have increased and for confirming those things which will please God. Therefore, by apostolic letters and through our beloved son Raymond, our chaplain, we command your entire body, under obedience, to come thither at the same time, putting aside every excuse, into our presence, so that, relying on your help and counsel, we may correct errors and, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, establish what ought to be established. [Col. 1285C] We also earnestly commend to you the aforesaid our chaplain and request that you receive him kindly and treat him honorably.

Given at Auxerre, on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

### CCXXXIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint John at Réôme. (1147, October 13, at Saint-Florentin.)

[Col. 1285D] [*History of the Monastery of Réôme*, according to Bréquigny, *Table chronologique*, III, 127.]

### CCXXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary at Jette. (1147, October 24.)

[Hugo, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, I, Preface, p. 511.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Walter, abbot of the church of Saint Mary at Jette, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

We are pleased to grant with a willing mind a desire shown to pertain to the purpose of religious life and to the salvation of souls, and to bestow fitting assistance upon the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive the aforesaid church of Saint Mary under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with God’s favor, by grants of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the altar of Geth with the chapel of Tansorna; the altar of Hembecca; the altar of Lewa; the chapel of Mosangen; the chapel of Himethea with all [Col. 1286B] their appurtenances; the tithe of Molbnick; one-third of the tithe at Volvrethem, from the gift of Odulph and his sons …; the mill at Geth; and the alder-grove beside the church, from the gift of Euwain and his sister …

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against [Col. 1286C] it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he or she makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, subscribe. [Col. 1286D] I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, subscribe. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, subscribe. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, subscribe. I, Gilbert, unworthy priest of the title of Saint Mark, subscribe. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, subscribe.

Given at Châlons through the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III, pope.

### CCXXXV. Privilege for the convent of Saint Mary at Hélder. (1147, October 25.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 676.]

[Col. 1287A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, Hildiard, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Hedera, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The care of venerable places admonishes us to consider diligently their peace and welfare; nor is there any doubt that, if we kindly comply with the petitions of God’s faithful, we find the Lord merciful toward our own needs. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, following the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of blessed memory, [Col. 1287B] we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, in which you are devoted to the divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with God’s favor, acquire by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

From the gift of Louis, king of the French, of illustrious memory: the land of Amaro-bosco and the whole land of Uno-villare, with all their appurtenances, free and exempt from every exaction; and eighteen sextaries of oats annually from his mill at Calliaco. From the gift of Louis, king and son of the aforesaid king: the land of Mansionillo-Ricuini. Likewise, in the same place, another tract of land, from the gift of Theoderic of Bouilla; and whatever *vinaticum* he held there at the village called Cons, together with whatever is rendered for that same *vinaticum*. Likewise, from the gift of the aforesaid King Louis the Younger: whenever the king is at Paris, a perpetual grant to you of a tenth of all bread brought to his court. Also, the mill near the monastery, free and exempt. From the gift of Hugh, son of Guarnerius: at his mill at Brennacum, one modius of wheat, or of whatever other grain is best there, and, each day, as much wood from the forest there as two asses can carry, for making fire. From the gift of Eremburgis: ten arpents of land at Succi, and an annual rent of six and a half solidi from the meadows of Bretimacum. From the gift of Stephen, bishop of Paris, of good memory: the church of Villa-abbatis with its tithe; the tithe of Gennaliacum; the tithe of Silviniacum; the church of Everiacum and its tithe; the tithe of Craumelle; the tithe of Athiis; the tithe of Calendie; the tithe of Concisso; the wine-tithe of Cons; the wine-tithe of Centeniacum; the church of Hedera and one-third of its tithe; the church of Altaria and its tithe; the tithe of Braium; the church of Locosanctum [Col. 1288A] with its tithe; two-thirds of the tithe of Darancium; and a portion of the wood at Monssiacum, the monastery of Gif with all its appurtenances. The same bishop also granted that the aforesaid monastery of Hedera should be free from every exaction. From the gift of Henry, archbishop of Sens: the tithes of Merboys and Monseunacum; the whole tithe of Bouilla; and the church of Villare. In the diocese of Chartres: from the gift of Simon of Gaserant and his sons, the place called Pomerium, in which G., bishop of Chartres, granted that a chapel might be built. Likewise, from the gift of the aforesaid archbishop of Sens: the tithe called the “small tithe” (*decima minuta*) of Cavannes, and the wine-tithe; the tithe of all the land which Hugh Guiretly holds in his demesne; the tithe of two arpents [Col. 1288B] of land which the same Hugh gave you; and the tithe of Chosel. From the gift of that same Hugh: half a modius of wheat and half a modius of barley annually from his granary, and a rent of six denarii. Moreover: four arpents of land upon which your monastery is founded; the land of Raveto; whatever Eustachia possessed at Cantalupum; seven sextaries of grain held by Count Frederic in the mills at the village called Valles; half of the mill of Pampiluna near Corbolium; a fourth part of the mill of Pontello of Saint Exuperius; half of the mill at Isona; a sixth part of the port of Villa-nova; at another Villa-nova, the tithe of Coutet; and also the tithe, so that no one may presume to demand tithes from your labor or from the sustenance of your animals.

No person whatsoever, therefore, may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he or she corrects the offense by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; [Col. 1288D] let that person be cut off from the most holy body and blood of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

And it was written in two small circles or roundels, in which there was a small cross: **SAINT PETER. SAINT PAUL. EUGENIUS POPE III. MAKE FOR ME, O LORD, A SIGN FOR GOOD.**

Thus subscribed:

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe. [Col. 1289A] I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, subscribe. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, subscribe. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, subscribe. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, subscribe. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, subscribe. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, subscribe. I, Ibald, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, subscribe. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title in Lucina, subscribe. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of Saint [Col. 1289B] Susanna, subscribe.

Given at Châlons through the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III, pope.

### CCXXXVI. Privilege for Christ Church, London. (1147, October 26.)

[Rymer, *Foedera*, I, 15.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Ralph, prior of Christ Church situated within the walls of London, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

[Col. 1289C] A pious petition ought to be fulfilled by the ensuing effect of the will, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves Christ Church, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with God’s favor, acquire by grants of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these [Col. 1289D] we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: namely, two parts of the revenue from the city of Exeter; the lands of Lectuna, which Simon de Molins and his wife Adelina granted to that place out of regard for divine mercy; the lands and *soke* of Angelische-cuithe-Gylde; the church of Bix with its revenues; the church of Tottenham; the church of Welcumestoa with its appurtenances; the tithe of Hehham; the church of Soresdich with its appurtenances; the church of Brumfeld with its appurtenances; the lands of Branbeleia, from the gift of William, canon of the same church; the lands of Brecbam; the land of Scelhgam, from the gift of Geoffrey de Magnavilla; land at Brachingis; from the alms of Stephen, illustrious king, and Matilda, his queen; land from the gift of Hubert the chamberlain in the same village; the land of Teia, from the generosity of the same man; and the tithe of Benedis.

[Col. 1290A] Upon the death of yourself, now prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any crafty intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, provide to be elected. We also grant that the burial place of that same place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

[Col. 1290B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he or she makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 1290C] The sign of Pope Eugenius III. Place of the monogram. **SAINT PETER. SAINT PAUL. EUGENIUS POPE THE THIRD. MAKE FOR ME, O LORD, A SIGN FOR GOOD.**

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Loverhad, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Gilbert, unworthy priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Arilicus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 1290D] I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Pastor. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Latalaum [read: Lateran] through the hand of Guy, cardinal deacon and [Col. 1291A] chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III, pope.

### CCXXXVII. He confirms certain tithes to the churches of Saint Mary and Saint John, situated above the river Materna near the castle of Gournay. (Fragment.—1147, October 27.)

[La Roque, *Histoire générale de la maison d’Harcourt*, IV, 1620.]

### CCXXXVIII. Privilege for the convent of the Holy Spirit at the Paraclete. (1147, November 1.)

[*Works of Abelard*, ed. Cousin, Appendix, p. 721.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1291B] daughters in Christ, Heloise, abbess of the monastery of the Holy Spirit, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life.

The care of the pastoral office has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, in order that we may labor to establish religious life pleasing to God and preserve it, once established, with exact diligence. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods in fields, vineyards, meadows, woods, mills, waters, tithes, or other things the same monastery now justly and canonically [Col. 1291C] possesses, or may hereafter, with God’s favor, acquire by grants of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit especially to record the following.

The land on which the monastery itself is built; the cultivated lands on Mount Limarsum; whatever you possess through the sale or gift of Milo; two jugera of land before the monastery itself; other land in the same place; the cultivated field at the spring of Amam; all the land that Rainald held in the parish of Quincey, on both sides of the little river Arduçon; the mill of Bruflet, the cultivated field, and certain other lands which Dean Hilduin, his brother Seguin, and their kinsmen gave to your monastery. [Col. 1291D] Half of the oven at Quincey, and Baboel’s vineyard at Calestra (Chalautre); whatever Arpinus of Mariac held from Milo’s fief on that side of the Seine where the monastery stands; the land of Busset; the lands which you possess at Fontanetum Petrosum (Fontenay-le-Pierreux), at Bocia Vagonis, and in the valley of Faiel; four *ochæ* of land at Ferroum (Ferreux); half of the whole wood and land of Furvelles; ten jugera of land at Bocennaium (Bocenay); a third share of the mill’s grinding and a sixth share of its milling, together with all the fishing rights which Maria of Balbusta held at Pontes, and land at Pomerulos (Pommereaux).
