Among these we have considered it proper to specify by their proper names: the parish church of Saint Stephen of Unsilia, with the chapel of Vallechia and its other chapels; the parish church of Saint Vitus of the Castle of Agnulfius; the parish church of Massa; the parish church of Saint Vitalis; the parish church of Saint Lawrence of Monte Libero; the parish church of Carraria; the parish church of Saint Mary of Sarzana; the parish church of Saint Andrew of Sarzana; the parish church of Saint Stephen of Cerreto; the parish church [Col. 1371D] of Saint Venerius; the parish church of Saint Vectianus; the parish church of Marnasco; the parish church of Saint Peter of Porto Venere; the parish church of Ceula; the parish church of Rubiano; the parish church of Cornia; the parish church of Pignone; the parish church of Saint Andrew of the Castle; the parish church of Bollano; the parish church of Saint Peter of the Castle; the parish church of Saint Lawrence; the parish church of Offlano; the parish church of Saint Cyprian of Capite Pontis; the parish church of Viano; the parish church of Soleria; the parish church of Saint Paul; the chaplaincy of Saint Mary of Pugnano; the church of Saint Margaret of Castro Verucula; the church of Saint Michael of Saxo Albo; the parish church of Saint Crispian; the parish church of Venelia; the parish church of Bagnione; the parish church of Vico; the parish church of Tarano; the parish church of Saint Cassian of Verteola; and the parish church of Vigniola with all its chapels, which you justly and canonically possess.

[Col. 1372A] We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, or take away its possessions, or retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any burdens or vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, anyone, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. Conrad, bishop of Sabina. Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New. [Col. 1372B] Ubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. Guido, deacon of Saint Lawrence and cardinal-priest of Saint Damasus. Julius, cardinal-priest of Saint Marcellus.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXXVI. Bull confirming for the Camaldolese hermitage the donations of Jerome, bishop of Arezzo.  
*(1148, 13 November.)*

[MITARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. III, p. 446, from the autograph of Fontebuono, § “Privileges,” no. 31.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1372C] sons AZO, prior of Camaldoli, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Care for venerable places admonishes us to think diligently of their peace and tranquillity, and to strengthen by the protection of our authority those arrangements which our brethren have reasonably established for their benefit. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery of Camaldoli, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, [Col. 1372D] gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit expressly to name those things granted to the Camaldolese hermitage by our venerable brother Jerome, bishop of Arezzo, and his predecessors: namely, everything which Bernard, son of Sidonia, or his father held from the church of Saint Donatus and from the bishops of Arezzo, as is contained in the privileges of those same bishops, etc.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid hermitage, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or burden it with any other molestations; but let all things be preserved whole [Col. 1373A] for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit [Col. 1373B] of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

**“Make for me, O Lord, a sign for good.”**

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have signed. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have signed. I, Gilbert, unworthy priest of the title of Saint Mark, have signed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, have signed. I, Aribert, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have signed. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have signed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Pastor, have signed. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have signed. [Col. 1373C] I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have signed. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New, have signed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have signed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New, have signed.

Given at Pisa through the hands of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXXVII. Bull for the convent of Saint Hilary, situated in the diocese of Fiesole.  
*(1148, 15 November.)*

[LAMI, *Delights of Learning*, 1737, p. 213.]

[Col. 1373D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ AGNES, abbess of the monastery of Saint Hilary situated in the diocese of Fiesole, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Since without the true worship of religion neither the unity of charity can endure nor fruit pleasing to God be produced, it is fitting for apostolic authority to foster religious persons and religious places by the protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, [Col. 1374A] receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that all castles, estates, rights, churches, courts, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands with their appurtenances—whatever the said monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means—shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

We further decree that the monastery itself shall remain forever in the same condition and in the religious observance of nuns in which it was established from its beginning, advancing daily in religious life. Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Alexander and Celestine, Roman pontiffs, we grant and confirm to you by apostolic authority the full tithes from cultivated and uncultivated lands and from your other property, for the use of the poor and pilgrims. You shall receive consecrations of altars or churches and ordinations of your clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

[Col. 1374C] We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been canonically admonished a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, and be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord [Col. 1374D] Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our God Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

+ In place of the circle.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have signed. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have signed. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ubald, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul. [Col. 1375A] I, Gilbert, unworthy priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Guido, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXXVIII. Bull for the monastery of nuns of Saint Martin of Agello.  
*(1148, 18 November.)*

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 997.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1375B] daughters in Christ AGNES, abbess of the monastery of Saint Martin of Agello, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

For prudent virgins, who, with lamps kindled through works of holiness, prepare themselves to meet the Bridegroom, apostolic protection should be at hand, lest some assault of rashness turn them from their purpose or weaken—God forbid—the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Martin of Agello—an institution belonging specially to the right of blessed Peter—in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order which is acknowledged to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord granting it, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to name expressly: the site itself on which your monastery stands, with all its adjoining lands and appurtenances; your lands, vineyards, tithes, revenues, and all other things known to belong to the said [Col. 1375D] monastery at Massa Marchionum; the church of Saint Pancras and the church of Saint Remigius; and all property or goods which Jolicta, widow of the late Ubaldo and Sigifred of Bozano, gave to the aforesaid monastery by way of donation or offering. We confirm these for the aforesaid monastery by this present document.

Moreover, no one may presume to demand tithes from you, according to the custom hitherto observed, from your lands which you now possess or shall possess hereafter, lawfully acquired under whatever right, or from lands which you newly cultivate or shall cultivate in the future. You may also receive free and unencumbered persons fleeing from the secular world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. Further, we decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the canonical portion of the testament remains reserved to those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1376A] We grant you freedom and immunity from the diocesan bishop. You shall receive the oil for the sick and ordinations of your clerics from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic; and we will that he furnish these freely and without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. You shall also have authority canonically to appoint priests in the aforesaid churches, as you are known lawfully to have possessed that authority until the present time.

We further command that no one shall disturb the churches belonging to the said monastery which you now justly and canonically possess or may acquire hereafter, or inflict injury or molestation upon those serving the Lord in them or upon their property, or presume to impose upon them new and unlawful exactions. Moreover, we hold valid the ancient liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs granted to your church and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain inviolate in future times.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things [Col. 1376C] be preserved inviolate and whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. Fare well. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed, etc.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends [Col. 1376D] of December, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXXIX. To the bishops of Auxerre and Soissons, and to Abbot Suger—Concerning the election of the bishop of Arras.  
*(1148.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 644.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren H., bishop of Auxerre, G., bishop of Soissons, and his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1377A] Our beloved son L., archdeacon of Arras, having come into our presence, gave a very different account to us and our brethren of what was done concerning our son Master H. from that which had been reported through Adam and his associates, canons of that same church. For he stated that certain canons of Arras had presumed, contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, to elect our son Master H. as bishop of Arras after an appeal had been made to us in their presence and hearing. Therefore, by this present writing we command you, after summoning both parties into your presence, to hear carefully the allegations on either side; and, if this is found to be true, to annul that election, setting aside the appeal. Moreover, since, as we have learned from the report of the aforesaid our son L. and his companions, they were despoiled of their revenues after the appeal had been made to us, we likewise command you by the authority of this present letter to cause what was taken from them to be restored in full.

Given at Pisa.

### CCCXXX. Bull for Guido, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Morrona.  
*(1148, 22 November.)*

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, III, 1163.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO, abbot of Saint Mary of Morrone, and his brethren, present and future, to be regularly appointed: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1377C] It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery of the blessed Mother of God Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit expressly to name: your share in the castle itself and its estate; the parish church and chapel of that same castle, with their tithes; whatever you possess in the estate of Aquisiana; the bathhouse and aqueduct as far as Cascina; the lands you possess in Palude and Pantano, with their tithes; the church of Thora with its appurtenances; the church of Montanino, with half of the castle and its appurtenances—without prejudice to the agreement made and confirmed in writing between Ubert, archbishop of Pisa of venerable memory, and Abbot Gerard. If any free and unencumbered person should wish during life or at death to enter the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 1378A] you shall have free authority to receive that person without any opposition, while preserving the right of the mother church.

We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, [Col. 1378B] know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints [Col. 1378C] Lawrence and Damasus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed.

Given at San Gimignano, through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and forty-eight of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius.

### CCCXXXI. Papal protection granted to the Scottish monastery of Saint James at Regensburg.  
*(1148, 29 November.)*

[RIED, *Diplomatic Codex of Regensburg*, I, 219.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1378D] sons CHRISTIAN, abbot of the monastery of Saint James of Regensburg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which seems consonant with reason and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and give appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery itself, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that the monastic order [Col. 1379A] established in that monastery according to the Rule of blessed Benedict shall there be preserved inviolate in future times. Moreover, whatever goods and possessions the monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the canonical right of the bishop of Regensburg. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to amend his or her offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1379C] I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Siena through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

*(Lead seal: Eugenius, Pope III.)*

### CCCXXXII. To Lord Abbot Suger—Concerning the affair of the church of Saint Geneviève.  
*(1148?)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 641.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1379D] son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, as the examined tenor of your letters has disclosed to us, you are shortly to send envoys and letters to our presence which will explain and set forth the affair of Saint Geneviève more fully, we have not thought it necessary to reply to you now through the bearer of this letter. But when your envoys, more fully making known that affair to us, appear before us, then, with the Lord as author, we shall do what must be done. Meanwhile, let your affection keep diligent watch, so that you may in no way permit what we have already accomplished for the most part by divine grace and with your assistance to be destroyed.

### CCCXXXIII. To Abbot Suger—Concerning the affair of the church of Saint Geneviève.  
*(1148?)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 642.]

[Col. 1380A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let it be known to your discretion that we associated with you our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, in the notification of our sentence, not because we have any distrust whatsoever of you—for past and strong deeds furnish evidence of constancy to come—but in order that the secular canons of Saint Geneviève might have no particular grounds for exercising hostility against you. We therefore thought fit to associate with you the aforesaid brother. It is accordingly your concern to remain steadfast in the good work begun, so that, as you appear to be the planter of religious life, you may likewise, with the Lord as author, be judged its preserver.

### CCCXXXIV. To Abbot Suger—That he provide Hugh of Saint-Victor with expenses for a journey to Rome; and concerning the affair of the church of Saint Geneviève.  
*(1148?)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 642.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having very great confidence in your affection, we do not hesitate at all to lay upon you all things which charity is accustomed to bear. Since therefore our beloved son Hugh, canon of Saint-Victor, is about to return to us, we ask your goodwill to provide him with one mount and the expenses sufficient for it and its rider on the return journey. On our behalf, instruct the abbot and brethren of Saint Geneviève that, from the revenues of the deanery which ought to be assigned to those brethren, they shall repay to the same Hugh twenty-five pounds of Provins currency, which he is known to have received from creditors for the work of the church. Moreover, we wish it to be known to your discretion that, in order that the grounds for hostility of the secular clerics of that church against you might be diminished, we associated with you the venerable Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, [Col. 1380D] as you could learn by examining the other letters which we sent you.

### CCCXXXV. To Abbot Wibald and the brethren of Corvey—That the deposed Henry find no refuge among them.  
*(1149, 1 January.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Collection*, II, 293.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot, and to the chapter of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How necessary it is to provide for the tranquillity of religious monks and to think diligently of their welfare is taught us by the office which we formerly held in governing an abbey; and God, Creator of all, made this still clearer when he took Mary’s side against Martha. Therefore, desiring, as far as we can and with justice accompanying us, to provide for your peace, we have commanded by apostolic letters the venerable brethren, archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout the German kingdom, that, so long as Henry, former abbot of Corvey—whom our beloved son Thomas, priest-cardinal of happy memory, deposed—persists in his purpose of perversity, they shall by no means receive him in their churches or furnish him with any aid or support against you and your monastery.

It is therefore your concern, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Wibald, to exercise your care and preserve by prayer and provident solicitude those entrusted to you, so that the lion seeking someone to devour may find no opportunity to tear them apart. Thus, when you have rendered those whose care you have assumed distinguished by religious observance and honourable conduct, the Mediator of God and humankind may, in his customary mercy, grant rewards to your labour and cause you to rejoice with his saints in eternal rest. And to all of you who belong to the community of Corvey we command by this present letter that you humbly accept and observe the admonitions of your abbot, our son Wibald, so that in his person you may appear to honour Christ, whose minister he is.

Given at Viterbo, on the Kalends of January.

### CCCXXXVI. He adjudicates the disputes between Ralph, bishop of Orte, and the canons of the Greater Church.  
*(1149, 2 January.)*

[UGHELLI, *Sacred Italy*, I, 736.]

[Col. 1381C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LEO, prior of the Greater Church of Blessed Mary at Orte, and his sons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In order that the darkness of forgetfulness may not, through disuse, be introduced into human minds concerning what has been judged or decided in disputes of cases, such matters should be committed to the due memorial of writing, so that posterity may thereby have what it may clearly recognize in future times. Therefore we command that the matters debated in our presence and determined by us concerning the disputes between you and our venerable brother Ralph, your bishop, be recorded in the tenor of this present document.

Accordingly, in accordance with the ancient customs of your church, we firmly decree that you shall have and peacefully possess the churches, lands, vineyards, and offerings concerning which the dispute arose, except in respect of four feasts, on which the bishop shall have a fourth part of the bread: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, on the first Sunday of Lent, at Easter, and at the Assumption of Blessed Mary. At the Nativity and at Easter he shall have the money, and on Maundy Thursday he shall provide hospitality for all of you. Further, you shall have half of the public penances, sacred rites, and ordinations, wherever the bishop performs them and throughout the whole diocese. When [Col. 1382A] the bishop goes out on feast days, he shall have with him a deacon, a subdeacon, and two others from among you; and when he goes through the county, he shall take with him two of you whom you, son Prior, and after your death your successors, shall choose for this purpose. Moreover, whatever other goods our aforesaid brother the bishop and you may justly and canonically acquire in the diocese, God being favourable, you and your successors, together with the bishop and his successors, shall henceforth possess peacefully and jointly. But if anyone should act contrary to this, etc.

Given at Viterbo, on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

### CCCXXXVII. To Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine, Canterbury.  
*(1149, 18 January.)*

[Chronicle of W. Thorn, in TWISDEN, *Historians of England*, II, 1808.]

[Col. 1382B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HUGH, abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine, Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The ancient enemy of the human race does not cease, with his customary malice, to lay snares for those who publicly profess themselves disciples of Christ; rather, with continual cunning he labours to deceive in every way souls serving the Creator of all and to bring them into hatred of their Creator. At his prompting, although you humbly accepted and observed the sentence of interdict proclaimed at our command by our venerable brother Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, your brethren nevertheless, setting aside consideration for monastic discipline, celebrated divine offices, as we have learned to be true. Therefore, lest so grave an offence remain unpunished and furnish many others with an occasion to commit the like, we command that, from the time you receive this present document, the monastery over which you preside abstain from divine offices for as long as such offices have been improperly celebrated there after the interdict.

Those who presented themselves before us, after we had accepted their satisfaction, we absolve from the bond of excommunication. But the prior and William, who were the leaders and instigators of this contumacy, and whom our brother the archbishop bound by sentence of excommunication, we have granted to him, by the grace of the Apostolic See, authority to absolve. We do not, however, wish that because we defer to him in this matter, he or his successors should hereafter impose any burden upon the monastery of Saint Augustine contrary to its ancient custom or to the privileges granted to it by the Apostolic See. Moreover, because of his rebellion and contumacy, we suspend the prior from the office of prior, on the condition that no one shall have leave to relax that same sentence without our command. The other monks who have incurred defilement through participation with the excommunicated we entrust to you for absolution.

Given at Viterbo, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

### CCCXXXVIII. Bull for the hermitage of Fonte Avellana.  
*(1149, 31 January.)*

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, IX, 28.]

[Col. 1383A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SABINUS, prior of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, and his brethren professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding effect, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid place, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the church of Holy Cross situated in the aforesaid hermitage [Col. 1383B] now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord granting it, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

We grant you free authority, without anyone’s opposition, to receive into the religious life clerics or laypersons who are free and flee the secular world. Moreover, no one whatsoever may presume to demand tithes from you from the produce of your labour which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. We also confirm for you, by the grant of the Apostolic See, the possessions which you have in the estate of Sorbitulo or may hereafter justly acquire, as is contained in the privilege of our predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, or take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, then, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall not make suitable amendment by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of February [31 January], in the sixth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of St Peter at Modena.  
*(1149, 8 February.)*

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, IV, 185.]

[Col. 1384A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PLACITUS, abbot of the monastery of St Peter, situated outside Modena, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

As devout and humble sons ought to be cherished by the comfort of paternal affection, so rebellious and proud men ought to be punished according to the deserts of their offences. Therefore, after taking counsel with our brethren, both cardinals [Col. 1384B] and other bishops, we deprived for ever the Church of Modena of episcopal dignity because of the obstinacy of the Modenese and the grave offences which they had long committed against the commands of the Apostolic See; and we divided its parish among the neighbouring bishoprics. We reserved to the right and ownership of the holy Roman Church the monastery of Blessed Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service. Therefore, receiving it with all its goods under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought the following worthy of express mention:

Namely, the land itself on which the said monastery is built, with its boundaries, as is contained in your documents. The church of St John the Baptist, and the tithes and burial rights which you have held from ancient times within the city. Two mills [Col. 1384C] with their watercourses near the city. The church of St Mary of Massa. The church of St Mary of Muniano. The church of St Geminianus of Saviniano. The church of St Mary of Ambiliano. The church of St Geminianus of the Tower. The church of St Mary near the Old Castle. The church of St Mary of the Wood. The church of St Michael of the Marsh. The castle of Adiano with the churches of St Michael and St Mary. The small estate called Abrica, with the church of St George. The church of Alliano. The fortress called Cornetulum, with the church of St Martin. The church of St Michael of Sorbetulo. The land which you hold in Crespellano and in the estate of Pragatuli. Whatever else you hold in [Col. 1384D] the bishoprics of Reggio, Ferrara, Verona, and Padua.

We decree, therefore, that no person may, etc., saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishops, etc.

Farewell.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed.  
I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of St Praxedes, have subscribed.  
I, In . . . . baldus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Jordanus, cardinal-priest of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed.  
[Col. 1385A] I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.  
I, Octavianus, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.  
I, Gregorius, cardinal-deacon of St Angelo, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal-deacon of St Mary the New, have subscribed.

Given at Viterbo through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February [8 February], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1149 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXL. To Henry, bishop of Moravia: he congratulates him upon the people’s return to obedience.  
*(1149, 1 March.)*

[BOCZEK, *Cod. diplom. Morav.*, I, 243.]

[Col. 1385B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable HENRY, bishop of Moravia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

While we were concerned for the condition of your brotherhood . . . we received your messenger, who reported that you had been visited by God with bodily illness and that the people who had withdrawn themselves from your subjection had returned to your obedience. Praying to the Lord for your health, we rejoice with paternal affection for your brotherhood in those things which prosperously befall you. Therefore, by this present writing we command your belovedness that [Col. 1385C] you should strive so to preside over and benefit the people entrusted to you that, with them, you may deserve, the Lord helping you, to receive eternal joys. Moreover, frequently inform us by your letters of your condition, which we always wish to be prosperous.

Given at Viterbo, on the Kalends of March [1 March].

### CCCXLI. To Henry, bishop of Moravia.—That he absolve Władysław, duke of Poland, from excommunication.  
*(1149, 3 March.)*

[Ibid., 245.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Moravia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1385D] As we believe has come to your knowledge, L., duke of Poland, having gathered a multitude of Saracens, invaded the land of Christians—something unheard-of and inhuman in our times—and with rash audacity committed in it many evils, countless and even abominable. Therefore our brother L., of blessed memory, archbishop of the Church of Gniezno, inflamed with zeal for justice, bound him with the bond of excommunication. But now, since that archbishop has entered upon the way of all flesh, and the duke himself requests absolution from us through his messengers and promises satisfaction, we command you by apostolic letters that, after summoning the duke before you, [Col. 1386A] you meet with him in a suitable place; and, if in your presence he gives an oath with his own hand that, concerning the matter for which he was excommunicated, he will receive and observe our command, whether made to him by ourselves, by letter, or through our messenger, you shall absolve him from that excommunication.

Once this oath has been received from him, inform us by your letters of the cause of excommunication, of the damages inflicted by him and through him, of the whole truth of the matter, and of what the duke himself may be liable to suffer as a result. Once we know the truth of the matter, we shall, with God as author, determine what ought to be decreed concerning it.

Given at Viterbo, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].  
[Note: [Col. 1385D] Read: March. JAFFÉ.]

### CCCXLII. He commands the clergy and people of Lemos and of other districts to obey the bishop of Lugo, to whom, by command of the Apostolic See, their churches had already been restored after previously being occupied by the bishop of Oviedo.  
*(1149, 17 March.)*

[RISCO (Florez), *España sagrada*, XLI, 307, from the Braga manuscript called the *Liber fidei*.]

[Col. 1386B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Lemos, Sarria, Flamoso, Páramo, both Neiras, Navia de Suarna, Burón, Balonga, Aviancos, Camba, and Elma, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since your churches had formerly been restored to the Church of Lugo by legates of the Apostolic See, and had again been unlawfully occupied by the Church of Oviedo, we commanded our venerable brother M., bishop of Oviedo, both by letter and orally, to restore those churches in their entirety to our venerable brother, the bishop of Lugo, within a fixed term. And indeed, as we have learned, he has now humbly obeyed our commands, as he ought. Since, placed in the seat of justice, we owe to all the preservation of their right, and ought, with the Lord’s help, beneficially to provide for the Church’s peace and tranquillity, [Col. 1386C] we command and enjoin your whole body by this present writing humbly to render obedience and reverence to the aforesaid bishop of Lugo, as your bishop and the shepherd of your souls.

Given at Viterbo, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March].

### CCCXLIII. To Henry, bishop of Moravia: he commends a certain person to him.  
*(1149, 25 March.)*

[BOCZEK, *Cod. diplom. Morav.*, I, 244.]

[Col. 1386D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, bishop of Moravia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The bearer of this letter has resolved to come into those parts on his own affairs. Since, therefore, we have great confidence in your prudence and integrity, we command your belovedness by way of request that, for reverence toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, you hold him commended to you and endeavour to assist him before the duke, consistently with our honour and your own.

Given at Viterbo, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March].

### CCCXLIV. To the archpriests of the diocese of Modena.  
*(1149, 8 April.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie Storiche di Modenesi*, III, 21.]

[Col. 1387A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the archpriests of St Martin in a Hundred Banks, Bajoaria, the New City, Ganaceto, St Thomas of Lama, Sorbaria, Solaria, St Felix, Masta, and Ponte Ducis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As is reported by rumours spreading through the regions of Italy, because of the grave obstinacy and offences of the Modenese we divided the parishes of that city among neighbouring bishoprics, but retained certain churches of that diocese specially within our own power. Since the Apostolic See is accustomed more readily to love and cherish humble and devout sons, and since we have considered the devotion of our venerable brother A., bishop, and of the people of Reggio, we have judged it fitting to grant your churches in perpetuity, with all chapels belonging to them, to that brother of ours and his successors, and through them to the Church of Reggio. Therefore, by this present writing we command and enjoin you [Col. 1387B] humbly to obey the aforesaid brother of ours as bishop and ruler of your souls, and likewise to receive and observe his admonitions and commands. If you disdain to do so, we shall, with God as author, ratify the sentence which our brother has justly pronounced against you.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixth day before the Ides of April [8 April].

### CCCXLV. Privilege for the monastery of St Peter at Salzburg.  
*(1149, 10 April.)*

[*Novissimum Chron. S. Petri Salzburg.*, p. 223.]

[Col. 1387C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BALDERIC, abbot of the monastery of St Peter at Salzburg, and his brethren, present and future, of the order of St Benedict, professing the regular life, for ever.

The care of the Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may cherish religious persons and strive in every way to promote the religious life pleasing to God. For no service is [Col. 1387D] otherwise rendered acceptably to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, with this concern for charity, and at the intervention of our venerable brother Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, we have judged your reasonable requests worthy of assent. We decree that the regular order introduced in that place according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict by St Rupert, formerly your abbot and bishop of Salzburg—and known to have been established there by him—shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Further, all rights and privileges with which, above other churches, you have been honoured because of your celebrated antiquity and the merits of the faith which have shone forth from you to many nations—namely, precedence in the more honourable place, [Col. 1388A] which you have always customarily held in stations and processions above the clergy and canons of that city by the command and institution of many archbishops of Salzburg and by the consent of those canons, as we have been fully informed through the letters of privileges of the archbishops and canons by our aforesaid venerable brother Eberhard—together with all other prerogatives which you have hitherto held in peaceful possession, shall remain unimpaired to you.

Moreover, we forbid any of you, cleric or layman, after having made profession, to dare to possess anything of his own or to leave the monastery enclosure without the permission of the abbot or community; and we fortify both you and all that is yours with the protection of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1388B] We confirm for you and your successors who remain in holy religion the perpetual possession of ecclesiastical benefices and all other goods which you now justly and lawfully possess or may hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, acquire through just means. And so that you may persist more tranquilly in that holy religion, we approve, confirm, and will to be inviolably observed in perpetual force everything which our venerable brother Conrad, archbishop of that see, established and ordained for the like preservation of your rights: namely, that your abbot for the time being shall always attend elections of the archbishops of Salzburg in your place, since such elections formerly belonged to you; and that the person whom he, together with the canons of the aforesaid see, has chosen shall be accepted as archbishop, without objection from anyone whatsoever.

We also approve and confirm what you reserved, with the consent of that archbishop, upon surrendering the parish church of the same city: [Col. 1388C] tithes sufficient to provide for your household of both sexes at Eastertime; and the right, as a sign of recognition of the ancient mother church, to baptize certain infants on Holy Saturday or Pentecost. We likewise approve, confirm, and will inviolably observed the sacred obligation owed to you by the aforesaid canons of the church of St Rupert, on account of the many goods, possessions, the transfer of the episcopal see to Salzburg, and the surrender of the said parish church, as is fully contained in the letters of our aforementioned brother Conrad, archbishop; together with the donation of the church at Mylbach and the tithes of twenty-four salt pans there, and many other goods which, in succession, [Col. 1388D] both the aforesaid archbishop and others, moved by pious consideration, bestowed upon you. Their purpose was that the persons serving the Lord in your monastery should not ever cease from religious observance because of the lack of temporal resources which you had incurred through the transfer of the episcopal see and the surrender of the aforesaid parish church, despite their assiduous pursuit of the devout life.

We decree, by force of the aforesaid obligation, that if the said canons should ever harass you in your rights or attempt anything contrary to the aforesaid ordinances, or to any one of them, then all the goods, possessions, and rights—including the archbishopric and the parish church—which had been transferred from you to them with great generosity shall have to return and devolve once more upon your church.

[Col. 1389A] Furthermore, we will and grant that your very ancient burial ground at that place shall remain free with every right of receiving whatever offerings are made at funeral rites, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, even if they are ministeriales or persons known to belong to the demesne of the aforesaid archbishop or canons—unless perhaps they are excommunicated or under interdict.

In addition, we decree that no person whatsoever shall have permission rashly to disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by wanton vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those [Col. 1389B] for whose governance and support they were granted, saving reverence for the proper metropolitan. Moreover, receive the ecclesiastical sacraments from the archbishop of Salzburg, your diocesan for the time being, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them to you freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may have recourse to whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

When you who are now abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, no one shall be placed over it through any cunning of usurpation or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, [Col. 1389C] shall elect from their own community or, if necessary, from another, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall receive blessing from his ordinary. Neither bishop nor abbot himself may give the goods of the monastery as a fief or benefice without the consent of all of you, or of the greater and sounder part; nor may they alienate, sell, squander, exchange, pledge, or grant them in benefice by any other means. Rather, the abbot himself, as a good steward, shall strive in every way to gather together the scattered goods of your church and preserve those gathered together. Nor shall any bishop have licence to impose upon you and your church forced services or other new exactions contrary to your canonical freedom and religious life.

If, then, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, [Col. 1389D] knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall not make suitable amendment by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

[Col. 1390A] Given at Troyes.  
[Note: [Col. 1389] Read: at Tusculum.]  
Through the hand of Guido, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of April [10 April], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1149 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCXLVI. He urges Guido, abbot of Bonnevaux, to admit the monastery of Vallemagne and its monks among the brethren of the Cistercian order.  
*(1149, 30 April.)*

[*Gall. Christ. nov.*, VI, 322.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., abbot of Bonneval, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1390B] Since the sons of holy Church are so kindled by an ardent desire through the prevenient grace of God that they desire those things to which they ought to be urged by pontifical admonitions, we ought to labour all the more diligently that their praiseworthy will may attain its effect, because the very things they desire accord with Christian religion and oppose the snares of the ancient enemy. Therefore, since the brethren of Vallemagne most earnestly desire to adopt and observe your order, we command your belovedness by this present writing to receive them among the brethren of the Cistercian order and to endeavour to provide for them, as for your special brethren, both spiritually and temporally.

Given at Tusculum, on the second day before the Kalends of May [30 April].

### CCCXLVII. To the abbots of Coxan, Bisuldun, and others.—That they obey G., abbot of St Victor at Marseilles, upon whom he bestows the blessing.  
*(1149, 30 April.)*

[MARTEN, *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 803, from the cartulary of St Victor.]

[Col. 1390C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., abbot of Coxan; the abbots of Bisuldun, Balneol, Gères, Vabres, Castres, and St Savin: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We graciously received in our presence our beloved son G., elected [Note: [Col. 1389] Guillaume, the first of that name, whose election Ruffius assigns to the year 1147.] of Marseilles, who came with letters of the chapter and brethren of the same monastery; and, having approved his election, we bestowed upon him the grace of blessing. Therefore, sending him back [Col. 1390D] to his own place with the favour of the Apostolic See, we command you by this present writing to render him due reverence and obedience as your master, and to obey his salutary admonitions in a salutary manner.

Given at Tusculum, on the second day before the Kalends of May [30 April].

### CCCXLVIII. To Conrad, noble margrave.  
*(1149, 3 May.)*

[SCHANNAT, *Videmiae litterar.*, II, 77.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman CONRAD, margrave, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1391A] We have graciously received the letters of your nobility and praise in the Lord the devotion which we perceive you bear toward Blessed Peter and the Church of God. Therefore, wishing to fulfil your praiseworthy request concerning the churches for which you petitioned, we have judged your petition worthy of assent. Accordingly, we have commanded our venerable brother, the archbishop of Magdeburg, in writing to endeavour to bring this into effect in accordance with your request to us. Furthermore, hold our beloved son, the provost of Meissen, and his canons especially commended to you, so that you may defend them from the assaults of wicked men and assist and support them in their needs.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].

### CCCXLIX. To [Hugh], archbishop of Sens, and [Hugh], archbishop of Rouen.—He admonishes them to compel their parishioners, who had inflicted damages and injuries upon the Church of Paris, to make satisfaction to that church.  
*(1149, 16 May.)*

[*Chartularium ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. I, p. 226.]

[Col. 1391B]

[lacuna]

Given at Tusculum, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May].

### CCCL. To H[ugh], archbishop of Vienne, to whom is entrusted the examination of the controversy between Henry, bishop of Autun, and Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, concerning the ownership of the churches of Poligny.  
*(1149, 20 May.)*

[*Bullar. Cluniac.*, p. 62.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother H., archbishop of Vienne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1391C] Wishing to bring to its proper conclusion the controversy being conducted between our beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, and the venerable bishop of Autun concerning the ownership of the churches of Poligny, we have judged it fitting to entrust that controversy to your brotherhood. Therefore, by this present writing we command your discretion that, having summoned both parties before you at a suitable place and time, you should endeavour, with the Lord as author, to determine the case by a canonical judgment.

Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June [20 May].

### CCCLI. To Hugh, abbot of the monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury.  
*(1149.)*

[TWSIDEN and SELDEN, *Hist. A. Script.*, vol. II, p. 1809.]

[Col. 1391D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Obedience and patience, required by the Christian religion in other persons, are especially expected from those known to have undertaken a more perfect life; and they ought surely to be judged so much the more blameworthy when they are provoked without cause to indignation or disobedience. Although, therefore, because your brethren presumptuously dared to violate our sentence, [Col. 1392A] we could have further aggravated our penalties against them and the aforesaid monastery under the rigour of the canons, nevertheless, since it is fitting that we be more merciful than severe, we have judged that they should be treated with such indulgence that their offence should not remain wholly unpunished, yet they should not be compelled to bear the penalty of disobedience longer than they deserve. Therefore, until the next Kalends of August [1 August], we prohibit the celebration of divine offices in the monastery of St Augustine; thereafter we grant permission for the customary and due offices to be celebrated there.

It is thus your concern, through your care and labour, so to provide that your brethren need not hereafter suffer anything of this kind because of their offences and incur the displeasure of Blessed Peter and ourselves. Concerning the portable altars upon which excommunicated persons [Col. 1392B] celebrated offices, we will that the severity which you customarily observe be maintained.

### CCCLII. Rescript to Theobald, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, concerning the absolution of Prior Silvester.  
*(1149.)*

[Ibid.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother THEOBALD, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we love your person with special affection, we honour you as far as justice permits. Moved, therefore, by this love of charity, and yielding to your brotherhood, we have entrusted to you for absolution the prior of St Augustine’s and the monk William [Col. 1392C] from the punishment which, in the rigour of justice, we imposed upon them because they had raised themselves against your interdict. Therefore, lest the favour of the Apostolic See shown to your charity prove detrimental to them, and lest they be forced to lament the aforesaid offence more than is right, we command your discretion by this present writing that you allow them by no means to be further tormented by this punishment; but at last, taking pity on them, absolve them from the sentence by which they are bound.

Furthermore, as has been reported to us, the men of the same monastery were compelled to make a payment for redemption because of participation with excommunicated persons, in addition to ecclesiastical punishment. This seems unusual and contrary to reason. For no one ought to be punished twice for the same thing—especially persons compelled to obey the commands of their lords. Since it is fitting that we be merciful rather than severe, [Col. 1392D] we command your brotherhood to cause everything taken from them on this occasion to be restored without harassment. For we do not wish novelties to be introduced into your Church.

### CCCLIII. To the archbishop and chapter of the Church of Tours.—He refuses to write to the churches of Dol and Saint-Brieuc, since they are excommunicated.  
*(1149, May.)*

[MANSI, *Conc.*, XXI, 690.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother the archbishop and to the chapter of the Church of Tours, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1393A] We have received your letters with due kindness and have diligently examined their contents. Nevertheless, we cannot write to the churches of Dol and Saint-Brieuc as you requested, since, as we remember, a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against them by you, brother archbishop, because of their disobedience and obstinacy; and it was subsequently confirmed by us at the Council of Reims. We decreed that it should remain in force until they repent of their obstinacy and return to obedience to the Church of Tours.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July [14 June].

### CCCLIV. To Conrad, king of the Romans.—He consoles him on his return from Jerusalem over the tribulations inflicted upon him and his army.  
*(1149, 24 June.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 629.]

[Col. 1393B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ CONRAD, by God’s grace illustrious king of the Romans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since in this world the order of change corrupts all things, we ought, trusting in divine mercy, neither to be exalted by prosperity nor broken by adversity. For the mediator between God and men, by a wonderful dispensation, customarily chastises with adversities every son whom he receives, so that, while by love he calls him to eternal rewards, [Col. 1393C] the present world may, through the troubles it brings upon him, repel his mind from itself; and that he may withdraw all the more easily from love of this age, the more he is impelled while he is called. This is figured in the people of Israel, in Moses calling and Pharaoh driving them on. Moses, indeed, was sent to call when Pharaoh was pressing them with harsh labours, so that the one might draw them by calling and the other drive them on by cruelty, and so that the people, shamefully fixed in servitude, might be moved either by the inducement of good things or by the pressure of troubles.

Moved, therefore, by this consideration, we admonish and exhort your discretion in the Lord to endure patiently the tribulations which almighty God has inflicted upon you and your army, and [Col. 1393D] to place your hope in him who permits whom he wills to be afflicted and is accustomed mercifully to deliver those who trust in him. For if you maintain patience and humility perfectly in adversity, you will be led fearlessly through the desert of this life under the protection of the pillar of cloud and fire—that is, under the consolation of patience and the ardour of charity.

Since, therefore, we love your person with true charity and have great confidence in you, it would surely have pleased us if, after your return, we had been able without delay to confer with you in mutual conversation concerning those matters known to pertain to the honour of holy Church and the kingdom. But since the circumstances of the time denied us that opportunity, and since we are concerned for your welfare, after we learned, by God’s working, that you had arrived safely in the regions of Lombardy, [Col. 1394A] we judged it fitting to send certain of our brethren to your serenity, as we informed you through our venerable brethren Artwic, archbishop of Bremen, and Anselm, bishop of Havelberg. They were to set before you the affection and goodwill which we bear toward you and to enable us to learn through their report what we desired to hear concerning you. Yet when they had proceeded as far as Tuscany and learned that you had passed into the German regions, fearing the length and difficulty of the journey because of the unseasonable summer heat, they returned to our presence.

[Col. 1394B] Moreover, because we desire to know your condition and that of our beloved son, King Henry the Younger—whom, after your departure, we have loved with paternal affection and whose actions we earnestly hope may prosper in the Lord—we are sending our faithful Franko, the bearer of this letter, and apostolic letters to visit your excellency, since our brethren could not complete the labour of so great a journey because of the heat of summer. We admonish and exhort your nobility in the Lord to endeavour to inform us through that same Franko of what is happening concerning you and him, and of the condition of the kingdom. At this time show the devotion which you bear toward your mother, the holy Roman Church, so that you may appear to respond fittingly [Col. 1394C] to our affection and may deserve, through the intercessions of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—to whom you ought to devote yourself wholly—to obtain a more abundant grace from our Creator.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June].

### CCCLV. To H., archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans.—On the same subject.  
*(1149, 8 July.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 643.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren H., archbishop of Soissons, and his suffragans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

With what devotion our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, undertook the journey to Jerusalem, you knew by your bodily presence, and it did not escape the greater part of the world that he left his kingdom under the protection of holy Church and ourselves. He earnestly begged both us and you to protect it against the assaults of wicked men. We have learned, however, that certain persons, by diabolical prompting, are disturbing the peace of the kingdom and maliciously assailing him, setting aside reverence for God and men. They do not consider that their king, too, has piously taken up his cross and followed Christ, and, leaving homeland and kingdom, hastened to the places where the Lord’s feet stood for the defence of the Christian faith. We bear this all the more grievously because we love his person with more particular affection and know that he is devoutly remaining in distant regions for God’s service.

[Col. 1395A] Since we cannot and ought not to fail so devout a son of holy Church and a most Christian prince in his need, we command you by this present writing to assemble together, summon before you those disturbing the kingdom, and strictly and carefully admonish them to desist altogether from harassing the kingdom and not presume to inflict any injury upon the men of the lord king. If they disdain to obey your admonitions, pronounce a sentence of excommunication against both them and their accomplices, with every pretext set aside. Furthermore, when those to whom the guardianship of the kingdom has been entrusted, or any one of them, admonish you, you shall, as lovers of peace and justice, provide them with temporal aid in accordance with the fidelity which you owe to that kingdom [Col. 1395B] and assist them in every way in its defence.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July].

### CCCLVI. To Abbot Suger.—Concerning the disturbers of the French kingdom.  
*(1149, 8 July.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 643.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letter that you sent us, and we sympathize with you in fatherly affection concerning the adversities and hardships which you reported yourself to be enduring. [Col. 1395C] And since we know that you bear them for the love of justice and fidelity toward our dearest son Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, we regard them as our own. Yet your discretion does not fail to know that all who wish to live devoutly in Christ and love peace must endure countless persecutions from the children of this age and from those who hate peace. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself came down not for the joys of the world, but to endure suffering and death for us. Therefore we must imitate him, our head; for if we suffer persecutions for his sake, secure in his promise, we shall be blessed in eternal recompense. Take courage, then, dearest son, and act manfully; and, trusting in the Lord, who is your helper, do not fear [Col. 1395D] what man may do to you. For our Savior, according to his promise, will by no means forsake his own until the end of the age; and we too shall take care, according to the authority granted us by him, to provide you aid and assistance. For, as you will be able to see from the letters which we are sending to our brethren the archbishops and bishops, we have ordered that those who disturb the peace of the kingdom be excommunicated unless they repent; and by exhortation we have instructed both them and the counts to stand by you and the others entrusted with the guardianship of the kingdom, helping manfully in its defense. Let it therefore be your concern to cause those same brother archbishops and bishops to assemble together at an appointed time, so that whatever must be done for the welfare of the kingdom [Col. 1396A] may be accomplished with the Lord’s help.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July].

CCCLVII. To Abbot Suger.—On the return of King Louis VII of France from overseas regions. (1149, 15 July.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 642.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Blessed be God, who does not forsake those who hope in him and who is accustomed mercifully to deliver those who trust in his mercy. For, as we have learned for certain, he has taken pity on our dearest son Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, after countless vicissitudes of tribulation; [Col. 1396B] he has brought him back from darkness to light and brought him to the nearer shores of the sea. His return, concerning which we had been anxious with fatherly affection, affords us the greatest joy and provides consolation amid the adversities which we have long endured. You therefore, as a faithful and prudent steward, should strive manfully to manage the affairs of the kingdom entrusted to you. For the time is near when you will receive the palm and reward of your labor. Henceforth let it be your concern honorably to prepare yourself, together with his faithful men, to meet the king. Our beloved son the king of Sicily subsequently informed us by letter that he had been told that the aforesaid our son, the king of France, had landed in his kingdom and was proceeding toward Sicily, intending to meet the queen, since he thought that she had arrived there from the regions of Barbary.

[Col. 1396C] Given at Tusculum, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August].

CCCLVIII. Letter concerning the election of Matilda, the second abbess of Fontevraud. (1149, 7 September.)

[Gall. Christ. nov., II, 362.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the nuns of the church of Fontevraud: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we gather from examination of your letter, your abbess of good memory, being called by the Lord, paid the debt of human mortality. Moved by fatherly sorrow at her death, we commend her soul to the Lord in our prayers. But you, [Col. 1396D] after her death, as you informed us in that same letter, canonically elected as your abbess M., sister of the noble count of Anjou; and you requested that she be blessed by our venerable brother G., bishop of Poitiers. Since he refused to do this without a promise of obedience, we shall not delay, in accordance with your petition, to bring this matter to a conclusion.

Moreover, by this present letter we admonish and exhort your whole community in the Lord to strive more diligently to persevere in your good purpose, and so to cleave to the divine service to which you are devoted that the fragrance of your good conduct, setting an example before many, may spread far and wide, as it has hitherto done. Thus may the good things which are praised in your community [Col. 1397A] not be attributed to the virtue or excellence of one or of only a few. Act, therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, and strive so to adorn your lamps with good works that, with Christ to whom you are betrothed, you may merit to enter into the eternal wedding feast.

Given at Tusculum, on the seventh day before the Ides of September [7 September].

CCCLIX. To King Conrad.—He confirms for his chaplain Thiebald the provostship of Xanten, provided that he relinquish the other provostship which he formerly held. (1149, 5 October.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Coll.*, II, 367.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ CONRAD, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letter of your excellence, [Col. 1397B] in which we have fully learned of the devotion and affection which you bear toward your mother, the holy Roman Church, and toward ourselves. On reading it, the reply of your kindness, filled with such great devotion, gave us much joy. Since we embrace you with the arms of charity as a special son and protector of blessed Peter, we desire to honor your person and, insofar as justice permits, grant your requests. Therefore, yielding to the prayers of your majesty, we have given our assent to the election made by the clergy of Xanten of our beloved son Thiebald, your chaplain. But since we cannot and ought not to act contrary to the decrees of the sacred canons and of the holy Roman Church, he must [Col. 1397C] be content with one provostship and relinquish the other which he formerly possessed. It is therefore for you, dearest son, to respond to the love and affection of your mother, the holy Roman Church, and to govern the kingdom entrusted to you by God with equitable judgment, so that she may rejoice that she has received the hoped-for fruit of your devotion, and that after the temporal kingdom you may merit to receive the everlasting one. We greet in the Lord our beloved son Henry the younger; and we pray him through whom kings reign that Henry may increase in age and wisdom before God and men.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Nones of October [5 October].

CCCLX. To Bermund, bishop of Béziers.—He directs him to allow Trencavel, viscount of Béziers, to build a chapel in his palace. (1149, 10 October.)

[MARTEN., *Thes. Anecd.*, I, 412.]

[Col. 1397D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother B., bishop of Béziers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The nobleman T., returning from Jerusalem and passing through our presence, humbly requested us to permit a chapel to be built in his palace on the following terms: that he should find a suitable chaplain, subsequently present him to you so that you may grant him the care of souls, and that during T.’s lifetime divine offices should not be forbidden there, unless T. himself or someone of his household should commit an offense. Since his request is tolerable, and so that no detriment may thereafter arise to your church on this account, we command you by this present letter [Col. 1398A] to allow the chapel to be built on the terms stated; and, when you are invited by T., not to refuse to consecrate it, while, of course, preserving intact in all other matters your own rights and those of your church.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixth day before the Ides of October [10 October].

CCCLXI. To Serlo, abbot of Savigny.—That he and all persons subject to his monastery should live according to the Cistercian observance. (1149, 21 October.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 813.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SERLO, abbot of Savigny: greeting and apostolic blessing.
