Although, by reason of the apostolic office enjoined upon us by God, we consider ourselves debtors to all ecclesiastical persons, [Col. 1398B] nevertheless we are especially bound to extend a more earnest care of charity toward those whom we know to be serving almighty God in the true habit of religious life. For the care of the pastoral office has been committed to us for this end: that we should labor to establish religion pleasing to God and, once established, preserve it with exact diligence. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, desiring that the religious life established in the monasteries over which you are known to preside may flourish in the Lord, we decree that in all monasteries which have proceeded from the monastery over which you preside, and in those which have sprung from monasteries issuing from that same monastery, you shall have free authority, concerning both the persons and the property of the monasteries, to arrange and order matters according to the institution of the Cistercian [Col. 1398C] brethren. Since many, led on by the evil spirit, rebel against obedience to their prelates and seek outside support in order to serve their own will more freely, we prohibit anyone, after making profession in those places, from withdrawing himself from subjection to you or your successors, or anyone else from retaining such professed persons or any persons from the monasteries. If anyone from those monasteries withdraws himself from your subjection and, having been admonished three times, refuses to return, you shall have authority to excommunicate him.

Given at Tusculum, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October].

CCCLXII. He laments the ill health of Henry, bishop of Moravia, and consoles him. (1149, 24 October.)

[BOCZEK, *Cod. dipl. Morav.*, I, 261.]

[Col. 1398D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Moravia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letter of your brotherhood and, as those who love you with special affection as a most devoted son of the holy Roman Church and embrace you among our other dearest brethren, we recall the devotion which you have always shown toward your mother, the Roman Church. We are anxious for your welfare and frequently desire with the greatest longing [Col. 1399A] to hear of it. It is pleasing to us that you are solicitous for the flock entrusted to you, strive to lead it by the paths of justice, and direct it according to the standard of ecclesiastical equity. Concerning those matters upon which your affection consulted us, we have decreed to answer you in accordance with the rulings of our predecessors. Clerics who have been degraded because their faults required it must not be restored to their former orders, even after reform of life. But the man who, having received no order, presumed to sing Mass is to be handed over to the secular ruler for punishment as a layman. No one may marry his sister-in-law after her death. And since the sacred canons do not allow crimes once alleged to pass without investigation, inquire diligently into the case of the cleric said to be a bigamist; and, if he is canonically [Col. 1399B] convicted, let him be deposed. Let him clear himself of this charge by the oath of seven men of his own order. If he cannot do so, let him be deposed. It pertains to your office, therefore, dearest brother, to advance by word and example those over whom you preside, so that together with the flock entrusted to you, you may attain eternal life. It grieves us that, worn down by age, you do not have confidence in the long life which we greatly wish for you. Yet we hope in the Lord that, with his help, we shall still see your face. But if, while we are alive, divine providence should call you from this world, it shall be our care to pour out prayers to God for you as for our dearest brother and frequently to remember you in our prayers. Moreover, because we know that you are concerned for our condition, we have thought it right to inform your affection of it. For although this year we have been burdened by bodily illness, the death of our brethren, and other adversities, nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, we have returned safely to the tranquility of peace. For your illness we are sending you a good electuary.

Given at Tusculum, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November [24 October].

CCCLXIII. To Henry, archbishop of Mainz.—He directs him “both personally and through his suffragan bishops to watch carefully and diligently for the wanderings of false messengers who travel about under his name and presume to harass the faithful of the Church by unlawful exactions; and, if any comes into his hands or those of his suffragans, especially Ildebrandinus, formerly a servant of Cardinal-Deacon Jacintus, to have him seized.” (1149, 25 October.)

[DENIS, *Cod. manuscr., theol.*, I, III, 2878.]

[Col. 1399D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

It has come to our ears that certain false messengers are travelling through your regions under our name and presume to harass the faithful of the Church by unlawful exactions. Since the audacity of such presumption is seen to redound to the disgrace of the holy Roman Church and of ourselves, we command you by this present letter to watch carefully and diligently, both personally and through the suffragan bishops of your church, for the wanderings of such persons; and if [Col. 1400A] any comes into your hands or those of your suffragans, especially Ildebrandinus, formerly the servant of our beloved Jacintus, cardinal-deacon, have him seized and keep him in custody until you learn by our letter what we wish to be done in the matter.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October].

CCCLXIV. To all the brethren of Fontevraud. (1149, 25 October.)

[NIQUET, *Hist. de Fontevrault*, p. 379.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the brethren of Fontevraud: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we are instructed by the manifest teachings of the holy Fathers, obedience alone [Col. 1400B] possesses the merit of faith; without it a man is shown to be faithless, even if he appears to be faithful. We have learned, however, that certain of you refuse obedience to our beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and prioress of Fontevraud; that without permission you presume to enter or open their enclosure; and that in other matters you are rebellious against justice. Since it is unworthy and wholly contrary to reason that due honor and reverence should be denied by subjects to the prelates of churches, we command and enjoin you by this present letter that all in your community who may be reproved on this account shall henceforth humbly render obedience and reverence to the abbess and prioress of that place; that they shall by no means presume to unlock or enter their enclosure without the consent of the abbess or prioress; [Col. 1400C] that they shall not presume, without consulting them, to establish abbesses in places where there have hitherto been none; and that they shall in no way neglect to assemble at their common chapter at appointed times.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [24 November].

CCCLXV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Lucius of Chur. (1149, 6 November.)

[MOHR, *Cod. diplom.*, I, 158.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son AIMON, prior of the Church of Saint Lucius of Chur, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1400D] The authority of the apostolic see, which, by the Lord’s bounty, we serve, and the bond of fraternal charity urge us to consent to the just desires of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable requests. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Blessed Lucius, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may in the future be able to acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your [Col. 1401A] successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the estate situated in the village called Maging; the estate in the village called Riunena; in the village called Avinne, an estate and vineyard; vineyards, fields, and meadows in the city of Chur; one estate in the village called Paiste; one estate in the village called Umbilico; the church of Saint Mary in the forest of Augeria, with all its appurtenances. We further decree that the canonical order established in your church according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, no one shall be set over it by any craft or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, shall see fit to elect according to God. Moreover, no one shall presume to demand from you tithes of the produce which you cultivate from newly cleared land by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the fodder of your animals.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations whatsoever; but that all things be preserved intact for the use and full benefit of those for whose governance and preservation they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, does not make fitting satisfaction and correct the offense, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, know himself or herself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But may all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of Saint Callixtus. I, Hugh, titular priest-cardinal of Lucina. [Col. 1401D] I, Wido, bishop of Ostia. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon. I, Jacintus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Boson, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of November [6 November], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1149 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CCCLXVI. To Abbot Suger.—That he settle in due judicial order the case of two excommunicated clerics. (1149, 7 November.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 644.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1402A] Our sons A. and Her., clerics of the Church of Meaux, recently came into our presence. Since they had confirmed by the solemnity of an oath the matter laid to their charge by Goslin, in fulfillment of our command we absolved them from the bond of excommunication. But because the opposing party was not present, we could not proceed in their case or decide anything definitively while preserving equity. We therefore refer them to the diligence of your discretion and command your affection by this present letter, after summoning both parties into your presence, that, if Goslin can prove according to the precepts of the canons what he charged against them, you shall determine the matter in due judicial order. But if the aforesaid Goslin fails in proof, receive the purgation of the aforesaid [Col. 1402B] clerics by the oath of seven men of their order; show and publicly announce to the neighboring brethren that they are free from the infamy charged against them. Cause also the revenues of the church which were taken from the aforesaid Goslin on this account to be restored to him in full. Moreover, firmly command the bishop and canons of the Church of Meaux on our behalf henceforth to maintain peace and brotherly concord with Goslin. If they do not do so and a complaint concerning it reaches our ears, we shall not be able to refrain from punishing their disobedience with due correction.

Given at Tusculum, on the seventh day before the Ides of November [7 November].

CCCLXVII. To Emperor Conrad.—At his request he again confirms the election of the provost of Xanten and postpones the deposition of the archbishop of Cologne. (1149, 28 November.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 684.]

[Col. 1402C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ CONRAD, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your clemency has recognized through very many proofs how great is our affection for your person and for the kingdom entrusted to you by God. Remaining unshakably in this disposition, we grant the requests of your excellence as far as we can with God, and, consistently with the honor of the Church, gladly give assent to your royal will, as to a devoted son of blessed Peter and special defender of the holy Roman Church. [Col. 1402D] Accordingly, receiving with fatherly affection the prayers of your highness concerning the election of the provost of Xanten, we have thought fit to grant your request as to our dearest son, although certain persons afterward reported matters wholly different from those signified in the letter of your affection. The case of our brother, the archbishop of Cologne, is grave; why this is so, since it would take long to relate, you can learn plainly from those about you. For if the discretion of your highness had known how much he had committed through negligence and proudly through disobedience in regard to his office, you would not, we believe, have spoken even a word for him. Therefore, in the council which, with God’s authorship, we held at Reims, he would have incurred a sentence of removal [Col. 1403A] had we not spared your royal absence, because we thought that some detriment might thereby come to the kingdom, a matter which we especially had to avoid. And after your return we had firmly resolved with you to strike him with a sentence deserved by his transgressions, had not the embassy of your majesty intervened first. Yet, yielding to your prayers as far as we can, we have for the present withheld our hand from his condemnation and granted him a respite until the Sunday on which is sung, “I am the good shepherd.” Since we could not in this matter comply entirely with the prayers of your excellence without grave injury to the holy Church and ecclesiastical discipline, let your royal clemency bear this patiently and, as we hope from your kindness, attend as a most devout lover of justice to those things incumbent upon the holy Roman Church, your mother, whose defender almighty God [Col. 1403B] has appointed you. We greet in the Lord our beloved son Henry, the younger king.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December [28 November].

CCCLXVIII. Bull to Obert, archbishop of Milan. (1149, 19 December.)

[GIULINI, *Mem. di Milano*, V, 594, from the archive of the Metropolitan Church.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother OBERT, archbishop, and to the beloved sons, the ordinarii of the Church of Milan, and to their successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider [Col. 1403C] of all good things, in order that we may strive for the condition of all churches and … [lacuna] … seek by every means … [lacuna] religion and integrity pleasing to the Lord. … For no service is ever rendered pleasing to God unless, proceeding from the root of truth, it has been strengthened by the purity of religion and integrity. Therefore we order that a quite reprehensible vice … [lacuna] … which, through sins demanding it, had grown up in your church, be eradicated: namely, that whereas among those who … [lacuna] … are there called ordinarii there ought to be one heart and one soul—as also, according to what is read concerning the assemblies of the apostles, there should be a community—on the contrary, there existed, in accordance also with the saying of the Apostle Paul: “… One indeed is hungry, another [Col. 1403D] is drunk.” But afterward, through your effort, brother archbishop, it came about that all revenues and all income of that church should henceforth be brought together into one fund, for the honor of God and for the common life of the canons who should reside in that place from time to time. And this has been openly confirmed also … [lacuna] … by an instrument of their own. We therefore, whose concern it is to correct what has been ill done and, by the authority of the apostolic see, to confirm what has been well done and accords with the venerable canons, confirm by the privilege of this present document what you have reasonably decreed concerning the maintenance of the common life: that the revenues of the church be divided in equal shares through the chapter among the canons for provisions, and that what remains thereafter be distributed equally for clothing. [Col. 1404A] As it is contained in your document, we decree that it shall remain ratified and inviolate, beyond contradiction, in future times. We command that you fulfill as soon as possible what is still known to be lacking for the maintenance of the common life: namely, that you eat in one refectory and sleep in one dormitory. Moreover, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, in which you serve almighty God. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future be able to acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your [Col. 1404B] successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: Cavacurtem, Gramorellam, Martaniam, Setezanum, Trecha, Arnugum, Novezatem, Habiascam, the valleys of Bellegnium and Leventina, the parish of Artizate, Sevisum, the estate of Curtadia de Leoco, Brivium, Gradi, Pulcoctum, Bulzanum, Salvanum; one holding at Caol, held by Ardicius of Carimate; and one hundred soldi of the new coinage, which your church is accustomed to receive each year from the monastery of Saint Simplician.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things be preserved intact for the use and full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see. If, therefore, anyone in the future, etc.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Guido, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Octavian, of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Aribert, of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, … [lacuna].

Given at the Lateran through the hand of … [lacuna], on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1148 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Eugenius III. [Col. 1404D]

CCCLXIX. On the annual celebration of the dedication of the church of Blessed Fridianus of Lucca. (1149, 19 December.)

[BALUZ., *Miscell.*, Lucca edition, IV, 594.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of God who have assembled out of devotion for the annual celebration of the dedication of the church of Blessed Fridianus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we believe has come to your knowledge, in reverence for the body which is believed to rest in it, we ourselves, with God as author, consecrated the church of Blessed Fridianus; and to those coming on the annual day of its consecration, who are under an imposed penance, we granted, trusting in the merits of blessed Peter and Paul, remission of forty days. [Col. 1405A] Therefore, to any who, impeded by some cause, cannot be present there on that same day but arrive within the octave of that dedication, we likewise grant the same remission on behalf of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December].

CCCLXX. To the archbishop of Braga.—He suspends him from episcopal office unless he renders obedience to the archbishop of Toledo. (1149, 29 December.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 674.]

A disciple of Christ does not fail to know how great is the power of obedience, and almost every page of sacred Scripture bears witness to it. [Col. 1405B] For since obedience itself is said to be the seasoning of the other virtues, it is more plainly evident that “to resist is as the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance is as the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15). Concerning your brotherhood, therefore, we can scarcely express our astonishment, and at the same time we grieve, because you despise obedience to the commands of the apostolic see. The command which we recently gave you orally—to render obedience to the primate of Toledo—has, as the repeated complaint of that church indicates, slipped all too quickly from your heart; and you seem, like a deaf asp with closed ears, to have persisted in this course. Yet no one ought to consider it unworthy to be subject to superiors who remembers that he is set over others. Would that those things known to belong to the glory of virtue [Col. 1405C] might be found in your brotherhood. Although contempt for so great a transgression ought to be weighed down by a more severe punishment, nevertheless, using apostolic mildness, we command and enjoin you by this present letter to strive humbly to render due obedience to the aforesaid archbishop by the next Sunday of Palm Branches; otherwise, from that time onward, until you fulfill what we have often commanded you, we again suspend you from episcopal office.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December].

CCCLXXI. To Alfonso, king of the Spains.—On the primacy of Toledo. (1149, 29 December.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 673.]

[Col. 1405D]

As we gather from examination of your letter and from the words of your messenger R., bearer of the present letter, the displays of honor and favor of the apostolic see which, yielding to the requests of your nobility and gentleness, we have frequently bestowed upon the churches and persons of your kingdom have not at all come to your knowledge. For at your request we have adorned the Church of Compostela with the special prerogative of carrying the cross before its metropolitan; and we have not failed to assist the metropolitan see of Toledo in recovering the right which it is said to possess over the archbishop of Braga. Indeed, as the whole Spanish Church knows, on account of this matter we suspended that same archbishop of Braga from episcopal office for a long time. Most recently, when he came into our presence in the regions of Lombardy, he was unable in any way to obtain absolution from us until, in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, he promised orally that, within the time fixed by us, he would humbly obey the Church of Toledo with due subjection; and that if he did not do so, he would remain under the same sentence of suspension until he complied. [Col. 1406A] Furthermore, whether after leaving us he obeyed the Church of Toledo in accordance with our command, or whether perhaps he persists in his rebellion, ought to have been reported to us by the archbishop of that church, upon whom the solicitude and care of that metropolitan see are known to rest. If, therefore, he has decided to remain silent through negligence and insufficient concern for the honor and dignity of the church entrusted to him, we, who by the Lord’s disposition, though unworthy, hold the place of a judge upon the watchtower of the apostolic see, ought not to become heralds or runners because of his insolence. But remembering the customary graciousness of your person and the devotion which your grandfather A. [Alfonso], king of Spain of illustrious memory, and you yourself have humbly displayed toward your common mother, the holy Roman Church, in the times of our predecessors and in our own, we gladly admit your prayers even now. Accordingly, in accordance with the desire of your petition, we have sent apostolic letters to the aforesaid archbishop of Braga; and unless he takes care, by the next Sunday of Palm Branches, to obey the primate of Toledo [Col. 1406C], we again suspend him from episcopal office until he fulfills what we have often commanded him.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Ides of January [31 December].

CCCLXXII. To Abbot Suger.—That he investigate the case of a priest excommunicated by an archdeacon, and excommunicate those who assaulted the priest. (1149?)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 645.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A certain priest, R., having come into our presence, complained that Archdeacon S., because he refused to pay him the money which the archdeacon demanded from him for the church entrusted to him, expelled him from the church. And because he appealed to our hearing concerning this, the same archdeacon caused him to be beaten by his own relatives with sacrilegious audacity. Since it is very unjust that, among those to whom authority to judge others is granted in the Church of God, a judgment of iniquity should be found, we command you by these letters that, after summoning both parties before you, you shall diligently investigate the case and decide it with justice as your companion. Publicly declare excommunicated those who laid violent hands upon the same cleric, and cause the excommunication to be observed until they present themselves before you in order to make satisfaction.

### CCCLXXIII. To H., Archbishop of Sens.—Concerning the same matter. (Year 1149?)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 645.]

[Col. 1407A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son H., Archbishop of Sens, greeting and apostolic blessing.

One of your priests, having come to Rome into our presence, complained that your archdeacon Stephen, because he refused to pay him the money which he demanded from him for the church entrusted to him, expelled him from that same church. And because he appealed to our hearing concerning this, the same archdeacon caused him to be beaten by his own relatives with sacrilegious audacity [Col. 1407B]. Since it is very unjust that, among those to whom authority to judge others is granted in the Church of God, a judgment of iniquity should be found, we command our beloved son Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, by our letters that, after summoning both parties before him, he shall diligently investigate the case and decide it with justice as his companion. Therefore cause that same archdeacon to go when summoned by the abbot, and cause what he shall decide thereupon to be observed. Afterwards, send him to appear before you to answer concerning these same offences. Publicly declare excommunicated those who laid violent hands upon the same cleric, and cause the excommunication to be observed until they present themselves before us in order to make satisfaction.

### CCCLXXIV. To Abbot Suger.—He appoints him judge in another ecclesiastical case. (Year 1149?)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 645.]

[Col. 1407C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the controversy and dispute known to be proceeding between Peter, bearer of the present letters, and Joscelin, canon of Meaux, each presented himself before us. First, Joscelin alleged that injury and violence had been inflicted upon him by the said Peter, and that on this account he had appealed him to our hearing. But after Joscelin’s departure from us [Col. 1407D], the same Peter came to us and wholly denied what had been said against him. Therefore, since we could not fully ascertain the truth of the matter, we have thought it necessary to refer the case to your discernment. By these present letters, accordingly, we command your belovedness that, after summoning both parties before you, you diligently hear the same controversy. If the opposing party cannot plainly prove the said Peter guilty of the violence alleged, and Peter suitably demonstrates his innocence, it accords with ecclesiastical moderation that his innocence should acquit him. But if he cannot prove himself free from the charge laid against him, you shall inform us by your letters as soon as possible, also stating how the case has proceeded.

### CCCLXXV. He confirms the canonical discipline of the brethren of Saint-Lô at Rouen. (1145–1150.—Fragment.)

[*Neustria pia*, 805.]

[Col. 1408A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons OSBERT, prior of Saint-Lô at Rouen, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brethren Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, and Algar, Bishop of Coutances [Col. 1408B], we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, which, by God’s grace and with the consent of the said brother of ours, the Bishop of Coutances, you have professed; so that it may be preserved inviolate in that church for all time. By this present decree we enact that henceforth no one shall be established there unless he is a regular canon, etc.

### CCCLXXVI. To the Prelates of Poland.—He rebukes them for not observing the sentence of interdict pronounced by his legate G., and confirms that sentence in order that they may amend. (1150, January 23.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 685.]

[Col. 1408C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout Poland, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Believe that we greet you with the address of blessing not because of your merits, but because of the benevolence of the Apostolic See. For whoever scorns to obey apostolic commands ought to be cast down by grief at the dishonour done to his own office. Since, in fulfilment of our office, we are solicitous for the welfare of you and of the people entrusted to you, we formerly sent our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, into your regions, so that, with the Lord’s help, he might restore peace between Duke W. and his brothers, and transact ecclesiastical business [Col. 1408D] as legate of the Apostolic See. As he had received command from us, he bound with the bond of excommunication the party which refused to obey his admonitions, and those who hold the land of that duke; and he prohibited the celebration of divine offices in that land. But, as we have learned, because he asserts that he did not do this by our command, you do not observe the sentence at all. Yet since he did this by our command, we hold valid both the sentence of excommunication and that of interdict, as pronounced by him; and we command that you observe it and cause it likewise to be observed. But you, brother archbishop, upon whom this especially rests by the duty of your office, shall make it known to all your suffragans and to the other prelates of churches [Col. 1409A], so that they may be without excuse; and you shall firmly observe the sentence and cause it to be observed. Know that if any of you refuses to observe this sentence, he shall not escape the vengeance of Blessed Peter and of the Holy Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January].

### CCCLXXVII. Privilege for the Monastery of Saint Martin of Anhausen. (1150, January 30.)

(PETRI, *Suevia ecclesiastica*, p. 92.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SIGEFRID, Abbot of Saint Martin of Anhausen, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life [Col. 1409B], in perpetuity.

Although we stand under an imposed obligation toward all venerable places, it is fitting that we support with greater zeal those which are known especially to belong to the right and protection of Blessed Peter and of the Holy Roman Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Walter, Bishop of Augsburg, and by yours, we graciously grant your just petitions. Following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, we receive under the protection of the prince of the apostles and under our own, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Martin, which was built on the freehold property of the aforesaid brother of ours Walter, then Bishop of Augsburg, and of his brethren, and was offered to Blessed Peter with all its appurtenances [Col. 1409C]. We decree that whatsoever possessions, tithes, or other goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the exchange which, by the agreement of both parties, was reasonably made concerning the tithes of the place in which the monastery itself is situated, together with the church of Saint Peter of Contingen, to whose parish they belonged. We further decree that the church of Saint Martin [Col. 1409D] of Nawa, in which your community had its beginning in the monastic life, by the Lord’s will, through Manegold, count palatine of illustrious memory—the father, that is, of the aforesaid Bishop of the Holy Church of Augsburg—on whose freehold it stood, shall remain subject in perpetuity to your monastery, together with its tithes and all its other possessions.

You may freely elect by common counsel an advocate whom you find useful for the defence of the same monastery; and, if he proves useless, remove him and appoint another whom you judge more useful. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any cunning of usurpation or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common counsel, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel [Col. 1410A], shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, provide to be elected.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We also grant that the burial-ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the burial there of any who choose it, unless they are excommunicated, saving nevertheless the rights of the mother church. As a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See [Col. 1410B], you shall pay one gold piece each year to us and our successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly profitable for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third warning should scorn to amend his presumption, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. [Col. 1410D] I, Guido, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cyriacus, have subscribed. I, Aubert, cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, John Paparo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Plebano, notary of the Roman Curia, the third day before the Kalends of February, indiction XIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1148 [1150], in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCLXXVIII. To the Bishop of Castello [Venice]. (1150, March 19.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 1240.]

[Col. 1411A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother, Bishop of Castello, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It ought not to be unknown to you that tithes should be divided into four portions. For, as the authority of the holy Fathers has decreed, one portion is assigned to the bishop, another to the clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth to the repair of church buildings. Therefore, by these present letters we command your brotherhood to cause the portion of the tithes which has fallen to the brethren of Saint Saviour by right to be assigned to them.

Given at the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April [19 March].

### CCCLXXIX. Bull for the Monastery of Saint Benedict of Piacenza. (1150, April 14.)

[CAMPI, *Ecclesiastical History of Piacenza*, I, I, 351.]

[Col. 1411B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son VITALIS, Abbot of Saint Benedict of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever that which is known to accord with reason and propriety is requested from us, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing mind and afford appropriate assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Vitalis, graciously assenting to your just requests, we grant to you, and through you to your monastery for administration, the oratory of Blessed Peter situated in the territory of Turin beyond the River Stura. Peter Podisii and Taurinus Rista, for the salvation of their souls, devoutly offered it to the Holy Roman Church through our hands [Col. 1411C]. We entrust to you the free management of that place, upon this condition: that in future the brethren of the Vallombrosan congregation shall continually serve there with diligent care; that the hospice established there for the service of the poor shall be carefully maintained; that boats for those crossing the river shall always be kept ready, as has been established; and that an annual payment of one gold piece shall be made to us and our successors. If you or your successors are unwilling to observe these terms, we or our successors may rightly remove you from the governance of that place [Col. 1411D].

Given at the Lateran, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April].

### CCCLXXX. He grants Guibert, provost, and the canons of Saint Lawrence of Genoa a broad confirmation of all their goods and rights, including Count Raymond’s donation. (1150, April 14.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 683.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIBERT, provost, and the other canons of the Church of Genoa, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to labour for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, wisely to provide for their peace and welfare [Col. 1412A]. For it is fitting and consistent with propriety that we who have been raised to the governance of churches should protect them from the malice of wicked persons and fortify them with the patronage of Blessed Peter and the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the church of Saint Lawrence, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you [Col. 1412B] and to your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name: the church of Saint Mary Magdalene; the church of Saint Saviour of Sanzano; the church of Saint James of Calignano; the church of Saint Bartholomew of Stajano; the church of Saint Mary of Quarto; the church of Saint Stephen of Pariesi; likewise the tithes which you lawfully possess throughout the entire diocese of Genoa; and three parts of the whole territory called Saint Romulus, with all its appurtenances, as these were reasonably granted to your church by Theodulf, Bishop of Genoa, of good memory, and confirmed by the authority of his document. Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you the island situated in the River Ebro near the city of Tortosa, lawfully granted to the same church by the illustrious Raymond, Count of Barcelona, and by the consuls [Col. 1412C] of your city.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and wholly profitable for your use and for that of others for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third warning should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour [Col. 1412D]; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer. But upon those who observe these provisions may there be peace, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, G., bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

[Col. 1413B] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Bosso, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, indiction XIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1150, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCLXXXI. Privilege for the Church of Fontevraud. (1150, April 20.)

[PAVILLON, *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, Proofs, p. 631.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters MATHILDA, abbess of Saint Mary of Fontevraud, and her sisters, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious petitions, so that pious devotion may obtain a swift effect [Col. 1413C] and the integrity of religious life may be preserved unshaken. For reason requires that the Apostolic See cherish honourable persons in the bosom of its mercy, and that it meet their just petitions with kindly favour, so that they may persevere firmly in their religious profession and advance therein. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, moved by this obligation of reason, we graciously assent to your just requests, confirm by apostolic authority the provisions known to have been established for you from regard for religion and by reasonable foresight, and fortify them by the assurance of this present writing.

We decree, indeed, and for the greater convenience of your religious estate command, that all virgins of your order who ought to receive the grace of blessing shall receive the blessing within the enclosure of the monastery in which they are devoted to service, from the diocesan bishop [Col. 1413D], provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide it freely, without burden or improper exaction. Otherwise, you may invite whichever bishop you prefer to perform this act; supported by our authority, he shall bestow the grace of blessing upon the virgins to be consecrated among you.

But because religious life cannot be preserved without the good of peace and concord, in order that every occasion of discord and rebellion may be entirely removed from your fellowship, and indeed that the unity of sincerity among you may be more fully preserved, let all look to the Abbess of Fontevraud as to their head and render her due obedience. Following also in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, we decree and strengthen by the protection of our favour that no person may dare establish a village or dwelling in the vicinity of your monastery unless it is separated from that monastery by at least half a league [Col. 1414A].

Therefore no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any other vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, wholly profitable for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it [Col. 1414B], and after a second or third warning should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [20 April].

### CCCLXXXII. To Abbot Suger.—Concerning King Louis’s plan for an overseas expedition. (1150, April 25.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 646.]

[Col. 1414C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The immense work of piety which divine mercy has inspired in our dearest son Louis, illustrious King of the Franks, causes us great anxiety. Recalling the grievous loss which the Church of God has suffered in our times to the Christian name, and the still recent shedding of the blood of so many men, we are shaken by great fear, and inconsolable sorrow is renewed. Yet the devotion of our said son and his divinely inspired charity somewhat mitigate the grief conceived and promise us hope [Col. 1414D] of consolation. Thus fear together with hope greatly troubles us, holding us in suspense between the two.

But lest so great an undertaking remain unfinished through any fault of ours, we command your prudence by these present letters diligently to examine the disposition of the said son of ours, the king, and of the barons and others of his realm. If you find them ready for so arduous an undertaking, securely promise them our counsel and assistance, so far as we are able, and remission of sins, as is contained in our other letters. Once we have been made more certain of their firmness and devotion of faith, laying aside our fear, we shall, with divine mercy favouring us, furnish them strength and assistance by whatever means we can. Let it further be your concern, after consulting wise men [Col. 1415A], promptly to inform us what of our assistance will be necessary for this purpose, and which ecclesiastical persons, besides those named, seem suitable to you.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April].

### CCCLXXXIII. To Abbot Suger.—That he cause the treasury of the Church of Saint Geneviève, which has been pledged, to be redeemed. (1150, April 28.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 646.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, Abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that it has escaped your prudence that it is a matter of great distress to us that the treasury of the Church of Saint Geneviève has been pledged. Since we do not wish that this church should suffer loss in this matter through negligence or contention, or be despoiled of its ornaments by anyone’s malice or cunning, we command you by these present letters to go to that place and diligently investigate the matter. Whatever of the same treasury has been pledged by the secular clergy since the change in the church came to their knowledge [Col. 1415B], compel them to redeem from their own resources. Whatever had been pledged before that time, cause to be redeemed from the common resources of both the regulars and the seculars, according to what belongs to each. Take diligent care that the church suffer no loss in this matter through anyone’s malice. If anyone is rebellious against you in this respect, subject him to excommunication by our authority.

[Col. 1415C] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April].

### CCCLXXXIV. He confirms the goods, possessions, and privileges of Saint Mary of Reno. (1150, May 13.)

[TROMBELLI, *Historical Memoirs of Reno*, Appendix, 367.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO, prior of the church of Blessed Mary of Reno, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, Popes Innocent and Lucius of blessed memory [Col. 1415D], we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing first that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Further, whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1416A]. Among these we have thought fit to specify by name: the church of Saint Saviour in the city of Bologna; at Turicella, the church of Saint Andrew; and the church of Saint Domini near Bagnuna.

We also prohibit any brother, after making profession there, from daring to depart from that cloister without the willing permission of the prior or the community; and no one at all may receive a departing brother without a common letter of authorization. But if any of the brethren dares to remain outside the cloister without the aforesaid permission and, after a second or third warning, perhaps scorns to amend, the prior of that place may pronounce against him, as his professed religious, a sentence of excommunication. You shall also have free authority, without anyone’s objection, to receive into conversion clerics or free laymen living in the secular estate. No one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the nourishment of your animals [Col. 1416B].

You shall receive holy oil and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. Upon the death of you, the present prior of the same place, or of any of your successors [Col. 1416C], no one may be set over it through any cunning of usurpation or force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine provide to be elected.

In addition, we decree that no archbishop, bishop, or any person whatsoever may impose an exaction upon the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary or inflict burdens upon the prior and brethren. We also grant that the burial-ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the right of the mother church.

[Col. 1416D] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, wholly profitable for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third warning should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer [Col. 1417A]; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

“Make for me, O Lord, a sign for good.”

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes [Col. 1417B], have subscribed. I, Manfred, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, John Paparo, cardinal-priest of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Bosso, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, the third day before the Ides of May [13 May], indiction XIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1150, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CCCLXXXV. Bull for the transfer of the monastery of Middelburg. (1150, May 23.)

[HUGO A. O., *Praem.*, II, p. 129.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WALTER, Abbot of Walcheren, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Just as assent must not be granted to unjust petitions, so a lawful request by those who desire something ought not to be denied. From the letters of our venerable brother Heribert, Bishop of Utrecht, we have seen that you have arranged to transfer your monastery to another place, where you may live more peacefully and serve the Lord more freely. The aforesaid brother of ours gave his assent to this arrangement and approved it by his writing, so that it might be lawful for you to carry it out in future [Col. 1418A]. We, whose concern it is to confirm well-accomplished acts, taking account of your vow . . . confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See the permission for the transfer reasonably granted to you by that same brother of ours. We decree, however, that nothing known to pertain to us shall be diminished in future for us or our successors on account of this change.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of June [23 May].

[Note: [Col. 1417D] This pontifical diploma, whose date is not fixed by any year-number, does not exceed the period of Heribert’s episcopate at Utrecht. Heribert succeeded Andrew of Cuijk in 1138; according to Beka, Andrew died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June]. Heribert, however, died in 1148. Jamingus adds two years [to this account]. Eugenius III ascended the pontificate in 1145; therefore the Roman pontiff’s grant must have been issued within the three following years, 1146, 1147, or 1148. The bull is addressed to Walter, Abbot of Walcheren, because Walter was the first prelate of the province [Col. 1418D] and his church enjoyed a certain primacy. William, King of the Romans, increased this primacy when he entrusted all the churches of Walcheren and Holland to the direction and care of the abbot of Saint Mary.]

### CCCLXXXVI. To the Canons of the Church of Orléans.—On behalf of Lord Philip, concerning the church of Saint Lætus, which he asserts belongs to his deanery. (1150, May 25.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 629.]

[Col. 1418B]

EUGENIUS, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Orléans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

On behalf of our beloved son Philip, brother of the illustrious king of the Franks, we have received a complaint that you are violently taking from him the church of Saint Léta, which he asserts belongs to his deanery, and are striving to deprive him of his right in it. [Note: [Col. 1418D] This Philip must be distinguished from Philip, the firstborn of Louis VI, king of the Franks, who died during his father’s lifetime, two years after he had been anointed king at Rheims. This Philip, however, the fifth son of Louis, long survived his father and was archdeacon of Paris; Pope Adrian IV refers to him in Letter 75 to King Louis, in Chesne, *Hist. Franc.*, vol. IV.]

Since we have received his goods, both ecclesiastical and temporal, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, we cannot and ought not permit them to be taken from him by anyone. Therefore, by these present letters we command you either to restore that church to him, [Col. 1418C] or to render him justice concerning it in the presence of our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

### CCCLXXXVII. To Abbot Suger.—That he should decide the ecclesiastical case already treated in Letters 372 and 373. (1150, 26 May.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 647.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

That priest R., who had come to us against Stephen, [Col. 1418D] archdeacon of Sens, recently returned to our presence with the messenger of that archdeacon. But, since it was by no means possible to proceed in the case itself as reason required, we ordered him to desist from his complaint and directed that the aforesaid archdeacon be presented before you [Col. 1419A] to purge himself canonically of the accusations brought against him. Therefore, by these apostolic letters, we command you to summon the same archdeacon again before you; and, if he can clear himself of the charges brought by the oath of five men of his order, dismiss him as acquitted of the suit of the aforesaid priest.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

### CCCLXXXVIII. To Peter, provost of Ulciensis.—He commands that in the church of Saint Mary at Secusium “henceforth no one whatsoever be ordained or admitted, nor that food be granted to anyone or clothing bestowed, unless he has first assumed the regular habit and professed the canonical life.” (1150, 27 May, Lateran.) [Col. 1419B]

[Cartulary of the Church of Ulciensis, p. 18.]

### CCCLXXXIX. He receives the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Angers under protection. (1150, 10 June, Lateran.)

[Abbey of Saint Nicholas of Angers, 76, according to Bréquigny, *Table chronologique*, III, 166.]

### CCCXC. To Abbot Suger.—Concerning the Eastern Church; the conference held by pope and king; and the Church of Compiègne. (1150, 19 June.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 648.]

[Col. 1419C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are grateful that you bear earnest concern for the distress of the Eastern Church, and we commend in the Lord the zeal of your devotion, since our own heart is likewise troubled by great sorrow and is grievously afflicted on that account. Thus, although it was very burdensome for us because of the frailty of the person in whom, by the Lord’s favor, the hopes of all converge, we nevertheless could by no means refuse assent to your request and to that of the others who wrote to us concerning this matter.

We therefore exhort your belovedness to apply diligent aid and effort to so great and illustrious a work, as a discerning and prudent man. Moreover, we wish your discretion to know that we held a personal conference with our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks, concerning the establishment of religious life in the land granted him by God, and he graciously gave his assent to our admonitions. Since, therefore, with the Lord’s help, we desire religious life to be promoted in the Church of Compiègne, by the authority of these present letters we enjoin upon you that you labor, with every diligence and earnest effort, to bring this about. We have imposed this charge upon you and upon our venerable brother, the bishop of Noyon.

Given at Albano, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

### CCCXCI. To Abbot Wibald.—That he should excommunicate Godebold, canon of Minden, unless he restores to Everard the church of Hemeringen which he took away. (1150, 22 June.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 435.]

[Col. 1420A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Everard, the bearer of these letters, has now approached our presence five times. On his behalf we commanded in writing our venerable brother H., bishop of Minden, under strict injunction to admonish his canon Godebold that, within twenty days after receiving our letters, he should restore in full to the aforesaid Everard the church of blessed P. at Hemeringen and other things [Col. 1420B] taken from him either personally or through persons sent by him, and should thereafter allow him to possess them in peace. If, however, within the prescribed time he should contemptuously refuse to obey the admonitions of that bishop, we directed that he then be excluded from entrance into the churches, and that he should not afterwards be absolved until he presented himself before us to make satisfaction for his offences.

But, as Everard’s repeated complaint indicates, none of this has been carried into effect: Godebold has neither come to us nor offered any excuse for burdening this poor man with such oppressions. Since, therefore, we have deep compassion for those oppressed and harassed, and cannot allow such contumacy to go unpunished, by these present letters we command you strictly to admonish the aforesaid Godebold to restore completely, within twenty days after being admonished by you, to Everard himself both that church and whatever has been taken by him or another, and thereafter to allow him peaceful possession. If he refuses to do this, publicly declare Godebold excommunicated; nor may he be absolved from the bond of excommunication until he comes before us to answer for so great a rebellion. Whatever you do in this matter, take care to inform us by letter as quickly as possible, together with the course of the case.

Given at Albano, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.

### CCCXCII. To Abbot Wibald.—He commends his zeal for the Roman Church and, at his request, writes to the bishop of Minden and the archbishop of Bremen. (1150, 24 June.)

[Same source, 436.]

[Col. 1420D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the letters of your belovedness with due kindness. Because you show earnest concern for your mother, the holy Roman Church, as a devoted son, this is pleasing to us, and we commend your devotion in the Lord. Concerning the Church of Camin, as you requested, we have written to the bishop of Minden regarding those said to be taking away its goods; but it ought not to be reconciled for the cause which you made known to us by your letter, since the event occurred neither through violence nor malicious intent. We have likewise written to the archbishop of Bremen in accordance with your request; and in other matters in which we can act according to God, we willingly admit your prayers.

We did not send our letters to the archbishop of Cologne for this reason: when he came to us, he did not receive the full measure of his office. It is therefore your concern, dearest son, that, as you have begun well, so with the work following you should continue vigilantly to labor for the honor and advancement of the Church of God and of the kingdom, so that you may deserve a fuller favor from blessed Peter and our greater goodwill.

Given at Alba, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July.

### CCCXCIII. To Henry, bishop of Minden.—That the Church of Camin does not require reconciliation because of the accidental death of a certain monk, and that he should cause its stolen property to be restored. (1150.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 437.]

[Col. 1421B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to H., venerable brother, bishop of Minden, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has reached our ears that, because a certain monk, while repairing the roof of that Church of Camin, fell by accident and thus died without bloodshed, you have caused it to cease from divine offices for almost a year [Col. 1421C] and intend to reconcile it. But if the matter stands thus, and the event occurred neither through violence nor malicious intent, we see no reason why that church should be reconciled on this account or should cease from divine worship.

Moreover, we command your brotherhood strictly to admonish Theoderic of Ricklinge, Reimbert, and Theoderic his sons, who are alleged to have presumed unjustly to seize and unlawfully retain the lands of that church, that, if this is found to be true, they restore those possessions to the church and wholly refrain from harassing that place. If they contemptuously refuse to obey your admonition, administer canonical justice upon them.

### CCCXCIV. To Hartwig, bishop of Bremen.—He commends Abbot Wibald to him and directs him to procure restoration of the lands taken from the Church of Camin. (1150, June.)

[Same source.]

[Col. 1421D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to H., venerable brother, archbishop of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is the duty of the episcopal office to cherish venerable places and persons and to support them in their needs. Therefore we have thought it right to ask your brotherhood, on behalf of our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, to honor and love him with fraternal charity, and, as your office requires, to assist in recovering and protecting the lands of the Church of Camin which lie [Col. 1422A] in your diocese, especially those which Abbess Judith presumed to alienate after her deposition.

### CCCXCV. To King Conrad.—He regards favorably the king’s embassy, in which matters of Church and kingdom are to be secured; he has entrusted the affair of the monastery of Murbach to the bishop of Lausanne; and he speaks of Otto who had cut off a cleric’s nose. (1150, June.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 686.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ CONRAD, illustrious and glorious king of the Romans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1422B] As we have learned from the first and second letters of your excellency, your serenity has resolved, with the common counsel of the princes of your realm, to visit your mother, the holy Roman Church, through eminent envoys, so that with them we may discuss and order the state and interests of the Church of God and of the kingdom. This is pleasing and acceptable to us and to our brethren. Since we were awaiting the arrival of these envoys, we would, as we believe, long ago have sent our own envoys to the diligence of your nobility.

For our desire is that those things which have been established between Church and kingdom by our predecessors and yours may, by the Lord’s help, be so strengthened between us and your majesty [Col. 1422C] that the universal Church, the bride of God, may peacefully enjoy her rights; that the Empire may retain its due strength; and that the Christian people may rejoice in welcome peace and pleasing tranquillity.

As for the business of the monastery of Murbach, concerning which you asked us most earnestly, before your royal letters reached us, having consulted our brethren, we had entrusted it for investigation and decision to our venerable brother, the bishop of Lausanne, in whose prudence and integrity we have great confidence. It therefore seemed to us and to our brethren contrary to equity to proceed in the case by any means at present while one party was absent. We have instead referred the matter to that same brother, who, as a discerning and prudent man trained for a long time in regular discipline, should beneficially correct the excesses of the monks of that place and, with God’s help, impose a canonical conclusion upon the case.

Moreover, with respect to that Otto who, setting aside reverence for God, did not fear in wicked boldness to cut off the nose of a certain cleric, we could by no means entertain a plan for absolving him from excommunication unless he presents himself before the apostolic presence in order to make satisfaction for so grave an offence. Surely the vigor of royal authority ought to have blazed out more sharply against him before the complaint of so great a crime reached the ears of our apostolate. [Col. 1422D]

### CCCXCVI. He receives the monastery of Ebrach under protection and confirms its goods. (1150, 23 October—Segni.) [Col. 1423A]

[Lang, *Regesta*, I, 197; *Brief Notice of the Monastery of Ebrach*, 67.]

### CCCXCVII. He receives the convent of Wechterswinkel under protection. (1150, 23 October—Segni.)

[Lang, ibid.]

### CCCXCVIII. To Pons, abbot of Vézelay.—On the same subject. (1150, 24 October.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 657.]

[Col. 1423B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PONS, abbot of Vézelay, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You will be able plainly to see from the copy of the letters what we have ordered by our letters to our venerable brother, the bishop of Autun, and to the noble duke of Burgundy, his brother, in your affair. Therefore, if the aforesaid bishop and duke wish to summon you concerning a monetary matter before our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, when summoned by him, appear before him, and hear and observe what he determines between you. But if the bishop of Autun wishes to proceed concerning the status of the monastery, we wish that controversy to be heard in our presence. [Col. 1423C]

Given at Segni, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.

### CCCXCIX. To the duke of Burgundy.—He rebukes him for being hostile to the monastery of Vézelay. (1150, 24 October.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 656.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the noble duke of Burgundy, greeting.

The more the clemency of divine providence has granted you and raised you higher in eminence, the more you ought to love churches, ecclesiastical persons, and Christ’s poor, and to defend them with watchful care against the attacks of wicked men. But, as we have learned, to our great grief, you are doing the opposite. You harass our beloved sons, the brothers of the monastery of Vézelay, with severe vexations, and have ordered their men and goods to be seized. You have also, through your messenger, formally defied those brothers as enemies. We had expected no such things from you.

Since we clearly recognize that these acts are being done to the destruction of your soul, and since we cannot and ought not fail the monastery, which belongs to blessed Peter, by these present letters we command you to make fitting satisfaction for the aforesaid losses and injuries inflicted, and henceforth to impose no burdens upon them. Rather, as a devoted son of the Catholic Church and a lover of justice, take care to assist those brothers, other religious men, and ecclesiastical persons [Col. 1424A] in their needs.

If, however, you believe you have any claim against those brothers, you may obtain what justice directs in the presence of our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre. When summoned by him, appear before him and firmly accept and observe whatever he judges between you. But if you contemptuously refuse to obey our commands, the hand of blessed Peter will without doubt be stretched out against you.

Given at Segni, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.

### CD. To Henry, bishop of Autun.—He rebukes him for being hostile to the monastery of Vézelay. (1150, October.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 655.]

[Col. 1424B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishop of AUTUN, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The clemency of the Apostolic See is accustomed to preserve for individual churches and ecclesiastical persons their dignity and justice. Hence we, whose special concern it is to bear care for all churches, ought to be solicitous for the monastery of Vézelay, which belongs to blessed Peter, and for the religious brothers of that place. We believe that we sent you letters on their behalf, directing you, according to your office and the power granted you by God, to defend these brothers against the attacks of wicked men.

Yet a grave complaint has reached us that you permit your men [Col. 1424C] and servants to harass that monastery in many ways. For, as we have learned, they violently take away its horses and oxen, seize its men with their goods and packs, and inflict many other losses and injuries. Moreover, the duke of Burgundy, your brother, after the fashion of enemies against whom war has been declared, ordered those brothers to be guarded by him and ordered their men and goods to be seized and detained.

Since we wish each person’s rights to be preserved, by this present injunction we command you to cause what has been taken by your men to be restored in full to the aforesaid brothers, and to make fitting satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted. But if you believe you have any rightful claim against them concerning a monetary matter, you may obtain what is just in the presence of our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre. Therefore, if summoned by that same brother, appear before him, and firmly accept and observe what he judges between you concerning this matter. But if the controversy concerns the status of the monastery, we wish it to be handled in our presence. [Col. 1424D]

### CDI. To Hugh, bishop of Auxerre.—On the same subject. (1150, October.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 656.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable [Col. 1425A] brother HUGH, bishop of Auxerre, greeting.

We have commanded by our letters our venerable brother, the bishop of Autun, who is said to have inflicted many evils through his men upon the brothers of the monastery of Vézelay, to cause what has been taken from them and their men to be restored in full, and to render fitting satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted. If he believes he has any rightful claim against those brothers in a monetary matter, we wish him to obtain what is just in your presence.

Therefore, by these present letters we command your discretion that, if he wishes to proceed, you summon both parties before your tribunal at a suitable place and time and, after examining and learning the case, decide between them with impartial equity. [Col. 1425B]

### CDII. He confirms all goods, donations, and exemptions of the monastery of Saint Quirinus at Tegernsee, which is declared subject to the ordinary bishop in spiritual matters. (1150, 21 November.)
