[Hundius, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, III, 400.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONRAD, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Quirinus by Lake Tegernsee, and his brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The authority of the Apostolic See entrusted to us exhorts us to grant the protection of guardianship to places and persons who duly seek its aid in devotion. For, just as no effect should be granted to those who seek unjust things, so the petition of those seeking what is lawful and just ought not to be delayed, especially those who rejoice to serve almighty God with uprightness of life and commendable ordering of conduct.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery, which was built on their estate by the noble brothers Adalbert and Occarius, illustrious counts, and endowed with the ancient privileges of the Roman emperors—namely, Pippin, Charles, and Louis—and in which, finally, the body of blessed Quirinus, obtained from our pious predecessor Pope Zachary of holy memory, bishop of Rome, [Col. 1425D] is said to rest.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Moreover, we likewise confirm to you the liberties and immunities reasonably granted and confirmed in writing to your monastery by bishops, kings, or princes; and by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to violate them or dare to grant them out as benefices.

In the parish churches [Col. 1426A] which you hold, choose suitable priests and present them to the bishop. If they are suitable, let the bishop, with the abbot’s consent, commit the care of souls to them, so that such priests may render account to the bishop concerning the care of the people, while giving you due subjection in temporal matters. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and is willing to provide these things freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of subterfuge or violence, except one whom the brothers, by common consent or the sounder part of the council, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. [Col. 1426B]

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of the uses for which they were granted—for the governance and support of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our enactment, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed.  
I, Manfredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Aribertus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed.  
I, Jordanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed.  
I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.  
I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Rolandus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman [Col. 1427A] Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDIII. To Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg.—That he should compel Otto, son of Count Palatine Otto, to make satisfaction to Otto, bishop of Freising, for the injury inflicted; or, if unwilling, excommunicate him; and that he should hold the brothers of Tegernsee monastery commended to his care. (1150, 21 November.)

[Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, I, 393, where this letter is wrongly attributed to Alexander III.]

To E., archbishop of Salzburg.

We have received a grave complaint from our venerable brother O., bishop of Freising, against Otto, son of Count Palatine Otto, [Col. 1427B] namely that, while he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, Otto treated him with serious insults and, setting aside reverence for God, behaved toward him disgracefully. How grave this is, and how sternly it ought to be punished, is not unknown to the discernment of those who think rightly.

Therefore, lest so great an offence remain unpunished in the Church of God and wicked men be afforded license to rage against ecclesiastical persons, by these present letters we command your brotherhood strictly to admonish the aforesaid Otto to render fitting satisfaction to our aforesaid brother for so grave an offence. If he contemptuously refuses to obey your admonitions, declare Otto excommunicated, [Col. 1427C] and maintain and cause the sentence of excommunication to be firmly observed until he makes fitting satisfaction to God and the Church for so grave an offence.

Moreover, we likewise command your brotherhood to uphold and defend in their rights, for the reverence of blessed Peter and of ourselves, our beloved sons Abbot C. and the brothers of Tegernsee monastery, and to render them due justice regarding the complaints which they lay before you.

Given at Segni, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

### CDIV. To P., prior of the church of Saint Fridianus of Lucca. (1150, 22 November.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucchese edition, IV, 595.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1427D] son P., prior of Saint Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is just and reasonable that the abundance of those who have plenty should supply the want of others. Our beloved son, the archpriest of the church of Montebellio, coming before us, stated that he desires to establish in that church an order of regular canons and to preserve there the Rule of blessed Augustine, which is endangered. He therefore humbly asked us to request your belovedness by apostolic letters to grant him for a time one or more of your brothers, who might instruct the brothers of the aforesaid church in the religious observance of the order.

Therefore, by these present letters, we request and command your belovedness to grant to them one or more of your brothers, who may teach them how they ought to observe that Rule and order. For a reward will be bestowed upon you and your brothers by the Rewarder of all good things. [Col. 1428A]

Given at Ferentino, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

### CDV. He confirms the privileges and immunities of the canons’ church of Saint Mary of Montebellio. (1150, 24 November.)

[Savioli, *Annals of Bologna*, Appendix, I, II, 221.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons N. N., archpriest, and his brothers in the church of Saint Mary of Montebellio, professing the regular life, present and future, forever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to labor for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to make beneficial provision for their peace and welfare. For it is recognized as worthy and fitting to honor that we, who have been appointed to the governance of churches, should protect them from the wickedness of evil men and strengthen them by the patronage of blessed Peter and the Apostolic See.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin. We have thought it necessary to set forth the following in their proper names: namely, the church of Luparolo; [Col. 1428C] the church of Bauzano, as it is to be adjudged to you by the judgment of our venerable brother Moses, archbishop of Ravenna; the church of Montalognio; the church of Saint Mary of Fagnano with all its appurtenances; the church of Pantiano; the church of Lupa Ahalaria; the church of Saint Peter of Savignano; the church of Saint Blaise of Lacumiano; the church of Saint Mary in Resiliolo; the church of Saint Nicholas in Roncheliis with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Doninus of Campere Maggiore; the church of Saint Paul of Palude; the church of Saint Mary of Prato Bonelli; the church of Saint Mark; the church of Saint Vincent; and the church of Saint Fabian by the River Lavino, together with the other churches belonging to [Col. 1428D] the parish church of Montebellio.

We also decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be kept there inviolate for all time. Further, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you from lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. We also prohibit anyone among the laity from daring in any way to exact, receive, or demand tithes from you from lands belonging to your church by right of ownership.

We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion or last will of those from the territory of your church who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving in all things the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1429A]

We therefore decree that no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it in any way by vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of the uses for which they have been granted—for the governance and support of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our enactment, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third admonition, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor, know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

**“Grant me a sign of favor, O Lord.”**

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theobaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes.  
I, Manfredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina.  
I, Aribertus, cardinal priest of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.  
[Col. 1429C] I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Angelo.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary the New.  
I, Guido, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico.  
I, Rolandus, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Hincarus, bishop of Tusculum.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Marinianus, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 1429D] in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDVI. Privilege for the church of the canons of Blessed Mary at Raitenbuch, in the diocese of Freising, under the Rule of Saint Augustine. (1150, 26 November.)

[Hund, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, III, 145.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son OTTO, provost of the canonry of Blessed Mary situated at Raitenbuch, and to his brothers, present and future, professing the canonical life, forever. Amen.

The authority of the apostolic see entrusted to us exhorts us to extend the protection of guardianship to places and persons that duly implore its aid with devotion [Col. 1430A]. For, just as no effect ought to be granted to those who seek unjust things, so the petition of those seeking lawful and just things ought not to be delayed—especially that of those who rejoice to serve almighty God with uprightness of life and a commendable ordering of conduct.

Therefore, beloved son Otto, provost in the Lord, graciously granting due and willing assent to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine [Col. 1430B] shall be preserved there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Upon your death, now provost of that place, or that of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect.

You shall receive consecrations of altars or churches [Col. 1430C], ordinations of clerics, chrism, holy oil, and the rest from the bishop of Freising, in whose diocese you are, provided that he is Catholic, possesses the favor and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to confer these things freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you choose and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, or have recourse to the apostolic see; and, supported by apostolic authority, he shall without hesitation grant what is requested.

We also prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, from leaving the cloister without the permission of his provost; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community. Further, we decree that the tithes of newly cultivated lands belonging to the same canonry shall belong to it [Col. 1430D], saving the rights of neighboring churches.

Moreover, we grant you Welf, your distinguished advocate or protector, and his sons after him, if, by God’s favor, they are such as may be useful to your church and executors of their father’s institution. But if not, it shall be at your discretion to choose whom you wish as a suitable protector for your church—one who shall vigorously and reverently provide this service through the power of God, without exacting secular profit.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid canonry, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be kept whole [Col. 1431A] and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted.

As a sign of this liberty received from the Roman Church, each year you shall pay to us and our successors, for our daily use, a white linen garment and a stole. If, therefore, any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, or any other person, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts in the future to violate rashly the text of this our privilege, and, after a second or third warning, does not make fitting amends by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself to be guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed [Col. 1431B]; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedis, have subscribed. I, Albanus, bishop, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Rolandus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and [Col. 1431C] Damian, have subscribed. I, Jordanus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Boso, writer of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CDVII. It enumerates the possessions of Lobbes Abbey, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Liège, and confirms and enlarges its privileges.  
*(A.D. 1150, December 2.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, II, 1169.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FRANCO, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever. Amen.

The authority of the apostolic see entrusted to us exhorts us to extend the protection of guardianship to places and persons that duly implore its aid with devotion [Col. 1431D]. For, just as no effect ought to be granted to those who seek unjust things, so the petition of those seeking lawful and just things ought not to be delayed—especially that of those who rejoice to serve almighty God with uprightness of life and a commendable ordering of conduct.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. Following the example of our predecessor Pope Innocent of blessed memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service [Col. 1432A], and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord prospering, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, contributions of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you.

Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

In the diocese of Liège: the estate of Bermerys with its altar; the estate of Ereheneis with its altar; also half the estate of Mathenoule; the estate of Tiguillers with its altar; Battiniacas and part of Alzonia; the estate of Castillon with its altar and the chapel of Mertinis; the estate of Feratis with its altar and the chapel of Viscort [Col. 1432B]; the altar of Hantis; the estate of Radionatis with its altar; the estate of Gillier with its altar; and the estate of Giniaco with its altar.

In the diocese of Cambrai: the altar of Blarignies; the estate of Huoi with its altar and appurtenances; the estate of Piscani with its altar; half of Perrone; the altar of Hyon; the altar of Meum and the chapel of Cipli; the estate of Brania with its altar; the estate of Monastery with its church and all things pertaining to it; the estate of Herstruz with two *manipuli*; half the tithe of Albys; the estate of Sanctis with its altar; the estate of Vergenoul with its altar; Geroldengias with its altar; the estate of Singulf with its altar; the estate of Tisenghien; the altar of Mortezele; the altar of Cotegna with all its appurtenances; and also the estate of Lerna.

Likewise, in the diocese of Cambrai [Col. 1432C]: the church of Anton with all its appurtenances; and the estate of Lobbes, with the church of Blessed Ursmar and all things pertaining to it. In the churches of Anton and Blessed Ursmar, just as the lordship over all prebends, the deanery, custody, and school is known to belong to the abbot, so we confirm that possession of all things belonging to the same prebends—whether in parishes or in other property—shall forever be subject to the disposition of the abbot or the ordering of the monks, as was instituted of old and has hitherto been observed.

By apostolic authority we also confirm to you all tithes from the demesne lands of the whole abbey, both from churches held as benefices and from those assigned to your maintenance [Col. 1432D], as these were granted to you by imperial munificence.

In the diocese of Tournai: the altar of Arcella, two *manipuli* at Tyrroda, and the altar of Ham with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Noyon: two *manipuli* at Colio; and in the diocese of Laon, the estate of Erclearo with its altar and appurtenances.

Further, we abolish that evil custom which had extraordinarily grown up under the name of the *personatus* until the time of our predecessor Pope Urban II of good memory. On the death of a priest serving any altar, we command that another suitable person be presented to the bishop through the abbot’s hand; he shall receive from the bishop the care of the parish with your assent [Col. 1433A], render account to the bishop for the care of the people, and show you due subjection concerning temporal matters belonging to the monastery.

We further decree that in all your parishes no one shall presume to build or hold a church or monastery without your assent. Moreover, because that place is consecrated in honor of St. Peter, whose office we exercise, and is especially distinguished by his relics, we have judged it fitting that its cemetery, as our holy fathers decreed and as has hitherto been observed, shall henceforth not be opened for the burial of any human corpse.

Since it is established that the rulers of the same place were bishops at its beginning—partly for the sake of preaching, partly because, having been nobly built by royal generosity, it was more nobly advanced by apostolic authority—we also, after the example of our predecessors, confirm the liberty reasonably granted to the aforesaid monastery: namely, that abbots may everywhere use a golden ring, sandals, gloves, and a subdiaconal tunic in the celebration of Mass [Col. 1433B].

They may also bless priestly vestments and altar ornaments; through that same blessed Peter, to whom Christ entrusted the keys of heaven and the power of binding and loosing, they shall have the power of binding and loosing, which through him was granted to us.

And because it belongs to religious men to establish religious observance in churches committed to them and to preserve what has been established with diligent care, we have commanded that, upon the death of clerics in the church of Blessed Ursmar, religious monks shall be substituted. Upon the death of the abbot of that place [Col. 1433C], no one shall be installed there by deceit or violence except one whom the brethren by common assent, or the sounder part of their counsel, in accordance with the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall judge should be elected, and whom the bishop of Liège shall set over them.

That bishop shall never lose the endowment of the abbey granted to him by the munificence of ancient kings and emperors; from it he shall preserve for the monks without disturbance the things they now hold or ought to hold, or will acquire hereafter. We altogether prohibit public visitations by the bishops of Liège and Cambrai from being held in that monastery, and prohibit them from coming there or imposing any burden by their arrival, unless they have been invited by the abbot or brethren [Col. 1433D].

Providing also for the rights of the Church of Lobbes, we decree that no monastery may presume, for the sake of conversion or burial, to receive anyone of its household without permission of the aforesaid church. We further decree that the advocacy of that monastery shall be altogether free, so that [lacuna] no advocate shall be appointed there except one whom the abbot and brethren appoint for the benefit of that place; and, when and where he is invited, that advocate shall protect the above-mentioned place with the brethren and without disturbance.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1434A], take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, let all things be kept unimpaired and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, attempts rashly to violate it, and, after a second or third warning, does not make fitting amends by due satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and [Col. 1434B] our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance.

But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the Church of St. Praxedis. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1434C] I, John Paparo, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Terentini, through the hand of Mariniani, writer of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDVIII. To the Abbot and convent of Lobbes.—That they are no longer to sit with the canons in the refectory, nor be in one choir.  
*(A.D. 1150, December 2.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 630.]

[Col. 1434D] EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son F., [Note: [Col. 1433D] Franco, who in 1149 succeeded Abbot Lambert, according to the short chronicle of Lobbes, vol. III, *Anecdota*.] abbot, and to the whole convent [Note: [Col. 1433D] The distinguished monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese [Col. 1434D] of Cambrai, founded by St. Landelin, whose first abbots also enjoyed episcopal rank.] of Lobbes, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has reached the hearing of the apostolic see that, contrary to the order of religious life and to the custom of those enrolled in monastic observance, you permit the canons of St. Ursmar to sit together with you in one choir and in one refectory. We have heard that from this there arise very many disorders disturbing the brethren’s peace and their purpose of holiness.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your care to strive to root out such confusion [Col. 1435A], and to protect the vows of pious life with such diligent care that your ministry may rightly be reproached in nothing. Thus, obtaining favor with God through the abundance of virtues, may you fill the hearts of those subject to you with the fragrance of good works and incite their minds more fervently to works of virtue.

Moreover, concerning those things belonging to the brethren’s prebend, by apostolic authority we command that you grant a prebend to no layman or cleric unless he becomes a monk or a convert; and if such a prebend was granted by your predecessors without the consent of the chapter, you are to recover it.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

### CDIX. Privilege for the monastery of St. Mary at Compiègne.  
*(A.D. 1150, December 13.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, X, Documents, 121.]

[Col. 1435B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ODON, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary situated at Compiègne, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

The Church recognizes that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was principally bestowed by God upon blessed Peter in the words in which the Lord himself addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” By the same divine author, both his own steadfastness and the confirmation of another’s faith are granted to him when it is said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail [Col. 1435C]; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren.”

It is fitting, therefore, for us, who, though unworthy, sit in the place of blessed Peter, according to the knowledge and power granted us by divine mercy, to correct what is wrong, confirm what is right, and so order the things to be ordered in the whole Church according to the judgment of the inner tribunal, that our judgment may proceed from his countenance and our eyes may behold equity.

Moved, then, by the obligation of this principle, we entrust to you, by apostolic authority, the governance and ordering of that monastery over which, by the Lord’s appointment, you are known to preside, in order to reform there the state of honorable life and religion. In it secular clerics have hitherto lived in a disorderly and insufficiently honorable manner. We strengthen this grant by the privilege of the present writing.

First [Col. 1435D], indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in the same place by us, through the favor and zeal of our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks, according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord granting it, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We likewise confirm to you the liberty and authority granted to that monastery by our predecessor pontiffs and established by writings of the apostolic see.

We also decree [Col. 1436A] that the monastery shall be subject to no archbishop or bishop, but only to the Roman pontiff. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from whatever bishop you prefer, provided he is Catholic and possesses the favor and communion of the apostolic see.

Upon your death, now abbot of the same place, or that of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall judge should be elected. The elected person shall then approach the Roman pontiff to receive the grace of blessing.

We therefore decree [Col. 1436B] that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, let all things be kept whole and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the apostolic see.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, attempts rashly to violate it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend such presumption by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment [Col. 1436C] let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the rewards of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Prison of Tullianus. I, John, cardinal prodeacon of St. Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo. I, Astaldus, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace. [Col. 1436D] I, John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary the New. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Rolandus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedis. I, Manfredus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Sabina. [Col. 1437A] I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cyriacus. I, Haribertus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Hubardus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bernardus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Clement. I, Jordanus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Boso, writer of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius.

### CDX. Privilege for the Church of Penne, at the request of Bishop Grimaldus.  
*(A.D. 1150, December 15.—Fragment.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, I, 1120.]

[Col. 1437B]

It reproduces word for word the privilege of Innocent II, issued in 1140 on the sixth day before the Kalends of November (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 451), as far as: “Given at Ferentino, through the hands of Boso, writer of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.”

Eleven cardinals subscribed.

### CDXI. At the request of Bishop Michael, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Monopoli.  
*(A.D. 1150, December 19.)*

[Same work, 964.]

[Col. 1437C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MICHAEL, bishop of Monopoli, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

Both the principle of justice demands and the order of reason requires that we should take more earnest care for churches and persons that adhere more closely to the apostolic see and are known to belong to the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff. For it is known to be worthy and fitting that we, who have been assumed to the governance of churches, should protect them from the malice of wicked people and fortify them by the patronage of Blessed Peter and the Holy Roman Church.

Therefore, beloved brother Michael, bishop in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. Following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Urban, Paschal, Calixtus, and Honorius, Roman pontiffs [Col. 1437D], we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Monopoli, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors forever. We also decree that this Church owes the reverence of subjection to no authority other than the apostolic see. We therefore decree that you [Col. 1438A] and your successors, enjoying the favor of this liberty, shall remain forever under the obedience of the apostolic see alone.

Upon your death, now bishop of the same city, or that of any of your successors, the clergy of Monopoli shall have the power, all impropriety set aside, to elect a bishop canonically; and the one elected shall approach the Roman pontiff for consecration.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, let all things be kept whole and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority and reverence of the apostolic see.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future [Col. 1438B], knowing the text of this our constitution, attempts rashly to violate it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend such presumption by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know himself or herself to be guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 1438C] I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, G.G., cardinal priest of St. Calixtus. I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Prison of Tullianus. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Boso, writer of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CDXII. He congratulates Godescalc on being made bishop of Arras.  
*(A.D. 1150.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., II, 169.]

[Col. 1438D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GODESCALC, bishop of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“A man’s way is not in himself. A man’s heart plans his way, but the Lord directs his steps.” We remember what you once sought with the greatest earnestness, and with joy and thanksgiving we behold that the divine right hand has raised you up. For when you were urgently seeking release from that bond by which you were held fast to the care of a little flock, through the agency of him beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed down, you have deserved to be bound by a closer and stronger bond to the guardianship of an innumerable people. This has been done by the Lord and is pleasing in our eyes [Col. 1439A].

He indeed gives snow like wool, when those who desire to sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet are, at the Lord’s prompting, turned back to the refreshment of peoples and the services of Martha. Hence we confidently trust that you will bring the ark committed to you through these waves of the sea to the harbor of rest all the better, because we more certainly judge that a governor has been provided for it who, according to the Apostle’s word, can be an example to his subjects in word, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity.

Furthermore, we have received a complaint on behalf of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of St. Vaast, that at the instigation of your clerics you are attempting to burden them contrary to the tenor of the privileges which they have obtained from the apostolic see and contrary to ancient custom. They have also informed us that they possess a certain parish chapel which is insufficient to contain its parishioners because of their number [Col. 1439B]. They therefore request that certain of them—namely, those who have begun only recently to inhabit the garden enclosure and orchard of the brethren—may, with your consent, transfer to another of their chapels, after a priest has been installed there, while your right in it, as in the other chapel, remains fully preserved to you.

Since, therefore, the higher you have risen, the more you ought both to attend to the welfare of those committed to you and to offer a more ready assent to the petitions of religious persons, by the present writings we command your brotherhood not in any way to burden them contrary to the tenor of our privileges and to ancient custom. But if their assertions rest on truth [Col. 1439C], permit those who inhabit their garden enclosure and gardens to transfer to their other chapel, in which your right, as in this one, shall remain fully preserved to you. If, however, there is anything which you believe may rightfully belong to you against them, take care first to make it known to us; and we, God being the author, shall preserve what is yours.

### CDXIII. To Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, etc.—That he restore monks to the church of Heidenheim after expelling the secular clerics.  
*(A.D. 1150?)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 662.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother EBERHARD, bishop of Bamberg, and to his beloved son Adam, abbot of Ebrach, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Gebehard, bishop of Eichstätt of good memory, inflamed by love of holy religion, grieved that service acceptable to God was not being rendered in the church of Heidenheim. Having peaceably removed the secular clerics from there, he arranged for religious brethren to be appointed there; provided, however, that the secular clerics then dwelling there should retain during their lives the benefices they had received, and that, upon their death, these should pass wholly to the use of the monks without anyone’s opposition.

But now, to our great sorrow, we state that, after he had been taken from these temporal things and called, God being the author, to eternity, and before [Col. 1440A] regular brethren had yet been introduced according to his intention, the archbishop of Mainz and the bishop of Eichstätt, with rash presumption, brought back the secular clerics. Your charity clearly and plainly recognizes sufficiently what punishment this act would deserve if we wished to exercise the rigor of justice.

Since it belongs to the office of our pontificate to revoke what has been wrongly done, and since we have great confidence in your prudence, by apostolic writings we command you to devote vigilant attention to this matter. Having expelled the secular clerics, strive to establish there the religion acceptable to God, according to the purpose of the aforesaid bishop.

Yet those to whom he left benefices for their lifetime, although they ought to be deprived of them by the rigor of justice, are nevertheless, because gentleness of kindness must be exercised toward all [Col. 1440B], to perceive that we mercifully grant them these benefices. But the rest, who are known to have been intruded there after the ordinance of that bishop, shall be driven thence as invaders, without receiving any benefice.

If they scorn to obey you in this matter, pronounce by our authority a sentence of excommunication against their persons, and a sentence of interdict against the place. Moreover, we earnestly commend to your charity the bearer of this letter, Ilsung, who has given this matter due attention. We ask that he may know that, in his needs, he finds our protection with you, and that he may receive your defense on our behalf in such a manner that he need neither regret his pious labor and zeal nor that fear and violence from wicked persons should restrain others [Col. 1440C] who have learned of it from undertaking a like purpose.

### CDXIV. To Henry, archbishop of Mainz.—On the same subject.  
*(A.D. 1150?)*

[Same work, 663.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly astonished and grieved that you have restored clerics to the church of Heidenheim and request that this be confirmed by our authority, since, by the office of the pontificate entrusted to you, you ought rather to plant, foster, and preserve religion more vigilantly [Col. 1440D], not to root it up, scatter it, and destroy it.

Gebehard, formerly bishop of Eichstätt, of good memory, inflamed by the fire of holy religion, peaceably removed the secular clerics from there in order to restore there, with the power of the Holy Spirit, religion acceptable to God. Since death prevented him from bringing so holy and commendable a vow into effect, your brotherhood ought to have labored to see that it was fulfilled, rather than presume to render it void and undermine it at the suggestions of anyone whatsoever.

Therefore, because it is known to concern us to revoke what has been wrongly done and, by the authority of the prince of the apostles, to advance worthy undertakings, we have instructed our venerable brother [Col. 1441A] Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, and our beloved son Adam of Ebrach, how they are to correct errors in our stead and bring to due completion what was commendably begun. By these present writings, therefore, we command your brotherhood in no way to resist them in this matter; but if they seek your assistance in anything, grant it to them, as you desire to retain the favor of the apostolic see.

### CDXV. To G[oswin] of Cîteaux and all the abbots assembled at Cîteaux.—He writes that, had his duties not prevented him, he would gladly have attended their assembly.  
*(A.D. 1150?—It survives among the letters of St. Bernard, prefixed to letter 273. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 476.)*

### CDXVI. To Suger, abbot of St. Denis.—Concerning the violence of the count of Anjou toward his brother Robert.  
*(A.D. 1145–1151.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 416.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of St. Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have seen in the letters of our dearest son, the abbot of Clairvaux, he recently received letters from the king of the Franks stating that the count of Anjou intends to enter the land of his brother Robert with an army [Col. 1441C] and violence. We therefore command your belovedness, should you judge it necessary, to inform us with haste; and, with God’s help, we shall take care to oppose his wicked design.

### CDXVII. To the same.—He commends the subdeacon Mo.  
*(A.D. 1145–1150.)*

[Same work.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of St. Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The prudence and devotion of your love, which we know you bear toward [Col. 1441D] us, urge us to write to you more often and, in honoring you, to burden you more frequently. Our beloved son and subdeacon Mo., whom we commended to you, has for some time been supported by the relief of your benefactions; but since he is weighed down by the burden of debt, while the necessary assistance is lacking, he is compelled to implore your aid still further. Therefore, as we instructed you in other letters, so by the present letter we command you by way of request: do not withdraw from him the hand of your generosity, but free him from the debt under which he is oppressed, and thus bestow still further the benefit of generosity already begun, so that he himself, with your assistance, may be able to advance in the pursuit of learning, and your generosity may make us more indebted to you on his behalf.

CDXVIII. To Abbot Suger.—He consoles him over the death of his nephew. (Year 1145–1151.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 636.]

[Col. 1442A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the death of our son John, your nephew, whom, as we have learned, you were sending into our presence on business of that Church, we sympathize with you in paternal affection, and commend his soul to the Lord in our prayers. Moreover, we do not believe that your love is unaware that the Lord visits and chastens those whom he loves, so that, through temporal scourges, [Col. 1442B] if they are borne with equanimity, the fruit of eternal blessedness may be gained. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, let not the adversity of this present life break you; let not earthly tribulation corrupt the sincerity of your heart. Fix the gaze of your mind upon the mountain whence help shall come to you, and, strengthened in the Lord, hold firmly to the purpose of your religious life and upright conduct. Nor on that account should you refrain from addressing the apostolic see concerning the needs of your Church and setting before it the state of your necessity. For we, loving that same Church and your person with sincere charity in the Lord, are prepared to heed your just petitions and to grant them insofar as we can according to the Lord.

CDXIX. He confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of the Savior and Saint Boniface at Fulda. (13 January 1151.)

[DRONKE, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 394.]

[Col. 1442C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MARCHWARD, abbot of the monastery of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Boniface, situated beside the bank of the river called Fulda, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

Although by reason of the office of the apostolate imposed upon us by God we are debtors to all ecclesiastical persons, it is especially fitting that we devote more earnest care to those who serve almighty God in the habit of religion [Col. 1442D] and are known to belong to the apostolic see by a special prerogative. For it is recognized as worthy and befitting our office that we, who have been appointed to govern the Churches, should both protect them from the malice of wicked persons and strengthen them by the protection of the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Marchward, we graciously grant your reasonable petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Innocent, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, over which by God’s ordering you are known to preside, and confirm it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of [Col. 1443A] pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have considered it proper to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, called Exajulum, situated at Rome near the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, called *ad Praesepe* [at the Manger], given by our predecessor Pope Leo, of happy memory, to your predecessor, the religious Abbot Hecbert, out of regard for affection, together with all its *caminatae* [uncertain: associated buildings or chambers] [lacuna] and the tithes of the faithful which you have possessed until now without opposition from any person. [lacuna] [Col. 1443B] you shall retain the primacy which you have hitherto held in every place and assembly. [lacuna] may they find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

(Sign.) I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cyriacus. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of Saint Sabina. [Col. 1443C] I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, John Paparo, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel. I, Astald, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace [Col. 1443D] near the Temple of Agrippa. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Jacintus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

[Col. 1444A] Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of January, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CDXX. Privilege for the monastery of Weissenau. (13 January 1151.)

[LANG, *Regesta*, I, 198.]

CDXXI. He confirms the churches and goods, which he enumerates at length, of the abbey of Saint Savior of Majella; protects its rights and vindicates its liberty. (24 January 1151.)

[*Bullarium Vaticanum*, I, 48, from a copy inserted in the volume of the Visitation of Giovanni Battista Corradi, marked with the letter D, fol. 26; preserved in the archive of the basilica among the records of abbeys.]

[Col. 1444B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALEXANDER, prior of the Hermitage of Majella, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the eremitical life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant the just desires of religious persons, so that faithful devotion may obtain a prompt effect. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Prior Alexander, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Paschal of happy memory, [Note: [Col. 1443D] This refers to a bull of Paschal II which has not yet come into our hands. It has therefore either perished or still lies hidden and inaccessible.] we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves [Col. 1444C], and confirm by the privilege of this present document, the church of Saint Savior, in which you have been devoted to the divine service; and we decree that the wilderness of your dwelling-place shall remain free from the jurisdiction and power of all persons, and that you may enjoy every tranquility in the service of the Lord.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have considered it proper to name expressly: the church of Saint Savior of Angre Castellar [Note: [Col. 1443D] The newly examined records of our archive place both fiefs—namely Castellar and Cephalia—in the province of Abruzzo Citeriore, beyond the River Pescara. In our own age these two estates, granted in emphyteusis by the chapter of Saint Peter, are possessed by the noble Valignana family.] with the dependent hill of Cefalia; the church of Saint Martin with its cells; the church of Saint Pancras; the *ara* of Pinna (read: Pinnae) [Note: [Col. 1443D] Eugenius’s bull enumerates here the *ara Pinnae*; the constitution of Alexander II mentioned above called it the castle named *la Penna*. It is therefore clear that the castle of Pinna Pedimontis is to be understood as subject to the abbey of Majella. Why Eugenius, and the Roman pontiffs who followed Eugenius—Adrian IV and Alexander III—call it not the castle but the *ara Pinnae* is not yet sufficiently known. Anyone who interprets *ara* as the church of Saint Sylvester, the principal parish church in the castle of Pinna, might perhaps be blamed for asserting this without any foundation. More worthy of consideration is the conjecture of one who understands *ara* as the proper name of the castle, so that the word *castrum*, used by Eugenius, is generic, whereas *ara Pinnae* expresses the individual name of the castle in the territory of Pinna. [Col. 1445A] In much the same way, when the castle of Guardia Grelis is named, the word *Guardia* [Col. 1445B] indicates the proper name of the place.] with the dependent hill of Famecchiano and its cells; the church of Saint Mary of Lavella with its cells; the church of Saint Angel and Saint [Col. 1445A] Peter [Note: [Col. 1445B] We discussed the church of Saint Peter in the castle of Laroma in the notes on the bull of Paschal II. One question remains: why does Eugenius here make subject to the abbey of Majella the church of Saint Peter which Paschal assigns to the monastery of Saint Martin of the Valley? We think that one and the same church, subject to a double obligation, could have served both abbeys; unless perhaps we should say that there were two churches of the same name within the same fief. The codex of the Visitation of 1604, fol. 184, records the church of Saint Angel as situated in the same fief of Laroma, but states that it had been worn down by age and ruins. Hence the title of this chapel, as also of another under the name of Saint Nicholas, which had suffered destruction through the devastation of the locality, was placed in the church of Saint Remigius, the principal church in the territory of Fara.] of the castle of Laroma; the church of Saint Clement with its cells; the church of Saint Blaise; the church of Saint Agatha; the church of Saint Procopius; the church of Saint Nicholas; the church of Saint Helena in the castle of Saint Angel in Trifinio, [Note: [Col. 1445B] The five churches listed in one continuous sequence seem to be referable to one and the same place. The last of them, dedicated to Saint Helena, is situated in the castle of Saint Angel in Trifinio; thus we may believe that the others were built in the same castle or in its territory. This conjecture is supported by their enumeration: a donation of Gerolf, priest, who gave the chapel to the monastery of Saint Savior of Majella in the year 1000, proves that the church of Saint Procopius, one of the five, is to be placed at Saint Angel in Trifinio. The already printed bull of Alexander II names the church of Saint Blaise of Saint Angel in Trifinio. Why should the remaining churches not likewise be placed there? Although this is, if not true, at least plausible, we are not yet permitted to establish with certainty the location of the castle in Trifinio. Not implausible is the conjecture which places that castle in the diocese of Chieti and within the jurisdiction of Guardia Grelis itself. For there, according to the precise description provided by the visitor Corradi, the churches of Saint Procopius, Saint Blaise, and Saint Helena are grouped together. Consult in our archive the codex marked C, [Col. 1445D] fols. 129, 203, and 215.] and there the villeins and holdings of lands and vineyards; likewise, at Fara, villeins, mills, holdings of lands and vineyards, and the church of Saint Cantiana [Note: [Col. 1445D] Here understand Fara Filiorum Petri, situated in the diocese of Chieti. All the records, especially that supplied by Corradi’s Visitation in codex D, fols. 139 and 150, place the church of Saint Cantian in the territory of this castle. They vary slightly in designating the church’s title: everywhere they call it the church not of Saint Cantiana but of Saint Cantian. In 1066 Peter, son of Amico, offered this very church to the abbey of Majella to possess.]; at Vacrum, the monastery of Saint Agatha and the church of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1445D] Both churches are situated in the province of Chieti near the not insignificant town of Vacrum, distinguished by the prerogative of a duchy. The former, under the dedication of Saint Agatha, stands on the hill called La Sterpara, according to the codex of the Visitation of 1640, fol. 312. The latter, dedicated to Saint Nicholas, is situated outside the walls of Vacrum, in the codex and folio just cited. In 1077 Agzarellus and William of Vacrum handed over the church of Saint Agatha to the prior of Majella. Concerning the acquisition of the latter church [Col. 1446A] we have thus far derived nothing from our records.] with its lands, vineyards, and possessions; at Preturium, the church of Saint Candida [Note: [Col. 1446B] In 1100 Count Gentilis of Monopoli is said to have given the church of Saint Candida. It stood at Preturium and, as was evident even from the ruins of the church itself, was built in splendid workmanship; we use words taken from the codex of the Visitation of 1598, fol. 30.], the church of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1446B] This church of Saint Nicholas denotes the parish church itself in the territory of Preturium, dedicated to Saint Nicholas. Consult the Acts of Visitation of 1598, fol. 27, and of 1604, fol. 101.], villeins, mills, holdings of lands and vineyards; [Col. 1446A] at Castellione, the church of Saint Justa and Saint Agnes [Note: [Col. 1446B] From the bulls of Adrian IV and Alexander III, which we shall publish below, we add here both churches, omitted from the copy of the present bull through the negligence of a scribe. According to Corradi’s aforementioned codex B, fol. 151, both churches—the one of Saint Agnes, the other of Saint Justa—exist in the territory of Castellione, included within the diocese of Chieti; but he describes both as decaying and near ruin. From 1074, by the donation of Peter of Arpa, the church of Saint Justa had passed to the abbey of Majella.] with villeins, lands, and vineyards; at Buclanicum, the church of Saint Mary of Mirabello, the church of Saint Mary of Bassano, and the church of Saint James and Saint Blaise, [Note: [Col. 1446C] To these churches situated at Buclanum, a noble and distinguished town in the diocese of Chieti, we add from the cited constitutions of Adrian and Alexander a fourth which bears the name of Saint Blaise. We thus count four in the jurisdiction of Buclanum, and indeed four are to be counted. The abbey of Majella reports that it had received the church honored with the title of Saint Mary of Bassano from Siginolfo, son of Siginolfo, already in 1142. Here is the condition of the churches, from the Acts of Visitation of 1640, p. 317: “Saint James, without a church; Holy Cross, without a church; Saint Mary of Bassano; Saint Blaise: there is a church there and Mass is celebrated there.”] villeins, mills, and holdings of lands and vineyards; at Saint Vitus, the monastery of Saint Angel [Note: [Col. 1446C] This same monastery of Saint Angel is mentioned by the bull of Paschal II and listed among the churches of the abbey of Saint Martin of Fara. It is now made subject to the abbey of Majella, and with better reason, since by the donation of Gerard, son of Transbert, in 1064 it ought to be assigned to the latter abbey. To reconcile the disagreement, we propose that one and the same monastery [Col. 1446B] could have been burdened with a double obligation, separately owed to two abbeys.] with its cells, villeins, mills, lands, and vineyards; at Pollutrum, the monastery of Saint Barbatus with cells, villeins, lands, and vineyards; at Gypsum of Domo, the church of Saint Mary with villeins, lands, and vineyards; and the church of Saint Mary of Calderar [Note: [Col. 1446D] Of the two churches placed by Eugenius III at Gypsum, the former is the parish church and provostship in the castle of Gypsum, called Saint Mary Major or Great. The latter church, Saint Mary of Calderariis, is situated in the territory of the same castle. Consult the codex of the Visitation marked D, fols. 144 and 195, and also the Acts of another Visitation in 1598, fol. 14.] with its cells; at Mount Morisco, the church of Saint Helena [Note: [Col. 1446D] Not far from the castle of Gypsum, which must be situated in Abruzzo Citeriore, there once existed, according to Corradi’s description in the repeatedly cited volume, fol. 149, the church of Saint Helena, which Eugenius places at Mount Morisco. It once existed, I say, since even in the time of the visitor Corradi it lay buried in ruins. Thus the church which the abbey of Majella had recognized as its own from 1144, by the gift of Marsilius, son of Robert, finally perished miserably.]; [Col. 1447A] at Gypsum, the church of Saint Julian [Note: [Col. 1447B] Here the surviving constitutions of the supreme pontiffs Adrian III and Alexander III differ from Eugenius’s bull: where Eugenius names the church of Saint Julian [Col. 1447C] at Gypsum, the others list the church of Saint Juliana at Atessa. The disagreement is easily reconciled if we distinguish the places and churches. Corradi, in the cited codex, fol. 149, mentions the church of Saint Julian outside the castle of Gypsum, in the place called *le colle di S. Juliano*, and states that the church of Saint Julian was destroyed. Another list of churches drawn up in 1489 agrees. But we shall show in the notes to the bull of Adrian IV, to be appended below, that the church of Saint Juliana is to be located at the town of Atessa. The difficulty is therefore resolved if we separate the different subject-matter of the bulls.]; at Casule, the estate called Colle Milone [Note: [Col. 1447C] From the inventory attached to the codex of the Visitation of 1604, fol. 139 and following, we have drawn the following concerning the fief of Colle Milone; it is useful to transcribe it in order to obtain a precise knowledge of the place: “Likewise, the said abbey holds and possesses in the territory of Casoli, in the place called Colle Milone, a fief where in ancient times there was a castle inhabited by citizens, called Colle Milone, in which the said abbey of Majella held civil and criminal jurisdiction. The said fief has been destroyed [Col. 1447D] and ruined by the men of Casoli.”], with its appurtenances; one hospital at Palazzano [Note: [Col. 1447D] This bull seems to us to indicate churches and hospital houses established in the territory of the city of Lanciano. Corradi affirms in the aforementioned codex, fol. 19, that Plazanum, named by Eugenius, is a part of that territory: in the margin of the page on which churches subject to the abbey of Majella are listed from a bull of Innocent III, he writes: “Plazanum near Septe in the territory of Lanciano.”]; at Septe another hospital and the church of Saint Pastor [Note: [Col. 1447D] From Corradi’s quoted words it is clear that the plain of Septe is to be placed in the district of Lanciano. It borders the territory of the River Sangro and once had the church of Saint Pastor together with the Hospital mentioned in the bull. Once, I say; for we read in the Acts of Visitation of 1598, fol. 38, that the chapel had already collapsed and its title had been transferred to the cathedral of Lanciano.]; at Lanzanum, one hospital [Note: [Col. 1447D] This hospital house lies closer to Lanciano, since it is situated outside the walls of Lanciano, at Arundinis, or in the city’s vineyards, in an inventory of our archive entitled “Index of Collations of the Churches Subject to the Basilica outside the City,” fol. 94. In the two codices of Visitation—the one of Corradi, fol. 152, the other of Binalducci, fol. 37—the church of Saint James is said to be connected with this house.]; at Rocca Morice, the church of Saint Mary and the church of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1448C] Corradi’s cited codex, fol. 135, mentions the churches of Saint Mary of Cerreto and Saint Nicholas in the territory of Rocca Morice, diocese of Chieti. But it lists no hospital house, and there is likewise no mention of one in the enactments of subsequent pontiffs. It may therefore be suspected that the house was either destroyed or transferred elsewhere. By the gift of Count Robert of Monopoli, both churches were already listed among the members of the abbey of Majella in 1122.]; at Ursonia, the church of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 1448C] The church of Saint Martin in the territory of Ursonia, commonly Orsogna, diocese of Chieti, was given in 1074 by Adeodatus, son of Peter, and Adam, son of Aeso. It is a familiar church, often mentioned both in the Acts of Visitation and in inventories of churches. According to Corradi’s testimony, fol. 148, this church became a simple benefice subject to the Vatican chapter.]; at Ilex, the church of Saint Angel [Note: [Col. 1448D] We note from Corradi’s codex, fol. 125, the following concerning the castle of Ilex in the diocese of Penne and the church of Saint Angel: “The church of Saint Angel of Jelice, which has the care of souls . . . is distant from the castle of la Jelice, and from the city of Penne by about two miles.” The castle of Ilex is subject to the abbey of Saint John in Venere.] with its cells, villeins, lands, and vineyards; on the bank of Corvara, the church of Saint Victorinus [Note: [Col. 1448D] Ripa Corvaria, today the castle of Corvajo, belongs to the county of Alba and Tagliacozzo in the Marsian region. Corradi, fol. 241, thus describes the distinguished church of Saint Victorinus named here: “The church of Saint Victorinus, in lands and vineyards, is immediately subject to the abbey of Saint Savior of Majella, as in the privilege of Pope Eugenius; that church is in the fief called Ripa Corvara, near the territory of Casale, diocese of Chieti.”] with lands and vineyards.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all [Col. 1447B] things be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. As a sign, moreover, of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to us and our successors one gold piece yearly. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make amends for such presumption by suitable satisfaction [Col. 1448A], let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, recognize himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to strict vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of that same hermitage, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. [Col. 1448B] I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cyriacus [Note: [Col. 1448D] The church of Saint Cyriacus at the Baths, once standing at the Baths of Diocletian and called Saint Cyriacus in Thermis, long ago fell into ruin. Pope Sixtus IV, according to Pauvinio, transferred its ancient title to the church of Saints Quiricus and Julitta.] have subscribed. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, [Guido], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pastor, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, (Gregory), cardinal deacon of Saint Angel, have subscribed. I, Astald, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. [Col. 1449A] I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Cosmas (read: Saint Mary in Cosmedin), have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1449D] Although the bull gives the year 1150, we calculate it as 1151 and have placed that year at the beginning of the bull. The discrepancy is easily reconciled if we observe the different dates from which the beginning of the year was reckoned. Some begin the year on 25 March, others on the Kalends of January. Both methods of reckoning are observed in bulls. We begin the year with January; hence we date to 1151 Eugenius’s bull [Col. 1450D] written on 24 January, as required by the years of Eugenius’s pontificate and by the indiction. We shall observe this continually in determining the chronology of the following bulls. It is enough to have given this warning once in advance, lest we uselessly repeat it later whenever the same chronological conflict occurs.], in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CDXXII. To the Archbishop of Sens.—That he should judge the controversy between the bishop of Orléans and the abbot of Vézelay. (26 January 1151.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 660.]

We have received the complaint of our beloved sons Pontius, abbot, and the brothers of the monastery of Vézelay against our venerable brother Manasses, bishop of Orléans [Col. 1449B]: namely, that he is unjustly taking from them and holding by force the church of Saint Machutus, which his predecessor gave them and confirmed by the authority of his written instrument. Since we have great confidence in the prudence of your discretion, we command your brotherhood by these present letters that, after summoning both parties before you at a suitable place and time, you diligently hear and investigate the case and settle it by the mediation of justice.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

CDXXIII. To M. [Manasses], bishop of Orléans.—On the same matter. (26 January 1151.)

[Ibid., 661.]

[Col. 1449C]

From the complaint of our beloved sons Pontius, abbot, and the brothers of the monastery of Vézelay, we have recently learned that you have unjustly taken from them and hold by force the church of Saint Machutus, which your predecessor He. gave them and confirmed by the authority of his written instrument. Since that monastery belongs to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter, and we can and ought not to fail it in its justice: we command you by these present letters that, if their complaint rests upon the truth, you either restore the church itself peacefully to the aforesaid abbot and his brothers, or render justice concerning it in the presence of our venerable brother Hu., archbishop of Sens.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

CDXXIV. Bull for the bishops of Orléans. (10 February 1151.)

[Gall. Chr. nov., VIII, *Instr.*, 510.]

[Col. 1449D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MANASSES, bishop of Orléans, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Whenever we are asked for something that seems consonant with reason and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind [Col. 1450A] and provide suitable support for the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by the authority of the apostolic see, and decree to remain valid in perpetuity, every liberty or immunity granted to you and your successors by our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, and strengthened by the protection of his written instrument: namely, that after the death of you or your successors, royal officials shall by no means take any iron or timber in the episcopal residences. When the bishopric of Orléans is vacant, they shall impose upon the land of that bishopric no exaction or *tallia* [levy], except those due at established times. That levy must not exceed [Col. 1450B] sixty pounds of that currency.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have considered it proper expressly to name: the abbey of Saint Maximin; the abbey of Saint Evurtius; the abbey of Balgentiacum; the church of Saint Lifard of Meung; the church of Saint Veranus of Gargonville; the church of Saint George of Pithiviers; the church of Saint Peter of the men; the church of Saint Peter of the women; the church of Saint Avitus; the church of Saint [Col. 1450C] Peter of Meung; the church of Craventium; the church of Ingrana; the castle of Pithiviers; the castle of Meung; the castle of Gargonville; Ingrana with its appurtenances; the estate of Strepetum with its appurtenances; Marolium with its appurtenances; Old Pithiviers with its appurtenances; the tithe of Craventium with its court; the land of the bishop of Orléans called Martirevim; the toll of Orléans; the church of Sully; the church of Rive Morentin; the church of La Ferté-Ebrouin; the church of Corneliacum; and the estate called Bullum.
