We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any disturbances; but that all [Col. 1450D] things be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make amends for such presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor [Col. 1451A], recognize himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to strict vengeance. But for all who preserve the just rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of Saint [Col. 1451B] Cyriacus. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Wido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pastor. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel. I, Astald, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. [Col. 1451C] I, Jacintus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

CDXXV. To Pontius, abbot of Vézelay.—Concerning his controversy with the bishop of Autun. (February 1151.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 657.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1451D] son PONTIUS, abbot of Vézelay, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Autun, having come into our presence, lodged before us and our brethren a complaint against you, in the presence also of your fellow monk whom you had sent to us: namely, that you are endeavoring unjustly to take from his Church certain things which it had peacefully held in your monastery until this time, and that you answered orally that you would do this entirely on his account. Since it especially belongs to our office to remove the scandals of brethren from the midst and preserve to each person his right, we command you by these present letters that on the next octave of Saint Martin, unless in the meantime you come to an agreement with that same brother of ours, you come into our presence, either in person or through sufficient representatives, with the evidentiary documents of your monastery, especially with the instrument of its founder, prepared to answer concerning these matters. Likewise, we command your diligence that, in the presence of our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, you render justice concerning those things which you and your men unjustly hold from him, having taken them from his men; for we have similarly ordered that same brother of ours, the bishop of Autun, to render justice in that same presence concerning those things which his men have taken from your men. In the meantime, we do not wish any molestation to be inflicted upon him in respect of what he possesses.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March.

CDXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Trinity and Saint Michael at Mileto. (24 February 1151.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 952.]

[Col. 1452B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, abbot of the monastery of Mileto, built in honor of the Holy Trinity and of blessed Michael the archangel, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

With all ecclesiastical persons we stand in the relation of debtors by reason of the office of the apostolate laid upon us by God; yet toward those places and persons which are known to have a more particular relation to the Apostolic See and to pertain to the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff, it is fitting that we should apply ourselves with a more earnest zeal of charity and graciously assent to their just desires. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, more kindly granting assent to your reasonable petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery, which was founded from its very foundations by Count Roger of illustrious memory and which, through the hand of Pope Urban II, our predecessor of happy memory, is known to have been offered in perpetuity to Blessed Peter and his Holy Roman Church, in right and guardianship; following the examples of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Paschal and Innocent of holy memory. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God being favorable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: in the territory of Mileto, the village of Saint Gregory, and there the church of Saint Nicholas; the church of Saint Gregory of Briatico; Saint John of Rayachio; Saint Mary of Medina; Saint Mary and Saint Clement of Arena; Saint Mary of Stilo; and Saint John and Saint Nicholas of Gerentia.

In the city of Giratio, three churches; the monastery of Saint Nicodemus of Patera; the church of Saint Nicholas of Falla with its appurtenances; the church of Mary of Demontorium with its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Peter near Bibona, [Col. 1453A] which Romeus held. Near Castellum Vetus, the church of Saint Nicholas of Caconit, the church of Saint John, and Saint Mary of Melicano. In the city of Squillace, the church of Saint Martin and Saint Nicholas of Prato. In the dependency of Agnelli, the church of Saint Philip, Saint Mary of Ponticella, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Hippolytus. In the territory of Alunantia, the church of Saint Angel of Stricto, Saint Barbara, and Saint Pessi. In the territory of the Cold River, the church of Saint Nicholas of Turiano; the church of Saint Philip near Monte Alto; the church of Saint Cassian; Saint Nicholas of Mave of Trabea; and, near the Black Pool, the church of Saint George and Saint Nicholas of Regina. In Sicily, the church of Saint John; Saint George of Mohac; Saint John of Calatiniseth; Saint Barbara of Calatebutor; Saint Nicholas of Caca; Saint John of Rocca [Col. 1453B] Maris; Saints Cosmas and Damian of Chetaludio with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Anastasia of Grateriis; Saints Innocents of Mistreto; Saint Stephen; Saint Basil of Naso; Saint Nicholas of Brutana; Saint Angel; Saint George; Saint Mary of Murra [lacuna]; and Saint Pessi of Melasio; and a portion of the town called Mestianum, which is known to have been offered by the aforesaid count to the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Trinity and Saint Angel. May the soul of Count Roger rest in peace.

Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be altogether free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict.

We prohibit Masses or public stations from being held in that place without the consent of the abbot and brethren, [Col. 1453C] lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of God’s servants. Furthermore, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you for the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks or clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. We further add that no bishop may, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, subject your house, or the monks or clerics dwelling there, to interdict or excommunication, or exercise any authority or molestation over them.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, [Col. 1453D] or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of usurpation or violence, save the person whom the brethren by unanimous consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the pontiff of the Apostolic See. We also add by the present clause that the same monastery, its possessions, and its monks shall be secure from every harassment of secular service; and, removed from every burden of worldly oppression, shall remain diligent and undisturbed in the observance of holy religion, nor be held subject on any ground to anyone other than the Roman and Apostolic See, to whose jurisdiction they belong.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its [Col. 1454A] possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to us and our successors one ounce of gold each year. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning does not correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 1454B] body and blood of God and of our Lord Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that same Church, may there rest the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis, have subscribed.  
I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of Saint Cyriacus, have subscribed.  
I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, [Col. 1454C] have subscribed.  
I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel, have subscribed.  
I, Astaldus, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius, have subscribed.  
I, Jacynthus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III. [Col. 1454D]

### CDXXVII. To Louis, King of the French.—Concerning the Church of Beauvais. (1151, 25 February)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 630.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the French: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although the diligence of a Catholic king honors and loves with due devotion all the Churches within his power, yet he embraces with greater love, reverences, and more willingly and promptly gives suitable assistance to those in which he sees his own flesh and nearer blood established in the office of prelate. For this twofold reason, therefore, your Highness ought to love the Church of Beauvais with a more affectionate concern: both because it is known to have been endowed and adorned by the lavish gifts of your predecessors, and because our venerable brother Henry, your brother by blood, exercises there the pastoral office.

Since, therefore, your said brother found that Church, upon entering office, greatly worn down and oppressed by the neighboring knights, he prudently refused those knights, on our advice, certain benefices which his predecessors had unlawfully granted them, and retained them for the use of his Church. On this account, as we have heard, those knights have been provoked and threaten to harass and persecute the said Church of Beauvais. Since you are bound both by the duty of government entrusted to you and by the obligation of fraternal affection sincerely to love and defend the aforesaid Church from the attacks of wicked men, we stir up, advise, and exhort the steadfastness of your nobility by this letter in the Lord: if any of these knights, on that account, should seize the goods of that Church or presume in any way to harass it, punish him temporally according to the power bestowed on you by God. For we have instructed our venerable brethren, the neighboring bishops, that if the aforesaid Church should happen to be harassed on this pretext by any one of those knights, they are to subject the offender to excommunication. Moreover, we admonish your vigor by apostolic letters, and impose it upon you for the remission of your sins, to endeavor, as a Catholic prince and lover of God’s Church, to restore to that Church the goods and possessions unlawfully alienated from it in the absence and without the counsel of the bishops of that place.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

### CDXXVIII. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—Likewise concerning the same matter. (1151, February)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, 631.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the letters and messenger of your brotherhood with due kindness, and we thank you for your visit. It is pleasing to us that, solicitous for the benefit of the Church committed to you, you willingly attend to its advantage and diligently seek its advancement. Yet it grieves us that the Church of Beauvais, through the weakness of your predecessors, has been burdened with certain revenues and compelled to pay annual benefices from the bishop’s treasury. But since royal power is sufficient to defend that Church in this affair, we do not wish it to be subjected, under the pretext of defense, to the power of others, or its goods delivered over to the plundering of many. For it is unworthy that royal power should permit you, undefended, to remain subject to lay domination and, what is unbecoming to royal offspring, to serve their demands.

Accordingly, we command our dearest son, the king your brother, to restrain by royal authority from such exaction those who seek to burden you with revenues of this sort. By the present letters we command you not henceforth to grant the aforesaid benefices, which your predecessors were forced by their weakness to pay annually; rather, according to the prudence given you by God, expend the goods of the Church entrusted to you for its benefit, [Col. 1456B] so that through your care that Church may from day to day receive growth pleasing to the Lord. It therefore concerns you, dearest brother, to proceed so prudently and moderately toward its advancement that almighty God may thereby receive the honor due to him and that Church may, with the Lord’s help, prosper through you unto better things. For we shall willingly take care to furnish you with such help and counsel as we know to be expedient.

### CDXXIX. To Hugh, Bishop of Auxerre, and Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.—For reconciling the king with the Bishop of Beauvais. (1151, 25 February)

[Ibid., 633.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of Auxerre, and his dearest son BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe it has escaped your notice with what sincere affection of heart we love our dearest son Louis, king of the French, and his brother, our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Beauvais; and how we desire that their actions may be directed and prospered by the Lord and always advanced from good to better. Thus, as their unanimity brings us joy and gladness, so, if we perceive that any resentment has arisen between them, we grieve with paternal affection, and their resentment or disturbance makes us no little sad.

Perceiving, therefore, that through the intervention of certain occasions their sincere charity and fraternal love have been somewhat disturbed, [Note: [Col. 1455D] This appears to refer to Saint Bernard’s Letter 305, to Pope Eugenius, and to Suger’s letter to Henry, bishop, chapter, and clergy of the Church [Col. 1456D] of Beauvais, published by us in *Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 422.] we are greatly astonished and more deeply grieved. Therefore, that we may uproot from their hearts the material of scandal, since we are quite unable to attend to this ourselves, we desire that your charity, in which we trust as in ourselves, should effectively devote labor and zeal to accomplishing it. Accordingly, we earnestly ask your holinesses to come together without delay into the presence of our aforesaid son Louis, king of the French; [Col. 1457A] and, having summoned to you our said brother Henry, bishop of Beauvais, diligently bring both parties, without commotion, to a stricter conference concerning their disputes. Remove the cause of litigation, and endeavor, with God as author, in our stead to reconcile them to concord and fraternal charity—so that royal dignity may be preserved in the integrity of its condition, episcopal honor may not be injured, and fraternal charity between them may be restored in perpetual love.

Given at Ferentino, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March.

### CDXXX. To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—Likewise concerning the harassment of the Church of Beauvais. (1151, 25 February)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 634.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother [Note: [Col. 1457D] This is that celebrated Hugh who, having been abbot of Reading, became archbishop of Rouen. We published his seven books of *Theological Dialogues* in [Col. 1458D] *Anecdota*, vol. V; and our Acherius published three books against heresies.] HUGH, archbishop of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Beauvais, coming into our presence, disclosed to us, when we carefully questioned him concerning the condition of his Church, that among the other burdens by which it is troubled he had found certain money-benefices—more properly called malefices—granted by the unlawful largesse of his predecessors to many knights and barons, without benefit to that Church. Having taken counsel with prudent men and with us, he refused these benefices to the knights and retained them for the use of his Church. On this account, as we have heard, the knights have been greatly provoked against [Col. 1457C] our aforesaid brother and threaten to harass and persecute the said Church of Beauvais.

Since, therefore, by the office of the apostolate committed to us by God, we must provide for the peace and tranquility of all Churches, we command you by the present letters: if any of the aforesaid knights dwelling in your diocese should on this account presume to harm or harass the aforementioned Church, take care to warn him strictly to cease altogether from molesting that Church and leave it in peace. But if, after your second or third admonition, he disdain to cease from his presumption, pronounce against him, as contumacious and rebellious, a sentence of excommunication and, in his land, of interdict; and cause that sentence to be firmly observed throughout your diocese until he renders worthy satisfaction for the offense committed.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

### CDXXXI. To G., Rector, and the People of Bologna.—That they should defend the inhabitants of Saint Cassian and Bishop R[udolph] of Imola against the wrongs of the people of Imola. (1151, 3 March)

[SAVIOLI, *Annals of Bologna*, Appendix, I, II, 224.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., rector, and the people of Bologna: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Many persons of diverse nations who have customarily dwelt among you have come more fully to recognize, by manifest experience, the ancient and lawful steadfastness of your predecessors; and the glorious fame of their name has been proclaimed through diverse regions of the world and spread far and wide. Therefore, if you wish to possess and retain their glory, you must firmly imitate their footsteps and, in paternal fashion, maintain perseverance in courage toward those who commit themselves to your defense until they attain the desired end. For virtue lies not in beginning good work, but in bringing it to completion.

The calamity of the men of Saint Cassian, who after God have placed their confidence in you, shows how they have been scattered and how grievously afflicted; and your discernment recognizes it. Although some of those of Saint Cassian may perhaps have joined with the people of Imola, being hard pressed by troubles or deceived by the malice of others, nevertheless, if you desist from your purpose of aiding the rest, who have always trusted in your protection, because you are weary, you will certainly lose your glory, and your labor will prove wholly useless. Therefore, that your exertions and toils may, with the Lord as author, attain a happy end, and that the malice and iniquity of the aforesaid people of Imola may be checked, we command you by these present letters to endeavor to raise up those who have fallen and gather together those who have been scattered. Apply yourselves with diligent effort, setting delay aside, so that the place may be restored and people gathered there; [Col. 1458C] and gird yourselves usefully against those sacrilegious persons as valiant warriors. Also render effective help and counsel to our venerable brother R., bishop, both in the defense of Bagnara and in the defense of the other places which still remain to him and the counts, so that you may obtain the blessing of almighty God and always be found worthier of the favor of Blessed Peter and of ourselves.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Nones of March.

### CDXXXII. Privilege for the Church of Beauvais. (1151, 7 March)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, X, Instrumenta, 259.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity, etc.

Venerable brother Henry, bishop, we graciously grant your just petitions and receive the Church of Blessed Peter at Beauvais, over which by God’s appointment you are known to preside, under the protection of that prince of the apostles and of ourselves; decreeing, etc., that they shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the abbey of Saint Symphorian, Saint Lucian, Saint Quentin, Saint Geremarus of Flay, Saint Mary of Breteuil, Saint Martin of Ruricourt, Saint Paul, the church of Saint Bartholomew, Saint Michael, Saint Lawrence, Saint Mary, and the church of Monthatere with all its appurtenances; moreover, the city, county, toll, forage-dues, and provostship of that city; likewise the cultivated land and mills, and the land of Maresco with the adjacent wood, its judicial rights, and its appurtenances; Hosdingum with all its dependencies; Lavercinum, Castanetum, Buriacum, Serronem, Saint-Just Bertacurt, and Congel with all their appurtenances.

Whatever liberty, immunity, or right of possession has further been granted to that Church by the pious devotion and reasonable foresight of the illustrious kings of the French or other princes, we likewise confirm to you and your successors. We decree that whatever has hitherto been unlawfully alienated from its property by the deceased bishop or by others shall entirely lack force and be revoked as void. We also prohibit anyone from presuming to hold, by hereditary right, the bishop’s table or the custody of the granary and cellar. Therefore we decree, etc.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Praxedis.  
I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Cyriacus.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Anastasia, etc.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman [Col. 1459C] Church, on the Nones of March, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDXXXIII. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—He replies to Henry’s letter asking to be released from the burden of episcopal rank, a request which neither Eugenius nor Adrian IV, who succeeded him after Anastasius IV, wished to grant. (1151, 8 March)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 635.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

So that you may receive privately our answer concerning what you first asked us after your departure, we have written with our own hand the letter which you read. Let, therefore, the sincere affection of your brotherhood know that neither in our chamber, when you received leave from us, nor at any other place or time when you spoke to us about that singular and secret petition of yours, did we grant you assent. Therefore harbor no scruple in your heart concerning our replies in this matter; but, setting that intention aside for the present, hasten your return to the Church committed to you by God, and labor diligently, prudently, and manfully for the gain of the souls of clergy and people, whose care, with the Lord’s favor, you once undertook. Fare well always in the Lord, dearest brother.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Ides of March.

### CDXXXIV. To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—Concerning Hugh of Gournay. (1151, 10 March)

[Ibid.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The report of our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Beauvais, has informed us that Hugh of Gournay, your parishioner, having received from a certain citizen of Bourges named Erqueric seventy-two pounds of Beauvais currency and two marks of silver, upon an oath given by him, refuses in bad faith to repay it. Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by this present writing, [Col. 1460B] if his statements in this matter are founded upon truth, to warn the aforesaid Hugh strictly that he restore that money to the aforesaid Gornaco without objection [an apparent inconsistency in the text]. But if he neglect to obey your admonition, restrain him with ecclesiastical severity in such fashion that no complaint need be brought to our ears because justice has failed.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

### CDXXXV. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—He refuses permission to lay down the episcopal office. (1151, 11 March)

[Ibid., 636.]

EUGENIUS, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1460C] blessing.

If every time that we speak or write to your brotherhood you develop a scruple, then either you must cease to doubt or we must cease speaking or writing. Therefore let your charity have the certain assurance, without doubt, that we by no means grant at present the release from the episcopate which you seek. Fare well in Christ, dearest brother; and that you may happily complete the return you have begun, we earnestly pray the Lord.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

### CDXXXVI. Privilege for the Monastery of Michaelstein. (1151, 11 March)

[LEUCKFELD, *Antiquities of Michaelstein*, 87.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROGER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael of the Rock, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Since without the true worship of religion neither the unity of charity can endure nor service pleasing to God be offered, we ought to devote ourselves with more earnest compassion to religious men and, lest they be disturbed in the observance of their order by anyone’s presumptions, defend their goods and places by the protection of our safeguard; so that they may cleave more securely to the purpose of holiness which they have chosen, in proportion as we have more vigilantly taken care to remove from them every undue burden. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we decree that the monastic order which, in the fear of God and according to the order of the Cistercian brethren, is known to have been established in that place, God being its author, through the care and direction of our beloved daughter Beatrice, abbess of the church of Saint Servatius at Quedlinburg, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same Church justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God being favorable, through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the place in which the abbey itself is situated, with its dependencies; the grange called Ervinkcrote, with its dependencies; the grange called Northolt, with its newly cleared lands and dependencies; the grange called Halsingen, with its dependencies; and the grange called Hevergodesroth, with its dependencies.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to exact from you any tithes from the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. Upon the death of you, beloved son Roger, abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any deceitful usurpation [Col. 1461C] or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common counsel, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine to elect in the fear of God and according to the order of the Cistercian brethren.

We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with vexations; but all things are to be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the canonical right of the Church of Quedlinburg. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum.  
I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano.  
I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis.  
I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement.  
I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.  
I, Wido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico.  
I, Jocundus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of March, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDXXXVII. Bull for Guarin, Abbot of Saint John in the Valley (Chartres). (1151, 17 March)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VIII, Instrumenta, 332, from the domestic cartulary of M. de Gagnières, in the Royal Library.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUARIN, abbot of the church of Blessed John of the Valley, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, in perpetuity.

Whenever this, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., we receive the aforesaid church under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing; decreeing that whatever possessions or goods, etc., shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: in the church of Blessed Mary of Chartres, the entire revenues for a full year of the prebend of every brother from the body of canons of that church, whenever he leaves it for any reason, so that, however the person may be changed, the prebendal benefice shall pass with all its integrity to the use of your church. The entire prebend which your church possesses in perpetuity in the church of Blessed Mary, which Abbot Albert of good memory held when he embraced the canonical rule; the church of Saint Stephen with its appurtenances, namely the altar of Morenciacum with the share of the synod dues pertaining to that altar; the church of Mondonisvilla with its appurtenances, free from every exaction, synod due, and *circada*; the church of Saint Faith with parochial right over the new borough called Castelleth; the church of Luciacum; and the portion of the fields from that land which Ivo, bishop of Chartres of good memory, had formerly possessed; the land of Osanivilla, both episcopal and canonical, with its offerings; the land of Ancherisvilla; in the village of Pontegodani, the priory of that village’s church with all episcopal houses, the whole fodder-rent in oats, all the bishop’s land which you possess beyond the river Audura, the square given to you by our venerable brother Goslenus, bishop of Chartres, the gift to your church of the altar of the church of Serneium by Goslenus, canon and provost of the church of Saint Mary, the gift to you from Hugh, viscount of Chartres, of the advocacy of the Valley and of all the land of Moncelli with all its customary dues; [Col. 1463A] all the land of Eddevilla with its customary dues and fiefs; the church of Ardelecth with all its tenants and land for two ploughlands; the church of Saint Nicholas of Curvavilla together with the church of Saint Peter of the same village; the church of Saint Dionysius of Putei; Saint Mary of Gohosvilla with its appurtenances; the church of Trembleium with tithes; the church of Blessed Mary of Teliu with tithes; the church of Braiosum with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saturninus of Camburciacum with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Loiniacum, with pannage for your pigs; the village of Armentarvilla with the tithe, which you received on lease from the church of Saint Benedict for three measures of wheat and four of oats, payable to it each year; the village of Arbereth and the village of Nerle; the land of Curvaulmus; and all other lands which you possess at Chartres; the church of Garneium with land for one ploughland, granted to your church by Nivardus of Nonancurte for the redemption of his soul; the church of Orrevilla with the tithe, given to you by Hugh, son of Guinemar, through the hand of the aforesaid Ivo, bishop of Chartres; in the place called Guoriart, one half with the meadows beside the river Audura; near Saint Priscus, a mill; the meadows which you possess at Ataias from the benefice of Blessed Mary; and the land which you hold by right of ownership near the village of Soors. Moreover, the rents of houses, lands, and vineyards, and the tithes of rye and vineyards, which belong to your right both in the city of Chartres and in its suburb.

Upon the death of you, beloved son Guarin, [Col. 1463C] abbot, no one shall be set over the house through any usurpation, craft, or violence, except the person whom the brethren shall determine to elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine. The person elected, however, shall be presented to the common chapter of Blessed Mary in order to receive the abbey and the grace of blessing from the bishop of Chartres; and he shall perform his week of service in the church of Blessed Mary, as do the other canons. Therefore we decree, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDXXXVIII. Bull for Theobald, Abbot of Saint-Cheron. (1151, 20 March)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VIII, Instrumenta, 334.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEOBALD, abbot of Saint-Cheron, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, in perpetuity.

For without observance of sacred religion neither do the members of the ecclesiastical body remain united in charity, nor is service pleasing to God rendered. It therefore becomes us to employ every diligence in founding religious houses and preserving those already founded, and to fortify them by the privilege of apostolic authority, lest they be shaken by the rash assault of wicked persons. [Col. 1464A] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the safeguard of this present writing. First, we establish that the canonical order which, by God’s agency, is known to have been instituted in that place according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, through the care and foresight of our venerable brother Goslen, bishop of Chartres, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just [Col. 1464B] means, God granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: the entire revenues of the prebends and of the provostship which the secular canons in your church are known to have held justly in the times of our aforesaid brother Goslen and of his predecessor, Gaufrid, bishop of Chartres, of blessed memory, and which that same brother Goslen has, by reasonable provision, assigned to your uses and needs; and the church of Dordan with its appurtenances.

Upon the death of you, beloved son in the Lord Theobald, now abbot of the same place, or of any one of your successors, let no one be placed over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, [Col. 1464C] except one whom the brothers, by common counsel, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall have provided to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine. The person elected, moreover, shall be presented to the bishop of Chartres, from whom he shall receive the abbacy and the grace of blessing.

We add also that, because, being as it were newly planted in religion, you have every need of the support of your elders, you shall have recourse with due devotion to the counsel and assistance of the bishop of Chartres in matters that may arise for you; and, humbly seeking in necessities his aid as your father and founder, you ought not, without his knowledge and counsel, in any manner to exchange, sell, or alienate the possessions of the Church.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever, etc.

[Col. 1464D] I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. (Several cardinals follow.)

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1150 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXXXIX. Confirmation of the privileges granted by Pope Innocent II to the monastery of Rott of the Order of Saint Benedict. (1151, March 30.)

[HUND, *Metropol. Salisb.*, III, 268.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LOTHAR, abbot of the monastery of Rott, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1465A] Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and give appropriate support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery of Rott, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the safeguard of this present writing. First, we establish that the monastic order which, by God’s agency, is known to have been instituted in that place according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods [Col. 1465B] that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: the place called Rott, where the abbey itself is situated, with its churches, tithes, boundaries, and other appurtenances; in the parish of Clemeringen, thirty holdings (*mansi*) with a share in the church of Saint Pancras, its tithes and appurtenances; Beusteten, Putingen, Aske, Miuvarn, with the church of that place, tithes, and appurtenances; Volchmaristorff, with vineyards and vintners’ fields; at Erigelteshusen, the church of that [Col. 1465C] place, tithes, and appurtenances; the estate called Rott, adjoining the river Glane, with the church of Saint George, tithes, and appurtenances; Harde Brumciuntal; a holding at Truhtheringen, Helpfendorf, Tontinhuscen, Warte, Veristeten, Wachreine, Durholz, Walse, Cholental; all of Bileresse, with the church of that place, tithes, and appurtenances; at Luichental, Stegen, Wisinchswanch, Criessonnowe, Gromsowe, and Barne; and whatever Cono the count palatine, of illustrious memory, founder of your church, had justly held from Strichen to Jagperch, and had granted you in pious devotion—except for one dwelling at Wisinchwanch; at Halle, a salt-pan and the site of the salt-pan; on the mountain called Ritino, one holding; at Bozen, a court (*curia*) [Col. 1465D] and vineyards; at Hartperch, six vineyards and fields; at Choftingen and Ratispona, a court near Saint Cassian, with the surrounding yard and buildings.

Furthermore, from the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals, let no one presume to exact tithes from you. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, while preserving nevertheless the rights of the mother church. Moreover, let no one presume to invade or usurp the advocacy (*advocatia*) of your house, except one whom the abbot and brothers shall choose according to the advantage of the Lord and of the monastery itself. Upon the death of you, now abbot of the same place, or of any one of your successors, let no one be placed over it by any [Col. 1466A] deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brothers, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall have foreseen to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishops. As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay yearly to us and our successors one gold Byzantine. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. [Col. 1466C] I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Otto, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Octavian, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Cencius, deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXL. Bull for the monastery of Saint Quiricus of Rosis. (1151, March 30.)

[MITARELLI, *Ann. Camald.*, III, p. 454.]

[Col. 1466D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANTONY, prior of the monastery of Saint Quiricus of Rosis, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the monastic life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and give appropriate support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and [Col. 1467A] of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Quiricus, to which you are devoted in divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire by reasonable means, God granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: namely, the church of Saint George in the castle of Fracta Guinildi, and that castle itself with the court of the same castle; whatever you possess in the court of Fojano; whatever your monastery possesses in the court of Marciano; whatever it possesses in the court of Liciguano; whatever you possess in the court of Puteo; whatever you possess in the court of Fracta Rainucci; whatever you possess in the court of Cese; whatever you possess in the court of [Col. 1467B] Donna; whatever in the court of Fracta de Paterno; whatever you possess in the village of Albula; whatever you possess in Broilo and in the court of Ficareto; whatever you possess in the village of Saint Lucy.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If anyone, therefore, etc. Amen.

“Make for me, O Lord, a sign for good.”

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. [Col. 1467C] I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title . . . [lacuna] have subscribed. I, Ubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Ubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Roland, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Otto, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and [Col. 1467D] Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Marianus, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXLI. He confirms to Robert, archbishop of Acerenza, the metropolitan rights and grants him the pallium. (1151, April 1.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 32.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROBERT, archbishop of Acerenza, and his successors canonically instituted: in perpetuity.

Placed, by the Lord’s disposition, upon the watchtower of the eminent Apostolic See, [Col. 1468A] we ought to love our brother bishops, both near at hand and far away, and to preserve for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their proper rights. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ Robert, archbishop, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Paschal of happy memory, fortify the holy Church of Acerenza by the authority of this decree. We confirm to you and your successors whatever is known to have belonged to it in past times by metropolitan right: namely, Venosa, Gravina, Tricarico, Tursi, and Potenza, so that you and your lawful successors may have the power to ordain and consecrate bishops in them canonically and in accordance with the decretals, without prejudice in all things to the authority [Col. 1468B] of the holy Roman Church.

Further, we establish and decree that whatever towns, villages, or parish churches are possessed by right by that same Church of Acerenza, and whatever goods it now justly possesses or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors—excepting, of course, those things fortified by special privileges of the Apostolic See.

Moreover, from the generosity of the Apostolic See we grant to your brotherhood the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to know that it may be worn only within the church, at the solemnities of Mass, on the following days: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Hypapante [Presentation], the three solemnities of Blessed [Col. 1468C] Mary, the Lord’s Supper, Holy Saturday, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the feasts of all the Apostles, of Michael the Archangel, the Commemoration of All Saints, and also those martyrs or confessors who rest in the Church of Acerenza; and at the consecration of churches, bishops, priests, and deacons.

We desire that you claim and maintain the character of this pallium in every respect; for the honor of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your brotherhood hasten to show himself, with all his mind, humble in prosperity and—should adversity ever come—upright with justice; a friend to the good and opposed to the perverse; never accepting anyone’s person against charity; never suppressing the person of one speaking for [Col. 1468D] truth; applying himself to works of mercy according to the capacity of his resources, yet desiring to go even beyond that capacity; compassionate toward the infirm, rejoicing with those who prosper; reckoning another’s losses as his own and exulting at another’s joys as though they were his own; piously severe in correcting vices, soothing the minds of his hearers in fostering virtues; maintaining judgment without anger when angry, yet not abandoning the censure of just severity when calm. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received. If you observe it diligently, you will possess inwardly what you show that you have received outwardly.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, [Col. 1469A] or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, to benefit in every place those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord [Col. 1469B] Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruits of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Martianus, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXLII. He receives under protection the nunnery of Saint Cyriacus at Gernrode and confirms its possessions, imposing upon the sisters an annual payment of one mark of silver. (1151, April 4.)

[BECKMAN, *Hist. von Anhalt*, I, 173.]

CDXLIII. To the abbots of Saint-Pons and Grasse.—That they should observe the decree of Urban II at the Council of Clermont. (1151, April 11.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 678.]

[Col. 1469C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Saint-Pons and Grasse: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of our venerable brother Peter, archbishop of Narbonne, and of the canons of his church, we have learned that, in the churches which you hold in his bishopric, you appoint chaplains without their knowledge, and receive persons excommunicated by them, in life and in death. This is recognized to be both contrary to reason and altogether opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers. Since, therefore, we can neither overlook nor ought to overlook an offense of such presumption, we command you by these present [Col. 1469D] letters that henceforth you receive none of their excommunicated persons; and that, concerning the appointment of priests in your parish churches which are in the same bishopric, you firmly observe the ordinance of our predecessor Pope Urban of holy memory: namely, that you yourselves elect the priests and present them to the aforesaid archbishop, who, if they are suitable, ought to commit to them the care of souls, so that they may answer to him concerning the care of the people, while rendering to you due subjection in temporal matters. Take care, therefore, to endeavor to carry out this command of ours in such a way that a renewed complaint about this matter need not reach our ears.

Given at Ferentino, on the third Ides of April.

CDXLIV. He consoles the nuns of Saint George at Prague concerning the death of Henry, bishop of Olomouc, their greatest benefactor, and gives thanks for the ornaments sent. (1151, April 15.)

[BOCZEK, *Cod. dipl. Morav.*, I, 264; from the original in the imperial-royal court archive at Vienna.]

[Col. 1470A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, B., abbess of Saint George, and her sisters: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The death of our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Moravia, of good memory, your kind patron and benefactor, has greatly saddened our heart. [Col. 1470B] His praiseworthy life, indeed, brought joy to us and timely comfort to you in your necessities. Yet we can receive consolation in this: that, withdrawn from temporal misery, he has been transferred to eternal blessedness. Meanwhile, however, we must give all attention to this, that whatever dust of the flesh may have clung to him may, through the Lord’s mercy, be forgiven, and that he himself may intercede more intimately for us before our Creator. For greater aid and greater consolation are now to be hoped from him than when he dwelt with us in bodily presence.

For our part, we cannot and ought not to be unmindful of his soul during the solemnities of Mass. For not only was he devoted to the Apostolic See and to us while he lived, so that he visited us with his gifts, but, when at the point of death, he offered to us with pious devotion and ordered to be brought to us those suitable ornaments which he had diligently caused to be made for the service of the altar by your skilled and expert hands. [Col. 1470C] Receiving these with due kindness, we pray the divine majesty more earnestly for his soul; and for your labor and work we render you many thanks. We exhort you to persevere more attentively in the purpose of your profession, according to the command and teaching of your aforesaid father, so that, through the merits of blessed Peter and Paul interceding, you may happily attain, by the Lord’s gift, the joys of eternal blessedness.

Given at Ferentino, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May.

CDXLV. He confirms the privileges of the hospital of Saint Blaise. (1151, April 21.)

[FRISI, *Memorie di Monza*, II, 61.]

[Col. 1470D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADAM, master of the hospital situated at Saint Blaise near Monza, and his brothers, both present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

We have been raised, by the Lord’s disposition, to the government of the Apostolic See so that we ought to assent to pious vows and incline our ears to just petitions. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Adam, considering your praiseworthy devotion, we receive with paternal kindness the aforesaid hospital, which, with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1471A] with the assent and counsel of Arnald, John, and the other neighbors of this place, you offer to Blessed Peter and to us under an annual payment of six denarii in old Milanese coin, to be paid to us and our successors. We establish that whatever possessions and goods the same hospital now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire by reasonable means, God favoring, shall remain secure and unimpaired for the hospital and its poor.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Ferentino, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

CDXLVI. He confirms the goods and privileges of the nunnery of Saint Peter Major at Florence. (1151, April 25.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 94.]

[Col. 1471C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ MAGDALENE, abbess of the monastery of Saint Peter Major, situated in the suburb of the city of Florence, and her sisters, both present and future, to be regularly instituted: in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, etc.

Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: the church of Saint Felix, situated near the Ema, and all the possessions which the noblewoman Gisla bestowed upon your monastery with prudent judgment and from a motive of devotion. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1471D] rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the canonical right of the bishop of Florence. If, therefore, in the future, etc.; but upon all, etc. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Ugo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, G.G., priest-cardinal of Saint Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Ubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title . . . have subscribed. I, Arisbertus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Julius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. [Col. 1472A] I, Ubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Octavian, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Roland, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Gerard, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, have subscribed. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Rodulphus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. [Col. 1472B] I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given by the hand of Bologninus, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXLVII. To the archbishop of Tarragona, legate of the Apostolic See.—That he recognize the primacy of Toledo. (1151, May 13.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 677.]

[Col. 1472C]

You yourself do not doubt, from your own subjects as well, how obedience or reverence ought to be rendered to superiors. In this matter it is highly useful and praiseworthy if what the rigor of discipline enjoins is observed, without compulsion, by commendable humility. You know, indeed, that our venerable brother Roderic [corrected: Raymond], archbishop of Toledo, rightly demands that the reverence due to him by right of primacy be shown by your brotherhood; fortified by many evidences, he firmly maintains that your predecessors rendered it to his predecessors. But because you have not yet wished to accede to his demands, he has recently, through his messengers, humbly sought the clemency of the Apostolic See, because, as he asserts, his church suffers injury in this matter, [Col. 1472D] and has with great urgency requested that we do him justice concerning it.

Moreover, as your brotherhood may remember, at Reims we called you to account concerning this case and commanded you not to withhold the obedience due to our aforesaid brother, the archbishop of Toledo, if you knew that your church had been accustomed to obey his church. But you then wished to plead to us your ignorance of this novelty, and promised that, with our permission, you would return to your church resolved to determine the matter. Since our aforesaid brother, the archbishop of Toledo, does not desist from his complaint, and since we, who sit—though unworthy—on the seat of justice, neither can nor ought to deny him his justice, we command you by these present letters [Col. 1473A] either to render to that same brother the obedience due which he requires of you, or, on the next feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, to come in person, or through sufficient representatives, into the presence of the Apostolic See, ready adequately to answer the aforesaid brother, the archbishop of Toledo, concerning this matter by authority or reason.

Given at Ferentino, on the third Ides of May.

CDXLVIII. Privilege for the Church of Imola. (1151, May 18.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, II, 625.]

EUGENIUS, etc., to his venerable brother RUDOLPH, bishop of Imola, and his successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1473B] Placed, by the Lord’s disposition, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are bound by the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God to love our brother bishops and to fortify with pious protection the places committed to their governance. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ Rudolph, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Imola, over which, by God’s agency, you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions and goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God favoring, [Col. 1473C] shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: the abbeys of Saint Mary in Regula, Saint Donatus, Saint Mary in Diacoma, Saint Apostle in the castle of Imola, Saint Peter in Sala, and Saint John in Senno; the hospice of Saint Vitalis in that city; the parish church of Saint Lawrence, and in it for you and your canons half of all the benefices arising from its entire parish in tithes, first-fruits, offerings, and bequests in the castle of Imola; the parish church of Saint Mary, with the chapel of Saint Theodore and the other chapels belonging to the same parish; the parish church of Saint Geminianus with its chapels; the parish church of Saint Sabinus with its chapels; the parish church of Saint Andrew and the chapel of Saint Paul in the castle of Albori; the Hospital of Saint James at Silero; [Col. 1473D] the parish church of Saint Mary in Gypso with its chapels; the chapel of Saxilio; the tithe of newly cleared lands in the forest of Pacto, within the boundaries of your bishopric; the parish churches of Saint Mary in Taussiniano, Saint Mary in Tyberiaco, Saint Martin in Colina, and Saint Angel in Campiano, with the chapels belonging to those parish churches; the parish church of Saint Stephen in Barbiano, with the chapel in the castle of Cunii and its other chapels; the parish churches of Saint Mary in Centum Licinia, Saint Patricius, and Saint Apollinaris, with the chapels belonging to them; the church of Saint Anastasius in Noredano; the parish churches of Saint Prosper and Saint Mary in Salustra, with their chapels.

The whole territory and court of Saint Cassian; the castle and court of Taularia; the castle and court of Acquaviva; the castle and massa of Boloniano; Massa Prata; Massa Campo; the castle and court of Caput [Col. 1474A] Silicum and its port, with its marshes, watercourses, and fisheries; the port of Petredulo; the *bachareta* of Runci; Libba Fenaria; the village of Zachara; the new castle of Fabriaci, with sixteen holdings; the castle of Bagnaria, with its entire court and all its appurtenances; Massa Adesso; Massa Sugarana; Massa Medecana; Massa Aureta; the estate of Peculini; the castle of Imola; Massa Plasignani; Massa Valeriani; Massa Cornarani; the castle of Galisterna; the castle of Toranelli; the court of Saint Martin in Sasso; the estate of Sasbiliani; the estate of Nunculia, called Casula; the court of Vallis Salvae; the castle and court of Monte Alto; Massa Saint Ambrose; the castle of Ronchum, with its entire court; the court of Macerata and the castle of Rocca; the village of Sorbedulum; the castle and court [Col. 1474B] of Corbaria; the castle and court of Fontes Ulicis; the castle and court of Tausiniano; the castle of Casale; the court of Publicum; the castle and court of Linarii; the castle and court of Podioli; the mountain of Saint Andrew with its appurtenances; the castle of Ducia with its appurtenances; the castle and court of Lavatoria; Massa Libanii; Massa Arsizi; Massa Galizani in the court of Vitriani; the estate called Capraria and four other estates; and, in that city itself, the toll and public dues.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to disturb the aforesaid Church, etc., as far as “without prejudice, of course, to the authority of the Apostolic See.” If, therefore, in the future, etc., as far as “let him be cut off.” But upon all, etc., as far as “they may find the rewards of eternal peace.” Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1474C] I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, etc. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, etc. I, Hubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, etc. I, Manfred, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina, etc. I, Aribertus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia, etc. I, Hubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, etc. I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of Pastor, etc. I, Roland, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark, etc. I, Gerard, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, etc. I, Otto, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, etc. I, George, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo, etc. [Col. 1474D] I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New, etc. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, etc. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, etc. I, Centius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro, etc.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXLIX. He adjudicates the controversy concerning the consecration of oil between the clergy of Saint John and Saint Sabina of the Marsi. (1151, June 6.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 748.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1475A] sons ODORISIUS, provost, and the canons of the Marsican church of Saint Sabina: greeting and apostolic blessing.

So that the darkness of forgetfulness may not be cast upon human minds concerning what has been adjudged in disputes, such matters ought to be committed to the memory of writing, so that by this means posterity may have something by which it may clearly know what occurred in times to come. Therefore we have ordered it to be recorded in the present written instrument how the controversy long debated between you and the clerics of the church of St. John concerning the consecration of oil was settled by our judgment.

The clerics of St. John maintained that the Marsican bishop ought to consecrate for them one separate flask of oil, asserting that they had received that flask by ancient [Col. 1475B] custom from the Marsican bishop. You, however, replying against this, said that, although this had been done in that church, Siginulfus, installed there by Bibert Louis, was the first to introduce it contrary to justice, and that it is altogether known to be contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers and to the venerable canons. Therefore, since we have recognized their petition to be superstitious and its very origin to have proceeded from the greatest arrogance, having taken counsel with our brethren, we hereby judge that henceforth only one flask of oil shall be consecrated in the mother church of St. Sabina and shall be divided equally, as is just, both through the church of St. John and through the other churches; and that this shall in every way be observed firmly and unshaken for all future time in perpetuity. [Col. 1475C] But if the aforesaid clerics should perhaps refuse to receive that oil, the Marsican bishop shall restrain them, as despisers and rebels, by severe disciplinary action.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth Ides of June, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDL. To Raymond, Archbishop of Toledo.—He rejoices that the Archbishop of Braga has submitted himself to his primacy; he rebukes him because he has invaded the latter’s boundaries and treated him harshly. (A.D. 1151, June 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 676.]

[Col. 1475D] Then does the Church of God rejoice in welcome tranquillity, when each person’s right is preserved and the order of reason maintained. Therefore, that true and unblemished peace and concord may be preserved among the prelates of the Churches, each must be content with his own right and must not attempt to invade another’s boundaries.

Accordingly, it pleases us, and we regard it favourably, that our true brother I., Archbishop of Braga, came to you in accordance with our command—although, as we have learned, you had embittered him—and humbly acknowledged you as his primate, thereby satisfying the just demands of your Church. But, as you desire that the honour and reverence due to you be rendered by him, so you are bound, with due regard for equity, to treat and love him as a brother and fellow bishop with fraternal charity, [Col. 1476A] and to preserve his rights unimpaired.

We are astonished, however, that, as we have recently learned from his complaint, you have unjustly occupied the boundaries of his province and, in the church of Zamora—which he establishes by many proofs and arguments to be situated within the boundaries of his province—you have unlawfully ordained the bishop who now presides over that Church. This you did, in contravention of an appeal made to the Apostolic See, by a violent settlement of the dispute—an agreement which, he asserts, was made between B., your predecessor, and A., Bishop of Asturias, in the presence of Lord D., cardinal-priest and then legate of the Apostolic See.

Therefore we, who, though unworthy, are seen to sit upon the seat of justice, wishing by virtue of the government [Col. 1476B] entrusted to us to preserve their rights to all Churches and ecclesiastical prelates, command you by this present judgment [variant: “these present documents”] that on the next feast of the Lord’s Resurrection you shall come, either personally or through sufficiently authorized representatives, into our presence, prepared to answer our aforesaid brother adequately concerning these matters. Furthermore, because your brotherhood is said to have excessively embittered that same brother of ours in demanding from him a profession of obedience, we nevertheless command you to come to an agreement with him concerning this matter with priestly moderation, so that henceforth he may have no just cause for complaint against you.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth Ides of June.

CDLI. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of St. Mary at Pongartenberg and receives it under his protection. (A.D. 1151, June 22.)

[KURZ, *Beiträge zur Geschichte des Landes Oesterreich ob der Enns*, Linz, 1805, octavo, III, 393.]

[Col. 1476C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FRIDERIC, abbot of St. Mary at Pongartenberg, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the monastic life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection should be at hand for those who choose the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them aside from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the monastery of Blessed Mary at Pongartenberg, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.
