Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the place in which the abbey itself is situated, with its appurtenances; the grange at Nodemestorf, with its appurtenances; the grange of Tymnich, with its appurtenances; [Col. 1477A] the grange of Gozoltingen, with its appurtenances; the grange of Teuphenbach, with its appurtenances; Modemefecche, with meadows and pastures; thirty holdings in the Northern Forest; the grange of Cremesa, with its fields and vineyards; and ten forest holdings at Nochelinge.

Moreover, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, nor on the sustenance of your animals. You shall receive the oil for the sick, the consecration of altars or churches, the blessing of the abbot, and the ordinations of monks who are to be advanced to holy orders, from the diocesan bishop—provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these freely and without improper exaction. [Col. 1477B] Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 1477C] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe.

The subscriptions of eleven cardinals follow.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, and in the seventh year of the pontificate [Col. 1477D] of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDLII. To [Eberhard], Archbishop of Salzburg.—He commands him to judge between the abbot of Baumgarten and [Conrad], Bishop of Passau, who are disputing over certain possessions. (A.D. 1151, June.)

[KURZ, *Beiträge*, etc., p. 388.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the abbot of Pawmgartennperg, appearing before us, lodged before us a complaint against our venerable brother, the Bishop of Passau: namely, that he was attempting unjustly to take from him certain movable goods of his church which the late nobleman Otto had left to it by testament for the redemption of his soul. [Col. 1478A] Since we neither can nor ought to tolerate that works of piety, especially those bestowed upon religious persons and Christ’s poor, should be nullified by anyone’s power or presumption, we command your fraternity by this present writing that, unless our aforesaid brother permits our aforementioned son and his brethren peacefully to possess all that had been bequeathed or assigned to them in that testament by the aforementioned man, you shall endeavour to summon both parties before your presence. Having summoned those who were present at the making of that testament, you shall make our aforesaid brother inviolably observe whatever they may be willing to testify concerning it under the obligation of an oath. [Col. 1478B] In these matters and in all their causes, we wish you to support the aforesaid brethren out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, so that through favour or power on the other side they may not find themselves deprived of their right, and so that in assisting them we may know what we ought to expect from your charity in carrying out pious dispositions.

CDLIII. To the Bishop of Passau.—He informs him of the mandate given to the Archbishop of Salzburg. (A.D. 1151, June.)

[Ibid., p. 289.]

[Col. 1478C] EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Bishop of Passau: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we embrace your fraternity in the arms of sincere love, we are not a little grieved that we so often see religious men dwelling in your diocese burdened by your fraternity in such a way that we are not without reason moved by it, and that you appear to derogate no little from the pontifical office to which divine grace has called you.

Our beloved son, the abbot of Pawmgartennperg, coming to the clemency of the Apostolic See, informed us by his complaint that you are attempting, through unsuitable witnesses, to take away certain property which the nobleman Otto, at the point of death, left by testament to his church for the redemption of his soul. [Col. 1478D] Since, therefore, it concerns an injury to the episcopal office and peril to your soul to take from religious men—who ought rather to be advanced with particular zeal by your fraternity from what is your own—goods granted by others in pious devotion, we command your affection by this present writing either to leave those goods to our aforesaid son and his brethren free and without any disturbance, or, when you have been summoned by our venerable brother the Archbishop of Salzburg, to appear before him and firmly accept and observe what he shall judge in this matter. Until the case is concluded by judgment, moreover, you shall in no way presume to take any of those goods from our aforesaid son.

CDLIV. He receives the Venetian convent of St. Zacharias under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms its possessions. (A.D. 1151, September 26.)

[CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XI, 373.]

[Col. 1479A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, GIRELDRUDA, abbess of the monastery of St. Zacharias, and her sisters, both present and future, to be regularly appointed: in perpetuity.

It belongs to the clemency of apostolic governance to cherish religious persons and to defend their places by the safeguard of pious protection. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously [Col. 1479B] assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established there according to the Lord and the observance of the brethren of Cluny shall be preserved inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery justly and canonically possesses at present, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: [Col. 1479C] the estate situated in the village called Petriolo, with the church of St. Thomas and all its appurtenances; the estate situated at the place called Cona, with the church of St. Mary and all its appurtenances; and whatever is held in Sacco, Lupa, Liquentia, and Laurentiaca, together with their appurtenances. We likewise confirm to you the tithes of all the tenants of those same estates, which you rightfully possess. We further forbid that any sister hereafter be admitted to that monastery who presumes to possess property in any fashion.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, [Col. 1479D] or harass it with any vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole and inviolate for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes amendment by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord [Col. 1480A] Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedis. I, Aribertus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Ubarldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bernardus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Clement. I, Urlandus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mary. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the [Col. 1480B] fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDLV. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Altenberg. (A.D. 1151, October 1.)

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta pontificum Romanorum*, 644, in the Düsseldorf archive, from Pertz’s notes.]

CDLVI. Privilege for the canons of Pistoia, from their own archive. (A.D. 1151, December 11.)

[ZACHARIA, *Anecdota medii aevi*, 231.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUENRIC, provost, and the other brethren of the church of Pistoia, both present and future, who shall remain in the observance of the regular life: [Col. 1480C] in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which appears consonant with reason and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, after the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander, Urban, and Lucius, we fortify by the authority of our privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed.

By this present decree, therefore, we establish that no living person may separate you and your successors from the fellowship of canonical life, nor may any of you, after profession, be free to depart from the community and follow the precipices of the broader way. [Col. 1480D] Accordingly, we decree that if any one of you deviates from his purpose, no person may hinder you, your successors, or the other superiors from correcting him and restraining him according to the discipline of the rule. At the death of you or the other rulers of your community of canons, no one shall be set over it through any stratagem of fraudulent procurement or by violence, except one whom the regular brethren, in the fear of God, shall elect—either from among themselves, if they find such a man among themselves, or from outsiders if necessary—with the counsel of the bishop who has been canonically elected and ordained through the Roman Church.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may [Col. 1481A] hereafter acquire, God being favourable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors who remain in the same religious life. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the parish church of Viliano with all its tithes; likewise the parish church of St. Quiricus; the other tithes granted to you by bishops, whether within or outside the city; the fourth portion of offerings made at the Litanies; the tithes of Gropole and Collina; the chapel of St. Saviour situated at Guido’s Gate; the chapel of St. Leonard in the borough of that same gate; the chapel of St. Mary in the borough of Guidterdus; the chapel of St. Vitalis at the Lucchese Gate; and the church of St. Blaise, [Col. 1481B] with lands situated at Aqua Vivola, Vizano, Falagrano, Barzani, and Glandaria, as Girardus son of Baronchus and Rolandus together with his son-in-law Davizus gave them; and the church of St. Andrew with its appurtenances.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that community of canons, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but all things shall remain whole for the benefit in every way of you and those for whose governance and support they have been granted. Yet this diligence and care must be employed: that you do not abuse an increase of possessions for freedom of the flesh and a cloak for wickedness, and that you do not in any way increase the possessions and diminish the number of brethren; rather, so great a number of canons shall be maintained as the resources of your place appear able to support, lest the Church suffer loss in religion and the service due to it. [Col. 1481C] In all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the Bishop of Pistoia are reserved.

You, therefore, ought to apply yourselves diligently to the institutions of the regular life and observe in all things the decrees of the Apostolic See, so that after the straits of the present life you may, with the Lord’s help, deserve to attain the glory of the heavenly expanse. But if hereafter any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, margrave, count, viscount, judge, castaldus, or any person, great or small, knowing this charter of privilege, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 1481D] But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Imarus, Bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, Bishop of Albano, have subscribed. [Col. 1482A] I, G.G., cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedis, have subscribed. I, Manfredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina, have subscribed. I, Aribertus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd, have subscribed. I, Gerardus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. [Col. 1482B] I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, through the hands of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of December, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDLVII. Bull of protection granted to the monastery of Esrom. (A.D. 1151, December 29.)

[Johannes TORKELIN, *Diplomatarium Arna-Magnæanum*, I, 248, from the Esrom diplomatic codex, fol. 1a. Copy.]

[Col. 1482C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Esrom, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. [Col. 1482D] We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery justly and canonically possesses at present, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: Widelingeruth with its appurtenances; Aveholm; whatever is held at Tanga; and Davidesthorp, given by our venerable brother Eschillus, Archbishop of Lund. Moreover, no one may presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate at your own expense or on the sustenance of your animals.

[Col. 1483A] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, or diminish them; but all things shall remain whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 1483B] But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callistus. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedis. I, Manfredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina. I, Aribertus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bernardus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Clement. I, Imarus, Bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 1483C] I, Nicholas, Bishop of Albano. I, Hugh, Bishop of Ostia. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDLVIII. To Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury.—That he may consecrate [Silvester], elected abbot of the monastery of St. Augustine. (A.D. 1151.)

[TWISDEN and SELDEN, *Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores*, II, 1811.]

[Col. 1483D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEOBALD, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your messengers whom you sent into our presence have been able to report to your fraternity, we discussed by searching examination in the presence of our brethren and cardinals, and diligently investigated, what malicious accusers were saying concerning the elected abbot of the monastery of St. Augustine. But since no one wished to proceed canonically against him in order to prove the charge, because we neither [Col. 1484A] could nor ought to do otherwise according to reason, we finally had recourse to the last remedy and, by the counsel of our brethren, received from him a purgation beyond what was required.

Therefore, since after he has made this purgation the ordination of the same elect ought neither to be denied nor delayed, although we could ourselves confer upon him the grace of consecration, nevertheless, wishing to show deference to your fraternity, we have thought fit to send him back to you. By this present writing we command that, according to the tenor of the privileges granted to that monastery by the Roman pontiffs, you shall go to that place and confer upon the aforesaid elect the office of consecration, with the grace of the Holy Spirit going before. For we do not wish that monastery to remain any longer without the comfort of its own shepherd, and consequently to suffer losses or inconveniences both spiritual and temporal. [Col. 1484B]

CDLIX. To Otto I, Bishop of Freising.—That he may support the monks of Tegernsee in the matter of an estate to be restored by Count Palatine Otto. (A.D. 1150–1151, November 16.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, I, 392.—This letter and the following one have been falsely attributed to Alexander III.]

To O., Bishop of Freising.

It belongs to our office to cherish venerable and religious places, and to support their rulers, both through ourselves and through our brother bishops, with the charity that is due, so that God may be honoured in us and that the peace and tranquillity of the Churches may be preserved, insofar as our [Col. 1484C] ability permits. Therefore we have thought fit to commend to your fraternity our beloved sons C., abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Tegernsee, who stand under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. We ask that you love and honour them and, when they have complained before you concerning the dispute over tithes and a certain estate which they have against O., the Count Palatine, render them the justice due to them and maintain and defend that place in its liberty.

Given at Segni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

CDLX. To Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg.—That he shall keep Count Otto excommunicated until he makes satisfaction to Tegernsee monastery concerning the tithes taken from it. (A.D. 1150–1151, November.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1484D]

To the Archbishop of Salzburg.

We have recently received a renewed complaint from our beloved son, the abbot of Tegernsee, against the nobleman Otto, Count Palatine: namely, that he violently takes from him certain tithes which, as the abbot asserts, belong by right to the Church entrusted to him, and refuses to restore them. Therefore, since we neither can nor ought to fail him in his right, we command you by this present writing strictly to warn the same count either to restore those tithes to the aforesaid Church or to render to that Church the justice due concerning them in your presence. [Col. 1485A] If he is unwilling to do either of these things, you shall subject him to the bond of excommunication and keep him bound under that bond until he is compelled to fulfil one of the aforesaid alternatives.

CDLXI. To the Archbishop of Ragusa [Andrew]. (A.D. 1145–1152, September 22.)

[FARLATUS, *Illyricum sacrum*, VI, p. 64.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother A[NDREW], Archbishop of Ragusa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having learned the condition of your fraternity through the bearer of this letter, S., your priest, who came to us under the Lord’s guidance, we sympathize with the weakness of your body with a fitting [Col. 1485B] weakness of heart; but we rejoice that in this furnace of fire the Lord, Creator of all, purging the rust of those whom he loves, deigns to place you among the number of his children.

But amid these things, … [lacuna; surviving “a”] … directing yourself toward the homeland, ponder with the eyes of your heart the hardships of the present exile … [lacuna] … and do not cease to govern and cherish by example the Lord’s people entrusted to your rule. Be vigilant in winning souls … [lacuna; surviving “r”] … be solicitous for uprightness; permit neither negligence nor fraud unjustly to cause the advantage of the Church to perish or deteriorate; and, through priestly solicitude, be so vigilant in assured good works, as the Lord grants, that, when you stand before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, you may present to the same Redeemer [Col. 1485C] of ours the fruit of good work belonging to your reward, in which he may rejoice.

As for that matter concerning which you diligently seek dispensation from us—namely, that by the obligation of an oath you are bound to visit the thresholds of the Apostles, but have hitherto been unable to accomplish this personally, hindered by grave illness—we remit it to your fraternity out of the kindness of the Apostolic See. But when divine clemency grants you an opportunity, if you are unable to come personally, endeavour through your messenger to visit with due devotion your mother, the holy Church, so that, by the Lord’s help, we may be informed of the state of your health, and you of matters occurring around us. Concerning … [lacuna] … for your visitation, we give thanks to your fraternity.

Given [at Ferentino?]—on the tenth day before the Kalends of October … [lacuna] …

CDLXII. To P., prior of the Church of St. Fridianus at Lucca. (A.D. 1150–1152, August 21.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchese edition, IV, 594.]

[Col. 1485D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son P., prior of St. Fridianus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son J., cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New, has frequently represented to us that his Church has been so disturbed inwardly and outwardly by many enormities and transgressions of the prior of that Church—as, we believe, is known to you—that, with the bond of charity dissolved, the entire structure of good work seems to totter and the goods of that Church to be wasted. Therefore, lest we allow through any dissimulation the good which our predecessors [Col. 1486A] planted there and which divine grace has watered until these times to be torn up, it is incumbent upon our solicitude to apply the hands of diligence and to recall with all zeal to the rule of rectitude whatever in that Church is said to exceed norm and order.

But because we have in no way thought that this should be done without the counsel of your affection, to whom the administration of that Church has been entrusted, we command you by this present writing, all excuse set aside, to present yourself before us by the next feast of St. Michael, so that we may be able with you to devote every effort to restoring concord in the aforesaid Church.

Given at Segni, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.

CDLXIII. To Conrad, vicar, and all the Roman clergy. (A.D. 1150–1152, October.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 690, from the notes of a manuscript of Gratian held by the Fathers of the Congregation of the Mother of God at Lucca.]

[Col. 1486B]

Furthermore, what you have decreed concerning those who presume to invade another’s parish and receive the parishioners of others contrary to the ordinances of the canons is likewise confirmed by the assertion of our authority: namely, that whoever hereafter is proved guilty of such presumption shall wholly lose the power of imposing penance in the Church of God and shall at the same time be deprived of ecclesiastical benefice until restored by the hands of the bishop.

Given at Segni, on the third Nones of October.

CDLXIV. To Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne.—Concerning confirmation of many rights and privileges long previously granted to the archbishop and to the priests and canons of the metropolitan church of Cologne. (A.D. 1152, January 8.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 634.]

[Col. 1486C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ARNOLD, Archbishop of Cologne, and to his successors canonically appointed.

In the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See [Col. 1486D], established by the dispensation of divine grace, we are bound, by the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God, to love our brother bishops with sincere charity and to preserve their due rights for the Churches committed to their rule and governance. For just as, in the structure of the human body, natural reason, providing for the welfare of each individual member, assigns to them their particular and proper functions while preserving the dignity of the nobler members, so apostolic providence, in the body of the Church, governs all Churches according to the enactments of the sacred canons, while safeguarding the worthier and more renowned in the prerogative of their rank. It is therefore equitable and reasonable that each Church’s own honor and proper rights should be confirmed by the protection of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, beloved brother in Christ, Archbishop Arnold, graciously assenting to your just requests and following the example of our predecessor Pope Leo IX of blessed memory, we receive under the protection of that prince of the Apostles, in whose place, though unworthy, we are seen to sit, and under our own protection, the Church of St. Peter at Cologne, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside [Col. 1487A], and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We likewise confirm for you and your successors the use of the pallium, the banner of the life-giving Cross, and the *naccus*, namely, the insignia of the festal horse, granted to your predecessors by our predecessors, to be borne at the proper time and place. We further add that [Col. 1487B] you are to be subject to no primate except the Roman pontiff alone. As a prerogative of fuller and more special favor, we have judged it fitting to grant you the consecration of the king within your province. And if the Roman pontiff or a legate of the Apostolic See holds a council in that province, you shall hold the first place among the others after them.

Moreover, we decree that seven suitable cardinal-priests shall be ordained in the aforesaid Church; clothed in dalmatics and adorned with mitres, they shall celebrate the solemnities of Mass, only on feast days, at the two principal altars of that Church, together with an equal number of deacons and subdeacons, to whom we grant the use of sandals. Therefore, that all the foregoing may [Col. 1487C] retain full force hereafter, as they are contained in the privileges of our predecessors, we confirm them by the authority of our favor for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, then, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor [Col. 1487D]; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity perpetrated; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 1488A] I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callistus. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedes. I, Manfredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Pastor. I, Bernardus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Clement. I, Gerardus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1488B] I, Rodulphus, cardinal-deacon of St. Lucy in Septisoliis. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Cencius, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Akyro.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151 [Col. 1488C], in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

### CDLXV. To the people of Cologne

He sends back to them Archbishop Arnold, consecrated by his own hand and adorned with the pallium, commanding them to obey him, etc. (1152, 8 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 502.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GU., provost; F., dean; the archdeacons, priors, and all the clergy and people of the Church of Cologne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with due kindness at the clemency of the Apostolic See our venerable brother Arnold, your elect [Col. 1488D], together with our beloved sons Wibald, abbot of Corvey; N., abbot of Siegburg [Note: [Col. 1487D] The monastery of Siegburg, a notable house of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Cologne, was founded by Saint Anno, archbishop; Nicholas was then its abbot.]; T., abbot of Kamp [Note: [Col. 1488D] Kamp is a distinguished Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Cologne, the mother of several monasteries, concerning which Juncelinus says more.]; Master Henry, notary of our dearest son Conrad, king of the Romans; A., provost; and G., dean of St. Gereon. Having carefully examined the election which you had unanimously made of him as a prudent and capable man, we held it valid, with the Lord as author; and although he resisted strongly, we consecrated him, as it were, by the hands of blessed Peter—our own hands—under the leading of the grace of the Holy Spirit, as your archbishop. [Col. 1489A] So long as he wished to remain with us, we regarded him as dear among our brethren, treated him honorably, and, by the customary generosity of the Apostolic See, conferred upon him the fullness of the pallium and of the pontifical office.

We have therefore thought it necessary earnestly to commend him to your whole community, as he returns to his Church and to you, adorned with the insignia of his pontifical office, accompanied by the grace of the Holy Roman Church and supported by our letters, with the Lord accompanying him. By these apostolic letters, therefore, we command you to receive him kindly and reverently, and humbly to render him, as Christ’s vicar and the shepherd of your souls, the honor, reverence, and obedience due to him, so that through his teaching and pastoral vigilance the grace of almighty God may work salvation in you. [Col. 1489B] May your Church, grievously weakened in both spiritual and temporal matters, by the Lord’s gift rise again to its state of wholeness; and may you obtain joy from him, and he from you a crown and abundant fruit in the sight of the Lord.

We likewise command you that, in order to restore the state of religion and propriety in that Church, and to recover its goods, possessions, and benefices which have been unlawfully granted away, dispersed, or alienated—whether from the table, treasury, or alms of the archbishop himself, from the table of his abbots, provosts, and abbesses, or from the prebends of his canons—you shall effectively provide strength and assistance as good and devoted sons. [Col. 1489C] Furthermore, we confirm by the authority of our favor the judgment recently and prudently promulgated at Cologne in the presence of our son Conrad, illustrious king of the Romans, concerning those things granted to laymen.

Moreover, since, as we have learned, some among you, after the aforesaid brother had begun his journey to us, violently and unjustly invaded or occupied certain of these possessions, we command by the authority of this letter that, unless within forty days after the warning of your aforesaid Archbishop Arnold they restore those possessions to the same Church, they shall be subject to the censure of ecclesiastical discipline.

Given at Segni, on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXVI. To King Conrad

He reports that he has honorably received Conrad’s envoys and complied in all matters with his wishes. (1152, 9 January.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 686.]

[Col. 1489D]

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to CONRAD, king of the Romans.

The more often we are informed, through letters and messengers of your magnificence, concerning the state of your welfare and the good will which you are said to bear toward blessed Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, and toward your mother, the most holy Roman Church, the more joy and gladness are daily increased in our hearts; our heart is more ardently kindled toward love of you, and we lend willing ears, insofar as we can with God, to hear your requests. Therefore, when our brother Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, and Master Henry, your notary—whom Your Serenity had sent to our presence—came to us, [Col. 1490A] we received them with due kindness as prudent and capable men, treated them honorably, and gave a favorable assent to your petitions, which we learned both through letters and from their own spoken words, insofar as we recognized this to be expedient for God’s honor and the good of the kingdom.

For we raised the aforesaid brother to the summit of pontifical dignity, the Lord being author, though he was unwilling, resistant, and shedding an abundance of tears. We also prolonged the terms fixed for our venerable brothers H., archbishop of Mainz, and A., archbishop of Bremen, to come to us; and by apostolic letters we carefully took care to warn and encourage both them and the other archbishops, bishops, and princes of your realm to support you and the expedition which, with divine clemency favoring you, you have arranged for the honor of God and His holy Church and for the exaltation of the kingdom. [Col. 1490B]

It is therefore your concern, dearest son, to exercise diligent care and solicitude for the honor and exaltation of the kingdom entrusted to you and of the holy Church of God, as the foremost and most eminent prince among the other Christian kings of the world, so that we may, by the Lord’s granting, receive with the desired fruit your coming, which we await for the advancement of the Church [Col. 1490C] and kingdom and for the salvation of the Christian people.

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXVII. To Henry, Bishop of Liège

That he compel the counts of Looz and Montaigu to restore what they have taken from the monastery of Stavelot. (1152, 9 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 504.]

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to HENRY, bishop of Liège.

We ought more readily to rise to the aid of those who rely especially upon our protection, and to punish those who harass them with fitting correction. We have received a grave complaint from our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, who came to the clemency of the Apostolic See, against L., count of Looz, and G., count of Montaigu: namely, that, at the devil’s instigation, they committed arsons, killings, and robberies upon the goods of the Church of Stavelot, and, though admonished concerning such great wickedness, are altogether unwilling to make satisfaction. [Col. 1490D]

Since we can neither leave an offense of such iniquity unpunished nor ought to do so, we command you by this present letter strictly to admonish the aforesaid L., count of Looz, and his accomplices to restore what they violently took from the brethren of Stavelot monastery and to make suitable satisfaction to those brethren for the injuries inflicted. If they should refuse to obey your admonitions, then, within two months after you receive this letter, let the aforesaid count and his supporters be struck by the sword of anathema. You shall also strictly admonish the count of Montaigu, who presumed to invade the goods of that monastery, to render due satisfaction to the brethren of the same abbey for the aforesaid losses. [Col. 1491A]

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXVIII. To H[artwic], Archbishop of Bremen

That he ensure the restoration of estates taken from the monastery of Kemnade by his parishioners. (1152, 9 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 504.]

Lord Pope EUGENIUS III to the Archbishop of Bremen.

[Col. 1491B]

From the complaint of our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, we have learned that certain of your parishioners—namely Odiko, Riebertus, Thederus, Rainerus, and Hermannus—have unlawfully received from Judith, formerly abbess, after she had been removed from the governance of the Church, certain possessions of the monastery of Kemnade which are known to lie in your bishopric; that they retain them contrary to justice; and that they utterly refuse to restore them to the aforesaid Church. Since it belongs to our office to correct errors, annul what has been done wrongly and contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers, and restore it to a state of right order, we command you by this present letter strictly to admonish those aforesaid parishioners of yours to restore the possessions to the monastery mentioned above [Col. 1491C] and to cease harassing that Church. Should they scorn to obey your admonitions, administer canonical justice upon them.

Furthermore, we likewise command you to ensure that what is just be rendered to the brethren of the Church of Corvey concerning the fishery of Hokwar, which, as we have learned, is unlawfully held by your parishioners.

[Note: [Col. 1491D] Conrad restored that fishery to Abbot Henry in 1145; see the *Annals of Paderborn*, book VIII, under that year.]

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Mainz

That he procure the restoration by his parishioners of what has been taken from the monastery of Corvey. (1152, 9 January.)

[Ibid., 506.]

The same pope to HENRY, archbishop of Mainz.

[Col. 1491D]

Natural law and the decrees of the holy Fathers alike testify that each person should remain content with what is his own and should not unlawfully stretch out hands toward another’s goods, much less toward ecclesiastical goods. Yet certain of your parishioners, putting aside the fear of God, have unlawfully and unjustly invaded the estate of Ostoph, which, as has been reported to us, is known properly to belong to the Church of Corvey; persisting in their wickedness, they utterly refuse to restore it to that Church. Since pastoral care ought especially to ensure that those who plunder ecclesiastical possessions may learn to desist from invading others’ property, we command you by this present letter to render due justice to our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, and his brethren against the invaders. [Col. 1492A]

Given as above.

[Note: [Col. 1491D] The same letter was sent to Conrad, bishop of Worms, as to the archbishop of Mainz. These words are appended to the preceding letter in the manuscript codex of Wibald’s letters preserved in the Royal Archive at Berlin. JAFFÉ. [Col. 1492D]]

### CDLXX. To Bernard, Bishop of Paderborn

That he compel Widikind, under threat of anathema, to restore what he has taken from the monastery of Corvey. (1152, 9 January.)

[Ibid.]

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to BERNARD, bishop of Paderborn.

[Col. 1492B]

Our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, appearing before us, lodged a grave complaint in our ears: Widikind, your parishioner, with certain of his retainers, violently entered the cemetery of Corvey monastery and, with sacrilegious audacity, carried off from it goods worth one hundred marks; moreover, he violated the chapel situated at the gate of that cemetery and presumed in criminal audacity to take away what he found there. Since it belongs to our office to correct errors and restrain the presumption of laymen with the bridle of justice, we command you by this present letter strictly to admonish the aforesaid Widikind and all those known to have been with him in the aforesaid wickedness, that they restore to the monastery what was taken [Col. 1492C] and make suitable satisfaction for so great a sacrilege. Otherwise, with the Lord as author, strike Widikind and his accomplices with the sword of anathema.

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXXI. To Hermann, Bishop of Utrecht

That he preserve estates of the monastery of Corvey located in his diocese. (1152, 9 January.)

[Ibid., 507.]

The same pope to HERMANN, bishop of Utrecht.

The authority of our office reminds and exhorts us to provide with paternal concern for the welfare of all the faithful, especially religious persons, [Col. 1492D] and, with the Lord as author, beneficially to make provision for their advantage. Accordingly, we admonish your brotherhood by this present letter to defend and protect, for the benefit of the brethren of Corvey, the possessions of the Church of Corvey known to be in your diocese: namely, the church of Linewert and the estate of Merthen, against those who seek to take them away. Moreover, endeavor to recover and gather back any of the same possessions which you learn have been alienated or encumbered; and henceforth we wish you to be so solicitous in this matter [Col. 1493A] that the Church of Corvey may suffer no loss in those possessions.

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXXII. To Ulric, Bishop of Halberstadt

That he restrain his parishioners who trouble the brethren of Corvey. (1152, 9 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 507.]

EUGENIUS, pope, to ULRIC, bishop of Halberstadt.

The authority of the government we have received exhorts us to be most ready defenders of ecclesiastical property and to oppose ourselves as a most secure wall to those attempting to despoil it. It has reached our ears that certain of your parishioners unjustly trouble the abbey of Corvey regarding the tithes at Gruninga and the tithes of the demesne land, which they violently take away from the aforesaid Church and presume unjustly to retain. [Col. 1493B] Since it belongs to the pastoral office to correct the excesses of evil men and to restrain them with the bridle of justice to a state of right order, we command you by the authority of this letter strictly to admonish the aforesaid parishioners of yours to desist from so great a presumption and henceforth to inflict no disturbance upon the Church concerning those tithes. If they should scorn to do so, administer canonical justice upon them.

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXXIII. To Henry, Duke of Saxony

He commends to him Wibald, abbot of Corvey. (1152, 9 January.)

[Ibid., 508.]

[Col. 1493C]

Pope EUGENIUS to HENRY, illustrious duke of Saxony.

Among the principal deeds of powerful men, there is nothing that makes them so acceptable to our God as seeing that they render due honor and reverence to Churches and their prelates. Therefore, since we love you with paternal charity and hope better things from the vigor of your virtue, we earnestly commend to your prowess our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, who is known to deserve honor for the prudence of his uprightness. By this present letter, we ask and exhort your nobility in the Lord to be a faithful and devoted helper, for our sake, in recovering and [Col. 1493D] preserving the goods of that Church.

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXXIV. To the Bishop of Verden

He complains that the bishop’s brother and other parishioners are invading the goods of the monastery of Kemnade. (1152, 9 January.)

[Ibid.]

The same pope to the bishop of VERDEN.

[Note: [Col. 1493D] Hermann, who was held in great renown and loyalty by Emperor Frederick I and by the whole court, as is read in the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Verden*, vol. II of the Brunswick writers. [Col. 1494D]]

If we carefully weigh the care of the universal Church, which, with God as author, we have undertaken to exercise, we must ensure that we preserve the due rights of all the faithful, especially of those known especially to fall under our protection, in such a way that, under the pretext that justice has been withheld, they may not be negligent in the strictness of their own duty. [Col. 1494A] From a recent representation by our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, we have learned, to our great surprise, that your brother Hungoldus, W. and Ge., and indeed certain other of your parishioners, violently take away and unjustly retain the goods of the Church of Kemnade, which are known to belong by right to that Church. Since ecclesiastical goods, especially those of the Church of Corvey and those pertaining to it, stand under our defense and protection, we command you by the authority of this letter strictly to admonish your brother and the other aforesaid invaders to restore what has been taken to the aforesaid Church and desist from harassing it. Should they refuse to obey your admonitions, administer due justice upon them. [Col. 1494B]

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXXV. To the Bishop of Minden

That he continue to act well toward the monastery of Corvey. (1152, 9 January.)

[Ibid., 509.]

The same pope to the bishop of MINDEN.

[Note: [Col. 1494D] Henry, formerly abbot of St. Maurice on the Island, of the Benedictine order.]

It is pleasing and acceptable to us that, as we have learned from the report of our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, you have been solicitous and well-disposed toward the advantage of that Church in accordance with the tenor of the letters which we sent you. [Col. 1494C] Since a reward is known to be due not to one who begins but to one who perseveres, we command your brotherhood by this present letter to endeavor to add greater increase to these good beginnings and to render due justice to our aforesaid son, the abbot of Corvey, against certain of your parishioners, both clerics and laymen, who presume to take away the goods of the Church of Kemnade.

Given at Segni, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### CDLXXVI. To the Abbot of Lüneburg

That Henry, deposed from the abbacy of Corvey, has not been restored to his office. (1152, January.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1494D]

The same pope to the abbot of Lüneburg.

We wish it to be made known to your charity that Henry, formerly abbot of Corvey, came before us and humbly requested that we restore him to his office. Since this appeared wholly inconsistent with reason, and the gravity of his fault appeared unworthy of such mitigation of punishment, you are to know that we have made no restoration whatsoever in his case. For it has been reported to us that, with rash audacity, he presumes to oppose the sentence of deposition pronounced against him by Thomas, cardinal-priest of blessed memory, then legate of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1495A] Anyone zealous for rectitude is by no means ignorant how contrary this is to reason and how wholly alien to the institutions of the holy Fathers. Since it belongs to our apostolic office to correct errors and root such criminal presumptions out of existence, we command you by the authority of this letter strictly to admonish the aforesaid Henry to desist from so great a presumption and not presume to oppose in any way the aforesaid sentence pronounced against him. If, however, he should thereafter attempt to harass or trouble the abbey of Corvey, restrain him with fitting punishment.

### CDLXXVII. To the Abbot of Lüneburg

He commands the Abbot of Lüneburg not to allow the monastery of Corvey to be harassed by Henry, the deposed abbot. (1152, 9 January.) [Col. 1495B]

[This letter of Eugenius is extant in the Bursfelde Cartulary preserved at Hanover, according to JAFFÉ, *Regesta Romanorum Pontificum*, p. 645.]

### CDLXXVIII. Bull for the monastery of Valciodorus

(1152, 12 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 819.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son THEODERIC, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary at Valciodorus, situated above the river Meuse [Col. 1495C], and to his brethren, present and future, regularly appointed in succession: in perpetuity.

It accords with the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious brethren with sincere charity in the Lord and to defend their places by the pious protection of apostolic faith. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; following the example of our predecessor Pope B. VII of blessed memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 1495D]

Upon the death of you, now abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any artifice of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of them, shall judge to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Furthermore, we also confirm to you the village called Hasteria, with all its appurtenances.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1496A], remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. If, then, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power or honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity perpetrated; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict [Col. 1496B] vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Manfredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina, have subscribed. [Col. 1496C] I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New, have subscribed. I, G., cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman [Col. 1496D] Church, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDLXXIX. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Aosta, in the province of Tarentaise

(1152, 15 January.)

[*Monumenta Historiae Patriae*, Charters I, 795.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ARNULF, bishop of Aosta, and to his successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Established, by the Lord’s disposition, in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are bound to love our brother bishops with fuller charity and more diligently to fortify with apostolic protection the places entrusted to their governance. Accordingly, venerable brother in Christ, Arnulf, bishop of the Church of Aosta, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid Church over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, and fortify it by the protection of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 1497A]

Among these, we have judged it fitting to set down expressly in their own names: in the city and borough of Aosta, the toll and the third part of the count’s levy, with the other revenues and investitures belonging to you; the meadow of Montanai; two vineyards; the Round Field; the village called Conia, with its alpine pastures and the other things there belonging to the episcopal household; the chapel of Donia, with its appurtenances and the other things belonging to the episcopal household in that village; the land which belonged to Aluis, with the other things belonging to the episcopal household in the village called Cinai; the chapel of Prociona, with its appurtenances and everything belonging to the episcopal household in that village; whatever right you hold in the village called Porreisan; whatever right you hold in the place [Col. 1497B] called Ovellanum; the alpine pasture of Formieria; two fields beyond the river Duria; and the right which you hold in the place called Palus.

Furthermore, we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See the liberty which Count Amadeus of blessed memory and his son Humbert granted, out of devotion, to you and to the canons of your Church, and strengthened by the guarantee of their writings; and we decree that it remain valid in future times. Thus, on the death of you, any of your successors, or the canons of that Church, no one shall by any rashness intrude upon ecclesiastical goods, but all things shall be preserved unshaken and intact for the benefit of the bishop or canon appointed there according to the Lord. [Col. 1497C]

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved unshaken and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, then, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second [Col. 1498A] or third time, does not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity perpetrated; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, G[regory], cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed. [Col. 1498B] I, Aribertus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Pastor, have subscribed. I, Bernardus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Clement, have subscribed. I, Rolandus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. George at [Col. 1498C] the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### CDLXXX. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, concerning the affair of Master Peter

(1152, 19 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 636.]

[Col. 1498D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We confidently invite to works of piety the zeal of those in whose devotion, prudence, and religion we have the fullest confidence in every respect. We have received letters on behalf of the bearer of these presents, Master Peter [Note: [Col. 1497D] This is that most celebrated Peter, called the Master of the Sentences, who, from being a canon of Chartres, became bishop of Paris. He resigned that dignity by death [Col. 1498D] not in 1164, as the Sammartani say, but in 1160, as is clear from two letters of Alexander III and other records.], from the lord of Clairvaux and many others, whose requests we can neither refuse nor ought to refuse. In them they earnestly begged [Col. 1499A] that, since for so long a time he has laboured usefully and honourably in scholastic studies through God's grace, yet has not hitherto deserved to be supported by an ecclesiastical benefice, he might obtain this through our intervention. Therefore, moved both by the prayers of so many persons and by the obligation of our office, we have decreed to entrust this work of mercy to your brotherhood, in which we have no distrust whatsoever, believing that you will carry it out all the better because we believe that your sufficiently devout mind is inflamed by the zeal of divine love for such matters even without our request. We therefore earnestly entreat your brotherhood by apostolic letters to grant him a prebend in your church, for the love of God, reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and the enhancement of the office of your pontificate, so that he may be more faithful to you and to us, may serve your church faithfully, and we may be bound to render thanks to your brotherhood.

Given at Segni, 14 Kalends of February [19 January].

CDLXXXI. To the same person.—On behalf of S., nephew of the abbot of Saint-Denis. (1152, 19 January.)

[MARTEN, *Collect.*, II, 637.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we know that your brotherhood is joined to us in true charity, we confidently commend to your care those whom we love. Our beloved son S. [Col. 1499C], on account of the devotion by which his uncle S., formerly abbot of Saint-Denis of venerable memory [Note: [Col. 1499] Suger, who died in January 1151; therefore this letter was written in the following year, or in 1153, since Pope Eugenius did not live longer.], was bound to the Apostolic See and to ourselves, is dear and acceptable to us. We wish to uphold and foster him as a special son of the Roman Church, both through ourselves and through those in whose charity we have the fullest confidence. Accordingly, the greater our confidence in your brotherhood, the more earnestly we appeal to you for his protection and favour, asking by apostolic letters that, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, you hold him and his people particularly commended to you; and, if any bitterness has arisen, that you forgive it for love of us, and henceforth show yourself so kindly toward them that they may be freed from the assaults of evil men under the shelter of your protection, and we may be bound to give thanks to your brotherhood on their account.

Given at Segni, 14 Kalends of February [19 January].

CDLXXXII. Rescript to Hugh, abbot of Saint-Remigius.—That he assist the needs of the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu. (1152, 21 January.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropol. Rem.*, II, 315.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot, and the monks of Saint-Remigius at Reims [Col. 1500A], greeting and apostolic blessing.

How greatly your abbot of venerable memory loved the religious brethren of Mont-Dieu and took care to exercise works of piety toward them has, we believe, not faded from your memory; nor is it unknown to us. Therefore, as you are the sons of so great a man in name, you wish also to prove yourselves such in affection and deed: cling more diligently to his good customs and their preservation, and devote yourselves with all charitable zeal especially to this work, so holy and praiseworthy. We therefore earnestly ask your beloved community, and exhort you with a parent's affection, that, for the love of Him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:6, 9), and for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, you love these aforesaid sons of yours with your whole heart. [Col. 1500B] And since, the more arduous the life they have chosen, the less they are entangled in secular affairs and the more they are exposed to many needs, attend to their aid and support in such a manner, open to them the bowels of mercy in such a manner, and supply them with the desired consolations of charity in such a manner, that we may be bound to commend your love because of the performance of pious deeds, and that you may furnish to all who learn of it the proof of living experience of how brightly charity shines in your hearts.

Moreover, to you, sons, as you hasten under a prelate's guardianship toward the homeland of life, we command by apostolic letters that you humbly render honour and reverence to our aforesaid son Hugh, whom divine clemency has at this time chosen to appoint as your abbot, as to a father and the ruler of your souls; and that you submit the necks of your pledged obedience to his salutary counsels and commands. Thus, by his diligence, he may, with the Lord's gift, profitably administer the office entrusted to him; and by the diligence of your obedience, you together with him may attain the joys of the heavenly kingdom. [Col. 1500C] That you may better devote yourselves to the matters which you must undertake, we have sent letters on your behalf for your support to our venerable brothers Samson, archbishop of Reims, and the bishop of Troyes; and, with the Lord's help, we shall hereafter take care to provide for your welfare with diligent concern.

Given at Segni, 12 Kalends of February [21 January].

CDLXXXIII. Fragment of a privilege to William, dean, and the canons of Vienne (of the Allobroges).—It confirms for them all the privileges and possessions of the Church of Vienne, enumerating among other things “Pupetum with its appurtenances; one third of the coinage of Vienne; the township called Conveniacum with its church and appurtenances; Charentonia with Chomondum; the borough called Villa; the estate of Saint-Clarus; the church of Reventinum; Saint-Victor; Saint-Peter of Sessiacum; the estate of Faramundus; the church of Saint-Genesius; Mount Solomon.”

[Col. 1500D]

Thus signed:

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

“MAKE FOR ME, O LORD, A SIGN FOR GOOD.”

[Col. 1501A] I, Vivarius, bishop of Tusculum. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Calixtus. I, Manfred, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina. I, Ambert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Julius, of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Pastor. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Clement. I, Roland, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saint George. I, Rodulf, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in the Seven Solar [churches; uncertain expansion]. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelus. I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico.

[Col. 1501B] (1152, 26 January. Given at *Eugenni* [read: Segni].)

[Joannes a Bosco, *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, left xystus, p. 83.]

CDLXXXIV. To the prelates, counts, and barons established throughout Germany.—That they assist Emperor Conrad in his Italian expedition. (1152, 27 January.)

[MARTEN, *Collect.*, II, 510.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops, and beloved sons the counts and barons established throughout Germany, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as two commandments of charity were chiefly established by God the ruler for the salvation of the human race, so likewise two powers have been established by him through which this world is governed: namely, the sacred authority of pontiffs and the imperial power. If these two agree well with one another and stand in the integrity of their own honour, religion is preserved secure and sacred to God in the holy Church, and the Christian people are beneficially governed both by the strength of justice and by the restraint of equity. [Col. 1501C] We have no doubt that it is known to all of you that our dearest son Conrad, king of the Romans, has determined at this time, by the Lord's grant, to come with a strong expedition to the royal city, relying upon your aid, in order to complete his honour, for the honour of God and the service of the Church, and for the vigour and exaltation of the whole kingdom. Since he is not sufficient for so arduous a work by himself [Col. 1501D], and his own strength does not suffice him, you ought zealously to render him service, according to your means, as to your prince. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord to gird yourselves manfully for the service of the kingdom and of our aforesaid son the king, and to prepare yourselves for that expedition with him in such a way that he may be able to make the intended journey with sovereign power, as befits so great a prince, and receive the fullness of his honour with joy and exultation; and that we, through the interceding merits of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, may receive with the desired fruit his arrival, which we await for the benefit of the Church and kingdom and for the salvation of the Christian people.

Given at Segni, 6 Kalends of February [27 January].

CDLXXXV. To the abbot of Réigny.—He appoints him judge in the controversy mentioned in the preceding letter. (1152, 28 January.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 661.]

[Col. 1502A]

We have committed to your discretion for hearing and determination the controversy known to be in dispute between our sons Pons, abbot of Vézelay, and G., abbot of La Chaise, concerning a tithe and the parochial right of a certain village belonging to the abbot of Vézelay himself, and concerning certain money which the same abbot of La Chaise is said to have borrowed from certain burgesses, G. and V. of Vézelay. We therefore command you by these present letters to summon both parties before you at a suitable place and time; and, after carefully hearing and fully examining the arguments on both sides [Col. 1502B], to decide the case by the mediation of justice.

Given at Segni, 5 Kalends of February [28 January].

CDLXXXVI. To the abbot of La Chaise.—Concerning the tithe which he had usurped at Vézelay, and the money he had borrowed. (1152, 28 January.)

[Same source.]

Our beloved son Pons, abbot of Vézelay, coming before us, complained of you: that you had violently taken from him a certain tithe and the parochial rights of the village of Prissy and unjustly retain them. He also complained that you refuse, contrary to reason, to return to his burgesses G. and V. of Vézelay the money which they are said [Col. 1502C] to have lent you. Since we are bound to all persons in the matter of their justice, we command you by these present letters to render justice concerning these matters to our beloved son, the abbot of Vézelay, in the presence of our beloved son S. [Stephen], abbot of Réigny. Therefore, when you have been summoned for this purpose by the same our son, the abbot of Réigny, you shall appear before him and accept and observe whatever he judges between you concerning this matter.

Given at Segni, 5 Kalends of February [28 January].

CDLXXXVII. To the bishop of Langres, etc.—Concerning the controversy of Pons, abbot of Vézelay, with the bishop of Autun. (1152, 29 January.)

[Same source, 658.]

[Col. 1502D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G. [GODEFREY], bishop of Langres, and to his beloved sons S. [STEPHEN], abbot of Réigny, and P. [PETER], abbot of Trinorc, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The case pending between our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Autun, and our beloved son Pons, abbot of Vézelay, could not be concluded by judgment in our presence, because our same brother said that he had certain witnesses who, worn out by old age or sickness, were unable to appear before us. Since, therefore, we have great confidence in your prudence and do not wish the case to be deprived on this account of its due conclusion, we command you by these present letters that, when requested by either party, you assemble together and go to the place where the witnesses can appear before you. Having received an oath from them, faithfully commit to writing whatever they testify concerning the same case. [Col. 1503A] When our aforesaid brother wishes to resume the case, transmit to our presence what has been reduced to writing and sealed by the impression of your seals. The form of the oath shall be this: “I, N., swear that I will disclose to you whatever truth I know concerning the case pending between Henry, bishop of Autun, and Pons, abbot of Vézelay; I will wholly conceal falsehood.”

Given at Segni, 4 Kalends of February [29 January].

CDLXXXVIII. To G., bishop of Langres.—That he excommunicate the count of Nevers unless he repents. (1152.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 654.]

[Col. 1503B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G. [GODEFREY], bishop of Langres, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that the cruelty and tyranny which the count of Nevers does not fear to exercise against the monastery of Vézelay, setting aside the fear of God, are known to you all the more because you are recognized as being nearer to him. Since that monastery has been recognized from its first foundation as the personal allod and patrimony of blessed Peter [Col. 1503C], we can neither endure nor ought to endure its destruction. And because we have great confidence in the prudence of your religious character, we command you by these present letters to confront the aforesaid count strictly and without long delay, so that he may restore in full the losses he has inflicted upon the monastery and leave that place in its peace and liberty. If he neglects to do this within thirty days after your admonition, go to a place from which it may come to the count's notice; gather religious and prudent men; light candles in the church; and, by our authority, pronounce a sentence of excommunication, without remedy of appeal, against his person and against the faithless burgesses of Vézelay. Throughout all his land, except for the baptism of infants [Col. 1503D] and penance for the dying, forbid the celebration of all divine offices. We further direct you, by your letters and on our behalf, to announce that this sentence is to be firmly observed by our venerable brothers P. [Peter], archbishop of Bourges, H. [Hugh], archbishop of Sens, and G. [Godfrey], bishop of Nevers, Henry, bishop of Autun, Henry, bishop of Troyes, and A. [Alan], bishop of Auxerre. For we have commanded them in other letters that, after your announcement, they shall cause the same sentence to be inviolably observed throughout their dioceses. Cause the letters which we sent to our aforesaid brothers, the bishops of Autun, Nevers, and Auxerre, to be presented to them by your messengers.

CDLXXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Bremet. (1152, 9 February.)

[*Hist. patriae Monum.*, *Chart.*, I, 797, from an authentic twelfth-century copy in the Turin archives; cat. 41, m. 1, no. 2 (D. P.).]

[Col. 1504A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAYNALD, abbot of Bremet, and the brethren to be regularly appointed after him, in perpetuity.

Established by the Lord's ordering in the government of the Apostolic See, we ought diligently to foster religious persons and, with religious care, those institutions belonging to the right of blessed Peter and specially pertaining to the Roman Church, by the protection of the Apostolic See.
