Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, … we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of blessed memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Bremet, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree … that all possessions and goods which that monastery now holds by the authority of our predecessors, or may hereafter acquire, God being propitious, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have judged it proper to specify the following by their proper names:

In the diocese of Pavia, the church of Saint Peter at Lomello; in the castle of Saint Saviour, the church of Saint Cecilia; [Col. 1504C] at Porciato, the church of Saint Saviour; at …, the church of Saint Alexander; in the diocese of Vercelli, at Pollicino, the church of Saint Mary; on Mount Nascio, the church of Saint Michael; at Bazola, the church of Saint Agatha; at Gabiano, the church of Saint Mary with its court; at Corneliano, the church of Saint Peter with its court; in the diocese of Asti, the church of Saint Peter of Nasto; at Morotum, the church of Saint Quiricus; at Clusa, the church of Saint Andrew; at Vulpilie, the church of Saint John; at Duodecimo, the church of Blessed Mary; at Casteggio, the church of Saint Quiricus and the church of Saint Maurice; the church of Saint Mary of Fubalnis …; likewise, the church of Saint Peter at Nizolasco [Col. 1504D], and the church of Saint Dalmatius; in the diocese of Ventimiglia, the church of Saint Mary of Dolceacqua and the church of Saint Lucy; in Campo, the church of Saint Margaret; in the diocese of Turin, the church of Saint Peter of Pollencio with its county, and the church of Saint George with its court; in Castro Sigifredi, the church of Saint Mary; at Cavalario, the church of Saint Peter with its court and the church of Saint Michael; at Paguo, the church of Saint Peter, the church of Valtinasco, and the church of Saint Firminus; at Villario, the church of Saint Andrew; at Suppunito, the church of Saint Peter and the parish church of Saint John; at Nodone, the church of Saint Lawrence and the church of Saint George; in the city of Turin, the church of Saint Andrew and the church of Saint Anilius; at [Col. 1505A] Gunzono, the church of Saint Peter and the church of Dalmatius with its court; at Moira, the church of Saint Mary; at Novalicio, the church of Saint Peter; at Ripeta, the church of Saint Peter; at Masio, the church of Saint Dalmatius; at Rupe, the church of Saint Alban and the chapel of Saint Mary; at Collegio, the church of Saint Christopher; near Campo Merleti, the church of Saint George and the church of Juvenalis; in the borough of Novalesi, the chapel of Saint Stephen; in the diocese of Maurienne, the church of Lance and the church of Villario; at Corberia, the church of Saint Peter; at Coria, the church of Saint Mary, the church of Saint Peter, and the church of Voclante; in the diocese of Geneva, at Villarie the church of Saint Mary and at Castillione the church of Saint Martin; [Col. 1505B] at Mauriniacum, the church of Saint Sulpicius; in the archdiocese of Nevers, the church at Murita; [a church?] at Planixia; and one church at Burniacum; in the archdiocese of Embrun, the church of Saint Maurice and the church of Saint Germanus; in the valley of the monastery of Briançon, the church of Saint Mary and Saint Peter with their chapels; in the city of Embrun, the church of Saint Mary of Actis; at Castro Falcone, the church of Saint Peter, the church of Saint Mary, the church of Saint Stephen, the church of Saint Michael, and the church of Saint Flavius; at Gauserio, the church of Saint Nicholas; at Rumulone, the church of Saint Peter and the church of Tenisi; in the archdiocese of Milan, the church of Saint Peter with its appurtenances; at Canobio, in the city [Col. 1505C] of Pavia, the church of Saint Gervasius; in the diocese of Gap, the church of Saint Peter of Ronuta; at Auriacum, the church of Saint John; at Faldene, the church of Saint Felix and the church of Mount Rovorco; in the valley of Ancilla, the church of Saint Martin; near Buxall, the church of Saint Julian, the church of Saint Mary, the church of Saint Lawrence, the church of Lain, and the church of Saint Bonitus, with the chapels belonging to them; at Cozbo, the church of Saint Peter with its chapels, the church of Aspere, the church of Saint Julian, the church of Salucia, and the church of Saint Relignus; at Ambella, the church of Saint Peter with its chapels; at Verano, the church of Saint Mary and Saint Peter with their chapels, and the church of Saint Mary of the Valley; in the diocese of Grenoble [Col. 1505D], the church of Saint Mary of Gartia, the church of Saint Desiderius and Saint Stephen, and the church of Naugerio, with tithes and the other appurtenances of the aforesaid churches.

But because that monastery pertains specially to the Roman Church, no archbishop, bishop, bishop [as printed], or any prelate may possess any grant in the aforesaid churches or their chapels, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. Moreover, no one at all may presume to demand tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. Nor may anyone interdict the aforesaid monastery of Bremet from divine offices without evident and reasonable cause. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place [Col. 1506A], or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any cunning of fraudulent procurement or by force; rather, you may freely elect an abbot, by common consent or by the decision of the sounder part, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, without anyone's opposition. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, and that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. We permit, moreover, by apostolic authority that baptism may be administered in those same churches. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to holy orders from whatever bishop, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See. Whatever other liberty is known by right to have been granted to your monastery, or to places belonging to it, by our predecessors, bishops of the Apostolic See, or by Catholic emperors, we likewise grant by the page of this present decree and confirm by the assurance of our favour. [Col. 1506B]

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions or goods, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the page of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third admonition, does not make amendment through suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.—Fare well.

[Col. 1506D] I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, G.G., priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Mainfred, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. I, Aribert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.

Done at Sigora, by the hand of Boson, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of February [9 February], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord's Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

I, Master Jacob, notary of the imperial court, [Col. 1507A] saw and read the authentic original of this copy, and it contained neither more nor less. It was sealed with the bull of Pope Eugenius III, and I subscribed it. (There follows the authentication of other notaries.)

CDXC. He receives the monastery of Heidenheim into his protection and grants it various privileges. (1152, 9 February.)

[FALKENSTEIN, *Cod. diplom. antiq. Nordgav.*, 33.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ADELbert [Note: [Col. 1507D] Adelbert. This Adelbert was the second abbot of Heidenheim after Wunibald. See vol. II of *Antiquitates Nordgaviae*, chap. 4.], abbot of the monastery of Saint Willibald at Heidenheim, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The care of the pastoral office has been entrusted to us by God for this purpose: that we should labour to establish religion pleasing to God and preserve it, once established, with exact diligence. Nor is there any doubt that, if we graciously comply with the just petitions of God's servants, we find the merciful Lord ready to meet our own needs. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, you who, at our command, have humbly moved to the aforesaid place for the restoration of the observance of uprightness and religion: we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive that monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been restored by you in that place according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. [Col. 1507C] Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the monastery now justly and canonically possesses there, or may in future acquire, God being propitious, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors.

Moreover, no one may presume to exact from you tithes on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. We also grant free burial in that place, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict [Col. 1507D], saving, however, the right of the mother church. [Note: [Col. 1507D] For the various meanings in which the word *justitia* (“right”) is commonly used, see, among others, Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*; here it denotes the right inherent in anyone in his own person; more specifically, the right belonging to the parish priest in the mother church. See Du Cange.] Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any cunning of fraudulent procurement or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder [reading perhaps to be supplemented: “father” or “part”], in accordance with the Lord and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall provide to be elected. We prohibit any secular person from presuming to conduct legal proceedings or maintain a dwelling within the enclosure of that monastery, lest an occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of God's servants. [Col. 1508A]

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and religious integrity they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the page of this our enactment, rashly attempts to act against it, let that person be admonished a second or third time. If that person does not make amendment through suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment [Col. 1508B] for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But may the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve what is right for that place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Umatus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Manfred, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. [Col. 1508C] I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of Pastor, have subscribed. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Rudolph, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelus, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, by the hand of Boson, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of February [9 February], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord's Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXCI. He commends Adelbert, abbot of Heidenheim, to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, and Burchard, bishop of Eichstätt, that they assist him in every way. (1152, February.)

[Same source, p. 131.]

[Col. 1508D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to EBERHARD, bishop of Bamberg, and BURCHARD, bishop of Eichstätt, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Blessed be the Lord and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who through your care and diligence, and in accordance with our admonition and the desire of our wish, has deigned to restore in the church of Heidenheim the observance of uprightness and religion pleasing to God. He has beneficially provided our beloved son Adelbert, bearer of these letters—indeed, as you affirm, a worthy man and of good reputation—as abbot and overseer in that place, so that where, through the demands of sins, the evil of every enormity and impurity long prevailed, there may henceforth flourish anew the regular order and the innocence of holiness, and service fragrant with a sweetness pleasing to God may be offered. Therefore, beloved brothers in Christ and most diligent fellow-workers in the cultivation of the supreme householder, we urge the zeal of your brotherhood by these present letters, and exhort and admonish you in the Lord, that the gift begun through zeal in the aforesaid church may not fail but always grow from good to better. [Col. 1509B] Hold our aforesaid son Adelbert the abbot particularly commended to you; for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, provide him strength and aid for the rebuilding and improvement of that church; and cause the money collected for the restoration of that place to be delivered into his hand and that of his brethren. Strive also to remove from that place the openly concubinary clerics who have their dwellings in the monastery itself.

CDXCII. He earnestly commends Adelbert, abbot of Heidenheim, and his brethren to Count Gerhard of Eichstätt. (1152, February.)

[FALREINSTEIN, *Cod. diplom. antiq. Nordgav.*, p. 32.]

[Col. 1509C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman GERHARD, count of Eichstätt, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is recognized as belonging to the diligence of noble and Catholic princes to love religious persons and foster their place out of regard for devotion, so that by such zeal they may be able to please their Creator, the Lord Jesus Christ, and deserve to attain the salvation of their souls. Therefore we particularly commend to your nobility our beloved son Adelbert, abbot of Heidenheim, and his brethren, who have humbly moved to that place at our command; asking you for the salvation of your soul and admonishing you for the remission of your sins that you love and honour them, and support and defend them from the attacks of evil men.

CDXCIII. He commands Adelbert, advocate of the monastery of Heidenheim, to support Adelbert, abbot of this monastery, and protect him from attacks. (1152, February.)

[Same source.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADELbert, advocate of the Church of Heidenheim, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Adelbert [Col. 1510A], abbot of Saint Wunibald, coming before us, reported very much good concerning you: that you kindly support and love him and his brethren, and provide him aid and counsel for restoring the state of religious life in that place. Since we know this to be pleasing to almighty God and most beneficial to the salvation of your soul, we admonish and exhort you with paternal affection in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of your sins, that, like a good guardian, you protect and defend him from the attacks wrongfully brought against him.

CDXCIV. To the archbishops of Rouen, Reims, and Sens, etc.—On behalf of the Church of Beauvais. (1152, 11 February.)

[MARTEN, *Collect.*, II, 632.]

[Col. 1510B] EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops of Rouen [Hugh], Reims [Samson], and Sens [Hugh], and the bishops of Paris [Theobald], Amiens [Theodoric], Noyon [Baldwin], Senlis [Theobald], and Soissons [Joscelin], greeting and apostolic blessing.

In preserving and distributing ecclesiastical resources, the more careful vigilance must be exercised because they have been gathered solely through the zeal of worthy men, in order that both the ministers of the Church may be supported by them, the needs of the indigent relieved, and church buildings repaired. Yet contrary to this, the Church of Beauvais is compelled to allot no small portion of its resources—which it ought to expend for the aforesaid purposes—to certain military persons, contrary to secular laws, canonical sanctions, and the decrees of the holy Fathers. For certain men who formerly held the episcopal see in that church, taking no care either to provide for their successors or for the needs of the poor, unlawfully granted to certain knights certain money-benefices, payable annually from the episcopal household; and by these the church itself is burdened to no small degree even now. Hence the venerable brother Henry, bishop of that place, prompted by the duty of his office and wishing to provide both for the freedom of the Church entrusted to him and for the need of the poor who ought to be supported from its goods, [Col. 1510D] acting on our advice and that of certain wise men, withheld the aforesaid benefices and denied them to those knights who had been accustomed unlawfully to receive them. But they, paying heed neither to the peril of their souls nor to the burden upon the Church of Beauvais, refuse to desist from their unlawful receipt of these same benefices. Indeed, some of them have inflicted many losses upon our aforesaid brother and, with reckless audacity, threaten him with still greater ones hereafter.

Therefore, since the chief concern of prelates of churches ought to be that disturbers of the Church be restrained from their presumptions, at least by the force of justice, by the authority of these present letters we command you strictly: against those known to have inflicted losses upon our aforesaid brother, and likewise against those who hereafter presume to inflict them, unless, having been sternly warned by you, they correct their rashness by suitable satisfaction within one month after your warning, pronounce a sentence of excommunication, and a sentence of interdict upon their lands; and cause that same sentence to be observed inviolably until they repent of their offences and render fitting satisfaction to our aforesaid brother. But because in cases of this kind certain persons commonly raise an appeal as a refuge against canonical punishment, thereby to foster their malice, if any one of these men appeals to the Apostolic See on this matter, nevertheless pronounce the aforesaid sentence against him and his land, and observe it firmly.

[Col. 1511B] Given at [Note: [Col. 1511D] Here a scribal error appears to have crept in through the copyist’s carelessness, for all those letters on behalf of the Church of Beauvais were issued on the same day, namely at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.] Segni, on the third Ides of February.

CDXCV. To Henry, bishop of Beauvais.—Concerning the church of Ruricourt. (Year 1152, February 11.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 638.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais, greeting and apostolic blessing.

How the church of Ruricourt [Note: [Col. 1512D] The church of Ruricourt, dedicated to St Martin, is a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, of the Gallican congregation, in the diocese of Beauvais; its abbatial estate is today possessed by the Fathers of the Society of Jesus.], although in former times it flourished in wealth and religious observance, has now through the negligence of those dwelling there been considerably ruined in both respects, has reached us through the reports of very many persons. We grieve all the more because it is fitting that we should apply ourselves with more earnest zeal to founding religious houses and preserving religious institutions. Therefore, because at the final judgment we fear that an account will be required of us if, through any lukewarmness, we leave uncorrected what we see needs correction in the churches entrusted to us, by these present letters we command your brotherhood to establish there religious brethren of canonical order, who may restore in that place the observance of religion acceptable to God and hold authority over the same place in both temporal and spiritual matters. We wish you to do this with such diligence that neither an appeal nor the intervention of any support may appear to hinder your zeal from carrying out this our command.

Given at Segni, on the third Ides of February.

CDXCV *bis*. Confirmation of all the possessions and liberties of the monastery of Rohr, of the Regular Canons of St Augustine in the diocese of Regensburg. (Year 1152, February 13.)

[HUND., *Metropol. Salisburg.*, III, 255.]

[Col. 1511D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son EBERHARD, provost of the church of Rohr, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may swiftly attain its effect. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, over which by God’s ordinance you are known to preside; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We likewise confirm to you, and through you to the church itself, all estates, vineyards, houses, building-plots, and other things that Henry, archbishop of Regensburg, has justly granted to your church out of devotional regard. [Col. 1512B] Furthermore, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that place according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall there be preserved inviolate for all time. In the parish churches which you hold, you shall choose priests and present them to the bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they render account to the bishop for the care of the people, while showing to you due subjection in temporal matters.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of St Callistus, has subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus, have subscribed. Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia, has subscribed.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXCVI. Privilege for the Church of Coventry, at the request of Walter, bishop. (Year 1152, February 14.)

[*Monasticon Anglic.*, III, 231.]

[Col. 1513A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUALTERUS, bishop of Coventry, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Placed, by the Lord’s ordinance, upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brother bishops with sincere charity in the Lord and preserve for the churches entrusted to them by God their rightful due. For it is equitable and reasonable that those known to be more devoted to blessed Peter and his Apostolic See, and who desire to be cherished under the patronage of the most holy Roman Church, should be nourished at the breasts of that pious mother and heard in their reasonable petitions. Therefore, beloved brother in Christ Walter, . . . . . in duly meeting your just desires with kindness, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of Coventry, over which by God’s ordinance you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names: [Col. 1513C] in the county of Stafford, Lichfield with its forests; part of Cannock; Cunifield with its assarts—which King Stephen of the English is known to have granted by reasonable provision to your predecessor Bishop Roger and his successors, and to have confirmed by the safeguard of his writing; Hints; Tibbington with its appurtenances; Haywood with its forest and all its appurtenances; Berchlewych with its wood and appurtenances; Brendam with Haye, its forest, and its appurtenances; Eccleshall with its forest and appurtenances; Sesteford with its appurtenances; the church of Penkridge with its appurtenances; the church of Stafford with its appurtenances; the church of Gnosall with its appurtenances; and the churches of Armitage [Atrewas] and Bromley with their appurtenances. In the county of Warwick: Chedelesont, Ychintuna, Chechelesbroc, and Caldecote, with all their appurtenances. In the county of Derby: Sallao and Bobendon with their appurtenances. In the county of Shropshire: Bettona, Prees, and Languenarum with their appurtenances; and the church of St Chad with its appurtenances. In the county of Chester: Trovam, Burtonam, Ferendonam, Bancheberiam, Wippenberiam, and Suttonam with their appurtenances. At Droitwich, two measures of salt yearly; in the suburb of Chester, the church of St John with its appurtenances and the village called Forieta; within the walls of Chester, four dwelling-houses; likewise in Staffordshire, Alacastona with its appurtenances.

Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Paschal of holy memory, we confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity the episcopal see at Coventry which he granted to your predecessors. Further, let the monks living in the monastery of blessed Mary at the same place always remain under the obedience of you or your successors, according to the terms of the agreement made in our presence between you and the monks of that place; and let them perform the due offices of divine worship in that episcopal church, as is believed to have been instituted in the Church of Canterbury by the blessed bishop Augustine of old, and established by the declaration of our most holy father and predecessor Gregory, doctor of the Catholic Church. Nor shall it be lawful for any of your successors whatsoever to remove men of monastic discipline from that church, or to take from them the possessions and other goods offered and acquired for the monks’ maintenance by Leofric, earl of illustrious memory, founder of that monastery, or by other faithful persons, or which, by the Lord’s ordering, may hereafter be offered. In addition, we decree that whatever the privileges of our predecessors Innocent and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, contain contrary to the terms of the aforesaid agreement shall be wholly without force.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Given at Segni [*Sing.*; *Signiae*], through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXCVII. To Bernard, bishop of Saintes.—That he should permit a new church to be built. (Year 1152, February 20.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 668.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother BERNARD, bishop of Saintes, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, appearing before us, showed us in his petition that the church of St Mary of La Rochelle, which is known to belong by right to his monastery, cannot contain the multitude of people who have newly come to live there; he therefore desires to build another church within its parish and humbly sought in this our favourable assent. Therefore, just as no effect ought to be granted to those who ask for unjust things, so we ought to respond with gracious consent to the desires of just petitioners. By these present letters we command and enjoin the charity of your brotherhood that you in no way hinder our aforesaid son the abbot from building a new church within the boundaries of the parish of the aforesaid church.

Given at Segni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March.

[Col. 1515B] This, however, took place in the year 1153 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

CDXCVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Souvigny. (Year 1152, February 20.)

[*Bullar. Clun.*, p. 62.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior of the monastery of Souvigny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which by the Lord’s bounty we preside, and the bond of fraternal charity exhort us to accede to the just desires of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable petitions. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting kindly assent to your just requests and following the example of our predecessor Pope Urban II of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves your monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names: in the diocese of Bourges, [Col. 1515D] the monastery of St Maurice; the chapel of Bourbon; the churches of Noyant, Chastellon, Colondan, Mariniac, Cressanges, Curtiliis, Bocheron, Bétiaq, Argiranda de Franciis; the churches of Lemelia, Madero, Vannat, Burginolio, Avalon, Cappis, comital Souvigny, Sardirliac, Bussecrias, Ferrerias; the chapel of Nicio; the churches of St Placidus, St Hilary, and St Marcellus; the church of Chirac; the monastery of Columbariense; the church of Monive; the chapel of Cella; and the churches of Dorequo, Commentry, Vordero, Feblineas, and Noro. In the diocese of Clermont: the church of Brenac, St Mazirian, St Martin; two chapels of Schola; the chapels of Sintrac, Genziac, Plaidac, Ledac, and Stoliac; [Col. 1516A] the monastery of La Ferté; the church of Altaripa; the chapels of Vernolio, Longa Prata, and Trebenno; the churches of Monasterio, Quintiniac, Melaro, Rungeriis, and Graniculis; the chapel above the castle of Montaigut; the church of St Julian of Vallibus; the churches of Olouzac, Souvigny of Teudonis, Conis, Marciac; two churches at Bocciac; the churches of Suspiriis, Briceolis, Chimiliac; and the chapel of Fagia. In the castle of Nobrio: two churches and the New Church. In the diocese of Autun: the chapel of Molinis and the church of Aversino. In the diocese of Nevers: the monastery of Champvoux with its appurtenances; the chapel of La Ferté; the church of Cantaneto; the monasteries of Montpied, Martio, Genestinis, Validomano, Novavilla, and Adiac; and the chapel of St Genesius. In the diocese of Limoges: the church of Manciac with all their appurtenances.

Moreover, following in the footsteps of that same predecessor of ours, we decree that, on account of a general interdict of the parish, the aforesaid monastery shall not cease from divine offices; rather, with doors closed, the excommunicated and interdicted excluded, and the voice subdued, you may celebrate the divine offices. Nor may anyone whatsoever within the bounds of the monastery itself or the adjoining village make an assault, plunder, or seize any person. We also decree that the burial-place of that site shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while nevertheless preserving the right of the mother church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, obedience in all things to the abbots of Cluny, and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops in the aforesaid chapels. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, G., cardinal priest of the title of St Callistus. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Julius, cardinal priest of St Marcellus. [Col. 1517A] I, Umbaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement. I, Roland, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark. I, Gerdredus, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Centius, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Agro.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1151 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Eugenius III.

CDXCIX. To Peter, abbot of Cluny, and the monks of Cluny.—He rebukes them for ingratitude and negligence because they did not restrain the monks of Gigny, violently hostile to the brethren of Miroir. (Year 1152, March 14.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 471.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot, and the whole convent of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Made drunk,” as Jeremiah says, “with wormwood and bitterness and surrounded with gall,” we are compelled to send you such letters as affection supplies and the greatness of our grief counsels. For a sad and mournful subject compels us to break forth in a sad utterance, and forces pains that cannot be contained in our heart, though late, to come forth openly. How greatly the Church of Cluny, both in its head and its members, has been loved by the Apostolic See from the time of its foundation until now; how greatly it has been helped in its necessities and always advanced to greater things—although you have consigned this to forgetfulness, it has not escaped our knowledge, and almost the whole Western Church acknowledges it. And, what we cannot say without deep sorrow, we see our prayers, exhortations, and commands brought into contempt by many among you, so that we may say with the prophet: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2).

How great a tyranny your brethren of Gigny have for many years now exercised violently against our own vitals, the brethren of Miroir, [Note: [Col. 1517D] This letter has the flavour of St Bernard’s style.] has clearly come to your notice—unless you are pretending not to know. [Note: [Col. 1517D] The cause of the dispute was the remission of tithes which Pope Innocent II had granted to the Cistercians, in order to repay St Bernard for his support of Innocent’s claim to the papacy. This stirred bishops, clerics, abbots, monks, and even laymen whom it could reach against them. See the letters of Peter the Venerable, nos. 33, 34, and 35 of book I, written in 1132.] And how earnestly our concern has sought to restrain their madness is demonstrated most plainly to right-minded people by the worsening of the evil. For after plundering orphans and despoiling the poor, their belly was not yet satisfied; but, after the property of the very granges had been seized and Christ’s servants savagely slaughtered with barbarian ferocity, so that nothing would remain to them, they have now turned into a wilderness of solitude that very little house in which Christ’s members lived in service of their Head. They burned its walls, carried off its spoils, and drove its inhabitants from their territory with swords and clubs. Alas, in this world the poorest servant is granted lodging beside his king’s palace, and a beast of burden rests beneath one roof with its master; but our own vitals were not permitted to establish their dwelling beside your brethren, nor even to attend divine worship in the same diocese, much less in the same village.

Moreover, if from earlier times your diligence had been directed to restraining them, and if our patience had not been abused for so long, amendment could neither have been delayed so greatly nor could our members have been torn so grievously. But because you regarded both your own offences and our miseries with a dissembling—or rather mocking—eye, a deed has occurred in our days which no one will believe when it is told, and whose like has not yet happened in Israel. Therefore, since neither does a mother forget her children nor can we fail to feel the pain of our own vitals, because you disdained to oppose such great evils, we now at least admonish you to be concerned for their correction. Since we cannot impose a punishment commensurate with so great a crime, what has fallen away must at least be restored to its proper state. Accordingly, by the authority of these present letters we command you, if you have confidence in our and the Apostolic See’s aid in your causes, to ensure that all things taken from our aforesaid sons of Miroir are restored, the losses inflicted fully repaired, and satisfaction for such great evils made in such a manner that you may be proved not merely in word but in deed and truth to grieve over the contempt shown to the Apostolic See and our affliction. Otherwise, know that the gravest vengeance will be taken upon you, so that you may at least be compelled unwillingly to render prompt obedience to our commands and to think more carefully of restraining those among you who walk disorderly.

Given at Segni, on the day before the Ides of March.

D. To Hugh [Humbert], archbishop of Lyons.—That under threat of excommunication he ensure the restoration to the brethren of Miroir of goods taken by the men of Gigny. (Year 1152, March.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 472.]

[Col. 1518D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH [corrected to HUMBERTO], archbishop of Lyons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The wickedness of those who at Gigny profess monastic life only in name but blaspheme it by the abomination of their deeds, and the extent to which they have for many years raged with madness against our beloved sons of Miroir and their goods, has come more fully to the notice of your brotherhood because the places themselves lie nearer to you. Certainly, both we and our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory have used great diligence that they might return to their senses and cease troubling our aforesaid sons. But they, full of filth, like ashes-baked bread that is not kept, confounding right and wrong alike, have kept before their mind’s eye neither the danger to their souls, nor the disgrace of their order, nor human respect, nor fear of God. Rather, turned into a crooked bow and following the desire of their heart, even after the agreement made between them through our dearest sons Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and Peter, abbot of Cluny, [Note: [Col. 1519C] We know that this agreement was negotiated from St Bernard’s Letter 283 to Eugenius; by what arrangement it was made we do not know. “We met,” he says, “at Cluny with the men of Gigny in hope of peace; much labour was expended for it, nothing achieved. For the whole labour of four days was followed at last only by the collapse of hope. In accordance with the tenor of your letters, reparation of losses and restoration of what had been offered were demanded; but in vain. Much was thought due from them, because they had done much harm: indeed, an accounting was made of more than thirty thousand solidi lost, since one abbey alone—to avoid ranging through every item—had been wholly destroyed. Yet we were prepared to relinquish much of such great losses; whereas they offered so little that the venerable abbot of Cluny, who laboured more affectionately than effectively to restore peace, did not judge it worthy of report. Thus no settlement resulted, because a ridiculous reparation was then offered. They said: ‘Certain malicious men among ours did all the harm; what has that to do with us? Let them see to it themselves.’ That too was ridiculous. It was clear throughout the whole region that this crime had been perpetrated by men of the Church; it was also clear that certain monks had been present and that all had assented. For up to this time we have heard that not even one person opposed the evildoers. Finally, the lord abbot himself openly refuted and disproved evasions of this kind, affirming that the Church rightly demanded back what was known to have been lost through the Church. Your final intervention is awaited in a matter which has been proved more than sufficiently to be capable of amendment only by a strong hand.”] seized by their accustomed fury, they added worse deeds to their earlier ones. Exercising barbarous rage against our aforesaid sons, both in person and through certain servants of the devil whose aid they begged, they did not hesitate with devilish audacity to attack their persons, plunder their goods, overthrow their houses, and perpetrate against them other indications of fury.

Although they have long deserved to be cut off from the body of the Church by the apostolic axe, we have endured them until now, believing that at some time they would return to their senses and cease persecuting our aforesaid sons. [Col. 1519C] But because they have now so rotted in their own dung that, unless Jesus utters a loud cry, there is no hope that they can in any way be drawn out from the stench of the tomb, by these present letters we command your brotherhood sternly to admonish them to restore to our aforesaid sons everything taken away, repair the losses inflicted, make full satisfaction for their injuries, and cease henceforth from harassing them.

[Note: [Col. 1520D] In the year 1155 an agreement was at last sanctioned on these terms: the brethren of Miroir paid to the lord of Cluny, through the mediation of Lords Eraclius, archbishop of Lyons, and Henry, bishop of Winchester, eleven thousand solidi of Lyons currency in respect of seventeen thousand solidi with which the aforesaid Cluniac house had ordered them of Miroir to be invested. Concerning all the tithes demanded by the men of Gigny, it was agreed that the brethren of Miroir should pay them sixty solidi of Lyons currency annually, and that in respect of these there should remain perpetual peace between them, etc. In the Sobusian Library, p. 113.] But if within twenty days after this warning they disdain to carry all these things into effect, we forbid from that point divine offices in the place itself and in all its cells and churches. We subject William the prior, Richard the hospitaler, Pons the dean, Hugh, William Cotarellus, and the others who are the leaders of this wickedness, together with all who consent to this wrongdoing, to excommunication; adding that they and those who presume to give them counsel or assistance shall be bound by the same sentence. When requested by our beloved son the abbot of Miroir to promulgate this sentence, you shall meet with our venerable brother Hugh (corrected to Humbert), archbishop of Besançon; and, an assembly of the church having been gathered and candles lit, you shall publicly announce this sentence and command that it be observed by all without contradiction.

DI. Privilege for the Church of Treviso. (Year 1152, May 3.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 511.]

[Col. 1520B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BONIFACE, bishop of Treviso, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we assent to the just desires of our brethren and lend an ear to their reasonable petitions, since, although unworthy, by the Lord’s disposition we are seen to sit as cultivators and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, beloved brother in Christ Boniface, bishop, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of that prince of the apostles and of ourselves the Church of Blessed Peter of Treviso, [Col. 1520C] over which, by God’s authority, you preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors, and through you to that same Church.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the church of Saint Mary of Asolo, with the castle, estate, and all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary of Muliane, with all its appurtenances; the consecration of the monastery of Saint Peter of Campreto; the parish church of Saint Mary of Montebelluna, with its castle and appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin of Cornuta, with fortress, estate, and appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Zeno of Ruvico, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Ciliano, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Balpago, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Cusignana, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Maurice of Stablucio, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Pauliano, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Romanus of Nigrisia, with castle, port, estate, and appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Maurus of Noenta, with [Col. 1521B] its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Peter of Piro, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Blaise of Caurillis, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Nicholas of Valio, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Lanzanigo, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Casale, with its appurtenances; the estate of Quarto, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Cassian of Paviliano, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Deso, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin of Tessaria, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Gervasius of Carpeneto, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Lawrence of Mestre, with castle, port, estate, and appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Theonistus of Burbiliago, with castle, port, estate, and appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Zulianigo, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint [—] of Zumiliana, [Col. 1521C] with its appurtenances; the parish church of Midranis, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Campo San Pietro, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Rustica, with castle, village, and appurtenances; the parish church of Aurelia, with village and its appurtenances; the castle of Stiliano, with village and its appurtenances; the parish church of Martiliago, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Zero, with its appurtenances; the parish church of the Three Basilicas, with castle, village, and appurtenances; the castle of Saint Ambrose, with church and appurtenances; the castle of Scorzadis, with village and appurtenances; the parish church of Quinto, with castle, village, and appurtenances; the castle of Settimo, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Postoima, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint John of Istruna, [Col. 1521D] with castle, village, and appurtenances; the parish church of Albareto, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Silva Rotunda, with castle and its appurtenances; the castle of Resana, with village, forest, and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Pieve Nuova, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin of Lavoro, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Godigo, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Bessica, with its appurtenances; the castle of Rosio, with parish church and appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Thomas of Costis, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Zeno, with half the castle and its appurtenances; the fortress of Sumozio, with village and all its appurtenances; the parish church of Fonte, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary of Cavasio, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Petra [Col. 1522A] Rubea, with its appurtenances; likewise the toll of the city, the riverbank, and the port of Treviso, with every lawful jurisdiction over the waters from the place where the river Sile rises as far as the salt waters.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act contrary to it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall not make suitable satisfaction and amendment, let that person lose the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Hubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis, have subscribed. I, Manfredus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. [Col. 1522C] I, Aribertus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of the Shepherd, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Gerardus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Rodulphus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Septa Solis, have subscribed. I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## DII. He grants privileges to the monastery of Fitero. (1152, 11 May.) [Col. 1522D]

[MANRIQUE, *Cistercian Annals*, I, 416.]

## DIII. He confirms certain possessions of the monastery of Heilsbronn. (1152, 16 May—Segni.)

[HOCKER, *Supplement to the Heilsbronn Antiquities*, II, 75.]

## DIV. To Emperor Frederick—He congratulates him on his election, hoping that he will complete what Conrad had begun for the exaltation of the Church. (1152, 17 May.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 683.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, FREDERICK, illustrious king of the Romans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having graciously and honorably received the messengers of your eminent nobility and your letter, and having carefully considered both their faithful and prudent account and the most diligent examination of that letter, we have plainly learned that you, whose person has long been dear to us, were raised, after the death of your uncle Conrad, king of the Romans of revered memory, to the summit of royal rank by the common wish and unanimous consent of the princes. We receive this with all the greater exultation because, through the report of our beloved son O., priest-cardinal, and the receipt of your letter, we had already held a more certain hope of your ability. Therefore, rendering from our heart due thanks to God, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present, [Col. 1523B] because, through the ordering of divine clemency, we have learned that this has taken place so harmoniously in consequence of your vigor, we approve it with the gracious favor of the Apostolic See.

For we believe that the good firmly promised to us and to the Roman Church by your aforementioned uncle and predecessor will, with the Lord’s help, obtain the effect desired by us through the zeal of your noble devotion. We, indeed, are earnestly intent, with heavenly grace cooperating, upon laboring, as the duty of the office entrusted to us requires, for the increase of your honor and exaltation. Therefore, having taken counsel with our brethren, we have resolved shortly to send a legate from our side to your Serenity, through whom we intend to disclose our purpose and intention to your glory.

Meanwhile, [Col. 1523C] we earnestly exhort your royal dignity always to contemplate with the penetrating light of your mind the pattern of royal profession; and untiringly and always to render prompt and due justice and protection to the Church of God and ecclesiastical persons. Bring peace and justice without delay to widows, wards, orphans, and all the people subject to your rule, so that, guarded by your protection and defense in keeping with the eminence of royal dignity, they may rejoice in devoted obedience to you; and that you, for your royal solicitude, may deserve to receive glory among men and, from Him through whom kings reign, eternal life with the holy kings.

Given at Segni, the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

## DV. To Stephen, bishop of Metz—That he compel Count Henry of Salm to restore the cell of Asmingia, which he had taken from the abbot of Saint Michael on the Moselle. (1152, 24 May.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 473.]

[Col. 1523D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Metz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned from the complaint of our beloved son M[anegaud], abbot of Saint Michael, that Count H[enry] of Salm, your nephew, has newly occupied by force the cell of Asmingia, which that abbot and his predecessors had peacefully held for many years; [Col. 1524A] and that, having expelled the monks, he has carried off its tithes and revenues and introduced there a priest according to the judgment of his own will. Therefore, by these present letters, we command your brotherhood that, if these things have occurred as stated, you strictly admonish that same count to restore to the aforesaid abbot that cell itself together with everything he has taken away. If he refuses to do so, prohibit divine offices in that cell and strike him with a strict sentence. Yet, if he believes that some right belongs to him against our aforementioned son, he may subsequently obtain it through the mediation of justice.

Given at Segni, the ninth day before the Kalends of June.

## DVI. To Henry of Salm—He orders him to restore to the abbot of Saint Michael the cell of Asmingia, which he had taken away; otherwise he is to be punished by canonical vengeance. (1152, 24 May.)

[Ibidem, 473.]

[Col. 1524B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman [HENRY], count of Salm, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We had expected, son, that reports concerning your nobility would reach us that showed you concerned for the salvation of your soul and would more readily move us to love and assist you, should circumstances require it. We have received the complaint, brought before us by the beloved son, the abbot of Saint Michael, Manegaud, against you: that you invaded with [Col. 1524C] your men the cell of Asmingia, which he and his predecessors had peacefully held for many years; that after plundering its goods by blameworthy presumption and expelling the monks, you intruded there a priest according to the judgment of your own will. If this is true, we are disturbed all the more because we had feared such conduct all the less from your character.

Therefore, by these present letters we command your nobility to restore that same cell, together with everything removed from it, to our aforementioned son. If you believe that you have any right against him, you may obtain it, if you wish, through the mediation of justice. Otherwise, we wish you to know that we have commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Metz, Stephen, to exercise canonical vengeance against you.

Given at Segni, the ninth day before the Kalends of June.

## DVII. To the bishops of Metz, Verdun, and Toul—He commands them to restrain Count Rainald of Bar from harassing the church of Saint Michael and to compel restitution of what was taken, under penalty of ecclesiastical censure. (1152, 25 May.)

[Ibidem, 474.]

[Col. 1524D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren STEPHEN, bishop of Metz, ALBERO, bishop of Verdun, and HENRY, bishop of Toul, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more, as the charity of many grows cold, wicked men abound in bishoprics by divine judgment, the more diligently must you, who have obtained there the office of oversight and governance, oppose them in the power of the word of the Lord. We have recently received the grave complaint of our beloved son, Manegaud, abbot of Saint Michael, that Count Rainald harasses him and the church entrusted to him in many ways, does not cease to plunder its goods, and afflicts its people with unlawful exactions, forced labor, and oppression.

Therefore by apostolic letters we command you strictly to admonish that same count to desist from harassing our aforementioned son and his church, to restore to him what has been unjustly taken, to repair the damages inflicted, and henceforth not presume to burden his people with any undue exactions or services. But if he refuses to obey your admonitions, restrain him by ecclesiastical censure in such a manner that the aforesaid abbot shall not henceforth be compelled to appeal to us because of a failure of justice. [Col. 1525B]

Given at Segni, the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

## DVIII. Privilege for the Church of Trier. (1152, 27 May.)

[GUNTHER, *Rhenish-Moselle Diplomatic Code*, I, 334.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HILLIN, archbishop of Trier, and to his successors to be canonically promoted, in perpetuity.

Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See, although by virtue of the office of apostleship imposed upon us by God we are debtors to all churches, near and distant, and to the prelates of churches, [Col. 1525C] yet it is fitting that we devote a more watchful and more ready zeal of charity to those places and persons known to have adhered to the holy and apostolic Roman Church with more devoted and abundant familiarity and service.

Therefore, beloved brother in the Lord Hillin, archbishop, considering the devotion and sincere affection of the Church of Trier, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and the due goodwill shown toward blessed Peter, toward our predecessors, and toward ourselves by your predecessors, we apostolically confirm to you and your successors the dignities, honors, and liberties granted to that Church by our predecessors—John XIII, Benedict VII, Leo IX, Victor II, and Innocent, Roman pontiffs of happy memory—or by emperors or kings; and we strengthen them by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically holds, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. In particular, we confirm the castle called Tris, with its ban and appurtenances, which the noble Count Odo, with the assent and will of his wife Gertrude, Countess Palatine, reasonably bestowed upon the said Church. [Col. 1525D]

We further decree, as established by the holy Council of Chalcedon, that no king, emperor, advocate, ecclesiastical person, or secular person may seize or plunder the goods of deceased archbishops, priests, or other clerics of the Church of Trier. Rather, such goods shall be freely preserved for the purpose of electing the bishop, according to the direction of the steward and clergy. Moreover, for the greater reverence and dignity of the Church committed to you, we also grant you by apostolic authority the privileges, granted by our predecessors of apostolic memory to the archbishops of Trier and confirmed by authentic privileges, both of riding through the stations with the *naccus* [uncertain term] and of having the cross borne before you.

We also confirm to you and your successors the right which Conrad, king of the Romans of illustrious memory, or his predecessors, are known to have possessed in the abbey of Saint Maximin, and which the same Conrad conferred or restored to your predecessor Albero of good memory and, through him, to the Church of Trier, as is reasonably contained in that king’s charter of restitution and confirmation. [Col. 1526B] We further decree that the peace, concord, or settlement concluded between your aforesaid predecessor and the noble Henry, count of Namur, in the presence of the said king, through the reasonable mediation of our dearest son Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and the princes of the German kingdom, and confirmed by the charter of that king, shall remain valid and unshaken in future times, as is set forth below.

For the count, making satisfaction in every respect to the aforesaid archbishop, again swore fealty to him; and concerning the aforementioned abbey he renounced in favor of that archbishop every claim arising from it. Thus he obtained absolution from the archbishop and, excepting the castle of Manderscheid with its appurtenances, received his fief in its entirety. The same count also swore that he would neither rebuild Rodolfisberg nor help anyone to rebuild it. If he should presume to act contrary to these terms and should refuse within eighteen weeks to make suitable amends, he pledged his land into the archbishop’s hand in such a manner that thenceforth the fief-holders should freely receive and hold their fiefs from that land from [Col. 1526D] the archbishop.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations. Rather, all shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act contrary to it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall not make suitable satisfaction and amendment, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Bb., priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus. I, Hibaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis. I, Oct. [Octavianus], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint [Col. 1527B] Cecilia. I, Manfredus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina. I, Cencius, priest-cardinal of the title in Lucina. I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, Otto, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Rodulfus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Septa Solis. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo. I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in [Col. 1527C] Cosmedin. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gerardus, deacon-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## DIX. Privilege for the monastery of Himmerod. (1152, 27 May.)

[HONTHEIM, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, I, 563.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RANDULF, abbot of Claustrum, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity. [Col. 1527D]

To grant effect to just petitioners is required both by the force of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ request and truth does not oppose it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring graciously in assent with your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the Lord’s favor, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the place called Claustrum, in which the monastery itself is situated, with its appurtenances; the grange called Winterbach; Bellum-campum; Hemmenrod; Valles; the grange called Hart, situated in the territory of the estate of Altreie; land for three ploughs, which you reasonably acquired from Cono of Maleberg in Rodesbusch, with the consent of the noble Count Henry of Luxembourg; the land called Molbach; the vineyards you possess in the territory of Wittlich, Noviant, Maranch, and Kestene; likewise the vineyards you possess at Kemetham, Cuvernam, and Ludenesdorph. [Col. 1528B]

The rights of use which you possess in the territory of the village of Cordula: namely, fishing in the water of the Kile as far as the Moselle, and rights of use in woods and pastures, etc. The rights of use which you possess in the wood called Saint Simeon’s, which you reasonably acquired from Fulmar, formerly provost of Saint Simeon’s of good memory, and from his brethren and the other possessors of the same wood. The rights of use which you possess at both Lidiche [Upper and Lower] in woods and pastures. The rights of use of the estate of Wittlich and the estate of Altreie in woods and pastures; and fishing in the water of the Lesere; and the house which you possess in the city of Trier beside the chapel of Saint Sulpicius, with the part of the garden adjoining that house.

Moreover, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals, except only in those matters for which, by voluntary will, through the hand of our venerable brethren Albero, former archbishop of blessed memory, Hillin his successor, and the Church of Trier, you have established an annual payment: namely, from the grange of Winterbach, for everything which ought to be tithed, six pence to the cleric and six *maldera* of rye to the layman; from the grange of Hemmenrodt, six pence to the cleric. For all that you possess in the territory of the estate of Wittlich and that ought to be tithed: one *malder* of rye and another of oats to the cleric; but to him who possesses two parts of the tithing, twelve pence. From everything which you possess in the territory of Noviant and Maranch: [Col. 1528D] six pence to the cleric. From the vineyards you possess at Kestene: twelve pence to the cleric. From the vineyards you possess at Kemetam: twelve pence to the cleric. From the vineyards you possess at Ludenesdorph: four pence to the cleric and eight to the layman.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved unshaken and whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act contrary to it and, after a second or third warning, shall not correct such presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, GG., priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus. [Col. 1529B] I, Hubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis. I, Octavianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Manfredus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Sabina. I, Cencius, priest-cardinal in Lucina. I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Equitius. I, Otto, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Radulphus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Septa Solis. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo. [Col. 1529C] I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## DX. Privilege for the monastery of Wadegossen. (1152, 27 May.)

[HONTHEIM, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, I, 564.]

[Col. 1529D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WALFRAM, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Wadegozingen, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the canonical life.

> **Note [Col. 1529D]:** There still exists in the archiepiscopal archives his written undertaking by which Walfram promised obedience to Archbishop Adalbero; in that obedience he and his successors remain subject to the bishop of Trier even today.

It is fitting that apostolic protection should be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps the assault of any person’s rashness either turn them back from their purpose or weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring graciously in assent with your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, is known to have been instituted there by the Lord’s authority, shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Further, whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the Lord’s favor, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you [Col. 1530B] and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names:
