The allod called Wadegozingen, in which the church itself is situated, which the noblewoman Gisela, widow of Count Frederick of Saarbrücken, with the consent of her son Simon—reserving only the ministerials—granted to you free and unencumbered, with its demesnes, dwellings with their holdings, all their rights, male and female dependents, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, and every right which she had in that place, in such fashion that she reserved to neither herself nor any of her heirs any advocacy or anything of right or lordship, apart from the ministerials.

> **Note [Col. 1529D]:** It lies in a wooded region, not far from the river Saar, two Roman miles above Saarlouis, on the borders of Lorraine, in a not unpleasant retreat, almost upon the military road by which the Triboci are reached from [Col. 1530D] Trier.

The allod lying before the aforesaid allod, which you bought from Cono and his sons for nine talents; at Wilre, the allod which belonged to Guntrann and his brother, and likewise to Albero, namely in woods and fields; at Habechesthal, the allod which belonged to Herbo, and the adjoining allod at Bredebach, purchased from Stephen for ten talents; at Kinderbura, the allod which belonged to Gervalius and his heirs Gisebert and his brothers; at Onesheim, the allod which belonged to the noble Count Frederick, Renerus, Bero, and Dithmar; at Escheringa, the allod which belonged to that same Dithmar, and other holdings which you possess there; at Wopenswilre, the allod which belonged to Udo, his brothers, and his sister; the allod which belonged to Roricus and Hadelugis; [Col. 1530D] at Burgalba, the allod which belonged to Count Sigebert, in waters, woods, and meadows.

> **Note [Col. 1530D]:** Situated on Weavers’ Street.

At Sulzasita, in the diocese of Worms, the allod which belonged to Henry and his wife Hirzeche, together with the other fields you possess there; in the nearby village of Hetdenetheim, the allod which belonged to Burchard; the fields and vineyards which you possess at Lambeleshim; in the city of Trier, the court, house, and adjoining vineyard, [Col. 1531A] together with the other vineyards which you possess there; at Heseningen, one holding and Leima, which you hold from the church of Herbodesheim, subject to a rent of seven shillings to be paid each year by you and your successors to that church.

> **Note [Col. 1530D]:** Doubtless this is the one concerning which Emperor Henry IV speaks in his diploma of 1080. For the counts possessed, besides their office, also allodial estates acquired through the liberality of emperors by the solemn formula: “We have conveyed [it] into private ownership.” Struve, *On Imperial Allods*, §§ 9 and 53. Hence, in the course of time, entire counties became allodial. This is affirmed of the neighboring county of Saarwerden by Goeddeus IV, *Marburg Opinion* 37, and by the Nassau memorandum against the duke of Lorraine of 1664, in Gastellius, chapter 31, p. 861 ff.; Burgoldensis, *On the Institutes of Peace*, dissertation 31, p. 501. See Ludolf Symphor., I, p. 1495.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority all the liberty which Adalbero, formerly archbishop of Trier of good memory, granted to you and, through you, to your church; and we decree that it shall remain unimpaired in future times. Thus no one at all shall presume to seize the advocacy of that place; rather, only the archbishop of Trier who is in office from time to time shall be your advocate. Yet he shall divert none of your church’s goods to his own uses, nor trouble it by any burdens or exactions. [Col. 1531B] You shall humbly remain only in his obedience, and shall never be subject to any chorepiscopus or to any person whatsoever under the archbishop of Trier; nor shall you be compelled to render to such a person obedience, rent, or any service on the ground that your church is parochial—except only the six denarii which you owe each year to the church of Blessed Peter at Trier.

We further add that, in accordance with the grant of the aforementioned archbishop, you shall have free authority, saving the right of the mother church, to preach to, baptize, and bury those who of their own will resolve to be buried in your church, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any trick of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of them, shall judge according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine to be elected. The person elected shall be presented to the archbishop of Trier, to receive from him, if qualified, the care of souls and the grace of blessing. [Col. 1531C] Moreover, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved unshaken and unimpaired, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act contrary to it and, after a second or third warning, shall not correct such presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; [Col. 1532A] and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct and, before the supreme Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, B[...], cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Manfred, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina, have subscribed. [Col. 1532B] I, Oct[avian], cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Censius, cardinal-priest of the title in Lucina, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Equitius, have subscribed. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Ralph, cardinal-deacon of St. Lucy in Septa Solis, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. [Col. 1532C] I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Signia, by the hand of Boso, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### DXI. Privilege for the Abbey of Springiersbach. (1152, 28 May)

[GUNTHER, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, I, 338.]

[Col. 1532D] EUGENIUS III, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Springiersbach: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more religious men, abandoning earthly things, burn with a fuller longing for heavenly things, the more diligently ought we—though unworthy, to whom the care of the universal Church has been entrusted—to devote ourselves to their peace, and by apostolic authority remove whatever seems likely to disturb them in their purpose. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Hillin, archbishop of Trier, and wishing, as our office requires, to provide for your peace and that [Col. 1533A] of your successors, we establish by the authority of these present letters that the abbot for the time being of your church shall receive the pastoral care of the church of Keymetha solely from the hand of the archbishop of Trier. The archdeacon, however, shall claim no parochial right there and exercise no exaction there, save only the payment which, by ancient right, must be made to him every fourth year.

Moreover, through you we confirm to you and to your church the allod situated between the stream Helze and the stream Lisere, in vineyards, fields, meadows, woods cultivated and uncultivated, which Sigefrid of Hifenburch and his wife Justina have lawfully conveyed to your church. Therefore let no person infringe the force of this our charter or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1533B]

Given at Signia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June [28 May].

### DXII. Bull by which a dispute formerly litigated before the bishop of Reggio by the abbess of the Brescian monastery of St. Julia against the bishop of Cremona concerning the church of Cicognaria is finally settled. (1152, 9 June)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 1029.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ RICHILDA, abbess of the monastery of St. Julia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1533C] By the Lord’s ordering, we preside in the seat of justice for this purpose: that, preserving to individual churches and ecclesiastical persons their rights, we may bring any dispute arising among them to its due conclusion.

Accordingly, at the petition of the same bishop, we entrusted for settlement to our venerable brother A., bishop of Reggio, the controversy which was being conducted between you and our venerable brother Obert, bishop of Cremona, concerning the church of Cicognaria. After both parties had appeared before him and the allegations and arguments on each side had been carefully heard and examined, and after seeking the counsel of many wise men, he pronounced the following judgment concerning the controversy: namely, that the people of the four villages—[Col. 1533D] Casale, Villa Ravennensium, Gurgo, and Scurolo—who from ancient times had been accustomed to come to the church of Cicognaria, should, as we direct on the testimony produced by both parties, come there by decree and receive spiritual ministrations from it.

But concerning the church of Cicognaria we decree as follows: the abbess shall choose and appoint a priest there, provided that she presents him to the bishop and that he receives the cure of souls from him. It shall retain by decree the fourth part of the tithes, as the church of Cicognaria has retained it hitherto. It shall receive chrism and holy oil from the parish of Casale Maggiore. It shall attend the Chapter and the Litany. It shall bring public penitents there to receive penance. We award temporal administration to the abbess. But the church which, as we have learned, was recently built without authority to the detriment [Col. 1534A] of the old church—we judge that it must be removed, also in order to avoid future scandal. We do not reopen Lord Aribert’s judgment concerning the churches of Calvatone and Alfiano.

From this judgment our aforesaid brother Obert, bishop of Cremona, appealed to our judgment. Therefore, after both parties had appeared before us; after the allegations and arguments had been stated orally before us; and after we had carefully inspected, and repeatedly reread, the allegations and attestations of both parties, transmitted under his seal by our aforementioned brother Regino, bishop of Reggio, we found that this judgment had been pronounced in its greater part contrary to the privileges granted by the Apostolic See to the monastery of St. Julia.

For in the privilege of Pope Paul we read among other things:

> “Therefore, because you have petitioned us that the venerable monastery of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, situated within the city of Brescia, which the most excellent queen Ansa is known to have recently founded, should be adorned with the privileges and insignia of the Apostolic See, we, with the agreement of our most reverend bishops, have decreed by common consent that the aforesaid monastery of the Lord Savior, and all monasteries with all basilicas belonging to it, which are known to have been lawfully built by the most devout Ansa, shall be adorned with the insignia of the privilege of the Apostolic See, which, by God’s aid, we serve.” [Col. 1534C]

And below:

> “Furthermore, concerning the consecration of each abbess of this monastery, we have decreed jointly that she may be consecrated by whatever bishop, from whatever city, she wishes. Clerics of whatever order, at the request of the same abbess, may likewise be sought from or kept by whatever bishop, from whatever city, she wishes. By a concordant ordinance we have also granted them permission, when need requires, to receive by apostolic grant chrism at the time of baptism, oil for celebrating the divine mysteries, or assistance in any special need, from whatever bishop they choose.”

And in the text of the same privilege we find:

> “Receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or basilicas, ordinations of the abbess or nuns, or of your clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, and whatever pertains to sacred ministry, from whatever Catholic bishops you prefer.” [Col. 1534D]

Therefore, desiring to restore to the norm of justice what is contained in the aforesaid judgment contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, and, as stated above, having carefully inspected the privileges, frequently and fully heard and examined the allegations of both parties, repeatedly read the attestations, and taken counsel with our brethren, we have judged as follows.

A priest shall be chosen by you for the church of Cicognaria in accordance with the tenor of the privileges, and shall be placed there. That priest, both for himself and for those subject to him, shall receive chrism, holy oil, and the other spiritual ministrations from whatever Catholic bishop he wishes, provided that bishop enjoys the favor of the Apostolic See. He shall be subject in no respect to the parish of Casale Maggiore.

All persons of the four villages—Casale, Villa Ravennensium, Gurgo, and Villa de Scurolis—except Banno, Lombarello, and the household of Camparello, Lupulus, and Albertus Ferrarius, shall go, both living and dead, to the aforesaid church of Cicognaria to receive all spiritual ministrations. From the village of Barcello, Stephen of Aggere, Modelena, and the households of Osbert, Doctor, and Barbalongus, together with the four houses of Barcello, and Abbot Peter and his kinswoman, shall be buried in that same church of Cicognaria. For all other divine services, however, both they and the other people of that village shall go to [Col. 1535B] the church of Fossa Capraria.

The church of Cicognaria shall always possess the fourth part of the tithes, as it has held it hitherto. We have also judged that the building constructed within the parish of Cicognaria, to the harm of the old church, under the name of a church and contrary to the sacred canons and to the formal prohibition of new work, must be wholly destroyed. But if the need of the people of the village of Barcello requires it, we permit the bishop of Cremona to build a church between that village and Fossa Capraria, outside the parish of Cicognaria.

So that there may be no confusion of parishes, we establish by this decree and by the authority of the Apostolic See that anyone from the aforesaid parishes who transfers his dwelling from one to another shall receive all divine ministrations from the church in whose parish he is shown to have transferred his dwelling. Therefore let no person whatsoever rashly infringe the text of this our determination or disturb it by any vexations. If anyone hereafter presumes to act against these provisions, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject at the eternal judgment to severe vengeance.

Given at Signia, on the fifth Ides of June [9 June], in the fifteenth indiction.

> **Note:** [Col. 1535B] In these documents is cited a bull of Pope Paul I, published by Margarini in vol. II of the *Bullarium Casinense*, constitution 9, upon which the origins of the exemption of the Brescian nunnery [Col. 1535C] are based. But, as I have already freely acknowledged in Dissertation LXIV, whenever privileges of such ancient liberty or immunity come before me, I immediately hesitate; fearing traps, I do not know what certainty to affirm.
>
> In that bull of Paul I the chronological data create obscurity for me. For it is said: “Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November [26 October], in the twenty-third year of the reign of Lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, great emperor, and in the tenth year of Leo, his son, as emperor, in the first indiction.” This is the year of Christ 762 if the new indiction is reckoned from September, or 763 if it began on the Kalends of January.
>
> Labbe, vol. VI of the *Councils*, p. 1689, prints letters of the same Paul I written “on the Nones of February [5 February], in the eleventh year of the reign of the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, great emperor, and in the twentieth (or nineteenth) year after his consulship, and in the seventh year of Leo, his son, as emperor, in the twelfth indiction.” There is also another [Col. 1535D] bull of the same Pope Paul I in Labbe, subscribed by many bishops as well as cardinals of the Holy Roman Church: “Given on the fourth Nones of June [2 June], in the forty-first year since Lord Constantine Augustus, crowned by God, great emperor, began to reign with his father, and in the twenty-first year after his consulship, in the fourteenth indiction.”
>
> I ask the reader to compare these acts, or these chronological data, with the Brescian document and determine whether all proceeds correctly. But perhaps Margarini, inaccurate in other matters, did not correctly transcribe the parchment here either.
>
> Yet one point remains which makes me more doubtful in this matter. The privilege of Paul I is subscribed by Apollinaris, Otto, Julian, Felix, and another Felix, all bishops perhaps from the province of Aquileia. These are precisely the persons who subscribe the privilege of Patriarch Sigualt, published in the same *Bullarium Casinense* and dated, as it is there read, “in the sixteenth year of King Desiderius and the fourteenth of Adulgis, in the twelfth indiction, on the third Ides of October [13 October],” that is, in the year of Christ 772 or 773—although [Col. 1536B] even these chronological data cannot be said to be wholly free from fault.
>
> I do not know whether it was customary in those times—for it was chiefly practiced in the twelfth century—for bishops to subscribe bulls [Col. 1536C] of this kind. Yet decide that as you please. Certainly it was customary that decrees of the Roman pontiff should receive the subscriptions of the bishops of the Roman province and of the cardinals. Why, then, do bishops of another province intrude here? Why are those same men, in the same number, present at Rome together, and ten years later confirm the documents issued by Patriarch Sigualt for the same Brescian nunnery? Moreover, why do they subscribe both charters in exactly the same words?
>
> I have assigned those bishops to the province of Aquileia, but only by conjecture; now I say that I find no trace of any of them anywhere, although Sigualt writes that he grants that privilege “with the agreement of our most reverend bishops,” and Pope Paul likewise declares that he did so “with the agreement of our most reverend fellow bishops.” For when Mabillon, in the *Annales Benedictini* under the year 772, said that “Apollinaris of Reggio and Julian of Piacenza” subscribed that charter, [Col. 1536D] he spoke conjecturally. And what business had the bishops of Reggio and Piacenza with the patriarch of Aquileia?
>
> Finally, it remains to ask why that privilege was obtained from Patriarch Sigualt, who possessed no jurisdiction over the diocese of Brescia, rather than from the archbishop of Milan, to whom the Brescian diocese was subject, or from the other archbishops in whose provinces were situated the other churches and monasteries attached to the Brescian religious house.
>
> However this may be, from the documents recently produced by me we have learned that in 1152 the privilege of Pope Paul I was approved at Rome as an authentic document, and that no right of the bishop of Cremona in the church of Cicognaria was mentioned as remaining. This certainly does not seem at all consistent with the decrees of the Council of Clermont and other papal letters. Moreover, even after those times, the rights of many bishops over monasteries and monks—and especially at Milan—are found to have remained in force.

Place of the appended seal, now lost.

### DXIII. Confirmation that the advocacy of the Abbey of Lower Altaich was transferred from the Empire to the bishop of Bamberg. (1152, 15 June)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XI, 168.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother EBERHARD, bishop of Bamberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whatever is lawfully done by kings or other Catholic princes from devotion and with reasonable provision, we wish to remain stable; and, that it may be firmly observed in future times, we strengthen it with the protection of our confirmation. Therefore, beloved brother in the Lord, favorably assenting to your reasonable petitions, we confirm by the guarantee of our favor the investiture and advocacy of the Abbey of Altaich, which belonged to the royal dignity, and those revenues which were annually paid from that abbey to the royal fisc. These had been taken from your predecessors and are now restored by our dearest son Frederick, king of the Romans, to you and, through you, to your church. We decree that they shall remain valid and unimpaired for all time, provided always that the rights and stipends due to the abbot and monks of that abbey remain at all times undiminished and inviolate, without prejudice to the right of the bishop of Passau. [Col. 1537B]

Therefore let no person whatsoever rashly infringe or in any way disturb the aforesaid restoration. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter presumes to attempt this, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject to the bond of excommunication.

Given at Signia, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June].

### DXIV. To Henry, bishop of Autun.—That, when summoned, he is to appear before G[odefrid], bishop of Langres, to answer for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Vézelay. (1152, 20 June)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 659.]

[Col. 1537C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishop of Autun: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The deeds reported to our hearing after your departure from us, concerning you and those who in every respect comply with your commands, confirm for us those words which, while you were staying with us, we heard issue from your own mouth: namely, that you would prefer the monastery of Vézelay to be utterly destroyed rather than not obey your command.

For a complaint has recently been sent to us by our beloved son Pontius, abbot of that place: that, after departing from the Apostolic See, you have grievously oppressed both him and the church entrusted to him, both through yourself [Col. 1537D] and through your agents; and that you enlist all whom you can to its injury and disturbance. Your brother also, at your instigation, wickedly attacks the church and its goods. He does not permit his people to go to the monastery, as is customary, for the sake of prayer; he seizes and plunders the people of the monastery; and certain persons under his jurisdiction have broken out into such audacity of presumption that they have not hesitated even to lay violent hands upon the monks themselves. Moreover, you are said to have so stirred up the count of Nevers to persecute the same church that, amid the shaking of such great storms, scarcely any place of peace remains there for our aforesaid son and his brethren to perform divine service. [Col. 1538A]

Since these matters are so grave that they ought neither to go unpunished nor uninvestigated, we have entrusted their examination to our venerable brother Godefrid, bishop of Langres. Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we command that, when summoned by him, you present yourself before him in order to render a full account in his inquiry concerning all these matters.

Those among your parishioners who are found to have laid violent hands upon any monk or cleric of that monastery, you shall publicly announce as excommunicated, with the congregation of the church assembled and candles lit. Until they appear before the Apostolic See with your letters in order to make satisfaction for so great an offense, you shall have them avoided throughout your diocese as excommunicates.

Henceforth take the utmost care not to presume to inflict any trouble upon our aforesaid son, his church, or his brethren, whether through yourself or through a subordinate person. Otherwise, by the Lord’s authority, we shall punish both you personally and your church in such a manner that all who hear of it may clearly understand how grave it is to seek tyrannically to seize things which ought to come to someone only by canonical judgment. [Col. 1538B]

Given at Signia, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June].

### DXV. Bull for Saint John of Sens. (1152, 21 June)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, Instruments XII, 40.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FULCO, abbot of the church of Blessed John the Evangelist, situated beside the walls of the city of Sens, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever something is petitioned of us that pertains to religion, etc. Among these we have thought fit to specify in their proper names: the church of St. George of Matrioles; the church of St. Sulpicius of Vicinies, with all their appurtenances; the church of Blessed Mary of Sosiac; the church of St. Peter of Carris; the church of St. Sulpicius of Nibella; the church of Blessed Mary of Vois; the church of St. Martin of Capriac; the church of St. Stephen of Château-Renard; the church of Blessed Genevieve; the church of St. George of Vico Novo; the church of St. Mary of Mont-Argis; the church of St. Leo [Col. 1538D] in the suburb of Sens; the church of Blessed Mary of Gresso; the church of St. Martin of Noem, with all their appurtenances; and, by gift of the chapter of Sens, the church of the Holy Savior.

In the diocese of Meaux: the church of Percio and the chapel of Meraldo, with all their appurtenances. In the parish of Orléans: the church of Blessed Mary called “between the wall and the ditch,” with all its appurtenances. We also confirm by the authority of our favor the annual revenues of the individual prebends of the deceased canons of the Church of Sens, as they have been prudently bestowed upon you by the common chapter of that church and confirmed by the text of its written instrument. We decree, therefore, etc.

[Col. 1539A] I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Gregory, cardinal of St. Vitus, etc. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of St. Praxedes. I, Aribert, cardinal-priest of St. Anastasia. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of Pastor. [Col. 1539B] I, Octavian, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Gerard, cardinal-priest of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill.

Given at Signia, by the hand of Hugh, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Eugenius III.

### DXVI. To All the Faithful. (1152, 22 June)

[MANRIQUE, *Annales Cistercienses*, II, 117.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful to whom these present letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[lacuna] Therefore, through these apostolic letters, we ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord to gird yourselves manfully for war against the unbelieving enemies of the Cross of Christ, and not hesitate to go with the noble man Raymond, count of Barcelona, etc.

Given at Signia, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July [22 June].

### DXVII. Rescript to Sylvester, abbot-elect of the monastery of St. Augustine of Canterbury. (1152)

[TWISDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, II, 1813.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SYLVESTER, abbot-elect of the monastery of St. Augustine, Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1539D] We sympathize with paternal affection over the labors and expenses of the monastery entrusted to you as our special house. That your cause has not yet, as we hoped, received its conclusion greatly displeases and grieves us.

The disturbance of the land and the unfavorable reports which we lately received from those regions compelled us, for no other reason, to retain your messenger with us so long. So that your business may obtain its desired result without delay, we have directed apostolic letters to our venerable brother Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, commanding that, if he can do so without danger to himself, he should come to your monastery, as is contained in your privileges, and, putting aside every appeal and pretext, bless you as abbot of that place, with the grace of the Holy Spirit present. [Col. 1540A]

If he perhaps demands from you a profession of obedience, we do not wish you to give it to him. But if, contrary to our expectation, that same brother of ours refuses, according to the tenor of our command, to come to your monastery and confer upon you the gift of blessing, it is our will that you bear this patiently; for, once you have canonically obtained the administration of that monastery through the authority of our confirmation, the withholding of that blessing will not give you less authority over the souls of the flock entrusted to you.

Given at Signia, etc.

### DXVIII. To Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury.—That he is to bless [Sylvester], the elect of the monastery of St. Augustine. (1152)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1540B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEOBALD, archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we have sent to your brotherhood the elect of the monastery of Blessed Augustine to be blessed, we did so not as a matter of right, but from the kindness of the Apostolic See. Yet you have not appeared, as was fitting, to heed or recognize the affection and kindness which we bear toward your person and the honor of the church entrusted to you; for you have, through a certain evasion, refused to confer the grace of blessing upon that elect according to our command, and indeed are known needlessly to trouble and grievously harass his monastery in the same matter. [Col. 1540C]

Therefore, because the care of the office entrusted to us obliges us to labor for the condition of all churches and, as far as we can with God’s help, to provide beneficially for their peace and tranquility, we command you through these present letters: if you can do so without danger to yourself, come to that place as is contained in their privileges and, setting aside every appeal and pretext, bless the aforesaid elect as abbot of that monastery, with the grace of the Holy Spirit going before.

Given, etc.

### DXIX. To the convent of St. Augustine, Canterbury.—That they are to obey Abbot Sylvester even if the archbishop refuses to bless him. (1152)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1540D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, to the convent of St. Augustine, Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

That the cause of your elect has not yet attained its desired conclusion has happened because of the disturbance recently arisen in our regions, not through our negligence. We indeed love you and your house with sincere charity in the Lord, and we desire that your right be kept and preserved for you in its entirety.

Accordingly, we recently directed apostolic [Col. 1541A] letters to our venerable brother Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, commanding that, if he can do so without danger to himself, he should come to your monastery, as is contained in your privileges, and confer the gift of blessing upon your elect, putting aside every appeal and pretext. But if, contrary to our expectation, he refuses to carry this into effect, we command you by the authority of these present letters that you nevertheless render no less the obedience and reverence due to that elect. For we do not wish him to possess less authority than if he had obtained the grace of blessing from that same brother of ours.

Given at Signia, etc.

### DXX. To Moses, archbishop of Ravenna.—That he should treat Bishop Plantius kindly. (1152, 28 July)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 666.]

[Col. 1541B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother M., archbishop of Ravenna: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your brotherhood clearly recognizes that our venerable brother L., bishop of Piacenza, has been exposed to immense dangers for obedience to the Apostolic See and for the restoration of the church of Ravenna. It is fitting, therefore, that in his difficulties and vexations, which he is known to endure for your church, you should offer him brotherly consolation.

Accordingly, through these present letters we command, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord to provide for that brother of ours in his necessities with due kindness and to open to him the fraternal bowels of charity, lest you should deservedly be reproached for excessive harshness and he should regret having humbled himself to your obedience. [Col. 1541C]

Given at Signia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [28 July].

### DXXI. To the Cistercians.—Confirmation of their constitutions. (1152, 1 August)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 669.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GOTHONIUS of Cîteaux, and the other brethren and monks, present and future, professing the regular life and the statutes of the Cistercian order: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1541D] The most holy Roman Church received from the Lord in Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the promise that it should be the foundation of the universal Church; and it received the command to strengthen those professing the Christian faith in faith, religion, and every holiness. Therefore it has always shown itself solicitous for the progress of all churches and has at all times been zealous for establishing, preserving, and promoting in every church the observance of holy religion. Thus religion may be derived from it, as from a fountain, to all the children of the Church; and what has been religiously and beneficially instituted by others who have received the first fruits of the Spirit may acquire through it unchangeable firmness.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, drawn by the reputation of your sacred religion, like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed, we graciously assent to your religious petitions and confirm by apostolic authority your regular ordinances. We have decreed that these should be set out under the specific chapters appended below.

You have established among yourselves that no abbey of your order shall be founded in the diocese of any bishop until that bishop promises to regard as binding the decree confirmed among the churches of your order for the maintenance of discipline. You have also established that the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed forever in all monasteries of your order as it is in the church of Cîteaux; and that no professed member of your order shall introduce into its reading any meaning other than the plain and common understanding, but that all shall understand it uniformly, as its provisions are known to have been defined, and observe it inviolably. You shall also maintain throughout all churches of your order precisely the same observances, chant, and books pertaining to the ecclesiastical office. No church or person of your order may dare to seek from anyone a privilege contrary to the common ordinances of that order, or in any manner retain one already obtained. [Col. 1542B]

It has also been ordained among you that all abbots of your order shall come every year to the general chapter at Cîteaux, setting aside every pretext, except only those whom bodily illness prevents from the labor of the journey. Yet these must appoint a suitable messenger through whom the reason for their delay may be reported to the chapter. Likewise excepted are those living in more distant regions who cannot appear at the chapter without serious and manifest difficulty. Such persons shall come at the time appointed for them in that chapter.

Moreover, if any dispute arises between any abbots of your order, or if such grave fault is reported of one of them that he deserves even suspension or deposition, whatever the chapter canonically determines concerning it shall be observed without any reopening. Nor shall any of your churches choose for its pastor a person from any religious order, just as you have established that no member of your order may be appointed abbot over other monasteries. [Col. 1542D]

These, indeed, beloved sons, we have selected from the many ordinances of your order and have taken care to set out under their own chapters. But because every individual provision which you have regularly established for the advancement of religion and the salvation of souls could not be appended to this present abridgment, we confirm by apostolic authority, together with the provisions written above, all that is contained in your charter called the *Charter of Charity*, and whatever you have regularly established among yourselves out of regard for religion. We decree that these shall be observed inviolably for all time by you, your successors, and all who profess your order.

[Col. 1543A] Furthermore, since you firmly intend to choose the places of your dwellings outside the society of secular persons, we establish that your granges, like the precincts of churches, shall be free and secure from the incursions and violence of wicked persons. By the power of the Holy Spirit we forbid anyone there to dare seize, despoil, beat, or rob a person.

We also enact that, because of general interdicts imposed upon lands, none of your churches shall be compelled to abstain from divine offices; rather, all members of your order may celebrate the divine solemnities with closed doors and in a low voice for their brethren, after excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons.

Likewise, we forbid any person whatsoever to dare summon brethren of your order before secular courts. If anyone believes that he has some legal claim against them, he shall have the right to pursue it before the judgment of an ecclesiastical judge. [Col. 1543B]

We therefore decree that no one may ever rashly oppose what has been confirmed and established in this charter by the authority of the prince of the apostles, or by any presumption infringe the force of this our decree. But if anyone, etc.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, etc.

Given at Signia, by the hand of Boso, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of August [1 August], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### DXXII. To the chapter of Magdeburg.—That they are not to support the bishop of Cice (Cicensis), invader of the Church of Magdeburg. (1152, 1 August)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 550.]

[Col. 1543C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the whole chapter of the Church of Magdeburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The report reached our ears that, after the election which all of you, save seven, made according to God, by the counsel of religious men, of the person of our beloved son your provost, the bishop of Zeitz, disregarding the propriety of his office, has endeavoured, contrary to justice and to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, to thrust himself into your Church by royal favour [Col. 1543D]; and, as we have learned, has not feared unlawfully to receive investiture therefrom the prince himself. How perverse and unworthy this is, no one possessed of zeal for rectitude can fail to know.

Therefore, since we neither can nor ought to suffer the liberty of the Church to be made a handmaid, ecclesiastical vigour to be confounded, and the constitutions of the holy Fathers to be rendered void, by these present letters we command and enjoin you that, should the aforesaid bishop attempt to intrude himself into your Church, you must on no account presume to support or favour him; rather, beware of him entirely as of an intruder. Know that whoever presumes otherwise will, without doubt, incur forfeiture of his office and benefice.

Given at Segni, on the Kalends of August [1 August].

DXXIII. To the bishops of Germany.—He disapproves the translation of the bishop of Zeitz to the archbishopric of Magdeburg. (1152, 17 August.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 631.]

[Col. 1544A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren EBERHARD, archbishop of Salzburg; HARTWIG, archbishop of Bremen; and HILLIN, archbishop of Trier; and to EBERHARD, bishop of Bamberg; HERMANN, bishop of Constance; HENRY, bishop of Regensburg; OTTO, bishop of Freising; CONRAD, bishop of Passau; DANIEL, bishop of Prague; ANSELM, bishop of Havelberg; and BURCHARD, bishop of Eichstätt: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letter which your prudence sent us concerning the cause of the Church of Magdeburg. But in reading and considering it, we were filled with great astonishment and wonder, because we saw that it contained something far different from what is incumbent upon you by reason of your pontifical office.

For, since by divine providence you have been set at the head of the Church, so that you ought diligently to drive from her midst what is harmful and preserve what is useful, in this matter, as became known to us from the representation contained in your letter, you have attended not to what benefits the Church of God, what accords with the decree of the sacred canons, or what would consequently be approved by the judgment of heaven, but to what pleases earthly princes. You, who ought to have turned their minds away from an unsound purpose and shown them where the way of the Lord lay, did not persuade them toward what is right, nor stand as a wall for the house of Israel. On the contrary, while they were building a wall, as the prophet says, you—though we can scarcely say it without deep bitterness of heart—coated it with mud without chaff (Ezek. 13).

The prince of the apostles did not think thus. By the confession of his faith he received that he should be the foundation of the whole Church; yet, when the children of this world threatened him and the apostles with death if they preached in the name of Jesus, trusting in the power of the Lord he answered: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 3). But you, lest you seem to disagree with earthly princes, bestow your favour upon a cause which is certainly believed to be opposed both by the authority of ecclesiastical ordinance and by the judgment of the divine will [Col. 1544D].

For whereas the oracle of divine law does not permit translations of bishops without evident proof of utility and necessity; whereas also a far greater concord of clergy and people than in other elections ought to precede such translations: none of these things is present in the proposed translation of our venerable brother Guicmann, bishop of Zeitz. The prince’s favour alone is awaited. Without examining the necessity of that church or considering the usefulness of the person, and with the clergy unwilling—indeed, as is said, with the greater part protesting—you are bringing him into the Church of Magdeburg to be intruded there.

We are all the more astonished at this because from the past we have learned the gravity and learning of that man, and accordingly do not wholly fail to know how useful he is to that Church [Col. 1545A]. Therefore, although others may be driven by the gusts of temporal favour, we are founded upon the solidity of that rock which merited to be placed as the foundation of the Church. As we ought not, so we are unwilling, to be carried about by every wind of doctrine or to depart under any pressure from the rectitude of the sacred canons.

By these present letters, therefore, we command that you lend this cause no further favour; and that by your exhortations you endeavour to bring it about with our dearest son Frederick, whom God has at this time raised to royal eminence for the preservation of the Church’s liberty, that he too desist from his purpose in this matter and lend no further favour to that cause against God, against the sacred canons, and against the duty of royal dignity. Instead, let him leave to the Church of Magdeburg, as to the other churches of the kingdom entrusted to him by God, free power to elect according to God whom they wish, and afterwards support that election with his favour, as befits royal majesty.

For if we saw that what he seeks to do concerning our aforesaid brother were supported by reason, we should not judge that either his will or your request ought in any way to be opposed. But against God and the enactments of the sacred canons, we can give consent to no request whatsoever.

Given at Segni, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August].

DXXIV. To Wibald, abbot.—He commends the cause of A. [Adelgot], bishop of Chur, and urges him to defend ecclesiastical immunities against laymen. (1152, 20 September.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 553.]

[Col. 1545C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

To those whose pure devotion we trust without hesitation, we confidently entrust what we desire to be brought to a worthy conclusion. Accordingly, we have thought it necessary earnestly to commend to your charity the cause of our venerable brother A., bishop of Chur, so that, supported by your counsel and aid and that of our brother bishops who shall assemble at the court of our dearest son Frederick, king of the Romans, he may not, with impunity, be treated dishonourably in word or deed, as happened on another occasion [Col. 1545D], nor may his Church, in accordance with the wishes of wicked men, be defrauded of its due justice.

[Note: Adelgot, made bishop from being abbot of Disentis; a man of great holiness.]

And do not suppose that in this cause, as though it were another’s, you should remain indifferent, as the poet says:

> Your own affair is now at stake when the neighbouring wall is on fire.  
> (HORACE, *Epistles* I.18.84.)

For a like cause has already produced enemies for you, or will shortly produce them.

Nor should you think that matter should pass over in silence which was maliciously introduced by laymen at the court held at Ulm, to the destruction of churches: namely, that those who are subjected to excommunication for plundering and arson inflicted upon ecclesiastical goods now, by a novel judicial procedure, themselves pronounce the excommunicated to be excommunicate only if a sentence of condemnation has first been issued in a lay court. If perchance both you and our brother bishops think this should be endured, it will unquestionably follow that no bishop in those regions will be permitted to exercise ecclesiastical discipline against anyone guilty of any crime. For when discipline ceases, the Christian religion will perish; and when religion ceases, the salvation of souls also will perish.

Therefore, dearest son, both in this and in other matters, whenever you assemble at courts and see the malice of wicked men devising measures against the honour of God, against the wholesome vigour of the Church, and against the dignity of the kingdom, resist them manfully and unanimously. Thus, through your prudent zeal and labour, wisdom may overcome malice, justice may overcome iniquity, and the condition of God’s Church and of the kingdom may be kept sound in its proper splendour [Col. 1546B].

Moreover, we make known to your holiness certain things recently undertaken in the City by a rustic mob, without the knowledge of the nobles and leading men, at the instigation of the heretic Ar.

[Note: Arnold of Brescia, formerly a disciple of Peter Abelard; Saint Bernard attacks him in Epistle 189, and Otto of Freising recounts his heresies in *The Deeds of Frederick the Emperor*, chapter 20.]

About two thousand persons have secretly conspired together, and on the coming Kalends of November they plan to create one hundred perpetual senators, men of evil works, and two consuls. One of these consuls is to arrange—or rather to gnaw away at—the condition of the commonwealth within the City, and the other outside it, by the counsel of those hundred. They also intend to create one whom they wish to call emperor, whom they hope will exercise deadly rule over those hundred men, the two consuls, and all the Roman people. Since by this they presume to assail the crown of the kingdom and the honour of our dearest son Frederick, king of the Romans, we wish this to be reported to him more privately through you, so that by mature counsel he may wisely provide what must be done.

Given at Segni, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October [20 September].

DXXV. Bull for the canonry of Blessed Mary at Fano. (1152, 27 September.)

[AMIANI, *Memorie Istoriche della città di Fano*, II, summary, p. IX, from the archive of the chapter of the Church of Fano.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BENEDICT, prior of the canonry of Blessed Mary of Fano [Col. 1546D], and to his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life: for ever.

A desire shown to belong to the religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay, when we graciously assent to the petitions made on behalf of our beloved sons. Therefore we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid canonry, in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that canonry now justly possesses, or may hereafter, God willing, acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names: namely, the parish church of Saint Caesarius, together with the *mansi* and lands which you lawfully possess in its territory; half of the parish church of Saint Paul, together with the demesne vineyard; the parish church of Saint Secundus with the chapel of Saint Bartholomew; whatever you possess in the church of Saint Angel in the episcopal estate; the church of Saint Peter outside the gate; the mill of Repulesio; the mill of Arzilla with vineyards; the vineyards of Pupilliano; the field of Gualdo; and the field near the church of Saint Stephen [Cols. 1547A–B].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid canonry, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept whole for the benefit and advantage of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Fano.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third warning and after being moved by excommunication, does not amend the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty of divine indignation for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment.

But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III [Col. 1547D].

(The subscriptions of eight most reverend lord cardinals are omitted.)

DXXVI. Bull for the monastery of Saint John in the valley of the Thur (near Toggenburg). (1132, 4 October.)

[NEUGART, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 83.]

[Col. 1548A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BURCHARD, abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist, situated in the parish of Constance, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for perpetual remembrance.

[Note: The monastery of Saint John in the valley of the Thur, near Toggenburg, was converted into a provostship and in the vernacular is called Alt-Sankt-Johann, to distinguish it from the new monastery of the same name, built two hours northward from there in 1629, after the old monastery had burned down in 1626.]

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized to accord with religion and honour, it is fitting that we grant it gladly and afford appropriate support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery presently possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter, God willing, acquire through grants of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names: Illnowo,

[Note: Ilnau in the county of Kyburg.]

Mogoldesberch,

[Note: Mogelsberg in the Neckar valley near Toggenburg.]

Pussenanch,

[Note: Busnang or Buslingen below Bischofszell in Thurgau.]

Hiltensowo,

[Note: Hiltisau, a village in the parish of Helfensweil in the county of Toggenburg.]

Haltenrieth,

[Note: Altenried, several farmsteads in the parish of Kilchberg in the same county.]

with their appurtenances.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or force, except the one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

We also forbid anyone to presume to usurp the advocacy of that place by hereditary right. Rather, according to the ordinance of the founder, you shall receive as advocate, on this condition, the man whom the abbot, by the common counsel of the brethren, provides to be set over that advocacy: that he must not rashly grant that advocacy or any other goods of the monastery as benefices, nor inflict any oppression upon you.

[Note: The founder is said in the records of the monastery of Saint Gall to be Wenzeslaus of Ganderswila, whom Bucelinus, *Germania Sacra*, part II, p. 49, calls Wezelius or Wezelinus, of the knightly Order of Saint John the Baptist.]

If he presumes to attempt this, and after a second or third warning does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, you may deprive him of that advocacy and appoint another suitable person in his place on the same terms [Col. 1548D].

[Col. 1549A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of honour and power; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment.

But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Callixtus, have subscribed.

I, Aribert, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed.

I, Octavian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed.

[Note: Later elected antipope under the name Victor IV, against Roland, by only two cardinals, 7 September 1159.]

I, Roland, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed.

I, Gerard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed.

I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.

I, Cencius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed.

I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, have subscribed.

I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed.

I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

I, Ildebrand, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, through the hands of Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

DXXVII. To Raymond, master of the Hospital of Jerusalem. (1152, 27 October.)

[*Codice diplomatico dell’ordine Gerosolimitano*, I, 308.]

[Col. 1550A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAYMOND, master of the venerable Hospital of Jerusalem, and his brethren serving in the ministry of the poor: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: Raymond of Le Puy, who died in 1160.]

As we are admonished by the administration of our office to settle the affairs of churches and pious places with a salutary conclusion, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, desiring in due charity to provide for your peace and tranquillity in the future, we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See, and decree to remain valid and unshaken for ever, the agreement made between you and the nobleman William, count of Forcalquier, concerning the castle of Manosque and its appurtenances, through our venerable brother G., archbishop of Embrun and legate of the Apostolic See, and confirmed by his written charter, etc. We have read the terms of that agreement set down in the same charter, etc.

Therefore let no one whatsoever dare rashly to violate this charter of our confirmation or disturb it by any vexations. If anyone presumes to attempt this and, after a second or third warning, does not correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment.

Given at Alba, the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October], in the year 1151.

DXXVIII. To Odo, duke of Burgundy, and the Burgundian nobles.—That the burgesses of Vézelay are to be regarded as excommunicated. (1152, 19 December.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 655.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the noblemen ODO, duke of Burgundy; HENRY, count; ARCHAMBAUD OF BOURBON; G., count of Chalon; R., brother of the duke; R., count of Joigny; G. OF DONZY; R. OF ROUGEMONT; D. OF LUZIAC; A. OF MONTRÉAL [Col. 1550D]; S., viscount of Sens, and his sons F. and B.; G., viscount of Châtillon; G. OF VIRY; ODO OF TILLES; and HUGH OF MONT-SAINT-JEAN: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that the excessive presumption and intolerable contumacy of the faithless burgesses of Vézelay has escaped your noble notice. In violation of the fidelity and oath which they had made to their abbot and lord, they have dared wickedly to expel him from his monastery and seek, though in vain, to take from us that place which from the beginning of its foundation is known to be the freehold and patrimony of blessed Peter.

Therefore, since powerful and noble men devoted to that prince of the apostles ought not to tolerate with impunity the boldness of such presumption, by these present letters we command your nobility utterly to exclude the aforesaid burgesses from all fairs in your land until they come to their senses and humbly render fitting satisfaction. Indeed, command that any of them whom your men find be seized and stripped of their goods as perjurers, traitors, and excommunicates [Col. 1551A].

Given at Saint Peter’s, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December].

DXXIX. To Hugh, archbishop of Sens; G. [Geoffrey], bishop of Langres; T. [Theobald], bishop of Paris; and Henry, bishop of Troyes.—That the burgesses of Vézelay are to be regarded as excommunicated. (1152, 19 December.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 654.]

[Col. 1551B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brethren HUGH, archbishop of Sens; G., bishop of Langres; T., bishop of Paris; and HENRY, bishop of Troyes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that the excessive presumption and intolerable contumacy of the faithless burgesses of Vézelay has escaped your brotherhoods’ notice. In violation of the fidelity and oath which they had made to their abbot and lord, they endeavour wickedly to expel him from his monastery and, though in vain, to take from us that place which from the beginning of its foundation is known to be the proper freehold and patrimony of blessed Peter.

Therefore, lest the audacity of such presumption remain unpunished and pernicious indiscipline break out into something worse, by these present letters we command you wholly to forbid the aforesaid burgesses, as perjurers, traitors, and excommunicates, to be received at the fairs and markets of your dioceses. Indeed, command that, if any of your parishioners find them, they be seized and stripped of their goods [Col. 1551C].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December].

DXXX. Privilege concerning all the properties of the monastery of Saint Mary of Bosau. (1152, 29 December.)

[*Thuringia Sacra*, 656.]

[Col. 1551D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary called Buzaugia [Bosau], and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery presently possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire from its own resources through grants of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names: Mount Bozowe, on which the monastery itself has been built; Podogrodiz; the village of Luconowe with the adjoining wood; six *mansi* in Gline; six in Provin; the tithe in Nuendorph; in Techibodiz, Molochosdorff; in the district of Geraha, the tithe of one hundred *Seobroni*; at Zwickowe, the church with two *mansi* and the tithe of that district; the village of Coarwiz with mill, meadows, and woods; the village of Waltrewitz; the village of Ozelz; the church and village of Hoychenwalt with the adjoining wood; in the district of Plisna, the tithe of one thousand *Scobroni*; four *mansi* in Rodowe; at Portin, the demesne with thirty-six *mansi*; in the district called Plima, half the tithe, and there also the tithe of all newly cleared land and of nine old villages; in the village of Borsix, a mill; the village of Techebodiz; the village of Rodowe with its appurtenances; in the village of Drogeliz, ten *mansi* and half the village of Golbin; the village of Lomezetz and another village of the same name; in the village of Gline, one *mansus*; the tithe of a certain demesne in the village called Crozelin; and the village of Milthendorph with its appurtenances [Cols. 1552A–B].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1552D]

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Samson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

DXXXI. To [Peter], abbot of Cluny.—That he grant the monastery of Silviniac to the exiled abbot of Vézelay. (1152.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 660.]

When our beloved son Pontius, abbot of Vézelay, your brother by blood, is placed amid the greatest vexations and straits, you ought, even without our exhortation and admonition, to sympathize with him in brotherly charity and to relieve his exile with kindly and timely consolations [Col. 1553A]. Therefore, since the duty of charity requires us to love our brethren in the Lord as ourselves and to provide for their needs with brotherly affection, by these present letters we command you to grant him the monastery of Silviniac, for so long as that exile endures, also out of reverence for Blessed Peter and for us.

DXXXII. To Arnald, archbishop of Narbonne.—That he restrain the bishop of Maguelone and Peter of Verona, hostile to the Cluniacs dwelling near Montpellier. (1145–1153.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 446.]

[Col. 1553B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ARNALD, archbishop of Narbonne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, appearing before us, made grave complaint against our venerable brother R[aymond], bishop, and the canons of the Church of Maguelone. He alleged that they have presumed publicly to forbid their parishioners of Montpellier, contrary to the duty of brotherly charity, from bestowing anything of their goods during life or at death upon his new monastery situated near Montpellier, or from directing that, when they die, their bodies be buried in that place. Moreover, contrary to the constitution of the Apostolic See, they nonetheless exact tithes upon the labour of its brethren. How perverse this is, and how wholly alien to religious observance, no one possessed of zeal for rectitude can fail to know.

Therefore, since it is our office to correct wrongs and preserve to every Church its justice, by these present letters we command you to go into those regions and, severely rebuking in our name our aforesaid brother bishop and the canons of Maguelone concerning these matters, strictly admonish them henceforth neither to exact from the brethren of the aforesaid monastery tithes of their labour or of the increase of animals which they raise, nor to presume to inflict injury or molestation upon them. Rather, just as they allow their parishioners to give alms to the monasteries of Aniane and Saint-Guilhem, and at death to give themselves to those houses, so they must by no means forbid them to benefit the aforesaid Cluniac monastery [Cols. 1553C–D].

If they refuse to obey your admonitions, publicly declare to their parishioners that they must not, because of the prohibition of that bishop or his men, refrain from benefiting that place as the Lord inspires them, and from committing themselves there for burial if they wish, while preserving the right of the mother church.

Furthermore, we command your brotherhood also strictly to admonish Peter of Verona, who has broken a certain mill of the aforesaid monastery and presumes unjustly to inflict molestation and hostility upon the brethren of that place on account of it, either to desist from molesting those brethren or to come with them before you for justice. If he is unwilling to do either, exercise against him the censure of ecclesiastical severity, lest through a failure of justice the aforesaid brethren should again be compelled to appeal to us concerning these matters [Col. 1554A].

DXXXIII. Privilege against the archdeacons of Paris, in support of episcopal authority. (1145–1153.)

[PETIT, *Theodori Poenitentiale*, II, p. 716.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEOBALD, bishop of Paris, and to his successors canonically appointed: for ever.

The duty of our office compels us to preserve justice for individual churches and ecclesiastical persons, and, by paternal solicitude [Col. 1554B], to provide that no discord concerning ecclesiastical matters may arise among them in the future. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Theobald, desiring to provide for the peace and tranquillity of you and of the church committed to you by God, by the tenor of this present writing we decree that the agreement made between your predecessor Stephen of blessed memory and Theobald, archdeacon of that same church, through Matthew, bishop of Albano, and John of St. Chrysogonus and Peter of the title of Callistus, then cardinal priests, and by mandate of our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory, and confirmed in writing by our venerable brothers Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Burchard, bishop of Meaux, shall be inviolably observed for all time between you and your successors and the present and future archdeacons of the Church of Paris [Col. 1554C]: namely, that archdeacons shall not be permitted to appoint priests in churches.

Rather, it shall belong to the bishop to provide churches with clergy, yet through the archdeacons as through his ministers: so that the bishop entrusts the care of souls to priests, while church and temporal goods are assigned to the churches through the archdeacons. Archdeacons shall in no way be permitted to suspend priests from office if the bishop is in the diocese; nor shall they be permitted at all to depose them, impose penances, or reconcile persons except by the bishop’s permission. Nor may archdeacons excommunicate or absolve any cleric except by mandate of the bishop.

Whenever expedient, the bishop shall summon his parishioners through the archdeacon and invite them to submit to justice. [Col. 1554D] If they despise this, and justice so requires, the bishop may excommunicate them; and the archdeacons shall observe the excommunication once imposed. Archdeacons shall not cause clerics to be promoted to orders except under the bishop’s mandate and seal, provided he is within the province. But if the bishop is absent and the archdeacons have his mandate, then, necessity being urgent, they may cause clerics to be promoted and may canonically provide churches with clergy.

The bishop shall not hold collections through the archdeacons’ parishes without the archdeacons, unless he is going to Rome, a council is being held in the province, or perhaps he is receiving the lord pope in his own church; even then he shall do so after consulting the archdeacons. In such collections, all expenses being borne by the bishop, the archdeacons shall have no share. [Col. 1555A] In other common collections, however, the archdeacons shall receive a third part, as is customary. Nor shall archdeacons be permitted to hold collections throughout the diocese without the bishop.

If an archdeacon wishes to give something from his own resources, whether at request or voluntarily, the bishop must by no means oppose it. If any cleric or layman in the diocese commits an injustice against the archdeacons or another person, and refuses to make amends through the archdeacons themselves, and if the bishop is present and wishes to hear the matter before himself, the archdeacons shall not proceed to sentence; rather, they shall refer their cause to the bishop, who shall observe canonical justice toward them in all things. But if the bishop is absent or unwilling to hear it, the archdeacons shall administer canonical justice, yet by mandate of the bishop; [Col. 1555B] and this applies to laypersons, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If anyone knowingly and rashly attempts to contravene this page of our confirmation, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. Amen, amen.

### DXXXIV. To R[aymond] of Maguelonne and A[delbert] of Nîmes. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 363.]

The laws of secular emperors and the ecclesiastical constitutions of the Fathers protect and defend religious men in the service of Almighty God, and do not permit any annoyance or disturbance contrary to the sacred order to be inflicted upon them. We have learned that certain advocates in your territory, on the occasion of deciding disputes that sometimes arise, demanded from the abbot and brethren of Franceval the oath against calumny, as from other men. This is unusual among brethren of that order, and we can neither compel nor ought to compel them to take it.

But lest, on this pretext, persons unlawfully appear to retain the rights of others, and lest the monks lose their case if the aforesaid oath is not taken on their side when the matter so requires, we direct them to appoint in their monastery, [Col. 1555D] as the imperial constitutions allow, an *oeconomus*—a steward—who may sue and defend on their behalf and, when necessary, take the oath against calumny.

### DXXXV. Privilege for the Monastery of Saints Lawrence and Hilary. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[LE BEUF, *Mémoires d’Auxerre*, II, p. 265.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of the church of the Blessed Lawrence and Hilary of the Abbey, and its brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life: in perpetuity.

The pastoral care entrusted to us by God has this purpose: that we should labour by every means to establish religion pleasing to God and preserve with exact diligence what has been established. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of the Apostolic See the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God favouring it, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.
