Among these we have judged the following to be named expressly: from Hugh, bishop of Auxerre of blessed memory, and his predecessors, as is contained in that bishop’s charter, [Col. 1556B] the church of Saint Eusebius of Auxerre; the church of Saint Mamertinus, subject to the aforesaid church of Saint Eusebius; the church of Saint Cyricus of Coslun; the church of Saint Symphorianus of Tracy; the church of Saint Domnolenus the Confessor; the church of Saint Martin of Troncy; the church of Saint Quentin the Martyr; the church of Saint Martin of Garchy; the church of Saint Symphorianus of Court; the church of Blessed Peter of Dompierre; the church of Saint Julian of Taury; moreover, the church of Saint Simeon, saving the right of the infirm; and the church of Tilly, saving the right of the bishop of Auxerre.

From the canons of the church of Saint Cyricus of Nevers, as their charter contains, the church of the holy confessors Lupus and Gildardus with all its appurtenances, which Hugh III, bishop of the church of Nevers of blessed memory, had granted them. Likewise, the canons of Nevers decreed that if one of them transferred himself to that church in order to serve God in a stricter life, he should, for the duration of his life, retain the prebend which he had held among them; while they granted to the church of Saint Gildard the prebend which they held in the monastery of Saint Mary for thirty days upon the death of one of their brethren. Likewise, by gift of the aforesaid bishop of Auxerre, the annual revenues of the canons of Saint Stephen. From Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges, the church of Saint Hilary of Gondilly.

Finally, Hugh, bishop of Nevers of blessed memory, granted to the aforesaid church of Saint Gildard [Col. 1556D] the church of Urzy; a house with orchard, land, meadows, and the other things which the canon Bruno had possessed; and the church of Saint Martin of Odilonville. Likewise Fromundus, successor of the aforesaid bishop, granted to the same church, for one year, the entire prebends of the canons of Nevers, whenever they should cease to hold them in whatever manner; unless one of them should change his mode of life at Saint Martin’s—for there he shall retain his prebend during his lifetime, but after death the prebend itself shall pass, as we have said, for one year to the canons of Saint Gildard. Furthermore, the church of Albigny, apart from what the monks of Diana possess therein; also the pond with its mill beside the same church; [Col. 1557A] and the house which belonged to Hugh, canon of Saint Cyricus.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church of Saints Lawrence and Hilary, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishops.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects himself by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

### DXXXVI. Bull for the Church of Coutances. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[Gall. Christ. nov., *Instr.*, XI, 239.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALGAR, bishop of Coutances, and to his successors to be instituted: in perpetuity.

By the apostolic office imposed upon us by God, we ought to love our brother bishops, whether near or far away, and preserve to the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their rights, so that, just as we are called fathers in name, we may likewise be proved such in deed. For this reason, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Algar, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Coutances, over which, by God’s ordering, you preside, and strengthen it with the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, God favouring, by the gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors, and through you to that church.

Among these we have judged the following to be named expressly: [Col. 1557D] one half of the city of Coutances, with one half of the toll and the mills which you have in the same place, the park, and the lands of the *pinceralae*; the mill-fee of Buinoldeville; one half of the fishery in the River Seine; the church of Saint Laud above the River Vire, together with the church of Saint Mary in the castle of that place; the church of Saint Giles; the churches of Verville and Lenneville, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Cherbourg, with the church of the Holy Trinity, the church of Saint Mary of Tourlaville, [Col. 1558A] the chapel of Flamengs, and the lands of Angot the chaplain, with all tithes and other appurtenances belonging to those churches; the entire tithe of the toll in the aforesaid castle of Cherbourg, with the holding of three burgesses and the liberties and immunities, both in the market and the woods of that castle, which you have hitherto lawfully possessed; the church of Saint Mary of Équeurdreville, with tithes, lands, houses, and its other appurtenances; the church of Aleran, with land for four oxen; the church of Saint Saviour in Gersey, with its lands, tithes, and other appurtenances; the church of Essert, with its tithes and land belonging to it; one ploughland of land at Krvarrey; the church of Saint Nicholas of Barfleur; two thirds of the tithes of Valognes, Yvetot, [Col. 1558B] and Huberville; houses among the brushwood; thirty acres of land which you have at Valognes, with liberties and rights of common in the count’s forest, for your use and that of your men, as you have hitherto lawfully possessed them; the church of Saint Mary of Poupeville, with cemetery, tithes, the land of Ralph of Spalda, and its other appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Bulmo; the chapel of Saint Nicholas, and the land in the same borough belonging by right to it, with the customs and liberties which you lawfully possess there; a fishery in the River Vire; at Méry, tithes of the *linguae cenarum* taken between the rivers Tar and Tarel; tithes of hunting in all the count’s forests throughout all the Cotentin and at Domfront; at Palles, [Col. 1558C] the castle of Saint Laud with all its appurtenances; Blainville, with its mill and other adjacent properties; Telle, with its appurtenances; Bonfossé, with its appurtenances; Caugey, with its adjacent properties; Saint-Ébremond, with its appurtenances; the fief of Ralph of Saint Giles; Robert’s fief, which is in the waters; the fief held from you by Richard; the fief held by Hugh Murdrac at Breuilly; the fief held by Robert of Sacey; at La Haye, Fodeville; the fowlers’ land at Zingreville; the land of Allod; the land of Crapolt Woods, with its appurtenances; and at Caen, four acres of meadow.

Moreover, by the authority of this decree we enact that the boundaries of the bishopric of Coutances shall henceforth be wholly undisturbed and preserved to you and your successors, as you and your predecessors have hitherto peacefully and lawfully possessed them. We further decree that the archdeacon of the Church of Coutances may conduct an ecclesiastical case in the court of any layman.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all shall be preserved intact for your use and that of Christ’s poor, to their benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to contravene it, then, by canonical sanction, unless he corrects his offence through fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour, let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

### DXXXVII. To the Clergy and People of Toledo—That the Mozarabs Shall Obey the Archbishop of Toledo and Not Differ from Him in Ceremonies. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 678.]

[Col. 1559B]

How grave the crime of disobedience is, and with how great a punishment it must be visited, the Lord, Creator of all, showed by punishing the disobedience of the first man; and the human race, set in the valley of tears, experiences it. It has been duly reported that certain persons called Mozarabs, refusing obedience to our venerable brother the archbishop of Toledo, receive churches from the hands of laymen; and that, in the sacraments of the Mass and other divine offices, and also in clerical tonsure and vestments, following their ancient custom, they presume to hold views differing from the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, such power has been bestowed by the Lord upon the Apostolic See that [Col. 1559C] what it has prescribed for sound doctrine, the morals of the faithful, and the Lord’s time must be accepted and maintained today, and what it has rejected must hitherto be regarded as ineffective, how much more ought those things which it is known to have instituted in the sacraments of the Mass and other divine offices, out of reverence for the Catholic faith, to be preferred with every honour and reverently adopted by all?

By these present letters we command your whole community strictly to admonish them that henceforth they shall not presume to differ from the Catholic Church in the sacraments of the Mass and other divine offices; and that, if they wish to remain in his province, they shall render due obedience to our aforesaid brother and reverently receive and observe his admonitions and commands.

### DXXXVIII. The Church of Saint Rumbold at Mechelen, Formerly Collegiate and Now Metropolitan, with All Its Possessions and Tithes, Is Received into Apostolic Protection. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opp. dipl.*, IV, p. 19, from the archives of the metropolitan chapter.]

[Col. 1559D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, dean of the church of Mechelen, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical [Note: From the opening of the diploma itself it is evident that the canons of Mechelen then lived in common life; this is said to have ceased only about the year 1215, when it also ceased in the cathedral church of Liège.] life: for the future.

A desire shown to concern the religious vocation and the salvation of souls must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without delay. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the church of Mechelen now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s grace assisting, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have judged the following to be named expressly: the altar [Note: Concerning the altar of Mechelen, see the diploma of the chapter of Cambrai, issued in 1134, in Miraeus, *Collectio diplomatica Belgica*, or vol. XIV, p. 964.] of the church of Mechelen with its appurtenances—namely, Muizen, Hanswijk, Battel, and Dungel—granted to you by the canons of the church of Cambrai at a rent of four marks and confirmed by the bishop; Haver, Hockensel, and Schelle, as granted to you by Bishop Nicholas and confirmed by his charter, we confirm by the page of our own writing; two thirds of the tithe of Hingene, Havesdonk, Heffen, Hombeek, Rumst [Note: Rumesta, commonly called Rumst, is today a parish of the diocese of Antwerp, at the confluence of the Dyle and the Nete; its lord is the prince of Ligne. The tithes of Rumst and Havesdonk were later acquired from the chapter of Mechelen, at an annual rent, by Godfrey, lord of Perwez and Rumst, in 1256.], Mortsel, Hanswijk, Hockensel, and Haver; one third at Hombeek (Hombeek of Saint Martin); one fourth at [Col. 1560C] Bolembeke and Kobbegem.

Your allodial estates with their rights of use in arable land, waters, and woods: namely, twelve *mansi* in the parish of Mechelen; at Leeghem, two *bonaria*; at Gherdeghem, one; a dwelling-place in Mechelen paying fourteen denarii; at Hombeek, two *mansi*; at Hockezela, fourteen *mansi*, with external perquisites; at Odeghem, five solidi, two denarii, and two rams; at Crondeghem, four solidi, two denarii, and one ram; at Bastela, twelve denarii; at Hingene, nine solidi; at Burna, two solidi and three denarii; at Liezela, fourteen denarii and a ram; at Kalsvoert, sixteen denarii; at Puderse, eighteen denarii; at Heffen, two solidi; at Herenthals, thirteen denarii; at Gersdeghem, ten denarii; at Kobbegem, eleven solidi; [Col. 1560D] at Lempst, twelve solidi, six denarii, and ten rams; [lacuna]; at Untho, ten solidi and six denarii, and four solidi in lieu of rams; at Baeleghem, ten denarii; at Haver, seven solidi and six denarii, a *panadium*, and external perquisites; at Hanswijk, three solidi and six denarii; at Hoigar, four denarii; at Aldeghem, four denarii; at Turnhout, twelve denarii; at Visplica, twelve denarii; at Mortsel, ten solidi and nine denarii, and thirty-two denarii in lieu of rams.

[Col. 1561A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amendment through suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood [Col. 1561B] of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given, etc.

### DXXXIX. He Confirms the Possessions and Privileges of the Abbey of Saint Cornelius of Ninove and Receives It under the Protection of the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opp. dipl.*, I, 530, from the archives of the metropolitan chapter.]

Whenever a request is made to us which is known to accord with religion and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and give suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Cornelius, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that all possessions and goods which that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God favouring, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have judged the following to be named expressly: [Col. 1561D] the entire tithe of the same village with its appurtenances; Herlincoven, with the entire tithe; the church of Liedekerke, with its entire tithe and its appurtenances, namely Lombeke and Strithem; part of the tithe at Menz; the estate of Netherwich, with meadow, fishing rights everywhere on the Tenena, and advocacy; two mills with holdings beside the church of Ninove; the estate of Rubroc with surrounding lands and woods; the land of Hugh of Ghent and of his brother Gislebert; the wood of Mentogh bought from Gerard the advocate; the estate of Wendecote with surrounding lands and meadows; the inheritance of Henry, lay brother of Herlincoven; the allod of Rosilar with the little wood of Stonbecca; the allod given by Herbrand of Merbeca; the land with wood of Walter of Curia; the land given by Theoderic [Col. 1562A] of Inferno; the land given by the castellan of Brussels, with the consent of Guy and Walter of Hosdem; at Senesia, the land given by Uffo the Poor, with the consent of his brother Gislard; and at Arken, the land given by Alberic, with wood and meadow at the same village.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on lands that you cultivate by your own hands or resources, or on the increase of your animals. We also forbid any brother, after making profession there, to dare leave that cloister without permission of his abbot; and no one shall presume to receive or retain a departing brother without letters of the community giving assurance.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 1562C] Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

### DXL. Privilege for the Church of Saint Lawrence of Genoa. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 865.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SYRUS, archbishop of Genoa, and to his successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

By the apostolic office entrusted to us by God, we must love our brother bishops, whether near at hand or far away, preserve to the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their rights, and prove in deed what we call them in name—our brethren. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Archbishop Syrus, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of the glorious martyr of Christ Lawrence and of Saint Syrus, over which, by God’s ordering, you preside, and strengthen it with the privilege of this present writing. We decree that all possessions and goods which you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire by lawful means, God favouring, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have judged the following to be named expressly: namely, the revenues from the sea and the tithes which you and your predecessors have from ancient times hitherto peacefully possessed from those men of the city and of the whole diocese of Genoa [Col. 1563A] who conduct maritime commerce, eastward from the port of Pisa and westward from the port of the Monk, whether in the land of Saracens or of Christians, beyond the aforesaid places; the castle of Saint Romulus with its appurtenances; the castle of Molacian with its estate, mills, and appurtenances; the estate of Bazali; the estate in the village of Molatio; the estate of Bavoli; the estate of Nervi; the castle of Medolico with its estate, appurtenances, and mills; the estate of Saint Peter of Arena with its appurtenances; the cultivated holding of Saint Vincent with its mills, and all that you possess at Corti; the estate of Saint Michael in Lavagna, the cultivated holding beside the sea, all that you possess in the valley of Lavagna and at Sestri, and one half of Roccatagliata with one half of Mount Comalio.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, etc., saving, etc.

If anyone, therefore, etc. Amen.

### DXLI. To Villanus, Archbishop of Pisa. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[GATTULA, *Hist. Casin.*, 155.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother VILLANUS, archbishop of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have frequently received the complaint of our beloved son Raynald, abbot of Cassino, against our venerable brother A., bishop of Sulci: namely, that he injures him in respect of six churches—Saint Vincent of Taverna, Saint Mary of the Warm River, Saint Martha, Saint Pantaleon of Olivano, Saint George of Tulvi, and Saint Mary of Palma—which he asserts belong by right to his monastery, and unjustly holds them by force.

Since that monastery is known to belong by special prerogative to the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter, we cannot and ought not fail it in its rights. Therefore, by these present letters we command your brotherhood to summon the aforesaid brother of ours before you on the next Kalends of May, in order to settle this controversy; and, after carefully hearing and examining the pleadings and arguments of both parties, to impose, God authorizing, a due conclusion upon the case, either by judgment or agreement. On the aforesaid date the said abbot shall take care to send suitable representatives before you for this case.

We also command you to endeavour to settle by justice the controversy which the archpriest of Torres brought against the monastery of Saint Mary of Tharros, concerning the church of Saint Peter within Cingla and Saint Mary of Tanache, before your predecessor Archbishop Baldwin of holy memory. Moreover, let your brotherhood cause the judgment which he is known to have rendered concerning the suit of the late Constantine of Athens against Saint Benedict to be put into due effect and firmly observed.

### DXLII. To the Archpriest of the Title of Saint Mark. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 629.]

[Col. 1564A]

Wishing to provide for the church of Saint Mark in the controversy concerning the obedience to be rendered which is known to be disputed between you and the chaplain of Pinea, we command you by these present letters strictly to admonish him not in any way to refuse to promise obedience to your church according to ancient and reasonable custom. But if he should scorn to obey your admonitions in this matter, we shall, God authorizing, hold valid the sentence which you have justly pronounced against him and the aforesaid church of Pinea.

### DXLIII. To Ardition, Subdeacon of the Roman Church, and Master Omnibonus. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[Ibid., 363.]

[Col. 1564B]

We kindly received your kindly letter, in which you asked whether, in the case pending before your tribunal between our venerable brother G., bishop of Bologna, and our beloved son the abbot of Padua, it is fitting that an oath against calumny be taken. Certainly, in cases concerning only the tithes of churches and spiritual matters, the Roman Church is accustomed neither to administer nor receive the oath against calumny. Such cases reach their proper conclusion not by the rigour of civil laws but by the equity of the canons. [Col. 1564C] The canons, moreover, impose the oath against calumny upon no one at all. Therefore, setting aside the dispute concerning the taking of the oath against calumny, let your brotherhood proceed to the further matters.

### DXLIV. To Aesculapius, Priest. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[Ibid., 326.]

That young man who married a girl not yet seven years old, although her age prevented it, nevertheless attempted, from human frailty, what he could not accomplish. Since, therefore, in doubtful matters we must hold to what we judge more certain, both for the sake of the Church’s honour—because the girl is said to be his wife—and because of the aforesaid doubt, we command you [Col. 1564D] to separate from him the cousin of that girl, whom he afterwards married.

### DXLV. To the Whole Clergy—Concerning Robbers and Violators of Churches, and When Ecclesiastical Burial Is To Be Refused after Penance Has Been Performed Unless They Give Security for Restitution of the Damage. (A.D. 1145–1153.)

[Ibid., 390.]

Concerning robbers of churches and priests who presume to impose penance upon them and receive their offerings contrary to our decree, we have established, after common deliberation with our brethren, and likewise confirm the constitution itself by the authority of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers. We decree that any of these robbers who, at the devil’s prompting, have violently risen up in the city and have been openly caught in robbery or violation of churches, or shall hereafter be so caught, shall be wholly denied the benefit of penance unless he first restores what was taken, if able, or gives full security that he will make restitution.

But if, God forbid, he persists in his obstinacy until death and, at the end of life, humbly seeks the remedy of penance, then, if he promises restitution or gives security for making it and provides suitable sureties who are to restore what was taken, penance and ecclesiastical burial shall be granted him. But one who, while in health, has not repented or made restitution with an obstinate mind, [Col. 1565B] and who at death cannot provide security and sureties as we have said—[perhaps supply: “to such a person”] the solemnity of penance seems, as we believe, of little benefit—shall nevertheless not be denied the viaticum. Yet no cleric may attend his burial or presume to accept his alms.

If any priest or cleric, contrary to our decree, presumes in life or death to impose penances, attend their burial, or accept their alms, or is found to have shared in robbery of this kind, let him suffer irrecoverable loss of his order and be deprived of ecclesiastical benefice.

DXLVI. On the witnesses to be employed in a case of separation on account of closeness of kinship. (A.D. 1145–53.)

[MANSI, Councils, XXII, 309.]

[Col. 1565C]

Whenever persons are separated on account of close kinship or consanguinity, the matter must be affirmed by three surviving witnesses of that same kindred; or it must be proved by two or three of the oldest and most reputable witnesses of that place. The examination of the witnesses, moreover, must take place under a twofold oath. For the witnesses must swear that they have not been induced to take this oath by private hatred or friendship, by gold, or by any transaction which they have had or expect to have. Thereafter they must swear that, as they declare, they have received the truth of the matter from their elders, and that it is so.

DXLVII. He determines the dispute between Theobald, bishop of Paris, and the canons of St. Geneviève concerning the parish of the church of St. John. (A.D. 1146–53, Jan. 8.)

[Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris, I, 30.]

[Col. 1565D]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to THEOBALD, bishop of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Lest the obscurity of oblivion, through human disuse, be introduced into human minds concerning what has been adjudged or decided in disputes of causes, it ought to be entrusted to the memory of writing, so that succeeding posterity may thereby have something which it may plainly recognize in times to come. We have therefore ordered it to be recorded in the sequence of the present document how the controversy which was being conducted between you [Col. 1566A] and our sons, the canons of St. Geneviève, concerning the parish of the church of St. John, was settled in our presence.

You maintained, brother bishop, that the aforesaid brethren by no means paid you the right which you possessed in that parish; and, since it was agreed that the parish belonged to you, you affirmed that the priest who ministered spiritual things to that parish ought to receive the care of souls from you. For you said that, if any persons in that parish were to be bound or loosed, the priest who governed that parish at the time bound or loosed them at your command. You also maintained that brides to be blessed received the blessing, women rising after childbirth received purification, and those held by open crimes received penance, in the mother church.

The canons, not denying what you asserted, said that the servants of the canons who resided in that parish had customarily been loosed or bound through the canons, and not by the bishop of Paris; and that the priest ministering in that church had received the care of souls from the dean of St. Geneviève, not from the bishop, for eleven years and before that time. Having therefore fully considered both your arguments and those of the aforesaid brethren, and after taking counsel with our brethren, we have judged that the priest who is to serve that parish, whether he be a regular canon or not, shall receive the care of souls from you, brother bishop, and shall bind and loose the aforesaid parishioners at [Col. 1566C] your command.

But if, for a cause arising, you pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against any person, or against all persons, of that parish, the priest shall not celebrate the divine offices either for the excommunicated or for those under interdict until that sentence has been relaxed. The same priest shall not presume to perform the blessings of brides, the purifications of women rising after childbirth, or public penances. Moreover, if the priest of the aforesaid chapel should at any time be found to be such a man as ought not to minister divine things, you must notify the abbot and his brethren of this; and they, having learned the truth, shall remove him and present another to you, to whom you may commit the care of souls. That priest, however, shall pay you neither the *circata* nor the synodal due.

[Col. 1566D] Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to infringe this page of our determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Ides of January [8 January].

DXLVIII. To Berthold, abbot, and the brethren of Zell near Würzburg. (A.D. 1146–1153, Jan. 11.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, Preface, p. 385.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERTHOLD, abbot of Zell, and his brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

At all times the most holy Roman Church has customarily been solicitous for the needs of religious persons, both temporal and spiritual; and the more it has seen them cast off concern for earthly things, the more gratefully it has always endeavoured to furnish them with the consolations of piety and mercy. Moved by the consideration of this habitual kindness, our predecessors, after due deliberation, mercifully decreed that religious men should not be compelled to pay tithes from their newly cultivated lands. Since, therefore, fraternal charity does not permit the benefits of piety—especially those bestowed upon the necessities of religious persons—to perish, and since the holy institutions of our predecessors must always remain unimpaired, we, sprinkled with the fragrance of your good religious life, by apostolic authority forbid anyone whatsoever to presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands or on the increase of your animals.

If anyone should presume to attempt this, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct his rashness by fitting satisfaction, let him incur the indignation [Col. 1567B] of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul, and at the final judgment be subject to the punishment of divine vengeance.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of January [11 January].

DXLIX. He rebukes Hugh, archbishop of Vienne, because he inflicts injuries upon the Cistercian and Cluniac brethren. (A.D. 1147–53.)

[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 902.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Vienne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more your person is known to be adorned with greater religious devotion, [Col. 1567C] the more grievously we take it when religious and God-fearing men are unjustly harassed by you; and on this account you are ill spoken of both by persons near at hand and by those far away. Although consideration of your habit ought to inflame you to love religion and urge you more earnestly to promote it, you do not protect, but attack, the Cistercian and Cluniac brethren, as frequent complaints show; and you nevertheless trouble the Cluniac brethren, whom you ought to love more devotedly.

DL. To John, bishop of Padua.—On usury. (A.D. 1150–53.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, Lucchesi edition, III, 377.]

[Col. 1567D] Concerning what your brotherhood asked of us—namely, whether those commit the crime of usury who receive the fruits from possessions pledged to them and subsequently receive the principal—we shall tell you briefly: all who receive more than the principal are liable to the crimes of usury; for whatever accrues to the principal is usury.

DLI. Privilege for the monastery of St. Sylvester on Monte Suavi. (A.D. 1152–1153.)

[MITARELLI, *Camaldolese*, III, p. 466.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved brethren of Monte Suavi, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1568A] Since without observance of religion you … neither unity of charity exists, nor is service pleasing to God rendered, it befits apostolic authority to establish religious observance and, once established, to preserve it with diligent care. Therefore, desiring, with the Lord’s help, to reform in your monastery the religious observance which, through the demands of sins, is known to have been greatly diminished, we entrusted the monastery itself to our beloved son R. …, prior of Camaldoli, to be ordered by him; decreeing that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery shall be observed there inviolate for all time, according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the constitutions of the Camaldolese brethren.

So that this order may be fulfilled more easily and suitably, we command you by these present letters, under obedience, that—as some of you did in our presence—you promise obedience to the aforesaid prior and his successors according to the Rule of Benedict and the Camaldolese order, and that you obey him without any contradiction both in temporal and spiritual matters, so that the aforesaid monastery may recover its former state of religious observance and you, with God’s cooperation, may be restored to the fruitfulness of a better life.

Given …

DLII. To the bishop of Langres.—That he judge those who communicated with the excommunicated men of Vézelay. (About A.D. 1153.)

[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 660.]

[Col. 1568C]

On behalf of our beloved son Pons, abbot of Vézelay, we have received a serious complaint against the archpriest of Avallon, R. of Domiciac, and I. of Chora, priests: that they knowingly communicated with excommunicated men of Vézelay and rashly presumed to celebrate the divine offices. Since we ought not to leave so grave an offence uninvestigated and unpunished, we command you by these present letters to investigate the matter diligently; and, if you find that the case is so, send the aforesaid archpriest and the other priests, suspended from their offices, to our presence. You shall also cause the letters which we are sending to the bishop of Autun to be presented to him by your [Col. 1568D] reliable and trustworthy messenger.

DLIII. Privilege for the church of St. Mary of Cappenberg. (A.D. 1153, Jan. 2.)

[NIESERT, *Münster Documentary Collection*, II, 183.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons OTTO, provost of the Church of St. Mary of Cappenberg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection at hand and receive the aid of our protection, lest an attack of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength [Col. 1569A] of sacred religious observance. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, Provost Otto and the other brethren gathered in the church of Blessed Mary of Cappenberg for God’s service, we mercifully assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we decree that the canonical order which, by God’s authorisation, is known to have been established there according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods in lands, vineyards, serfs, rents, tithes, [Col. 1569B] mills, waters and watercourses, meadows, pastures, woods, fields, hills, valleys, or any other things that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter obtain, God being propitious, by concession of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: Cappenberg, Curedo, Wisele, Wesheim, Werne, Hele, Alstede, Mengede, Nette, Hilbeke, Sorbecke, Langere, Wetmare, Stikelevic; the estate called Velmede; and whatever Winemar granted you from his own right by a reasonable disposition. Also, by concession of our venerable brother Frederick, bishop of Münster, the church called Werna and the church called Alnon, together with the tithe in the aforesaid church of Werna.

Moreover, desiring to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority any ecclesiastical or secular person to occupy Cappenberg and its precinct by force or fraud, to fortify it as a castle, or to remove religious men from it. Nor may any of your brethren, after making profession there, leave the place itself; and no one may dare retain one who departs without letters of the community’s permission.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, or take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and entire, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of authority and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to stern [Col. 1570A] vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Hincmar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of St. George, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of the Schola Graeca, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of St. Mary across [Col. 1570B] the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Humbald, cardinal priest of St. Praxedes, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of SS. John and Paul, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth Nones of January [2 January], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

A lead seal is appended on silk cords of red colour.

DLIV. At the intercession of Rainald of Dassel, provost, he confirms Ringelheim Abbey to the church of Hildesheim. (A.D. 1153, Jan. 3.)

[*Origines Guelficae*, III, 440.]

[Col. 1570C] EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, bishop, and to his beloved sons of Hildesheim, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Set by the Lord’s ordinance upon the lofty watchtower of the Church, we ought to attend with diligent care to the revenues of all churches, and to strengthen by the confirmation of our writing and apostolic authority those things which, by God’s gift, accrue to them lawfully. Our beloved son Rainald, provost of your church, coming into the presence of the Apostolic See and of ourselves, declared in a hearing that Conrad, once king of the Romans, of illustrious memory, illuminated by the radiance of heavenly light, for the salvation of his soul relinquished to you—and through you to your church—the abbey at [Col. 1570D] Ringelheim, free and undisturbed, together with whatever he himself appeared to possess there by the custom of his predecessors. And lest what he had thus done should in the course of time be assailed by anyone’s rashness, or any of his successors should inflict injury upon you or your successors with respect to that church or exercise there by force anything under pretext of some customary right, he strengthened this act by the safeguard of royal authority, with the consent of his court officials and the ministerials of that church present.

Since the aforesaid son, the provost, requested that this be established by the confirmation of our writing, and since we judged it fitting to grant consent to his petition and to provide more carefully for the honour of your church, we confirm the act itself by the authority of the Apostolic See and decree that it shall remain valid in time to come. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted by any presumption to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act against this act. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Nones of January [3 January].

DLV. To Peter, archbishop of Bourges.—He commands him to restore to the monastery of St. Denis the church of La Maison-Major and the goods of its deceased priest, wrongfully taken. (A.D. 1153, Jan. 8.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, vol. XV, 476.]

[Col. 1571B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Bourges, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When the order of justice is thrown into confusion and the decrees of the canons disturbed by those persons who ought to be their defenders, and when what they ought most diligently to correct in the Church of God is presumed to be undertaken against them by those same persons, we are bound by the duty of our office to restore what has been wrongly done to its proper state, so that neither scandal may arise from it in the Church nor an occasion for similar presumption accrue to the more simple-minded.

Accordingly, our beloved son Odo, abbot of St. Denis, appearing in our presence, laid before us a complaint against your brotherhood: after he had come into the presence of the Apostolic See on the business of his church, you despoiled his church of La Maison-Major, not so much by justice as at your own discretion; and when the priest of that church—who, upon being appointed there, had decreed that everything which he could lawfully acquire there, God granting, should be granted to that church—was taken from this life, you applied all his goods to your own uses. If this is true, we are the more astonished because we see that our authority has been disregarded in this matter, canonical enactments set aside, and the order of reason in great part confused.

Moreover, your prudence, unless we are mistaken, does not fail to know what the sacred canons permit priests and all prelates of churches to dispose of at their death. Since, therefore, what has been done contrary to the canons ought by their force to be declared void, we command your brotherhood by these present letters that, if his complaint is supported by truth, you restore in charity that church and those things which came to you from the goods acquired by its priest in the service of that church, or, if they were taken by another, cause them to be restored. Thus he may not find that his journey to the Apostolic See has harmed him, and your brotherhood may not appear to wish improperly to burden those churches which belong especially to the right of blessed Peter and are especially under his protection. Likewise, with respect to his other wrongdoers residing in your diocese, render them such full justice that they are not compelled further to be troubled by a failure of justice.

We command your brotherhood [read: fatherhood], on our behalf, to enjoin upon our brother S[tephen], bishop of Clermont, that he is in no way to trouble Brother R., prior of Mont-Firmin, because the latter appears to have opposed his advancement; and, as he does not wish to incur our indignation, neither personally nor through his agents may he presume, on that account, to inflict any annoyance upon him or his men.

[Note: [Col. 1571] Stephen of Mercœur, who was elected bishop of Clermont in 1151.]

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution or in any manner rashly to oppose it. If anyone should attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation [Col. 1572B] of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Ides of September [8 September].

DLVI. Bull for the nunnery of St. Saviour at Évreux. (A.D. 1153, Jan. 23.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, Documents, XI, 134.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, HILARY, abbess of St. Saviour of Évreux, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, etc. …

It is fitting that prudent virgins who, beneath the religious habit, with lamps kindled according to the Gospel saying, show themselves ready to enter the marriage-feast with their bridegroom Jesus Christ, should have apostolic protection at hand, lest an attack of any rashness recall them from their devout purpose or—God forbid—break the strength [Col. 1572C] of sacred religious observance. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we mercifully assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter obtain, God being propitious, by concession of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and those who shall succeed you.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: by the gift of Count Richard, two mills at Évreux, one a grain-mill and the other a tannery-mill, with the land belonging to those mills; and the tithe of the mills, rents, and fishpond of Trozcomitissae; and the tithe of all revenues and profits of the whole forest of Évreux; the tithe of honey from that forest, of hunting, and of the money from clearings (*essarts*) that shall be made in that forest; and, finally, whatever the count possesses at Asnières in his demesne, excepting the fiefs of knights, the wood, and the water.

Yet in the water he gave the fishery popularly called *Croignum Clavillae*; land for half a ploughland; Hundoville and all that belongs to it; the mill-dues of Daubol; and Escauville of Gravigny; the tithe of the mills and of the entire count’s demesne, except the grain tithe at Guitebuet; the tithe of the demesne of the same count—that is, of wool, cheeses, and wax candles made there. At Alba Via, the tithe of wool, cheeses, tolls, rents, and every money revenue; eight tenant holdings and land for half a ploughland. At Bavent, one hundred shillings. Beyond the Seine, the tithe of all revenues and profits whatsoever of the forests of Tractu, Cravenchon, and Caudebec, and the tithe of the mills of Maisnil and Cravenchon. At Dourenc, the tithe of the mills, tolls, burgesses’ rents, the stabling-dues of pigs, and the grazing-dues of sheep held by the burgesses; and two sheaves from the burgesses’ gardens, of flax, hemp, and every other thing; likewise the tithe of the land called Troz-comitis, two sheaves from the peasants’ land, and two sheaves from the clearings.

By the gift of Count William, six marks of silver in England, which the prior and monks of Nogent-sur-Andelle are to pay you annually. By the gift of Count Amaury, the fair of St. Leodegar at Évreux; the tithe of his pigsties in the forests of Guaz; and the entire tithe of old and newly cleared lands belonging to Guaz, in the forests of Tractu, Cravenchon, and Caudebec; likewise the tithe from the *Haia de Lentot*, of everything there which is tithed. By the gift of Anschetil of Autoly, the mill of Alba Via, one vineyard, and two tenant holdings at Foville; from Helmaci of Autoly, the water of Gravigny; by the gift of Richard son of Herluin, the tithe of the mills of Garennes; the tithe of St. Andrew, by the gift of Osenna; by the grant of Ralph son of Otto, two burgesses in the street of St. Taurin, free of every customary due.

In the diocese of Évreux: all churches and the grain tithe of the forest of Évreux; the church of St. James of Essarts, with the tithe of woodland and arable land; the church of Caugeio, with its tithe and thirty acres of land in the same village; the church of Guichenville with its tithe; the tithe of Buissondrœlin and Folmuchon; the church of Neuville [Col. 1573D] with its tithe and thirty acres of land in the same village; the church of Ferrières with its tithe; the church of Lacelle with its tithe, land there for half a ploughland, and the tenant holdings which you have there; the church of Boore, with the right which belongs to you in the tithe of that church in the diocese of Lisieux; the church of Boissey, with the tithe of that village and sixty acres of land in the same village; the tithe of Lamberville, given by the wife of Wauquelin from her patrimony; half of the village called Capelle; and the right which you have in the church of that village. In the diocese of Chartres, by the gift of Amaury of Domorotunda, half the village of Orviller.

Furthermore, because the aforesaid Count Richard, for the salvation of his soul, granted to your servants the immunity which the servants of his household enjoyed, and rendered your church free and undisturbed from every customary due and burden imposed by himself or his successors; and because, after granting to William, then bishop of Évreux of good memory, the fairs held on the Annunciation of the Lord in the forecourt of the church of Blessed Mary—reserving only the care of souls to him and his successors—he exempted it from every wrongful custom and episcopal exaction, we also confirm this by apostolic authority and decree that it shall remain unshaken in future times.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit in every way of the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of authority and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here [Col. 1574C] the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, W., cardinal priest of the Lateran church. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedes. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of St. Sabina. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Roland, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. [Col. 1574D] I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. I, Ismar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints George and Bacchus. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman [Col. 1575A] Church, on the tenth Kalends of February [23 January], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

DLVII. To Henry, bishop of Autun.—He rebukes him because he is hostile to the monastery of Vézelay. (A.D. 1153, Jan. 27.)

[MANSI, Councils, XX, 658.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Autun, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The fact that we make you a participant in the apostolic blessing proceeds not from your merits but from the kindness of the Apostolic See. For, as has been reliably reported to us by many persons, all the troubles and vexations which the burgesses of that town of Vézelay have wickedly presumed to inflict upon our beloved son Pons, abbot of Vézelay, had their origin in your instigation and incitement; and you do not fear to encourage and support them in such great wickedness against God, against the episcopal office entrusted to you, and against the salvation of your soul.

For it is said that you even presume to communicate with those same excommunicated burgesses, admit them yourself to the divine offices, and permit and command your priests to celebrate the divine offices for them. Since, therefore, we can neither can nor ought to leave so grave and excessive an offence unpunished, we command you by these present letters that, on the next feast of St. Luke, you come into our presence without excuse, both to settle the controversy which is being conducted [Col. 1575C] between you and the aforesaid abbot and to give us a sufficient answer concerning the wrongs which you are said to have inflicted upon that abbot.

Meanwhile, do not presume in any manner to inflict disturbance or annoyance upon that abbot. Take diligent care that none of the aforesaid excommunicated or interdicted persons be admitted by you or your priests to the divine offices; rather, wherever any one of them may come within your parish, no one there may presume to celebrate the divine offices so long as that person is present. But if you neglect to come to us at the appointed time, or have presumed, or shall presume, to violate these provisions or others laid down by us or our brethren for the punishment of the aforesaid burgesses, know for certain that the cause itself will take its course as justice dictates, and that you will incur danger to your office.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Kalends of February [27 January].

DLVIII. Privilege for the Church of Arras. (A.D. 1153, Feb. 5.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, Lucchesi edition, II, 170.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GODESCALC, bishop of Arras, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

The authority of our office exhorts us to be solicitous for the condition of the Churches and, with the Lord’s salutary assistance, to provide for their peace and welfare. For it is judged worthy and consonant with propriety that we, who have been appointed to govern the Churches, should both protect them from the wickedness of evil persons and fortify them by the patronage of blessed Peter and of the apostolic see. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Godescalc, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Arras, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of the apostolic see. Thus, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Urban, Paschal, Gelasius, Calixtus, and Innocent, Roman pontiffs, confirming by the present page the episcopal dignity of the same Church as it exists today, we decree that whatever blessed Remigius granted to the aforesaid Church—namely Orcos and Sambucetum—and whatever that Church justly and lawfully possesses or may acquire hereafter, is confirmed to you and your successors.

Among these we have added the following, to be specified by their proper names: two archdeaconries, namely that of Arras and the other called Ostrevant. We also decree that the boundaries between the Churches of Arras and Cambrai shall be those shown to have existed from ancient times either by documentary records, by the division of territories, or by certain other evidences, so that, with God’s assent, the peace of the Churches may not be disturbed on any pretext and what has been established for the salvation of the faithful may endure in unshaken stability for all time. We further command that the abbeys situated within the boundaries of the bishopric of Arras—namely, St Peter of Hasnon, Holy Saviour of Anchin, St Vindician of Mont-Saint-Éloi, St Ragenfredis of Denain, St Rictrudis of Marchiennes, St Mary of Estru(n), together with the others situated within the aforesaid boundaries, and the monastery of St Praejectus of Béthune—shall be subject to you and your successors, and that their abbots or abbesses shall render canonical obedience. But the abbot of St Vedast of Noyelles and his successors shall promise obedience to you and your successors by hand, and shall show due reverence and subjection in respect of the things known to be possessed from the Church of Arras.

Likewise, [we confirm] the part of the deanery of Vals situated within the boundaries of the territory of Arras: namely, the churches of Bajoncourt, Vallibus, Migerol, Chaom, Brodovilla, Caxenignicuth, Sarving, Halcurth, Schulsa, and Hailcourt, with their appurtenances. Moreover, for the maintenance and table of the bishop of Arras: the altars of Avions, Culcis, Menricourt, and the altar of St Martin of Hénin-Rainard; also Mareolum, with woodland, land, water, mills, oven, tenants, and all the jurisdiction of the entire village; the mills of Schenfolt; and another mill within Arras, with two ovens, a cambo, and tenants; together with lands and the fishpond of Bronnis. All these things, because your predecessor Bishop Alvisus, of revered memory, is known to have held them in his lifetime, we likewise confirm to you.

Furthermore, the altar of Monci, Gamapis, the altar of St Martin, [Col. 1577A] the altar of Atluth with its appurtenances, Vulpi, Wlgeval, the altar of Raincourth with its appurtenances, the altar of Miralmont and of St Mary of Postumviller, Bagunils, Bulgy, Hangra, Ruyth, Berry, Cornay, Bruay, Hesdinvil, Camblin, Maresch, Hanubiis, Tungry, Herlu, Obertio, Harmenteriis, Salty, Belona, Carency, and Novavilla; the altar of Athis in Ostrevant, Syrici, and the church of Berberiis with its appurtenances. In addition, we confirm for your use and domestic needs the custody of the Church of Arras and the revenues pertaining to it and to its lights: namely, the altar of Curcelles, Gummicurt, Hervilert, and the altar of Vimy.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; rather, all shall be preserved intact, to benefit in every way those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third warning should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, recognize himself or herself as guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But may all who preserve what is right for that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Ymarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed.  
I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed.  
I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes, have subscribed.  
I, Aribertus, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia, have subscribed.  
I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement, have subscribed.  
I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia, have subscribed.  
I, Roland, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark, have subscribed.  
I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed.  
I, John Paparo, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Peter and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, [lacuna] [Col. 1578A]  
I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of the title of St George, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of St Angelo, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.  
I, Odo, cardinal deacon of the title of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.  
I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of [Col. 1578B] Boson, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

### DLIX. He exhorts the canons of Arras to maintain their ecclesiastical duties.  
*(A.D. 1153, February 5.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucae edition, II, 170.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1578C] Just as a natural mother desires to be supported by the children whom she has endeavoured to nourish, so the spiritual mother, the Church, urgently demands due service from those to whom she supplies necessities according to her means; nor does she willingly bestow her benefit on those who withhold the service owed to her. For those do not wish to pay what reason requires who, idly eating the bread of the Church, grow slothful and absent themselves from her service without a definite and reasonable cause.

And because we have heard that among you there are some who, though they live from the altar of the Church entrusted to you, are unwilling to serve that Church and indeed, with no definite or reasonable cause intervening, withdraw themselves from the service of your Church to the peril of their souls, by these present letters we command you [Col. 1578D] that, unless a definite and reasonable cause should at some time arise, you be so constant in the Church’s service that the aforesaid Church is not defrauded of its due service. But if any of you, unless an evident and honourable cause intervenes, should perhaps refuse to labour in the service of your Church, since it is written that whoever does not work shall not eat, we wish you to know that, by God’s authority, we shall hold firm and ratified whatever sentence our venerable brother Godescalc, your bishop, shall canonically pronounce against him with the counsel of the sounder part of your chapter.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of February.

### DLX. To the clergy and people of Arras.—He declares beforehand that he will approve the sentence which their bishop pronounces against heretics of his diocese, and orders them also to obey it.  
*(A.D. 1153, February 5.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 689.]

[Col. 1579A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When there is so great a union of charity between prelates and subjects that the prelates provide with diligent attention for what is salutary to their subjects, and the subjects submit themselves to their prelates in all obedience and humility, then the Church of God is without doubt directed in its proper course [Col. 1579B] and rejoices in tranquil peace and gladness. We therefore received with due kindness our venerable brother Godescalc, your bishop, when he came to the clemency of the apostolic see; and while he remained with us, we treated him among our brethren and fellow bishops with fraternal charity, especially out of regard for his integrity.

Since certain matters concerning the state of the Church entrusted to him had reached our hearing, matters which permit neither us nor him to be negligent in investigating and correcting them, we charged him orally to be so ready and strict in correcting them and preserving integrity and religious observance in that Church that he may appear to have fulfilled his office in these matters and that no adverse report arising from them may any further trouble our mind. Among other things, that same brother reported to us something which we relate not without great sorrow of heart. For he informed us that the wickedness of certain persons in the Church entrusted to him has so increased that they are ensnared in the net of heretical depravity; they do not even shrink from spreading the snares of heretics with certain others, so that they may have more companions in their destruction and condemn themselves together with many souls. Certainly the rigor of ecclesiastical severity must be opposed to such persons more strictly. Therefore, by God’s authority, we shall hold ratified the sentence which the aforesaid brother, your bishop, shall pronounce against them on the advice of religious men; and we strictly command you to observe it firmly.

Accordingly, just as [Col. 1579D] our said brother has been more earnestly exhorted by us concerning the care of the flock entrusted to him and the urgency of his office, so you must be exhorted by the admonitions of our letters to obey and venerate him. As that same brother returns to his Church and to you, the Lord guiding him, with the support of the apostolic see and our letters, we have judged it right to commend him earnestly to your whole community, commanding you by these present letters to receive him reverently and honourably, constantly show him filial reverence and honour, and humbly obey his salutary commands, both concerning the matters stated above and concerning other matters among you requiring correction. Thus [Col. 1580A] he may, by God’s gift, receive the crown of everlasting glory for the pastoral office bestowed upon you, and you, through the merit of obedience, may enter with him alike into the joys of eternal blessedness.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of February.

### DLXI. To the nuns of Denain.—He states that he has entrusted their reform to the bishop of Arras.  
*(A.D. 1153, February 5.)*

[Ibid., 688.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the nuns of Denain: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Believe that we greet you with the address of apostolic blessing not because of your merits, [Col. 1580B] but because of the customary kindness of the apostolic see. For such things are reported to us concerning your manner of life as do not move our mind to confer upon you the grace of apostolic blessing. For, as we have heard from the report of certain persons, you run after your desires with such loosened reins that the memory of your vow seems wholly to have fallen away from you, and you appear to be going backward when you ought with all your strength to be pressing forward.

Indeed, the small spark of charity, which is recognized as the kindling and nourishment of uprightness, has, because of the demands of your sins, grown so cold among you that your monastery has been greatly diminished both spiritually and temporally. Therefore, since we desire, with the Lord’s help, that your condition be reformed for the better, [Col. 1580C] we have instructed our venerable brother Godescalc, bishop of Arras—whose integrity and religious devotion we trust, since he is known to be fully qualified in these matters—to endeavour to restore among you a form of religious life pleasing to God and to bring your monastery back to the fruitfulness of a better life.

Accordingly, by these present letters we command and order you to obey the aforesaid brother of ours with due humility in matters concerning the amendment of your life and the correction of monastic discipline; to receive kindly his admonitions and salutary commands; and to observe them without contradiction. Know that if hereafter you despise obedience to his salutary admonitions, we shall, by God’s authority, hold ratified whatever sentence he shall pronounce against [Col. 1580D] you on that account.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of February.

### DLXII. To the people of Douai.—That they render due obedience to the bishop of Arras.  
*(A.D. 1153, February 5.)*

[Ibid.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the greater and lesser inhabitants of Douai: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us, we must be concerned for all and diligently call back to the way of truth the Church’s children known to stray from the path of rectitude. From the account of our venerable brother Godescalc, bishop of Arras, who came into our presence, we learned that you are unwilling to show him the due reverence owed to your father and bishop; and that, when you commit some offence and are summoned by him, you rashly refuse to come before him. Indeed, on the pretext of some institution of your own, when you ought unanimously to cleave to your head, you abandon that head and endeavour to separate yourselves from him, though without him you cannot live. For members cannot live without a head, even if some persons may perhaps consider them to be members of some head. Therefore members ought to cleave to their own head, from whom they receive life and without whom they cannot live at all.

So that you may receive the teaching of salvation from your head, and that your head may obtain a reward for the teaching bestowed on you, we command and strictly enjoin your whole community by these present letters [Col. 1581B] to show the aforesaid brother, as the father and bishop of your souls, due reverence and obedience; and, when summoned by him for the correction of offences, never to disdain to come before him. Know that if any of you should prove contumacious and rebellious toward him and, when summoned by him, disdain to appear in his presence, we shall, by God’s authority, hold ratified and firm whatever sentence that same brother pronounces against that person for this reason.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of February.

### DLXIII. He exhorts Count Theodoric of Flanders to restore to Godescalc, bishop of Arras, the men of the village of Mareolum.  
*(A.D. 1153, February 5.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucae edition, II, 171.]

[Col. 1581C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman THEODORIC, count of Flanders: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as one who reasonably uses the authority granted him by the Lord will without doubt receive a reward, so conversely one who, on the pretext of authority received, acts contrary to reason will suffer no slight punishment. From the complaint of our venerable brother Godescalc, bishop of Arras, who came to the thresholds of the apostles [Col. 1581D] and into our presence, we have learned that in his village called Mareolum you inflict many burdens upon him and, contrary to justice and to the will of that same brother of ours, keep in your own territory the people of that village.

Certainly, since you have many villages and villeins, you ought not to seize another’s property, especially that of your bishop, or grievously and unjustly offend the very man whom you ought to love as a father with filial devotion and to defend more earnestly against the disturbances of others. For temporal authority has been conferred upon you by the Lord so that in the land entrusted to your care you may preserve justice and restrain by the bridle of equity those who do injustice. [Col. 1582A] But unless your nobility is willing to keep the path of justice itself, and unless it chooses to desist from disturbing and unjustly occupying the Church’s property, then from that for which it ought to have gained reward at the strict judgment it will without doubt find punishment prepared for itself.

Since we cannot with a clear conscience endure the oppressions and injuries done to that brother of ours, and since we are unwilling henceforth to defend you against him, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters to restore his dependants to the aforesaid brother and inflict no further annoyance upon him in this matter. If you should refuse to do so, know that we have instructed our venerable brother Samson, archbishop of Reims, to endeavour to punish such presumption severely, both against your person and against [Col. 1582B] your land.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of February.

### DLXIV. To Sibylla, countess of Flanders.—That she dissuade her husband, the count, from injuries against Godescalc, bishop of Arras.  
*(A.D. 1153, February 5.)*

[Ibid.]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ SIBYLLA, countess of Flanders: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, beloved daughter in the Lord, we believe your devotion to be solicitous in matters pertaining to the Lord, [Col. 1582C] we have thought fit to honour you with apostolic letters and earnestly urge you, for the salvation of your soul and of your husband’s, to assist our venerable brother Godescalc, bishop of Arras. For if that brother of ours is freed from your husband’s oppression through your efforts, you will receive a double reward from this very fact: for you will have endeavoured to rescue your own soul, which is certainly bound by the same sin when you are able to oppose it but neglect to do so, from the devil’s snare. For it is written: “A loving wife is her husband’s crown.”

Indeed, as we have learned from the complaint of the aforesaid brother, your husband harasses him in many ways in the sole village which he has, and unjustly and violently takes away from him the men—namely, his dependants—of that village. Therefore, since we trust in your devotion, prudence, and discernment, we command your nobility by these letters prudently to admonish your husband to desist from harassing the aforesaid brother and restore to him the men whom he retains. For those things which he is known to have taken from our brother are not the possessions of a man, but belong to God and to His Church. Therefore, unless he should be willing to restore them, we have instructed our venerable brother Samson, archbishop of Reims, to endeavour severely to punish such wickedness, both against his person and against his land.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Nones of February.

### DLXV. To Samson, archbishop of Reims.—That he withdraw Count Theodoric of Flanders from inflicting damage on the bishopric of Arras and, should he not desist, punish him and his land.  
*(A.D. 1153, February.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 687.]

[Col. 1583A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SAMSON, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Reason persuades us, and the obligation of fraternal charity compels us, to furnish kind assistance to all, and especially to our brother bishops. Our venerable brother Godescalc, bishop of Arras, coming into our presence, laid before us a complaint against the nobleman Theodoric, count of Flanders: [Col. 1583B] that he takes from him, contrary to justice, his men in the village called Mareolum and, though repeatedly called upon, refuses to desist from his presumption.
