We also grant and confirm that the burial of nobles may take place freely in your monastery, and that at Aderstade—indeed, in all parish chapels established under the right and ownership of your monastery—monk-priests shall be appointed by the abbots of your house, according to the decrees of the apostolic popes Leo, Gregory, Agapetus, and Boniface, to celebrate divine offices for the people, while the due reverence of the Church of Halberstadt is preserved. Therefore, lest any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter presume rashly to disturb in any manner your monastery, with all its property and persons, placed under the protection of apostolic clemency, by violating anything (the reading is uncertain: “to be corrected, or whatever”) of the matters set forth above in the privilege granted by our predecessors or by us, we forbid it by apostolic authority under threat of perpetual anathema and eternal damnation. May peace be in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ with all who foster and defend you. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, cardinal bishop of the title of Saint Rufina. I, Octavian, cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. [Col. 1611A] I, Hubald, bishop of Ferentino, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal of the title of Saint Adrian, have subscribed.

Present and assisting were the bishops John of Ostia, Guido of Palestrina, Samson of Reims, Gisibert of Poitiers, Adalbero of Trier, Hartbert of Utrecht, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

Given at Reims through the hand of Roland, chancellor, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [23 March], in the year of the Lord 1148, the eleventh indiction, and happily in the fourth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius III.

DXCII. Bull confirming the Premonstratensian institute at Roth and the possessions of the same monastery. (A.D. 1152, December 15.)

[HUGO, *Premonstratensian Annals*, II, 446.]

[Col. 1611B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons OTTHINO, abbot and prelate of the church of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God, and of the virgin Saint Verena at Roth, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity.

Since without the observance of true religion neither can the Church stand secure nor service pleasing to God be rendered, it is fitting that, wherever we can, we establish the sacred observance of religion and, once established, preserve it with exact diligence. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed virgin Verena at Rotha. It was built on her own allodial estate by the venerable [Col. 1611C] matron and widow named Hemma and her son Chuno, free persons; it was offered to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, subject to an annual payment to the most holy Roman Church of one Byzantine gold coin; and you have been devoted there to divine service. We decree first of all that the canonical order which, by the Lord’s authorship, is known to have been established there according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, shall be observed there for all time.

Moreover, we confirm the possessions, whether ecclesiastical or secular, belonging to it: namely, the church on its own foundation at Rotha [Col. 1611D], with every endowment, every ecclesiastical right, its own allodial estate, and the other properties in that village with all their appurtenant rights; likewise the church of Schopflohc, with its rent-paying people, every endowment, every ecclesiastical right, and the allodial estate in the same village with all its rights; likewise the chapel church of Nertenbuech and the allodial estate there with all lawful rights; and the allodial estate of Tempsheim and the properties in the villages of Hoggenberd, Veldstettim, Grabenstet, and Grabenstetten; also the church of Steinbach, with its rent-paying people, every endowment, every ecclesiastical right, and the other properties in that village with all lawful rights; likewise the properties in the villages of Dathofen, Mazenhofen, Harde, Hausen, [Col. 1612A] Oye, Crawinkel, Mamper, Maiselstein, and Stirenhosen; the chapel church of Ruthina, with its own allodial estate and the vineyard planted there. In the village called Amodes, in the territory of Chur, one estate; in the village of Wilperch, one estate; the chapel church of Mowiler and the allodial estate there with all lawful rights; in the village called Upper Mowiler, one estate. Welmanswiler, Dieplshofen, Richenhofen, Bunofen, Steinethala, Mitthenrieth, Haslach, Murwangen, Habbesegg, Conradiswiler, Chonen, Welants, Spinnelwag, Zell, Binroth, Eicheberg, Bonlanden, Bachen, Halden, Egelsec, Obsingen, Rothum, Herbruchts, Waltenwyler, Bermeswiler, Manzenwiler, Oufdndorf, Lophaim, Hitishaim, Dalmafinger, Schaffhusen, Berg; and likewise whatever other goods, whether acquired by exchanges or by any other price, in small villages or little estates situated far or near, that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or shall possess in the future. [lacuna]

So that you may be able to serve almighty God more peacefully, we decree that the same place shall remain free and undisturbed by every authority or lordship of an advocate or of any lay person. Further, concerning your labours, which [are performed] by your own hands or at your own expense, [lacuna] We also decree that burial in that place shall be free. [lacuna] But when any provost of the same place dies in the Lord, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deceit or by force, except the man whom the brethren have elected by common consent. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [lacuna] As a sign that the same church belongs to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and of the holy Roman Church, you shall pay one Byzantine gold coin each year to us and to our successors.

Then, to all apostolic men who bear with us Christ’s yoke in turn—namely bishops, priests, members of Christ, and those armed with spiritual weapons—we command by apostolic blessing, request in the true charity of Christ, and enjoin that, wherever the aforesaid church and the aforesaid brethren of Roth, belonging to the holy Roman Church, need your assistance, you shall, in our stead—indeed in the stead of almighty God—more sternly rebuke, excommunicate, and anathematize perverse persons inflamed against them by the tinder of envy and hatred and inflicting upon them the violence of a stronger power, as you would aid yourselves; and such persons shall be compelled most strictly to the apostolic see, unless perhaps aid is given by the common consent and request of the brethren, if that is expedient. [Cols. 1612C–D]

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our ordinance, should attempt to act against it through any cunning deceit, violence, or accursed pretext of advocacy—which they should know is forbidden by our apostolic authority to themselves and to every person henceforth, except the royal person alone—by plundering their goods, inflicting any coercive force, whether at the place of their original foundation itself or in their possessions, small villages, or little estates belonging to them far or near [Col. 1613A], or by subjecting their people to their own services: after a second or third warning, unless such a person makes due satisfaction and corrects the offence, let that person be deprived of rank and office. [lacuna] Moreover, let all who adhere to, favour, or consent with such a person be subject to the bond of excommunication and anathema by apostolic authority—indeed, by the authority of almighty God, of all supreme pontiffs, and of priests. At the end of their lives let them be deprived of communion with all the faithful; we forbid, under holy obedience, that they be visited by any priest; rather, let them be buried with the burial of an ass, as they have well deserved, so that even at the last judgment they may be punished by the recompense of strict and eternal vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may it be from our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1613B] that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. I, Gg., priest-cardinal of the title of St Callistus. I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of St Chrysogonus. [Col. 1614A] I, Theobald, priest-cardinal of the title of St Praxedes. I, Gilbert, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia. I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Baradus, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church. I, John, deacon of St Mary. I, Peter, deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. [Col. 1614B] I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Boso, scribe of the holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1152 from the Incarnation of the Lord; in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III.

## VARIORUM LETTERS TO POPE EUGENIUS

[Col. 1613]

### I. Conrad, emperor, to Eugenius.—He requests confirmation of the election of Wibald, who was absent and reluctant, as abbot of Corvey, and of the union of Keminade and Visbeke with the monastery of Corvey. (Year 1146.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 198.]

[Col. 1613C]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

We wish Your Holiness to know that, after the deposition of Henry, formerly abbot of Corvey, who had been exceedingly useless to that church, the brethren of the aforesaid monastery chose as their abbot a certain Henry, provost of the same church. Not long afterward he died; and the whole church of Corvey, bereft of its spiritual father, by equal vote and unanimous consent chose for itself as father and shepherd of souls Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, so that through his diligence and our assistance that noble church—which through the negligence of preceding abbots had declined greatly from its former greatness—might, with God’s mercy going before, be restored in some measure. Since the aforesaid faithful servant of ours, the abbot of Stavelot, was not only absent when these things were done concerning him but also far away, we summoned him by royal authority while he long resisted and protested; and, at the petition of the entire church of Corvey, compelled him, wholly unwilling, to undertake the burden to which he was called, so that in the monastery of Corvey the religious observance of divine worship might be restored through him, and the service owed by the kingdom for the defence of God’s holy Church might thereby be rendered more readily and more abundantly.

Nearby there were two small convents of women which supplied no support to the kingdom or to us, either in military service or in any other service. They were so disordered and without discipline that it is better to be silent than to speak about the way of life and conduct of their inhabitants. Therefore, long instructed by your many exhortations concerning the reform of such places, we granted to the church of Corvey by right of ownership these two places, namely Keminade [Col. 1615A] and Visbike, so that divine religion might be reformed there and the abbey of Corvey might, during the tenure of this abbot, be increased by us in honour and wealth.

> [Note: [Col. 1613D] The foundation of the convent of Keminade on the river Weser by Countess Imma and Count Gero was published by us in vol. I from an autograph document which we found in the archives of the monastery of Corvey. Wisbeke, or—as the Saxon Chronicle which we are to publish calls it—the convent of girls of Wisbeke, owes its origin to the Empress Adelaide and her daughter Matilda, abbess; it was built by them about 992.]

Concerning this matter we earnestly admonish and request your sincerity, in which we place great confidence, that you not refuse to strengthen by the written privilege of your authority what we have confirmed for that abbot and the monastery of Corvey, by a lawful grant in the text of our charter, concerning the two aforesaid cells; and that you incline a kindly ear of hearing to the abbot in his needs. For it is fitting that those whom we have received into our favour with a more gracious bond you should embrace in the arms of benevolent love; and that those whom, conversely, you intend to support, we should endeavour to defend against every attack and ought fittingly to honour.

### II. Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to Eugenius.—He complains concerning Henry, archbishop of Mainz. (Year 1147.)

[HERMANN, *Episcopatus Bambergensis*, Proofs, p. 104.]

[Col. 1615B]

To his most reverend lord, father, and creator [Note: that is, consecrator], EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Catholic Church: EBERHARD of Bamberg, with his whole body of fellow-members and brethren, offers the humble work of his hands—such as it is by divine and apostolic grace—due obedience in Christ and every devotion within his power.

Blessed is God, who has blessed His whole Church at your accession and, after the great lights of the firmament that ruled the night had been extinguished, has kindled in your person the greater light to rule the day. Truly, in your times and through your merits, light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart: indeed, a light for the illumination of the nations and the glory of the people Israel. Enlightened by this light, the faithful work through love in faith, while unbelievers are gathered into the unity of faith by the arm of divine power. We believe that this common joy of the whole earth touches us with special force because we are subject to you by a closer bond of service and obedience. [lacuna]

Moreover, your mercy, most clement father and lord, is always before our eyes, [Col. 1615D] because you have anticipated all our merit with blessings of sweetness. Therefore we humbly render to Your Holiness before the sight of the divine majesty not such thanks as we owe, but such as we can; and whatever good is in us, after God, we attribute to your fatherhood.

But lest we should be proud amid prosperity, divine providence has ordained that adversity should not be lacking to us. The lord archbishop of Mainz is acting toward us not judicially [Col. 1616A], but ruinously persecuting us, because we prefer obedience to you over obedience to him; because, in receiving episcopal consecration, we presumed to share in the fullness of your grace; and because we preferred to drink from the fountain rather than from the stream. The enormity of this matter has grown so great that the people of Mainz dare to threaten us, your servants and sons, if we may say so, with danger of death and threaten your Church with destruction. In all these things, taking in you the sole refuge of our hope, we depend upon the sentence of your authority in such a way that neither death nor life can separate us from obedience to you. May almighty God order your days in His peace and grant you tranquillity of times for the consolation of all the faithful.

### III. Conrad, emperor, to Eugenius.—He informs him that his son Henry has been elected king of the Romans by the common acclamation of the princes, and that he himself, having taken up the cross, is preparing for the expedition to Jerusalem. (Year 1147.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 204.]

[Col. 1616B]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

We received with the greatest gratitude the letters of Your Holiness sent through your legate, a man whom we must name with every affection and honour, T., bishop of Santa Rufina; and what they contained we have carried into effect with filial and heartfelt charity.

> [Note: Theodewin the German, cardinal created by Innocent II and sent by him as legate to Germany. According to Otto of Freising, he crowned Conrad himself with the imperial diadem at Aachen, since the archbishop of Cologne, to whom that office belongs by right, had recently been elected and had not yet received the pallium.]

For concerning the ordering of the kingdom granted to us by God, about which you took care to admonish and exhort us with fatherly solicitude, we dealt carefully and effectively, God granting it, at a frequent assembly of princes at Frankfurt, where we held a general court. Having established and secured a firm peace throughout every part of our kingdom by common agreement, we have decreed, with divine mercy going before, to crown our son Henry—chosen king and successor to our sceptre by the unanimous agreement of the princes and the eager acclamation of the whole kingdom—during this coming Lent at the palace of Aachen.

> [Note: The monk of Gembloux, cited by Miraeus, writes that this was done in 1147, so that after the emperor’s departure the kingdom might not remain without a prince.]

Certainly, your statement that we had undertaken so great a matter—namely, the sign of the life-giving cross and the purpose of so great and long an expedition—without your knowledge, proceeded from the great affection of true love. But the Holy Spirit, who blows where He wills and is accustomed to come suddenly, did not permit us to delay in seeking your counsel or that of anyone else. Rather, as soon as He touched our heart with His wondrous finger, He impelled the whole intention of our mind to follow Him without any intervening delay. Since we have learned, both from your letters and through your legate, that you are coming into the regions of Gaul, we invite your venerable fatherhood with the greatest affection and earnest admonition to come to the Rhine, so that, being together, we may by God’s mercy jointly discuss and arrange those matters by which the peace of the churches and the order of Christian religion may be increased by fitting advances, and the condition of the kingdom given us by God may be established by expedient decrees with an increase of our honour. And because at the point of our departure no lengthy time is available to us, we desire to see your longed-for face at Strasbourg on the Friday which falls in Easter week. We commend to your sincerity our envoys—men prudent and discerning, lovers of the holy Roman Church and of the kingdom, and most dear to us—namely Buco, bishop of Worms, Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, and Wibald, abbot of Corvey, so that you may hear what they say to you as from our own mouth, and may not refuse to discuss and settle matters concerning the holy Roman Church and the kingdom with them in due form.

### IV. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, to Eugenius.—He asks the pontiff to uphold the liberty of the monastery of Vézelay. (Year 1148.)

[*Spicilegium*, folio edition, vol. II, p. 512.]

[Col. 1617C]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: HUGH, humble priest of Rouen, due obedience and reverence.

We are confident that what the holy Roman Church, by provident dispensation of law and dignity, has granted to any churches is held ratified by that Church itself and can never afterward be violated by anyone. For the church of Vézelay, which is yours, is, as we hear, grievously attacked by the lord bishop of Autun, who strives to annul what has been granted to it in liberty and dignity by the gratuitous favour of the Roman pontiffs. As for the assertion which the same brother bishop is said to make—that in Vézelay no bishop other than himself, or without his consent, can celebrate ordinations or consecrate altars—we remember that, at the prayer and request of the abbot and convent of that church, we ourselves performed each office there; and that many other bishops have done like things by the authority of the privileges of the holy Roman Church held there. We therefore entreat your pious fatherhood for that same church of yours at Vézelay: deign to preserve it in the liberty and dignity in which your predecessors preserved it, and do not permit it, dearest father and lord, to be diminished in its right or unjustly deprived thereof.

### V. Henry, king of the Romans, to Eugenius.—He excuses the archbishop of Mainz for not having attended the council of Reims, and commends him as he sets out for the pope. (Year 1148.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 268.]

[Col. 1618A]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: HENRY, by God’s grace junior king of the Romans, son of the great Conrad, renowned victor, king of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

Our dearest father, a cultivator of the Catholic faith, when departing from us and from his kingdom, gave us these final commands, deeply impressed upon our memory: that we should embrace your person with the highest affection of love; that we should cherish our most holy mother, the Roman Church, with especial diligence; and that, wherever opportunity offered, we should not neglect to guard and defend her possessions. Receiving these most pious admonitions of our religious father neither with a deaf ear nor with sluggishness of heart, we have taken care to carry them into effect with diligent devotion. Henceforth we are so intent that, as age and wisdom increase in us through divine favour, we may strive to increase and perfect all things for the better.

We do not think that your prudence is ignorant of the custom of the kingdom bestowed upon us by God: namely, that the archbishop of Mainz, by an ancient privilege of his church and dignity, is recognized as guardian and administrator of the kingdom during the prince’s absence. Our glorious father, following the institutions of earlier kings in this as in other matters, entrusted our youth and the governance of the kingdom to our reverend father Henry, archbishop of Mainz, with the favourable concurrence of all the princes and with great care. Your understanding knows very well how disadvantageous the absence of this venerable archbishop is to the entire kingdom and to our person, for the conditions of Belgian Gaul, which is for the greater part subject to our sceptres, and of all Germany are not unknown to you. Therefore, when you celebrated your synod in the city of Reims, by the favour of divine clemency, for the advancement of the whole holy Church, the same archbishop could not come into the presence of Your Holiness: he could not safely enter the borders of another kingdom, and—since we and the counsel of many princes objected—he could not, without prejudice to his faith and honour, abandon our affairs, which are the more difficult to govern the greater they are through God’s mercy.

But since, repeatedly summoned by you, he was now hastening to appear before your exalted presence, we, on the previous Nativity of the Blessed Mary, held a court, by God’s inspiration, in the town of Frankfurt. There, with a great assembly of our princes gathered, we discussed at length, after prolonged deliberation, both the absence of the archbishop himself and his safe journey to you. Accordingly, as he now sets out for the presence of Your Sublimity, contrary to the advantage of ourselves and of the whole kingdom, we commend him with filial and affectionate recommendation. We earnestly ask your most pious fatherhood, proved toward us in good things, graciously to receive him; and, having treated him honourably out of regard for our petition, to send him back to us soon with joy, strengthened by the grace of your blessing.

### VI. The same to the same.—He asks for the pontiff’s protection. (Year 1148.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 230.]

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, EUGENIUS [Col. 1619B], supreme and universal pontiff: HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans, the sincerity of due love and service.

Blessed is God, who has deigned to raise the discernment of your sincerity to the office and administration of the supreme pontificate. For, as religious persons think of you, you love justice and truth and diligently attend to what concerns the adornment of God’s house. Therefore we are indeed ready to obey your sincerity in this: that in our time the material sword and the spiritual sword may work together fruitfully in the Church. For our father, your most devoted son, who bears the cross of Christ for the enlargement of the Church, when he last departed from us repeatedly commanded us to rely on justice, embrace the pattern of religion, and protect with the greatest diligence the dignity of the Church and the honour of the kingdom. Therefore, under the protection of our father, who carries the dignity of the Roman Empire through foreign kingdoms and, exposing himself to every danger even to the shedding of blood for the enlargement of the Church, has made a perpetual covenant with the Church, we confidently seek your protection, you who are the special father of the Church; for, according to God and our father’s command, we are ready to obey your fatherhood in all things.

### VII. The same to the same.—That he may graciously receive Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and others travelling to the pope; absolve the duchess of Poland from excommunication; and regard Abbot Wibald as commended to him. (Year 1148.)

[MARTENE, *ibid.*, col. 232.]

[Col. 1619D]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme and universal pontiff: HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

[Col. 1620A] With all the powers of our mind we render many thanksgivings to your sincerity because you received our envoys and letters with fatherly affection; by your most gracious replies you kindly instructed our youth in the worship of divine religion and love for the holy Church; and you provided pious and effective consolation concerning the absence of our illustrious father, your most devoted son. Therefore, through your merits interceding with God, insofar as we are able through His grace to advance in age and capacity, so much do we grow in love for your person and the most holy Roman Church, and in the defence of the whole Catholic Church. For our father, departing from us beneath the banner of the holy cross, left us these final commands, many times repeated: that we should love you as himself with filial and intimate affection, and expect from you, as the most faithful guardian of our youth, true counsel and suitable help in every need.

Remaining steadfast in the purpose of the discipline entrusted to us by him, we greet your fatherhood, held by us in reverence, with pious devotion, asking you to admit our petitions, set out below, to the effect of a hearing. First, that you graciously receive our beloved father, teacher, and helper, the venerable Henry, archbishop of Mainz, as well as the other archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, and other persons from the kingdom of our father—to whose succession we have been appointed by God’s mercy—who pass into your presence; and that you do not refuse to exhort them with earnest admonition to bear patiently and courageously the absence of our father and strive to guide our natural disposition, so that they may themselves return joyfully to their own lands in the proper standing of their dignity, await our father’s return with gladness, and furnish the due service of loyalty and counsel for our needs and those of the kingdom.

> [Note: He was made archbishop of Mainz from being provost in 1142, and was deposed by order of Pope Eugenius III in 1151. St Bernard’s Letter 323 to him survives. The annalist of Paderborn, under the year 1153, says of him: “Henry, archbishop of Mainz and our metropolitan, was deposed; whether guilty or innocent is not agreed among writers. In other respects he was a good man, and simpler than the craftiness of politicians could tolerate.” For that reason St Bernard had taken him under his protection. But the hatred and accusations of the clergy whom he had undertaken to reform prevailed; he went into exile at Embeck in the duchy of Brunswick, where he died that year and lies buried. His familiar saying was: “I was a rich canon, a poor provost, and a beggar bishop.”]

Our aunt, the duchess of Poland, suffers both from the sentence of excommunication which you pronounced against her and from the absence of our father, who was her lord and brother; she is compelled to live in exile from her land and from the honour of her duchy. Your discernment should remember well in this matter that our father entrusted that same sister of his to your chancellor, a man wise, honourable, and most dear to us, and through him earnestly commended her to your exaltedness, so that you might deign to apply gracious effort toward her restoration.

We too commend to your gentleness Abbot Wibald of Corvey, faithful both to ourselves and to our kingdom, who was personally entrusted, with equal care and similar earnestness, to the hand of your aforesaid chancellor by the hand of our illustrious father, so that you may graciously protect him in every need—especially in securing the two small abbeys, namely Kaminata and Visbike. Since these had nearly collapsed and been destroyed alike in religion and in possessions, our most gentle father granted them by right of ownership to the monastery of Corvey and to the aforesaid abbot, so that through his diligence divine order might be restored there and, once the dispersed possessions had been recovered and preserved, the places might not be utterly destroyed as they had begun to be.

### VIII. Henry, duke of Saxony, to Eugenius.—He praises the merits of Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, and asks that the pope ratify the union of Kaminata with the monastery of Corvey. (Year 1148.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 234.]

[Col. 1621B]

To EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman Church: HENRY, duke of Saxony, devotion of prompt and dutiful service.

We commend to your fatherhood our beloved lord, the venerable Wibald, abbot of the church of Corvey, whom we understand has come before your majesty on the affairs of his church. Although we do not doubt that he has found favour in your sight, yet because of the affection with which we love him, we also support him with our recommendation. We therefore beseech your fatherhood graciously to hear him in his petitions, especially concerning the church of Kaminata. There he has reformed the worship of divine religion, as a religious man fearing God; and, like an energetic man, with God’s help and ours, he has recovered almost in full and restored to the uses of the church the lands and possessions of that church which Abbess Judith, after her deposition, had granted in benefice to her supporters and favourites—more than one hundred *mansi*.

> [Note: Concerning the lands alienated by Abbess Judith after she was deposed, we found the following in a certain schedule of the monastery of Stavelot: “Lady Judith, abbess, gave the following from the estates of the church of Kaminata after she was deposed. From the manor of An, she gave one *mansus* at Cadenbero, with six serfs, to the advocate Odiko. Likewise, from the same manor, she gave two *mansi* to Thieder. Likewise, one *mansus* and twelve solidi to Reinher. Likewise, three *mansi* to the wife of Sigehard. Likewise, five solidi of oats and five solidi of gifts to Helprad. From the manor of Cokerbike she gave to the advocate Odiko one *mansus* and one serf named Bado. Likewise, to the same man, a woman named Seburg with her three sons. Likewise, one *mansus* and the serf Radulf to Hermann. Likewise, one *mansus* and the serf Borgodo to Odo. Likewise, one *mansus* with the serf Mane to the advocate Rikbert. Likewise, one *mansus* with the serf Huico to the same man. Likewise, one *mansus* with the serf Reinolf to the same man. Likewise, nine serfs to the same man, who are called *Enlope* in German. Likewise, five serfs to Walding. To Henry of Botwide she gave five *mansi* with their serfs, which are the benefice of Helprad, our steward. Likewise, to the same man, four *mansi*, of which one is from the benefice of Tankerad and three from the benefice of Bruno. Likewise, one *mansus* belonging to us to Arnold. From the manor at Heppenstide she gave two *mansi* to the advocate Henry, one *mansus* to the advocate Odiko, and one *mansus* to Eppo. From the manor of Inwidele she gave two *mansi* to the advocate Odiko; four *mansi* to the advocate Ricbert; one *mansus* to the advocate Hermann; three *mansi*, which are the benefice of Helprad, my steward, to the advocate Henry; and one *mansus*, the benefice of the cleric Henry, to Tezzo. Likewise, twenty-four serfs to the advocate Rikbert, who are called *Enlope* in German. Almost all these things belong to the sustenance of the community. At Bardenwich she gave three marks in benefice. In the manor of Wichmannesburg she gave thirty-nine *mansi* in benefice; and from the demesne land, twelve *mansi* with three houses and their enclosed yards. She further gave twenty Slavic villages belonging to the same manor. Between Bodenhusen and Sutherburg she gave twenty-five *mansi* and, from the demesne land, eight *mansi*, with two houses and their enclosed yards, and thirteen and a half Slavic villages. Likewise, three *mansi* to Walthard, subadvocate; and two *mansi* to Gerart.”]

You will therefore provide us a salutary example and admonition for the future protection and aid of churches if, in accordance with the petition of the aforesaid venerable abbot, you make stable and firm by your authority the good which we have begun in that church to the praise of God. Farewell.

### IX. Henry, count of Namur, to Eugenius.—He declares himself ready to observe the arrangements made at Trier in the pope’s court concerning the case between himself and the archdeacon of Verdun. (Year 1148.)

[MARTENE, *ibid.*, col. 244.]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: HENRY, count of Namur and Luxembourg, the devotion of a son together with faithful service.

As was arranged between me and Richard, archdeacon of Verdun, in your court at Trier through the mediation of the abbot of Clairvaux, and confirmed in the presence of your company, so I afterward wished in every way to observe and fulfil it on the appointed day, under the witness of the bishop of Verdun and the abbot of Corvey.

> [Note: That is, St Bernard, who was then at Trier with Eugenius.]

> [Note: Namely Bishop Albero and Abbot Wibald.]

But that archdeacon Richard began very ingeniously to seek pretexts for withdrawing from the proposed conditions. He diligently incited a certain Anselm, my free man, and certain others, not to become his men and not to receive from his hand the benefices which they hold from me. Out of reverence for your apostolic office, I wish to remain without deceit or fraud in the aforesaid conditions and agreement; provided that, if it could be done with your favour [lacuna], he should summon me in this case before my own judge, and should wish to litigate it in the court to which this jurisdiction belongs, he would find me ready in every way. Therefore, with humble supplication, I entreat your fatherhood not to issue a sentence against me, who am obedient to you and desire to observe the terms set down above, nor place my land under any interdict, so that I may be able to love the excellence of your person all the more [Col. 1623A] and be more devoted to the defence of God’s Church.

### X. Conrad, emperor, to Eugenius.—That he may deign to confer the provostship of Xanten upon Thiebald, his canonically elected chaplain. (Year 1149.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 365.]

The letters of your paternal eminence, full of most tender affection, joy, and congratulation, we have decided to answer more fully on another page and through other messengers; there we shall also communicate more precisely to your greatness certain matters concerning our condition and the administration of the kingdom entrusted to us by God. But meanwhile, as the fire of unfeigned charity toward you burns within us, we greet your blessedness with filial and sincere affection and earnestly ask that our first request, after our return, may find a hearing with your holiness. The archbishop of Cologne [Note: Arnold, who, at the Council of Rheims, was accused of simony together with the archbishop of Mainz and is said in *Gallia Christiana* to have been deposed by the supreme pontiff, although here he is described only as suspended from his office.] has been suspended from the episcopal office by your equity; and therefore we believe that whatever pertains to pontifical and canonical right in his bishopric belongs to the ordering of your hand. And since, after the death of their provost B., the clergy of Xanten, with almost unanimous feeling and canonical voice, elected as their provost your son—namely our beloved chaplain Thiebald [Note: He was archdeacon of Cologne, as we learn from Wibald’s letter to him cited below.]—except for a very few whose age and judgment are to be counted for nothing, we earnestly urge and request your kindness, for the sake of our affection, not to refuse to confer the aforesaid provostship upon our aforementioned cleric, whom the canons of the church of Xanten had once elected, when that provostship was then vacant, without any objection whatever. Formerly the provost H. held that same provostship by the grant of Pope Innocent of blessed memory, while the see of Cologne was vacant upon the death of Archbishop Hugh [Note: Concerning him Alberic writes in his Chronicle under the year 1138: “Hugh, elected archbishop of Cologne after Bruno, while travelling to Rome to be consecrated, died abroad; having held life and priesthood for two months, he rests at Melfi in Apulia.”]; and we do not doubt that it is both lawful and fitting for your holiness to act in a similar manner.

## XI. The Same to the Same

—He writes on behalf of Thiebald, provost of Xanten, and the cleric Otto. (A.D. 1149.)

[MARTEN., ibid., col. 339.]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

It is very pleasing to us, and we retain it in the secret of our heart with grateful remembrance, that, in consideration of our affection and intercession, you have promoted our beloved chaplain Thiebald to the provostship of Xanten. For we judge it worthy and just that, while preserving the institutions and laws of your predecessors and ours—men indeed most holy and most wise—we should take care to love and exalt those persons who are more graciously cherished by the mercy of your holiness in the bosom of our most holy mother, the Roman Church; just as your kindness is solicitous to honour and advance those whom our clemency deigns to raise with more abundant favour. And because virtue consists not in beginning but in completing, we earnestly urge and request your eminence that the same blessed and generous hand of yours, which laid good foundations of favour and honour in the aforesaid person, may not refuse to build to completion: namely, if the archbishop of Cologne obtains your mercy and recovers the fullness of his office, let him not harm the provost, who has been invested and promoted by your hand as by the hand of blessed Peter.

Moreover, since your discernment, as you wrote to us, cannot and ought not to act contrary to the sacred canons and the ordinances of the holy Roman Church, we do not wish to trouble your prudence concerning matters which must be established and confirmed. Yet what ought not to be confirmed may be tolerated, so that by the moderation of dispensation the fruit may be multiplied in an increase of recompense. We say this because we consider it unfitting that anyone in the Church of God should maintain the strictness of the canons regarding this person whom you have exalted, as though following in your footsteps, while in the case of other persons whom you do not know he relaxes that strictness at his own discretion. Therefore, if any church, with equal desire and unanimous consent, wishes to take this same man so that it may remove his reproach, it ought to be the more inclined toward him in a dispensation of favour, the more certainly it is known that he is more acceptable to your holiness through the intervention of our affection.

Moreover, as we recently requested your sublimity to cause a certain free man of ours, Otto, who has been accused before your discretion of having cut off the nose of a certain Würzburg cleric, namely Conrad, to be absolved from the excommunication by which he is bound on this account—because, having been accused by that same cleric concerning this matter in our court, he proved by oath, according to the judgment of his people and of our court, that he was innocent—so now we make the same earnest request, asking you to write back through the present messenger, both to us and to the bishop of Bamberg, concerning the same affair. Your beloved son in Christ, Henry the Younger, king of the Romans, greets your beloved fatherhood.

## XII. The Same to the Same

—That he may receive Archbishop Arnold of Cologne kindly and send him back restored to his see. (A.D. 1149.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 384.]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

How pleasing to your sacred mind are the condition of our honour, the safety of our person, and the peace and tranquillity of the kingdom bestowed upon us by the heavenly Majesty, was clearly shown by the words of your greatness which we received first after our return from the expedition to Jerusalem. For our part, stirred by an equal zeal of devotion toward you, we bear heavily and grievously whatever is done wrongly against your venerable person and against the affairs of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, whose defenders we have been appointed by God. Yet we delayed answering those letters of your blessedness until, with the Lord’s help, we might shortly send to your sublimity such envoys as ought to make your holiness fully certain, both by our letters and by their spoken words, of all our purpose.

For the present, however, the substance of our urgent and dutiful request is this: because holy mother Church never closes her bosom to those who return, receive with paternal kindness the venerable Arnold, archbishop of the church of Cologne, when he comes to you; and, for the sake of our affection, send him back to us with his honour unimpaired. [Note: This letter had no effect; for the pope could by no means be persuaded to restore the archbishop to his rank.] For it must not be supposed that he refused to present himself to you out of contumacy; rather, since he is worn out both by old age and continual illness, he was unable to undertake so great a journey—especially since during his absence no small disturbances and irreconcilable conflicts might arise, capable of bringing troublesome labours upon our person and no slight inconveniences upon our kingdom. It remains that you should love us, as you do, with all the affection of devotion, and that you should expect from us the counsel and assistance of a devout good son.

## XIII. The Same to the Same

—He commends to him the bishop of Regensburg, setting out for Jerusalem. (A.D. 1150.)

[MARTENE, ibid., col. 401.]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection and the reverence due in Christ.

[Col. 1626A] Our faithful man, the son of your holiness, the bishop of Regensburg, though he would be exceedingly useful and advantageous to us in the affairs of our kingdom, nevertheless could by no means be held back from setting out for Jerusalem beneath the sign of the Crucified, because of the ardour of faith and his desire to fulfil his vow. When he comes into the presence of your eminence, receive him with paternal kindness for the sake of our affection; assist him in whatever his need may require, both by the protection of your hand and by the support of your faithful; and, strengthened by your blessing, send him forth joyfully to fulfil his purpose. For the statement on account of which he became suspect to your holiness filled his soul with bitterness. Concerning it we testify truthfully on his behalf that he neither sold nor betrayed the Christian army, nor in any respect diminished the dignity of our most holy mother, the Roman Church.

## XIV. The Same to the Same

—He sends envoys to him and asks him to confirm Eilulf, abbot of the monastery of Murbach, and to absolve the cleric Otto. (A.D. 1150.)

[MARTENE, ibid., col. 404.]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

After, by God’s favour guiding our frailty, we had returned from the Jerusalem expedition, we intended to visit your blessedness and our most holy mother, the Roman Church, through our distinguished envoys. But, while God stretched out His hand in requital, we were afflicted by so severe and prolonged a bodily illness that we were compelled to desist from public affairs. Now, however, having recovered health through the indulgence of divine mercy, and persisting in the purpose of that same intention, we have decided, after consultation with the princes, to send those same envoys into the presence of your eminence, so that we may discuss and arrange with you such matters concerning the condition and welfare both of the Church and of the kingdom as may enable the Christian people to live in peace and fear of God, and the Roman empire, with God as its author, to be restored to the strength of its former dignity.

You may learn more fully from the bearers of this letter, men certainly religious and prudent, the affair of the monastery of Murbach. It was long debated and diligently examined in the sight and presence of the bishop of Basel, in whose diocese that monastery stands, and also of the bishops of Constance, Bamberg, Eichstätt, and Speyer, as well as the abbot of Corbie and many other abbots and religious and learned men; and it was brought, in accordance with the order of law and reason, to this conclusion: because the community of the aforesaid monastery, united in evil though some of them opposed it, had elected a person congenial to their vices, we, instructed by the authority of the Rule of Saint Benedict and with the support of bishops and abbots, did not permit the consent of the wicked to prevail. Therefore, in order to reform religious life and restore the honour of our kingdom, we placed over that monastery the venerable and religious man Eilulf, abbot of Erlach, through whose industrious effort the aforesaid monastery may be cleansed of its former foulness. We earnestly urge and request that this action be strengthened by the blessing of your holiness; and do not incline your ear to those censorious pseudo-monks, who have appealed to your presence against the bishop of Basel, although he had taken no action in the same affair. For such rash appeals overthrow all ecclesiastical discipline and confound the whole order of law.

Furthermore, we earnestly request your sublimity to have a certain free man of ours, Otto, absolved from excommunication. He has been accused before your discernment of cutting off the nose of a certain Würzburg cleric, namely Conrad; but, having been accused by that same cleric in our court concerning the same matter, he proved that he was innocent by the judgment of his people and our court. Your son, our friend Cardinal Guy, was present at those proceedings.

## XV. The Same to the Same

—He commends to him Peter, archbishop of Capua, through whose aid he had recovered his health. (A.D. 1150.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 406.]

[Col. 1627C]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

As God in His favour governs our affairs and disposes the course of our life through adversity and prosperity, after our return from the Jerusalem expedition we lay ill with a severe and prolonged sickness. Yet the same grace of divine goodness, providing for our recovery, had provided us with Peter [Note: There is profound silence in *Italia Sacra* concerning this archbishop’s pontificate, although he ought to have a place there between Geoffrey, who appears to have died in 1138, and Alphanus, who is said to have held office from 1163 to 1183.], formerly archbishop of the church of Capua, a man unquestionably most skilled in the art of medicine. Therefore, with divine mercy helping us and with the endeavour and diligence of the aforesaid man cooperating, we rejoice that we have recovered complete health; and, our strength restored, we apply ourselves with all the intention of our mind to administering the affairs of the empire, which we had interrupted because of the obstacle of illness.

Accordingly, we earnestly urge and request your fatherhood, whom we love with true affection and in whom we greatly trust, that our aforementioned physician may obtain from your eminence, in both honour and advantage, the same benefit that he conferred upon us through his art; and that he may possess peacefully and honourably his church, which Pope Innocent of blessed memory granted him in the city of Rome, together with all his other possessions; nor allow any annoyance to be inflicted upon him in any matter belonging to him.

## XVI. The Same to the Same

—He sends to him as envoy Master Henry, notary of his court. (A.D. 1150.)

[MARTENE, ibid., col. 410.]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

Since gracious divinity brought us back safe and sound to our own lands from the regions of the East after many perils undertaken by land and sea, and since we were not permitted to behold your holy and venerable fatherhood face to face with bodily eyes, we had intended to send certain of our magnates to you, so that through familiar and intimate inquiry we might receive the judgment of your most discerning counsel concerning both the state of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, and of the other churches, and the restoration of the dignity of the Roman empire. But first a severe illness, given us by God for correction, detained us; it afflicted us for almost six months so greatly that we were nearly unfit for conducting more important affairs. This occasion nourished the audacity of some and stirred up the seeds of certain disturbances. When we had obtained health through the gift of heaven, we girded ourselves with all vigilance of mind to quiet and restrain them. And now, hoping through God’s grace for an appropriate conclusion from good beginnings, we have presently sent to your eminence Master Henry, notary of our court, a prudent and honourable man, and, as you know, familiar and acceptable to us. Beyond the contents of this letter, he will communicate orally to your discernment certain matters concerning our purpose and affairs; you should not hesitate in any way to trust him.

## XVII. Baldwin, Bishop of Noyon, to Eugenius

—He relates how, amid troubles and reproaches, he introduced religious monks into the church of Compiègne in place of canons of infamous life. (A.D. 1150.)

[DUCHESNE, *Historiæ Francorum Scriptores*, IV, p. 544.]

To the most holy father and lord EUGENIUS, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, BALDWIN, unworthy minister of the church of Noyon: whatever good prayer or affection can offer.

As lord and master, you have burdened weak shoulders so heavily that, under the pressing anxiety of carrying out the work enjoined, strength was almost exhausted and gave way. For it is neither light nor small a matter suddenly to transform the famous, celebrated church of Compiègne, supported by so great an authority, into another state, however eminent; especially when in men such as these clerics—if indeed they are clerics—ancient custom rules, and what has become familiar through corruption pleases and delights more than what is unfamiliar through improvement. But behold: you have tested us at the waters of contradiction, where that venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, the faithful and prudent servant of your holiness, was troubled. We have experienced the wondrous swelling of the sea; but more wondrous and far more powerful on high is the Lord, and His supreme pontiff, who sent us.

Finally, pressed by your holy obedience, and knowing it written: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is worthy shall be beaten with many stripes,” we adhered more eagerly to your will, endured the reproaches of clerics who reproach God and you, and initiated a place truly holy into religious life and order. We assigned monks, established an abbot—a religious and vigorous man, canonically elected—and, on the feast of the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian, the greatest celebration there, solemnly blessed that abbot. He shall be blessed, God willing and your favour confirming it. Thus that true saying of the Lord was fulfilled: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up.” The tree was cut down which even occupied the ground, and a fruitful olive tree was planted in the house of God; it hopes greatly in your mercy and at present has very great need of it.

The hand of the lord king, your son and glorious prince, was with us. In this work we truly found him to be a servant of the living God, able to say: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house,” and: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.” How he strove; how he burned with the fire of God, that this change might be effected by the right hand of the Most High! He also drank with us from the torrent, received humiliation, overlooked injury, and deferred the exercise of majesty. On the first day he summoned the clerics with us to chapter; they did not come. On the following day he went himself, and they came only with difficulty, compelled by him. The letters which you had sent through me, as you know, to the aforesaid abbot for this very undertaking were read; but not even your authority was respected. There we saw “the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud.” I pass over what that criminal hand afterwards did, and how, deceitfully and at an untimely hour, it entered the church and attempted to carry away the holy relics. This it partly accomplished: it cut the hanging ropes, lest perhaps the people should assemble at the ringing of the bells. The bearer of this letter will explain all these things better to your holiness.

Why say more? It remains, lord, that your authority should endeavour to establish, fortify, and confirm for ever what, by God’s will and yours, has received a good beginning. The monks have nothing on which to live. The clerics, both outsiders and residents, who hold benefices, are unwilling to share anything with them; indeed, they seem rather to rely on the Jordan’s flowing into their mouths. The watering of the new plantation lies in your hand, lord: lest it wither, lest it fail—which the enemy is wholly striving to bring about. Set apart a willing rain for the inheritance of God and yours.

## XVIII. Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius

—That he may confirm the election of Hermann, bishop of Utrecht, and absolve the count of Are from excommunication. (A.D. 1151.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, p. 483.]

To his most beloved father, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

When the bishopric of Utrecht became vacant after the death of Bishop Haribert of pious memory, we sent our envoys to that church with instructions, by our authority, to forbid the rash disturbances which commonly arise in such matters and the plundering of ecclesiastical goods. We also commanded the clergy, distinguished persons, and people of that city, laying aside partisan zeal, to prepare themselves for the coming election in a spirit of concord and humility, and not in contentious animosity to commit anything by which the liberty of canonical election might be shown to have lost its lawful freedom.

But they, taking the liberty granted in piety by the Fathers as a cloak for wickedness, began to throw the whole affair into confusion through dissensions and ambition, and for a long time allowed so great a power, in both spiritual and temporal matters, to remain without a ruler and tossed about. At length the provost of the greater church and the dean of the same church, together with the remaining clergy and all the nobles, agreed unanimously upon Lord Hermann, provost of the church of Saint Gereon at Cologne, a man of upright life and approved reputation. But certain ministeriales of that church, having raised a tumult and brought in arms, compelled some of the clergy to nominate and in some fashion elect Fritheric, provost of Saint George at Cologne, a man below the required age and orders, whose ignorance his supporters might exploit for the ruin of the church.

Moved by merciful compassion at the downfall of so great a church, we again sent envoys to them with royal commands, ordering them, once every pretext had been set aside, to appear before us during the Lent which has now passed, there to receive, in accordance with royal custom, an end to their contention and the lord of their city who should be supported by the better votes. Accordingly, the aforesaid Hermann came before us with his electors; but those who had chosen the young man, behaving youthfully, neither came nor sent a canonical or lawful excuse—except that, of the aforesaid Provost Fritheric [lacuna], namely Count A., came without attestation from clergy and people, and with definite written mandates asked that the matter be deferred.

But we, having taken counsel with bishops, princes, prudent and religious men, judged that the electors of the aforesaid Provost Hermann were of sounder counsel and had chosen a person not at variance with canonical institutions. All the nobles and powerful men of that land assented to them with great zeal; in peace they honour the church of Utrecht by their laws, and in war defend it by arms. Therefore, because in our presence no objection according to the order of law was raised against this election, although the whole church had been summoned into our presence, the bishops and princes judged that we ought not to delay the well-grounded wishes, but should promote the person elected without force or any evil contrivance and found, in his sacred orders, to be of suitable age.

Therefore we earnestly urge and request the eminence of your priesthood, which we embrace with true charity in the Lord, that you may not refuse to complete and confirm with the blessing of your sacred hand the work honourably begun by us, and support the ruin of the declining church of Utrecht with a swift blessing. We further request your holiness, on behalf of our kinsman the count of Are, whom a certain cleric named Jonathan procured to be excommunicated by you through deceit, that you have him absolved by the bishop of Liège, with this moderation of justice: after he has been absolved, let him be summoned before a synod, and let the case concerning a certain church which is being litigated between them be decided by canonical judgment.

## XIX. Henry, Bishop of Liège, to Eugenius

—He asks that the election of Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, be confirmed. (A.D. 1151.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, p. 487.]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme and universal pontiff of the holy Roman Church, H., by the grace of God humble minister of the church of Liège: obedience at once as devoted as it is due, in all subjection, and ready and faithful service in all things.

After the death of A., archbishop of Cologne of good memory, the church of Cologne summoned us and the other suffragans of that metropolitan see to the day of election for the future bishop according to canonical order. After fasting and the supplications of the litanies had preceded, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked and He entreated from whom comes every good gift and every perfect donation, who makes those dwelling in a house to be of one mind, it elected for itself—every private interest having been removed—by the common not merely favour and assent, but desire and acclamation, of all, Arnold, major provost of the same church and chancellor of the royal court: a man suited to priestly office in character and birth, order and age, and in every respect of prudent judgment, able through merit of life and learned knowledge alike to benefit and to govern.

Indeed, the brevity of that act at the time was so great that it seems rather to have been wished for than carried out, and he himself to have been seized rather than elected. For in the very matter in which he might then have seemed liable to accusation, he resisted beyond the measure of regular modesty and almost became disobedient; he was forced to be dragged and compelled rather than called. Therefore, prostrate at the knees of your holiness, we pour out supplicatory prayers to your clemency: deign, in this person sought by the wishes of all, to relieve the manifold calamities of the church of Cologne and, through the hands of blessed Peter and your own, to restore to its former estate of dignity one of the fairest daughters of our most holy mother, the Roman Church. For we fear—and believe ourselves certainly to have understood—that unless he is aided and strengthened by your mighty hand, he will altogether refuse to bear the burden; casting at the feet of your eminence the linen cloth in which he seemed wrapped, he will flee from you naked.

## XX. The Church of Cologne to Eugenius

—Concerning the election of Arnold, provost of the greater church of Saint Peter, as archbishop of Cologne. (A.D. 1151.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 488.]

To its most reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, W., dean; the archdeacons, abbots, provosts, clergy, distinguished persons, and all the people of the church of Cologne: obedience at once as devoted as it is due, in all affection and subjection.

We do not believe that it has escaped your eminence’s notice that our mother, the church of Cologne—one indeed of the illustrious daughters of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, over which now, with God as author, you happily preside—served with ready and eager steadfastness, indeed not merely with steadfastness but with effectiveness, at the time when that same Roman Church was compelled, for the defence of truth, orthodox religion, and holy constitutions, to take up arms against tyrants, to defend itself vigorously, and to vindicate itself into its own liberty. In that conflict, to the extent that the universal condition of the Catholic Church appeared to receive strength and growth, our own domestic affairs suffered loss from afar, both through the disturbance of our peace and the diminution of our resources. For our homeland must be considered to have fallen when, its defenders of justice having been extinguished, it was left unarmed and without a protector; and its collapse was to be the greater because it had possessed a higher glory in its exaltation.

For, by the negligence of its prelates and by our common negligence, it descended from eminence to abasement, from rule to abuse, from riches to poverty, from tranquillity to disturbance, from splendour to disgrace, from nobility to infamy. This indeed occurred through the most holy and just judgments of divine providence, wholly beyond our understanding, although at almost every death of our Fathers our mind and purpose had been concordant, that, with God as author, we might elect as Fathers and shepherds of souls such men as were judged sufficient and suitable to bear so great a burden and adorn so great a dignity. For when every head is sick, the whole heart must be sorrowful; and from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in the same body. But the wisdom of the divine order, which reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly, turned our wills at its pleasure, so that the agreement of our election proceeded not to building up but rather to our destruction.

Yet by the suffrages and chief desires of all, the man who has now, through God’s mercy upon our affairs, been elected was sought already for the third time; for, as is read of the patriarch Jacob, “He was a man prospering in all things.” But because he displayed his humility too importunately, he was offending, as we believe, the heavenly Majesty. But why have we said “elected,” when he was drawn and compelled not only by the tears and prayers but even by the violent hands of all? For after the death of our father Archbishop Arnold, the church of Cologne, which for a long time had hungered for its safety and protection, proclaimed a three-day fast in accordance with the desire of all. The bodies of the holy confessors Severinus, Cunibert, and Ailulf—who while living in the flesh had planted the church of Cologne and enlarged it in divine charity—were carried through every street of the city; and the people besought the clemency of almighty God with humble prayer and sincere devotion, that the eternal Shepherd, through the merits and intercessions of the aforesaid shepherds, might deign to show and appoint for His sheep such a shepherd as, by imitating their footsteps, could both govern the people of God usefully and benefit them effectively.

On the day when the election of the future bishop was to be made, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked with greater devotion and attention, with concordant wishes and the equal acclamation of all ranks, we drew forward for enthronement the venerable man, the son of your holiness, Arnold, provost of the greater church. He had so ministered that he deserved a better rank; having previously been faithful in a little, he might afterward be placed over much and finally enter into the joy of his Lord. But resisting and protesting, he excused himself, pleading the weakness of his powers more humbly than truthfully. He recalled the manifold ruin and devastation of our church, grieving especially over those losses whereby the church of Cologne appeared wholly stripped and despoiled of almost every dignity and power which it had gloriously received in former times from the apostolic see. Although the whole body of our brethren had long wasted away in the same sorrow, yet trusting in your mercy we consoled him with good hope, not doubting that your clemency would by no means abandon his desire and our petition.

We therefore send to the feet of your sublimity one of the elders of Israel, whom we know to be an elder and teacher of the people, not merely by lawful bodily age but also by maturity of mind and priestly gravity, so that the operation of divine power, through the grace of your blessing, may give him from your spirit, that he may bear with you the burden of the people. For if, God forbid, he is not kindly received by your favour and clothed in the first robe, which the church of Cologne has long lamented that it lost, he will choose to be abased in the house of his God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners; and thus the fruit which has already appeared in most abundant blossom will perish, and our land will be crushed with a double destruction.

## XXI. Emperor Conrad to Eugenius

—Concerning the election of Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, which he asks to be confirmed. (A.D. 1151.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 491.]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and the reverence due in the Lord.

[Col. 1634B] The Church of Cologne, which by its size and splendour surpassed almost all the Churches of Germany and Gaul, had fallen, through the negligence of its pastors [Note: [Col. 1633D] Especially Arnold, whom Eugenius III suspended from office for simony.], into such calamity that it was seen miserably stripped alike of all religion and all dignity. Therefore, as God governs human affairs and has mercy on whom He wills, the bishop A. of that same Church was removed from this life, during whose time it had been very greatly shattered and worn down. Then the faithful sons of the aforesaid Church cried to the Lord in their tribulation, that He might deliver them from their necessities.

God, hearing their devout prayers from the hidden depths of His mercy, sent them a spirit of consolation and unanimity, so that with an equal vote, an equal judgment, and [Col. 1634C] the harmonious acclamation of all, they might choose as father, shepherd of their souls, and lord of the city of Cologne, Arnold [Note: [Col. 1633D] From this letter of Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius, and from others preceding and following, *Gallia Christiana* must be corrected. It places Arnold II’s election in 1155, whereas Conrad died in February 1152; and in the instrument of 1151 concerning Walciodor, quoted above, Arnold is called bishop-elect of Cologne.], major provost of that city and chancellor of our court. They hoped, through his learning and integrity, with God’s help, your blessing, and our protection, both that peace would be restored in the land, brigandage restrained, laws reformed, and morals improved.

Yet he protested and resisted, beyond the requirements of humility and obedience, because he judged himself weak and unequal to repairing so many and such manifold ruins within and without. He declared that he would rather die or go into perpetual exile than, with himself set over her as prelate, see his mother torn apart and laid low by wicked men. Therefore, when clergy, nobles, [Col. 1634D] and people alike rushed upon him, he was violently dragged into the church; and, although he resisted, he could not be enthroned according to the proper custom or order, saying that he wished to defer the whole matter and decision of this counsel until the assent and command of Your Sublimity.

At that time we had gone down into those parts of Lotharingia to repress warlike disturbances and punish the raids of brigands, who had thrown the whole district of that bishopric into disorder by plundering and burning, and had filled everything with an irreparable dread of devastation. When, therefore, we entered the city of Cologne, which was wholly [Col. 1635A] crowned with joy, hope, and eagerness because of so unanimous an election of so eminent a person, and because of our speedy arrival to confirm the same matter, the electors, by a certain reverent and humble compulsion, prevented us from leaving the church in which we had been received until we had confirmed, in royal fashion, the election canonically and unanimously made, and had advanced and assisted the elect in restoring peace and administering secular justice.

But he persisted, with his customary zeal, in refusing, asserting that he was in no way sufficient to heal their wounds. The whole Church of Cologne lay prostrate at his feet in a tearful spectacle, weeping and beseeching him, as a loving son, to lend his hand to his mother as she slipped and fell. We therefore, relying upon your [Col. 1635B] goodness, which we love exceedingly in the Lord, promised both the Church of Cologne and him that we would obtain by every means from Your Sublimity that the Church of Cologne should be strengthened both in its ancient privileges—neglected indeed, but now to be renewed and confirmed through the bounty of your blessing—and that his person should be invested with its former dignity, according to the precedent of his predecessors.

And divine clemency attended these good beginnings, increasing them with better results; for at his entry, with our clemency cooperating, both the trumpet of war fell silent, and the band of brigands, terrified by the hand of such strength, hid itself in the secret places of its wickedness. We therefore earnestly exhort and ask your sincerity [Col. 1635C] that, in regard for our affection and petition, you graciously receive the same elect when he comes before Your Meekness; and, consecrated by the grace of apostolic blessing, speedily send him back to us with his privileges renewed and enlarged. For since, by virtue of the office of the Church of Cologne, he is chancellor in the Italian kingdom, and since in the regions on this side of the Alps he will undoubtedly be useful and serviceable to us both because of the greatness of his principality and because of long familiarity, it seems favourable and beneficial alike to our most holy mother, the Roman Church, and to our empire, if a suitable person is advanced by you with greater augmentations and a greater prerogative.

## XXII. From the same to the same.—He announces that he is preparing an Italian expedition for the benefit of the Church, and commends the Archbishop of Bremen and Abbot Wibald. (A.D. 1151.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, col. 499.]

[Col. 1635D]

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

As we have often experienced, both formerly and now, the goodwill of your fatherhood in all our affairs and those of our people, so we do not doubt that we shall continue to feel it in all things. We promise Your Highness this: that we shall always be ready, with whatever diligence we owe, to promote the honour of the Church of God and your honour. Accordingly, we held a general court at Würzburg in the middle of September; and there, after receiving the faith and oaths of the princes who had assembled, we effectively arranged an Italian expedition. Since in carrying this out properly we neither ought nor wish to be without the presence and counsel of our beloved Har., venerable Archbishop of Bremen, we earnestly and kindly ask Your Holiness to remit to him the day and term appointed for preserving the dignity of the Church of Bremen, and to defer his cause until our arrival, subject to this condition: that upon our arrival the same cause shall be concluded in your presence according to the tenor of truth and [Col. 1636B] justice.

For, relying on your sincerity and trusting the counsel of our beloved O., your cardinal, who was then present, we retained the aforesaid archbishop with us when he was already prepared for the journey, so that in so great and rapid an expedition we might have him more readily at hand. We earnestly commend to Your Holiness Wibald, Abbot of Corbie, most dear to us: a man indeed prudent and in every respect most faithful both to you and to our most holy mother, the Roman Church. In regard for our affection and petition, graciously receive him, kindly grant his requests both for confirmation of his privileges and in his other petitions, and, distinguished by some prerogative of your blessing and grace, [Col. 1636C] send him back to us more speedily with joy.

## XXIII. From Emperor Frederick I to Eugenius.—He informs the pontiff of his election and coronation. (A.D. 1152, March.)

[PERTZ, *Monum. Germ. hist.*, Laws, vol. II, p. 89, from Wibald’s Malmedy manuscript.]

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, FREDERICK, by the grace of God King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

It befits the father of his country diligently to observe the venerable institutions of ancient kings and steadfastly to adhere, with earnest endeavour, to their sacred ordinances, so that he may know how to adorn the kingdom entrusted to him by God with laws and customs no less than to defend it with arms and war. Therefore, following the solemn custom of the Roman Empire transmitted to us from our forefathers, namely emperors and kings, we have taken care to send to the presence of Your Holiness and to the City our legate E., a venerable bishop of Bamberg, a man both prudent and upright, accompanied by H., Archbishop-elect of Trier, and A., Abbot of Ebrach. Thus, both through the information of this present letter and by their own living speech, you may be more fully informed about our advancement and the condition of the whole Church and kingdom.

Accordingly, when it pleased Him who is terrible, terrible to the kings of the earth, and who takes away the spirit of princes—He in whose hand [Col. 1637A] are all powers and all the rights of kingdoms—to summon from this present life our uncle and foster-father, Conrad, the glorious King of the Romans of blessed memory, all the princes of the kingdom, as though stirred by the divine Spirit, came together on the seventeenth day after his burial at the town of Frankfurt, both in person and through honoured representatives. Without any interval of delay, on that same day, with great harmony granted by God, the princes themselves and the other nobles, with the favour and joyful eagerness of the whole people, elected us to the summit of the kingdom.

Five days later, that is, immediately after the middle of Lent had passed, with one and the same consent and with the people’s favourable acclamation, they anointed us royally in the town of Aachen with the oil of consecration by the most holy hands of your devoted son Arnold, metropolitan of Cologne, [Col. 1637B] and of venerable bishops; and they placed us, with a solemn blessing, upon the throne of the kingdom.

For our part, clothed in the manifold ornaments of royal dignity with which we have been invested partly through the services of lay princes and partly through the venerable blessings of bishops, we have assumed a royal spirit. With all the strength of our mind we strive, according to the formula of our profession, which we received from orthodox bishops upon the royal throne itself and at the sacred anointing, to show you honour and love, and to afford to our most holy mother, the Roman Church, and to all ecclesiastical persons prompt and due justice and protection; and to establish and preserve law and peace for widows, orphans, and all the people committed to us.
