For since there are two powers by which this world is chiefly governed, namely the sacred authority of bishops and royal power, we are prepared to submit devoted necks to the obedience of all Christ’s priests, so that, by the favour of the Divinity, during the time of our rule the word of God may run unhindered, and no one may dare, without punishment by a more grievous penalty, to violate the rules and decrees of the Fathers defined by most holy councils. Thus, through the urgency of our effort, the Catholic Church may be adorned with the privileges of its dignity, and the loftiness of the Roman Empire, with God’s assistance, restored to the former strength of its excellence.

And because we know that the mind of Your Blessedness is not without reason disturbed by the death of the aforesaid most serene prince, we steadfastly promise you, as to a dearest father, that as we succeeded that glorious king of old upon the throne of the kingdom, so we have undertaken an inherited love, wholly special toward your person, and a most ready and devoted defence of our most holy mother, [Col. 1638A] the Roman Church. This is the ordering principle: whatever he had purposed and arranged for the liberation and honouring of the Apostolic See, we shall steadfastly strive to accomplish, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s blessed promise to the holy man, we may be enemies to your enemies and afflict those who hate you.

We earnestly commend the aforesaid legates of ours to your kindness, that for the sake of our affection you may treat them graciously and kindly grant their requests. We also most earnestly ask that you send back to us freely the lord Abbot of Ebrach, who is necessary to us both in divine and human affairs.

(The reply of Eugenius may be seen above among his letters, [Col. 1638B] no. 504.)

## XXIV. Compact of Emperor Frederick I with Pope Eugenius III

[Note: [Col. 1637D] The compact made by Frederick’s and the pope’s legates is found among the letters of Abbot Wibald, in Martène, vol. II of the *Amplissima Collectio*, letter 385; we have corrected its text with the aid of the Malmedy manuscript. Baronius first published the royal confirmation under the year 1152, p. 378, from the Vatican manuscript of Cencius; but it is so full of errors that you may rightly judge our version, based on Vatican manuscript no. 2040, parchment, fourteenth–fifteenth century, where it is read on folio 53, to be far more corrected. Yet we do not maintain that even in this way everything has been healed; for the date at which we read that the compact was confirmed by the king needs correction, so that it should be assigned to the year of the Incarnation 1153, the second year of the reign, first indiction. Frederick was at Cologne on 23 March 1152, while Eugenius’s legates—apparently bearers of the compact—Bernard, cardinal-priest of St Clement, and Gregory, cardinal-priest of St Mary in Trastevere, as is clear from the pope’s letters to Wibald, did not cross the Alps and arrive in Germany until February or March 1153. —PERTZ, *Monum. Germ. hist.*, Laws, vol. II, p. 92.] (A.D. 1153, 23 March.)

[PERTZ, ibid., p. 92.]

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is the form of concord and agreement established between Lord Pope Eugenius and Lord Frederick, King of the Romans, through the mediation, on the pope’s side, of Cardinals Gregory of St Mary beyond the Tiber, Ubald of St Praxedes, Bernard of St Clement, Octavian of St Cecilia, Roland of St Mark, Gregory of St Angelo, Guy of St Mary in Portico, and Abbot Bruno of Caraville; and, on the king’s side, of Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, [Col. 1638C] Hermann, Bishop of Constance, Ulrich of Lenzburg, Guy of Werra, and Guy, Count of Blandrate.

The lord king shall cause one of his ministeriales to swear upon the king’s soul; and he himself, giving faith with his own hand in the hand of the legate of the lord pope, shall promise that he will make neither truce nor peace with the Romans, nor with Roger of Sicily, without the free consent and will of the Roman Church and Lord Pope Eugenius, or of his successors who shall be willing to keep the tenor of the subscribed concord with King Frederick. To the full extent of the kingdom’s powers he shall labour to subject the Romans to the lord pope and the Roman Church, as they have ever been during the previous hundred years and earlier.

As a devoted and special advocate of the holy Roman Church, he shall preserve and defend against men, to the best of his power, the honour of the papacy and the regalia of blessed Peter which it now possesses. What it does not now possess, he shall help to recover to the best of his power; and what has been recovered he shall defend. Nor shall he grant any land on this side of the sea to the emperor of the Greeks. If that emperor should invade, he shall endeavour, with the forces of the kingdom, to expel him as quickly as possible. He shall do and observe all these things without fraud or evil intent.

The lord pope, by word of apostolic authority, together with the aforesaid cardinals in the presence of the aforementioned envoys of the lord king, has promised, and shall observe, that he will honour him as the dearest son of blessed Peter; that, when he comes for the completion of his crown, he will crown him emperor, so far as lies in his power, without difficulty or opposition; and that he will help, as required by the duty of his office, to maintain, increase, and extend the honour of the kingdom. Whoever presumptuously dare to trample upon or overthrow the justice and honour of the kingdom, the lord pope, when apprised by the royal dignity, shall canonically admonish them to make satisfaction. If they disdain to render justice to the king, after apostolic admonition, concerning royal right and honour, [Col. 1639B] they shall be bound by a sentence of excommunication. Nor shall he grant land on this side of the sea to the emperor of the Greeks; should he dare to invade, the lord pope shall endeavour, through the power of blessed Peter, to expel him. All these things shall be observed by both sides without fraud and without evil intent, unless they are altered by the free and common consent of both.

### Royal Confirmation

To the venerable father in Christ, EUGENIUS, by God’s grace pontiff of the Apostolic See, FREDERICK, by the grace of God Augustus, Emperor of the Romans, filial love [Col. 1639C] and due reverence in Christ.

The dignity of royal majesty requires us to establish with earnest care what is known to concern the good of peace and concord, and to labour with diligent effort and exact care that this good may endure forever, between kingdom and priesthood, in indissoluble charity. Therefore, in view of this consideration, we order that the concord recorded below, established between us and you by God as author, shall be set down in the same words in the present text, just as it has been confirmed and ordered by both parties, lest we appear to have altered anything by our own judgment.

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is the form of concord, etc., as above, down to the words: “unless they are altered by the free and common consent of both.”

[Col. 1639D] The witnesses are those whose names are seen written below:

Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne; Hermann, Bishop of Constance; Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg; Arditio, Bishop of Como; the Bishop of Chur; Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot; Albert, Dean of Cologne; Master Henry, notary; Godfrey of Viterbo, the king’s chaplain. Among the laity: Duke Welf; Margrave Hermann of Baden; Count Ulrich of Lenzburg; Count Werner of Lenzburg; Anselm, chamberlain and ministerial of the kingdom.

The sign of the lord Frederick, most invincible Emperor of the Romans.

I, Arnold, chancellor, have authenticated this.

[Col. 1640A] Given at Constance, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [23 March], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, in the first year of the reign of the glorious lord Frederick, King of the Romans.

## XXV. Letter of Cardinals Bernard and Gregory to Eugenius.—They commend to him the bearer of the present letter. (A.D. 1153.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Coll.*, II, 561.]

To the reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, B., priest, and G., deacon, cardinals of the holy Roman Church: duty in all things.

The bearer of this letter is a nobleman and, as we have learned from the report of many, well behaved and very devoted to the most holy Roman Church. Coming to the thresholds of the apostles for prayer and to the feet of Your Holiness, he requested that we commend him to your compassion by our letter. Therefore, commending him to Your Majesty, we ask that you receive him with your customary kindness and, by your paternal admonition, provide greater incentives for his devotion toward the Apostolic See.

## XXVI. From Robert, Bishop of Exeter, to Eugenius.—Against Hugh of Cotes, who had left the order of regular canons. (A.D. 1148–1153.)

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. GILES, vol. II, p. 131; see *Patrologia*, vol. CXC.]

[Col. 1640C]

To the most reverend and most holy lord and father EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff, R., by the grace of God humble Bishop of Exeter and servant of Your Holiness: greeting and due obedience with every devotion.

At the request of our venerable brother and friend Gilbert, of the Church of Hereford and of the monks of Gloucester, and especially in order that the truth may be made known, we wrote to the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, the truth that we know concerning Hugh of Cotes; and at their request we truthfully write the same to you.

Having, as we heard, abandoned the order of regular canons, he became, as we knew for certain, a recluse among us; but he did not conduct himself among us as we should have wished. To say nothing of other matters, he was publicly notorious also for sexual incontinence, and, as we believe, not without cause. For a cleric, beside whose church he had his cell, asserts that he found in Hugh’s cell a woman who had entered it through the cell-window; and since there was no other entrance or exit, she left by the same way. When he questioned her about the reason for her entry, she could give no fitting or honourable reply.

Although men of great respectability and good reputation made every effort to quiet this dishonour and infamy of his, it was never fully settled. Many times he wished to leave his cell and, abandoning also this second purpose of religious life, pretended that he wished to enter the monastic order. And indeed, although he was long detained by the honourable and religious compulsion of upright and religious men, at last [Col. 1641A] he left without our knowledge or permission, taking with him, as we heard, no small sum of money. Yet he neither assumed the monastic habit nor returned to the cloister of canons from which he had departed.

After much wandering, however, he returned to us and asked whether, in our parish and on another property, he might live under the guise, I know not whether, of a hermit or a canon. We did not permit this in any way without the authority of you or of your legate, both because of his instability and because of his former notoriety. When he learned this, the aforesaid Hugh returned to us after a long time and said that he had visited Your Presence, revealed to you the entire course and truth of his life, and had thus returned to us under your authority with this request and intention. But he was proved beyond doubt to have lied about this, since he could neither produce your letters as testimony nor establish by any true or plausible evidence that he had seen you or when he claimed to have visited you. For one of our clerics convicted him, having stayed at that time, when Hugh said that he had visited you, in your court with the lord Robert, your chancellor of blessed memory.

We have written to you these few matters out of many which it seems more decent to leave unmentioned, lest he deceive you by the persuasive words in which he abounds, or by the false appearance of religion which he puts forward. May Your Holiness prosper.

[Col. 1641] See the letters to Pope Eugenius III of Saint Bernard, Peter the Venerable, Suger, and Abbot Wibald among their respective works.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1148: ULGÉRIUS, BISHOP OF ANGERS

[Col. 1641]

## NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, p. 302)

[Col. 1641] Although Ulger’s birthplace is not recorded in any monument, it is very probable that he was born in Anjou [Note: [Col. 1641] *Gallia Christiana vetus*, vol. II, p. 132; Liron, *Singularités historiques*, vol. I, p. 387.], since from childhood he is found among the pupils of the school of Angers. The regularity of his conduct and the progress he made in letters first earned him a canonry. He subsequently obtained the office of schoolmaster after Geoffrey Babion’s retirement, and in 1113 according to some, or 1119 according to others, added to it the dignity of Archdeacon of Outre-Loire [Note: [Col. 1641] *Histoire universelle d’Anjou*, vol. I, p. 88; Liron, ibid.].

The great reputation Ulger acquired through his lectures drew the flower of French youth to the city of Angers. William Quadradi, son of the Baron of Jonsac, elected Bishop of Saintes in 1127, was among his first and most devoted pupils [Note: [Col. 1641] Egas. Bul., *Historia Universitatis Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 216.]. The historian of the University of Angers reports a letter that he wrote Ulger soon after his election, in which one observes marks of tender and lively gratitude. Time has doubtless deprived us of many similar testimonies to the gratitude of his other pupils. For the praises bestowed upon him in his own time show that he had gained a claim upon the hearts as well as the minds of all who had passed through his hands.

After governing the school of Angers with such success, he was judged worthy to be placed at the head of the diocese when Bishop Renaud de Martigné left it to become Archbishop of Reims. The chronicles of Saint-Florent of Saumur and Saint-Aubin of Angers place his ordination in 1125, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, that is, 20 September. Hardly had he been installed when he found himself obliged to go to Rome for a reason not stated by history [Note: [Col. 1641] Lobineau, *History of Brittany*, vol. II, p. 279.]. Guy of Étampes, Bishop of Le Mans, and William, Bishop of Poitiers, accompanied him on that journey.

On his return he renewed the dispute of his predecessors with the abbots of Vendôme over the redemption of altars. What has already been said above [Note: [Col. 1641] *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI, pp. 204–206.] to explain the nature of this controversy need not be repeated. Ulger pressed his claim vigorously and always encountered resistance equal to his efforts. Opposed to him was a man who yielded to him neither in learning, firmness, nor influence, and who moreover possessed the advantage of right: the celebrated Geoffrey of Vendôme.

The papal legates instructed the prelate as many as four times to cease his proceedings, because the Abbot of Vendôme could invoke a canon of the Council of Clermont condemning the redemption in question as an illicit and simoniacal agreement [Note: [Col. 1643] Gauffr. Vindoc., book III, letter 12.]. Far from yielding, Ulger, urged on by his archdeacon Richard, assembled his synod in order to enlist all the clergy of Anjou in his quarrel. There he complained bitterly about the alleged rebellion of the Abbot of Vendôme and about the rashness he believed the abbot had shown in summoning him before the legate. The assembly entered into his views. Consequently, he laid an interdict upon all the abbey’s churches situated in his diocese.

Geoffrey appealed to Rome. Pope Honorius II delegated the Archbishop of Tours and the Bishop of Le Mans to settle the dispute. But Ulger intercepted the letters addressed to those prelates and thereby prevented their effect. The letter which the pontiff wrote to Ulger himself, exhorting him to peace, had equally little success. Abbot Geoffrey did not live to see the outcome of this affair; but his successor Fromond, through the mediation of Pope Innocent II, made the following agreement with Ulger [Note: [Col. 1643] Liron, *Singularités historiques*, vol. I, p. 392.]. The Abbot of Vendôme renounced the offerings from baptismal fonts in his churches within the diocese of Angers; and the bishop granted him for the future those connected with purifications and weddings, as he had enjoyed them in the past.

Another dispute, which occupied our prelate during the greater part of his episcopate, in which he displayed the same vehemence, and which he left to his successor to settle, was the one he had with Pétronille de Chemillé, Abbess of Fontevraud [Note: [Col. 1643] Cosnier, *Exordium Fontis-Ebrardi*, p. 192.]. Its object was of little consequence, since it concerned only several small estates which the bishop disputed with the abbey. Nevertheless, there was no way to bring him to a settlement. Good people lamented it. Saint Bernard, without entering into the merits of the lawsuit, could not refrain from informing the prelate that his conduct in this matter scandalized the public. His letter was otherwise seasoned with testimonies of the highest esteem for Ulger’s merits.

Pope Innocent, whose protection the nuns of Fontevraud had invoked, summoned the Bishop of Angers to Rome, where he was obliged to appear in 1137. He returned without allowing himself to be moved either by the pontiff’s prayers or by his threats. His resistance was punished by a suspension from the exercise of his functions, which Innocent caused to be served upon him the following year.

But at the prayer of the Abbot of Clairvaux, who could not bear to see a prelate otherwise so estimable in disgrace, he was quickly restored [Note: [Col. 1643] Bernard, letter 340.]. Among Hildebert’s poems (p. 1337) appears a short piece composed on the occasion of this interdict. It represents Ulger as a bishop whose courage was proof against everything when faithfulness to duty was concerned. Its title is: “A Disputation between the Roman Pontiff and Bishop Ulger.”

Amid these troubles and all the concerns attached to the episcopal ministry, Ulger did not neglect the schools of his diocese. He took care to provide them with outstanding masters, both in morals and ability. More than one taught simultaneously in the city of Angers. We possess a letter of Herbert [Note: [Col. 1643] Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 767.], one of them, to Hilary, a teacher at Orléans, in which he names five other colleagues who were teaching at the same time during Ulger’s episcopate. Their emulation was encouraged by Ulger’s care to reward their labours. It will suffice to name Bohemond, who rose from schoolmaster to archdeacon, and Veslat, who appeared in the same dignity at the Council of Reims in 1131, where he accompanied the prelate.

This illustrious bishop, after gloriously completing a long career, ended it by an edifying death on 17 October 1148. That is the date given in the chronicles of Saint-Florent of Saumur and Saint-Aubin of Angers [Note: [Col. 1643] *Historia Universitatis Andegavensis*, p. 121.]. We have all the more reason to believe them on this point because no act of Ulger later than that year is found. His body was buried in the nave of the church, before the chapel of Saint Mathurin, near the cloister door. There, even today, one sees his figure in enamel, with his epitaph on a copper plaque attached to the wall. The figure depicts him in pontifical vestments, with a mitre upon his head; but this is an unusual mitre, less like those of today than like a doctor’s cap.

History attests that he carried to the grave the universal regrets of his people, for whom he had always possessed a father’s tender compassion and the watchful, active zeal of a true shepherd. The epitaph reads:

> Here lies Ulger, accustomed from tender years  
> To bear fruit for God in speech, mind, and hand.  
> His work was to benefit many, to teach the young,  
> To root out wickedness and strengthen faith;  
> To console the weeping, clothe the naked, break  
> The proud, harm no one, and follow what is right.

Ulger is one of the twelfth-century prelates whose learning was most celebrated by contemporary authors [Note: [Col. 1643] *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, p. 345; Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 882; Bernard, letter 340.]. To judge the fruitfulness of his pen from this, one might be inclined to believe that it produced a great many volumes. Yet only a small number of rather brief writings by him survive, and not many others are known to have fallen prey to time.

Among these writings, the most remarkable—and, properly speaking, the only one in which perceptible traits of that rare genius attributed to him may be seen—is his pleading, or report, on the case being pursued at the Roman court between the abbey of Vendôme and that of La Roë concerning the church of Saint-Nicolas de Craon. It is brief, but clear, methodical, vigorous, eloquent—in a word, such as might still serve today as a model. Baluze, who published it in the second volume of his *Miscellanies*, calls it a *gravissimam et elegantissimam relationem*: “a most weighty and elegant report.” Ulger delivered it before Pope Innocent II in 1136. Its opening follows:

> “Father and sole Lord of this world,” he said, addressing the pope, “compassion and charity oblige me to speak for poor Abbot John and his most poor house, whom the abbot and monks of Vendôme, aided by the convenience of their proximity and the weight of their excessive resources, seek to crush. This poor man, having at last reached us with exhausted wings, sent no one ahead, brought no one with him, and expects—nor has expected—no one who had agreed to follow him. He is alone, powerless, and poor. Alone, he is assailed by many; powerless, he is surrounded by powerful men; poor, he is hemmed in by rich adversaries. His spirit is distressed within him. This moves me to help him, because it is neither the part of an honorable man nor of a Christian to refuse aid to an oppressed innocent person. This man is your servant and ready to give you every mark of devotion within his power. He is a regular canon of the church of Saint Mary of the Wood, which among holy churches is held to be the holiest, but among poor ones is known to be the poorest. Thus, I say, this poor son of a poor mother, prepared at once to fight for his poor mother, prays and supplicates at the feet of your majesty; and we, with him and for him, pray and supplicate that you may deign to turn the ears of your head and heart toward the arguments of his defence. For it is not our intention to detain the serenity and reverence due to your gravity with idle speeches. Let rhetoric belong to Cicero and the Ciceronians. But, most holy Father, I propose to set before your eyes, as also before those of this august court before which I have the honor to speak, pure truth—whose evidence must secure the salvation of my party—and the simple and succinct statement of what is essential to the cause I defend.”

The advocate then sets out the facts. The matter, as has been said, concerned the church of Saint-Nicolas de Craon, which each side claimed as its own. Ulger briefly recounts the history of this church. At first it was a chapel or oratory which the lords of the place had built for themselves and their household. It then possessed neither parishial title nor revenues; but these same lords, wishing afterward to have the divine office celebrated there, endowed it with several portions of their fief for the maintenance of a number of chaplains. Some time later they decided to give it, with all its dependencies, to the abbey of La Roë. This gift was confirmed not only by Renaud de Martigné, then bishop of Angers, but also by Pope Paschal II.

Nevertheless, the same Renaud, from whose hands Albin, abbot of La Roë, had received investiture of this church, changed his mind after he had been made archbishop of Reims. By the counsel of Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, and other eminent persons, he invested the abbot of Vendôme with it. The reason for this change was that the chapel in question lay within the boundaries of the parish of Saint-Clément, which belonged to that abbot. The legates of the Holy See, among whom was Innocent II, then a cardinal, approved this new investiture, and Pope Calixtus II ratified it. Yet all this did not cause the monks of La Roë to yield. They protested against the injustice and remained in possession. Ulger undertakes to show that their possession was legitimate and secure, being founded on an incontestable title of property. He vigorously refutes the objections of the monks of Vendôme. It must be remembered that he was then himself in litigation with them; and one may say that, if passion is needed for eloquence, his personal resentment served him admirably on this occasion. In the end he gained a complete victory over his adversaries, whose claims were dismissed. It is very likely that Ulger delivered similar pleadings in the cases in which he acted in his own name; but no trace of them remains.

We have seven letters of this prelate. Two are addressed to Pope Lucius II in volume IV, pp. 769–770, of Duchesne’s *Historians of France*. In the first Ulger casts himself in spirit at the pope’s feet to commend to him Odo, dean of Saint-Martin of Tours, who had been obliged to go to Rome in consequence of a very severe summons. He does not explain the matter that occasioned this journey; but he declares that the entire chapter of Saint-Martin is ready to bear witness before the Holy See to the dean’s innocence. The second is on behalf of Robert, prior of the monastery of Saint-Cosmas at Tours, who was to deliver it personally to the pope. The bishop of Angers asks him to receive Robert kindly, grant what he is about to request, and send him back satisfied to France. At the end he adds that he will shortly dispatch to Rome Peloquin, his official, with tokens of his complete devotion to the Holy See: *cum intersignis servitutis meae*, “with the tokens of my service.”

The same editor placed after these two letters a mandate, or pastoral letter, of Ulger to all the clergy of his diocese, recommending to their charity the representatives of the Order of the Templars, whom he greatly praises. This mandate is also found in Duboulay’s *History of the University of Paris*.

Among Suger’s letters published in the same volume, the third is from our prelate. It was written to that abbot, then regent of the kingdom during Louis the Younger’s journey to the Holy Land. Ulger asks Suger, whom he calls “majesty,” to confirm the election which the monks of Bourgueil had made of Robert as their abbot after Peter’s death. Robert, who himself delivered this letter to the regent, also brought one from his chapter requesting the same favour. But because this election had been made without first seeking the court’s permission, Suger, a good statesman, approved it in his reply only with the reservation *salvo regni jure*, “without prejudice to the rights of the kingdom”: “so that,” he says, “if it in any way infringes royal dignity, the electors shall be bound to answer before the king’s court when he has returned, or before us, who have the honour of holding his place.”

The fifth letter, published by Souchet in his notes on the *Life of Saint Bernard of Tiron* (p. 302), is addressed to William, abbot of that house. Its purpose is to persuade him to consent that the priory of Asnières in Anjou, dependent on Tiron, should be raised to an abbey, without however ceasing to depend upon the mother house. This letter contains high praise of the monks of Asnières and of Tiron. It is dated 1139.

We know the sixth only from what Dom Liron reports of it [Note: [Col. 1645] *Singularités historiques*, vol. I, p. 401], having read it in the manuscript *History of the Abbey of Saint-Nicolas of Angers*. It was, he says, an agreement made by the prelate between that house and the nuns of Ronceray concerning a corpse brought into the church of Saint-Nicolas. The nuns, at the instigation of the parish priest of Saint-Jacques, claimed burial of the body; they came with their people to carry it away by force. In this affair acts of violence were committed on their part which did honour neither to their sex nor to their religious state. The matter was likely to have consequences; but Ulger’s wisdom forestalled them by the settlement of which we speak. We have called it a letter because it is addressed to the parties in epistolary form. Perhaps “charter” would better deserve to be its title.

It is uncertain whether the seventh letter, which has never been published any more than the preceding one, still exists [Col. 1647] [Note: [Col. 1647] *Hist. Univ. Andegav.*, p. 116]. What is certain is that Babin, chancellor of the University of Angers, had held the original in his hands; but it has since disappeared. This letter is our prelate’s reply to one Saint Bernard had written to urge him to end his dispute with the abbey of Fontevraud.

Ulger held the abbey of Marmoutier in singular esteem and affection. Proof of these sentiments is found in a charter whose original the monastery preserves. It records the foundation, for the monks of Marmoutier, of the hospice of Saint Eligius in the parish of Saint-Étienne at Angers. It ends as follows:

> “This donation was made while Louis was reigning in France and Geoffrey, son of Fulk, king of Jerusalem, was count of Anjou; it was issued by the hand of Vaslet, master of the schools and chancellor, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November.”

But it is appropriate to reproduce part of the text of this act, for reasons that will appear below.

> “To give joyfully,” says Ulger, “and by the magnificence of one’s alms to induce others to do the same—this is what a priest, and especially a bishop, should make his glory. . . . Therefore I, Ulger, though unworthy bishop of the church of Angers . . . having learned that the most holy church of Marmoutier owned no dwelling in our city where its monks could be lodged and fed, have resolved, in order to remedy so great an inconvenience, to give them in alms—and by these present letters do indeed give them in perpetuity—an orchard which I held as bishop and which lies in the parish of Saint-Étienne. This was done with the counsel of Richard the dean, Grafion the cantor, the archdeacons Normand and Raoul, Master Vaslet, Master Gordon, and many other canons, who asked our brethren of Marmoutier to accept the said orchard in order to build there a suitable hospice. For it is unfitting that monks of so holy and venerable a monastery, which has so many different hospices elsewhere and which, in the number of its establishments, surpasses the other regular houses, should have no place of refuge in so great a city as this—or should have one only by borrowing it.”

In the remainder of the act, Ulger assigns revenues for the maintenance of the obedientiaries of this hospice. Normand de Doé, his successor, united the priory of Vern to it in 1152. Pocquet de La Livonière, in his *History of the University of Angers*, maintains that the purpose of this foundation was to enable the monks of Marmoutier to come and study in that city’s schools. But this does not appear, either directly or remotely, in the act just quoted. It is much more likely that Ulger had in view solely the convenience of Marmoutier’s officers, whose business drew them to Angers. Besides, who could persuade himself that an abbey so celebrated did not have within its own community several persons as capable as the Angevin professors of lecturing on the principal branches of learning? Has it not been shown in the discourse on the state of letters in that century [Note: [Col. 1647] *Hist. lit.*, vol. IX, p. 36] that it itself had a flourishing school, a substantial library, and learned monks who daily held conferences for their brethren? It is surprising that Dom Rivet, author of this discourse, adopted La Livonière’s opinion concerning the antiquity of monastic colleges in the school of Angers.

The same historian reports another charter of our prelate, by which he bound each of his successors to entertain the beadles of the Academy on the day of the ceremony of licences, as he himself practised. This foundation is likewise recalled in the thirty-fifth of the statutes of that university, published in 1373 under the scholastic Peter Bertrandi. Thus, as observed above, the licence, or authority to teach, was already conferred with a certain ceremony.

The Messrs. de Sainte-Marthe published in their *Gallia Christiana* (vol. II, p. 134) Ulger’s testament from a mutilated original lacking its end. At the beginning, its author speaks of the length and hardships of his exile, a circumstance of his life otherwise unknown. He says that, despite this misfortune and other adversities he had suffered during his episcopate, he had nonetheless recovered a fairly large number of churches and estates, which he lists. He gives them all to his canons, addressing Richard, their dean. The act is rather well written and contains lofty sentiments of humility.

It would be useless, for our purpose, to review the other charters of our prelate, of which a great number survive in the archives of the churches of Anjou. They indeed praise his wisdom, beneficence, and charity; but since they contain no point bearing on literature, that is sufficient reason to omit them.

Only a word need be said of his poetry. In the discussion of Marbod [Note: [Col. 1647] *Hist. lit.* vol. X, p. 438 (*Patrologiae*, vol. CLXXI)] we have seen the two epitaphs which Ulger dedicated to the memory of that prelate. They are the only fruits of his poetic vein in public hands. Baillet [Note: [Col. 1647] *Table Critique*, 13 September, no. 3], who calls him Oulger, makes him the author of a verse *Life of Saint Maurilius*. But it has been shown elsewhere that it belongs to Marbod. Ménard, in his manuscript *History of Anjou* (p. 47, col. 2), attests that he saw various short poems by Ulger in praise of the saints—works, he says, written in a coarse style, and which he therefore did not judge proper to transcribe. At least he ought to have indicated their titles and the repositories in which they are preserved.

Finally, according to the testimony of John of Salisbury, Ulger composed a work entitled *Venalitium disciplinarum*, “The Venality of the Disciplines,” which has not come down to us [Note: [Col. 1647] *Metalogicon*, bk. II, ch. 19 (*Patrologiae*, vol. CXCIX)]. It is the only known work of his whose loss seems, judging by its title, to deserve our regret.

[Col. 1649]

## Ulger, Bishop of Angers: Report to Pope Innocent II on Behalf of the Monastery of La Roë against the Monks of Vendôme

(Baluze, *Miscellanies*, folio edition, vol. III, p. 15, from the cartulary of the church of Saint-Lézin of Angers.)

[Col. 1649A]

“Unique Father and Lord of the world: charity and compassion impel us to answer on behalf of poor John and his most poor house, whom the abbot and monks of Vendôme seek to suffocate, my lord Pope Innocent, by the advantageous position of their proximity and by the weight of their resources, which they possess in excessive abundance. When this poor man finally reached us with exhausted wings, he sent no one before him, brought no one with him, and expects—nor has expected—anyone who was to follow by prior arrangement. He is alone, powerless, and poor. Alone, he is attacked by many; powerless, he is surrounded by powerful men; poor, he is surrounded by rich men. His spirit is distressed within him. Therefore I desire to help him, because it is not the part of a free man or a Christian not to assist the oppressed.

“This man, indeed, is your servant and faithful according to his power; he is a regular canon [Col. 1649B] of the church of Saint Mary of the Wood, which among holy churches is held to be most holy, but among poor ones is known to be the poorest. Thus, I say, her poor son, about to fight at once for his poor mother, prays and supplicates at the feet of your majesty; and we, with him and for him, pray and supplicate that you may deign to turn the ears of your head and heart toward the arguments of his defence. For we have no intention of detaining the serenity and reverence due to your gravity with idle speeches. Let Cicero and the Ciceronians keep their rhetoric. But we have proposed to lay before you and your present court, simply and briefly, pure truth, which will set him free, and only those things necessary for this business.”

[Col. 1649C]

**II.** A certain nobleman of our country built two churches: one as an abbey for regular canons, who from that time to the present have most devoutly served God in it; the other he built as a chapel and oratory for himself and his own household. While it was being built, he is said—and this is acknowledged by the adversary—to have granted this chapel to that regular church of which we spoke above. Now this chapel possessed absolutely nothing from the revenues of parochial right. But, with the permission of the regular canons already mentioned, that same lord assigned to it his chaplains, whom he had held and had already held for a long time as feoffees, in order that they might celebrate the divine office there according to canonical custom in honour of God [Col. 1650A] and of most holy Nicholas. Their possessions were in rents, arable lands, market dues, ovens, mills, and in what had been taken from the demesne and household provision of that lord—things which he could freely have given to any one of his knights or dependants, had he wished, or to a mime or actor, had he wished to behave frivolously.

Afterward, the grandson of that man, understanding that the regular church was in very great need because it was situated in barren country, in marshy and wooded places—from which the church itself is called “of the Wood”—turned his mind toward completing what his ancestor had begun. To supply the needy food and clothing of the poor brethren, he gave the repeatedly mentioned chapel, together with the whole chaplaincy, to the repeatedly named [Col. 1650B] abbey. But in order that this wish might proceed by the right path and take effect in due order, he entirely renounced whatever lordship and authority he had over it, placed it in the hand of my lord Renaud, formerly the venerable bishop of Angers and now archbishop of Reims, and earnestly requested that he both restore and grant this deposit to the regular monastery of which we have spoken so often.

**III.** My lord the bishop, then greatly rejoicing at so great an increase for that needy church, received it from the nobleman’s hand and invested that poor little abbey with this chapel through the hands of Abbot Albin. He gave him the keys of the chapel, the ropes of its bells, [Col. 1650C] its charter of foundation, as well as its books and whatever else there was. The chaplains assigned to the service of the chapel consented to this and surrendered themselves and their chaplaincies—or, if you prefer, their prebends—into the abbot’s hand and disposition. Renaud, the archpriest of that place, consented to this, as did our dean Normand and our chapter, to which the chapel was subject for rent. I, Ulger, who at that time, though unworthy, administered the office of archdeacon, also consented, on condition that the number of ministers should not be diminished.

**IV.** In order that this whole work might attain its most complete fulfilment, my lord bishop sent Abbot Albin himself [Col. 1651A] to our blessed lord Pope Paschal, praying and beseeching him to lay the right hand of his condescension upon this alms, and to give and grant this chapel to the abbey of which we speak, and to confirm it by apostolic authority. Inclined, as was his custom in kindness, by petitions so worthy and prayers so just, he granted what was requested. By apostolic letters—which we have gladly produced before you, and which we show and offer to you: look, look at them—he confirmed this chapel to that abbey, and sent Albin and his companions, more than sufficiently happy—may his soul be most joyful—back to their own home.

**V.** From that day the abbot of Saint Mary of the Wood held the chapel, not as though it were his own, but truly as his own; and he had and exercised in it the fullest right of abbot and lord, celebrating there privately and publicly at his pleasure, on feast-days and on ordinary days. Whenever any of the chapel’s chaplains died or departed, the abbot put in his vacant place, by his own right, whomever he chose: a secular clerk when he wished, or a regular [Col. 1651B] when he pleased. That abbey held and possessed this chapel, not to mention the ancient gift, in the lifetime of our lord Pope Paschal, in the days of our most noble lord Pope Calixtus, in the days of my sweetest lord Pope Honorius, and in your days, most reverend Innocent.

**VI.** Up to this point polished and learned advocates should not reproach us because, upon hearing the arguments of our adversaries, we did not immediately fly upon them and hasten to cut them down. For by this path of narrating what was done, we shall approach them more freely and briefly, step by step; we shall show that precisely those points in which our adversaries place greatest confidence are useless and empty, and shall overthrow them with the battering-ram of reason—or shall prove that whatever force and legal right they possess stands more on our side than on that of our adversaries.

**VII.** The abbot of Vendôme argues against the abbey of Saint Mary of the Wood and against this its poor daughter as follows: “You unjustly hold the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Craon, and unjustly take it from us.” John’s reply is: “We neither take it from you nor hold it unjustly. It is ours by legal right and by length of undisturbed possession.”

The abbot of Vendôme, to prove his case, produced the claim that Renaud, archbishop of Reims, formerly bishop of Angers, and Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, with Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, and other wise men associated with them, adjudged to the church of Vendôme the investiture of the chapel of Saint Nicholas; and that Pope Calixtus, as also our lord Innocent and Peter Leo during the time of his legation, confirmed the same. Further, the abbot of Vendôme asserts that our lord Renaud, bishop of Angers, judicially invested his predecessor Geoffrey with that chapel and issued him sealed letters as witnesses of the judgment and investiture; [Col. 1652A] and that the chapel had been built within the parish of Saint-Clément, which is his.

**VIII.** John here invalidates all these claims. What you call a judgment or adjudication—if it may be so called without offence to the majesty of my lord the archbishop of Reims—was not, and ought not to be called, a judgment, but rather a prejudgment or an alien judgment. Or it was not a just judgment, because it was not made before the person before whom it should have been made, nor by those by whom it should have been made, nor in the manner in which it should have been made, nor in the place, nor at the time, nor concerning those persons concerning whom it ought to have been made.

It was not made before the person before whom it should have been made. This matter, which the most illustrious Pope Paschal had given, granted, and confirmed by letters and the seal of his authority, should have been adjudicated only before the pope, not before any other person. It was not made by those by whom it should have been made, because it ought first to have been made by the pope and, after him, by his cardinals and by those whom he had admitted, and not by others. Hence it ought not to have been made either by the archbishop of Tours or by the bishop of Le Mans.

Moreover, they still say that the archbishop of Tours adjudged that infamous investiture—indeed, rather an “inversion”—to the monks. We reply that the case did not come before that archbishop and was not referred to him; rather, he came to the case at the urging and under the guidance of the abbot of Vendôme. The abbot drew the archbishop away from the unfinished feast of Saint Maurice and brought him from Tours to Angers at his own expense. The abbot maintained him as his advocate on the day before [Col. 1652B] the case was heard and throughout however long he had been at Angers; he came with the abbot from the abbot’s lodging to the case, and returned with the abbot from the case to the abbot’s lodging. At that time he did and could do whatever he knew and could do for the benefit of the abbot of Vendôme. For this reason he was suspect to us.

It was not done in the manner in which it should have been done, because the feast of Saint Bartholomew had passed when the bishop fixed a day for proceedings, namely, the day after the then imminent feast. Those whom the bishop summoned to the case pleaded the shortness of this term and the harshness of the lord of Craon, who often seized their goods and sometimes did not permit a canon whom he had captured to depart unless he was ransomed. They also said that the chapel for which they were summoned to the case belonged to the abbey of the Wood. They would indeed come to the case on the appointed day, but would not enter upon the cause unless it were first judged whether those reasons were sufficient to obtain for them a safe and more convenient term.

When both parties had assembled on that date and the abbot of Vendôme sought judgment concerning the said chapel, the opposing party replied that it would not enter upon the case until it had first been judged whether the reasons above stated were sufficient, lest on that day they might be compelled by law to plead, as they themselves had stipulated when that term was fixed. Moreover, they were not summoned a second or third time.

It was not done in the place where it should have been done, because it was not done before the pope. Nor was it done at the place ordered, because the clerics who were being sued could not obtain a six-month delay to plead concerning their livelihood—namely, their prebends, from the usufruct of which they were to live in God’s service and to whose service they had been ordained. [Col. 1653A]

It was not done concerning those persons concerning whom it ought to have been done, because it was not done concerning the abbot and regular canons of Saint Mary of the Wood, whose alone were both the ownership and possession of the repeatedly mentioned chapel, given and confirmed by the bishop of Angers, the archdeacon, the archpriest, the dean and chapter of Saint-Maurice, the chaplains of the chapel now under discussion, and, to crown all, by our magnificent and wondrous lord Pope Paschal, whose authority far surpasses and exceeds all the gifts and confirmations of others.

Therefore, trusting in the mercy of the highest Judge and in yours, and likewise in the justice of God, of ourselves, and of these poor men, we confidently say that, since these regular canons were neither summoned to the case nor judged, what is here called a judgment was not made concerning those persons concerning whom it ought to have been made. Nor ought these regulars to be condemned or for that reason excluded from the case, even if those secular chaplains—being the vicars and officers of the said regulars, and [lacuna] their instrument—lost the case through their own fault and default. Rather, we hold that, if the adversary’s arguments were effective, they could remove the secular chaplains; they would not harm the regulars [Col. 1653B] but would benefit them, since the removal of the seculars would be the admission of the regulars, and since it belongs to the regulars themselves, and to no other person, to enter the vacant place of the chapel and either retain it for themselves or give it to another whom they choose.

**IX.** To the adversaries’ statement that, after this judgment, the bishop of Angers made an investiture of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, with the chapel, we reply that an investiture resulting from such a judgment is not to be approved. We desire—and in desiring pray—the apostolic dignity and the authority of its holy court to judge whether an investiture made and adjudged before such a person, by such persons, in such manner, at such a place, at such a time, concerning such persons, ought to be or to be called an investiture, or rather an “inversion”; since no investiture except a canonical one is to be admitted or reckoned as an investiture by the pope and his court, and since what they call an investiture was only in words and verbal, not real or material, and more headlong and hasty than considered.

**X.** To the adversaries’ assertion that Renaud, bishop of Angers, invested Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, with the chapel by its key, we reply that this argument—or rather, this clever and arguable lie—is met by the publicly known fact, apparent to many clerics and very many laymen, that the priest Alberic redeemed his son, the monk Pagan, from the intolerable yoke of the monastery of Vendôme. He did so by taking the said key from his belt and offering it, together with his own [property?] and twenty pounds promised to the abbot of Vendôme; after redeeming him, he restored him to the abbey of Saint-Alban. [Col. 1654A]

**XI.** Their statement that the bishop of Angers made them a charter as evidence of the judgment and investiture seems more harmful than helpful to them, because it was not composed by the man who had formerly been master of the schools. For no charter concerning matters belonging to the church of Angers is customarily received in that church unless it has been drafted and approved by the master of the schools. We add that this charter does not contain the former privileges of our church; and any charter which lacks them not only loses authority but also deserves to be challenged.

**XII.** Against their assertion that Pope Calixtus, you, and Lord Peter Leo confirmed such a judgment and such an investiture, it is no wonder that you confirmed these matters, since you heard no one arguing the case against them. Yet the Roman Church must always exercise such discernment that, if someone has obtained from it an unjust confirmation of something by introducing falsehood or concealing truth, then, once the truth is known, it ought not on that account to deprive anyone of his possession.

Lord Abbot Geoffrey, who was very prudent, learned, and eloquent, sufficiently showed that he did not greatly trust or press these arguments. At Tours, where you, the abbot, and we were with you, he made no outcry concerning this chapel; likewise, at the most famous council of Reims, where the archbishop of Reims on whom these men rely was present, and where we were with you, he brought no outcry or complaint concerning what they now proclaim to the ears of your Holiness. Finally, the regulars who now possess it are prepared to prove that this chapel was given to the church of Saint Mary of the Wood thirty or forty years ago, with no lawful objection raised against it. [Col. 1654C]

**XIII.** Now, most reverend Father, examine the case of our adversaries and ours. Compare authorities with authorities, supporters with supporters, procedures with procedures, places with places, times with times, plaintiffs with defendants; and, judging rightly, adjudge to the repeatedly mentioned abbey of the Wood this very small consolation of its own—something which you would do even if we had not asked it of you. But if the prayer of our littleness carries no weight with your highness, let the poverty of this brother and the humility of his poor church move your bowels of compassion; for you are the sustainer of the poor, father of orphans, and their advocate. You are the judge of the judges of the earth; your sentence decides all things. There was no respect of persons with Christ, and there ought to be none with you, his vicar. It is yours to confirm what has been rightly established. Henceforth I cast the care of this poor man’s case and of his brethren into the bosom of your mercy. Henceforth, have care of this poor John and his other brethren. For, Lord, the poor man is left to you. I shall not say that you will be the helper of orphans, but that you may be their helper.

[Col. 1655]

## Letters of Ulger

**I. To Pope Lucius II.—He commends Odo, dean of Saint-Martin of Tours.**

[Col. 1655A]

(See under LUCIUS II, among the letters of various persons addressed to him, *Patrologiae*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 2.)

**II. To the same.—That he may kindly receive Robert, prior of Saint-Cosmas of Tours.**

(See above, no. 3.)

**III. To the clergy of Angers.—He commends the Knights of the Temple of Jerusalem.**

(Duchesne, *Script. rer. Franc.*, IV, 770.)

Ulger, by unworthiness called bishop of Angers, to the archpriests, archdeacons, priors, priests, [Col. 1655B] and all the clergy established in the bishopric of Angers: life which knows no end of blessedness.

Commanding, requesting, and entreating you, we ask that, when these our brethren come to you, you receive them kindly and affectionately; that you make your churches available to them for preaching; and that you most generously incline the hearts of your parishioners to bestow their alms upon them. For these are the messengers, officers, and fellow-soldiers of those who fight for Christ in the most holy Temple of the Lord at Jerusalem, whose warfare is beyond doubt true and most pleasing to God. Having cast aside worldly desires—namely, the joys of marriage and every kind of pleasure—and being without private property, they have professed an arduous religious life, in order to attain eternal blessedness; they have chosen to fight against the enemies of God, who persecute the holy city of Jerusalem and other regions of the East. Nor do they hesitate to give their lives and shed their blood, in order to destroy and root out the impious heathen from the most holy places which the Lord chose for His birth, passion, and earthly sojourn. We, moreover, desiring to share in their blessedness and lot, grant that, if churches to which they make their way are under interdict, then at their arrival, once a year, on one day, with bells solemnly rung in honour of God and of them, the divine office may be celebrated in those churches, all parishioners being admitted, except the excommunicated; and if there are any brethren of theirs who bear their sign or habit or observe their manner of life, should they die, they may on that occasion be buried. The Roman Pope, the whole Roman Church, and all who love God cherish and embrace these men. To all, indeed, who extend their benefactions to them, we remit a fifth part of the penance for sins which they have confessed. Farewell.

IV. To Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis.—Having received news of the death of Peter, Abbot of Bourgueil, he asks him kindly to receive Robert, his successor.

(It stands third in the collection of Suger's letters. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, col. 1348.)

[Col. 1655]

# ULGER’S TESTAMENT

(*Gallia Christiana*, old edition, vol. II, p. 134.)

[Col. 1655C] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. ULGER, least of bishops, to RICHARD, dean of the church of Blessed Maurice of Angers, and to its whole community, for ever.

By the patience of the merciful God, having been placed, despite our character and life, in charge of the see of Angers, although impeded by the burden of exile and many other disadvantages, striving beyond our strength, we acquired by God’s grace certain churches and villages, and, through our labours, built up not a little. Terrified by the nature and quantity of our sins, which we frequently recalled to mind, and drawn by that saying, “Give, and it shall be given unto you” (Luke 6), we choose to give to the church of Blessed Maurice—out of whose resources and revenues came the expenditures necessary and effective for this purpose—to it and to our successors, the things written above:

[Col. 1656C] The oven of Calomna, which Turpin of Ramoforti and his wife Villana gave us as alms; the mill which is at the weir of Robert of . . . .; the rents at the gate of Angers which belonged to Helenot; Lagenarium of Transmeduana; half of the church of Saint Clement of Platea; the church of Saint Maurice in the Wood, near Bellamnoa; the church and village of Saint Philip with their appurtenances; the lordship of the Church of Grugii, which Philip of Sauconay gave us, together with the dues levied by its priest; the church of Castello, apart from that portion held by the abbey of Saint Albinus; the church of Saint Quentin with its chapel; the land which we have there in the new village of Samonac; the church of Loigniac; and the village of Saint Giles with its church, [Col. 1656D] after the death of Ralph the archdeacon; the church of Poimelles; the church of Alençon and of Chemerario; [Col. 1657A] the church of Monteboherii; the church of Solemniis; and the church of Saint Martin in the Wood. Moreover, we give the church of Jallia and the chapel which is nearby, and what we possessed in the church of Parisiaco. Further, the church of Saint Peter of Priscinniac; half of the church of Valleio, of Laigniac, of Chineiac, and of Disseium; and what we possessed in the church of Saint Symphorian. We give all these things to you, saving the rights of the archdeacons and archpriests. Further, [Col. 1658A] we give whatever we possess in the new castle, in Helonium, and in Chyreium; the half-shareholding at Salviniac, called *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”); one burgess assessed at five shillings; at Columa, from Albert; fifteen shillings from Philip of Gresolla; and fifteen from Walter of Le Mans . . . . . . The remaining words of the parchment have been lost.

[Col. 1657]

XXXVIII.—That selling or buying a church or tithes is Simoniac heresy. 948 CHAP. XXXIX.—That modern Simonists strive to buy the Holy Spirit in sacraments as Simon did in miracles. 949 CHAP. XLI.—That no good fruit can arise from the beginning of Simony. 950 CHAP. XLII.—That the Holy Spirit does not shine in Simonists’ sacraments. 951 CHAP. XLIII.—That the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought. 951 CHAP. XLIV.—That almsgiving cannot be made even from the price of Simony. 952 CHAP. XLV.—That Simony harms those who know of it and consent to it. 952 CHAP. XLVI.—That one who permits himself to be ordained by someone whom he does not doubt is a Simonist must be deposed. 953 CHAP. XLVII.—That one must burn with zeal vehemently against Simony. 953 CHAP. XLVIII.—That Simonists must be persecuted or avoided. 954 CHAP. XLIX.—That Simony must also be fought against. 954 CHAP. L.—That a sacrament, though truly a good thing for the good, becomes a great evil for the wicked. 954 CHAP. LI.—That the Lord was transfigured twice in the flesh. 955 CHAP. LII.—That in the baptism of heretics, though it is granted to be valid, the Holy Spirit is not to be believed to be possessed unless imposition of hands follows. 955 CHAP. LIII.—That whoever defiles himself by heretical communion ought no longer to be promoted. 956 CHAP. LIV.—How heretics’ sacraments are said to be invalid and untrue, though they are true and holy. 956 CHAP. LV.—That some sacraments concern dignity, others necessity. 956 CHAP. LVI.—That one who is illicitly ordained must be condemned on account of place, time, or promotion. 957 CHAP. LVII.—That such a bishop is permitted to administer the other sacraments, though forbidden to confer orders. 957 CHAP. LVIII.—That one who surpasses others in dignity ought to surpass them in holiness. 957 CHAP. LIX.—That Pope Anastasius was condemned together with his decree, by which he sought, contrary to the authority of the saints, to absolve those ordained by the condemned Acacius. 958 CHAP. LX.—The decree by which Pope Felix condemns Acacius. 958 CHAP. LXI.—Likewise Gelasius condemns [him]. 959 CHAP. LXII.—Likewise Hormisdas. 959 CHAP. LXIII.—That Anastasius’s decree was contrary to Innocent’s decree. 959 CHAP. LXIV.—That Acacius was condemned. 959 CHAP. LXV.—That although, before Christ’s coming, persons of the Church were kings and priests, nevertheless after the coming of that same king and priest, kingship was divided from priesthood. 960 CHAP. LXVI.—That no one ought to absolve except the one who binds, unless perhaps by consent. 961 CHAP. LXVII.—That an inferior cannot absolve a superior. 961 CHAP. LXVIII.—That by a fraudulent absolution the guilty do not absolve the guilty. 961 CHAP. LXIX.—That secular power must not judge divine matters. 961 CHAP. LXX.—That, although kingship and priesthood are the two principal powers, nevertheless, just as priests are subject to kings in temporal matters, so kings must be subject even more to priests in divine matters. 961 CHAP. LXXI.—That the Apostolic See is set over all priests and Churches. 962 CHAP. LXXII.—That no power of an imperial city can alter the prerogative of ecclesiastical dignity. 962 CHAP. LXXIII.—That a king who sins must be publicly rebuked by priests. 962 CHAP. LXXIV.—That every heretic must be rebuked according to the rule applicable to him. 963 CHAP. LXXV.—That the Apostolic See must be appealed to by all Churches; it itself, however, ought neither to appeal nor to be judged by any. 963 CHAP. LXXVI.—That heretics must be deposed by the authority of the Apostolic See alone. 963 CHAP. LXXVII.—That a heretic condemns himself by his own judgment. 963 CHAP. LXXVIII.—That guilt cannot be remitted without correction. 964 CHAP. LXXIX.—That the judgment of any heresy must not be reopened, but action must be taken concerning it, without any examination, according to the tenor of the ancient constitution. 964 CHAP. LXXX.—That, without any examination by a synod, the Apostolic See can condemn and restore whom it ought, since it is permitted to judge all persons and no one may judge it. 964 CHAP. LXXXI.—That those are heretics who are placed above living Catholic priests in any respect, or communicate with persons so placed above them. 965 CHAP. LXXXII.—That anyone who has confessed his crime both in writing and orally ought not to be heard further. 965 CHAP. LXXXIII.—That the sacraments of any evil priest, heretic, or condemned person are true. 965 CHAP. LXXXIV.—That anyone who gives or receives sacraments illicitly must be punished unless he repents. 966 CHAP. LXXXV.—That avarice alone commends Simony. 967 CHAP. LXXXVI.—That no one may be silent concerning the condemnation of Simony. 968 Notice on the following little work. 968 LITTLE BOOK ON FREE WILL. 969 CHAP. I.—What Adam’s free will was like before and after the Fall. 969 CHAP. II.—Neither the predestination of the good to reward nor the foreknowledge of the wicked for punishment hinders free will. 970 CHAP. III.—God’s eternal vision, by which he has always held all our actions present before himself, imposes no necessity upon them, but leaves them wholly free. 971 CHAP. IV.—Whether predestination can be obtained by our merits and prayers. 972 [Col. 1669] CHAP. V.—That our will is now free in such a way that it can will evil from itself alone, but good only through grace. 972

HENRY OF SALTRY.

Notice. 972 TREATISE ON THE PURGATORY OF ST PATRICK, APOSTLE OF THE IRISH. 973 Preface to the Reader. 973 Prologue. 975 CHAP. I.—On the name, existence, and location of purgatory. 977 CHAP. II.—On the manner and rite of making a pilgrimage to this purgatory in these later centuries. 983 CHAP. III.—On the discovery of purgatory and the rite formerly observed in its pilgrimage. 987 CHAP. VIII.—On the flame-devouring pit and the very high bridge to which the knight was led by the demons. 995 CHAP. IX.—On the heavenly glory and earthly paradise shown to the knight, and his conversation with the pontiffs. 996 CHAP.
